title: Seven finalists named for Sangamon County Sheriff. Here's the list
author: Steven Spearie
description: Seven finalists, including four internal candidates, have been named for the Sangamon County Sheriff opening. Here's what to know.
content:
Seven finalists, including four internal candidates, have been named for the Sangamon County Sheriff opening.
A new sheriff possibly could be confirmed at a special county board meeting on Sept. 18.
There were 15 applicants, according to Sangamon County spokesman Jeff Wilhite. Interviews with the finalists will begin this week, with each candidate undergoing a comprehensive background check.
Sheriff Jack Campbell retired on Aug. 31 in the wake of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman and mother of two children who had called 911 about a possible prowler.
Sean P. Grayson, a former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy, faces murder charges. He is in custody.
Campbell had been sheriff since 2018.
The new sheriff will serve out the remainder of the term, which is up in 2026.
Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon is serving as sheriff in a temporary capacity.
The finalists are:
Timothy Becker, Athens Police Chief; Retired Chief of Staff from the Illinois State Police
Bryce Benton, Illinois State Police, Division of Criminal Investigation, Intelligence Command, Special Agent/Task Force Officer
Paula Crouch, Sangamon County Chief Deputy Circuit Clerk; retired lieutenant from the Springfield Police Department
Nancy Finley, Sangamon County Sheriff's Office Sergeant
Mike Harth, Sangamon County Sheriff's Office Sergeant
Chris Mueller, Sangamon County Central Dispatch Executive Director; retired lieutenant from the Springfield Police Department
Bryan Pruitt, Retired from the Illinois State Police, Captain of District 10/Troop 7
The Sheriff Applicant Review Committee is being chaired by retired Seventh District Circuit Court Judge and former state's attorney Patrick Kelley. It also includes two county board members: Joel Tjelmeland Jr. of District 14 and chairman of the jail committee and Linda Douglas-Williams of District 20, the ranking Democrat on the jail committee.
The county board will meet Tuesday though it will be largely procedural. The special meeting at the Bank of Springfield Center will cover all September business, public comment and the possible sheriff's confirmation.

title: Presidential debate fact check: Analyzing Trump, Harris on abortion, immigration, more
author: Joedy McCreary
description: The USA TODAY Fact Check Team analyzed claims on abortion, immigration, guns, inflation and more. See where each candidate erred.
content:
Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Donald Trump took the stage tonight in Philadelphia for their first presidential debate of the Nov. 5 election season.
The USA TODAY Fact Check Team investigated claims from the nominees and added context where it was missing on issues including abortion, immigration, guns and inflation.
Read on for our analysis of statements that exaggerated, mislead, misrepresented or otherwise strayed from reality. Our team uses primary documents, trustworthy nonpartisan sources, data and other research tools to assess the accuracy of claims.
Donald Trump claim: 2020 election lawsuits failed only on 'technicality'
'They said we didn't have standing. That's the other thing. They said we didn't have standing. A technicality.'
Trump has repeatedly and falsely claimed his 2020 election defeat to Joe Biden was 'rigged.' He continued down this line during Tuesday's debate, claiming his election lawsuits challenging the results failed on 'a technicality' of not having 'standing,' a legal term for the right to bring a lawsuit based on one's connection to the issue at hand.
But that's not true. Dozens of cases brought by Trump and his allies appeared before judges in hearings, including 30 that were heard on the merits, USA TODAY reported. Every case but one failed.
Eight conservative legal experts published a report in 2022 that reviewed evidence in 64 cases in six swing states, finding that Trump and his supporters didn't provide evidence of widespread election fraud.
'These cases provided the forums in which Trump and his supporters could and should have proven their claims," the report concluded. "This report shows that those efforts failed because of a lack of evidence and not because of erroneous rulings or unfair judges."
Of the 64 cases brought by Trump and his supporters, 20 were dismissed before a hearing on the merits, 14 were voluntarily dismissed by Trump and his supporters before a hearing on the merits, and 30 cases included a hearing on the merits, according to the report.
-Andre Byik, Erin Mansfield
Kamala Harris claim: Number of new manufacturing jobs under Biden surpasses 800,000
'We have created over 800,000 new manufacturing jobs.'
This claim – which echoes one President Joe Biden made in 2023 – is not quite right anymore. Since Biden took office in January 2021, the U.S. added about 739,000 seasonally adjusted manufacturing jobs, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data.
Previous estimates did put the job growth well over 800,000, but the Labor Department lowered it during its annual preliminary revision of its data. The department estimated that 115,000 fewer manufacturing jobs were created during the 12-month period that began in March 2024. Its final revision is expected in February 2025.
Harris claim: SCOTUS ruled Trump would be immune from misconduct while president
'The United States Supreme Court recently ruled that the former president would essentially be immune from any misconduct if he were to enter the White House again.'
This overstates the content of the ruling.
Harris is referring to a Supreme Court ruling from July that concluded in a 6-3 decision that presidents, including Trump, are at least partially immune from prosecution for crimes committed while in office. But the court's decision isn't as clear cut as Harris' remarks make it seem. It declares that 'official' acts by presidents are protected, but steps taken as a candidate are not.
The ruling also leaves room for presidents to be prosecuted under a narrow set of circumstances, related to responsibilities 'within the outer perimeter' of presidential duties, or to unofficial acts, as USA TODAY previously reported. The ruling did not grant Trump blanket immunity.
'The President enjoys no immunity for his unofficial acts, and not everything the president does is official. The president is not above the law,' Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the conservative majority in the ruling.
Trump is the first president – former or current – to be criminally charged.
- Brad Sylvester, Chris Mueller
Donald Trump claim: Migrants eating cats, dogs in Ohio
'In Springfield, (migrants are) eating the dogs. The people that came in, they're eating the cats. They're eating... they're eating the pets of the people that live there.'
This claim echoes allegations made by Trump's running mate, J.D. Vance, who has accused Haitian immigrants of stealing and eating cats in his home state of Ohio.
But Springfield city officials, including the city manager, say there is no evidence of any cats or other pets being harmed or eaten by Haitian immigrants, USA TODAY reported.
There was an incident in Canton, Ohio, about 170 miles northeast of Springfield, involving a 27-year-old woman who was arrested in August on suspicion of killing and eating a cat, but the woman was not a Haitian immigrant, according to the Cincinnati Enquirer.
-Andre Byik
Donald Trump claim: Biden took $3.5 million from Moscow mayor's wife
'Between (Joe Biden) and his son, they get all this money from Ukraine, they get all of this money from all of these different countries, and then you wonder why is he so loyal to this one, that one, Ukraine, China, why is he - why did he get $3.5 million from the mayor of Moscow's wife? Why did she pay him $3.5 million?'
Trump has made similar claims before, including during his first debate with Joe Biden in 2020. It's a reference to a report released that year by the Republican-controlled Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
In a section called 'key findings,' the reports claims, 'Hunter Biden received a $3.5 million wire transfer from Elena Baturina, the wife of the former mayor of Moscow," as USA TODAY previously reported. A later section instead attributes this transfer to a company: "Rosemont Seneca Thornton, an investment firm co-founded by Hunter Biden, received $3.5 million in a wire transfer' from Baturina. The report's source for the claim is a confidential document it says is on file with the committees, but it does not elaborate.
Hunter Biden's lawyer, George Mesires, told CNN at the time that his client was not an owner of Rosemont Seneca Thornton.
'Hunter Biden had no interest in and was not a 'co-founder' of Rosemont Seneca Thornton, so the claim that he was paid $3.5 million is false,' Mesires said.
Trump has tried before to link the claim to Joe Biden, who is Hunter Biden's father.
- Chris Mueller
Catch up on our convention, debate fact-checks
We fact-checked key speakers throughout the Republican and Democratic conventions. Catch up here on what was false, what was true and what was in between from Kamala Harris, Donald Trump, JD Vance, Tim Walz and a host of others.
-Eric Litke
Donald Trump claim: No American casualties in Afghanistan in 18-month period during his presidency
'For 18 months, we had nobody killed (in Afghanistan).'
Trump made this claim during an exchange about his negotiations with the Taliban that preceded the chaotic withdrawal of U.S. troops from Afghanistan in August 2021.
Trump didn't specify the 18-month period he was referring to, but there is no such period in his presidency during which no U.S. troops were killed in Afghanistan, according to the Defense Department's Defense Casualty Analysis System.
In 2017, 14 total deaths – including 'hostile' and 'non-hostile' ones – were recorded, according to the data. In 2018, there were 15. In 2019, there were 23. And in 2020, there were 11.
PolitiFact reported there was an 18-month stretch between February 2020 and August 2021 when no U.S. service member died 'in combat,' but the period overlaps with President Joe Biden's term in office.
This claim has also been debunked by multiple independent fact-checkers.
-Andre Byik
Donald Trump claim: Harris was first candidate to leave the presidential race in 2020
'And when she ran, she was the first one to leave because she failed.'
This is wrong.
While Harris did run unsuccessfully for president in 2020, she was not the first Democratic candidate to drop out of the race. More than a dozen Democrats vied for the party nomination, which ultimately went to President Joe Biden.
Harris ended her campaign on Dec. 3, 2019, citing a lack of financial resources. Other Democratic hopefuls who called it quits before her included California Rep. Eric Swalwell, then-Colorado Gov. John Hickenlooper, Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, Massachusetts Rep. Seth Moulton, New York Sen. Kristen Gillibrand, then-New York Mayor Bill de Blasio, then-Ohio Rep. Tim Ryan, former Texas Rep. Beto O'Rourke, former Pennsylvania Rep. Joe Sestak and then-Montana Gov. Steve Bullock.
- Brad Sylvester
Kamala Harris claim: Trump invited Taliban leaders to Camp David
'And (Trump) at the time invited the Taliban to Camp David, a place of storied significance for us as Americans.'
Harris is right, but it's worth noting that such a meeting never actually took place.
In September 2019, Trump revealed he had planned to meet with Taliban leaders and Afghan President Ashraf Ghani at Camp David to continue peace negotiations. But it didn't happen – Trump suspended peace talks after the Taliban claimed responsibility for a car bomb that killed 12 people, including an American.
At the time, Democratic and Republican leaders criticized Trump for planning to bring Taliban members to the U.S., and specifically to Camp David, which has long been used as a presidential retreat. He was also rebuked for the timing of the meeting, which was set to happen days before the 18th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.
- Chris Mueller
Donald Trump claim: Harris proposed to take guns from all firearm owners
'She has a plan to confiscate everybody's gun.'
This is false, and it echoes a claim we previously debunked that Harris would 'end the Second Amendment."
While Harris has been a proponent of stricter gun control measures, there is no credible evidence of any plan to confiscate firearms from all gun owners.
Her campaign's policy platform outlines gun control proposals that include bans on assault weapons and high-capacity magazines, universal background checks and red-flag laws. But it makes no mention of confiscating guns from all Americans.
The campaign website credits the Biden-Harris administration for enacting 'the first meaningful gun safety reform in decades,' referring to a bipartisan bill President Joe Biden signed into law in June 2022, a month after the elementary school shooting in Uvalde, Texas. That law enhances background checks on gun buyers who are 18–21 years old, encourages states to develop better "red flag" laws and adds dating partners to the list of domestic abusers who are prohibited from buying firearms.
– Joedy McCreary
Donald Trump claim: Worst inflation in US history happened under Biden
'She is Biden – (responsible for) the worst inflation we've ever had.'
The highest year-to-year inflation rate since the consumer price index was introduced was in 1917, when it hit 17.8%, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.
While the inflation rate has been consistently higher under Biden's administration than it was under Trump, it still remains far below that number.
The highest monthly rate during Biden's presidency was 9.1% in June 2022, compared to a peak of 2.9% under Trump in June and July 2022, according to consumer price index data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The average annual inflation rate is about 5.7% under Biden, according to an Investopedia analysis that found the average rate under Trump was 1.9%.
-BrieAnna Frank
Donald Trump claim: Harris wouldn't meet with Netanyahu when he addressed Congress
'She wouldn't even meet with Netanyahu when he went to Congress to make a very important speech. She refused to be there because she was at a sorority party of hers.'
This is misleading. It's true that Harris, in her capacity as vice president, didn't preside over Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's July 24 address to Congress in order to attend a previously scheduled campaign event, USA TODAY reported.
That event was the Zeta Phi Beta sorority's national convention in Indianapolis, the Indianapolis Star reported. The sorority is among the country's oldest historically Black Greek-lettered organizations.
Harris did, however, meet with Netanyahu at the White House the following day, as numerous news outlets reported. The vice president 'reiterated her longstanding and unwavering commitment to the security of the State of Israel and the people of Israel' during the meeting, according to a White House news release.
-BrieAnna Frank
Kamala Harris claim: Trump said there will be a 'bloodbath' if he loses the presidential election
"Donald Trump the candidate has said in this election there will be a bloodbath if the outcome of this election is not to his liking"
Harris is misrepresenting what Trump said, as Trump himself pointed out moments later. Harris is referring to a comment Trump made at a rally he held in Vandalia, Ohio, in March.
While speaking at the event about the auto industry, Trump said it would be a 'bloodbath' for the industry if he were to lose the election.
' We're going to put a 100% tariff on every single car that comes across the line, and you're not going to be able to sell those guys if I get elected,' Trump said during the speech. 'Now, if I don't get elected, it's going to be a bloodbath for the whole – that's gonna be the least of it. It's going to be a bloodbath for the country. That'll be the least of it.'
The full context of the comment shows he was warning about a metaphorical bloodbath for the auto industry, not promising violence if he doesn't win the election.
'If you actually watch and listen to the section, he was talking about the auto industry and tariffs,' Steven Cheung, a spokesman for Trump's campaign, told the Washington Post. 'Biden's policies will create an economic bloodbath for the auto industry and autoworkers.'
- Brad Sylvester
Kamala Harris claim: Trump told Putin to 'do whatever the hell he wants'
'It is well known that he said of Putin, that he can do whatever the hell he wants and go into Ukraine.'
This is technically accurate but an oversimplification by Harris, who made a similar claim during her speech last month at the Democratic National Convention.
It's a reference to a remark Trump made during a Feb. 10 campaign rally in South Carolina, where he suggested he might not aid NATO members attacked by Russia if they weren't contributing enough money to the alliance, as USA TODAY previously reported.
'One of the presidents of a big country stood up and said, 'Well sir, if we don't pay and we're attacked by Russia, will you protect us?'" Trump said. 'I said, 'You didn't pay? You're delinquent?' He said, 'Yes, let's say that happened.' No, I would not protect you.'
He added, 'In fact I would encourage them to do whatever the hell they want.'
At the time, NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg said Trump's comments could endanger lives and undermine the security of NATO members, including the U.S.
-Chris Mueller
Donald Trump claim: Department of Justice played role in his four criminal prosecutions
'Every one of those cases was started by them against their political opponent.'
Trump has long sought to paint President Joe Biden and his administration as orchestrating his prosecutions.
But under the Constitution, the administration did not have authority over the state of New York's prosecution of Trump, who was convicted on 34 felony charges of falsifying business records related to a hush money payment to an adult film actress ahead of the 2016 election.
Nor does it have that power in the former president's case in Georgia, where he and others have pleaded not guilty to charges of trying to steal the 2020 election. That case is on hold while an appeals court reviews a ruling that allows Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis to remain on it.
'When you're dealing with state prosecutions, it's district attorneys elected by the voters of their jurisdiction,' said Allan Lichtman, a professor of history at American University. 'That has nothing to do with the federal government.'
Additionally, when the Justice Department had the authority to pursue a case against Trump over the hush money circumstances, it chose not to do so.
The federal classified documents case against Trump was dismissed in July with U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon saying Justice Department special prosecutor Jack Smith – appointed in November 2022 in part to add a layer of separation between the investigation and the administration – was improperly appointed. Smith in August filed a new indictment in Trump's federal election interference case to address the Supreme Court's July decision that Trump had broad immunity from charges related to official acts as president.
Trump is due to be sentenced in New York on Nov. 26 – three weeks after the election.
– Joedy McCreary
Donald Trump claim: Crime has soared under Biden and Harris
'Crime here is up and through the roof.'
Trump's claim conflicts with the latest available data.
Earlier this year, the FBI released preliminary data that showed sharp declines in violent crime in the first three months of 2024 compared to a year earlier, continuing a trend ongoing since a pandemic surge. Murder and rape were both down 26%, robbery was down 18% and aggravated assault fell by 13%, the Associated Press reported. But some experts have cautioned that the data is still preliminary and likely overstates the drop.
Many cities in the U.S. have reported declines in homicides from 2023 to 2024, Axios reported in April. Similarly, the number of murders in the first three months of 2024 fell by nearly 20% in 204 cities analyzed by AH Datalytics, a criminal justice consulting firm.
The most recent FBI data, which dates to 2022, shows the country's violent crime rate at 370 per 100,000 people, the third-lowest rate in the last 50 years, behind only 2014 and 2019, according to PolitiFact. The FBI hasn't released the final 2023 violent crime figures, which come out each October.
-Chris Mueller
Kamala Harris claim: Project 2025 calls for abortion monitor to track pregnancies, miscarriages
'In his Project 2025 there would be a national abortion monitor that would be monitoring your pregnancies, your miscarriages.'
This significantly overstates the nature of the monitoring called for in Project 2025.
The playbook does support anti-abortion policies, and it laments the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention abortion surveillance and reporting systems, calling them 'woefully inadequate.'
Fact check: False claim Trump said he'd force government monitoring on pregnant women
It calls for the Department of Health and Human Services to use every available tool 'to ensure that every state reports exactly how many abortions take place within its borders, at what gestational age of the child, for what reason, the mother's state of residence, and by what method.' But that's not the same as "monitoring your pregnancies." It appears to be calling for states to regularly report cumulative totals, not specific instances.
It says reliable statistical data about abortion, abortion survivors and abortion-related maternal deaths 'are essential to timely, reliable public health and policy analysis.'
Harris also repeats a common overreach by calling Project 2025 Trump's plan. Trump allies worked on the plan, but Trump has repeatedly said he does not support all elements of the plan and wasn't directly involved in creating it.
-Andre Byik
Donald Trump claim: Tim Walz supports abortion in the ninth month (updated)
Corrections & Clarifications: This item was updated Sept. 11 to clarify the timeline and nature of Walz's actions on abortion as Minnesota governor, which included signing a bill that removed any restrictions based on gestational duration.
'Her vice-presidential pick says abortion in the ninth month is absolutely fine.'
There is no evidence Walz said this, though he signed a bill that removed limits to abortion based on gestational duration.
Walz said in 2022 that he supported 'maintaining the timelines outlined by current law,' which at the time allowed abortions until the time of viability, around 24 weeks, for elective abortions, according to the Guttmacher Institute. That viability standard was then removed from state law in 2023 through a law Walz signed.
Walz has taken other steps to protect abortion rights in the state. He signed a bill enshrining the right to abortion and other reproductive healthcare into Minnesota state statutes in January 2023, seven months after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Months later, Walz signed a bill that protected people traveling to Minnesota for abortion care, as well as the professionals providing that care, from legal repercussions from other states.
However, USA TODAY found no record of Walz quotes expressing support for abortion in the ninth month of pregnancy.
There is no current restriction or ban on abortion based on gestational duration in the state, according to the Guttmacher Institute and Kaiser Family Foundation.
Nationally, only 1% of all abortions occur at or after 21 weeks of pregnancy, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation.
-BrieAnna Frank
Donald Trump claim: The economy and stock market improved under the Trump administration despite the COVID-19 pandemic
'We handed them a stock market and economy that was higher than it was before the pandemic.'
Trump is right about the stock market, but the economy as a whole was worse off when he left office than it was before the pandemic.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average (a popular stock market index) was up by about 8% (about 2,300 points) from February 2020 (the month before the COVID-19 pandemic was declared) to January 2021, when Trump left office.
But the overall economy was still reeling from the impact of the pandemic. U.S. GDP was down from where it was prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, and the unemployment rate had spiked as millions of Americans had lost their jobs. The unemployment rate was at 3.5% in February 2020 compared to 6.4% when Trump left office in January 2021, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data.
- Brad Sylvester
Kamala Harris claim: Trump left one of highest trade deficits in US history
'The Trump administration resulted in a trade deficit, one of the highest we've ever seen in the history of America.'
This is accurate.
The country's trade deficit reached its highest level since 2008 under Trump, who had promised to reduce it during his 2016 campaign. In 2020, the combined U.S. goods and services trade deficit increased to $679 billion, up from $481 billion in 2016, before Trump took office, Politico reported. A trade deficit happens when a country imports more than it exports.
However, the U.S. trade deficit has been higher before, including in 2006, when it reached $764 billion under former President George W. Bush. In 2007, it dropped to $711 billion, remained about the same in 2008, then fell sharply to $395 billion in 2009 as a result of the recession, according to Factcheck.org, which cited data from the U.S. Census Bureau.
- Chris Mueller
Kamala Harris claim: Trump tariffs would cost families $4,000 per year
'Economists have said that that Trump sales tax would actually result, for middle-class families, in about $4,000 more a year.'
Harris also brought up this number during her speech at the Democratic National Convention in reference to Trump's proposed tariff of between 10% and 20% on imported goods. Her estimate is at the high end of the economic estimates.
While Trump has described it as a way to raise revenue, economists say it would mostly be passed along to consumers, effectively making it a tax. But they disagree on the additional cost families would face.
A study by the nonpartisan Tax Policy Center found that tariff, and one of 60% on Chinese goods that Trump has also proposed, would lower the average post-tax incomes of American households by about $1,800. Another think tank, The Peterson Institute for International Economics, says the larger tariff would cost households more than $2,600 per year.
But a projection from the conservative American Action Forum falls closer to the figure Harris cited, saying the 20% tariff and 60% tariff on Chinese goods would amount to a tax increase of $3,900 for a middle-class family.
– Joedy McCreary
Donald Trump claim: Immigrants in the country illegally have highest rate of 'criminality'
'(Immigrants in the country illegally are) destroying our country. They're dangerous. They're at the highest level of criminality, and we have to get them out.'
Immigrants are 60% less likely to be incarcerated than the broader U.S.-born population in recent years, according to a 2023 National Bureau of Economic Research paper.
The paper, co-authored by Stanford University researcher Ran Abramitzky, used U.S. Census data and focused on immigrants present in the Census regardless of their legal status and on men between the ages of 18 and 40, according to a news release about the study.
Fact check: No, 51M 'illegals' have not entered US under Biden, Harris
Alex Nowrasteh, vice president for economic and social policy studies at the Cato Institute, in a Feb. 24 report, examined homicide conviction rates between those who entered the country illegally and native-born Americans in Texas. Nowrasteh found that those entering illegally had a lower homicide conviction rate (2.4 per 100,000) than native-born Americans (2.8 per 100,000) in 2015.
-Andre Byik
Donald Trump claim: Inflation was at 21% under Biden
'We have inflation like very few people have ever seen, probably the worst in our nation's history. We were at 21%.'
This is wrong, according to consumer price index data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The highest year-over-year inflation rate during Biden's presidency was 9.1% in June 2022. The rate as of July 2024 was 2.9%.
By contrast, the highest rate during Trump's presidency was 2.9%, which happened in both June and July 2018. The lowest rate was 0.1% in May 2020, amid the COVID-19 pandemic.
-BrieAnna Frank
How we pick and research fact checks
Ever wonder how fact-checkers do their work? We've got you covered.
Check out our process explainer to see how we pick claims, research them and edit them. This includes a rundown of how we cover live events like tonight's debate.
And if you've ever wondered who fact-checks the fact-checkers, you might want to read this op-ed explaining our emphasis on transparency. Because the answer is you! We use the format and approach precisely so that everyone has the ability to check our work.
-Eric Litke
Debate background: Rounding up our recent claims on Donald Trump
Former President Donald Trump has long been at the center of online misinformation.
That was especially true in the summer of 2024, when rumors swirled about Trump's ties to Project 2025, the assassination attempt against him in July and the former president's unprecedented conviction on 34 counts in his New York criminal hush money trial.
Here are some of USA TODAY's latest fact-checks on claims related to Trump:
Claim: Trump posted about military relationship, interaction with 'Civil War soldier' (False)
Claim: Image shows Secret Service agents weren't wearing earpieces during Trump assassination attempt (Altered)
Claim: Trump warned mpox will be used as an excuse for electoral fraud and lockdowns (False)
Claim: Trump mistakenly addressed North Carolina at Pennsylvania rally (False)
Claim: Trump said cereal costs $100 a pound at press conference (False)
Claim: Image shows Trump falling asleep at the 2017 NATO summit (False)
Claim: Image shows 'Trump train' truck crashed into bridge (Altered)
Claim: Trump couldn't land in Bozeman, Montana, because he owed the airport $12,000 (False)
-BrieAnna Frank
Where to find our fact checks
In addition to live events like tonight's debate, the USA TODAY Fact Check Team publishes about 100 checks each month on the most viral and significant claims circulating online. Here's how to find our work.
Subscribe to our Checking the Facts newsletter to have get the latest updates in your inbox each morning.
Follow our Facebook page to get our latest work in your feed.
This landing page always has our most recently published work.
- Eric Litke
Debate background: Rounding up our recent claims on Kamala Harris
In the weeks since the Democrats selected Vice President Kamala Harris to replace President Joe Biden at the top of their ticket, an array of false or misleading claims about her circulated.
Many centered on her background, her record as vice president or her campaign platform. Some have been around for years, dating to Biden's pick of Harris as his running mate in 2020. Newer ones center around her role in addressing immigration and where she and her running mate, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, stand on gun control and taxation.
Among the false or misleading claims related to Harris that USA TODAY has debunked:
– Joedy McCreary
Video series: Follow our work on TikTok, Instagram
USA TODAY's video fact-check series debuted in March and highlights our team's most impactful work, from debunking viral pieces of false news to fact-checking high-profile political events.
A new fact-check video is published most weeks on USA TODAY's social media accounts and website.
Here are some of our recent fact-check videos:
- Andre Byik
Debate background: Immigration a key issue even as encounters at southern border drop
Immigration has been one of the top issues for voters during the presidential campaign season. Under President Joe Biden, illegal border crossings reached record highs, averaging more than 2 million per year from 2021 to 2023, according to Customs and Border Protection. But more recently, illegal crossings – or 'encounters' – at the southern border fell to the lowest total in nearly four years only months after Biden announced broad restrictions on asylum.
Vice President Kamala Harris was never put in charge of the southern border or made "border czar," contrary to some posts on social media, but that hasn't stopped former president Donald Trump and other Republicans from attacking her immigration policy. In 2021, Biden announced Harris would lead his administration's diplomatic efforts with Mexico and the Central American countries of Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador to slow migration to the southern border. At the time, Harris said the administration 'must address the root causes that cause people to make the trek, as the president described, to come here.'
Trump, meanwhile, has promised the largest deportation effort in U.S. history if he is elected again. He also said he would reinstate strict immigration policies from his first term, limit asylum access at the U.S. southern border and eliminate automatic citizenship for people born in the U.S. to immigrant parents.
In February, Republican lawmakers blocked an immigration bill that would have revamped the country's immigration and border policies. Biden and Harris have blamed the bill's failure on opposition from Trump. Harris has vowed to bring back the bill and sign it into law if elected.
- Chris Mueller

title: LL Flooring changing name back to Lumber Liquidators, selling 219 stores to new owner
author: The State Journal-Register
description: LL Flooring signed an agreement to sell 219 of its stores to F9 Investments, while the company's new owner says it will rebrand back to Lumber Liquidators.
content:
"It's just getting back to basics." Tom Sullivan, founder and former CEO of LL Flooring said in a FloorDaily.net interview. "It's just something about the Lumber Liquidators that works."
LL Flooring has signed an agreement to sell 219 of its stores to F9 Investments, the company announced on Friday.
The agreement comes days after the retail company announced it would be closing over 400 stores nationwide.
LL Flooring filed a Chapter 11 bankruptcy claim on Aug. 11 after the company "spent several months" trying to resolve liquidity concerns and refinance debt obligations, according to court documents filed in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Delaware.
The retail company announced on Sept. 6 that it would be closing its stores and starting closing sales. Now, the company has an agreement in the works.
'We are pleased to have reached this agreement with F9 Investments for a going-concern sale following significant efforts by our team and advisors to preserve the business and maintain ongoing operations,' Charles Tyson, LL Flooring's president and chief executive officer, said in the press release.
'As we move through the court-supervised process toward the approval and completion of this transaction, we remain committed to continuing to serve our valued customers and working closely with our vendors and partners,' Tyson said.
In addition, the retail company will work with Hilco Merchant Resources, LLC, on the store closing sales at 211 of its locations. The stores include the recently initiated 117 LL Flooring store closings and the 94 store closings that was previously announced before the store's Chapter 11 filing on Aug. 11.
USA TODAY reached out to F9 Investments for comment.
Here is what you need to know about the LL Flooring's agreement.
What are the terms of the LL Flooring agreement?
F9 investments will 'acquire 219 stores, inventory in those stores and in the Company's Sandston, Virginia, distribution center, LL Flooring's intellectual property and other company assets," the release states.
This transaction is expected to be finalized by the end of September and is 'subject to approval by the Bankruptcy Court and other closing conditions,' the release said.
Who is taking over LL Flooring?
In an interview with FloorDaily.net, Tom Sullivan, F9 Investments chairman and former CEO and founder of LL Flooring, confirmed that he and the F9 Investments CEO, Jason Delves, will be taking over the 219 LL Flooring stores.
The agreement also includes the warehouse and intellectual property, Sullivan confirmed.
Sullivan said the change back to Lumber Liquidators was not just for nostalgic purposes, rather, it was a decision that was made for their customers.
"How this company grew was the people in the stores that were all motivated to make the company successful," Sullivan said.
The change back to the black and yellow logo felt like the right thing to do and a way for the private company to "turn it around pretty quick," Sullivan said.
"It's just getting back to basics." he said. "It's just something about the Lumber Liquidators that works."
LL Flooring's history
LL Flooring, formerly known as Lumber Liquidators, started from humble beginnings, the company says, launching "out of a pickup truck" in Stoughton, Massachusetts, about 21 miles south of Boston.
The company changed its name to LL Flooring in 2020 after stock prices fell, Floor Covering Weekly reported.
A 2015 investigation by CBS' "60 Minutes" revealed the company's products contained high levels of formaldehyde, a known cancer-causing chemical.

title: Week 3 preview: Here are the top 4 football matchups and predictions around Springfield
author: Bill Welt
description: The Springfield area will be treated to one of the biggest games in the state between Byron and Williamsville, plus other top matchups and predictions
content:
The Central State Eight Conference kickstarts conference play this weekend, but Paul Jenkins Field will be the site of the biggest game of the week between perennial Class 3A titans Byron and Williamsville.
Here are the top four matchups this week, along with predictions for the rest of the Springfield area. All games kick off Friday at 7 p.m., unless noted otherwise.
🏈 TOP KEY MATCHUPS
Byron at Williamsville: Byron comes to town after Riverton bowed out of the varsity season due to low numbers. The Tigers won their second Class 3A state title in the last three years and third overall last season and return a pair of formidable running backs: Caden Considine and Brayden Knoll. Both ran for over 1,000 rushing yards last season. Williamsville faithful likely remember capturing the program's only state title with a last-minute 46-42 victory over Byron in 2019. Byron 34, Williamsville 28
Jacksonville at Sacred Heart-Griffin: Jacksonville has knocked off SHG twice in the playoffs in 2004 and 2010 but just once in the regular season in 1998 since the formation of the CS8. SHG sophomore backup QB Cameron Brinkman replaced starter Trent Caldwell due to injury in last week's 43-22 win over Mascoutah. Jacksonville is 2-0 following wins over Pittsfield (26-14) and Decatur Eisenhower (65-12). SHG 49, Jacksonville 14
Litchfield at North Mac: Senior Roark Lewis and junior James Graves have combined for 516 rushing yards and six TDs in North Mac's 2-0 start after going 1-8 last season. Litchfield figures to be its toughest test yet. The Purple Panthers rebounded with a 30-6 win over Piasa Southwestern. Junior QB Ethan Saathoff threw for 210 yards and three TDs on 10 of 21 passing, while rushing for 57 yards. North Mac 28, Litchfield 26
Kincaid South Fork at Pawnee, Saturday, 1 p.m.: South Fork won the inaugural Hanlon-Kratochvil Coal Miner's Cup 34-6 last season. Both teams return ample experience at 2-0. title: Illinois Republican claims new state flag would 'advance the far-left's political ideology'
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: The Illinois Flag Commission began accepting submissions of new flag designs last week, but not everyone is on board with changing the flag.
content:
The Illinois Flag Commission began accepting submissions of new flag designs last week, opening up a process that could result in a change to a 55-year-old flag.
The original flag, designed by Rockford native Lucy Derwent in 1915, featured the state seal in front of a white background. It has remained the same since with exception for the addition of the word "Illinois" placed below the seal in 1969.
State lawmakers could ultimately decide to keep the flag as is, Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, noted during a press conference last week in Springfield. After a constituent of hers introduced the idea, she and Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, led the legislation which created the commission later signed into law by Gov. JB Pritzker.
But at the very least, she sees the discussion as a healthy way to activate young people across Illinois to get involved in state government.
"I have always said that history is living, breathing and ever evolving, and I think we need to ensure that government is also evolving so people are engaged," Turner said.
Following a public vote starting Jan. 1, the commission will submit 10 flags in addition to the current flag with the Illinois General Assembly by April 1, 2025. They are expected to take-up a vote on the matter during the spring session.
Not all state lawmakers are enthusiastic at the prospect of a new state flag.
Certainly not is Rep. Adam Niemerg, R-Dieterich, who is leading a petition to fight a new state flag. He believes a new flag could "advance the far left's political ideology," while Buckner noted on X, formerly known as Twitter, the commission is composed of Republicans and Democrats alike.
"Will we highlight the Governor's efforts to partner with Chinese-owned companies? Or will the flag become a state-sponsored tribute to the Pride flag?," Niemerg, a member of the far-right Illinois Freedom Caucus, said in a statement. "We need patriotic citizens to take a stand against this clear attempt to rebrand our state."
As for Turner, a change is something she could get behind.
"The seal represents the government," she said. "And I believe that the flag should be a symbol that represents the people and not the government."
A Secretary of State official said there have been more than 370 designs submitted so far. Submissions will be accepted until Oct. 18.

title: Williamsville, Jacksonville turn the page, and other Week 3 football takeaways
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Williamsville had the top team in 3A on the ropes in the first quarter, plus other takeaways from around Springfield for Week 3 games
content:
Here are the top takeaways around Springfield for Week 3 in the high school football season:
Bullets fade after promising start
Williamsville will turn the page.
The Bullets (2-1) could have put Byron in an early hole, but a couple drives stalled in or around the red zone that ultimately yielded just one field goal in the 41-3 loss.
Williamsville quarterbacks Jackson Sanders and Kaden Entwistle split time handling snaps throughout the night, as in the previous two games. Sanders finished 9 of 12 for 81 yards while Entwistle threw for 26 yards on 3 of 6 passing.
'We've got two guys who we feel are both good at their jobs, so that's what we've been doing,' Williamsville coach Aaron Kunz said of Sanders and Entwistle. 'I thought early we had the ball at the (Byron) 3 first down, we jumped twice. That was a killer and we settled for three points.
'I really thought the first quarter was ours and obviously they beat us up a little bit after that. There were definitely some bright spots and then there's some things that we know we're going to have to get better at and we will.'
More late drama for Athens
Athens found itself in another close Sangamo Conference battle.
Last week, Pittsfield stunned the Warriors 14-7 with a go-ahead touchdown pass on fourth down in the final five minutes of the game.
Pleasant Plains also nearly stole another win away from Athens on Friday. The Cardinals, who trailed 20-0 during the second quarter, rallied ahead 21-20 following a pair of touchdown passes from Cooper Schallenberg to Grady Grisham in the fourth period.
Schallenberg, who finished 8 of 17 for 138 yards and two scores, dialed up a 35-yard TD pass to Grisham to take the lead with under six minutes left and present Athens with the dire prospect of beginning 0-3 after reaching the Class 2A state finals last season.
But Gage Honn answered with a 25-yard TD run with 3:52 remaining for a 26-21 victory and give the Warriors their first win of the season. Luke Tapscott, Talon DGiovanna and Brady Shipp scored in the first half for Athens.
Young Crimsons still learning
Jacksonville coach Mark Grounds says Friday's 35-10 Central State Eight Conference loss at Sacred Heart-Griffin will give the coaching staff an opportunity to reinforce some things to a team that has 27 freshmen and sophomores.
"We have a lot of people that are touching the ball, a lot of people that are doing some good things, but then there's a lot of kids who when they aren't touching the ball, we have to continue to coach to get more out of them when they don't have the ball and that's young guys," Grounds said.
"The standard is, what do you do when you don't have the ball in your hands? When the ball is in their hands, they're doing some great things. They're doing less bad things each time out when they don't have the ball: their blocking, the angles, those are the subtleties of the position they have to master."
Jacksonville (2-1 overall, 0-1 CS8's west division) used seven different ball carriers before the Cyclones put the game away. Early, it allowed the Crimsons to chew up the clock and take a 10-7 lead into halftime. After needing just two punts in the first half, the Crimsons booted the ball away five straight times in the second half.
"We forced them to make adjustments, they forced us to make adjustments, and it was a game of chess throughout much of the game," Grounds said. "We just can't give up 60-yard touchdowns, we can't go three-and-out, or have negative-16 (yards) on a scramble play that puts you behind the chains."
Jacksonville had 11 plays go for negative yardage, not including penalties.
"We are an on-schedule offense," said Grounds, the CS8's dean of football coaches. "When you're on schedule, you take time off the clock, you give body blows and you force the defense to play the entire width of the field.
"At times, we did that, but in the second half, I give (SHG's) defense some credit: it stiffened up, forced us into some three-and-outs. A couple of quick touchdowns and the game got out of hand."
Unbeaten Nokomis running wild
Nokomis, which improved to 3-0 after routing Villa Grove 62-13 on Friday, is churning out the ground yards at a fast pace.
NHS has run for 1,221 yards through three games and is showing no signs of putting the ball in the air. In two of its games, Nokomis has thrown for zero yards. In a 49-0 victory over Argenta-Oreana in Week 2, quarterbacks Kannon Jones and Kadynn Petty combined to complete just three passes for 76 yards.
Meanwhile, Nokomis is riding the backs of junior running backs Daryl Evans and Nolan Herpstreith en route to its perfect start. With his 190 yards against Villa Grove, Herpstreith has a team-high 407 yards with five touchdowns. Evans has rumbled for 404 yards and leads the team with eight TDs. The team has finished with 358, 390 and 473 rushing yards in the three games.
Nokomis has outscored its opponents 138-23, including a 27-10 win over Arcola in Week 1. NHS hosts winless Cerro Gordo in Week 4.
Here they come
➤ North Mac has put last season out of its rearview mirror. The Panthers dispatched Litchfield 26-14 at home to improve to 3-0 after going 1-8 last season. That puts them in a tie for first place in the South Central Conference standings with defending champion Greenville and Pana. North Mac visits Pana for its Week 4 matchup.
➤ Springfield High continues to make a push back to its first playoffs in three years. Brody Scheffler threw for 213 yards and five TDs with just one pick to dispatch Lanphier 51-12 and remain unbeaten at 3-0. The Senators, who collected a key 21-7 win over Decatur MacArthur the previous week, next meet 0-3 Southeast.

title: Erin Turk, Kylie Sullens highlight top swimmers at Chatham Glenwood and Springfield area
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: The Chatham Glenwood girls swimming and diving team is in "good shape" after second-place showing at Capital City Classic on Saturday
content:
It's a girls swimming and diving meet that can help gauge the season, and Springfield area coaches will have time to look over the data before the championship competition begins.
Chatham Glenwood coach Scott Brandt acknowledged that the Titans aren't where they want to be after their second-place finish at the Capital City Classic Invitational on Saturday at Eisenhower Pool.
2024 football coverage: High school football in the Springfield area: Complete coverage from the 2024 season
Glenwood finished with 248 points, and Edwardsville claimed 10 of 12 events while rolling up 401 points en route to the title. Mahomet-Seymour was third with 222, followed by fourth-place O'Fallon (130).
'It's our first meet that we've had a lot of competition,' Brandt said. 'Edwardsville is always a tough team, and Mahomet-Seymour has got some good swimmers, obviously that we saw today.
'We've got a good solid team, a good number of swimmers that are good, but we've got some work to do to catch those two schools. We've been working hard in practice, and the girls are a little tired, so I think we're in really good shape at this point of the season.'
With some good individual swims from freshman Paityn Brady, senior Izzy Canny and juniors Karigan Books and Hope Speiser, Sacred Heart-Griffin was sixth with 101 points. Springfield High finished eighth with 80 points with the core of senior Mary O'Brien, sophomores Lily Allen and Abby Myers and freshman Chloe Scheffler.
Kylie Sullens goes back-to-back
Sullens, a small but mighty Glenwood sophomore, won her second straight 200-yard IM race at the classic. She clocked in at 2 minutes 17.59 seconds to break Edwardsville's streak of winning the first four events. Sullens was second last season in the IM at the Edwardsville Sectional.
'It was really fun,' said Sullens of winning Saturday's IM. 'I like being able to see my teammates cheer me on, and it pushed me to go farther to do what I can do. It's a little difficult sometimes because (the other swimmers) are really good, but when we race against them, I feel like it pushes us to go farther because we see them close to us.'
Brandt is a fan of his sophomore.
'Kylie's tough, she's a mentally tough swimmer and has really good speed,' he said. 'I think she has a really good chance of winning the IM at sectionals and making it to state this year. For her age, she is one of our best swimmers.'
Sullens scratched her second event — the 100 butterfly — which sat two events after the IM. It resulted in a disqualification.
'I was really exhausted from the IM, and I wasn't in a good state to swim,' Sullens said. 'I decided to sit that out and save it for the relays, and that was better.'
Along with Sullens, junior Sydney West and seniors Ashleigh Maender and Erin Turk, Glenwood placed second in the 400 freestyle relay, jumping over Mahomet-Seymour, which was disqualified for an early takeoff. The Titans finished third in the 200 free relay.
Turk, The State Journal-Register's two-time All-Area Swimmer of the Year, placed fourth in the 200 freestyle (2:04.70) and grabbed third in the 500 free (5:37.12).
'I wasn't where I wanted to be with my times, but I think I placed higher than I was seeded in all of them, which was nice,' Turk said. 'A lot of us might not have been super happy with our times, but as a team we were still performing and placing well.'
Maddy Yom to return
According to Brandt, Yom hit her head on the bottom of the pool at the Illinois State swimming pool. She has been in concussion protocol for about 1 ½ weeks, but Brandt is hoping for her return by the end of next week. Yom won the 100 butterfly at last season's Central State Eight Conference Meet and placed third at sectional.
'The bump wasn't too bad, so she should be in good shape, and we're looking forward to having her for the big meets at the end of the season,' said Brandt of the junior. 'I think she's going to be just fine. She's one of our top swimmers, and it definitely shows when she's not here.'
Adding more depth
Brandt said he is 'happy' with the team numbers that include a full array of talent in each event. He pointed out newcomers in sophomore Lainey Ryan and freshmen Joyce Lee and Josie Kegg, while relying on other contributors, West and Jenna Lutchka.
'We've got a good sized team,' he said. 'Hopefully, we've got some top swimmers to carry us over the top.'
🏊Top Swimmers and Divers
➤ Delaney Batton, Chatham Glenwood
The junior compiled a score of 297.10 for a third-place finish at this season's Capital City Classic in 1-meter diving. She took second at the sectional and third at conference last season.
➤ Paityn Brady, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The freshman could be a solid contributor in the 200 medley relay by swimming the butterfly, backstroke or breaststroke for the Cyclones — an event the team won at last season's CS8 meet. She has shown she can swim the 200 and 500 freestyles as well.
➤ Izzy Canny, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The senior started this season in sixth place in the 100 backstroke and eighth in the 100 butterfly at the Capital City Classic. She was fourth in the backstroke and seventh in the fly at last season's sectional.
➤ Ashleigh Maender, Chatham Glenwood
The senior will continue her journey as a sprint swimmer, namely racing in the 50 and 100 freestyles. Maender is also a big contributor in the relays for the Titans.
➤ Abby Myers, Springfield High
The junior was the prime anchor for the Senators last season, and will get some help with O'Brien, and the additions of Allen and Scheffler. Myers consistently swam the 200 and 500 freestyles last season but can swim the 100 free. She was seventh in the 100 butterfly at the Capital City Classic Invite this season.
➤ Hannah Poppenhouse, Chatham Glenwood
The senior gives the Titans even more depth in individual events and relays. She placed fifth in the 100 backstroke and sixth in the 500 freestyle at the Capital City Classic.
➤ Hope Speiser, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The junior has played a prominent role early in the season, anchoring the Cyclones' 200 medley relay and 400 freestyle relay. Speiser mostly swam the 500 freestyle and 100 breaststroke last season, taking second in both at the CS8 meet.
➤ Kylie Sullens, Chatham Glenwood
Her breakout freshman year could carry the sophomore to new heights. Sullens placed second in the 200 IM at the Edwardsville Sectional last season, and the goal is to take another step forward to a state swimming and diving berth.
➤ Erin Turk, Chatham Glenwood
The senior won the All-Area Swimmer of the Year award the past two seasons. The only thing missing for Turk is a trip to state in her signature events — the 200 and 500 freestyles. She is also key in the 200 and 400 freestyle relays.
➤ Maddy Yom, Chatham Glenwood
The junior will be counted on to deliver for the Titans in the big meets, especially during the championship season. She was a mainstay on the 200 and 400 freestyle relay teams last season and swam to a first-place finish in the 100 butterfly at the CS8 meet.

title: A project to build a tiny-home community for homeless veterans is on hold. Here's why
author: Claire Grant
description: Some aldermen argued that homeless shelters, housing and services seem to all be in certain parts of the city.
content:
A proposal to build a community center to serve a tiny-home community on the city's east side came to screeching halt Tuesday night after City Council members argued with each other over the city's approach to homelessness and whether it's saturating certain neighborhoods with homeless people.
'You see success out there, but we don't see success in ward 2,' Ward 2 Ald. Shawn Gregory said speaking to the disparity in housing types in different wards.
Ordinance 2024-333 would authorize an agreement with Be Neighbors Affordable Housing for Veterans Inc. with the city for the construction of a community center on the east side of town, at 2835 Stanton St. to benefit a tiny home neighborhood of 18 places for unhoused veterans.
The ordinance was originally held on Sept. 3, with the absence of Gregory.
The ordinance requested up to $400,000 for the construction of the facility that would include a computer lab as well as other amenities.
Concentration of homeless services
Teresa Haley of Ward 2 spoke before the council on Sept. 17 saying members of the community are worried that the 18 tiny homes will bring down property values.
'It was sold to us that these tiny homes would be permanent homes, and they would be owned by these veterans,' Haley said. 'But during our neighborhood association meeting, we were told that these homes would receive vouchers from the housing authority, which would have to be renewed every year. That sounds more like public housing than permanent housing.'
Gregory and Ward 3 Ald. Roy Williams argued that homeless housing, shelters and services appear to be getting concentrated on the city's east side.
'Please make it clear. We don't need any more facilities in two, three or four – in the east,' Williams said. 'We have yet to respect the east side cause we keep finagling and finding ways to put (shelters) over there anyways.'
Fifth Street Rennaissance and Inner City Mission are two of the agencies Gregory said he already works with in his ward.
'The issue is that we're wanting to take a population of people who have chronic issues — the people who Fifth Street Renaissance cannot get in housing by their choice — and put them over here,' Gregory said. 'There's four unhoused veterans at Helping Hands that are refusing the housing. ... Fifth Street Renaissance is not at capacity right now, and I'd rather see this money be invested into services we have now.'
Ward 7 Ald. Erin Conley said the Park Street Apartments project, a 24-unit apartment complex for permanent supportive housing to the homeless, has been a success in her ward and that the supportive services like a community center are key. But it all needs to be communicated properly to existing residents.
'This speaks to the bigger issue," Conley said. "We need to have a joint conversation with the city of Springfield, the continual care, our frontline service providers and make a coordinated organized approach."
'Time for the rest to step up'
The ordinance with Be Neighbors Affordable Housing for Veterans Inc. was held in committee.
According to the project website, Be Neighbors Affordable Housing for Veterans Inc. was founded in 2010 by veteran Harvey Hall.
The organization incorporated in 2020 to support B e Neighbors Veterans Community, its first development project. The mission of the organization is to provide permanent supportive housing for American veterans in Springfield.
In 2023, the Be Neighbors Veterans community received $4.8 million from the Illinois Housing Development Authority to facilitate the building of the over two dozen tiny homes on Stanton Street.
The Springfield Zoning Board approved the tiny-home construction, but plans cannot commence without the city moving forward on the $400,000 Learning, Technology & Resource Center at the heart of the project.
The community center would offer onsite health, wellness and employment services for residents.
'This is not a problem about the unhoused," Williams said. "It's about we have our share, and we're doing our part. It's time for the rest to step up.'

title: Third-and-three: Routt duo Creviston and Olson hook up thrice in 3Q to beat Beardstown
author: Ryan Mahan
description: A brief but windy downpour of rain helped prevent Beardstown from taking a halftime lead, then Routt turned on the jets in third quarter.
content:
JACKSONVILLE — With one touchdown in the second quarter under its belt, Beardstown was looking for its second with the ball inside the red zone.
Unfortunately for the Tigers, everything came together to create the perfect storm in Jacksonville Routt 's 41-8 Western Illinois Valley Conference North Division win at Freesen Field on Saturday.
Beardstown coach Elliott Craig had used all three of his timeouts. The clock was in the final minute with the Tigers trailing Routt 13-8. Plus, a sudden wind-driven rain was making the field and the ball slick. A team that is methodical, slow and ground-based needed a quick strike.
But two fumbled snaps in a row cost the Tigers.
'I burned my timeouts early when it was hotter than crap,' Craig said. 'I felt like we needed water; we needed a break. I had to burn them so then down there, we couldn't quite get it spiked in time; that's on me.
'Maybe if we score at the end right before halftime (it's a different game). We felt good at halftime. (Routt's) good; they average 30-some points per game (scoring).'
Creviston's chemistry with receivers
In the third quarter, with dryer and far-less windy conditions, Routt was able to do what it does best — air it out — as quarterback Kellen Creviston and Eli Olson combined for three touchdown passes to take a dominant 34-8 lead.
After Olson caught a 60-yard pass to open the third quarter and give the Rockets (3-1 overall, 2-0 WIVC North) a 20-8 lead, Routt quickly got the ball back on Beardstown's 28-yard-line after the Tigers couldn't convert a fourth-and-3 from their own 27. Olson caught an 18-yard pass to setup first-and-goal from the 10. The Rockets were still facing fourth-and-goal from the 10 when Creviston rolled to his right and found Olson just inside the right pylon of the end zone for a touchdown.
'We've been preparing all week,' Olson said. 'We've got a good receiver group with me and Jace (Lautemann), Samuel (Long), Dalton (Brown). We find ways to get open and Kellen just finds whoever is open.
'We practice that a lot where I line up inside and kind of fade to the outside. (Creviston) threw a good ball there. Kellen is known for throwing good balls (and) he's known for throwing some crazy balls, but he hit me there, so that was good.'
Surprisingly, the Routt QB thought he would've given kicker Brock Runyon an opportunity for a field goal in that spot.
'I actually wanted to kick it because in walkthrough (Friday), Brock actually hit like a 40-yarder,' Creviston said. 'I was like, 'OK, we can use him more instead of taking these risky options.''
Routt coach Barry Creviston has six receivers with at least one catch this season to account for more than 1,000 yards receiving.
'(Kellen Creviston), Eli, Jace, Declan (Lahey) and Sam Long, just like any football team, we've taken all the small steps in summer football, in practice, and now in games,' coach Creviston said. 'Eli gets more yardage than anyone else, but it's not by design; we throw it to whoever's open.'
Olson caught five passes for 113 yards and three touchdowns. Creviston was 12-for-22 for 207 yards and four TDs, including a 25-yarder to Jace Lautemann on the Rockets' first drive for a 7-0 advantage.
Brown had three catches for 50 yards.
Young Tigers still learning
It was just the second time this season Beardstown (0-4 overall, 0-2 WIVC North) scored. The Tigers lost 46-6 in Week 1 at Carrollton and were shutout the next two weeks by Pleasant Hill and Camp Point Central.
'We got the lead there early, our kids are resilient, we just didn't play a good second half,' Craig said. 'First-and-20 (on a holding penalty deep in Beardstown's territory), with what we're trying to do this year, just puts us in a major hole. It just seemed like every fourth down that they went for, they converted. The bottom line was we just didn't get the job done in the second half.'
There are positives to take in the loss, especially given Beardstown can play the what-if game about the loss of timeouts and the weather at the end of the second quarter.
'We're an extremely young football team,' Craig said. 'We have three seniors who've done this before. The other eight guys you see out there, this is their fourth game at the varsity level. You can see we're getting better. Our kids are starting to get it, they're grinding and we've got some pretty tough kids.'
But one thing did leave a sour taste in Craig's mouth: Routt's 85-yard touchdown run by Charlie Alan, scored with just seven seconds left on the clock.
'I thought they'd take a knee with seven seconds,' Craig said, 'but that didn't happen.
'I just felt like, he's got a good team: put your subs in, the game's over.'

title: From Oktoberfest to Miami, there's surprises in store in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: Even if it isn't sweater weather just yet, Springfield is gearing up for fall with fun events for the whole family.
content:
September is still kicking with summer heat, with temperatures staying in the 80s through the weekend and a high of 89 degrees on Friday.
Even if it isn't sweater weather just yet, Springfield is gearing up for fall with fun events for the whole family.
Check out these five things to do around Sangamon County this weekend, from murder mysteries to solve with friends to Oktoberfest.
Summer in Miami murder mystery
What: Step into Miami, in the heat of 1979. The lights are dimmed save for the candles flickering at the table, as guests join for an unforgettable night of deception and intrigue with a cocktail of surprises in store.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Imagine this: a sweltering summer night in Miami, where love is in the air, and betrayal is just around the corner. Dress in your Miami best and prepare to uncover the truth in a classic whodunit!
The night has in store prizes for the supreme detective who can crack the case, a four course dinner at The Pasfield House and other prizes for solving clues.
When: 6:30 p.m. Saturday Where: 525 S. Pasfield St., Springfield
More: This is a 21+ event, with tickets at $46.13 per person after fees for the dinner, detective work, and gifts. Tickets can be found online at The Culture Experience website.
Chatham Oktoberfest
What: Is there truly a better combination than beer, brats, bands and weiner dogs? Chatham's got them all and more at their local Oktoberfest.
Grab a celebratory stein at the vendor village before heading to the ceremonial keg tapping to announce the start of the festival! Try your hand in sausage toss or the stein hoist, before enjoying a night with lively music from the Brandy Kristin Band.
When: All day Saturday
Where: 700 S. Main St., Chatham
More: This is a kid friendly event for all ages, with a kids area open from noon to 5 p.m.
Out of the Darkness Walk
What: There is hope in Illinois, one step at a time.
94% of adults in the U.S. think suicide can be prevented. People throughout Springfield and Sangamon County plan on walking to end the fight against suicide at the Out of the Darkness Walk.
The walk gives an opportunity for people impacted by suicide to come together so they can support and connect one another.
Since the first walk was held in 2004, the Out of the Darkness Community Walks have provided a platform to create awareness about mental health issues as well as raise funds, which are split between Illinois and national efforts.
When: 2 p.m. Saturday
Where: 2251 Richard Wright Drive, Springfield
More: There is no fee to register for an Out of the Darkness Walk. Individuals wishing to participate can find the registration page for their local walk at afsp.org/ILTogether.
Vintage Clothing pop-up
What: Ditch the crop tops and get down with denim this weekend for a vintage clothing fest to fill your wardrobe with autumn essentials!
Visit over 20 different vendors from across central Illinois who are setting up at Dumb Records in downtown, for Illinois Vintage Fest.
This may be the only chance to find that windbreaker you tossed away in the 90s.
When: 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Saturday
Where: 418 E. Monroe St., Springfield
Edwards Place Fine Arts Fair
What: Tour the Historic Edwards Place house in the capital of Illinois, as part of the Annual Edwards Place Fine Art Fair.
Around the historic house, guests to the building will find a used book sale benefiting the Michael Victor II Art Library in Springfield, a live music stage, with food and beverage vendors just around the corner.
Across the house and grounds will be artwork created by artists across the U.S. while supporting the Springfield Art Association.
When: 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday and Sunday
More: The SAA is a nonprofit visual arts community center established in 1913, which regularly provides free events to the public for all ages.

title: FBI responds to Springfield Board of Elections building for suspicious mail
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Board of Elections building in Springfield received a suspicious parcel Friday, prompting presence from the FBI and a hazmat team.
content:
The FBI responded to the Illinois State Board of Elections building in Springfield after a suspicious package was found.
Election offices across the U.S. have been receiving suspicious mail, in upwards of 15 states, according to a report Tuesday from Associated Press.
Matthew Dietrich, a spokesperson for the Board of Elections, said the Springfield Police and Fire Departments responded to the building at 2329 S. MacArthur Blvd. until FBI arrived.
Employees became suspicious when they read an odd-looking return address on the parcel.
"We were expecting to get something like this, based on the fact that so many other state election offices around the country had already received them this week, so we were on the lookout for it,' Dietrich said. 'We knew if anything halfway suspicious came in, we knew not to open it, so when it arrived, we did not open it.'
About 20 people were inside the building when the package arrived and everyone evacuated.
Nationally, the FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service on Tuesday were investigating the origin of suspicious packages were sent to or received by elections officials, according to the AP report, but there have been no reports of injuries or hazardous materials found within the parcels.
Public Affairs Officer for FBI Springfield, Becky Cramblit, provided the following statement:
'The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to election officials in several states. Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident and safely collect the letters. We are also working with our partners to determine how many letters were sent, the individual or individuals responsible for the letters, and the motive behind the letters. As this is an ongoing matter we will not be commenting further on the investigation, but the public can be assured safety is our top priority. We would also like to remind everyone to exercise care in handling mail, especially from unrecognized senders. If you see something suspicious, please contact law enforcement immediately.'

title: Former cellmate of man who pleaded guilty in 2021 triple murder case takes the stand
author: Steven Spearie
description: Joseph Hembrough's former Jacksonville cellmate testified that he left his gun clip at the murder scene by accident.
content:
A Jacksonville man and the former Morgan County cellmate of Joseph Hembrough, who pleaded guilty in a 2021 triple murder case in Springfield's Harvard Park neighborhood, told a Sangamon County jury Monday that Hembrough shared with him particular details about the shootings and robbery, including his leaving his gun clip at the house where it occurred.
On the stand, Michael S. Pullings admitted that he told a Springfield detective that Hembrough "might be lying," and that Hembrough disparaged one of two men on trial for the murders, Kelton Galmore of Jacksonville, with racial epithets.
The murder trial of Galmore and Larry McClain Jr. of Springfield has reached its second week with the state putting on witnesses.
Those included Tannya Martin, McClain's one-time girlfriend, and Det. Ryan Maddox of the Springfield Police Department and the lead investigator in the case.
Savante English, 27, and Keyera Gant, 25, of Springfield, and Bryant K. Williams, 27, of Houston, Texas, were all fatally shot in a house in the 2500 block of South 10th Street on Aug. 9, 2021.
Hembrough pleaded guilty on the eve of the trial and was sentenced to 20 years in the Department of Corrections. He testified against Galmore and McClain on Friday, saying while he was present and packing a gun, he didn't shoot any of the victims.
The three had gone to the 10th Street house to buy drugs.
Pullings, who has a criminal record out of Morgan County, was a surprise witness and the subject of an open-court discussion before taking the stand.
Special prosecutor Derek Dion pointed out that defense attorneys for Galmore and McClain, Monroe McWard and Mark Wykoff, referred to Hembrough as "an opportunist" and "a liar" during his testimony Friday.
"We should be able to rehabilitate that," Dion told Presiding Circuit Judge Ryan Cadagin.
Pullings shared a cell with Hembrough, who was originally arrested on a theft charge in October 2021. On a search of Hembrough's house, Morgan County detectives found firearms, including a Polymer 80, commonly known as a "ghost gun."
Pullings said Hembrough threatened to kill him if he told anyone about the particulars of the case he shared with him. Pullings testified that he has known Hembrough since he was a kid.
Hembrough told Pullings that he left the clip or magazine at the crime scene by accident. Pullings said that Hembrough was worried about it.
"(Hembrough) showed me how to release the clip," Pullings told assistant state's attorney Meghan McCarthy on re-examination. "He dropped the clip. He didn't mean to lose it."
Hembrough told police in an interview in October 2021 that the clip wouldn't come back to him, but he later testified that it was his.
Maddox said the clip was fully loaded, and none of the live rounds matched any of the 22 casings found at the scene.
On cross, McWard reminded Pullings that he described the gun as "an Uzi."
Pullings also told McWard that Hembrough referred to Galmore as "N**s," though he also used the pejorative "N****r." Pullings told Maddox about Hembrough's name-calling.
Miller testified that around McClain's Dec. 13 birthday in 2021, he made comments to her about being involved in a robbery though she said he didn't give details.
Miller, who lived with McClain, said he "regretted it" and that he was crying.
Maddox testified to Hembrough saying initially that he wasn't present for the shooting and robbery, that only Galmore and McClain were there.
In a Feb. 22, 2022, interview, Maddox said, Hembrough admitted he was there and armed.
The state also played clips of outgoing calls from the Sangamon County Jail where Galmore talked about McClain "taking his weight" and "taking his charge," meaning he needed to take responsibility for what happened.
Maddox will again take the stand Tuesday morning. The trial is expected to wrap up sometime this week.

title: Will Hurricane Helene impact the Springfield area?
author: Tom Ackerman
description: While much of Florida's Gulf Coast braces for what is predicted to be Hurricane Helene, the storm may impact Springfield. Here's what to know.
content:
While much of Florida's Gulf Coast braces for what is predicted to be Hurricane Helene – a Category 3 storm – it is not ruled out that Springfield will be impacted by the storm.
Here's what you need to know.
Where and when will storm reach the Springfield area?
The hurricane's track, known as the 'cone of uncertainty', will arrive at I-57 general area by Saturday morning, said Meteorologist John Bumgardner with the National Weather Service based in Lincoln.
How much rain might Springfield receive?
As of Tuesday afternoon, some models indicated Springfield may see a couple of inches of rain, Bumgardner told The State Journal Register.
Will Springfield see wind gusts?
While the weather models still have time to change, Bumgardner said that strong wind gusts are predicted mainly to the southeast. The gusts are possible if the remnants of the hurricane move further west.
If wind gusts reach Springfield, the wind speed would be less than 39 miles per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center and Central Pacific Hurricane Center.
How does the storm actually reach the Midwest?
According to Bumgardner, most "guidance" or weather predictors are showing the low-pressure system making landfall in the Florida panhandle.
"Then there's already an upper-level, low pressure system – kind of what we call a cutoff low, meaning it's like cutoff from the flow aloft. It's lingering across the heartland and basically the hurricane gets pulled northward into that low, and they kind of spin around each other Friday into Saturday," he said.

title: An asteroid known as a 'mini-moon' will join Earth's orbit for 2 months starting Sunday
author: Max Hauptman
description: A small asteroid will join Earth's orbit around the sun for two months beginning Sunday, becoming a 'mini-moon.'
content:
Beginning Sunday, Earth's skies will soon have a temporary visitor.
On September 29, an asteroid dubbed 2024 PT5 will become a " mini-moon" of sorts, temporarily entering Earth's orbit for almost two months before the forces of gravity return it to a vast field of space rocks known as the Arjuna asteroid belt that follows a similar orbital path around the sun as our own home planet.
Scientists discovered the object Aug. 7 using the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System in Sutherland, South Africa during routine monitoring, according to a study published in the journal Research Notes of the American Astronomical Society.
What is a mini-moon?
"Mini-moon" events are when pieces in space like an asteroid or floating pieces of space junk temporarily participate in orbiting the Earth with some completing a full revolution.
In order to be considered a mini-moon, an incoming body must reach Earth at a range around 2.8 million miles (4.5 million km) and at a steady space of about 2,200 mph (3,540 km/h), according to Universidad Complutense de Madrid professor Carlos de la Fuente Marcos.
Previous mini-moon events occurred in short-lived mini moon in 1981 and 2022, according to researchers.
Marcos told Space.com earlier this week that the asteroid will enter Earth's orbit at 15:54 ET on Sunday, and depart at 11:43 ET on Nov. 25.
Can I see the mini-moon?
At just 37 feet wide, 2024 PT5's presence in Earth's skies won't be visible unless one is a professional astronomer, or at least has access to a powerful telescope.
"The object is too small and dim for typical amateur telescopes and binoculars. However, the object is well within the brightness range of typical telescopes used by professional astronomers," Marcos told Space.com. "A telescope with a diameter of at least 30 inches plus a CCD or CMOS detector is needed to observe this object; a 30-inch telescope and a human eye behind it will not be enough."
