title: Defendants in 2021 triple homicide in Springfield found guilty on all counts
author: Steven Spearie
description: Two defendants charged in a 2021 triple homicide in the Harvard Park neighborhood in Springfield were found guilty on all counts Wednesday.
content:
Two defendants charged in a 2021 triple homicide in the Harvard Park neighborhood in Springfield were found guilty on all counts Wednesday, capping an eight-day trial in Sangamon County court.
Kelton Galmore of Jacksonville and Larry McClain Jr. of Springfield both face life in prison. Sentencing before Presiding Circuit Judge Ryan Cadagin is on Dec. 9.
Savante English, 27, and Keyera Gant, 25, of Springfield, and Bryant K. Williams, 27, of Houston and formerly of Springfield, were all shot multiple times in a house being rented by English in the 2500 block of South 10th Street. They were found on Aug. 9, 2021.
Galmore and McClain were on trial for two types of murder counts: accountability for all three victims and accountability for only the victims they individually shot.
Galmore was charged with shooting Williams and McClain was charged with shooting English. Both were charged with shooting Gant. The three victims were found in different rooms in the home.
Galmore and McClain were also found guilty of armed violence and armed robbery.
The seven-man, five-woman jury took a little over two hours to render the verdict.
A third defendant, Joseph Hembrough of Jacksonville, pleaded guilty on Sept. 9 and was sentenced to 20 years in the Illinois Department of Corrections and a three-year mandatory supervised release term. He testified against Galmore and McClain on Friday.
"The evidence showed this was a joint venture," said special prosecutor Derek Dion in his closing statement.
English and Williams, a budding rapper in the Houston area who went by the name BK Yola, were childhood friends in Springfield. Williams was scheduled to return to Texas the day of the murder.
Williams had returned to Springfield to attend a Celebration of Life event, marking the one-year anniversary of the death of De'Arius Equan Jones of Springfield.
A number of people had attended an after-party at the 10th Street home after the Celebration of Life, including McClain. In the trial, the connection was made that Williams knew McClain.
On the way to the 10th Street house late on Aug. 8, Hembrough and Galmore picked up McClain in Springfield. Hembrough said he did not know McClain at the time.
McClain, Galmore and Hembrough entered through the front door around 1 a.m. on Aug. 9. It was English, Hembrough said, who brought out bags of methamphetamine and scales to complete the sale.
When Williams appeared, he started yelling at McClain for showing up unannounced and bringing other people with him, Hembrough testified.
Galmore produced a Glock 34, which had a switch on it to make it fire automatically, Hembrough said. Williams tried to knock the gun out of Galmore's hand before he was shot multiple times, Hembrough said in testimony.
McClain then shot English in the kitchen, Hembrough testified. Both Galmore and McClain shot Gant.
Attorneys for Galmore and McClain did not put on any witnesses after the prosecution rested its case Tuesday. Neither defendant took the stand.
Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser applauded law enforcement and legal teams for putting together a case to hold McClain and Galmore accountable.
Several family members of the victims openly wept after the verdict was read by Cadagin.
"I can imagine what their families are going through," Milhiser said afterwards. "They had to sit through not only this happening but justice to happen, then the vivid details and descriptions of what happened to them."
Both attorneys in the case--Monroe McWard for Galmore and Mark Wykoff for McClain--continued to punch holes in Hembrough's statements and testimony, calling him "an opportunist" and "a liar."
"With Hembrough's testimony, we expected a different result," McWard said outside the court. "But the jury heard the evidence, and they decided."
In closing remarks, Dion said the jury "didn't have to trust Hembrough," but that the evidence--surveillance video, phone logs and GPS data--would prove Galmore and McClain guilty.

title: 'It's time for him to pay': Families of Texas serial killer's victims welcome execution
author: Amanda Lee Myers
description: Garcia Glen White confessed to killing five people: Bonita, Annette and Bernette Edwards, Greta Washington and Hai Pham. These are their stories.
content:
Two of Garcia Glen White 's victims were identical twin sisters who had just celebrated their sweet 16th birthdays the day before they were killed. Another victim was a hard-working dad with big dreams who had just moved his family to the U.S. from Vietnam and left behind seven children.
In all, White confessed to murdering five people in a six-year period and will be executed for his crimes on Tuesday. He will be the sixth man executed in the U.S. in 10 days and the fifth inmate put to death in Texas so far this year.
The families of most of his victims have waited 35 years for White's execution day, which has been delayed repeatedly despite his confession. He was even scheduled for execution in 2015 but won a reprieve with less than 24 hours to spare.
"He has lived longer in prison than my sister lived on this Earth," said Dewanta Washington, a 60-year-old schoolteacher in Houston whose beloved sister, Greta Williams, was beaten to death by White in 1989.
"If you know he did it, he admitted to it, why have all these appeals?" she questioned, saying that her parents died waiting for the execution to happen. "It's time for him to pay the piper. He just needs to go meet his maker."
Now that White's execution appears to be moving forward, USA TODAY spoke with family members of his victims to learn more about their loved ones. These are their stories.
Greta Williams: A pint-sized free spirit who dreamed of being a mom
White's first victim was Greta Williams, a 27-year-old who grew up in Chicago and had only lived in Houston for a few months when she was beaten so "beyond recognition" that the family couldn't have an open casket, her sister told USA TODAY.
Dewanta Washington said she and Williams were only two years apart and looked so much alike, people thought they were twins.
The girls loved their two brothers, dancing to Michael Jackson songs, playing house with baby dolls and riding bikes.
"Greta, she was my best friend," Washington said. "We shared a room, and we talked about when we got bras, what we were gonna do, and, 'When I get married I'm gonna have this many kids. I'm gonna have a husband,' that kind of stuff."
As they got older, Washington said she was the boring one while her sister was a "free spirit" and "party girl," who was just an acquaintance of White's. The sisters were living together again in Houston when Williams decided to go out one night. Washington said she had a bad feeling.
"The night that she left I told her, 'Don't leave, we're going to find you dead,'" Washington said. "Her last words were, 'I'll be fine, I love you.'"
Washington said that she still has her sister's ashes and has been waiting for the day White is put to death in order to spread her ashes back in Chicago.
"My sister wont be truly free until he's executed, until he pays his debt," Williams said.
Bonita, Annette and Bernette Edwards: Killed in triple murder
Identical twin sisters Annette and Bernette Edwards knew they were living in a dangerous situation with their mother, who used crack cocaine and would allow questionable people into their apartment, according to court records.
The day before they were all killed, the girls had turned 16 and begged their grandmother to let them come live with her, Harris County prosecutor Josh Reiss told USA TODAY.
It's unclear why the girls were still in their mother's home the next day when White came over. He later told police in a confession that he and Bonita Edwards were using crack cocaine while the girls were in their room. He said he and Edwards got into a fight.
"She reached for a knife, and I took the knife and stabbed her," White said, according to court records. "Some kids come out. I went into the bedroom after them ... I stabbed one in the bedroom and one in the living room
The Edwards' bodies were found just a few weeks before Christmas. They were riddled with stab wounds in various states of undress, and strong evidence showed that Bernette had been sexually assaulted, court records show. Among the many disturbing details at the crime scene: A bloody sock was found under the Christmas tree.
On top of White's eventual confession, his DNA was a 99.9999 % match to semen found on Bernette, who had a pink shirt wrapped around the back of her neck and through her mouth as a gag, court records show.
USA TODAY was unable to find out more about the girls or their mother. The court records are 35 years old and limited, and the Edwards' family members haven't responded to requests for comment.
But prosecutor Reiss said about their case: "Two dead 16-year-old girls kind of speak for themselves in terms of the savageness of these crimes."
Hai Pham: A hard-working Vietnamese immigrant with a dream
Hai Pham moved his wife and his four youngest children to the U.S. in September 1994. Nine months later, White killed him in the middle of the day in the convenience store where he worked while his 14-year-old son napped nearby, according to one of Pham's other sons, Hiep Pham.
Hiep Pham told USA TODAY that his father had been teaching his children English even before they left Vietnam, and that his big dream was for his other grown children to eventually reunite with the family in the U.S., and for everyone to have successful careers.
"My dad believed we would have a better life in the states," said Hiep Pham, who was just 17 when his father was killed and is now a 47-year-old Houston salesman with a daughter of his own. "But that whole dream was just went down the drain."
As Hiep Pham grew up in Houston without his dad, struggling to learn English, dropping out of school to work two jobs and help put food on the table, he said he eventually realized how big of a deal Father's Day is here. It made him miss his own dad that much more.
"I feel angry still," said Pham, fighting tears. "We never celebrated Father's Day for my dad. And I always dreamed of that, having a beer with my dad."
If Hai Pham had lived, he would have been a grandfather of 12. His three oldest children remain in Vietnam while his four youngest have carved out their lives in the U.S. His wife no longer has a memory after a debilitating cancer fight.
Like Williams, Pham plans to witness White's execution.
"When I got the call (about the execution) I felt relief. I went back home and told my family during dinner that night: 'I don't know about y'all, but I'm going,'" he said. "It's hard to see somebody die, but I think its justice for my dad."

title: Here's a breakdown of when leaves will change colors in Springfield
author: Tom Ackerman
description: While it may not totally feel like fall yet, it may begin starting to look like it soon.
content:
While it may not totally feel like fall yet, it may begin starting to look like it soon.
According to the 2024 Fall Foliage Prediction Map, which annually predicts the fall color changes, Springfield residents should start seeing colors change beginning on Sept. 30.
Here's a breakdown for when colors will begin changing in the Springfield area according to the map on Smokymountains.com.
When will leaves begin to change?
Leaves will begin turning a pale-yellow color around Sept. 30. This type of change in color is described as "minimal."
What about orange and red leaves?
Orange and red leaves on trees will be seen throughout much of October, according to the map. The site says residents may start seeing orange leaves beginning Oct. 7 and last for a couple of weeks before turning more red around Oct. 21.
When will we see peak colors this year?
According to the map, Springfield residents should start seeing peak red colors around Oct. 28, which will last for about a week.
Why do leaves change color?
The timing of color changes and the reason they fall is primarily regulated by the calendar and as nights become longer, according to the U.S. Forest Service.
"None of the other environmental influences – such as temperature, rainfall, food supply – are as unvarying as the steadily increasing length of night during autumn," the website reads. "As days grow shorter, and nights grow longer and cooler, biochemical processes in the leaf begin to paint the landscape with Nature's autumn palette."
Why are certain colors specific to autumn foliage?
Trees store certain sugars for the winter dormant period, according to the page from the U.S. Forest Service.
Three types of pigments are involved in autumn color:
Carotenoids: Produces yellow, orange, and brown colors in such things as corn, carrots, and daffodils, as well as rutabagas, buttercups, and bananas.
Anthocyanin: Gives color to such familiar things as cranberries, red apples, concord grapes, blueberries, cherries, strawberries, and plums. They are water soluble and appear in the watery liquid of leaf cells.
Chlorophyll: Gives leaves a basic green color. It is necessary for photosynthesis, the chemical reaction that enables plants to use sunlight to manufacture sugars for food.

title: Iran launches missile attack on Israel
author: Tom Vanden Brook
description: A direct attack by Iran on Israel will carry 'severe consequences for Iran,' a White House official said. A shelter in place order was issued by the US embassy.
content:
This story has been updated to add new information.
WASHINGTON — Iran launched missiles toward Israel, Israel's Defense Forces said in a short statement Tuesday as it urged Israelis to enter bomb shelters.
The move was the latest escalation in a weeks-long skirmish between Iran-backed Hezbollah and Israel, and comes days before the the one-year anniversary of Hamas' Oct. 7 attacks on southern Israel. It also comes just as the Jewish high holiday Rosh Hashanah begins at sunset on Wednesday.
Few other details were immediately available.
Sirens were sounding across Israel. The IDF said it was working to intercept the missiles.
The IDF said on Tuesday evening that it determined people could leave protected spaces in areas across the country, following a situational assessment.
There were no reports of injuries from the missiles, Magen David Adom, Israel's emergency medical service, said on Tuesday.
The White House said President Biden had directed the U.S. military to aid Israel in defending against the attacks and shoot down missiles targeting Israel. Earlier, a White House official warned that Iran was preparing to launch an "imminent" ballistic missile attack on Israel.
The Pentagon is actively supporting Israel in its preparations to defend against the attack, according to the official who was not authorized to speak publicly. A direct attack on Israel will carry "severe consequences for Iran," the official said.
The U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem on Tuesday directed government employees and their family members to "shelter in place until further notice."
A short while before Iran launched its attack there were multiple casualties in a shooting incident in Tel Aviv that police said appeared to be terror-related. Police said on Tuesday that six people were dead, including the two shooters, but the death toll was "dynamic" and could rise.
The indications of an imminent attack follow Israel's aggressive airstrikes and covert attacks against the Iranian-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement that the missile attack was revenge for the deaths of several Hezbollah leaders, including its top leader Hassan Nasrallah. It warned that it would launch greater attacks if Israel reacts.
Earlier on Tuesday, Israeli troops crossed into Lebanon for the first time since 2006. The Israeli military said it was conducting a "localized and targeted" ground operation on Hezbollah command posts and weapons storage sites.
Iran has also been threatening to attack Israel since August, when Hamas political leader Ismail Haniyeh was assassinated in a Tehran apartment building.
Israeli military spokesman Rear Adm. Daniel Hagari said on Tuesday that the U.S. informed Israel of Iran's intention.
He said Israel has dealt with Iran's "threat" in the past, adding, "we'll deal with it now." Israel's military is "patrolling the skies" and, along with the U.S., is watching developments in Iran closely, he added.
'Iranian fire on the state of Israel will have consequences,' he said.
In a statement, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu urged Israelis to follow military directives. Israel's restrictions on large gatherings would be tightened, he said.
Israel hammers Hezbollah, 1,000 dead
Israel killed Hezbollah's longtime leader, Hassan Nasrallah in an airstrike on Sept. 27.
Israel has pummeled Lebanon with airstrikes in the last two weeks, killing more than 1,000 people, according to the country's health ministry. The escalation between Israel and Hezbollah, the largest in nearly a year, was triggered by an Israeli operation that exploded thousands of pagers and walkie-talkies across the country.
In April, Iran launched a barrage of more than 300 missiles and drones at Israel. With U.S. and western allies, Israel shot down almost all of them.
Supreme Leader Khamenei moved to secure location
Iran's Supreme Leader Sayyed Ali Khamenei called for five days of mourning on Sept. 28 for his ally Nasrallah and was moved to a secure location, a second U.S. official said.
Tehran has in the past used mourning periods for operational planning, this person said.
Even as Israel, the U.S., and other allies prepared for a ballistic missile strike on Tuesday, an official noted Tehran could take longer to respond − opting to rebuild Hezbollah's leadership before striking back.
For almost a year, the Iran-backed militant group has intensified firing of rockets into northern Israel. Tensions on that border have increased since the October 7 attack by Hamas on Israel that killed 1,200 people. Israel responded by launching military strikes on Gaza that have killed about 40,000 Palestinians, according to the Hamas-run Gazan Health Ministry.
U.S. officials are concerned that a ratcheting up of tensions could lead to a broader regional conflict in the Middle East and have been trying to negotiate a cease-fire.
Hezbollah is financially backed by Iran and is part of its "axis of resistance," a network of groups across the region that it funds and provides with weapons, including the Houthis in Yeman and Hamas in Gaza.

title: Springfield business owner wins Hispanic Heritage Month award from Illinois Treasurer
author: Claire Grant
description: 'I'm trying to get (Hispanic people) to feel comfortable to come downtown and be a part of the community,' Monica Zanetti said.
content:
At 10 o'clock in the morning, Wild Rose Artisan Gallery owner Monica Zanetti unlocks the shop right across from the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and sets out her shirts while prepping to greet guests.
Monarch butterflies on painted canvases cover the walls, an homage to their migration south from North America to South America. The store is more than an art gallery to Zanetti, who's made it a welcoming spot for Springfield's Latinx community.
'I'm trying to get (Hispanic people) to feel comfortable to come downtown and be a part of the community,' Zanetti said. 'It's all about seeing yourself somewhere.'
Zanetti, whose roots are Zinapecuaro Mexican descent, moved to Springfield from the San Francisco Bay area over 15 ago to relocate for her husband's career while developing her decades-long passion with art in the capital city. Her art style is bright with strong fluorescent blues and creamsicle orange, painting roses around Lincoln, monarch butterflies in Springfield and words of support in Spanish on canvas.
'There's just so much culture with indigenous people,' Zanetti said, 'There's Day of the Dead, we get colorful and it's all about living your life and with community. When I go to Mexico it's all about community, so when I come here that is what I try to do.'
Springfield's Hispanic population is only 3.10% according to estimates from the U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey.
In honor of Hispanic Heritage Month from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15, Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs hosted a celebration on Sept. 18 to commemorate the month and honor the work of community leaders across the state.
Zanetti was one of eight Latino leaders to receive the outstanding award, for her craftsmanship and outstanding achievement in arts and humanities, like establishing the Wild Rose Scholarship Fund to help local children develop an understanding with Latino music and culture. In 2022, the fund helped run an event for children to listen to a mariachi play traditional music and talk about the culture behind the songs.
'What I love about my events is that you're going to see diversity,' Zanetti said. 'I ask, 'where's the diversity?' and they're like 'they don't come', well are you making them feel special when they come?'
Five years ago, Zanetti fulfilled a lifelong dream of owning a retail shop to display her art drawing from her Mexican roots through purchasing the Wild Rose from its original owners in 2020. Since then, she has provided more than 20 local artists a venue to display their passion projects with a portion of sales found toward the fund. Her work has been featured in San Francisco's historic City Hall, Mexican Historical Museum Gift Shop, Sacred Art and Pilsen Outpost and has held a speech at the Illinois State Museum.
To celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month with the city, the Wild Rose will hold a fiesta all day long on Saturday, Oct. 5, with party games and good food from scratch. Guests can try their hand at loteria, a Mexican bingo game, and try out different games every hour.
'I love my community so the best way to grow it is to be a part of it,' Zanetti said. 'The more we volunteer to make it better is manpower.'
A full list of awardees for this year can be found on Illinoistreasurer.gov.

title: Why were USPS workers rallying in Springfield? Here's what you need to know
author: Claire Grant
description: USPS workers across the country rallied Tuesday evening. Here's what you need to know about the rallies and if your mail service will be impacted.
content:
There's a good chance you saw men and women holding picket signs outside of the Post Office on Cook Street Tuesday afternoon.
Members of the American Postal Workers Union in Springfield joined USPS workers across the country in a rally demanding for better service at the post office as negotiations for a new contract are underway.
Here's what you need to know.
What are postal workers rallying about?
Johnny Bishop, Locale 239 president of the American Postal Workers Union in Springfield, cited poor working conditions. Bishop said he's had people working 12 hours a day since May, and the union wants safer conditions.
What are the demands of the union?
The APWU is demanding greater transparency from the Postal Board of Governors and for public comment in board meetings along with more investment in its workforce citing high turnover and short staffing rates.
Will rallies like this impact my mail service?
The APWU says barring the exception of election mail, which is prioritized, mail service has been noticeably slower for millions of customers due to postal management's implementation of modernizing facilities, known as the Delivering for America plan, which was halted until 2025 on May 15.
What is the Delivery for America Plan?
The change in mail processing is part of the Delivering for America plan proposed in March 2021. The decade-long proposal would slash Packaging and Distribution Centers, or PDCs, nationwide to save the company between $1.7 to $2.2 million annually with the plan. The PDCs would be transformed into Local Processing Centers which would move mail processing to larger distribution centers and for Springfield's case, over state lines to the PDC in St. Louis, Missouri.
The plan implemented by Postmaster Louis DeJoy is three years into the making and also slowed delivery standards for rural communities. Mail delivery in rural areas may take an additional 12 to 24 hours. Service previously guaranteed three-day delivery but in 2024, standard delivery is one to five days.
The 10-year plan came to a halt in May of this year, following a slew of senators sending letters to Postmaster General Louis DeJoy citing concern about the plan's implementation of LPC.
What is election mail and why won't it be impacted?
Bishop said election mail monitors are working around the clock to make sure ballots won't be impacted. Ballots and other election mail are moved ahead of other mail in priority ahead of the Nov. 6 election date. The USPS also has authorized extra deliveries, collections, transportation, and overtime for this purpose. In previous election cycles, the USPS took a similar approach toward fast-tracking ballots. In 2020, 97.9% of ballots were delivered to election officials within three days.

title: CS8 stunner: U-High beats Glenwood for first time since joining league
author: Ryan Mahan
description: The Normal U-High offense jumped out to a big lead and stymied Glenwood almost the entire night to earn first CS8 win over Titans.
content:
This story will be updated.
NORMAL — If last year's win over Decatur MacArthur turned the page for the Normal U-High football team, then Friday's stunning victory over Chatham Glenwood started a new chapter.
U-High quarterback Alek Weiland threw five touchdowns and finished with 316 yards passing as the Pioneers beat Glenwood 33-13 in a Central State Eight Conference east division game at Illinois State University's Hancock Stadium.
When Weiland found AJ Holden for a 1-yard touchdown with 1 minute, 44 seconds left in the first half, it gave U-High a 26-0 lead.
The Titans (4-2 overall, 3-1 CS8 east) found their offensive groove long enough to cut the deficit in half, when Brady Dwyer scored a 1-yard touchdown run with 12 seconds left in the second quarter and junior quarterback Colten Knoedler found Jonathan Helm for a 21-yard score on the Titans' first possession of the second half.
Glenwood's defense held the Pioneers (4-2, 3-1 CS8 east) scoreless for almost the entirety of the second half but couldn't get any closer. U-High cemented the win when Weiland and Holden connected on an 18-yard strike with 2:40 to play.
Heading into Friday's game, Glenwood was 7-0 against U-High since the Pioneers entered the CS8 in 2017. That first season, Glenwood pulled out a 37-36 overtime win, but since then, the Pioneers haven't been within a mile of the Titans with Glenwood holding a 326-106 scoring advantage in the series.
Glenwood fans were heard starting to get restless after the Pioneers went up 12-0 on Weiland's second TD throw to Cade Cunningham, this one a 19-yard pass after the two connected on a 34-yard score to start the game.
Twice in a row, Glenwood had to punt out of its own end zone in the second quarter. The first time, U-High couldn't convert a fourth down from the Glenwood 3. Four plays later, the Titans had a fourth and 11 from their own 2. After a 25-yard punt, Weiland found Carson Stevens for his third TD throw, and U-High found itself up 19-0.
Glenwood committed a holding penalty on first and 10 from its own 9-yard line, then had to again punt from its own 3. The Titans' defense committed a pass interference on first and 10 from the Glenwood 20, and three plays later, Holden and Weiland put the Pioneers up 26-0.
One week ago, U-High lost 38-30 to Rochester. Brody Walworth said it was important to protect against the emotional rollercoaster football can be after tough losses. He added that it will be important to do the same thing after this momentous win.
Knoedler finished 22-for-39 for 236 yards and two interceptions. He found six different receivers, including Gavin Simmons, who caught 11 passes for 131 yards.
U-High forced Glenwood into a one-dimensional team on Friday. The Titans rushed 16 times for just 42 yards and one touchdown. Glenwood also committed seven penalties for 57 yards, while U-High was whistled four times for 30 yards.

title: Official: Witnesses say boy, 10, wasn't intended target in fatal shooting
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Witnesses have told officials the boy who was fatally shot in Peoria who had ties to Springfield was not the intended target. Here's the latest.
content:
A botched drug deal may have led to the fatal shooting of Torres L. Johnson II, a 10-year-old boy who lived in Peoria but had ties to Springfield.
Witnesses said the shooting happened after a drug deal involving cannabis went wrong and led to an attempted armed robbery between the suspect Maurice Sargent, 33, and two juveniles, according to the Peoria County State's Attorney's Office.
The State's Attorney's Office said Johnson not involved in the drug deal and was simply walking by when the shooting occurred in the middle of an attempted robbery.
Sargent was charged with first-degree murder and armed habitual criminal in the shooting.
'My office will do everything we can to get justice for Torres and his family,' Jodi M. Hoos, Peoria County State's Attorney, said in a news release.
Peoria Police said that in addition to Sargent, a 14-year-old boy was identified as a suspect in the case. The teen was arrested for attempted armed robbery.
Johnson was shot at an apartment complex Sunday evening in Peoria. He was found, lying in the grass with a gunshot wound to the chest.
Police took Sargent into custody on Oct. 1.

title: Man arrested, charged in connection to homicide of boy, 10, with ties to Springfield
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A man has been arrested and charged in connection in of the killing of a 10-year-old boy in Peoria who had ties to Springfield.
content:
A man has been arrested and charged in connection in of the killing of a 10-year-old boy in Peoria who had ties to Springfield.
Maurice D. Sargent, 33, was arrested for first-degree murder in the case of Torres L. Johnson II. Police said the boy was shot at an apartment complex Sunday evening.
During the course of the investigation, Peoria Detectives identified Sargent as a suspect in the case, according to a news release sent Wednesday afternoon.
Police took Sargent into custody on Tuesday while conducting a motor vehicle stop at Farmington Road and Sterling Avenue, according to the release.
Sargent was taken to the Peoria Police Department and later charged with murder and unlawful possession of a weapon by a felon.
Sargent was taken to the Peoria County Jail.
The release also said a 14-year-old boy was arrested a day later for attempted armed robbery. The SJ-R reached out to police for clarification if there was a connection between the homicide and the alleged robbery, but police did not respond.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: Looking for a taste of fall? Check out one of these Springfield-area breweries and wineries
author: Claire Grant
description: Oktoberfest season is here, and central Illinois is already filling tankards in biergartens, while vineyards across the region are pulling out their fall-festive wines.
content:
Oktoberfest season is here, and central Illinois is already filling tankards in biergartens, while vineyards across the region are pulling out their fall-festive wines.
Springfield is a hotbed for breweries to microbreweries.
Toast to the Bavarian culture, and then toast to the fall season even after the lederhosen come off, sample some signature IPAs and wines across the region.
Don't worry, we made a bucket list for you to try 10 breweries and five wineries within an hour from Springfield.
Engrained Brewery
What's on the menu: Brombier Blackberry Lage r with real blackberry puree at the bottom, Lokal Hop with a citrus-like flavor and aroma, Fulsome Irish Red, Brazilian Bombshell pale ale and a peachy Lucious Fuzz Belgian farmhouse ale.
Where: 1120 W. Lincolnshire Blvd., Springfield
Hours: 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday; 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. Monday and Tuesday.
Anvil and Forge
What's on the menu: Very cherry Hibiscus sour fruit ale, Hefe Doodles lemon drop hops ale, Keller Clown German style lager, Why Not Lager with a hint of caramel.
Where: 619 E. Washington St., Springfield
Hours: 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday; 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday; 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Sunday.
Buzzbomb Brewery
What's on the menu: Orange Whip cream ale, Hoppy Bukkake Mosaic IPA, Angry Red Head American amber ale, Walk of Shame Milkshake IPA, The Marzens Are Coming Marzen and Nanner, Nanner, Nanner wheat beer.
Where: 406 E. Adams St., Springfield
Hours: 3 to 11 p.m. Tuesday; 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. Wednesday and Thursday; 11a.m. to midnight Friday; 8 a.m. to midnight Saturday; 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Sunday.
Obed and Isaac's
What's on the menu: Strawberry Blonde ale, Ditzy Blonde bright ale, Isaac's IPA with sweet malt back boning and orange hues, Hefenator Hefeweizen banana German beer, Mother Road APA, Upside Coffee Brown Ale and many, many more.
Hours: 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily.
Springfield Beer Co.
What's on the menu: The Juicy Hop Bomb, Russian Imperial stout at 11.5% ABV, Brunch hard seltzer with orange, tangerine and coconut tastes, Hurricane Smoothie sour smoothie, Mosaic IPA with west-coast hops and other IPAs ranging from 4% to 11.5% ABV.
Where: 3788 Wabash Ave., Springfield
Hours: 5 to 11 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday; noon to midnight Friday and Saturday; and noon to 8 p.m. Sunday.
Sangamo Brewing
What's on the menu: A bright Summer Shandy, Old Indian Trail blonde ale, Vanilla tart Cherry blonde golden ale, the Salted Cream Caramel Scottish ale and a basic stout. ABV percentages range from 9.3% to 4%.
Where: 109 E. Mulberry St., Chatham
Hours: 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday; 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday.
Hand of Fate
What's on the menu: There are over 15 different brews on tap handmade by the Hand of Fate itself, featuring notes of peach fuzz, cookies and cream, milky sweet stouts and cream ales, and holiday flavors like the latest Pumpkin Pie Dream Ale.
Where: 107 E. Douglas Ave., Petersburg
Hours: 5 to 10 p.m. Wednesday and Thursday; 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Friday, Saturday; 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Sunday.
Limerick Brewing
What's on the menu: Take a sip from Limerick's nine different ales, featuring the summer Jandy Cream Ale, a peachy Kolsch, Yo Quiero Mexican Lager, to their Oktoberfest with their Marzen Harvest Prost Oktoberfest 7.5% ABV beer.
Where: 509B Pulaski St., Lincoln
Hours: 4 to 10 p.m. Wednesday through Friday; noon to 11 p.m. Sundays.
Opera House Brewing
What's on the menu: Ranging from 4% ABV to 9%, these ale s offer sweet like the Booh Bee Beer, to peanut butter chocolate with Here Comes the Nuts to a more German style altbier with Cntrl-Alt-Repeat.
Where: 405 S. Main St., Hillsboro
Hours: 5 to 11 p.m. Friday; noon to 11 p.m. Saturday and Sunday
Red Rooster Inn
What's on the menu: Looking for something unique? Red Rooster Inn offers a place to stay, as well as sample homemade brews on the grounds. Tackle Odin's Eye-PA with piney tingles to blood orange-soaked hops in Chavah Wheat beer, or maybe a midnight lounger dark lager with toasted malt.
Where: 123 E. Seward St., Hillsboro
Hours: Hours of operation run from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. according to the menu website, but Friday and Saturday doors are open until 11 p.m.
Wineries and wine bars
West of Wise Winery
What's on the menu: From case to cask to your glass – West of Wise is serving reds, whites, and sweet ciders to taste. The website lists strawberry lemon ciders, a Church Lady concord red, Blackberry Sangria, Jordan Creek Chardonel to Strike the Gold Traminette and the specially made Tina's Bourbon Barrel Red Blend. The red blend is aged in a Four Roses bourbon barrel for 7 months, giving a nose of dark, red fruit and bourbon with some smoke from the charred barrel. This blend is crisp and full bodied with layers of flavorful spice.
Hours: Noon to 5:30 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday
Hill Prairie Winery
What's on the menu: Take a sip of freshly casked Peach Sangria with a touch of citrus added to their classic white wine, to the semi-sweet Vignoles which gets it's name from the grapes. Prairie Dew is a medium sweet wine made in Germanic style, while Adam's Apple blends Illinois apples into the flavor profile. Try Prairie Barn in blush rose, sunshine white, or red.
Where: 23753 Lounsberry Road, Oakford
Hours: 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday; noon to 5 p.m. on Sundays.
Ad Astra Wine Bar
What's on the menu: There's just too many to list and fit on one page – so take it from the expansive menu at Ad Astra, there's a drink for all wine aficionados. Try unique blends like the Almond Infusion white wine, to the sweet spice of the Avignonesi Nobile with hints of raspberry and cherry. The Ferrari Carano merlot is a red ride with maple, cinnamon and cherry with toast and vanilla, sure to remind tastes of past fall afternoons. White, rose and red too plain? The bar hosts a rotating cocktail menu, including non-alcoholic versions.
Where: 308 E. Adams St., Springfield
Hours: 4 to 10 p.m. Wednesday through Friday; 2 to 10 p.m. Saturday and early closing at 7 p.m. on Sundays.
Danenberger Family Vineyards
What's on the menu: Looking for the vineyard appeal of sipping on a pinot noir while surrounded by stretching vineyards? Why not kick back with some musical performances to boot? The menu at the vineyard is simple yet delectable, using French-American hybrids, and American hybrid grapes.
Cabernet Franc red wine tastes of clove fill, spice and pepper. Oberlin Noir, Marquette, Arandell and Regent are other vinted red wines on shelf at the vineyard.
Hours: 5 to 9 p.m. Thursday, 3 to 10 p.m. Friday, noon to 10 p.m. Saturday and noon to 6 p.m. Sundays.
Bloom Wine Bar
What's on the menu: Bloom curates wines from around the world, for fans of exotic wines looking for a glass or bottle to reminisce on – this wine bar is a must try. The menu lists white wines from Portugal, Italy and South Africa just to name a few countries, and offers wine flights with four wine samplers for $25.
Where: 2 S. Old State Capitol Plaza, Springfield
Hours: 3 to 10 p.m. Wednesday through Friday, 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. Saturday.

title: Top performers: Chatham Glenwood's Ellie Surges remains perfect in CS8 girls tennis
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Ellie Surges and Chatham Glenwood edged Sacred Heart-Griffin in a key CS8 girls tennis match, plus other top performances this week
content:
This is a daily list of top performers from Springfield-area high school sports teams for the week of Oct. 7-12, compiled from information provided to The State Journal-Register by coaches, athletic directors and team statisticians.
To have your team's athletes included, email results to sports@sj-r.com.
Monday, Oct. 7
⭐ Game of the Week
CHATHAM GLENWOOD 5, SACRED HEART-GRIFFIN 4: Chatham Glenwood took the top three singles matches and pulled out a pivotal No. 1 doubles match, leading to a 5-4 victory over Sacred Heart-Griffin in a girls dual tennis meet at SHG on Monday.
Glenwood junior Ellie Surges put her perfect Central State Eight Conference record on the line and defeated SHG senior Caroline Sheehan 6-2, 6-0 in the No. 1 singles match.
At No. 2 singles, Samantha Shankland got a point for Glenwood with a 6-0, 6-0 victory over Laney Aleman, while Lydia Ryherd gave the Titans a third singles point by stepping in at No. 3 to post a 5-7, 6-0, 10-5 win over Brooklyn Budd.
Glenwood's big point came at No. 1 doubles when Kiki Mander and Natalie Alexander edged Brooklyn Budd and Katherine Karns 7-6 (5), 7-5. Surges and Ryherd provided the second doubles point after securing a 6-4, 6-2 win over Sheehan and Aleman at No. 2.
Catalina Mosquera and Lucia Hassebrock kept SHG in striking distance by supplying three team points. Mosquera won her No. 5 singles match 6-1, 6-2 over Kylinn Wood and Hassebrock defeated Alexander 6-2, 6-2 at No. 6. Mosquera and Hassebrock notched a third-set tiebreak win at No. 3 doubles with a 4-6, 6-4, 10-4 triumph over Shankland and Wood.
Karns got the final point for SHG by beating Mander 6-4, 6-3 in the No. 4 singles slot.
🏌Girls Golf
Izzy Hassebrock/Maddy Johnson, Sacred Heart-Griffin: The tandem just missed the individual Class 1A Rochester Sectional title in a playoff after ending with rounds of 2-over 74 in regulation at Lincoln Greens Golf Course. Carlyle's Sarah Hyten prevailed as the medalist. The Cyclones, however, came away with the team sectional title by 37 strokes.
Alaina Ervin, Pleasant Plains: The four-time Sangamo Conference champion tied for ninth place at the 1A Rochester Sectional. She fired a 78.
🏌Boys Golf
A.J. Charpentier/Colton Barr, Jacksonville: Charpentier tied for fifth place individually at the University of Illinois Golf Course and the Crimsons missed the team 2A sectional title by just one stroke behind Normal U-High. Charpentier shot 1-over 73, while Barr finished just one stroke behind.
Sam Schwab, Litchfield: The junior missed the individual Class 1A Zeigler-Royalton Sectional title by one stroke. The junior forged a round of even-par 71 behind Effingham St. Anthony junior Jack Swingler.
🏐 Volleyball
Kinley Stolte, Nokomis: Finished with 10 assists, four kills and two service aces to help Nokomis defeat Pawnee 25-11, 25-10 in an MSM Conference match to improve to 21-3 overall and 6-0 in league play.
Meaghan Marshall, Jacksonville Routt: Had eight kills, seven blocks and an ace in a 26-24, 22-25, 25-21 loss to Jacksonville.
Isabella Tiburzi/Braley Wiser, Carlinville: Tiburzi ushered five kills, nine assists, six digs and two aces in a 25-9, 25-11 win over Jerseyville. Wiser also had five kills.

title: Popular fast-food restaurant temporarily closes one of its Springfield locations
author: Claire Grant
description: If you're looking for a quick bite to eat in Springfield, you'll have one less place to go for now.
content:
There's one less late-night fast-food spot in town.
The Taco Bell on Adlai Stevenson Drive next to Starbucks and Jaalsa has temporarily closed its doors to the public.
Before fans of Chalupa Supremes and value boxes with chips, cheese and guac mourn the loss of the store – the closing won't forever, according to Tri-Jen of Springfield LLC, owner of the location.
Tri-Jen employee Heather Burch confirmed the building closed early October for interior renovations, such as upgrading the seats in the establishment.
Two building permits were issued by the City of Springfield Building and Zoning Department to Tri-Jen on October 1st and 3rd, reiterating the restaurant would only be temporarily closed for renovations.
The permits are for a new sign installation in front of the location and a restaurant interior remodel. The contractor is WM Aupperle 4 Sons Inc., working with electrical contractor Shwartz Electric.
With the temporary closure of this location, only three Taco Bell locations are still serving the city. The locations remaining open are on Toronto Road, West White Oaks Drive and North Dirkson Parkway.

title: SHG gets best of Washington Street rivalry over Springfield High
author: Adrian Dater
description: With just a 14-7 halftime lead, Sacred Heart-Griffin was even better in the second half to beat Springfield High 35-7.
content:
The Cyclones were missing two starting defensive ends and playing on enemy turf against maybe the hottest quarterback in central Illinois. So, naturally, Sacred Heart-Griffin went out and dominated defensively in a 35-7 rout of previously red-hot Springfield High on Pajama Night at Memorial Stadium.
While the Senators' student body came dressed loose and casual, the Cyclones were all business in a tremendous performance for their fifth win of the season, making them playoff-eligible once again under coach John Allison.
'It was all gas, no brakes,' said 5-foot-11, 260-pound SHG senior nose tackle Edisson Charles, who played a great game against the run and in getting in on Springfield quarterback Brody Scheffler (454 yards passing last week with four TD throws) on many occasions. 'I had my blood pumping the whole time. I didn't want to get off the field.'
The Cyclones (5-2, 4-1 CS8) got outstanding performances from many players, even the punter/kicker Tom Davis. You might not think the punter would have mattered much in a 35-7 win, but Davis played a starring role for the Cyclones. He made some booming punts, none bigger than a 55-yard kick from deep in his own end zone when SHG held just a 14-7 lead late in the first half. Davis also salvaged good defensive field position when a bad snap forced him to grab the ball at about his own 15-yard line, with a great kick into Senators' territory when SHG was up only 7-0.
'You can't really look up in those situations; you've just got to get it off,' Davis said of his retrieval and soccer-style punt. 'We had a great week of practice. Our defense was phenomenal, and offense played well. We can celebrate this one for a bit, but we've got a big week of practice and a tough game next week (at Chatham Glenwood).'
The Cyclones took firm control of the game early in the third quarter. Up by just a touchdown, the SHG defense forced a three-and-out Springfield punt, which junior Drew Ward — who also played a great defensive game in the backfield — grabbed at midfield and ran down the right side to the Senators' 23. From there, Cyclones' sophomore QB Cam Brinkman ran it in from 14 yards to make it 21-7.
The Senators (5-2 overall, 3-2 CS8 West Division) came right back down the field, getting to the Cyclones' 11-yard line after a 63-yard pass from Scheffler to junior wide receiver Deandre Brown. But, on a 4th-and-3 from the SHG 4-yard line, Springfield's Kale Thurman was stuffed at the line of scrimmage.
After an exchange of punts, SHG went 44 yards on four plays, capped by sophomore Mikey Groesch's 4-yard run to make it 28-7.
'Our defense played lights out,' Allison said. 'To win without some of the guys we had out was pretty impressive. We wanted to come out in the second half and establish the run game more than we did in the first half, and we took care of the ball too, which was key. For us now, it's about better playoff seeding. We don't want to be a 5-4 team playing a 9-0. That will be a key for us to get to (Normal for the state championship) and get to where our goal is.'
Junior Emery Greene also played an excellent game on the defensive line with two starters out. He and Charles seemed to be in on most every tackle of a Senator in the game.
'They're solid players. Edisson has been in there most of the year and Emery has been working his way in quite a bit,' Allison said.
Springfield coach Jon Hebb tried to accentuate the positive after the game, telling his players in a postgame gathering to 'put it behind you.'
'We definitely had some missed opportunities. We felt like we had guys running open, but it just seemed like, when it was there, we maybe ran a wrong route or had some miscommunication or dropped a pass,' Hebb said. 'On the defensive side of the ball, we had some trouble tackling. I don't necessarily want to say this was a letdown game. But I do feel like we were pretty loose this week. We knew coming in that the pressure was on SHG, and they were fighting to get into the playoffs. It was pretty obvious, by the end of the night, that they wanted it more than we did.'

title: Monday is Columbus Day. Here's what's open and closed in Springfield
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Are schools in session? Is my bank open? Here's a look at what's open and closed in the Springfield area on Columbus Day.
content:
Monday is Columbus Day, which is a federal holiday, meaning federal offices are closed and mail is not delivered.
The state of Illinois has kept Columbus Day as a holiday, while Illinois lawmakers in 2017 designated the last Monday in September as statewide Indigenous Peoples' Day.
Here's a look at what's open and what's closed on Monday.
Banks
Some banks in Springfield are closed, such as: Prairie State Bank & Trust, Clock Tower Community Bank, and INB. Heartland Bank and Trust Company is closed but over the phone customer support is available.
Other banks are open such as Bank of Springfield and United Community Bank.

title: Start smiling: Southeast wins first game under new coach Borders, beats Lanphier
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Marcell Jerome returned the opening kickoff 81 yards to put Southeast on top quickly and the Spartans kept the lead all game.
content:
Finally, the Spartans can smile, and it didn't take long.
Marcell Jerome returned the opening kickoff 81 yards to put Southeast on top quickly, and the Spartans kept smiling all the way through a 52-0 Central State Eight Conference win over crosstown rival Lanphier at Memorial Stadium on Saturday afternoon.
It gave Nate Borders his first win as the Southeast coach, so naturally, he shared in his team's smiles after the game — even after he was doused with the team's Gatorade cooler, which left him not only wet but a prime attraction to the swarm of bees that were buzzing around the Southeast sideline.
'It feels great,' Borders said before he laughed and added, 'sticky, but great.'
It took the Spartans seven weeks to pick up their first win.
'It's one of those feelings were you see all the work coming to fruition, getting that first win with a program, that's always a good feeling,' Borders said. 'Now with them, I think that's a building block for the rest of the season and next season.'
Easton McGlathery scored four rushing touchdowns for the Spartans (1-6 overall, 1-5 CS8 West Division). He finished with 130 yards on eight carries. Southeast quarterback Tony Boyd finished with three touchdown passes: two to Jordan Gillum and one to Jerome.
'It feels great,' McGlathery said. 'This whole year, we've been struggling to keep the same line. We finally had a steady line, and they were able to execute and make me able to get in the end zone.
'I think it's great for the offensive line to get the confidence in this game, because once they see (when) they do (their) job, we can get some points on the board and win some games.'
Lanphier had chances in the red zone, getting inside the Spartans' 20-yard line four times, but each time Southeast's defense — and untimely Lanphier penalties — kept the Lions out of the end zone and the Spartans' shutout intact.
'When our backs are against the wall, we are still going to fight,' Borders said. 'With (Lanphier) scoring no points despite being in the red zone four times, that shows that.'
Brandon Miller, Lanphier's first-year coach, said he noticed some growth by his 0-7 Lions, and moving the ball against the Southeast defense was one of those areas.
'A lot of big improvements that I've seen in this game that I felt could have went our way, especially in the red zone, offensively,' Miller said. 'Like I said, we didn't execute well enough to try to get it in, and that's something that we're slowly, but surely, trying to turn the corner on and get better at.
'The improvements of us moving the ball and getting in the red zone helped out a lot.'
Everything going Blue and Gold
It was quite the change for Southeast to win by the running clock, which had been imposed on the Spartans three times this season.
After Jerome returned the opening kick for an 8-0 lead, McGlathery scored a 10-yard touchdown for a 14-0 Southeast advantage. In the second quarter, the Spartans tacked on three more scores. Boyd found Gillum for a 45-yard touchdown pass with 9 minutes, 13 seconds left in the half.
The Spartans were flagged for an excessive celebration personal foul on the score. Despite the kickoff being backed up 15 yards, Southeast successfully pulled out an onside kick attempt, and on the next play, Boyd hit Jerome for a 65-yard score for a 28-0 lead.
'First win of the season, got to feel good,' Boyd said. 'We've been doing great things and getting better every week, but bro, I feel like we could've been doing this, but it takes more time with a new coach, new team. I feel like the next year and the rest of this season, we're going to come out and do what we're supposed to do.'
Southeast finished with 601 yards of total offense, but Jerome was also pleased with the defense's work, especially the Spartans' bend-but-don't-break mentality in the red zone.
'It was great to see,' Jerome said. 'I just think our guys were just seeing that (Lanphier) was moving the ball, so they started locking down and stopped (the Lions) from scoring.'
One key for the Spartans was the team playing unselfishly and everyone being on the same page, Gillum suggested.
'We stayed together the whole game: no bad fights or anything came out on offense, and I feel like we just stuck together the whole time,' Gillum said.

title: Springfield homicide victim identified
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon has confirmed the identity of a man who was shot and killed early Sunday morning.
content:
Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon has confirmed the identity of a man who was shot and killed early Sunday morning.
39-year-old Antoine Williams of Springfield died shortly after his arrival to HSHS St. John's Hospital emergency room.
Williams died from multiple gunshot wounds, according to an autopsy done Monday.
Police found Williams in the front seat of a vehicle with a gunshot wound in the area of 17th and Cook streets just after 1 a.m.
The death remains under investigation by the Sangamon County Coroner and the Springfield Police Department.
This is the eighth homicide in Springfield for 2024.

title: Here are 10 pumpkin patches to check out in the Springfield area this fall
author: Claire Grant
description: With plenty of pumpkins to go around, we've put together a list of 10 pumpkin patches around central Illinois you can check out this fall.
content:
What does your fall bucket list look like? Does baking bread, going on a hiking trail and trying a new warm, cozy soup make the list? How about a classic trip to a pumpkin patch?
Illinois is the king of pumpkins, producing almost more than twice as many pumpkin acres compared to the other top five producing states in 2022 with over 17,600 acres dedicated to gourd growing.
According to the USDA, the most recent available data indicate that almost 80 percent of pumpkin acres in Illinois are devoted to varieties destined for pie filling, which tend to be smaller, sweeter and cheaper than jack-o-lantern pumpkins.
On average Illinois grows about 37,500 pumpkin pounds per acre per year.
With plenty of pumpkins to go around, we've put together a list of 10 pumpkin patches to check out within an hour of Springfield.
Bomke's Patch
What: With roots in a small Christmas tree farm, Bomke's has expanded into a place for families to visit every fall season. The farm features a pick it yourself pumpkin patch over 10 acres of land, with a common play area for kids and a corn maze. For little ones, a bean maze on two acres is challenging for kids, who'll want to visit the petting zoo after or go on a wagon ride. One thing you have to try? The pumpkin cannon – load and shoot your own pumpkin up to a quarter mile away for only $5.
Hours: 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday and Sunday, until Oct. 26.
Jefferies Orchard and patch
What: This is your one stop shop for all food and decorations. Sample homegrown tomatoes, cabbage, cauliflower, broccoli, raw honey and over a dozen types of apples at Jeffries Orchard. For decorations, guests can pay and pick flowers on the farm, as well as Indian corn shoots.
Where: 1016 Jefferies Road, Springfield
Hours: 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. every day except Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Apple Barn
What: Apple Barn grows and sells apples, Indian corn, pumpkins, gourds, mums, and more. Whether you are celebrating Halloween or just need some fresh delicious apples, Apple Barn has what you need just a short drive away from the city.
Where: 2290 E. Walnut St., Chatham
Hours: 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily.
Kristin's pumpkin patch
What: Maybe you've driven by this patch before and never even noticed, since this gem is easy to miss. Family run for over 30 years, the farm relies on guests who are happy to get hands-on with wheelbarrows, cutters and walks through the patch. Pumpkins are picked and weighed at 70 cents a pound, with self-pick flowers also available for purchase for a dollar a stem. Find the orange tent on the corner and grab a wheelbarrow for picking, or a ticket to the corn maze and hayride at $2 each.
Where: 6300 Wind Tree Road, Springfield; the address is actually in a neighborhood, there should be an orange tent and silo.
Hours: 2 to 6 p.m. Friday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturday and 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Sunday.
Pumpkin Creek Farms
What: For tickets as little as $6, guests can enjoy all the attractions at Pumpkin Creek. Attractions include an interactive corn maze GPS game, two corn bins, haystack mountain, self-picking pumpkins, hayrides, a petting zoo and barrel train rides. For younger crowds, a spider web trampoline is available, as well as other playhouse activities around the farm.
Indian Creek Farmstead
What: Every weekend, Indian Creek is welcoming guests to their pumpkin patch featuring tractor-pulled wagon rides around the farm. Activities range from a kids area to play in the barnyard, roping corrals, wagon rides and grain slides.
Hours: 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday and Sunday
Gail's Pumpkin Patch
What: Come taste the fresh honey, baked goods and apples at Gail's Pumpkin Patch after picking your favorite pumpkin on the farm. According to the business' website, the patch offers fun with farm animals, popcorn wagon rides, a tunnel maze and giant games like gourd bowling.
Where: 1709 2000 Ave., Beason
Hours: Noon to 5 p.m. Monday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday.
Indian Knolls Pumpkins
What: This beautiful centennial farm is nestled along the Sangamon River in extreme northern Christian County. Surrounded by rolling pastures and timber, Indian Knoll offers one of the most picturesque fall venues in the area. Drop by the artisan shop with locally made items for sale at the barn, before heading out to the patch on seven acres of land. Face painting, a barrel train, bale climbing and other fun for the family will be available for guests.
Where: 2850 N. 1000 East Road, Mechanicsburg
Hours: 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday and Saturday, noon to 5 p.m. Sunday.
Black Bart's Patch
What: Open until Halloween, this small pumpkin patch has fun for the kiddos with a mini haunted house, a pirate ship play area, a goat petting zoo to the classic corn maze. On the weekend, barrel rides are available for a $2 ticker per person.
Hours: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. every day, except Sundays 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Greene Field Farms
What: Greene Field Farms is asking guests to simply skip the parking fees and in return, bring a trailer to take home as many pumpkins as they could ask for. This is the place to go for guests looking to make the most out of their day and cross out at least a few lines in their fall bucket list. Try your hand at apple picking and pumpkin picking, before heading over to the concessions with fresh apple cider slushies and hot steak sandwiches. From small enough to carry in your pocket to pumpkins over 100 pounds, dad will be dragging out a pumpkin heavier than most fifth graders for only $25.
Hours: 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday and Saturday, noon to 5 p.m. Sundays.

title: One person killed in crash outside of Springfield
author: Tom Ackerman
description: One person was killed in a car crash outside of Springfield Monday morning. Here's what we know.
content:
One person was killed in a car crash outside of Springfield Monday morning.
Illinois State Police said the crash happened at the intersection of Illinois 29 and East Hartgrave Street, just outside of Athens.
Karen Fox, 70, of Athens, was pronounced dead at the scene, said Menard County Chief Deputy Sheriff and Coroner Ben Hollis on the department's Facebook page late Monday afternoon.
