title: Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum celebrates 20 years in new building
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum celebrated the 20th anniversary of the library's opening to the public.
content:
The Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum celebrated its 20 th anniversary since they opened their doors to the public in October of 2004.
The museum and library were officially dedicated in April 2005, which Former President George W. Bush attended with his wife, Laura, among other notable attendees.
The library in 2004 had moved from the basement of the Old State Capitol and into the nearly 100,000-square-foot facility on the 200 block of North Sixth Street.
A celebration of the library was held on Oct. 16 gave people a chance to reflect on the importance of the museum.
Executive Director Christina Shutt spoke about continuing the legacy of the organization and its mission of preserving Illinois and Abraham Lincoln history, as well as moving forward efforts to engage with online audiences by digitizing the library's documents.
Former Library Services Director Kathryn Harris who now serves on the organization's board of trustees spoke about progression to construction in the late 1990s.
'My fondest memory comes from the work that was done by the staff at that time. And I see many of those staff members here, which makes my heart go pitter-patter,' she said.
Amanda Helm, a 25-year employee of the organization attended the reception with her son Gabriel. Helm appreciates that people continue to utilize the library.
She emphasized that the library has documents containing Illinois history in addition to that of Abraham Lincoln.

title: Illinois lawmakers pushing for more stringent gun storage laws. What you need to know
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: A recent school shooting in Georgia is prompting discussion in Illinois for how to improve gun storage safety. Here's what you need to know.
content:
The 14-year-old suspect who shot 11 people and killed four in a Georgia high school last month had access to a semiautomatic assault-style weapon legally purchased by the shooter's father, prompting questions nationwide for how to address youth firearm safety.
The deadliest school shooting in Georgia history, children having easy access to firearms in their homes is far from an anomaly, studies show, and the consequences could be deadly. Last year alone, there were more than 400 unintentional shootings by children per research by the anti-violence group Everytown for Gun Safety.
Three deaths have been recorded in Illinois in 2024 so far, including a two-year-old boy in Chicago's South Side this January. Now, Illinois lawmakers are pushing legislation that would strengthen gun storage laws.
Here's what you need to know.
What would the legislation do?
The Safe Firearm Storage Act, filed under Senate Bill 3971 and House Bill 5891, would prohibit the possession of a firearm outside its owner's "immediate possession or control" and increases the age to 18 from 13 where safe storage in homes are required.
In the case of a lost or stolen firearm, Senate Bill 3973 and House Bill 5888 would require the owner to report it with local law enforcement within 48 hours instead of the original 72. It comes after reports show that approximately 380,000 guns are stolen per year nationwide.
What happens if a gun owner violates these laws?
Gun owners who fail to properly store their firearms could see penalties up to $10,000 if a minor, at-risk or person prohibited from owning a firearm gained access and used it to injure or cause the death of a person. If an unauthorized person gains access, the penalty ranges from $500 to $1,000.
They could also be subject to losing their Firearm Owner Identification Card on a second violation of failing to report a lost or stolen firearm within the new 48-hour window.
When is veto session?
Illinois lawmakers are scheduled to return to Springfield for a six-day veto session. They will meet from Nov. 12 to Nov. 14 and Nov. 19 through Nov. 21.
For this legislation and any other pieces of legislation to go into immediate effect, a super-majority vote is required in both chambers. Democrats hold those margins in the House and Senate.

title: Down the wire: How did Springfield-area golfers fare at the state finals?
author: Bill Welt
description: Sacred Heart-Griffin's Izzy Hassebrock, Pleasant Plains' Alaina Ervin tied for second place at this year's 1A girls golf state title on Saturday
content:
DECATUR — Sacred Heart-Griffin senior golfer Izzy Hassebrock couldn't be too disappointed.
The defending Class 1A state champion matched the same score as last year and tied for second place with Pleasant Plains senior Alaina Ervin at Red Tail Run Golf Course on Saturday.
Hassebrock and Ervin entered the final round first and second place, respectively, and finished behind none other than Mount Carmel's Zeme Moore, who was state runner-up last year. Hassebrock and Ervin delivered 3-over 147 totals, while Moore won even-par after a torrid final round of 3-under.
Sophomore teammate Maddy Johnston placed 17th individually and the Cyclones achieved second place as a team for a second straight season. Junior Natalie Zak followed in 29th while senior Macie Petropoulos rounded out the team score in 38th. SHG earlier claimed its second consecutive regional and sectional team titles as well.
"I'm definitely proud of all the work I've put in this year and last year," Hassebrock said. "It's not the result that I wanted, but again, I played the same as last year, so there's not much else I could've really done except make some putts today. That would've been nice."
During the regular season, Hassebrock not only captured the Central State Eight Conference individual championship 1-under 71 at Lincoln Greens Golf Course but also spurred the team to first place.
Hassebrock said she will remember all the laughs and fun times the most.
"We practiced really hard every day," Hassebrock said. "We had great coaches who led us here. Everyone worked really hard, especially in the postseason. Everyone just knows what they need to work on and how to practice in order to improve."
Hassebrock will keep her golf career alive in college, but she still has the basketball season to look forward to this winter. As for this past golf season, she harbored a positive mindset not just to be a role model for her younger teammates but also to cope with loftier expectations after becoming the first female state champion from the city since Springfield High's Tracy Tate in 1981.
She persevered and was embraced by her teammates on the 18th green.
"I'm proud of us for doing it two years in a row," Hassebrock said of the team's banner season. "I think that's very special. It's my senior year and I know it's a couple other girls' senior year, so it definitely means a lot to us this year."
Ervin takes another step forward
Pleasant Plains' Alaina Ervin quit competitive softball in order to pursue golf.
'I think it's the best decision that I've ever made,' Ervin reflected after reaching second place alongside Hassebrock at the Class 1A state finals.
The four-time individual Sangamo Conference champion said she squarely focused on each shot throughout the tournament and added she made her biggest strides mentally this year. Ervin said she perhaps didn't finish the way that she wanted to but was proud of her overall performance — perhaps not unlike Hassebrock.
She previously took seventh place with a 9-over total at last year's 1A finals.
'I think my biggest thing is that I wanted to stay in the moment,' Ervin said. 'That was the biggest goal. I felt confident and I was excited to get some good competition out here.'
Ervin fully intends to resume golf after high school.
'I'm very happy about it,' Ervin said of her high school career. 'I don't even know what else to say about it, I've had so much support over the past couple years and especially this year. It's surreal.'
Other top performers
Sam Schwab, Litchfield: The junior finished 12-over 156 to end in a tie for 21st place in the Class 1A boys state finals at Prairie Vista Golf Course. He shot 4-over in the final round.
Reed Fretueg, Rushville-Industry: The senior shot 15-over and tied for 30th place in the 1A boys state finals.
Anderson Thielen, Pleasant Plains: The senior tied for 50th place in the 1A boys state finals. He shot 22-over.
A.J. Charpentier, Jacksonville: The junior shot 17-over and led the area by tying for 44th place in the 2A boys state finals at Weibring Golf Club. Junior teammate Elias Martin tied for 50th place.
Derek Dulceak, Chatham Glenwood: The senior tied for 76th place for the area's top finish in the 3A boys state finals at The Den at Fox Creek Golf Course. He shot 23-over.

title: Boeing strike: Machinists' union to vote on contract proposal with 35% pay hike
author: David Shepardson
description: Machinists will vote next week on Boeing's contract proposal with a 35% pay hike over four years and other benefits. It could end a month-long strike.
content:
Striking machinists at Boeing, will vote Wednesday on a new contract proposal that includes a 35% pay hike over four years that could end a costly five-week-old strike, the company and union said Saturday.
Around 33,000 of Boeing's unionized West Coast workers, most in Washington state, have been on strike since Sept. 13. The work stoppage has halted production of the plane maker's best-selling 737 MAX and its 767 and 777 widebodies, putting added pressure on the company's already fragile finances.
The latest offer includes a $7,000 ratification bonus, reinstated incentive plan and enhanced contributions to workers' 401(k) retirement plans including a one-time $5,000 contribution plus up to 12% in employer contributions, International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers Local 751 said.
Boeing said Saturday it looks "forward to our employees voting on the negotiated proposal." Still there is no guarantee workers will approve the proposal after they overwhelmingly rejected an initial proposal. "The future of this contract is in your hands," the union told workers Saturday.
Boeing on Oct. 8 withdrew its enhanced offer that included a 30% wage increase over four years, after talks also attended by federal mediators broke down. The union has been seeking a 40% hike and restoration of a defined benefit pension, which was not offered in the new contract proposal.
In September, nearly 95% of the West Coast workers rejected Boeing's contract offer of a 25% pay rise over four years that had been endorsed by union officials, prompting the strike.
That earlier deal also had a $3,000 signing bonus which some Boeing workers told Reuters was too low, given that prior deals had bonuses of at least $5,000.
Labor Secretary Julie Su joins Boeing strike negotiations
The union said on Saturday in a social media post that with the help of Acting U.S. Secretary of Labor Julie Su they had received a "negotiated proposal" and telling striking workers it "is worthy of your consideration."
On Monday, Su was in Seattle for her first in-person effort to help reach a new Boeing contract and returned on Thursday night to resume efforts after a trip to Detroit.
While some reaction on social media sites on Saturday morning were favorable to the new deal, it's not yet clear how the workers will vote.
A spokesperson for the White House said 'President (Joe) Biden believes the collective bargaining process is the best way to achieve good outcomes for workers, and the ultimate decision on a contract will be for the union workers to decide.'
Last Friday, Boeing announced it would cut 17,000 jobs, or 10% of its global staff and take $5 billion in charges, continuing a year of tumult for the company since a new Alaska Airlines 737 MAX 9 airplane suffered a mid-air emergency.Boeing announced a window for up to $25 billion in stock and debt offerings over the next three years on Tuesday, as well as a $10-billion credit agreement.
Boeing has been facing ongoing pressure since a door panel flew off a new 737 MAX 9 jet in midair in January prompting the Federal Aviation Administration to bar the plane maker from increasing production. The FAA opened a new safety inquiry into Boeing on Friday.
In July, Boeing agreed to plead guilty to a criminal fraud conspiracy charge and agreed to pay at least $243.6 million after breaching a 2021 deferred prosecution agreement.
The labor strife is expected to have a negative impact on October's employment report, which will be published days before the Nov. 5 U.S. presidential election.
Economists estimate that the strike and rolling weekly furloughs of non-striking workers as well as temporary layoffs at Boeing's suppliers subtracted as many as 50,000 jobs from nonfarm payrolls this month. The economy added 254,000 jobs in September and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2% in August.
.

title: ‘Unreal': Sangamon Valley football dispatches Villa Grove to become playoff eligible
author: Bill Welt
description: Sangamon Valley rushed for over 300 yards and celebrated its first playoff eligibility since 2016
content:
NIANTIC, Ill. — Niantic Sangamon Valley football coach Carl Spath hoisted a 2024 placard and plastered it to the playoff banner.
The Storm became playoff-eligible for the first time since 2016 with a 34-14 Lincoln Prairie Conference victory over Villa Grove on Saturday.
Sangamon Valley (5-3) marched inexorably down the field throughout the night and 337 yards later celebrated the long-awaited moment.
'This moment is unreal,' junior fullback Hunter Martin said. 'It's something that I thought would come, but I didn't realize how unreal it would feel. We're so excited and ready to go celebrate with friends.'
Martin churned up 109 rushing yards and a touchdown, while senior quarterback Jaeger Hill had 102 rushing yards and three TDs to go along with three completions for 41 yards.
Sangamon Valley claimed a 28-0 lead in the third quarter following Brody Beals' short touchdown plunge.
'It's a big deal to a lot of our players, coaches and community,' Spath said. 'This one's special. This group is special and these kids just work really hard to represent their school. They're the best we got, I'm just proud to be their head coach.'
Senior quarterback Lukas Shadwick led Villa Grove (1-7) with 150 passing yards and a score on 14 of 25 passing. Noah Wilcoxon had eight catches for 109 yards. Hunter Butts rushed for 90 yards and a touchdown in the loss.

title: New name, same place: Springfield cidery rebrands
author: Claire Grant
description: The name may be new, but the food will be familiar at this Springfield cidery.
content:
7th Street Cidery is getting a new name, and familar food pairings to go with the perfect cup.
Conn's Hospitality Group, the owner of 7th Street Cidery, announced on Oct. 17 the restaurant would rebrand to Obed & Isaac's The Cidery, as a combination with Obed & Isaac's, a local microbrewery also owned by the Conn family.
7th Street Cidery sits at 503 S. 7th St. just across from Lincoln's Home and has on tap 20 different types of craft ciders, meads and perry's.
The taproom is set inside a historic home much like Obed & Isaac's, which is settled in the Booth-Grunendike house.
According to owner Karen Conn, the rebrand represents a shift to a seamless affiliation with Obed & Isaac's, creating a single destination where guests can enjoy a variety of food, beer and cider offerings.
Customers can order food from Obed & Isaac's and enjoy it at The Cidery, making it a prevailing spot for a full dining and drinking experience.
The Cidery, the parlor room at Obed & Isaac's are joining Vinegar Hill Mall and the Inn at 835 as available private event booking in the city at connshg.com.

title: How these Riverton seniors found solace despite missing varsity football season
author: Bill Welt
description: Tristan Tolley and Andrew Watson came out for the Riverton JV football team not just for the love of the game but something more altruistic
content:
RIVERTON — Tristan Tolley and Andrew Watson envisioned their senior year differently.
The Riverton football team canceled the varsity season due to insufficient numbers over the summer. Tolley and Watson came out undeterred regardless. They were still just grateful to have a JV season, and it was more than just for the love of the game.
The senior linemen wanted to build a springboard for the future.
Watson had played football since he was 4 years old. He emphasized giving not just his teammates but also his two younger brothers currently in the JFL the chance to play varsity even if that was not granted to him this year.
'I want to help this program to what it could possibly be to help them get the chance that they deserve,' Watson said.
Ditto Tolley.
'Everyone is out here performing,' Tolley said. 'Everyone is doing the things they need to do. We're all working together.'
They have helped foster pivotal success along the way. It's a necessity if they want to generate enthusiasm around the program and bolster its numbers.
This budding JV team most recently scored a 46-13 win over Auburn's JV to improve to 6-1 with only two games remaining.
'I'm more than proud of these guys,' Watson said. 'They've put in so much work. I personally feel like this is the best offensive line we've had in years since I was at least a sophomore. With the people who are showing up here every day, I think this program will go far over the next couple of years.'
Tolley agreed.
'I feel like we've already achieved so much,' Tolley said. 'What Andrew was saying how the program was a couple years ago, I honestly think this year we've stayed together so mentally well. These kids have done amazing this year.'
According to head coach Colton Piper, the experience has transformed Tolley and Watson into genuine leaders.
'The seniors have been awesome,' Piper said, 'they've both matured a ton throughout the season and they're playing really well. There's just been a lot of positivity that we've never had before. The culture and people speaking up is nice to see, it's trending in the right direction.'
During practices, Watson and Tolley will act as mentors while yielding reps to their younger teammates. Tolley described that teaching aspect as a learning experience.
'It's been really helpful because you get to look back and think how you were back around that time and try to help them in the areas they need help,' Tolley said.
With 26 kids, Piper said the program still isn't where it needs to be to compete on the varsity level, especially in positions that require more strength and size.
'But I think if we keep winning and it's an atmosphere that people are looking forward to practice, it's only going to get better,' Piper said.

title: Seriously, Stormy Daniels bringing stand-up comedy act to central Illinois
author: Steven Spearie
description: Adult film star Stormy Daniels is coming back to the Springfield area next month as the headliner of a comedy show.
content:
Adult film star and director Stormy Daniels, whose alleged tryst with Donald Trump in 2006 led to the former president being found guilty of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records as part of a conspiracy to unlawfully interfere in the 2016 election, will headline a comedy show at the Backroom Lounge in Riverton on Nov. 11.
A 6 p.m. show quickly sold out and owner Jeb Brown added a 9 p.m. show.
The venue seats 50 people. Tickets are $100.
Trump, in a neck-and-neck race with Vice President Kamala Harris in the Nov. 5 election, paid the actress $130,000 as part of an agreement in which Daniels would keep quiet about the alleged sexual encounter.
Trump has denied the affair with Daniels, whose real name is Stephanie Clifford.
The former president is awaiting sentencing.
In March 2019, Daniels made several stops in Springfield, including at Déjà Vu Showgirls nightclub. She also appeared at the Abraham Lincoln statue at the Illinois Capitol railing against the Live Adult Entertainment Surcharge Tax, or "pole tax" leveled against dancers.
Joining Daniels at the Riverton show will be nationally touring comedians Copenhagen Bandit and Nina Kern.
Brown said the show has received some national attention. On Monday, he did a 15-minute interview with MSNBC host Rachel Maddow about booking Daniels.
Maddow recently reported that a Trump attorney allegedly tried to work out a deal about what Daniels owes Trump over a 2018 failed defamation suit if she agreed not to talk about Trump leading up to the election.
"Some people have let politics completely take over their lives and they've forgotten how to laugh," Brown said. "I'm sure there are going to be some political jokes in her segment. We're glad we can all come together and get some laughs out of the deal."
Brown said he originally had thought about scheduling the show on election night but thought the better of it.
All of the comedians are donating, after costs, proceeds to local veterans groups, Brown said.

title: Rochester football doesn't miss a beat despite missing head coach in win over SHG
author: Bill Welt
description: Derek Leonard may not have been on the field, but that did nothing to stop Rochester's hot start in win over Sacred Heart-Griffin
content:
ROCHESTER — Rochester football coach Derek Leonard wasn't on the field.
The Rockets still kept humming along in a 41-27 Central State Eight Conference victory over rival Sacred Heart-Griffin at Rocket Booster Stadium on Friday.
Offensive line coach Derrick Nelson acted as the interim coach after Leonard was suspended earlier the same day for one game following a hazing investigation.
Rochester (7-2, 5-1 CS8) claimed a 14-0 lead in the first five minutes before extending the margin to 24-0 in the second quarter. It started auspiciously when junior receiver Tristan Stanton's fumble at the goal line after turning up field on a pass from junior quarterback Tanner Beal was recovered by sophomore teammate Eli Cox in the end zone for the opening score.
Junior running back Kaiden Stout then added two rushing touchdowns before finishing with 17 carries for 104 yards.
"That's the character of this team because the man that leads this team is coach Leonard," Nelson said. "They did it for him and they know how to play. I'm just glad they came out the way they did. That is truly how we should be coming out every single game."
Rochester senior receiver Mason Jacobs caught a 71-yard touchdown pass from freshman Khordell Gregory on a trick play early in the third quarter and ended with six catches for 109 yards, while also rushing for 22 yards.
Rochester, which won a share of the inaugural CS8 East title with Normal U-High and Chatham Glenwood, pulled out another trick play on Gregory's second TD pass to Stout for the team's largest lead of the game, 38-7.
Its special teams and defense also played at a high level. That included two fumble recoveries on kickoff returns, a Ty Durocher interception and five sacks — two apiece from Dylan Durocher and Connor Broughton.
"We played like our hair was on fire," said senior linebacker Holt Zeidler, who had the other sack. "We flew around today."
SHG QB Cam Brinkman went 25 of 39 for 322 yards and four touchdowns with one pick, which came after his TD pass to Jamarion Bardwell on a screen play was called back on a holding call. Bardwell recorded nine catches for 107 yards and a TD, while Seamus O'Brien notched 10 grabs for 106 yards and two scores.
"We're still doing some things that I'd hope at this point of the year we might clean up," SHG coach John Allison said. "By Week 9, our sophomores got to start playing a little bit more like juniors. Some of them have.
"If anything has told us the last three weeks is there are about three or four kids that we can count on and they've started to show their faces again and again, and we've got to figure out ways to get those guys that we can trust the ball more and that will help our offense go, too."

title: City of Springfield will resume showing faces of public commenters at meetings
author: Steven Spearie
description: After two weeks, the city of Springfield is reversing course when it comes to showing public commenters on video at city council meetings.
content:
Show Caption
The city of Springfield will resume showing faces of public commenters at its committee of the whole meeting Tuesday.
For the past two meetings, the city preempted video but not audio during public commentary citing "unauthorized recording and sharing of meeting content."
Haley Wilson, a spokeswoman for the city, told The State Journal-Register last week the move was "temporary" and may be lifted.
The decision not to show faces coincided with more heated discourse over a variety of topics, including the clearing of an unhoused encampment near Fifth Street and North Grand Avenue on Sept. 26 and the Sept. 9 arrest of recently retired Springfield Police Sgt. Michael Egan.
Ward 6 Ald. Jennifer Notariano said last week the city wasn't be transparent in its decision. She added that city council members weren't consulted by Mayor Misty Buscher regarding either decision.
"I think the mayor made the right choice in her reversing the decision," Notariano said.
Notariano said she was hoping to get clarification from the city attorney regarding the Open Meetings Act.
The city broadcasts its meetings on Channel 18 and YouTube, with closed captioning available on both platforms.
The city will continue to adhere to rules and procedures at the city clerk's website.

title: Springfield girls tennis players end season at IHSA state tournament
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Glenwood, SHG and Rochester all were represented at this year's IHSA girls tennis tournament. See how they fared during the first day of action Thursday.
content:
All seven competitors from the Springfield area were eliminated after the first day of the Class 2A/1A Illinois High School Association girls tennis state finals.
Here is how the area players fared.
Chatham Glenwood bows out in 2A
The top two singles players in the area — senior Samantha Shankland and junior Ellie Surges of Chatham Glenwood — combined to go 1-4 for the Titans on Thursday.
Shankland, the Central State Eight Conference champion and a second-place finisher at the Glenwood Sectional, lost her opening round match to Lily David of Downers Grove South 6-1, 6-0. Shankland won a consolation match by beating Vicki Lipinski of Palos Hills Stagg 6-1, 6-3. She ended the tournament with a 6-1, 6-3 loss to Deerfield's Liza Gleyzer.
Surges, second in the CS8 and third at sectional, finished 0-2. Hampshire's Isabella Kowalak posted a 7-5, 6-2 straight sets win over Surges in the first round. Deerfield's Maya Stolarsky knocked out Surges with a 6-2, 6-0 victory in the consolation's first round.
SHG, Rochester ends season in 1A
Sacred Heart-Griffin sent one singles player and a doubles team to the Class 1A finals and both won a match for the Cyclones.
Senior Caroline Sheehan, the Jacksonville Sectional singles champion, opened the tournament with a 6-2, 6-0 win over Maroa-Forsyth's Isabella Griffiths. Sheehan then ran into the No. 1 seeded player, Chloe Goins of Darien Hinsdale South, and lost 6-0, 6-0 in the second round. In her first consolation match, Sheehan fell to Isabella Gomez of LaGrange Park Nazareth 6-0, 6-4.
The SHG doubles team of sophomore Lucia Hassebrock and freshman Catalina Mosquera finished 1-2.
The Cyclones lost their first-round match to 5-8 seed Anna Probst and Adi Davidson of Teutopolis 6-0, 6-0. Hassebrock and Mosquera responded by beating Joliet Catholic's Georgia Buza and Madeline Darley 6-2, 6-2 in consolation play. Emma Davis and Abigail Harms of Bethalto Civic Memorial defeated Hassebrock and Mosquera 6-3, 6-2 in the consolation's second round.
It was the second time the Bethalto team had beaten Hassebrock and Mosquera in a week. They knocked off the Cyclones in the sectional semifinals before winning that championship on Saturday. The SHG duo ended with a fourth-place sectional finish.
Rochester had advanced senior Julia Musgrave and junior Cora Haupt to state after the tandem finished second at the Jacksonville Sectional.
But Musgrave, who has been battling an illness this season, had to withdraw and was replaced by sophomore Molly Eichholz. Eichholz and Haupt opened the tournament with a major task and lost to No. 1 seed Shane Delaney and Clare Lopatka of Lisle Benet Academy 6-0, 6-0.
The Rochester duo closed out the tourney with a 6-0, 6-1 defeat to Joliet Catholic's Megan Ardaugh and Alondra Espino in the consolation's first round.

title: Halloween parade among 5 festive things to do this weekend in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: We're days away from Halloween which means spooky spectaculars are picking up in Springfield.
content:
Show Caption
We're days away from Halloween which means spooky spectaculars are picking up in Springfield.
This weekend, the streets of downtown will be transformed into a scene right out of Halloweentown with the Halloween Parade.
From chili with pups to performances as chill as the weather, here are five things to do around the capital this weekend.
Annual Halloween Parade
What: The Parent Place is hosting its seventh Annual Halloween Parade in downtown on Fifth and Sixth streets. Families will line the street as floats, children and other special Halloween guests parade the streets. Floats, musical performances and dancers will take on the streets of Springfield, right as the sky starts to darken for Jack-o-Lanterns to shine bright.
When: 7 p.m. Saturday
Where: The route starts on Jefferson to Fifth Street, Monroe to Sixth Street to Washington.
More: This event is free; more information can be found online at tppos.org.
Chili and Paw Paw Patch Bazaar
What: The Animal Protective League presents the annual APL Chili Supper and Paw Paw Patch Bazaar, offering baked goods and unique seasonal crafting opportunities. One ticket will buy a bowl of boiling hot and spicy chili with or without meat, cornbread or a hotdog, a dessert and of course a drink to go along with the dinner. All proceeds from the event benefits the sick, injured and homeless animals in APL's care. Animals within the Mobile Adoption Unit will also be available for adoption onsite.
When: 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Sunday
Where: 2200 Meadowbrook Road, Springfield
More: Tickets are $12 for entry to the event and included food. Tickets must be purchased at apl-shelter.org.
Halloween Ghost Hunt
What: If you've ever been interested in the paranormal, or if you're a more experienced investigator, here's your chance to visit one of the most haunted locations in Illinois. James J. Eldred Historic Site is hosting a night of history and paranormal takes place at one of Greene County's original haunted treasures. Join other ghost adventurers in a two-hour paranormal tour of four key areas in this historic home.
When: Two-hour tours go from 7 to 11 p.m., with a premium ghost hunt from 10 p.m. to 1 a.m. Saturday and Sunday
Where: 742 NW 100 St., Eldred
More: Tickets are $20 to $35. All proceeds from the event will go toward the restoration and preservation of the historic Eldred home, on behalf of the Illinois Valley Cultural Heritage Association nonprofit.

What: Put your artistic creativity to the test with the Springfield Art Association with a holiday-themed craft session. You don't need to be a professional welder to make a stained glass treat, anyone can with the assistance of a professional artist. Make and take home your own stained glass bat ornament at the end of this workshop.
When: 9 a.m. to noon Friday
Where: 700 N. Fourth St., ​Springfield
More: Tickets are $45 for nonmembers, and $35 for SAA members.
Hallow-Palooza
What: The downtown Kidzeum is celebrating the spookiest time of the year with plenty of family friendly activities. Join the museum on East Adams for a spook-tacular carnival with Halloween-themed games, sinister science demonstrations with our resident mad scientist, frightening face-painting, and much more!
When: 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday
Where: 412 E. Adams St., Springfield

title: High school volleyball playoff schedule, results: Taylorville gears up for another run
author: Bill Welt
description: Taylorville's Mazie Fleming, Sami Breckenridge lap up final season, plus the complete high school volleyball schedule with results for the Springfield area
content:
The Taylorville volleyball team views the regular season as one big practice for the postseason, and it's finally here.
The Tornadoes herald another potent lineup ahead of the Class 3A playoffs with a cluster of seniors who go as far back as first grade.
That includes 6-4 hitter Mazie Fleming and 5-8 setter Sami Breckenridge.
Fleming recently committed to NCAA Division II University of Illinois Springfield. Also a basketball standout, Fleming said she went the other route because she enjoys the intensity and camaraderie that comes with volleyball.
'I'm super excited and I think it's going to be a great fit for me,' Fleming said.
Fleming said she has improved in all facets of the game over the past four years under head coach Kim Peabody, especially blocking. She was strictly a middle hitter before injuries on the team led her to become an outside hitter last season. She can now handle both positions.
'We do a lot of blocking at practices,' Fleming said. 'Coach Peabody likes to really crack down on it because it's a really big part of the game. It's a lot easier for our passers to get those hard hits if we get a touch on it.'
Fleming indeed led the team in kills (156) and blocks (43) prior to the weekend.
Breckenridge has a wealth of other options with four other players with at least 90 kills, including juniors Alayna Vincent (149) and Ella Appel (116) and seniors Liv Havera (102) and Lia Champley (92). That doesn't even include junior Robyn Ward, who was injured at the start of the season.
'I'm very confident in my hitters," Breckenridge said. "When I set them up, I have the mindset they are going to put the ball down and they're going to be smart about it. Even if it's not a really good set, they're going to do something with the ball that will make a change.'
Breckenridge has morphed into an assertive leader over the past two seasons, while contributing 562 assists and 192 digs this fall. She also performed gymnastics, specifically trampoline and tumbling, until about a month ago.
She represented USA Gymnastics abroad over the last three years in England (2023), Bulgaria (2022) and Azerbaijan (2021). Breckenridge said she first attempted gymnastics as young as 3.
'My mom (Josi) put me into that because I was really shy and she was hoping that would open me up a little bit,' Breckenridge said. 'It didn't really help my shyness, but I was just a natural at it and did really well.'
Maybe not initially, but over time it cultivated Breckenridge into the proverbial quarterback she is now. She intends to resume volleyball in college.
'I feel like it's a really big opportunity for you and it's really changed the person that I am today,' Breckenridge said of her time with Team USA. 'I've become more responsible because of that. And because I'd go without my parents and be a leader for younger people, I think that's helped me in volleyball becoming a leader.'
Fleming and Breckenridge certainly share a history of success together that also extends to their teammates.
They finished 18-0 in eighth grade, in fact. Although the Illinois Elementary School Association state finals were nixed due to the COVID-19 pandemic that year, Fleming became a key contributor on Taylorville's first-ever run to the Illinois High School Association state finals in 2022.
"I'm really grateful to have her as my setter," Fleming said of Breckenridge. "She's really talented and knows where to put the ball. She's got great timing and I'm really thankful to have her back being my full-time setter for a second year. And the friendship that we have since we've played together for so long just makes the connection so much better."

title: Rhetoric ratchets up in election for Sangamon County Recorder
author: Steven Spearie
description: Rhetoric is ratcheting up in the race for the Sangamon County Recorder. The subtext may be the 2023 Springfield Mayor's election.
content:
The idea of merging the Sangamon County Recorder's office with the county clerk has become a hot button campaign issue between incumbent recorder Josh Langfelder and challenger Frank Lesko in the Nov. 5 election.
Those aren't the only sparks flying.
Fallout from a contentious 2023 mayoral campaign, involving Josh Langfelder's brother, Jim Langfelder, still may be lingering.
Lesko, the current city clerk for Springfield, has touted in ads"Hire me so you can fire me" and claims the merger of the two offices could save county taxpayers $250,000 annually. Other counties, like Cook and Champaign, have gone that route, Lesko said.
Langfelder, who has been in the office since 2008, said merger talk is "a terrible idea" and that Lesko is "defrauding voters" by claiming there will be a savings when there won't be. Those offices that have merged have "regretted it," Langfelder countered.
The recorder's office is the official land records depository for the county. Instruments filed with the office include deeds, mortgages, releases and assignments, property liens, as well as assorted federal, state and local liens. Other documents include veteran's discharge papers, corporation papers and instruments pertaining to the Uniform Commercial Code.
While having the offices separate is "an outlier," the current clerk, Don Gray, said there is "a lot of legwork" yet to be done around any potential merger.
If talk gets more serious, Gray said, the public would have to weigh in through a binding referendum.
"I would almost demand an independent third-party entity analyze its specifics to what the cost savings would be and what that structure would look like," Gray said. "I don't want to step into something with unknowns."
Lesko, 64, said the recorder's staff would be merged into the new office, so no one would lose his or her job. Under the plan, Lesko said the recorder would leave the office at the completion of the merger.
"It's the right thing to do for the people," Lesko contended. "It's the right thing to do for the county. As elected officials, these aren't jobs. They elect us to look out for their best interests. We have to put the people first. It's a government by the people.
"I see this as government waste and a way to save money for the taxpayers."
But Langfelder sees it as something else.
"It's not going to be a tax savings," he said. "What they're doing is political maneuvers to eliminate an individual in that office because they, one, can't beat them in an election, or, two, those individuals haven't done a great job.
"I've done a great job in that office, saving taxpayer money by returning back to the county anywhere from $600,000 to $1 million for other offices to operate."
Langfelder, 54, criticized a second TV commercial as "an attack ad" against him. The ad, paid for by the Sangamon County Evening Republicans Club, claimed Langfelder "(made) more than $2 million from taxpayers."
"That's basically a salary over 16 years," Langfelder said. "This is coming from a guy who has been on the government payroll his entire life. He's gone from working in various positions in the city to the county to the state to holding three elected offices (city clerk, Ward 4 alderman and park board trustee)."
Lesko said he hadn't seen the ad and didn't know who paid for it.
"I don't think it's an attack ad when you're telling the truth and you're talking about saving money," he said.
Langfelder said he was turned off that Lesko started passing petitions to run for recorder months after being sworn in to his third term as city clerk in May 2023.
Lesko's candidacy, he said, may be tied to the 2023 mayoral race when city treasurer Misty Buscher defeated Jim Langfelder, denying him a third term for the city's top spot.
"For him to run for this office after he just got elected basically tells you he's not in it for the right reasons," Langfelder said. "He's in it for the money and in it to get back at my family, for whatever reason, just because individuals did not care for how my brother ran the city."
Lesko said the timing was just part of "the election cycle" and that the recorder's officer "seemed like a natural progression for me being the keeper of the record for the city of Springfield."
Asked if the matchup with Langfelder was any hangover from that election, Lesko said "there was no motive on my part from that. My motive was to save money for the taxpayers.
"It's nothing personal about the Langfelder family. Would there be effects from that election? I guess we'll see (Tuesday), but I don't know."

title: Volleyball regional results: Taylorville, Lincoln, SHG advance to finals
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Volleyball rivals Taylorville, Rochester to meet for Decatur MacArthur Regional final on Thursday
content:
Here are high school volleyball regional updates from around Springfield:
Tuesday's results
Top seed Taylorville and fourth seed Rochester won their semifinal matches in straight sets on Tuesday and will play for the Class 3A Decatur MacArthur Regional volleyball championship.
Taylorville defeated No. 9 seed Southeast 25-15, 25-16 and Rochester beat No. 7 Decatur Eisenhower 25-12, 25-14.
The Tornadoes play the Rockets at 6 p.m. on Thursday.
The two teams split a pair of matches this season. Taylorville defeated Rochester 25-22, 25-23 at Taylorville in the first match of the season on Aug. 26. Rochester then nipped Taylorville 25-15, 20-25, 15-13 on Sept. 28 at the Champaign Central Invite.
At Lincoln
Third seed Lincoln survived No. 5 Springfield High 18-25, 25-20, 25-21, while No. 2 seed Chatham Glenwood posted a 25-12, 25-13 win over No. 6 Jacksonville in the semifinals on Tuesday.
Glenwood and Lincoln play for the championship at 6 p.m. on Thursday.
Lincoln earned a 25-22, 25-22 home victory over Glenwood in a Central State Eight Conference match on Sept. 17.
Class 2A
Top seed Sacred Heart-Griffin and No. 5 Pleasant Plains both needed three sets to pull out semifinal wins at the Class 2A Sacred Heart-Griffin Regional volleyball tournament on Tuesday.
SHG downed sixth seed Lutheran 25-19, 20-25, 25-20 and Plains handed fourth seed Petersburg PORTA a 25-22, 23-25, 25-20 loss in the other semifinal.
SHG meets Plains for the regional title at 6 p.m. on Thursday. The Cyclones defeated Plains 25-18, 25-11 in a nonconference match earlier this season on Sept. 11 at Plains.
At Auburn
Second seed Williamsville and third seed Athens both picked up semifinal wins to advance to the championship match at 6 p.m. on Thursday.
Williamsville beat No. 10 Pittsfield 25-12, 25-13 and Athens ousted No. 7 Auburn 25-10, 25-18.
Williamsville, the Sangamo Conference champs, has beaten Athens once this season, outlasting the Warriors 25-19, 24-26, 25-22 in a conference match at Williamsville on Sept. 24.
At Carlinville
Second seed Carlinville beat No. 9 Piasa Southwestern 25-17, 25-17 and third seed Pana knocked off No. 11 Gillespie 25-21, 27-25 in the semifinals to advance to Thursday's 6 p.m. title match.
Braley Wiser had six kills and 11 digs and Isabella Tiburzi provided 16 assists, 10 digs and three blocks for Carlinville.
Izzy Reed had 20 assists in Pana's win. Kennedy Bowker collected 10 digs and Reagan McGlauchlen served eight aces. Phoenix Pope recorded a team-high nine kills for Pana.
Carlinville defeated Pana 25-16, 25-16 in a South Central Conference match on Oct. 17 at Carlinville.
At Litchfield
Staunton, the South Central Conference champs and top sectional seed, handled No. 6 seed Litchfield 25-17, 25-14 in the semifinals to advance to the regional championship match.
Staunton will face No. 5 Shelbyville for the title at 6 p.m. on Thursday. Shelbyville defeated fourth seed Hillsboro 25-19, 27-25 in the other semifinal.
Class 1A
Mackenzie Mehochko recorded eight kills and 11 digs and second seed Nokomis defeated 11th seed Altamont 25-13, 25-7 in the quarterfinals of the Class 1A Effingham St. Anthony volleyball tournament on Monday.
Becca Hill led NHS with 12 assists and three aces.
Nokomis (31-4) will play sixth seed Brownstown/St. Elmo at 6 p.m. on Wednesday in the semifinals. Third seed Carrollton plays No. 5 Effingham St. Anthony in the second semifinal at 7.
At Franklin
Fourth seed New Berlin defeated White Hall North Greene 25-8, 25-15 and No. 5 South County downed Pawnee 25-11, 25-20 in a pair of quarterfinal matches.
New Berlin plays South County in the semifinals at 7 p.m. on Wednesday. Sixth seed Calvary plays top seed Decatur Christian in the other semifinal at 6.
Calvary defeated Jacksonville Routt 25-21, 22-25, 25-22 in the regional's quarterfinals on Monday.
At Mount Olive
Raymond Lincolnwood, seeded fourth, swept Bunker Hill 25-15, 25-17 and seventh seed Greenfield beat Mount Olive 25-19, 25-16 in the quarterfinals.
Lincolnwood meets Greenfield in the semifinals at 7 p.m. on Wednesday.
At Mount Pulaski
Mason City Illini Central, the 11th seed, overcame a one-set deficit and rallied for a 18-25, 25-18, 26-24 victory over No. 7 seed Edinburg in the quarterfinals on Tuesday.
Illini Central plays third seed Greenview in the semifinals at 7 p.m. on Wednesday. Greenview also needed three sets to edge 13th seed Delavan 23-25, 25-14, 25-20 in the quarterfinals.
At Havana
Fifth seed Rushville-Industry won in straight sets, 25-22, 25-11 over Astoria South Fulton in Tuesday's quarterfinals.
The Rockets will play No. 4 seed Concord Triopia — which defeated Griggsville-Perry 25-10, 25-13 — in the semifinals at 7 p.m. on Wednesday.
No. 11 seed Havana moved on to the semifinals after winning a thriller by upsetting sixth seed Bluffs 25-9, 20-25, 26-24 in a quarterfinal match on Monday. Havana plays No. 1 seed Augusta Southeastern in Wednesday's first semifinal at 6.

title: Springfield Rail Improvement Project gets $157M to help get to the finish line
author: Springfield State Journal
description: The latest round of funding is expected to help get the Springfield Rail Improvement Project to the finish line.
content:
The Springfield Rail Improvement Project has received more than $150 million in federal funding to help finish the massive project.
Officials announced $157.1 million in federal funds have been garnered for the project. $156.3 million of that money is coming to the city of Springfield from the Federal Rail Administration, which is part of the U.S. Department of Transportation.
Incoming money is expected to finish the $475 million project, moving all passenger and freight traffic from Third Street to Tenth, and creating the $111 million HUB transportation center. A series of overpasses and underpasses has also been constructed.
The HUB will be home to Amtrak and bus service along with a parking garage, art exhibits and dining.
Last December, the U.S. DOT's denial of a $138 million grant stymied some of the work. Other work continued, like the construction of underpasses.
The hiccup delayed overall progress by more than a year, but the project is now on schedule for completion in August of 2027, said Nate Bottom, Chief City Engineer for the city.
Fresh dollars will resume construction of the HUB as well as tackle the North Grand Avenue underpass.
Money will be fairly evenly distributed among those two remaining projects, Sangamon County Board Chairman Andy Van Meter told The State Journal-Register.
"The project is going to be done as originally intended by the community. It's just a stunning announcement for the community," he said of the announcement of the funds.
The finish line will demonstrate what a community can do when it pulls together and focuses on one goal, he added.
The Springfield Rail Improvement Project was originally formed in 2010 as the Springfield Railroad Corridor Study. The city of Springfield and Sangamon County conducted the study to rethink how best to accommodate passenger rail traffic through Springfield.
It also aims to address issues of public safety, traffic congestion, and commercial improvement of the current railways system in the city.
Sergio "Satch" Pecori, CEO of Hanson Professional Services who has partnered with the city in the project, said in August that August and September would be spent tying down "odds and ends" as the project nears completion.
Pecori said bid documents to construct the HUB will go out once getting authorization from the FRA. The contract will be awarded in either January or March.

title: County-wide, county board seats up for election. Here are some key races on the ballot
author: Steven Spearie
description: Half of the 14 Sangamon County Board seats up for election are contested races. Here's what you need to know.
content:
The fatal shooting of Sonya Massey by a former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy in her home on July 6 and reforms in law enforcement have very much been on the minds of county voters.
Those voters will decide a number of contested county-wide races on Nov. 5.
That includes seven races for spots on the Sangamon County Board, which approved the Massey Commission. The commission was formed to produce a comprehensive report outlining findings, recommendations and proposed actions within a year.
The county board has staggered terms, so 14 of the 29 seats are up this time.
Three county officeholders face opposition, while Auditor Andy Goleman and Coroner Jim Allmon are running unopposed.
Here's what to know:
Sangamon County Board
A.D. "Andy" Van Meter, who has spent 30 years on the county board and 24 years as chairman, is locked in a rematch with Maureen Duffy Bommarito. The two are neighbors in Leland Grove.
In 2022, Van Meter won by a little less than 13 percentage points in the District 24 race.
Three Republican incumbents--Tom Madonia Jr. in District 9, Greg Stumpf in District 16 and Abe Forsyth in District 27--try to return to their seats. They are matched against Democrat challengers Dana Stoerger, Garret Selinger and Kamilah Renee Webb, respectively.
In District 12, Democrat incumbent Marc Ayers faces challenger Colleen Lucas Cavanagh.
Jennifer Ghesquiere Deaner in District 25 and Justin Davsko in District 26, both Republicans, were appointed to their seats earlier this year and are making bids to stay on.
Ghesquiere Deaner takes on Democrat Jennifer Merritt and Libertarian Russ Clark. For a two-year unexpired term, Davsko faces Democrat Rick Thompson.
Other county-wide races
In one of the more intriguing races, incumbent Recorder Joshua Langfelder, the only Democrat to hold a county-wide office, seeks reelection against Springfield Clerk and former Ward 4 Alderman Frank Lesko.
State's Attorney John Milhiser, a Republican who was sworn in on Nov. 14 replacing Dan Wright, takes on Kimberly Talken, a Springfield trial attorney.
Joe Roesch, the Republican circuit clerk since Oct. 1, 2023, when he succeeded Paul Palazzolo by appointment, will face Democrat challenger Juwanda M. Burrage, an Illinois Department of Human Services caseworker.

title: Here are the top volleyball players to follow this postseason in the Springfield area
author: Bill Welt
description: Here are just a few names to follow as the volleyball playoffs begin this week in the Springfield area
content:
CARLINVILLE — The Staunton volleyball team certainly carries a little target on its back in the South Central Conference.
They still reign supreme following a 25-23, 25-22 win over Carlinville at The Big House on Thursday. It not only clinched a fifth straight league crown but also extended the conference winning streak to 52 games.
It wasn't achieved through any one particular individual but rather numerous sources. Four different hitters — seniors Grace Bekeske, Gianna Bianco, Ele Feldmann and sophomore Jenna Staggs — cashed in at least five kills, while senior Lilly Troeckler and junior Mallory Lucykow combined for 26 assists.
'We did very well hitting our middles and our right-sides tonight,' said Feldmann, who also contributes to the back row. 'Everywhere was playing well and we just put the ball down when we needed to. It was a good game for us.'
Fellow seniors Lilly Bandy and Samantha Fulton combined for three kills, while freshman Kadyn Legendre chipped in two herself.
That core of seniors has played under coach Jeanene Lucykow since sixth grade. Jeanene, who reached 500 career wins earlier this season, said each rotates as a captain because each deserves it.
'It's like my kids out there and they know who's going to get what because they've been playing together for so many years,' Jeanene said. 'I cannot be more proud of this group.
'They all play hard and they're all great athletes. There's not one player who I can say who wins it for us. It's truly a team effort.'
That senior connection also extends to basketball and softball. Last winter, Staunton claimed its second straight Class 2A hoops regional title.
'It's honestly so easy,' Bekeske said of their chemistry, 'because I have a main group of girls who I've grown up with and trained with. It's like family out there.'
They now enter the postseason as the No. 1 seed in the 2A Litchfield Regional semifinals on Tuesday.
'I love playing with these girls, they mean everything to me,' Feldmann said. 'It's great and it's pretty sad that this is our last year.'
Here are other top names primed for a deep postseason run around the Springfield area beginning with Class 3A:
🏐 Alexis Neumann, Chatham Glenwood
The sophomore hitter has continued to dominate the net to help give the Titans to the No. 2 seed in the Class 3A Lincoln Regional. Through Oct. 22, she had already amassed 300 kills, 161 digs, 41 blocks and 33 aces.
🏐 Peyton Sasse, Lincoln
This prolific senior outside hitter and Marshall University commit also looms in the 3A Lincoln Regional as the No. 3 seed. The reigning Large School Volleyball Player of the Year, Sasse set the school record for most career kills earlier this season and posted 321 kills, 150 digs, 35 aces and 33 blocks through Oct. 22. The Railsplitters settled for third place in the Central State Eight Conference standings behind champion Normal U-High (10-0) and runnerup Sacred Heart-Griffin (9-1).
🏐 Rachel Becker, Springfield High
The junior hitter supplied eight kills and three digs in the 2-0 win over Rochester last week to bring her total to 234 kills, 39 digs and 32 aces as the No. 5 seed in the Lincoln Regional.
🏐 Peyton Zeidler, Rochester
The sophomore outside hitter recently delivered 11 kills and six digs in a 25-21, 25-20 loss to Springfield High on Oct. 22 to reach 269 kills and 152 digs. The Rockets have the No. 4 seed in the 3A Decatur MacArthur Regional.
🏐 Mazie Fleming, Taylorville
The senior hitter recently committed to NCAA Division II University of Illinois Springfield brandishing 156 kills and 43 blocks through Oct. 22. Her senior setter, Sami Breckenridge, has also starred with 562 assists, 192 digs and 60 kills. The Tornadoes hold the No. 1 seed in the MacArthur Regional.
🏐 Ava Hillyer, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The senior setter led the Cyclones to a second straight City title and entered the final week of the regular season with more than 2,000 career assists with a bevy of potent hitters that include seniors Josie Mack and Macie Rolf. The Cyclones grabbed the No. 1 seed for its tough home 2A regional that also includes No. 4 Petersburg PORTA and No. 5 Pleasant Plains.
🏐 Cassie Cox, Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central
The senior hitter has assembled another prolific season with 230 kills and 101 blocks (57 solo) to go along with 84 digs prior to the regular-season finale. The Bluejays will seek back-to-back regional titles after claiming their first-ever regional last season.
🏐 Izzy Lynch, Pleasant Plains
The senior libero has anchored the back row with 330 digs entering the final week of the regular season. The balanced Cardinals won their seventh straight Sangamon County title this season.
🏐 Addie Stadsholt, Athens
An all-state honoree last season, the senior outside hitter led the Warriors with a staggering 359 kills and 209 digs through Oct. 21. Athens holds the No. 3 seedbehind only No. 2 Sangamo Conference rival Williamsville in the 2A Auburn Regional.
🏐 Britni Walters, Williamsville
The senior outside hitter has rebounded from a basketball injury with more than 1,000 career kills. Her senior setter, Riley Holliday, also touts more than 2,000 career assists. They led the Bullets to a third straight Sangamo Conference title.
🏐 Reagan McGlauchlen, Pana
The junior hitter totaled 11 kills in a recent 25-12, 25-17 win over Litchfield while senior setter Izzy Reed had 17 assists and five digs. The Panthers earned the No. 3 seed behind No. 2 host Carlinville in their 2A regional.
🏐 Isabella Tiburzi, Carlinville
The senior setter leads the team in assists (373), kills (225) and aces (46) in addition to 229 digs through Oct. 24. She starred in the showdown against Staunton with 12 assists and seven kills.
🏐 Tatum Christian, Hillsboro
This senior hitter, along with fellow senior teammate Addison Lowe, has registered more than 200 kills as the Hiltoppers approach the 2A Litchfield Regional as the No. 4 seed behind No. 1 Staunton. Both have also combined for more than 210 digs.
🏐 Mackenzie Mehochko, Nokomis
The Class 1A all-state honoree helps present a big 1-2 punch alongside junior Addison Glenn. Both have combined for more than 457 kills after each had six kills in a 25-16, 25-13 win over Calvary to secure a second straight outright MSM Conference title. Mehochko has also tallied 231 digs and 20 blocks, while Glenn has a team-high 56 blocks prior to the weekend. NHS picked up the top No. 2 seed in the 1A Effingham St. Anthony Regional.
🏐 Kierstyn Denney, Raymond Lincolnwood
The senior hitter and 1A all-state second teamer already matched last season's kill total (219) amid the final week of the regular season. That doesn't include the 142 assists and 168 digs for the No. 4 Lancers in the 1A Mount Olive Regional.
🏐 Myleigh Barton, Greenview
This senior hitter mustered 12 kills, eight digs and three assists in a two-set win over Calvary Christian Academy to up her total to 175 kills and 203 digs. She will lead the No. 3 Bulldogs into the 1A Mount Pulaski Regional that also includes No. 2 juggernaut Hartsburg-Emden.
🏐 Jenna McGath, New Berlin
The versatile sophomore can handle any job. She contributed 11 kills, 13 digs, two aces and a block in a 25-23, 26-28, 25-21 win over Athens late in the regular season. The Pretzels are the No. 4 seed in the 1A Franklin Regional.

title: Who are the boys and girls cross country state qualifiers in the Springfield area?
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Chatham Glenwood, Williamsville won girls cross country sectional titles on Saturday
content:
Here are the boys and girls cross country state finalists for the Springfield area:
Volleyball playoffs: Who's advancing to volleyball sectionals: SHG wins first regional since 2017
Class 2A girls
Chatham Glenwood put three runners in the top 10 and edged Rochester 50-74 to win the girls team title at the Class 2A Olney Sectional cross country meet at Olney Central College on Saturday.
Glenwood and Rochester both advanced their teams to the state meet at Detweiller Park in Peoria next Saturday.
Sophomore Ali Londrigan took fourth to lead Glenwood in 18 minutes, 27.38 seconds. Junior Ashlyn Chopra (18:34.84) was seventh and junior Ally Knudson (18:38.47) came in ninth for Glenwood.
Defending champs:
Rochester senior Brooke Zeibert had the best finish for all area runners, placing third in 18:19.38, and sister Ashley Zeibert, a junior, was sixth in 18:29.80.
No other entries from the area was able to qualify for the state meet individually. Taylorville freshman Elayna Harker was the closest with a 16th-place finish in 18:53.90.
Class 1A girls
Behind a pair of sisters, Williamsville captured the Class 1A Elmwood Sectional title, sending the girls team to the cross country state meet at Detweiller Park.
Senior Louisa Wilson placed third in 18:01.17 and sophomore Joelle Wilson (18:25.62) took ninth, helping the Bullets finish the sectional with 76 points at Maple Lane Country Club.
Williamsville had five runners place in the top 30 that included Hannah Nation (26th), Brooklyn Turley (28th) and Kaylea Hollinshead (30th).
Pleasant Plains ended with 143 points and also sent its team to state with a fifth-place finish. Junior Alaina Hawker (18:21.05) led the way for Plains, coming in seventh place.
By one place, Sacred Heart-Griffin (180 points) missed the state cut with a seventh-place team finish, but will be sending freshman Paityn Brady to Peoria. Brady finished fourth individually in 18:02.78.
Jacksonville Routt freshman Millie Schumacher also advanced to state with an eighth-place showing in 18:23.32.
At Toledo Cumberland, Carlinville failed to reach the Class 1A state meet when the Cavaliers finished 20th with 564 points at Lake Land College.
Individually, Pana freshman Kadence Rochkes (21:49.2) placed 66th and Litchfield sophomore Rilynn Younker (22:24.4) was 80th.
Class 2A boys
Chatham Glenwood totaled 180 points at the Olney Sectional and placed fifth in the standings to earn a spot at the Class 2A boys state cross country meet next Saturday at Detweiller Park in Peoria.
Junior Van Schneider (15:53.47) had the best finish for Glenwood, coming in 18th place. Other contributors for Glenwood included junior Brady Moser (25th) and seniors Carter Simmons (36th) and Mason Daley (45th).
With its 205 points and eighth-place finish, Taylorville did not advance to state, and sophomore Liam Bettis came up two places short of going Individually. Bettis finished 12th overall in 15:39.50. Senior Brody Harker of Taylorville got 15th place in 15:47.87.
Class 1A boys
Gillespie junior Chaz Oberkfell won the Class 1A Toledo Cumberland Sectional at Lake Land College and the Miners got the final team spot to advance to the state meet at Detweiller Park.
Oberkfell finished the race in 15:11.8, nearly 9 seconds ahead of second-place finisher Evan Cook (15:20.06) of Decatur St. Teresa. Gillespie junior Carter Sies was 44th in 16:56.7 as the Miners finished with 228 points.
At Elmwood, Pleasant Plains advanced its team to the 1A state meet when the Cardinals finished in fifth place with 151 points at Maple Lane Country Club.
Junior Elijah Teefey (15:20.73) sparked Plains with a third-place finish.
Auburn did not advance to state, taking seventh place in the team standings with 183. Junior James Baisden did make the state cut individually and was seventh in 15:32.98.
Class 3A boys and girls
Springfield High, the lone team representing the area in Class 3A, did not advance to state in the boys and girls races at the Normal Community Sectional at Parkside Junior High.
The boys placed 15th with 365 points, and Springfield junior Alexander Ratz having the top time of 16:07.66 to finish 54th.
The girls finished 17th as a team with 506 points. Senior Mia Volpert (19:36.04) had the best time and placed 58th.

title: Benton football breaks first-round hex with win over New Berlin in 3A playoffs
author: Bill Welt
description: New Berlin football hopes the playoff loss can be a springboard for the future, while Benton moves on in the Class 3A bracket
content:
NEW BERLIN — It was a big moment for all of Benton's seniors.
Senior quarterback Tiffin Kouzoukas totaled five touchdowns and the Rangers dispatched New Berlin 48-7 in the Class 3A playoff opener after enduring first-round exits the past two seasons.
'This season, we've had some ups and downs,' Kouzoukas said. 'We knew if we lost, we would go home and turn in our pads on Monday. We were like, 'No, not this year,' especially my senior year.'
Benton (7-3) scored on seven of its nine possessions — including its first three — after New Berlin junior QB Brady Crews threw a 15-yard touchdown pass to junior teammate Charlie Neuman on the game's opening drive.
The Pretzels (7-3) subsequently didn't pick up another first down until the final seconds of the game.
AJ Craven first scored a nine-yard touchdown run before Kouzoukas connected with senior receiver Grant Owens for the go-ahead 34-yard touchdown pass to begin the second quarter. Benton led 21-7 at halftime after a short Kouzoukas keeper.
Kouzoukas completed 9 of 11 passes for 119 yards and three touchdowns while rushing for two scores. Owens had four catches for 56 yards while senior teammate Jesser Zepeda had three receptions for 48 yards and a score. Senior Lucas Kinsman had the other TD grab.
Senior running back Clark Nelson led New Berlin with 68 rushing yards on 17 attempts. He departs with 1,307 rushing yards and 19 TDs. The Pretzels were making their first playoff appearance since 2015 in coach James Dambacher's second season at the helm.
'This whole senior class, they're the ones who bought in,' Dambacher said. 'I think that's what led to our success this year. Obviously Clark (Nelson) and Gabe (Lyons) are great. Our offensive line worked their butts off. I'm going to miss this senior class.'

title: 4A shake-up: Peoria Notre Dame bounces nine-time state champ Rochester in first round
author: Adrian Dater
description: A blocked extra-point kick in overtime led to Rochester's first-round ousting by Peoria Notre Dame.
content:
ROCHESTER — Ben Mullens seemed almost in shock when he limped to the Peoria Notre Dame bench while his teammates celebrated on the battered turf of Rocket Booster Stadium following his team's unbelievable 59-58 Friday night victory that ended the season of defending Class 4A champion Rochester. Mullens, it turned out, wanted to take it all in for just a few more moments, to comprehend what his team had just pulled off.
In one of the most epic playoff games probably in all of state history, the visiting No. 13-seeded Irish just barely outlasted a valiant, banged-up Rockets squad in a game that both teams seemed to have locked up just a few minutes earlier. In the end, it went the Irish's way thanks to Mullen's quarterbacking, the running of halfback Jack Hanley, and the right leg and right arm of fullback, linebacker and kicker Lawson Alwan.
'That was such a great game. I'm going to remember this game forever,' said Mullens, whose white and Kelly green uniform was caked in dirt. 'It's just an unbelievable feeling to actually win it.'
For the first time since 2008, the nine-time state champion Rockets are bounced in the first round. Not only was it the first opening-round playoff loss for No. 4 Rochester in that span, but the Rockets had not failed to make at least the quarterfinals in any playoff run since 2008.
While Hanley probably deserved the game ball after scoring five touchdowns, including one on a 33-yard run with 3 minutes, 7 seconds left in regulation, the Irish's real hero at the end was Alwan. Not only did he kick a 30-yard field goal with 1.8 seconds left in regulation to tie it at 52-52, but he then blocked the extra point after Rochester's Tanner Beal scored on the Rockets' first possession in OT to keep the Irish six points back with four downs from the 10-yard line to get seven points.
On fourth down, about three inches from the goal line, Mullens called an audible and handed the ball to Alwan, who barely got the ball over the white stripe. With the score now tied 58-58, Alwan booted the extra point well past the uprights.
Rochester players fell to their knees, while Irish players danced in jubilation along with a sizable contingent of fans that made the drive from Peoria.
Alwan credited junior lineman teammate Jacob Khoury for helping him block the extra point in OT.
'He got the guard opened up a little bit and gave me a small, little window and I was able to get my right hand up and block it,' Alwan said. 'After that field goal to tie the game, that (extra point kick) was easy. I felt the nerves go away and I knew we had it.'
Rochester, which lost starting quarterback Bryan Zulauf at the start of the season, became an offensive juggernaut as the season wore on. The Rockets were averaging 39 points a game entering this one. But, no, the defense just wasn't as good as last season's dominant squad. Not that the effort wasn't there.
'This is a young team, and they played their butts off,' Rockets coach Derek Leonard said. 'We just didn't play our best game tonight. They were physical and out-physicaled us, but you know what man? I love these kids and love these seniors and people can't assume that winning just happens. It doesn't, and I think this was a real lesson for everybody.'
The first half saw touchdowns on the first 11 combined possessions, with the Irish holding a 42-38 lead. Rochester's defensive line got much tougher in the second half, and it took the Irish more than 15 minutes to get another point. The Irish's running game was just too tough for Rochester to deal with in the end, as the visitors ran for 460 yards. Mullens only threw three passes in the game, but they were big ones toward the end, for 56 yards.
Kaiden Stout had a strong game for the Rockets, running for 127 yards on 19 carries and a 9-yard TD run in OT. Tanner Beal scored three touchdowns for the Rockets, and three quarterbacks combined for 230 yards on 12-for-19 passing.
Hanley not only ran for 212 yards, but he also caught a big pass on the Irish's field-goal drive that tied it 52-52. He also ran back a kickoff 88 yards for a touchdown.
'He's our superstar,' Alwan said. 'That's our guy. He does it all for us. But it was a team effort for us all the way through.'
Rochester finished the season 7-3. The loss snapped a five-game win streak.
'In the playoffs, there are no good lessons, but this will be eventually for some of our young kids," Leonard said. "For our seniors, they can walk off this field with their heads up high.'

title: Low and nonalcoholic wines are growing in popularity. Here are some to get in Springfield
author: Jay Kitterman
description: Some may be looking to cut back on alcohol consumption ahead of the holiday season. Try one of these low or nonalcoholic wine options.
content:
Would you be willing to spend more than $100 on a bottle of non-alcoholic sparkling wine? I recently read an article in the Wall Street Journal announcing that Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessey (LVMH), the owner of such prestigious brands as Dom Perignon and Moët Hennessey, was introducing a non-alcoholic champagne called French Bloom that would sell for $100.
This is when I knew the low and non-alcoholic liquor business was no longer just a fad, but truly a trend.
French Bloom sources its grapes from the Languedoc region of southern France, where the sunny climate results in grapes with naturally high alcohol.
To remove the alcohol, French Bloom uses a technique called 'cold-vacuum distillation.'
Generational trend
From my research, low and non-alcohol wine is truly a generational and lifestyle trend. The low and non-alcohol wine category is currently being driven by Gen X (demographic cohort 1965-1980) and Millennial (1981-1996) consumers.
A major player in this market is Bota Box. When Bota launched their Breeze products in 2021, research showed that more than 40% of consumers were looking for lower-alcohol wines.
These Gen X and Millennial consumers are upper income, educated and want their wine to fit into their healthy lifestyle.
Bota Box light wines is now the number one brand of low alcohol wine category by volume in the U.S. The box is produced from recyclable materials, stays fresh 30 days after opening and each box is equivalent to four bottles making it very budget friendly.
Many of the Bota Box varieties are also available in the tetra packs, making them very convenient for traveling. I recommend their Chardonnay.
Bota Box research shows this trend tracks closely with long-term consumer trends around food. Consumers want options that align with health-conscious lifestyle choices, in beverages and food, and wine is no exception.
The company states, 'The point of light wine is not to compete with traditional wine; it's to offer an alternative to traditional wine that fits into the lifestyle choices that are important to consumers today.'
Local recommendations
John Russo, who works part-time at the Corkscrew Wine Emporium in Springfield, has researched this topic extensively and reports, 'calorie reduction is a major benefit of non-alcoholic or low alcohol wines.'
A 5 oz. glass of wine, which is one serving, contains 120-130 calories, depending on grape variety and residual sugar. Low alcohol wine has 70-90 calories/serving and non-alcoholic wine has 20-30 calories/serving.
I asked David Anderson at The Corkscrew and Zach Sweet at "It's All About Wine" for their recommendations.
It's All About Wine is currently carrying two wines from Oddbird. Oddbird is a Scandinavian company that started in 2013. Today, they reign as Scandinavia's premier producer of wines, beers and spirits. The wines are matured for up to 12 months and then 'gently liberated from alcohol.'
In 2016, King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden awarded Oddbird an entrepreneurship award. It's All About Wine currently carries Oddbird Red Blend and Oddbird Blanc de Blancs Sparkling.
Their commitment to purity means that their wines contain no artificial colors and no synthetic aromas.
Blanc de Blancs is from Languedoc-Roussillon and made from Chardonnay and Colombard, giving tones of crispy Granny Smith apples, honey and lime. It is described as, 'a youthful and elegant Chardonnay blend with high complexity and delicate bubbles.'
Blanc de Blancs is matured for 12 months before 'being gently liberated from alcohol.'
The Red Blend, which is a combination of Grenache, Syrah and Mourvedre from Saint-Chinian, south of France, is characterized by its acidity and earthy notes with fruity touches. Both are priced at $32.00 a bottle.
Anderson also introduced me to ARIEL Vineyards Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon. Owned and operated by J. Lohr Vineyards & Wines, ARIEL Vineyards is on California's Central Coast.
Their ARIEL Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon and ARIEL Vineyards Chardonnay are batched and fermented like any other wine.
Using a reverse osmosis method, which uses a pump to push their fresh wine through special membranes, the alcohol and water are separated from the wine. Their California Cabernet Sauvignon is described as black currant, velvety chocolate and dark cherries.
Notes for their California Chardonnay describe, 'On the nose, there is a hint of sweetness, with hints of fresh-cut pear, apple, butterscotch and French oak.' These two wines have 45-calories per 8 oz serving and both are priced at $11.99.
In addition, The Corkscrew also has these low or non-alcoholic wines in stock:
Giesen Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc and Rose from New Zealand, $16.99
Selbach Funkel Wurtz Zero Sparkling from Germany, $19.99
Fre Sparkling Brut from California, $14.99
Codorniu Zero Sparkling from Spain, $14.99
Low and nonalcoholic wines are growing rapidly and no longer just located in the back corner of your wine store. Powerhouse brands such as Yellow Tail, Kendall-Jackson, and Kim Crawford have all launched lower-alcohol lines.
My thanks to David Anderson from The Corkscrew, Zach Sweet from It's All About Wine and Calvin Jacey from Bota Box for their assistance with this article.
(This story has been updated to add new information.)
Jay Kitterman is a culinary and special events consultant and adjunct instructor at Lincoln Land Community College.

title: Springfield could have new $40M water distribution facility, public works facility
author: Claire Grant
description: Discussions are being had for a new water distribution facility and public works building in Springfield. What you need to know.
content:
Springfield may be getting a new water distribution facility.
The city's Planning and Zoning Commission met on Oct. 16 to discuss a petition for a new water distribution facility for City Water, Light and Power and building for the Public Works department on the east side of Springfield.
The estimated cost of the project is $40 million.
The parcels for 2101 and 2021 Clear Lake Ave. petition for a reclassification of the property to I-1 light industrial for plans to build a new center for the Office of Public Works including a warehouse, municipal offices and garage on a 38-acre lot the city already owns.
In the parcel, the city of Springfield petitions that the current distribution facility for water does not have appropriate space for daily operations to serve power customers in the area.
Nearly 7 acres of the 38-acre lot would be allotted for the Water Distribution Facility, which will be to the southwest section of the acreage.
CWLP previously planned on building at 401 N. 11 St. but shifted locations due to the 1908 Race Monument becoming designated as a national park service site.
The new distribution facility would be 22,000 square feet with warehouse space near a 30,000-square-foot equipment garage to house snowplows and as a parking lot used by employees of CWLP.
The petitioned new office of Public Works would be 75,560 square feet and will include a wash bay along the north side of the building and have outdoor storage for trailers and equipment used by Public Works, along with other new amenities according to city engineer Nate Bottom.
'We will have offices in there for street superintendent, 24-7 dispatch and zone managers," Bottom said. "We'll also have the traffic sign making facility, as well as our inventory facility."
Public works says its current office at 301 N. 17th St. is outdated. If Public Works gets its new facility, the current building will be used for storage according to Bottom – who says in the distant future the building will be razed.
The offices will take around a year and a half to build, however a date to start construction has not yet been set in stone according to Bottom, who says city council must first approve the budget hearings for the buildings in January to February of next year. If approved, earliest construction would begin in spring of 2025.
