title: Who is winning 2024 US presidential election today? Current Election Day polls, odds, results
author: Chris Sims
description: Happy Election Day 2024! Who's winning the latest U.S. presidential election? Current polls and results on Election Day.
content:
Election Day 2024 has officially arrived as presidential candidates Donald Trump and Kamala Harris are dueling neck-and-neck across the country.
Illinois looks to favor a Harris presidency, but there are several swing states that could impact the presidential election.
Here's what you need to know:
Who is leading 2024 US presidential polls on Election Day today, Tuesday, Nov. 5?
The polls and odds are constantly in flux, but you can find the latest polls we could find for each candidate as of 6 a.m. on Nov. 5, 2024:
ABC News project 538: The final poll shows Harris with a 48.0% to 46.8% edge over Trump.
270towin: Showing a composite of the latest national polls, Harris currently leads Trump by 1.2%.
Realclearpolling: Here are the latest betting odds, which are currently in favor of Harris winning with the spread giving her an edge at +.1 How are odds changing? The edge went to Trump at +0.3 on Friday, +.01 Monday morning and by Monday afternoon were an even stalemate.
Who is winning the 2024 Election Day polls for president in Illinois right now?
The Democratic candidate, as in the last two presidential races, appears to have a commanding lead of the U.S. presidential election in Illinois. Here's where each candidate stood as of 6 a.m. on Nov. 5, 2024:
Who is historian Allan Lichtman's 2024 US presidential election prediction to win on Election Day − Donald Trump or Kamala Harris?
Distinguished American University, Washington, D.C. history professor Allan Lichtman has correctly predicted 9 out of the last 10 U.S. presidential elections. Lichtman earned his doctorate from Harvard, specializing in modern American history and quantitative methods.
This year, Lichtman has predicted Vice President Kamala Harris will win the 2024 U.S. presidential election. "I've been doing this for 42 years and every four years I have butterflies in my stomach," he told USA Today. "This year, I think I have a flock of crows in my stomach."
2024 presidential election predictions: Allan Lichtman vs. Nate Silver — Who will accurately predict the 2024 election?
When will 2024 US presidential election results winner be announced for President of the United States?
Do not expect final results on Election Night.
Election workers have never completed ballot counting on Election Day at any point in the country's history. This year, local and state certification deadlines range from two days to more than a month after Nov. 5.
In recent decades, news outlets have typically called the presidential race late on election night or the morning after, with two notable exceptions. In 2000, a famously close race and legal challenges dragged out the process — things likely to affect this year's cycle. In 2020, a rise in mail-in ballots during the COVID pandemic delayed results.
This year, state laws still in place in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin prohibiting election workers from counting early votes until Election Day are expected to delay results again.
When is Election Day 2024? When to vote in the U.S.?
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024, for the U.S. general election.

If you're not sure where your polling place is, or want to make sure it hasn't changed since the last time you voted, the address can be found by searching the Illinois polling place lookup here. You will need your ZIP code and home address.

The polls opened at 6 a.m. today in Illinois and will close at 7 p.m. If voters are in line by 7 p.m., they can still vote.

If a voter is already registered at their current home address, they do not need to bring ID. It could be helpful to bring a photo ID in case issues arise.

title: Election: Rockford, Springfield, Champaign report technical issues at polls this morning
author: Corina Curry
description: Some Illinois cities experienced technology problems during the first couple of hours of voting this Election Day. Here's what happened.
content:
Rockford, Springfield, Champaign and other cities across Illinois experienced technical issues Tuesday morning shortly after they opened their polling places for the 2024 General Election.
According to election officials across the state, election judges were temporarily unable to access voter registration databases online to check voters in to vote at polling places.
This lasted for about two hours before the system was back online. Officials in Rockford and Springfield said voters were still able to vote and voting did not stop.
"We had to use paper logs of registered voters to check people in instead of being able to access voter registration information using our laptops. That added some time onto the check-in process," said Jorge Paredes,, executive director of the Rockford Board of Election Commissioners. "It was an unfortunate inconvenience for voters and for our election judges, but we train for this and we have backup systems in place."
According to Sangamon County Clerk Don Gray, the connectivity issues also did not affect voters in the Springfield area.
"'It's not affecting any type of voter who's already registered to vote. Even in voter registration, it's just taking a little longer," Gray said. " What you need to keep in mind is that any registered voter in Sangamon County is not affected at all. ... They have a paper application assigned, and there's a ballot for them to vote. They won't know that there's any issue at all."
Gray remarked that some other counties that relied more heavily on electronic voter information may not have been as lucky.
"Some of my colleagues do electronic poll books and check in and they're being affected much greater than we are," he said.
In Champaign County, State's Attorney Julia Rietz has filed a motion for injunctive relief asking that voting hours be extended to 9 p.m. Tuesday to compensate for this morning's issues saying that voters could not vote.
A hearing will be held at 1:30 p.m. at the Champaign County Courthouse.
'We were having problems similar (to Sangamon County). We were not able to search for voters through our voter registration program," said Champaign County Clerk Aaron Ammons. "We have electronic poll books (where Sangamon County has paper poll books)."
Platinum Technology Resource, a Batavia, Illinois-based election service provider, called Tuesday's system error "a temporary issue that affected the speed of voter searches and not a system outage."
In an email to the Rockford Board of Elections Tuesday morning, Platinum explained that its database, which stores and protects the city's electronic voter registration log, locked up causing an error message.
"A non-critical function running during the general election caused database locks, resulting in search times exceeding 30 seconds and, in some cases, leading to timeout errors," Platnium COO Jay Bennett said in an email. "Upon identifying the issue, we promptly disabled the non-critical function, and search times have since returned to their normal speed of under 2 seconds.
We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused and appreciate your understanding as we work to ensure a smooth and efficient voting process."

title: Why the Illinois basketball roster will have a new look for the 2024-25 college season
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The Illini opened with a big win, but learned a returning starter will sit out for the 2024-25 college basketball season.
content:
Illinois basketball looked good Monday night in its 112-67 season opening victory against Eastern Illinois. The Fighting Illini roster also looked a little different.
Returning starter Ty Rodgers did not play Monday and has decided to redshirt the 2024-25 season, team spokesman Derrick Burson told the Champaign News-Gazette and coach Brad Underwood confirmed in a postgame news conference.
Underwood also said the program is looking into redshirt options for 6-foot-10, 210-pound freshman Jason Jakstys, who was the only Illini to suit up Monday and not play.
Why did Ty Rodgers redshirt?
Underwood said discussions about a possible redshirt took place over the last few weeks, since practice started, and through the exhibition loss to Ole Miss. Rodgers was scoreless in 14 minutes of the 91-74 road loss to the Rebels.
"The thing about young people is, they have goals, things they want to try to reach," Underwood said Monday night. "We feel he could continue to grow ... offensively. ... He has areas of his game he wants to work on, and we support that development."
Rodgers was by far the most experienced returning player for Illinois. He started every game last season in a run the NCAA Elite Eight, averaging 6.2 points, 5.3 rebounds and 2.0 assists. Underwood called Rodgers decision "a loss," but also said he was a winner and a nice young man with a kind heart.
Will Ty Rodgers transfer from Illinois?
This is a similar situation to last season, when Sencire Harris decided to redshirt before the season; he ended up transferring to West Virginia. Underwood hopes the program can keep Rodgers, but knows the transfer portal is a possibility.
"It's the world we're in," Underwood said with a shrug. "I think he's an Illini. I think he's our guy. We love Ty to death, but our world doesn't have any guarantees in it now."
Who will replace Ty Rodgers for the Illini?
If Monday night was any indication, the Illini have some depth on the wing to replace Rodgers. Louisville transfer Tre White started and provided some stability, but freshman Will Riley and sophomore Dra Gibbs-Lawthorn came off the bench and dominated.
Riley, a five-start recruit from Canada, played 25 minutes and scored 31 points — the most by a freshman in an Illinois debut. He was 10-for-13 from the field including 5-for-6 from 3-point range. Gibbs-Lawthorn finished with 21 points in 21 minutes on 5-for-10 shooting.

title: A werewolf and a crawfish walk into a voting poll: Unique 'I Voted' election stickers
author: Julia Gomez
description: Some states have very unique stickers that voters can receive after they cast their ballot.
content:
Some people might say the most exciting part about voting is the rush and sense of pride they feel when completing their civic duty but for others? The best part is the stickers, and states did not disappoint with this year's designs.
Obviously, that's a joke. Voting is crucial to our democracy. But stickers are definitely a great bonus. Even President Joe Biden sported his sticker when he voted early this election season.
In Florida, counties like Miami-Dade gave voters red, white, and blue stickers with "I VOTED!" written in Spanish, English, and Haitian Creole. The sticker is cute and shows Miami residents' cultures and backgrounds.
Other states gave out stickers with "I Voted!" printed on top of an American flag.
But compared to Michigan's werewolf voter sticker, it makes these designs look a bit generic.
Michigan's 'I voted' stickers
Michigan held contests for residents to submit their designs for the 2024 "I voted" sticker, and the nine winners were chosen to be handed out to voters after they cast their 2024 ballot.
The winners were split into three groups, and three designs were chosen from each:
Elementary and middle school winners- The werewolf sticker; a simplistic sticker with"I voted yay" written on a blank background and some letters flipped the wrong way; and a sticker that has a man saluting the flag and a happy face with "I'm cool," written on top and "I voted" on the bottom.
High school winners- A sticker with a little guy surrounded by confetti says "Hooray," with "I voted" written on the bottom; A buck with multi-color sunglasses and a baseball cap. "I" is colored in to look like the American flag, and "voted" is written in red, white and blue; and a sticker with " I voted" written in the beam of light coming from a lighthouse at sunset.
General entry winners- A patriotic cat with a red, white and blue top hat carrying a picket sign that says "I voted;" A sticker with "Ope, I voted," written on a swirly red and purple background; A fish with "I voted" written on its scales.
"The wolf one is a fan favorite," said Mell Stoner, 18, a history student at Central Michigan University and first-time voter.
The sticker, which is pictured above, has taken the internet by storm. On it, a muscular werewolf with a visible eight-pack of abs and large biceps is ripping off his tank top while he howls in front of an American flag. "I voted" is written on top in blue and red.
The sensational sticker was created by a Brownell Middle School student in Grosse Point, Michigan.
"I love the stickers," said Stoner. "I think it was a really good idea, and I'm really glad [the state] got multiple age groups to participate."
Stoner's favorite sticker is the fish sticker, with "I voted" written on its upper half, pictured to the right of the werewolf. They're glad they and other Michiganders got to vote on the stickers.
"It's a really great way to get everyone involved in the election without just putting politics in their face," they said.
Stoner was one of the first people to vote during the early election and received all nine of the sticker designs.
North Carolina's eye voted sticker
Some voters were surprised by the interesting stickers they received when they cast their ballot.
The sticker a poll worker gave Kiersten Maresca, 30, was not what she expected. So, she jumped on TikTok to tell the story because "it was so funny," and the video went viral.
Maresca thought she was going to get a regular, "patriotic" "I voted" sticker with the American flag in the background, she told USA TODAY. Needless to say, she didn't.
"I went to put on my cute little patriotic sticker, and I saw it," she said. "And I was like, 'that is an eyeball...'"
An eyeball that is out of its socket with pink and red tissue attached to the back of it. It takes up most of the sticker. Below it is the word "voted."
The punny " eye voted" sticker looks more like something one would find at a horror movie or Halloween convention, not a voting poll.
"Did you vote in a Hot Topic?" one person asked in the comment section of Maresca's video.
"They're really in the spooky spirit over there," said another.
But she isn't "ungrateful" for the unique sticker, as some in the comment section of her video said.
"It was an actual shock," Maresca told USA TODAY.
Maresca, born and raised in New Jersey, moved to Brunswick County in North Carolina, where she said the residents seem "very traditional." It's her first time voting in the area
"I couldn't believe that was the sticker," she said.
"I need to frame it now."
A 'patriotic' crawfish
Maresca isn't the only one who wants to frame her sticker. Robby Marshall, a Louisiana native who lives in Baton Rouge, wants to do the same for his, too.
This year's sticker "felt personal to Louisiana," Marshall told USA TODAY.
The state's "I voted" sticker has a red crawfish, a staple in Louisiana, wearing a blacktop hat, shoes and a white and blue suit.
"It's a crawfish in a blue suit, so it represents the red and blue, and it's still patriotic," he said.
Louisiana's Secretary of State Nancy Landry asked Academy Award winner William Joyce, who was born in the southeastern state, to design the sticker for the 2024 election season, Joel Watson, Lousianna's Deputy Secretary of State for communications, told USA TODAY.
Joyce, who wrote and illustrated children's books like "Rolie Polie Olie," "A Day with Wilbur Robinson" and more, changed up the usual "I voted" sticker for 2024.
"It's very different," said Watson. "You know, most of [states' previous stickers] are very unique to one another, but this one is certainly, I would say, most unique."
Feeling 'hopeful'
Marshall wants to frame his sticker not only because he likes the design but also because of its meaning and the hope this year's election gives him.
"For me, it was being able to vote for the first female person of color for president," said Marshall. "That's something that's very historic."
Marshall wanted to keep his sticker from 2016, when he voted for former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, but the polling place had run out of stickers when he cast his ballot, he said.
"Regardless of whether or not [Harris] wins, I was able to play a part."

title: IHSA volleyball sectionals: SHG, Nokomis remain as Springfield area's last teams
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Sacred Heart-Griffin will meet Quincy Notre Dame in the Class 2A sectional finals, plus other results on Tuesday.
content:
Top seed Sacred Heart-Griffin rallied in the first set and then sealed a sweep with a 25-23, 25-19 win over third-seeded Tremont in the Class 2A Riverton Sectional semifinals volleyball tournament on Tuesday.
SHG (26-10) will play the other top seed, Quincy Notre Dame, for the sectional title on Thursday at 6 p.m. QND (35-2) edged third seed Athens 18-25, 25-12, 27-25 in the second semifinal.
The Cyclones used a 6-0 spurt in the first set, highlighted by Ava Hillyer, who served five straight points to give SHG a 20-18 lead. The Cyclones closed out the set on kills by Lauren Johannes and Kendall Stotlar.
Stotlar's kill and block early in the second set gave SHG a 13-7 advantage and later Johannes' service ace pushed the lead to 20-12. Tremont got within 22-19, but kills by Stotlar, Johannes and Macie Rolf ended the match.
Athens bowed out with a 30-8 record but pushed QND to the brink. The Warriors had a match point at 25-24 before the Raiders reeled off three straight points for the win.
CLASS 1A
At Farina South Central
Nokomis Def. Glen Carbon Father McGivney 25-22, 25-9: Mackenzie Mehochko chalked up eight kills and eight digs and No. 2 subsectional seed Nokomis defeated the top seed to advance to the sectional title match.
Nokomis (34-4) will play Hardin Calhoun for the championship at 6 p.m. on Thursday. Kinley Stolte compiled 11 assists and Becca Hill had nine for NHS. Lizzy Hill and Grace King served four aces apiece and Madison DeWerff collected eight digs.
CLASS 3A
At Mahomet-Seymour
Levyn Snow had ten kills, and Amanda Freehill collected 13 digs and served three aces as the top-seeded Pioneers downed their Central State Eight Conference rivals, Chatham Glenwood, 25-8, 25-11 in the semifinals.
Lola Clayton dished out 17 assists for U-High, which will play No. 2 seed Mahomet-Seymour for the championship at 6 p.m. on Thursday.
Glenwood ended the season 28-9.
Mahomet-Seymour (35-3) won the second semifinal over top seeded Taylorville 25-12, 25-20. Taylorville finished 30-8.
CLASS 2A
At Staunton
Second-seeded Columbia dropped top-seeded Staunton 25-17, 25-15, and No. 1 seed Breese Mater Dei beat No. 2 Carlinville 25-15, 25-13 in the semifinals.
Columbia (31-6) will face Mater Dei in the championship match at 6 p.m. on Thursday. Staunton finished 27-11, and Carlinville ended 28-8-1.

title: Pritzker to Trump: 'You come for my people, you come through me'
author: Claire Grant
description: During a news conference Thursday, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker told Donald Trump, \
content:
Show Caption
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker reassured residents he will continue to protect them once President-elect Trump takes office in 2025.
Speaking during a news conference Thursday morning, Pritzker said he will continue to protect people within his state in a Trumpian era.
'To anyone who intends to come take away the freedom and opportunity and dignity of Illinoisans, I would remind you that a happy warrior is still a warrior,' Pritzker said. 'You come for my people, you come through me.'
The statement comes after the loss of Vice President Kamala Harris to President-elect Donald Trump Tuesday night. Illinois was one of 19 states which voted blue at the time the Associated Press called the race.
Pritzker championed Vice President Harris as a campaign contributor and has previously used his podium before to comment on Trump's last presidency, calling it 'wreckage to clean up.'
Pritzker said his administration is ready to fight against policies which could harm Illinois' most vulnerable populations including LGBT+ people, reproductive rights, immigrants and people with disabilities.
'We will continue to advance a positive, productive and inclusive agenda of our own,' Pritzker said. 'One that brings opportunity to Illinois and helps uplift the nation as a whole.'
The governor urged a peaceful transition of power into Trump's presidency, when Trump will be sworn in at his inauguration. The presidential inauguration is always held on Jan. 20, as specified by the Constitution's 20th Amendment.

title: Store allowing children to buy, wrap and tag gifts reopening soon in Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: The popular store allowing children to buy, wrap and tag gifts for parents, grandparents and more reopens for the season soon in Springfield.
content:
The Mini O'Beirne Crisis Nursery Holiday Store returns to Fairhills Mall, 1919 W. Monroe St., beginning Nov. 30.
The store allows children to purchase, wrap and tag gifts for parents, grandparents, siblings and even their pets with the assistance of volunteer shoppers.
The gifts range in price from $1 to $15.
Here are all the details:
What are the shopping times and dates?
The store is open from Nov. 30 through Dec. 21.
Shopping times are from 4 to 7 p.m. Thursday and Friday; 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturday and noon to 6 p.m. Sunday.
Special hours can be scheduled for groups.
Is the store looking for volunteers?
Yes. Shopping assistants or elves must 14 years of age or older. You can sign up at the Holiday Store website MOCN.org or call 217-525-6800, Ext. 5 for more details.
Does the store have another location?
There will be a pop-up store at Chatham United Methodist Church, 104 W. Chestnut St., from 6 to 8:30 p.m., on Dec. 6. There will be carriage rides, hot cocoa, carolers and the lighting of the tree.
Are there other ways to help the nursery?
New this year is a holiday cash raffle with a grand prize of $2,500.
Tickets are $25 each and available online, by mail or in person at the Holiday Store. A limit of 500 tickets will be sold.
What does the Crisis Nursery do?
Founded nearly 40 years ago, the Crisis Nursery, 1011 N. Seventh St., provides free, 24-hour emergency childcare to families in need. It also offers family support services, like parenting education classes, and has a basic needs pantry with items like diapers, wipes and formula.

title: Downtown Italian restaurant racks up 23 health code violations in October
author: Claire Grant
description: Overall, Sangamon County establishments did well in October, as only nine of the 224 establishments inspected had over 10 violations.
content:
An upscale Italian restaurant racked up 23 healthcode violations in October for improper paperwork during inspection and missing food handler licensing.
Di Piero's at 518 E. Adams St. in Springfield was inspected on Oct. 3, and during inspection norovirus and allergen training paperwork for all employees was not available, nor was a certified food manager with a license present at the restaurant.
Venturing into the preparation cooler, the inspector found the walls of the cooler soiled with food and dirt debris.
A follow-up inspection was conducted on Oct. 11 to Di Piero's and no additional violations were marked.
Overall, Sangamon County establishments did well in October, as only nine of the 224 establishments inspected had over 10 violations.
How violations work
Food establishments are inspected by the Sangamon County Department of Public Health on an annual schedule that is determined by assigned risk type. The risk types are high, medium, or low risk, as defined by the Illinois Food Service Sanitation Code. These are determined by the complexity of food preparation taking place at the facility. Routine inspections are conducted unannounced. Follow up and complaint inspections are conducted as needed.
Critical violations concern hygiene, food temperatures, sanitizing procedures, and cross contamination. Non-critical violations concern the maintenance and cleanliness of a facility.
Here are the Sangamon County restaurants that received more than 10 violations from the health department during the month of September.
Circle K
Location: 1801 E. North Grand Ave., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Oct. 2, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 18 violations, five risk factor.
Notes from inspection: Repeat violations from 2022 filled out the report on how the building is cleaned and maintained, describing wet rags in locations where they should not be, an unsealed soda counter which could cause accumulation and caulking issues with a triple sink. On the service front side, the inspector observed the customer microwave was heavily soiled with food debris. Food and slushy refuse were also found in the front cashier area, under the iced coffee machines and underneath the soda fountains.
Popeye's Chicken
Location: 2496 Wabash Ave., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Oct. 15, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 14 violations, five risk factor.
Notes from inspection: According to the inspector's notes, the facility was observed to be soiled with accumulated grease and food debris in areas where food is being stored, prepared, and served. There is potential for cross-contamination due to the overall lack of cleaning. Of particular concern is the areas within the walk-in cooler, preparation cooler, and upright coolers. See that these areas where fans are blowing soiled dust and soiled around are clean. The entire facility is observed in poor cleaning condition. From the lobby to the rear mop sink there is observed gross chicken debris, spilled grease, food crumbs, splash, equipment leaking, and soil.
Road Ranger
Location: 700 King Road, New Berlin
Date/inspection type: Oct. 9, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 14 violations, 3 risk factor.
Notes from inspection: No certified food protection manager was present during the inspection duration. The main issue was milk; it appears in the notes left, indicating whole milk and creamer dispensers were missing key date marks. Gaskets on the creamer dispenser were observed to be soiled with mold accumulation as well, while the floor under the milk storage was soiled and needed a thorough cleaning.
Locals Tavern
Location: 605 Douglas St., Pawnee
Date/inspection type: Oct. 2, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 13 violations, five risk factor.
Notes from inspection: The inspector observed employee finish cutting chicken, remove gloves, and begin removing clean dishware from the dishwasher. In the back as well, rice was found stored on the floor during the inspection, which could lead to forms of contamination from pests. Areas of the kitchen need to be cleaned including: the storage drawers with clean cutlery, shelving for plates and pans, cookware lids and the interior and exterior of the prep coolers.
Replay Lounge
Location: 217 S. Fifth St., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Oct. 22, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 12 violations, three risk factor.
Notes from inspection: The best place to store raw shrimp is in fact, not above ready to eat foods – so the inspector reported inverting the setup immediately to prevent contamination. The entrance piece of metal to the walk-in cooler is observed to not be attached to the floor, while the walk-in freezer door gasket is observed to be in a state of disrepair where there are gaps present from the gasket not being sealed properly. Paint is peeling from the ceiling in the freezer, which could flake onto frozen food storage.
Marco's Pizza
Location: 3211 W. Iles Ave., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Oct. 8, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 12 violations, two risk factor.
Notes from inspection: Violations included food handler certificates were not available during inspection, as well as the person in charge did not have a food allergen certification. In a repeat violation, the person in charge was not a certified food protection manager. Beside paperwork other violations came from the gap in the double doors, and sanitizer buckets with a low concentration of cleaner.
Mission BBQ
Location: 2401 Wabash Ave. Suite B, Springfield
Date/inspection type: Oct. 15, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 11 violations, four risk factor.
Notes from inspection: The facility has a number of spatulas that are observed with chipped or ripped ends. One spatula was pulled for cleaning because an entire fry was stuck within an opening of the handle. Moving to the sinks, employees were observed to be switching tasks without proper handwashing and a roll cart was stored in front of a sink, making accessibility to the waterspout obstructed.
Dew Chili Parlor
Location: 301 W. North Grand Ave., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Oct. 9, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 11 violations, five risk factor.
Notes from inspection: According to the inspector's notes, multiple areas of the location needed cleaning inside the prep cooler, the cookline and hood of the fryer covered in grease, the shelf holding dry goods and the freezer. A number of fruit flies were observed by the dishwasher and in the dry storage room.

title: Springfield area's 32 high school girls basketball players to know for the 2024-25 season
author: Bill Welt
description: Here are the 32 high school girls basketball players to know around Springfield as the season kicks off this week
content:
Last winter was something to remember with not just one but two Central State Eight Conference girls basketball teams in the Class 3A state finals.
It culminated in Lincoln's first ever hoops title following a 60-44 victory over Chatham Glenwood. Senior point guard Kloe Froebe led the Railsplitters to a 38-0 record as the Gatorade Illinois Girls Basketball Player of the Year to boot.
Froebe, now at Colorado State University, has since departed, along with the rest of Lincoln's starting lineup, while Glenwood has largely retained its roster from last season.
Taylorville, which nearly knocked off Glenwood in the regional finals, also returns with a strong core.
Here are the top girls basketball players to know in the Springfield area for the 2024-25 season, listed in alphabetical order by school:
🏀 Lydia Hart, Athens
The sophomore guard tallied 5.7 points and 4.6 rebounds per game. Sophomore guard Ava Bee also supplied 4.6 points and 2.7 rebounds per game. They are among a group of 16 sophomores and freshmen on the roster.
🏀 Addison Wheatley, Auburn
The senior all-Sangamo second teamer is among five seniors on the lineup. Others include Karlissa Clark, Chloe Crissey, Kianna McGraw and Graysen Allen. Wheatley has been named all-Sangamo first team in softball the past three seasons.
🏀 Bella Palmer, Beardstown
The senior forward/center is tabbed as the team leader averaging 5.7 rebounds per game in the paint. Other returning starters include junior guard Camila Salazar (11.8 ppg.), senior guard/forward Brandy Mendoza (6.8 ppg.) and senior forward Dafne Mariscal (3.2 ppg., 3.5 rpg.). The Tigers begin the season playing eight games in 12 days.
🏀 Isabella Tiburzi, Carlinville
The versatile senior is set to play at Lincoln Land Community College next school year. The SJ-R all-area honoree already owns school records for most blocked shots in a season (56) and assists in a career (362). She wound up with 12.2 points, 8.4 rebounds and 4.9 assists per game last season and is not only approaching 1,000 career points but also 1,000 rebounds and 500 assists.
🏀 Alexis Neumann, Chatham Glenwood
The sophomore guard/forward racked up a team-high 11.8 points and Central State Eight Conference-best 8.5 rebounds en route to the team's first ever Class 3A state finals appearance and The State Journal-Register's all-area girls basketball team. She was also among the top volleyball hitters over the fall with 426 kills, 218 digs and 46 blocks this past season.
🏀 Ava Bobb, Chatham Glenwood
The sophomore guard/forward ranked third on the team with 5.2 points per game. She was also tied for second-best alongside fellow sophomore Hope Gilmore with three rebounds per game. Bobb and Gilmore became key catalysts in Glenwood's deep playoff run. Senior guard Katelyn Lehnen, who has signed for track and field at University of Illinois, also returns with 5.1 ppg.
🏀 Mia Brawner, Gillespie
The senior forward/guard has already eclipsed 1,000 career points. She also owns multiple school records in a season for points (501) and steals (132) — not to mention in a game for points (45). She finished with 16.2 points, 6.1 rebounds, 4.3 steals and 2.4 assists per game last winter to end up on the SJ-R's all-area team.
🏀 Josie Hughes, Havana
The senior guard has twice been named to the SJ-R's all-area team. Last season, she overcame a shoulder injury and averaged 15 points, five rebounds and four steals. Junior teammate Kaydi Miller posted nine points, six rebounds and three steals per game.
🏀 Tatum Christian, Hillsboro
The senior guard earned all-SCC second team with 10.2 points, 6.5 rebounds, and three steals per game.
🏀 Zara Harper, Jacksonville
The junior forward put up 8.4 points and 7.6 rebounds to lead the Crimsons in both categories last season. She was all-CS8 honorable mention.
🏀 Angelina Ippolito, Kincaid South Fork/Edinburg
The junior guard produced 15 points, three steals and two assists to reach the SJ-R's all-area team. She shot 42% from the field and led the Ponies to their most wins in program history at 20-12.
🏀 Lilly Wake, Kincaid South Fork/Edinburg
The senior point guard has signed to play at NJCAA Division II Lake Land College. The all-MSM Conference first teamer averaged 10 points, six assists, five rebounds and four steals per game, sinking 32 3-pointers. Senior teammate Jara Shoulders also chipped in 12 points, seven rebounds and three steals per game.
🏀 Aubrey Beavers, Lanphier
The junior point guard and all-CS8 honorable mention summoned 13.8 points per game with 17 3-pointers in 21 games. Junior teammate Lovely Jackson averaged seven points per game as well. Key newcomers include freshman Amiyah Jarrett, junior Shawtianna Walker, junior Laparionna Collins and senior Thomasina Moore.
🏀 Piper Whiteman, Lincoln
The senior guard/forward stepped up as a key reserve player in Lincoln's 74-1 record the past two seasons. She averaged six points per game last season to help come away with the Class 3A state title.
🏀 Megan Hughes, Mason City Illini Central/Greenview
The junior guard contributed 8.7 points and 3.1 rebounds per game. Junior teammates Addie Wilcoxon and Alyvia Morrow pitched in 6.9 and 6.4 points per game, respectively. Senior guard Taylor Keihn is returning back to the floor from injury.
🏀 Alyson Murphy, Mount Pulaski
The prolific junior guard scored 41 points in a Class 1A regional semifinal win and finished with 17.5 points, five assists, 4.5 steals and three rebounds per game. The SJ-R all-area honoree poured in at least 25 points in eight games as the Hilltoppers reached 20 wins for a third straight season.
🏀 Natalie Brownback, Nokomis
The senior guard and all-MSM Conference first teamer ushered 8.4 points, 2.9 assists and 2.5 assists per game. She led a balanced lineup. Senior starters Grace DeWerff (6.8 ppg.), Becca Hill (3.9 ppg.) and Lizzy Hill (1.5 ppg.) also come back as MSM Conference champions, complemented by a deep bench that includes junior forward Kinley Stolte (6.9 ppg., 7.8 rpg.), sophomore forward Alivia Sabol (6.3 ppg., 5.7 rpg.), junior guard Camryn Engelman (4.9 ppg.) and sophomore guard Cloey Dirks (2.9 ppg.).
🏀 Joey Laker, Pana
The junior was on the SJ-R's all-area team with 10.3 points, three rebounds and 2.5 steals per game.
🏀 Ava Rodriguez, Pawnee/Lutheran/Calvary
The junior guard led the team across the board with 9.8 points, 6.4 rebounds, 2.3 assists and 2.3 steals per game. Senior guard Greenlee Dust provided 8.7 points and 3.2 rebounds per game as well.
🏀 Carson Arthalony, Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central
The senior center averaged 10.8 points and 5.7 rebounds per game. The four-year starter was named to the SJ-R's all-area team for a second straight season. She will play at Illinois College. title: Massey Commission endorses resolution for county mental health board
author: Steven Spearie
description: Sonya Massey, who was shot to death on July 6, was the subject of a mental health call the day before the fatal shooting.
content:
Meeting with full membership for the second time Monday, the Massey Commission passed a resolution throwing its support for the creation of a 708 Mental Health Board in Sangamon County.
The referendum could go before voters on April 1 if it passes the Sangamon County Board.
Those same voters could also consider implementing "recall authority" for the sheriff's office.
The citizens commission, formed in the aftermath of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey by a Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy on July 6, also welcomed a U.S. Department of Justice investigation of the sheriff's department initiated last week.
The commission recently sent a letter to the DOJ requesting a full review of the sheriff's department, though co-chair Dr. Jerry Kruse couldn't say if the investigation was a result of the letter.
"We were pleased with the Department of Justice document," Kruse said afterwards. "They will be very thorough."
The eight-page letter directed to Sheriff Paula Crouch and State's Attorney John Milhiser among others and dated on Nov. 14 "raises serious concerns about (the sheriff department's) interactions with Black people and people with behavioral health disabilities" along with a host of practices and procedures.
Commission co-chair JoAnn Johnson said the sheriff's department, the Emergency Telephone System Department and the State's Attorney's Office should answer all of DOJ's questions "so that we can all understand what exactly happened before, during and after Sonya Massey was killed by a Sangamon County deputy. These answers will help inform our work as we continue to research reform ideas and recommendations at the Massey Commission to make sure a tragedy like this never happens again."
Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman and the mother of two children, called 911 about a would-be prowler at her home in an unincorporated area of Woodside Township early on the morning of July 6. Just hours earlier, Massey was the subject of a 911 call made by her mother, Donna Massey, who said she was having "a mental breakdown."
708
According to a League of Women Voters website, there are over 90 708 Community Mental Health Boards around the state, including Christian and Montgomery counties. The "708" refers to House Bill 708, also known as "the Community Mental Health Act."
Such boards "evaluate needs, allocate funds, and coordinate a comprehensive system of services for mental health, intellectual and developmental disabilities and substance use disorders in order to benefit citizens," according to the website.
Speaking Monday, Ryan Croke pointed out that the Mid-Illinois Medical District Commission, which includes stakeholders from Springfield Memorial Hospital, HSHS St. John's Hospital, Springfield Clinic and the SIU School of Medicine, passed a resolution in favor of a board on Aug. 29.
"We at the Medical District Commission have heard over and over again that our community is in need of stronger mental health resources to support not just the medical establishment, but families, the law enforcement community, our social services safety net community, all of whom would benefit from stronger mental health infrastructure (in the county)," said Croke, the commission's chair. "The resolution, I think, speaks for itself."
Sheriff's recall
The question on the sheriff's recall would also have to pass the county board.
Board member Sam Cahnman had earlier proposed an advisory question about the fate of Sangamon County Sheriff Jack Campbell, who initially refused to resign from the office, but eventually retired before that question went to the board.
But Cahnman pointed out that Campbell retired voluntarily and that under current law, there is no way to remove an elected sheriff from office.
"The way I see recall," Cahnman said, prior to the vote, "is that it provides a safety valve when the people lose confidence in their sheriff."
Emotions were heightened at the end of the meeting when a former Springfield City Council alderwoman called out the city for offering to name a bridge after Massey.
"The county building should be named after her," said Gail Simpson, who was joined by Sontae Massey, a commission member and Sonya Massey's cousin, during public comment. "This is what happens. We'll give (her family) this much so they won't ask for this much.
"It's an insult. I know the family, in their grief, may have said 'yes.' But I hope they say 'no.' It's a bridge to nowhere."
The dedication is scheduled for Dec. 6.

title: Media company that bought Neuhoff buys 4 more Springfield-area radio stations
author: Claire Grant
description: Four more radio stations in the Springfield area have been sold. Here's what you need to know.
content:
The same media company that bought the Neuhoff stations in Bloomington and Springfield in October has now acquired the Mid-West Family radio group in Springfield.
Woodward Communications, Inc. announced an agreement with Mid-West Family radio to purchase four radio stations in the Springfield market. Springfield now is WCI second radio market, alongside Appleton, WI.
Under the acquisitions, WNNS-FM, WQLZ-FM, WMAY-FM and WMAY-AM will operate under WCI.
These four radio stations join WXAJ-FM, WFMB-FM, WCVS-FM and WFMB-AM in Sangamon County, which were previously owned by Neuhoff Family Limited Partnership before being acquired by WCI on Oct. 1.
WCI is an employee-owned company which owns 15 radio stations and Insight Publications in Northeastern Wisconsin.
WCI said in a news release the purchases were strategic and that by merging the two operations, listener and customer experiences will be enhanced as well as advertiser value.
'We are excited about this opportunity and look forward to integrating Mid-West's solid brands into our Springfield operations,' Tom Woodward, CEO and President of WCI said. 'Over a period of time our plan is to co-locate all of the stations and related operations into Mid-West Family's current office and studios, which we believe will create synergies that will benefit our employee owners, our customers, and the community.'
In order to conform with Federal Communications Commission ownership rules, WCI has entered into an agreement to divest WCVS-FM.
WCI also has entered into agreements to divest two of its recently acquired radio stations in Bloomington, IL: WIHN and WWHX. Further, WCI has entered into a Local Marketing Agreement, or LMA, with Great Plains Media to operate WBBE.
Great Plains Media currently owns and operates three radio stations in Bloomington, IL. WCI stated the divestitures and the LMA agreement in Bloomington will allow it to better focus its resources in the Springfield marketplace.
Kevin O'Dea, market manager for Woodward's Springfield marketplace, will continue in his role with the company following the acquisition. O'Dea started his radio career in 1978 as an account executive with Mid-West Family Broadcasting's WMAY-AM in Springfield and has since been awarded the Illinois Broadcaster Association's 2024 'Vincent T. Wasilewski Broadcaster of the Year.'
O'Dea said in an interview that the radio team had met with Woodward already online and will keep their jobs under WCI. The new broadcasting schedule once cleared with the FCC might not be exactly what's on the radio today, but will be "best local programming we can," according to O'Dea.

title: Fire Chief: Squatters were inside abandoned Springfield home at time of fire
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A vacant home went up in flames Monday morning in Springfield. Fire Chief Ed Canny told the SJ-R squatters were inside the home at the time of the fire.
content:
Two people were hurt after a fire at an abandoned house in Springfield Monday morning.
Authorities said the fire happened at an empty house in the area of 11th Street and Phillips Avenue.
Three people were inside the abandoned house at the time of the fire, a city spokesperson said. All three people were considered to be squatters, Springfield Fire Chief Ed Canny told The State Journal-Register.
The house had been boarded up for at least a year, but a neighbor told the fire department that unhoused people went in and out of the house frequently.
Canny said people living in abandoned houses is unsafe because there are not usually working smoke detectors. The boarded windows and doors also make exiting harder in such an emergency.
The cause of the fire is still under investigation.
The status of the two people who were taken to the hospital are not known.
The house was torn down following the fire, officials said.

title: April election: Who is running for Springfield school board, park district and more
author: Steven Spearie
description: Only one of the three School District 186 seats up for election on April 1 will be contested.
content:
Only one of the three School District 186 seats up for election on April 1 will be contested.
Anthony "Tony" Mares, the former board president who was first elected in 2017, will be matched against political newcomer Kristin Barnett in Subdistrict 1.
Board president Micah Miller in Subdistrict 2 and vice-president Erica Austin of Subdistrict 6 are both running for re-election in uncontested races. Miller first won election to the board in 2019. Austin was elected for the first time in 2021.
All seats are for four-year terms.
Also filing over the last two weeks were candidates for other area school boards, the Springfield Metropolitan Exposition and Auditorium Authority (SMEAA) board and the Springfield Park District board.
Two newcomers have filed for seats on SMEAA, which governs the Bank of Springfield (BoS) Center.
Robert "Bob" Mizeur and Alyssa Haaker both filed in District 1, along with SMEAA chairman Mike Coffey Jr. Three seats, all for four-year terms, are up in the district.
In District 2, SMEAA treasurer Jeanette Goza will seek another term.
Mary Beth Rodgers and Nancy Eck are running as incumbents for the park district.
Trustee Mallory Westcott did not seek another term. Ali Coffey Farmer is running for a third open spot on the board.
The three seats are all for four years.
For the Pawnee school board, Travis Simpson and TJ Walker are seeking four-year terms. There are four open seats.

title: 'It's cheaper than therapy': From toys to handbags, consumers are drawn to mini products
author: Felecia Wellington Radel
description: Miniatures — whether tiny toys or usable items — are appealing to consumers, but why? Collectors — and psychologists — weigh in.
content:
Miniature versions of popular products like makeup and toys are growing in popularity.
Consumers are drawn to the collectability, affordability, and stress-relieving aspects of miniatures.
The trend is particularly popular on social media, where collectors share their hauls and connect with others.
For about $10, shoppers can pick up several of some of the most popular makeup, hair and skin care items at Ulta – as miniature toys.
Beauty retailer Ulta and toy company Zuru recently collaborated on a Mini Brands line of capsules containing five mystery mini replicas of brand-name beauty products.
Do you prefer toy food over foundation? MGA's Miniverse released a Target Food Favorites themed Make It Mini where buyers can create tiny replicas of snacks, such as Bullseye cookies or lava cakes – for collecting and displaying, not eating.
MGA is also the company behind the LOL Surprise line of collectible mini dolls, accessories and playsets, first released in 2016.
It's not just toys.
Luxury brands like Hermes and Fendi have also released micro versions of their handbags in the past few years, with other brands, such as Coach, Longchamp, Lululemon and Dagne Dover, selling pocket-sized bags, charms and backpacks. Many box stores, beauty stores and pharmacies have sections dedicated to trial, travel and tiny-sized versions of many products.
Miniatures – whether tiny toys or practical items – are appealing to consumers. According to an industry report by market research firm Circana, the category of exploratory and other toys, which includes mini toys, had the second highest growth rate – 16% – for toy categories in 2022 and had seen positive growth since 2019. Tiny crafts and micro-sized toys also were among the Toy Association's 2023 top toy trends.
But what draws shoppers to small things?
Crafting, collecting and connecting with community
Collecting or creating tiny toys isn't new, or even just for the young. For decades, one of the more popular miniature-related pastimes has been crafting dollhouses.
"It's not just a child's hobby anymore. It can be with a small dollhouse, of course, but a lot of adults are collecting," said Mary Johnson of Wall, New Jersey, who has worked on dollhouses for years. Johnson is one of the founding members of the Jersey Shore Miniature Society, which started in 1986 and is part of the National Association of Miniature Enthusiasts. The society meets weekly, and the group has online classes and chats.
"The details have become so amazing, and they're not cheap anymore," Johnson said. "Things can get quite expensive, especially if they're handmade. But it's nice to see that there are younger people becoming interested in the hobby."
Creating dollhouses is not only a fun, artistic expression, but it can be a stress reliever, Johnson said.
"It's satisfying to create something so small in your own style, in your own imagination," Johnson said. "We use all different forms of crafts. We work with clay, wood, 3D printing, laser-cutting. We paint, we wallpaper, we landscape, we make flowers. You can do whatever you want. And I think that's what a lot of people need now."
Jo Barker, known on social media as The Little Bean, has been sharing her collection of mini handbags and beauty products with her followers since she started her accounts in 2021.
"I've always loved mini items, specifically mini makeup," Barker said. "I found that when I would share those types of items in my content, it would resonate a lot with my viewers, namely because they're just so cute, especially the brand name miniatures."
Aside from the cuteness, there are practical benefits to mini items, she said, such as obtaining unique items and sustainability.
"Having a mini version might be a way to try out a product without fully investing in a larger version," Barker said. "It's something that they can try and fully use, given it's a much smaller amount, and then not feel like they're going to waste large amounts of product before something expires."
Kayla Lam, who lives in the San Francisco Bay Area, would buy miniature toys here and there, but she really began building her collection earlier this year.
"I was so stressed," Lam said. She was finishing her master's degree in biostatistics, and purchasing and items from Miniverse Make It Minis and Mini Brands gave her "a stress-free way to escape," she said.
"With Miniverse, you put it all together yourself, and that really appealed to my crafty side, and it sucked me in," Lam said. "And a big thing for me was all of the people I've met in the community. They're all so nice, and people are trading, and they're all supporting each other."
Lam began sharing items in her collection on social media in March. While she doesn't have a firm number on how many miniatures she's collected, she said she has an entire full-sized fridge full of Miniverse, items she hasn't created yet and Miniverse on hair clips and keychains.
"It's cheaper than therapy," Lam said.
Experts on why people like miniatures
Humans are biologically wired to like mini things, psychologists say.
"Miniatures make us happy," said Kristina Durante, a psychologist and marketing professor at Rutgers Business School. "We feel like we can have a sense of control over these tiny things."
"When times are tough, we like to have things around that make us feel good," Durante said.
Even seeing photos or videos of miniatures on social media can be satisfying.
"When we see miniatures, it brings up more of that feel-good neurochemical that keeps us going back, those dopamine hits of, 'this is so cute.' That's why we follow it on social media," said clinical psychologist and author Carla Marie Manly. "We're getting hit after hit after hit that makes us feel good in an otherwise often disappointing or dismal world."
For many people, looking at or purchasing mini items can remind adults about childhood or "bring up a childlike sense of wonder," Manly said.
"It takes us out of that place of being the responsible adult and reminds us of our ability to play, to be in a flow state, to feel carefree and to feel charmed by things in life, which we often forget," Manly said. "We forget that beauty, that delight of feeling charmed by something."
The low price of miniature items compared to their larger counterparts can be encouraging to shoppers, especially as some shoppers look to tighten budgets.
Consumers may do what's called mental accounting while shopping, Durante said, which is a person's way of trying to convince themself to make a purchase through mental gymnastics, such as justifying buying a $15 tiny lipstick instead of a $40 regular-sized lipstick, even if the cost per volume doesn't make financial sense.
Owning items on a smaller scale still "fulfills that desire to possess it," Manly said.

title: Looking for a new holiday breakfast? Can't go wrong with this classic
author: Joshua Dineen
description: Looking for a new breakfast idea for the holiday? Or just a nice Sunday morning? Check out this biscuit and gravy recipe.
content:
At our house, we always have biscuits and gravy on holiday mornings. For my wife and I, biscuits and gravy provide a fun memory that spans the length of our marriage.
I think I mentioned in an earlier article that when we were first married, I was completely focused on ultra fancy foods and really struggled making more traditional home cooked dishes. I spent the first several years correcting that idea and learning to cook all the things she grew up eating.
I eventually was making versions of those dishes that were specifically adjusted to her tastes … which may or may not change from day to day. Eggs Benedict, waffles, pancakes, crepes, hashbrown variations, and biscuits and gravy were among the favorites that I perfected for her and have now become favorites for our children.
My wonderful kids are not morning people, but if I announce to the house that I have made any of these items even before the sun rises, they all quietly shuffle to the kitchen to enjoy their breakfast before they begin their days.
I have only attempted to skip biscuits and gravy once on a holiday morning, and the only response was a question about what I needed from the store to remedy the mistake.
My wife also teaches here at Lincoln Land Community College. One of the classes she teaches is Introduction to Baking. In that class, she teaches the students to make biscuits with a ridiculous number of flaky layers and covers them in honey butter. They are amazing! But when she eats sausage gravy, she wants it to be a super-hydrated drop biscuit that I make with no layers and barely holds its shape.
Sausage gravy is a simple idea, but I have had many versions that often surprise me with their unique methods. In its simplest form, it is browned sausage mixed with flour and butter, and then milk is added until the sauce is the desired thickness and the seasoning is correct.
For those who love classic French food, this is a Béchamel sauce with browned sausage. I have had versions where the sausage is added to cream of mushroom soup, then a little milk to get the right viscosity. Occasionally, I add spices to the sauce to give it a regional feel. Coconut milk, red curry paste and fresh cilantro supplied a fun Thai spin on the gravy.
Thanksgiving is next week, and I always make extra biscuits, which I use in my stuffing. It gives the stuffing a delicious buttery taste, and they absorb lots of liquid. If I am really in a good mood, I will use biscuits, croissants, brioche and sourdough to make my Thanksgiving stuffing.
I like my stuffing made with onions, carrots, celery, dark turkey meat, eggs, homemade turkey broth and more butter. It is arguable that stuffing is just a savory bread pudding. We like the crispy top and corners of the stuffing the best.
So, years ago, I started baking my stuffing on a sheet pan or cookie sheet.
Biscuits and Gravy
2 cups all-purpose flour
6 tablespoons unsalted butter, chopped small
2 teaspoons baking powder
1/2 teaspoon baking soda
1/4 teaspoon salt, not iodized
Buttermilk, as needed
1 pound breakfast sausage
2 tablespoons bacon grease
2 tablespoons unsalted butter
1/2 cup all-purpose flour
2-3 cups milk
1/8 teaspoon apple cider vinegar
1/8 teaspoon ground black pepper
Salt to taste
Optionally:
1/4 teaspoon onion powder
1/4 teaspoon garlic powder
Pinch of sweet paprika
Directions
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees.
Combine the flour, 6 tablespoons butter, baking powder, baking soda and ¼ teaspoon salt in a bowl, and work together by hand until the butter is in tiny pieces and mixed well with the flour.
Add enough buttermilk to make the dough come together, but do not over mix the dough.
Use a spoon to scoop about 2 tablespoons of dough onto a cookie sheet sprayed with cooking spray.
Brush the tops of the biscuits with a little buttermilk.
Bake for 10-12 minutes, or until the bottoms are very golden brown and the insides are dry.
Place the bacon grease and the sausage into a pan and brown the sausage.
Turn the heat to medium/low, and add the butter and flour, stirring to combine.
The mixture will have a 'raw' flour smell. Stir occasionally and cook until the flour smells cooked. It should take 3-5 minutes.
Add the milk (start with 2 cups) and stir on medium heat until the sauce thickens.
Add the vinegar, salt and pepper, and turn the heat to low. It takes about 5 minutes for salt to fully set in to the flavor; wait until then to add more salt if needed.
If you want to add the other dried ingredients, do this now, and adjust to your tastes.
Check the salt one last time.
Ladle the gravy over a couple hot biscuits and enjoy!
Joshua Dineen is the chef specialist at Lincoln Land Community College.

title: How kindness 30 years ago inspired decades of giving back at this Springfield restaurant
author: Claire Grant
description: Ziyad Samara gives back every year to the community that welcomed him with Thanksgiving meals for those who would go without.
content:
It's been over fifty years since Ziyad Samara left the West Bank and found his new home in Springfield, leaving college and his brother up in the Chicagoland area to pursue being a business owner.
With success and a few decades, Samara gives back every year to the community that welcomed him with Thanksgiving meals for those who would go without. This year will be his 25th anniversary of giving out free Thanksgiving and Christmas dinners.
The free meal of turkey and all the fixings is available to all and can be enjoyed either as dine-in or take-out from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Sgt. Pepper's Cafe on Stevenson Drive.
If the name doesn't ring a bell, Beatles memorabilia covers the walls in Ringo, Paul, John and George in honor of the Beatles eighth studio album, 'Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band".
Pickup orders must call between 10 to 11 a.m. with information about the number of meals required and pick-up time to (217) 525-5939. Take-out is limited to two meals per person.
The reason for the kindness? As a restaurant owner, it's just something Samara has always wanted to do for his community.
While Samara wasn't planning on ever going into the restaurant business when earning a degree in engineering, an opportunity came in 1977 to move to a place he'd never been before – but had high hopes for.
'My brother … he said, 'you want to move to Springfield?' and I said yeah why not? Let me go see! So, I came down and fooled around for one day and went back,' Samara said. 'I said man, it's a beautiful city, it's nice! So, he said, 'you sure you want to leave Chicago and go to Springfield,' and I said yeah, I'm sure!'
By 1978, Ziyad was operating a Lums in the city, before selling it to Hardee's in 1994 and choosing to open his mainstay place in town: Sgt. Pepper's Cafe at 3141 Baker Drive in 1999.
Samara got the idea from an act of kindness during his time at college. He had only been in the U.S. for two years and wasn't able to spend the time off with his brother in Carbondale, so a woman named Lydia offered for him to spend Thanksgiving with her family.
'There were about 25 people coming together for the holidays and to me that was impressive,' Samara said. 'Really from that day on in my own mind I came up with the idea I wanted to give away a free meal on Thanksgiving. 2001 it happened – after thirty years in restaurants it happened.'
It was that kindness that sparked Samara's spirit to give away anywhere from 12 to 14 home cooked turkeys and all the fixings from his restaurant every November.
This year, the ovens are already broiling in the back of his restaurant with big dishes of stuffing, potatoes, yams, greens and even pumpkin pies being prepared. The prep starts on the Sunday before with three turkeys being cooked per day, but it's a work of pride he does anyway.
This Thanksgiving, as a Palestinian business owner, Samara would love to see peace in his homeland for families like his and pushes pro-peace in the Middle East.
'I've been in America for fifty-plus years, and it is definitely the number one country in the world that has all aspects of freedom and trying to make a living,' Samara said. 'That's why the U.S. will always be (that way) as long as we hold our values.'

title: 'A serious miscarriage of justice': Hearing set for Sean Grayson's release conditions
author: Steven Spearie
description: A hearing has been set regarding the conditions of Sean P. Grayson's release from jail after the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey.
content:
Circuit Court Presiding Judge Ryan Cadagin and attorneys for the State and for former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy Sean P. Grayson will take up the "least restrictive conditions" of his release at a hearing in Sangamon County court at 2:30 p.m. Friday.
A Fourth District Appellate Court decision overturned a lower court decision last week, meaning that Grayson, charged with first-degree murder in the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey inside of her home, will be released from detainment prior to his trial.
Grayson, sitting with one of his attorneys, Daniel Fultz, appeared by Zoom from the Macon County Jail in Decatur at Monday's hearing. Grayson agreed to appear by Zoom at Friday's hearing.
Outside of the county building before Grayson's hearing, about 15 to 20 protesters called for Grayson, 30, to continue to be detained.
Late Monday morning, State's Attorney John Milhiser filed a motion to stay the appellate court's mandate.
James Wilburn, Massey's father from Pine Bluff, Arkansas, called Grayson's possible release "a serious miscarriage of justice."
Cadagin twice ordered Grayson to be detained under the Pre-Trial Fairness Act.
The appellate court opinion was written by Justice Eugene Doherty. Justices James A. Knecht and Craig H. DeArmond joined in the opinion.
It took exception with Cadagin's ruling that "no conditions of release would be adequate to mitigate the threat (Grayson) posed to the safety of the community."
The trial court's focus on Grayson's failings as a law enforcement officer, the opinion noted, "distracted from the central question of how to address any risk he posed after being stripped of his office."
Conditions for Grayson's release could include home confinement and some sort of monitoring process.
Sheriff's deputies were called to Massey's home in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield on July 6 for a report of a suspected prowler. A conversation between Grayson and Massey over a pot of boiling water quickly escalated, leading to Grayson drawing his service weapon and firing at Massey, striking her in the face.
Massey was the subject of a 911 mental health call made by her mother, Donna Massey, the day before the shooting.
Last month, the U.S. Department of Justice launched an investigation against the Sangamon County Sheriff's office, noting "serious concerns about (the sheriff department's) interactions with Black people and people with behavioral health disabilities," along with a host of practices and procedures. The office has until Dec. 14 to provide DOJ necessary documents.

title: Hearing for potential release of ex-deputy in Massey shooting is delayed

The new hearing date is Jan. 2, 2025, pending further action by the Illinois Supreme Court.
The appellate court decision overturned a circuit court decision last week, meaning that Grayson would be released from detainment prior to his trial.
Circuit Court Presiding Judge Ryan Cadagin twice ordered Grayson detained.
Grayson is being jailed at the Macon County Jail in Decatur.
Sheriff's deputies were called to Massey's home in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield on July 6 for a report of a suspected prowler.
A conversation between Grayson and Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman and the mother of two children, escalated quickly over a pot of boiling water, leading to Grayson drawing his service weapon and firing at Massey, striking her in the face.
The released body cam footage and case has garnered international attention.
Last month, the U.S. Department of Justice launched an investigation against the Sangamon County Sheriff's office, noting "serious concerns about (the sheriff department's) interactions with Black people and people with behavioral health disabilities," along with a host of practices and procedures. The office has until Dec. 14 to provide DOJ necessary documents.

title: How this iconic Mount Pulaski coach proved that small-town farm girls can play volleyball
author: Bill Welt
description: Donna Dulle's name will grace the Mount Pulaski court following last week's ceremony celebrating the volleyball program's storied past
content:
MOUNT PULASKI — Donna Dulle surveyed the crowded bleachers.
She recognized everyone like family — not just the former players under her watch at Mount Pulaski but also the faintest acquaintances.
They packed the new multi-purpose high school gym the night before Thanksgiving to celebrate her prodigious coaching career after Mount Pulaski was hailed as the fourth best volleyball program in IHSA history — the highest among public schools.
'It was overwhelmingly surreal,' Dulle said.
They not only reminisced over the heady days that stretched from 1981 to 2021 but also soaked up the revelation that Donna Dulle Court will soon become a reality at Ed Butkovich Gym in the coming months.
'Those were some awesome times, a really good family group and a great community,' Dulle said. 'They just really backed us, it was wonderful.'
High expectations
Dulle ranks second in IHSA history with 1,189 wins and led the Hilltoppers to 14 state appearances with a pair of state titles in 1989 and 2007.
Illustrious players litter the Dulle era, including two-time all-state first team hitters Tina Rogers-Smith (1988 and 1989) and Dulle's daughter Bethany (2002 and 2003).
Rogers later competed at University of Illinois while Bethany attended Bradley University, but countless others also possessed collegiate talent.
That includes Bethany's former teammate Mary (Olson) Link, who played at Western Illinois University.
'She has a great legacy and we would not be known for volleyball without Donna and she proves that small-town farm girls can play ball,' Link said.
And the pick is in: Signings and commits around Springfield so far, including Chatham Glenwood girls hoops
Link said her favorite memory was becoming tournament champions against far larger schools from the Chicago area.
Dulle's teams indeed never shuddered from a challenge, 1999 graduate Donna Vaughan said.
'She never really praised us as much as she critiqued us to become better players and ultimately that's what will make a team better is by always having something higher to reach for,' Vaughan said. 'You may be County champions, great, but that's not what we want. What is our goal? We want to win regionals. Now what's our goal? Our goal is to win state.
'We always had goals — and we always had high goals. That's how she got us to eventually participate after a long day of school.'
Link's sister, Ellen (Olson) Knauth, said playing for Dulle was fun but also rigorous.
'She knew if we worked as hard as we possibly could and left it all on the court, it didn't matter the talent that we played,' said Knauth, a 2010 graduate. 'It didn't matter how talented we were because we were going to outwork everybody and all through the season we were going to outwork people. So when we did get to the state tournament, we were able to beat the talent that was there.
'We knew it took everybody on the team whether you played or not. It was everybody on the team practicing against each other and working together as a team.'
That was just as true on Dulle's grade school teams, according to 2014 graduate Cady Lowery.
'I would be in fifth grade, and she's got her stat sheet out and she's charted the defense of the other team,' Lowery said. 'You're nine or 10 years old digesting what that means, but that's the level of excellence. It's like, 'Yeah, you're 10 years old, figure it out now. I just told you they run this certain type of defense.' It really is a standard of excellence she expects everyday.'
Dulle subsequently appeared at Downs Tri-Valley where her daughters, Kathy and Bethany, also helped out. The high school team went a combined 61-10-1 over two seasons, while the seventh-grade team won the Illinois Elementary School Association state title last spring.
'I think what I remember the most is her presence,' Lowery said. 'When you walk into an opposing gym, it's very clear everybody knows who she is. I feel like now the lessons from playing for her and being taught by her, too, is something you can't really put into words because she did expect a level of excellence, hard work and attention-to-detail that has prepared a lot of people for everyday life — a true definition of a coach and someone who has really implemented a team atmosphere.'
'Best cheerleader'
Her presence was ubiquitous not only as a volleyball coach but also as a P.E. teacher and track coach.
Dulle was just always there and treated everybody the same. If you're part of the team, you're part of the family, Link said.
It's why everybody showed up to the ceremony, Bethany said.
'She was always thinking of other people and buying kids kneepads and shoes,' Bethany said. 'Even when I was little, I considered the girls that I played with on the court as my sisters and when I started coaching, I thought of these girls kind of as my daughters.'
Top players in boys hoops: Springfield area's 42 high school boys basketball players to know for the 2024-25 season
Lynn (Clementz) Flach, a 1988 graduate, also embraced a long coaching career in volleyball and track at Mercer County, Kentucky. It wasn't by pure chance.
'She is so loving and kind, and very knowledgeable,' Flach said. 'She was always on the forefront of the game. She was always developing and doing things that no other schools or coaches were doing yet. She was just a leader. She was ahead of her time and the game, and she would teach us and do things that no one else was doing. I think to be as successful as she has been, she's continued that on for 40-plus years.
'She never really yelled at you, she never scared you. She was always just a supportive, loving coach.'
Dulle deferred credit, of course.
'It's unbelievable,' Dulle said of the court being named after her. 'Just wow, I guess. The kids did it. The kids played those games with their hearts and they're the sole reason this is happening. They played, I was the best cheerleader.
'I just want to thank the community for all their support today — and the last 40 years.'

title: The Jaycees Holiday Lights Parade highlights a festive weekend in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: Want to get out and do something this weekend? The State Journal-Register has you covered with these five things to do around town.
content:
Show Caption
After surviving the talks at the Thanksgiving table, boxes of holiday lights are being dragged up from cellars to mark the start of the season.
Want to get out and do something this weekend? The State Journal-Register has you covered with these five things to do around town.
Jaycees Holiday Lights Parade
What: You know what they say – Santa Claus is coming to town. The Springfield Jaycees are bringing him and the holiday spirit this weekend with the annual Holiday Lights Parade to kick off the season in stunning lights bigger and better than last year. The route will follow west on Jefferson starting at Seventh Street, turn south on Fifth Street, head east on Monroe Street, north on Sixth Street and end at Sixth and Washington streets.
When: 5:30 p.m. Saturday
Where: West Jefferson and Seventh streets, downtown Springfield
More: A Facebook page about the event contains more information and an active discussion thread.
Zoo Lights at the Henson Robinson
What: Enjoy the winter season with dazzling incandescent lights, twinkling in the snow. Enjoy a hot chocolate on your stroll through the Henson Robinson Zoo, hanging out under the tent to enjoy a s'more after roasting a marshmallow over the fire pit. Beyond the candy cane-colored lights there will be caroling, performances to remember and moments for young ones to meet with Santa.
When: 5 to 9 p.m. all weekend
Where: 1100 E. Lake Shore Drive, The Henson Robinson Zoo
More: Tickets can be purchased online at Springfield Park District website and are $7.50 before taxes for adults, $5.50 for children 12 and under.
The Nutcracker Ballet
What: Presented by the Springfield Clinic, the Springfield Youth Performance Group is ready to entertain for a weekend of magic wonder with a classic Christmas play. The Nutcracker is a two-act classic ballet by Russian composer Pytor Tchaikovsky; set on Christmas Eve, a young girl befriends a nutcracker which comes to life and takes her to a dream land to wage battle against an evil Mouse King. The story is based on 'The Nutcracker and the Mouse King', written in 1816 by E. T. A. Hoffman.
When: 2 and 6 p.m. Saturday, 2 p.m. Sunday
Where: 1200 W. Washington St., SHG Auditorium
More: Tickets are $25 for adults and $15 for children 13 and younger and can be purchased online at sypgfoundation.org.
Caroling at the Carillon
What: Kick off the Holiday season with Caroling at the Carillon with a family friendly event, entirely free. Bundle up in your warmest winter gear and bring your friends to the Carillon at Washington Park to sample warm cookies, hot chocolate and apple barn cider. After stuffing your face with free snacks and goodies, try your hand with ornament making or sit by the bonfires listening to caroling while kids play scavenger hunt. Finish off the day with a picture to remember in the holiday photo booth – you may even get a picture with ol' Saint Nick.
When: 3 p.m. Sunday
Where: 1740 W. Fayette Ave., Thomas Rees Memorial Carillon
More: This is a free event; a floral holiday show will be inside of the Washington park Botanical Garden as well.
Frostbite Festival Race
What: What do you think you can take? A 10-mile, or a two-mile race? No matter the answer, run until your legs frost off (but not really) at the 61st annual Frostbite Festival this weekend. Led by the Springfield Road Runners Club, this race will take runners up the same roller coaster hills with the start and finish line but will be held at the AMF Springfield Lanes. Race registration is open up until race day for bibs and packets until 8:45 a.m. just before the race. The 2024 Frostbite Festival will have an in-person and virtual option, to run the race online.
When: 9 a.m. to noon Sunday
Where: 2660 W. Lawrence Ave., AMF Springfield Lanes
