title: Two long-serving cabinet members retire from Springfield school district
author: Steven Spearie
description: Two longtime members of School District 186 Superintendent Jennifer Gill's cabinet have recently retired.
content:
Two longtime members of School District 186 Superintendent Jennifer Gill's cabinet have recently retired.
Arwah Franklin, the assistant director of human resources, exits in December after the director of operations and maintenance, Darrell Schaver, retired earlier in the fall.
"Bringing new people into our cabinet always gives us new life," Gill recently said. "It's always a moment of refresh as you say goodbye to somebody you've worked alongside."
Franklin, who worked for the district for 29 years, was both a special education teacher and administrator.
As community based programs supervisor, she received the 2020 Horace Mann Administrator of the Year.
Gill said in her current role, Franklin assisted the district with personnel recruiting and with its non-certified staff.
"She served our district nobly for many years and her family are great supporters of the work that we do," Gill said of Franklin, who were classmates at Springfield High School. "It's weird to say you're proud of someone retiring, but she's done great things for District 186, and I know in retirement she will continue to serve our community in many, many ways."
Schaver, who has an architecture background and worked for the district for over 20 years, was at the center of a building boom in the district the last few years, brought on by the windfall of a 1% sales tax increase voters approved in Sangamon County in 2018.
Gill said Schaver also oversaw builds of Enos, Ridgely and Matheny-Withrow elementary schools that used Health/Life Safety dollars.
"It's been very exciting to have him alongside me and helping me 'dream that dream' and plan and keep us on budget and on time," Gill said of Schaver. "We will miss him greatly."
Mike Grossen moves into the director's spot after serving as an assistant director. Jennifer Hanson-Russell, principal at Lindsay Elementary, is the interim assistant director of human resources.

title: Illinois Supreme Court rules Grayson remain jailed until it takes up State's petition
author: Steven Spearie
description: The Sangamon County State's Attorney filed a petition asking the Illinois Supreme Court take up an appellate court ruling over Sean Grayson's jailing.
content:
The Illinois Supreme Court entered an order Tuesday staying the release of the former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy charged with the murder of Sonya Massey on July 6 until it takes up or denies the State's Petition for Leave to Appeal, or PLA.
Sean P. Grayson will remain detained for now in the Macon County Jail in Decatur.
Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser last week filed the PLA asking the state's high court address the Fourth District Appellate Court's ruling from Nov. 27 that cleared the way for Grayson's pre-trial release.
The appellate court said in essence that the circuit court had ruled improperly about denying Grayson's release under the Pre-Trial Fairness Act, part of the Safety, Accountability, Fairness and Equity-Today, or SAFE-T Act.
Grayson and another sheriff's deputy responded to a 911 call from Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman and the mother of two children, about a possible prowler around her home in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield.
Grayson, who is white, shot Massey in the face, with the actions caught on body camera.
Grayson was later terminated from his job prior to his indictment on the murder charges.
'The trial court's focus on (Grayson's) failings as a law enforcement officer, while understandable, distracted from the central question of how to address any risk he posed after being stripped of his office,' the opinion, reached by a three-justice panel, read in part.
The ruling from the appellate court bound the circuit court to set a hearing for Grayson's release with "the least restrictive conditions." The appellate court later stayed that mandate until Jan. 2.
Massey's family members and other supporters gathered in the Illinois Capitol Rotunda last week demanding that Grayson be kept behind bars.
"I'm going to fight to keep my daughter's killer in a jail cell," said James Wilburn, Massey's father. "I don't ever want to see him walk free amongst any of us."
The shooting has grabbed international headlines, leading the U.S. Department of Justice last month to launch an investigation into the sheriff's department and other offices.

title: Springfield man in custody after allegedly threatening to kill President Biden
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A Springfield man is in custody after he allegedly made threats against President Biden, former President Barrack Obama and more politicians.
content:
Show Caption
A Springfield man is facing federal charges for allegedly threatening to kill several politicians, including President Biden.
Jacob Sterr, 36, has been jailed and faces charges for allegedly making threats against President Joe Biden, successors to the presidency, former presidents, and other people protected by the U.S. Secret Service, according to a criminal complaint that was filed in the United States District Court for the Central District of Illinois.
A sworn statement from a Task Force Officer with the U.S. Secret Service attached to the complaint provides images of 'tweets' on the social media platform X, which is formerly known as Twitter, where Sterr allegedly posted explicit, life-threatening messages to accounts representing Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas, Former President Barrack Obama, and First Lady Dr. Jill Biden.
All of the posts appear to be from Nov. 25.
The Task Force Officer, Timothy Zajicek, is also a detective with the Springfield Police Department. He confirmed Sterr's identify in the statement.
Zajicek has seen Sterr in person and was able to identify him in a video he filmed of himself and broadcast on X.
Sterr is in jail. A detention hearing took place Wednesday before Magistrate Judge Karen L. McNaught.
Sterr and his attorney, Robert J. Scherschligt, Assistant Federal Public Defender, have filed a motion for a psychiatric exam to determine Sterr's competency to stand trial.

title: Springfield-area dive bar named one of best in nation for food
author: Claire Grant
description: America's grungiest dive bars for food have been named and a Springfield-area bar cracked the top 100.
content:
America's grungiest dive bars have been named – and Southern View's own Curve Inn has one of the best for food across the country.
In a recent poll from Geek Nexus, an entertainment and media website, 3,000 adults across America were surveyed to uncover the best dive bars in their locale for unexpected menu items and reasons to return again, and again, and again.
In total, 120 dive bars were named among the best for food, including four total in Illinois.
According to Geek Nexus, dive bars have adapted over the past two and a half decades from just cheap drinks and gritty charm to food destinations as well.
The Curve Inn, 3219 S. Sixth St. Road, is a historic bar and grill established in 1932.
Bought in 2002 by husband-wife duo Ray and Ami Merchant, the locale is known for its vibrant atmosphere, the love of all things grunge, pony shoes and national acts on its state-of-the-art beer garden stage.
'(Ami and Ray) are proud to be a dive bar and they revel in that,' marketing representative for The Curve Perry Zubeck said. 'Ray and Ami were the first ones to have live entertainment and they started doing that ten, twelve years ago and now there's so many bars.'
The Merchant family dig into the vibes and all things dive about their bar, which had a scandalous history offering prostitution and illegal gambling in the fifties, before turning into a piano bar in 1972. The current iteration of The Curve Inn still features live music on stage weekly.
The menu at Curve features American fare, including burgers, lasagna, and fish tacos.
Amenities such as live music, darts, karaoke and staff that've been there for decades contribute to its reputation as a favored spot for both locals and visitors.
'When you walk in and you just kind of know that feeling when you're there,' Zubeck said. 'Most people will tell you they're on a first name basis and if you don't know anybody there you will very soon. And that's what makes it a good dive bar.'
The Curve Inn is currently open from 11 a.m. until 3 a.m. but will soon be closing at 2 a.m. after the village of Southern View voted to reduce bar hours in the area to follow suit with Sangamon County.
Of the four Illinois locations that cracked the top 120, The Curve Inn is the only one in the central Illinois area.

9. Dugout Café: Boston, Mssachusetts
8. The Green Door Tavern: Chicago, Illinois
7. Old Shillelagh: Detroit, Michigan
6. McSorley's Old Ale House: New York City, New York
5. Triple Nickel Tavern: Colorado Springs, Colorado
4. Port of Call: New Orleans, Louisiana
3. Flora-Bama: Perdido Key, Florida
2. Rudy's Bar and Grill: New York City, New York

title: Court reverses murder conviction of Springfield teenager, new trial set in juvenile court
author: Steven Spearie
description: The Fourth District Appellate Court has ordered the murder conviction of a Springfield teenager reversed.
content:
The Fourth District Appellate Court has ordered the murder conviction of a Springfield teenager reversed.
The court, in its ruling last month, said the juvenile court "abused its discretion" in transferring Kamyjah Bias to criminal court and that the trial be re-set for juvenile court.
Bias was convicted in the Nov. 17, 2021, fatal stabbing of Lanphier High School senior Pierre V. Scott Jr. outside of the school. She was sentenced to 43 years in the Illinois Department of Corrections.
Bias was a 15-year-old student at Douglas-PREP at the time of the stabbing, though she attended classes in the afternoon at Lanphier.
The case was initially filed in juvenile court because of Bias' age, but then-Sangamon County State's Attorney Dan Wright petitioned to transfer the charges to adult criminal court. That petition was granted on April 12, 2022.
According to the order, the juvenile court "did not have sufficient evidence and/or information regarding several statutory and nonstatutory factors it was required to consider before transferring (Bias)."
State's Attorney John Milhiser said the State planned to petition the juvenile court to have Bias transferred to adult court. If she is transferred, "we will be prepared to try the case."
The appellate court decision was authored by Justice Amy C. Lannerd with justices James A. Knecht and Thomas M. Harris concurring.
Bias also was convicted for the attempted murder of Daquan R. Dunn, another Lanphier student, who was stabbed in the chest just after Scott was fatally stabbed.
At trial, Bias' attorney, Gregory Sronce, argued that she acted in self-defense and that there was "objective evidence" that Scott, Dunn and others intended to confront her after school.
Bias testified that she didn't know either Scott or Dunn but admitted that her younger brother attended Washington Middle School with Scott's younger brother and the two "had a beef with each other."
Then-first assistant state's attorney Derek Dion labelled Bias' trial testimony "flatly incredible and patently self-serving," adding that Scott didn't pose a threat to Bias, nor did he have a weapon on him.
Bias remains in custody.

title: From festive lights to old world markets, these destinations are worth the drive from Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: From light displays to holiday markets, these Midwest events will put you in a festive mood and are worth the drive from Springfield.
content:
From light displays to holiday markets, these Midwest events will put you in a festive mood.
Kids can meet Santa Claus, in a town named after him. Families can glide along the ice or even duck the cold weather in a heated igloo.
Check out these holiday destinations, all within short drives of Springfield.
Christkindlmarkt
Christkindlmarkts ("Christkind" translates into "Christ child") date back to the early 18th century in Germany.
Belleville replicates the Nuremburg Christkindlmarkt on the Public Square (Illinois 159 and Main Street) through Dec. 23.
Some 20 vendors will be featuring unique European and handcrafted items. The are German bands and folk dancers; gingerbread creation displays; horse-drawn trolley rides; a cookie stroll, a petting zoo and Santa on the Square.
The Christkindlmarkt operates from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Thursday through Saturday; 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Sunday and 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Dec. 23.
Visit bellevillechristkindlmarkt.com for more information.
A Christkindlmarkt in Carmel, Ind., about 45 minutes north of Indianapolis, features German artisans and craftsmen, an ice-skating rink, German food and drink and a children's area in the town's center. A 33-foot-tall "Christmas pyramid" features over 3,000 lights.
It runs through Christmas Eve. For days and hours of operation, visit christkindlmarkt.com.
Chicago's Christkindlmarket in Daley Plaza, 50 W. Washington St., runs through Dec. 24.
The market is open from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Friday and Saturday.
Way of Lights, Belleville
The Way of Lights at Our Lady of the Snows, a Catholic shrine in Belleville operated by the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate, uses over 1.5 million lights to depict the journey of Mary and Joseph as they travel to Bethlehem.
Other activities include area bands and choirs; camel, donkey and pony rides for the kids; a LEGO brick display; a selfie stand and a food stand.
The drive-through display is open nightly from 5 to 9 p.m. through Dec. 31. Donations are accepted.
Santa Claus, Indiana
How can you go wrong with a town named after the Big Guy himself?
Located at the southwestern tip of the Hoosier State and about a four-and-a-half-hour drive from Springfield, family-friendly favorites include a 1.2-mile Christmas light drive-through at Sun Outdoors Lake Rudolph ($20 per vehicle through Dec. 23) and a live reindeer exhibit at Santa's TOYS.
There's also a Santa Claus Christmas Parade (Dec. 14) and ongoing activities like Christmas cookie decorating, dinner with Santa and roasting chestnuts.
Since the post office there gets letters to Santa from all over the world, it's a tradition for "volunteer elves" to reply to children's letters with a postmark from Santa Claus, Ind.
For more information, visit santaclausind.org
East Peoria Festival of Lights
The East Peoria Festival of Lights celebrates its 40th anniversary this year with the lighted display running through Jan. 5.
Forty floats that made up the Nov. 23 parade are now part of the drive-through portion at 123 Par 3 Lane.
Crowd favorites include a 160-foot Steam Train, a replica of a Clydesdale horse team pulling a wagon, a Chinese Dragon and a Giant Blue Whale.
Admission is $10 per regular vehicle. You can also see the display via a horse-drawn wagon.
For more all the details, visit folepi.org or call 1-855-833-5327.
Winterfest in St. Louis
Winterfest returns to Kiener Plaza in St. Louis through New Year's Eve.
There's ice skating, s'mores stations, holiday-themed karaoke and even heated igloos for rent underneath 100,000 twinkling lights.
For more information, visit archpark.org.
While in St. Louis, there are holiday light displays at Grant's Farm (10501 Gravois Rd.) and the Anheuser-Busch Brewery (721 Pestalozzi St.), both drive-through and walk-through, and Missouri Botanical Garden (4344 Shaw Ave.), walk-through.

title: Three Springfield restaurants landed a spot on Tripadvisor's Choice Awards list
author: Claire Grant
description: Three Springfield restaurants scored a spot on Tripadvisor's Travelers Choice Awards for best restaurants.
content:
Three Springfield restaurants scored a spot on Tripadvisor's Travelers Choice Awards for best restaurants.
Every year, Tripadvisor's Best of the Best Restaurant Awards showcase travelers' top recommendations for sustainable dining, quick bites and vegan & vegetarian, hidden gem, open air, pet friendly option, date night, fine dining and overall restaurants.
Mariah's Steak House, Obed & Isaac's Microbrewery and Engrained Brewing Co. all secured a spot on the list for 2024 as destinations to visit while in the capital city.
Mariah's Steakhouse is currently Springfield's No. 1 destination for food on Tripadvisor, serving upscale dining and of course, steak options to the public. Obed and Isaacs and Engrained both make their own beers to sell on-site, with a lively pub atmosphere.
In the United States, That's Amore, an Italian restaurant in Miami Beach, Florida was the best rated casual dining spot, while Osteria Positano, another Miami Beach Italian joint, took the second top spot.
Methodology
Awards are determined based on the quality and quantity of traveler reviews and ratings posted on Tripadvisor over the 12-month period between June 1, 2023, through May 31, 2024, as well as an additional editorial process.
The Travelers' Choice awards honor travelers' favorite destinations, hotels, restaurants, things to do and beyond, based on the reviews and opinions collected from travelers and diners around the world.
Travelers' Choice, formerly Certificate of Excellence, recognizes businesses that earn consistently great reviews. Travelers' Choice award-winners are among the top 10% of listings on Tripadvisor.
Traveler's Choice differs from Tripadvisor's Best of the Best award, which is given to winners among the top 1% of listings on Tripadvisor.
About Tripadvisor
Tripadvisor is one of the world's largest travel guidance platforms in the world, helping travelers plan and book trips using the website and app to see the best places to eat, stay and play.
The travel website has been providing the Traveler's Choice awards since 2002, covering hotels to destinations to food.

title: Hundreds of new laws coming to Illinois in 2025. Here are 10 you need to know about
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Some of the changes include minimum wages increasing and it being easier for you to cancel your gym membership. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Hundreds of laws and amendments will go into effect in Illinois in 2025.
A higher minimum wage will be implemented. Legislators crack down on youth vaping, and several health insurance mandates are added.
Here are a few changes coming after the Times Square ball drops.
Minimum wage
Minimum wage in the state will climb to $15 per hour, coming from $14 per hour.
Employees who receive tips will see a rise in minimum wage to $9 per hour from $8.40 per hour.
Pay transparency
Employers with 15 or more employees will be required to disclose pay scale and benefit information in job postings.
The change is result of an amendment to the Equal Pay Act of 2003 that was contained in HB 3129, passed by the General Assembly and signed into law by Governor JB Pritzker in 2023.
Canceling gym memberships
A new law will make it easier for you to cancel your gym membership. House Bill 4911 passed in the summer and will allow people to cancel gym memberships either via email or their gym's website.
Landlord retaliation
It is against public policy of the State for a landlord to take retaliatory action against a tenant. The law spells out that a landlord may not evict someone, increase rent, decrease service, or file a lawsuit against them provided that the tenant acts in ways that are outlined.
Youth vaping
The amendment to the Preventing Youth Vaping Act restricts a manufacturer, distributor, or retailer from advertising, marketing, or promoting an electronic cigarette "in a manner that is likely to cause a parent, legal guardian, teacher, or other adult to mistake the electronic cigarette for a product that is not a tobacco product."
Purchasing e-cigarettes
Electronic cigarettes can no longer be shipped through the mail or other remote methods to anyone under 21 years old.
Digital driver's licenses
The law allows the Secretary of State to issue digital drivers licenses or state IDs. The digital ID would be issued in addition to a physical ID. The law allows agencies and private entities to choose if they want to accept electronic IDs in place of physical ones, but upon request by law enforcement, physical ID must be presented.
Epinephrine injectors
Insurance companies must limit the total price for medically necessary epinephrine injectors for children and teens to $60 for a twin-pack.
Hearing devices
Insurance plans must now provide coverage for medically necessary hearing instruments for all individuals, rather than just those under the age of 18.
Strengthening community media
A local news organization will be required to provide written notice 120 days before a sale occurs to affected employees and the county government, as well as any Illinois nonprofit 'in the business of buying local news organizations.'
The law also will create a Journalism Student Scholarship Program to encourage academically talented Illinois students to pursue careers in journalism, especially those in underserved areas of the state.
For a full list of new laws, go to the Illinois General Assembly website.

title: Expired food, mold, found in Springfield-area restaurants in November
author: Claire Grant
description: An upscale Japanese restaurant racked up 20 health code violations in November, getting hit for repeat violations from previous inspections.
content:
Show Caption
An upscale Japanese restaurant racked up 20 health code violations in November of this year, getting hit for repeat violations from previous inspections.
In August, Osaka Japanese showed up in The State Journal-Registers Public Health Reports for a routine inspection which landed the authentic Asian restaurant with 24 violations, 15 of those being risk factors.
On Nov. 22, a Sangamon County health inspector found 8 risk factor violations, with five repeat violations from last time that had not been corrected.
Repeat violations included employees not washing hands before preparing food and storing raw meats on top of raw fish in the storage cooler, which could lead to cross contamination.
How violations work
Food establishments are inspected by the Sangamon County Department of Public Health on an annual schedule that is determined by assigned risk type. The risk types are high, medium, or low risk, as defined by the Illinois Food Service Sanitation Code. These are determined by the complexity of food preparation taking place at the facility. Routine inspections are conducted unannounced. Follow up and complaint inspections are conducted as needed.
Critical violations concern hygiene, food temperatures, sanitizing procedures, and cross contamination. Non-critical violations concern the maintenance and cleanliness of a facility.
Here are the Sangamon County locations that received more than 10 violations from the health department during the month of November.
Popeye's Louisiana Chicken
Location: 2496 Wabash Ave., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Nov. 22, complaint
What: Inspection found 15 violations, three risk factor.
Notes from inspection: According to notes left by the inspector on duty, dipping wells in the floor were clogged causing water to pool on the front cooking line. The water constantly moved around by staff could cross contamination and according to the inspector, if the clogging was not repaired, the store should not open. Mold was found throughout the inspection on the shelves of the walk-in cooler, the ice bin and rust was forming throughout the shelves.
In a follow-up inspection on Nov. 26, the inspector noted a new manager had just taken over the location and the restaurant was in desperate need of repair, leading to a short-term closure.
'The emphasis of the closure today is to allow for uninterrupted cleaning and maintenance to this facility,' the inspector wrote. 'There are corners and hinges that are observed soiled with accumulated food debris.'
Qik n' EZ
Location: 4401 W. Wabash Ave., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Nov. 21, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 15 violations, five risk factor.
Notes from inspection: Shelves in the walk-in cooler were observed with an accumulation of dust and mold, with milk residue on the floor under the milk shelves. During the inspection, the person in charge could not locate the employee reporting agreement and upon inspector's arrival, the hand sink near the 3-compartment sink was observed with soda fountain nozzles in the basin.
All Star Grocery
Location: 806 E. Black Ave., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Nov. 22, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 14 violations, six risk factor.
Notes from inspection: There are holes in the drywall, right next to the meat and cheese. During the inspection, a slew of issues was found by the health inspector including but not limited to hot dogs past their use by date by multiple weeks, raw eggshells above milk and cheese in storage and the absence of bleach within the facility for cleaning.
The issues were corrected during inspection, and a reinspection has not been issued since.
Dolphin Foods
Location: 2613 Adlai Stevenson Drive, Springfield
Date/inspection type: Nov. 20, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 12 violations, eight risk factor.
Notes from inspection: The main points of the inspection were the lack of cleaning items for employees to use during shift, resulting in cross contamination possibility. During the visit, the inspector noted no soap was available at the hand sink, and no paper towels. Other violations included no sanitizer was available for the location which is crucial to cleaning throughout the shift as well as employees putting on gloves without washing their hands first.
Jifi Stop
Location: 3062 Adlai Stevenson Drive, Springfield
Date/inspection type: Nov. 14, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 12 violations, four risk factor.
Notes from inspection: The location needs a deep clean according to the inspector's notes, as the pop machine nozzles, milkshake mixer and slushy dispenser were all heavily coated in food debris. Besides the drink nozzles, the roller grill also was found coated in food buildup. Throughout the inspection, violations were corrected through cleaning.
Two follow up inspections were conducted, with no notes taken or violations assigned.

title: Winter weather forecast: See maps of projected snowfall around Midwest states
author: Eric Lagatta
description: A winter storm dumped snow and ice on a portion of the Midwest while bringing strong winds and severe cold to millions of Americans.
content:
A winter storm dumped snow and ice on a portion of the Midwest while bringing strong winds and severe cold to millions of Americans in a region bracing for winter weather this week.
While much of the wintry mix had tapered off by Friday morning, slippery roads were expected to complicate road conditions in several Midwest states. The National Weather Service said in its Friday morning forecast that a storm heading southeast from Canada was forecast to weaken along the lower Great Lakes "with lingering periods of snow across much of the region."
A general 1-3 inches of dry, fluffy snow was expected to fall across southern North Dakota and much of Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan, according to Accuweather. However, higher totals were predicted for some parts of the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley regions.
A region from eastern North Dakota to central Minnesota was in a zone susceptible to larger snowflakes that have the potential to pile up in a hurry. And both Minneapolis and Fargo, North Dakota, may have ended up with a half-foot of snow, Accuweather said.
Amid the winter weather, the state highway patrol said 15 people were injured early Thursday in North Dakota, six of them seriously, when a truck attempting to stop at an intersection slid on an icy road, causing a crash with a van and an SUV. The crash happened amid high winds, blowing snow and sleet near Reeder, about 115 miles southwest of Bismarck, according to the highway patrol.
A snow plow was also hit Thursday by a passing car, the patrol said.
The North Dakota Highway Patrol issued a " no travel advisory" urging motorists to stay off the roads, which temporarily included a complete restriction for larger vehicles and "oversize loads."
Northeast wind was also expected to produce lake-enhanced snow in the Lower Peninsula of Michigan's northeastern coast.
The Detroit area remained under a winter weather advisory Friday morning as the region was expected to get up to another 3 inches of snow through Friday night, the weather service said. Temperatures were also forecast to dip significantly into Saturday.
Another inch of snow was expected in the Chicago area Friday morning, causing untreated roadways to potentially become covered or slick, the weather service said.
The winds are forecasted to push the storm swiftly through the Northeast into Friday night.

title: Looking for a sweet treat this holiday season? Check out this homemade fudge recipe
author: Joshua Dineen
description: Looking for tasty treat this holiday season? Check out this homemade fudge recipe.
content:
One of my grandmothers was known for her fudge during the holiday season.
She would make a batch and distribute it out in small tins to a special few, and the rest was put out on a platter for Christmas Eve dinner, where it would greedily be devoured. I remember being encouraged to bring a little home when my sister and I visited for the holiday meal.
I have always been a little picky when it comes to sweets but have held a dear place in my heart for anything that involved chocolate. My grandmother did not share this recipe with me, but I know a thing or two about food and science, so I figured it out on my own like so many family recipes.
I haven't made fudge in years, as I don't make a lot of sweets at home since my wife is a pastry chef, and all four of my children work at the amazing bakery, Incredibly Delicious.
When I do make pastries, I try to do things I don't see my wife make or old favorites that you can't get anymore. If you have read a couple of my articles, I love making pastries and bread just as much as any savory food. One of these days, I will have to share some fun bartending science, but that is yet another article.
The easiest way to make fudge uses chocolate, sweetened condensed milk and vanilla. You just melt it all together, add any mix-ins, pour it into a pan and let it chill for three hours.
The more traditional way to make fudge is more in the realm of candy making. Sugar, cocoa powder and salt are combined and cooked to a particular temperature. While doing this, it is important to not stir the mixture as it will form sugar crystals, which will seize the fudge and ruin it.
Once it comes to temperature, butter and vanilla are added but not stirred in, once again to avoid crystallization. Once the mixture gets to 115-130 degrees, the fudge is agitated until a particular opaque consistency is met. At this point, mix-ins are added quickly, and then it is all moved to a lined pan to set.
As far as ingredients go, you can substitute the cocoa with chocolate if you prefer.
If you add a tablespoon of corn syrup or honey, it will discourage crystallization. You can add a little chocolate with the butter if you enjoy both cocoa and chocolate flavors together.
For those of you who like to play with your food, substituting different sugars might be fun as well as other fats other than butter. Vanilla is usually alcohol based, and so adding another spirit is fun too.
From what I understand, fudge is an American confection; however, Britain has their clotted cream fudge, and France has caramel chocolate candies, which share similar science. This French connection seems possible as the story goes that a recipe for caramels was 'fudged,' or a mistake was made, and fudge was born.
For me, fudge will always bring me a good bit of joy and fond remembrance of childhood holidays and one of the grandmothers who instilled in me my deep love of cooking.
Traditional Fudge
Ingredients:
3 cups sugar
1 ½ cups milk
2/3 cup cocoa
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/4 cup butter
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
Directions:
Combine sugar, milk, cocoa and salt in a heavy bottomed pan. With a spoon, stir to combine.
Bring to a boil over medium heat without any stirring. Cook to 240-245 degrees.
Add butter and vanilla; DO NOT STIR. Let cool until 130 degrees.
Stir by hand until it starts to lose its shine. Optionally, place in a mixer fitted with a paddle, and beat on medium low.
Quickly place into a pan lined with parchment and press flat. Let cool completely. Slice into small squares and enjoy!
Joshua Dineen is the chef specialist at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management and Baking/Pastry, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: Illinois man on federal death row has sentence commuted by President Biden
author: Steven Spearie
description: A Chicago podiatrist convicted in the 2002 shooting of a church worker had his federal death sentence commuted by President Joe Biden.
content:
A Chicago podiatrist convicted in the 2002 shooting of a church worker had his federal death sentence commuted by President Joe Biden.
Ronald Mikos, 76, is housed in the federal penitentiary in Terre Haute, Ind. Mikos was one of 37 people who had their death sentences commuted. None of the 37 will be eligible for parole.
The action comes on the heels of the largest single-day act of clemency in modern history on Dec. 12 when Biden commuted the sentences of nearly 1,500 people and issued 39 pardons.
The president also earlier pardoned his son, Hunter Biden, who was convicted on federal gun charges and pleaded guilty to federal tax charges.
While pardons and commutations are forms of clemency, a commutation shortens a sentence while a pardon provides complete forgiveness.
Under Biden in 2021, U.S. Attorney General Merrick Garland ordered a moratorium on federal executions to allow for a federal review of death penalty policy.
'In good conscience, I cannot stand back and let a new administration resume executions that I halted,' Biden said in a statement, referring to President-elect Donald Trump, a supporter of expanding capital punishment.
In July 2020, the Trump Administration ended a 17-year hiatus on federal executions when it executed Daniel Lewis Lee. Six more executions followed a little over two months.
Mikos was convicted in 2005 of fatally shooting Joyce Brannon, a 57-year-old nurse turned church secretary.
Brannon was a patient of Mikos'. In 2002, Mikos was under a federal grand jury investigation for Medicare fraud, specifically for inflating bills for surgeries he had not performed.
Brannon, who refused to go along with Mikos' scheme had been scheduled to testify before the grand jury on Jan. 31, 2002, but was murdered four days before.
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Springfield, commended Biden for his "justice and mercy.' Durbin has long advocated for the abolition of the federal death penalty.
Three men remain on federal death row: Robert Bowers, convicted in the attack on the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh that left 11 worshippers dead; Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, convicted in the Boston Marathon bombing that killed three people and injured more than 260 people in 2013 and Dylann Roof, convicted of fatally shooting nine people at Mother Emanuel Church in Charleston, South Carolina, in 2015.

Residents can also drop off branches year-round at Evans Recycling, located at 2100 J David Jones Parkway. Proof of residency, such as a driver's license, is required. For additional information, call Evans Recycling at 217-370-3780.
See more information about branch pickup on the city's website.
Private services
Lake Area Disposal & Recycling offers the service to their customers for a small fee. The company asks that customers call in advance at 217-522-9317. The trees can be picked up on customers' normal day of trash pick-up.
INDR is collecting trees for fish habitat
The Illinois Department of Natural Resources will be collecting live Christmas trees to be used as fish habitat in local lakes.
Once collected, trees will be bundled together, weighted, and submerged at lakes, 'providing critical habitat for multiple fish species and promoting algae growth for insects that attract fish for anglers,' the agency stated.
The trees will naturally decompose over time.
Visit the INDR Office of Fisheries website for drop-off location information and instructions, along with more about the program.

title: With 2024 coming to an end, here are some food trends to know for 2025
author: Jay Kitterman
description: The new year is right around the corner, so what food trends will be left in 2024? Here are some trends we're watching for 2025.
content:
Today's article is my annual review of food trends for 2025. Eating out at a restaurant and dining at home have become more expensive. Shoppers are relying more on private store brands/labels rather than national ones. Aldi has benefited from this trend and recently announced they will be opening 240 new stores in 2025 compared to their typical annual rate of around 100. Over the next five years, Aldi's is investing 9 billion to open 800 groceries in the U.S.
Personal health will continue to be a major influence on what we eat in 2025. Protein is no longer just a tool for bulking up; it's increasingly sought after by customers looking to maintain energy levels throughout the day and support overall health. While popular staples like chicken, yogurt and cottage cheese have staying power, retailers predict a growing interest in collagen and a greater incorporation of plant-based proteins such as beans, lentils and hemp seeds into daily diets.
Hot and spicy — customers have shifted from chasing the highest Scoville ratings to now exploring how heat maximizes flavor. And delving into spices and peppers — like Calabrian chiles and guajillo peppers — from international cuisines.
Hail Caesar! Caesar salads continue to make a strong innovative revival. Beyond traditional salads and wraps, recipes featuring Caesar dressing on pizza, pasta and a variety of leafy greens beyond romaine lettuce are gaining popularity. You can look forward to creative combinations of the umami-rich dressing with flavors like miso, tahini and black garlic as customers breathe new life into the century-old recipe.
Everyone is busy, and everyone is stressed; but no one wants to deal with excessive food delivery fees. In 2024, the variety and quality of frozen and prepared foods is higher than it's ever been, and the stigma of cooking with them has all but disappeared. Thus in 2025, we might see a rise in what Nestlé Food Company refers to as 'flavor done fast' — home cooking that relies on premade sauces, marinades and prepped ingredients, like cubed root veggies, to create something comforting in as little time as possible. With restaurant prices being what they are, the prediction that more of us will cook at home is a safe bet.
The reusable water bottle culture is upon us, but consumers want more from their water these days. They are seeking added electrolytes and hydration in more innovative forms. New items include popsicles with electrolytes, sparkling coconut water, chlorophyll water and even protein water. Look for cactus waters that contain antioxidants and electrolytes, and better-for-you competitors to sugary and artificially colored sports drinks. Even kids can get in on this trend with new and tasty beverages in fun formats, like pouches and mini coconuts.
Coconut water is receiving a lot of hype. Coconut water is the clear fluid inside coconuts and not the same as coconut milk. Unflavored coconut water is low in added sugar and calories. The water is high in electrolytes and includes potassium, sodium and manganese. It does have calories, about 45-60 calories in an 8-ounce serving. In a review, Mayo Clinic listed the pros and cons of coconut water and stated that plain water is still the smart choice. 'Once Upon a Coconut' (onceuponacoconut.com) is a new company that offers coconut water in many flavors, including chocolate and watermelon.
During the pandemic, we saw a sourdough resurgence with at-home bakers trying their hand at the classic fermented bread. Now we're seeing this trend move into grocery aisles in both traditional and innovative ways — pizza crusts, flatbreads, brownies, crackers, chocolate and more — with customers looking for the benefits and flavor that sourdough offers without spending hours in the kitchen. There's also a variety of innovative sourdough breads launching, including pumpkin turmeric, Bionaturae organic sourdough spaghetti (launching February 2025) and Jesha's sourdough pancake & waffle mix.
If you want the fun of baking without the hassle of dealing with yeast, visit the Martha Stewart website. You will find recipes for baked goods that include muffins, biscuits, scones, cornbread and loaves. They are leavened with baking powder and/or baking soda instead of yeast. This baking technique yields fast results because you can pop your bread directly into the oven without allowing time for the dough to rise, a step that's always required when baking with yeast.
From crispy grains and granolas to sprouted and fermented nuts to roasted chickpeas and mushroom chips — consumers are increasingly reaching for these items to enhance meals and add texture to breakfast, lunch and dinner. Brands are creating crunchier versions of the ever-popular chili crisp, while new seasonings marketed for their texture are stars of salads and roasted veggies. Dehydrated fruits and candy are taking over social media, with consumers seeking that light, airy crunch. This trending texture can also be seen in beverages and desserts like crème brûlée espresso martinis or pistachio-topped pastries.
On behalf of my family, I wish everyone happy holidays, plus a healthy and prosperous new year. Remember to include in your New Year's resolutions to dine out at a new restaurant monthly and to be very kind to their staff.
Bon appétit and see you back here in 2025!
Jay Kitterman is a culinary and special events consultant and adjunct instructor at Lincoln Land Community College.

title: Staunton's Isiah Laux, Bryce Coalson find their mark in first holiday title since 2009
author: Bill Welt
description: Isiah Laux and Bryce Coalson helped make history for the Staunton boys basketball team on Saturday.
content:
CARLINVILLE — It certainly appears to be an harbinger of even bigger things to come.
Staunton's Isiah Laux and Bryce Coalson combined for nine 3-pointers and the Bulldogs captured their first Carlinville Holiday Tournament since 2009 with a 52-47 win over defending champion Hardin Calhoun on Saturday.
"It's huge for us, it's really exciting for all of us," Coalson said. "We've worked so hard offseason and to win it is great."
Laux drained five 3s and finished with a team-high 18 points, while Coalson had 17 points. Coalson, a junior, drained the go-ahead trey with six minutes left in regulation. The team totaled 11 3s in the win and the Bulldogs improved 12-2 overall after a 16-16 campaign last season.
"They both can absolutely shoot it," said Staunton head coach Ty Laux, Isiah's dad. "They go against each other just about every day in practice, they hate losing to each other in our shooting drills. It just shows the work they put in the offseason.
"There's no reason to not be a great shooter. If you want to be a great shooter, you just got to put in the work and they've definitely done that."
Junior guard Aaron Bodner sealed the win with a layup in the final 20 seconds and chipped in nine points.
Lane Eilerman led Calhoun (6-5) with 15 points.
Girls championship result
HARDIN CALHOUN 41, CARLINVILLE 33: The Warriors opened the third quarter with a key 9-0 run en route to its third straight Carlinville Holiday Tournament title.
Senior forward Kate Zipprich triggered the sequence with an assist to senior guard Anna Oswald and scored six of her game-high 15 points in the frame. Oswald and Sadie Kiel had eight points apiece for Calhoun, which improved to 10-3.
Senior guard Isabella Tiburzi led Carlinville (12-3) with 13 points. Senior teammate Jordyn Loveless added eight points.

title: Ex-deputy charged in fatal Sonya Massey shooting has court date rescheduled
author: Steven Spearie
description: Sean P. Grayson's scheduled court date for Jan. 2 has been moved according to a docket entry made by Presiding Circuit Court Judge Ryan Cadagin.
content:
Sean P. Grayson 's scheduled court date for Jan. 2 has been moved to Jan. 13, according to a docket entry made by Presiding Circuit Court Judge Ryan Cadagin.
Grayson, a former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy, was charged with first-degree murder in the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield.
The Illinois Supreme Court, which returns to session on Jan. 13, hasn't taken up or denied a petition filed by the State called a Leave to Appeal, or PLA.
On Dec. 10, the Supreme Court entered an order staying the release of Grayson until it decides what to do in the case.
Grayson is being held at the Macon County Jail in Decatur.
The PLA, filed by Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser, asks the state's high court to address an earlier ruling from the Fourth District Appellate Court that would have cleared the way for Grayson's release from detention before his trial.
That would have come with some conditions for Grayson, possibly house arrest or some type of monitoring device.
The appellate court ruled the day before Thanksgiving, infuriating Massey's family members and other supporters.
In short, the appellate court, in an unanimous three-justice decision, said that the circuit court had erred in denying Grayson's release under the Pre-Trial Fairness Act, which is part of the Safety, Accountability, Fairness and Equity-Today, or SAFE-T Act.
Cadagin said Grayson's callousness during and after the shooting, including not rendering help to Massey, was one of the reasons he ordered Grayson to continue to be detained.
The appellate court decision particularly incensed Massey's father, James Wilburn of Pine Bluff, Arkansas.
"My message to those three judges who ruled Sean Grayson is not a danger to the people of Springfield...If there's a house for sale on your block, let him move on the block where you live and we'll see how quickly that (not in my backyard) attitude comes out in you," Wilburn said in a Dec. 5 rally in the Illinois Capitol Rotunda.
In a news release announcing the PLA filing, Milhiser said Grayson had demonstrated that he "cannot comply with conditions and is a danger to the community."
But Mark Wykoff, an attorney for Grayson, said the State's arguments in the PLA appeared to be "a regurgitation of the arguments that were unpersuasive in the appellate court."
Two former emergency medical services workers, both charged with the December 2022 first-degree murder of Earl Moore Jr., were ordered released pending trial under the SAFE-T Act.
Grayson and another sheriff's deputy responded to a 911 call from Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman and the mother of two children, about a possible prowler around her home.
Grayson, who is white, shot Massey in the face, after words over a boiling pot of water quickly escalated. A body camera activated by Grayson's partner captured the fatal shooting, which was later released to the public.
The shooting has grabbed international headlines, leading to the retirement of Sheriff Jack Campbell. In November, the U.S. Department of Justice launched an investigation into the sheriff's department and other county offices.

title: Top performers: Mia Clark, Lincoln girls hoops upset Morton, plus other basketball results
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Lincoln's Mia Clark made the go-ahead free throws against ranked Morton, plus other week's top performers
content:
This is a daily list of top performers from Springfield-area high school sports teams for Jan. 2-4, compiled from information provided to The State Journal-Register by coaches, athletic directors, and team statisticians.
Results can be emailed to sports@sj-r.com.
Girls holiday results: Girls basketball holiday schedule, results for the Springfield area
Saturday, Jan. 4
Girls Basketball
Game of the Night
LINCOLN — Lincoln jumped out to a 14-0 lead at the end of the first quarter but battled down the stretch to pull out a 52-50 win over state-ranked Morton at Roy S. Anderson Gymnasium.
Mia Clark made two free throws with 7.5 seconds left to give Lincoln the go-ahead score. Morton tied the game 50-50 when Ellie VanMeenen hit a layup with 19.5 on the clock.
Abby VanMeenen put up a contested shot at the buzzer, but Lincoln survived when the shot missed.
Paige Selke got Morton on the board with a putback basket on the Potters' first possession of the second quarter. By halftime, the Potters had trimmed the Railsplitters' lead to 22-14.
Makinley Knapp and Clark both scored 18 points apiece to lead Lincoln (8-6). Meanwhile, Lily Holmes scored 10 for the Railers.
Ellie VanMeenen led Morton (12-4) with 17 points, Abby VanMeenen had 12 and Salke finished with seven.
Morton was tied at No. 8 in the most recent Associated Press Class 3A high school girls basketball poll. Lincoln, the 2024 undefeated state champion in 3A, is unranked.
Morton defeated Chatham Glenwood 43-30 on Friday.
Izzy Hassebrock/Reese Watson, Sacred Heart-Griffin: Hassebrock and Watson buried three 3-pointers each and combined for 29 of SHG's points in a 41-34 defeat to Bloomington. Hassebrock led with 17 points and Watson scored 12.
Boys Basketball
Game of the Night
Lanphier rallied back from a 15-point deficit to beat Collinsville 67-59 in a nonconference boys basketball game at Lober-Nika Gymnasium.
Shaunassey Hatchett Jr., scored 16 of his game-high 26 points in the third quarter to spark the Lions' run. Collinsville (7-8) led 35-25 at halftime.
Lanphier forced Collinsville into 18 turnovers and outscored the Kahoks 23-6 off giveaways. Hatchett also led Lanphier with six rebounds and was 9-for-12 at the free-throw line.
JaiQuan Holman scored 13 points for the Lions (10-6) while Soriano Hayes contributed 12 points.
Lanphier outshot Collinsville 52.5% (21 of 40) to 44.0% (22-for-50), despite going 2-for-12 from behind the 3-point line. But the Lions scored 23 of their points at the free-throw line.
Donovan Coates led Collinsville with 23 points and had 11 rebounds. Collinsville outrebounded Lanphier 38-18, including 14 offensive boards. Evan Wilkinson added 10 points for the Kahoks.
Lanphier has alternated wins and losses over its last seven games. The Lions started the season 5-0 before suffering a three-game losing streak.
Blake Horn, Lincoln: He led Lincoln with 14 points in a 43-42 nonconference win over Rockford East at Roy S. Anderson Gymnasium. Brody Tungate was fouled by Rockford East with 1.6 seconds left, missed his first free throw before intentionally missing the second. Rockford East's Brian Harper attempted a full-court shot to win the game, but the heave fell harmlessly short of the basket. Karson Komnick scored 12 points off the bench for Lincoln and Gabe Smith added 10 points. The Railers nearly shot 50% and finished 17 of 35 (48.6%).
Cooper Schallenberg, Pleasant Plains: The Plains' senior scored 15 of his 17 points on five 3-pointers to lead the Cardinals past Warrensburg-Latham 50-41 in a nonconference game on Saturday. Grady Grisham poured in 10 in the win.
It is Warrensburg-Latham's third straight loss after a 14-0 start to the season. Two of the losses have come against Sangamo Conference teams: Pleasant Plains and Williamsville in the Williamsville Holiday Tournament championship game on Monday. Plains improved to 6-7.
Nathan Southern led Warrensburg with 12 points.
Owen Paluska, South County: The Vipers' junior led the team with 15 points in a 48-36 MSM Conference win over Nokomis. Paluska went scoreless in the first quarter but had five in the second and scored eight in the fourth, including going 6-for-8 at the free-throw line. Leo Bergschneider added 10 for the Vipers.
Ian Keller, Nokomis: The Nokomis senior scored 11 points before fouling out in the team's 48-36 loss to South County in an MSM Conference game.
Julian Rice, Riverton: The sophomore guard ushered a game-high 20 points in a 64-50 win over Pana.
Madyx Angel, Pana: The junior hit two 3s in the first quarter and finished with 19 points in the loss to Riverton.
Friday, Jan. 3
GIRLS BASKETBALL
Game of the Night
Senior guard Kyleigh Heimsness hit a couple key 3s and Taylorville's 1-2-2 zone defense clamped down to withstand Springfield High's gritty comeback in a 63-56 win at Dolph Stanley Court.
The Senators (6-9) trailed 36-17 at halftime before clawing back within one possession, 48-45, on an Aniyah Rhinehouse layup with six minutes left in regulation.
A Grace Rogers steal and subsequent Heimsness 3 helped the Tornadoes (9-6) regain control in the final four minutes.
Taylorville senior guard Addison Tarr knocked down three 3s in the first half for a team-high 19 points. Heimsness and Rogers each had 15 points. Senior forward Mazie Fleming had nine points and eight rebounds.
'We started off strong and then Springfield finally found their rhythm and they were making a lot of shots,' Tarr said. 'We just had to come back together and play hard. It comes first on the defensive end. We rebounded well pretty well, I thought. We didn't give them a lot of second chances, so I think that helped a lot for sure.'
Freshman guard Abigail Malit sparked the Senators off the bench and scored 17 of her game-high 21 points in the second half. Senior forward Ariana Williams also carried the banner and shot 7 of 9 from the field for 17 points before fouling out in the fourth period.
SHS coach Brad Scheffler hopes that second-half effort can be a springboard for next week.
'The No. 1 team in the state is Washington (in Class 3A) and over Thanksgiving we were ahead of them the whole second half and they hit a 3 at the buzzer to beat us (52-50),' Scheffler said. 'I know if we can play with them, we can play with anybody. It's just being consistent and playing 32 minutes of good basketball. Right now with this group, we're mixing different lineups and trying different things to see what has success.
'Tonight we had success in the second half, so hopefully we'll continue that on to next week.'
— Bill Welt
Taylor Keirs/Fynlee Hart, North Mac: Keirs dropped a game-high 21 points and Hart followed with 16 in North Mac's 62-27 home victory over Bunker Hill.
BOYS BASKETBALL
Game of the Night
Sacred Heart-Griffin sophomore Tereik Hurd spurred a comeback with 12 points in the fourth period and the Cyclones rallied to beat Quincy Notre Dame 58-55 in a nonconference game at Jim Belz Gymnasium.
QND had its biggest lead of the game at 51-44 with 4 minutes, 21 seconds remaining in the fourth. Hurd then went on an 8-0 run by himself, scoring eight straight points that included a pair of 3-point plays to give the Cyclones a 52-51 advantage with 2:49 to go.
Surrounded by two free throws from Hurd, QND's Jace Allensworth scored a pair of baskets as the Raiders went ahead 55-54 with 43.7 left. SHG's Zion Lee then stuck a jumper and the Cyclones went back in front 56-55.
After a QND miss on its next possession, Myles Montgomery snared a rebound and was fouled and the sophomore drained two free throws with 9.8 remaining for a 58-55 SHG lead. The Raiders attempted a game-tying 3-pointer, but the shot was short as time expired.
Hurd finished with a team-high 18 points and he scored the first 12 points of the fourth quarter for the Cyclones. Lee scored 13 points, Cam Brinkman added 10 and Montgomery ended with six.
QND led 17-16 after one quarter before SHG went into halftime with a 34-31 lead. The Raiders went on a 9-0 run during the third period and led 45-42 heading into the fourth.
Allensworth netted a game-best 21 points for the Raiders (8-5).
Griffin McClure, Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central: The senior guard delivered a team-high 16 points in a 57-44 win over Rushville-Industry. Jett Kerrick (12), Gavin Gronewald (11) and Drew Marr (10) also reached double figures.
Bennett Fretueg, Rushville-Industry: The senior drained two 3s and finished with a game-high 17 points in the loss to PORTA.
Eli Cox, Rochester: The sophomore scored 16 points to lead the Rockets to their seventh win in a row with a 63-45 nonconference decision over Lexington. Rochester (10-3) has also won nine of their last 10 games. Nate Swaney, Khorbin Gregory and Kai Bruce all had eight apiece for the Rockets.
Ethan Saathoff, Litchfield: The Purple Panthers ' junior scored a team-high 13 points in a 57-34 nonconference loss to Troy Triad.
Caden Colwell, South County: In Bluffs, Colwell scored a team-high 12 points for the Vipers, but Winchester West Central avenged a 22-point loss to South County on Monday by beating the Vipers 44-33 on Friday. West Central (12-4) trailed 19-14 at halftime but outscored the Vipers (7-8) 22-4 in the third quarter to take a 13-point lead into the fourth.
Sawyer Hill/Carson Moscardelli, Athens: The duo combined for 12 of the team's 14 points in the first quarter and each finished with a game-high 14 points in a 67-23 win over Havana. Trevor Schilling supplied 12 points.
Brock Brown, Taylorville: The freshman drained four 3s to lead the Tornadoes with 17 points in a 60-36 win over Charleston. Drake Howard had 16 points.
Thursday, Jan. 2
GIRLS BASKETBALL
Game of the Night
Gillespie outscored Nokomis 13-3 in overtime and pulled out a 60-50 win in a nonconference home game.
Senior Mia Brawner, who finished with a game-best 21 points, scored four in OT to pace Gillespie (12-5). Sophomore Amari Vickery made a 3-pointer and scored four in overtime to finish with 13. Teammate Delaney Taylor hit one of her two 3s in the extra period and ended with 11.
After trailing 26-19 at halftime, Nokomis got within 36-33 after three quarters. NHS forced overtime by outscoring the Miners 11-8 in the fourth period, and the game was tied at 47 apiece at the end of regulation.
Junior Kinley Stolte and senior Natalie Brownback led NHS with 11 points each. Senior Grace DeWerff scored the only points for Nokomis in OT with a 3-pointer, finishing with two 3s in the game and 10 points. Sophomore Alivia Sabol added 10 points in the loss.
Aubrey Vogel, Carson Arthalony, Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central: Vogel nailed two 3-pointers and finished with a game-high 22 points, and Arthalony made five field goals with a trey while hitting 8 of 10 free throws for 19 points in PORTA's 51-39 home win over Hardin Calhoun.
Addison Wheatley, Auburn: The senior netted 12 of her team-high 14 points after halftime, and the visiting Trojans defeated Kincaid South Fork 45-36. Graysen Allen scored 12 points for Auburn.

title: Former Sangamon County Coroner who resigned amid controversy passes away
author: Steven Spearie
description: A former Sangamon County Coroner who resigned in 2011 after county officials threatened to eliminate the office has died.
content:
Susan Boone, who served as Sangamon County Coroner for 14 years, but resigned in 2011 after county officials threatened to eliminate the office, died Dec. 30.
She was 76.
First elected coroner in 1996, Boone's office became the subject of a criminal investigation after The State Journal-Register reported that two pathologists had determined that a two-year-old had died from abuse in 2008, not cancer.
Boone signed off on Anakin Credit 's death certificate based on an autopsy by Dr. Jessica Bowman, who was not a board-certified forensic pathologist.
Top county officials thought that Boone had agreed to stop using Bowman, but that turned out not to be the case.
Sangamon County Board Chairman Andy Van Meter threw his support behind a resolution to abolish the coroner's office and assign Boone's duties to then-Sheriff Neil Williamson. That forced Boone's resignation.
In 2023, Coroner Jim Allmon amended the death certificate for Credit through the Illinois Department of Public Health's Vital Records Major Corrections division.
Two independent pathologists determined that Credit died of strangulation or a blow to the abdomen.
The boyfriend of Credit's mother was sentenced in 2013 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to aggravated battery of a child.
Allmon also worked to change the death certificate of Patrick Burns, who died in January 2010, days following a struggle on the city's north end with sheriff's deputies during his arrest following a home invasion.
Boone and Bowman said that Burns died from "excited delirium," a condition marked by bizarre behavior, paranoia and super-human strength that can coincide with drug use and is now refuted by the National Association of Medical Examiners (NAME).
Two forensic pathologists, however, concluded that Burns died of "prone restraint asphyxia," with his manner of death now reflected as "a homicide."
Allmon noted then that he wanted the death certificates "to be right. It wasn't my decision back then. Now I guess it is my decision."
Boone was coroner when Allmon joined the office as a deputy coroner in 2003. Allmon became coroner in 2020, succeeding Cinda Edwards, who had replaced Boone in 2011. Edwards and her husband, former Springfield Mayor and alderman Frank Edwards, and businessman John Evans of Glenarm died in an airplane accident on Jan. 28, 2020.
Allmon said Boone "worked to comfort families during their most difficult moments, and she was a strong vocal advocate for organ and tissue donation. Our thoughts and prayers are with her family and friends during this time."

title: Four takeaways from Rochester's CS8 boys basketball loss to Eisenhower
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Rochester roared back from an eight-point deficit to tie Eisenhower at halftime. Rochester couldn't answer the bell in the second half. What changed?
content:
ROCHESTER — With 3-pointers dropping for Decatur Eisenhower's Garryon Henderson in the first half, the Panthers threatened to take a commanding lead.
Down nine points, Rochester fought back over the final 6 minutes, 35 seconds of the half to go to the locker room tied.
When Eisenhower put together another strong quarter in the third, this time Rochester didn't have answers in Eisenhower's 70-57 Central State Eight Conference win at the Rochester Athletic Complex on Friday.
The loss snapped the Rockets' seven-game win streak.
Eisenhower (8-6 overall, 2-1 CS8) got 18 points from Marcus Page and 17 apiece from Henderson and TiShawn Clemmons.
It was a game Eisenhower coach Rodney Walker said before it began his Panthers needed to win.
'It's been up and down, a rollercoaster,' Walker said of the first half of the season. 'We're right there where we need to be, but we still haven't gotten that rhythm yet, two or three games in a row. We're playing good ball — enough to win but enough to lose as well.'
Rochester's 6-foot-3 senior Jack Melton led the Rockets with 13 points and he added five rebounds.
Here are four takeaways from Friday's game.
Rochester adapted well in the first half
Henderson connected on four of six 3-pointers over the first 9:23, much to the chagrin of Rochester coach Tony Gavin. He called a timeout moments after Henderson's fourth gave Eisenhower a 25-16 lead.
Gavin's message to his team? Guard Henderson, know where Henderson is, don't let Henderson shoot wide-open 3s.
The message worked. Henderson was held without a shot for the rest of the half and wouldn't score again until a fourth-quarter free throw and the game's final basket in the last minute.
Then Rochester, with 6-5 sophomore Eli Cox on the bench with two fouls, started hitting shots of its own. Melton came out of the timeout and buried a 3-pointer to spark a 15-6 run.
'I felt really good (at halftime),' Gavin said. 'I felt like our pressure was really good in the second quarter (and) I thought that led to some easy buckets and then shots started to fall.'
Eisenhower's Jayden Lane had the Panthers' lone three buckets over the final 5:32 of the half and kept the Panthers treading water.
Meanwhile, Rochester had seven points in the quarter from Melton, four from Khorbin Gregory and two apiece from Nate Swaney, Brooks Gavin and Tanner Beal.
'I was just looking for my shot a little more there but still spreading the ball,' Melton said of his second period.
Discipline works for Eisenhower
While Walker saw his team's lead slip away, he hoped his halftime adjustments would allow Ike to get back in front again. Page and Clemmons carried the Panthers in the third.
Page, a 6-foot-5 junior, used his large frame to muscle his way to 11 points in the quarter while Clemmons had seven.
'Our strategy is pretty much energy: everything is based off energy, from defense to offense,' Walker said. 'When those guys are hitting their spots, doing what they're supposed to do, we're an effective team but when we're under control, we're even better.'
At the same time, Eisenhower's defense forced Rochester into five turnovers in the period after the Rockets committed just four in the entire first half.
'The pressure finally did catch up to them a little bit,' Walker said. 'We pride ourselves on our Panther pressure.'
Rochester finished with 12 turnovers, but they came at inconvenient times.
'(Eisenhower) is a very good team; they've beat some good teams already this year and you just can't give them those opportunities,' Gavin said. 'Every possession counts and when you're turning the ball over, they're going to take advantage of it. They've got guys that can score and when you turn it over, you're just missing empty possessions and asking them to go on runs at that point.'
Eisenhower also got extra possessions with nine offensive rebounds. Page finished with nine boards, including four on the offensive end.
'Everybody has to rebound: we don't have 7-footers,' Walker said with a smile. 'We're not blessed (with height). Everybody has to crash with us.'
Eisenhower pleased after long layoff
Eisenhower has won its last two games, but they were spread out over nearly two weeks. The last time the Panthers suited up was Dec. 29 with a 61-36 win against Granite City in the Collinsville Holiday Tournament 's consolation third-place game.
Walker said he wasn't exactly sure what to expect.
'We executed when we needed to, we ran when we had to, we slowed it down when we had to, which I wasn't sure how our legs were going to be,' Walker said. 'I didn't want us to get too excited out there in the first half and not have anything left in the second half. It was good that the boys were able to turn it on still in the second half.'
It can get a little mundane with nothing but constant practice.
'It's hard to keep those guys motivated and going at practice,' Walker added. 'Trying to simulate the game is tough.'
Rochester and Eisenhower will meet again on Jan. 24 in Decatur. He hopes to have a full lineup, but still expects to see new wrinkles from Gavin.
'We're not all the way healthy yet,' Walker said. 'We have one of our key players out right now (J.T. Moore).
'Good teams will always adjust. They've seen us play a couple of times, I'm sure coach will get back in the lab and throw a few tricks at us.'
Rockets still positive
Since Rochester joined the CS8 in the 2010-11 school year, the Rockets have just one finish above .500 (2022-23, 17-15) and won its first regional title since 2005 a season ago. A 10-4 record is still celebrated there.
Melton said the team needs to learn from the loss but quickly put it in the rearview mirror and get back to what's carried the team: everyone contributing.
'We're just seeing everyone involved (when Rochester plays well),' Melton said. 'You look at a lot of our wins ... we're getting everybody involved: we're getting me, Kai (Bruce), Eli, Khordell (Gregory), Khorbin — we're all borderline double digits, scoring is spread out, we're playing great defense and forcing a lot of turnovers.'
Rochester has a quick turnaround before a Saturday game against Eureka in Clinton.
'I just said, 'Don't let one loss turn into two' and that has to be our mindset tomorrow,' Gavin said. 'We're going to see teams like that throughout the conference; our conference is very good and very even. We've got to be ready next week and (Saturday). We're going to have a gauntlet here coming up and we're going to see that kind of competition every game now, so we've got to be ready.'
