Emmy-winning talk show host Conan O'Brien is host of the 2025 Oscars. He takes over for Jimmy Kimmel, who hosted the show the last year.

title: New Springfield restaurant has a friendly staff and good food, but confusing menu
author: Kathryn Rem
description: This new business offers a variety of dishes with generous portions. But, our restaurant reviewer thought there could be some improvements.
content:
Name: Pinoy Pride Cuisine
Address: 2501 Wabash Ave., Springfield (White Oaks Mall food court)
Phone: 217-685-2832
Credit/debit cards accepted: Yes
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Hours: 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Friday and Saturday, noon to 6 p.m. Sunday
Entrée price range: $5.99-$13.99
Children's menu: No, but there is a grilled cheese sandwich and a chicken salad sandwich on the menu.
My order: This new business offers a variety of Filipino dishes, including Pork Adobo ($11.99), considered by many the star of the cuisine of the Philippines. This version featured a generous portion of marinated and braised pork chunks in a garlic sauce over white rice and with a whole cooked egg in the center of the dish. My friend dined on an order of vegetarian Pancit Noodles ($9.95), which were mixed with carrots and green beans. She thought the dish would have been better without the large amount of oil in it. I also got the Halo Halo ($4.99 for the small size), a blend of tropical fruit, ice cream and shaved ice, which was quite delicious.
Likes: The staff was helpful in explaining what each dish was.
Dislikes: There are many different menus and promotions on the front counter, which I found confusing.
What would I order next time? Eight pieces of fried lumpia (spring rolls) are $8.99.

title: Springfield-based hospital names new CEO, president
author: Claire Grant
description: Weeks after it was announced the president and CEO of a Springfield-based hospital was leaving, we now know who will be taking over for them.
content:
HSHS Central Illinois Market and HSHS St. John's Hospital will have a new president and CEO come the spring.
Dr. Leanne M. Yanni will take over the role at HSHS on March 17, 2025.
Yanni will take over for Matthew Fry. Earlier in January, the SJ-R reported Fry will be leaving in early March to assume leadership duties at a Missouri-based health system.
More: President, CEO of Springfield-based hospital is leaving his position
Yanni is a collaborative physician executive with over 20 years of progressive leadership experience in navigating change and transformation in matrixed organizations.
In her new role, Yanni will have strategic and operational responsibility for HSHS Medical Group, Prairie Cardiovascular, Physician Clinical Integration Network, PCIN, HSHS ACO, and Prairie Education & Research Cooperative.
Before joining the team at HSHS, she worked at the Bon Secours Mercy Health, which operated 13 hospitals and medical centers in Kentucky, Virginia and South Carolina, Yanni served as Market Ambulatory Chief Medical Officer for the Bon Secours Richmond, Virginia hospitals.
Concurrently, she has been serving as Chief Medical Officer for St. Mary's Hospital in Richmond.

title: 'More questions than answers.' White House memo sends Springfield agencies scrambling
author: Steven Spearie
description: A federal judge on Tuesday issued a stay against a Trump Administration memo ordering a halt to federal funding and grant programs that left city and county officials scrambling.
content:
A federal judge on Tuesday issued a stay against a Trump Administration memo ordering a halt to federal funding and grant programs that left city and county officials scrambling.
Judge Loren L. AliKhan for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia blocked the order until at least Monday.
If reenacted, the federal funding freeze could affect everything from highway programs to medical research labs. It does not affect Social Security benefits, Medicare benefits and food stamps
One project that still could be left in the lurch is the Springfield Rail Improvements Project, according to U.S. Rep. Nikki Budzinski, D-Springfield.
Budzinski called Trump's freeze on federal funding "reckless."
"We're left with more questions than answers," Budzinski posted on Facebook.
She wasn't the only one searching for answers.
"We don't have a whole lot of information on (the freeze) right now," said city of Springfield spokeswoman Haley Wilson earlier Tuesday. "We're trying to get it figured out."
Wilson confirmed that Mayor Misty Buscher met with State officials about the policy on Tuesday.
"We've talked to all of our departments to give them a heads up on what could be coming down the pike," Wilson said. "We've contacted all agencies we partner with who we think may be affected."
"We don't know yet what departments within the county might be affected," added Sangamon County spokesman Jeff Wilhite.
Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul led a lawsuit Tuesday to prevent the White House from instituting the funding freeze.
Continuum of Care Coordinator Josh Sabo said it and other agencies dealing with homelessness in the Springfield area, like M.E.R.C.Y. Communities, Helping Hands of Springfield, Fifth Street Renaissance/SARA Center and Youth Service Bureau, get an allocation from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.
Everybody was in a holding pattern Tuesday, Sabo said.
"Hopefully, it's a short-lived freeze, otherwise it will make life really difficult for these programs," Sabo said.
Rail project manager Michael Mendenhall said he is also playing the waiting game.
"We have not received anything yet from (the Federal Railroad Administration) that the city of Springfield has the (rail project) grants through," Mendenhall said. "I'm sure they're in the process of trying to evaluate everything and figure out a plan of action here."
U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., said Trump's executive order freezes billions of dollars in grants that help fund programs run by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
The order, Duckworth said, would jeopardize "critical and life-changing VA grants that support community-based suicide prevention efforts, rural telehealth access and more."

title: Springfield High's Riley Herr forges own path to swimming success
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Springfield High's Riley Herr is one of the best swimmers in the area, but he's not content. With the postseason looming, he aims to improve.
content:
Just as a loving mother would do, Elisha Beard dropped everything to watch her son Riley Herr swim the 100-yard breaststroke at the Boys City Swimming and Diving Meet at Eisenhower Pool on Tuesday.
Beard, formerly known as Herr, wears many hats. She has been the diving coach for all the area high schools for 13 years and the coach at Illinois College. Her busy schedule and passion for swimming and diving is one reason why her son is one of the top swimmers in the area at Springfield High.
'We put him in the pool, and he never got out,' said Beard of Herr. "He's been in the Eisenhower environment with the Springfield High School swim team since he was like 4-years-old. He used to come with me (during the Olympian) Ryan Held era and watch swim meets. He's dreamed of swimming for Springfield High School since way back then.'
Beard, herself, is an all-around gymnast, swimmer and diver. Her younger brother, Matthew Woodson is an assistant coach for the boys programs and was a diver for Springfield High and Illinois College. Beard said she has no regrets that Herr didn't follow in the footsteps of his mother and uncle.
'He started out diving, but he just loved swimming more,' she said. 'I'm very proud of him."
Herr, who eventually won the 100-yard breaststroke at City, gave his own reason that attributed to his quick exit from diving.
'I recently tried to dive and do a flip and landed straight on my back and it was red for 10 minutes,' the junior said. 'I've just always been a swimmer.'
The breaststroke is Herr's signature event, and said he likes swimming the 500 freestyle to boot. He noted dropping the 200 IM, an event that he won at the Central State Eight Conference Meet and came in sixth place at the Champaign Centennial Sectional last season.
Everything, however, hinges on how well he can improve his time and placing in the breaststroke. He placed sixth in the event in 1:03.32 at last season's sectional.
'(Currently), I am seeded second at sectionals and could possibly win my event and go to state,' Herr said. 'I also think our medley relay (where he swims the breast) has a chance to go.'
Third-year head coach Eric Sommer had many positive thoughts on Herr.
'He's a great kid,' Sommer said. 'He's very mild, somewhat quiet. But overall, when it comes to leadership, he is always there to be a helper for the younger kids and a leader for the other kids. He's a dream to have on the team.'
Sommer also stated that if all things go right, Herr could be on the sectional podium and heading to the Illinois High School Association state meet.
'Through the season he has definitely improved, and it's really been the little things that we're working on,' Sommer said. 'It's all details now — the fitness is there and everything else is there. I think he's got a shot — on any given day, he's got the ability and knowledge to do it. It's a matter of, he's got to show up and be on his A game. Everybody else has to show up and he just has to beat them.'
Maybe Herr will get to experience what some of his favorite past swimmers were able to accomplish.
'(They) influenced me with what I've done (in high school),' Herr said. '(Springfield graduate) Matthew Knox and (Sacred Heart-Griffin grad) Ryan Held were very fun to watch.'

title: Big 3 turn up big in Lanphier's boys basketball win over Sacred Heart-Griffin
author: Bill Welt
description: "Shaunassey Hatchett was a man-child out there," said Lanphier coach Blake Turner after a boys basketball win over Sacred Heart-Griffin on Saturday
content:
Lanphier teammates Shaunassey Hatchett Jr. and Soriano Hayes were humming in the first half, while JaiQuan Holman was tethered to the bench due to early foul trouble.
It wasn't long until they all found their groove in an 82-60 Central State Eight Conference boys basketball victory at Sacred Heart-Griffin on Saturday.
The 6-4 senior Hatchett and 6-3 junior Hayes combined for 24 points in the first half for a slim 35-33 deficit and never eased off the throttle.
'We're both fast and tall, and we can handle the ball and shoot, so we just try to set screens for each other and create mismatches,' Hayes said.
'We both have talks before the game and tell each other what to do and give each other tips here and there, so we pretty much know what we're doing going into the game.'
Hatchett led the Lions with a game-high 27 points, five rebounds and two blocks, while shooting 9 of 11 from the floor and 2 of 3 from 3-point range — not to mention 7 of 10 from the free throw line. Hayes, shooting 8 of 9 from the field, furnished a double-double with 18 points and 10 rebounds.
'Shaunassey Hatchett was a man-child out there today,' Lanphier coach Blake Turner said. 'Big challenge for him playing against these guys and he stepped up to it.'
Holman, The State Journal-Register's reigning Large School Boys Basketball Player of the Year, scored all his 17 points after the break, including a perfect 8-for-8 on free throw attempts.
'Shanaussey and JaiQuan are our leaders and Soriano is that third wheel and when all three of them are going, we're tough to beat,' Turner said. 'I'm not surprised that we won by more than 20 points. Like I told the guys in the locker room, I think we're 20 points better than anybody when everybody is clicking like that. The key to that is to get everybody clicking like that, which isn't easy.'
Lanphier (16-9, 3-5 CS8) trailed most of the way — but not by much — until Holman's 3 with just over three minutes left in the third period.
Other weekend results: Owen Johnson's heroics give Plains win over Riverton, plus more
Senior guard Amari Anderson's go-ahead 3 in the frame's final seconds triggered a sudden 8-0 burst and the Lions outscored SHG 29-9 in the fourth period. Tourion Rice and Kenyon Greer added six points apiece.
'He only played three minutes in the first half and didn't score,' Turner said of Holman. 'He was asking me to put him back in and I told him no. At this point of the season, you've got to depend on other guys to step up. I was proud of the other guys stepping up.'
Sophomore guards Terrion Wallace and Cam Brinkman each led SHG (11-10, 3-4) with 15 points. Myles Montgomery and Jamarion Bardwell chipped in eight and seven points, respectively.
Bardwell and fellow senior Chuck Lanier were also saddled by early foul trouble. Both picked up their fourth fouls late in the third.

title: Springfield-area top performers: Jaiyden Wilson, Elijah Wade lead Springfield High to win
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Pleasant Plains got a big play from Owen Johnson to rally for a win over Riverton, plus other top performances around Springfield this week:
content:
This is a daily list of top performers from Springfield-area high school sports teams for Jan. 27-Feb. 1, compiled from information provided to The State Journal-Register by coaches, athletic directors, and team statisticians.
Results can be emailed to sports@sj-r.com.
Girls City champions: SHG beats SHS to force three-way tie for Girls City Tournament trophy
(Correction: Ali Fleischli's first name in Wednesday's girls basketball game of the night was incorrectly reported.)
Saturday, Feb. 1
Boys Basketball
Stars of the Night
Jaiyden Wilson/Elijah Wade, Springfield High: The duo combined for 42 points and led four Springfield players in double figures in an 83-50 win over Southeast at Willard Duey Gym. Wilson scored 22 points and Elijah Wade netted 20, while the Senators got 17 and 14 points, respectively, from Mayango Jallah and Noah Wade.
Dom Alepra, Carlinville: The senior guard found the range with six of his seven 3-pointers in the first half, and he finished with a game-best 25 points in Carlinville's 68-43 home win over Athens. Tate Duckels scored 15 and Sawyer Smith added 12 points.
Luke Blackford, Calvary: The junior shooting guard poured in a game-high 35 points, but Calvary fell to Peoria Richwoods 71-58 at the Peoria Manual Shootout. Joshua Long added 11 points.
Jack Kaylor/Chaz Oberkfell, Gillespie: The pair of Miners teamed up to each score 14 points apiece in Gillespie's 55-49 South Central Conference win over Pana. Kaylor scored 12 of his in the second half as the Miners outscored the Panthers 33-25.
Cash Lynch, Pana: The junior connected for a pair of 3-pointers and finished with a game-high 16 points in the Panthers' 55-49 South Central Conference road loss to Gillespie. Madyx Angel and Tyler Rench both finished with 10 points apiece for Pana.
Ian Keller, Nokomis: Keller put in 12 of his 14 points in the second half and NHS defeated host Raymond Lincolnwood 54-43. Kannon Jones made one field goal, went 9-for-10 from the foul line and scored 11 points.
Girls Basketball
Stars of the Night
Anna Weber/Grace Sabatka, Pleasant Plains: Weber erupted in the third quarter with eight of her game-high 14 points as the Cardinals beat Chillicothe IVC 59-22. Sabatka opened with a 3-pointer in the first quarter, then had 10 of her 13 in the middle quarters. Madison Burke netted 10 for the Cardinals.
Addi Jones/Addison Wheatley, Auburn: The Trojans got 11 points from Jones and 10 from Wheatley as Auburn beat St. Joseph-Ogden 46-32 in the Sangamo vs. Illini Prairie Shootout.
Carson Arthalony, Petersburg PORTA: The senior center scored 13 of her game-high 25 points in the third quarter in PORTA's 55-38 victory over Tolono Unity at the IPC/Sangamo Shootout. Freshman Regan Heubner and senior Cassie Cox added 10 points each.
Jordyn Durham, Riverton: The senior guard scored 20 points in a 53-36 loss to Paxton-Buckley-Loda.
Megan Hughes, Mason City Illini Central: The senior provided 14 points in a 44-22 win over Fairbury Prairie Central.
Callie Wagner, South County: She hit a pair of 3-pointers and finished with 12 points in South County's 52-45 win over Pontiac.
Natalie Brownback/Hannah Tarter, Nokomis: The senior/freshman tandem made two 3-pointers each and finished with 10 points apiece in Nokomis' 63-45 loss to Carrollton in the third-place game of the Carrollton Lady Hawk Tournament.
Boys Swimming and Diving
Sawyer Lobmaster, Southeast: The junior had two second-place finishes to account for all of Southeast's points in a triangular swim meet at Eisenhower Pool on Saturday morning. In the 50-yard freestyle, Lobmaster finished in 28.61 seconds. In the 500-free, he placed second in 7 minutes, 25.14 seconds.
Friday, Jan. 31
Boys Basketball
Game of the Night
Pleasant Plains 40, Riverton 39
Owen Johnson converted the go-ahead 3-pointer with under 20 seconds remaining and the Cardinals held on for the Sangamo Conference win.
The junior led the Cardinals (13-9, 3-0 Sangamo) with 14 points, while Cooper Schallenberg and Grady Grisham each had nine.
Plains trailed 39-35 with under a minute left until Schallenberg supplied two free throws and a steal to set up the game-winning 3.
Julian Rice led the Hawks (17-5, 0-3) with 14 points, while Jaxson Miller had 10.
Stars of the Night
Karson Komnick, Lincoln: The junior guard scored nine of his 20 points in the fourth quarter in a 43-30 win over Mattoon. Frank Sanders had eight points.
Jett Karrick, Petersburg PORTA: Karrick made five field goals with one 3-pointer and finished 9-for-10 from the foul line for 20 points in PORTA's 62-39 victory over Maroa-Forsyth. Griffin McClure contributed 12 points and Drew Marr tallied 10.
Amaree Burries, Jacksonville: The senior dropped a team-high 17 points, but the Crimsons lost to Decatur MacArthur 64-46 at The Bowl. Latrell Hemphill hit three 3-pointers and scored 13 points.
Cash Lynch, Pana: The Panthers' junior scored seven points in the second quarter and nine in the fourth to finish with a game-high 21 in Pana's 43-41 South Central Conference win over visiting Piasa Southwestern.
Carter Wexstten/Kannon Jonas, Nokomis: The duo combined to score 33 points as NHS downed Macon Meridian 60-53 in a nonconference game. Wexstten had 17 points to go along with his team-leading seven rebounds. Jonas scored seven of his 16 points at the free-throw line as Nokomis improved to 11-14.
Nate Schaake, Litchfield: He connected on three 3-pointers in the fourth quarter and finished with 19 points in the Purple Panthers' 50-46 South Central Conference loss to Hillsboro. Ethan Saathoff added 10 points for Litchfield.
Nathan Matoush, Hillsboro: The senior led the Hiltoppers with 23 points as Hillsboro downed Litchfield 50-46 in a South Central Conference matchup. Fellow senior Jackson Tuetken added 10 points for the Toppers.
Isiah Laux, Staunton: The sophomore shooting guard delivered a game-high 13 points and the host Bulldogs defeated Carlinville 49-39 in the South Central Conference. Bryce Coalson (two 3-pointers) and Ethan Sharp chipped in eight points apiece.
David Bard/Brody Folkes, Mason City Illini Central: The Cougars' dynamic scorers combined to score 43 points in Illini Central's 58-53 Sangamo Conference win over New Berlin. Bard, a senior, finished with 25 points. Folkes, a junior, had 18.
Aydin Littig, New Berlin: The Pretzels got 21 points from the junior in a 58-53 loss to Mason City Illini Central in a Sangamo Conference clash. Junior Reid Hepperly added 15 points for the Pretzels.
Luke Blackford, Calvary: The junior had 26 points as Calvary beat Lutheran 67-55 in an MSM Conference game between in-city rivals at Our Savior's Lutheran Church. Joshua Long added 14 to the Saints' cause while Josiah Reynolds finished with 13.
Parker Cloyd, Lutheran: The senior led the Crusaders with 19 points in Lu-Hi's 67-55 MSM Conference loss to Calvary at Our Savior's Lutheran Church. Teammate Jeramy Daniel, a sophomore, scored 13 and junior Connor Hilligoss added 11.
Owen Paluska, South County: He scored 19 points, including eight in the opening quarter, as the Vipers topped Concord Triopia 59-56 in a nonconference tilt. Bishop McDannald added 11 and Caden Colwell finished with 10.
Girls Basketball
Games of the Night
Lincoln 57, Taylorville 45
Grace Schneider drained a game-tying 3 before the buzzer to end the third period and Lincoln outscored the Tornadoes 18-6 in the final period.
Mia Clark led Lincoln (13-10) with 24 points, while Mesa McCloud (13) and Lily Holmes (11) also reached double figures. Schneider had four points.
Addison Tarr paced Taylorville (12-9) with 20 points. Kyleigh Heimsness and Mazie Fleming each had eight.
Chatham Glenwood 47, Rochester 30
Macy Martynowski shot 6 of 12 from the field and led the Titans with 18 points.
Alexis Neumann and Rowann Law provided 10 points apiece in the Central State Eight Conference win.
The Titans (17-8 overall, 8-1 CS8) can clinch a share of the CS8 title with a win over Southeast at home on Saturday at 1:30 p.m. before the CS8 finale at Lanphier on Tuesday, Feb. 11. Glenwood next welcomes Troy Triad (19-6) on Tuesday, Feb. 4 at 7 p.m.
Stars of the Night
Ariana Williams/Keziah Toran, Springfield High: The pair of seniors teamed up to score 38 points as the Senators downed Southeast 70-53 at Herb Scheffler Gymnasium in a Central State Eight Conference game. Williams finished with 20 points — including 10 in the third quarter — while Toran netted 18. Junior Aniyah Rhinehouse pitched in with 11 points.
Navehua Collier, Southeast: The sophomore guard led Southeast with 22 points, a game-high total — in the Spartans' 70-53 loss to Springfield High in a Central State Eight Conference game at Herb Scheffler Gymnasium. Zaria Weston added 13 points while Chloe Crawford chipped in with 12 for the Spartans.
Thursday, Jan. 30
Girls Basketball
Stars of the Night
Anna Weber, Pleasant Plains: The junior forward made 11 shots and was the only scorer in double figures with a game-high 23 points as Plains defeated Rochester 48-22 in a nonconference game at the Rochester Athletic Complex.
Aubrey Vogel, Petersburg PORTA: The junior guard provided a team-best 13 points in a 46-34 victory at Stanford Olympia. Seniors Carson Arthalony and Cassie Cox chipped in 10 points apiece for PORTA (20-5).
Kaitlyn Reels/Jordyn Loveless, Carlinville: The duo made two 3-pointers apiece and combined for 32 points in Carlinville's 59-27 victory at Piasa Southwestern. Reels led the team with 17 points and Loveless had 13 of her 15 in the first half.
Taylor Keirs, North Mac: The senior guard racked up a career-high 28 points as North Mac defeated host Greenville 66-60 in South Central Conference play. Brittnee Lange had 17 points and Fynlee Hart tallied 13.
Ava Bee/Addie Stadholt, Athens: Bee led with 12 points and Stadholt scored 10 as Athens defeated visiting Auburn 41-34.
Karlissa Clark, Auburn: She scored 11 points in Auburn's 41-34 Sangamo Conference loss to Athens.
Delaney Taylor, Gillespie: Taylor connected on three 3-pointers, hit 10 of 12 free throws and finished with a game-high 21 points in Gillespie's 60-51 South Central Conference home win over Hillsboro. Maggie Heyen added 10 points.
Tatum Christian, Hillsboro: The senior led four Hillsboro scorers in double figures with 12 points in the loss to Gillespie.
Mia Root, Williamsville: The junior scored a game-high 17 points with five 3s in a 40-9 win over Riverton.
Alyson Murphy, Mount Pulaski: The junior guard tallied 20 points in a 55-35 win over Niantic Sangamon Valley/Buffalo Tri-City.
Lauren Bailey, Mount Olive: Bailey recorded 24 points in a 62-54 win over White Hall North Greene.
Boys Basketball
Stars of the Night
Treyton Davis/Alex Peacock, Edinburg: Davis led the Wildcats to a 70-65 nonconference win over Greenfield. Meanwhile, Peacock, a senior, scored 25 points to help Edinburg get their 20th win of the season.
Bishop McDannald, South County: He knocked down four 3-pointers and accumulated a game-high 27 points in South County's 64-35 win over Beardstown at the Triopia Tournament. McDannald made three 3s in the first quarter.
Sawyer Smith, Carlinville: Smith posted a double-double with 20 points and 13 rebounds in Carlinville's 66-48 home win over Pawnee. Tate Duckels (18), Triston Thompson (15) and Dom Alepra (10) also scored in double figures.
Jett Kerrick/Griffin McClure, Petersburg PORTA: The tandem both made two 3-pointers and scored 13 points apiece in PORTA's 63-42 win over Pittsfield. Clayton Hoke added 11 points.
Wednesday, Jan. 29
Boys Basketball
Game of the Night
Rochester 54, Springfield High 48
Kai Bruce buried five 3-pointers in the first half and Rochester built a big halftime lead in claiming a nonconference road victory at Willard Duey Gymnasium.
Bruce made two 3s in the first period and Nate Swaney scored five points to give the Rockets a 19-14 lead after one. Bruce added three more treys in the second frame to provide Rochester (16-6) a 40-27 advantage at intermission.
The Senators slightly cut their deficit by outscoring Rochester 6-3 in the third quarter to make it 43-33. Springfield's Elijah Wade then scored 12 of his game-best 16 points in the fourth period but the comeback fell short.
Rochester's Khordell Gregory helped cap the win, netting seven of his 10 points in the final quarter. Bruce finished with 15 points and Swaney notched 10.
Noah Wade tallied 11 points and Victor Komalafe ended with 10 first-half points for Springfield (13-11).
Stars of the Night
Jett Karrick, Petersburg PORTA: The junior made 10 field goals and compiled a game-high 21 points in PORTA's 53-45 victory over Athens. Drew Marr added 14 points.
Trevor Schilling, Athens: The Warriors' freshman scored 12 points to lead Athens in a 53-45 Sangamo Conference loss to Petersburg PORTA.
Girls Basketball
Game of the Night
Chatham Glenwood 40, Sacred Heart-Griffin 35
The Titans outscored the Cyclones 12-6 in the fourth quarter and recorded a nonconference victory at SHG.
Alexis Nuemann and Rowann Law had four points each in the final period. Neumann finished with a team-high 13 points, making four field goals and going 5-for-6 from the free-throw line. Law scored 11 and Ava Bobb added 10 points.
SHG (13-14) jumped out to a 14-6 lead after one period when Ali Fleischli got going by hitting a pair of 3-pointers. Glenwood (16-8) answered by holding the Cyclones to three points in the second quarter to even the game at 17 points apiece at intermission.
Fleischli had six more points in the third stanza, helping SHG take a one-point lead into the fourth quarter. Fleischli led the Cyclones with 13 points and Izzy Hassebrock contributed nine.
Stars of the Night
Angelina Ippolito, Kincaid South Fork: The junior scored her 1,000th career point and finished with a game-high 14 as Kincaid defeated visiting Piasa Southwestern 44-24. Ippolito made four field goals and finished 6-for-6 from the free-throw line.
Lauren Bailey, Mount Olive: She scored her 1,000th career point and finished with 14 total points in Mount Olive's 59-51 loss to East Alton-Wood River. Sami Roeske and Bella Lueken also scored 14 points.
Callie Wagner, South County: The sophomore made a pair of 3-pointers and scored 12 points as South County edged Pawnee 31-30 at Franklin.
Alivia Sabol, Nokomis: The sophomore posted a double-double with 15 points and 12 rebounds and NHS defeated Jerseyville 58-54. Grace Dewerff chipped in 13 points and Kinley Stolte and Natalie Brownback contributed 10 apiece.
Tuesday, Jan. 28
Boys Basketball
Games of the Night
Auburn 58, Riverton 44
Auburn came up with the stops down the stretch.
The Trojans, ranked No. 1 in Class 2A by The Associated Press, started the fourth quarter on a 15-1 run to put away host Riverton.
The Hawks (17-4, 0-2 Sangamo Conference) led 38-37 by the end of the third quarter following a Jaxsen Trager 3-pointer before the buzzer. Auburn (21-1, 2-0) then forced nine turnovers in the final period.
'I'm just proud of the guys for gutting it out,' Auburn coach Seth McCoy said. 'Everybody knows what this conference is. Throw out records, whatever. We have great coaches and great players in this conference.'
Senior guard Cooper Carter led the Trojans with 18 points, while senior teammate Carter Hunley had 15 points. Senior forward Ryan Lash added 11 points.
Riverton was missing two starters, leading-scorer Julian Rice (illness) and Grady Hartlaub (knee). Coach Matt Mead expects to have both back for Friday's game against Pleasant Plains.
Senior guard Jaxson Miller paced the Hawks with 17 points.
'Overall, I'm proud of our guys,' Mead said. 'We've got to learn how to play four quarters and we're getting closer against some really good teams.'
— Bill Welt
Pleasant Plains 33, New Berlin 30, OT
Sean Lowder hit a 3-pointer in overtime to give Pleasant Plains the lead and Owen Johnson made a pair of free throws to add to the Cardinals' lead in a Sangamo Conference matchup.
Cooper Schallenberg scored 13 points to lead the Cardinals (12-9 overall, 2-0 Sangamo). He had 10 points in the opening period as the Cardinals opened up a 12-7 lead.
Reid Hepperly led New Berlin (9-9, 1-1) with 13 points. Gabe Molloy had the only points for the Pretzels in overtime when he scored a 2-point basket.
Champaign Centennial 64, Lanphier 58
The glow from the City Tournament win didn't last long after the Lions dropped a nonconference road game on Tuesday.
Lanphier got 45 points combined from Soriano Hayes, JaiQuan Holman, and Shaunassey Hatchett Jr., in the Lions first on-court loss of 2025. Lanphier (16-9) had to forfeit two games after a fight broke out against in-city rival Southeast on Jan. 7.
Hayes led Lanphier with 16 points while Holman finished with 15, including a team-high three 3-pointers. Hatchett posted a double-double with 14 points and 13 rebounds.
Centennial's Sherrod Clark led the Chargers (11-10) with 27 points despite playing limited minutes with foul trouble and then picking up his fifth foul. Isaiah Allen added 15 points for Centennial and Kayden Peat had 10.
The Lions will face Sacred Heart-Griffin for the second time in nine days on Saturday in a Central State Eight Conference matchup. Lanphier beat SHG 62-56 on Jan. 23 in the boys City Tournament opener at the BOS Center. The Lions then beat Springfield High and Southeast to sweep the tournament and win the outright title.
Stars of the Night
Luke Blackford, Calvary: The junior gave the Saints 29 points — with 26 coming in the middle quarters — as Calvary downed Litchfield 81-52 in a nonconference game at home. Antione Hunter added 18 for the Saints while Josiah Reynolds finished with 15.
Nate Schaake, Litchfield: The senior poured in 20 points but the Purple Panthers dropped an 81-52 road nonconference decision to Calvary. Sophomore Brody Dykema added 10 for Litchfield.
Eli Cox, Rochester: He scored a team-high 13 points to lead the Rockets to a 59-46 nonconference home win over Taylorville. Khornell Gregory had 11 for Rochester and Khorbin Gregory added 10.
Baron Odam/Drake Howard, Taylorville: The pair of Tornadoes each scored 11 points in Taylorville's 59-46 nonconference road loss to Rochester.
Gage Shafer, Buffalo Tri-City/Sangamon Valley: The Tornadoes' senior scored 22 points to help carry Tri-City to a 58-49 MSM Conference win over Mount Olive. R.J. Sullivan added 11 points in the win at home.
David Schoen, Mount Olive: Schoen scored 13 points to lead the Wildcats and added five rebounds in a 58-49 MSM Conference road loss to Buffalo Tri-City. Matthew Bywater had nine points and led the team with 10 rebounds and four assists.
Madyx Angel/Cash Lynch, Pana: The pair of Panthers combined for 27 points in a 53-38 nonconference loss to Mattoon. Angel connected three times behind the 3-point arc and finished with 14 points while Lynch had 11 of his 13 in the middle quarters.
Caden Colwell/Owen Paluska, South County: Colwell, a junior, had 16 points and connected on four 3-pointers and Paluska had 13 points in a 57-40 nonconference win over Rushville-Industry.
Carter Fretueg, Rushville-Industry: He led the Rockets with 14 points in a 57-40 nonconference loss to South County.
Sawyer Smith/Dom Alepra, Carlinville: Smith led all scorers with 22 points as Carlinville beat Lutheran 56-43 in a nonconference game. Alepra added 16, including 12 points off four made 3-pointers, to help the Cavaliers' cause.
Parker Cloyd/Connor Hilligoss, Lutheran: Cloyd scored four points in each of the first and third quarters and finished to lead the Crusaders with 11 overall in a 56-43 nonconference loss at Carlinville. Hilligoss added 10 points while Brayden Cabell netted nine.
Luke Alexander, North Mac: Alexander was dialed in early and hit three 3-pointers in the first quarter to lead the Panthers in a 46-36 nonconference loss to Winchester West Central. Payne McLean added 11 points for North Mac.
Girls Basketball
Games of the Night
Springfield High 77, Lincoln 72, OT
Amiyah Rhinehouse scored five points in the extra period and helped provide the Senators with just enough separation as SHS pulled out a Central State Eight Conference win in overtime at Willard Duey Gymnasium.
Springfield High's Ariana Williams scored on an out-of-bounds play with 1.9 seconds to send the game to overtime.
Rhinehouse gave Springfield High 30 points overall and was one of four Senators to finish in double figures. Abigail Malit had 19 points for the Senators while Morgan Leininger and Williams each had 10 apiece.
Makinley Knapp led Lincoln with 23 points and Mia Clark netted 20 for the Railers. Piper Whiteman and Grace Schneider each finished with 11 for Lincoln.
Rochester 42, Lanphier 40
Delaney Farris scored six of her team-high 14 points in the fourth and the Rockets held on for a Central State Eight Conference victory.
The win snapped a four-game losing streak for Rochester (8-16 overall, 5-4 in the CS8).
Taylor Offer also added six of her 12 points in the fourth to hold off the Lions.
Lanphier (7-14, 2-6 CS8) got a game-high 18 points from freshman Amiyah Jarrett and 16 from junior Lovely Jackson. Jarrett had eight in the second and six in the fourth while Jackson scored seven in each of the final two periods. Lanphier has dropped four games in a row.
Stars of the Night
Meadow Gribbins/Angelina Ippolito, Kincaid South Fork/Edinburg: Gribbins scored 20 points and Ippolito had 19 as the Ponies topped White Hall North Greene 58-32 in nonconference action. Gribbins helped South Fork jump out to an 18-6 lead after one quarter when she jump-started the Ponies' effort with 10 points in the opening quarter. Ippolito had nine points in the third. Teammate Paisley Swinger had all five of her points in the first period.
Boys Swimming and Diving
Oliver Havey/Kishan Ugrappa/Riley Herr, Springfield High: Havey (50 and 500-yard freestyles) and Ugrappa (100 freestyle, 100 backstroke) won two events each and Herr was a winner in the 100 breaststroke as the Senators won the City meet with 149 points over Sacred Heart-Griffin (70) and Southeast (6) at Eisenhower Pool.
Andrew Kotner, Springfield High: The junior won the 1-meter diving competition with a score of 222.35 at the City meet.
James Maeda, Springfield High: The sophomore won the 100 butterfly and was on the winning 200 medley and 400 freestyle relays to help Springfield High win the City meet.
Monday, Jan. 27
Girls Basketball
Games of the Night
Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central 40, Carlinville 26
Aubrey Vogel totaled a game-high 14 points and the Bluejays (19-5) held Carlinville to just two field goals in the first half.
Vogel had seven points in the first half for a 12-8 halftime lead. Allison Vogel had six of her eight points in the second half, while Carson Arthalony added seven points.
Ruthie Reels led Carlinville with nine points. Hannah Gibson added eight.
South County/New Berlin 42, Gillespie 39 (OT)
Brielle Johnson and Callie Wagner each sank a 3-pointer in overtime to complete the comeback win.
South County trailed 27-23 by the end of the third quarter. Johnson, Wagner, Natalie Dennis, and Jacee Alexander each had seven points, while Jenna McGath went 5-for-6 from the free throw line to lead the Vipers with eight points.
Amari Vickery led the Miners with nine points. Mia Brawner had seven.
Stars of the Night
Taylor Keirs, North Mac: The senior guard amassed 27 points in a 50-22 win over Niantic Sangamon Valley/Buffalo Tri-City.
Anna Weber/Bailey Leach, Pleasant Plains: The duo combined for 27 points in a 48-28 win over Athens. Weber had a team-high 14 points and Leach had 13. Madison Burke added nine points.
Ava Bee, Athens: Bee led the Warriors with 12 points in the loss to Pleasant Plains.
Graysen Allen/Reese Megginson/Addison Wheatley, Auburn: Each player scored 11 points in a 50-45 win over Mason City Illini Central. Emme Divjak added nine points.

title: Grammy winners full list: Beyoncé, Kendrick Lamar, Chappell Roan take top awards
author: Clare Mulroy
description: Beyoncé won her first album of the year for "Cowboy Carter," plus Kendrick Lamar took home two "Big Four" awards. Here's every 2025 Grammy winner.
content:
Music's biggest night has concluded. In the "Big Four" categories of the 67th Grammy Awards, Chappell Roan was crowned best new artist and Kendrick Lamar took home both record of the year and song of the year.
Beyoncé and "Cowboy Carter" won both best country album and album of the year, the night's biggest award. She's the most decorated winner in Grammy history and lead with 11 nominations this year for "Cowboy Carter," but this is her first AOTY.
Who else took home a gramophone trophy? And who got snubbed? Here are the biggest winners of the night (in bold):

title: Springfield-based health system names new president and CEO
author: Claire Grant
description: The new president and CEO will be taking over for Ed Curtis, who has been with the health system since 1975.
content:
The new president and CEO of Memorial Health in Springfield has been announced.
The health system announced Mandy Eaton will be the new president and CEO beginning April 1. Eaton will take over for Ed Curtis who is retiring at the end of March.
Before coming to Memorial, Eaton served as executive vice president and chief operating officer of Cone Health, a non-profit healthcare organization that includes five hospitals and numerous outpatient locations serving a five-county area in North Carolina.
'I'm honored to be joining Memorial Health and looking forward to getting to know the organization and the communities it serves,' Eaton said in a news release. 'I'm impressed with Memorial Health's commitment to excellence, compassion and collaboration, and am excited to build upon the strong tradition that exists at Memorial.'
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Eaton holds her undergraduate and graduate degrees from the University of North Carolina, holding a Bachelor of Science degree in public health and a Master of Science degree in healthcare administration, before earning a doctorate degree in leadership studies from North Carolina A&T State University.
In March of 2024, Memorial Health president and chief executive officer Ed Curtis announced he would be retiring in 2025.
A Springfield native, Curtis spent his entire career with the health system, starting out as a register nurse at Springfield Memorial Hospital, then known as Memorial Medical Center, in 1975 before becoming president and CEO in 2008.
Memorial operates five hospitals located in Decatur, Jacksonville, Lincoln, Springfield and Taylorville, as well as 70 primary care, urgent care and specialty care clinics; behavioral health services; and home health services. It is based in Springfield.

Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon confirmed the identity of one person shot at a home just east of Petersburg Saturday.
Allmon, in a release issued around noon Tuesday, said that Richard Withers, 40, was pronounced clinically dead at 5:12 p.m. Sunday.
The Illinois State Police have not given an official update on the other person shot at the home in the 15000 block of Tice Road just after noon on Saturday.
On a Facebook post, the PORTA School District invited its students to wear "camo" clothing in support of the Withers family.
PORTA Superintendent Shannon Duling said counselors were deployed throughout the district's schools, along with some therapy dogs.

Allmon said an autopsy will be scheduled.
The death remains under investigation.

title: Indiana shouldn't want Illinois' poor counties
author: Michael J. Hicks
description: No, Indiana doesn't really want these Illinois counties — though it is easy to see why Illinois might not want them either.
content:
If Illinois' secessionist counties were their own state, it would be the second-poorest state in the union, right between Mississippi and West Virginia.
| Contributing Columnist
Show Caption
It is hard to resist trolling Illinois, especially Chicago. I've done so myself on occasion.
After all, Chicago is a city with too many governance flaws to list in a single column. But it also enjoys a few strengths. The Chicago metro area is bigger, richer, better educated and its workers substantially more productive than Indiana as a whole.
Still, it's fun to troll a place like Chicago, and Indiana House Speaker Todd Huston, who must be ranked among the most serious and effective legislative leaders in the country, did so earlier this month. The story is worth telling.
Many downstate Illinois residents dislike Chicago's strong influence in the state. Last year, a total of 33 counties voted to secede from Illinois and form their own state. Huston invited those counties to join Indiana. He even created a commission to study the possibility.
That's first-rate trolling.
I thought it'd be fun to think through the prospect of Indiana picking up these 33 counties. Would it be good for Indiana? Would it be good for those counties? Would it be good for the remaining 69 Illinois counties?
Which Illinois counties would Indiana get?
The "secessionist" counties in Illinois are in the southern part of the state, with many bordering Indiana. This one-third of counties comprise only 6.6% of the Illinois population, and only 4% of the state's economy.
Per capita income in the secessionist counties is $54,381. If it were a separate state, it would be the second-poorest state in the union, sliding right in between Mississippi and West Virginia. The remaining counties in Illinois have a per capita income of $73,228.
Adding the secessionist counties to Indiana would cut our per capita income enough for us to move from 14th to 11th place from the bottom. Only 18.6% of adults in these counties have completed college, while the Illinois total is 36.7%. This new post-secession Indiana would instantly be the least well-educated state, and would be right about where the U.S. as a whole was in the late 1980s.
Economic growth in the secessionist counties has been at about half the rate of the rest of Illinois so far this century. And, while the rest of Illinois has experienced very modest population growth of about 1.4%, these secessionist counties have lost a whopping 5.2% of their population.
If the secessionist parts of Illinois were their own state, they'd have the worst 25 years of population loss of any state in U.S. history. So, it's pretty easy to see why these counties might be unhappy about their economic conditions. They are truly dismal.
Bad vibes borne of ignorance
But how much of this is the fault of Illinois state government? After all, the other Illinois counties are doing much better. That includes Chicago, where the economy continues to be robust, even as population growth has stalled. Is it possible that these counties are somehow being robbed of economic opportunity by Illinois?
Nope. As it turns out, these counties are essentially welfare queens of the state of Illinois.
A pair of researchers at Southern Illinois University's Paul Simon Public Policy Institute publish reports every couple years on the flow of public budgets across Illinois. This very detailed work by John Jackson and John Foster makes it possible to see where the tax dollars are flowing across Illinois. And, for what it is worth, that is very much like a study I did for Indiana more than a decade ago with colleagues Dagney Faulk and John Ketzenberger.
As it turns out, residents in these secessionist counties pay about $2,986 per person each year in state taxes. That would make them the fourth lowest-taxed residents in the nation. But here's the rub: They receive $5,430 per person each year in support from residents of the other 69 Illinois counties.
In contrast, the rest of the state collects $4,485 in state taxes each year and gets back $4,217 per person in state spending. So, each resident of the secessionist counties gets $2,444 more state dollars spent in their county each year than they pay in taxes. On top of that, they pay only 66.6 cents for every dollar of taxes residents in the other 69 Illinois counties pay.
Federal taxes and spending tell a similar story. A recent study of mine calculated the share of taxes and transfer payments made at the county level to the federal government. You guessed it, the secessionist counties pay a lower federal tax rate, but receive more in Social Security payments and in other types of transfers (TANF, SNAP, etc.) than the counties that did not vote to secede from Illinois.
Rural voters are failing themselves
There are some useful lessons here.
First, the secessionist counties of Illinois pay low state taxes but are beneficiaries of enormous transfers from the rest of Illinois. It is hard to pinpoint just what these Illinois secessionist counties are angry about. Most likely it is bad vibes borne of ignorance. There's compelling evidence of that.
If they do come to Indiana, Hoosier taxpayers will need to pony up almost $2 billion more per year to match the fiscal largesse those secessionist counties receive from the rest of Illinois. It is worth noting that those taxes are going to come primarily from urban areas, like Fishers, Carmel and Indianapolis.
So, no, we don't really want them — though it is easy to see why Illinois might not want them either.
Second, neither the red state and blue state models of rural development have worked. The secessionist counties of Illinois look just like 40 or 50 declining rural counties in Indiana. Both Illinois and Indiana policymakers are failing their rural counties, though most of the blame for economic decline belongs squarely with the voters of those rural counties.
Finally, the real political divisions in America are geographic. So far this century, a whopping half of all the population growth this century has occurred in just 75 out of 3,143 U.S. counties, or 2.3%. Fully 45% of U.S. counties have lost population this century.
This deep economic divergence has gripped the U.S. for four decades. It is not between red or blue states, or places with high taxes or woke policies. It is primarily between urban and non-urban counties, and reflects the desire of most Americans to live in places with strong local public services — great schools, low crime and businesses that offer a mix of goods and services.
Places that offer these do well; those that do not will look more and more like rural Illinois.
Michael J. Hicks is the director of the Center for Business and Economic Research and the George and Frances Ball distinguished professor of economics in the Miller College of Business at Ball State University.

title: County board OKs $10M Massey settlement; critics say it was 'woefully inadequate'
author: Steven Spearie
description: The agreement to the payout comes a little over seven months since the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey.
content:
The case was mediated by a retired Illinois judge.
A Sangamon County administrator said taxes won't be raised for the payout.
Some criticized the settlement as 'woefully inadequate.'
The Sangamon County Board unanimously agreed to a $10 million out-of-court mediated settlement with the estate of Sonya Massey.
The dollar amount, worked out last week in sessions last week in Chicago, was quickly criticized by some board members and Massey family supporters, though they hoped the settlement would move the family forward in the grieving process.
Sontae Massey, a cousin to Sonya Massey, who was fatally shot in her home by a Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy, said he was "disgusted" by the proceeding and left with his fiancée, Margaritta Fultz, before the vote.
Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represented the Massey family, has a scheduled news conference Wednesday morning. Crump will be joined by members of the Massey family.
Crump was also expected to address legislative efforts of State Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, to strengthen background checks and increase transparency in law enforcement hiring.
Sangamon County Assistant State's Attorney Joel Benoit and two outside attorneys represented the county. The settlement was mediated by retired state judge Kay Hanlon, who is employed by ADR Systems.
Sean P. Grayson, who responded to Massey's home in an unincorporated area of a Springfield neighborhood, shot Massey, a Black woman and the mother of two children, in the face.
Grayson was charged with first-degree murder and remains jailed.
Massey would have turned 37 years old Wednesday.
The settlement, said County Administrator Brian McFadden, will be paid through cash reserves.
The county has 100 funds which have reserves, he said.
"We will not be raising taxes. We will not be issuing additional debt. We will not be cutting services," McFadden insisted.
Marc Ayers, a Democrat who represents District 12, said the payout, believed to be the largest in Sangamon County history, was "woefully inadequate."
"I am pleased how quickly this did come to a settlement and that the family did sign off on the settlement," Ayers said. "I'm at least pleased that there is an end in sight for the family and that they might be able to move on somehow. We shouldn't have been here in the first place and that is the pressing thing about tonight's vote."
Teresa Haley of Haley & Associates also didn't think the settlement was enough.
"Sonya's life was worth so much more because this part of her life, that history, this legacy will go on for generations to experience," she said.
"How can you provide restitution or make whole someone or family that has experienced a significant loss?" asked Reggie Guyton, who was sworn in as a new board member representing District 21. "There's no way to make whole when someone has been needlessly, senselessly taken."
While the settlement is a start, Guyton acknowledged, "we need to consider there is much distrust, much hurt that a community at large is feeling and we have an obligation to make things right."
Ayers hoped it was a wakeup call to the community, to attend more county board and Massey Commission meetings.
"We owe it to taxpayers and the Massey family to not stop this fight and to continue these reforms wherever we can," he said.
Guyton appointed to the board
Guyton, an actor and singer, now represents which encompasses the south-central part of Springfield.
Guyton's predecessor, Clyde Bunch, was recognized as the longest-serving county board member in Illinois when he died on Dec. 3. Bunch was first elected to the board in 1978.
Turner presented a proclamation about Bunch from Gov. JB Pritzker to the board.
Guyton has been vocal in calling for police reform.
"I feel I can provide a different perspective and hopefully sway the board to make some choices that are beneficial in the long run," Guyton said Monday, prior to the Massey Commission meeting. "I think people know me as at least thoughtful.
"We have to do work, and I want to dig in."

title: Springfield coffeehouse offers plenty of variety with favorable prices
author: Kathryn Rem
description: This Springfield coffeehouse has a variety of coffees, teas and smoothies to go along with some baked goods.
content:
Name: Stella Coffee & Tea
Address: 1135 W. Governor St.
Phone: 262-622-3151
Website: stellacoffeetea.com
Credit/debit cards accepted: Yes
Hours: 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Monday through Saturday
Item price range: $2.74-$3.50
My order: Stella is a neighborhood coffeehouse where one can tuck into a chair or sofa and stay comfortably for a long time. There's a variety of coffees, teas and smoothies, plus a limited number of baked goods. I had a sweet cinnamon chai tea with almond milk and my friend had Draco Puerto Rican coffee, both satisfying. We split slices of spinach bake, sausage-egg bake and a cherry scone (each $3.50). The sausage-egg bake was the best; the others seemed slightly old.
Likes: Special events and activities abound here. There are musicians, speakers, poets, craft demos, workshops, a book club and more. Patrons can play board games and puzzles and use coloring books, all on hand. The decor is warm, inviting and quirky. And there are no disposable utensils or dishes used.

title: No. 3 Williamsville boys basketball reloads thanks to reunited group of senior guards
author: Bill Welt
description: There are familiar names, and a new one or two, for the Williamsville boys basketball team, which has reloaded after just missing out on last year's state championship
content:
AI-assisted summary
Blake Shoufler, starting point guard for the Williamsville Bullets, is back after a broken ankle sidelined him for most of his junior season.
Senior guard Carson Doran has also been instrumental in Williamsville's success, averaging a team-high 14.7 points and 6 rebounds per game.
Doran transferred to Williamsville from Chatham Glenwood and has played travel basketball with Shoufler since the fourth grade.
WILLIAMSVILLE — The Williamsville boys basketball team made its second state finals appearance last season — sans starting point guard Blake Shoufler.
Shoufler was averaging a team-best 15.9 points and 4 assists per game until his junior season was halted by a broken ankle in December. It would be another nine months and uncountable hours of rehabilitation and training until his next game.
'When you go out with an injury like that,' Shoufler said, 'it sucks and you can't go out there and play. But you can still contribute to the team. I tried my best by being the coach and that also played to my advantage when I came back. Being a point guard, you're already kind of the coach on the floor, so I got a different perspective.'
Impact players: Here are the top breakout performers in boys basketball around Springfield
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Shoufler said he had to settle in at first this winter but is now shining, with averages of 14.4 points, 5.2 assists, 3.1 rebounds and 1.7 steals per game this season as the Bullets (24-2, 6-0 Sangamo Conference) are once again among the top ranked teams in Class 2A — now No. 3 in the latest Associated Press poll — with a replenished backcourt that also includes senior guards Carson Doran and Brayden Saling, The State Journal-Register's reigning Small School Boys Basketball Player of the Year.
'We've had a target on our back all year and we've shown that we can handle anything thrown our way,' Shoufler said. 'Hopefully we can finish off strong.'
Another big addition
Shoufler has always been all about basketball with his dad, Clay.
The former Milford High School and Illinois College point guard regularly served as Shoufler's travel ball coach at B.I.G. Time until last summer due to the injury.
Shoufler's physical therapy program included visiting a specialist in St. Louis every two weeks for the first five months of recovery.
'Ever since I was born and played basketball,' Shoufler said, 'I've always been in that point guard role and learning from (his father). He coached my travel basketball team, so he's kind of passed down those coaching thoughts to me.'
'A true North Side kid': Meet Lanphier's star forward Shaun Hatchett Jr.
Doran has also provided a good measure of respite.
Shoufler said Doran sometimes steps in at point guard, but his teammate does so much more. Doran averages a team-high 14.7 points, 6 rebounds, 3.5 assists and 1.4 steals per game.
Doran starred in the Sangamon County Tournament championship game and generated a game-high 17 points with five 3-pointers in a 32-29 loss to Auburn, currently ranked No. 4 in 2A.
'Whatever they need me to do, I just try to do that to the best of my ability and help the team win,' Doran said.
Doran transferred from Chatham Glenwood but has been acquainted with Shoufler through B.I.G. Time since fourth grade. That travel ball team also included Saling and senior forward Reid Bodine — not to mention Pleasant Plains senior standout Cooper Schallenberg and Maroa-Forsyth senior Mitch Williams.
Doran said the chemistry was already there.
'It's been amazing this year,' Doran said, 'just playing with my boys is a great feeling.'

title: New bill seeks more thorough review of officer candidates' past employment
author: Steven Spearie
description: An Illinois Senator has introduced two measures in response to the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey last year.
content:
A bill would require law enforcement agencies to conduct a more thorough review of a prospective officer's past employment.
The proposed measures come months after the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey.
State Senator Doris Turner, D-Springfield, has introduced two measures in response to the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield last July.
Senate Bill 1953 would require law enforcement agencies to conduct a more comprehensive review of a prospective officer's past employment to ensure that candidate is physically and psychologically fit for duty.
The proposed legislation would include the creation of sheriff's merit boards and sheriff's merit commissions for counties with a population of at least 75,000.
Turner's Senate Bill 1954 would allow the recall of a countywide elected official to be put on the ballot by either the county board or a petition.
The recall would then go on the ballot for voters to approve. It must be passed by a simple majority.
'Since that fatal day, I have worked with state and county officials, law enforcement and community members to ensure this doesn't happen again," said Turner, who grew up knowing members of the Massey family.
Former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy Sean P. Grayson, 30, of Riverton has been charged with first-degree murder, in the shooting of Massey in her face inside of her home.
Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman, had called 911 because of a possible prowler.
Massey had been the subject of a mental health call in Springfield just hours before the fatal shooting.
In the aftermath of the shooting, Turner and county board chairman Andy Van Meter helped create the Massey Commission to address systemic issues in law enforcement practices, mental health responses and community relations.
Both legislative efforts came directly from the commission, Turner said.
Grayson's hiring by the county in 2023 has come into question. His criminal history includes two DUIs before he became a police officer and a separation from the U.S. Army that listed "misconduct (serious offense)" as the reason.
People also have questioned the number of agencies Grayson worked for before coming to Sangamon County and the way he was hired. One of Grayson's references was longtime deputy Scott Butterfield, the father of Grayson's now-fiancée.
Sangamon County Sheriff Paula Crouch, hired in September after the retirement of Sheriff Jack Campbell, implemented a four-person merit commission and a mandate that investigators review records in person if an applicant worked at another law enforcement agency.
The merit commission would review the written test scores of applicants and recommend if the sheriff should proceed with the background process. It would also determine whether the applicant goes on the merit list.
On Jan. 13, the Sangamon County Board voted down recall for the office of sheriff over a recommendation by the Massey Commission.
'I've been committed to making the necessary changes to ensure our community has trust in those who are elected to serve,' said Turner. 'My hope is that the legislation will honor Sonya's life by showing our commitment to enhancing that trust.'
Turner's measures await committee assignments in the Senate.

title: Pittsfield girls basketball withdraws from Williamsville Regional tourney after accident
author: Bill Welt
description: Pittsfield girls basketball will not play in the local regional tournament, but the superintendent provided positive news for two players after tragedy
content:
The Pittsfield girls basketball team will not participate in the upcoming Class 2A Williamsville Regional following a fatal accident, the school's superintendent announced on Facebook on Friday.
A freshman on the team, Reese Ramsey, was killed in a motor vehicle collision on Tuesday, according to reports. A 68-year-old woman from Pittsfield also died in the crash.
Two other members of the team were airlifted from the scene, Muddy River News reported. Pittsfield superintendent Todd Fox said on social media that freshman Lincoln McCartney was released from hospital care on Thursday, while sophomore Deeghan Allen remains at HSHS St. John's Hospital but walked unassisted for the first time on Friday.
The team will not play in the postseason after being directly involved in the decision on Friday morning, Fox said.
'There is no wrong or right in this situation, and this decision needs to be supported,' Fox said.
Pittsfield, a No. 3 seed, was scheduled to play its regional semifinal on Monday. Saturday's quarterfinal winner between No. 6 Sacred Heart-Griffin and No. 12 Riverton advances to the regional final, the IHSA confirmed on Saturday.

title: Historic Decatur theater announces closure
author: Claire Grant
description: One of Decatur's last family-owned theaters is closing and ending its over 100-year history, following the death of the venue's owner.
content:
One of Decatur's last family-owned theaters is closing and ending its over 100-year history, following the death of the venue's owner.
The Avon Theatre posted to social media on Feb. 11 the death of owner Skip Huston on Jan. 31.
The movie theater has been also handling an accumulation of debt. Citing the debt and the death of Huston, the family-owned theater is planning to shutter doors.
A planned closure has not been announced; the line connected to the business office of the Avon has been disconnected for incoming calls.
'The Avon Theatre wasn't just a business—it was a home for our family,' the theater posted to social media. 'Thank you for all the years of support. This is the end of an unforgettable chapter, but the memories we've made here will live on forever.'
Huston was a movie aficionado in his family's words, who called him a community treasure and lifelong movie enthusiast. Following his death and memorial services, in lieu of flowers the family set up a GoFundMe for funeral and other costs.
'Despite the incredible support from our community through GoFundMe,' The theater posted online. 'The financial burden was just too great. This was the hardest decision we have had to make, and it marks the end of an era.'
The theater first opened in 1916 as Kerasotes Theater - a spot for Vaudeville acts in central Illinois before changing hands several times, and landing in the hands of the Huston family since 1999.
When opened, Avon Theatre had one of the largest screening walls for a theater outside of Chicago borders, making it a unique staple in the central Illinois region.
Under Huston and his wife Susan, two adjacent storefronts were added to the theater for smaller screening rooms.

title: 'Critical moment in history': Protests across US today target Trump, Musk
author: John Bacon
description: Discontent has intensified across the nation as the administration moves to lay off thousands of federal workers.
content:
Groups opposed to President Donald Trump's agenda and his top adviser Elon Musk converged on cities across the nation Monday to express outrage with slogans such as "Not My President's Day" and "No King's Day."
The rallies, led by the 50501 Movement and other organizations, come less than two weeks after the last round of widespread rallies and street marches.
"We witness, with growing alarm, how our constitutional rights are trampled upon, how the authority of the President is being usurped by those who seek to consolidate power for personal gain," 50501 said in a statement on its website. "Meanwhile, President Trump systematically dismantles thevery guardrails designed to ensure accountability across the branches of government."
The 50501 Movement − 50 states, 50 protests, one day − was started by grassroots organizers spreading the word on Reddit forums, Instagram, Bluesky, Discord and other social websites. 50501 has 115,000 members on its Reddit page.
Developments:
∎ Thousands gathered to protest outside the U.S. Capitol, waving flags, carrying protest placards and chanting "This is what democracy looks like!"
∎ In New York City, hundreds of protesters marched behind a banner reading "Stop the GOP coup" and chanted several slogans, including "No one elected Elon Musk!"
∎ In Texas, a crowd gathered in Austin chanting "Hey hey, ho ho, Elon Musk has got to go!" and "No justice, no peace!"
∎ In Colorado, a few dozen protesters gathered outside Rocky Mountain National Park carrying signs such as "I speak for the trees" and chanting "No king, no crown, we the people won't back down."
NAACP group holds 'buy in' demonstration
In Denver, the Rocky Mountain chapter of the NAACP held a "buy in" at a Costco store, drawing at least 30 supporters who went shopping to their support for the company's decision to maintain its commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion. NAACP is a nonpartisan civil rights group.
Group supporters posed for photos amidst big-screen TVs, and said they hoped Costco noticed the increased spending following their visit.
"This isn't a Black thing. This isn't a white thing. It's a green thing," said Portia Prescott, the regional president. "One power we do have in America is buying power. Diversity brings income to corporations. We need to make sure corporations understand how valuable diversity is."
– Trevor Hughes
Florida protestors shout 'Who keeps us safe?'
In Tallahassee, dozens protested in front of the Florida Historic Capitol building. It was one of at least 15 planned protests expected across Florida on Monday.
The protesters in Tallahassee, some as young as teenagers to others in their late 60s, held signs and chanted "Who keeps us safe? We keep us safe!"
Among them was 16-year-old Leah Terrazas who held a sign and shouted at passing cars to join them. The teen said it is important to use their voice to fight for change.
"I'm here because I care about my family who are immigrants and have lived in this country and provided so much for this country," said Terrazas, who stood alongside her mother and father. "For my mother and every other woman in my family who deserves to feel safe in their own home, in their own country."
Another protester, Phil Pouliot, 66, a former state park ranger held a sign that said, "Keep your paws off my national parks."
"We want to pass down the country the way we remember it," said Pouliot, wearing his state park jacket. "Our number one principle is to protect the resources. Secondary is allowing (the) public to have access to the resources."
– Alicia Devine, Tallahassee Democrat
'Our leaders here can listen to us'
More than 100 people chanted "Stop the coup" and "No dictators" outside Cincinnati's City Hall in freezing temps Monday to make sure their concerns about Trump and Musk were seen and heard.
Protest organizers said while Trump and Musk obviously weren't in attendance, they had to start somewhere.
"We wanted to make sure people in Cincinnati have a voice, to make sure our leaders here can listen to us as well, to channel all this energy into their actions," said protest organizer Jack Cunningham, 26, a Democratic activist from nearby Clifton, Ohio.
Protester Veronica Bishop, 58, of Finneytown, Ohio, said she's concerned about how much influence Musk has with overseeing the Department of Government Efficiency or DOGE. The agency is spearheading the Trump administration's effort to downsize the government and has backed thousands of federal workers losing their jobs.
"It's like where are the checks and balances?" Bishop said. "How can a private citizen have so much power in our government?"
However, Hamilton County (Ohio) Republican Party Chairman Russell Mock said there is nothing unusual in a president having an adviser like Musk.
"I don't know how this is a dictatorship," Mock said. "I don't think people understand what that means. We held a lawful election in November. President Trump won, overwhelmingly. And he's doing exactly what he said he's going to do."
– Scott Wartman, Cincinnati Enquirer
Angst intensifies as Trump eliminates federal jobs
The movement has emphatically opposed Trump's executive orders, such as cracking down on illegal immigration and pardoning people involved in the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol. The group also seeks reinstatement of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion efforts.
Discontent has intensified as the administration moves to lay off thousands of federal workers in an effort to shrink government and cut costs.
"We stand firm at a critical moment in history, demanding that the American people be heard andthat the White House be governed by the true will of the people, not by a tech billionaire whoseeks to buy influence and control," the group said in a statement on its website.
Protesters want to 'take back the flag'
The 50501 group, in a social media post, urged protesters to wave an American flags "like your life depended on it." They suggested protesters wear blue because it represents "vigilance, perseverance, and justice." The post said the protesters were trying to save the country because they love it.
"If you have any American flags or patriotic apparel, bring them and wave them proudly,," the post said. "It's an excellent way to take back our flag."
Sen. Hollen to join Annapolis rally
U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said he would attend the rally in Annapolis. Van Hollen attacked "Trump and Musk's efforts to harm the merit-based civil service in order to implement a system of political cronyism."
Van Hollen said he will express his commitment to fight for federal workers and "defend critical services to the American people under threat by the Trump-Musk Administration."
Similar protests were held Feb. 5. In Washington, protests near the U.S. Capitol drew hundreds bearing signs and shouting dissent. The protesters marched from streets around the Capitol to the Department of Labor building on Constitution Avenue − where Elon Musk's DOGE officials were visiting for the day. Musk, a staunch Trump ally, has been executing Trump's cost-cutting initiative to reduce the size of the U.S. government.

title: 'It's a lot of fun that we get to have him around.' Springfield WWII veteran turns 105
author: Steven Spearie
description: Bob Dyson served in World War II, building runways in Burma and India. Dyson celebrated his 105th birthday on Sunday in Springfield.
content:
Dyson is one of a little more than 2,500 World War II veterans living in Illinois.
Among the sports he played were golf, bowling and fast-pitch softball.
A few years ago, Monica Dyson recalled missing a birthday party for her grandfather, George Robert "Bob" Dyson of Springfield, who had just turned 100 years old.
She had been around a co-worker who was diagnosed with COVID and was unsure if she had it herself.
"My dad's comment was, 'It's fine, you'll get the next (birthday party)," Monica Dyson said. "We laughed, but that was three years ago, and here we are all, still. It's a lot of fun that we get to have him around."
Sunday marked the 105th birthday for Bob Dyson, a lifelong resident of Springfield.
Four generations of family members attended a small get-together at Cedarhurst of Springfield with pizza and cake.
Dyson, a former construction worker and home builder, still begins his day with 'Bob's Breakfast'—a toasted muffin with butter, grape jelly, and bacon, alongside two cups of coffee—and stays sharp by reading by reading The State Journal-Register and working crossword puzzles.
His secret to a long life? "Take it easy, love your neighbor and love yourself."
Dyson's son, Robert George "Bob" Dyson," said longevity is in the genes. Dyson's mother lived to be 95. An uncle lived to be 102.
Bob Dyson, 81, said his father was always into sports. He bowled in several leagues, including one with his wife, Alice, who passed away in 1990, and played in a fast-pitch softball church league.
Another son, Kirk Dyson, said his father also coached his brother and him in youth baseball.
Later in life, Dyson took up golf, playing in a league at Bunn Park. Bob Dyson said his father still follows the professional golf on TV, especially rooting for Jordan Spieth.
Dyson worked for both Vrendenburgh Home Builders and von Behren Builder after the war. He went to school with and was lifelong friends with Bob von Behren.
A couple of years ago, the director at Cedarhurst put together a luncheon for Dyson's birthday.
"People started showing up," Bob Dyson recalled. "Four or five people from the American Legion in uniform, from the VFW. Mayor (Jim) Langfelder came. He brought a proclamation.
"Dad sat there and said (to the mayor), 'I knew your dad (former Springfield Mayor Ossie Langfelder). I worked on your dad's house. We both lived on Whittier Avenue.'
"Dad built the house on Whittier and that's where we grew up. (Back then) there were only three houses on the block (between Outer Park and Lenox) because it was all new. There were (farm) fields (to the south)."
After graduating from Springfield High School, Dyson served in the U.S. Army, building runways in Burma (the present-day Myanmar) and India.
Bob Dyson said he didn't know if his father was the oldest living military veteran in Springfield, but he has a pretty good claim.
According to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, a little over 66,000 Americans who served in World War II were still living as of 2024. Some 16.4 million Americans served in the war.
There are 2,531 WWII veterans living in Illinois.

title: Building of closed popular steakhouse in Springfield has been sold. Here's what we know
author: Claire Grant
description: The sale of the closed steakhouse in Springfield was one of just multiple commercial buildings sold in Sangamon County last month.
content:
One of Springfield's closed steakhouses may be repurposed very soon, according to recent Sangamon County records.
Here's what we know.
What building was sold?
The property of Alexander's Steakhouse was sold.
Who bought the building?
The property was bought by an independent buyer. The name of the buyer has not been released at this time.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
When was the building sold?
The building at 620 N. Bruns Lane was reported as sold on Jan. 16, 2025, according to Sangamon County property sales. The building was one of nine commercial and retail locations sold throughout the month.
How much was it sold for?
According to the documents, the 5,000 square foot building was sold for $825,000 and was previously listed on both Coldwell Banker as well as Realty.com.
When did Alexander's Steakhouse close?
Alexander's Steakhouse closed after nearly 40 years of operation on Feb. 29, 2024.
Why did the steakhouse close?
President of Mercedes Restaurants Ron Helms, which owns Alexander's Steakhouse, cited poor customer retention, inflation of service costs and competition between other steakhouses.
What other commercial buildings sold last month?
These buildings, but not necessarily the businesses inside, were sold in January.
