title: Springfield teacher remembered as one who went above and beyond for students' success
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A longtime Springfield teacher known for helping her students go above and beyond died after a battle with leukemia. She was 46.
content:
(This story was updated to correct a misspelling/typo.)
Lauren Engelke-Smith is largely remembered as a special education teacher and educator who always went the extra mile for her students.
The 46-year-old teacher died Monday after a battle with leukemia that was initially diagnosed in 2021.
Kris White commented on Engelke-Smith's online obituary, sharing that her grandson JaTron Bevly, who has dyslexia, would not be where is today if his teacher had not pushed and encouraged him.
'Despite his struggles with learning, he will be graduating from college in a year and getting to play the sport he loves, football,' White wrote. 'Some people told him he was too small to play college football. Lauren said 'don't listen to them. You can do it if you really try.' Thank you, Lauren, for your belief in your students and everyone else.'
Bevly also made the Dean's list. He will be graduating from Lakeland University in Plymouth, Wisconsin, this year.
Bevly was paired with Engelke-Smith in a resource class from grades six through eight at Washington Middle School, White said.
For their first two years together, Bevly complained that his teacher was always assigning him too much work, but by the third year, Bevly wrote Engelke-Smith a letter thanking her, to which she cried tears of joy, White said.
White, a former public education teacher herself, emphasized that Engelke-Smith was interested in figuring out how each individual student learns. Engelke-Smith found solutions for Bevly such as utilizing books on tape for reading assignments, and in seeking smaller schools and smaller class sizes as he graduated to high school and college. She was part of the reason that White chose to place Bevly at Sacred Heart-Griffin, and why he chose the university that he did.
This story is no anomaly to Engelke-Smith's family and the Lauren that they knew. She was simply a person who liked to help people, they said.
The family was grieving in anticipation of funeral services, but they sat around the kitchen table, sharing stories and laughing about the memories. They appreciated Engelke-Smith's sense of humor.
She also held a passion for haunted houses and paranormal activities, and she was active with her church.
Her husband, Aaron Smith, lovingly remembered his wife's blue eyes, which their daughter, Ebby, partly inherited.
The table was stacked with photographs, letters, and newspaper clippings, all helping to tell who Engelke-Smith was.
'She went to every one of his football games,' Smith said, referring to Bevly. He held a framed photograph of Bevly and Engelke-Smith at a football game and one at a graduation.
She also advocated for Individualized Education Plans for her students, the family said. She helped parents through that process, and she stood up for them if there was any issue with administration.
'She got in trouble with admin more than once,' Smith said. 'She cared about the kids; she didn't care about rules.'
Chelsey Ziebler, Principal at Jefferson Middle School, where Engelke-Smith most recently worked, wrote in an email that 'Mrs. Smith was an extraordinary educator whose unwavering dedication to her special education students left a lasting impact on everyone she encountered. With a warm smile and an open heart, she created a nurturing environment where each child felt valued and understood. ... She believed in their potential, celebrating every small victory with enthusiasm and encouragement, fostering their confidence both academically and socially. Her legacy lives on in the countless lives she touched, inspiring her students to dream big and believe in themselves.'
Engelke-Smith taught special education for both Springfield and Ball-Chatham Schools among others over the last 17 years or so. She earned her master's degree from the University of Illinois Springfield. She also was a vice principal at Beardstown. She is originally from Maryland, and moved to Springfield after having met Smith, who is from southern Illinois.
Services are being held this week. Memorial contributions are being accepted to: Lauren Engelke-Smith memorial for her children's college fund.

title: New sheriff in town: County board officially approves Crouch nomination
author: Steven Spearie
description: Sangamon County Board chairman Andy Van Meter cited Paula Crouch's \
content:
Show Caption
A nearly 25-year veteran of policing will officially take the reins of the Sangamon County Sheriff's Department.
In doing so, Paula Crouch breaks the glass ceiling, becoming the county's first female sheriff. Two of the seven finalists were females.
Crouch's nomination was approved by the county board at a special meeting at the Bank of Springfield Center Wednesday.
There was further history when the board officially adopted a resolution establishing the Massey Commission in the aftermath of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey by a former sheriff's deputy who now faces murder charges.
The Massey Commission held its first public listening session on Monday.
An amendment to the resolution which would have put in place some additional hiring criteria and processes of sheriff's deputies and correctional officers was tabled as were resolutions entering into agreements with a communications company and a consulting firm as part of the commission.
Restoring trust
Crouch, 51, was sworn in by Seventh Circuit Judge Raylene Grischow as her husband, Robert, the police chief of Riverton, and her two sons looked on.
Crouch held multiple roles with the Springfield Police Department from 1999 to 2023, including serving as the Sangamon/Menard County Crime Stoppers coordinator, a neighborhood patrol officer and a detective.
Crouch was also assigned to the Child Advocacy Center before her retirement, where she investigated cases of child abuse.
Board chairman Andy Van Meter cited her "incredible breadth of experience with almost every aspect of policing and managing."
Van Meter downplayed any notions that the process was rushed, but did note that Coroner Jim Allmon was serving as temporary sheriff and was trying to run two offices.
Public speakers had hopes for Crouch, from restoring trust in the community to addressing hiring practices to being visible to the Black community.
Crouch succeeds Sheriff Jack Campbell, who declined to step down in the weeks after Massey's shooting, then retired on Aug. 9.
"There is a lack of trust in this community in this department and in police in general, so restoring that trust (is paramount)," said Jenna Broom.
Nepotism and hiring practices in the sheriff's department are also big problems, Broom said.
Grayson, who was hired on in Sangamon County in 2023, has been accused of being a "nepo" hire after he used his fiancée's father, former county deputy Scott Butterfield, as a reference.
Deputy hires up to this point should be reviewed, Broom said.
Teresa Haley said the new sheriff should willing to meet with the Black community on a regular basis.
"The Black community is a big part of this community," Haley said. "If we are one Springfield, one community, then our voices must be heard, and I don't believe they're being heard."
While lauding Crouch's extensive background in areas like child forensics, hostage negotiation and community policing, Breonna Roberts said she was concerned about the absence of some critical training areas.
"There was no mention de-escalation techniques, crisis intervention or cultural competency, which are issues we've mention repeatedly as things that we need to implement in our sheriff's department," Roberts said. "How do we know she's committed to integrating these essential components into her leadership?
"This isn't a statement of opposition, but a reflection of apprehension because I still think we need a leader who can build a more community-centered, compassionate and equitable department."
Hiring amendment tabled
A proposed amendment that would have addressed temporarily some of the issues critics pointed out about the Grayson hiring was tabled.
It would have put department and Sangamon County Deputy Merit Commission eyes on applications and background check information for deputies and other hires.
In addition to the normal background check, the joint review would FOIA the personnel files of any current or past employers
It also addressed applicants' convictions for DUI or other Class A misdemeanors.
Grayson had two DUIs on his record.
While well-intentioned, Van Meter said the proposal was "inimical to the spirit of the Massey Commission. The concept behind the Massey Commission is to let it do its work and make its recommendations, not to have this board suggest or propose what solutions it may choose to adopt."
Board member Marc Ayers argued the proposal "was a common-sense thing."
"We found out through FOIA and through the press about Sean Grayson," he added. "What a shameful moment in this county's history (voting this down)."

title: Video puts suspect car at the scene of 2021 triple homicide in Springfield neighborhood
author: Steven Spearie
description: A detective testified a Springfield man was in the home where a triple homicide took place hours before victim's fiancée.
content:
Video obtained by Springfield Police from several residences around a house in the 2500 block of South 10th where three people were found fatally shot on Aug. 9, 2021, showed one of the suspect's vehicles around it near the purported time of the shooting.
The vehicle, a Mercury Milan, was totaled when it was driven by Taylor Rosenberger, the girlfriend of Joseph Hembrough, at Fifth Street and South Grand Avenue three days after the homicide, a Springfield detective testified at in Sangamon County court Thursday.
Larry McClain Jr. of Springfield and Kelton Galmore of Jacksonville are standing trial for the murders of Savante English, 27, and Keyera Gant, 25, of Springfield, and Bryant K. Williams, 27, of Houston, who were all shot multiple times in a house being rented by English.
A Morgan County detective testified that two firearms, including a Polymer 80, commonly known as a "ghost gun," were found at Hembrough's Jacksonville residence via a search warrant a month after the murders.
Hembrough pleaded guilty last week and was sentenced to 20 years in the Illinois Department of Corrections and a three-year mandatory supervised release term.
Hembrough is expected to testify against McLain and Galmore.
Springfield Police Det. Jason Sloman said he was asked to canvass for "anything that could help the case. The video from private residences was collected from across English's home, along Oberlin Avenue, Bryn Mawr Boulevard and Eighth and Ninth streets.
Video played for the seven-man, five-woman jury shows the vehicle turning west on Bryn Mawr at 12:58 a.m. on Aug. 9. Timestamps show it was in the area as late at 1:51 a.m.
Earlier Thursday, Springfield Police Sgt. Adam Westlake testified to responding to the two-car crash involving the Mercury Milan.
The car sustained front end damage and caught fire. The car was towed and Rosenberger, Sloman said, signed the car over to the tow company.
Springfield Police Sgt. Michael Fannin acknowledged the car was processed in relation to the crime, though a report memorializing that went missing.
Fannin said log records survived.
Sloman testified the one other person, Letravian Medley of Springfield, was in the house before Williams' fiancée, Shunderika Price on Aug. 9.
Medley was in the house around 10:30 or 11 a.m., about three hours before Price stopped by there.
Medley testified to that effect Wednesday.
The state's case is expected to go into early next week.

title: Southeast side grocery store closing in November
author: Claire Grant
description: A southeast side grocery store is shutting down. Here's what's going on at Kent Plaza.
content:
(This story has been updated to because an earlier version included an inaccuracy.)
A grocery store the serves neighborhoods on the city's southeast side is shutting its doors in early November.
According to Niemann Foods director of consumer affairs Gerry Kettler, the County Market store at 2777 S. Sixth St. has not been able to renew its lease.
Staff was given notice of the closing on Sep. 12. Employees were then contacted by Niemann Foods that when the store closes, employees will be transferred to other County Markets in the area.
'The good news will be that all of our associates will be employed at our stores,' Kettler said. 'We're not necessarily closing it. We are, but we don't have a lease. We can't operate.'
The store plans to close Nov. 2, 2024, according to employees. If stock runs out, they may close earlier, they said.
The store is located in Kent Plaza.
Cleeman Realty Group arranged the $6,300,000 sale of Kent Plaza in July of 2020 in an off-market transaction to a private investment firm based out of Maryland.
Cleeman Realty's Michael Cleeman and Sam Seelenfreund represented both the buyer and the seller of the 94,260 square-foot center during the sale.
Kettler said the owners of Kent Plaza want to perform upgrades, including improvements in the space occupied by County Market.
'I don't know what they were going to be fixing but I know there are a lot of problems with the electronic things and the doors,' said County Market associate Meg Alexander. 'It's just an old store. This happens. Things get worn out. … I think Neimanns is trying to take care of their valued employees because they have a record of doing that.'

title: Shiny happy Senators: Smiles plentiful for 4-0 Springfield High football team
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Winning can cure a lot of things, and curing a lot of mistakes can lead to winning. It's been a circular process for the 4-0 Springfield High football team.
content:
There's always an unwritten level of machismo in football, an understood need for stoicism.
But when a team is 4-0 for the first time since the players were in preschool, there's also a time for a few more smiles and lightheartedness. Not too much, Springfield High football coach Jon Hebb cautions: there's still plenty of work ahead for the 4-0 Senators.
Even Monday's constant drizzle of rain during a walkthrough ahead of Friday's Central State Eight Conference meeting at Memorial Stadium against Quincy Notre Dame couldn't damper the spirits of SHS players, who have taken care of business through four games for the first time since 2010. For senior linebacker Keyshaun Harris and junior receiver Kale Thurman, they were just 3-year-olds that season, which was also the last time the Senators appeared in the quarterfinals of the Illinois High School Association playoffs.
Winning is infectious, Harris said.
'It's getting better,' said Harris, who leads the team with 28 tackles. 'The group energy keeps rising after every win. I think (winning has helped the players rally) together. It's better to be together as a group and not as individuals to keep the energy going.'
No letting up
No one on the team has to be reminded that now is not a time to relax. QND (3-1 overall, 2-0 CS8's west division) comes to town fresh off upending Sacred Heart-Griffin 37-7 in Week 4. And with playoff contenders Jacksonville, SHG, Rochester and Chatham Glenwood to finish out the season, Hebb knows even one more win — and a potential playoff berth — isn't guaranteed. He wants to get six wins.
'In my head, we've got to get two (more) to make sure that we're in' Hebb said. 'It's going to be a gauntlet. We've got great respect for coach (Jack) Cornell at Quincy Notre Dame and (Jacksonville) coach (Mark) Grounds comes to town after that. You've got five outstanding head coaches (ahead) with coaching experience and playing experience. It's not going to be easy: our staff knows that, and I think our kids know that.
Brody Scheffler, in his second year guiding the Senators, was asked how close the team is to its ceiling.
'We are so far,' the junior signal-caller said. 'We have not played anywhere near our potential. That's a good thing and a bad thing. (It's bad because) we've got to fix it fast, but we have so much room to grow and so much more we can do right.'
Problems fixed
Sophomore Bryce Bryant, an outside linebacker and occasional running back, wasn't on the varsity team last year, but he could tell something was amiss.
'I could see from a distance, there was a lot more attacking people on the team than this year,' Bryant said.
He also added that a lot those issues have so far been a thing of the past due to the team's, 'discipline, keeping it the way we've been keeping it, everybody staying together (and) nobody playing for themselves, but the team.'
Everybody seemingly could point to a different issue last year. Harris said there were 'a lot of missed tackles,' while Thurman said it was the old adage of trying to put an 'I' in team.
'I'd say our route-running and playing as a team,' Thurman said of what's better. 'We had a lot of 'self' players last year. I think that's changed a lot this year. Everybody really just understood that. Always about the stats (last year): that's not this year at all.'
Perhaps those things don't always show up on the stat sheet. Scheffler said he understood one glaring stat he wanted to improve: turnovers. Despite throwing for 1,706 yards and 16 touchdowns, he did not like seeing 17 interceptions thrown on his stat line.
'Last year, I was lousy with the football: too many turnovers and it led to a lot of our losses,' said Scheffler, who has completed 68% of his passes for 808 yards, nine touchdowns and just two INTs so far in 2024. 'In the offseason, I talked to coach that we've got to fix that to get better.'
What's it like being around the Senators on a day-to-day basis?
'A lot (of smiles),' Thurman said. 'We're having a lot more fun, too.'
With a tough five-game stretch to close out the season, Hebb doesn't want to let any potential loss derail the good vibes the team has going.
'I think the goal stays the same,' Hebb said. 'We're fighting for the playoffs right now and we know it's not going to be easy over the next five weeks. We've got to be focused and make sure we don't lose sight of what the goal is.'
Few players on the Senators were even in high school when the team last made the playoffs in 2021, in Roy Gully's final season as coach. But the players see something special with the group.
'We've got something going for us this year,' Thurman said.
When reminded that Monday's wet, cool weather could be a precursor for what playoff practices might look like — especially deeper into the postseason — Bryant smiled.
'I don't like playing in the cold, but I hope that we do,' he said. 'I know we will.'

title: 'Heart for the game': How the run game has carried Nokomis football to 4-0 start
author: Bill Welt
description: Nolan Herpstreith is one of the standout juniors on the Nokomis football team.
content:
NOKOMIS — Nolan Herpstreith venerates former NFL star running backs Marshawn Lynch and Barry Sanders.
The Nokomis junior running back is a challenge to bring down in his own right and has averaged 139.3 rushing yards per game in a 4-0 start in the Lincoln Prairie Conference.
He lately summoned 150 rushing yards and three touchdowns on 15 carries in a 55-7 Week 4 win over Cerro Gordo-Bement after amassing 190 yards and two scores on just 12 touches in a 62-13 win over Villa Grove.
'He's just hard to get down,' NHS coach Paul Watson said.
He is just part of a prolific junior class that also includes fellow teammates Daryl Evans and Kadynn Petty. Evans has twice rushed for over 100 yards himself to begin the season, including 175 yards and one TD on 15 attempts in a 27-10 season-opening win over Arcola.
Petty, meanwhile, has been appearing as both a quarterback and slot receiver.
'I think a lot of us just have a heart for the game,' Herpstreith said. 'We've been doing this together since probably fifth grade — a lot of ups and downs, but it's been real fun.'
A healthy number of juniors have started since freshman year, including Herpstreith defensively. He ended up getting some touches toward the end of his freshman season due to injuries before assuming the lead role offensively the following year.
Herpstreith finished with 1,621 rushing yards and 20 TDs last fall and Nokomis reached the playoffs before bowing to Greenfield/Northwestern in the first round, 52-13. That somber finale continues to resonate with NHS this season.
NHS visits Oakland Tri-County (1-3) on Saturday before hosting Arthur-Lovington-Atwood-Hammond (4-0) and Sullivan/Okaw Valley (4-0) the next two proceeding weeks for conference supremacy.
'Our goal is to make a deep run in the playoffs,' Watson said. 'I think what really kind of inspired us and gave us extra fire is that playoff game at Greenfield. We started a lot of sophomores and juniors and went over there and they were more physical than us, and that's kind of the thing we've been preaching all offseason and this season as well. We don't want to get that feeling again to a team that's just more physical than us.'
Herpstreith and Evans certainly complement each other. Herpstreith perhaps brings a certain elusiveness and shiftiness in the vein of Lynch or Sanders, while Evans could be described as the bruising type.
Herpstreith deferred credit to the offensive line and the coaching staff. That veteran line includes seniors Atticus Bertolino, Kyle Reynolds, Conner Wilson and Drake Taylor, junior Riley Reynolds and sophomore Hunter Arkebauer.
'We had most of our O-line come back and it's been great having them upfront,' said Herpstreith, who also plays cornerback. 'They've gotten to the linebackers and safeties sometimes and it just makes it easy for me.'

America's most loved grocery store
Hy-Vee has been voted the Best Grocery Store in America, taking the top spot among the most-loved grocery stores in the country. Previously the company ranked within the top three spots, but this is the first time on the golden podium for the Iowa-based company.

The State Journal-Register is part of USA Today. The USA TODAY's 10Best Readers' Choice Awards is conducted annually. A panel of experts nominates 20 grocery stores as the best in the U.S. for their offerings, selection and great service.
USA TODAY readers, like you, are then encouraged to cast their votes during a 28-day voting period. The nominated stores who received the most votes are designated as the Readers' Choice for their category.
About Hy-Vee
Founded nearly 95 years ago, Hy-Vee has become known for its quality, variety and Chinese takeout section. The retail giant operates more than 570 business units across the U.S. and is one of the largest employee-owned companies in the nation.
The business operates across nine Midwest states with sales of more than $13 billion annually.

title: Hurricane Helene: Workers from Springfield head to Georgia for assistance
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Springfield will be in a wind advisory starting at 1 p.m. Friday thanks to Hurricane Helene. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Show Caption
Crews from the City Water Light and Power division of the City of Springfield are heading to assist people with the effects of Hurricane Helene in Georgia.
Two crews and a supervisor left Thursday afternoon to assist in Douglas, Georgia. The crews were initially headed to assist the City of Marietta but were reassigned. They were originally tasked to assist with power restoration from Hurricane Helene making landfall, according to CWLP.
The hurricane was expected to hit the area around 3 a.m. to 5 a.m. Friday morning.
"Through mutual aid agreements like this, utilities are able to pool resources to restore power more quickly while staying safe when a big disaster hits," said Amber Sabin, director of customer and media relations at CWLP.
This mutual aid agreement is through the American Public Power Association and the Illinois Municipal Utility Association, she said.
Springfield is in a wind advisory
The National Weather Service has issued a wind advisory from 1 p.m. Friday until 1 a.m. Saturday.
Wind gusts will be at least 40 to 45 miles per hour but could be as high as 50 mph, according to Meteorologist John Bumgardner with the NWS based in Lincoln.
The peak of the winds will be from 5 p.m. to 1 a.m., he said. Weather effects from the hurricane will taper off after that.
Springfield will likely see light rain throughout Friday with intermittent showers on Saturday.
Bumgardner advises people to secure lawn items and to drive cautiously.
University of Illinois Springfield's Homecoming Pep Rally Block Party has been canceled due to the weather.

title: Springfield man sentenced for trying to kill his ex-girlfriend
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Authorities said the suspect cut his ex-girlfriend's throat with a boxcutter before running off and later being arrested in Colorado.
content:
A Springfield man has been sentenced to 40 years in prison for trying to kill his ex-girlfriend.
Clarence Hopson was sentenced on Oct. 3 after being found guilty of attempted first-degree murder, home invasion, aggravated battery and aggravated stalking in July.
Prosecutors argued that Hopson had stalked his ex-girlfriend and ultimately tried to kill her two years ago.
The woman testified that Hopson broke into her Springfield home around 5:30 a.m. on Nov. 12, 2022, when he and cut her throat and chin with a boxcutter, in addition to slashing her wrist.
After cutting her, Hopson ran out of the house, and the woman called 911.
Authorities said Hopson then went to Chicago and Las Vegas before being arrested in Colorado.
But Hopson left his box cutter at the crime scene, and lab results showed his DNA on the handle, according to a news release from the Sangamon County State's Attorney's office.
Phone records and social media data showed Hopson was at the woman's home around 1 a.m., several hours before the attack. Authorities also said Hopson called the woman 39 times and sent several text and Facebook messages between 1 a.m. and the time of the attack.
'You broke into that house with the intent to murder her; I have no doubt in my mind about that,' said Judge Adam Giganti, according to the press release.
Giganti said there were numerous opportunities to stop what he was doing, and he articulated that Hopson had stalked and harassed the victim for weeks prior to the attack.
Hopson represented himself at the trial and the sentencing hearing. The case was prosecuted by Special Assistant State's Attorney Derek Dion and Assistant State's Attorney Meghan McCarthy.

title: Camp Point Central escapes with close win over Jacksonville Routt after wild ending
author: Bill Welt
description: Jacksonville Routt's upset bid was dashed in the final seconds against Class 1A defending champion Camp Point Central
content:
JACKSONVILLE — An offsides penalty erased Jacksonville Routt's succesful go-ahead field goal attempt in the waning seconds in a 22-21 loss to Class 1A defending champion Camp Point Central at Freesen Field on Saturday.
Brock Runyon drilled a 27-yard field goal attempt through the uprights with nine seconds left, but confusion immediately reigned on the field with the offsides flag against the Panthers.
The Rockets initially celebrated amid the uncertainty, but the pre-snap penalty nixed the initial attempt and moved the ball forward for a second attempt from 22 yards out. This second field goal attempt missed the mark and No. 5-ranked CPC (5-1 overall, 4-0 Western Illinois Valley Conference North) escaped with the win.
"We told our guys jump the snap count," CPC coach Brad Dixon said. "They're going to kick it anyway, so we went offsides and of course it's loud. The official blows the whistle because offsides in high school is a dead-ball penalty. In the NFL, it's a free play and in high school once you encroach the line of scrimmage, it's a dead ball. The referee didn't get the information from the side judge I'm assuming, so we told them, 'Hey, that's a dead ball,' and it was and they had to try to make it again."
Week 6 takeaways: New Berlin, Springfield High come up clutch, and other Week 6 football takeaways
Routt (4-2, 3-1) moved the ball with ease on its final possession in the final 86 seconds, led by senior quarterback Kellen Creviston. The Rockets reeled off three first downs and reached as close as the CPC 7-yard line with 27 seconds left before settling for a field goal attempt.
Routt was initially stopped at midfield on its previous possession, but the defense forced a three-and-out to allow one more chance to win.
Creviston completed 24 of 40 passing attempts for 333 yards and two scores. Senior receiver Jace Lautemann caught a 52-yard TD pass down the near sideline in the first quarter and finished with five receptions for 95 yards. Senior wideout Eli Olson had eight catches for 85 yards while senior running back Charlie Alan had four catches for 74 yards and a score.
"It was just a series of things we've done in practice a 100 times with our hurry-up offense," Routt coach Barry Creviston said of the final drive. "We just go up and down the field and everybody's kind of on their heels, so get the ball down the field, get out of bounds and stop the clock. We put ourselves in a position to win the game and it just didn't work out for us.
"It's going to be a hard one to swallow. But it's football and it's a life lesson. We're going to have to definitely bounce back because it doesn't get easier in the next three weeks."
CPC initially trailed 14-0 but quickly rebounded with Zack Wear's 80-yard TD run early in the second quarter before finally rallying ahead on Nate Peters' 3-yard touchdown run with 5:38 left in the fourth quarter to cap a 16-play drive.
Wear led the Panthers with 92 rushing yards on eight carries. Elijah Genenbacher ushered 51 rushing yards while Kadin Niekamp had 47 yards and the team's other score.
"It was a big grind every single play," Peters said. "Their defense is really good. They've got No. 54 (Trey Gause) and 68 (Henry Rawe) on the edge — they were blowing us up all day. Their offense has gotten so much better, too, with No. 2 (Eli Olson) and 88 (Jace Lautemann) as their receivers. They're really good."

title: Thurman, Scheffler lead last-minute drive as Springfield High football beats Jacksonville
author: Adrian Dater
description: Jacksonville took a 29-28 lead with 62 seconds left. That turned out to be plenty of time for Brody Scheffler and Kale Thurman in Springfield High's win.
content:
Trying to describe Springfield High's 36-29 victory over Jacksonville Friday night? You definitely had to be there, because words alone make that difficult.
Having just taken a 29-28 lead with 1 minute, 2 seconds left in the game following a gutsy decision by Crimsons coach Mark Grounds to go for a 2-point conversion, the Crimsons' sideline and Memorial Stadium's visiting partisan crowd were euphoric. Just prevent a Senators touchdown, and the Crimsons would be a 5-1 team celebrating a huge win on the road in this Central State Eight Conference matchup.
Springfield quarterback Brody Scheffler and receiver Kale Thurman would not let that happen. Going 80 yards in four plays — all catches by Thurman, including a 40-yard TD reception with 35 seconds left — the Senators pulled out the improbable victory to improve to 5-1 overall (3-1 CS8's west division) and become playoff-eligible.
'Listen, they punched us in the mouth, but we responded,' said Thurman, whose final TD reception was after a gorgeous timing-pattern by Scheffler down the right sideline that hit him fully in stride. 'The offense really just came together at the end. I mean, it couldn't have been a better pass by Brody.'
Scheffler's eye-popping statistics: 27-for-37, 428 yards and four TD passes.
'I put the ball in the air and trust my guys to come down with it, and that's what they did,' said Scheffler. 'We were in the same situation last week, but stalled out at the 20-yard line. Tonight, we finished the job. I couldn't be more proud of my teammates.'
Talk about a game of contrasting styles: Jacksonville 4-2 (2-2 CS8's west division) had 408 yards of total offense, but 316 of them came on the ground. Springfield had 454 yards of total offense, but only 36 came on the ground.
Jacksonville seemed to have the game won when Jeremiah Jackson (121 yards, 15 carries, and two TDs) ran it in from 7-yards out to make it a 28-27 game, then Jacksonville got the two-point conversion — and the lead — after a La'Marion Williams run.
But then Scheffler and Thurman combined to steal the show. Four plays, 80 yards. Still time on the clock for Jacksonville, but valiant Crimsons QB Braden Hutchison's Hail Mary attempt fizzled at the buzzer.
Normally, Springfield coach Jon Hebb calls the offensive plays on behalf of Scheffler. But not on the game-winner.
'Brody called that one,' Hebb said. 'That call takes some guts, but he made a perfect throw. A credit to our kids. They finished tonight.'
Asked if his 5-1 team has exceeded his expectations to this point, Hebb said: 'Maybe a little bit. But these guys have really grown. They've taken some huge strides toward the culture that we're trying to build here at Springfield High. They exemplified it tonight.'
The Crimsons had 182 yards of offense at the half — all on the ground. Hutchinson had 80 of the yards on just seven carries, doing much of the work on a drive in which Williams, a senior, capped with a 2-yard TD run.
Behind 6-foot-5, 290-pound center Ryan McCombs, Jacksonville runners had big holes to jump through. Jacksonville looked like it would take a 13-0 lead when it got the ball deep into the red zone on its next possession, but Springfield defensive back Jaiyden Wilson made a drive-stopping tackle near the goal line.
Springfield got down to the Jacksonville 2 on its first drive, but QB Brody Scheffler nearly was picked off on passes on third- and fourth-down. Mehki Newman, however, got the Senators even at 7-7 with a 49-yard touchdown run down the left side.
Williams ran for 75 yards and two TDs for the Crimsons, who only attempted eight passes in the whole game. For the Senators, Armanze Lewis had the second-most crowd-pleasing play of the night. Lewis, a big fullback, only ran the ball one time in the game, but it was for 65 yards and a touchdown that gave Springfield a 21-14 lead as the third-quarter buzzer expired.
The buzz, clearly, is back with the Senators' program after a few tough years. Can it continue on toward a great state playoff position?
'We're learning more as a team, I think,' Scheffler said. 'What we've been through before is starting to help us now.'

title: CS8 stunner: U-High beats Glenwood for first time since joining league
author: Ryan Mahan
description: The Normal U-High offense jumped out to a big lead and stymied Glenwood almost the entire night to earn first CS8 win over Titans.
content:
NORMAL — If last year's win over Decatur MacArthur turned the page for the Normal U-High football team, then Friday's stunning victory over Chatham Glenwood started a new chapter.
"I think that's probably a fair statement," U-High coach Brody Walworth said. "Last year against MacArthur was pretty special, too. That was a corner-turning win last year and now we're in a situation where we think we're competitive with the best teams in the league. To finally get over the hump in (a big game) is awesome."
U-High quarterback Alek Weiland threw five touchdowns and finished with 318 yards passing as the Pioneers beat Glenwood 33-13 in a Central State Eight Conference east division game at Illinois State University's Hancock Stadium.
When Weiland found AJ Holden for a 1-yard touchdown with 1 minute, 44 seconds left in the first half, it gave U-High a 26-0 lead.
"I think we knew we had it in us and we knew we could play with these guys and I knew we could beat them," Weiland said. "A lot of people didn't think we could win this game, but coming in, I think we all thought we were just as good, if not better, than them."
The Titans (4-2 overall, 3-1 CS8 east) found their offensive groove long enough to cut the deficit in half, when Brady Dwyer scored a 1-yard touchdown run with 12 seconds left in the second quarter and junior quarterback Colten Knoedler found Jonathan Helm for a 21-yard score on the Titans' first possession of the second half.
Glenwood's defense held the Pioneers (4-2, 3-1 CS8 east) scoreless for almost the entirety of the second half but couldn't get any closer. U-High cemented the win when Weiland and Holden connected on an 18-yard strike with 2:47 to play.
But, Glenwood coach David Hay said, that defensive play in the second half wasn't good enough.
"They just beat us: flat-out beat us," Hay said. "We didn't show up to the game until maybe somewhere in the third quarter. We can't do that. If we think we're good enough to do that, I think we just found out that we're not.
"We had places where we played well, but this is a team sport, a team game and that's not good enough."
Heading into Friday's game, Glenwood was 7-0 against U-High since the Pioneers entered the CS8 in 2017. That first season, Glenwood pulled out a 37-36 overtime win, but since then, the Pioneers haven't been within a mile of the Titans with Glenwood holding a 326-106 scoring advantage in the series.
Glenwood fans were heard starting to get restless after the Pioneers went up 12-0 on Weiland's second TD throw to Cade Cunningham, this one a 19-yard pass after the two connected on a 34-yard score to start the game.
Twice in a row, Glenwood had to punt out of its own end zone in the second quarter. The first time, U-High couldn't convert a fourth down from the Glenwood 3. Four plays later, the Titans had a fourth and 11 from their own 2. After a 25-yard punt, Weiland found Carson Stevens for his third TD throw, and U-High found itself up 19-0.
"The biggest thing defensively is, we know we've got the right guys — we can play — but we've got caught in a trap of playing what I call, 'Hero ball,' where we try to do too much," Walworth said. "I think tonight was a great example of when you have 11 guys playing disciplined football, doing their jobs.
"We played really well (on the defensive) side. The pressure was great, but forcing them to be one-dimensional (was key). (Glenwood) wants to run the ball, they like running it and I think we did a great job up front controlling the line of scrimmage, as well."
Glenwood committed a holding penalty on first-and-10 from its own 9-yard line, then had to again punt from its own 3. The Titans' defense committed a pass interference on first and 10 from the Glenwood 20, and three plays later, Holden and Weiland put the Pioneers up 26-0.
Holden's second touchdown was the final touch.
"That last play, we knew what we had to do to drive that nail, so we just go out there and executed," Holden said. "Now, we know we can beat the best teams in the state and in the conference."
U-High managed to run for 129 yards to finish with 447 yards of offense. After the game, Hay was asked what his team did right. Hay had some thoughts.
"Maybe a couple of drives, we got a couple of stops on defense, but generally, we didn't cover, we missed tackles, we didn't block, at times we didn't catch and at times, we didn't throw," Hay said.
U-High made the playoffs five straight seasons from 2011-15, but didn't make it back to the postseason until last year. Now, a win away from playoff eligibility has the Pioneers excited, but not content.
"I think we can build a ton off this," Weiland said. "Even though we won, we still have things to improve on and we're going to go watch film (Saturday) and improve on those things in practice next week."
Knoedler finished 22-for-39 for 236 yards and two interceptions. He found six different receivers, including Gavin Simmons, who caught 11 passes for 131 yards.
U-High forced Glenwood into a one-dimensional team on Friday. The Titans rushed 16 times for just 42 yards and one touchdown. Glenwood also committed seven penalties for 57 yards, while U-High was whistled four times for 30 yards.
"That's a good football team," Hay said of U-High. "I don't want anyone to misunderstand. A good football team, they're playing great, Brody does a hell of a job, but we expect more of ourselves."

title: Reason to smile: How Lincoln Land women's soccer staged a big turnaround with local talent
author: Bill Welt
description: Lincoln Land failed to produce any wins last season. Here's how these local players changed the narrative of the nascent women's soccer team
content:
It was in the heat of the summer that Mack Elam detected something brewing in the air.
The Lincoln Land Community College women's soccer team was assigned a sweltering four-mile run for the first week of practice. But in those stifling conditions, a new camaraderie was forged.
'We were all dying, and it was horrible,' the sophomore midfielder/forward said, 'but in the end we all were cheering each other on as we came back together, and that's what kind of clicked for me is that this is going to be a team.'
Building blocks
Coach David Meyer knows first-hand as a former player on the LLCC men's soccer team — which folded in 2019 to make way for the women's team — that there's nothing better than playing soccer with your friends. It's ultimately why LLCC first beckoned to Meyer more than 20 years ago, and it's as true now as it was then.
The Loggers (9-1) quickly flushed away last season's 0-16-4 woes by winning their first eight matches with a roster laden with local talent. That includes Meyer's daughter, Kaleigh, who won the Class 2A state title while at Chatham Glenwood.
'It was a shock, but it's nice,' Kaleigh said of the torrid start. 'We know we can do it.'
Lincoln Land certainly presented a balanced attack in a recent 6-1 win over Morton with goals pouring from all directions.
Sophomore forward and Riverton/Buffalo Tri-City product Kyndel Moore opened the onslaught from long distance before Meyer, Elam and freshman Adi Frasse each extended the margin 4-1 by halftime.
Fraase's former teammate at Pleasant Plains, Sophia Smith, added another goal before Hillsboro graduate Kinley Richardson tacked on the final score.
'I really love that part about the team because it's not just one person who carries all the goals,' said Elam, who graduated from Springfield High.
Moore wields a team-high nine goals through the first 10 matches, while Richardson has six goals and three assists. Meyer (6 goals, 2 assists), Smith (5 goals, 4 assists) and sophomore Tetee Jallah (5 goals, 4 assists) each ranked third on the team with 14 points to boot.
'You can really rely on all of our teammates,' Richardson said. 'Everyone takes their fair share of turns. You don't feel so much pressure for yourself because I know if I pass it to my teammates they can finish it just as much at a high rate as everyone else.'
Richardson decided to resume soccer at the next level after recovering from an ACL tear in high school. Jallah, another Springfield High alum, similarly missed last season due to an ACL tear.
'The recovery was very hard,' Jallah said, 'but then when I started running again, I got cleared, and I worked hard for the four months, and my spring season last semester I came back stronger than I was.
'I really took it for granted, and I'm glad to be back on the field.'
Jallah and that back line add an extra dimension to the offense.
'It all starts back on the defense with Adi Fraase, Teetee (Jallah), Tatyana (Mehundrew) and Libby (Maddox),' Richardson said. 'They all bring it up, and our midfield really serves out good passes. All the offense has to do is finish.'
Meyer said she fills the field wherever needed — except goalkeeper, she says with a laugh stemming from her experience first playing in the YMCA. She said everyone on the team is hungry 'and we know that we want to be out there winning.'

title: Central Illinois first responder dies in two-vehicle crash
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A first responder in central Illinois died after being involved in a crash last week. Here's what we know.
content:
A first responder in central Illinois died after being involved in a crash last week.
Chelsie M. Sonneborn, 32, was an emergency medical technician in Franklin. Sonneborn was driving on IL Route 104 near Ress Station Road on Oct. 3 when her vehicle collided head-on with a pickup truck, according to the Morgan County Coroner's Office. The crash happened around 4 p.m.
The coroner said Sonneborn died at the scene of the crash.
Sonneborn worked as an EMT for seven years for America Ambulance while she worked towards becoming a paramedic.
'She absolutely loved being a first responder and helping others,' her obituary reads.
Sonneborn graduated from Jacksonville High School in 2010. She also worked for the Murrayville Fire Department for two years, as well as volunteering for the Murrayville Woodson Ambulance Service for a few years.
'Chelsie was not just a co-worker but was a friend to many in our community, and her loss has come with a tremendous amount of grief and devastation,' according to a Facebook post from America Ambulance. 'Chelsie's dedication and expertise as an EMT will be sorely missed by all that knew her. We ask that you keep her family, friends, and EMS family in your thoughts and prayers.'
A funeral service is set for Oct. 9 at 12 p.m. at the Buchanan & Cody Funeral Home in Jacksonville.
The crash is being investigated by the Illinois State Police and the Morgan County Coroner's Office.

title: Glenwood junior Surges onto CS8 tennis scene
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Ellie Surges might be Glenwood tennis' No. 1 singles player, but the junior says teammate Samantha Shankland is the No. 1 role model.
content:
Chatham Glenwood junior Ellie Surges admitted that her senior teammate Samantha Shankland has been a great example during her high school tennis journey.
'Sam is a team leader and my biggest role model on the team,' Surges said. 'I remember when I started, I saw her, and I was like, 'I want to be like her.'
"She's so nice, so sweet, so athletic and so fast; I've looked up to her.'
Now Surges has a chance to replicate Shankland's accomplishments as the No. 2 singles seed at the girls Central State Eight Conference Tournament this weekend at the Velasco Tennis Center in Washington Park. Shankland was awarded the top seed after she defeated Maroa-Forsyth's Ella Sandgren in a third-set tiebreak in a quad meet on Aug. 24.
The CS8 tournament begins at 1 p.m. on Friday and concludes Saturday with a start at 9 a.m.
Surges has gained some serious momentum this season, coming into the tournament undefeated in the CS8 while playing in the No. 1 singles spot for Glenwood. She rallied for a 6-1, 5-7, 10-8 victory over Normal U-High's Haley Martin on Oct. 3 in a dual meet before following that up with a 6-2, 6-0 triumph over Sacred Heart-Griffin senior Caroline Sheehan on Monday. Earlier this season, Surges took down The State Journal-Register's defending All-Area Player of the Year, Julia Musgrave of Rochester, 6-2, 6-0 in a dual meet on Sept. 11.
Surges credits her father and mother for introducing her to the game. As a sophomore, Surges made a push late in the year and finished fourth at the Class 2A Belleville West Sectional and advanced to the Illinois High School Association's state finals, where she went 0-2.
'All the girls that I've played have been amazing players; they've been great people,' Surges said. 'I think that coach Sonthana (Thongsithavong) and my dad (former Glenwood coach Eric Surges) have really boosted my confidence this year.'
'They've helped me improve strategically and fundamentally, and I'm definitely more confident going into the postseason this year than I was last year. It's a little bit of added pressure, but I'm excited to see those nice (players) again and prove myself again in the tournament.'
Thongsithavong has noticed the difference and maturity in Surges' play this season after Shankland held Glenwood's No. 1 singles position since her sophomore year.
'Ellie took a big leap and took that No. 1 singles and just ran with it,' Thongsithavong said. 'Ellie's methodical, she has a lot of variation to her shots; a very smart player. It frustrates the other player, but she has some weapons too that she didn't have. She hits passing shots now and her serve has got a little more pace to it.'
Glenwood narrowly defeated U-High, 26-25, to win the CS8 tournament last season. Shankland and Surges played a big role in Glenwood's title run when Shankland outlasted Surges 4-6, 6-0, 6-1 in the singles championship match.
'If it was anybody but Sam, I would've been upset, but I love Sam,' said Surges of her loss in the title match. 'If I can't be the winner, I would want it to be Sam. I was happy for her and the team.'
Being top-heavy in singles is a bit of a switch for Glenwood, Thongsithavong said.
'Normally our program is heavy on doubles so this is the first year that my top two players are going in singles,' he noted. 'That's something new for me and something exciting to go into conference.'
Shankland, who started playing tennis at 7 years old, became a protégé of Thongsithavong in her early tennis years. She still has something to prove as the top CS8 seed while supporting the team to another conference championship.
'We've been strong for the past few years,' Shankland said. 'Sonthana has done a good job keeping that up for everybody. I feel confident going into the conference. I think we'll do just as good or even better than last year with the way we've been playing lately.'
As for the differences between her and Surges' game, Shankland appreciates both.
'Ellie gets to a bunch of balls, she's crazy fast on the court,' Shankland said. 'She gets to everything, and she never gives up on the ball. I think that aspect of our game is similar — I also try to go after every ball and never give up. I think I attack the ball a little bit more, try to play a little more aggressively, but both strategies are good.'
Thongsithavong vehemently said he knows where the two are very similar.
'Off the court, I don't know anybody who is more liked than these two,' he said. 'They care for each other, it's not really competitive at all. You can ask anybody on the team. They look up to these two off the court on how they portray themselves and how they carry themselves. They're good role models for the players, and I can say that about both of them, probably two of the nicest players I've ever coached.'

title: Glenwood junior Surges onto CS8 tennis scene
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Ellie Surges might be Glenwood tennis' No. 1 singles player, but the junior says teammate Samantha Shankland is the No. 1 role model.
content:
Chatham Glenwood junior Ellie Surges admitted that her senior teammate Samantha Shankland has been a great example during her high school tennis journey.
'Sam is a team leader and my biggest role model on the team,' Surges said. 'I remember when I started, I saw her, and I was like, 'I want to be like her.'
"She's so nice, so sweet, so athletic and so fast; I've looked up to her.'
Now Surges has a chance to replicate Shankland's accomplishments as the No. 2 singles seed at the girls Central State Eight Conference Tournament this weekend at the Velasco Tennis Center in Washington Park. Shankland was awarded the top seed after she defeated Maroa-Forsyth's Ella Sandgren in a third-set tiebreak in a quad meet on Aug. 24.
The CS8 tournament begins at 1 p.m. on Friday and concludes Saturday with a start at 9 a.m.
Surges has gained some serious momentum this season, coming into the tournament undefeated in the CS8 while playing in the No. 1 singles spot for Glenwood. Earlier this season, Surges took down The State Journal-Register's defending All-Area Player of the Year, Julia Musgrave of Rochester, 6-2, 6-0 in a dual meet on Sept. 11.

'Ellie took a big leap and took that No. 1 singles and just ran with it,' Thongsithavong said. 'Ellie's methodical, she has a lot of variation to her shots; a very smart player. It frustrates the other player, but she has some weapons too that she didn't have. She hits passing shots now and her serve has got a little more pace to it.'
Glenwood narrowly defeated U-High, 26-25, to win the CS8 tournament last season. Shankland and Surges played a big role in Glenwood's title run when Shankland outlasted Surges 4-6, 6-0, 6-1 in the singles championship match.
'If it was anybody but Sam, I would've been upset, but I love Sam,' said Surges of her loss in the title match. 'If I can't be the winner, I would want it to be Sam. I was happy for her and the team.'

title: For the team: Braddock Cates, veteran offensive line carry Williamsville football
author: Bill Welt
description: Williamsville's veteran offensive line has had to learn a new set of drills and plays — and they have jelled at the right time
content:
ATHENS — Braddock Cates tells his offensive linemen all the time.
''My touchdowns are your touchdowns,'' Cates said. 'They work hard for me, so I give them all the credit. That's all there is to it. Without them, there is no me.'
The senior running back barreled ahead with 125 rushing yards and three touchdowns on 14 carries and the Williamsville football team dashed to a 52-6 win over Athens last week to remain unbeaten in the Sangamo Conference at 5-1 overall and 5-0 in the league.
'It's really nice having dudes out there that you know who are going to get the job done,' Cates said, 'you can trust them. They're just your guys. If worst comes to worst, you know that somebody out there is going to have your back.'
The Bullets have gravitated more to the run game over the past two seasons, even brandishing the wishbone and Wing-T. They ended up assembling 404 rushing yards as a team against Athens, with senior Gage Paul and junior Matthew Miller also emerging out of the backfield.
Paul churned out a 91-yard rushing touchdown in the second quarter and finished with 123 yards and two scores on just three carries. The previous week, Paul ran for 87 yards and a TD on 12 attempts in a 27-12 win triumph over Stanford Olympia.
Williamsville coach Aaron Kunz said they started implementing the wishbone last season before ushering the Wing-T, something the Bullets are quite acquainted with defensively against the likes of Class 3A top-ranked Byron, Pittsfield, Olympia and Athens this season alone. New Berlin (6-0) and its strong penchant for the run game also looms this Friday at Pretzel Field.
'We said, 'Let's try to run a couple of these things,' and they were really good tonight,' Kunz said after the Week 6 win at Athens. 'It was a good little addition to the playbook for sure.'
And why not with a prolific running back such as Cates and a host of other playmakers, not to mention a slew of experienced linemen? Last season, Cates was tabbed to the Illinois High School Football Coaches Association Class 3A all-state team with 1,437 rushing yards and 16 touchdowns.
Senior left tackle Matthew Crouch was also named all-Sangamo first team that year. Crouch, as well as seniors Corbin Stewart and Carson Beattie, have started upfront since sophomore year when the Bullets reached the Class 3A state championship game. Senior lineman Caden Kahl additionally became a starter last season.
Their experience is invaluable, Kunz said, and they've learned to jell at the right time.
'It kind of puts a little more of a priority on us to make sure we're doing everything right,' Crouch said of the transition to the run game. 'We can't take any plays off because if we don't do our jobs, then it's going to go wrong in the backfield, so it's on us to play every play until the whistle and do the best we can.'
Crouch doesn't need to search far and wide for the right source of motivation.
'The biggest thing for me along the way has been the team itself,' Crouch said. 'That's your family — you've got to trust that everyone is going to do their job. I'd say that's my biggest motivation: do it not for yourself but for the whole team.'
That attitude also extends to the backfield.
'Our coaches really help us and we have some great guys like Braddock,' Stewart said. 'He cheers us on. He tells us when we do our job, he gets in that end zone and we celebrate with him, so he gets us hyped. We really do it for our running backs and our team.'
Stewart handles both center and guard. Junior Zach Graber also plays center depending on the formation.
Stewart said he lives and breathes the offensive line and has battled his share of injuries. He broke his collarbone as a sophomore before tearing his ACL in basketball.
He said it's good to get games under his belt this year.
'We're pretty run heavy this year, but we're still the same old Bullets,' Stewart said. 'We get the ball moving, we get hyped.'

title: Teammates battle: Shankland beats Surges in all-Glenwood CS8 tennis meet
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Chatham Glenwood, the defending champion, took second place with 25 points and Sacred Heart-Griffin was third with 23 at Saturday's CS8 girls tennis meet.
content:
Normal U-High put both of its doubles teams into the championship final and the Pioneers rolled up 31½ points to win the Central State Eight Conference girls tennis tournament on Saturday at the Velasco Tennis Center in Washington Park.
Chatham Glenwood, the defending champion, took second place with 25 points and Sacred Heart-Griffin was third with 23. Upstart Jacksonville was next with 15½, followed by Rochester (15), Lincoln (9), Springfield High (9) and Southeast (6).
Here are four takeaways from the two-day tournament:
Glenwood goes 1-2 again
Chatham Glenwood teammates Samantha Shankland and Ellie Surges squared off for the conference singles title for the second straight season, and it was Shankland repeating as champ with a 6-4, 6-3 victory.
Shankland, the No. 1 seed, reached the final after beating unseeded Angel Yin of Normal U-High 6-2, 6-2 in the semifinals. Surges, seeded second, posted a 6-0, 6-2 victory over third seed Caroline Sheehan of SHG in the other semifinal.
The Titans, top-heavy in singles this season, received 20 points in the draw. Glenwood got five points in the doubles draw when unseeded Lydia Ryherd and Stella Lopp got to the quarterfinals. Fifth seed Natalie Alexander and Kiki Mander, however, were sent to the back draw after a 3-6, 7-5, 6-4 loss to unseeded Norah Alexander and Finley York of Jacksonville in the second round.
Sheehan proving her status
After losing to Surges in the semifinals, Sheehan rebounded with a resounding 6-0, 6-0 victory over Yin in the third-place match.
The senior has been a solid No. 1 for the Cyclones and confirmed that missing the tennis postseason last fall was due to her primary sport of soccer where she will continue to play for SHG in the spring as a center midfielder.
'I missed a couple tournaments for soccer (practice), and we had a lot of seniors last year, so coach Hayden (Esker) wanted to give them an opportunity to play since I missed,' Sheehan said. 'Someone else got to play singles and they moved our doubles team up, so they got to experience that.'
Sheehan appears grateful for the opportunity this season. She placed second in the No. 1 singles draw at the Central Illinois Invitational, defeated Rochester's best, Julia Musgrave, at a dual meet, and helped the Cyclones beat Quincy 5-4 in a meet with a win in doubles.
'Honestly, I was just wanting to have fun this year,' Sheehan said. 'I've played varsity since my freshman year I joined, just to have fun for a fall sport. I've always been able to move well. I've gotten better with my shots and my placement and gotten more consistent.'
Sheehan said she started playing tennis during the winter of eighth grade, and didn't have state tournament aspirations before this season.
'I can get to state if I work hard and do well, so I'm excited about that but it's not entirely my goal,' she said. 'I'm really happy with how well I did overall in the (CS8) tournament. I think sophomore year I got fourth, so I was glad I got to improve on that.'
U-High's depth leads to title
Top seed Haley Martin and Emma Eovaldi defeated teammates and sixth seed Risha Patel and Alison Storm 6-4, 6-1 in the doubles title match.
Patel and Storm got by the second-seeded team of Musgrave and Cora Haupt of Rochester 4-6, 6-3, 6-3 in the semifinals. Martin and Eovaldi downed unseeded Lucia Hassebrock and Catalina Mosquera of SHG 6-0, 6-1 in the semis.
Thanks to Yin's fourth-place finish in singles, the Pioneers were able carve out the title.
Area teams bracing for tough sectionals
Shankland and Surges will be two of the top singles players when Glenwood hosts the Class 2A Sectional that includes traditionally tough schools in Edwardsville, Belleville West and Alton.
Shankland, who did not qualify for the IHSA state finals after a loss in the quarterfinals at last season's Belleville West Sectional, said this time will be a great opportunity for her and the team to make some noise.
'I'm really excited that we're hosting sectionals this year,' Shankland said. 'It's definitely a higher level of competition than conference, but ever since we've been in 2A, it's good to play stronger people. It makes me stronger and everyone else gets better after playing them. They are definitely tough.'
With their strong CS8 showing, the Cyclones may have put themselves as one of the favorites to win the Class 1A Jacksonville Sectional. Quincy Notre Dame and Jerseyville usually put themselves in the running.
With Sheehan, Hassebrock and Mosquera and sixth-place singles finisher Laney Aleman, SHG has a core of players to compete.
Jacksonville's fourth-place finish has put the Crimsons on the map. Olivia Dobson reached the quarterfinals before losing to Sheehan, while Norah Alexander and York also advanced to the quarters before falling to Springfield High's Myla Shannon and Madisyn Williams 1-6, 6-2, 10-8 in the fifth-place doubles match.
Rochester still has Musgrave and Haupt in doubles to go with Grace Winkler and possibly Hannah Eichholz in singles.

title: Majority of Illinois teachers considering leaving profession, survey finds
author: Tom Ackerman
description: As teacher and support staff shortages impact Illinois, a new survey shows nearly 3 out of 5 teachers in the state are considering leaving the profession.
content:
As teacher and support staff shortages impact Illinois, a new survey found nearly three out of five teachers in the state are considering leaving the profession.
The Illinois Education Association recently released data from a Red for Ed membership poll, which surveyed 500 active IEA members in the middle of June.
The poll found 59% of teachers, higher education professors and education support staff are considering leaving the profession.
Of those 59% of educators, 65% say they are considering changing fields because they are not making enough money, 65% say there is a lack of respect for the profession, and 62% say their workload is increasing.
'This data should set off massive alarm bells for parents, students and community members,' IEA President Al Llorens said in a news release regarding the findings. 'We are in a dire situation with teacher and support staff shortages. We know districts cannot attract and retain enough talented adults to work with our students.'
One in four IEA members has at least one additional job, according to the survey results.
The survey also found 94% of IEA members work additional hours outside of their contractual workday with 97% of IEA members spending their own money on supplies for their students and classrooms. One in four teachers spend at least $500 on things like pencils, furniture and hygiene products, according to the survey.
The report cited the #RedforEd movement that saw teachers striking in places like West Virginia and Arizona, wearing red and advocating for higher teacher pay and more K-12 education funding.
IEA is a union of more than 135,000 members composed of Illinois elementary and secondary teachers, higher education faculty and staff, educational support professionals, retired educators and college students preparing to become teachers, according to their website.

title: 'A proud day for Springfield.' City celebrates race riot site as newest national monument
author: Steven Spearie
description: "This is a proud day for Springfield. This is a great day for Springfield."
content:
In her first term as a U.S. Representative, Nikki Budzinski said the push to make the site of the Springfield 1908 Race Riot a national monument was "the single largest ask of the Biden Administration."
On Wednesday, Budzinski and others joined in a celebration at HSHS St. John's Children's Hospital nearly two months after President Joe Biden made the designation official through the Antiquities Act.
"I'm so excited to see it come to fruition after so many years of community pushing for this recognition," said Budzinski, a Springfield Democrat. "This is a proud day for Springfield. This is a great day for Springfield."
Many who have been with the effort longer, including past Springfield NAACP presidents Teresa Haley and Judy Johnson, and U.S. Sens. Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth, were also on hand for the celebration.
Among the other guests at Bunn Auditorium Wednesday were Lindsay Harney Price and Amanda Staab Londrigan, who as Iles Elementary School sixth-graders in 1991, presented a petition of more than 250 signatures to the Springfield City Council asking for it to memorialize the race riot.
The violence perpetrated by white mobs claimed the lives of at least five people, caused millions of dollars of damage to Black-owned businesses and uprooted thousands of Blacks from the city. Two Black men — Scott Burton and William Donnegan — were lynched.
The NAACP was formed in the aftermath of the riot.
Durbin said one of the seminal moments in beginning the work to get the site its status was when an archaeological team from Fever River Research, led by Floyd Mansberger, found seven homes, five of which were burned during the riot as the Springfield Rail Improvements Project was in its infancy. Mansberger, who was in the audience Wednesday, found a trove of artifacts in the unearthing.
"(It was as if) the voices- were saying, 'Don't forget us,'" Durbin said.
Durbin, who first introduced legislation about the site in the Senate with Duckworth in 2019, said he was aware that Biden's signing of the act came just a month after the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey at the hands of a now-former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy sent shockwaves throughout the country.
"It was certainly a reminder," he said, "that the forces of hate and violence that were so dominant during the Springfield Race Riot are still in our community. We have to work together, all of us, to bring that to an end."
Massey's family is related to William Donnegan.
Durbin and others recognized that it was the pull of the community that brought the project to the finish line.
"This is what you dream of, community coming together for the right reason, to send the right message," Durbin told the media afterwards.
Brian Mitchell, director of research and interpretation at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum, said the ALPLM is creating a database that chronicles every Black household that was in the city in 1908.
Researchers, he said, "want to know who was in every house that was burned down. We want to know the organizations they belonged. We want to know who their families were. We want to know every serviceman that was there and we want to celebrate their stories of resiliency."
Mitchell, who has researched race riots in other cities, said Springfield "is the one community that I have seen that has come together: Black, White, business, regardless of partisan position and they have worked together to make this (designation) happen."
Shannon Estenoz, assistant secretary of the U.S. Department of Interior for Fish and Wildlife and Parks and part of listening in Springfield in June, said the National Park Service will join the Springfield community "to use the power of place to bring 1908 out of the misty distance and into focus for this and future generations.
"The park service is the nation's premier storytellers."
It will be the second National Park Service site in Springfield. It also manages the Lincoln Home National Historic Site.

title: See which Springfield-area girls tennis players qualified for the IHSA state meet
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Seven players from the Springfield area reached the girls tennis state meet. Here is how they fared in both sectional classes.
content:
Sacred Heart-Griffin won the Class 1A Jacksonville Sectional and Chatham Glenwood advanced its top two singles players to the Class 2A Illinois High School Association girls state tennis finals.
In all, seven players from the Springfield area qualified for state. Here is how they fared in both sectional classes.
Samantha Shankland, Ellie Surges bound for state
The top four placers in both singles and doubles advance to the state tournament and Shankland, a Glenwood senior, spent more than three hours on the Velasco tennis court in a quarterfinal match on Friday while stamping her ticket to the Class 2A finals at the Glenwood Sectional in Washington Park.
Shankland, seeded fifth, defeated fourth-seeded Gabi Hill of Edwardsville 3-6, 6-4, 7-6 (3) in the quarterfinal. The roller-coaster match ended with drama when Shankland went up 5-1 in the third and final set, only to lose the next five games to Hill and trail 6-5.
Shankland evened the third set at six apiece before winning the tiebreak 7-3. Shankland got a little revenge from Hill after she lost to her 6-2, 6-3 at the Belleville West Sectional in last season's quarterfinals and missed going to state.
Friday's win catapulted Shankland into the semifinals and she took out second seed Natalie Spihlman of O'Fallon 7-5, 6-0 on Saturday. Edwardsville's Dia Kannan, the No. 1 seed, downed Shankland 6-1, 7-5 in the title match.
Surges, a sixth-seeded junior, also needed a three-set win in the quarterfinals. She lost the first set to No. 3 seed Toby Hawkes of Collinsville but rallied for a 6-7 (1), 6-0, 6-3 victory.
Kannan defeated Surges 6-0, 6-0 in the semis, but Surges rebounded and won the third-place match 6-3, 5-7 after Spilhman retired before the third set due to a rolled ankle.
Edwardsville won the sectional title with 32 points and Glenwood was second with 21. Belleville West had two doubles teams in the third-place match and finished third with 19. Notably, Springfield High ended up tied for seventh with Alton and Granite City with four points each.
Caroline Sheehan, doubles team pace SHG
Sheehan, the No. 1 singles seed, rolled to the title and advanced to her first Class 1A state tennis finals.
Sheehan defeated Bunker Hill's Samantha Anderson 6-0, 6-1 in Friday's quarterfinals and beat fifth seed Neely Goetten of Jerseyville 6-2, 6-1 in Saturday's semis. She won the singles title with a 6-2, 6-0 victory over No. 2 seed Kiley King of Jerseyville in the championship match.
Sheehan did not play in the postseason during her junior year because of some missed tournaments during the regular season. She has been with the team the whole way in her senior season.
As the fifth seed, Lucia Hassebrock and Catalina Mosquera of SHG reached their first 1A state finals with a fourth-place finish.
Hassebrock and Mosquera beat fourth seed Leah Range and Abby White of Jacksonville 6-4, 1-6, 6-1 in the quarterfinals before losing to top seed Emma Davis and Abigail Harms of Bethalto Civic Memorial 6-3, 6-2 in the semis. The SHG team then lost to third seed Morgan Zanger and Kaitlyn Brown 6-2, 6-1 in the third-place match.
Rochester doubles advance, take second
Senior Julia Musgrave, The State Journal-Register's All-area Player of the Year last season, paired with teammate Cora Haupt and the duo finished runner-up in the 1A doubles draw at Jacksonville.
Musgrave and Haupt knocked out unseeded Finley York and Norah Alexander of Jacksonville 6-2, 6-3 in the quarters, and then defeated third seed Morgan Zanger and Kaitlyn Brown of Quincy Notre Dame 6-4, 6-4 in the semis.
Davis and Harms posted a 6-2, 6-1 win over the second-seeded Rochester tandem in the title match. It will be Musgrave's fourth trip to state. She went in doubles her freshman year and qualified in singles during her sophomore and junior seasons.
Near-misses and notables
At the Glenwood Sectional, the unseeded doubles team of Myla Shannon and Madisyn Williams from Springfield High, came up short in the doubles quarterfinals, falling to sixth-seeded Morgan Seagle and Gabrielle Patterson of Belleville West 6-1, 6-2.
Unseeded Lydia Ryherd and Stella Lopp of Glenwood also dropped their quarterfinal match, succumbing to Sophie Byron and Katie Woods of Edwardsville 6-0, 6-0 in the quarters. Bryon and Woods, the overwhelming No. 1 seed, won the doubles title by beating their third-seeded teammates Veda Kommineni and Bina Selimi 6-0, 6-1 in the championship match.
At Jacksonville, SHG could not send a second singles player to state when sixth seed Laney Aleman lost her quarterfinal match to third seed Alyssa Ley of Quincy Notre Dame 7-5, 6-2.
Rochester's Grace Winkler won her first-round match in straight sets and was beaten by fifth seed Neely Goetten of Jerseyville 6-2, 6-0 in Round 2. Jacksonville's Olivia Dobson also fell in the second round, losing to No. 4 seed Maddie Waters of Alton Marquette 6-0, 6-2.
