title: Springfield restaurant displaced by fire appears to have found new home
author: Steven Spearie
description: A Sept. 16 fire displaced the popular late-night spot on North Ninth Street, but it appears the restaurant will be reopening soon.
content:
A "coming soon" sign for California Kitchen now greets motorists along North Ninth Street.
But the new building is just across the street from the old fast-food eatery, popular with late-night crowds chowing down on fried fish and chicken, Philly cheesesteak sandwiches, gyros and kebabs, among other selections.
The new location at 1111 N. Ninth St. is the former home of KFC. Two other KFC restaurants in Springfield at 3150 S. Sixth St. and 1850 W. Jefferson St., also have closed.
A fire at 1132 N. Ninth on Sept. 16 displaced California Kitchen. There were no injuries reported from the fire.
An "occupancy prohibited" sign has hung in a window since Sept. 26.

title: Presidential library historian who voted against purchase of controversial flag out of a job
author: Steven Spearie
description: A former presidential library and museum historian said a committee took a vote on a controversial flag after it had been purchased.
content:
A historian and director at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum who voted against the ALPLM's purchase of a controversial flag last year was fired last week.
Brian Mitchell ran a number of community-based history projects in the area around the 1908 Springfield Race Riot, the New Philadelphia National Historic Site and the Freedom Corridor, linking together a number of Underground Railroad sites, in addition to his work as director of research and interpretation at the ALPLM.
Chris Wills, a spokesman for the ALPLM, confirmed by email that Mitchell "recently vacated his position."
The 56-year-old Mitchell was fired in a meeting Thursday after a scathing performance evaluation, which he provided to The State Journal-Register.
The other member of the collections committee who voted "no" to the purchase of the 21-star flag whose provenance, or origin, has been disputed by some experts, ALPLM registrar Eldon Yeakel, was fired in May.
Both Mitchell and Yeakel confirmed that an e-mail vote was taken after the flag had already been purchased.
Mitchell, a noted expert on Reconstruction after the Civil War and the author of two books, was a history professor at the University of Arkansas-Little Rock to come to Springfield in 2022.
Mitchell had been encouraged to apply for the position by current ALPLM executive director Christina Shutt, who previously ran an African American museum of history and culture center in Little Rock where Mitchell frequently delivered speeches and organized symposiums.
"I gave up tenure to come here, and I've done everything they told me I was supposed to do, so I'm feeling like anybody would who came to work and did their job," Mitchell told The State Journal-Register Wednesday. "I'm feeling I've been wronged and it's not fair."
Mitchell said he's also concerned about the ALPLM's "brain drain" within the past couple years, with the exodus of the Jacob Friefeld, a research historian; Toby Trimmer, senior public service administrator; Lauren Dodge, development director, and Melissa Coultas, human resources director, among others.
"The museum is a beautiful place," Mitchell said. "When I arrived there, it was filled with professionals who knew their jobs. They were educated. They had experience. They were fantastic people. However, they all felt abused and largely abused by the upper management."
After their "no" votes, both Mitchell and Yeakel received poor evaluations that led to their dismissals.
Mitchell's evaluation cited his "unwillingness to act as a front-line supervisor."
Mitchell and Yeakel independently said the flag purchase, first reported by The Associated Press in May, was largely orchestrated by Ian Hunt, chief of acquisitions and special projects.
Mitchell said he asked for a report on the flag's provenance, at the Dec. 7, 2023, collections committee meeting, but was told one hadn't been drafted.
Some believed the flag dated back to 1818, the year of Illinois' admission into statehood, while others believe it is from the 1860s.
According to the AP story, the museum paid $15,625 for the flag at an auction. That went above the threshold of a museum policy that calls for advance consideration for the purchase by the collections committee.
Mitchell said that Shutt maintained that the policy "didn't apply to her, that it was merely a suggestion, that her authority superseded policy."
Wills didn't make Shutt immediately available for an interview.
The purchase led to an investigation by the Office of the Inspector General, which hasn't issued its final report yet.
"It was going against what they wanted," Yeakel said of the "no" votes. "It's kind of interesting that the only two people who voted 'no' aren't (at the ALPLM) anymore."
Now a collections curator at a Kansas City museum, Yeakel said he was frustrated that neither he nor Mitchell were contacted by Hunt before the purchase.
"You usually go to the people that are going to have more knowledge or are going to interpret it or care for the objects first and get their opinions," he said.
The centerpiece of a 1,400-piece collection once at the ALPLM, a stovepipe hat generally believed to be worn by Lincoln, was discredited by a 2019 study.
Mitchell said he was told shortly after his arrival in Springfield that "one of my primary responsibilities was to make sure those sorts of things don't happen. Four people told me that, including Christina Shutt.
"They told me these regulations are in place to protect the institution and to ensure we don't waste taxpayers' money by buying anything that's fake again."
Among those who was incensed about Mitchell's departure was Lincoln scholar and author Harold Holzer.
"I have the highest regard for Brian," said Holzer, reached in New York Wednesday. "I know he left a faculty position to come to Springfield. He deserves to be working at an institution of history somewhere.
"I'm sad for Springfield, sad for the library and I'm a big supporter of Brian Mitchell."

title: Ready to clock in? Stream 'Severance' on Apple TV+ before season two drops
author: Kasey Caminiti
description: Catch up on all ten episodes of the first season of 'Severance' on Apple TV+ before Adam Scott and Patricia Arquette return for season two on January 17, 2025.
content:
— Recommendations are independently chosen by our editors. Purchases you make through the links below may earn us and our publishing partners a commission.
Trying to achieve a healthy work-life balance is on most people's list of priorities. In the Apple TV+ series "Severance," that concept takes a dramatic leap far beyond anyone's usual 9-to-5. Adam Scott stars in the hit show as Mark Scout, an unassuming man who works at a biotech company that is performing medical experiments on employees to surgically separate their work and personal lives. As Mark uncovers a mystery about his job and himself, the experiment in "work-life balance" is questioned. Hooked? Same. Before the show's highly anticipated second season returns to Apple TV+ on Friday, January 17, you're going to want to catch up on all the mystery and drama. Learn more about "Severance" and how to stream on Apple TV+ below.
Stream "Severance" on Apple TV+
When does season two of "Severance" start?
Season two of "Severance" will premiere on Friday, January 17, 2025 on Apple TV+.
How many episodes will the second season of "Severance" have?
There will be ten episodes of the second season of "Severance." After the first episode premieres on Friday, January 17, 2025, the remaining eight episodes will air weekly until the finale airs on Friday, March 21.
What is Apple TV's "Severance" about?
Directed by Ben Stiller, following his work on Showtime's "Escape at Dannemora", the nine-episode first season of the Apple TV+ series 'Severance' features Adam Scott as Mark Scout, a pretty unassuming individual. After his wife's tragic death in a car accident, Mark secures employment at Lumon Industries, a biotech corporation that is immediately depicted with dystopian undertones. Lumon Industries uses a medical procedure known as "severance" to separate the consciousness of their employees when an implanted chip is activated. The chip activates when entering restricted (read: severed) floors to prevent leaks of classified work.
Mark spends his days working at a desktop computer in the windowless, minimally furnished Lumon Industries office under the strict supervision of his boss, Peggy, played by Patricia Arquette.
Apple TV+ has confirmed that Adam Scott, Patricia Arquette, John Turturro, Christopher Walken, Britt Lower, Tramell Tillman, Zach Cherry and Dichen Lachman will return for the second season. New cast members will include Sarah Bock, Bob Balaban, Gwendoline Christie and more.
The series premiered on Apple TV+ on February 18, 2022

title: Here are The State Journal-Register's All-Area girls swimmers and divers of the year, team
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Here are the 20 girls swimmers and divers on The State Journal-Register's all-area team, plus the swimmer of the year
content:
Chatham Glenwood Kylie Sullens polished off another positive season and the sophomore might have more to prove after becoming The State Journal-Register's All-Area Girls Swimming and Diving Athlete of the Year.
Sullens helped Glenwood win the Central State Eight Conference meet in Normal with wins in the 200-yard IM while turning in her best time in the 100 breaststroke in 1 minute 9.67 seconds. She was a member of the victorious 200 medley and 200 freestyle relays.
Sullens was able to drop time in the IM (2:15.31) and touched in fifth place at the Chuck Fruit Aquatic Center of the Edwardsville Sectional. She was fourth in the breaststroke (1:10.34).
At the Capital City Classic — one of the city's biggest meets during the regular season at Eisenhower Pool — Sullens won the IM.
Here is the rest of the all-area team in alphabetical order. No individual, team relay or diver made the IHSA state finals this season.
Delaney Batton, Chatham Glenwood
She placed second at both the sectional (342.05) and CS8 conference (328.95) meets in 1-meter diving. She was third at the Capital Classic with a score of 297.10. The junior did not have enough points to reach the state diving finals by her sectional score.
Brooke Bonitzer, Taylorville
The sophomore placed third in the 200 IM (2:19.45) and fifth in the 100 freestyle (56.05) at the Urbana Sectional.
All-area golf: Here are The State Journal-Register's All-Area boys, girls golfers of the year and teams
Karigan Books, Sacred Heart-Griffin
She played a big part in SHG's City victory at Eisenhower Pool. Books won the 200 IM (2:25.17) and 100 freestyle (59.84). She was on the 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay teams. Books got third in the IM at conference.
Paityn Brady, Sacred Heart-Griffin
While also running cross country, the freshman contributed for the Cyclones in the pool. She was fourth in the 200 freestyle (2:15.10) and third in the 100 butterfly (1:08.73) at conference. Brady helped the Cyclones win City, getting first in the 500 freestyle (5:52.70) and second in the 200 free, while swimming legs on the winning 200 medley and 400 freestyle relays. She got 10th in the butterfly at the Edwardsville Sectional.
Marlow Burger, New Berlin
The freshman compiled a score of 341.75 at the Edwardsville Sectional and finished third, but didn't have the points to reach the state finals in 1-meter diving. She also swims the 100 breaststroke.
Izzy Canny, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The senior was one of the steadiest and most reliable swimmers on the Cyclones' team. She was second in the 100 butterfly (1:06.18) and fourth in the 100 backstroke (1:06.59) at conference. Canny was sixth in the backstroke at the Capital Invite, and she was a double winner in the fly and back at City, including swimming in two winning relays.
Calista Gardner, Rochester
The freshman nearly reached the IHSA state finals when she swam a 24.88 in the 50 freestyle at the Urbana Sectional. The state qualifying time was 24.38. Gardner was third in the 100 backstroke (1:01.56) and the state time was 58.56.
Reese Jennings, Springfield High
Jennings ended her senior season with a fifth-place finish in 1-meter diving at the Edwardsville Sectional with a score of 306.80. She was fourth (3:14.80) in the conference, sixth (273.85) at the Capital Invite and won the City title with 218.85.
Ella Lundin, Taylorville
Lundin, a freshman, swam to an eighth-place finish in the 100 butterfly (1:07.02) at sectional.
Ashleigh Maender, Chatham Glenwood
The senior was sixth and eighth in the 50 freestyle at the Capital Classic and sectional, respectively. She dropped time in the 100 freestyle (56.91) and was seventh at sectional. Maender led off the 200 freestyle relay for the first-place Titans and anchored the 200 medley relay to go with a second-place finish in the 50 free (26.34) at conference.
Abby Myers, Springfield High
The junior cut her time in the 100 butterfly (1:08.40) and came away in eighth place at sectional. She was second in both the 50 free and butterfly at City and helped the Senators win the 200 freestyle relay.
Olivia Paul, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The senior notched a fourth-place finish in 1-meter diving at sectional with a score of 309.40. She took third in both the conference (315.15) and City (207.75) meets.
Hannah Poppenhouse, Chatham Glenwood
The senior led off the winning 200 medley and 400 free relays at conference and individually was second in the 500 free (5:44.23) and third in the 100 backstroke (1:06.21). She dropped her backstroke (1:04.68) and 500 free (5:42.42) times at sectional, taking fifth and sixth, respectively.
Laynie Ryan, Chatham Glenwood
The sophomore came on and closed the season by taking sixth in the 100 freestyle (56.86) and fourth in the 100 backstroke (1:04.31) at sectional. She won the backstroke, was second in the 200 free (2:04.87) and swam third on Glenwood's winning 400 freestyle relay at conference. Her 50 free (26.98) time got her fifth place at the Capital Classic.
Chloe Scheffler, Springfield High
The freshman became one of the Senators' top swimmers after having her best time in the 200 free (2:09.62) at City. She was second in the 100 backstroke (1:05.47) and third in the 200 free (2:13.38) at conference before finishing 10th in the freestyle (2:11.87) and seventh in the backstroke (1:05.33) at sectional.
Hope Speiser, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The versatile swimmer swam from the 50 freestyle to the 500 freestyle. She took sixth place in the 50 free (25.44) at sectional and was third in the 500 free (5:51.59) at conference. The junior was fourth in the 200 IM at the Capital Classic before taking two wins at City, one of the victories was in the 100 breaststroke (1:14.74).
Lucy Tucker, Rochester
The junior took seventh place in the 200 freestyle (2:08.25) and fifth in the 500 freestyle (5:44.12) at sectional.
Erin Turk, Chatham Glenwood
The two-time All-area Swimmer of the Year got a third-place finish in the 500 free (5:23.24) and was eighth in the 200 free (2:03.35) at sectional. The senior guided the Titans to the conference title with wins in the 200 and 500 free and anchoring both the winning 200 and 400 free relays.
Maddy Yom, Chatham Glenwood
After recovering from a head injury early in the season, the junior finished third in the 100 butterfly (1:00.64), just missing the state cut of 58.38 at sectional, while taking seventh in the 50 free (25.67). She won the 50 free and butterfly and was part of the winning 200 freestyle and 200 medley relays at conference.

title: Lincoln girls basketball stands alone as top sports story around Springfield for 2024
author: Bill Welt
description: Lincoln has always been synonymous with basketball. Its storied past became richer in 2024.
content:
Caitlin Clark captivated audiences across the nation and lured scores of new viewers to the WNBA.
Kloe Froebe and the Lincoln girls basketball team also raised the bar of excellence at the high school level.
The Railsplitters dominated to such an overwhelming degree they will surely be remembered as not just one of the top teams in the history of girls basketball in The State Journal-Register coverage area but across all sports.
Lincoln not only romped to the Class 3A state title with a perfect 38-0 run but also won by an average margin of 37.2 points per game and triggered a running clock throughout the playoffs until the state semifinals.
The all-Central State Eight Conference state championship game against Chatham Glenwood presented a clash of the area's best female athletes.
Kloe Froebe became the first player in CS8 history to win Illinois Ms. Basketball, now proudly displayed at the city limits.
Then there was Becca Heitzig, who won the SJ-R's Female Athlete of the Year award for a second straight year. Her superlative résumé extended beyond basketball to cross country, track and even volleyball.
Heitzig first won the individual Class 2A cross country title over the preceding fall. She simultaneously teamed up with Froebe to help the volleyball team to its best season ever as state runners-up in 3A. She later mopped up a third gold medal in the 2A 800-meter run over the spring and still harbors the state meet record from 2022.
On the other side, the Titans featured 3A state sprint champion Katelyn Lehnen and a host of talented freshman such as Alexis Neumann, who recently became the SJ-R's Large School Volleyball Player of the Year.
Lincoln ultimately prevailed 60-44 for the school's first basketball state title.
It far from marked the end of Froebe's basketball career. She is quickly making an impact at Colorado State University and was named Mountain West Conference Freshman of the Week in November, while Heitzig continues to run at Iowa State University.
Lincoln has always been synonymous with basketball. That illustrious past became even richer in 2024.

title: Meet the SJ-R's Small School Football Player of the Year: Williamsville's Braddock Cates
author: Bill Welt
description: Williamsville senior running back Braddock Cates even threw a TD pass and is the SJ-R's Small School Football Player of the Year
content:
WILLIAMSVILLE — Braddock Cates would crank out one hit after another on seemingly every down, whether as a power back in the Wishbone or Wing-T offense or as a linebacker on defense.
'If we needed yards, I was the guy that got the ball to run people over and hit them,' Cates said. 'If I didn't, I wasn't doing my job. They put me in to push people around, and I got some yards for them. I feel like I did a pretty good job of that this year.'
The senior standout indeed piled up 1,650 rushing yards and 20 touchdowns this season and became the first player in Williamsville history to be named to the Class 3A all-state team for a second straight season by the Illinois High School Football Association.
He is also The State Journal-Register's Small School Football Player of the Year.
Cates said the team initially wasn't too sure about switching to a more smashmouth approach at the beginning of the season, but the Bullets (9-2) learned to adapt and won their first Sangamo Conference title since Cates' freshman year.
Cates said he couldn't have flourished without the offensive line, which found a good footing down the stretch under assistant coach Will Peters.
'I'm just thankful they were fast learners and got the job done,' Cates said.
Cates also learned to be an effective lead blocker for other teammates such as senior Gage Paul and junior Matthew Miller, who combined for 817 rushing yards and 14 scores. It was hardly an unattractive proposition for Cates.
'I learned not to take anything selfishly this year and last year,' Cates said. 'It's a team game. I couldn't do it without the rest of the guys. I'm just as happy for them as I am for myself whenever good things happen.'
Cates also led the offense with 18 catches for 282 yards and three scores and finished with 3,479 career rushing yards, 4,416 all-purpose yards and 48 TDs.
On defense, he delivered 52 tackles, including six for loss. He was unanimous all-Sangamo first team both ways.
His résumé also includes a Hail Mary pass to Miller to eventually claim a key 39-7 win at New Berlin. He perhaps took a page or two from his older brother Josh, who was the starting quarterback last year.
'I got put in last year, and I remember I was 1-for-1 passing for a 30-yard reception by Mason Lyttaker, so I knew there was a possibility that I could throw the ball this year,' Cates said. 'I was just waiting for the time to come, and we needed a quick score, and that was the last resort play. It somehow worked out, and we got a touchdown out of it.'
Ever since starting JFL in third grade, Cates said both his dad, J.D., and brother taught him to leave everything on the field. Gage Paul's dad, Ronnie, served as another coach over the years as well.
Cates said he wants to be a welder. When he realized this was his final season of football, Cates wanted to supply the team with all he could, not just in games but also practices. He wasn't above helping the scout teams either.
'I learned a lot from the guys that I played with, and I also taught a lot of things to the younger players on the team the last couple of years,' Cates said. 'I think I left a good impact on our program, and I hope what I've seen these younger kids do translates to next year, and I hope they have a great season. I think they have a lot of potential.'

title: History preserved: How a longtime Springfield manufacturer is being remembered
author: Steven Spearie
description: After closing last spring after nearly 150 years, the history of this Springfield-based business will be preserved in the presidential museum.
content:
The Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum has acquired an extensive collection of documents and artifacts from a Springfield-based tent manufacturer that ceased operations in the spring of 2024 after nearly 150 years.
Armbruster Manufacturing Co., now part of Traube Tent & Structures in Columbia, Ill., was a one-time global leader in the industry, producing tents for state fairs, movie sets, circus companies, military operations during both world wars and the Red Cross.
At the time of its closing in early June, it was the country's oldest family-owned tent maker.
Hellar Armbruster, a fourth-generation family owner who became president in 2005, donated the company's archives to the ALPLM. The Palm Road (Old Route 66) site of the former company is set to be part of a Roto-Rooter franchise, according to SangamonLink, the online history of the Sangamon County Historical Society.
Armbruster has been at the location on the Interstate 55 Frontage Road since 1978, after being in downtown Springfield for 68 years.
Founded in 1875 by German immigrant Rudolf Herman "R.H." Armbruster, the canvas, awning and upholstery shop began by creating covers for Conestoga wagons used by westward pioneers.
A current exhibit, located outside the museum's 'Ghosts of the Library' show, features tools and products created, sold or rented by the company, including a collapsible feed bucket, antique pulleys, an industrial size sewing machine and company stencils.
The exhibit, which runs through April 8, 2025, is included with regular museum admission.
"When we made the decision to close, it was important to us to preserve our company's rich history,' Hellar Armbruster said. 'Trusting the ALPLM with our legacy was an easy choice, and we're grateful for the work they're doing to share our story with future generations."
The ALPLM, 212 N. Sixth St., is open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

title: Where can I park during a snow emergency? Here are some reminders
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The city of Springfield is under a winter storm watch for Sunday and some municipalities have already declared a snow emergency.
content:
The Springfield area may be seeing its first major snowfall this weekend.
Several inches of snow are being predicted for the area on Sunday, and a winter storm watch was issued on Friday evening.
Usually when there's a snowstorm, a municipality will declare a snow emergency.
Here are some reminders of what happens during a snow emergency.
Where can I park during a snow emergency?
During a snow emergency, parking is not allowed on designated snow routes. This allows plows and crews to work quickly and safely. The city's snow emergency route map along with the city's snow and ice removal policy is at springfield.il.us/snow.
What determines the order in which plows clear the roads?
The city will plow primary roads first before tending to secondary roads and trouble spots, according to the city's website. Side streets in neighborhoods and subdivisions are tended to as weather and time permits. Primary streets are defined as main thoroughfares that connect the different quadrants of the city.
Can I shovel snow into the street?
No, residents should avoid shoveling snow into streets when clearing their driveway or sidewalks. It's against Springfield city ordinance. Residents and business owners should have sidewalks cleared by 10 a.m. during the snow events.
What happens if I don't?
Residents or businesses could be subject to a $250 fine for refusal to comply with city ordinances regarding the matter.
See more about the city's snow and ice removal policies on their website.
How to prepare for severe weather
During snow emergencies and other severe weather emergencies, it's handy if you are stocked with things like bottles of water, nonperishable food, a portable phone charger, flashlights and batteries, a can opener, first-aid supplies, hand sanitizer, prescriptions, pain reliever, warm clothing and blankets, a battery-operated radio, money, and baby and pet supplies if required.

title: Superintendent of Rochester schools put on paid administrative leave
author: Steven Spearie
description: The superintendent of Rochester's schools has been placed on paid administrative leave.
content:
The superintendent of Rochester's schools has been placed on paid administrative leave.
A letter dated Monday from board of education president Amy Reynolds and acting superintendent Suzanne Keller cited an investigation against Dan W. Cox, though it did not offer specifics.
"It is the practice of the Board of Education and the District not to discuss pending investigations and personnel matters," the letter stated.
Keller is the district's Director of Educational Services. Reynolds replaced Christina Margolis as board president on Dec. 11.
Cox was hired at Rochester for the 2020-21 academic year.
Cox was superintendent of the Staunton Community Unit School District from 2015 to 2020. Before that, he was superintendent of Jasper County Community Unit School District in Newton for five years.

title: Why basketball is king for this three-sport standout at Carlinville
author: Bill Welt
description: This Carlinville senior has raked in all-area honors in three different sports from the SJ-R but basketball reigns supreme
content:
CARLINVILLE — Hannah Gibson baited fellow Carlinville classmate Isabella Tiburzi into trying track and field.
It just never found a place in Tiburzi's heart, but she certainly has a knack for other athletic endeavors.
'She's definitely better than me,' Tiburzi said with a laugh alongside Gibson, a state medalist in the discus throw. 'She kind of got me to do it so she wouldn't be alone.'
Tiburzi's competitive fire envelops basketball, volleyball and softball.
Last spring, she was named to The State Journal-Register's all-area softball team boasting a .432 hitting average with 41 hits, 17 RBIs and 24 runs. This past fall, she was tabbed to the SJ-R's all-area volleyball team for a second straight season with nearly 1,900 career assists. The prolific setter/opposite hitter also summoned 240 kills and 244 digs to lead the Cavaliers to their first regional title since 2017.
The 5-foot-10 senior brings perhaps even more versatility to the girls basketball team. She not only harbors more than 1,000 career points but is also pursuing 1,000 rebounds and 500 assists to boot.
She was already the school's all-time career assists leader with 362 at the start of the season in addition to most blocked shots in a season with 56.
She ultimately averaged 12.2 points, 8.4 rebounds and 4.9 assists per game last season to be distinguished with yet more all-area honors.
Tiburzi takes a certain level of pride in being a player that can do everything, including being the primary ball handler.
'She's always kind of been the one that was handling the ball,' Carlinville coach Darrin DeNeve said. 'It's not like she was one of the littler ones. She's always been big and strong, but since middle school she's been the one that's sort of their ball handler. She's got a lot of experience.'
Tiburzi said she looked up to former teammate Jill Stayton, while her older brother, Ayden, also helped her become stronger with the ball.
'He was always the defensive type and I was more the offensive type, so he's kind of one of those people who pushed me to be better,' Tiburzi said. 'Playing in the driveway he was always the person who defended me and got me better. He's probably the best defender I've ever played against, so that helps.'
Her myriad ball skills will certainly come in handy at Lincoln Land Community College, currently 14-0 and ranked No. 5 in NJCAA Division II. Pushing the ball up the floor is one of the Loggers' hallmarks at the next level.
'Basketball's just kind of the thing that I've played since I was younger,' Tiburzi said. 'I didn't start volleyball until seventh grade, so basketball was just always the thing that I had in my head that I was going to play. I started volleyball and I loved it. I obviously still love it, but basketball is just what I decided to do in college.'
'Great fun': Lincoln girls basketball coach sees progress in new team after state run
Tiburzi, Gibson, Braley Wiser and Jordyn Loveless form a senior nucleus that stretches as far back as first grade across different sports and it's no coincidence that each team champions a winning pedigree thanks to that enduring connection.
Gibson is notably a four-sport athlete who simultaneously participates in softball and track over the spring. Loveless similarly stars in volleyball and soccer to name just a few multi-sport athletes on the girls basketball roster.
'We really encourage our players throughout the whole school to be three-sport athletes, so they've taken it to heart,' said DeNeve, also the school's athletic director. 'They're good athletes, good kids and good competitors. I'm very excited to have that going for us.'
Gibson said they've been around each other for so long they can anticipate their next move on the floor to generate points and rebounds.
Tiburzi added they know how to pick each other up and work cohesively.
'I feel like we have the perfect pieces,' Tiburzi said. 'We have every position we need to do well.'

title: Frozen Open, cooking class and more among 5 things to do in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: We know there was a snowstorm a few days ago and you may be looking to stay inside and stay warm, but if not, here are 5 things to do in Springfield.
content:
I know after the snowstorm this past weekend; you may be wanting to stay inside to stay warm. Others may be looking to get out and about as 2025 officially rolls on.
Here are five things to try out this weekend.
25th Annual Frozen Open
What: For a quarter of a century, the Springfield & Boat Club have brought the community together with parties and putts for charities. Golfers will have the opportunity to play 12 holes at the following participating clubs: Anchor Boat Club, Aqua Sports Club, Blue Ridge Club, Elks Lodge #158, Firefighters/Postal Lake Club, KC Lake Club, Lake Press Club, Prop Club, Sangamo Surf Club, Motor Boat Club TRN Club and the host club, Ski & Boat Club. This year's charities for benefit are the Military Families Together & Sangamon County Inter Veterans Burial Detail, with all registration fee's proceeds going to the charities.
When: The doors open at 10:00 a.m. Saturday with registration and sign up at the host club Ski & Boat Club, or the club of your choice.
Where: 268 Maple Grove, Springfield
More: Sign up by Thursday to be entered to win. Tee-off is at 10:30 a.m. at the club where you signed up. The Cost to play is $15.00 per player or $60 per team of four. After putting, come back to the main club by 5:30 p.m. for awards.
Sacred Heart Covenant Chapel Tours
What: Enjoy an intimate look at the Dominican Sisters' magnificent mid-century modern chapel. The convent chapel, completed in 1968, is one of Springfield's' most significant examples of mid-century modern architecture, art, and design. The 2025 schedule includes four free public events. The first tour is scheduled for this Sunday, so guests can see the chapel's 40-foot vaulted basilica-like frame providing the setting for 4,000 square feet of faceted slab glass designed by French glass artist Gabriel Loire. The mosaics, reminiscent of Byzantine iconography, were commissioned by Deprato Rigali Studios in Chicago and crafted by Italian guild artists from Venetian glass.
When: 1:30 p.m. Sunday
Where: 1237 W. Monroe St., Springfield
More: This is a free event, but registration is required before the tour. Guests can register at springfield.org/events or at 217-787-0481.
Mommy meet up at The Wakery
What: Looking to make some new friends outside your usual circle? Or maybe you're just looking for a place to grab some drinks after work with your girls after a long day. Join the team at The Wakery for a chance to sit and sip with other local moms. Coffee and non-alcoholic drinks will be available for purchase in the shop, as well as conversation starter flashcards to help guide chats when you're drawing a blank.
When: 4:30 p.m. Saturday
Where: 5 W. Old State Capitol Plaza, Springfield
More: A Facebook event has been made by The Wakery to promote the event.
FA Cup at Trish and Mary's
What: The Football Association Challenge Cup, more commonly known as the FA Cup, is the annual football – or soccer in the states – competition for English teams across the pond. It's a tradition to watch over a pint of beer so Trish & Mary's Public House will be open bright and early Sunday morning for another round of games.
When: 9 a.m. Sunday
Where: 107 W. Cook St., Suite A, Springfield
More: Learn more about the FA Cup here.
Kimchi making class with downtown local business
What: Learn the benefits of Kimchi and how to make traditional kimchi from Taste of Seoul owner Kimsimone Manning. In this two-and-a-half-hour class, explore Korean spices and pickling processes making traditional fermented kimchi as well as quick Kimchi – which does not need to be fermented for long periods. Kimchi is a traditional Korean dish of fermented vegetables, usually cabbage or radish, covered in a spice blend of garlic, ginger, chili peppers, salt and fish sauce. Manning wants to let guests know ahead of time to bring their own pickling container and four smaller containers for the non-pickled version of the dish.

title: Springfield officially appoints new director of Planning and Economic Development
author: Claire Grant
description: Some Springfield aldermen had questions about who the city appointed to be the new Planning and Economic Development director.
content:
Springfield officially has a new Director for the Office of Planning and Economic Development.
Amy Rasing was approved for the position at Tuesday night's city council meeting with a 9-0 vote.
Ward 2 Ald. Sean Gregory had several questions before appointing Rasing, bringing up her qualifications in business development for the city with her background primarily in nonprofit work.
'Business development is something that falls into the rolls I've had over the years,' Rasing said. 'I have partnered with businesses and helped businesses develop marketing plans. Working in a nonprofit many of you know nonprofits are looking for ways to promote themselves and promote the good things they do.'
Gregory also asked about how to go about the application and offering of cannabis grants to businesses on the east side. Rasing didn't have numbers on hand and wasn't equipped to speak that evening.
'February first we're supposed to open (cannabis grants) back up, we went from 69 applications to 18 applications in the second year,' Gregory said. 'This has been available for four to five years and we've only gotten two years out of it. People are losing faith in the city to deliver.'
Rasing was the city's operations coordinator for state and federal grants to head the Office of Planning and Economic Development before accepting her new role.
As grant manager for the city, Rasing joined OPED in November of 2023 and previously worked in Central Illinois Arthritis Foundation and the Illinois Presbyterian Home Community.
Rasing takes over for Val Yazell who officially retired at the end of 2024.

title: Taylorville Shootout notes: Dilley appreciates chance to coach on familiar floor
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Taylorville was the host of seven games on Saturday in its sixth annual shootout. Here are some observations from the day.
content:
It's been a while since Steve Dilley has called Taylorville home. But even after 21 seasons coaching the Buffalo Tri-City/Sangamon Valley Tornadoes, Taylorville remains special to the 1987 Taylorville graduate and 2018 inductee into the Taylorville Sports Hall of Fame.
Even Saturday's 67-59 loss to Stanford Olympia couldn't damper Dilley's experience, his third time being a head coach on the Dolph Stanley Court after appearing in three Taylorville High School Basketball Shootouts.
'You come back, and my dad and my sister are over there and friends and this place is special,' Dilley said. '(There are) a lot of memories here, a lot of memories in this locker room as a player and as a coach. Seeing people from Taylorville that I still see and just the gym and the atmosphere.
'I'm so glad our boys get to play here and just experience it because I think it's one of the most special gyms in the state and we get to come do that. What it means, I can't explain to you.
'I'm at a loss for words believe or not. I'm a little emotional here because it's special. It's special and it means a lot.'
Dilley served as an assistant basketball coach at Taylorville from 1995-2003. The venerable gym reminds him of so many things. Even trying to answer a question about what it means to be back had Dilley's emotions going haywire.
'No, I never dreamed of it, so I really owe (Taylorville athletic director) Jason Hadley and the Taylorville administration a huge gratitude of thanks for inviting us to come play in this,' Dilley said. 'I'm just blessed to be able to coach here and coach at Tri-City and have a group of players and a community that I think supports us and are behind us. It's just special and I don't care who we play. And I told Jason that.'
Tri-City battled all the way to the end against a bigger Olympia team and despite missing two starting post players: senior Gage Shafer and Hill Muir. Muir only played a few minutes.
With the County Tournament starting Monday, his Tornadoes gave Dilley enough to stay optimistic.
'This group plays so hard and they're so much fun and enjoyable to coach,' Dilley said. 'We don't ever quit, and we scrap — we do, we fight, we battle. It's hard to get on them sometimes (because) ... they play so hard and you saw it today. Now, we didn't overcome it, but we get down and then all of a sudden, we get back in.
'We knew it was going to be tough whether we were healthy or not, but I really like how our guys battled today and played.'
Riverton's bench boosts Hawks
Riverton opened the seven-game event with a 53-46 win over South County in the only matchup involving two teams from The State Journal-Register's coverage area.
The Hawks (15-1) won their 12 th -straight game thanks to an impressive second quarter and 14 points off the bench. In that period, Riverton got eight points from senior Jaxson Miller and seven from sophomore Jaxsen Trager to take a 31-24 halftime lead.
South County had leads in the opening quarter of six points (twice) and five points. The closest the Vipers would get the rest of the game was three points.
Riverton forced South County into 21 turnovers, including one shot-clock violation.
'To be honest, I kind of forgot it was on there until we got a shot-clock violation, the buzzer sounded and our guys were looking around,' Riverton coach Matt Mead said about his approach to playing with a shot clock.
'I always felt like a shot clock, the way we play, is never going to impact us because we don't really hold it. Defensively, I think we can grind people for that long.'
Trager, at 6 foot 2, is just one of three players on the Riverton roster taller than 6-1. He had 12 of the Hawks' 14 bench points and didn't miss a shot: 5-for-5 — including a pair of 3-pointers.
'Whatever I can help my team get going, whatever's fine with me,' Trager said about whether he prefers to shoot from the outside or work inside.
The only thing was Trager picked up three fouls in the first half to keep his minutes limited. Mead said he isn't worried. Those blocking fouls will eventually turn into charges taken.
'He's got some good rhythm about him and I think he's just starting to see how good he could be,' Mead said of Trager. 'He's got a lot of good skills, but it's a matter of getting somebody who is a sophomore and young guys to play hard for long periods of time. I was thrilled with the way he played today. I thought he came in and gave us some production on offense, played hard on defense, but got a couple of tough-luck fouls early, but I liked his energy today.
'I felt like he was at the wrong spot at the wrong time. Again, he's a sophomore, he's not got a lot of varsity experience yet so the game's still moving a little bit fast, so once that slows down, those fouls will become charges when he's moving his feet a little bit quicker.'
Trager even displayed his ability to impress with his passing skills. On the final play of the game, leading by five, Trager got his hands on the ball at midcourt and found a streaking Gage Werner with a behind-the-back pass.
That's a first for him in a high school game.
'Split decision,' Trager said about the pass. 'Maybe during summer basketball, but not for my high school team. It definitely did feel good, especially coming to the teammate Gage Werner. I love him; I love my teammates.'
Mead laughed at the play that took him by surprise.
'I'm glad that got caught by a Riverton Hawk, or we might've had a different conversation,' Mead joked.
Taking (a) charge
Owen Johnson knows it could hurt, but he does it anyway.
The Pleasant Plains 6-foot-0 junior won a team award for leading the Cardinals last season in charges taken. He showed that bumps and bruises still don't deter him.
In the third quarter of Plains' 49-37 win over Charleston, Johnson stepped in front of a driving Trojans' player, took a hard hit, fell to the floor but won the call. About a minute later, another Charleston ballhandler thought he could drive to the bucket, but once again, Johnson was there.
'I won an award for most charges on the team (last season) and coach really preaches help defense, so I knew my guy was in the other corner, I saw him drive and I made sure to get in help defense and take the charge,' Johnson said. 'I'm feeling it right now. It's worth it, though, for the win.'
Plains (8-7 overall) was trailing in the first half, but with Cooper Schallenberg's 18 points and 13 from Trager Shultz, the Cardinals' offense was covered. With plays like Johnson's, so was the defense.
'I think our ability to play defense and help each other out (is key),' Johnson said. 'We have lots of guys who can shoot the ball and it's a lot of fun to play with these guys.'
In the other games on Saturday, Champaign St. Thomas More beat Manito Midwest Central 53-46, Teutopolis beat New Berlin 58-34, Aurora Waubonsie Valley topped Sacred Heart-Griffin 65-41 and host Taylorville lost 59-44 to Maple Park Kaneland in the finale.

title: Springfield man is charged with arson at apartment complex that burned several units
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A Springfield man is being charged arson in connection to an apartment complex that was set ablaze earlier this week.
content:
A Springfield man is being charged with arson in connection to an apartment complex that was ablaze earlier this week.
Cyrus Banks, 22, has been charged with aggravated arson, residential arson, and criminal damage to property, following a fire that displaced at least six tenants and their families from the 2900 block of South Taylor Avenue on Wednesday.
Banks is scheduled for a preliminary hearing on Jan. 16.
No occupants were injured in the fire.
The apartment complex, Village Green Condominiums, burned on its south end. Out of 36 units in the building, six units saw significant damage and six other units experienced minor damage.
Fire crews were called to the building around 5 a.m. on the day of the fire, Springfield Fire Chief Ed Canny said.
Crews evacuated the building when they first arrived on scene.
Canny said the fire quickly spread in the building to places firefighters did not have access to.
Crews contained the fire to the south end of the building.
The American Red Cross was at the complex Wednesday to distribute food and blankets. Springfield Mass Transit District provided buses to keep people warm during the freezing temperatures.

title: More than 100 new US citizens take oath at Springfield ceremony
author: Tom Ackerman
description: 'I appreciate the opportunity that we've been given. ... We love the constitution, and we're ready to go along with you in that journey.'
content:
Over 100 people officially became U.S. citizens in Springfield.
109 excited and proud faces from 42 countries took the Oath of Allegiance at a naturalization ceremony at the Hoogland Center for the Arts on Jan. 8.
The ceremony was presided over by Judge Colleen R. Lawless of the U.S. District Court for the Central District of Illinois.
Tafadzwa Mamvura, a woman from Zimbabwe who was with her husband and three kids, woman was emotional.
'I appreciate the opportunity that we've been given,' she said. 'We value the traditions of the United States. We love the constitution, and we're ready to go along with you in that journey.'
Mamvura and her family waited for about three years to first come to the U.S. before having to wait five years to become permanent residents. Then, they were able to apply for citizenship.
Her family lives in Chatham, where they have lived for around five years. Mamvura works as a registered nurse.
For Rishabh Chalam, who is originally from India, the citizenship status signifies freedom and a cemented identity as an American.
The 25-year-old has lived in the U.S., and primarily in the Midwest since he was around six years old. In that time, he has learned to live as an American, but he appreciates the opportunities that come with citizenship.
'The concept of immigration is, you learn that you are a different person when you're here. You are becoming not even American – you're becoming someone who values the true spirit of freedom," he said.
Chalam lives in Bloomington and is pursuing a career in filmmaking since he graduated from university in Carbondale. His parents encouraged him to go through schooling and to learn about life and culture in the U.S. while they all worked towards citizenship.
Chalam's parents are proud, and they too will likely take their constitution tests.
For Ephraim King, who first came to the U.S. in 2019 with his wife and two kids from Cameroon; the move was a cultural shock, but he wanted to see the America that everyone was talking about.
'When I was in Africa, I used to hear a lot about the United States in general – the land of opportunities. I was wondering, how can I see this beautiful country that everybody is talking about?', he said.
When he arrived, he faced challenges being in a new place. But now, King is working in his dream job as an HVAC technician. He and his wife also gave birth to another child while living in the U.S.
'I'm very proud to be an American citizen,' King said.

title: Feeling lucky? Springfield alderman wants to revive talk about a casino here
author: Steven Spearie
description: An alderman wants to revive discussion about the possibility of Springfield getting in line for a casino license from the State of Illinois.
content:
A Springfield alderman wants to revive discussion about the possibility of Springfield getting in line for a casino license from the State of Illinois.
A resolution that the city be included for consideration of receiving a casino license was shelved by the Springfield committee of the whole in 2022.
But possible revenue streams and jobs has Ward 2 Ald. Shawn Gregory more than interested in the venture.
The issue could be brought up at a scheduled Jan. 14 meeting.
A downtown casino, proposed by then-Mayor Jim Langfelder, had a unique look, with table games like blackjack and craps and roulette and sports betting, but minus video gaming.
That was because of a proliferation of video gaming terminals spread throughout the city.
A solution to that, Gregory told The State Journal-Register Thursday, would be limiting the terminals to the restaurant area of the proposed casino.
Gregory said he would be willing to work with the Central Illinois Licensed Beverage Association (CILBA), which in 2022 opposed consideration for casino licenses in Springfield.
"I like the people from the beverage association," Gregory said. "I want to work with anyone, work with the council, work with (Mayor Misty Buscher), work with all the stakeholders in Springfield to make this come to fruition. We can work it out.
"Our city likes to gamble. That's their prerogative. Some people don't, so they don't have to go."
The 2022 proposal eyed downtown Springfield, but Gregory said he would be open to looking at other locations, like the Crowne Plaza, which is in Ward 3.
Decatur has shown recent interest in a casino and a horse racing track.
"I think Springfield, as a state capital, surely has to be open to saying, hey, we want one if the state's going to open up the application and opportunity for one in central Illinois," Gregory said. "We want the opportunity to make the pitch, too.
"I just look at the industry and the jobs. We need this revenue source to add to our tax bases, so I think we need to be open to that."

title: Harm reduction drive through coming soon to Springfield thanks to $60K grant
author: Claire Grant
description: Springfield's first harm reduction drive through, offering testing strips to plan B, is right around the corner in 2025.
content:
Springfield's first harm reduction drive through, offering testing strips to plan B, is right around the corner in 2025.
Nestled into the north side in Enos Park is a small business front with an unusual sight still for many people: A distribution box of Narcan, an over-the-counter drug which can reverse opioid overdose. Past the doors is a room with colorful murals on the walls, racks of donated children's coats and pregnancy tests for free across the counter.
Intricate Minds, a harm reduction organization specializing in providing services to people of color and LGBT, has been operating out of 619 North Grand Ave. since 2024.
The organization provides a myriad of free services such as access to the internet, clothes, shoes and hygiene kits and Monday barber sessions. In January of this year, the organization received a $60,000 grant from 2025-2027 from Springfield Memorial Hospita l, to improve and expand the program.
Funding will also go toward more staff and adding a ramp at the location for people living with disabilities to have better access to care.
Tiara Standage, who lost her own mother to a fentanyl overdose in 2022, is a single mom who started the group back in 2023. She says her first plan with the funding will be to make a drive-thru window for service.
'We'll be providing our same harm reduction supplies and services through the drive through for the convenience of people to drive up and get what they need,' Standage said. 'I put in a community support request just to be able to be able to purchase some harm reduction supplies and the lady who helped me emailed me … it caught me by surprise thinking she wanted to talk about some things and telling me they wanted to offer some support.'
Intricate Minds also offers help to people who use drugs with clean syringes, fentanyl testing strips and life-saving overdose medication education.
Standage says her organization is an alternative to the '12-step' program commonly used in shelters relying on abstinence from substances to not fail the program. The 12-step program Standage says doesn't work for all people in active use of drugs, and those who fall through the cracks are failed by it; Intricate Minds doesn't push for abstinence before action – the first step is to house and help give a reason for those using drugs to become sober.
'We're attacking the symptoms and not the root cause of the problem,' Standage said. 'Once we can identify the root cause of why people are unhoused, we can get over the fact some people are different – some people have mental disabilities or boundaries that prevent them from being in programs already existent. Instead of punishing them, we need to make new programs they can be involved in regardless of hangups. There's still a lot of people falling through the cracks.'
The people who walk through the doors of the storefront are are diverse as their needs. Young girls come in for 'Period Pooh' classes to learn about puberty, periods and is partnered with Planned Parenthood.
Another version of the class aimed for highschoolers teaches about safe sex and sex education.
Men and women of all ages, unhoused or not, can get a set of clothes and a haircut to be ready for an interview. The program isn't just meant for those unhoused, but as a way to break past barriers that would prevent growth, Standage says.
'What I do is very rewarding work, I see immediate results every day,' Standage said. 'When my participants compare me to other harm reduction agencies, they say that they like it here and they feel like people here and don't feel judged or discriminated against. So, I think that's my main goal is to make people feel comfortable here.'
This is the first large-level of funding the organization has received.
Standage, who is the sole employee and relies on volunteers to help keep things running, says her goal is to have enough resources so people come in from off the street and by the time they leave, are interview ready.

title: Second-half separation: Springfield High grabs lead over Lincoln for good in third quarter
author: Ryan Mahan
description: The Wade brothers, Eli and Noah, led Springfield High with 26 combined points in a win over visiting Lincoln on Tuesday.
content:
With the City Tournament's No. 1 seed already in hand, Springfield High shot nearly 60% from the field to beat Lincoln 47-32 in a Central State Eight Conference game at Willard Duey Gymnasium on Tuesday.
Junior Eli Wade led all scorers with 15 points while his brother, Noah Wade, scored 11 to lift the Senators over Lincoln's 1-3-1 zone defense. Even though the Railsplitters ' defense successfully sealed off the lane from the Senators' half-court offense for much of the game, the Senators (11-9 overall, 4-2 CS8) still shot 18 of 31 (58.1%), including 3-for-7 on 3s.
'They hit their shots, we made them turn it over,' Lincoln coach Neil Alexander said. 'We done what we wanted to do defensively, first half. Second half, we didn't once we got down and they spread the floor on us, it made the difference.'
Lincoln junior Karson Komnick sank a 3-pointer to start the third quarter to give Lincoln (10-6, 2-3 CS8) a 22-19 lead. It was all Springfield High after that.
Valor Komolafe, Noah Wade, Logan Peach and Mayango Jallah kicked off a 9-0 run that put the Senators in front for the rest of the game. Eli Wade hit a layup midway through the fourth quarter that gave Springfield High an 18-point lead, its largest of the game.
'We just had to stay locked in on what we had done against everybody else (SHS opponents this season),' Noah Wade said. 'It's the same with (Lincoln) and other teams moving forward.'
But missed free throws allowed Lincoln to get within 41-32 with 1 minute, 46 seconds left. The Senators were 7-for-18 from the line in the fourth quarter and eight of 21 overall.
Eli Wade, who was still sore after taking a hard fall in the final 67 seconds, had no doubt he and his teammates would get better at the line.
'That's one main thing we've got to work on,' Eli Wade said. 'I'd say when we're in practice, that's the main thing we focus on, is free throws, because that's the main thing we struggle at.'
The short-handed Railers, still missing Drew Hayes and Frank Sanders, just didn't have enough offense. Komnick led the way for Lincoln with 10 points while Brody Tungate finished with seven.
With those notable absences — not including Komnick, who missed approximately three weeks with a broken wrist last month — some Lincoln players are getting more minutes, but Alexander said he's still hoping to see more improvement quickly.
'At times (he sees progression), but it's not consistent enough to be where we want to be,' Alexander said. 'We just have to keep working at it; we'll keep plugging away.'
Lincoln struggled to make baskets all night, going 11-for-38 overall and three of 21 from behind the 3-point line.
The four City Tournament coaches met on Monday to seed next week's four-day event at the Bank of Springfield Center and Springfield High was seeded No. 1. The Senators haven't won a City Tournament title since 2009, their only City Tournament championship this millennium.
SHS coach Marques Warfield was pleased with his team's ability to bounce back from a less-than-stellar second period.
'Overall, we kind of had a funky second quarter that could've doomed us — and for most teams, it does — so I liked their response, I liked how they responded to the timeouts (and) I liked how they responded to halftime,' Warfield said. 'This was a collective win; it really speaks to our togetherness."

title: Promise kept: Voters in April will weigh merging county recorder, clerk offices
author: Steven Spearie
description: Sangamon County Recorder Frank Lesko ran on a "hire me to fire me" platform in the November election. Now, it's up to the voters.
content:
Sangamon County Recorder Frank Lesko ran on a "hire me to fire me" platform in the November election.
Sangamon County Democrats wanted to make sure the Republican got his wish.
Voters, though, will have the last word, with a referendum going on the April 1 ballot that would transfer duties and responsibilities of the recorder to the county clerk by Dec. 1, 2026.
The vote of the Sangamon County Board Monday ended up in favor of the resolution 17-9.
Despite calls from the Massey Commission, formed in the aftermath of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey by a former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy on July 6, the board voted down giving voters a referendum to recall the election of the sheriff.
On another vote, the board signaled its approval for a commission to study the formation of a 708 Mental Health Board with the idea that it would go before the voters in 2026.
'A campaign promise'
Lesko, the former Springfield Clerk who eked out a win over Democrat incumbent Josh Langfelder, previously told The State Journal-Register he started researching at the start of his political run how other counties in Illinois had successfully abolished the office.
Lesko never mentioned a date when he saw the office collapsing, if his campaign was successful.
"I'm talking about however long it takes to get the job done," Lesko said about the merger.
Mike Ingram said he left the Champaign County Recorder's office on Dec. 31, 2021, a little over a year after being elected to the office. Ingram spoke to the board Monday during the public comment section and sat in on both parties' caucuses.
Board member Tom Madonia proposed amendments that would have put the referendum to voters in 2026 and merged the offices in 2028. It also provided contracting with a firm to study the proposal.
But board member Tony DelGiorno asked why the board would delay the issue
"I'm just trying to help the guy keep his campaign promise," he told reporters afterwards.
Sheriff recall, Mental Health board votes
Board member Sam Cahnman said giving the voters the opportunity to recall an elected sheriff was "a safety valve" if things went awry in the future.
Despite calls from Gov. JB Pritzker and other officials, Sheriff Jack Campbell initially rebuffed resigning in the aftermath of Massey's murder before opting to retire on Aug. 31.
The board voted down having Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser ask the Illinois Attorney General's office for its opinion on recall.
The establishment of a Mental Health Board also had the blessing of the Massey Commission. A nine-person committee was given $50,000 to study the issue.
Such boards "evaluate needs, allocate funds, and coordinate a comprehensive system of services for mental health, intellectual and developmental disabilities and substance use disorders in order to benefit citizens," according to the Illinois League of Women Voters website.
There are over 90 such boards around the state, including in Christian and Montgomery counties.
Another vote by the board would consider an annual tax to provide the facilities and services.

title: New year means new menu at this student-run restaurant in Springfield
author: Joshua Dineen
description: Looking for a quick bite to eat? You'll enjoy the new menu at Bistro Verde in Springfield. Here's what you can expect.
content:
Here we are again! After a very fun and busy fall semester, we are ready to start a new class of students in Bistro Verde. We will begin service again on Tuesday, Jan. 28. This menu will be available until Thursday, Feb. 27. After that, we will enjoy a quick spring break and come back to start another new menu to finish out the spring semester.
The first menu is composed of quick service items all packaged 'to go.' They can be enjoyed in the restaurant, but the idea is to teach the students fast-paced foods and how to package them well to ensure a better chance of travelling back to the office while maintaining a delicious lunch.
The first menu category is 'Handhelds.' As the name suggests, they are items meant to be eaten with your hands. The first item is a vegetarian and gluten free option — crispy potato and cheese filled tacos. The students will practice making homemade tortillas and stuffing them, as well as making homemade salsas.
The next lesson will be about braising. We will make pulled pork with a Vietnamese flavor influence using a technique of caramelizing sugar and then gently cooking the pork in the caramel with lemongrass and garlic. We will make homemade pickles to accompany this sandwich. For the grilled cheese, we are offering a classic pairing of strawberries and balsamic vinegar, adding mozzarella and parmesan on brioche.
This will be a fun vegetarian option and a selection for anyone wanting to try something a little playful. A chicken parmesan sandwich is the next offering, which teaches students how to bread and fry meats appropriately. The last sandwich is our version of a gyro, which gives them the opportunity to learn this unique method for preparing meats as well as a delicious yogurt sauce.
We always offer three soups in this class. Loaded parlor chili is a classic and a great opportunity for the students to learn this traditional method. We are making wonton soup for which we will make hundreds of mini chicken wontons and a delicate broth, and it will have noodles and baby bok choy. The third soup comes from Honduras, called sopa marinera. It is coconut broth soup with seafood and vegetables.
I also really like having some version of sushi in this class. This time we are doing chirashi sushi, which translates to scattered sushi. All the fillings are arranged on a bed of sushi rice with seaweed on the side.
We are offering a crispy orange chicken salad with snow peas, tomato, pineapple, carrot, scallions, red cabbage, mixed greens, a lightly spicy vinaigrette and crispy wontons. Both dishes provide great practice in knife cuts for several ingredients, in different methods for breading and frying, and in making dressings and sauces.
We have two hot dishes on the regular menu, and one is always pasta. This time I wanted to show the students how to use Persian flavors. We will be taking the idea of a kofta kebab and shaping it into meatballs.
It will be served with a saffron cream sauce over fettuccini with a drizzle of pomegranate molasses, a sprinkling of ground sumac and grilled cherry tomatoes. For the final dish of the regular menu, we are offering teppanyaki foods — quickly seared chicken and beef, noodles, fried rice, cabbage pancake, vegetables, yum-yum sauce and okonomiyaki sauce.
The last is a sweet and rich, soy-based sauce traditionally paired with the cabbage pancakes, which are known as okonomiyaki. This dish will be challenging to execute as there are so many components, but I always put one hot dish like this to really show them how to multitask successfully.
Additionally, each student will create and execute a chef's special that will run each week. This is a good-sized class, so this semester we may offer a couple each week. For more information on Bistro Verde, visit llcc.edu/bistro-verde.
Kofta Kebab
5 lbs. ground beef
3 onions, grated
4 tablespoons paprika
2 tablespoons + 1 teaspoon cumin
2 tablespoons + 1 teaspoon salt
1 ½ teaspoons pepper
¼ teaspoon cayenne
1 ½ teaspoon cinnamon
1 ½ cups parsley, chopped
1 ½ cups cilantro, chopped
¼ cup + 2 tablespoons mint, chopped
Combine all the ingredients. Let sit covered in the fridge for at least 1 hour or overnight.
Shape into meatballs or onto skewers.
Bake the meatballs at 400 degrees until done, 20-25 minutes. For skewers, grill until done.
Enjoy these as an appetizer or with bread.
A quick sauce I have used is a little mayo with a bit of tahini, lemon juice and black pepper. Cucumbers, fresh tomatoes, onions, lettuce and fresh herbs would be delicious too.
Enjoy!
Joshua Dineen is the chef specialist at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management and Baking/Pastry, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: What sets Lincoln's Dawson McConnell apart, plus other top wrestlers around Springfield
author: Bill Welt
description: This Lincoln senior has twice set the school record for most pins in a season, plus other top boys and girls wrestlers around Springfield
content:
LINCOLN — Jason Lawrence boasted the most career wins in Lincoln wrestling history for nearly three decades until Austin O'Donoghue set the new record with 158 in 2021.
It may not last much longer.
Lincoln senior Dawson McConnell already surpassed 100 career wins last season. The future NCAA Division III Wisconsin-Platteville wrestler said he wants this last season to be memorable, but he just wants to soak up the experience more than anything.
'I just want to go out here, have fun, and show people what I'm about,' McConnell said.
McConnell loves wrestling wholeheartedly. He possesses a diverse array of moves and is by no means a conservative wrestler, according to Lincoln coach Justin Dietrich. That entrepreneurial spirit may sometimes make Dietrich uneasy, but that's also what makes McConnell such a prolific and talented wrestler.
'He's just the type of kid who wants to be in the room all of the time,' Dietrich said. 'He wants to be trying different stuff. If you watch him wrestle, he's a lot of fun because he's hitting a lot of different moves from a lot of different positions.'
He has cultivated his own brand of wrestling since second grade. Originally from Nebraska, he moved to Lincoln around sixth grade and has enjoyed the community's support over the years. McConnell said O'Donoghue helped with his development in eighth grade. He has also trained with former two-time University of Iowa national champion T.J. Williams out of the Peoria area since that time.
'He pushed me so hard and I'd get so mad because he would beat me all the time,' McConnell said of O'Donoghue, 'but it helped me grow and figure out who I am.'
McConnell earned fourth place in the Class 2A state finals at 165 pounds with a 44-8 tally last season (just two wins shy of Isaac Decker's 2023 record) and proceeded to win the Brian Keck Memorial Preseason Nationals title at 175 pounds in Des Moines, Iowa this past October.
Among his attributes include getting pins through different techniques such as the chicken wing and — the latter he recently showcased on Wednesday against El Paso-Gridley.
It's by no accident that McConnell set a season school record with 30 pins as a sophomore before topping that mark last winter with 33.
'He's not real comparable to a lot of kids,' Dietrich said. 'I'd imagine he's kind of hard to game plan against because he has such a wide repertoire of moves.'
McConnell is currently ranked fifth by Illinois Matmen at 175 in Class 2A. His experience at last year's state finals exemplifies how there's little separation at the top. McConnell said it's important to stick with what works.
'You never know what's going to come at you,' McConnell said. 'You just got to do your best to overcome it.'
Here are other ranked boys wrestlers in the area beginning with Class 2A, according to Illinois Matmen. Also included are the top girls wrestlers based on last year's all-area team.
Class 2A boys
Joe Reif, Jacksonville
The junior is ranked No. 2 at 157 pounds by Illinois Matmen. After winning a sectional title at 150 last season, Reif is now 20-4 overall after reaching second place in Lincoln's Floyd Bee Memorial Holiday Tournament. His only loss at Roy S. Anderson Gym was against top-ranked Tyson Raker of Highland.
Max Wiezorek, Chatham Glenwood
The senior is ranked No. 2 at 175 pounds, just ahead of Lincoln's Dawson McConnell. He took fifth place at last year's 2A individual state finals at 190 while assisting the Titans to third place at the dual-team state finals. He will wrestle at NCAA Division II Southwest Minnesota State. He already has a couple of tournament titles to his résumé, including the Floyd Bee Memorial and Tyler Cox Memorial at 190.
Cody Moss, Chatham Glenwood
The junior comes in No. 4 statewide in the heavyweight division. He went 40-13 last season at 215, including two wins at the state finals. He moved to 18-4 overall following a second-place showing at the Joe Bee Memorial and garnered second-team honors at the Don Flavin Dual Team Invitational at the end of December.
Class 1A boys
Vincent Moore, Litchfield
The junior finished 34-10 last season with a win at last year's 1A state finals. He is currently No. 9 at 120 pounds after winning Toledo Cumberland's Skull and Crossbones tournament in December.
Zach Bryant, Petersburg PORTA
The junior is No. 10 at 132 in the co-op which also includes A-C Central, Greenview, and Havana. He won PORTA's Rex Avery Invite before taking second at the Joe Bee Memorial to move to 16-3.
Logan Baker, Petersburg PORTA
The junior is slotted No. 9 at 150 and won the Joe Bee Memorial title with a 17-3 mark.
Justin Zimmerman, Petersburg PORTA
This other junior is ranked No. 4 at 157. He won the Rex Avery Invite with a narrow 8-7 decision over Cumberland's No. 5-ranked Owen McGinnis as well as the Joe Bee Memorial title for an unblemished 18-0 record.
Braxton Kieffer, Litchfield
The junior is No. 7 at 157 after placing second in the Skull and Crossbones tournament. He lost via pin to the aforementioned McGinnis to go to 14-2 overall.
Girls
Kadi Wilbern, Chatham Glenwood
The sophomore had a blazing 23-2 freshman season with two wins at last year's state finals and won both the Crimson Ladies Holiday Invite and Murdale titles at 105 to reach 22-1.
Rilynn Younker, Litchfield
The sophomore took home fourth place at last year's state finals and recently achieved second place at the co-ed Skull and Crossbones at 113 pounds.
Alexis Seymour, Jacksonville
The senior already holds two state medals, including fourth and sixth place. She recently nicked Morton's Karen Canchola with a 5-4 decision to win Jacksonville's own Crimson Ladies Holiday Invite in the 130-pound bracket at the end of December.
Jenna Tuxhorn, Chatham Glenwood
The junior took fourth at last year's state finals and won 145-pound titles at the Crimson Ladies Holiday Invite and the Murdale tournament via pins to improve to 22-1 overall.

title: What we learned from Southeast's CS8 hoops loss to Normal U-High
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Southeast boys basketball came up short against Normal U-High, but not without positives moving forward
content:
Normal U-High weathered Southeast's sparkling spirit in the early going, and with a big third quarter, collected a 55-45 Central State Eight Conference victory at Herb Scheffler Gymnasium on Tuesday night.
Here are two takeaways from the Pioneers' road win:
Second-half surge paves the way
U-High outscored Southeast 35-25 in the second half after the game went into intermission tied at 20 apiece. Junior guard Dallas Smith and sophomore forward Owen Kirby picked it up after halftime and the duo combined for 42 points as the Pioneers (11-8 overall, 2-3 in CS8) forged ahead.
U-High drained five 3-pointers in the third period, outscored Southeast 22-12 in the frame and led 42-32 after three quarters.
'In the third quarter, we did a good job of finding our shooters against their zone and Owen Kirby made those shots and started attacking the basket as well — that kind of opened things up for us,' U-High coach Andrew McDowell said. 'But it started with us getting more defensive rebounds that led us to get out a little bit in transition.'
Kirby buried 6 of 9 3-point attempts and finished with 20 points. Smith, a slashing guard, led all scorers with 22 points, hitting 6 of 8 shots while going 9-for-12 from the free-throw line.
'Dallas did a great job tonight,' McDowell said. 'When he's on balance, he does a really good job of making the right decision whether he's going to dump it down, kick it out or finish. Owen (Kirby) is only stepping into who he is going to be as a sophomore right now.'
The Pioneers committed just three turnovers in the second half after having 10 miscues in the first 16 minutes.
'Every time we come here to Southeast it's always a battle,' McDowell stated. 'They play so well here; it's such a hard place to play. The crowd got going when they made a little run back at us. We expected a fight from them. Our guys did a good job of responding in the second half. We're just trying to get a little bit better every game, and every CS8 game you can win you got to take it and get out the door, especially on the road.'
Spartans starting anew while still learning
Southeast , coming off its second win of the season — a 66-57 triumph at Bloomington on Saturday — showed promise against U-High. It appears the Spartans are putting the past behind them after a skirmish with rival Lanphier on Jan. 7 that led to two forfeited games.
'That's what we've been preaching, building this house brick by brick and we've been trying to lay bricks every game,' Southeast coach Wayne Hamilton said. 'For the most part, we have been doing that.'
The Spartans (2-14, 0-5) committed just one turnover in the first period and led 13-7 after one. Sophomore guard Josiah Turner had six points in the first quarter and junior forward Aaron Holman scored five. Turner finished with a team-best 17 points to go with seven rebounds, while Holman tallied seven points and eight boards.
Turner, who saw some valuable minutes as a freshman last season, is one of the primary cogs as the Spartans attempt to mesh, said Hamilton.
'We're a really young team and had been inexperienced but with all the games we've played they've gained some experience, and Josiah is a huge piece of that,' he said. 'You've got to keep him on the floor and out of foul trouble.'
The Spartans had six miscues in the second quarter and didn't make their first basket of the period until junior Pharez Carter hit a jumper at the halftime buzzer to knot the score 20-20. Carter drilled two 3s and joined junior point guard Inigo Angeles with eight points apiece.
'They did a pretty good job in the first half, fighting hard and playing the way we wanted to play, making smart decisions and working together,' Hamilton said. 'We started turning the ball over and things got away from us from there. Kudos to (U-High) for knocking down the shots, but we gave up too many open looks and they knocked them down.'
Southeast, which trailed 49-35 in the fourth quarter, went on a 10-0 run to get within four points with 1:58 remaining. But six free throws by U-High and a pair of turnovers by the Spartans sealed the Pioneers' victory.
Hamilton noted Southeast still has a lot to play for with three games at Evansville this weekend and Monday's game on the holiday of Martin Luther King Jr. Then it's City Tournament time at The Bank of Springfield Center on Jan. 23-25.
'We've got a packed January,' Hamilton said. 'We've got business to attend to on Friday evening.'
