title: Grayson appears in court while Illinois Supreme Court mulls state petition
author: Steven Spearie
description: The former deputy charged in the killing of Sonya Massey had his court date rescheduled. Here's what to know about Grayson's court appearance Monday.
content:
The former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy charged with first-degree murder in the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield has a new court date while the Illinois Supreme Court decides whether to take up a State's petition over his pre-trial detention.
Sean P. Grayson of Riverton again appeared before Presiding Circuit Court Judge Ryan Cadagin by Zoom Monday morning as Massey's family members and supporters, including her mother, Donna Massey, packed the small courtroom in the Sangamon County Complex.
Grayson, who is being jailed in Decatur, was seated next to defense attorney, Daniel Fultz and spoke only to greet Cadagin.
The case was re-docketed to March 24, but Grayson could be in court before then based on the state's high court's ruling on a Petition for Leave to Appeal, or PLA, filed by Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser.
The PLA asks the Supreme Court to address a Nov. 27 ruling from the Fourth District Appellate Court that would have cleared the way for Grayson's release from detention under the Pre-Trial Fairness Act, which is part of the Safety, Accountability, Fairness and Equity-Today, or SAFE-T Act.
On Dec. 10, the Supreme Court ordered Grayson remain jailed until it decides what to do in the case.
The March 24 date stands, said Mark Wykoff, Grayson's other attorney, if "it isn't guided by the Illinois Supreme Court."
Milhiser appeared for the State in the 90-second or so hearing.
Teresa Haley, the founder of the community-based organization Visions 1908, said afterwards that Massey family members anticipated the hearing being brief but work under the premise that "justice delayed is not justice denied.
"We will show up every time there is a court hearing to ensure Mr. Grayson stays behind jail," she added.
Haley said civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who also represents the Massey family, was informed about the proceeding.
Family members met with Milhiser following the hearing.
Haley insisted "a loophole" in the SAFE-T Act was found to potentially spring Grayson.
Two former emergency medical services workers charged with first-degree murder in the case of Earl Moore Jr. of Springfield have been released from jail prior to their trial.
Crump also represented Moore's family in a civil suit in the county.
Haley admitted she was "a cheerleader" for the SAFE-T Act, especially when it came to the "no cash bail," but has talked to members of the Illinois Black Legislative Caucus about other issues concerning the act.
"We believe we need to go back and revisit the SAFE-T Act and close that loophole (regarding release)," Haley said.
Other Massey family members, including her father James Wilburn of Pine Bluff, Arkansas, have spoken forcefully about keeping Grayson jailed.
Grayson and another sheriff's deputy responded to Massey's residence for a purported prowler early on the morning of July 6.
Grayson shot Massey in the face while in her home, even as Massey put her arms in the air and said "I'm sorry" while ducking for cover. Grayson aggressively yelled for Massey to put down a pot of boiling water.
Body worn camera footage of the shooting sparked international outrage.
Grayson has pleaded not guilty to all counts.
Haley is hoping a trial date can be set by later this summer for Grayson.

title: 'Once in a lifetime opportunity': Springfield police sending officers to Inauguration
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Nearly a dozen Springfield Police officers are heading to the nation's capital to boost security during the presidential transfer of power.
content:
Nearly a dozen Springfield Police officers are hitting the road and heading to the nation's capital to boost security during the presidential transfer of power.
Ten officers and one lieutenant from the Springfield Police Department have been called to support law enforcement at the Presidential Inauguration.
The Springfield officers, who are part of the Mobile Field Force team locally that specializes in crowd control, will likely be working along the Inaugural parade route, said Lieutenant Joe Phillips, who is commander of the Mobile Field Force team in the Springfield region.
The Springfield officers will be working with and supporting the Metropolitan Police Department who are more familiar with the laws in Washington D.C.
The Springfield team will also join around 4,000 officers who are traveling to the nation's capital from across the U.S.
Phillips said the opportunity maybe comes once in a lifetime or in the career of a police officer.
Why are Springfield Police officers being sent?
Authorities contacted Springfield Police Chief Ken Scarlette who chose to send the Mobile Field Force team, Phillips said.
In addition to crowd control, the team specializes in mutual aid response, which is when emergency responders agree to help one another.
What other major events has the team been called to assist?
In recent years, they have beefed up police presence at the Democratic National Convention as well as the Republican National Convention. They also worked at the G20 Summit in Pittsburgh.
The team mostly puts their training to use in Springfield at events where there are large crowds.
Do assisting departments get paid to help?
The trip and its expenses will be reimbursed by the Metropolitan Police Department.
Springfield police are also looking to learn from the experience. While the Springfield officers are well-versed with crowds and political figures, Phillips said he and the team will be looking to learn from the police there who routinely protect the president and other high-profile politicians.
Will the event affect policing in Springfield?
No, the attending officers are from different divisions and units within the department, and there are enough officers in Springfield to cover the shifts.
The Illinois National Guard is also sending troops
Approximately 140 Illinois National Guard members are deploying on federal orders.
Around 110 Soldiers and 30 Airmen from the Illinois National Guard will attend.
The Illinois National Guard force will include 100 Military Police Soldiers from the 933 rd Military Police Company, based in Fort Sheridan, and about 30 Security Forces Airmen from the 183rd Wing based in Springfield, the 126th Air Refueling Wing based at Scott Air Force Base, and the 182nd Airlift Wing based in Peoria.
There will also be a few service members in the 5 th Civil Support Team (CST), based in Bartonville, and the 126 th Air Refueling Wing, based at Scott Air Force Base.

content:
You've probably been trying to keep warm most of the week with the bitter cold. But there are still plenty of things to do in the Springfield area this weekend.
Here are five things we found to do.
Revel in Red at Motorheads
What: Sometimes, you don't know what you've been missing until it's right in front of you. This may just be the case with Revel in Red. This six-piece rock band is hitting the stage at Motorheads with the skill and presence to keep you singing and dancing all night.

Performed by local actors, these original works showcase creativity and storytelling at its finest. This event is sponsored by Carol Herzog. For a full list of plays, check out the ticket section below.
More: Tickets can be purchased at UIS PAC website. Tickets bought before the event are $17, while day-of are $21.
Pot painting with Ceramics by Rosie
What: Two local businesses are coming together for Springfield's first paint-a-pot at It's All About Wine to paint a piece of pottery handmade by artist Rosie. Bring yourself, a friend, a date, a whole crew of pals and join us to get creative, enjoy food and drinks, and paint a handmade pot to keep and use. title: Culture changers: Springfield High boys eye first City Tournament title since '09
author: Ryan Mahan
description: "When I started the season, the message to our team was, 'We're the best team in the city; we're not the best individuals,'" SHS coach Marques Warfield says ahead of this year's event.
content:
There's a feeling of optimism inside the walls of Springfield High's Willard Duey Gymnasium as the Senators' boys basketball team hopes to do something that hasn't happened since they were just toddlers: win a City Tournament.
While the 76th annual Boys City Tournament, which begins on Thursday at the Bank of Springfield Center — a day after the Girls City Tournament gets underway at the same venue — is by no means Springfield's to lose, the Senators' players have no intention to be happy with just the No. 1 seed.
The last time the Springfield High boys basketball team brought home a City Tournament title was in 2009, when the Senators had names like Benjamin Mathis, Kendall Murdock, Mark Gilchrese, Isiah Hale and Derek Wilkerson.
Barack Obama had barely finished his oath of office as the newly-sworn-in president of the United States. Stephen Curry hadn't yet entered the NBA, Lebron James was still seeking his first NBA title and the Boston Celtics' hope for a multi-year title dynasty was still alive before Kevin Garnett hurt his knee in February that year and missed the playoffs.
Springfield High sophomore Noah Wade was born the year before; his brother Elijah Wade, a junior, was born in 2007. They don't need to knock on SHS social science department chair Jeff Lightfoot's door for a history lesson: They want to make a bit of it themselves.
The Senators are 12-10 overall and 5-2 in the Central State Eight Conference. Of their 10 losses, five were by two points or less, including Monday's 59-57 setback to Chicago Hope in the second annual MLK Day Classic at Lanphier.
The players credit second-year coach Marques Warfield as the driving force behind the improvement and the raised expectations. Warfield, who had been an assistant at both Southeast and Lanphier, said he thought a major shakeup was in order when he was hired.
'A lot of people didn't want the job because they fear the past, essentially,' Warfield said. 'There hasn't been any culture for a long time. The main thing I wanted to address was culture.'
Springfield's 6-foot-6 senior forward Valor Komolafe is a big believer in Warfield's ability to get the players to believe.
Last season, the Senators started 0-7 before a 7-20 finish. This season's start didn't seem much better, record-wise — 0-2, 1-3, 2-5 — but Komolafe said there were reasons for hope.
'This year we lost our first two games, but I think we were able to correct it quicker and be able to bounce back and win more,' said Komolafe, who added that he's won just a single City Tournament game in his career.
Junior Eli Wade plays for Warfield's summer team as well.
'I say everything, for real,' Eli Wade said of what's changed. "I mean, we all love the game of basketball. Even if we're down (or) up, we're always going to show some grit."
Eli Wade started playing basketball in sixth grade, but due to COVID-19 restrictions, Noah Wade didn't start until his seventh-grade season. Noah said it's been a 'long journey' for him to get to where he is now individually. For the team, however, the work began in earnest last summer.
'We came in and practiced in the summer,' Noah Wade said. 'We knew what we had to do if we wanted to be the best in the city; now we've got to go out and show it.'
Warfield saw the potential of his squad, despite that it only has three seniors: Komolafe, point guard Jaiyden Wilson and Kevin Salimtoua. Warfield said the potential had to be matched by the effort, however.
'I believe in strength in numbers,' Warfield said. 'When I started the season, the message to our team was, 'We're the best team in the city; we're not the best individuals. We're the best team.'
'Everything that we try to get done is collectively. And I think that's what makes us a hard draw because we don't care who scores. One night you might have Elijah Wade have 20; the next night it might be Logan Peach. The next night it might be someone else. So for us, it's just strength in numbers. It's, can you do the job? And then the other part of us is we try to take pride in defense. Everything is defense first.'
A month after the conclusion of the City Tournament, the Senators will seek the end of another long drought: a postseason plaque for the first time since 1999.
'I think it's the mentality you have to have ... you've got to have the dog mentality, the mentality that you're going to win every single game,' Wilson said. 'It's just more to come for us; more than the city. We want a regional, we want a sectional, we want a state.
'We've got our eyes on the prize.'

title: Best independent coffee shop in Illinois is found in Springfield, new report finds
author: Claire Grant
description: The best independent coffee shop in Illinois is found in Springfield, according to a new report. What's your favorite coffee shop in Springfield?
content:
Where's your favorite place to grab a cup of coffee and catch up? According to Springfield residents, it's a little shop on the corner of West Cook and Spring Street, just a block away from the Illinois State Museum.
It's the vintage charm of Vinegar Hill Mall and classic, cozy feel that gives Wm. Van's Cafe a bustling cult following.
Not just a cult following, but now a position on America's best independent coffee shops, as Illinois' top caffeine spot.
Serving breakfast, brunch and aesthetics worth a picture or two, Wm. Van's average rating was 4.46 out of five.
General Manager Sydney Huffman said the growing interest in local coffee spots comes from the experience and that it really does matter if your barista knows you.
'Not only are you supporting your local community, but you have more personable experiences when you're at your local shop,' Huffman said. 'Your morning coffee run becomes more than an iced latte; it's a chance to connect with the familiar faces.'
The business regularly rotates the drink menu depending on season and place an emphasis on quality over quantity – Huffman says in the past nine months she's been GM, the most important part is seeing what sticks in the menu and strikes a chord with coffee fans and finding a way to add it to the next menu.
The top three local coffee spots nationwide are The Espresso Bar in Taos, New Mexico at 4.93 stars out of five, Prestogeorge Coffee and Tea in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania at 4.90 and Iris Bagel and Coffee House in Arlington, Texas with 4.86.
Big is out - small is in
According to OnDeck, big chain cafés are saving money by opening smaller premises to minimize costs and concentrate on walk-through trade. Meanwhile, independent cafés are capitalizing on their already cozy premises by delivering personality, quality and good company to customers looking to sit down with a brew and a pastry — and maybe even return to the counter for more.
The specialty coffee shop market is tipped to grow by $39.17 billion from 2022 to 2027, driven by the indie sector. The same follows suit for Springfield; the city has seen a growth in locally-owned coffee shops in the past year trying to enter the market.
Methodology
The rankings are put together by OnDeck, a platform offering loans for small businesses, using publicly available Tripadvisor pages for rankings. Building a list of the major cities in every state, the five-star rated local establishments were isolated from chains.
Lastly, cities were ranked based on the weighted average five-star rating across all independent coffee shops in that city.
This analysis was completed in October 2024.

title: Lanphier upsets SHG, Springfield High cruises past Southeast as boys open City Tournament
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Lanphier held off a late charge from Sacred Heart-Griffin in the first boys basketball game of the City Tournament. Springfield High cruised past Southeast.
content:
Lanphier junior Soriano Hayes was on a mission from the opening tip.
Hayes scored the first six points for the Lions and added 15 more in the second half en route to a game-high 21 as Lanphier controlled No. 2 seed Sacred Heart-Griffin 62-56 in the first game of the City Boys Basketball Tournament at the BOS Center on Thursday.
Lanphier, seeded third, has reeled off four straight wins since its skirmish with crosstown rival Southeast on Jan. 7 that led to forfeiting two games. Hayes received a four-game suspension due to the altercation, and he appears to have a renewed mindset for the second half of the season.
'I came out to help my team,' said Hayes, who made eight of 11 shots and had seven rebounds and three assists. 'I was suspended four games, so I was just trying to take that and use that as motivation. I just wanted to make sure that we get this game and look forward to the game on (Friday).'
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Lanphier coach Blake Turner immediately put Hayes back into the starting lineup on Thursday, and he was needed against the Cyclones. He scored 10 points in the third period to help Lanphier build a 46-34 advantage after three, and his three-point play with 11.4 seconds remaining in the final period salted away the victory.
'He's a huge part of what we do,' Turner said of Hayes. '(His suspension) was a tough situation, and everybody knows it was a tough situation. He really matured a lot. He didn't pout; he was one of our hardest workers in practice. He was our most vocal person on the bench for those four games. I thought that he was great out there (on Thursday).'
Lions seize momentum
SHG led 17-15 after one quarter, getting seven points from sophomore guard Terrion Wallace. Lanphier answered and got a combined 13 points from seniors JaiQuan Holman (15 total points) and Shaunassey Hatchett Jr. (11 points, seven rebounds) in the second frame to go into intermission with a 32-29 lead.
Lanphier's execution in the third period sparked a big run as Hayes had several alley-oop layups to help the Lions outscore the Cyclones 14-5 in the stanza and forge ahead 46-34 going into the final eight minutes. The Cyclones had three turnovers to start the second half and didn't attempt a shot until sophomore Tereik Hurd made a basket at 4 minutes, 38 seconds of the quarter.
'We're playing the way that we expected to be playing all season,' Turner said. 'We hit a couple bumps, and we kind of lost our way a little bit, but I think we are finding our way. We're a team that thrives on defense, and right now I like our defense. We're doing a much better job rebounding the ball. Offensively, I think we are being more efficient and taking better shots.'
SHG makes final push
Lanphier (14-8 overall, 3-3 in CS8, 1-0 City) built its biggest lead of 16 points when Hatchett threw down an alley-oop dunk early in the fourth quarter. But his dunk resulted in a technical foul for hanging on the rim, and after picking up his fourth foul, Hatchett went to the bench as the Cyclones chipped at the lead.
'You must be disciplined in those type of moments because stuff like that can make (the other team) go on a run,' said Hayes of Hatchett's technical. "Stay disciplined, dunk the ball, get back on defense and look forward to the next play.'
SHG (11-10, 2-4, 0-1 City) responded, getting within four points twice and had a chance to get within two but missed a close layup with :40 to go before Lanphier sealed it. Sophomore Myles Montgomery hit a pair of 3-pointers in the fourth and scored a team-high 15 points for the Cyclones. Hurd added 14, followed by junior Zion Lee (12) and Wallace (11).
As for Hayes, it's on to the next matchup for Lanphier.
'We won last year, and I was here,' he said. 'I'm just soaking it all in and not trying to get satisfied with one win. We win all three — we win the City — then I'll be satisfied. The job ain't finished. When we win all the games, then we can celebrate. Right now, no celebrating, just move on to the next game.'
Springfield High 66, Southeast 31
The Wade brothers — junior Eli and sophomore Noah — combined to score 41 points as the top-seeded Senators beat No. 4 Southeast in a game that finished with a running clock.
Eli Wade scored 22 points on 7-for-14 shooting. He also led the Senators with eight rebounds and five steals. It was his second game back after he injured his ankle against Lincoln on Jan. 14, and he said he was roughly 90% healed on Thursday.
'Coming into this game, we just have to prove a point,' Eli Wade said. 'Play with discipline. Coming into every game, our coach is on us about defense.'
Noah Wade finished with 19 points on a perfect 7-for-7 from the floor, including hitting his one 3-point attempt. His only blemish was a missed free throw on five tries.
Springfield High outrebounded Southeast 28-12, including 17-3 on the offensive glass. SHS also won the turnover battle 23-11, which turned into a 33-8 scoring edge in points off turnovers. Second-year SHS coach Marques Warfield said his players are aware of the seriousness they need to have in this event.
'I think they understand now, because look at the type of environments we've been in,' Warfield said. 'We've played at Illinois College twice — we've played at a lot of neutral sites — the Pekin Holiday Tournament, the BOS (Center floor near the beginning of the season). We're used to play on bigger floors and what it takes to play at that level and just being in shape.'
Valor Komolafe, a Springfield High senior who said prior to the City Tournament he had won just one time in the tournament, finished with nine points for the Senators.
Aaron Holman led Southeast with eight points.

title: New multimillion dollar warehouse one step closer to reality in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: A new multimillion dollar warehouse that could bring hundreds of jobs to Springfield is inching closer to the finish line of final approval.
content:
A new distribution warehouse could soon be on its way to Springfield.
Project Cardinal, or better known as the Frito-Lay distribution hub, has been placed on the consent agenda for the Feb. 4 City Council for the development process.
Ordinance 2025-023, which approves the large-scale development of Project Cardinal for the Office of Public Works, was overwhelmingly voted onto the Springfield City Council consent agenda on Jan. 28.
Where will the warehouse be?
The land is on the southwest corner of I-55 on the Chatham interchange.
The development is located on the east side of Palm Road and the west side of On-Ramp 88S for Interstate 55. On the southern end of Springfield, beneath the lake.
What will the warehouse look like?
The planned building will be a warehouse and while the city has not formally confirmed who will use the building, sources told The State Journal-Register last year that Frito-Lay, a subsidiary of Pepsico, will use the location. Pepsico produces snacks like chips, pretzels and popcorn.
How big would the warehouse be?
The almost 227,000-square-foot warehouse will have associated trailer parking, a 12,000-square-foot office space, a bulk truck parking, a 5,180-square-foot garage, a 10-foot site security fence and landscaping surrounding the lot.
Who currently owns the land to be developed?
Houston, Texas resident John Kovski, who is listed as manager for Lakeview Acres LLC, is listed as the owner of the large-scale development project on the 30-acre lot. Martin Engineering is listed as the engineer in the project.
How many jobs will the warehouse bring?
While the number has not been confirmed, an average warehouse of that size could bring anywhere from 100 to 200 employees to the city.
Why was the development put on consent?
Part of why the warehouse has been placed on consent could lend to the Dec. 5, 2024, Land Subdivision Committee of the Springfield-Sangamon County Regional Planning Commission. In a letter sent to Mayor Misty Buscher on Jan. 7 from the commission, Project Cardinal was recommended for approval for a 234,842 square-foot industrial warehouse building along Palm Road.

title: Hall of fame football coach comes out of retirement to fill Pana opening
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Mark Ramsey, who is fifth all-time in Illinois football coaching wins, is returning to the sidelines to take over the Pana football program.
content:
Mark Ramsey, who is fifth all-time in Illinois football coaching wins, is returning to the sidelines to take over the Pana football program.
Ramsey, who retired from coaching after guiding Decatur St. Teresa to the 2022 Class 2A state championship — his second in his career — was approved by the Pana school board at Monday's meeting.
'I think that Pana football is really exciting,' Ramsey said in a statement released by the Pana Community Unit School District on Monday. 'There's great support from the school board, administration, and the community. It's a great situation to come into and to continue the success of the program.'
He replaces Pana's all-time winningest coach, Trevor Higgins, who finished 78-18 over nine seasons. Higgins stepped down in December, citing time constraints with his job and family.
When Higgins heard the rumors that Ramsey was interested in the job, he was happy to know the program he left would be in good hands. Higgins has plenty of history with Ramsey: Higgins, who graduated from Moweaqua Central A&M in 2003, played on the 2001 runner-up team Ramsey coached, and his Panthers lost to St. Teresa in the 2022 2A quarterfinals.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
'I never would have guessed that it would have been him to be next, but I'm excited for the kids to have the experience that I did to play underneath him, and I mean, why wouldn't you go after him, right,' Higgins said by phone on Tuesday. 'Hall of Fame coach, multiple state runs, multiple state championships, and I'm excited for the kids and the community, and I'll be their No. 1 fan on the outside of the fence.'
With 332 wins (against 113 losses), Ramsey brings a wealth of knowledge and experience to the Panthers' program, which has qualified for the postseason the last nine straight full seasons, including reaching the quarterfinals in four of the last five seasons.
Ramsey began his career in 1983 at Moweaqua High School. Moweaqua and Assumption combined in 1991 to become Central A&M. In 1992, Ramsey reached the state title game for his first time, losing 20-6 to Richmond-Burton in the Class 2A championship. Following two more runner-up finishes in 1995 and '96, the Raiders broke through in 1997 and beat St. Joseph-Ogden 35-28 to cap a 14-0 season and win his first state championship. He led the Raiders back to second place in the state in 2001.
Following the 2012 season, Ramsey went to Shelbyville and helped the Rams make the playoffs in 2014 and 2015 and left for St. Teresa, where he immediately took the Bulldogs to the 1A playoffs and finished second to Forreston. In his final season, he won his second state championship and beat Downs Tri-Valley 29-22, for his second 14-0 finish.
So, what can Pana fans expect?
'(Ramsey is a) very detail-oriented, terrific X-and-O guy, understands the game of football and taught it really well to the players, and then surrounded himself with other coaches who were experts at their positions,' Higgins said. '(That is) another reason why I think that's a perfect fit for him, to be able to have the coaching staff down there, also for him to bring coach (Mike) Conlon, who was also my defensive coordinator when I was in high school, to bring him along too, I just see a win-win for Pana football.'
The Illinois High School Football Coaches Association class of 2007 Hall of Fame inductee sits nine wins away from passing longtime Sterling Newman coach Michael Papoccia for No. 4 on the state's all-time wins list.
'This is obviously something that he's been born to do,' Higgins said of Ramsey. 'He's been coaching a long time, and I'm just happy that he gets another shot at it.'
Taylorville Shootout notes:
In another interesting twist, Pana opens its season with a Week 0 scrimmage against Central A&M.
This story will be updated Wednesday.

title: Illinois Supreme Court will take up State's petition on Sean Grayson's detention
author: Steven Spearie
description: The petition filed by the Sangamon County State's Attorney centers around an appellate court decision saying Sean Grayson should be released.
content:
The Illinois Supreme Court has agreed take up a Petition for Leave to Appeal filed by Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser regarding the detention of a former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy charged with first-degree murder in the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey.
Oral arguments will be heard by the high court after the State and defense attorneys for Sean P. Grayson file briefs.
The petition, or PLA, asks the Supreme Court to address a Nov. 27 ruling from the Fourth District Appellate Court that would have cleared the way for Grayson's release from detention under the Pre-Trial Fairness Act, which is part of the Safety, Accountability, Fairness and Equity-Today, or SAFE-T Act.
A March 24 hearing for Grayson in Sangamon County Court will stand.
On Dec. 10, the Supreme Court ordered Grayson remain jailed until a decision is made in the case. He is currently jailed in Decatur.
Grayson and another sheriff's deputy responded to Massey's residence for a purported prowler early on the morning of July 6.
Grayson shot Massey in the face while in her home, even as Massey put her arms in the air and said "I'm sorry" while ducking for cover. Grayson aggressively yelled for Massey to put down a pot of boiling water.
Body worn camera footage of the shooting sparked international outrage.
Grayson has pleaded not guilty to all counts.

title: New task force looks to target gun violence in Springfield
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Springfield Police Department has announced an initiative to formally partner with a federal agency to tackle gun violence.
content:
The Springfield Police Department has announced an initiative to formally partner with a federal agency to tackle gun violence.
The SPD is joining forces with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives to form a Springfield Firearms Task Force that aims to more quickly and effectively identify and arrest people illegally purchasing, selling and using firearms.
The task force has been working since this past fall and is made up of officers from the SPD, special agents from the ATF, and also Springfield police officers who have been sworn as federal task officers for the team's purposes.
During a news conference last week, Springfield Police Chief Ken Scarlette reiterated that the city has seen an increase in gun crime in Springfield.
'I made it very clear when I took over as Chief of Police almost three years ago that it would be my goal and my mission and the mission of the men and women of Springfield Police Department to combat gun violence and do whatever we can to keep our community safe,' he said about the need for the partnership.
While the ATF has a presence in Springfield, the partnership has given certain Springfield Police detectives the same tools and resources that ATF agents have, Jason Gore, Assistant Special Agent in charge of the ATF Chicago Field Division said.
Scarlette said he would ideally hope to see the team meeting with each other on a regular basis, also in collaboration with state and federal prosecutors. The effort aims to streamline the process of reviewing gun cases and reviewing evidence, so law enforcement can more quickly find leads and make arrests.
Who will the task force target?
The agencies want to crack down on gun violence, but they also want to focus on illegal trafficking of guns, and specifically 'straw purchasers,' who are people who buy guns for others.
The task force is also looking for felons who illegally possess guns and drug traffickers who have guns.
The agencies are also concerned with aftermarket devices that convert handguns and rifles into automatic firearms, as opposed firing bullets in a semi-automatic manner.

title: Plane collides with helicopter, crashes into DC river; bodies reportedly recovered
author: Thao Nguyen
description: An airplane collided with a helicopter while trying to land at the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Wednesday night, officials said.
content:
Editor's note: This page reflects news of the plane crash near DC on Wednesday, Jan. 29. For the latest updates on the search for survivors, please read USA TODAY's live coverage of the rescue and recovery efforts on Thursday, Jan. 30.
WASHINGTON — A passenger jet with 64 people aboard collided with an Army helicopter above Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport Wednesday night, and a major search-and-rescue operation is ongoing in the nearby Potomac River.
Authorities said American Airlines flight 5342 from Wichita, Kansas, was preparing to land at the airport before it "collided in midair" with the helicopter around 9 p.m.
At least a dozen bodies were recovered as authorities late Wednesday rushed boats into the water to search for survivors, according to NBC and CBS.
Area officials have not said how many people died or were injured in the collision. "We can't provide any more information about recovery efforts,' Washington D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser said in the early hours of Thursday morning. Bowser and other area leaders will give another update at 7:30 a.m.
President Donald Trump was briefed on what he called a "terrible accident" and was monitoring the response.
"May God Bless their souls,' Trump said in a statement. "Thank you for the incredible work being done by our first responders."
Catch up with live updates from the USA TODAY Network.
American Airlines provides phone numbers for family members
American Airlines wants people who believe they may have loved ones on board Flight 5342 to call toll-free at 800-679-8215. "Those calling from outside the U.S. can visit news.aa.com for additional phone numbers," the airline said in a statement. "Family members in Canada, Puerto Rico or the U.S. Virgin Islands can call 800-679-8215 directly."
− Swapna Venugopal Ramaswamy
Washington-area residents stunned by crash
When Arlington, Virginia, resident Habihor Rabby heard about the crash, he and a group of friends decided to observe the search and rescue efforts.
Rabby, 26, said he first tried nearby Hains Point, which was blocked off by police, and then moved to the marina on Daingerfield Island in Alexandria, Virgina, where a sea of flashing lights from emergency vehicles could be seen across the river early Thursday.
Though he frequently flies from Washington, D.C. to Kentucky, Rabby said the incident hasn't made him nervous about traveling. While officials have not said how many people died or were injured, the crash has already taken an emotional toll on the local communities.
"That really hurt," he said. "It's really sad."
–N'dea Yancey-Bragg and Thao Nguyen
Air traffic control audio: 'I just saw a fireball'
Air traffic control audio recorded the final moments before and after the crash of an American Airlines regional passenger jet and a U.S. Army Black Hawk helicopter.
Audio from LiveATC.net, a respected source for in-flight recording, captured the final communications between the three crew members of the helicopter – call sign PAT25 – before it collided with the jet carrying 64 passengers and crew.
"PAT25, do you have a CRJ in sight? PAT25, pass behind the CRJ," an air traffic controller said at 8.47 p.m. on Wednesday. Seconds later, another aircraft called in to air traffic control, saying, "Tower, did you see that?" apparently referring to the crash.
"I don't know if you caught earlier what happened, but there was a collision on the approach into 33. We're going to be shutting down operations for the indefinite future," another controller remarked.
"Both the helicopter and the plane crashed in the river," a third air traffic controller can be heard saying.
"It was probably out in the middle of the river," the controller said. "I just saw a fireball and then it was just gone. I haven't seen anything since they hit the river. But it was a CRJ and a helicopter that hit."
– Reuters
U.S. Figure Skating says athletes, coaches and family members were on flight
U.S. Figure Skating, the sport's American governing body, confirmed in a statement to USA TODAY that "several members of our skating community were sadly aboard American Airlines Flight 5342."
"These athletes, coaches, and family members were returning home from the National Development Camp held in conjunction with the U.S. Figure Skating Championships in Wichita, Kansas," the statement said. – Marina Pitofsky
Airport to remain closed until 11 a.m.
Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport will remain closed for flights until at least 11 a.m. Thursday, said Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority CEO Jack Potter.
The airport halted all takeoffs and landings after the collision occurred around 9 p.m. Wednesday. Aircraft were rerouted to Washington Dulles International Airport.
'Obviously, that will be fluid,' Potter said. 'We'll learn more, but we wanted to advise passengers who might be coming to the airport in the morning that we will be closed until at least 11 o'clock.'
− Thao Nguyen
'My heart goes out to those people and their families'
Minutes before an American Airlines flight collided with a military helicopter, Anthony Rosado landed at the DCA on another American Airlines flight coming in from Florida.
He saw the flash of emergency lights on the tarmac, but initially didn't think much of it. When he learned his connecting flight to Buffalo was canceled, he thought it might be due to weather.
Rosado, 24, said he didn't realize the gravity of the situation until he got into the terminal, called his wife and learned of the crash.
'She's like, 'that could have been you,'' he said. 'It's kind of very surreal. I'm very grateful that that wasn't me. My heart goes out to those people and their families.'
Rosado was among a small group of stranded passengers waiting at the airport into the early hours of Thursday morning, some trying to sleep, some waiting in line rebook their flights and others watching a press conference on the crash. Rosado said he tried to leave the airport, but Uber drivers were unable to pick him up and he couldn't navigate the Metro due to the heavy police presence.
− N'Dea Yancey-Bragg
Senator refers to losing 'over 60 Kansans'
Officials early Thursday did not confirm specific numbers of survivors or fatalities after the shocking crash hours earlier. However, a Kansas senator referenced losing "over 60 Kansans simultaneously."
'When one person dies, it's a tragedy, but when many, many, many people die, it's an unbearable sorrow,' U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., said at an airport press conference. 'It's a heartbreak beyond measure.'
'It's really hard when you lose probably over 60 Kansans simultaneously,' he said.
U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said he lobbied for the nonstop Wichita-to-D.C. flight that started last year. He said he's been a passenger on the route many times himself.
'It is certainly true that in Kansas and in Wichita in particular, we're going to know people who are on this flight, know their family members, know somebody. So, this is a very personal circumstance as well as an official response.'
− Joey Garrison
Emergency officials say hundreds of first responders in area
Emergency responders were alerted of an aircraft crash at 8:48 p.m., according to D.C. Fire and EMS Chief John Donnelly. First units arrived at the scene at 8:58 p.m. and discovered the aircraft in the water.
Authorities immediately began rescue operations, Donnelly said. He noted that incident is 'growing' and there were currently about 300 responders working the incident.
'The conditions out there are extremely rough for the responders,' Donnelly said at a news conference. 'It's cold. They're dealing with relatively windy conditions.'
American Airlines CEO says the focus is now on passengers, crew members and their families
Robert Isom, CEO of American Airlines, said the aircraft involved in the tragic collision Wednesday night was operated by PSA Airlines, a wholly owned subsidiary of the company.
He said the company's efforts are now 'focused entirely on the needs of our passengers, crew members, partners, first responders, along with their families and loved ones."
The flight had four crew members and was carrying 60 passengers for a total of 64 people on board, he said.
'We are actively working with local, state, and federal authorities on emergency response efforts,' he said.
Isom said he will be heading to Washington D.C. shortly and that the company was cooperating fully with the National Transportation Safety Board in its investigation.
− Swapna Venugopal Ramaswamy
Military opens own investigation into crash, defense secretary says
The Army and the Defense Department "immediately" opened an investigation into the crash, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in a post on X early Thursday morning.
The military typically conducts at least two investigations whenever a fatal mishap occurs, according to an Army handbook.
The Army Combat Readiness Center at Fort Novosel, Alabama, investigates all fatal accidents involving Army personnel or equipment. Their investigations solely focus on improving safety practices.
A parallel administrative investigation determines the facts surrounding the accident for use in discipline, public information, legal claims and more. If necessary, a third, criminal investigation occurs as well.
−Davis Winkie
Trump says collision 'should have been prevented'
After the White House released Trump's formal written statement, the president raised questions about the crash in a post on Truth Social, referencing video of the collision and saying it appears it 'should have been prevented.'
Trump said the American Airlines jet was 'on a perfect and routine line of approach to the airport' and the helicopter was 'going straight at the airplane for an extended period of time.'
'It is a CLEAR NIGHT, the lights on the plane were blazing, why didn't the helicopter go up or down, or turn. Why didn't the control tower tell the helicopter what to do instead of asking if they saw the plane. This is a bad situation that looks like it should have been prevented. NOT GOOD!!!'
− Joey Garrison
Metrobuses will transport people to their vehicles at airport
In the aftermath of the tragic midair collision at , multiple public transit options are available for residents in the area. The Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority announced that its Silver Line metro service has been extended from the Washington Dulles International Airport to Metro Center, a major transit hub in Washington.
The Metrobuses will be available at Metro Center to transport customers back to the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport to their vehicles, the WMTA said.
− Swapna Venugopal Ramaswamy
Hypothermia a concern for possible survivors and first responders, AccuWeather says
Hypothermia is a 'major concern' for possible survivors and first responders of the plane crash, according to AccuWeather meteorologists.
Water temperature ranging between 33 to 36 degrees were reported in the Potomac River near the crash site on Wednesday night, AccuWeather said.
'At these frigid water temperatures, the human body's core temperature quickly drops. Exhaustion or unconsciousness can occur in as little as 15 to 30 minutes,' AccuWeather Senior Director of Forecast Operations Dan DePodwin said in a statement.
DePodwin noted that the waters in the river has been 'much colder' than they were at this time last year due to 'persistent blasts of Arctic air' in the D.C. area.
− Thao Nguyen
'All we can do is pray'
At Wichita's Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport, City Councilmember J.V. Johnston encouraged families to call the American Airlines help number or come to the airport where they have volunteers to speak impacted loved ones.
"There's going to be some tough times ahead. Hopefully there are survivors. All we can do is pray," Johnston said. "We're all going to know someone who is on that plane, whether a friend or family member."
− Alice Mannette
Flights to Washington airport diverted, delayed or canceled
Shortly following the crash, several dozen flights to and from DCA have been delayed or canceled, with others diverted.
Tyler Kim, a passenger on Delta Flight 2729 from Orlando International Airport to DCA, said the pilot announced a last-minute diversion to Washington Dulles International Airport due to an accident. 'It was pretty scary because we didn't know what was the cause of the crash yet,' Kim told USA TODAY.
Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority said it is running extra Silver Line trains and extended its hours to accommodate travelers whose flights have been diverted to IAD, according to a post on X by Randy Clarke, general manager and CEO of WMATA. It has also deployed warming buses to support rescue efforts.
− Kathleen Wong
History repeats itself: Second plane crash in the Potomac River
This is the second time a commercial plane has crashed into the Potomac River leading to tragic consequences.
On Jan. 13. 1982, 74 people were killed when Air Florida Flight 90 crashed into the 14th Street Bridge connecting Arlington, Virginia, Washington, D.C. and fell into the frozen Potomac River. The flight was in the air and crashed shortly after taking off from the Washington National Airport, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. The flight was headed to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport.
− Swapna Venugopal Ramaswamy
What do we know about the Army helicopter from the crash?
The military helicopter that collided with the plane was an Army-piloted Black Hawk on a "routine training flight," said Joint Task Force-National Capitol Region media chief Heather Chairez. Three soldiers − the aircraft's standard number of crew − were aboard the helicopter.
JTF-NCR oversees military operations in the greater D.C. area. Chairez said the helicopter belonged to B Company, 12th Aviation Battalion, which is headquartered at Fort Belvoir, Va., about 10 miles from DCA.
The 12th Aviation Battalion frequently flies military VIPs around the D.C. area in specialized Black Hawks. No VIP officials were aboard the aircraft at the time of the crash, though, according to an Army official who spoke with FOX News and POLITICO.
− Davis Winkie
Police control traffic at airport, helicopters heard flying
Police have blocked off at least one exit leading toward Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, where a handful of passengers are waiting outside to be picked up or trying to find their way out on foot.
Helicopters can be heard flying overheard and the flashing lights of emergency vehicles crowded around the Potomac River can be seen from the windows of the media staging area set up inside the airport's Terminal 1.
− N'Dea Yancey-Bragg
'Shocked and saddened': Aviation unions respond to crash
Aviation unions that represent both the pilots and flight attendants at PSA, the regional affiliate airline of American that was operating the flight involved in the crash, issued statements about the incident.
'While we mobilize to support the families and crews directly affected by this incident, we are also sending strength to all first responders doing everything they can to bring survivors to safety,' Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants said in a statement. 'We ask the public to keep the families in your thoughts and respect efforts to get information to loved ones first as everyone clings to hope for survivors. Please avoid speculation at any time.'
'We are shocked and saddened by the tragic accident at DCA tonight. Our thoughts are with those affected by this tragedy and ALPA's accident investigation team is responding to assist the National Transportation Safety Board in their investigation,' a statement from the Air Line Pilots Association said.
− Thao Nguyen and Zach Wichter
In a post on X shortly after 9 p.m., the District of Columbia Fire and Emergency Medical Services Department said an aircraft was "down in Potomac River" and fireboats were on scene. The department later said there was "no confirmed information on casualties at this time."
Local police and other agencies were also responding to the scene, according to the Metropolitan Police Department. The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board are investigating the incident.
"Tonight, we received devastating news of what can only be described as nothing short of a nightmare," U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, said in a statement. "A plane, traveling to the Nation's capital from Wichita, KS carrying roughly 60 passengers collided with a Military helicopter. My prayer is that God wraps his arms around each and every victim and that he continues to be with their families."
What aircraft were involved in the crash?
American Airlines said the plane, operated as an American Eagle flight, had 60 passengers and four crew aboard. It left Wichita at 5:18 p.m. local time, and was due to land at DCA at 9:03 p.m.
The military helicopter that collided with the plane was an Army-piloted Black Hawk on a "routine training flight," said Joint Task Force-National Capitol Region media chief Heather Chairez. JTF-NCR oversees military operations in the greater D.C. area. Chairez said the helicopter belonged to B Company, 12th Aviation Battalion, which is headquartered at Fort Belvoir, Va., about 10 miles from DCA.
"Our concern is for the passengers and crew on board the aircraft. We are in contact with authorities and assisting with emergency response efforts," American said in a statement.
American Airlines said that people who believe their loved ones were aboard the flight should call 800-679-8215 for more information.

title: An Illinois legislator is asking IDOC staff to let her know about undocumented immigrants
author: Tom Ackerman
description: An Illinois legislator asks staff at prisons in the state to contact her if they know about undocumented immigrants that she can report to ICE.
content:
An Illinois legislator has publicly asked staff at prisons in the state to contact her if they know about undocumented immigrants that she can report to Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
State Sen. Terri Bryant, R-Murphysboro, posted last week on X, which is formerly known as Twitter, a memorandum from Illinois Department of Corrections Legal Services to all agency staff about guidelines for cooperating with immigration enforcement.
'IDOC staff are prohibited from notifying or cooperating w/ICE so no way for ICE to know the offender is incarcerated,' she wrote on the social media platform on Jan. 22. 'If you are IDOC staff who wants ICE to know of an illegal immigrant in IDOC call or message me.'
Sen. Bryant also posted that 'I won't rat you out. I will notify ICE. I will also, refile the REPEAL of the Trust Act.'
The TRUST Act limits state and local law enforcement's participation in federal immigration enforcement, according to the American Civil Liberties Union of Illinois.
Bryant said she took to X because IDOC staff could be fired if they choose to personally share information about undocumented immigrants who are prisoners.
'What I'm concerned about is that someone is about to be released into our community, a murderer or a rapist who, under federal law, can now be deported because they're a felon,' State Sen. Bryant told The State Journal-Register.
Bryant said she and her office would not ask for the name of the IDOC staff sharing the information.
'All we want is the offender's name, institution number and the institution at which they're being held,' she said, adding that that is the information ICE would likely need to get a federal warrant.
Bryant worked for 20 years in IDOC, starting in 1994 and until she retired and was elected in 2014.
For IDOC staff, unless presented with a federal criminal warrant or otherwise required by federal law; the staff may not participate, support, or assist in any capacity with an immigration agent's enforcement operations, according to the memorandum, in addition to other listed directives.

title: Springfield nonprofit continues helping women recovering from substance abuse
author: Claire Grant
description: Wooden It Be Lovely provides transitional employment, education, community networking and a safe community for women recovering from substance abuse.
content:
Almost every day, Taylor Williams goes to work on the second floor of the Douglas Avenue Methodist's Church second building.
Walking through brightly painted halls up to the Wooden It Be Lovely art studio, she starts her day with a group session sharing thoughts with other women in her program recovering their lives from addiction, before setting up her crafting station. She'll make dozens of candles a day for pay.
It's been an uphill battle, like many people overcoming addiction, for Williams the past several years, but she's coming out on top.
Williams has been part of the Wooden It Be Lovely nonprofit program for three and a half years, which provides work and aid for women to recover from addiction and homelessness. The job is part time but helps toward her goa of owning a house.
Williams is one of 15 women who are part of the nonprofit's recovery program meeting on weekdays.
The nonprofit was founded by Executive Director Rev. Margaret Ann Jessup providing transitional employment, mentoring, recovery tools and a safe community for women recovering from substance abuse. In 2021, the nonprofit opened a housing program, which saves girls in the home 70% of their income.
'When I got out of seminary, I wanted to start something to benefit this community to help women other people couldn't or wouldn't help,' Jessup said. 'When you're in recovery and you have any criminal past or have problems with the courts, probation, all of those require you to meet with people at certain times, do outpatient rehab, do drops at different times … there's a lot of barriers to success.'
Homelessness is a reoccurring topic in Springfield, with regular calls made by speakers to Springfield City Council about a need for more unhoused support. Many people living on the streets or in emergency shelters struggle with use of drugs, which can lock users out of 12-step programs to recovery.
In a 2023 impact report, WIBL had over 78 applications to the program, but only 20% of applicants were hired.
Since the program's creation in 2016, Jessup says around 150 women have passed through the doors of the studio.
Through donations, fundraising and grants WIBL's funding was just over $570,000 in 2023, plus $184,000 in sales of the furniture and decorations the women make at the location; however, Jessup says funding is a constant issue holding the organization back from bringing more women into the program and expanding.
'We don't want to repeat services other nonprofits do locally, so we network with a lot of current nonprofits for care,' Jessup said. 'Mainly we connect them and make sure they get the services they need in the community. If the community has a hole, we try to fill that.'
Martie Blaylock has been with the WBIL program for two years and says the nonprofit has saved her life. Through remission and return to recovery, Blaylock uses her experiences and lessons learned on the road to recovery.
In May of last year, Blaylock finished her Certified Recovery Support Specialist, or CRSS, training program at SIU Medicine. She'll go on to use her certification to help other people who use substances.
In the same 2023 impact report from WIBL, 80% of the women employed in the program maintained sobriety, two women started college courses, several women completed rehab, and three women purchased houses.
Three days out of rehab, Kara Malott had a job. It's been almost three months since she joined the program, she said was saving her. Her goal is the same as Blaylock's: to become CRSS certified.
"I had my second interview here and through my excitement I just was ecstatic to be coming here," Malott said. "I love the idea of the program and the sisterhood here with other women who know my experience and have been there as well. They've made it so much easier to be here."
Holding back some much-deserved tears, Malott wants more women to know about WIBL because "I love the idea there's going to be a future for this place, and I'm not going to be the only one."
Options for women dealing with homelessness, addiction
M.E.R.C.Y Communities, another Springfield nonprofit dealing with family homelessness aids in women transitional and permanent housing programs with weekly accountability checks. Addiction is a qualifying disability to enter the permanent housing program and for those living on the street, M.E.R.C.Y offers a rapid re-housing program for HUD-recognized women living in emergency shelters, unsafe locations or fleeing domestic violence.
Executive Director of M.E.R.C.Y Communities Amy Voils says the success rate for families in their programs is 94%, representing the people who move from transitional or permanent housing programs into permanent living situations with a home to call their own. Many clients in the program move through the Springfield housing authority public housing program or through emergency voucher programs.
'Barriers to full time employment can include disability, whether it be diagnosed or undiagnosed, often undiagnosed mental illness, transportation and childcare issues,' Voils wrote over email. 'The families we serve are not necessarily 'unhoused' – many are in our permanent housing program … where they are still technically 'homeless', they have more stability including a home address.'
Other groups which help unhoused people find stability in Springfield include Contact Ministries, I nner City Mission, Intricate Minds, Helping Hands of Springfield, Fifth Street Renaissance, among many others. Intricate Minds, which recently received a $60,000 grant from Memorial Health for 2025-2027, offers hygiene kits, clean needles, clothes and other interview-ready necessities for unhoused individuals - whether or not they are currently using substances.

title: Taylorville gets Lincoln's Horn: senior carries Railers' offense early in win
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Blake Horn says he's just one of the guys, but games like Saturday's win over Taylorville shows his recent increased value to Lincoln.
content:
LINCOLN — Karson Komnick was asked if there was a silver lining to the numerous injuries and lost playing time for Lincoln's boys basketball team this season.
Without hesitation, the junior pointed directly to his teammate, 6-foot-3 senior Blake Horn.
'(Horn) stepped up in a big role, really, scoring the ball,' Komnick said, 'he had a good stretch in basketball games.'
Horn scored 10 of his 11 points in the first half as the Railsplitters' offense otherwise sputtered in Lincoln's 40-30 win over Taylorville in a nonconference game at Roy S. Anderson Gymnasium on Saturday.
'I never felt any pressure because I'm fully confident that we put five guys out on the floor that can do basically anything,' Horn said. 'And I'm very willing to score, but I'm always very willing to step back. I'm willing to do whatever this team needs to be great.'
Komnick wasn't the only one to rave about Horn's performance of late.
'Tremendous. I mean, you know he's going to play, but his minutes went up significantly with all the injuries and sickness that we've had,' Lincoln coach Neil Alexander said. 'And he's helped us out, he's won us some games and, he's a hard worker and deserves it.'
The give-and-take injuries cause
It has been an up-and-down season for the Railers (15-8), who have battled a multitude of injuries as well as illnesses. Alexander was battling some sort of minor bug on Saturday and Lincoln had to do without its two top point guards, junior Brody Tungate and senior Brady Miller, against the Tornadoes.
Those absences led to a sloppier brand of offensive basketball on Saturday than Lincoln is used to.
Komnick, who finished with a game-high 12 points, said without Miller and Tungate, it was more difficult to get the ball to inside-presence Drew Hayes, who had seven points — all in the second half.
'I thought we played really well, and without two of our point guards — both of them actually — we really put Drew in a hard spot for our offense to run, and I thought he did a good job,' Komnick said.
Besides Komnick, who had a broken wrist, Lincoln has also missed Hayes and Frank Sanders for long stretches this season. Komnick and Alexander both said while having other teammates step up has been a big plus when the postseason comes, right now the Railers need more cohesion on the court. That only comes with more practice and more games fully healthy.
'It's different, it's weird, yeah, we haven't had a full practice with all five of our guys to practice since the first part of the year,' Komnick said. 'It's been different, it's been hard for us to be a one (group), to play together and play hard.'
The returns of Komnick, Sanders and Hayes have helped the Railers win five straight games. But Alexander wants to see his players jell as a unit together before the postseason begins on Feb. 24.
It has created more depth for us, where the kids can step up and help us out, but we need to be able to get into a flow. We've got no flow right now.'
'Where we're losing is we're not getting the flow that we need,' Alexander said. 'That's what we're going to be missing. But (with the added depth aided by players who have needed to fill certain roles), those guys can come in tough spots (or if) somebody gets hurt and we're able to step in.
Taylorville struggled against Lincoln's defense
The Tornadoes' offense couldn't get much going against Lincoln's 1-2-2 zone press and managed just two points in the first quarter and six points in the entire quarter.
'That's how it (Lincoln's defense is) designed and well I thought we defensively, for the most part, covered them up and covered their shooters,' Alexander said. 'We've played some really good shooters here of late and we've really held them in check.'
Taylorville's leading scorers, senior Drake Howard and freshman Brock Brown, were held to just 10 points combined.
'We wanted to punch (the ball) to the middle (of Lincoln's defense),' Taylorville coach Ryan Brown said. 'We're not a great 3-point shooting team this year, so we got to get middle touches. We did it, and unfortunately, we had to sacrifice some turnovers and steals for them because we were so committed to trying to get it in the middle.
'But that's our formula for trying to beat Lincoln this year. We had to get it in the middle against them.'
One bright spot was the performance of senior Owen Younker, who led the Tornadoes (12-12) with nine points and seemingly had his hand on many of the loose balls on both ends.
Younker's ability to come in off the bench and give Taylorville some energy has been a welcomed addition, Brown said.
'A lot of people say that about him, just giving us a spark,' Brown said. 'He's that guy off the bench that we really need to do that, and he fills that role extremely well. We've talked about it off and on during the season, but here lately he's just really turned it on in the last three weeks scoring.
'It's nice getting six or eight points off the bench here and there and then adding great defense. When you've got a nice quality sub like that, it's nothing more than a relay race: you just hand off the baton to Owen, and then he tries to just go as hard as he can and that kind of thing. So, yeah, Owen was really good tonight.'

title: State Police investigating shooting just east of Petersburg
author: Steven Spearie
description: Menard County Sheriff's deputies initially responded to the call Saturday afternoon.
content:
Menard County Sheriff's deputies located two men with gunshot wounds early Saturday afternoon in response to a 911 call.
In an email Sunday morning, an Illinois State Police spokeswoman Trooper Genelle Jones said the two were taken to area hospitals "with life threatening injuries."
Deputies were called to the residence in the 15000 block of Tice Road at approximately 12:30 p.m. Saturday.
The address is just off Illinois 123, east of Petersburg and about half an hour northwest of Springfield.
The sheriff's department requested the help of ISP's Division of Criminal Investigation to handle the shooting investigation.

title: Egg costs predicted to rise in 2025, despite Vance saying 'prices are going to come down'
author: Jonathan Limehouse
description: The price of eggs is expected to rise throughout 2025 due to the bird flu outbreak that killed 17.2 million egg-laying hens in November and December alone.
content:
Making eggs for breakfast might become more challenging as the common grocery item is expected to become pricier throughout the year, despite Vice President JD Vance recently saying otherwise.
According to the Department of Agriculture's price outlook, egg prices are predicted to increase about 20% in 2025, compared with about 2.2% for overall food prices. The USDA attributed the rise in egg costs to an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza, or bird flu, which has caused a strain in supply.
The rise in prices is not sudden, as eggs cost 36.8% more in December 2024 than in December 2023, but prices were still below the peak in January 2023, according to the USDA. The outlook says retail egg prices climbed 8.4% in December 2024 and continued to experience volatile month-to-month changes.
Beef, coffee and orange juice are also expected to cost more in 2025, but none will rise to the degree of eggs, according to the USDA's price outlook. During an interview on CBS News' ' Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Vance said gas and grocery prices will come down at some point.
'Prices are going to come down, but it's going to take a little bit of time,' Vance told Brennan in the interview, which aired Sunday. 'The president has been president for all of five days. I think that in those five days, he's accomplished more than Joe Biden did in four years.'
Here is what to know about the increasing egg prices and how they became so high.
How bad is the bird flu outbreak?
The bird flu outbreak strain, H5N1, emerged among poultry flocks and wild birds in Europe in the fall of 2020 before moving to the U.S., Africa, the Middle East and Asia. The disease has grown to become the largest such outbreak in the U.S.
The USDA Agricultural Marketing Service reported on Jan. 3 that grocery stores were seeing record-high prices in retail markets nationwide because of the "significant outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in commercial table egg layer flocks through December."
By Jan. 17, the virus had infected more than 136 million poultry across 50 U.S. states since January 2022, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Because of the spread, infected birds have been selectively slaughtered across the U.S., sometimes millions of birds at a single location.
Though some states avoided last year's outbreaks, many have recently reported a resurgence of the virus, which the USDA reported killed about 17.2 million egg-laying hens in November and December. This accounted for nearly half of all birds killed by the virus in 2024, the federal department said.
How much did eggs cost a month ago?
With egg prices expected to rise, consumers could see a significant jump from December. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the average price of a dozen large grade-A eggs was $4.15 in December, which was up from $3.65 in November.
Egg prices also shot up more than 36% year-over-year in December, according to the Consumer Price Index.
During Vance's interview, he said several of the executive orders signed by Trump will help drive prices down, adding that they 'have caused, already, jobs to start coming back into our country, which is a core part of lowering prices.'
'More capital investment, more job creation in our economy, is one of the things that's going to drive down prices for all consumers, but also raise wages so that people can afford to buy the things that they need,' Vance said.
When will egg prices come back down?
It's unclear when the cost of eggs may drop, but it could be after 2025.
One of the main determiners of egg prices will be farmers and producers and how long it takes them to recover their stocks of healthy laying hens.
Supply and prices will stabilize only when farms and producers can recover their stocks. The USDA forecasts table egg production going down in 2025, "reflecting a smaller laying flock as a result of losses to Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI), as well as lower lay rates."
'No one can predict the future, but bird flu remains an ongoing threat to our egg farms, and egg farmers are working around the clock to protect their birds, replenish supply and keep those eggs coming," Emily Metz, president and CEO of the American Egg Board, told USA TODAY this month. "On a positive note, she said, farmers have a lot more experience fighting the disease now, meaning farms are able to recover faster."

title: 'Oh my gosh!' Hunter's massive game helps lift Calvary past Edinburg
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Luke Blackford may have led Calvary with 30 points in a win over Edinburg, but the Saints were left surprised by Hunter's big night.
content:
EDINBURG — Four times in the second and third quarters, Calvary took 17-point leads, and that was before Edinburg senior Alex Peacock fouled out with less than a minute left in the third quarter.
Down its only 1,000-point career scorer before the night began and the Wildcats' tallest player (6 foot 2), Edinburg mounted a fourth-quarter charge to get within four points — twice.
However, Calvary's final four minutes were nearly flawless as the Saints pulled out an 85-66 MSM Conference win on Tuesday night.
Naturally, Calvary's leading scorer was junior Luke Blackford. The Saints' 6-foot-4 star racked up 30 points and had 11 rebounds in the win.
But it was sophomore Antione Hunter who may have dazzled the most. Hunter scored 28 points to go with his 19 rebounds — including eight on the offensive end — to give coach Tives Gardner's small roster another boost, just weeks before the Class 1A postseason begins. That was even after playing much of the junior varsity game right before the varsity one.
'Really just to keep scoring and keep my team in it, and just really just to step up,' Hunter said of his motivation on Tuesday. 'Especially since our best player (Blackford) was hitting his shots. I was making my shots; we just all came together.'
Hunter wows teammates, coach
As a reporter read off Hunter's statistics off to Gardner, the Calvary coach interrupted: 'He had what?' While the same reporter interviewed Hunter, one of his teammates overheard that Hunter had 19 rebounds and yelled, 'Oh my gosh, Antione! No way!'
The team was in a very joyous mood as the Saints moved to 17-8 and 5-1 in the MSM.
'I didn't know the stats, I didn't know he had 28,' Gardner said after he gathered his thoughts. 'I'll tell you what: we'll take it.'
Calvary dressed just nine players on Tuesday. The team doesn't worry if Blackford can get his points, but Gardner said Hunter's recent emergence will help bolster the team.
'We're playing well as a team,' Gardner said. 'Beginning of the year, the other guys thought this was just going to be the Luke Blackford show, because he was the only guy with that experience.
'I always talk about he needs a supporting cast and we talked about that before tonight's game. Every big game that we've lost, our supporting cast didn't show up. When Luke scores under 26, we win; he scores more than 30 we lose.'
It also helped Calvary that the Saints made 28 of 59 shots, including 9-for-19 from the 3-point line. Both teams had foul trouble, with Peacock and Ian Dial picking up five fouls each for Edinburg while Calvary's Joshua Long and Aaron Wilson also got disqualified with five apiece. Of the 35 offensive rebound possibilities, the Saints came down with 20 and 49 total boards.
Blackford scored 11 of his points at the free-throw line and was a perfect 10-for-10 there in the second half. He also remembered giving an interview during last month's Sangamon County Tournament where he told the same reporter the Saints had issues on defense.
'You know how I said we don't play no defense,' Blackford asked with a smile. 'We're starting to play a little bit of defense now; we're winning games and it shows.'
Davis, Edinburg nearly rally
A couple of times, Calvary threatened to take nearly insurmountable leads, but the Wildcats (20-3, 5-1) kept fighting back.
Blackford hit a jumper to give Calvary a 52-35 lead — the fourth time the Wildcats found themselves down by 17 — with 4 minutes, 27 seconds left in the third quarter.
Treyton Davis, on the night he surpassed 1,000 points in his career, helped spark an 11-2 run over 1:21 to cut the deficit to 54-46. With 1:11 left in the third, Peacock hit a turnaround to get Edinburg back within eight points, but 13 seconds later, Peacock picked up his fifth foul.
Edinburg didn't give up, even down 12 after three periods. Senior Finn Swinger banked in a 3-pointer then hit one from in front of the Edinburg bench to sandwich four Davis points as the Wildcats got within 66-60 with 5:51 left. Then, Colton Puccetti knocked down a pair of free throws to cut Calvary's lead to four. Blackford and Davis then alternated free throws as Edinburg stood within 68-64.
'I'm always on those sophomores, those juniors, and even a couple of the freshmen, telling them, 'Next year, it's going to be you, you're going to be in this position, so when you're called upon, you've got to step up, and I think they did a good job at that,'' Edinburg coach Rashawn Jones said.
'Ian came off the bench in the second half, and he was a spark, handling the ball, and running the offense, and getting those guys set up. Then Miles (Norris) up top, he was (applying) super pressure and defensively, they turned it on. If they did that in the first half, it'd be a different ballgame.'
But over the final four minutes, it was all Calvary. Hunter had a putback, followed by a Blackford steal and fast-break layup before Josiah Reynolds — who finished with 14 — pushed the Saints' lead back to double digits as part of a 12-0 run.
