title: Two business owners, longtime friends team up to buy former Alexander's Steakhouse
author: Claire Grant
description: Two longtime friends, business owners have purchased the former Alexander's Restaurant location in Springfield.
content:
The owners of several coffee locations across Illinois are the new owners of a former popular steakhouse location in Springfield.
According to Sangamon County property tax records, Marcus McGlasson and Andrew Cochran of Pleasant Plains have purchased the old Alexander's Steakhouse at 620 N. Bruns Lane.
If one of those names ring a bell for readers, Marcus McGlasson and his wife, Lauryn, run several franchised Scooter's Coffee locations across Illinois and Indiana, including the Springfield-area Scooters and the still in development Chatham Scooter's Coffee.
McGlasson also co-owns Just Right Easing, a meal delivery service in Edwardsville and Springfield and is a financial advisor for LPL Financial. According to the Illinois Secretary of State, Cochran, Brian Brewer, Stephanie Johnson and Dominic Podeschi are listed as managers for the meal prep kit business.
Cochran, who is a homebuilder in Springfield and owns Andrew Cochran Construction, has been lifelong high school friends with McGlasson.
'We bought it as an investment and haven't finalized plans yet,' Cochran said. 'We look to get together mid-March and come together with some (business) options.'
The two friends' choice to go all in on purchasing the close to million-dollar building is an investment into the future, while keeping a part of the local food scene's history active and not left to sit on the market.
The steakhouse business closed a year ago this month of Feb. 29, 2024, citing poor customer retention, inflation of service costs and competition between other steakhouses as the reason. The 5,000 square foot building was sold to Cochran and McGlasson on Jan. 16, 2025.
Before closing, Alexander's Steakhouse had been open for almost four decades and been a piece of Springfield's high profile dining experiences for customers.
In the following weeks, Cochran said to expect an update on the commercial direction the building will take and what the two friends cook up for the area.

title: Audit: Illinois' noncitizen health care programs far outstripped original cost estimates
author: Hannah Meisel
description: The report also found more than 6,000 people enrolled in the state-funded programs were classified as 'undocumented' despite actually having social security numbers.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Two Illinois healthcare programs for noncitizens cost the state $1.6 billion, far exceeding initial projections.
Governor Pritzker proposes defunding the program for adults aged 44-64, citing high costs and potential for work-based coverage.
The audit highlights discrepancies in enrollment data and the need for more accurate cost estimations in the future.
A pair of health care programs that benefit noncitizens – one of which is already on Gov. JB Pritzker's budgetary chopping block – far outstripped its original estimated price tag and cost the state of Illinois $1.6 billion through last summer, according to a new audit of the programs published Wednesday.
The report also found more than 6,000 people enrolled in the state-funded programs were classified as 'undocumented' despite actually having social security numbers. Some of those people were green card holders who would have instead qualified for health coverage like Medicaid or traditional insurance.
The audit, which lawmakers requested in late 2023, comes one week after Pritzker delivered his annual budget proposal to the General Assembly. The governor's plan would defund the newer of the two programs, which is aimed at noncitizens aged 44 to 64, while leaving in place the smaller program for noncitizen seniors aged 65 and older.
Asked about the audit at an unrelated Chicago news conference Wednesday, Pritzker defended the Department of Healthcare and Family Services' work on redeterminations in the program over the last year, which has brought down total enrollment in addition to the administration's freezes on enrollment in the programs in 2023.
'It's some evidence, anyway, that there are an awful lot of people out there who need coverage, who aren't getting it, or who will do anything to get it,' Pritzker said after reiterating his support for universal health care coverage. 'And I think that's a sad state of affairs in our society.'
Republicans, who've long criticized both the programs' ballooning costs and what they've characterized as a lack of transparency, said the audit proves them right about Illinois' first-in-the-nation programs.
'We're the only state that puts this burden on Illinois tax on their own state taxpayers taking this on and to not run it properly and to have these large cost overruns, that's how you end up with a budget deficit,' Senate Minority Leader John Curran, R-Downers Grove told reporters Wednesday at the Capitol. 'That's what's crowding out spending on education. That's what's crowding out spending on other components of the state budget. That's why we need an audit.'
Vastly underestimated costs
When progressive lawmakers first pushed for the creation of the Health Benefits for Immigrant Seniors, or HBIS, program for noncitizens aged 65 and older in the first few months of the COVID-19 pandemic, officials relied on advocates' $2 million cost estimate for the program's first year. Though that projection was later doubled to $4 million as the program was being set up in the latter half of 2020, the actual cost ended up at more than $67 million after HBIS began accepting enrollees in December of that year.
But while actual costs for the seniors' program in its first three years – $412 million – ended up being 84% higher than original estimates, the price tag for the expanded program for adults aged 44 to 64 was many times larger.
The Health Benefits for Immigrant Adults, or HBIA, program covered noncitizen adults age 55 to 64 and was later expanded to cover those as young as 44. It cost $485.3 million over its first two years – roughly 284% more than the combined original estimate for both programs.
The programs were designed with the same income eligibility thresholds as Medicaid. But since federal Medicaid dollars can't be spent on many types of non-citizens, the state has had to foot the bill itself instead of receiving a roughly 52% federal match like it does for traditional Medicaid coverage.
The audit noted that HFS began seeking federal reimbursement for some emergency services last year, which would be retroactive to mid-2022. But Pritzker last week said part of the reason he was proposing axing the program for adults – which would save an estimated $330 million next year – was due to the Trump administration signaling it would soon halt that reimbursement.
Enrollment has also far outstripped original estimates, especially in the program for adults aged 44 to 64. For fiscal year 2023, nearly 54,000 adults enrolled in the program – about twice the original projection of 26,800.
In 2023, after the Pritzker administration acknowledged the programs' cost had grown to $1.1 billion, the governor asked the General Assembly for authority to impose spending controls. After lawmakers followed his request, Pritzker quickly paused enrollment in the program for adults in July of 2023, followed by a pause in the program for seniors in November of that year.
The programs have not accepted any new enrollees since those pauses and redetermination efforts have decreased their headcounts in the last year. The audit cited an enrollment decline in the adults' program from a high of 53,936 in fiscal year 2023 to 41,537 in fiscal year 2024, which ended June 30.
The day after the second enrollment pause in November 2023, lawmakers approved a resolution calling for an audit of the programs, which authorized Auditor General Frank Mautino's office to begin work on the report published Wednesday.
Pritzker last week proposed defunding the program for adults, telling reporters that those aged 44 to 64 are still of working age and could get jobs with health care coverage.
Axing the program renews a disagreement between the governor and progressive members of the General Assembly's Latino Caucus, who opposed enrollment pauses and efforts to require co-pays for program participants.
But the governor framed his proposal as one of shared sacrifice.
'If you come to the table looking to spend more, I'm going to ask you where you want to cut,' the governor told lawmakers in his Budget Address. 'I have made difficult decisions – including to programs I have championed, which is hard for me, just as I know some of the difficult decisions you will have to make will be hard for you.'
Mis-enrollments
The audit also found inconsistencies in enrollment data, sometimes relying on misreporting from program participants.
Of the 6,098 enrollees with social security numbers who'd been mislabeled as undocumented, nearly 400 people had been in the U.S. for the five years it takes for legal permanent residents to qualify for Medicaid, according to the audit. Meanwhile, other green card holders who hadn't yet reached that five-year threshold but were enrolled in the state-run programs would have been eligible to purchase health coverage from the Affordable Care Act's insurance marketplace.
HFS last spring issued new rules clarifying that those noncitizens were not eligible for the state health coverage programs, and the agency's redetermination process has identified and disenrolled many.
Others who had social security numbers are in the U.S. legally but are not eligible for green cards. The HBIA and HBIS programs were designed to cover them but were not intended to cover asylum-seekers who've been sent to Illinois from southern border states in recent years.
Those mis-enrollments, which also included nearly 700 people who received coverage under the program for noncitizens 65 and older despite being too young to qualify, drove some of the ballooning costs in the health care initiative. But the audit points to the Pritzker administration relying on vastly underestimated figures when setting up the programs in 2020, 2021 and 2022.
'Actual enrollment and actual costs exceeded the initial program estimates for both the HBIS and HBIA program,' the audit said.
Jade Aubrey contributed.

title: Vinzant, Bellemare come up short at IHSA boys state swimming and diving finals
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Andrew Bellemare of Niantic Sangamon Valley and Chatham Glenwood's Jackson Vinzant did not advance to Saturday's competition of the IHSA boys state swimming and diving finals.
content:
Senior Andrew Bellemare of Niantic Sangamon Valley and Chatham Glenwood senior Jackson Vinzant did not advance to Saturday's competition of the Illinois High School Association boys state swimming and diving finals at the FMC Natatorium on Friday in Westmont.
To advance to Saturday, a swimmer must place in the top eight to swim for a state championship. Placers 9-16 swim in the consolation finals.
Bellemare and Vinzant both reached state in the 200-yard freestyle after wins in their respective sectionals. Bellemare won the Urbana Sectional with a time of 1 minute, 45.35 seconds, and Vinzant tied for first place in 1:49.59 with Edwardsville's Jackson Suhre at the Edwardsville Sectional to advance.
Bellemare finished 29th in Friday's state preliminaries with almost the exact time as in the sectional in 1:45.36. Vinzant took 33rd in 1:50.87.
Bellemare also won the 500 freestyle at sectional in 4:51.55. He swam a 4:55.32 in the state preliminaries and placed 31st.

title: Water bills for Springfield residents are about to spike again. What you need to know
author: Steven Spearie
description: A second year of water rate hikes will be felt by City Water, Light and Power customers this spring. Here's what you need to know.
content:
The 32% hike in April was part of a plan approved by the Springfield City Council in 2024.
The rate increase comes out to about 15 cents per day for consumers.
A second year of water rate hikes will be felt by City Water, Light and Power customers this spring.
Like last year, water rates will go up 32% and will be reflected on bills arriving in April.
Last year's increase, approved by the Springfield City Council by a 7-3 vote, was the first time bills had been hiked in 13 years.
Here's what to expect.
Why the rate increase?
A state-mandated replacement of lead water service lines in the city is one reason.
According to CWLP's FY26 budget, $10.8 million will go to water main and lead service line replacements. Some service line replacement is grant funded through the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency State Revolving Fund Program and remaining American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) dollars.
Since that rate increase was announced, the federal government passed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI), a rule which requires all lead service line replacements to be completed over a 10-year period. That legislation is currently being challenged by the industry's leading advocacy group, the American Water Works Association (AWWA).
The overall cost to the city for switching out lead lines with copper lines was estimated to be about $150 million.
Some of money from the rate increase also will go towards the utility's Water Fund.
The increase in a nutshell
Like last year, the rate increase comes out to about 15 cents per day. As previously reported, for a household using on average five units (on 5/8-inch meters), or 3,740 gallons of water a month, the bill would go from $19.51 to $25.75.
To figure out the new rate, multiply the total CWLP 'Water Charges' line on your bill by 1.32.
Payment plans
Customers who get behind on bills can request a payment plan, said CWLP spokeswoman Amber Sabin. A customer also can set up a level payment plan to pay the same amount each month.
Those requests can be made through Customer Service by calling 217-789-2030.
CWLP's Energy Services Office can help customers reduce their water usage and assist with finding and fixing water leaks.

title: Seeing double: Bard, Folkes give Illini Central top-tier deep-shooting threat
author: Ryan Mahan
description: When David Bard and Brody Folkes are on fire, Illini Central fans are in for quite a show, and opponents are likely in for a headache.
content:
When Mason City Illini Central senior David Bard is in the zone, the Cougars have a chance at winning.
When Illini Central junior Brody Folkes' shots are on target, the Cougars also have a winning chance.
When the two of them are on fire, coach Ryan Burks and the Cougars' fans are in for quite a show, and opponents are likely in for a headache.
The pair of 3-point lethal shooters combine to score 37.7 points per game, both hitting 33% of their shots from outside and Bard, Folkes, Burks and the Cougars are in the Class 1A Brimfield Sectional semifinals, the deepest run for Illini Central since winning the 2013 Class 1A state championship.
'I think early on in the summer, we kind of realized that we were going to be pretty tough to guard with David Bard and Brody Folkes,' Burks said. 'Just both being really good scorers and kind of having the green light. I think our biggest challenge was trying to figure out how to defend and get some of the younger guys to be able to play at the varsity level. Honestly, some of the guys came on a lot quicker than we thought and were able to put us in that position.'
No. 3 seed Illini Central (17-16) faces No. 1 Peoria Christian (25-9) in the Class 1A Brimfield Sectional semifinals on Wednesday at 7 p.m.
'This season's been incredible; it's been awesome,' Folkes said. 'We were underrated at the start of the season, weren't supposed to win a championship, that's for sure.
'The whole town, everywhere we go, everyone's just congratulating us. It's been awesome.'
Prolific shooters
Bard leads the Cougars with 19.9 ppg with 78 made 3s (33.9%) and 42.2% shooting overall from the field. Folkes has connected for 102 3s (33.4%) and 37.6% from the field.
Illini Central lost four straight games as the Cougars headed into the Illini Central Regional quarterfinals. In the first game, IC beat Astoria South Fulton 69-39 before a nail-biting 52-51 win over Manito Midwest Central — where Burks graduated from in 2005 — in the semifinals. On Friday, the Cougars beat Mendon Unity, 46-37. Being one of the smallest schools in the Sangamon Conference means IC is facing some of the strongest teams in the state in 2A. The players and coach agree that those regular-season challenges can payoff in the smallest postseason class.
'That was actually my biggest thing with the team all season, was telling them that all these times that we're getting beat by 40, we're getting better,' Bard said on Saturday, minutes after getting off work at a local landscaping company. 'No matter what, we're getting better at something.
'Everything will be easier in regionals coming out of the Sangamon Conference because that's a conference for 2A schools.'
As Bard's career advanced each season, Burks could see Bard, who moved from Ohio in first grade, taking the steps necessary to shoulder the responsibility of driving the team with his talent, shot making and leadership.
Burks saw fearlessness in Bard when Bard was a sixth grader playing up on the seventh and eighth grade teams. He saw a kid who didn't mind taking the ball and letting it fly.
"I'm like, holy smokes, this isn't normal,' Burks said.
Last year, due to a couple of injuries, Bard's role on the team took on a bigger importance.
"He was scoring, going one-on-one and making shots and I thought, 'Man, this is going to be fun next year,' Burks said. 'Watching him all summer and watching how hard he worked. He just did really good, and I knew he's a winner, so, you combine a lot of talent with a kid that just refuses to lose — it's going to be fun to watch.'
Seeing is believing
When Burks arrived to take control of the IC program 2019, he was told there was a fifth grader he needed to check out named Folkes. Fine, Burks thought, but the kid is in elementary school. How good could he be? What Burks saw left him excited for the future.
'I'd go watch and he'd make six 3s as a fifth grader; he's just always been an unbelievable shooter,' Burks said. 'As a freshman, he was able to just hit open shots right away. He's tough to guard because he's kind of taller and lankier and he's left-handed. So that's kind of awkward for people (to guard).
'And he's more kind of calm and collected and just kind of the silent guy. This year, he's had to take on a bigger role, and (Friday) night, he just took over the game and just kept hitting deep 3s.'
Burks describes Folkes as quieter than Bard, but the two players have much more in common than not. They describe the other as great friends and the two not only split the shooting guard and point guard duties, but their chemistry with each other — and their teammates — is superb.
'When we're both going, we're very hard to stop, and we don't like to lose,' Bard said. 'I think our competitiveness takes us a long way.'
Both players would love to play college basketball. Bard said the interest just hasn't come yet, but he remains hopeful.
For now, though, the players are focused on just one thing: Peoria Christian.
'We're just going to go to this game and leave it all on the court, give it all we got,' Folkes said. 'I think an upset ... anything's possible when we're all leaving it out on the court.'

title: OT: Oh Titans. Glenwood rallies to force overtime, beat Central in 3A sectional semifinals
author: Adrian Dater
description: Todd Blakeman just kept shaking his head when asked how in the world his Glenwood basketball team won Tuesday night's Class 3A Decatur Eisenhower Sectional playoff game.
content:
DECATUR — Todd Blakeman just kept shaking his head when asked how in the world his Chatham Glenwood boys basketball team won Tuesday night's Class 3A Decatur Eisenhower Sectional playoff game over Champaign Central.
'I don't know, man, I don't know,' the Titans' coach said, after his team's 57-45 overtime victory. 'All I know is, we're playing again Friday night.'
No. 3 seed Chatham Glenwood will play the winner between No. 1 Lincoln and No. 2 Mount Zion in the Class 3A sectional title game on Friday at 7 p.m. on the Bob Witt Gymnasium floor.
There have undoubtedly been more improbable comebacks in Illinois high school basketball history than this one. Terming it a miracle would be overstating it. But not by much.
The Titans overcame a 13-point late third-quarter deficit, found a way to tie it with 10.5 seconds left in regulation, and then literally had everything go right in a 12-0 OT period that sends them into Friday's sectional final.
Jonathan Helm's reverse layup with 10.5 ticks left in the fourth quarter finally got the Titans even after several frustrating missteps beforehand, and senior Cam Appenzeller scored the first four points over OT in finishing a most improbable victory.
'I said, 'Find a way', and they found a way,' said Blakeman, still shaking his head. 'We just hung in there. We stayed with our game plan, even when things looked bleak for us. I tell you what, we had a lot of guys play well for us, but Johnny Helm….'
Helm was, indeed, the best player in this game. He scored 26 points, with nine rebounds and three blocked shots. After he and his teammates forced a bad pass and turnover by the Maroons with time running out in regulation, Helm missed a first shot but grabbed his own rebound and put in the reverse layup to send the game to OT at 45-45.
Glenwood (22-9) had a 25-24 lead at the half — after falling behind by nine points — and then went the first 6 minutes, 20 seconds of the third quarter without scoring a point. With 1:40 left, the score was Champaign Central 38, Glenwood 25.
'I don't know what happened with us, but we just couldn't do anything right in that third. We were sloppy and had a lot of turnovers,' Helm said. 'We started to play better defense after that, I think, and started to force some turnovers by them. That helped us get back in it.'
The Titans scored the final seven points of the third to cut the Maroons lead to 38-32, but Champaign Central had a 45-43 lead and the ball with 38 seconds left. But the Maroons threw the ball away, setting up the chance for Glenwood to tie. Actually, Glenwood had a chance to win at the buzzer following another CC turnover but settled for OT.
Appenzeller scored off a lefty drive to open the OT scoring, then followed up his own miss with another basket for the 49-45 Titans lead. From there, teammates such as Helm, Mason Neumann and Gavin Simmons all scored baskets, and the Titans danced off the floor in exultant high-fives. Glenwood's defense did a great job in the final minutes of regulation and OT, with Neumann, Helm and Appenzeller blocking shots and getting every rebound off Maroons misses.
Over in the stone-silent Champaign Central dressing room, coach William Keaton could only shake his head as well, when asked how the game slipped away for his team.
'We were just a couple of rebounds away from putting a lid on it,' Keaton said. 'The ball just didn't bounce our way at the end. We played well for good stretches tonight, but they made a lot of big plays at the end and we didn't.'
Appenzeller had 10 points for the Titans, with Simmons adding 11. Neumann had eight points and eight rebounds, with three blocks. For the Maroons, senior Chris Bush led the way with 21 points.
Blakeman said: 'We're going to have to play better than this if we want to win Friday night. But I'm proud of our kids tonight. We found a way. I don't quite know how they did it, but they found a way.'

title: Auburn boys basketball avenges Pleasant Plains in Class 2A Greenville Sectional win
author: Bill Welt
description: Clayton Kessler and Ryan Lash scored Auburn's first eight points for the early lead and spark a revenge win over Pleasant Plains in the Class 2A boys basketball sectional semifinals.
content:
GREENVILLE — The Auburn boys basketball team made some adjustments based on its previous matchup against fellow Sangamo Conference foe Pleasant Plains.
The Trojans quickly took control with its lengthy forwards and 1-3-1 zone defense en route to a 50-39 win in the Class 2A Greenville Sectional semifinals on Tuesday.
Auburn (30-4) advances to the sectional finals on Friday at 7 p.m. against Wednesday's winner between Williamsville and Staunton.
Auburn exploits height advantage
Six-foot-six senior forward Clayton Kessler and 6-5 senior forward Ryan Lash combined for 14 points in the first half, while the defense thwarted Plains from scoring any points in the second quarter for a 16-5 halftime lead.
Auburn fell to Plains 51-43 during the regular season but took away a couple of lessons from the Feb. 4 meeting. That included feeding the post and finishing inside.
'That was a big emphasis for us,' Kessler said. 'We knew we had a size advantage, so coach (Seth McCoy) was stressing that from the beginning that we needed to get it inside and get good looks and just be patient because we have a lot of options. The offense will come to us as long as we're patient.'
Kessler led the Trojans with 16 points and seven rebounds, while Lash had eight points and three rebounds. Senior guards Carter Hunley and Cooper Carter had nine points apiece.
'We challenged those guys all week,' McCoy said of Kessler and Lash. 'If that's the advantage, we have to make it an advantage.'
Auburn goes zone
Auburn pulled ahead as much as 18-5 early in the third quarter to complete a 14-0 run, while Plains' scoring drought lasted nearly 13 minutes. Junior guard Grady Grisham ended the dry spell with 6:30 left in the third period.
'They absolutely torched us in the first game man-to-man,' McCoy said of the previous meeting. 'We went 1-3-1 in the second half and I believe they scored 14 points in the second half. We knew they would have something ready to go for it, but I'm super, super proud of the intensity that we played with tonight.'
It wasn't just down low. Auburn's guards also wreaked havoc defensively, including junior Jacob Barth and senior Brady Boylen. McCoy described Boylen as one of the team's top defenders.
'He's a guy who didn't get to play the entire year last year because of a labrum tear,' McCoy said. 'He's a guy who we trust in big time spots. We trust all our guys, but that's another senior just stepping up when his name is called.'
Cardinals still hang around
Grisham paced the Cardinals (22-11) with 15 of his 17 points in the second half. Senior guard Trager Shultz added nine points.
Plains reached as close as 32-27 with under six minutes left by attacking the basket. It also generated open looks behind the arc and the Cardinals converted four of their five 3s after the break.
'Credit just the 1-3-1,' Plains coach Kyle Weber said. 'We knew it was coming and we still looked tentative and passive against it. They're long out there, so we threw a couple passes out of bounds just worrying about guards tipping it up top. You miss a couple shots in there, too, and it starts compounding a little bit.'
Plains bows out after winning a third straight regional title.
'It's always tough losing that last one,' Weber said. 'We're going to miss Cooper (Schallenberg), Trager (Shultz) and Sean (Lowder). Those kids have done so much for us and Pleasant Plains basketball over the course of our four years.
'It's not going to feel good for a couple days, but looking back they had some big moments where they won some games that probably a lot of people didn't think they could. That only happens because they're determined kids. They hung in there, battled through the ups and downs and kept grinding.'

title: Major construction underway on I-55 near Springfield. Here's what to know.
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A multi-million-dollar construction project underway north of Springfield could impact commuting. Here's what you need to know about the project.
content:
A multi-million-dollar construction project underway north of Springfield could impact commuting.
Here's what you need to know about the nearly $30 million project on Illinois 55 and how it will impact your commute.
What will the construction accomplish?
Builders began widening the bridges last week as a step towards adding a northbound and a southbound lane to the bridges, as well expanding a stretch of the interstate. The bridges are just north of the northbound RailSplitter rest area.
The project will also add safety and capacity improvements to the interstate, according to the Illinois Department of Transportation.
The construction is a part of a series of projects that will lead to the expansion of the interstate from Sherman to the Illinois 54 (Sangamon Avenue) interchange. The state plans to add an extra lane in each direction, according to IDOT.
What's the timeline for the project?
This bridge is expected to be widened and improved by 2026.
Afterwards, builders will replace overpasses at Bissell Road, Andrew Road, and Sudduth Road, starting in 2026.
Starting in 2028, the state plans to expand the portion of the interstate to three lanes in each direction, which may be completed in 2030.
How will this impact travelers?
Starting Monday, a work zone with concrete barriers will be created.
Two lanes of traffic will be open for travel in each direction with the use of the shoulders as adapted lanes. There will be intermittent lane closures throughout the summer.
'Motorists can expect delays and should allow extra time for trips through this area. Drivers are urged to pay close attention to flaggers and signs in the work zones, obey the posted speed limits and be on the alert for workers and equipment,' a news release from IDOT read.
Why is this being constructed?
The projects are part of Gov. JB Pritzker's bipartisan $25.4 billion highway construction plan.

content:
Show Caption
Name: Gabatoni's Restaurant and Cocktail Lounge
Address: 300 E. Laurel St.
Phone: 217-528-9629
Website: gabatonispizza.net
Credit/debit cards accepted: Yes
Hours: 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. seven days a week
Entrée price range: $7.99-$18.95 (pizza prices vary)

My order: Gabatoni's has been operating in Springfield since 1951. Indoor dining had been suspended for several years, but it recently resumed under a new owner. title: Six students arrested following separate fights at Lanphier High School
author: Steven Spearie
description: Police officials told The State Journal-Register six students were arrested after separate fights broke out Wednesday afternoon. Here's what we know.
content:
Six students were arrested following two separate fights at Lanphier High School, 1300 N. 11th St., around 12:50 p.m. Wednesday.
Responding officers, said Commander Sara Pickford of the Springfield Police Department, were directed to the high school's atrium once they were on the scene.
The atrium is in the middle of the school and is a connector for students to take to get to different parts of the building, said School District 186 spokeswoman Rachel Dyas.
Lanphier security and administrators initially responded to two students engaged in a fight in the atrium.
While they were able to stop that altercation, four other students came up on the scene and became involved in a separate fight, Dyas said. Those students also were eventually separated.
Dyas confirmed that two school administrators were taken off the campus for medical evaluation. She did not say where they were taken.
Pickford confirmed that two ambulances were requested at the scene.
All six students were taken to police headquarters, where they were processed and then taken to the Sangamon County Juvenile Detention Center because of meeting system points, Pickford said.
Dyas said Lanphier faculty and staff and families were notified of the fight.
"Fighting and aggressive behavior are not acceptable and do not align with our values of respect, responsibility, and kindness," Lanphier principal Alicia Miller wrote in an email, which was provided to The State Journal-Register. "This type of behavior will not be tolerated.
"Our staff and students need to come to school without worry of injury or chaos caused due to reckless behavior."

title: Moving forward: With prosthetic legs and arms, Springfield teacher regains 'normal-ish' life
author: Steven Spearie
description: In 2023, K.J. Reid was so close to death that two nurses at Springfield Memorial Hospital were assigned to him around the clock.
content:
Springfield High School teacher K.J. has been fitted with computerized and AI-assisted prosthetic legs and arms.
Reid returned to teach full-time at SHS last fall.
Reid hopes to be able to drive using his prosthetic legs in a couple of years.
With physical therapist Bill O'Connor on his right side and a walker in front of him, K.J. Reid takes steps on his "C-Legs" down a hallway at Memorial Therapy Center on Koke Mill.
The German-engineered prosthetics, which Reid was fitted with from Hanger Clinic in Springfield, have microchips in them with Artificial Intelligence (AI) programs--the "C" in "C-Legs" stands for "Computerized"--so when he lifts his legs, they are propelling themselves forward trying to match his gait.
The AI is so advanced that if Reid loses his balance, the knees will lock up to try to prevent him from falling.
With time and more therapy, Reid said he envisioned walking like his old self.
"I have not stood up on legs and knees in two years," said Reid, the Springfield High School chemistry teacher whose legs and arms were amputated after being diagnosed with a "flesh eating" strep infection in early 2023. "My body just doesn't know how to walk again. It's really weird because I walked for 39 years and literally within two and a half weeks, the muscle was gone.
"That's one of the hard things."
Reid, who wears myo-electric arms that also run on microchips and AI, returned last fall to teaching in the classroom, a place, he admitted, where he finds comfort.
Still, Reid's initial worry was that some of the students would look at him and wonder what happened. Reid has sometimes had to endure stares in public or answer questions from strangers about his situation.
"The kids have been incredibly great and understanding," Reid said.
James Covey taught with Reid at Lanphier High School before moving over with him to SHS. Having him back, Covey said, has uplifted everyone.
"He's by far our best (Advanced Placement) chemistry teacher and one of the best teachers we have in the building," said Covey, the science department chair. "Nobody can do the things that he does as well as he does them, even in the limited capacity that he has.
"The kids really enjoy having him and he's good at getting the best out of them."
Managing the frustration
Reid, 41, was diagnosed with a virus on a visit to a rapid-care clinic on Feb. 13, 2023. He was turning a shade of blue when his wife, Kenna, later rushed him to Springfield Memorial Hospital.
The condition wreaked havoc on Reid's internal organs, leading to kidney and liver transplants. He was on a ventilator and was hooked up to as many as 17 IVs.
During his four-and-a-half month hospital stay, Reid was so close to death that two nurses were assigned to him around the clock.
"I was unconscious for about two and a half weeks," Reid pointed out. "Most of my muscle degenerated. I literally didn't have the ability to roll over."
Nerve impulses control the use of the prosthetic arms from muscles left in Reid's arms. It's an early version of the model, but he can use them to write on an i-Pad, eat with a fork and pick up or move anything around.
While the arms are letting Reid be a "normal-ish type person again," he told O'Connor and other therapy team members that he wanted to walk first and minimize the use of an electric wheelchair.
"My knees being lost made it to where it was a lot more energy to walk, so I would tire out pretty quickly at therapy in the beginning," Reid said. "I can still tire out, but it takes a little more time."
Still, Reid has a timeline in mind: anywhere from six months to a year and a half to be walking; a year and a half to two years to be driving and one to two years to be fully independent.
"There's still a lot of frustration, but I'm getting better at managing that frustration," Reid admitted. "As time goes on, I'm walking more at therapy and I'm becoming like a normal person again. Things are getting better mentally and emotionally.
"I'll be walking around again someday. It's just a matter of time, but you just have to not dwell on the negatives as best you can and move forward."
'A scary thing for everybody'
Brooke Lyons took an honors chemistry class with Reid her sophomore year.
Lyons said she was going to take an AP chemistry course her junior year, but she held off, waiting to see if Reid would return sometime.
She got her wish in the fall.
"He's still the Mr. Reid that I know and enjoyed having as a sophomore," said Lyons, now a senior. "It was really cool to see how this experience didn't really knock him down."
Olivia McGuire took the same honors chemistry course as Lyons.
McGuire remembered the day she heard that Reid had been hospitalized.
"It was definitely hard for the students because we were only sophomores," McGuire said. "Learning was a challenge (without him), but I feel like the teachers made it work and some of the other science teachers would try to help us as much as they could."
"A lot of kids who knew (Reid) from previous classes have moved on to college now," Covey added. "(The ones who were here) when this first happened, I think it was really good for them to see him come back and be successful.
"It was a pretty scary thing for everybody."
Like Lyons and McGuire, Lillian Shaffer is headed towards a science-oriented major in college. All three said they were directly influenced down that path by Reid.
Even though she isn't taking any courses from him, Shaffer still drops by Reid's classroom to see her former teacher.
"It always puts a smile on his face when his old students go talk to him because it truly shows they still care he's here," Shaffer said. "I know he has gone through so much and he still is going through so much. The fact that he can still do it with a smile on his face and he can still have his personality, that's inspiring."

title: Federal funding cuts hitting Illinois farmers, foodbanks
author: Claire Grant
description: The most recent round of cuts from the Trump Administration are hitting Illinois farmers and foodbanks.
content:
AI-assisted summary
The Local Food Purchase Assistance Program and the Resilient Food Systems Infrastructure Program, funded by the USDA, have been discontinued, leaving millions of dollars in outstanding reimbursements for Illinois.
The cuts will significantly impact Illinois farmers, particularly those from historically underserved communities, and limit access to nutritious food for those in need.
The most recent round of cuts from the Trump Administration are hitting Illinois farmers and foodbanks.
The Illinois Department of Agriculture, or IDOA, announced on March 4 the end for two grant programs as part of the Trump Administration's federal cuts.
The Local Food Purchase Assistance Program, or LFPA, and the Resilient Food Systems Infrastructure Program, RFSI, had funding cut without explanation by the United States Department of Agriculture.
'This program requires Illinois farmers to invest in upfront input costs which is no longer possible given that the federal government has said they will no longer provide reimbursements,' said IDOA Director Jerry Costello II. 'Without federal funding, the program that has helped to create local food systems in Illinois is unfortunately no longer able to operate.'
The USDA informed states it is ceasing reimbursements for any costs incurred after Jan. 19, 2025.
States were notified by USDA that LFPA and RFSI invoices are being processed only for costs incurred on or prior to Jan. 19, 2025. Reimbursement claims submitted for costs incurred after that date are being returned with no explanation or timeline for reimbursements to resume.
Capitol News Illinois reported the funds are part of the $2 billion the federal government is withholding from the state.
Local Food Purchase Assistance Program
The USDA established the LFPA program to strengthen statewide food systems, using federal funds to buy food from growers and producers at fair market value that is distributed to communities in need at no cost.
The Illinois-Eats program is funded by the LFPA with federal funds to buy produce from farmers at the fair market value before distributing to foodbanks in areas across Illinois needing the most.
In Illinois, 883 community sites have distributed food from 176 farmers, 58% of whom meet the USDA definition for new farmers.
Illinois was approved to distribute $43 million under the course of the multi-year LFPA agreement and $17.8 million remains outstanding from the federal government. Illinois is also the only state sourcing 100% of products from socially disadvantaged farmers.
Resilient Food Systems Infrastructure Program
The purpose of the RFSI program is to expand the middle of the food supply chain capacity for locally and regionally produced foods to offer better market opportunities and new streams of revenue to small and mid-sized agricultural producers.
IDOA says it was in the process of selecting grantees for the RFSI program, which would have provided $6.4 million in grant funding to entities.
Illinois agricultural impact
Illinois is the third largest exporter of agricultural commodities in the U.S. Total exports from Illinois in 2023 were estimated at $81 billion, of which $13.7 billion was attributed to agriculture.
According to the USDA Global Agricultural Trade System in 2024, Illinois accounted for over $12.4 billion of agricultural product exports, including $3.6 billion worth of products to Mexico ($2.5 billion) and Canada ($2.1 billion).
Similarly, according to the U.S. Department of Commerce, in 2024 Illinois accounted for over $784 million in agricultural product imports.
'This loss in support for our farmers, especially those from communities that have historically been disinvested in, is a loss for everyone in our state,' said IDHS Secretary Dulce M. Quintero. 'Access to nutrition is a human right.'

title: Roaches (dead and alive), mouse droppings found in Springfield-area kitchens in January
author: Claire Grant
description: Health inspectors found a variety of issues across Sangamon County kitchens in January. Here's a look at the eateries with 10+ violations last month.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Several Sangamon County restaurants were cited for health code violations in February.
Violations ranged from improper food storage to pest infestations.
A popular burger chain was hit with multiple health code violations last month in Springfield.
On Feb. 14, a food safety complaint was investigated by the health department at Red Robin Gourmet Burgers & Brews at 2881 S. Veterans Parkway. The inspection found 16 violations at the establishment on Valentine's Day, with five risk factors.
According to the inspector's notes, thawed salmon was seen still in its packaging, when the label clearly stated the salmon had to be removed before or immediately after thawing. Reduced oxygen packaging can risk botulism from Clostridium botulinum, which thrives in low-oxygen environments like vacuum-sealed packages. If frozen fish is left to thaw at room temperature, these bacteria can produce spores that release botulinum toxin.
Raw egg shells were also seen stored above pickles in the walk-in cooler, which would require separation between raw animal products and produce like veggies.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Other notes from the inspection include a repeat violation of a sink not properly attached to the wall, food debris inside the bar shelves and coolers, and the prep cooler near the southern end of the kitchen not working.
Ten days later on Feb. 24 a reinspection occurred, with no repeat violations.
In February, almost 180 establishments across Sangamon County were visited by the Public Health Department.
How violations work
Food establishments are inspected by the Sangamon County Department of Public Health on an annual schedule that is determined by assigned risk type. The risk types are high, medium, or low risk, as defined by the Illinois Food Service Sanitation Code. These are determined by the complexity of food preparation taking place at the facility. Routine inspections are conducted unannounced. Follow up and complaint inspections are conducted as needed.
Critical violations concern hygiene, food temperatures, sanitizing procedures, and cross contamination. Non-critical violations concern the maintenance and cleanliness of a facility.
Here are the Sangamon County restaurants that received more than 10 violations from the health department during the month of February.
Finley's Tap House
Date/inspection type: Feb. 26, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 15 violations, 10 risk factor.
Notes from inspection: There wasn't a Certified Food Protection Manager present at the start of the inspection. Shortly after the start of the inspection however, they arrived. The inspector said the facility is inconsistently date marking foods. Several of the foods were labeled with the creation date and others were dated with the discard date. A container of oven cleaner was stored over plates, pans and salt, meaning chemicals had been stored in range with food equipment.
The floors, walls, and ceilings throughout the facility need cleaning. There is grease accumulating in the corner by the gas canisters to the left of the cookline, according to the inspector. The floor in the walk-in cooler is thickly coated with soil beneath the conduit lines.
Homestyle Cafe
Date/inspection type: Feb. 13, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 14 violations, three risk factor.
Notes from inspection: Raw hamburger was observed stored above cut vegetables in the under-counter cooler, while raw chicken was found stored over sausage and bacon in the under-counter cooler as possible cross contamination.
Both a living and dead cockroach were found in one of the two glue traps in the kitchen. A possible way of entry is the back door, which was not tightly fitted to the frame of the wall.
A follow-up inspection was done on Feb. 27, with one violation noted for pest entry through the back door which had not been fitted.
Fire & Ale Tavern
What: Inspection found 12 violations, four risk factor.
Notes from inspection: Two live cockroaches were found in the utility sink and several dead pests were found scattered around the kitchen and storage areas.
While the location makes their own sauces and dressings home made, certain sauces were dated back to January during the time of inspection and had been used after the seven-day safety regulation, or the labels had stayed on from past sauces used in the bottles.
In the inspector's words, the facility has been lacking general cleaning as well as detail cleaning. Soil was observed on most of the surfaces throughout the kitchen, dish machine, wait station, bar and back storage areas. Plumbing lines, storage tubs, and shelving were seen soiled with accumulated grease and dust. The grease accumulation remains on the fryers in the kitchen.
The reinspection noted above came following a complaint filed and investigated on Feb. 13, with five overall violations.
Tasty's Cafe
Location: 110 Villa Parkway, Sherman
Date/inspection type: Feb. 28, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 11 violations, four risk factor.
Notes from inspection: Mouse droppings were found by the inspector on top of a flour container in the outside walk-in dry storage.
Besides employees on their phones without changing gloves or a stored bottle of ibuprofen mixed in with other food items on shelving, the store is in need of cleaning near the kitchen sinks and fans.
Eggs were alo observed to be stored over cooked bacon and peeled cooked potatoes in the walk-in cooler. The potatoes were observed to be open without appropriate covering.
Yummy Yummy Hibachi Express
Location: 2901 Ridge Ave., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Feb. 18, spot check at a mobile unit
What: Inspection found 11 violations, five risk factor.
Notes from inspection: In one month, Yummy Yummy Hibachi was inspected three times.
Multiple items in the standing cooler entering the unit were stored in contact with or over items that allow for cross contamination prohibited by code, including raw chicken stored directly over broccoli, shrimp over cooked noodles and scallops over carrots.
The main issue is there is no running water in the mobile unit. Most of the unit was found with food soiling from the previous day and upon entering the unit, the inspector saw a large quantity of fried rice was in the process of being cooked, while there is virtually no place for prep within the unit.
Trustwell Living of Springfield
Location: 2451 W. White Oaks Drive, Springfield
Date/inspection type: Feb. 21, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 11 violations, two risk factor.
Notes from inspection: The main issues found at Trustwell living included food debris accumulation on the microwave, blender and freezer while numerous dented cans were pointed out in the dry storage area.
No sanitizer was prepared upon inspection in the dim lit kitchen, which required a protective cover for the lightbulbs.

title: Need a yummy dessert for Passover? We have you covered
author: Jay Kitterman
description: Passover this year begins at sundown Saturday, April 12 and ends after nightfall on April 20.
content:
Why are those macaroons and other Manischewitz products on the grocery shelf this year different from all other traditional Manischewitz products? It's a question that many American Jews may add to the traditional four questions asked on Passover. The answer is how they are packaged.
Gone is the tired, beige and blue, and now there is rusty orange with playful cartoon figures. Gone also are the macaroon canisters. They have been replaced with resealable bags. Manischewitz, the 136-year-old brand, has been a staple in Jewish homes for generations and has rebranded and expanded its product lines.
Passover this year begins at sundown Saturday, April 12 and ends after nightfall on April 20. Similar to Easter, the date is based on a lunar calendar and changes year to year.
If you have seen the movie 'The Ten Commandments,' then you are familiar with the story of the Israelites' exodus from Egypt. The holiday commemorates the 'passing over' of the forces of destruction, or the sparing of the firstborn of the Israelites.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
During the holiday, only unleavened products are eaten. The matzo symbolizes both the Hebrews' suffering while in bondage and the haste with which they left Egypt in the course of the exodus.
Many people ask me what kosher means. The word kosher is derived from the Hebrew word for 'proper' or 'correct.' The kashrut laws have to do with the cleanliness and sanctity of the food, including the production process.
It is traditional to gather with friends and family for the festive holiday meal called the seder. The word "seder" means "order" and refers to the very specific order of things that happen during the meal.
Centered on the table is the seder plate, which consists of the symbolic foods for the holiday. Non-symbolic classics for a seder include matzo balls in chicken soup, gefilte fish (a dish made from a poached mixture of ground deboned fish, such as carp, whitefish or pike), tender beef brisket and, of course, Manischewitz macaroons.
During the seder, four cups of kosher wine are consumed. Kosher wine is produced in accordance with Jewish dietary laws (kashrut). It must be handled by Sabbath-observant Jews throughout the winemaking process, and no non-kosher additives are allowed. Today Kosher wine is produced around the world and not just in Israel.
Flourless chocolate cake is a popular modern dairy Passover dessert. This cake tastes like a complex restaurant dessert but comes together effortlessly in one bowl. Chocolate chips save you the messy step of chopping chocolate bars. If you don't have a springform pan, a regular cake pan lined with foil all around makes it easy to lift out the delicate cake, which melts in your mouth when served warm or at room temperature. Refrigerated or frozen leftovers take on a candy-like chewiness, but a quick zap in the microwave will return it to just-baked softness.
My thanks to the New York Times for the following flourless chocolate cake recipe. On behalf of our family, I wish you a happy Pesach!
Flourless Chocolate Cake
Yield: 8 to 12 servings
Ingredients
3/4 cup (168 grams) unsalted butter, cut up, plus more for greasing the pan
1 cup (173 grams) bittersweet or semisweet chocolate chips
1/2 cup (50 grams) unsweetened natural cocoa powder
3/4 cup (150 grams) granulated sugar
4 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
Whipped cream or ice cream, for serving (optional)
Directions
Heat oven to 350 degrees.
Generously butter the bottom and sides of an 8-inch springform pan; or press a large sheet of foil into the bottom and up the sides of an 8-inch round cake pan (smoothing the sides) and generously butter the foil.
Bring a few inches of water in a large saucepan to a simmer over medium heat. Set a large heatproof bowl over the saucepan and add the chocolate. When the chips look soft and melty, stir gently until smooth.
Turn off the heat and add the butter to the bowl. Stir gently until melted and smooth.
Add the cocoa powder and stir until smooth; then take the bowl off the saucepan.
Stir in the granulated sugar until incorporated.
Add the eggs, one at a time, and beat well after each addition. Stir in the vanilla. Then scrape the batter into the prepared pan and smooth the top.
Bake until crackly and dry on top, and a toothpick inserted 2 inches from the edge comes out clean (40 to 50 minutes.) A toothpick inserted in the center should come out with some crumbs attached.
Cool in the pan on a rack. Then remove the sides of the springform pan or lift the cake out of the cake pan using the foil overhang.
You can slice and serve warm or at room temperature. Or, to cut very neat slices, freeze the cooled cake until firm. Slice, and warm up in the microwave or oven, if preferred. Serve the cake with whipped cream or ice cream, if you'd like. The cake can be wrapped and kept at room temperature for up to three days, in the refrigerator for up to one week or in the freezer for up to one month.
Jay Kitterman is a culinary specialist at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management and Baking/Pastry, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: Dead body found identified as missing Springfield woman
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The woman who was found dead in a field in Springfield Tuesday has been identified by the coroner.
content:
The woman who was found dead in a field in Springfield Tuesday has been identified by the coroner's office.
Georgia A. Holder, 51, of Springfield, had missing for more than a month.
Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon confirmed Holder's identity after conducting an autopsy Wednesday, which also showed no evidence of injury or trauma. The official cause of death is pending further studies, he said in a news release.
Holder was found dead in a field near the 3200 block of Ridgley Road in Springfield on Tuesday afternoon. The location is northeast of the village of Grandview and west of Illinois 55.
Holder was last seen on Feb. 8 around 5:30 a.m. near the area of North Dirksen Parkway and Ridge Avenue, according to the Springfield Police Department in a Facebook post last month. The post sought the community's help in locating Holder.
Multiple searches had been organized in recent weeks to find Holder.
The death remains under investigation by the Sangamon County Coroner and the Springfield Police.
(This story has been updated to add new information.)

title: A slice of Springfield history is for sale
author: Natalie Morris
description: A Springfield restaurant that opened in 1951 is now for sale. here's what we know.
content:
Johnny Lewis first encountered pizza while serving in the Marines as a cook during World War II. Lewis, known for his gift of gab, decided to pass the introduction along when he returned home to Springfield and opened Gabatoni's Restaurant.
'I think we were the third (business in Springfield) to serve pizza,' his daughter Rosalie Beck recently recalled. 'There was also Saputos, then called the Twin Corners, and The Plantation and us.
'Mom and dad thought we needed an Italian name. Dad was very, very friendly and people called him Gabby. So, they made it up. It took right off.'
That slice of Springfield history is now up for sale.
Last week The Real Estate Group listed the green-roofed restaurant at 300 E. Laurel St., furniture, fixtures and equipment along with the Gabatoni's name and secret recipes including the parlor's signature thin crust for $895,000.
Beck has had her hand in the day-to-day operations since her parents, Johnny and Rosemary Lewis, opened the business in 1951. That is, until the past year.
'I'm 90. I worked my whole life there,' Beck said when asked about her decision to sell the business.
Gabatoni's has operated solely as a takeout/delivery operation since shutting the dining room in 2020 during the coronavirus pandemic.
'We need to get it back open. And I can't be there.'
General manager Bob House will continue daily operations until a buyer is identified.
Gabatoni's ranks among Springfield's culinary staples that have stood the test of time like Maldaner's Restaurant (1884), Maid-Rite Sandwich Shop (1924), Saputos (1948), the Cozy Dog Drive In (1949) and the home-grown chili parlors – Dew Chilli (1909) and The Den Chili Parlor (1945), now operating as The Chili Parlor.
Since Gabatoni's served its first pie more than seven decades ago, pizza has gone from a culinary novelty to a dining staple. Beck's thoughts on how that happened?
'All pizza is good, but some is better than others,' said Beck, whose personal preference is sausage, pepperoni, green peppers and onions on Gabatoni's thin crust, of course. 'It's our dough that sets us apart.'
Business reopens
Loukinens' on 4th has reopened with Keith and Laurie Loukinen at the helm of their namesake business.
The husband-wife team are back serving customers just shy of a month after unexpectedly closing the restaurant at 517 S. Fourth St. just before Valentine's Day in what the couple termed a 'temporary' situation on social media.
'We had a few things we had to work through,' chef Keith Loukinen said Monday. 'Everything is back to normal. We're pleased to be open, thank the community for their support and look forward to serving exceptional food in the future.'
Loukinen said the business, which had been listed with The Real Estate Group last month, is no longer on the market.
Lunch hours at the casual fine dining establishment are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Tuesday through Friday and dinner hours 5 to 9 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday.
Menu change
Luminary: Kitchen & Provisions is taking its fried chicken, carryout dinner March 20 south of the border.
The entree features fried chicken served with Mexican creme, avocado, lime, cilantro and onions. Side dishes include green chili cheddar grits, Mexican street corn and potatoes, tortilla soup, Spanish rice and charro beans and for dessert a churro cheesecake with cajeta caramel.
The meal costs $85 and serves 4. A gluten-free option is available. Orders can be placed online at luminarychefs.com under the events tab. Pick up at 3121 Hedley Road March 20.
Decorating event
Want to decorate your own Easter cookies without the kitchen mess? Three Twigs & Co. is having a cookie decorating event March 23 at the 6221 Chatham Road establishment.
Kits include 8 Easter-themed sugar cookies, buttercream icing in three different colors and sprinkles for $25. Stay and complete your edible artwork at the eatery in Montvale Junction or opt for a to-go box.
Three Twigs & Co. opens at 8 a.m. but the cookie decorating party doesn't start until 9 a.m. Photos available with the Easter Bunny from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Area restaurants offering Easter Sunday specials will be featured in the March 24 print edition. Businesses interested in participating should submit information by March 18.
The A La Carte column highlights restaurant openings, closings, renovations and relocations, as well as personnel changes and business news. Natalie Morris can be reached at 217/737-7254 or by email at natalie.sjr@gmail.com.
