title: Why the giant, inflatable IUD that set DC abuzz could visit your town this year
author: Julia Gomez
description: The 20-foot IUD that debuted in DC the day Right to Contraception Act was brought before the Senate will travel to different cities across the country.
content:
A giant, inflatable IUD is going to travel across the country to help educate people about birth control this coming election season, after it made its first appearance in Washington, D.C., before the Senate voted against the Right to Contraception Act.
Americans for Contraception inserted the IUD, a form of birth control, last week to "educate, inform and empower the American public on what is under threat," Chris Fleming, a spokesperson for the group, told USA TODAY.
The 20-foot inflatable made its first appearance in front of D.C.'s Union Station. It garnered a lot of attention online when people began to post photos of it and jokes on social media.
"I hope Union Station took an ibuprofen before getting its giant IUD," posted one account to X, formerly known as Twitter.
"What if we kissed under the giant inflatable IUD?" posted another.
Why an IUD?
"It was an attention-grabbing way to educate the public, and it worked," said Fleming. He adds that the reaction has been overwhelmingly positive.
AFC inserted the IUD on Wednesday, the day the Right to Contraception Act was brought before the Senate.
"It's going to be making appearances across the country in important areas and states for a member election," said Fleming. "It's also gonna be in places where folks might not expect to see it, like in the South."
Jenny Marten, the health training manager at Planned Parenthood of Metropolitan Washington, DC, said she saw the IUD.
"I think it is a great opportunity for us to bring attention to a very important topic," Marten told USA TODAY.
Fleming did not reveal where exactly the IUD would pop up but said that it would continue to travel throughout the election year.
What is an IUD?
An IUD, or Intrauterine Device, is a form of reversible birth control. It's a plastic device that's shaped like the letter T and the size of a quarter, according to Marten. Doctors can place it in a person's uterus, and it can temporarily prevent future pregnancies.
"It's one of the most effective forms of birth control available," said Marten.
It's also growing in popularity.
Between 2006 and 2010, only 8% of women relied on an IUD for birth control, but, between 2015 and 2019, the number jumped to 20%, stated Marten.
While it works well to prevent pregnancies, people with IUDs can get them removed whenever they want to. Those who decide to have a baby can get it removed and immediately start trying to conceive.
"Every patient is different, but typically a person can get pregnant once the IUD has been removed," said Marten
Different types of IUDs
There are five different brands of IUDs, according to Planned Parenthood's website:
Paragard - Copper, works for up to 12 years
Mirena - Hormonal, works for up to eight years
Liletta - Hormonal, works for up to eight years
Kyleena - Hormonal, works for up to five years
Skyla - Hormonal, works for up to three years
Some IUDs, which are fully plastic, prevent pregnancy by administering a hormone called progestin. Other IUDs, like Paragard, are nonhormonal and are wrapped in copper. Both work by changing the way sperm cells move in the uterus and prevent them from reaching an egg.
Emergency contraception
IUDs can also be used as a form of emergency contraception.
Similar to Plan B, they can be used to prevent pregnancy for up to 5 days after having unprotected sex, according to Marten.
However, despite common misconceptions, IUDs do not induce an abortion.
"Research has shown that IUDs are very effective and they're safe," she said. "Research has also shown that IUDs do not induce an abortion."
Right to Contraception Act
The Right to Contraception Act set out to protect a person's right to access birth control, and a medical provider's right to prescribe it.
However, Senate Republicans blocked the bill.
Sen. Marco Rubio and other Republican senators who voted against the bill, signed a letter that explained why they opposed the bill.
"There is no threat to access to contraception," states the letter. It adds that the bill infringes on parental rights.
The senators who signed the letter called it a "stunt legislation."
"Why do you need a law to address a problem that doesn't exist?" asked Rubio at a press conference that was posted on X.
However, Democrats disagree. President Joe Biden said GOP lawmakers have already attacked access to contraception by proposing to defund the Title X Family Planning Program, the only program that is only dedicated to family planning.
"Dangerous and extreme abortion bans are putting women's health and lives at risk, and disrupting access to critical health care services, including contraception, as health care providers are forced to close in states across the country," said Biden. "Attacks on contraception are an affront to women's dignity and their ability to make their own decisions about their lives."
Though the bill was rejected,. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., changed his vote to "nay," which will allow him to bring the legislation to the floor again in the future.

title: Embrace the moment: Zanger, Washko, Giannuzzi eager for chance to coach all stars
author: Ryan Mahan
description: The first all-star coaching nominations for Giannuzzi and Zanger while Washko rides off into sunset at Baseball Classic.
content:
Three coaches at Tuesday's Baseball Classic All-Star game at Lincoln Land Community College's Claude Kracik Field will remember it for a long time.
For Central State Eight Conference coach Kevin Zanger, the Sacred Heart-Griffin assistant baseball coach will have veteran coaches — whom he played against — behind him.
Area coach Joel Washko may be spending his last game as a high school baseball coach. After 10 seasons at Mount Pulaski, Washko has accepted a job to become a dean of students at Lincoln.
Litchfield's second-year coach, Rocky Giannuzzi, is wrapping up one of the most packed high school seasons he'll ever have as the Area team's assistant coach.
All three coaches say they are extremely grateful for this opportunity.
'I thought that there's got to be a trick to this, and it doesn't seem like there is,' chuckled Zanger, who helped lead SHG to a Class 3A runner-up title as a senior in 2014.
The game begins at 6 p.m.
Hectic, but not Rocky
There's not much more Giannuzzi could've fit into his spring season. The Litchfield physical education teacher and baseball coach was wrapping up his master's capstone project, a 30-page paper, during the season. His wife, Kelsey, was pregnant with their first child until she gave birth, to Mia Jane, on May 14. The family was discharged from HSHS St. John's Hospital on May 16, and Giannuzzi had just enough time to get his family settled at home before his team beat Pana 8-0 in the Class 2A Gillespie Regional semifinals to set the school record with its 25 th win.
The Purple Panthers ended up with 28 wins and advanced to the Springfield Supersectional before a 10-4 loss to Maroa-Forsyth on the same field as Tuesday's all-star game.
It was nearly a blur for Giannuzzi.
'My nights were coming home, basically eat, go to sleep, do it all over again,' he said. 'I've just been so busy.
'During the year, after I'd eat, I'd try to work on an hour of homework. I'd usually catch myself; my eyes are closing and I'm dozing off.'
Giannuzzi will share a field one last time with two of his seniors who made the turnaround from a nine-win team in 2023 to a school record this season: seniors Drake Gasperson and Tate Dobrinich.
Anticipation for Zanger
The CS8 team expects to have several current head coaches serving as assistants, but Zanger said he's really looking forward at picking the brain of Springfield High's Jim Steinwart — the current dean of conference baseball coaches.
'It'll be a fun game to play with Steinwart, because he's been the veteran of this all-star game for quite some time,' Zanger said.
Zanger is in his fourth year coaching at SHG under Nick Naumovich. Naumovich was originally asked to be the head coach for the CS8 team, but a conflict prevented it and Naumovich asked Zanger if he wanted the chance.
'Getting kids in and out of the lineup is going to be honestly fun with how many athletes we have there,' Zanger said, acknowledging the complexity is part of the enjoyment.
After he graduated from St. Ambrose University in Iowa, he started helping his younger brothers improve at the sport. Now, he helps train roughly 20 kids from 8-16 years old, outside of his coaching job at SHG.
'I taught my brothers summer teams for two years,' Zanger said. 'And then at that point, I was really ready to get into either high school or college and kind of settle in here around the Springfield area.'
He said it was a 'dream' to get into coaching, especially putting on the hat of his alma mater.
'The bigger games still give me goosebumps every time we get ready for them,' Zanger said.
Washko's successful career capstone
In 10 seasons with the Hilltoppers, Washko's teams went 168-101 with four regional titles and a Class 1A fourth-place finish in 2021, the school's first trip to the baseball state tournament. Mount Pulaski has more than 20 wins in each of the last five seasons.
The Hilltoppers didn't manage more than six wins in the five seasons before Washko's arrival. But Washko says his proudest accomplishment is the overall quality the program achieved.
'The thing I'm most proud of is, this was a program that was, I mean, we were bottom of the barrel,' Washko said. 'There's no getting around it. When we came in, there was, I think, 10 kids in the program, like they were coming off a four-win season.
'We figured out sort of a formula that was successful and building a program culture, different ways of doing things and different ways of teaching things that I think really just gelled and worked. And once we got it rolling, there was still talent that kept coming through, and we had a lot of success.'
Washko, a 2006 SHG graduate, will miss spending those spring days on the baseball diamond with the Hilltoppers.
"I'm still trying to mentally to kind of wrap my head around that I'm not going to be the baseball coach at Mount Pulaski anymore,' Washko said. 'It'll be strange, because that was a big part of my life ... going back to when I was five or six years old.'

title: Sangamon county Fair among 5 things to do Father's Day weekend in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: From the Sangamon County Fair to some yacht rock, Father's Day weekend offers plenty of ways to hang out with dad.
content:
If dad is a Jimmy Buffett fan, this Father's Day is going to be a memorable one.
Looking for something to do with the whole family? Whether it's deep diving into history with the kiddos, enjoying live music, or diving across a bar for another round, there's plenty to do in Springfield this weekend.
Here are five things we found to do.
Sangamon County Fair
What: An annual favorite is back in the area with concerts, ride and more to beat the heat in the middle of June. This year's fair brings back typical Fair food along with some new events, like a car show.
Where: 318 W. Birch St., New Berlin
Capital Area Concert Band's 50th Anniversary Performance
What: For their golden anniversary, the Capital Area Concert Band has pulled out all the stops with a program celebrating the band's history and performing favorite compositions of founding members. Interim Conductor Andy VanDeVoort features selections of favorite composers of the current band, former members and a set to highlight honoring the nations and veterans as the event falls on Flag Day.
When: 6:30 p.m. on Friday
Where: Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum, 212 N. 6th St., Springfield
More: This is a free concert for the entire community, but registration for seats must be made ahead of time at presidentlincoln.illinois.gov.
Henson Robinson Zoo Day
What: The City of Springfield proclaims June 15 as Henson Robinson Zoo Day, so to celebrate all ages have free admission into the park from open to close.
When: 10 a.m. Saturday
Where: 1100 E. Lake Shore Drive, Springfield
More: A map of the park and exhibits can be found online under the Springfield Park District.
Juneteenth Celebration in downtown
What: Part of Juneteenth Inc Springfield celebration, Comer Cox Park is being transformed for the holiday into a lively stage for music, over 20 vendors and more. Play games to win prizes or check out the car and bike show, artist Morris Day and the Time will play enough music to keep Springfieldians going all day.
When: 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Saturday
Where: Comer Cox Park on South Martin Luther King Jr. Drive
Chicken Fry and tropic rock with the Boat Drunks
What: Voted the Top Rock Band of the Year seven times by Trop Rock Music Association, The Boat Drunks are bringing out the saltshakers and maracas to bring Springfield a taste of comfort, while transporting them to the tropical beaches of Margaritaville. A little bit of original music and a little bit of Jimmy Buffett, The Boat Drunks are taking over the Firefighters Lake Club right off the water in a sure to be packed clubhouse.

title: Springfield area under a severe thunderstorm watch; Sangamon County Fair show paused
author: Steven Spearie
description: The National Weather Service said a few tornadoes in the Springfield area are possible. Here's what we know.
content:
Sangamon County is under a severe thunderstorm watch until 10 p.m. Thursday, according to the National Weather Service in Lincoln.
A hazardous weather outlook from NWS indicated that damaging winds gusts, large hail and a few tornadoes are possible.
Heavy rain also could lead to flash flooding, especially in urban areas.
The storm dampened the Levitt AMP Springfield Music Series concert at the North Mansion Block after opening act, Zuh-Cari, completed her set. The featured act was featuring Curley Taylor and Zydeco Trouble, in partnership with Juneteenth Inc.- Springfield, IL.
At about 7:45 p.m., Sangamon County Fair officials put the Grandshow "on pause," according to board member Jessie Burrell.
The headliner is Priscilla Block.
Brown, Cass, Logan, Menard, Morgan, Scott and Schuyler counties are also under the severe thunderstorm watch.
The Springfield area is expected to get some temperature relief Friday and Saturday with highs in the low to mid-80s with heat building back on Sunday.

title: Springfield motorcyclist killed in crash identified
author: Steven Spearie
description: A motorcyclist killed in a two-vehicle accident at North Dirksen Parkway and Sam's Place early Friday afternoon has been identified.
content:
A motorcyclist killed in a two-vehicle accident at North Dirksen Parkway and Sam's Place early Friday afternoon has been identified.
James Hoskins, 40, of Springfield, died after being taken to HSHS St. John's Hospital, said Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon.
An off-duty Springfield firefighter had been administering CPR to Hoskins, Deputy Chief Sara Pickford said, when Springfield Police officers arrived.
Allmon said Hoskins was pronounced dead by hospital staff at 1:30 p.m. Friday.
Hoskins was northbound on Dirksen, Pickford said. The driver of a Cadillac XTS was making a left turn onto Sam's Place.
The driver of the Cadillac was transported to Springfield Memorial Hospital with non-life threatening injuries.
Pickford said no citations have been issued so far.
An autopsy, Allmon said, was scheduled for Monday.
Springfield Police are handling accident reconstruction.

title: Here are the SJ-R's girls track and field athletes of the year and all-area team for 2024
author: Bill Welt
description: Athletes from Chatham Glenwood, North Mac highlight the SJ-R's all-area girls track and field team
content:
Here are The State Journal-Register's girls track and field athletes of the year and the other members of the Springfield all-area team.
The two winners are listed first, followed by the rest of the all-area team.
Katelyn Lehnen, Chatham Glenwood
Katelyn Lehnen immediately starred as a freshman by winning the 200-meter dash in Class 3A at the girls track and field state finals in Charleston.
The Chatham Glenwood junior can now add the 100 and 400 to her list of state golds and is The State Journal-Register's Large School Girls Track and Field Athlete of the Year.
Lehnen started off by winning the 100 in 11.69 seconds before claiming the 400 in 54.81 this past May. She finished the afternoon with fourth place in the 200 in 24.37.
Last season, Lehnen pulled her hamstring at the indoor Illinois Top Times meet but still recovered in time to finish third in both the 200 and 400 and fifth in the 100 at the outdoor state meet.
"I definitely got wiped out a little bit," Lehnen said following the 200. "It's a hot day, but I gave it my all. I had a tough field to go up against. We have girls that are running 23s (in the 200). That's insane, so being able to run against those girls has been awesome. I just have to keep getting better — one more year."
Emma Crawford, North Mac
Emma Crawford initially didn't want to sign up for track in sixth grade.
But coach Brian Carman's persistence paid off and ultimately prodded Crawford to become one of the area's top female sprinters and hurdlers.
The North Mac junior assisted the winning 4x100 relay to a new Class 1A state meet record of 48.50 seconds before landing third place in both the 4x200 relay (1:42.91) and the 100-meter hurdles (15.36) this past May.
A police escort subsequently welcomed Crawford back home in Virden, along with relay teammates Kaelyn Swift, Alexis Bowman and Addison Earley.
'It was really exciting to feel that pride coming home like that,' Crawford said.
Last year's all-area team: Here are the SJ-R's girls track and field athletes of the year and all-area team for 2023
Crawford, The State Journal-Register's Small School Girls Track and Field Athlete of the Year, initially attempted the long jump and the relays before pivoting to the individual sprints and hurdles in eighth grade.
She earned ninth place at last year's state finals in the 100 hurdles but made even bigger strides this season. She particularly worked with Brian's wife, Alyssa, in mastering the three-step method.
It wasn't until the South Central Conference meet that she was able to perfect it and set a new personal best by a significant margin.
'She's the best,' Crawford said of Alyssa. 'We started working back in October with the basics before we attempted the three-step again and she worked so many long hours with me.
'It was just really relieving finally putting it all together.'
As for next year, Crawford intends to focus on the hurdles and sprints. She actually held the school's 100-meter dash record before Swift and later Bowman eclipsed the mark this season.
Crawford still holds a number of other records to boot.
Ditto Swift, also a junior. She placed ninth in the 100 (12.54) and 200 (26.34) in addition to the sprint relay medals at state. The victorious 4x100 relay was the school's first track gold medal since the consolidation between Virden and Girard.
'It's so good to have someone like that in practice and meets,' Crawford said of Swift. 'Me and Kaelyn, we've been running together since sixth grade and I just think we've always been right there neck and neck, so to have a person like that can really push you and make you better.'
Natalie Alexander, Chatham Glenwood
The senior claimed eighth place in the 3A 300-meter hurdles in 45.35.
Becca Heitzig, Lincoln
The senior mopped up her third straight gold medal in the Class 2A 800-meter run. She crossed the finish line in 2:09.55 for her best run of the season. Last year's time of 2:08.48 remains as the 2A state meet record. Last year's Girls Track Athlete of the Year and overall Female Athlete of the Year, Heitzig also won her first ever 1600 in 4:58.82 and was ninth in the 4x400 relay. Heitzig, who won the 2A girls cross country state title in the fall, will run at Iowa State University.
Madison Kacevicius, Greenview
The senior grabbed second place in the 1A long jump with a distance of 17 feet, 9 inches.
Jaida Linn, Hillsboro
The freshman reached second place in the 2A high jump with a height of 1.61 meters (5-3).
Macie Rolf, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The junior earned seventh place in the 2A 300-meter hurdles (46.95) and third place in the 4x400 relay (3:56.71) with teammates Antonette Bartletti, Maria Bartletti and Maggie Fleischli.
Addie Stadsholt, Athens
The junior captured first place in the 1A discus throw with a distance of 130-9 ¼.
Kendall Stewart, Litchfield
The senior secured third place in the 1A 300-meter hurdles in 46.49.
Kaelyn Swift, North Mac
The junior participated on the winning 4x100 relay and third-place 4x200 relay. She was also ninth individually in the 100 and 200.
Reese Wolfe, Chatham Glenwood
The junior won the 3A pole vault with a height of 3.80 meters (12 feet, 6 inches) on her first attempt for her first ever gold medal. She reached fourth place last year.
Brooke Zeibert, Rochester
The junior ascended to fourth place in the 2A 800 in 2:15.88.

title: Fruit flies, expired condiments, mold found in Springfield-area kitchens in May
author: Claire Grant
description: Nine restaurants in Sangamon County received more than 10 violations during health inspections in May, including fruit flies and mold being found.
content:
A new Springfield restaurant racked up almost 40 health inspection violations in May, including 19 risk factors to public safety.
On May 22, for the first routine inspection after it's pre-open on April 19, Mr. Hibachi on East Ash Street received 39 violations divided into three categories: risk factor, non-compliance and repeat violations.
Some of the violations, according to the report, show the facility did not have the needed paperwork from the supplier for the fish used for sushi preparation at the time of the inspection. The fish was then observed over raw vegetables in the standing cooler in the kitchen. A container of bleach was observed on top of a container of soy sauce in the dish room, which was removed during the inspection.
The inspection found all three hand sinks without paper towel and soap for drying hands, as well as no signs to notify employees to wash hands, as per according to Illinois Food Code.
Follow up inspections done by Spegal on May 28 and 31 after the initial visit found all violations were corrected at the restaurant.
Food establishments are inspected by the Sangamon County Department of Public Health on an annual schedule that is determined by assigned risk type. The risk types are high, medium, or low risk, as defined by the Illinois Food Service Sanitation Code. These are determined by the complexity of food preparation taking place at the facility. Routine inspections are conducted unannounced. Follow up and complaint inspections are conducted as needed.
Critical violations concern hygiene, food temperatures, sanitizing procedures, and cross contamination. Non-critical violations concern the maintenance and cleanliness of a facility.
Here are the Sangamon County restaurants that received more than 10 violations from the health department during the month of May.
Cancun
Location: 420 S. Crossing Road, Sherman
Date/inspection type: May 23, routine inspection.
What: Result found 26 violations with 9 risk factors.
Some notes from the inspection: The ice machine is observed to have an accumulation of mold/soil on the ice baffle. PIC was made aware of this build-up and will be cleaning and sanitizing its surface. The utensil drawer along the prep station is observed to have a significant number of soil/debris in the bottom of the drawers and on the walls of the drawers.
Scoop Du Jour
Location: West Plummer Blvd., Chatham
Date/inspection type: May 15, routine inspection.
What: Result found 17 violations with 5 risk factors.
Some notes from the inspection: Observed an open bottle of Comet sitting on a shelf above food contact utensils and bowls. Discussed with person in charge and relocated. Observed the following areas in need of repairs: Sections of the counters in the front house area are being held together with duct tape. Duct tape is not an approved material for construction in food service. Areas should be repaired so counter is not fraying or coming away and tape is no longer used.
Di Piero's
Location: 518 E. Adams St., Springfield
Date/inspection type: May 2, routine inspection.
What: Result found 16 violations with 8 risk factors.
Some notes from the inspection: There was accumulated food debris observed during multiple inspections on floors and sides of equipment. The kitchen sink was not functioning during the inspection and multiple foods were not marked with dates. Observed a number of condiments in the dish machine room to be outdated and turning rancid. Two mustard bottles were from 2020 and were opened and definitely had a strong vinegar odor. Discarded during inspection. Then a bulk Worcestershire bottle was observed half used and from 2017. That bottle had mold around the lid. The bottle was discarded. Owner mentioned the bottle was from the previously owner.
Cuatro Amigo
Location: 14758 Old Route 54, New Berlin
Date/inspection type: May 3, routine inspection.
What: Result found 17 violations with 8 risk factors.
Some notes from the inspection: A food employee was observed entering the kitchen and immediately handling clean dishes without washing hands. A food employee was also observed moving from handling dirty dishes to clean without washing hands. A sanitizer bucket was not prepared for the inspector and was corrected when the person in charge arrived at the restaurant.
Jaalsa
Location: 3114 S. 6th St., Springfield
Date/inspection type: May 2, routine inspection.
What: Result found 21 violations, with 11 risk factors.
Some notes from the inspection: Observed several containers of food in walk-in cooler to not be covered. Food containers were covered with foil during inspection. A bowl of raw chicken wings and box of raw chicken to be stored directly on floor in dry storage, which were discarded. Observed both soda gun nozzles at bar to be heavily soiled with debris. Soda gun nozzles were cleaned and sanitized during inspection. Observed several items in walk-in cooler to not be date marked. Items included: one container of chicken legs, two containers of lamb and one container of mixed vegetables. All items were discarded during inspection.
Piper Glen Golf & Social Club
Location: 7112 Piper Glen Drive, Springfield
Date/inspection type: May 2, routine inspection.
What: Result found 10 violations, with 2 risk factors.
Some notes from the inspection: Repeat offenses included no employee health reporting agreements, the baffle of the ice machine to have an accumulation of mold and no probe style thermometer for the facility. Observed the hot dog cooker to not have any overhead cover. Discussed with PIC.
Abelardo's Mexican Fresh
Location:1610 W. Jefferson St., Springfield
Date/Inspection type: May 10, routine inspection
What: Result found 9 violations, with 3 risk factors.
Some notes from the inspection: Frozen shrimp was observed in a pan of water on the counter. The shrimp was still about 41 degrees Fahrenheit on the surface and frozen in parts. After reviewing thawing methods, person in charge moved the shrimp to the walk-in cooler to continue thawing. A tub of cooked pork was observed at 66 degrees Fahrenheit (probed) on the kitchen counter. Employees stated that the pork was removed from the walk-in cooler at 7 a.m. (about 1.5 hours prior to the temperature observations) with the intention of portioning it into bags and freezing it. The facility was out of bags, so the pork was returned to the walk-in cooler. When the temperature was checked again at 10:30 a.m., the pork was 65 degrees (probed) and was voluntarily discarded. A container of pork was observed with its date label reading 'pollo rojo.' Several other containers in the walk-in cooler were similarly mislabeled, causing confusion regarding the accuracy of the date labels (though all dates were in the appropriate time frame, the foods did not correspond with the contents of the container). Containers were relabeled to reflect their contents and prep dates during the inspection.
Popeye's #823
Location: 2801 East S. Grand Ave., Springfield
Date / inspection type: May 8, routine inspection.
What: Result found 15 violations, with 9 risk factors.
Some notes from the inspection: The May 8 inspection prompted two follow up visits, May 10 and June 10. During the May 8 inspection, no one was observed washing hands. There are a number of drain flies and fruit flies around the mop sink. Inspector tapped the chemical dispenser and at least a dozen flew from the unit. Several more were observed around the walls. Observed a number of coolers to not be working within the facility: the preparation cooler was holding mayonnaise at 49 degrees (unit at 67) and the upright freezer adjacent to the preparation cooler was holding temperature at 56F. A number of foods were discarded from these two cold-holding units.
In follow-up inspections, the hot holding well was observed to still be broken but significant improvement to the restaurant had been made.

title: A Springfield high school has finalized a deal to build a new multimillion dollar school
author: Steven Spearie
description: Lutheran High School has finalized a deal to purchase 25 acres on the city's far south side where it intends to build a new school.
content:
Lutheran High School has finalized a deal to purchase 25 acres on the city's far south side where it intends to build a new school.
The property was purchased from Cherry Hills Church, 2125 Woodside Road. It is just north of the church structure and located off Chatham Road.
The school had reached an intent to purchase agreement with the church on the property in December.
George Perkins, chairman of the school's board, did not disclose a purchase price.
The school, which had an enrollment of 145 students this year, has operated out of Springfield First Church of the Nazarene, 5200 S. Sixth St. Frontage Road East, since mine subsidence issues forced it from its former home at 3500 W. Washington St.
In June 2022, school officials started noticing separation of walls and dropping of floors around the buildings.
There have been several mine subsidence incidents in the area of LuHi over the past several decades, including at Lewis Memorial Christian Village and in neighborhoods further west.
Subsidence is the sinking of land surface, commonly resulting from underground mining.
Perkins said a building committee is being formed and will look to raise $15 to $20 million for the project, though he acknowledged it could be built in phases like the former school.
Fencing went up around the Washington Street school on Monday. Perkins said he expected it to be demolished in the next several weeks.
The Illinois Department of Natural Resources is paying for the demolition, Perkins said.
Lutheran High School received, according to Perkins, a payout of $750,000 from its mine subsidence insurance.
The new space will have room for soccer, baseball and softball fields as well as a track. Perkins said the school will continue to use the fields and track at the Washington Street campus until the new facility is built.
Perkins wouldn't speculate on a timeline for completion but added that the association recently extended its lease agreement with Church of the Nazarene for three more years.
"I'm excited," Perkins said. "It's a step forward, but there are some tough steps ahead. There was some doubt about whether Lutheran High School could continue, and this tells you we will continue."

title: Trump, Pritzker trade swipes as conventions loom
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: Over the weekend, former President Donald Trump and Gov. JB Pritzker once again traded swipes at one another.
content:
Former President Donald Trump took a jab at Gov. JB Pritzker on social media Sunday, the latest in an ever-growing feud between the Democratic governor and the presumptive Republican presidential nominee.
Trump posted on his social media site, Truth Social, that Pritzker had "presided over the destruction and disintegration of Illinois" and urged voters to elect a new governor. The next gubernatorial election isn't until 2026 where it remains unknown whether Pritzker will seek a third term.
"Unless a change is made at the Governor's level, Illinois can never be Great Again!," Trump said, losing the state by more than 10 percentage points in the 2016 and 2020 elections.
His comments came after The New York Times profiled Pritzker earlier last week regarding the governor's prominent role in the campaign against Trump.
As The Times noted, few Democrats have gone to the extent that Pritzker has attacked the former president following his conviction in Manhattan last month.
'I can't mince words when it comes to talking about who Donald Trump is,' Pritzker is quoted in the article. 'It's important, I think, for people to really refocus on the idea that: Do they really want a president who is a felon who faces jail time?'
Throughout the presidential campaign, the governor has served as a top political surrogate for President Joe Biden and will likely take the stage at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago this August. Trump, on the other hand, sparked controversy when he reportedly called Milwaukee, the host of next month's Republican National Convention, a "horrible city" — a quote Wisconsin Republicans said was taken out of context.
Pritzker made note of Trump's comments made to Congressional Republicans in the neighboring state.
"Gosh - the convicted felon insulting me and Milwaukee in the same week. Is it because we are both hosting conventions full of people who can't stand him?," he posted on X, formerly known as Twitter.

title: A Springfield favorite is teaming up with a local farm to provide sweet treats this summer
author: Natalie Morris
description: A Springfield bakery has been tempting your sweet tooth in the mornings since 1932. Now, the store is helping you beat the heat in the summer.
content:
Mel-O-Cream has been making mornings a little sweeter in Springfield since 1932. Now the local franchise has teamed up with a Greenville dairy farm to tempt your sweet tooth in the afternoons too.
Mel-O-Cream's store at 4411 W. Yucan Drive has begun carrying hand-dipped ice cream made by the century-old family dairy farm, Rolling Lawns Farm.
Mel-O-Cream franchise operator Amanda Crossland said she is testing the expanded menu and operating hours on the westside with an eye to copy the process at other locations throughout Springfield.
'We've been working with Rolling Lawns (Farm) a couple of years,' Crossland said. 'They provide our milk. And people have been asking for a place to get their ice cream in town too.'
Mel-O-Cream will offer six ice cream flavor staples (vanilla, chocolate, strawberry, butter-pecan, mint chocolate chip and cookie dough) and two varieties that will rotate seasonally. Lemon curd and cookies and cream are the current seasonal selections.
Other seasonal offerings listed on Rolling Lawns' website range from Bond County Sweet Corn to Pawpaw, Harvest Peach to Pumpkin Cheesecake, Double Dark Raspberry to Peppermint Bark
A scoop of ice cream is available in a cup or served in a cake or waffle cone. The frozen treat also can be purchased in a milkshake, traditional sundae or a sundae with a donut base. Sundaes are served with house-made whipped cream and caramel and chocolate sauces.
The Yucan Drive store is now open from 5:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. Original hours (5:30 a.m. to noon) remain for Monday and Tuesday.
Mel-O-Cream will sell doughnuts throughout the day, as well as breakfast and lunch sandwiches and ice cream. The new lunch sandwiches feature a choice of turkey or ham with cheese on either a bismark doughnut shell or Italian bread. The lunchbox special includes a sandwich, donut, chips and drink for $9.99.
The Turley family has raised registered Holstein cows in Greenville for four generations. Michael and Jennifer Turley, current owner/operators of Rolling Lawn Farm, expanded the business in 2018 with the addition of a processing plant, known as The Milk House. Fresh milk from Rolling Lawns Farm is turned into milk, cream and ice cream at the Greenville processing plant.
Test kitchen
The proprietors at Whimsy Tea Company are following their own fancies as they explore a food menu for the downtown tea house.
Scratch-made selections created in-house at the 316 E. Adams St. business are available on Saturdays from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. for the next month while husband-wife owner/operators Gordon and Laura Davis finalize what will be on Whimsy's permanent menu of edibles.
'Right now what we're doing is a sort of test kitchen,' said Gordon Davis. 'And our offerings are surprises, Come see what we have going on.
'This is the culmination of everything I wanted this to become when we started Whimsy five years ago.'
Early entries featured cream filled choux puffs and limoncello-raspberry fairy cupcakes. Savory selections also are planned.
Davis said these Saturday surprises will eventually lead to a permanent food menu for the tea house later this summer.
Whimsy Tea Company began as a booth at the Old Capitol Farmers Market before finding a brick-and-mortar home in downtown Springfield in 2020.
Calling Springfield home again
Cured Catering once again is calling Springfield its home base after fire gutted its temporary home in McClelland Dining Hall on the MacMurray campus in Jacksonville June 9.
Owner Brian Reilly said Cured Catering is currently sharing kitchen space at 2232 S. Sixth St. where food for The Railyard is prepared.
'Our clients are our No. 1 priority,' Reilly said. 'We are continuing. Anything we had on the books will be completed.'
Cured Catering began in 2017, sharing kitchen space with McCormick's Catering on Springfield's north end. It even called Riverton home for a while, operating from the kitchen at The Venue before finding a home at the closed college campus in Jacksonville for the past two years. Reilly said the fire damaged all the company's equipment, except its vehicles.
Ironically, Cured Catering played a role in the creation of its new home base.
Plans for The Railyard, the al fresco food court at 2242 S. Sixth St. that opened this spring, were placed on hold to search for a new kitchen after then-partner Chip Kennedy announced in 2022 he was selling off most of his Springfield holdings.
That included his 5Flavors Catering/Secret Recipes Catering headquarters at 3086 Normandy Road, which was originally supposed to serve as the kitchen for The Railyard's eateries.
Cured Catering was poised to purchase the Normandy Road facility. Reilly said the deal fell through. But by then Jefferis already had begun converting his Sixth Street warehouse into a commercial kitchen.
Reilly said the shared kitchen is a temporary solution.
Ground was broken last week for Cured Catering's permanent home in Dawson, he said. A fall opening is expected for the catering kitchen.

title: Springfield home sells for more than $1M in May. Take a look at the home
author: Claire Grant
description: All 10 of the Springfield area's most expensive homes sold for at least $500,000 in May, including one home selling for more than $1 million.
content:
For the first time since January, a home in Sangamon County sold for more than $1 million.
Of the ten most expensive homes sold in May, nine of them were located in Springfield. Here's a look at the top 10 homes sold.
10. 3724 Stone Road, Springfield
Price: $500,000
Date: May 13
Size: 3,336 square feet
Description: A rare historical find from 1900, this house screams historical beauty the only way Springfield can display. The four-bedroom and four-bathroom welcomes guests by winding gravel paths through a tree-lined lawn. Seated on six acres of land and minutes from the city, the two-story brick home has kept its authentic features, needed updates like a new roof, attic fan and replaced windows keep it up to date while still staying rustic. The historic home was originally occupied by Harriet Knudson who is best known as the founder of Lincoln Memorial Gardens at Lake Springfield in 1936.
9. 5716 Kelley Point Drive, Springfield
Price: $530,000
Date: May 30
Size: 3,366 square feet
Description: Less than 10 years old and still looking fresh as its garden, this 2017 ranch style has the privacy of nature on its side to keep personal life personal. Built to overlook Centennial Park and the nature habitat, the backyard boasts no neighbors. The home does have a theater room and exercise room to keep guests entertained. Featuring four beds and three baths, black and brass accents decorate the lighting fixtures and doors to the house.
8. 1900 Bent Creek Road, Springfield
Price: $530,000
Date: May 24
Size: 4,557 square feet
Description: Located in the new section of the Mill Creek neighborhood, this open concept ranch style house offers plenty of living space. A new build from 2019, the home has four bedrooms and four bathrooms. Elegant but still functional, the house has a warmth leading through the hearth room up to the covered deck and patio outdoors.
7. 5229 Wildcat Run, Springfield
Price: $600,000
Date: May 22, 2024
Size: 4,509 square feet
Description: Right at the end of the cul-de-sac, this house overlooks Panther Creek Golf Course. The home has four bedrooms to match the four bathrooms. The expansive formal dining room has a built-in custom hutch featuring lighted, glass-front cabinets.
6. 1305 Woods Farm Lane, Springfield
Price: $615,000

title: Letter: Springfield's new fire station warrants multiple thank-you's
author: Jim Langfelder
description: Springfield's new fire station on Rickard Road is a reminder of who we need to thank, according to resident Jim Langfelder.
content:
Recently, Springfield reached a new milestone with the ribbon cutting and opening of the new Fire Station No. 8, located on Rickard Road, west of Veterans Parkway. This is a post-pandemic, 'state of the art" fire station and an historic modernization that will have a useful life serving public safety for the next 50-75 years.
It was great to see numerous city and state office representatives come out in unison to celebrate this important historic event. Unfortunately, two people, who were critical to building not only this new firehouse but two other new stations now under construction, were not recognized—U.S. Senators Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth.
Both should be commended and thanked for these critical public safety facilities that will serve the citizens of Springfield for decades. Approximately 50% of the funding for these firehouse modernizations came from the American Rescue Plan Act funds (ARPA), which passed the U.S. Senate by only one vote.
Regardless of your party affiliation - if you support the fire department, Senator Durbin and Senator Duckworth should be given our thanks and gratitude. They were the critical votes to pass ARPA, which not only brought approximately $34 million to Springfield, but also tens of millions to School District 186 and Sangamon County, and hundreds of million dollars via ARPA to the State of Illinois.
We look forward to the future openings of the new Station No. 6 on 11th and Ash Streets and the new Station No. 13 off of Veterans and Woodside Road.
We should also thank the community and taxpayers of Springfield for supporting our Class 1 Fire Department and making this critical step to improve public safety for our community possible.

title: How hot will it be in Illinois this summer? Here's what the Climate Prediction Center says
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: Most of Illinois saw high temperatures last week. It's trend we're likely to see all summer, according to the Climate Prediction Center.
content:
Get ready to use your air conditioners, Illinois.
Temperatures throughout most of the state last week surpassed 90 degrees. With summer official underway, that'll likely be the case for the next few months.
AccuWeather 's long-range forecast team projected last month that June through August temperatures will be two to three degrees above the historical average in the state. It's much the same per the National Weather Service Climate Prediction Center who also foresees a hotter summer.
Here's what you need to know.
How hot will it get in Illinois?
The Climate Prediction Center predicts the chance for temperatures to be above average in June, July and August to be anywhere from 33% to 40%.
As for what a typical summer weather day is in Illinois, the University of Illinois state climatologist office says highs are usually in the 80s with lows in the 60s. Days above 90 degrees are more common the further south in the state, where that total per year ranges from 10 days to 40 days.
While they are less common, Rockford and Chicago have already had multiple 90 degree-plus days this week with more likely. Temps in Springfield and Peoria also approached record highs on June 16 and June 17.
How much will it rain this summer?
Those hoping to rely on Mother Nature's help to avoid watering the grass this summer should probably keep on hoping. Outside of a sliver of southern Illinois, the majority of the state will not receive any additional precipitation than normal according to the NWS.
This holds consistent with data from the state climatologist. Northern parts of the state, on average, receive 32 inches of precipitation per year while portions of southern Illinois can receive more than 48 inches of rain.
Through May, NWS found Springfield and Peoria had received nearly an extra inch of precipitation compared to the city's average since 2000.

title: Here is The State Journal-Register's all-area baseball team for 2024
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Nine IHSBCA All-State selections litter The State Journal-Register's all-area baseball team.
content:
The State Journal-Register has selected 24 members for its annual area high school baseball teams. This year, there were 10 selections for the Large School Team and 14 picks for the Small School team.
The players and their stats are listed below, in alphabetical order, beginning with the Large School team.
LARGE SCHOOL TEAM
CAM APPENZELLER, Chatham Glenwood
When this junior got the ball and headed to the mound, it was probably going to be a good day for the Titans. This University of South Carolina commit led the Central State Eight Conference with a 0.65 ERA and a 5-0 record in 43 1/3 innings pitched. He also had a brilliant 85 to 15 strikeouts to walks and allowed just four earned runs and 18 hits. At the plate, he hit .265 (18-for-68) in 28 games with 21 RBIs and led Glenwood with 11 stolen bases. He was also an Illinois High School Baseball Coaches Association All-State pick.
TYSON BINION, Rochester
The senior second baseman hit .348 (40-for-115) and drove in 20 runs for the 20-win Rockets. He scored 35 runs and stole 12 bases.
CRU ERICKSON, Chatham Glenwood
The senior center fielder earned The State Journal-Register 's Large School Baseball Player of the Year honor, as well as an IHSBCA All-State selection, by batting .462 (54-for-117) with 38 RBIs and four home runs for the 30-win Titans, who were a perfect 10-0 in the Central State Eight Conference. He scored 32 runs and added five stolen bases. He will play at Lincoln Land Community College next season.
COLBIE GLENN, Lincoln
The Railsplitters' senior center fielder tied for the Central State Eight Conference lead by belting five home runs and had 33 RBIs and a .429 batting average (48-for-112). He gave Lincoln 41 runs, and his 20 stolen bases were tied for second-most in the league. In 26 2/3 innings on the mound, he had a 1-2 record with a 3.94 ERA. He struck out 28 and issued just 13 walks. He will play at LLCC next season.
HAYDEN HICKS, Jacksonville
The Crimsons' senior outfielder and pitcher hit .390 (41-for-105) with a .488 on-base percentage, drove in 17 RBIs, scored 35 runs and swiped 16 bases. In 48 innings pitched, he was 7-0 — including a seven-inning shutout over Rochester for Jacksonville's first regional title since 2007 — with a 0.73 ERA, 75 strikeouts and 34 walks. He also had one save in three relief outings.
SETH IMPSON, Springfield High
The last remnant from the Senators' 2021 Class 3A state championship, the senior batted .357 (30-for-84) with 14 extra-base hits, 20 RBIs, a .429 on-base percentage and a .619 slugging percentage. On the mound, he was 4-1 with wins over Lincoln, Southeast, Sacred Heart-Griffin and Rochester and had an eight-inning no decision against Normal U-High with one earned run allowed. He carried a 1.58 ERA over 35 1/3 innings and finished with 41 strikeouts against 10 walks and a .192 opposing batting average. He will play at LLCC.
JAKE KEPLER, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The Cyclones' senior right fielder led the Central State Eight Conference with a .477 batting average (31-for-65) and drove in 23 runs and scored 22 times. He stole 19 bases — tied for fourth-best in the CS8 and helped SHG finish with 23 wins, including a Class 2A regional title.
CHARLIE LINDERMAN, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The Cyclones' pitcher and shortstop hit .400 (42-for-105) with 32 RBIs and 33 runs scored. He tied Lincoln's Colbie Glenn with 20 steals for No. 2 in the Central State Eight Conference. On the mound, he was 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 28 1/3 innings pitched. He allowed six earned runs and struck out 23 against 10 walks. He will continue his career at Heartland Community College.
JACK SWANEY, Rochester
The Rockets' Northern Illinois University-bound had a heck of a senior season. He tied Lincoln's Colbie Glenn with five home runs for the top spot in the Central State Eight Conference. He hit .383 (41-for-107) with 32 RBIs and finished with 15 stolen bases. When he wasn't at first base, he was probably on the mound, where he provided the Rockets a 2-3 record with a 3.60 ERA in 37 innings pitched. He struck out 42 hitters and walked 29. He will play baseball at NIU.
ENRICO VEACH, Springfield High
The Senators' senior shortstop and pitcher hit .412 (35-for-85) with 18 extra-base hits and 20 RBIs. He only struck out twice in just 108 plate appearances and walked 17 times. The Wabash Valley College commit added 11 stolen bases. In 30 2/3 innings on the mound, he was 2-4 in 19 relief appearances, but had a 2.51 ER and struck out 44 batters.
SMALL-SCHOOL TEAM
DREW ATWATER, Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central
The Bluejays' senior center fielder hit .469 (45-for-96) and had a .563 on-base percentage out of the PORTA leadoff spot. He also finished with 13 stolen bases, 18 RBIs and drew 21 bases on balls. His average was second-best in the Sangamo Conference.
LUXAS BIXBY, New Berlin
The Pretzels' senior left-handed pitcher and first baseman ended his four-year career with a .392 batting average overall. As a senior, he hit .376 (44-for-117) with five home runs, 26 RBIs, a .447 on-base percentage and a .632 slugging percentage. He also stole a career-best 11 bases and finished with 18 total extra-base hits. The Illinois High School Baseball Coaches Association Class 2A All-State selection, he carried a 1.38 ERA across 61 innings pitched. He was 8-3 and fanned 108 batters against just 19 walks and allowed 12 earned runs in 14 appearances, including one save. He helped New Berlin go from just seven wins as a freshman to back-to-back 22-win seasons in 2023-24.
MATTHEW BYWATER, Litchfield
The Purple Panthers' sophomore shortstop, who is from Mount Olive, hit .394 (41-for-104) to help get Litchfield to a program-best 28 wins. He also finished with a .537 on-base percentage and hit two home runs as part of his 12 extra-base hits. He drove in 11 runs, scored 44 and walked 22 times.
CONRAD CHARPENTIER, Jacksonville Routt
The State Journal-Register's Small School Baseball Player of the Year was a two-way threat as the senior pitcher and first baseman helped guide the Rockets to a Class 1A third-place state tournament finish. He, along with teammate Nolan Turner, were named IHSBCA Class 1A All-State players. He finished with a .374 average (46-for-123), drove in a team-high 45 runs, hit three home runs, stole 16 bases and had a .521 on-base percentage. On the mound, he was 9-3 with a 1.41 ERA in 79 2/3 innings, including winning his last six decisions. He struck out 104 against 22 walks and held opponents to a .201 batting average.
JONAH ELVIDGE, Raymond Lincolnwood
The Lancers' junior pitcher and shortstop led the team with a whopping .514 average (54-for-105) and had a team-high 37 RBIs. He had an on-base percentage of .560 and led the Lancers with 19 stolen bases. On the mound, he was 3-6 with a 2.90 ERA in 58 innings pitched and posted 81 strikeouts against 27 walks.
AIDEN HATALLA, North Mac
The Panthers' junior shortstop shined at the plate with a .517 batting average, a .625 on-base percentage and just five strikeouts in 84 plate appearances. He drove in 24 runs and scored 26. He also had a .980 fielding percentage on 88 attempts.
NATHAN MATOUSH, Hillsboro
The junior pitcher and first baseman did all he could for the six-win Hiltoppers. He had a 2-3 record and a 0.66 ERA in 42 2/3 innings pitched with an impressive 94 strikeouts against 16 walks while getting close to throwing 90 mph. He allowed just four earned runs and came in to make two saves. He was also the team leader at the plate with a .393 average (33-for-84) and tied for the team lead with 18 RBIs and had half of the team's four home runs. He struck out just eight times in 99 plate appearances.
CHANCE PAYNE, Mount Pulaski
A Class 1A IHSBCA All-State selection, the Hilltoppers' junior left-handed pitcher and first baseman had a 7-0 record with a 0.45 ERA and 94 strikeouts in 47 innings pitched. He surrendered only three earned runs and 17 hits. At the plate, he hit .456 (36-for-79) with a .551 on-base percentage and totaled 38 RBIs, nine doubles, three triples, three homers, seven stolen bases and drew 19 walks against seven strikeouts. The Hilltoppers won a Class 1A regional title.
ETHAN SAATHOFF, Litchfield
The Purple Panthers' sophomore pitcher and third baseman helped his team to an 11-0 start en route to a program record 28 wins. He was 6-1 with two saves and a 1.67 ERA in 46 innings pitched. He fanned 43, walked 24 and helped Litchfield get to the Class 2A supersectional round for the first time since 1985. He batted .343 (34-for-99), had a .461 on-base percentage, doubled 13 times, had 27 RBIs and scored 21 runs.
COOPER SCHALLENBERG, Pleasant Plains
The Cardinals' junior third baseman and pitcher hit .398 (41-for-103), drove in 26 runs and scored 32 runs in 37 games. He also had 17 stolen bases. In 31 1/3 innings pitched, he was 1-2 with a 1.79 ERA and struck out 27 against eight walks. Plains brought home another Class 2A regional title, along with a Sangamo Conference banner.
TRAGER SHULTZ, Pleasant Plains
The Cardinals' junior center fielder earned IHSBCA Class 2A All-State honors by leading the Sangamo Conference with a .477 batting average (41-for-86). He also had 16 RBIs, 32 runs scored and tied teammate Grady Grisham with a league-best 22 steals for the 29-win Cardinals.
NOLAN TURNER, Jacksonville Routt
The senior shortstop carried the Rockets to a Class 1A third-place finish with a .386 average (56-for-145). He accumulated 29 RBIs, 57 runs scored, 23 extra-base hits and stole 29 bases. He, along with senior teammate Conrad Charpentier, were each selected to the Class 1A IHSBCA All-State team. He and Charpentier will stay teammates next season at Lincoln Land Community College.
TRISTEN WARGO, Gillespie
The senior shortstop and pitcher for the Miners batted .414 (41-for-99) out of the leadoff spot with 18 RBIs, 32 runs scored and 16 stolen bases. In 46 innings pitched, he finished 7-0 with a 0.97 ERA and had a pair of saves in 13 appearances. He fanned 63 and walked 10.
CARSON WORT, Pawnee
The junior catcher and second baseman posted a .485 average (48-for-99) and drove in 44 runs with 17 extra-base hits in 33 games. He walked 14 times, had just six strikeouts, stole 37 bases, scored 42 runs and belted two homers to earn IHSBCA All-State honors in Class 1A.

title: SEC baseball hopeful named SJ-R Boys Athlete of the Year for 2023-24
author: Bill Welt
description: Chatham Glenwood's Cam Appenzeller was one of the state's top pitchers as a junior — and more this past school year
content:
Baseball is certainly a staple at Chatham Glenwood, and being one of its top luminaries is not lost on Cam Appenzeller.
The junior left-handed pitcher committed to South Carolina in October and didn't disappoint this spring.
He was not just among the top pitchers in the Central State Eight Conference but also the state, with a 0.65 ERA and 5-0 mark in 43 1/3 innings. He totaled 85 strikeouts while allowing just 15 walks, 18 hits and six runs (four earned).
It wouldn't be a stretch to describe Appenzeller as a top prospect nationwide next season.
'When he was on, he was unhittable,' Glenwood coach Casey Erickson said. 'I had multiple coaches and umpires come up to me in the middle of a game or after a game and tell me that's the best pitcher they've seen all year. He's really special on the mound.'
Appenzeller particularly trained with Brett Huber at the Maximum Pitching Lab in Edwardsville over the offseason.
'He was an ex-pro baseball player and he's just really helped me and knows what he's talking about. He got me into the gym doing all of my stuff and making sure I stay on top of getting better," Appenzeller said.
'I think that's what really made me a lot better this year and I found my control with all of my pitches. I used to be kind of wild around the zone, but this year I kind of found it and started throwing strikes.'
That physical strength could also be attributed to other sports, including golf and basketball. He excelled on all fronts to become The State Journal-Register's Male Athlete of the Year.
He won the individual and team CS8 boys golf titles as the only player to shoot under par at Weibring Golf Course in Normal before leading the boys basketball team with 12 points and 6.5 rebounds per game.
It shows on the diamond, Erickson said.
'Cam's a special athlete,' Erickson said. 'He's very talented like you saw in basketball. He can shoot, he can dribble by guys, he can throw it down at the rim. He plays great golf in the fall and obviously in the spring he's a five-tool guy.
'He's got a great arm, he's got plus speed, plus power and he plays really well defensively, so obviously the kid's just a very talented athlete.'
Appenzeller recalled once winning the Drysdale junior golf tournament as a kid before focusing on baseball. He started using the clubs again after his family moved next to a golf course.
Appenzeller said he knew this year's golf team was going to be special.
'It made me play better knowing that I had people on my team trying to catch up to me and we were all competing for the (No.) 1 spot and everybody was close,' Appenzeller said.
Golf and baseball require Appenzeller to keep his emotions in check — but not basketball.
'Basketball's always been fun,' Appenzeller said. 'I think playing it keeps me athletic and it just helps me in baseball even more running and staying in shape. I think I move pretty well for my size, if I can just help the team handling the ball, getting rebounds or whatever it is, I think it's just my job.'
The 6-foot-5 Appenzeller wants to reach at least 195 pounds by next baseball season. The strength he's already added led him to reach as high as 93 miles per hour on his fastball this spring.
He hopes to hit those high marks consistently next season while helping the team's newcomers get up to speed to forge another playoff run. He may perhaps become a mentor like his dad, Kyle, who was a pitcher himself at Lewis and Clark Community College and Francis Marion University, which also happens to be in South Carolina.
'I'm pretty sure he's the reason I'm a lefty,' Appenzeller said. 'He would hand me the ball in my left hand and that's what I started throwing with. I think he knew that lefties are a little bit more sought after.'

title: Arby's franchisee Miracle Restaurant Group files Chapter 11 bankruptcy. Are stores closing?
author: Chris Sims
description: Arby's franchisee Miracle Restaurant Group filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy ... again. Are locations closing in Illinois, Indiana and Texas? What to know
content:
Arby's franchisee Miracle Restaurant Group has once again filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and could sell multiple stores in three states, according to court documents.
Court documents show Chapter 11 bankruptcy was filed by Miracle Restaurant Group on June 20, 2024. The business was formed in 2005 and currently own and operates 25 Arby's restaurants across Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas.
Several restaurants have been filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy or closing stores in 2024, including Red Lobster, Hooters, Tijuana Flats and Alamo Drafthouse to name a few.
The court documents for Miracle Restaurant Group state:
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
"In September 2023, the Debtor sold three of its stores located in Indiana and used the proceeds to pay down its notes with First Franchise Capital Corporation ('FFCC'), the LH Mortgage, and the U.S. Small Business Administration ('SBA'). The Debtor's remaining two stores in Indiana remain operating."
Additionally, stores in other states are also being impacted:
"The Debtor intends to continue to market and sell its seven Texas Stores, eight Illinois Stores and two remaining Indiana Stores through the Bankruptcy Process, and to focus on its Louisiana and Mississippi Stores. To accomplish this, the Debtor has retained Peak Franchise Capital, LLC as financial advisor to assist in marketing the Debtor's stores."
CEO Donald Moore declined to answer questions about the bankruptcy when contacted by phone. In the filing, Moore notes he has "experience in senior officer roles at public and private restaurants since 1990."
Here's what to know:
Is Arby's filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy?
No. Franchise operator Miracle Restaurant Group is filing for bankruptcy and owns 25 Arby's locations in Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas.
Who owns Arby's?
Arby's is owned by Inspire Brands. They own several restaurants including Baskin Robbins, Buffalo Wild Wings, Dunkin', Jimmy John's and SONIC.
Are Arby's restaurant locations closing via Miracle Restaurant Group's Chapter 11 bankruptcy?
No. Miracle Restaurant Group is attempting to sell the remaining locations in Illinois (8), Indiana (2) and Texas (7), according to court documents.
Has Miracle Restaurant Group filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy previously?
Yes, this is Miracle Restaurant Group's second Chapter 11 filing. The franchisee used to own 60 Arby's franchise locations before filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2010, according to court documents. A number of stores were closed after the plan was confirmed and all creditors were paid in full under the plan.
What Arby's restaurant locations could be closing in Illinois, Indiana and Texas?
Miracle Restaurant Group has not confirmed a list of store closings or which restaurants are being sold. Below is a list of locations posted on the website at mrgarbys.com/locations.htm. Three Indiana locations were sold in September 2023, but which stores were sold is unclear.
