title: 10 fall festivals and outings in the Springfield area you won't want to miss
author: Steven Spearie
description: From carving pumpkins to walking in Lincoln's footsteps, fall festivals and outings in the Springfield area are on tap.
content:
Check out some fine art, tour a historic (and some say haunted) mansion or be part of a bicentennial celebration.
There's a fall festival or outing for you in and around Springfield.
Here's a sampling of what's going on.
Edwards Place Fine Art Fair
The 36th annual Edwards Place Fine Art Fair features artists from around the country exhibiting a variety of media Sept. 21 (10 a.m. to 5 p.m.) and Sept. 22 (10 a.m. to 4 p.m.)
There are tours of the historic Edwards Place, a 190-year-old Italianate mansion. The fair features live music and food and beverage vendors. A used book sale benefits the Michael Victor II Art Library. 700 N. Fourth St. springfieldart.org. 217-523-2631. Free.
While in the neighborhood, visit historic homes in the Enos Park neighborhood in various stages of renovation. Tours are from 1 to 5 p.m. Sept. 21. Tickets available at the booth at the art fair. 217-553-4629. $10.
Clayville Fall Festival
Visitors to the Clayville Fall Festival Sept. 21-22 (10 a.m. to 5 p.m.) can join in on the bicentennial celebration of the Broadwell Inn and Tavern. The inn, according to an online history, served as a stagecoach stop and public house catering to stagecoach passengers, freight caravans, freight carriers, cattle drivers, circuit riders and others.
The name stems from Whig Party statesman Henry Clay and the Broadwells, the namesake of the inn, were prominent Whig participants. An 1842 Fourth of July celebration there drew another early Whig advocate, Abraham Lincoln.
The fall festival includes Civil War camps with the 10th Illinois Infantry Regiment, the 108th Illinois Infantry Field Hospital and others. Chris Camp (The Whip Guy) will be giving demonstrations and Batterton and Edwards will provide the music. Pleasant Plains, Illinois 125. clayville.org. 217-481-4430. Free.
Buzz Bomb Oktoberfest
Oktoberfest in September? Why not, especially when Buzz Bomb Brewing Company will be serving up several German styles of beers, along with other local breweries, and the musical headliner is the legendary Supersuckers.
The Sept. 21 outdoor festival will also include food, vendors, games and children's activities.
Other bands include Left Lane Cruiser, Aage Birch, Sonic Sunday, Master Bastard and Prairie State of Mind. Minors are allowed outside but must be accompanied by a parent/guardian to go inside Buzz Bomb. 406 E. Adams St. buzzbombbrewingco.com. 217-679-4157. $10.
International Route 66 Mother Road Festival
The Mother Road Festival routinely draws some 1,200 classic and antique cars and other vintage vehicles to downtown between Washington and Capitol streets and Fourth and Seventh streets Sept. 27-29.
It kicks off with the Route 66 City Nights Cruise from the Capitol City Shopping Center on Dirksen Parkway to downtown at 6:15 p.m. Friday. Dennis Gage will be filming an episode of Motor Trend TV's "My Classic Car on Saturday. Chris Jacobs, a host of "Overhaulin'" on Motor Trend TV, will also be appearing.
There's a burnout competition, a 5K run and a Miss Mother Road contest. Wowie Zowie, Wreckless Whiskey, Pizzazz Dance Band and Horizon Band will provide the music over Friday and Saturday. Route66Fest.com. 217-553-5271. Free to spectators.
Oak Ridge Cemetery Walk
Dead men (and dead women) do tell tales. Some of the best will be heard on 'Echoes of Yesteryear: A Walk Through Oak Ridge Cemetery' sponsored by the Sangamon County Historical Society.
Actors dressed in period costumes will portray figures at his or her gravesite. That includes con artist and international hustler Reed 'Kid' Waddell (1860-1895), who actually sold the Brooklyn Bridge. He will be portrayed by Pat Foster. Ellen Huntington Henkle(1853-1919) was, in her day, considered to be Springfield's best singer. She will be portrayed by Linda Schneider.
The walk between gravesites is about half a mile. Sept. 29. Noon. Oak Ridge Cemetery, 1441 Monument Ave. sangamonhistory.org. 217-525-1961. Free but donations are welcome.
Fall Harvest Festival
Lincoln Memorial Garden's annual Fall Harvest Festival includes artisan demonstrations and exhibits and gets started on Oct. 12 with a concert by duo Tater Tots (Kristi Lecocq and Micah Walk).
It runs Oct. 12 (9 a.m. to 4 p.m.) and Oct. 13 (10 a.m. to 4 p.m.) Lincoln Memorial Garden, 2301 East Lake Shore Drive. lincolnmemorialgarden.org. 217-529-1111. $8.
Artisan & Antique Market
The Artisan & Antique Market, put together by the owners of the Ursuline Music Conservatory, the Dream Center and the Brinkerhoff Mansion, offers up over 150 vendors, food trucks, a jump house, live music and more from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Oct. 5.
Some say the mansion, built for a contemporary of Abraham Lincoln's and known as "the Castle," is haunted by George Madoc Brinkerhoff Sr. himself.
Sixth Street between Keys Avenue and Eastman Avenue. Visit the Brinkerhoff Mansion Facebook page. Free.
Carve for the Carillon/Jack-O-Lantern Spectacular
Bring your carving tools and your imaginations to Carve for the Carillon from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Oct. 12-13 as a run-up to the Jack-O-Lantern Spectacular the following weekend around the Thomas Rees Memorial Carillon and Washington Park Botanical Garden.
The Springfield Park District supplies the pumpkins (while they last). It's a free event, but donations will be accepted.
The pumpkins will be on display from 6:30 to 9:30 p.m. Oct. 18-19. On Oct. 20, you can take away a decorated pumpkin for a donation. 1740 W. Fayette Ave. carillon-rees.org. $7-$10 (discount tickets at Ashley HomeStore Outlet, 1987 Wabash Ave.).
Springfield Area Highland Games & Celtic Festival
You can experience Scottish culture without having to cross the pond at the Springfield Area Highland Games & Celtic Festival at the Sangamon County Fairgrounds in New Berlin Oct. 19.
Athletes compete in traditional Scottish sporting events like the caber toss, hammer throw and stone put. Enjoy live performances of bagpipe music and Scottish dances, food and drink, like haggis and single malt whisky, plus crafts and storytelling.
316 W. Birch St., New Berlin. centralillinoiscelts.com. $8-$20.
New Salem Fall Festival
Period-clothed interpreters demonstrate daily tasks at the reconstructed village, such as candle dipping, soap making, blacksmithing, spinning wool, gardening and natural dyeing at the Fall Festival at Lincoln's New Salem from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Oct. 26.
Abraham Lincoln spent about six years of his early adulthood living in the village, about 20 miles northwest of Springfield.

title: Music acts help 2024 Illinois State Fair set attendance record
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: Aided by favorable weather conditions and new attractions, the 2024 Illinois State Fair had record attendance.
content:
Aided by favorable weather and new attractions, it was another year of record-breaking attendance at the Illinois State Fair.
More than 773,000 people attended the 11-day event in August, topping last year's record by nearly 66,000, per an announcement made by Gov. JB Pritzker and the Illinois Department of Agriculture on Monday.
"Each year, the hardworking team at the Illinois Department of Agriculture manages to improve the Illinois State Fair with innovative new offerings, bigger and more diverse entertainment options, and an unwavering commitment to spotlighting Illinois agriculture," said Pritzker in a news release.
Big-name musical acts like the Jonas Brothers, Keith Urban and Miranda Lambert drew large crowds. The big draw to the Grandstand was Lil Wayne, who broke the attendance record by selling more than 15,000 tickets.
The fair also serves as a way to showcase one of the state's leading industries — agriculture — where the Governor's Sale of Champions experienced record-high sales. The Grand Champion Steer sold for a combined $110,000, and the Land of Lincoln Grand Champion Steer sold for $65,000.
Among new attractions to this year's fair was a naturalization ceremony where the governor welcomed nearly 200 new citizens to the United States from 49 countries around the world. The ceremony finalized the process to integrate into American society and accept the rights and responsibilities of U.S. citizenship.
According to the Regional Economics Applications Laboratory at University of Illinois, the fair is estimated to generate $86 million in local economic impact in addition to $2.6 million in sales tax revenue for the state.
The 2025 Illinois State Fair will be held from Aug. 7 to Aug. 17.

title: 'You will not die. The terrorists will not find you.' Survivor of Hamas attack speaks out
author: Steven Spearie
description: 'One bullet went near my neck and another under my legs,' recalled Hamas attack survivor Amit Ganish. Ganish shared her story Sunday in Springfield.
content:
Escaping the rocket attacks and gunfire from Hamas forces at the end of the Supernova open-air music festival in southern Israel on Oct. 7, Amit Ganish, a 24-year-old law student, found herself hiding out in a bush in an orchard with her best friend.
With the battery on her cellphone running low, Ganish texted her mother and her boyfriend that she loved them. She also sent pictures of the hideout, desperate to get the attention of authorities, even with the enemy roaming around.
Ganish, telling her harrowing tale at the Chabad Jewish Center in Springfield Sunday afternoon, said she remained resolute in her surroundings, even with being deprived of food and drink.
"I told myself, 'You will not die. The terrorists will not find you. You will fight. You will do what you need to do, but you will survive. I will survive for my family, for my boyfriend,'" Ganish told the 100 or so people gathered Sunday. "That was the decision that I took."
After nine hours, a local farmer, credited with saving the lives of hundreds of music festivalgoers, coaxed Ganish and her friend, Zohar, out of hiding.
Walking out of the orchard, they were met with a phalanx of Israeli TV cameras. That's how, Ganish said, her family learned that she had survived the ordeal.
This is Ganish's second speaking tour in the U.S. since last year's music festival attack, which claimed the lives of some 360 concertgoers. In all, nearly 1,200 people were killed in the Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, included at least 43 Americans.
A documentary about the attack, "We Will Dance Again," which will include the experiences and anecdotes of survivors like Ganish, is set to debut later this month.
The militant group's attack triggered hostilities that have been felt region wide. The Gazan Health Ministry claimed over 40,000 Palestinians, fighters and civilians, have been killed in Gaza and around 90% of Gaza's population has been displaced. U.S. officials have been engaged in peace talks they hope can include a two-state solution.
"October 7 was a terrible reminder that the opposite of good — evil — is something that still exists in the world," Rabbi Mendy Turen told the audience before Ganish's remarks. "That's something that we always have to remember. It's something that has to be on our mind. Our job, of course, is to spread good, to spread light, to spread positivity to the world."
Ganish, who lives just outside of Tel Aviv, said she had a premonition about the music festival, which drew around 3,500 people not far from Gaza, but decided to go anyway.
Ganish said she wasn't panicked even as she saw rockets from Gaza in the early morning hours of Oct. 7. But as she was about to go to sleep after a night of dancing and partying, a voice warned of terrorists shooting.
Running towards the main road, Ganish, Zohar and her boyfriend got a ride from a stranger. Nine people crammed into the car, minus Zohar's boyfriend, who they later learned was gunned down.
"One bullet went near my neck and another under my legs," recalled Ganish, as she and her friend ditched the car and zig-zagged their way into the orchard.
Even there, they could hear enemy voices trying to pry them out, Ganish said.
Rami Davidian, a 58-year-old farmer from the area, finally got them out of hiding and to safety.
About a week after the experience, Ganish said she re-upped for the military.
Psychological counseling and the speaking engagements, cathartic in their own way, have helped Ganish deal with the trauma.
"It helps me a lot to share my story and get all this love and support from other Jewish communities," Ganish told The State Journal-Register afterwards. "This is my honor to do it."

title: How this Rochester senior plans to live up to high expectations this girls tennis season
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Meet the SJ-R's defending Girls Tennis Player of the Year, plus other top players in the Springfield area this season
content:
It's early in the fall girls tennis season and Julia Musgrave has a specific goal in mind.
'I think I just need to play more,' said the Rochester senior. 'I hadn't been able to play that much this summer because I teach tennis, worked 40-hour weeks, basically. I want to play more and have fun for my senior season. Most importantly, it's about being consistent for myself and having a positive attitude.'
Musgrave — The State Journal-Register's 2023 All-Area Player of the Year — had a mild setback on playing more when she fell ill for several weeks. As the top singles seed, she had to pull out of the Central Illinois Invitational on Sept. 7, which was won by second seed Ella Sandgren of Maroa-Forsyth.
In addition, Musgrave suffered a 6-2, 6-0 defeat to Chatham Glenwood junior Ellie Surges in a dual meet at Chatham on Wednesday. Glenwood, the top team in the area, won the match 9-0.
Third-year Rochester coach Rolando Salazar noted that it was a 'tough match' for Musgrave while praising Surges and senior teammate Samantha Shankland.
'Glenwood has a really good program, bringing up those two, Ellie and Sam,' Salazar said. 'It's not the last time we'll see Ellie, she played well. (Musgrave) is just now getting over her sickness that she's been having for the past month, so I think that had a little bit of play into it. The best thing that we can do is go back to the drawing board, practice and hit it from there.'
To boot, Musgrave hinted that being the returning player of the year can bring some higher expectations.
'There is definitely some pressure,' Musgrave said. 'I wasn't expecting to get (the award) last year at all. I was expecting (Shankland) or (Springfield High graduate Nischi Korrapati) to get it. I'm really grateful for it. I hope I can live up to that title for this year.'
Musgrave's run to her award as a junior started with private lessons from current Glenwood head coach Sonthana Thongsithavong at about 9 years old. She said she quit playing volleyball to focus solely on tennis and also worked with Decatur's Chuck Kuhle and took many classes around Washington Park.
Musgrave's dedication paid off last season when she finished second at the Class 1A Alton Marquette Sectional and advanced to the Illinois High School Association state tennis finals, winning two matches in the consolation bracket to finish 2-2. She earlier had two second place finishes at the Springfield High Invite and at the CII, respectively. Musgrave and Rochester graduate Raleigh Meneghetti took third place in doubles at the Central State Eight Conference Tournament.
'It would be really great if I could make it to state again, that's always the goal,' Musgrave said. 'If I win a tournament, that would be great, too. It would be a great way to finish off the season.'
Salazar said he wants to see Musgrave finish with a winning record at state and admires her work ethic.
'Just the fact that she doesn't stop, she doesn't stop fighting,' Salazar said. 'She doesn't give up too easily and has grit and hunger. If she wants something, she'll go after it. She feeds that off to my other players as well. I'm looking forward to her senior season.'
Regarding Rochester's team, Musgrave praised senior and No. 2 singles player Grace Winkler and her doubles partner, junior Cora Haupt.
'She worked the entire summer, played every day and really worked hard at it,' said Musgrave of Winkler. "She can definitely win some games for us. Cora still has room to improve, but I think she has really come a long way.'
Salazar has a bigger goal in mind for Rochester.
'I feel really confident this season, going for a sectional title,' he said. 'I think we have the right group to do it — it's just a matter of how bad we want it. The response I got from most of the girls is that they really want a sectional title, and it would be great for the girls and the school.'
Including Musgrave, here are the top area players to watch for the 2024 season.
Samantha Shankland, Chatham Glenwood
The senior started this season with a big 4-6, 6-1, 10-3 victory over Sandgren at the Maroa Quad Meet on Aug. 24. Shankland, last season's CS8 conference singles champion, also picked up a pair of straight sets wins at the Belleville East Invite with victories over Belleville East and Morton at No. 1 singles on Sept. 7. She has a chance to right the ship after missing out on a state berth last season with a loss in the quarterfinals of the Class 2A Belleville West Sectional.
Myla Shannon, Springfield High
The senior ended 2023 with a combined 16-13 record in singles and doubles while teaming with sophomore Madisyn Williams. Shannon defeated Sacred Heart-Griffin graduate and Class 1A state qualifier MK Christie 6-4, 6-1 for fifth place at last season's CS8 tournament. She won her first match at the Class 2A Belleville West Sectional before losing to Surges in the second round.
Caroline Sheehan, SHG
The senior became one of SHG's top players in both singles and doubles last season, but did not play in the postseason due to 'extra-curricular' activities, said SHG coach Hayden Esker. She and Lily White tied for fifth in the No. 1 doubles draw at last season's Central Illinois Invite, a meet that SHG won in 2023. Sheehan has started 2024 positively by getting to the No. 1 singles title match of the CII and placing second after falling to Sandgren 6-4, 6-1.
Ellie Surges, Chatham Glenwood
The junior has begun the season with a 6-0 start, including beating Musgrave 6-2, 6-0 at No. 1 singles in a dual meet. The majority of her matches have been in the No. 2 singles spot, namely posting a 7-5, 6-2 win over Quincy's Mary Dodd in a dual meet on Sept. 3. She is also expected to contribute at the No. 1 doubles slot, said Thongsithavong, with junior teammate Lydia Ryherd. Surges is currently 6-1 in the Nos. 1 and 2 doubles flights this season. She finished second at the CS8 tournament last season, falling to Shankland in three sets and — with a fourth-place finish at the Class 2A sectional — she qualified for state and went 0-2.

title: Big-sized win: Glenwood bullies Rochester in marquee CS8 matchup
author: Adrian Dater
description: After Friday's 45-17 win over Rochester, Glenwood quarterback Colten Knoedler had one date in mind: November 30.
content:
CHATHAM — Standing under the Friday night lights, and big prairie skies of Chatham Glenwood High School, Colton Knoedler had admirers young and old surrounding him after a game he'll surely never forget.
'Now that was a performance,' said one of the elders in the crowd to the junior Titans quarterback.
It surely was. Knoedler threw for five touchdown passes in Glenwood's 45-17 thrashing of defending Class 4A state champion Rochester in front of an overflow crowd. Completing 15 of 22 passes for 246 yards, Knoedler was the leading man in the Titans' triumph — just the third in 16 total meetings with the Rockets.
With his offensive line affording him ample time in the pocket all night, Knoedler picked apart a Rockets team that lost most of the veterans from last year's dominant club — but was still considered a top contender in the Central State Eight. If Friday's game made a 'statement,' it was this: Glenwood (3-1 overall, 2-0 CS8 East Division) now looks like the big, new bully on the block.
'November 30. That's all I got,' said Knoedler, when asked for thoughts on his team's future.
That's the date of the Class 6A state title game, and if the Titans keep looking like they did Friday, they have a legitimate chance of playing then.
'I don't know, it's Week 4,' Titans coach David Hay said. 'We won Week 4, now we got to win Week 5. Last year, we lost to (Decatur) MacArthur, and now we've got to go back there. But we did a lot of little things right tonight that made a bigger difference in the outcome. Our offense did a great job executing and making big plays.'
Perhaps the biggest came early in the third quarter.
Rochester (2-2, 1-1 CS8 East) scored as time expired at halftime to get themselves back in the game, 17-7. In one of Knoedler's few bad throws in the game, Rochester seemingly had an interception near midfield, but the ball was dropped. On the next play, Knoedler hit senior receiver Gavin Simmons down the right side for a 77-yard TD pass. Instead of a 17-7 game, and Rochester having the ball, it was 24-7 Glenwood.
That was a major turning point in the game.
'You never know when the big plays are going to happen, and when they do, you've got to be a difference-maker. (Simmons) was selected to be a captain this week, and he showed leadership out here,' Hay said. '(Knoedler), he's a playmaker, and just cool as could be out there tonight.'
Said Knoedler of the long TD to Simmons: 'He ran a great route and kind of kicked it into another gear speed-wise. He's a great athlete and made a great play.'
Rochester's miserable night included injuries to some top players, including starting QB Eli Carlson. He was on crutches by halftime, after a second-quarter injury to his left foot. Tanner Beal, a 6-foot-5 junior, did an admirable job in relief, completing 11 of 18 passes for 130 yards, but Glenwood's strong pass rush made things tough on all Rockets' backfielders.
The Titans have a new weapon in 6-foot-7 tight end Mason Neumann, who caught six passes for 112 yards and two touchdowns. The first, an 11-yard catch, was essentially a jump ball between him and Rockets defenders, and the towering Neumann won that battle.
Neumann, the starting center on the Titans' playoff basketball team, showed a willingness to be physical on plays despite his wiry frame.
'Having smaller guys on me, it means I've got to work my hands more, to get off the line,' Neumann said. 'But the jump balls? Yeah, that's my go-to. It's kind of hard to guard.'
The Titans also got strong games from Springfield High transfer Herchel Walker, who ran for 54 yards on 16 carries, and placekicker Mia Gerger, who booted a 23-yard field goal to open the scoring and converted on seven extra points.
Before he left the game, Carlson ran for 68 yards on five carries and threw for 29 yards on 6-for-10 passing.
Adrian Dater is a freelance writer for The State Journal-Register. He can be reached through the sports department at sports@sj-r.com.

title: Quincy Notre Dame sends emphatic message in CS8 football race against SHG
author: Bill Welt
description: How could Quincy Notre Dame handle the big boys in the Central State Eight? Consider that question answered in shocking fashion Friday night.
content:
(This story was updated to add new information.)
QUINCY — Quincy Notre Dame made a statement, loud and clear.
The Raiders can play with the best football teams in the Central State Eight Conference.
QND senior Wyatt Mueller threw three touchdown passes and ran for two more scores in a 37-7 win over Sacred Heart-Griffin on Friday. Mueller hurled a 68-yard TD pass to junior Gavin Doellman on a trick play to open the first quarter, then dashed for two TD scores to jump ahead 18-0 in the first half.
"He's a Swiss army knife," fellow running back Oliver Triplett said of Mueller. "He can do everything for our offense — put him in when we need him and he can do the job 100%."
SHG's Cam Brinkman threw a 24-yard TD pass Seamus O'Brien to shave the deficit 18-7 at halftime.
An Oliver Triplett interception and Mueller's second TD pass to Doellman reassured the momentum stayed on QND's side after the break. Triplett became the primary ball carrier after Ivan Hun went down with an injury in the first half and ran for 141 yards on 27 carries.
"I'm excited the way all our guys played tonight," QND coach Jack Cornell said, when asked of the Hun injury. "I loved how all our guys had to step up for some dudes and we got to see what they could do."
Doellman finished with two interceptions on defense and returned a punt 69 yards for a TD in addition to his two TD catches. Mueller finished 3-for-3 for 128 yards, all on scoring plays. Starting QB Hunter Schuckman completed 8 of 15 passing attempts for 74 yards and two picks. QND (2-1) committed all three of its turnovers in the first half.
"Our coach emphasized the whole week that we have to make a statement coming into the Central State Eight," Triplett said. "I feel like we really made that statement. SHG is a very respected program. I feel like we really answered the call today."
SHG (2-2) struggled to move the ball on the ground, with only 42 rushing yards. That was compounded by costly penalties. Brinkman went 13-for-28 for 205 yards and one TD with four interceptions.
"We've got to fix the O-line obviously," SHG coach John Allison said. "When we can't run the ball for three or four yards, then the whole offense is going to struggle. We've got to get back to basics and find out who wants to be part of the solution and not part of the problem and go from there."

Crucifixio Mitchell and Jacksonville's defense
Mitchell opened the game with an 80-yard kickoff return and he added a 29-yard touchdown reception as the Crimsons rolled Lanphier 76-14 in a Central State Eight Conference game. Jacksonville had four interceptions, including three returned for touchdowns by Jeremiah Jackson (32 yards), Darren Henry (26 yards) and Jason Brown (30 yards). Asher Greene returned a fumble 18 yards for a TD in the win.
Nolan Herpstreith, Nokomis
The junior back rushed 15 times for 150 yards and two touchdowns as Nokomis improved to 4-0 with a 55-7 win over winless Cerro Gordo in a Lincoln Prairie Conference game. Herpstreith opened the scoring with a 50-yard TD run and added a 2-point conversion to get Nokomis going.
Cooper Schallenberg, Pleasant Plains
The senior quarterback ran for two touchdowns and threw for two more, including a game-winning 50-yard TD pass to Grady Grisham with 39.5 seconds remaining in the fourth quarter in Plains' 28-25 Sangamo Conference win at Auburn. He finished 11-for-16 for 194 yards and one interception.
Isaiah Harbert, Pana
Pana's senior running back had four touchdowns and 142 yards rushing on 20 carries in Pana's 51-24 win over North Mac to improve to 4-0 overall and in the South Central Conference. His 4-yard run with 1 minute, 47 seconds left in the third quarter capped off a 98-yard drive and gave Pana the lead for good, 30-24. Cash Lynch intercepted North Mac quarterback Payne McLean, a senior, on the 2-yard line, to set up the possession.
"I saw Cash pick it and it was so much relief," Harbert said. "We knew it was go-time for our offense. Props to our offensive line: they started moving those guys. Everyone was clicking. We had our pass game and we had our run game and they didn't know where the ball was going."
Noah Byots and Tate Duckels, Carlinville
Byots, a senior quarterback, totaled 238 yards and scored the game-winning touchdown on a 6-yard run with 3 minutes 9 seconds left in the fourth quarter of Carlinville's 20-13 South Central Conference win at Staunton. He completed a 63-yard TD pass to Duckels, who caught 7 passes for 98 yards. Byots finished 16-for-25 with 180 passing yards to go with 58 ground yards on 15 attempts.
Caden Venrick, Auburn
The senior running back ran for three scores in Auburn's 28-25 loss to Pleasant Plains. His TDs covered 5, 11 and 74 yards.
Pana's defense in second half
After North Mac headed into the locker room leading 24-15 at Pana's Brummett Field, not only did the host Panthers know their offense needed a spark, but so did its defense.
Mission accomplished.
Cash Lynch intercepted Payne McLean at the Pana 2-yard line to set up the host Panthers' go-ahead touchdown. North Mac's offense ended the game with a turnover on downs, a punt, another turnover on downs and two interceptions. The visiting Panthers had just four first downs in the second half, and only one following Lynch's INT.
"As soon as we punched it in, got a stop, and punched it in again, you could see through their body language and their expressions, they knew they were on their heels," Pana running back Isaiah Harbert said of North Mac.

title: 'It's a joke.' Woman pillories Massey Commission, which gets final approval from board
author: Steven Spearie
description: On an evening where the Sangamon County Board officially voted in the Massey Commission to address police practices in the aftermath of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey, one Springfield woman had strong objections to its setup.
content:
(This story has been updated to add new information.)
On an evening where the Sangamon County Board officially voted in the Massey Commission to address police practices in the aftermath of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey, one Springfield woman had strong objections to its setup.
"I believe it's a joke," Teresa Haley told The State Journal-Register, after pillorying the commission as "fake" in public comments made at a special board meeting at the Bank of Springfield Center Wednesday. "I believe it was put together really quickly to check the box, to say we're doing something."
The commission was called for last month by Sangamon County Board Chairman Andy Van Meter and State Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, with an eye towards addressing systemic issues in law enforcement practices, mental health responses and community relations.
Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman and mother of two children, called 911 in the early morning hours of July 6 because she thought she heard someone outside of her house, which is in an unincorporated area of Woodside Township.
Former sheriff's deputy Sean P. Grayson shot Massey in the face after a situation over a pot of boiling water quickly escalated.
Grayson's hiring by the sheriff's department has been called into question. He jumped from agency to agency before landing in Springfield in 2023. His criminal history also show he had two DUIs and a questionable discharge from the military.
The commission, co-chaired by Jerry Kruse, dean and provost of the SIU School of Medicine; the Rev. T. Ray McJunkins, pastor of Union Baptist Church and Nina Harris, chair of the Illinois Commission on Equity and Inclusion, held its first listening session Monday.
While its 12 commissioners haven't publicly been named yet, McJunkins said following Monday's meeting that nine members are aboard, including a member of the Massey family.
Others let loose with other concerns Wednesday.
Jenna Broom said that with a lack of subpoena power, "this commission really is nothing. I hope there's a way that all records and documents requested are received."
Breonna Roberts added that "transparency in who is appointed" is needed and appointees with questionable backgrounds or insufficient experience risk the commission making "the same mistakes that got us here."
Roberts also urged the board to reconsider the commission's co-chairs.
"Sangamon County deserves better," she said.
Haley, who has her own public relations firm, is allied with the Massey family. Several Massey family members, including Sonya Massey's mother, Donna Massey, attended the meeting.
Haley said it was "disrespectful" for a commission to be formed and co-chairs named without allowing letting the commissioners decide who they want to be co-chairs.
"That's bold transparency," Haley said. "That gets people to buy into it."

title: Springfield's Jefferson Bridge officially renamed to honor Sonya Massey
author: Claire Grant
description: Springfield's City Council has officially changed the name of the Jefferson Bridge to honor Sonya Massey.
content:
"This and our Black Lives Matters signs we put up permanently that we all signed up to, are more than symbolic."
Those were the words Ward 2 Ald. Shawn Gregory said at the Springfield City Council meeting on Sept. 17, after the aldermen unanimously approved the vote to rename Jefferson Bridge to the Massey Memorial Bridge.
Sonya Massey was fatally shot in her home by a former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy in an unincorporated part of Woodside Township after reporting a possible intruder on July 6.
Former deputy Sean P. Grayson, 30, was charged with Massey's murder. Grayson has pleaded not guilty.
Ordinance 2024-364 was originally requested by Gregory, and all other members of the council requested for the vote to pass. The ordinance authorizes the creation of murals on select areas of the bridge over Clearlake Avenue and Jefferson Street.
The council approved on Sept. 10 to commission a mural for the Jefferson Bridge, and work with IDOT to rename the bridge in her honor. This final vote on Tuesday night sealed Sonya Massey's name, and impact on the city for future generations to acknowledge.
Massey's mother, Donna, was in the crowd when the ordinance passed.
'Those that pushed for us did it,' Massey said. 'She deserves it, and I thank you guys very much.'
The inspiration for this vote comes from the resounding mural of Sonya Massey, painted by Springfield artist Austin Wells in late July of this year.

title: Emotional testimony by fiancée of triple homicide victim opens Springfield murder trial
author: Steven Spearie
description: Opening of murder trial takes witnesses back to Aug. 9, 2021, the night Savante English, Keyera Gant and Bryant K. Williams were shot to death.
content:
What started out as a celebration of life turned into the loss of three lives, argued Sangamon County assistant state's attorney Meghan McCarthy Tuesday as the murder trial of Larry McClain of Springfield and Kelton Galmore of Jacksonville began in earnest.
Savante English, 27, and Keyera Gant, 25, of Springfield, and Bryant K. Williams, 27, of Houston, were all shot multiple times in a house being rented by English in the 2500 block of South 10th Street. They were found on Aug. 9, 2021.
"All three had lives stolen," said McCarthy in her opening statement.
A seven-man, five-woman jury, seated on Monday, and families of all three victims saw gruesome crime scene photos as former Springfield Police Det. Lori White described accounting for 21 shell casings in the home in the Harvard Park neighborhood.
All three of the victims were found in different rooms of the house.
A third defendant, Joseph Hembrough of Jacksonville, pleaded guilty last week and was sentenced to 20 years in the Illinois Department of Corrections and a three-year mandatory supervised release term.
Hembrough will have to serve the sentence at 100%.
Hembrough was expected to testify against McClain and Galmore. The state's case could go into next week.
In an emotional testimony, Shunderika Price of Springfield, who was engaged to Williams, said she had stopped by the house on the afternoon of Aug. 9 after failing to reach either Williams or English.
Price said the back door was already open and she walked into the house, encountering English's body almost immediately.
She said she saw Williams on the floor in the dining room, which was when she called 911.
"I touched Bryant because I was sad," Price said.
A construction worker at the house next to English's also called 911.
White, who is now a retired crime scene investigator, testified that she also found a fully loaded magazine in the house, in addition to the shell casings, which came from several different manufacturers.
Family members left the courtroom after photos of the victims were shown.
Former Springfield Park Police Sgt. Brian Crolly testified to being the first first responder at the scene. Crolly was patrolling around Bunn Park at the time.
Crolly said the house was in disarray and was concerned that there might be other people still in the house after he arrived. He also recalled escorting Price out of the house.
Williams, a budding rapper who went by "BK Yola," was a childhood friend of English. Gant and English were cousins.
Williams had been moving from California to Texas and was set to return to Houston the day his body was found.
In separate opening statements, Monroe McWard, Galmore's attorney, and Mark Wykoff, who represents McClain, alerted the jury to Hembrough.
"He's highly motivated to present a version of facts (that suits him)," McWard said.
Wykoff quoted from the Illinois Pattern Jury Instruction (Criminal), telling the jury that Hembrough's testimony should be considered "with caution and suspicion."

title: As a nod to Hispanic Heritage Month, try this simple cocktail that is a dance of flavors
author: Sheridan Lane
description: Could Fernandito Fridays be the next Taco Tuesday?
content:
Sept. 15 marks the start of Hispanic Heritage Month, which runs through Oct. 15 and aims to celebrate and recognize the histories, cultures and contributions of Hispanic and Latino Americans. Because culture and heritage are so closely tied to culinary influences and traditions, it is just plain fun, if you are open minded and willing to learn, to study how food and beverage evolves when societies grow and change. When the heritage flavors and techniques are modified or adjusted to match what is accessible in a new location, the heritage, the journey and the outcome are just plain exciting to experience.
The culinary influence of Hispanic and Latino impressions on modern-day cuisine in the United States is quite literally everywhere. According to an article published in spring 2023 on the consumer analytics platform, Civic Science, Mexican food has emerged as the now favorite heritage cuisine among the 18-54 age group, edging out the baby boomer's preference of Italian.
Mainstream Mexican cuisine, especially here in the Midwest, is largely influenced by northern Mexican cuisine, and northern Mexican cuisine was heavily influenced by European explorers and conquistadors so many years ago. The culinary melting pot is certainly far from being ephemeral. Millennial and Generation Z adults are the most diverse culinary prospectors of worldwide cuisine here in the U.S., and that trend is not expected to slow down according to the same Civic Science publication.
So, let's propose a toast this month to explore at least one new gastronomic journey inspired by the transitions of brave groups of people adding to the diversity of our nation. Let's explore, undercover and dabble, and those of us that fall in the millennial and Gen Z market sector are noted as being more willing to do so, with yet another culinary collision where global influence morphs into a countrywide tradition in South America. I introduce to you the Argentinian Fernandito — a cocktail made with Fernet-Branca and Coke.
While the preparation of this cocktail is a so called 'no brainer,' even for those hesitant to try to make new things at home (also said to be a characteristic of Gen Z and Generation Alphas in the above mentioned Civic Science publication), this cocktail has a rich history as an example of an ingredient that made a jump to a new location and slowly became interwoven as a mainstream source of enjoyment.
According to the company's website, Fernet-Branca claims to be the OG Italian amaro with roots that date back to 1845 in Milan, but its popularity does not reside in Italy. Argentina claims to drink roughly 75% of the company's Fernet-Branca and mostly as a liquor mixed with Coke.
If you are not familiar with Fernet-Branca, it is an Italian amaro, a bitter digestif, self-proclaimed as the 'preferred spirit of bartenders and industry folks.' From experience, it does have a unique flavor, well, actually 27 unique flavors combine to make this special recipe, which has been passed down from headmaster distiller to headmaster distiller through generations of ironclad secrecy. Its bitter uniqueness does absolutely balance a very sweet Coca-Cola quite well. It may be a so called 'acquired taste,' but it does kind of hit the spot as a sort of self-deprecating pick me up.
Could 'Fernandito Fridays' be the next 'Taco Tuesday' colloquialism? I have no idea, but I will do my part this Friday to find out.
Fernandito
1 part Fernet-Branca (best chilled in the freezer ahead of time)
3 parts Coca-Cola
Ice
Lemon, for garnish
Fill a highball glass with ice and add one part Fernet-Branca to three parts soda. Gently stir the mixture to combine the ingredients evenly. Garnish with a twist of lemon.
Sheridan Lane is director of culinary programs and operations at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management, Baking/Pastry, and Value-Added Local Food, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: How newcomers like Lutheran grad Makenna Cox have sparked torrid start for UIS volleyball
author: Bill Welt
description: It's been a promising start for the University of Illinois Springfield volleyball team with setter Erica Sledge and Lutheran grad Makenna Cox
content:
Coach Kamille Jones loves her Harley-Davidson motorcycle.
She even offered junior setter Erica Sledge the opportunity to take motorcycle lessons.
Jones also has the University of Illinois Springfield volleyball team humming to a roaring 7-1 start — its best since joining the Great Lakes Valley Conference in 2009.
There's certainly a new aura around the program, which traces its only NCAA Division II tournament appearance to 2018. UIS, in fact, is just two wins shy of last year's win total.
'I definitely think that we really mesh well,' Sledge said. 'The new girls honestly fit right in immediately. You could already tell how different the dynamic was.
'We all get along, we all want the same goal of having intense practices and being intense on the court because we know how you practice is how you play, so we all have that same mindset. Literally, at 5 or 6 a.m., we're all ready to get after it at practice. That makes a huge difference.'
Perfect blend
UIS swept all four matches in the season-opening Hilltopper Classic in Austin, Texas. Sledge was named tournament MVP while redshirt freshman transfer Makenna Cox also reached the all-tournament team.
Everyone connected from Day 1, Jones and Sledge said. That's despite just three seniors on the roster: outside hitter Eirini Glynou, middle/outside hitter Carly Michels and defensive specialist Haley Allen.
Top volleyball teams for 2024: Here are the top 17 high school volleyball teams in the Springfield area for the 2024 season
Glynou, of Athens, Greece, led the team with 419 kills last season. Michels, a Lincoln Land Community College transfer, tallied 117 kills while Sledge accumulated 837 assists.
The spate of newcomers, including Cox and freshman outside hitter Anna Laincz, have blended right in to say the least.
'Eirini has been great,' Cox said. 'We just throw stuff off each other and help each other out in the game, too. Like say I'm getting blocked, she's like, 'You've got this open.' We help each other out and tell each other what's open. Erica has been great obviously and is a stud out there — just have fun out there, really.'
Back home
Cox currently leads the team with 120 kills and is tied for second-best alongside Laincz with 76 digs through the first eight matches. Laincz is third with 49 kills as well. Glynou has a team-high 81 digs and a second-best 89 kills.
Some may recall that Cox led Lutheran High School to the 2022 Class 1A state finals and was The State Journal-Register's Small School Volleyball Player of the Year.
She subsequently had ankle surgery and took a redshirt at Missouri Western State before returning home.
'It had its ups and downs,' Cox said, 'but I think it helped me overall to be a better player ... We have some girls who are injured this year and I know what it's like to go through that, so just being able to be there for them and help them go through it.'
Lutheran volleyball: For this Lutheran High School family, volleyball is more than just a sport, it's a legacy
She immediately clicked with Sledge during summer camp. Cox, Sledge and the rest now even complete their own sentences.
'We've had so much fun with each other,' Cox said, before Sledge added, 'I feel like that makes a huge difference is the fact that we want to see each other outside (the court).'
Cox may be described as a workhorse while Sledge is the quarterback. The latter has been a setter ever since elementary school. That first day as a setter will always have a special place in her heart, she said.
'My fourth-grade coach, it was our first practice and we were warming up and she pulled me aside and she was like, 'I want to put you in the 1,'' Sledge said. 'I thought I was in trouble, 'First practice, what did I do?' But she put me in the 1 and had me do setting work and she was like, 'Yeah, I want you to be a setter.'
'I just love being able to distribute and seeing my teammates shine and get their kills, I'm so happy for them.'
The Prairie Stars are indeed inseparable and hope that leads to more positive results in the always daunting GLVC. UIS kicks off conference play against Missouri S&T at home on Friday at 6 p.m. and Maryville on Saturday at 3 p.m.
Jones said she doesn't need to worry about the team's energy or confidence.
'I already know all the girls will find it and we know with conference play coming up, we know how we want the rest of our season to look like,' Jones said.

title: Bob Gray, 2009 SJ-R First Citizen who was co-founder of Citizens Club, dies at 84
author: Steven Spearie
description: Robert \
content:
Robert "Bob" Gray, an educator and administrator and co-founder of the Citizens Club of Springfield who was The State Journal-Register First Citizen in 2009, died Monday.
He was 84.
A platform dedicated to civic engagement and local improvement and modeled after the City Club of Chicago, Gray helped establish the local club in 2006 with the late Rudy Davenport, the SJ-R's 2001 First Citizen, James Forstall, Kenley Wade Jr., Willis "Bill" Logan, John Allen and Ward 9 Ald. Jim Donelan.
"In a time when positions are argued primarily by shrill volume, Bob has changed the conversation through the Citizens Club over the last three years to assist in public understanding and encourage public participation in civic issues," wrote Allen in his nomination of Gray.
Gray was also the club's longtime president before passing the mantle in 2022.
The Citizens Club discusses a wide range of topics from high-speed rail to race relations to education in Springfield. It is set to meet at the Hoogland Center for the Arts on Friday.
The First Citizen Award, established by the SJ-R in 1963, recognizes a person's contributions to the good of the Springfield area.
Gray earned bachelor and master degrees from Southern Illinois University Carbondale.
A native of West Frankfort, Illinois, Gray taught at Proviso West High School, The Ohio State University and served as a school administrator in the Dundee School District. Gray and his wife, Judy, moved to Springfield in 1967, and he had a long career in Illinois state politics and government, retiring in 2002.
Gray was a longtime Sangamon County Republican Precinct Committeeman. He served as president of the Illinois Jaycees and the Springfield Jaycees and inducted to the Illinois Jaycees Hall of Fame in 2022. Gray was also a member of the American Business Club.
He is survived by a son, Kent Gray of Springfield, and grandsons, Harrison and Oliver Gray.
Gray's funeral is at Butler Funeral Home, 900 S. Sixth St., at 3 p.m. on Sunday. There is a visitation from 3:30 to 6 p.m.

title: Aramark workers at 3 Philadelphia sports stadiums are now on strike. Here's why.
author: Max Hauptman
description: Aramark service workers at all three of Philadelphia's major sports complexes are now on strike.
content:
Show Caption
Food and beverage workers from three Philadelphia sports complexes went on strike Monday morning in an effort to secure increased wages and healthcare coverage.
Unite Here Local 274, which represents over 4,000 workers including cooks, servers, bartenders, dishwashers, concession workers, cleaners, retail workers and warehouse workers at Citizens Bank Park, the Wells Fargo Center and Lincoln Financial Field, announced the strike on September 22.
The striking workers are employees of Aramark, which provides food and facilities services at all three locations.
According to a statement from the union, the strike 'is part of an ongoing campaign to win family-sustaining wage increases and healthcare coverage for stadium workers at all three stadiums.'
Striking workers are from three sports stadiums
Teamsters Joint Council 23, which represents food and beverage truck drivers, announced that it was sanctioning the strike. This means that union members can refuse delivery jobs to the three Philadelphia sports complexes.
'Before we even talk about building a new arena, we need to make sure that stadium food service jobs are good jobs,' Tiffani Davis, an Aramark concessions workers employed at Citizens Bank Park, Wells Fargo Center and Lincoln Financial Field said in an announcement by Unite Here Local 274. 'Year-round work should come with benefits like healthcare and family sustaining wages.'
Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker endorsed a plan to build a new arena for the city's 76ers basketball team on September 18.
While many Unite Here Local 274 workers are employed at all three sports complexes, according to the union those workers have their hours counted separately for all three locations, affecting their health insurance eligibility. The union's statement calls for Aramark to aggregate hours worked at all of its stadiums.
'In the five-week period since the union rejected our offer, they have chosen to strike without making any substantive changes to their position. They continue to engage in non-productive tactics choosing to strike again and continuing to seek a boycott of Aramark's services,' Debbie Albert, a spokesperson for Aramark, told the Philadelphia Inquirer on September 22.
The strike was announced earlier this month
The union announced the strike earlier this month, as reported by the Philadelphia Inquirer, saying that 84% of its members had voted in favor of striking.
Citizens Bank Park is set to host the Philadelphia Phillies and Chicago Cubs beginning Monday. The Wells Fargo Center is scheduled for concerts by singer-songwriter Maxwell on September 24 and Charli XCX on September 25 along with a Philadelphia Flyers pre-season hockey game on September 26. Lincoln Financial Field will host the Temple University-Army football game on September 26, while the next Philadelphia Eagles game at the stadium is scheduled for October 13.
Aramark employees at the Wells Fargo Center previously held two strikes in April, as reported by the Philly Voice. Aramark workers also protested outside of Aramark's Philadelphia headquarters in June.

title: Sonya Massey's cousin named a new co-chair of Massey Commission in leadership shake-up
author: Steven Spearie
description: The new leadership for the Massey Commission will delay a scheduled Sept. 30 listening session. Here's a look at the changes.
content:
Show Caption
After only one listening session, the Massey Commission has new leadership.
One of the newest co-chairs is Shadia Massey, a cousin of Sonya Massey, the namesake of the commission, who was fatally shot by a now former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy in her home in an unincorporated part of Woodside Township on July 6.
In light of the leadership change, a Sept. 30 gathering has been postponed.
Yet to be publicly announced are the 12 commissioners.
JoAnn Johnson, the first Black woman to reach the rank of colonel with the Illinois State Police and a law enforcement trainer in police bias, is the other new co-chair.
Dr. Jerry Kruse, dean and provost of SIU School of Medicine and CEO of SIU Medicine, will serve as the other co-chair.
More than two dozen speakers addressed the Sept. 16 session on issues like police reform, accountability, training and crisis intervention in Monday's open forum.
But some of those speakers also scrutinized the leadership of the commission and called for members of the Massey family to be included in the commission.
Also in question are resolutions that doled out over $78,000 to two different communications and consulting companies. They were tabled at a Sept. 18 special meeting of the county board.
'As we have been from the beginning, we will continue to be responsive to community voices in this process," said State Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, who helped form the commission, along with Sangamon County Board chairman Andy Van Meter.
The commission seeks to address systemic issues in law enforcement practices, mental health responses and community relations, with the goal of creating "tangible, practical and equitable solutions for the betterment of all who call Sangamon County home."
It will look to produce a comprehensive report outlining findings, recommendations and proposed actions within a year.
'Have to have a direction'
Johnson was with the State Police for nearly 30 years and came to Springfield in 2010.
Speaking at the session on Sept. 16, Johnson said she helped, through a company she now works for, train Springfield Police officers in "implicit bias."
Implicit bias is any bias a person holds on a level that they are not consciously aware of and can affect a person's behavior and decision-making without realizing it.
Johnson said the commission "will not get far if it is just a group of angry voices. We absolutely have to have direction, focus, come from a place of composure and bring these important issues to the forefront."
The commission, Johnson added "has to be diverse not only in race gender, culture and background, but also experience and expertise."
Johnson said she was one of just 200 people who applied to be on the commission.

title: Oktoberfest, Route 66 Festival among 5 things to do in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: There's plenty going on in the Springfield area this weekend, including Oktoberfest and Route 66 Festival.
content:
Unpack those decorations and toss on your best sweater because fall is officially under way!
Springfield is celebrating German style this weekend, but there's plenty of other ways to enjoy the first foray into the season around the capital city.
Here are five things to do around town this weekend.
Oktoberfest
What: Come on down to one of Springfield's most beloved breweries to sample ciders, ales and meads galore, for two days of beer, pretzels and brats. Engrained Brewing Company is celebrating the start of the autumn season with their Oktoberfest setup, so dress in your dirndl or lederhosen, head on down to the brewery and make some memories celebrating.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.

Where: 1120 W. Lincolnshire Blvd., Springfield
Route 66 Mother Road Festival
What: Cruise on down to the Isringhausen Imports main stage between Sixth and Washington streets for a few hours to enjoy country music, as part of Route 66 Fest. Decatur-based country band Wreckless Whiskey will be playing for the duration of the event. Immediately following the event, a burnout competition will take place between Seventh and Washington. The winner will be named by audience reaction.
When: 1 to 3 p.m. Saturday
Where: 619 E. Washington St., Springfield

Backyard Bash in Chatham
What: Think you can tame the wild bull? What about a mechanical one? Try your hand and steady balance at Spartan Sports park for an adult night of fun with music, food and drinks for a good cause. While the event is free admission, donations are suggested as all funds raised will go toward the Ball-Chatham Educational Foundation to help students and staff members.
When: 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. Saturday

Free movie day at the Hoogland

More: The full movie itinerary can be found online on the Route 66 Flicks website.
Walk to End Alzheimer's

title: Then there was one: Greenville wins SCC battle of unbeatens over Pana
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Remnants of Hurricane Helene made it windy and rainy, and despite an early injury to Greenville's top running back, it was Pana which slipped up in SCC race.
content:
GREENVILLE — The wet football turf at Greenville was bound to cause some issues on the same night as the remnants of Hurricane Helene made central and southern Illinois a wet, windy mess.
On the first play from scrimmage, Greenville's top running back, Dayton Oliver slipped for a 2-yard loss. On the next play, he had to be carried off the field.
While the Comets had to play the other 47 minutes without their star rusher, senior Declan Graber stepped up for two touchdowns and 129 yards on 23 carries to keep Greenville undefeated with a 21-7 win over Pana in a game that could likely determine the South Central Conference championship.
"It feels great," Graber said. "That's not usually my spot where I run, but too bad Dayton had an ankle injury and I stepped up."
The Comets were ranked No. 8 in Class 4A in the latest Associated Press statewide poll.
Greenville coach Todd Hutchinson was proud his team didn't lose focus following the early injury. Oliver was taken away from the field on a cart.
"We have great kids," Hutchinson said. "I love them, they do a lot of things right, they stay locked in, they practice well, they take care of business on and off the field and in the classroom. That's their character. Dayton's a special player, we're family. But he goes down and it's next-man-up. We were playing for D.O. (after the injury)."
Before Pana had a chance to touch the ball, Graber, a senior, caught two passes for 27 yards before sprinting into the end zone for a 12-yard touchdown with 9 minutes, 40 seconds left in the opening quarter. Gavin File made the first of his three point-after kicks, despite the crosswind, to give the Comets (5-0 overall, 5-0 SCC) a 7-0 lead.
By the time the quarter was out, Greenville put up another score when senior quarterback Ben Hutchinson found fellow senior Eli Shadowens for a 46-yard touchdown pass. It was the second time in three plays the QB and receiver hooked up for a big gain. On first-and-five from the home team's 22, Shadowens ripped the ball away from Pana defensive back Cash Lynch to turn back an interception for a 32-yard gain.
"We had the two touchdowns right off the bat and that really put a damper on (Pana's) offense and defense," Graber said.
The wind gusts didn't prevent Hutchinson from finishing with 152 yards passing and the one TD while completing 12 of 19 passes.
Pana's red zone blues
Three times in the first half, the Panthers (4-1 overall and in the SCC) found themselves in the red zone. All three times, Pana came away with no points.
Pana looked to tie Greenville early when the Panthers had first-and-10 from the Comets' 16 after Sam Sims picked up a 50-yard rushing gain. After Cayden Durbin moved the down marker up three yards, Pana had two negative-yardage plays in a row before quarterback Wyatt Kile's fourth-and-11 pass fell incomplete.
"Our coaches do a great job: our defensive coaches and our offensive coaches, alike," Hutchinson said. "We've got a great staff that takes care of our kids, works hard and puts guys in the right spot. And then you've got to give all the credit to our kids, who were out there performing and working their tails off."
With Greenville ahead 14-0 in the second quarter, the Panthers had a first down at the Greenville 15, but Pana cost itself on fourth-and-six with a 5-yard false start penalty. A Greenville defender tipped Kile's pass at the goal line for another turnover on downs.
Finally, Pana got the ball back with 2:41 left in the half at its own 31. On fourth-and-four from the Greenville 45, Kile hooked up with Parker Moore for a 6-yard gain. On third-and-six from the 11, Lynch caught a 6-yard pass for a first-and-goal from the Comets' 5. But a spike to stop the clock and two incompletions left Pana going into halftime still searching for its first points.
"I was just hoping that our guys were going to be more physical than what we came out," Pana coach Trevor Higgins said. "We got out-physicaled for the first time this season and that's sad to see."
Harbert fights through injury
Pana senior running back Isaiah Harbert, who had been battling a leg injury suffered in last week's 51-24 win over North Mac, gutted out a 71-yard effort on 18 carries.
"When we say we got out-physicaled, we've got a couple of guys who came in and (played hard)," Higgins said. "Harbert just has that last name you can depend on. We're trying to get him (healthy) for playoffs, as well. We would've loved to have had him in all game, but long term, for his health, we need him healthy for the playoffs."
Harbert said he'd love to have another chance at Greenville after losing the last two matchups, including 20-6 last year with four Pana turnovers.
"It was a mental battle the entire game; you just have to keep pushing and pushing," Harbert said. "I'd give anything in the world for another Greenville game. We're right there — they are a very good football team, I'm not taking anything away from that — but whenever something like that happens, you always want the extra chance."
Kile finished 12-for-34 with 122 yards and one touchdown. The wind made it difficult on both quarterbacks, but Higgins felt like there were some unfortunate dropped passes.
"We had our opportunities to make plays and we had big drops and missed blocks at times and you've got to capitalize on them against a good team," Higgins said.

title: An asteroid known as a 'mini-moon' will join Earth's orbit for 2 months starting Sunday
author: Max Hauptman
description: A small asteroid will join Earth's orbit around the sun for two months beginning Sunday, becoming a 'mini-moon.'
content:
Beginning Sunday, Earth's skies will soon have a temporary visitor.
On September 29, an asteroid dubbed 2024 PT5 will become a " mini-moon" of sorts, temporarily entering Earth's orbit for almost two months before the forces of gravity return it to a vast field of space rocks known as the Arjuna asteroid belt that follows a similar orbital path around the sun as our own home planet.
Scientists discovered the object Aug. 7 using the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System in Sutherland, South Africa during routine monitoring, according to a study published in the journal Research Notes of the American Astronomical Society.
What is a mini-moon?
"Mini-moon" events are when pieces in space like an asteroid or floating pieces of space junk temporarily participate in orbiting the Earth with some completing a full revolution.
In order to be considered a mini-moon, an incoming body must reach Earth at a range around 2.8 million miles (4.5 million km) and at a steady space of about 2,200 mph (3,540 km/h), according to Universidad Complutense de Madrid professor Carlos de la Fuente Marcos.
Previous mini-moon events occurred in short-lived mini moon in 1981 and 2022, according to researchers.
Marcos told Space.com earlier this week that the asteroid will enter Earth's orbit at 15:54 ET on Sunday, and depart at 11:43 ET on Nov. 25.
Can I see the mini-moon?
At just 37 feet wide, 2024 PT5's presence in Earth's skies won't be visible unless one is a professional astronomer, or at least has access to a powerful telescope.
"The object is too small and dim for typical amateur telescopes and binoculars. However, the object is well within the brightness range of typical telescopes used by professional astronomers," Marcos told Space.com. "A telescope with a diameter of at least 30 inches plus a CCD or CMOS detector is needed to observe this object; a 30-inch telescope and a human eye behind it will not be enough."
Anthony Robledo contributed to this report.

title: Illinois-Penn State 'College GameDay' predictions: Who picked Illini, Nittany Lions?

description: Here's who the 'College GameDay' crew picked between Illinois and Penn State.
content:
After plenty of talking and pregame drama, the Illinois and Penn State football teams are ready to meet on the field Saturday night.
For coach Bret Bielema and the No. 21 Fighting Illini, Saturday's game will be a chance to assert themselves as a legitimate threat to contend in the Big Ten after a 31-24 overtime win last week against Nebraska. Penn State, No. 8 in the US LBM Coaches Poll, remains a contender for the new 12-team College Football Playoff and in the Big Ten.
Though their game didn't earn the 'College GameDay' treatment — ESPN's popular pregame show was broadcasting from Tuscaloosa, Alabama, ahead of Saturday night's game between No. 4 Alabama and No. 2 Georgia — the matchup between Illinois and Penn State is one of the biggest on the Week 5 calendar. The game is scheduled to kick off at 6:30 p.m. from Beaver Stadium in University Park, Pennsylvania. The game is broadcast on NBC and streams on Peacock.
What did 'GameDay' say about Illinois-Penn State?
Pat McAfee of the "College GameDay" crew was excited about the Illini, pointing out their solid quarterback play behind Luke Altmyer and receivers Pat Bryant and Zakhari Franklin. He said the large point spread put the Illini and Bielema "right where they want to be."
Host Rece Davis brought up Bielema's oft-discussed comment about " White Out energy, whatever the hell that means" (but left out the full context). Fellow panelist Desmond Howard jumped in and said the Illini were about to "eff around and find out," highlighting the Penn State offense behind QB Drew Allar.
'I love what I see from this Penn State offense," Howard said. "It's gonna be a great game tonight in Happy Valley.'

title: Boy, 10, killed in Peoria shooting was from Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: A 10-year-old boy who died in a shooting in Peoria Sunday evening was from Springfield. Here's what we know.
content:
A 10-year-old boy who died in a shooting in Peoria Sunday evening was from Springfield.
Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood identified the victim as Lamar T. Johnson II, of the 400 block of South Grand Avenue.
A post from the coroner's office Facebook page said Johnson "likely died within seconds" of suffering the wound to his chest.
Peoria Police responded to an apartment complex in the 600 block of West Romeo B. Garrett Avenue just after 7:30 Sunday after a Shot Spotter alert of two rounds having been fired.

Peoria Police haven't released any suspect information.

title: Police: Ohio man's death now being investigated as a homicide in Springfield
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The death of a 29-year-old Ohio man is now being called a homicide in Springfield. Here's what we know.
content:
(This story was updated to add new information.)
The death of a 29-year-old man in Springfield is now being called a homicide.
Springfield police said the man, identified as Telley Palmer of Columbus, Ohio, was found with multiple gunshot wounds in the 400 block of South Illinois Street around 2:30 a.m. Palmer was taken to the hospital where he died from his injuries.
In a news release, police said the shooting happened after a fight involving multiple people at a Springfield bar earlier in the night. Police said they were not notified of the fight.
Police said at least three different guns were used and officers found 35 shell casings in the area.
Police have not said if they have any suspects as of Monday afternoon.
The shooting is under investigation.

title: Unhoused people return to encampment site after city of Springfield removes items
author: Tom Ackerman
description: People who were staying at a homeless encampment site returned to the area a day after the city removed items from the area.
content:
People who were staying at a homeless encampment site returned to the area a day after the city removed items from the area.
People were seen on lounging in chairs or on bicycles in the area of North Grand and Fifth Street, some who had items taken by the city a day prior.
One of those people was Dwayne Chapelle, who said he witnessed public works employees with the city removing his belongings, including his clothes, winter coat, drawing supplies and bicycles, some of which he said he was trying to fix up so he could sell.
Chappelle now only owns a suitcase he said as he motioned to the luggage beside him as he sat on someone's sleeping bag that was sprawled on the grass.
City officials emphasized during a news conference Thursday items that were removed how items were removed with people's consent who were present at the time of the removal.
"When public works arrived on the scene, I let them know to not touch anything until the individuals let us know what was not theirs," Shannon Allen, community care coordinator for the city of Springfield, said. "Then public works preceded to discard the items that were abandoned."
The mayor's office released a statement Wednesday afternoon that the large tents posed safety risks to the unhoused individuals near the roadside, and cited "tragic incidents, including loss of life, reports of battery and increased drug activity" as reasons to remove the unhoused campground.
Director of community relations Ethan Posey said Thursday that a member of the unhoused community died in proximity to a business close to the camp, but did not provide additional details.
When asked about possible drug needles because of the 'drug activity' mentioned, Michael Newman, a Homeless Outreach Team Coordinator said the following:
'You're not going to find a lot of specifics about exactly was in the trash because when we're dealing with a situation where there's any kind of potential hazardous material, the last thing you want to do is send somebody digging through the trash where you can't see whether or not something might cut you or there might be something that could poke you, or there may be something that someone is simply allergic to.'
Kelsi Booker, who works at a nearby business, observed that some of the individuals who have stayed at the corner location may have mental challenges. Others have simply gotten comfortable, she said.
'I don't know the best thing to do but at the same time, just having them out here, just laying around and just making a homeless utopia – that's not okay,' Booker said.
Multiple people brought food to the seven or so people present in the morning, carrying bags of Lunchables, sandwiches, bottled water and doughnuts.
'We're not supposed to close up our bowels of compassion and not help,' said Michelle Myers who handed out sandwiches she had made. 'It becomes very political and so forth… but we are still supposed to help. And that's just being a Christian and a humanitarian.'
Myers is a member of the Knox Knolls Free Methodist Church at 2251 W. Monroe St.
Others in the church support Myers in this type of outreach, in addition to friends of hers at churches of other denominations and local agencies, she said. Some people bring her donations so that she can pass them out, and some comes out of her pocket, she said.
