title: Fundraising efforts begin for 10-year-old boy fatally shot with ties to Springfield
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Fundraising efforts are officially underway to help pay for funeral costs for a boy, 10, with ties to Springfield who was shot and killed in Peoria.
content:
Fundraising efforts are officially underway to help pay for funeral costs for a 10-year-old boy with ties to Springfield who was shot and killed in Peoria.
Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood identified the victim as Lamar T. Johnson II. Hardwood said one of the boy's parents lived in Peoria while the other lived in Springfield. The boy was living with the parent in Peoria at the time of the shooting, according to Hardwood.
A GoFundMe has been started with a goal of $15,000.
'It is with a heavy heart that I reach out to all of you today,' the fundraiser reads. 'Our community is mourning the tragic loss of 10-year-old Lamar T. Johnson, II, a bright young soul whose life was taken far too soon.'
GoFundMe has verified the legitimacy of the fundraiser that is organized by Briggett Carter-Meachem, who said she does not know the family but wanted to help.
Carter-Meachem will also be opening a memorial account at Busey Bank where donations can be made directly. She is the Senior Vice President of Treasury Management at the bank.
'Lamar's life, though short, touched the hearts of many. Let us come together as a community and show his family that they are not alone,' the fundraiser reads.
Peoria Police responded to an apartment complex in the 600 block of West Romeo B. Garrett Avenue just after 7:30 Sunday after a Shot Spotter alert of two rounds having been fired. Johnson was taken to the hospital where was pronounced dead.
A post from the coroner's office Facebook page said Johnson "likely died within seconds" of suffering the wound to his chest.
The shooting is under investigation.

title: Illinois woman sentenced to probation, must pay $600K in restitution for stealing from YMCA
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The theft was discovered when the YMCA switched to an internet-based accounting software, officials said.
content:
A Taylorville woman was sentenced to three years of probation and ordered to pay $600,000 in restitution to the Christian County YMCA after pleading guilty to five counts of wire fraud.
Lori Zeitler, 65, pleaded guilty to stealing at least $292,336.29 from the Taylorville YMCA. According to a news release from the U.S. Attorney's Office of the Central District of Illinois, Zeitler was responsible for $600,000 in losses.
Zeitler's theft was discovered when the YMCA switched to an internet-based accounting software, the release stated.
Zeitler worked at the YMCA for 32 years in various roles, including bookkeeper.
Det. Rob Thompson of the Taylorville Police Department told The State Journal-Register in a 2019 report that the missing funds came to light in March 2018 and that shortly afterward he met with the YMCA's executive director and CEO, Chris Weittenhiller.
A forensic audit of current and previous accounts from the YMCA was part of the investigation.
'The impact of the defendant's deception is wide reaching, as the money she stole deprived the Christian County YMCA of funds that should have gone towards needed facility improvements and to support programs for members,' said Assistant U.S. Attorney Sierra Senor-Moor.
Zeitler pleaded guilty before U.S. Magistrate Judge Karen L. McNaught on March 28.
The Springfield FBI, the Taylorville Police Department and the Illinois State Police investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Sierra Senor-Moore represented the government in the prosecution.

title: Capital city to host basketball coaching clinic after Jumper, Turner jump-start idea
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Jim Jumper had a thought: Springfield was a desert when it came to basketball coaching clinics. Then he and Blake Turner made one happen.
content:
With all the successful basketball coaches who have come through the Springfield area, Lanphier boys basketball coach Blake Turner was stunned when Jim Jumper told him there hadn't been a basketball coaching clinic here before.
'I couldn't believe it and when Mr. Jumper contacted me, my first response was, 'Wow,'' Turner said.
Then, Jumper asked Turner if the new Lober-Nika Gymnasium would like to host the first one.
'My second response was, 'Sure, I'd love to do it. Tell me where we start,'' Turner said. 'I followed his guidance, and he's got a lot of basketball knowledge and wisdom and he's been around the block a few times. It was a great experience just sitting back and listening to him and going off his expertise.'
The plans have culminated in the Capital City Basketball Coaches Clinic on Saturday at Lanphier from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. It is open to all basketball coaches from grade school through high school. The cost is $30 per person or $20 if a group from the same school signs up for the seven-speaker event.
'I thought, 'Let's have it in Springfield, let's give coaches — or anyone interested — a chance to get more information about how to coach basketball, and why not bring in the best people you can,' Jumper said.
Jumper and Turner both said it was important to get a broad range of topics and speakers. The day begins with Chatham Glenwood girls basketball coach Alyssa Riley, who led the Titans to the Class 3A runner-up title earlier this year. The day ends with former University of Illinois star and NBA player Dee Brown, who is in his third year coaching at the NCAA Division II Roosevelt University.
Also speaking will be Tim Allen, who guided Sacred Heart-Griffin to its first state boys basketball championship in 2022. Riley will speak about building a program, Allen's topic will cover basketball culture and practice planning while Brown will talk about transition offense and defense.
'I always felt if I could pick up one or two ideas, it was a great clinic,' said Jumper, who coached for 37 years, including the final seven leading the Mount Pulaski boys program until 2009. 'We've got people who can speak on just about every facet of the game of basketball.'
Also speaking will be former Lanphier and Illinois player Rich McBride, who is currently an assistant at Eastern Illinois; Altamont's John Niebrugge, University of Illinois Springfield men's coach Matt Broc k and Turner.
'Rich McBride was a great offensive player, so what should we have Richard talk about? Offense and special plays,' Jumper said. 'John was my assistant at Mount Pulaski for years and he's from (Teutopolis), which is a hotbed of basketball ... and John's had great success down at Altamont (a 264-95 record in 12 seasons). He is as good of a defensive man-to-man coach as you'll find anywhere in the state.
'I wanted full-court stuff, so I said, 'Blake, why don't you speak about (defensive) presses.' Trapping, pressing defenses is one of the things that he's known for. Matt Brock, whose teams have done very well in his stay out at UIS, we've got him talking about how to build an offense.
'And then we've got Dee Brown and Dee Brown is known for fast-break type of basketball, so we've got him talking about transition offense and defense, and how to get from one end of the floor to the other end of the floor (quickly) without turning it over, but then he'll also be talking about how to defend that.'
Jumper added that clinics have lost some attention over the years as the internet has made it easier to quickly find topics of interest, but Jumper says the right clinic, with a variety of topics, can still have importance.
'I've wanted to do it for a long time,' Jumper said. 'When I was coaching, I would go to clinics every year; I was a student of the game. A lot of guys did, and then along came a thing called Google ... plus, you can watch clinics online.
'So, clinics started going by the wayside, or they started doing other things: there are roundtables now ... where a few coaches get together and they talk about stuff. I wanted to bring back (clinics).'
Already, Turner has his eyes on doing it again next year.
'I feel like we put together a good lineup and we've got a good field set,' Turner said. 'I feel like we put together a good group of people, we've got some great topics, we've got some speakers people know around here, and people are going to be excited about it.
'We're committed to doing it and making it better. However it turns out for us this weekend, we'll just try to make it better next year.'

title: 'A complete misdirection': Speakers lash out at city council over unhoused encampment
author: Steven Spearie
description: A barrage of speakers at Tuesday's city council meeting insisted city workers and Mayor Misty Buscher whitewashed the clearing of an unhoused encampment last week.
content:
Capping a five-hour Springfield City Council meeting Tuesday, a barrage of speakers insisted city workers and Mayor Misty Buscher whitewashed the clearing of an unhoused encampment near Fifth Street and North Grand Avenue last week.
Buscher countered that it was a public safety issue and that she was satisfied with actions after reviewing Springfield Police body cam footage.
But Buscher acknowledged that the city doesn't have enough health care providers addressing mental health or addiction issues and that more outreach officers are needed budget-wise.
Some speakers were especially critical of the clear out noting that it happened in the shadow of the withdrawal of a controversial ordinance addressing unhoused encampments on public property. That ordinance, sponsored by Buscher and Ward 5 Ald. Lakeisha Purchase, came in light of a U.S. Supreme Court ruling this summer that bans prohibiting unhouse individuals from camping on public property are not unconstitutional.
Others saw the action last week as the city trying to put on its best face with the International Route 66 Mother Road Festival in town last weekend.
Anu Paruchuri said it was indigestible that Public Works had a backhoe and a dump truck handy at the scene.
"The story we were fed was absurd," Paruchuri said. "That encampment has been there for years."
Phelan Chappell, who lives at Fifth and North Grand, said he lost art supplies, which he called his "meditation."
"I don't want to fight with the police, so I had to remove myself and after that, they didn't give me no options and they took everything," Chappell said at the meeting. "Just because we're homeless, that doesn't mean we're not people and don't have morals and values."
Addressing the media after the meeting, Buscher said she didn't see what Chappell reported.
"I did hear from some of the people here tonight, including Mr. Chappell, that possibly when a police officer comes up and talks to them, they are intimidated and they agree to things because of the uniform," she said. "I understand that, and we will look at how we do that."
Reggie Guyton said he no longer had confidence that city leadership was in tune with the reality of the citizens of Springfield.
"To say that people are promoting misinformation or have some type of agenda is a complete misdirection (by the city)," Guyton said.
The meeting also included a presentation by community care coordinator Shannon Allen and Springfield Police homeless outreach officer Michael Newman.
Buscher said Allen recently met with U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Springfield, about her work.
Allen said the city could use two or three more community care workers.
"We have to address funding of how to pay for people to get the help that's needed," Buscher said.

title: Unemployment claims in Illinois increased last week
author: Staff reports
description: Here's a look at how weekly unemployment claims changed in Illinois last week compared with the week prior.
content:
Initial filings for unemployment benefits in Illinois rose last week compared with the week prior, the U.S. Department of Labor said Thursday.
New jobless claims, a proxy for layoffs, increased to 7,873 in the week ending September 28, up from 7,545 the week before, the Labor Department said.
U.S. unemployment claims rose to 225,000 last week, up 6,000 claims from 219,000 the week prior on a seasonally adjusted basis.
Iowa saw the largest percentage increase in weekly claims, with claims jumping by 41.8%. Virgin Islands, meanwhile, saw the largest percentage drop in new claims, with claims dropping by 61.3%.

title: CS8 stunner: U-High beats Glenwood for first time since joining league
author: Ryan Mahan
description: The Normal U-High offense jumped out to a big lead and stymied Glenwood almost the entire night to earn first CS8 win over Titans.
content:
NORMAL — If last year's win over Decatur MacArthur turned the page for the Normal U-High football team, then Friday's stunning victory over Chatham Glenwood started a new chapter.
"I think that's probably a fair statement," U-High coach Brody Walworth said. "Last year against MacArthur was pretty special, too. That was a corner-turning win last year and now we're in a situation where we think we're competitive with the best teams in the league. To finally get over the hump in (a big game) is awesome."
U-High quarterback Alek Weiland threw five touchdowns and finished with 318 yards passing as the Pioneers beat Glenwood 33-13 in a Central State Eight Conference east division game at Illinois State University's Hancock Stadium.
When Weiland found AJ Holden for a 1-yard touchdown with 1 minute, 44 seconds left in the first half, it gave U-High a 26-0 lead.
"I think we knew we had it in us and we knew we could play with these guys and I knew we could beat them," Weiland said. "A lot of people didn't think we could win this game, but coming in, I think we all thought we were just as good, if not better, than them."
The Titans (4-2 overall, 3-1 CS8 east) found their offensive groove long enough to cut the deficit in half, when Brady Dwyer scored a 1-yard touchdown run with 12 seconds left in the second quarter and junior quarterback Colten Knoedler found Jonathan Helm for a 21-yard score on the Titans' first possession of the second half.
Glenwood's defense held the Pioneers (4-2, 3-1 CS8 east) scoreless for almost the entirety of the second half but couldn't get any closer. U-High cemented the win when Weiland and Holden connected on an 18-yard strike with 2:47 to play.
But, Glenwood coach David Hay said, that defensive play in the second half wasn't good enough.
"They just beat us: flat-out beat us," Hay said. "We didn't show up to the game until maybe somewhere in the third quarter. We can't do that. If we think we're good enough to do that, I think we just found out that we're not.
"We had places where we played well, but this is a team sport, a team game and that's not good enough."
Heading into Friday's game, Glenwood was 7-0 against U-High since the Pioneers entered the CS8 in 2017. That first season, Glenwood pulled out a 37-36 overtime win, but since then, the Pioneers haven't been within a mile of the Titans with Glenwood holding a 326-106 scoring advantage in the series.
Glenwood fans were heard starting to get restless after the Pioneers went up 12-0 on Weiland's second TD throw to Cade Cunningham, this one a 19-yard pass after the two connected on a 34-yard score to start the game.
Twice in a row, Glenwood had to punt out of its own end zone in the second quarter. The first time, U-High couldn't convert a fourth down from the Glenwood 3. Four plays later, the Titans had a fourth and 11 from their own 2. After a 25-yard punt, Weiland found Carson Stevens for his third TD throw, and U-High found itself up 19-0.
"The biggest thing defensively is, we know we've got the right guys — we can play — but we've got caught in a trap of playing what I call, 'Hero ball,' where we try to do too much," Walworth said. "I think tonight was a great example of when you have 11 guys playing disciplined football, doing their jobs.
"We played really well (on the defensive) side. The pressure was great, but forcing them to be one-dimensional (was key). (Glenwood) wants to run the ball, they like running it and I think we did a great job up front controlling the line of scrimmage, as well."
Glenwood committed a holding penalty on first-and-10 from its own 9-yard line, then had to again punt from its own 3. The Titans' defense committed a pass interference on first and 10 from the Glenwood 20, and three plays later, Holden and Weiland put the Pioneers up 26-0.
Holden's second touchdown was the final touch.
"That last play, we knew what we had to do to drive that nail, so we just go out there and executed," Holden said. "Now, we know we can beat the best teams in the state and in the conference."
U-High managed to run for 129 yards to finish with 447 yards of offense. After the game, Hay was asked what his team did right. Hay had some thoughts.
"Maybe a couple of drives, we got a couple of stops on defense, but generally, we didn't cover, we missed tackles, we didn't block, at times we didn't catch and at times, we didn't throw," Hay said.
U-High made the playoffs five straight seasons from 2011-15, but didn't make it back to the postseason until last year. Now, a win away from playoff eligibility has the Pioneers excited, but not content.
"I think we can build a ton off this," Weiland said. "Even though we won, we still have things to improve on and we're going to go watch film (Saturday) and improve on those things in practice next week."
Knoedler finished 22-for-39 for 236 yards and two interceptions. He found six different receivers, including Gavin Simmons, who caught 11 passes for 131 yards.
U-High forced Glenwood into a one-dimensional team on Friday. The Titans rushed 16 times for just 42 yards and one touchdown. Glenwood also committed seven penalties for 57 yards, while U-High was whistled four times for 30 yards.
"That's a good football team," Hay said of U-High. "I don't want anyone to misunderstand. A good football team, they're playing great, Brody does a hell of a job, but we expect more of ourselves."

title: New business brings locally, organically grown groceries right to your door
author: Claire Grant
description: A group of central and southern Illinois farmers are bringing their new business directly to the doors of Springfield and neighboring cities.
content:
A group of central and southern Illinois farmers are bringing their new business directly to the doors of Springfield and neighboring cities.
The Farms Of Illinois is a supply chain delivery system launched by farmer and entrepreneur Clint Bland, whose goal is to bring organic produce to your door without skimping on farmer's livelihood.
'I'm taking a different approach here and trying to promote each of these businesses and keeping their name,' Bland said. 'Twin Willows processes their pork, and the farms sell Twin Willows pork. It has their farm name on it and it's more of a promotion, that's why I call it an alliance.'
The new farm to door delivery system is an 'alliance' between eight Illinois farms, who are utilizing modern day technology to compete with online food delivery platforms. Bland, who previously worked for Dot Foods, used his experience in supply chain management with the company to start connecting farmers together under the new business.
How does the business work?
The system works similarly to competing grocery delivery app, Instacart. Customers can go to the Farms of Illinois website, order online and select through fresh chicken, pork, eggs and produce to add to their cart. Ordering before Sunday means guaranteed Tuesday morning deliveries and orders over $100 get free shipping. Subscriptions can also be set up for recurring deliveries – so shoppers don't forget to add milk to their cart every week.
How is the price decided?
While there are different price markups on wholesale or home delivery, the farmers set the price of purchase for The Farms of Illinois to buy the needed product. While some produce may have multiple farms selling, the farmers choose a set price together for the overall item.
Direct orders equal less waste
The ordering ahead helps smaller farms, according to Bland. Usually at farmer's markets, small businesses gather an assortment of fresh produce to sell and whatever doesn't get sold, goes bad. By giving an exact number to gather produce, less food waste is created while saving farmers money.
'If I say I need 24 pounds of spring mix, (the farmer) is cutting that directly to order," Bland said. "At a farmer's market, you'd cut all that and hope to sell as much as you can.'
Does the business work with retailers?
Yes, the brand works with 30 different retailers already across Illinois, including Harvest Market on South Veterans Parkway. Bland says the app works as a one stop shop for retailers rather than reaching out to several different farms.
'If you allocate a certain portion of your field growing this crop, we'll move it,' Bland said. 'That gives them a stronger security knowing that.'
Expanding the farm network
Bland plans on expanding the farm network up to 30 farms over time, but requirements to join are strict. Farms cannot produce by using chemicals and GMO food for animals to be in line with company values and pass an inspection by Bland. Farms also get to keep their name on packaging when selling through the business, instead of labeling their produce under a different supply chain management.
The Farms of Illinois participating farms
Abundant Pastures in Claremont
Oak Tree Organics in Ashland
Mueller Family Farm in Bluffs
Heirloom Haus in Pawnee
Twin Willow Farms in Roodhouse
Lemay Mushroom Opera in Springfield
Bland Family Farms in Jacksonville
Buckhorn Dairy in Mount Sterling
More information about each farm can be found on the Farms of Illinois webpage.

title: Crane collapses into building where Tampa Bay Times is located: Watch damage from Milton
author: Max Hauptman
description: As Hurricane Milton slammed into the Florida coast, video shows a massive crane that was toppled in downtown St. Petersburg.
content:
As Hurricane Milton slammed into the Florida coast Wednesday evening, video captured the aftermath of a crane that collapsed near a building construction site in downtown St. Petersburg, Florida.
The crane was reportedly being used to construct a large luxury condo building. As it fell, it left a gaping hole in an office building that houses several businesses, including the Tampa Bay Times newspaper. No injuries were reported.

St. Petersburg assessing damage following crane collapse
'The public is urged to continue to shelter in place' but avoid the area, the city of St. Petersburg said in a statement.
"We can confirm one crane cab in the upper section of the mast has fallen," said John Catsimatidis, the CEO of Red Apple Group, which is developing the skyscraper, the Tampa Bay Times reported. "We are working with city officials and others to assess the situation."
John Bacon, Trevor Hughes, and Thao Nguyen contributed to this report.

title: Taco Bell returns Double Decker Tacos to its menu for limited time. When to get them
author: Mike Snider
description: Thursday, Oct. 10, marks the return of a Taco Bell favorite to the menu: Double Decker Tacos, made with a taco wrapped in a bean-filled tortilla.
content:
Taco Bell has a special treat coming to its menu leading up to Halloween: the return of a fan favorite, the Double Decker Taco.
The Double Decker Taco, made with a hard shell taco wrapped in a bean-filled tortilla, has been on and off the Taco Bell menu since its 1995 debut. The Double Decker Taco and Double Decker Taco Supreme will be available nationwide now through Oct. 30.
Also appetizing: Perhaps in a nod to the value meal price competition, the Double Decker Taco costs $2 (310 calories), nearly one dollar less than it cost when it made its last menu appearance in December 2023 at $2.99. The Double Decker Taco Supreme (330 calories) – comes with diced tomatoes and reduced-fat sour cream – is priced at $2.69, a $1 below its price in December 2023.
More at Taco Bell: Disha Hot Discovery Box, Big Cheez-It
The Disha Hot Discovery Box ($8.99, prices may vary), a recently-launched collaboration with Mexican-American musician Omar Apollo, includes a Cheesy Gordita Crunch, Nacho Cheese Doritos Locos Taco, Crunchy Taco, Chips and Nacho Cheese sauce, medium drink and three packets of Disha Hot Hot Sauce – based on the "Ivory" singer's family recipe.
You can add individual 20-cent packets of the sauce to your order; it's made with toasted tomatillos, white vinegar, tomatoes, onions, peppers, lime juice and a "family-secret spice blend."
Also recently added to the menu: the Big Cheez-It Crunchwrap Supreme ($5.49) and Big Cheez-It Tostado ($2.99), which made their debut in late May-early June.
Other options include an à la carte Big Cheez-It ($1), which is 16 times the size of a traditional Cheez-It cracker, and a Big Cheez-It Crunchwrap Combo ($9.99), which includes a Big Cheez-It Crunchwrap Supreme, a Beefy 5-Layer Burrito, Nacho Fries and a medium fountain drink.
Contributing: Anthony Robledo.

title: Frozen food delivery service announces closure, 119 Illinois employees to be laid off
author: Claire Grant
description: How do you get your frozen food delivered right to the door? For some Springfield locals, it's time to find another delivery system.
content:
How do you get your frozen food delivered right to the door? For some Springfield locals, it's time to find another delivery system.
Yelloh, formerly known as Schwan's Home Delivery, announced last month it's closing its delivery service this November. The company cited multiple insurmountable business challenges for the decision, including economic and market forces, as well as changing consumer lifestyles.
In a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification, or WARN act, filed to the state of Illinois on Sept. 30 by parent group Cygnus Home Service, LLC, 119 Illinoisians will be affected across the state from the layoff. The final day of work for employees will be Nov. 22 of this year.
Yelloh has an address in Springfield listed on Google Maps at 2440 Colt Road under Schwan's Home Delivery, but the location's phone is disconnected. Questions about the location and how many Springfield households it served were not answered by Yelloh.
About Yelloh
Founded in 1952, the Minnesota-based frozen food delivery giant has grown to nationwide size as a leader of the country's largest fleet of yellow freezer trucks. The business operates as a direct-to-consumer frozen food service, with 1,100 employees nationwide. The company changed its name from Schwan's to Yelloh in 2023 after their yellow-colored vehicles.
Yelloh Board Member Micahel Ziebell said in a statement the food supply chain disruption during the pandemic affected the business, alongside other challenges to maintain operation in a digital landscape.
'The current Yelloh team has worked hard against external headwinds such as the nationwide staffing challenges and crushing food supply chain disruption caused by the pandemic,' said Ziebell. 'These challenges, combined with changing consumer lifestyles and competitive pressures that have been building for over 20 years, made success very difficult. Digital shopping has replaced the personal, at-the-door customer interaction that was the hallmark of the company.'
The last day products purchased by the iconic yellow trucks will be Friday, Nov. 8, 2024.

title: How these sisters work seamlessly together on the Williamsville volleyball team
author: Bill Welt
description: Williamsville's Britni Walters recovered from an ACL tear to share final season with extended volleyball family
content:
WILLIAMSVILLE — Brianna Walters is proud of the way her older sister, Britni, bounced back.
Britni indeed not only recovered from an ACL tear that she encountered over the basketball season but also has continued to perform at a high level on the Williamsville volleyball team.
'It's definitely a blessing coming back two months early, I'm very grateful for that,' Britni said.
The senior outside hitter recently supplied 13 kills and 12 digs in a 25-11, 26-24 win over Maroa-Forsyth to nudge the Bullets ever so closely toward a third straight outright Sangamo Conference title with only New Berlin standing in the way from another unblemished 9-0 conference mark.
'Britni's my biggest supporter and I love her being on the court with me, and I'm definitely going to miss that,' Brianna said. 'We connect really well and we're just really close with one another.'
Last year, Britni led Williamsville in kills (380) and digs (268) for a second consecutive season and currently ranks second on the team in both categories entering this week with 273 kills and 193 digs despite wearing a knee brace.
Brianna, a junior libero, leads the back row with 278 digs. Previously a six-rotation outside hitter, defense has always been one of Brianna's many attributes. She made the transition to make room for senior setter Riley Holliday's younger sister, Hannah, who joins the lineup as a freshman outside hitter.
The four together resemble a volleyball family.
'It's definitely been better with my sister on the court,' Hannah said of her first varsity season, 'and I've grown up with all these girls. It's a lot more comfortable than what it normally would be. We're pretty much always together 24/7. There's not really a point in time when we're not.'
Hannah said her older sister makes it clear what needs to be done on and off the court.
Earlier this season, Riley served up 29 assists in a 25-19, 24-26, 25-22 win over Athens and eclipsed 2,000 career assists in the process.
'We talk a lot about games and practices,' Riley said of Hannah, 'and just how we can figure things out with her and Britni being our game producers. And Brianna being the libero, it's kind of the four of us who communicate the most, so we just try to figure it out.'
They certainly didn't show a hint of panic despite trailing late in the second set against Maroa.
'Most of us have played with each other club-wise for a while now,' Riley said. 'We were real successful in junior high when we played together and now we're all coming back up here and Hannah and Bri are with us, we're jelling pretty well.'
Riley and Britini have been playing club volleyball together since they were 10 years old. Both all-state honorable mention last season, they know how to run things.
'They've kind of been the foundation of turning the program back around,' Williamsville coach Courtney Beard said. 'They just have a certain competitiveness that you can't teach. I think it shows on the court.'
Much the same could be said of their younger counterparts.
'We all pick each other up when we're down and we're just there for each other,' Britni said.

title: Springfield getting early taste of winter with freeze warning for Wednesday
author: Tom Ackerman
description: For those of you hoping temperatures would cool down, you're getting your wish early Wednesday morning.
content:
Springfield is getting its first taste of fall and winter.
The National Weather Service issued a freeze warning from 1 to 8 a.m. Wednesday morning.
Residents can expect to see frost on the grass as temperatures will reach the mid 30s overnight. After the brisk morning, temperatures are expected to reach near 60 degrees on Wednesday.
Fall outlook
Most of Illinois is predicted to experience 'above normal' temperatures this fall and early winter, according to the three-month outlook forecast from the NWS.
The forecast from October through December predicts a 33% to 40% chance for most of the state to see above normal temperatures, other than the northernmost part of Illinois. The northernmost part of the state predicts equal chances, or average temperatures.
This prediction does not quantify the temperature other than above normal, average (equal chances), near normal, or below normal.
For precipitation over the next three months, Illinois is predicted to see average amounts.
Winter outlook
From January through March, the forecast predicts a 33% to 40% chance that half of Illinois, including Springfield will see above average temperatures.
For precipitation, the forecast predicts a 40% to 50% chance for most of the state to experience above normal amounts. A part of the northwest section of the state sees a 33% to 40% chance of experiencing above normal amounts.
For a small portion of western Illinois and most of Indiana, the forecast predicts a 50% to 60% chance of experiencing above normal amounts of precipitation.

title: Who is on the Massey Commission? A closer look at the 14 members
author: Brian Wojcicki
description: The first hearing of the Massey Commission will be Monday. Here's what the meeting will entail and a closer look at the 14 commission members.
content:
The first hearing of the Massey Commission will be held at Memorial Learning Center, 228 W. Miller St., at 6 p.m. Monday.
The commission, an outgrowth of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey by a former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy on July 6, recently seated its members and named two new co-chairs, JoAnn Johnson and Shadia Massey, Sonya Massey's cousin, replacing the Rev. T. Ray McJunkins and Nina Harris after an initial listening session.
Dr. Jerry Kruse is staying on as the third co-chair.
During the hearing, the co-chairs plan to present the scope of the commission's work. The commissioners will discuss and consider approval for the draft mission and values, workgroup titles and proposed members.
The commission will hear testimony regarding a proposal for an independent review of the Sangamon CountySheriff's department's procedures. Kelly Hurst, the equity and inclusion strategist for SIU School of Medicine will present on the language and values of antiracism work.
There will be a public comment section and sign-up is at the meeting. The meeting will be live streamed on youtube.com.
Here is a look at the commission members:
JoAnn Johnson, co-chair
A South Side native and the daughter of a Chicago Police officer, JoAnn Johnson became in 2016 the first Black woman to reach the rank of colonel of the Illinois State Police, when she was in charge of the division of internal investigation in Springfield. Johnson started as a patrol officer, worked in criminal investigations and served as an undercover narcotics officer in a joint-jurisdictional drug task force. Johnson retired in 2018.
Dr. Jerry Kruse, co-chair
Dr. Jerry Kruse is dean and provost, SIU School of Medicine and CEO of SIU Medicine. He joined the medical school in 1984 as a practicing family physician. He established the Office of the Associate Dean for Equity Diversity and Inclusion in 2016 and later assisted the medical school in its declaration to strive to be an anti-racist organization.
Shadia Massey, co-chair
The cousin of Sonya Massey, Shadia Massey has likened herself to Massey's older sister. The two practically grew up together and had, Shadia Massey said, "an unbreakable bond." She was the first family member, along with Jimmie Crawford Jr., the father of Sonya Massey's daughter, to arrive at Massey's home the morning of the July 6 fatal shooting in an unincorporated part of Woodside Township. Massey is a certified nursing assistant.
Gerry Castles
Sgt. Gerry Castles spent nearly three decades in law enforcement, including 24 with the Springfield Police Department before retiring in 2019. As a neighborhood police officer and crisis intervention team sergeant, he was cofounder of SPD's co-response teamed with mental health program, and founder of SPD's homeless outreach team (H.O.T.). Castles is currently certified as an instructor for officer mental health, well-being and crisis intervention.
Calvin Christian III
A popular blogger, Christian's never-ending battles over Springfield Police internal affairs records have been well chronicled, including the "Shredgate" affair in 2013, which netted him a six-figure sum from a federal lawsuit with the city and led to the downfall of a police chief.
Sunshine Clemons
Sunshine Clemons, along with Khoran Readus, organized the Springfield Chapter of Black Lives Matter (BLMSPI) in 2016. BLMSPI staged a procession of about 3,000 vehicles around Springfield days after the murder of George Floyd at the hands of Minneapolis Police officer Derek Chauvin. Clemons is a member of the Springfield Police Community Review Commission. She is the Diversity, Equity & Inclusion Officer for the Illinois Department of Public Health.
Veronica Espina
Veronica Espina is founder, co-chair and board president of the Springfield Immigrant Advocacy Network. The network supports immigrants and refugees in Springfield and the surrounding areas, advocating for immigrants' rights, encouraging immigrants' full participation in civic, cultural, social and political life and educating the public about issues that affect local immigrant communities. The native of Chile works for the Illinois Department on Aging.
Harvey Hall Sr.
Hall is president of Be Neighbors Affordable Housing for Veterans and is a U.S. Marine Corps veteran. A community activist and business owner for over 30 years, Hall is actively involved in building inclusive communities for homeless veterans and families toward self-advocacy, to maintain independence and advancing inclusive systemic changes.
Kathryn Harris
The former division manager of library services at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum, Harris most recently served as interim head of the city's public library. She serves on the board of the Springfield and Central Illinois African American History Museum. Known for her work in the community with study circles on race, the city's zoning commission and the Illinois Humanities Council, Harris was named the SJ-R First Citizen in 2020.
Sontae Massey
A cousin of Sonya Massey, Sontae Massey serves as the asset manager for the Springfield Housing Authority. He has decades of experience in sales and customer service in Springfield and is trained in cultural competence and diversity.
Rev. Susan Phillips
Phillips became the first female pastor at First Presbyterian Church in downtown Springfield in 2017. Nationally, Phillips is known for her innovative worship services and leads workshops on design worship and liturgical dance and maintains a popular website, Faithful Spaces. Phillips co-chairs the Illinois Poor People's Campaign and has been active with the Springfield Coalition on Dismantling Racism and the Greater Springfield Interfaith Association.
Kristin Rubbelke
Rubbelke has been lobbying since 2016 and has her own consulting firm. She is also a licensed social worker and policy advocate with a background in racial justice initiatives. As a former co-chair of the National Association of Social Workers-Illinois Racial Justice Task Force formed after George Floyd's murder in 2020, Rubbelke helped develop police reform recommendations.
Bob Wesley
Before retiring in 2018, Wesley was the SIU School of Medicine's principal administrator responsible for rural outreach, telehealth development and implementing community service programs. The U.S. Marine Corps veteran is a member of Frontiers International, the American Legion Post 32 and the Community Health Roundtable and is a current board member of SPARC.
An attorney, Wojcicki is the CEO of Illinois Capitol Group, a Springfield lobbying firm. He has served on the board of The Outlet, Springfield Ball Charter School and Downtown Springfield Inc.

title: Budzinski hopeful for farm bill passage after prior deadline passes
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: Congress has unfinished legislative business to attend to after Election Day, legislation that millions of Illinoisans rely on for farming and food assistance.
content:
Congress has unfinished legislative business to attend to after Election Day, legislation that millions of Illinoisans rely on for farming and food assistance.
Already renewed for one year, the 2018 Farm Bill expired on Sept. 30 but has largely kept its main provisions such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program in-tack. That program is also at the heart of the divide between Democrats and Republicans in Washington.
An earlier version of the Farm Bill passing in the House Agriculture Committee would have paved way for a $30 billion cut over the course of a few years per an analysis by the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office. As of the latest data, SNAP provided food assistance to more than 2.8 million Illinoisans in August 2021 according to the state Department of Human Services.
This cut was part of the reason why U.S. Rep. Nikki Budzinski, who sits on the committee, could not support it. The Springfield Democrat and most others in her party were opposed to this version of the bill.
"SNAP is utilized by people that do have jobs, are working every day, struggling to provide for their families," she said on Oct. 7 in her Springfield office. "A $30 billion cut over five years is too much and so that was a bright red line, I think, for a lot of us on the committee."
Budzinski also told The State Journal-Register she felt the bill played "geographic favorites" benefiting peanut, rice and cotton growers in the South rather than corn and soybean growers in the Midwest. Her congressional district, stretching from the Metro East to Champaign, makes up some of the most productive farmland in the state.
The immediate future for the freshman congresswoman is vying for a second term to represent Illinois Congressional District 13, facing off against Republican challenger Josh Loyd of Virden. But after that, Congress returns to the national's capital on Nov. 12 with goals to pass a five-year farm bill and not another extension.
SNAP and other key programs have funding guaranteed through the end of 2024, but once a new crop year begins in January, they would revert to 'permanent law,' sending crop supports back to policy from the 1938 and 1949 farm bills reports States Newsroom.

title: Williamsville football topples No. 1 Maroa-Forsyth for Sangamo lead
author: Bill Welt
description: Mayson Buckman, Anthony Beckman drummed up big defensive plays to spark Williamsville football to key Sangamo win over Maroa-Forsyth
content:
(This story was updated to add new information.)
WILLIAMSVILLE — The Williamsville football team's defensive line grabbed the spotlight Friday with pivotal plays to cement a 28-21 Sangamo Conference win over Class 2A top-ranked Maroa-Forsyth at Paul Jenkins Field.
Senior lineman Mayson Buckman tipped a pass at the line of scrimmage to set up Griffin Liles' interception deep in Maroa territory before Matthew Miller capitalized with a short touchdown run with just 12 seconds left in the second quarter to even the score 14-14 at the break.
Junior lineman Anthony Beckman later had a critical sack that prompted a Dylan Farris interception to preserve a two-touchdown lead.
"This defensive line since the start of the season has stepped up, it's done amazing," Buckman said. "Every single week we've progressed and taken a step forward. It's honestly amazing how great this defensive line has progressed."
Maroa (7-1, 6-1) forged a 96-yard scoring drive with just over five minutes left in the fourth period, but Williamsville (7-1, 7-0) drained the clock with its potent run game to clinch at least a share of the Sangamo title for the first time since 2021.
Maroa won the previous two meetings en route to consecutive Sangamo titles.
"I feel like it was senior night and the entire setting with all our parents behind us," Buckman said, when asked what sparked the Bullets after falling behind 14-0 by the end of the first quarter. "We've lost to Maroa these past two years, we just wanted to finally beat them and get it done."
Williamsville's rushing attack asserted itself after going three-and-out on its first possession.
Senior running back Braddock Cates led the Bullets with 199 rushing yards and a score on 26 carries, while Miller had 69 rushing yards and a TD. Fellow senior Gage Paul had 57 yards and two scores on the ground as well.
Although Maroa's DeAngelo Owen came down with an interception in the end zone on Williamsville's promising third drive, Buckman and Liles answered with the key interception to quickly regain the momentum. Cates delivered the go-ahead TD run to begin the third quarter while Paul exploded through the line of scrimmage for a 27-yard scoring run on the ensuing possession.
"That was an incredible play," Williamsville coach Aaron Kunz said of the Buckman/Liles INT. "Mayson's been doing really, really well. That was a big play to get back and get that score. We felt when we threw that pick (to Owen), it kind of felt like we squandered an opportunity even to not score but to give them ball back with three minutes to go, it was a double whammy. Mayson tipped, Griff got it — it was a pretty special play and something they'll always remember."

title: Springfield woman accused of interfering with man's medical device before he died
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A Springfield woman is in custody and charges have been filed after she allegedly interfered with a man's medical device that led to his death.
content:
A woman is in custody and charges have been filed after she allegedly interfered with a man's medical device that led to his death.
Kavita Lettimore, 39, of Springfield, is charged with involuntary manslaughter. The Morgan County State's Attorney's Office filed the charges.
Lettimore allegedly cut the Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter line that was attached to Randy Lettimore, which unintentionally caused his death, according to charging documents. The document also said the two were family or household members.
Illinois State Police arrested Lettimore for the Class 2 Felony on Oct. 15, which is the same day she was charged.
The Waverly Police Department on Feb. 21 requested ISP to investigate the death of Lettimore. He died on Feb. 18 in the 300 block of West State Street, according to a news release from ISP.
The state police investigation led them to believe that someone had interfered with the man's medical device that led to his death.
Lettimore is being held at the Sangamon County jail and awaiting transfer back to Morgan County, where she will make her first court appearance.
This story has been updated to include new information.

title: Prison employees picket over drug safety concerns across Illinois
author: Erich Murphy
description: Union members at 23 Illinois Department of Corrections facilities walked out on Thursday over safety concerns.
content:
An explosion of drug use in Illinois prisons has drawn the attention of corrections officers and others working inside the walls of the state's correction facilities.
Members of AFSCME Council 31 walked an informational picket line at 23 Illinois Department of Corrections facilities from Vienna in southern Illinois to Dixon in the northern part of the state on Oct. 17.
In a statement from Anders Lindell of AFSCME Council 31, the prison employee union members demonstrated in a call for safer working conditions. A major problem as of late, Lindell said, is the drug issue overtaking virtually all of the prisons in the state. Not only is it affecting inmates, but employees have been exposed as well.
In a written statement, Lindell noted that 'Safety Matters,' adding that 'AFSCME members are calling on the Department of Corrections to prevent illegal substances, enforce policies requiring clear consequences for offenders abusing substances or assaulting staff, and expedite hiring for safe staffing levels."
'AFSCME members should not have to face violent assaults, illegal drugs and chronic staff shortages as common occurrences when just doing their jobs,' Council 31 Executive Director Roberta Lynch said. 'We demand that leadership of the Department of Corrections step up and do more to make this essential work safer.'
William Lee, president of AFSCME Local 494, said that the drug issue has become a bigger problem in recent years. The main issue is inmates getting drugs through the mail, particularly legal mail, which is mail coming to inmates from their attorneys.
An AFSCME Council 31 report notes the growing problem of drugs in IDOC. The report notes incidents from employees at various correctional centers. One incident took place at Menard, a maximum security facility near Chester along the Mississippi River in southern Illinois.
The report cites an August incident at the Menard Correctional Center where 12 staff members were taken to the hospital after a mass exposure event.
The report also cites an April incident at the Henry Hill Correctional Center in Galesburg where a correctional lieutenant was attacked by an inmate over two pieces of paper which tested positive for fentanyl.
A quote in the report from an unidentified Sheridan Correctional Center employee stated, 'It's been getting worse over the past couple years, so much of it, it's overwhelming.'
Lee said he met with leaders discussing the Pontiac Correctional Center and possible solutions.
'Everything was talked about at the table,' Lee said. He pointed out what he called 'a very simple solution,' which would be to scan the inmate mail.
'It's an easy solution but who's going to push the button to make it happen?' Lee said. 'At some point, DOC and the governor and everybody who has the power to change everything needs to use their power and ability put it to something useful, like staff and help the safety of everybody who works in their facilities.'

title: Video shows police officers saving man from radio tower hundreds of feet in the air
author: Saleen Martin
description: Police rescued the man from a 250-foot radio towe in Eagan, about 16 miles southeast of Minneapolis.
content:
Police in southeastern Minnesota saved a man from a 250-foot radio tower this month, and a video captured shows the daring rescue.
Authorities made the rescue in Eagan, about 16 miles southeast of Minneapolis. The footage was released on Oct. 17, but the rescue was made on Oct. 10, according to a news release issued by the Eagan Police Department and Storyful, where the footage was shared.
Neighbors called Eagan police around 5:51 a.m. on Oct. 10 for a welfare check. They told police they heard someone yelling for help, according to the press release. When officers arrived, they found a 51-year-old man at the top of the radio tower.
Watch officer rescue man from radio tower
To the rescue
Eagan Fire and Dakota County Special Operations Team (SOT) were called for help. An SOT officer climbed to the top of the tower and rescued the man by rappelling him down.
According to Eagan police, the man was "in a mental health crisis and had been exposed to the cold weather." He was taken to the hospital for treatment. Authorities were not able to offer any updates on the man's condition Wednesday afternoon.
The Rosemount Police Department also helped that day. Rosemount Police Chief Mikael Dahlstrom said Wednesday afternoon that the man was in the early stages of being hypothermic when he was rescued.
"In order to access the tower, he had to climb over a fence that included barbed wire across the top of the fenced sections," Dahlstrom said.
The six-minute body cam video of the rescue shows an officer climbing the tower to reach the 51-year-old man, securing himself to the tower so he didn't fall. According to television station KVRR, a Dakota County Special Operations Team member was also there and used high-angle rope rescue techniques to climb the tower and save the man.
The body cam footage was shot from the perspective of a police officer helping with the rescue.
'Alright, let's take a break,' the officer said in the video, briefly resting his arms on the tower's bars before resuming his climb.
'You're doing awesome buddy'
As the officer inched closer to the man, he told him 'You're doing awesome, buddy" and reminded the man to keep breathing.
As the wind picked up, the man appeared to yell, prompting the officer to comfort him and let him know they were doing everything they could to get him down to safety.
The video also showed the man clinging and attached to a rescue team member.
The task seemed to have worn out the officer involved, who said his arms were 'dead' and later added 'I need an IV bag' once he was closer to the ground.
'I don't need to work out for the next two months,' the officer said at the end of the video.

title: Think tank gives Pritzker average grade when it comes to taxes and spending
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A think tank site recently graded all 50 governors when it comes to taxes and spending. Here's what the report said about Gov. Pritzker.
content:
A think tank site promoting libertarian ideas in policy debates has given Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker an average grade when it comes to taxes and spending.
The Cato Institute recently graded all 50 governors in its Fiscal Policy Report Card on America's Governors report.
Governors receiving an A are those who have cut taxes and spending the most, whereas governors receiving an F have increased taxes and spending the most, according to the think tank.
The think tank gives governors a score from 0 to 100 with higher scores equaling a higher grade. Gov. Pritzker received a score of a 45 and a C grade.
'Governor Pritzker scored poorly on past Cato fiscal reports because of his huge tax increases but he was more restrained on tax and spending increases for the period of this report,' the report read.
The governor's report highlights his fiscal policies in recent years in a mostly chronological narrative.
'Pritzker seems unconcerned that Illinois is losing workers, entrepreneurs, and retirees, who are fleeing to warmer and lower-tax states,' the report reads. 'IRS data show that Illinois has the worst ratio of in-migration to out-migration of any state except New York. Illinois loses more than two households earning more than $200,000 per year for each one moving in. To reverse the migration outflow, the state needs to reduce taxes and embrace leaner government.'
Cato credits Gov. Pritzker for giving taxpayers a break in 2022 but said that 2023 and 2024 again saw tax increases.
'While Pritzker favors higher taxes on businesses in general, he hands out narrow breaks to big corporations. In 2023, for example, he awarded $213 million of incentives to a Chinese battery maker that is building a facility in Illinois. Because 'the company is making a minimum investment of at least $1.5 billion, it's also eligible for exemptions from state and local sales tax on building materials, utility tax, and telecommunication excise tax.' This sort of favoritism for large corporations is both unfair and distorts the economy,' the report read.
The report also criticizes Gov. Pritzker for touting the state's $2 billion Rainy Day Fund in his 2024 state of the state address.
'That figure is correct, but compared to state spending it is the second smallest rainy-day fund in the nation,' the report read, adding that Illinois also has the highest level of unfunded pension obligations of any state.
All six of the A grades given out by the institute were given to Republican governors.

title: Family of fallen Illinois State Police trooper releases statement
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The family of the fallen Illinois State trooper released a statement, mourning the loss of their 28-year-old husband, son, brother and friend.
content:
The family of fallen Illinois State trooper Corey S. Thompsen released a statement, mourning the loss of their 28-year-old husband, son, brother and friend.
The trooper was killed by a truck driver in Champaign County on Oct. 18.
'Our world has been shattered, and we will never be the same,' the family said. 'But we take comfort in knowing that he lived life to the fullest, he loved his family and friends deeply, and he died doing what he loved.
'We could never begin to thank law enforcement or the thousands from our community who have reached out to us to express their love and support,' the family said.
Thompsen was part of a motorcycle patrol and a Special Operations Group. He had served with the ISP for nearly five years.
Thompsen was on-duty finishing a traffic enforcement detail and traveling east on East Leverett Road last Friday afternoon.
A truck, driven by Helen Torres, 32, of Thomasboro, was traveling south on County Road 1300 East and stopped at the intersection at Leverett Road when she pulled into the roadway, hitting Thompsen's motorcycle.
A witness provided aid until first responders arrived and took Thompsen to an area hospital where he died of injuries.
It is the first fatal crash involving a state police trooper this year.
A visitation will be held Oct. 26 from 1 to 5 at St. Joseph-Ogden High School. The funeral will be held Oct. 27 at Faith United Methodist Church in Champaign.
Instead of flowers, the family is asking for donations to the Trooper Corey S. Thompsen Scholarship fund that will provide a scholarship to St. Joseph-Ogden High School students entering the field of Criminal Justice. Donations can be made to any University of Illinois Credit Union branch.
