title: Family of fallen Illinois State Police trooper releases statement
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The family of the fallen Illinois State trooper released a statement, mourning the loss of their 28-year-old husband, son, brother and friend.
content:
The family of fallen Illinois State trooper Corey S. Thompsen released a statement, mourning the loss of their 28-year-old husband, son, brother and friend.
The trooper was killed by a truck driver in Champaign County on Oct. 18.
'Our world has been shattered, and we will never be the same,' the family said. 'But we take comfort in knowing that he lived life to the fullest, he loved his family and friends deeply, and he died doing what he loved.
'We could never begin to thank law enforcement or the thousands from our community who have reached out to us to express their love and support,' the family said.
Thompsen was part of a motorcycle patrol and a Special Operations Group. He had served with the ISP for nearly five years.
Thompsen was on-duty finishing a traffic enforcement detail and traveling east on East Leverett Road last Friday afternoon.
A truck, driven by Helen Torres, 32, of Thomasboro, was traveling south on County Road 1300 East and stopped at the intersection at Leverett Road when she pulled into the roadway, hitting Thompsen's motorcycle.
A witness provided aid until first responders arrived and took Thompsen to an area hospital where he died of injuries.
It is the first fatal crash involving a state police trooper this year.
A visitation will be held Oct. 26 from 1 to 5 at St. Joseph-Ogden High School. The funeral will be held Oct. 27 at Faith United Methodist Church in Champaign.
Instead of flowers, the family is asking for donations to the Trooper Corey S. Thompsen Scholarship fund that will provide a scholarship to St. Joseph-Ogden High School students entering the field of Criminal Justice. Donations can be made to any University of Illinois Credit Union branch.

title: Sneak peek: Take a look at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum's new exhibit
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A new exhibit pays tribute to the late Illinois sculptor Richard Hunt at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum. Here's what to expect.
content:
A new exhibit pays tribute to the late Illinois sculptor Richard Hunt at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum.
Visitors can now explore 'Freedom in Form' that offers insight to Hunt's story as an African American artist whose work was often inspired by issues of Civil Rights. Hunt also professed freedom artistically.
'An art exhibition of this scale is a new challenge for the ALPLM, but we thought the idea was too good to pass up,' said the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum Exhibits and Shows Director Lance Tawzer.
'We had an Illinois artist who built an international reputation exploring themes of race, justice and Civil Rights in America – basically, looking at where this nation stood 150 years after Abraham Lincoln wrestled with those same issues,' he added.
It is a unique exhibit for the museum because it is primarily an art exhibit, but it also touches on history and tells the story of a prominent artist from the state.
Hunt died last December at the age of 88.
Hunt lived and worked in Chicago all his life, producing more public sculptures than any other artist in American history. They can be found in plazas and parks from Champaign and Peoria to Washington and New York.
Hunt's work is also prevalent in Springfield, living in such places as the Illinois State Capitol and the Illinois Department of Natural Resources building.
Last year, First Lady MK Pritzker honored Hunt and declared the day April 24, 2023, Richard Hunt Day in Illinois.
About the exhibit
Visitors at the library and museum may have noticed the 22-foot-tall, 2,000-pound stainless steel sculpture by Hunt in 2013 (Steel Garden) that was installed in August as a teaser to the opening. It will travel to London before the ALPLM's indoor exhibit ends on April 20.
The exhibit itself showcases additional large and medium scale works as well as miniature prototypes of massive sculptures, known as maquettes.
The exhibit also focuses on Hunt's creative process and explores history that inspired him.
On display are tools from Hunt's studio and books from his library, as well as video interviews. Hunt was an avid reader, with interests ranging from poetry to civil war and Lincoln history, African American history, and of course art history, Tawzer said.
Visitors will be able to see the artist's 1956 sculpture Hero's Head, that was inspired after Hunt at 19 years old saw the battered body of Emmett Till, the Chicago teenager who was murdered in Mississippi.
Also on display is Maquette for Hero Ascending, which is among the last pieces for which Hunt may be credited. A monument to Emmett Till, the full-scale version will be installed at Till's childhood home, the Mamie and Emmett Till-Mobley House Museum and Theater in Chicago.
In the spring, the exhibition will move to the Loyola University Museum of Art in Chicago.
Hunt passed before he could view the exhibit
The ALPLM met with Hunt a year and a half ago to talk about creating an exhibit. The group kicked around a couple ideas, but freedom was a theme that rang true for Hunt, Tawzer told the State Journal-Register.
'He used a walker, but then he sat down in his walker, and he would put his face shield on, and he would start grinding and working on sculptures,' Tawzer said.
The group talked about the possible project when Hunt took a break from the artwork.
Tawzer said Hunt's death came as a surprise to the museum.
'We knew he was 88 years old; we knew that he had had some health issues, but our expectation was that he was going to be here to see the opening. I'm sure it was his as well,' he said.
Tawzer said the exhibit felt important before the artist's passing, but it became more important after he passed.
In addition to Steel Garden, patrons can view the piece John Jones at no cost within the library.

title: Low and nonalcoholic wines are growing in popularity. Here are some to get in Springfield
author: Jay Kitterman
description: Some may be looking to cut back on alcohol consumption ahead of the holiday season. Try one of these low or nonalcoholic wine options.
content:
Would you be willing to spend more than $100 on a bottle of non-alcoholic sparkling wine? I recently read an article in the Wall Street Journal announcing that Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessey (LVMH), the owner of such prestigious brands as Dom Perignon and Moët Hennessey, was introducing a non-alcoholic champagne called French Bloom that would sell for $100.
This is when I knew the low and non-alcoholic liquor business was no longer just a fad, but truly a trend.
French Bloom sources its grapes from the Languedoc region of southern France, where the sunny climate results in grapes with naturally high alcohol.
To remove the alcohol, French Bloom uses a technique called 'cold-vacuum distillation.'
Generational trend
From my research, low and non-alcohol wine is truly a generational and lifestyle trend. The low and non-alcohol wine category is currently being driven by Gen X (demographic cohort 1965-1980) and Millennial (1981-1996) consumers.
A major player in this market is Bota Box. When Bota launched their Breeze products in 2021, research showed that more than 40% of consumers were looking for lower-alcohol wines.
These Gen X and Millennial consumers are upper income, educated and want their wine to fit into their healthy lifestyle.
Bota Box light wines is now the number one brand of low alcohol wine category by volume in the U.S. The box is produced from recyclable materials, stays fresh 30 days after opening and each box is equivalent to four bottles making it very budget friendly.
Many of the Bota Box varieties are also available in the tetra packs, making them very convenient for traveling. I recommend their Chardonnay.
Bota Box research shows this trend tracks closely with long-term consumer trends around food. Consumers want options that align with health-conscious lifestyle choices, in beverages and food, and wine is no exception.
The company states, 'The point of light wine is not to compete with traditional wine; it's to offer an alternative to traditional wine that fits into the lifestyle choices that are important to consumers today.'
Local recommendations
John Russo, who works part-time at the Corkscrew Wine Emporium in Springfield, has researched this topic extensively and reports, 'calorie reduction is a major benefit of non-alcoholic or low alcohol wines.'
A 5 oz. glass of wine, which is one serving, contains 120-130 calories, depending on grape variety and residual sugar. Low alcohol wine has 70-90 calories/serving and non-alcoholic wine has 20-30 calories/serving.
I asked David Anderson at The Corkscrew and Zach Sweet at "It's All About Wine" for their recommendations.
It's All About Wine is currently carrying two wines from Oddbird. Oddbird is a Scandinavian company that started in 2013. Today, they reign as Scandinavia's premier producer of wines, beers and spirits. The wines are matured for up to 12 months and then 'gently liberated from alcohol.'
In 2016, King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden awarded Oddbird an entrepreneurship award. It's All About Wine currently carries Oddbird Red Blend and Oddbird Blanc de Blancs Sparkling.
Their commitment to purity means that their wines contain no artificial colors and no synthetic aromas.
Blanc de Blancs is from Languedoc-Roussillon and made from Chardonnay and Colombard, giving tones of crispy Granny Smith apples, honey and lime. It is described as, 'a youthful and elegant Chardonnay blend with high complexity and delicate bubbles.'
Blanc de Blancs is matured for 12 months before 'being gently liberated from alcohol.'
The Red Blend, which is a combination of Grenache, Syrah and Mourvedre from Saint-Chinian, south of France, is characterized by its acidity and earthy notes with fruity touches. Both are priced at $32.00 a bottle.
Anderson also introduced me to Ariel Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon. Owned and operated by J. Lohr Vineyards & Wines, Ariel is on California's Central Coast.
Their Ariel Cabernet Sauvignon and Ariel Chardonnay are batched and fermented like any other wine.
Using a reverse osmosis method, which uses a pump to push their fresh wine through special membranes, the alcohol and water are separated from the wine. Their California Cabernet Sauvignon is described as black currant, velvety chocolate and dark cherries.
Notes for their California Chardonnay describe, 'On the nose, there is a hint of sweetness, with hints of fresh-cut pear, apple, butterscotch and French oak.' These two wines have 45-calories per 8 oz serving and both are priced at $11.99.
In addition, The Corkscrew also has these low or non-alcoholic wines in stock:
Giesen Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc and Rose from New Zealand, $16.99
Selbach Funkel Wurtz Zero Sparkling from Germany, $19.99
Fre Sparkling Brut from California, $14.99
Codorniu Zero Sparkling from Spain, $14.99
Low and nonalcoholic wines are growing rapidly and no longer just located in the back corner of your wine store. Powerhouse brands such as Yellow Tail, Kendall-Jackson, and Kim Crawford have all launched lower-alcohol lines.
My thanks to David Anderson from The Corkscrew, Zach Sweet from It's All About Wine and Calvin Jacey from Bota Box for their assistance with this article.
Jay Kitterman is a culinary and special events consultant and adjunct instructor at Lincoln Land Community College.

title: Springfield could set record high temperature on Tuesday
author: Tom Ackerman
description: While you may have been enjoying the fall like temperatures, you may want to consider breaking out the shorts on Tuesday.
content:
While you may have been enjoying the fall like temperatures, you may want to consider breaking out the shorts on Tuesday.
A high of 83 degrees is predicted for Tuesday, but if temperatures reach 84 degrees in Springfield, it'd be a new record high for Oct. 29.
Daryl Onton, a meteorologist at the NWS in Lincoln, said there is a strong chance of Springfield breaking that record.
According to the National Weather Service, Springfield has hit 83 degrees three times on Oct. 29, including 1937, 2004 and 2016.
Tuesday's warm temperatures will be met with overcast skies and comes about a week after the city was filled with a weird smell.
Social media users complained about a foul smell in the area the morning of Oct. 23.
Most people theorized that it had something to do with farmers fertilizing their fields, or farm products in some capacity.
But a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Lincoln said the best and simplest explanation is a phenomenon known as petrichor, which is an earthy smell that occurs after a rain, especially after a dry period.
That smell can be perceived as chemical or oily, and as radiating upward from the ground, said Mike Albano, a staff meteorologist with the NWS.

title: Oberkfell, Gillespie soar up the cross country charts
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Chaz Oberkfell had never run cross country before, and yet his arrival helped boost Gillespie to conference championship and, hopefully, beyond.
content:
There is something strange about the top runners on the Gillespie boys cross country team: none of them thought they'd be this good this fast, and most couldn't even fathom running three miles at a time.
A group that is two years removed from finishing last in the South Central Conference cross country meet is now a back-to-back conference champion, with eyes set on even larger prizes.
The next journey began with Gillespie's third-place finish in the Class 1A Shelbyville Regional on Saturday. The Miners advanced to the Toledo Cumberland Sectional on Saturday at 11 a.m. The girls race is first at 10 a.m. If Gillespie can finish in the top-six teams at sectionals, the Miners will head to the Class 1A state meet at Detweiller Park in Peoria on Saturday, Nov. 9.
Gillespie coach Jay Weber put together a ragtag group of first-time long-distance runners and gave them the confidence they needed.
The Miners are led by junior Chaz Oberkfell, whose time of 14 minutes, 20.8 seconds in the 30 th annual East Alton-Wood River Invitational on Oct. 12 has him ranked No. 1 in the state's Class 1A rankings. Fellow juniors Marshall Garwood, Hank Fletcher and Carter Sies give Oberkfell more company at sectionals this season after the Miners' top runner was the team's sole qualifier out of regionals last year.
Oberkfell finished third overall at the Shelbyville Regional in 15:13.57.
Oberkfell's journey
Oberkfell took a surprising path to get to being a state contender. It all began with a sibling rivalry.
'I ran my P.E. mile, and my brother (Collyn Oberkfell) was in my P.E. class, and I had to just beat him because I had to prove that I could beat him,' Oberkfell recalled. 'I don't even think he went all out in the P.E. mile, but I full-sprinted. I went as hard as I could, and I beat Collyn.
'I went to their cross country banquet, because (of) my brothers, and (Weber) met me, he walks out and goes, 'That P.E. mile was the worst mistake of your life.''
Oberkfell also remembered saying something most running coaches wouldn't want to hear.
'I told him I thought running was dumb,' Oberkfell admitted. 'I just wasn't really big into running.'
But Weber saw potential.
'It's really interesting,' Weber said. 'Freshman year in the fall, that kid would've told you distance running was stupid and he would never do it in his entire life.'
During the 2023 track and field season, Weber approached Oberkfell — whose older brothers Collyn and Cadyn were on the team and a part of the eventual 4x800-meter relay state qualifying team — and suggested to his freshman that he stretch out his sprints to a little longer distance races. Eventually, Oberkfell qualified for the Class 1A state meet in the 1,600-meter run as a freshman. But when Weber approached Oberkfell about the upcoming cross country season, Oberkfell made Weber a deal.
'I told him if he'd bring me honey buns to practice, I'd run,' Oberkfell said. 'Weber would bring honey buns. Then I started doing it, it was fun. Running with all them just made it enjoyable.'
Competitive genes run in the family
Oberkfell doesn't just share a unique name with a former third baseman for the 1982 World Series champion St. Louis Cardinals. He and Ken Oberkfell also share DNA.
His grandpa, who spent 16 seasons in Major League Baseball with six teams, played with the Cardinals from 1977 to 1984. He was 7-for-24 with an RBI and two stolen bases as St. Louis beat Milwaukee in seven games to win the 1982 championship.
But shockingly, Ken Oberkfell had to bribe his own grandson to claim he rooted for the Cardinals.
"I'm a Cubs fan," Oberkfell said. "He'd give us like a dollar if we'd say we were Cardinals fans. I'd get my dollar."
Now retired, the elder Oberkfell — born in Highland — currently lives in Gillespie.
"He still only watches sports," Oberkfell said of his grandpa's viewing habits. "That's all he watches."
There is a little bit of a friendly competition with his grandpa, Oberkfell said.
"I'm trying to beat him in (Alton) Telegraph articles," Oberkfell said with a laugh. "My goal is one day, whenever I look up Oberkfell, I just want to see my name instead of his."
Oberkfell also gets some of his athletic genes from his mom, Anne Mitchell, who ran track and field when she was at Edwardsville High.
Teammates surge
Garwood has the second-best time on the team, according to athletic.net. All of the top-six Gillespie runners hit their season best in the East Alton-Wood River Invitational. Garwood's time of 16:04.1 is the best of the three teammates — including Fletcher and Sies — who are all sub-17 minutes.
"This year is kind of the year their goal is to try to get to state, then we look at it as we're returning everyone (in 2025)," Weber said. "We know the work we put in, and these guys want to take their shot at being right up at the top of state next year and being able to compete at the state meets."
Garwood started running in eighth grade, and he too claims he was reluctant.
"I did some running eighth grade year for track and I didn't really want to do track, but (Weber) convinced me to do it," Garwood said. "Once I got done with track season, I was totally ready for cross country. I was really pumped up about it.
"Eighth grade year looking back, I definitely did not think I'd be here by now. Thought I'd probably have passed out on the track by now."
Garwood went from not having much competitiveness in his personality to getting a thrill to pass other runners.
"The practices are great. I want to come out to practice," Garwood said. "I love running with (Oberkfell). Like the encouragement I get from him is like really strong.
"I was not competitive at all. When I go out there and race, I really want to beat everyone I can."
Sies has a similar story. He gave up baseball his freshman year to run in the fall and spring.
"I think it was worth it," Sies said. "I think it's just like the community in cross country and the friends with it."
Weber doesn't care how much running experience kids have when they come out for the team. As long as they'll put in the work, so will he.
"What Carter and Marshall represent — probably more than anyone I've ever coached in my life — is they are just super kids," Weber said. "I mean, these are straight-A, they're going to be valedictorian students. These are guys who are part of everything. These are the nicest, most responsible, solid kids you'll ever see.
"They had no running ability. But I've always kind of had this mantra that if you give me the right kid, you can make him a distance runner, because distance running is all about the work you'll put in. What's happened over the last couple of years is, these guys spent most of the summer putting in 50-mile weeks and just putting in the work. When you start doing that, you start to see gains."
Fletcher ran track throughout junior high as a hurdler. Again, distance running was not seemingly in the cards.
"It took some time because I'm not a fan of the heat (and) running in the heat in summer is pretty rough," Fletcher admitted. "The first time, I was kind of nervous because the mile, I felt like that was a lot. Three miles is a lot more."
If Gillespie makes it to the state meet as a team, the runners will also have something to return.
"We had no reason to believe freshman year," Weber said. "I think Carter and Marshall were running 22, 23, something like that. We didn't have Chaz on the team yet. Hank was running like 20ish. And no reason to believe.
I go to the state meet every year, no matter what, and that year I brought back a whole bag of leaves from Detweiller. And I told those guys, 'Hey, there's something special here.' But crazy a sixth-place team in the SCC conference is going to think there's something special. But I told them all to grab a leaf and keep it safe because it was going to be their job to get back to Detweiller and return it to its to its home."
The Miners have sophomore Lucca Kapp and freshman Nolan Hostettler in its top-six as well.

title: Boy, 16, accused of stealing vehicle in Springfield released to parent
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A 16-year-old boy was released to a parent after abandoning a stolen vehicle on a railroad track in Springfield.
content:
A teenager who allegedly stole an SUV and drove into oncoming traffic in Springfield before abandoning the vehicle had been accused of stealing a vehicle before.
According to the Springfield Police Department, a 16-year-old was found after allegedly stealing a vehicle over the weekend wearing a non-functioning ankle monitor from a previous vehicle theft.
So, what happened when the boy was arrested this time?
'He met the criteria for incarceration, however placement was not available at any state juvenile facility, so he was released to a parent,' the police department said in a press release.
Despite being released to his parent, the boy was charged with motor vehicle theft, theft of property, aggravated unlawful possession of a stolen vehicle, aggravated fleeing and eluding, criminal damage to property, and reckless driving.
The new charges were filed after police said the boy stole a GMC Acadia around 8 a.m. on Oct. 26 from the 2500 block of Griffiths Avenue.
The SUV was then found abandoned on the railroad track under the Clearlake overpass near 19th and Washington streets and a boy was seen running from the vehicle, Springfield police said. He was arrested in the 1700 block of East Reynolds Street.
The charges come not long after Springfield Police Chief Ken Scarlette spoke publicly about the impacts of the closure of the Sangamon County Juvenile Detention Center last year.
'We have juveniles who are becoming emboldened, who are being arrested with firearms, who we have to turn around and release back to their guardians and go back home, and I think that sets a terrible precedent and a bad message for what we as citizens expect in our community," Scarlette said at a recent city council meeting.
The Sangamon County Juvenile Detention Center has been approved to reopen once enough staff are hired to operate the facility.

title: Comic book convention, hot soup fundraiser and more: 5 things to do in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: Even though candy buckets will still be sitting out on the dining room table from Halloween, there are plenty of sweet things to do in Springfield.
content:
This weekend marks the end of spooky season and the start of giving thanks across the prairie state with the start of November.
Even though candy buckets will still be sitting out on the dining room table from Halloween on Thursday, there are plenty of sweet things to celebrate downtown.
Go ahead and give these five things to do around town a try, if you aren't tired from all the Trick-or-Treating.
Springfield Comic Book Convention
What: The Springfield Comic Book Convention will be held this weekend at the Route 66 Hotel & Conference Center and is free to the public. According to the convention website, it costs dealers a lot less to set up at smaller venues compared to larger conventions, meaning customers can often find some really good deals. Unlike buying things online, customers will get to see the comic before buying it, so they'll know what shape it is in without trusting the seller's judgment.
When: 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Sunday
Where: 625 E. Saint Joseph St., Southern View
Souper Friday Fundraiser
What: The Souper Friday soup fundraiser benefiting Catholic Charities St. John's Breadline will be serving up fresh soups to go this weekend with made fresh from scratch soups to warm the soul. The soup options include chicken noodle soup, steak & vegetable, and chili. The suggested donation is $10 for 32 oz. of soup. All proceeds will benefit the St. John's Breadline.
When: 3:30 to 5:30 p.m. Friday, until sold out.
Where: 1615 W. Washington St., Springfield
More: For more information, you can visit the Catholic Charities Diocese website at cc.dio.org.
Lilacs and Letters
What: The Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum has brought back two powerful theatrical productions throughout fall to the museum's Union Theater, telling a compelling tale in one act about the sacrifices, struggles, and resilience of the people experiencing the Civil War. Written and performed by Nation, "Lilacs & Letters" portrays one of America's most influential poets, Walt Whitman, as he processes the assassination of Abraham Lincoln and tends to wounded Civil War soldiers. The play, which consists of a single actor alone on a stage, is set at the Armory Square Military Hospital in Washington, D.C. In the shadows of an early morning in 1865, Whitman, a hospital volunteer, sits among the sleeping wounded as he reflects on national grief and puts the finishing touches on poetry eulogizing President Lincoln.
When: 1:15 p.m. Friday
Where: 212 N. Sixth St., Springfield
More: Tickets are free with regular admission to the museum.
Brews and Mews
What: What pairs best with a warm apple cider? Is it an apple fritter, or maybe a furry critter? Join Buzzbomb Brewing Co. and Forever Home Feline Ranch for a night of bubbling witches brew and celebrate the black cats in attendance for Halloween. There will also be merchandise for humans and four-legged friends available.
When: 2 to 6 p.m. Sunday
Where: 406 E. Adams St., Springfield
More: A Facebook post has been made for the event.
A Samhain Night of Magic
What: Weave a little magic into the season at Ad Astra. Samhain, or summer's end, is a Gaelic festival marking the end of the harvest season and the beginning of winter on Nov. 1. Ad Astra has taken a step into enchanting the new year with multiple vendors, special drinks and group rituals in their downtown wine and tapas bar. Foxfire Fantasies will help intrigued customers creature protection braid and crystal bracelets, with every knot a wish for safety and strength. The Gallery Hair Salon will enchant with a hair braiding bar, while Ad Astra itself will have potions brewing – in the forms of unique sangria.
When: 4 to 8 p.m. Saturday
Where: 308 E. Adams St., Springfield
More: This event is just part of a weeklong Samhain celebration; for more information about the events taking place, Ad Astra's Facebook page has all the information you could need.

title: Opinion: Utility companies taking advantage of Illinois families, consumers
author: Cornel Darden Jr
description: Cornel Darden Jr. believes major utility companies are taking advantage of Illinois families and consumers.
content:
Have you ever wondered why your utility bill seems to climb higher and higher each year? Electricity distribution fee increases have outpaced inflation across the country, and Illinois is no exception.
Illinois electric utility ComEd, which raised its rates on Jan. 1, 2024, has filed a multiyear rate plan seeking further increase s in the fees they charge for delivery of electricity, which the Illinois Commerce Commission expects to decide in early December.
Every year, utility companies ask for rate hikes from regulators on the grounds that they must spend this money to improve or expand their systems to deliver electricity.
Yet, at the same time, they promise record profits to their Wall Street investors. The truth is that utility monopolies in Illinois, like ComEd, are taking advantage of the system to boost their profits, leaving families and small businesses to foot the bill.
Unlike most industries where companies cut costs to stay competitive, utility companies' unique positions as monopolies in their region allow them to benefit from spending more.
They make more profit the more they invest in infrastructure—whether it's really needed or not. By spending money unnecessarily, companies are not only guaranteed to recoup their investment, but they are allowed to add extra fees on to customers' monthly bills.
When these companies pour money into the grid, too often they make unnecessary additions or replacements of equipment that will not make any meaningful improvements in service or reliability for customers.
This process of upgrading the grid when it is already reliable enough is called 'gold-plating,' and it has delivered exceptional results for the shareholders of ComEd's parent company Exelon.
For example, ComEd must replace worn or damaged utility poles to ensure continued service, but they are now proposing to install polls for fiber optic cables to support communications without sufficiently demonstrating the need for the upgrade.
Exelon has promised up to 7% higher earnings each year through 2027. These results are only possible if ComEd continually gold-plates the grid.
That is why Illinoisans are facing this new 'multiyear rate plan,' where customers will be held hostage to increasing rate hikes year after year. The more ComEd invests in the grid, the more profits they rake in, and the more Illinois families are left holding the bag.
Adding insult to injury, while most companies make charitable gifts from their profits, ComEd and a few other utilities have the unique ability to use funds collected from customers to donate to causes and organizations the company selects with no input from those customers – and the utility gets the good PR that comes with it.
In fact, ComEd has charged its customers an additional $7 million per year for this purpose, and millions of additional dollars are included in the annual rate hikes it is seeking through 2027.
Customers have no ability to control where these 'donations' go. While some may be for the public good, some have been given to charities that have supported legislation supported by ComEd.
Illinois families cannot afford ComEd's schemes. While billionaires and CEOs rake in massive profits, approximately one in three Americans said they have avoided paying for basic necessities in order to pay their utility bills.
Nearly one-fourth said they could not pay their utility bill. We must urge our public officials to reject these new rate hikes from ComEd. Only lawmakers and regulators can end this never-ending cycle of increased fees and give customers the help they need.
Dr. Cornel Darden Jr. is the Chairman of the Board of the Chicago Southland Black Chamber of Commerce & Industry. a Professor of Information Science, a family man, entrepreneur, and an economic advocate.

title: CWLP proposes 4-year contract to lock in coal prices but not everyone is on board
author: Claire Grant
description: Springfield's coal supply may soon be doubling the distance it takes to get the city. See why some alderpersons and residents are concerned.
content:
Springfield's coal supply may soon be doubling the distance it takes to get the city, at an apparent lower price point.
CWLP was proposed the contract by Foresight Coal Sales LLC, for the purchase of coal in a four-year contract for $85.6 million from Foresight's Hillsboro mine, more commonly known as Deer Run.
The contract would set the price of coal at $40 per ton until 2027, when the price would increase to $44.50 per ton and $46.75 per ton in 2028; however, the contract would not include the cost of hauling the coal over fifty miles from Hillsboro to Springfield.
CWLP chief utility engineer Doug Brown said Knight Hawk Coa l, which owns Viper Mine, the current mine CWLP uses for fossil fuel, raised their prices from 2020 $45 per ton to $65 per ton. Brown said CWLP has instead looked to the fossil fuel market and was offered two different proposals, one of which was Foresight.
McKiernan said at Tuesday's Committe of the Whole meeting that Foresight Energy has an extensive history of mistreatment of the environment and before entering a contract, should perform an Integrated Resource Plan.
An Integrated Resource Plan, or IRP, is a strategic framework plan for the next 20 years of future energy needs and considers the environmental impacts of resources used. The plan should be renewed every five years McKiernan says, and that CWLP has not performed an IRP since 2018.
'Uncertainty, price volatility, change in technology if mines are closing or maybe they're not closing are not reasons to delay the integrated resource process - it's precisely why it's needed,' McKiernan said.
'I feel trapped'
Ward 3 Ald. Roy Williams Jr. voiced concern about the longevity of accepting a bid from Foresight Energy for four years; in 2020, or four years ago, the energy company filed for bankruptcy.
'I feel trapped, I feel like I have no choice but to go with the contract because we need coal,' Williams Jr. said. 'This is why it's so important and I said way back last year this is why we need a plan in case what things (ward 2) Ald. Gregory was asking you. This company we're getting ready to sign with doesn't have a good reputation in my opinion.'
Local environmental activists also raised concerns.
'CWLP has gotten utility into a precedent where our energy sources are not reliable and they don't have a long-term plan on resolving this,' local environmental activist Lori McKiernan said Tuesday night.
The Sierra Club of Illinois, who McKiernan is part of, earlier this October created a petition urging City Council to develop a medium- and long-term plan to transition the community to clean energy.
Other concerns about the energy provide date back to 2022 when Illinois attorney general Kwame Raoul sued Foresight Energy for allegedly dumping 46,000 gallons of PFAS into the Sugar Camp mine in Franklin County in 2021 to try and curb a mine fire.
Foresight then told state officials the foam used at the mine was biodegradable, in a report from The Chicago Tribune in October of that year.
'Foresight has so many problems and then to get told that's the environment of coal mines nowadays, that's even more evidence we need an IRP,' Williams said.
Brown said part of the uncertainty of renewing a contract with Viper mine are recent unconfirmed rumors of the location shutting down, and mixed with the raised rates, the city could save $39 million over the length of the contract with the lower rates at Foresight.
The contract would also have no minimum purchase, meaning CWLP would not have to purchase coal more often than it needs to.
CWLP estimates the coal burn of Dallman 4 at 500,000 tons per year.
The Springfield City Council will discuss and is scheduled to vote on the ordinance at Tuesday's City Council meeting.

title: Seamus' spark: O'Brien boosts SHG offense in first-round upset of Mahomet-Seymour
author: Ryan Mahan
description: With an empty backfield, the pressure was on SHG quarterback Cam Brinkman. He and Seamus O'Brien lifted the Cyclones to a playoff victory.
content:
MAHOMET — There were plenty of reasons to doubt the outcome of Friday's Class 5A first-round playoff football game for both Mahomet-Seymour and Sacred Heart-Griffin.
In the first half, the host Bulldogs had plenty of success moving the ball but had just seven points to show for it. Sacred Heart-Griffin, which had offensive struggles early in the season, couldn't move the ball and settled for a Tom Davis 29-yard field goal late in the second quarter for the Cyclones' only points.
When No. 3 Mahomet-Seymour (7-2) scored back-to-back touchdowns midway through the fourth quarter to put the Bulldogs back on top 21-17 — thanks to a recovered onside kick — it could've deflated No. 14 SHG.
But the Cyclones had more tricks up their sleeves, both offensively and defensively.
With 3 minutes, 59 seconds left in the game, sophomore quarterback Cam Brinkman bought enough time to find Seamus O'Brien down the visitors' sideline for a 78-yard go-ahead touchdown. Davis' point-after kick was good to ultimately give SHG a 24-21 upset victory over Mahomet-Seymour.
'I think that last drive we had in the first half was a good offensive-builder even though we only got three points out of it,' Brinkman said. 'We found a lot of stuff that we were running, and that's what worked, really, the rest of the game.'
SHG (6-4) will face either No. 6 Joliet Catholic (6-3) or No. 11 Jacksonville (6-3) in the second round. JCA and Jacksonville kickoff at 7:30 p.m. on Saturday. SHG will host Joliet Catholic while Jacksonville would host the Cyclones.
'We've played some tough teams,' SHG's Chris Link said. 'Our record doesn't show who we are at all. We knew it was going to be a good football game, and we knew we were going to be victorious.'
The Cyclones sealed the victory when sophomore defensive back Andrew Wolters picked off Mahomet-Seymour quarterback Lucas Dyer's pass attempt at the SHG 15-yard line with 2:04 to play. It was Wolters' first interception of the season.
SHG needed just one first down to run out the clock and take the final play out of the victory formation.
Dyer entered the game with just five interceptions through nine games. SHG took two from the senior QB — both coming in the fourth quarter. Junior Drew Ward had the first, which came on first and 10 from the SHG 33 — eight plays after Brinkman lost a fumble to give the Bulldogs the ball down 10-7 with 11:14 to go.
Meanwhile, it was Brinkman who shined with SHG's empty backfield. He finished 22-for-33 with 292 yards and three touchdowns. He found Seamus O'Brien 10 times for 196 yards and two scores.
Brinkman also did the brunt of the Cyclones' work on the ground with 19 carries for 30 hard-fought yards. SHG's other running backs finished with four carries for minus-5 yards.
'We've had two (close games): Chatham and this one; I'm just glad we came out on top in this one,' SHG coach John Allison said.
The Bulldogs put the first points on the board halfway through the second when Dyer found Gavin Hammerschmidt for a nine-yard touchdown pass to cap a 13-play, 98-yard drive for a 7-0 lead. The Cyclones then put together a matching 13-play drive of their own that began at the 17. It was on this possession that Brinkman and O'Brien first hooked up when O'Brien caught a pass for eight yards. O'Brien was the sixth SHG player to catch a pass, but it wasn't long before he became Brinkman's primary target.
"I loved the script for this week,' O'Brien said. 'First half, we just didn't get the look we thought we were going to get from them: we were expecting man, we were expecting press. Once we got used to it, we got to half, we looked over some things, and it obviously worked when we came out for the second half.'
By the time the half was over, O'Brien had three catches for 37 yards before Davis ended the Cyclones' drought with his field goal.
'Seamus is a playmaker,' Allison said. 'The more he touches the ball, the better we are. (As a quarterback), if you trust the guy, that's huge. You trust the guy that, if I put it up there, I know he's either going to catch it, or it's going to be incomplete.'
SHG took its first lead with 4:37 left in the third when Brinkman found Demetrius Roberson for a 10-yard score. Davis' PAT gave SHG a 10-7 lead.
Momentum went back and forth in the final period after Brinkman lost a fumble on first and goal from the 5-yard line. Mahomet-Seymour drove to its own 33 before Dyer was picked off by Ward. One play later, Brinkman and O'Brien put SHG up 17-7 with a 29-yard touchdown throw with 8:03 left in the game.
For a game that struggled to produce scoring drives in the first half, the fourth quarter made up for that with four scores in quick succession.
The Bulldogs' Cade Ashby scored a 1-yard touchdown midway through the final quarter to pull Mahomet-Seymour within 17-14, then the hosts recovered an onside kick at the SHG 49 and needed four plays to regain a lead when Dyer found Wade Manuel for an incredible 48-yard TD on fourth and nine.
Mahomet-Seymour's senior defensive captain, Brock VanDeveer, said he was still proud of the Bulldogs' efforts all night.
'We didn't expect them not to run it at all,' VanDeveer said of SHG's empty backfield. 'They did their QB sneaks a little bit, but they were empty the whole game, and they obviously have their pass game worked out. We knew they were going to pass a lot, but we were shocked they didn't run at all.'
SHG, shaken but not stirred, put a hush over the home bleachers with that 78-yard touchdown pass from Brinkman to O'Brien for the 24-21 lead. Wolters' pick with 2:04, plus a Brinkman pass to O'Brien for a first down, sealed the upset victory.

title: State, Cook County use similar arguments to defend assault weapon bans
author: Peter Hancock
description: Ruling on state ban expected soon in Southern District as Cook County prepares for 7th Circuit arguments.
content:
Attorneys in the offices of Attorney General Kwame Raoul and Cook County State's Attorney Kim Foxx made similar arguments in recent court filings as both defend bans on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines against constitutional challenges.
In separate cases at different levels of the federal court system, both offices are trying to make the case that the laws under challenge – a state law enacted in 2023 and a county ordinance that dates to 1993 –fall within the bounds of the U.S. Supreme Court's most recent interpretation of the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms.
Raoul's office filed its final written arguments Monday, Oct. 21, in the Southern District of Illinois, where an in-person trial was held in September on multiple challenges to the state's Protect Illinois Communities Act. That's the weapons ban state lawmakers passed in 2023 in the wake of a mass shooting at a Fourth of July parade the previous summer in Highland Park.
Foxx's office made its argument in briefs filed with the 7th Circuit Court of Appeals, where a three-judge panel will hear oral arguments Nov. 12 in a challenge to the county's assault weapons ban.
First adopted in 1993, that law was strengthened in 2006, and again in 2013. It is now known as the Blair Holt Assault Weapons Ban, named after a Chicago teen who was killed in a 2007 shooting while protecting a high school classmate.
Both cases are among the numerous challenges to assault weapons bans that have been filed in recent years in Illinois and elsewhere. Those cases come as state and local governments look for ways to control the proliferation of increasingly deadly weapons on their streets while a conservative majority on the U.S. Supreme Court takes an increasingly expansive view of the Second Amendment's protection of gun rights.
The court's current standards for judging Second Amendment cases are spelled out in the 2008 decision District of Columbia v. Heller, and the 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen.
The Heller case held the right to bear arms is an individual right, not a collective right, and that the Second Amendment protects an individual's right to own and carry weapons such as handguns that are commonly used for self-defense and other lawful purposes.
In the Bruen decision, the court went further to say that for a gun control law to pass constitutional muster, the government must show that the law is consistent with the nation's 'historical tradition of firearms regulations.'
In both pending cases, attorneys for the plaintiffs argue the weapons banned under the laws are among the most popular firearms in America and are commonly used for self-defense and other legal activities such as hunting and target shooting.
Attorneys for the state and Cook County, however, argue the assault weapons covered under the laws are modern variations of guns first developed in Nazi Germany during World War II, the Sturmgewehr 44. That weapon's design was later adapted and modified by the U.S. military into a weapon known as the AR-15, which was later 'rebranded' as the M-16 rifle.
Briefs filed in both cases also offer graphic descriptions of mass shootings in which assault weapons have been used to illustrate how their lethal power is many times that of smaller weapons like a 9 mm handgun.
Cook County's brief, for example, begins with a description of the 2022 mass shooting at Robb Elementary School, in Uvalde, Texas, where 19 children and two teachers were killed by a man wielding an AR-15.
'Afterward, a pediatrician observed that the children 'had been pulverized by bullets fired at them, decapitated,' their 'flesh had been ripped apart' to such an extent 'that the only clue as to their identities was blood-spattered cartoon clothes still clinging to them,'' the county's brief states.
Cook County's brief also includes a list of 17 mass shootings in the United States involving assault weapons between 1984 and 2022, as well as the July 13, 2024, attempted assassination of former President Donald Trump.
The state's brief begins with a description of the Highland Park mass shooting, noting that '(i)n less than 60 seconds, the shooter fired approximately 83 shots into the families and community members gathered to celebrate the nation's birthday. Seven people died, and an additional 48 people were wounded.'
Both the state and county argue the military origins of assault weapons, combined with their lethal impact when used in mass shootings, place them in the category of 'dangerous and unusual' weapons which, under the Heller decision, are outside the scope of Second Amendment protection.
Both the state and the county also argue there is a long, historical tradition of regulating weapons that posed particular threats to public safety. They both cite laws from the first half of the 19 th century banning Bowie knives, as well as later laws regulating pistols, revolvers, and 'Tommy guns.'
Plaintiffs in both cases, however, argue there is a fundamental difference between the assault weapons banned under the state and county laws and the type of weapons used in the military – namely, that the laws ban 'semiautomatic' weapons, which fire only one round with each pull of the trigger, while the military uses weapons that can fire in either semiautomatic or fully automatic mode, meaning they fire continuously with a single pull of the trigger until the trigger is released or the ammunition is depleted.
In earlier proceedings, Judge Stephen P. McGlynn, who is presiding over the case in the Southern District of Illinois, issued a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of the Protect Illinois Communities Act, saying the plaintiffs were likely to win on the merits of the case.
But the 7th Circuit Court of Appeals reversed that decision and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to review the case at this juncture, opting instead to remand it back to district court for full proceedings. The trial in that case ended Sept. 19, and McGlynn is expected to issue his ruling soon.
In the case challenging the Cook County ordinance, U.S. District Judge Rebecca R. Pallmeyer ruled March 1 in favor of the county, noting the 7th Circuit has ruled several times that assault weapons bans are constitutional, including an earlier challenge to the Cook County law. The plaintiffs are now appealing that decision. The appellate court will not release the names of the three judges assigned to hear the case until the morning of oral arguments Nov. 12.
Both lawsuits have backing from national gun rights organizations such as the Second Amendment Foundation, the Firearms Policy Coalition, Federal Firearms Licensees, and the National Shooting Sports Foundation.
National gun control advocates such as Everytown for Gun Safety and Giffords Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence have also filed briefs in support of the weapons bans.

title: Pumpkin smash, circus among 5 things to do in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: It may have been a more stressful week than normal. Relax with these five things to do in the Springfield area this weekend.
content:
Feeling a bit of tension on your shoulders following the presidential election?
You aren't alone. Across Springfield, there's plenty of ways to relax in the style that suits you best.
Whether relaxation in your eyes is a day at the spa getting your back massaged or exploding ripe pumpkins – check out these five things to do around Springfield this weekend.
Ansar Shrine Circus
What: The Ansar Shrine Circus is coming back to town for another season of stunts, art and animals. Celebrate art and fund the Shriner's goals for hospitals to provide care to families whether they can pay or not.
When: 11 a.m. Saturday
Where: 1 Convention Center Plaza, Springfield
More: General admission tickets are $15 per person, $8 per child before fees and can be purchased on Ticketmaster.
Winter Clothing Swap
What: Want to freshen your wardrobe for the coming season? Skip the box store lines and find a unique piece you'll wear all season long at the clothing swap. Hosted at The Keep Store in downtown, guests can bring up to seven pieces to trade for new winter wardrobe staples.
When: 2 p.m. Sunday
Where: 312 E. Adams St., Springfield
More: Stay fashionable and sustainable. No ticket is required but a donation of $5 at the door for The Keep Store is appreciated.
Luminescence
What: Have a night of art therapy at the Pharmacy Gallery this weekend. This glass and other mediums exhibit named after the Latin word for light challenges guests to explore the different reflections of light and the colorful shadows it casts. Guest artist Michael Houser's large energetic paintings will be on display as well, showing fragmented movements in time.
When: 6 to 9 p.m. Friday and Saturday
Where: 623 E. Adams St., Springfield
More: This event is free to the public.
Annual Pumpkin Smash
What: Ready for the winter season already but keep staring at that droopy, goopy gourd sitting on the edge or your porch every morning? The City of Springfield waste and recycling team is here to help you throw out your pumpkin before it turns to mush, smashing it into dust. Now that's a form of meditation. Set up that ghoulish face slowly rotting away onto a tree trunk and work out built-up stress with a baseball bat. The event will host indoor and outdoor activities around the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum, with a free useable tote bag for the first 100 visitors.
When: 10 a.m. Saturday
More: For more information, a Facebook page has been set up for the event.
Lick Creek Live
What: Saddle up for a weekend of drinks, good food and one of central Illinois hottest country bands at Motorheads Bar and Grill. Mixing electric bluegrass with classic country, Lick Creek is a meshing of 6 rock and country musicians putting their love for both genres into one sound that has been making a buzz since the first show. They have performed in their home state of Illinois, and all over the Midwest.
When: 8 p.m. Saturday
Where: 600 Toronto Road, Springfield
More: The event is free to the public, make sure to check out Big Ron, the latest attraction to Route 66.

title: In tight Sangamon County Recorder's bid, Lesko leads Langfelder
author: Steven Spearie
description: In a taut race, challenger and Springfield Clerk Frank Lesko edged out incumbent Sangamon County Recorder Josh Langfelder by 68 votes Tuesday.
content:
In a taut race, challenger and Springfield Clerk Frank Lesko leads incumbent Sangamon County Recorder Josh Langfelder by 68 votes.
But there are still 3,510 votes by mail still outstanding, said Sangamon County Clerk Don Gray.
"This election's not over yet," Gray said. "Additional work needs to be completed in terms of finalizing the results."
Additionally, any qualified ballot postmarked by Tuesday and returned no later than Nov. 19 will be added to the returns.
All provisional ballots that are qualified, Gray added, also will be added, though he didn't know that number. The provisional ballots will be counted Wednesday.
The Republican Lesko, serving a third term as city clerk, gathered 48,934 votes to Langfelder's 48,866 votes.
Langfelder has been recorder since 2008 and was the only Democrat to hold a county-wide seat.
Lesko had touted in ads"Hire me so you can fire me," in reference to the merger of the recorder's office with the Sangamon County Clerk.
Lesko claimed the merger of the two offices could save county taxpayers $250,000 annually. Other counties, like Cook and Champaign, have gone that route, Lesko maintained.
Langfelder said merger talk was "a terrible idea."
The recorder's office is the official land records depository for the county. Instruments filed with the office include deeds, mortgages, releases and assignments, property liens, as well as assorted federal, state and local liens. Other documents include veteran's discharge papers, corporation papers and instruments pertaining to the Uniform Commercial Code.
Lesko, 64, said the recorder's staff would be merged into the new office, so no one would lose his or her job. Under the plan, Lesko said the recorder would leave the office at the completion of the merger.
Lesko said he would take "a business approach" to running the recorder's office. He is the owner of Abe's Tradin' Post, 2704 N. Peoria Road.
(This story has been updated to add new information.)

title: Clerk: Nearly half of Sangamon County ballots were early voting and mail-in ballots
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Voter turnout in Sangamon County was strong for this year, but still below previous years, including the 2020 election.
content:
Voter turnout in Sangamon County was strong again for the Nov. 5 election, but still fell short of previous elections.
100,219 voters made their voice heard in the county, which accounts for nearly 72% of the registered voters.
That number is down slightly from past presidential elections, like in 2020 when 76% of registered voters cast their ballot, said Sangamon County Clerk Don Gray.
Part of the reason for that dip could be the rain, Gray said. Polling places saw a slow morning but then ramped up quickly in the mid-morning and stayed consistent until their close at 7 p.m.
But polling locations have also drawn less crowds in recent years as voters turn to early voting and voting by mail, Gray told The State Journal-Register.
Of the 100,219 ballots cast in the county, 41,617 were from early voting and mail-in ballots.
'It certainly administratively makes (election day) more smooth…even though it was steady and a steady pace, it was never overwhelming,' Gray said.
Gray and his team will continue to process late arriving mail-in ballots. The mail-in ballots will likely play a role in deciding some of the county's local races, which include the County Recorder race which was separated by just 68 votes at the end of election night..
Kenny Naughton, exiting So. Side Christian Church, after voting Nov. 5, 2024.
Kenny Naughton of Springfield talks about the anxiety and divisiveness of the nation going to the polls on Nov. 5, 2024.
Gray also observed that rural areas of the county voted heavily, and particularly in southern parts of the county like Chatham and Rochester.
'The city of Springfield was definitely a little slower in pace,' he said.

title: A procrastinator's guide to Election Day in the Springfield area
author: Andy Carrigan
description: Have you waited until today to cast your ballot? What you need to know in the Springfield area.
content:
In case you may have missed it, Tuesday is Election Day.
While plenty of you may have voted early, we know some of you may be stragglers.
Here's some fast facts you need to know.
When can I vote?
You can cast your vote between 6 a.m. and 7 p.m.
Am I registered to vote?
Residents can check to see if they're registered to vote online at ova.elections.il.gov. If you're not registered, you can register at your polling location if you still need to register. Simply bring two forms of ID with at least one showing your current Illinois address.
Where is my polling place?
You can find your polling place online at ova.elections.il.gov.
What are some big races to watch today?
In Illinois, two of the largest races are for congressional seats. Incumbent Rep. Nikki Budzinski, D-Springfield, faces a challenger in Josh Loyd for the U.S. House District 13 seat. In northern Illinois, Republican challenger Joe McGraw looks to knock off incumbent Democrat Eric Sorenson for the U.S. House District 17 seat.
In Sangamon County, 15 of the 29 county board seats are up for grabs, with seven contested races. Incumbent Recorder Joshua Langfelder, the only Democrat to hold a county-wide office, seeks reelection against Springfield Clerk and former Ward 4 Alderman Frank Lesko.

title: Music titan Quincy Jones, legendary producer of Michael Jackson's 'Thriller,' dies at 91
author: Kristin McGrath
description: The man who made stars collide for "We Are the World," Quincy Jones had a long career as a composer and producer who broke down racial boundaries.
content:
Quincy Jones, best known as the architect of Michael Jackson 's " Thriller" and the man who made stars collide for 1985's " We Are the World," had a long career as a composer and trumpeter who broke down racial boundaries in music and film.
Jones died on Sunday, his publicist said. He was 91.
Jones won an astonishing 28 Grammy Awards throughout his career as an arranger and producer, and his legacy intersected with those of Frank Sinatra, Ella Fitzgerald, Duke Ellington and Lesley Gore.
Born March 14, 1933, to Sarah and Quincy Delight Jones, he and his younger brother, Lloyd, grew up in gang-riddled Great Depression Chicago. His mother suffered from mental illness and was institutionalized when he was 5, and his father moved the family to Bremerton, Washington.
When he was 11, Jones broke into the Armory recreation center in Bremerton to steal food. Inside, he found an upright piano. As he would later say in interviews, this was the moment that led him from a childhood of petty crime to a life of music.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
His chance encounter with the piano led Jones to try a medley of instruments before settling on the trumpet. By age 14, he was playing the club circuit with 16-year-old friend Ray Charles, freewheeling from jazz to big band to bebop. After high school, Jones toured the world with jazz greats Lionel Hampton and Dizzy Gillespie.
This whirlwind life as a traveling musician deposited Jones, who was broke, back in the States in 1961. He repaid his debts by working at Mercury Records, where he was eventually promoted to vice president at the otherwise white company.
When dreams of scoring films lured Jones to Hollywood in 1965, executives were shocked to learn he was Black after they'd hired him for the Gregory Peck film "Mirage." He soon racked up two Oscar nominations (best original song for "The Love of Ivy" and best original score for the film "In Cold Blood") in 1968 and became the first Black musical director at the Academy Awards in 1971. He would executive produce the show in 1996.
Yet Jones suffered from health problems. He had two nearly fatal brain aneurysms in 1974. The resulting metal plate in his head ensured he would never play trumpet again. Yet he continued making music, scoring "The Bill Cosby Show," "Sanford and Son" and the 1977 miniseries "Roots," for which he won an Emmy.
Gloria Estefan, Colman Domingo and more honor icon Quincy Jones: 'A genius has left us'
Then, while scoring the film "The Wiz," Jones met Jackson. He produced Jackson's "Off the Wall" album in 1979, ascending to music royalty alongside the King of Pop in a partnership that also generated mega-sellers "Thriller" and "Bad." In 1985, the pair collaborated on the star-studded charity song "We Are the World," which won three Grammys.
Star power of 'We are the World'
He co-produced "The Color Purple" and helped introduce Oprah Winfrey to a national audience (He also produced the Broadway version). In 2013, Winfrey induct Jones into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
His name appears as a producer, composer, conductor, arranger, or performer on more than 400 albums. He composed roughly 35 film scores.
Quincy Jones paid tribute to his daughter in final Instagram post: Who are his 7 kids?
Jones leaves behind seven children: Jolie Jones Levine (with former wife, actress Jeri Caldwell), Martina Jones and Quincy Jones III (with second wife, model Ulla Andersson), Kidada Jones and "The Office" actress Rashida Jones (with third wife, "Mod Squad" actress Peggy Lipton), Rachel Jones (with Carol Reynolds) and Kenya Julia Miambi Sarah Jones (with actress Nastassja Kinski).
In his later years, the force that propelled Jones from jazz musician to music mogul never seemed to die out. He formed the production company responsible for " Fresh Prince of Bel-Air." He published an autobiography in 2001. He partnered with Lionel Richie for a second installment of "We Are The World" after the Haiti earthquake in 2010.
In 2018, daughter Rashida and director Alan Hicks chronicled Jones' generation- and genre-spanning career in the Netflix documentary "Quincy." Rashida called the two-hour film "a starter pack," saying she shot 800 hours of footage and worked through 2,000 hours of archives.
Netflix's Quincy Jones doc
"He's lived such a big life," Rashida told USA TODAY in a joint interview with Jones at the time. "I just cannot believe all of this experience is contained in this one human being who just happens to be my dad."
Jones, who admitted to tears every time he's seen the film, said the message of his life comes through in the movie: family, love and keeping perspective.
"Don't never give up," he said. "Keep the humility with the creativity. And grace with the success. Just because you're behind a No. 1 record does not make you better than anybody."

title: Ike Young, Monticello pass game carves up Williamsville in second round 3A playoff game
author: Bill Welt
description: Monticello's Ike Young totaled six touchdowns to carry the Sages past Williamsville in second round of 3A playoffs
content:
(This story was updated to add new information.)
WILLIAMSVILLE — Monticello's pass game quickly ignited.
The Sages scored on four of their first four possessions en route to a 42-14 victory over Williamsville in the second round of the Class 3A playoffs at Paul Jenkins Field on Saturday.
Senior quarterback Ike Young totaled six touchdowns. He nearly had one pass picked off on Monticello's opening drive but still caromed its way to junior receiver Nolan Buehnerkemper for a first down. He dialed up a 63-yard touchdown pass to senior wideout Carter Foran just a couple of plays later.
"Every week, they put in new things," Williamsville coach Aaron Kunz said of Monticello. "It's impressive all the things they do and how many formations they run, how many motions they run, and how many trick plays they can put in. It's a very impressive offense. We didn't get stops, but it wasn't really anything they tricked us on. We just didn't make plays at times."
Monticello (9-2) advances to its first quarterfinals since winning the 3A title in 2018. It draws Benton next.
"We haven't been here in a while," Young said. "It feels really great. I love my community, they support us a lot, so it's been fun."
A 76-yard pass to Foran set up Young's go-ahead touchdown keeper for a 14-7 advantage with less than a minute left in the first period. The Sages barreled ahead 28-7 by halftime with Young going 9 of 12 for 281 yards and three scores in the first half, either to Foran or Buehnerkemper.
Young finished 14-for-18 for 355 yards and five touchdowns while also rushing for 115 yards. Foran had nine receptions for 237 yards and three scores, and Buehnerkemper had five catches for 116 yards and two touchdowns.
"A lot of the attention comes to me, but they're really good receivers and they get open for me, and I just do my job," Young said.
"Carter's really fast. I can always give him the ball. I know he's going to get open."
Williamsville senior running back Braddock Cates' 50-yard run set up junior quarterback Jackson Sanders' 14-yard touchdown throw to senior Gage Paul in the first quarter. Cates finished 26 carries for 124 yards.
Williamsville finishes 9-2 overall, including as the Sangamo Conference champion.
"I'm proud of our kids for winning the conference, that's something we haven't done in two years," Kunz said. "That was a big deal. We won some big games and did some great things, so overall, it's not where we wanted to end, but I'm proud of our effort."

title: City Council approves $85.6M for new coal supplier for City Water, Light & Power
author: Claire Grant
description: The four-year coal contract with Foresight Energy passed in a vote 9 to 1, with Ward 3 Ald. Roy Williams Jr. voting no.
content:
The nearly $86 million contract with Foresight Energy to power Springfield's coal power plant passed in city council chambers Tuesday night.
The four-year coal contract with Foresight Energy passed in a vote 9 to 1, with Ward 3 Ald. Roy Williams Jr. voting no.
The contract would set the price of coal at $40 per ton until 2027, when the price would increase to $44.50 per ton and $46.75 per ton in 2028; however, the contract would not include the cost of hauling the coal over fifty miles from Hillsboro to Springfield.
That would be a separate contract.
Changing Springfield's coal supplier
City Water, Light and Power chief utility engineer Doug Brown previously said Knight Hawk Coa l, which owns Viper Mine, the current mine CWLP uses for fossil fuel, raised their prices from 2020 $45 per ton to $65 per ton. Brown said CWLP instead looked toward the fossil fuel market for competitors to Knight Hawk and was offered two different proposals, one of which was Foresight and the other Peabody Energy.
CWLP estimates the coal burn of Dallman 4 at 500,000 tons per year.
Brown previously said part of the uncertainty of renewing a contract with Viper mine are recent unconfirmed rumors of the location shutting down, and mixed with the raised rates, the city could save $39 million over the length of the contract with the lower rates at Foresight.
Integrated Resource Plan concerns
During an Oct. 29 committee of the whole meeting, local environmental activist Lori McKiernan voiced hesitation about the city entering an agreement with Foresight Energy without an Integrated Resource Plan, or IRP, to plan for the future energy needs of the city and the environmental impact of resources, like coal in this case, used.
At Tuesday's city council meeting, Anne Logue of Sustainable Springfield said it was time for an outside insight into the city's environmental plans with an IRP.
Nick Dodson of Helping Hands Springfield said there was a level of cognitive dissonance between CWLP and constituents of wards about the need of an IRP.
'Let's also remember that the last IRP reportedly saved CWLP and ratepayers tens of millions of dollars over the last five years,' Dodson said. 'If an IRP offers such clear financial benefits, why is it missing from the priorities of this council and CWLP's leadership? Ignoring the potential benefits as a new IRP seems at best disingenuous and at worst, deceptive.'
Dodson and several other environmental activists have organized a petition to tell City Council to plan Springfield's utility feature, which has accrued close to 400 signatures since its creation.
Dodson says the plan should include public engagement, consultation with independent energy experts, evaluations of the most cost-effective way to move to clean energy and away from coal.
The plan suggested by activists would pass an ordinance this year for an IRP in the next budget and to be completed in 2025.

title: Joliet Catholic football overwhelms Sacred Heart-Griffin in Class 5A playoffs
author: Adrian Dater
description: Sacred Heart-Griffin football just didn't have the size or strength to match Joliet Catholic in the second round of the 5A playoffs
content:
Francis Ruettiger is the strength and conditioning coach of the Joliet Catholic Hilltoppers. Francis' brother, Dan, was immortalized in the film 'Rudy' about a pint-sized nobody who made the Notre Dame Fighting Irish as a walk-on.
There weren't many Rudy-looking guys on the Hilltoppers Saturday at Ken Leonard Field. A team with many hulking, well-muscled players, the Hilltoppers squashed Sacred Heart-Griffin 49-0 to advance to the Class 5A quarterfinals. The Cyclones, whose season ended at 6-5, just didn't have the size and strength to compete with Joliet Catholic.
'We didn't match their intensity,' said senior Jamarion Bardwell, one of the only Cyclones players to do much of anything offensively. 'It's a tough loss for the SHG community, but I'm sure they'll bounce back next year. This community has done so much for me. I'm just thankful to be part of it.'
How big is Joliet Catholic? Senior lineman Cam Jurcich is 6-foot-5, 330 pounds – and he can run some. Senior lineman Michael Lynch is 6-5, 300. Junior lineman Ian Campbell is 6-3, 230. Nine other players are listed at 240 and above.
The Cyclones have two players listed at a high of 260 pounds.
'We've got some lifting to do,' Cyclones coach John Allison said. 'Between the trenches, we didn't have a lot of answers. We tried match protection, we tried seven-man protection, but they still got to us.'
The Cyclones, who got only five first downs in the game, are a young team that some say overachieved getting this far in the playoffs, so Allison is upbeat about the near future.
'We've got some great young skill kids. We've got some great young arrivals. We started probably five or six freshmen and sophomores today,' Allison said. 'But honestly, we gotta big bigger and stronger in the trenches. That's really what it comes down to.'
'Yeah, they're big boys, but I think what really sets us apart is our strength and conditioning program in the off-season, led by Francis Ruettiger,' Hilltoppers coach Jake Jaworski said. 'The atmosphere he creates is … I mean, it's just a man cave with weights. It's got all the memorabilia on the wall from the '60s, '70s, '80s, and on with Joliet Catholic stuff. The kids kind of see what other teams have achieved. It's kind of the culture center for our program. Our guys are there four days a week – the Monday our season ends all the way through the next summer.'
The Hilltoppers (7-3 overall) got three touchdown passes from junior quarterback Lucas Simulick, but on the ground is where they did the most damage. Hilltoppers running backs such as Nate Magrini and Vince Bremmer had strong days, each of whom weigh more than 200 pounds.
Joliet Catholic had a 28-0 lead at the half. The Hilltoppers, who never had to punt in the game, stopped the Cyclones on fourth down on two subsequent drives, and each time they went down the short field for scores. Magrini scored twice as part of the first-half scoring.
Cyclones sophomore QB Cam Brinkman had a good season, but a final game he'll never remember fondly. Brinkman, usually a strong runner up the middle, had nowhere to go on most plays. Joliet Catholic's defensive line simply bulldozed their way into Brinkman's kitchen on more plays to count. Brinkman was sidelined by the third quarter, with the Cyclones getting 'clocked' (a 40-point deficit triggers a running clock) on their home field for the first time in more than anyone could remember.
'We just couldn't get anything clicking,' Bardwell said. 'That's a good team over there.'
Said Jaworski about his team's championship hopes: 'I think our conference prepares us well for the playoffs, the grind of getting through that conference. We played a team today with a great program, so it says a lot about how our kids played. We know we're going to have a very tough opponent (Peoria) next week, so that's all we can focus on after this one.'

title: Racist text messages spamming Black Americans across US, including Illinois
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Illinois is the latest state to have Black Americans reportedly receiving racist text messages. Here's what we know.
content:
Illinois is the latest state to have Black Americans reportedly receiving racist text messages.
The widespread messages are being reported in multiple states and screenshots are going viral on social media sites. The messages vary in detail, but follow the same basic script.
Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul confirmed students in the state have received some of these text messages.
'Hate has no place in the state of Illinois," Raoul said in a news release. "Full stop. I am outraged by reports of these offensive, racist texts and am particularly saddened to learn these hate-filled messages have even been received by students, including in Illinois.'
Raoul's office did not provide additional information on the text messages.
A spokesperson for the University of Illinois Springfield said there have been no instances reported at UIS. The Illinois NAACP and the Springfield branch of the NAACP were unable to be reached for comment.
The Southern Poverty Law Center, which tracks hate incidents nationwide, is investigating the messages, according to a report from the Columbus Dispatch. So are authorities in Texas, Ohio, Alabama, South Carolina and other states.
At least some of the messages claimed to have come from, "a Trump supporter."
Raoul encouraged residents who may have received a racist text to contact local law enforcement or the Help Stop Hate Helpline at 877-458-4283. People can also file a complaint with the AG's Civil Rights Bureau.

title: 'Best of both worlds': Chatham Glenwood senior shines in slot ahead of football quarters
author: Bill Welt
description: Gavin Simmons has totaled nearly 1,500 receiving yards over the past two seasons with the Chatham Glenwood football team.
content:
The Chatham Glenwood football team will figuratively throw anything at you.
Senior Gavin Simmons said the playbook itself contains hundreds of plays — so much, he said, 'I can't even count how many plays we have.'
That extensive playbook is complemented by a gamut of players who each bring something different to the table. It starts with junior dual-threat quarterback Colten Knoedler.
Knoedler can turn to speedy slot receivers Simmons and junior Blake Lehnen or bigger targets such as 6-7 senior Mason Nuemann and 6-4 senior Jonathan Helm.
That doesn't even include the tailback combo of electric junior Grady Mueller and bruising senior Herchel Walker.
'We have a little bit of everything that you could ever want in the offense,' Simmons said.
Last season, Simmons led the Titans with 53 receptions for 725 yards and nine touchdowns. This season has been much the same in the slot with 50 grabs for 767 yards and nine TDs.
Simmons has dabbled a little bit of everywhere over his career, but the slot is unquestionably his preferred position with jet sweeps and screens potentially in the offing.
'It's more of a hybrid receiver/running back player compared to the outside,' said Simmons, who has ambitions to play at the next level, 'so I'd say I like it a little bit more because you get the best of both worlds playing running back and slot.'
Mueller is also a threat in more ways than one.
He has a team-high 699 rushing yards and nine scores on 122 carries. He is also second-best on the team with 26 catches for 507 yards and six scores. He began the season as a slot receiver before pivoting back to what he considers his more natural position.
'I knew that was my spot,' Mueller said of being a running back. 'I just kept at it and kept working.
'Herchel Walker, he's been competing with me all year. We definitely help each other get better.'
Last week, Mueller rushed for 217 yards and three touchdowns on 22 carries in a 42-21 win over Oak Forest in the second round of the Class 6A playoffs. In Week 8, he totaled three touchdowns — including a 98-yard kickoff return — and 165 rushing yards in a 34-31 overtime victory over Sacred Heart-Griffin.
'I've just been working hard every day at practice — shoutout to my line, they're just working hard as me,' Mueller said. 'We've been getting better every week.'
Knoedler has been shattering records along the way himself. He went 23 of 31 for 475 yards and six touchdowns in the 49-34 win over Crete-Monee in the playoff opener to set a record for most completions and passing yards in a game while also tying for most touchdowns. Last week, he broke his own record for most passing yards in a season with 2,430.
Lehnen's return has further galvanized the offense. He missed most of the season due to injury.
The No. 5-seeded Titans (9-2) next welcome top-seeded East St. Louis (10-1) in the 6A quarterfinals on Saturday at 2 p.m.
Glenwood lost the last meeting 50-28 in the 2019 6A semifinals before the Flyers captured the state title. East St. Louis has subsequently returned to the state finals the past three seasons with one additional title in 2022 — a stretch only interrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic.
Simmons is keenly aware of the challenge ahead but said the team's mental approach remains the same.
