title: Federal appeals court strikes down FCC net neutrality rules. What this means for you.
author: Jessica Guynn
description: The FCC's net neutrality rules prevented internet service providers from throttling or blocking some content or charging more to deliver it.
content:
A federal appeals court has struck down the Federal Communications Commission's net neutrality rules that prevented internet service providers from throttling or blocking some content or charging more to deliver it.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit said Thursday that the FCC lacked the authority to reinstate the Obama-era rules, dealing a final blow to a decade-long effort to gain greater oversight over the internet.
Long the source of partisan tensions, the net neutrality rules were repealed in Donald Trump's first term. President Joe Biden signed a 2021 executive order encouraging the FCC to reinstate them, which the FCC voted to do along party lines in April.
Net neutrality decision early win for Trump
Democrats want greater oversight of internet service providers while Republicans reject the idea that they should be regulated like phone companies.
The appeals court's decision is an early win for the incoming Trump administration which has vowed to roll back Biden regulations.
Brendan Carr, tapped as the new FCC chair by Trump, has been a key critic of net neutrality.
'While the work to unwind the Biden Admin's regulatory overreach will continue, this is a good win,' Carr said Thursday on X.
Former FCC Chairwoman Jessica Rosenworcel had called net neutrality 'a necessity for daily life.' She said Thursday that Americans still want 'fast, open, and fair' internet service and called on Congress to take action.
The decision does not affect state laws in California, Colorado and Washington.
What is net neutrality?
Neutrality refers to the idea that internet service providers should treat all content flowing through their systems equally. The term was coined in 2003 by Columbia University law professor Tim Wu.
Net neutrality rules are opposed by telecommunications giants like AT&T, Comcast and Verizon.
Internet service providers praised Thursday's ruling. 'Our fight to stop the government's unwarranted internet takeover has resulted in a major victory,' Grant Spellmeyer, CEO of the cable trade group ACA Connects, said Thursday.
Consumer advocacy groups are major backers of net neutrality, arguing the rules are needed to keep internet service providers from abusing their power. These advocates warned Thursday that consumers could be subject to higher fees or slowed or blocked services.
'Today's decision will let the incoming Trump FCC abdicate its responsibility to protect internet users against unscrupulous business practices,' Free Press Vice President of Policy and General Counsel Matt Wood said in a statement.

Springfield Police had responded to the area at approximately 11:40 a.m. for the report of a shooting. Upon arrival, officers found the woman who was shot, according to Springfield Police officials.
It is an ongoing investigation.

title: Sheriff: Springfield man fatally shot was inside vehicle at time of shooting
author: Steven Spearie
description: A Springfield man was the victim of a fatal shooting in a chaotic scene on East Carpenter Street Saturday evening.
content:
A Springfield man was the victim of a fatal shooting in a chaotic scene on East Carpenter Street Saturday evening.
Lajarvious Smith, 31, was pronounced dead at HSHS St. John's Hospital just after 8:30 p.m. after being shot multiple times.
Through a Sangamon County spokesperson, Sheriff Paula Crouch said that Smith was in a blue Dodge Charger with a 23-year-old unidentified female, who had non-life-threatening gunshot wound.
Crouch said Smith was in the driver's seat while the woman was in the passenger's seat.
Smith arrived at St. John's in the Charger.
Detectives from the sheriff's investigations division processing the scene and talking to witnesses determined over 50 shots were fired. They believe a dark, four-door sedan, last seen driving east on Carpenter Street, was involved in the shooting.
Anyone with information on the shooting can contact the sheriff's office at 217-753-6840, or Crime Stoppers of Sangamon and Menard Counties at 217-788-8427.

title: Here's a recipe for how to lighten up in 2025
author: Sheridan Lane
description: We all tend to look to make improvements at the start of the new year. Here's a recipe to how to lighten up in 2025.
content:
According to history.com, humans have been setting New Year's resolutions for some 4,000 years dating all the way back to the ancient Babylonians.
Ringing in a new year with celebration and a mindset to make improvements was central to even those early New Years' celebrations; yet from Forbes to U.S. News and World Report, statistics indicate that most of the resolutions we set in the modern-day are foiled by the end of February.
Why do we place so much emphasis on doing something to which we fail year after year? Psychologists, scholars, researchers and the like suggest that it is because we are bad at making realistic goals.
Since we are bad at setting goals for ourselves, I turned to AI for some help with my resolution this year rather than think one up on my own. AI's response gave me quite a chuckle.
'Lighten up' was its advice. Ironically enough, that phrase has echoed in my ears for years as it is something my parents used to say to me as a kid when I was too wrapped up in one thing or another.
While AI may know me mysteriously well, its recipe for how to achieve its proclaimed New Year's resolution to 'lighten up' is one in which we might all be able to enjoy and find success. I can even weave in AI's suggestion for 'top five food trends of 2025' right along with the ways in which I can accomplish a life that is a little lighter.
AI's recipe for how to lighten up in 2025
Practice 'digital minimalism' while enjoying 'functional hydration.'
Certainly, I am guilty of the so called 'doom scrolling' on social media, binge shopping on Amazon and of never drinking enough water; but I do believe I can achieve this mini goal in 2025 on my way to lightening up. My phone tracks just how much time I am on each of those apps, so I will just set a specific goal, which is the recommendation for actually achieving the goals we set. And while I like seeing posts with pictures of people I don't see often enough, I am going to enjoy a hot cup of tea from Whimsey Tea to wind down before bed instead of my nightly 'thumbs up,' 'likes' or 'hearts.'
'Laugh more,' and 'move more.' I am going to accomplish this goal by trying to incorporate a comedy series into my daily commute and by actually standing at the standing desk I got two years ago for my office. These two little things are just that — little things that AI suggests will help us in our overall mission to lighten up in 2025.
'Delve into experiences,' 'rediscover creativity' and enjoy 'experiential dining.' These two mini goals as well as the one top food trend are easy for all of us to achieve. Just join us at Lincoln Land Community College during the spring semester for Bistro to Go, Bistro Verde (www.llcc.eldu/bistro-verde) or one of LLCC Community Education's many culinary offerings that are available (www.llcc.edu/culinary-offerings). Make a plan to join us with a friend and/or to book at least one class or dinner, and we can check off this mini goal as complete!
Best wishes for a joyous and light 2025 from all of us at LLCC Hospitality Management and Culinary Arts.
Sheridan Lane is director of culinary programs and operations at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management and Baking/Pastry, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: Author and historian Michael Burlingame to address Abraham Lincoln Banquet
author: Steven Spearie
description: Michael Burlingame is the author of one of the most definitive biographies on Abraham Lincoln. Here's when he'll be in Springfield.
content:
Renowned Abraham Lincoln scholar, author and professor Michael Burlingame will be the featured speaker at the Abraham Lincoln Association (ALA) Birthday Banquet at the President Abraham Lincoln Hotel on Feb. 15.
The free Benjamin P. Thomas Symposium will be held the same day.
The author of the two-volume "Abraham Lincoln: A Life," one of the most definitive biographies of the 16th president, Burlingame is the Chancellor Naomi B. Lynn Distinguished Chair in Lincoln Studies at the University of Illinois Springfield.
A former Springfield resident, Burlingame has been a proponent for building a replica of the 1844 Lincoln cottage, the original six-room cottage before it was expanded by the Lincolns at Eighth and Jackson streets in 1856.
In 2023, U.S. Sens. Dick Durbin, D-Springfield, and Tammy Duckworth, D-Chicago, introduced legislation to expand the boundary of the Lincoln Home National Historic Site to include the proposed replica and the Elijah Iles House.
Burlingame's banquet speech is titled 'Adventures and Misadventures of a Lincoln Scholar.'
Burlingame taught at Connecticut College for many years. He was at the Lincoln Studies Center at Knox College before joining the UIS faculty in 2009.
The symposium, also at the President Abraham Lincoln Hotel, begins at 10 a.m.
Presenters include Timothy S. Good, Edward Robert McClelland and Kate Masur, all who have written widely about Lincoln.
The Thomas F. Schwartz Symposium Luncheon speakers will be Jonathan W. White and William J. Griffing, authors of " A Great and Good Man: Rare, First-Hand Accounts of Abraham Lincoln." White, professor at Christopher Newport University and a director of the ALA, is also the author of " A House Built by Slaves: African American Visitors to the Lincoln White House," co-winner of the Gilder Lehrman Lincoln Prize.
The luncheon is at the President Abraham Lincoln Hotel at 11:30 a.m. Cost is $45.
Burlingame will lead a roundtable discussion with all symposium speakers at the hotel at 2:15 p.m. followed by a book-signing. Books will be available for purchase on site.
The ALA banquet begins at 7 p.m. preceded by a reception at 6 p.m. Tickets are $100 each and can be obtained online at abrahamlincolnassociation.org, by calling 217-546-2656 or by emailing KaySmith.ala@gmail.com.

title: It's a boy! Baby boy's arrival marks first baby born in Springfield in 2025
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The mom of Springfield's first baby has a New Year's resolution: to see her child grow to be happy and successful, and to give her kids the best life.
content:
The mom of Springfield's first baby has a New Year's resolution: to see her child grow to be happy and successful, and to give all her kids the best life that she can.
Aar'ion Henderson was born on New Year's Day at 9:40 a.m., weighing five pounds, 8.8 ounces and measuring 18.75 inches long.
The mother, Arion Malone, held Aar'ion in their room at HSHS St. John's Hospital where the two rested. She said she felt blessed to hold the healthy baby boy.
Having the year's first baby was unexpected, she said, but the birth of all her babies has been special. At home, she has two young boys and one young girl.
'All my babies are special and unique…they all came out beautiful and healthy. So, it's the same to me, and I'd do it again," she said.
Malone unfortunately faced a complication known as preeclampsia, meaning that very high blood pressure led to a two-week hospital visit before she was induced. That led to the child being born nearly a month before the due date.
Malone wanted for the baby to come a day sooner as was planned, but Aar'ion chose to meet the world on New Year's Day.

title: Madigan to take witness stand in his corruption trial
author: Hannah Meisel
description: In a turn of events, former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan will take the witness stand in his corruption trial.
content:
Former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan will take the witness stand in his corruption trial – an unexpected revelation that will likely stretch the already lengthy trial into late January.
The longtime House speaker's decision to testify is a risk, but it's also a surprise, given the quiet demeanor that was emblematic of his five decades in Springfield, including 36 years as the longest-serving legislative leader in the country.
Madigan faces 23 counts in a case that frames his power in government, politics and as a partner in his law firm as a 'criminal enterprise' meant to maintain and increase his power and enrich his allies. His co-defendant, longtime Springfield lobbyist Mike McClain, is accused on six related counts. Before the holiday break, McClain waived his own right to testify.
Prosecutors rested their case the week before Christmas after calling 50 witnesses and playing for the jury more than 150 wiretapped phone calls and videos secretly recorded by FBI cooperators. Attorneys had just finished questioning the eighth defense witness on Tuesday morning before the parties discussed a matter during a sidebar.
When U.S. District Judge John Blakey returned to the courtroom after a post-sidebar recess to his chambers, he asked Madigan if he could approach the bench. But he then changed his mind after attorneys said they needed to further research case law regarding whether the former speaker could testify in his own jury trial but not testify in a possible forfeiture bench trial if he is found guilty.
'So he'll testify now?' Blakey asked Madigan attorney Dan Collins, who indicated that the former speaker would be the next witness.
Prior to the revelation, Madigan's former law partner, Vincent 'Bud' Getzendanner, was expected to testify on Tuesday. But Madigan's time on the witness stand could take days or even weeks.
The former speaker has had at least one family present each day of trial
Madigan was indicted in March 2022 on nearly two dozen counts of racketeering, bribery, wire fraud and extortion. The feds allege Madigan helped electric utility Commonwealth Edison and telecom giant AT&T Illinois pass key pieces of legislation through Springfield in exchange for jobs and contracts for Madigan allies. Additionally, prosecutors say Madigan used his positions to recruit work for his property tax law firm.
McClain was charged alongside him, alleged to have acted as the conduit – and sometimes muscle – for multiple bribery schemes even beyond those pertaining to ComEd, which was his largest client as a contract lobbyist.
The former speaker's trial began in October after two weeks of jury selection. Despite the high-profile nature of the case, most of the 12 jurors and six alternates ultimately chosen had never heard of Madigan.

title: Sangamon County preview: How this Auburn senior is adding to family's basketball legacy
author: Bill Welt
description: Carter Hunley's uncle holds the Auburn boys basketball scoring record, plus what else to know about this week's Sangamon County Tournament
content:
Auburn senior guard Carter Hunley comes from a big hoops family that even includes his grandfather, Tom.
Hunley's uncle, Brett, still holds the boys basketball team's all-time scoring record with 1,664 career points, while dad, Paul, also lends a hand.
'My uncle was a basketball star at Auburn, he likes to keep telling me about that and how he scored the most points for all the boys and he likes to keep it in my ear,' Hunley said.
County bracket, results: Here are the 2025 Sangamon County Tournament boys basketball schedule and results
Hunley has also helped cement basketball history himself at Auburn. He was recently named to the all-tournament team, along with senior forward Clayton Kessler, after the Trojans captured their first Waverly Holiday Tournament since 2009.
It was another major milestone for the program after Auburn ended an even longer drought last season in which Auburn won its first Sangamon County Tournament title since 1986. Hunley appeared on that all-tournament team as well.
Auburn, currently ranked No. 9 in Class 2A by The Associated Press with a 16-1 overall record, is the No. 2 seed in this year's County tournament and meets either No. 7 Calvary or No. 10 Lutheran in the quarterfinals on Tuesday at 8 p.m. Williamsville, the top seed, is ranked No. 2 by the AP.
Hunley certainly takes a measure of pride in setting a legacy for future players.
'You just want to elevate the whole program,' Hunley said.
That winning mentality also extends to his teammates.
'We love playing together,' Hunley said. 'We've been playing together since we were five years old. We've always been best friends since kindergarten, it's a great chemistry and a great team.'
They all love sports in general.
Hunley was named to The State Journal-Register's all-area small school football team as a receiver and defensive back and over the spring won the fifth-place medal in the 4x400-meter relay at the Class 1A boys track and field state finals on a group that also included senior guard Jacob Barth.
Kessler also played receiver on the football team and was a state qualifier on the 4x800 relay, which also included Barth.
'Basketball has always been my favorite sport, it's definitely the sport that I've put in the most work in the offseason,' Kessler said. 'We just all have a really fun time playing together. We've been playing basketball since we were little kids and I think that's elevated our chemistry on the court.'
Kessler has undoubtedly developed a bigger presence in the frontcourt, alongside fellow senior forward Ryan Lash. They mesh seamlessly with guards Hunley, Barth and Cooper Carter. Four of those players reached double figures in a recent 84-66 win at Calvary on Tuesday.
It's indeed hard to single out one player.
'Every kid has taken a big stride and it's kudos to their work ethic,' Auburn coach Seth McCoy said. 'They don't take any days off. Our attendance was outstanding this summer and we challenged ourselves this summer with the teams that we played like Moline and Lanphier. It's a mature group, a great group of kids who work their tails off so I'm not surprised to see that jump.'
Here's what else to know about the tournament:
How to watch
The Sangamon County Tournaments returns to Cass Gymnasium on the campus of Lincoln Land Community College beginning Monday. Admission is $5 at the door and $2 for seniors.
Click here for the schedule and results.
Nearly a century ago...
Pawnee knocked off New Berlin 18-15 to win the first Sangamon County Tournament title on Feb. 28, 1925. Pawnee's John Fenoglio scored 12 points, while Bill Jabsen led New Berlin with eight points. The tournament resumed in 1927 and has been held at Cass Gymnasium virtually every year since 1976. This will be the 99 th County tournament.
Most championships
Plains has 19 County titles and had won four in a row until Auburn defeated New Berlin 51-38 in their first-ever championship meeting.
Riverton has 17 County titles, while New Berlin and Auburn each have nine. Chatham Glenwood, which dropped out of the tournament beginning in 1993, is third with 11.
Returning all-tournament players
Several players from last year's all-tournament team return to the floor, including Auburn senior guards Cooper Carter and Carter Hunley. The list also includes Calvary junior guard/forward Connor Brown, Riverton sophomore guard Julian Rice and Williamsville senior guard Blake Shoufler.

title: Trump's inauguration is Monday. Here are the Illinois lawmakers that will, won't attend
author: Tom Ackerman
description: President-elect Donald Trump will be sworn into office for a second time on Monday. Which Illinois representatives will be attending?
content:
President-elect Donald Trump will be sworn into office for a second term on Monday at the Presidential Inauguration.
The news outlet Axios reported that more than a dozen congressional Democrats are not planning to attend the inauguration. What Illinois Congressmen and Congresswomen will attend, and who won't? \
Here's what we found out.
What U.S. senators in Illinois plan to attend?
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Springfield, will attend.
U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Chicago, has not responded to inquiries.
What U.S. House representatives in Illinois plan to attend?
U.S. Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Highland Park, will attend.
U.S. Rep. Mike Bost, R-Murphysboro, will attend.
U.S. Rep. Mary Miller, R-Oakland, will attend.
U.S. Rep. Nikki Budzinski, D-Springfield, will attend.
U.S. Rep. Lauren Underwood, D-West Chicago, will attend.
U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood, R-Peoria, will attend.
U.S. Rep. Bill Foster, D-Naperville, will attend.
What U.S. House representatives in Illinois do not plan to attend?
U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Chicago, will not attend. The congresswoman told Axios that she "doesn't feel safe" to be present with supporters of the president-elect. Rep. Ramirez was sworn into Congress in 2023, so this would be her first opportunity to attend a presidential inauguration.
U.S. Rep. Sean Casten, D-Downers Grove, will not attend. Rep. Casten was sworn into Congress in 2019, which was after President-elect Trump was inaugurated, but he attended President Joe Biden's inauguration. Rep. Casten wrote in a statement to the SJ-R that he has a great respect for the office of the president, but he has found President-elect Trump "consistently failed to recognize that all of us who are in elected office succeed only to the extent that we hand our position off to our successor in better shape than we found it."
U.S. Rep. Jan Schakowsky, D-Evanston, will not attend because she will be recognizing MLK Day with her constituents. The representative did not attend the president-elect's first inauguration. Rep. Schakowsky attended President Biden's inauguration. "I know many of my constituents are concerned about the direction our country is headed in, and I want to assure them that anybody who goes after the people of the 9th Congressional District will have to come through me!", Rep. Schakowsky wrote in a statement to the SJ-R. "You have got a fighter on your side, and I will continue to push for a more just society, one in which our systems work for everyone, not just a wealthy few."
U.S. Rep. Jesús 'Chuy' García, D-Chicago, will not attend because he will be attending the MLK Breakfast hosted by the Rainbow PUSH Coalition. Rep. Garcia was sworn into Congress in 2019, which was after President-elect Trump's first inauguration, but he attended President Biden's inauguration.
U.S. Rep. Robin Kelly, D-Matteson, will not attend because she will be observing MLK Day with constituents. She attended the president-elect's first inauguration and also President Biden's inauguration. The representative said in a statement to the SJ-R that she chose to attend events honoring Martin Luther King Jr. to continue his work toward racial justice and civil rights while serving the people of her district, including feeding the hungry and donating blood. "As we enter the next Trump Administration, I hope the President will also recognize the need to advance civil rights for all, not just the select few. I look forward to working in Congress with colleagues on both sides of the aisle to make MLK's dreams a reality," Rep. Kelly wrote.
Who did not respond?
Some offices of representatives did not respond, and some did not know whether their respective official would be in attendance by the time of publication. Those delegates are:
U.S. Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Chicago, did not respond.
U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley, D-Chicago, did not respond.
U.S. Rep. Danny K. Davis, D-Chicago, did not respond.
U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Schaumburg, did not respond.
U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen, D-Moline, did not respond.

title: Edinburg stays unbeaten in MSM as Davis, Peacock lead Wildcats past Nokomis
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Treyton Davis went 5-for-10 from the 3-point line and Alex Peacock recorded a double-double as Edinburg topped Nokomis in an MSM Conference matchup.
content:
EDINBURG — It's been a long time since the MSM Conference's boys basketball title has gone through this small town in Christian County, not far from the Sangamon County line, but Edinburg got a key victory on Friday in the Wildcats' chances to make that happen.
Edinburg (17-2 overall, 4-0 MSM) got 21 points from junior Treyton Davis and 19 points and 18 rebounds from senior Alex Peacock to beat Nokomis 51-36.
Davis scored 15 points on his 5-for-10 shooting from behind the 3-point line. If he missed, there was a good chance the 6-foot-2 Peacock was there for the offensive rebound. Seven of his game-high 18 boards came on the offensive end.
After the game, Davis said it was the first time he's beaten Nokomis since junior high.
'It feels great,' he said. ' It (17-2) is the best start Edinburg's had in a long time... it feels really good (because) we've worked hard for it, and we know we can do it.'
Edinburg, which last had a 20-win season in 2006-07, is succeeding under second-year coach Rashawn Jones, who has installed a phrenetic defensive press and an up-tempo, always-moving-the-ball offensive system.
The Edinburg basketball program has just three regional championships: 2002 and 2006 were both Class A titles in the two-class system; the Wildcats won a Class 1A regional in 2013. The players aren't shy about sharing their goals.
'It's a big accomplishment for all of us as a team,' Peacock said of the win over Nokomis and the 17-2 mark. 'We knew coming into this season that we want to win something big, like a regional championship; we want to hang a banner up. We want to break the scoring record.'
Tuesday's 68-60 win over a Class 2A team, Litchfield, helped prepare the Wildcats for their date with Nokomis, coach Rashawn Jones said.
'I let them know Litchfield was pretty good,' said Jones, who was a freshman in the Lanphier program when the Lions finished fourth in the 2012 Class 3A state tournament. 'They scored back and forth with us for a little bit, but I let them know when you play Nokomis, they're going to be in your face. Defensively, you better be prepared for that 1-2-2 (zone press). I let them know you've got to be ready defensively. We know that they usually do a good job handling pressure, but we always talk about getting in their jerseys and that's what we want to do.'
Nokomis committed 22 turnovers, many of which led to Edinburg transition buckets.
'Taking care of the ball has been an issue for us more often than not this year,' Nokomis coach Dan DeWerff said. 'Sometimes we think we turn the corner and we've it figured out, but then you have a game like tonight where you have 11 turnovers in the first half. We have the kids; we just haven't turned the corner.'
Though Edinburg only won the turnover battle by five, DeWerff stressed there was a difference between the type of turnovers committed and the result.
'(Edinburg) can shoot it, they're skilled,' DeWerff said. 'I think we forced them into (17) turnovers, but our turnovers typically led to points for them, and we really didn't do much converting their turnovers into points for us."
Ian Keller led Nokomis (9-11, 2-2 MSM) with 13 points. Edinburg also had 21 free-throw attempts while Nokomis had six.
Nokomis got within 17-16 when Kannon Jonas hit a contested jumper in the paint midway through the second quarter before Davis connected on a deep 3-pointer. In the second half, it was all Edinburg. Peacock scored nine points in the third period while Davis had eight. That offense was enough for Edinburg to take a 39-27 lead into the final quarter.
Edinburg was 7-for-25 from behind the 3-point line; Nokomis was just one of 18 from deep. Finn Swinger and Keagan Getz each added a 3-pointer each for the Wildcats.
'They're skilled, they've got good shooting and they can score,' DeWerff said of Edinburg. 'You've seen the points they can put up against good teams. I'd just like to see us — we've got good kids — but I'd like to see more sense of urgency. Sometimes we do, sometimes we don't.
'We've got a better idea what we need to do on the offensive end. Defense is, at times, solid. We've just got to put it together for four quarters and that's been our issue: there's been eight, maybe 10 minutes, maybe even a half where we know what's going on and what we need to do, but then there's another half where that's not the case. We're having some inconsistency.'
A small community and some lean years due to success meant the Wildcats didn't always play in front of big crowds, even in their own gym. Davis has noticed that's starting to change.
'Now there's pretty much a packed house almost every home game we have,' Davis said.

title: State colors: Public voting begins for possible new Illinois flag. Here's how to vote.
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Following a state commission that narrowed down thousands of the public's flag designs to 10, the public can now vote for their favorite.
content:
Following a state commission that narrowed down thousands of flag designs to 10, the public can now vote for their favorite.
Residents can vote multiple times through Feb. 14 for flags they want to see waving across the state. Here's what you need to know.
How do I vote?
Head to ilsos.gov/stateflag.
Where can I see the new designs?
You can view the 10 designs at the ilsos.gov. website.
Can I vote for the existing state flag?
People can vote for one of the 10 new designs, or for one of the three former flag designs including the current state flag, the 1918 Centennial Flag and the 1968 Sesquicentennial Flag.
People can vote more than once?
Residents can vote for one flag every 24-hour period. They can also vote for different flags each day if they want. Votes cannot be altered once they are cast.
When will the winning flag be known?
After the public voting ends, the Illinois Flag Commission will count votes and report its findings and recommendations to the Illinois General Assembly by April 1. Members of the General Assembly will vote on whether to adopt a new flag, return to a previous iteration of the flag, or retain the current flag.
Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias' office is conducting the public vote.

title: Springfield man pleads guilty to fatally shooting couple in home near Southwind Park
author: Steven Spearie
description: A Springfield man pleaded guilty Wednesday in the fatal shooting of a couple near Southwind Park in September 2022.
content:
A Springfield man pleaded guilty Wednesday in the fatal shooting of a couple near Southwind Park in September 2022.
Mark N. Crites, Jr. was sentenced to natural life in prison in the shooting deaths of John and Gloria Norgaard in the 500 block of Southwind Road.
Under Illinois law, a life sentence is imposed if there are two or more deaths.
Circuit Court Judge John "Mo" Madonia found that Crites, 25, suffered from a mental illness at the time of shootings, leading to a "guilty but mentally ill" finding.
Crites will receive mental health treatment in the Illinois Department of Corrections.
Illinois Compiled Statutes defines mentally ill as "a substantial disorder of thought, mood, or behavior which afflicted a person at the time of the commission of the offense and which impaired that person's judgment, but not to the extent that he is unable to appreciate the wrongfulness of his behavior."
According to a news release from the Sangamon County State's Attorney's Office, Crites apologized to the Norgaard family members in court Wednesday.
Springfield Police reported Crites was involved in a fight with his brother late in the afternoon of Sept. 10, 2002, leading him to pour gasoline throughout their home in the 100 block of Genoa Drive. He then set the house on fire and fled.
Crites wandered into the Norgaards' home about a mile away. He did not know the couple.
The couple's bodies were discovered in their residence by a family member, who then called 911 around 8 a.m. on Sept. 11.
Crites was found sitting in the Norgaards' 2008 black Dodge Charger in Benld, a town of about 1,400 people about an hour south of Springfield the morning of Sept. 12.
A caller alerted the Gillespie police about the vehicle, which was found just off Illinois 138.
The firearm used in the murders was found in Crites' possession.
It was not determined why Crites had driven to Macoupin County.
John Norgaard was the owner and operator of Norgaard Paint and Body. Gloria was employed by Springfield Clinic. The couple had been married 45 years.
Their daughter, Elizabeth, said in court that "(Crites) took good people from us."
Crites' attorney, Daniel Fultz, did not offer comment.
State's Attorney John Milhiser said his thoughts and prayers were with the Norgaard family.
"Hopefully, the convictions and sentence today help to bring them closure," he said in the release.

title: Springfield bar offering subscription service for a latte savings
author: Claire Grant
description: Looking to save on some sips? A local coffee shop is trying a new payment model for customers. Here's what to know.
content:
Looking to save on some sips? A local coffee shop and non-alcoholic bar is trying a new payment model for customers.
Instead of paying $6 to $7 for a latte every other day, The Wakery at 5 W. Old State Capitol Plaza says don't even bring out your wallet – just pay a lump sum yearly for coffee at a discount.
The subscription service was first advertised on Jan. 7 on the business' Facebook page as a means to help purchase new kitchen equipment to expand the menu.
The subscription service spans from $75 for one drink a month to a whopping $895 for 20 coffee a month; a $25 subscription for the month of March is also available, with up to four redeemable drinks of choice.
Guests can get one coffee drink of any size and flavor per month and must make it a call pickup order to redeem. Subscription signup will close on Feb. 10 and start on March 3, running until Feb. 28, 2026.
Walking into the emerald green painted shop, jewel tones and gold cover the counter where business owner Elizabeth Wake offers a menu with a cheery owl on it.
The non-alcoholic bar serves mocktails, mixers and proofless drinks during the night, but most days the sales consist of the classic latte.
The bar expanded hours in the new year, the new hours are 7 a.m. to 11 a.m. and 4 p.m. to 10 p.m. Monday through Friday, after a tumultuous last year seeing the business reduce schedule to stay open.
The non-alcoholic bar in 2024 had two major Gofundme campaigns following a break-in at the store on Sept. 1, and the aftermath of the Adams Street fire in June, which caused the business to shutter doors for 10 days due to smoke damage and loss of inventory.

title: Central Illinois pawn shop owners, employees charged in retail crime operation
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The alleged crime operation happened at pawn shops in Springfield, Bloomington and Normal. Here are the details.
content:
Owners of some central Illinois pawn shops, along with employees have been charged for allegedly reporting merchandise as stolen and then reselling those products.
A Bloomington family that owns and operates several Monster Pawn shop stores is being charged, along with people in the Springfield area.
Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul said that the Pierce family and associates ran an organized retail crime operation at the stores, including the two Monster Pawn shops in Springfield, between November 2023 and July 2024.
The family, along with shop managers and employees allegedly bought new merchandise and then reported it as stolen. They allegedly resold the items online, below market value, according to a news release.
Raoul's office investigated the case along with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Investigations; the Illinois Department of Revenue Criminal Investigations Division; and the Bloomington, Chatham and Springfield police departments.
The crime allegedly happened at these stores:
Monster Pawn Springfield North LLC at the 200 block of North Grand Ave. E., in Springfield.
Monster Pawn Springfield Inc. at the 2300 block of South MacArthur Blvd. in Springfield.
Midwest Exchange Inc. at the 1400 block of East Empire St. in Bloomington.
Monster Pawn, Inc. at the 1600 block of R.T. Dunn Dr. in Bloomington.
Monster Pawn Normal Inc. at the 1400 block of S. Main St. in Normal.
Who is being charged?
Edwin Pierce, 65, is charged with being the organizer of a continuing financial crimes enterprise, for being the manager of organized retail crime, and other related felonies. He is also charged with eight counts of theft between $500 and $10,000. He is also charged with solicitation of theft and two counts of money laundering.
Everson Pierce, 28, is charged with being the organizer of a continuing financial crimes enterprise and for being the manager of organized retail crime. He is also charged with four counts of theft between $500 and $10,000 and two counts of money laundering.
Kathleen Pierce, 58, is charged with three misdemeanor counts of theft under $500.
Thomas O'Donnell, 57, of Normal, is charged with two counts of theft between two counts of money laundering, as well as misdemeanor charges.
Steven Mileham, 71, of Springfield, is charged with solicitation of theft and one count of theft between $500 and $10,000, as well as a charge for being the manager of organized retail crime.
Jessica Cloyd, 34, of Mechanicsburg, is charged with one count of theft between $500 and $10,000, as well as misdemeanor charges.
Carter Walker, 25, of Chatham, is charged with one count of theft between $500 and $10,000 and a misdemeanor charge.

title: If you're a foodie and like the water, this cruise might be for you
author: Jay Kitterman
description: The family-oriented ship features some 18 restaurants, 20 bars, two shows and many other activities.
content:
'Are you here with your husband?' This is a question I recently overheard — from a fellow traveler to a young lady on the Norwegian Cruise Line Cruise Ship Bliss. We celebrated New Years and our anniversary with the family and 5,800 other passengers and staff in the Western Caribbean.
The Norwegian Bliss started sailing in 2018 and just entered dry dock for a three-week complete refurbishment. It is part of the Breakaway-Plus class and has the capacity to hold over 4,000 passengers with 2,200 cabins. The ship has an overall length of 1,094 feet (or approximately three football fields), width of 136 feet and 20 decks. It has a height equivalent to a 15-story building.
The family-oriented ship features some 18 restaurants, 20 bars, two shows and many other activities. It took me a couple of days to figure out where everything was. My daily routine was rowing while overlooking the ocean portside in their massive gym, getting coffee for Carol (they even had a Starbucks) and placing towels to reserve chairs around the pool. Then it was breakfast at a buffet, which included my daily, fresh croissant.
The Bliss is a foodie traveler's dream ship. Numerous restaurants on board come with unique cuisines and atmospheres. Their 'Freestyle Dining' program allows you flexibility with no fixed dining times or pre-assigned seating. Dress up. Dress down. Sit with your friends, or make new ones.
Dine inside or oceanside along the waterfront. There are various dining and beverage plans to consider when booking. All the restaurants had the same wine list with a wide range of prices and wines The dining staff are international, and at a session I attended on 'Managing a Floating Hotel,' I learned that most of the chefs were from India. The Garden Café buffet featured numerous Indian dishes.
There is no longer a midnight buffet but 'The Local' is a 24-hour eatery on Deck 7. The Local offers classic pub fare in a relaxed pub atmosphere. With popular dishes like chicken pot pie, fish n' chips and daily dinner specials like prime rib, The Local has all your favorite comfort foods.
The Garden Café is a massive buffet on Deck 16. Whatever you're craving, you will find it at the Garden Café. This indoor restaurant serves breakfast, lunch and dinner — and the floor-to-ceiling windows provide picturesque ocean views. You also have the option to bring your food from the buffet out to the pool deck where there are tables.
The three main inclusive, white-tablecloth dining rooms are the Savor, Taste and Manhattan. The dinner menus were the same for the three and changed nightly. We were a group of eight and never had to wait more than 10 minutes for a table.
Specialty dining restaurants have fees and/or are included with premium dining packages. We dined at two of them, Teppanyaki and Le Bistro.
Teppanyaki featured flying shrimp, onion volcanoes, twirling knives and group singing led by the chef. We all sat around a lively shared table as the skillful chef sliced, chopped and grilled steak, seafood and chicken on a large steel grill right before our eyes.
Romance was in the air as Carol and I celebrated our anniversary in their signature French restaurant, Le Bistro.
Situated toward the top of the ship among floor-to-ceiling windows, the restaurant offers spectacular views. Elegant interiors, crisp white linens and attentive servers make this an intimate dining experience.
Other themed, specialty restaurants on the ship were Cagney's Steakhouse, Italian dining at La Cucina and Ocean Blue for seafood. Room service is available for a small service charge.
We did not try it, but Coco's, which serves chocolate treats on Deck 6, looked interesting. It has savory chocolate pralines, crepes, coffees and more types of divine treats than there are days of your cruise.
For those planning a cruise, I would recommend selecting a cabin that is mid-ship (above and below other rooms), close to the elevators and not a room above or below any of the restaurants or bars. I would also avoid being underneath the pool deck. If you have any motion sickness issues, mid-ship cabins are more stable.
For the kids and families, there is a racetrack, multiple water slides, bowling, laser tag, miniature golf, family karaoke and kids' camps.
For adults, I counted 16 bars, a comedy club, a club with Beatles impersonators and live entertainment everywhere. We saw the full production of the Jersey Boys with a very talented cast in the ship's theater. In the casino, Carol won 37 cents one night on the penny slots.
In a session I attended led by the captain, he was asked why the ships are getting so large. His response was, 'It's all about demand. It was not long ago that around 2,500 people would be cruising weekly in Alaska, and now in-season, there are over 100,000.' I can see why. The service provided by the staff was exceptional. I think they are trained to try to never say 'no' to a request. A cruise provides a weeklong vacation with new adventures daily and never having to repack your luggage.
One final note — next time you complain about your gas mileage, keep in mind that our captain reported theirs was 17 feet for every gallon of fuel.
Bon voyage, and I hope to see you on a future cruise!
Jay Kitterman is a culinary and special events consultant and adjunct instructor at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management and Baking/Pastry, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: One of the country's fastest growing coffee shops is opening in Chatham
author: Claire Grant
description: A new coffee shop is opening later this year in Chatham. Here are the details.
content:
Noticed something new about Chatham? A big old moving sign on the Country Financial place marker and flags to set the stage for the village's latest coffee stop.
Popping up this spring with the flowers will be Scooter's Coffee, one of the largest expanding chains currently in America. The building will be finished in the spring and is expected be opening in the summer.
Taking over the Country Financial office acreage at 1220 N. Main St., franchise owner Lauryn McGlasson says the lease process is finalizing for the offices, and the new coffee location will be built in the front.
In 2024, Scooter's Coffee was named the second fastest-growing brand by Yelp after the coffee giant had a 53% jump in net new locations. The tiny coffee model was the top growing brand in the Midwest with more than 850 stores across 31 states.
McGlasson, who owns the business with her husband Marcus, are multi-time Scooters franchise owners. The couple from Pleasant Plains opened their first location in Taylorville back in 2021 when Lauryn was a PRN nurse, before opening two Springfield locations.
'We were traveling on vacation and wanted to stop for coffee,' McGlasson said. 'Our only options were Starbucks or Scooters Coffee. We had never tried Scooters Coffee so decided to give it a try, we were impressed with the quality of coffee we were served through a drive through coffee shop so decided to look into franchising.'
McGlasson said when signing an agreement with Scooter's Coffee, part of the agreement was to open four locations.
Chatham just happened to be in the territory for expansion and as a growing community, the couple chose the spot at the right moment.
'The last two years we have been trying to put a location in Chatham but finding the perfect location,' McGlasson said. 'Purchasing the perfect location and permitting takes a lot of time.'
Once constructed, a Scooter's tends to employ anywhere from 15 to 20 baristas.
Commenters on Facebook have pledged worry about Chatham's local coffee and ice cream shop, Scoop Du Jour, losing business over the opening of the new location. McGlasson said every time the couple has previously built a store they have encountered pushback but it is important for them as entrepreneurs to open their franchise like their own small business.
'Someone will always have an opinion, positive or negative, and they are entitled to that opinion,' McGlasson said. 'We are entrepreneurs, just like any other small business owner, but we choose a Scooter's franchise because they provide a support system to help us run our business.'

title: Lions bite down: Lanphier cruises past Southeast to claim City title; SHS takes 2nd
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Lanphier might not be used to having the No. 3 seed in the City Tournament, but the Lions are more than accustomed to winning the title.
content:
Lanphier's 56-23 matinee victory over Southeast got the party started early for the Lions on Saturday.
And the party might have gone deep into the night after Lanphier secured their second straight boys City basketball tournament championship on the floor of the Bank of Springfield Center.
The third-seeded Lions ran the table, taking down No. 2 seed Sacred Heart-Griffin 62-56 on Thursday and then defeating top seed Springfield High 54-48 on Friday.
The Lions eased past the Spartans on the final night with a 28-1 run that started in the first quarter and spilled late into the second period. Lanphier led 35-8 at the half and forced 17 Southeast turnovers.
The igniters during the spurt were seniors Shaunassey Hatchett Jr. and JaiQuan Holman and junior Soriano Hayes. The trio combined for 43 points in all. Hatchett Jr. led the way with 17 points and eight rebounds, Hayes scored 15 with six boards and Holman tallied 11 points.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
'It's really exciting. I knew we could do it,' said Hatchett while wearing the championship basketball net around his neck. We just had to lock in — we played some tough opponents, and I feel like we really came through with it.'
Lanphier felt slighted coming into City as a third seed.
'That gave us more aggression and we felt like we had something to prove,' Holman stated. 'We came in here with a chip on our shoulder and handled our business.'
With the triumph, the Lions (16-8 overall, 4-3 in CS8) extended their winning streak to six games and Holman commented on the current state of the team.
'Everybody had high hopes for us, and we didn't start off how we wanted to start,' Holman said. 'We're getting back together as a team and we're only going to get better. We want to go on a run, we've got big expectations late in the season. We want to extend our season until March and go to state.'
Holman and Hatchett Jr. have been running mates since sophomores in coach Blake Turner's lineup. This City title felt a bit sweeter, Holman alluded.
'I wouldn't want to share this with nobody else,' he said of Hatchett Jr. 'He's a good teammate and I couldn't ask for a better partner.'
Senior leadership, as Turner explained, has been stressed throughout his coaching career at Lanphier, and for this season that included seniors Torioun Rice and Amari Anderson.
'Our senior leadership — I wasn't as happy with it at the beginning of the year — but it's come on strong late,' Turner said. 'When you're a good leader, your teammates don't want to let you down. I think that JaiQuan and Shaunassey are playing like men on a mission. The team knows what it means to those two and I don't think they want to let them down, and they are playing like it.'
But it will take even more if Lanphier wants to make a deep run into March.
'Our bench has been huge,' Turner said. 'We're starting to form a rotation of guys off the bench that can contribute — knowing their roles, knowing the way we want to play, putting defense ahead of everything and putting our team first. I think those are the things that are going to make us a hard out in the postseason.'
Southeast (2-20, 0-7), in rebuilding mode, finished the tournament 0-3. Senior guard Tim Herrington had a team-high six points and four rebounds to lead the Spartans.
Springfield High 47, Sacred Heart-Griffin 41: Eli Wade and Noah Wade combined for 25 points as the Senators took control with an 11-2 first quarter and never trailed to finish the City Tournament with a 2-1 record.
It wasn't the finish the Senators wanted when they came to the BOS Center with the No. 1 seed, but after losing 54-48 to No. 3 Lanphier on Friday, SHS coach Marques Warfield reminded his team that postseason seeds and Central State Eight Conference standings are still up for grabs.
"The Central State Eight is a tough conference. We don't get the respect that we deserve," Warfield said. "Chatham's a good team, Lanphier's a good team, Griffin's a good team, we're a good team, Rochester's a good team. I'll put our conference up against anybody in the state of Illinois, and I mean that."
SHS senior Valor Komolafe finished with two of his three career City Tournament wins. For that, the 2025 tournament will be memorable.
"Our team had more energy than the years before," Komolafe said. "We came with a different energy. Did you see how we came out: 11-2 after the first quarter."
Eli Wade, a junior, led SHS with 13 points while sophomore Noah had 12.
Zion Lee led SHG with 12 points and Myles Montgomery finished with 10.
2025 City Tournament final standings

Chefs, restaurants and restaurateurs from Illinois have been an announced for the annual James Beard awards.
The finalists were recently announced.
The competition is considered to be one of the nation's most prestigious honors in the food industry.
Here's what to know.
What semifinalists were nominated from Illinois?
Frontier and Ina Mae Tavern, Chicago - Best Restaurant Semifinalist
Lee Wolen of Boka, Chicago - Outstanding Chef presented by Hilton
Galit, Chicago - Outstanding Restaurant presented by Acqua Panna Natural Spring Water
Jacob Potashnick of Feld, Chicago - Emerging Chef presented by S.Pellegrino Sparkling Natural Mineral Water

Marika Josephson and Aaron Kleidon of Scratch Brewing, Ava - Outstanding Professional in Beverage Services
Thomas Kakalios of Asador Bastian, Chicago - Outstanding Professional in Beverage Services
Are there any ties to Springfield?
Yes. Boka Restaurant Group was founded by Rob Katz and Springfield native Kevin Boehm in 2002. Boehm has established himself as one of the world's foremost hospitality visionaries, opening 40 restaurants over the past three decades.
About the James Beard Awards
The James Beard Awards recognizes exceptional talent and achievement in the culinary arts, hospitality, media, and broader food system, as well as a demonstrated commitment to equity, community, sustainability, and a culture where all can thrive.
What do winners receive?
Along with the prestige of winning, all James Beard Award winners receive a certificate, and a medallion engraved with the James Beard Foundation Awards insignia.
When will winners be announced?
The list will be narrowed down in the coming weeks, with the final nominees made public in April. The winners will be announced in June in Chicago.

title: Trump orders United States to exit WHO again. Health experts warn of danger.
author: Eduardo Cuevas
description: The day-one executive order fulfills a campaign promise. Health experts worry it puts US health at risk.
content:
NEW YORK — President Donald Trump is pulling the U.S. out of the World Health Organization for a second time, the White House announced late Monday.
The day-one executive order fulfills Trump's campaign promise to reject global institutions. Health experts worry it isolates the U.S. with consequences for pandemic and disease response and diplomatic relations worldwide.
The U.S. is and has historically been the largest funder of the global health agency headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. WHO, part of the United Nations, is tasked with preparing for and fighting health emergencies. The U.S. has strongly influenced the agency since its founding after World War II.
Trump criticized WHO for its handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, even as his administration faced scrutiny for being slow to respond to the crisis. In 2020, at the height of the pandemic, he began the process of pulling out from WHO.
Despite his promise, he failed to do so under U.S. law governing the timeline for withdrawal and funding obligations to the agency. Former President Joe Biden reversed Trump's decision after taking office and restored funding to WHO.
Trump's executive order — on the first day of his second term rather than the last year of his first presidency — allows him to actually carry out his decision.
The order said the U.S. was withdrawing "due to the organization's mishandling of the COVID-19 pandemic that arose out of Wuhan, China, and other global health crises, its failure to adopt urgently needed reforms, and its inability to demonstrate independence from the inappropriate political influence of WHO member states." It also cited the "unfairly onerous payments" the U.S. has made to support the organization.
During the Biden administration the U.S. continued its role as the largest funder of the agency, which has a budget of $6.8 billion in the current fiscal year. Nearly a fifth of WHO's budget in 2023 came from the U.S.
The U.S. has been a part of WHO since 1948, the same year the organization launched, and the departure would make the nation the only major power that's not a member of the 194-country body.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has said the agency will do everything to cooperate with the incoming Trump administration to continue to strengthen for global health security, Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson, said in an email. The partnership between WHO and the U.S. has "as protected and saved millions of lives in America and around the world," Jašarević said, citing the director-general.
'Grave strategic error,' health experts say
Trump's announcement had been expected by health experts. In public and private, officials and academics raised concerns about the decision, which they said endangers the health of the nation and the world.
In December, Dr. Ashish Jha, the Biden White House's former COVID-19 response coordinator, called it a 'catastrophic mistake' for the global community and a 'terrible mistake' for the U.S.
'This is going to be a grave strategic error that will make America less healthy and less safe,' Lawrence Gostin, a global public health expert and the faculty director of Georgetown University's O'Neill Institute for National and Global Health Law, told USA TODAY.
'The withdrawal itself is going to isolate the United States,' Gostin said. 'It'll isolate us diplomatically, and it'll isolate us in pandemic response.'
How will U.S. withdraw from WHO?
Trump's order will require arduous disentangling of American and global health institutions woven together for 75 years.
WHO's constitution, drafted in New York, doesn't have a clear exit method for member states. A joint resolution by Congress in 1948 outlined that the U.S. can withdraw with one year's notice. This is contingent, however, on ensuring that its financial obligations to WHO 'shall be met in full for the organization's current fiscal year.'
The U.S. is the only member state to have made such an exit strategy, Jašarević, of WHO, said. The former Soviet Union withdrew from WHO in 1949 during Cold War tensions, though returned years later.
Questions remain on how the U.S., and the rest of the world, will interact and respond to health emergencies in the future.
The U.S. leaving WHO would grievously weaken the global health agency from responding to outbreaks, conduct surveillance and cooperate closely, Gostin said.
'Our public health agencies would be flying blind,' he said.
For example, the Pan-American Health Organization, WHO's regional office for the Americas, is based in Washington, D.C. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also has staff at WHO and elsewhere globally.
American response alongside WHO has been key in fighting diseases such as polio, which has been nearly eradicated, and HIV/AIDS, under a President George W. Bush-era program that has helped curb transmission in several countries. The Bush program is considered a success both in public health and diplomatic relations.
Even more technically, information-sharing between the U.S. and WHO has been key not only to disease response, but also pharmaceutical developments to rapidly innovate and create life-saving vaccines and treatments, Gostin said.
Gostin now worries of other emerging diseases and pandemic threats that could leave the U.S. weaker and more vulnerable.
This includes a mpox, which has killed at least a thousand people in Africa in 2024, and bird flu circulating in the U.S. American officials assessed that bird flu has 'moderate' risk of becoming a pandemic, and just one or two mutations in the avian influenza viruses that have been circulating could make it more contagious or severe in humans.
Gostin cited Operation Warp Speed, the accelerated COVID-19 vaccine effort, which was led by the U.S. during Trump's first administration. Then, the U.S. provided vaccines to its entire population before offering them to vulnerable people elsewhere, which struck many around the world as unfair.
'In the next pandemic,' Gostin said, 'we might find ourselves at the back of the line, on the outside looking in.'

title: Video shows cold iguana falling from tree in Florida then getting bit by cat: Watch
author: Kinsey Crowley
description: Cold weather in Florida made lizards fall from trees. One green iguana fell from a tree in North Miami Beach, as caught on camera.
content:
Show Caption
Amid a cold snap that brought snow to Southern states, Florida got so cold that lizards fell out of trees.
Often mentioned as an indicator of how cold it is for the Sunshine State, invasive green iguanas become immobilized as temperatures approach freezing and fall from their sleeping places on tree branches.
On Jan. 22, Avrohom Eliezer Friedman's security camera captured this phenomenon in North Miami Beach, where temperatures dipped to the low 50s, according to AccuWeather. The stunned iguana also had a run-in with another animal, as caught on camera.
Watch cold iguana fall from tree, get bit by cat
The security camera footage shows the iguana suddenly falling from the tree and landing on the concrete driveway. It appears to bounce slightly and move its legs before resting there.
Later in the footage, a cat shows up, crouched near the iguana. The cat sniffs the iguana's tail and appears to bite it, startling the iguana. The two creatures jump in opposite directions, and the cat stays back from the lizard in the video.
The lizard slowly walked away the next morning, a resident said.
Why do Florida iguanas fall from trees when it gets cold?
Green iguanas are an invasive species originally introduced from warmer climates in Central and South America, according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). They live on the ground, in shrubs or in trees anywhere, including suburban developments and urban areas. And they don't handle cold well.
"When temps dip to near freezing, nonnative green iguanas can temporarily lose all muscle control, sometimes even falling out of trees," the FWC said in a social media post last week.
They don't actually die and they don't freeze solid, but when temperatures drop far enough, iguanas become immobilized. And if they were sleeping in a tree, they may lose their grip and drop to the ground.
Like all cold-blooded animals, iguanas can't generate their own heat so as the surrounding temperatures drop, so does theirs. They survive cold weather by slowing down their blood flow, circulation and heart rate.
But the paralysis is temporary most of the time. When the temperatures rise again, the stunned iguanas will usually get up and resume their business.

title: Some Illinois residents are able to file taxes for free this year. Here's what to know.
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Tax season is officially upon us and some Illinois residents will be able to file their taxes for free this year. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Tax season is officially upon us.
Illinois residents can start filing taxes Jan. 27.
Some Illinois residents will be able to file their 2024 federal tax returns for free.
Here's what you need to know.
Who can file their federal taxes for free?
Check to see if you are eligible by visiting https://directfile.irs.gov.
How can it be free?
Illinois is participating in the Internal Revenue Service's Direct File program this year. Through the program, the eligible taxpayers would be filing their federal returns directly with the IRS.
"It offers a range of benefits for taxpayers, including free federal tax return filing, step-by-step guidance, and real-time online support," a spokesperson wrote.
Direct File has no income limits for filers.
For those who choose to file a federal return using Direct File, the program afterwards will connect taxpayers to Illinois' free state income tax filing system, MyTax Illinois, where people can file and complete their Illinois state returns.
Do I have to file with Direct File?
No, people can still choose to file using tax-prep software, a tax professional, or the paper Form IL-1040.
How quickly can I receive a refund?
Taxpayers who file an Illinois return electronically with no errors should receive a direct deposit refund in about four weeks. The Where's My Refund? tool, which is updated each night, is the simplest way to track your refund within 24 hours of e-filing. For taxpayers who filed a paper return, refund information is normally available after four weeks.
When is the tax filing deadline?
April 15, 2025.
What is the deadline to file an extension?
The deadline to file for an extension is April 15, according to the IRS. That gives taxpayers until Oct. 15 to file without penalties.

title: How this star pitching prospect elevated Chatham Glenwood boys basketball to win over Rochester
author: Adrian Dater
description: Cam Appenzeller, signed to the University of Tennessee baseball team, is currently the epicenter of the Chatham Glenwood boys basketball team's rise
content:
CHATHAM – Cam Appenzeller is 6-foot-5 and one of the most dominant big men in the Central State Eight Conference. The lefthanded senior with Chatham Glenwood can play above the rim, as his many dunks and swatted opposition shot attempts attest. By necessity, Appenzeller is now the tallest point guard in the CS8 — and it's working out quite well for the Titans.
Appenzeller, a three-sport star and a potential Major League Baseball first-round pick as a pitcher, was moved to the backcourt earlier this season when senior Mason Marshall was lost — probably for the season — with a left leg injury. While Marshall watched from the bench still encumbered by a brace, Appenzeller was the ball general in host Glenwood's 51-36 victory Saturday afternoon over Rochester.
Appenzeller has usually played on the wing in coach Todd Blakeman's offensive system, but Marshall always brought the ball up and made the first pass. Now, Appenzeller hangs back when his team gets the ball and brings it up. He is proving quite capable of making such a big adjustment.
'It really sucks with Mason out, but someone's got to take care of the ball and make plays, and I'm willing to do that for the team,' said Appenzeller, who had eight points, seven assists and nine rebounds for the Titans (15-6, 5-1 CS8). 'I know we've got other guys who can run the offense, but I know the plays and feel like I can run the point guard well and get everybody else shots.'
Appenzeller protects the ball well, always spinning his way up the court. With his long strides, he can get by opponents quickly on the first dribble. His size makes him a handful for opposing guards, not just in the backcourt but also when shots go up. The lefty, who has signed to attend the University of Tennessee on a baseball scholarship, will frequently crash the boards on misses while fellow guard Gavin Simmons rotates up high defensively if the ball goes the other way.
When Marshall went down early in the season, Blakeman knew Appenzeller's versatility made a logical choice as a replacement.
'We needed somebody to bring the ball up, and Cam's really fit that role,' Blakeman said. 'I'm very happy with what he's done and kind of taken the team under his wing. He's playing really well right now. He did a good job today getting in the middle of the zone and getting other guys shots.'
The Titans had a balanced attack, with 6-7 senior center Mason Neumann scoring a game-high 14 points, with Simmons adding 13 and 6-4 senior forward Jonathan Helm 11. The difference in the win over Rochester was Glenwood's considerable size advantage, with Neumann, Appenzeller and Helm making it prohibitive for Rockets players to get shots off in the paint.
Glenwood raced to a 7-0 lead, and the game was never closer than five points from there. Senior Jack Melton was the only Rockets player to reach double figures, with 11 points. The Rockets fell to 16-7, 4-4 in the conference.
Neumann, who said he is 'talking to a couple of (colleges) right now', said the difference between this season's team and the up-and-down one of last season: defense.
'One of our goals this year was to keep teams under 40 points, and we did that today,' Neumann said. 'If we do that, it's hard to lose a game. We've got a lot size, so we need to use that to our advantage.'
By having Appenzeller play up top defensively, instead of the 5-11 Marshall, teams are finding it harder to get by him and into the paint. If anyone does, he, Neumann and Helm are often there to either reject shots or make opponents have to contort themselves just to get them off. Missed Rochester shots Saturday were akin to big slabs of red meat to hungry lions for the tall Titans trio.
'I took off two years, and last year was really the first introduction to our style of defense and our style of play,' Blakeman said. 'When guys went down at the beginning of the year (including Neumann for a while), I think guys just got an idea that if you want to win, you've got to guard people. I think we're doing that, and getting more of an identity.'

title: 33 Illinois counties explore formation of a new state. Here's what could happen
author: Steven Spearie
description: More than 30 Illinois counties are looking to leave the state and join another state. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Thirty-three counties are exploring the possibility of forming a separate state, distancing themselves from Cook County.
The Illinois Separation Movement is efforting to get more counties and municipalities to weigh in on separation.
Indiana has crafted a bill setting up a commission to consider boundary adjustments with Illinois.
Two Springfield-area counties have passed referendums voicing a preference to explore the possibility of forming a separate Illinois by distancing themselves from Cook County.
Now a separatist movement wants even more voters to weigh in on that issue in 2026.
In all, 33 counties in downstate Illinois have voted affirmatively to explore formation of a new state.
Illinois isn't alone in that movement.
Counties in eastern Oregon have made noise about joining Idaho. Upstate New York could also separate, and conversations are being had in Minnesota, Colorado, Maryland and California.
The speaker of the House of Representatives in Indiana has appeared to roll out the welcome mat for dissatisfied Illinois counties, although Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker thought the move was "a stunt."
Here's a look at the situation:
'They've lost their voices'
Greene County, about 45 minutes southwest of Springfield, was among seven counties to approve a non-binding referendum in November. Other counties included Calhoun, Jersey, Iroquois, Clinton, Perry and Madison.
Northwest of the Springfield area, Brown County voters endorsed the referendum in 2022.
G.H. Merritt of New Illinois, a non-profit and educational group that helps create county committees to further the work, said the issue of separation is less an ideological one than a rural vs. urban divide.
"In numerous states, the rural people are underrepresented, and, in some cases, you could make the argument that they've lost their voices," said Merritt, who lives in Lake County. "We look at this as a civil rights issue."
Don't call it 'secession'
Merritt and Loret Newlin, director/coordinator of Illinois Separation Movement, are both aware of the connotation of "secession" regarding the Confederacy during the Civil War.
Newlin said her group, which efforts to get referendums on ballots, uses "separation" or 'state split' because Article IV, Section 3 of the U.S. Constitution "allows us to form a new state from within a state without withdrawing from the Union. It doesn't require a Constitutional amendment."
Merritt said, "nobody looks at Maine and thinks, 'what a bunch of secessionists.' They went through this process because their needs weren't being met."
Maine, once part of Massachusetts, came into the Union through the Missouri Compromise of 1820 as "a free state" keeping the balance when Missouri was admitted as "a slave state."
'It's not going to happen'
None of the 33 counties voted on anything other than having their county boards look at the possibility of separating and becoming its own state, "never about joining another state," said Newlin, who lives in Jasper County. Neither has her movement advocated for that, she added.
Eric Ivers, a member of the Jersey County Board, said his personal preference would be to see some of the counties go to Indiana, some to Missouri and possibly others to Kentucky, Iowa and Wisconsin.
"That would be entirely up to the counties and the various states they would like to join," Ivers said.
Creating a new state, Ivers said, "would be nearly impossible for political reasons." It would upset the long-term balance of the U.S. Senate because those senators would likely be Republican, and national Democrats, he said, "would work hard to keep the Illinois government from approving that."
Ivers said there is "a political realignment happening in the U.S. (and)...it makes sense to also have a geographical realignment."
Any boundary change is a heavy lift, requiring the approval of the legislatures of the states involved, plus the U.S. Congress.
Merritt said at least people like Indiana House Speaker Todd Huston, whose bill creates a so-called "Indiana-Illinois Boundary Adjustment Commission," "understands the dynamics of what is going on and why (some Illinoisans) are dissatisfied."
Pritzker seemed to stymie such talk.
"It's not going to happen," Pritzker said recently. "I'll just say Indiana is a low-wage state that doesn't protect workers, a state that does not provide health care for people when they're in need, and so I don't think it's attractive for anybody in Illinois where wages are higher, where the standard of living is higher, and we do provide health care for people in need."

title: Pritzker calls Trump 'incompetent', says Illinois families will feel impact of new tariffs
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Governor of Illinois has taken to both national TV and social media to voice concerns about the new presidential administration.
content:
Gov. Pritzker calls Pres. Trump "incompetent."
The governor has been vocal about tariffs, citing Candada and Mexico as significant trading partners to Illinois.
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt spoke about the governor in reference to statements he made.
The Governor of Illinois has taken to both national TV and social media to voice concerns about the new presidential administration.
Gov. JB Pritzker in one posting on social media called President Donald Trump incompetent.
'I know these are challenging times – and the Trump administration is trying to confuse the American people,' Gov. Pritzker posted on X. 'That's why it's so important we speak plainly: Donald Trump is incompetent.'
Gov. Pritzker also spoke up about tariffs, posting a clip of him speaking on a segment of MSNBC theweekend that aired on Saturday.
When prompted to talk about tariffs that Pres. Trump imposed, Gov. Pritzker said the people of Illinois and the U.S. are going to pay the price.
'Mexico and Canada are our two largest trading partners here in Illinois. We get most of our natural gas and also gasoline North, from Canada. So, when you impose a 25% tariff, you're imposing that tariff on working families in Illinois," he said.
Illinois exported over $20 billion to Canada in 2023, according to the Illinois Department of Commerce. Second to Canada, Illinois exported nearly $13 billion to Mexico in that year.
He went on to label the tariffs as well as the 'Trump tax.'
'The Trump tax goes right along with the Trump tax of taking away things like Meals on Wheels, the freeze that he put in place, taking away head start and childcare from working families so they can't hold down a job because there's nowhere to take their kids. Our seniors who are in nursing homes have Medicaid taken away from them… these are the Trump tax.
The governor also spoke on immigration raids happening in Chicago in the MSNBC interview.
An anchor asked Gov. Pritzker to comment on White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt recently speaking about Pritzker in reference to statements he has made that he would not comply with Pres. Trump's immigration policy.
"We here in Illinois follow the law. They don't seem to believe in that at the white house. Consistently, they've been breaking the law, and they've put in place unconstitutional orders," he said.
Gov. Pritzker said he wants to see arrests made and the deportation of violent criminals who are undocumented immigrants, but he advocated for immigrants who live in the state legally.
"Frankly, I don't want them in my state or in the country. Those laws are on the books already. But we also have laws on the books that say that people who have been here a long time who are following the rules, who are paying their taxes, who are holding down jobs -- who happen to be undocumented -- we're not going to have our police here locally coordinating with federal officials to have them taken away. We want people like that in this country. We're a country of immigrants, mostly, and we ought to abide by that principal."

title: 'Wherever he goes, good things happen': Springfield's Daly seeks seventh Super Bowl ring
author: Steven Spearie
description: If the Kansas City Chiefs win Super Bowl LIX on Sunday, Springfield's Brendan Daly will be on par with Tom Brady with seven rings.
content:
Springfield's Brendan Daly has coached in nine of the last 11 Super Bowls.
A win in Super Bowl LIX Sunday would put Daly on equal footing with Tom Brady with seven rings.
Jim McMann said he always saw "drive" in Brendan Daly.
But a six-winning Super Bowls kind of "drive?"
"There was nothing given to him at all," said McMann, a Springfield Fire Department captain who came to Sacred Heart-Griffin as a football assistant under Ken Leonard in 1990, Daly's sophomore year. "A lot of guys could've hung it up. But when you have that drive and sometimes you get hooked up with the right coaches and you all keep moving on together, that's huge."
Daly, who still has family in Springfield, has been part of the National Football League's two biggest dynasties this century.
As an assistant coach, he has won three rings with both the New England Patriots and the Kansas City Chiefs. The linebackers coach punched his ticket to another Super Bowl after his Chiefs beat the Buffalo Bills in the AFC Championship Game.
Daly has coached in nine of the last 11 Super Bowls. The two times he didn't make it, his team was one game away from getting there.
A win Sunday against the Philadelphia Eagles would give the Chiefs and unprecedented "three-peat" and give Daly his seventh ring, on par with Tom Brady, widely regarded as the greatest quarterback of all time.
"It's hard to fathom what that would take, and you have to also be lucky in some of those games," McMann, 56, said in a recent interview at SHG. "All it takes is one bad play, one bad call, one bad anything and it's over. You have to be lucky, and you have to be really, really good and he's on a really, really squad."
If McMann didn't see the next Dick Butkus in Daly as a player at SHG, he did see a relentless worker who served as a role model for SHG's younger players.
Daly went on to play football at Drake University, where he would return as a graduate assistant and tight ends coach.
Daly's nomadic coaching career had an inauspicious start at Ridgewood High School in New Port Richey, Florida, in 1997 when the team didn't win a game.
"That's the stuff," McMann said, "people need to find and know about."
McMann has kept in contact with Daly all along and has been to games and training practices at Daly's invitation.
Daly is usually one of the first to text McMann after an SHG win or loss and McMann reciprocates after Chiefs games.
"(Those) are a lot more congratulatory," McMann laughed.
In a more sobering moment, Daly, McMann recalled, was one of the first ones to check in on him when he heard about McMann's house fire July 4.
"That text meant a lot to me," McMann admitted.
Pat Selinger said Daly hasn't forgotten about Springfield.
For the last several years, Daly has donated a Chiefs ticket package and post-game on-the-field activity to Christ the King Parish 's annual auction, Selinger said.
When Christ the King School recently named Daly its distinguished alum, he sent an encouraging video that was played at an all-school Mass.
"To me, the biggest thing that blows me away is how humble he is," said Selinger, who went to school with Daly's younger brother, Tim. "A guy who's been in nine of the last 11 Super Bowls, it's humble pie. He's a good dude."
McMann said he will be at home with his family watching Sunday's Super Bowl, cheering on Daly, naturally.
"It's been a fun ride," McMann said. "Who knows how many more he could get?
"Wherever he goes, good things happen."
