title: Four recently closed Subways in Springfield are anticipated to reopen with new owners
author: Natalie Morris
description: While a four Subways have closed, a Springfield-based business is expanding and opening its third location.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Four Subway locations in Springfield, Illinois have closed after the franchise owner retired.
Springfield-based HAE's Bakery & Coffee Shoppe is expanding with a third location in Sherman, Illinois.
Four Subway locations have been shuttered in Springfield. But it is anticipated most will reopen under new ownership.
Vern Evans – sole owner of VCM Inc. franchise, which owned the four sites – said he has retired after operating as a Subway franchisee for 25 years in the Springfield market. His Springfield holdings at 1827 W. Jefferson St., 607 E. Adams St., 2359 W. Monroe St. and 417 South Grand Ave. E. – all closed Jan. 14.
'I closed them to retire, but I believe a new owner will be reopening them eventually,' Evans said. 'My impression is most will be reopened.'
A Google search lists all but the South Grand Avenue business as 'temporarily closed.'
Evans was one of four franchise operators for the Connecticut-based sandwich chain operating in the Springfield market before his retirement. The Chatham resident said he was not at liberty to name who will be taking over his former locations, but that none of the other Springfield franchise operators will be enlarging their footprint with the transition.
Springfield-based business expanding
HAE's Bakery & Coffee Shoppe is expanding beyond the Springfield market.
Owners of the Springfield-based business announced plans this week for a third location on track to open in Sherman this summer.
'They don't have a coffee shop in Sherman and our (food) truck did really well there,' said Amy Benad, who co-owns the business with her husband Christian. 'We figured (the next) brick and mortar would do best there.'
Benad said HAE's will be located in the yet-to-be-built strip mall at 290 Crossing Drive in Sherman – tucked between the Fairlane Diner and Casey's convenience store. Construction is expected to begin later this month.
Hae's Bakery & Coffee Shoppe food truck operated from the same site the fourth quarter of 2024 before closing shop to allow groundwork to begin for the new construction project.
Reggie Sadiku, who owns the property and is building the two-unit, 3,000-square-foot strip mall, said a May completion date is the goal. Sadiku, who also owns the Fairlane Diner, purchased the Sherman Car Wash at 290 Crossing Drive in 2024 before demolishing the building last spring.
Benad said HAE's Bakery & Coffee Shoppe will occupy roughly 1,500 square feet and have a drive-through window and a lobby.
The Benads opened their first brick-and-mortar location at 917 W. Jefferson St. in 2022 after the bakery got its start online as a pandemic hobby that evolved into a business. A second location opened at 3844 Wabash Ave. a year later.
The business, named after the couple's daughters: Hadley, Avery and Emma, is known for its selection of scratch-made treats, grab-and-go eats and caffeinated drinks.
More food trucks in the works
The Lumpia House has opened its doors on MacArthur Boulevard to welcome guests. But that doesn't mean the food truck that first introduced Springfield to its Filipino menu is being parked.
In fact, Rolando Cabral – who owns the business with his wife Myrna Balabag – has plans for a whole fleet.
'We're going to build more trucks to send to other communities,' Cabral said. 'I want to provide access to our food and the (food trucks') objective is to identify areas for a more permanent presence.'
For now though, Cabral is focused on one address in particular: 1731 S. MacArthur Blvd.
The menu at The Lumpia House is more extensive than that available from its forerunner, The Lumpia Truck. Of course, there are still the namesake lumpia – a Filipino take on spring rolls – and barbecued meat skewers.
The Lumpia House offers more than just a taste of Filipino cuisine, but also Filipino culture. Cabral said the full-service restaurant also features music and art from his native land.
Operating hours are 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 8 a.m. to 11 p.m. Friday and 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Saturday. Dine in, take out and curbside pick-up service available. Orders can be placed online at thelumpiatruck.us. Phone: 447-448-8262.
Di Piero's reappearing soon
Di Piero's will soon reappear at Danenberger Family Vineyards in New Berlin after the Italian restaurant closed its downtown Springfield location in December.
Owner Peter Praia said he plans to begin serving a scaled-down version of his standard menu from the kitchen at the New Berlin vineyard later this month. Grab-and-go salumi trays – the Italian take on a charcuterie board with a variety of cured meats, cheese, fruits, briny snacks and crackers – also will be available.
The restaurant, initially, will only be open to the public during scheduled events at the vineyard. Praia said he is taking bookings for private events with family-style meals. Regularly scheduled operating hours will eventually be added, he said.
Di Piero's closed its 518 E. Adams St. restaurant Dec. 28, two months shy of its fifth anniversary. A social media post for the establishment said it was closing 'to seek out a new location.'
Di Piero's is the latest eatery to operate from the New Berlin vineyard. Its arrival marks a return to Italian fare after recent tenants that offered everything from Mexican to home cooking to health food.
Winter hours in place
CD BBQ's has switched to winter hours after a brief holiday break.
Operator Cecil Turner said the eatery at 725 North Grand Ave. W., will serve its signature barbecue from 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Wednesday through Thursday and 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday and Saturday.
Barbecue chicken and Polish beef sausage will join the menu on weekends.

title: Two surgeries later, Taylorville star savors final high school season with senior core
author: Bill Welt
description: Addison Tarr has always been a leading scorer for Taylorville girls basketball, but not without adversity
content:
TAYLORVILLE — Not one.
Not two.
Taylorville features three 1,000-point scorers this season. They include seniors Addison Tarr, Mazie Fleming, and Kyleigh Heimsness.
Tarr reached the milestone last year, while Fleming and Heimsness joined the exclusive club this past January.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Senior guard Lia Champley and sophomore guard Grace Rogers complete the starting lineup. Each of those four seniors has a camaraderie that stretches back to fourth grade.
'It's been real fun coaching them the past four years,' Taylorville coach Hayden Eldred said. 'I'm excited to see how it ends up here.'
Two surgeries later
Tarr has averaged double figures each of the past three seasons even as a freshman — injuries notwithstanding.
She missed the end of her sophomore year due to an ACL and partial meniscus tear. She still averaged 14.9 points, 6.3 rebounds, 2.4 assists, and 2 steals per game the following season despite not being 100% before she encountered another meniscus tear on the same knee during an AAU tournament.
'It's definitely been a tough journey for her the past couple of years,' Eldred said. 'Last season, she probably wasn't at full strength and needed another surgery over the summer. But this year has been much better.
'Just getting her confidence back in that leg each game has been big. She's really persevered over a lot of it and her determination is second to none.'
Girls hoops breakout stars: See what new names are making an impact in girls basketball around Springfield
The recovery process requires more than just rehabilitating the knee.
'Everything has to work together and I've been building muscle in that leg my whole life and then it really atrophied when I tore it,' Tarr said. 'Just building that muscle back and getting that strength back has been the biggest part.'
It's why staying healthy is a top priority this season before going off to play at NCAA Division I Southeast Missouri State University.
'It's been my dream since I was a little girl,' Tarr said of playing at the next level. 'I'm really proud of myself for just sticking with it and I'm really thankful for all the people who have helped me along the way — all the surgeons, trainers, coaches, teammates and my parents. Huge shoutout to my parents (Blake and Lisa), they're so supportive. I thank all of them.'
That retinue also includes former Lanphier and Northern Illinois University standout Marke Freeman. Tarr has worked with Freeman since fourth grade.
'She's like family, she's awesome,' Tarr said.
Combo guards
Tarr can score in a variety of ways. Ditto Heimsness, who will resume basketball at NCAA Division III Millikin University. Fleming will play volleyball at DII University of Illinois Springfield.
Heimsness averaged 10.9 points and 3.6 assists last season. As a freshman, Heimsness took sixth place in the IHSA 3-Point Showdown before that was discontinued the following season.
'It definitely boosted me up knowing I could get there and do that well,' Heimsness said. 'You have to go so far to even get to that point.'
Heimsness knows how to handle pressure, both mentally and physically after growing up with four brothers.
'They taught me how to be tough because they would always push me around outside and we have a rock driveway,' Heimsness said.
She checks all the boxes as the team's primary ball-handler and distributor.
'We go how she goes,' Eldred said. 'Trying to get into our offense under pressure is probably one of the toughest jobs on the floor. She's definitely been vital for us.'
Tarr similarly said Heimsness is a great passer.
'I don't think she realizes it either,' Tarr said. 'She can easily average 10 assists a game, I really think so. She has a great 3-point shot and Lia (Champley) will sometimes come out and play guard depending on our lineup, too. She's really fast and quick on her feet.'

title: 'We would call it a coup': Watchdogs and Dems attack Elon Musk Treasury Department takeover
author: Josh Meyer
description: The dramatic power play began Friday, continued through the weekend -- and poses extraordinary and unprecedented threats to US security, lawmakers say
content:
WASHINGTON – Democratic lawmakers and government watchdog groups are pledging to fight back against Elon Musk's takeover of the federal government's payment system, which they say may be the biggest privacy and security breach in American history.
"If we were watching this happen in Venezuela or Malawi and we saw a billionaire seize the money supply and the checkbook of the government, we would call it a coup," said Lindsay Owens, executive director of the Groundwork Collaborative economic policy group and a former Senate senior economic policy advisor.
Musk, the world's wealthiest person, is an unpaid advisor to President Donald Trump. Musk's Department of Government Efficiency has been tasked with finding ways to cut spending and regulations.
Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., in an exclusive interview with USA TODAY, said that Musk sent young DOGE computer programmers into the Treasury Department's headquarters, where they allegedly strong-armed civil service workers to gain full access to the system that cuts checks for all congressionally authorized government payments.
Reports emerged over the weekend that Musk's DOGE operatives were at Treasury, going through the payment systems and that they had effectively ousted the top civil servant at the Treasury Department, David Lebryk, after he refused to grant access to Musk's emissaries.
And they ultimately pressured Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to 'turn the keys over' to them, said Wyden, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee.
The payment system, traditionally managed by career civil servants and non-political staff, handles trillions of dollars annually, including Social Security and Medicare benefits and tax credits.
Wyden said his staff found out about the events on Friday and independently confirmed them through whistleblowers and internal sources.
By Monday, the Senate staffers had concluded that the DOGE workers spent the weekend accessing the Treasury Department's massive federal payment system, Wyden said, including 'the personal information of hundreds of millions of Americans, bank accounts and tax data, Social Security numbers and home addresses.'
'We got on it, and what is clear now is that unqualified and unaccountable people have seized control of the flow of taxpayer funds and a trove of very sensitive data, and they are seizing the tools they need for a coup,' Wyden said.
'Treasury officials are breaking the law every hour,' Musk says
Musk appeared to condone the activities of DOGE personnel working at Treasury in a Feb. 2 post on X, the social media platform he owns.
'Career Treasury officials are breaking the law every hour of every day by approving payments that are fraudulent or do not match the funding laws passed by Congress,' Musk posted. 'This needs to stop NOW!'
Musk later posted information about some of the DOGE personnel at Treasury, and others going through similar databases at the Office of Personnel Management, or OPM. He said they have degrees from Stanford, UC Berkeley, & MIT and work experience at Google and companies he owns like Tesla and SpaceX.
'Time to confess: Media reports saying that @DOGE has some of world's best software engineers are in fact true,' Musk wrote in a Monday afternoon @X post.
Musk also defended his team's actions at Treasury by saying, "The @DOGE team discovered, among other things, that payment approval officers at Treasury were instructed always to approve payments, even to known fraudulent or terrorist groups. They literally never denied a payment in their entire career. Not even once."
A Democratic staff official on the Senate Finance Committee told USA TODAY on Monday that Musk's comment suggests a fundamental misunderstanding of how the process works. The system, he said on the condition of anonymity, is basically the U.S. government's checkbook for payments already approved by Congress. To find waste, fraud and abuse, the staffer said, Musk would need to go to the agencies that are actually spending the money.
The White House did not return an email seeking comment. But on Monday in the Oval Office, Trump told reporters he agrees with the steps Musk has taken "for the most part."
'Elon can't do and won't do anything without our approval, and we'll give him the approval where appropriate. Where it's not appropriate we won't," Trump said. "But he reports in and he, it's something that he feels very strongly about, and I'm impressed because he's running, obviously, a big company.'
On @X, Musk also said that, the " @DOGE team discovered, among other things, that payment approval officers at Treasury were instructed always to approve payments, even to known fraudulent or terrorist groups. They literally never denied a payment in their entire career. Not even once."
An extraordinary breach by the 'Musk hatchet brigade'
Wyden said the breach poses an extraordinary and unprecedented threat to U.S. national security given the nature of the information contained in the Treasury system that is now in the hands of Musk's staffers.
'The Musk hatchet brigade has infiltrated a gold mine of data that every foreign spy and corrupt actor would love to see,' Wyden said. 'It is a prescription for nightmares.'
After news broke that Musk's DOGE crew was at the Treasury department, some journalists and open source investigators posted identifications − and photos − of some of them deployed to the Treasury, OPM and elsewhere. WIRED magazine reported that the young men were engineers between 19 and 24 years old, most linked to Musk's companies, with one purportedly still in college.
Wyden and others interviewed by USA TODAY Monday said the DOGE staffers had not been given congressionally authorized jobs, hadn't passed the required background checks or obtained security clearances needed to access at least some of the material.
Wyden said he was especially concerned about the fact that the Treasury data – and personnel data at OPM – contain highly sensitive information about government workers and programs and payments to government contractors, including those that compete with Musk-owned companies for billions of dollars in government contracts.
What's more, Wyden said, Musk's vast business interests in China, including a factory that builds many of his Tesla electric vehicles, could cause even more problems.
Faced with mounting outrage among Democrats, Wyden and other senators held a news conference Monday afternoon where they called on Republicans to join them in fighting for Musk's DOGE personnel to relinquish the reins of the Treasury payment system.
If Bessent doesn't revoke DOGE's access, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. said, Democrats will introduce legislation to "stop unlawful meddling in the Treasury Department's payment systems."
Both Wyden and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., also sent separate letters to Bessent over the weekend demanding answers.
Wyden's letter posed several questions to the Treasury Department, including whether officials linked to Musk or DOGE have requested or been granted access to Treasury's payment systems, and if they have, under what legal authority and for what purpose. The senator also inquired about any vetting processes conducted by the Treasury Department regarding potential conflicts of interest due to Musk's business operations in China.
'The press has previously reported that Musk was denied a high-level clearance to access the government's most sensitive secrets,' Wyden wrote in his letter to Bessent. 'I am concerned that Musk's enormous business operation in China ... endangers U.S. cybersecurity and creates conflicts of interest that make his access to these systems a national security risk.'
Warren told Bessent she was "alarmed by reports" of the 'extraordinarily dangerous' DOGE takeover at Treasury, including allowing Lebryk – who was acting Treasury secretary before Bessent's confirmation – to be pushed aside. Lebryk, Warren noted, is "the key official responsible for managing the extraordinary measures the Department of the Treasury is taking to avoid a default on U.S. debt."
Thus his sidelining, "risking missteps that could result in a global financial meltdown that costs trillions of dollars and millions of jobs," Warren wrote.
Most congressional Republicans have not yet commented on the issue, but in response to Warren's complaints, Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, replied on @X, "I disagree with your characterization of the facts. Other than that, this is exactly what we voted for. Who's with me on this?"
'Seizing critical systems' and 'rooting through them'
The Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC), a legal and constitutional watchdog group, was marshaling legal resources to fight DOGE's accessing of the Treasury and OPM systems on Monday.
'We haven't made any decisions yet, but we're looking at many pieces of this, and what the legal implications are,' John Davisson, EPIC's director of litigation, told USA TODAY.
'This is an extremely irregular, unprecedented act of seizing critical systems and handing it over to people who, to a certainty, lack the training or have no prior familiarity with systems, are not charged with their safe keeping, and are really just rooting through them, identifying data points and combining data sets, it appears, for their own ends of dismantling the federal government,' Davisson said.
Former Republican Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois called on congressional lawmakers to go to Treasury headquarters around the corner from the White House and find out for themselves what, exactly, is going on inside.
'Send members of Congress to go into the building and investigate what these people are doing,' Kinzinger said in a video posted on @X. 'Dare them to stop you because they can't.'
Later Monday, two major federal employee unions filed seeking to block DOGE access to Treasury Department payment database.
"The scale of the intrusion into individuals' privacy is massive and unprecedented," the lawsuit by the American Federation of Government Employees, AFL-CIO and Service Employees International Union, AFL-CIO, said. "Secretary Bessent's action granting DOGE-affiliated individuals full, continuous, and ongoing access to that information ... means that retirees, taxpayers, federal employees, companies, and other individuals from all walks of life have no assurance that their information will receive the protection that federal law affords."

title: Jeepers, Mr. Peepers! Springfield's Chris Kattan part of 'SNL' 50th anniversary docuseries
author: Steven Spearie
description: Chris Kattan reflects on the iconic Saturday Night Live sketch \
content:
Show Caption
Chris Kattan of Springfield has been part of the run-up to the 50th anniversary of "Saturday Night Live."
Kattan was part of the "More Cowbell" sketch, which premiered on April 8, 2000.
Chris Kattan of Springfield has been part of the run-up to the 50th anniversary of "Saturday Night Live," including appearing in an episode of the Peacock docuseries "SNL50: Beyond Saturday Night" focusing on the "More Cowbell" sketch.
Next month, Kattan, an SNL cast member from 1996 to 2003, and his fiancée, Maria Libri, will be on hand for the reunion weekend at New York's Radio City Music Hall.
Here's more about the sketch and Kattan's reflections on it:
'Hard to be serious'
Written by Will Ferrell and known as "Recording Session," the idea for the sketch had been "germinating for decades" in his head, Ferrell told Parade Magazine. It had been pitched to guest host and former SNL cast member Norm MacDonald but then shelved.
Premiering on April 8, 2000, the sketch re-imagines Blue Öyster Cult's "Don't Fear the Reaper" recording session with Kattan as Donald "Buck Dharma" Roeser, Ferrell as cowbell-playing Gene Frenkle and Christopher Walken as music producer Bruce Dickinson. Walken's plea for "more cowbell" gave rise to an oft-quoted line.
At one point in the sketch, Kattan gives Ferrell, whose enthusiastic playing is sabotaging the session, a shove, pushing his already too-tight shirt up further.
"It's hard to be serious," Kattan told the docuseries, "when you see that stomach."
Later on, Walken promises members of the band that, with the success of the record, they're going to be wearing "gold-plated diapers."
"What does that mean?" a baffled Kattan asks.
"Never question Bruce Dickinson," Walken shoots back.
'In the moment'
While cast members Darrell Hammond and Jimmy Fallon, who appeared as the drummer in the sketch, have talked about how the sketch "connected" with the audience when it was first performed, Kattan said its success caught everyone by surprise.
'We were just in the moment doing what we should be doing,' Kattan told WTOP-TV, "and that is performing in a sketch and just doing our roles as scripted. We were just doing the scene and had no sense of foreshadowing.'
Mr. Peepers
Viewers of the docuseries also get a peek at another of Kattan's recurring SNL characters, the Amazon rain forest primate, Mr. Peepers.
On his YouTube channel "Hey Kattan," he shows the introduction of Mr. Peepers from The Groundlings improv group. The sketch also features Ferrell.
Mr. Peepers shared the SNL stage with Tom Hanks, Sting and The Rock, as Papa Peepers.
How to watch
"SNL50: The Anniversary Special" airs on NBC and Peacock at 7 p.m. on Feb. 16.

title: Titans' turnaround: Healthier Glenwood girls squad erases memory of four-game losing skid
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Though the Titans have had to face adversity this season, it hasn't been all in vein. Glenwood looks to finish regular season healthier, more confident.
content:
CHATHAM — As Alyssa Riley has had more consistency with her Chatham Glenwood High School girls basketball lineup, the Titans have had better consistency in the win column.
The Titans wrapped up at least a share of the Central State Eight Conference title with a 52-37 win over Southeast on Saturday afternoon. Glenwood also hit the 20-win mark.
The sophomore trio of Ava Bobb, Hope Gilmore and Alexis Neumann, who helped the Titans to a Class 3A runner-up finish in last year's state tournament, combined for 36 points and 22 rebounds and allowed Glenwood (20-8 overall, 8-1 CS8) to grab a healthy lead in the first half and win for the 11 th time in 13 games.
The Titans can win the CS8 outright with a win at Lanphier on Tuesday. Springfield High finished its conference schedule 8-2, Decatur MacArthur is 7-2 with a conference game at home against Southeast on Tuesday.
Southeast coach Jasmin Woolfolk remains impressed with Glenwood and said the Titans offer her team something to aspire to mimic.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
'I think the biggest challenge is just that they are relentless,' Woolfolk said. 'Finished in second place last year for state: That's a great accomplishment.
'They're going to come out and play hard no matter what. They don't hit all of their shots either, but they come out and play hard. As I watch them against other teams, they are relentless. They're going to keep coming at you no matter what and you have to be able to match that energy.'
Neumann finished game-highs with 13 points and 11 boards. Gilmore powered the Glenwood offense early as all 12 of her points came in the first half. Bobb was 5-for-6 at the free-throw line and netted 11 points.
By no means were the Titans whole on Saturday. They were without the services of senior guard Katelyn Lehnen, who was seen in a walking boot and moving around on crutches. Following the game, Riley had no comment if Lehnen, the 2022 Class 3A 200-meter state champion in girls track and field, would be available for the postseason.
Riley is confident that her group grew from being without both Gilmore and Neumann at different times this season.
'They've had to face some adversity,' Riley said. 'I don't know if we've had the same starting lineup for any of our games, and they continue to come to practice and work hard and fill roles where roles are needed, and each individual continues to get better.'
Though only a sophomore, the 6-foot-1 Neumann gives the team an option the rest of the players can trust.
'I think that she helps everybody stay composed, because they trust her with the ball, even though she's your post player,' Riley said.
From Jan. 3-9, Glenwood lost four games in a row: half of the Titans' total losses so far this season. Now, the Titans are on a six-game win streak.
'I think it was just a lot different because we haven't had the same starting lineup for a really long time,' Neumann said of how her team has rallied after the losing streak. 'For us to finally get into the groove of having that starting lineup, then we finally realized that we can do it together, even if we're missing an important piece of our team.'
Glenwood outrebounded Southeast 39-20 and outshot the Spartans (47.2%, 17 of 36 to Southeast's 28.3%, 13 of 46). But Glenwood lost the turnover battle, 22-14, and sent Southeast to the free-throw line 17 times.
Bobb, however, is glad that the team still has room to get better, and going against Southeast's pressure defense a week before the postseason begins will give the Titans some lessons if they face a similar team in a one-and-done situation.
'Yeah, it definitely made us better,' Bobb said. 'I think it was good for us to have that pressure to be able to handle the ball more. It definitely will help us get better with our ball handling going into the postseason.'
Southeast sophomore Naveahua Collier led the Spartans (14-13, 5-4 CS8) with 11 points. She also led the team with four boards.
'I think that's one of our primary identities is just pressure defense, just to turn them over.' Woolfolk said. 'On that end of it, we got what we wanted; we just have to do better at getting the ball in the hole.'

title: Government workers sue to stop Trump from dismantling USAID
author: Maureen Groppe
description: The suit says the administration's actions are costing thousands of jobs, threatening national security interests and causing a humanitarian catastrophe.
content:
WASHINGTON − Groups representing foreign aid workers are suing the Trump administration to try to stop the dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development, calling what's happening to the humanitarian agency an "unlawful seizure."
"It's a genuine moral crisis," said Lauren Batemen, an attorney with Public Citizen Litigation Group, which is helping represent the American Federation of Government Employees and the American Foreign Service Association.
The suit, filed in Washington, D.C., federal court on Thursday, says the administration's stop-work orders, funding freeze and staff reductions are costing thousands of jobs, threatening U.S. national security interests and causing a humanitarian catastrophe.
President Donald Trump has accused the agency of being corrupt by spending money on projects the White House has called ridiculous.
About 10,000 USAID employees were told this week that they will be placed on administrative leave at the end of Friday.
The only exception is for designated personnel responsible for "mission-critical functions, core leadership and specially designated programs."
Fewer than 300 will remain.
About two-thirds of USAID employees work overseas across 60 countries. Bringing the employees home could cost more than $20 million, said Randy Chester, president of the American Foreign Service Association.
"Kids will be pulled from schools. Spouses are losing jobs, and families are thrown into uncertainty with no clear plan," Chester said, "not to mention the cost to American taxpayers of this sudden, disorganized, chaotic departure."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this week that the administration would have preferred to handle its review of USAID in a "more orderly fashion."
"But we had no cooperation, and in fact insubordination, and so it required us to work from the bottom up," he said.
The suit claims that under current law, only Congress can dismantle USAID.
"Dismantling USAID is very different from a strategic review, which could be undertaken to improve coherence of the government's mission by an incoming administration," said Rachel Beatty Riedl, professor of government and director of Cornell University's Center on Global Democracy,
But Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow with the conservative Heritage Foundation, said the internal structure of USAID is not set in statute.
'And that also would extend to who the employees are and how many employees are there,' he said. 'So if (Trump) wants to turn it into a hollow shell ... he can do that.'
Any structural changes to USAID are supposed to be done in consultation with Congress, according to the Congressional Research Service.
Scott R. Anderson, a former U.S. diplomat and government attorney now at the Brookings Institution, said the administration took steps this week to try to satisfy that requirement by notifying Congress it intended to work with lawmakers on a reorganization.
"If it's actually abided by it in good faith, they may be on better legal grounds," he said. "It still could be a a disaster from a policy perspective."

title: Trump accuses USAID of being 'corrupt'; implies the agency's days are numbered
author: Swapna Venugopal Ramaswamy
description: USAID, a federal humanitarian agency, has been in turmoil as the Trump administration considers folding it into the State Department
content:
Show Caption
President Donald Trump confirmed Tuesday that he will be winding down the U.S. Agency for International Development, saying the humanitarian agency 'had to be corrupt' to approve certain initiatives.
Trump's comments came a day after the White House said more than 600 USAID employees had been put on administrative leave and more than 700 personal service contracts had been terminated, prompting Democrats to question the legality of the actions.
On Monday, the White House released what it called a list of 'pet projects of entrenched bureaucrats' approved by USAID. The list, which the White House described as 'ridiculous' and 'malicious," included items such as $1.5 million to "advance diversity equity and inclusion in Serbia's workplaces and business communities"; $70,000 for production of a "DEI musical" in Ireland; $47,000 for a "transgender opera" in Colombia; and $32,000 for a "transgender comic book" in Peru.
'It has to be corrupt. Nobody could approve that,' Trump said Tuesday as he signed a new batch of executive orders from the White House.
USAID, an independent government agency that distributes foreign aid, oversees around $40 billion a year in spending and was created in 1961. In fiscal year 2023, USAID funding went to everything from women's health in conflict zones to clean water, HIV/AIDS treatments, energy security and anti-corruption work, according to Reuters.
As of Monday morning, the government website was unavailable, but the archived website states the agency's mission is to "promote and demonstrate democratic values abroad, and advance a free, peaceful, and prosperous world."
One of Trump's closest advisors, billionaire tech entrepreneur Elon Musk, who runs the newly formed Department of Government Efficiency, disclosed Monday that he and Trump were planning to shut down the agency. Musk has been tasked with helping to slim down the federal bureaucracy.
USAID has been in turmoil as the Trump administration considers folding it into the State Department. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been the agency's acting head since Monday, and Trump said he could see him running it in the long term. The agency had a staff of more than 10,000 people.
Rep. Gerry Connolly, D-Va., the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee said in a post on X that neither Musk nor Trump had the authority to shut down USAID. He said the Executive Branch cannot dismantle an agency Congress created by statute.
"We ask a lot of our civil servants," he wrote. "Today, we ask of them another task ‒ show up to work. Continue to serve."

title: Illinois, Chicago sued by Trump administration over immigration laws that 'thwart' feds
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Trump administration has sued Illinois and Chicago, alleging its laws are impeding on federal efforts to enforce immigration laws.
content:
The Trump administration, DOJ sues Illinois and Chicago over some of its immigration laws.
The lawsuit argues that the government has authority to regulate immigration, but it needs to work with state and local partners.
Chicago and Illinois have some of the strongest protections for immigrants in the nation.
The Trump administration and the U.S. Department of Justice sued the State of Illinois and the City of Chicago Thursday, including several of its officials, alleging that its sanctuary city designation and other protections for immigrants are impeding on federal efforts to enforce immigration laws.
The lawsuit takes issue with state laws that prohibit Illinois law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration agents. The suit also cites laws and ordinances in Chicago like the Welcoming City Ordinance that limits Chicago police officers from arresting on the basis of immigration status.
'The conduct of officials in Chicago and Illinois minimally enforcing — and oftentimes affirmatively thwarting — federal immigration laws over a period of years has resulted in countless criminals being released into Chicago who should have been held for immigration removal from the United States,' according to the lawsuit that has been filed in Chicago's federal court.
The administration argues in the suit that the U.S. has authority to regulate immigration matters, per the Constitution, numerous acts of Congress, and U.S. Supreme Court precedent. Further, they say that consultation and communication between federal, state, and local law enforcement officials is necessary for federal officials to carry out federal immigration law.
Gov. JB Pritzker who has been highly vocal and critical about President Trump, said the state has always complied with the law.
'Unlike Donald Trump, Illinois follows the law,' Pritzker's office said in a statement. 'Illinois will defend our laws that prioritize police resources for fighting crime while enabling state law enforcement to assist with arresting violent criminals. Instead of working with us to support law enforcement, the Trump Administration is making it more difficult to protect the public, just like they did when Trump pardoned the convicted Jan. 6 violent criminals. We look forward to seeing them in court."
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson has defended the city's sanctuary laws. He and other may plan to testify next month at a congressional hearing on sanctuary cities, according to Associated Press.
Chicago in recent months has helped host trainings for people to learn their rights when it comes to immigration agents and publicized the information at public transit stations.
President Donald Trump has often singled out Chicago and Illinois, which have some of the strongest protections for immigrants in the nation, AP reported.

title: Argentina President Javier Milei pulls out of World Health Organization, following Trump
author: Cybele Mayes-Osterman
description: Argentinian President Javier Milei cited similar complaints as President Donald Trump when he pulled out of the World Health Organization.
content:
President Javier Milei pulled Argentina out of the World Health Organization, citing right-wing complaints about COVID lockdowns, weeks after President Donald Trump, his close ally, also removed the U.S. from the organization.
In a statement released Wednesday, Milei faulted the organization for its response to the COVID pandemic, saying it "failed in its greatest test" by promoting lockdowns.
Echoing Trump's accusations, Milei's statement claimed the organization's prescriptions were the result of "political influences, not based on science."
Manuel Adorni, a spokesperson for Milei, said he withdrew Argentina from the organization because of "deep differences" and "a lack of independence from the political influence of other states."
Milei has propagated many of the same right-wing complaints against global organizations as Trump. At a United Nations speech, he called COVID lockdowns, which scientists at the organization recommended to stop the disease's spread, a "crime against humanity."
Trump pulled out of the organization on the first day of his new term. He faced his own criticisms for his administration's handling of the pandemic in 2020 during his first term, as the disease quickly spread through the U.S., killing more than a million Americans.
Trump also took issue with the U.S. giving what the order called "onerous payments" to the organization – the U.S. gave the most money of any country worldwide during the Biden administration.
The move caused concern among health experts, who said it could impair worldwide disease response and readiness for a future pandemic. WHO's work with the U.S. has " protected and saved millions of lives in America and around the world," said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson.
Trump and his allies have called for a "herd immunity" approach to COVID – allowing some parts of the population to catch the disease so that they become immune. Global health experts say the approach runs contrary to science and could put large swaths of people in danger.

title: Indiana shouldn't want Illinois' poor counties
author: Michael J. Hicks
description: No, Indiana doesn't really want these Illinois counties — though it is easy to see why Illinois might not want them either.
content:
It is hard to resist trolling Illinois, especially Chicago. I've done so myself on occasion.
After all, Chicago is a city with too many governance flaws to list in a single column. But it also enjoys a few strengths. The Chicago metro area is bigger, richer, better educated and its workers substantially more productive than Indiana as a whole.
Opinion: No, Illinois counties won't secede to Indiana. Here's why.
Still, it's fun to troll a place like Chicago, and Indiana House Speaker Todd Huston, who must be ranked among the most serious and effective legislative leaders in the country, did so earlier this month. The story is worth telling.
Many downstate Illinois residents dislike Chicago's strong influence in the state. Last year, a total of 33 counties voted to secede from Illinois and form their own state. Huston invited those counties to join Indiana. He even created a commission to study the possibility.
That's first-rate trolling.
I thought it'd be fun to think through the prospect of Indiana picking up these 33 counties. Would it be good for Indiana? Would it be good for those counties? Would it be good for the remaining 69 Illinois counties?
Which Illinois counties would Indiana get?
The "secessionist" counties in Illinois are in the southern part of the state, with many bordering Indiana. This one-third of counties comprise only 6.6% of the Illinois population, and only 4% of the state's economy.
Per capita income in the secessionist counties is $54,381. If it were a separate state, it would be the second-poorest state in the union, sliding right in between Mississippi and West Virginia. The remaining counties in Illinois have a per capita income of $73,228.
Adding the secessionist counties to Indiana would cut our per capita income enough for us to move from 14th to 11th place from the bottom. Only 18.6% of adults in these counties have completed college, while the Illinois total is 36.7%. This new post-secession Indiana would instantly be the least well-educated state, and would be right about where the U.S. as a whole was in the late 1980s.
Economic growth in the secessionist counties has been at about half the rate of the rest of Illinois so far this century. And, while the rest of Illinois has experienced very modest population growth of about 1.4%, these secessionist counties have lost a whopping 5.2% of their population.
If the secessionist parts of Illinois were their own state, they'd have the worst 25 years of population loss of any state in U.S. history. So, it's pretty easy to see why these counties might be unhappy about their economic conditions. They are truly dismal.
Bad vibes borne of ignorance
But how much of this is the fault of Illinois state government? After all, the other Illinois counties are doing much better. That includes Chicago, where the economy continues to be robust, even as population growth has stalled. Is it possible that these counties are somehow being robbed of economic opportunity by Illinois?
Nope. As it turns out, these counties are essentially welfare queens of the state of Illinois.
A pair of researchers at Southern Illinois University's Paul Simon Public Policy Institute publish reports every couple years on the flow of public budgets across Illinois. This very detailed work by John Jackson and John Foster makes it possible to see where the tax dollars are flowing across Illinois. And, for what it is worth, that is very much like a study I did for Indiana more than a decade ago with colleagues Dagney Faulk and John Ketzenberger.
As it turns out, residents in these secessionist counties pay about $2,986 per person each year in state taxes. That would make them the fourth lowest-taxed residents in the nation. But here's the rub: They receive $5,430 per person each year in support from residents of the other 69 Illinois counties.
In contrast, the rest of the state collects $4,485 in state taxes each year and gets back $4,217 per person in state spending. So, each resident of the secessionist counties gets $2,444 more state dollars spent in their county each year than they pay in taxes. On top of that, they pay only 66.6 cents for every dollar of taxes residents in the other 69 Illinois counties pay.
Federal taxes and spending tell a similar story. A recent study of mine calculated the share of taxes and transfer payments made at the county level to the federal government. You guessed it, the secessionist counties pay a lower federal tax rate, but receive more in Social Security payments and in other types of transfers (TANF, SNAP, etc.) than the counties that did not vote to secede from Illinois.
Rural voters are failing themselves
There are some useful lessons here.
First, the secessionist counties of Illinois pay low state taxes but are beneficiaries of enormous transfers from the rest of Illinois. It is hard to pinpoint just what these Illinois secessionist counties are angry about. Most likely it is bad vibes borne of ignorance. There's compelling evidence of that.
If they do come to Indiana, Hoosier taxpayers will need to pony up almost $2 billion more per year to match the fiscal largesse those secessionist counties receive from the rest of Illinois. It is worth noting that those taxes are going to come primarily from urban areas, like Fishers, Carmel and Indianapolis.
So, no, we don't really want them — though it is easy to see why Illinois might not want them either.
Second, neither the red state and blue state models of rural development have worked. The secessionist counties of Illinois look just like 40 or 50 declining rural counties in Indiana. Both Illinois and Indiana policymakers are failing their rural counties, though most of the blame for economic decline belongs squarely with the voters of those rural counties.
Finally, the real political divisions in America are geographic. So far this century, a whopping half of all the population growth this century has occurred in just 75 out of 3,143 U.S. counties, or 2.3%. Fully 45% of U.S. counties have lost population this century.
This deep economic divergence has gripped the U.S. for four decades. It is not between red or blue states, or places with high taxes or woke policies. It is primarily between urban and non-urban counties, and reflects the desire of most Americans to live in places with strong local public services — great schools, low crime and businesses that offer a mix of goods and services.
Places that offer these do well; those that do not will look more and more like rural Illinois.
Michael J. Hicks is the director of the Center for Business and Economic Research and the George and Frances Ball distinguished professor of economics in the Miller College of Business at Ball State University.

title: Massey family, Sangamon County reach agreement to $10M settlement
author: Steven Spearie
description: Sangamon County has reached an agreement with the family of Sonya Massey through mediation on an out-of-court settlement. Here's what happens next.
content:
Show Caption
The agreement between the county and the Massey family will be taken up at Tuesday's board meeting.
The settlement would be paid from "reserves and contingency lines within the various funds of county government."
Sangamon County has reached an agreement with the family of Sonya Massey through mediation on an out-of-court settlement.
The settlement, in the amount of $10 million, would need final approval from the county board at its Tuesday meeting.
The agreement followed extensive confidential discussions involving legal representatives for the county and the Massey family.
A memo discussing the parameters and timeline of the settlement was obtained by The State Journal-Register Friday.
The settlement, agreed upon by both parties on Feb. 4, could avoid a potentially protracted lawsuit.
Through a county spokesman, Sangamon County Administrator Brian McFadden said the settlement would be paid from "reserves and contingency lines within the various funds of county government."
The county, McFadden added, is able "to establish and maintain reserves to cover situations such as this, a large one-time expense outside the normal operations of county government. We anticipate for such instances, and we plan accordingly."
Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman and the mother of two children, was fatally shot in the face inside of her home in the 2800 block of Hoover Avenue of in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield the morning of July 6.
Sangamon County Sheriff's deputies were dispatched to the home after Massey called 911 about a potential prowler.
Now former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy Sean P. Grayson shot Massey even as she put her arms in the air and said "I'm sorry" while ducking for cover. Grayson aggressively yelled for Massey to put down a pot of boiling water.
Grayson, who is white, has been charged with first-degree murder. He is currently being jailed in Decatur and is next due in court on March 24.
Video of the shooting, captured on another deputy's body-worn camera, has caused international outrage.
The shooting led to the formation of the Massey Commission, which meets Monday, and an investigation by the U.S. Department of the Justice into race and disability discrimination in policing and dispatch services by the sheriff's office and other county entities.
Under a memorandum of agreement reached with the DOJ on Jan. 16, the sheriff's office will "review and update policies, rules and procedures" with the State's Attorney's Office.
The agreement requires the sheriff's department, dispatch and the county to make reports every six months to the DOJ about any complaints it receives.
In December, speaking before the Massey Commission, Sangamon County Sheriff Paula Crouch outlined an investigation manual for new hires, including the creation of a sheriff's merit commission.
Grayson's hire drew scrutiny because of two DUI offenses before he became a police officer and a separation from the U.S. Army that listed "misconduct (serious offense)" as the reason.
The memo regarding the financial settlement, written by Chairman Andy Van Meter, "takes into account county finances and the use of public dollars and acknowledges what county taxpayers can realistically afford. Due to the long-standing fiscal responsibility of Sangamon County, the settlement will not result in a tax increase, additional debt, or cuts to county services."
Van Meter noted that "no price paid can take back the actions of a rogue former deputy, but this agreement is an effort to provide some measure of recompense to the Massey family for their unimaginable loss. The county remains committed to working with the community to strengthen policies to try to ensure tragedies like this never happen again."

title: Jacksonville business closes after 75 years of being open
author: Claire Grant
description: After being open for 75 years, a Jacksonville business has closed its doors. Here's what we know.
content:
It's never easy walking down the street and seeing a much-beloved business dark on the inside.
For Jacksonville residents, that feeling is all too fresh walking down East State Street and seeing the telltale lights off and paper printed sign taped to the door of Bill Wade Photography.
According to the note left by the photography team, the historic Bill Wade Photography studio at 229 E. State St. closed early Tuesday, Feb. 5. Clients still looking to schedule appointments were given a number to call at 217-371-4319 for Kurt Wade, one of the two brothers who run the business.
Wade says both of the brothers are in their sixties and realized it was time for retirement. Both began working at their fathers shop in the early seventies.
For Kurt Wade, his lifelong journey into photography started at 11 and according to him, has been a job he's always loved, and is learning to step away from.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
'I see a lot of obituaries with people my age and think if I don't quit, I'll never quit," Wade said. "I have not forgotten how to do things and one thing about my job is I really like working - I've been blessed having a job I like to do.'
The brothers have eventual plans to sell the building with the business in it still dark, but mentioned freelancing for specific photography sessions indoors.
'After 75 years we are closing our doors,' the sign from Bill Wade says. 'We have loved being part of your lives.'
Bill Wade Photography was started in 1950 by Bill Wade, who attended Illinois College in the early 1940's before leaving to fight in World War II. Following the war, Wade used the G.I. Bill pursued photography in Santa barbara California attending Brooks Institute of Photography.
Returning to Jacksonville and setting up shop, the studio expanded in the following decades experimenting and creating their own wedding style photography.
Both Bill and Kurt hold a master's degree in photography.

title: Plains girls basketball wins Sangamo title, plus other conference champions around Springfield
author: Bill Welt
description: Pleasant Plains edged Petersburg PORTA for the Sangamo title, plus other conference champions in the Springfield area in boys and girls hoops
content:
PLEASANT PLAINS — The Pleasant Plains girls basketball team soaked up another championship moment on Thursday night.
The Cardinals warded off Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central 43-35 for their third outright Sangamo Conference title in the last four years.
'This was our next goal and we did it,' Plains junior guard Bailey Leach said. 'PORTA's a good team, credit to them. We played our game, got some steals and made our shots.'
Leach reeled off a couple key baskets late in the third quarter for a 32-26 cushion before the Cardinals ultimately put away PORTA at the free throw line.
Junior forward Anna Weber led Plains with 14 points and 14 rebounds, while Leach had nine points. Junior forward Madison Burke overcame early foul trouble and finished with eight points.
'We're known for our defense — work hard, get some stops, double the ball and just play our game,' Leach said. 'Once we get defensive stops, we'll get offensive scores.'
Plains contains Arthalony
Plains especially circled around PORTA senior forward Carson Arthalony, who posted nine of her 11 points in the third quarter. Both Weber and Arthalony are returning all-area forwards from last season.
The Bluejays just missed open opportunities down the stretch, PORTA coach Derek Schnapp said.
'I'm proud of the girls, they didn't back down,' Schnapp said. 'We both went on some streaks, even took a little lead (in the second quarter). Pleasant Plains, you've got to give them credit. They're good, they're deep and they're balanced. They're going to make a good postseason run and we knew that.
'Our girls wanted that conference championship one more time (after winning last year's title), but they gave it all they got and I'm proud of them.'
Nolan Scott vaults Plains to OT win: Pleasant Plains junior reserve gets hot at the right time in OT win over Petersburg PORTA
PORTA junior guard Aubrey Vogel generated a team-high 14 points while her cousin, Allison, had seven points and team-best 15 rebounds.
Which Springfield-area teams won conference basketball titles this winter?
Here is a list of conference champions and leaders in boys and girls basketball around Springfield through Thursday's games:
CENTRAL STATE EIGHT
BOYS: Decatur MacArthur ― The Generals clinched their second straight outright CS8 title following Friday's win over Rochester with an 8-1 record ahead of the conference finale against Lincoln on Friday.
GIRLS: Chatham Glenwood ― The Titans won the outright CS8 title following Tuesday's win over Lanphier with a 9-1 record.
SANGAMO
GIRLS: Pleasant Plains ― The Cardinals won their third conference title in the last four seasons following Thursday's win over Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central with an unbeaten 8-0 record.
BOYS: With one week to go, Williamsville, ranked No. 3 in Class 2A by The Associated Press, remains unbeaten at 6-0 ahead of Friday's showdown at Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central, which is tied for second place at 5-1 with Auburn and Pleasant Plains.
SOUTH CENTRAL
GIRLS: Gillespie ― The Miners won the outright title with a 55-52 win over Pana on Thursday to go unbeaten in the league at 9-0.
BOYS: Staunton can clinch at least a share of the title at 7-0 with a win at Litchfield on Friday. They close out the conference schedule against Greenville on Tuesday and Hillsboro on Thursday.
MSM
GIRLS: Nokomis ― NHS finished unbeaten in the MSM for a third straight season at 7-0 after Monday's win over South County/New Berlin.
BOYS: Calvary can clinch at least a share of the title with a win at Raymond Lincolnwood on Friday to move to 7-1. They meet Pawnee in the MSM finale on Feb. 21 for a chance at their second straight outright title.
APOLLO
GIRLS: Taylorville ― The Tornadoes won a share of the league title at 8-2 following Tuesday's win over Mount Zion. Taylorville won an outright title last season.
BOYS: Jacksonville Routt, ranked No. 7 in 1A, dropped a game to co-leader Greenfield/Northwestern on Feb. 7 but can clinch at least a share of the title with a win at Mount Sterling Brown County on Friday.

title: Illinois State Fair announces two more headlining acts. Here's what you need to know
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Two more headliners have been announced for the Illinois State Fair in August. Here's what you need to know .
content:
Two more Grandstand headliners have been announced for the Illinois State Fair.
Sheryl Crow and Turnpike Troubadours will perform on Aug. 12 and Aug. 17, respectively.
Here's what to know about the performers and how to get tickets.
Sheryl Crow
Sheryl Crow is a nine-time Grammy winner with a soft rock or alternative rock-style.
'Her music lifts people up, brings them together, and we can't wait for that to happen at the Illinois State Fair,' said Jerry Costello II in a news release, who is Director of the Illinois Department of Agriculture.
Crow last performed at the state fair in 1996 in a performance with John Hiatt.
Tickets for Crow will go on sale Friday via Ticketmaster, ranging from $40 to $105.
Turnpike Troubadours
Turnpike Troubadours is an American country music band from Tahlequah, Oklahoma, that started making music in 2005.
The group has achieved 1.5 billion streams globally and is selling out arenas and headlining festivals, according to a press release from the fair.
'Turnpike Troubadours perform a unique kind of music that we are happy to have at the Illinois State Fair,' Jerry Costello II stated. 'This band will feel right at home here in central Illinois.'
Tickets for the show will go on sale Feb. 15 at 10 a.m. via Ticketmaster, ranging from $55 to $125.
Who else will perform?
The fair has so far announced four headliners, meaning that they will announce six more.
Def Leppard and country star Megan Moroney are set to perform.

title: Forbes named the best employers in the U.S. Here are 54 from Illinois on the list
author: Mike Kramer
description: Forbes has recognized 31 large businesses and 23 midsized companies based in Illinois as some of the nation's best employers in 2024.

The state of Illinois is home to more than 50 of the best employers in the United States, according to annual rankings released recently by Forbes.
Here is a look at how the list was made and which Illinois businesses made the cut.
How did Forbes make the list of best employers?
Forbes partnered with market research firm Statista to survey over 217,000 employees nationwide. Respondents rated employers based on salary, advancement opportunities, work environment and training programs.
After tallying and analyzing the data, Forbes gave each employer a score and placed a total of 1,199 organizations on either a Best Large Employers 2025 list or a Best Midsized Employer 2025 list. title: Plain to see: How these guards moved Pleasant Plains boys basketball into title contention
author: Bill Welt
description: How did Pleasant Plains boys basketball become one of the best in the Sangamo Conference? It's plethora of guards
content:
PLEASANT PLAINS — Pleasant Plains junior guard Owen Johnson comes from a competitive household.
His mother, Elizabeth (Schilling), previously played volleyball under former distinguished Mount Pulaski volleyball coach Donna Dulle and routinely participates in Owen's shootarounds.
'She just rebounds all the time, throws it to me and tells me when something is going wrong,' Johnson said.
Johnson has lately found the right touch.
It's a product of constant repetition after suffering a baseball injury as a freshman. It not only required eight months to recover, but he also still had to adjust to a revamped shoulder.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
'I'm really happy with the results that I've been getting in games and coach (Kyle Weber) trusts me to shoot, so I'm going to shoot them and thankfully they're going in,' Johnson said.
All kinds of shooters
Johnson poured in the go-ahead 3 and game-high 14 points in a 40-39 win over Riverton before twice contributing 16 points with seven 3s combined in subsequent Sangamo Conference wins over state-ranked Auburn and Petersburg PORTA/A-C Centra l.
Senior guard Cooper Schallenberg remains a focal point with 14.5 points per game, but other returning starters such as Johnson, junior Grady Grisham and senior Trager Shultz are now making their mark.
Grisham ranks second on the team with 9.8 points and first with 5.4 rebounds per game, while Johnson is averaging 8.9 ppg.
Grisham described this season as a breakout year after largely serving as a facilitator last winter. The 6-foot guard became the team's top rebounder following the graduation of 6-5 forward Liam Hatfield.
Grisham, who also plays baseball with the rest of the starting lineup, said he uses his speed and plyometric jumping exercises from P.E. to clean up the boards.
'That's what coach (Weber) talked about,' Grisham said, 'he said we're all going to have to step up and we've just been moving the ball and now all of us are more confident than we were last year. We all know we're going to step up and make shots in games.'
It also extends to the bench. In the 67-63 overtime win over PORTA on Tuesday, junior reserve Nolan Scott doled out five 3s and 19 points, while four others produced at least nine points.
'We're just a lot of shooters,' Scott said.
Big Time guards: No. 3 Williamsville boys basketball reloads thanks to reunited group of senior guards
Basketball roots: How this Auburn senior is adding to family's basketball legacy
The Cardinals (18-10, 6-1 Sangamo) thus remain just one game behind Class 2A No. 3 Williamsville in the conference race despite their 46-41 loss to the Bullets and have won eight of their last nine games after Schallenberg drained the game-winning 3 in Saturday's 49-46 win over El Paso-Gridley.
'We were struggling early on in the season with our tough schedule but as we play more together, it's been more cohesive, so we're playing well together and we know where everyone's going to be at one time,' Johnson said. 'It's great playing with these guys basically my whole life.'

title: Unlicensed massage parlors may face additional legal actions in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: Days after being forced to close by the city, some massage parlors may still be illegally operating in Springfield.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Despite the closure of 11 massage parlors in Springfield for failing to apply for necessary permits, some businesses, like Q2 Asian Massage, are reportedly still operating.
The city is aware of these violations and is prepared to seek civil court orders to prohibit occupancy.
This closure is part of an ongoing effort by the city to address concerns about human trafficking and prostitution, ensuring that all massage parlors adhere to local laws and licensing requirements.
The door may still be swinging at least one of Springfield's now closed massage parlors, and the city's next step toward keeping the business closed could be coming soon.
On Feb. 4, the city of Springfield released the names of 11 massage parlors across the city which closed on Jan. 31 after a slew of inspections.
Red Bean Spa, Fitness Massage and Q2 Asian Massage were among the near dozen businesses shuttered for failing to apply for necessary permits. Each business shut down was stamped with a bright green plaque for order to not operate.
Q2, one of the closed spas on West Lawrence, however, may still be operating. Images of the parlor were posted on social media of cars in the parking lot with people accessing the building.
City attorney Greg Moredock said the city was aware of the situation and has put another sign on the building for no operation. The business owners by choice plastered to the building window their 2024 business license, but according to Moredock, the license is expired for the previous year, and was issued before the new inspection process was rolled out.
'We are aware of what's being said and what they've posted on their doors,' Moredock said about Q2 massage. 'We have the ability to seek civil court orders at any time now to prohibit occupancy moving forward.'
Moredock said the city has received reports on other closed parlors and has followed up on the calls, but could not comment further on the subject.
'On the civil side we can't get an injunction over the weekend,' Moredock said. 'We are keeping an eye on that location and all the locations we have placards at.'
The closure restricts the parlor from operating in Springfield, as result of ongoing efforts by the city to make sure the parlors are adhering to local laws and licensing requirements.
The new licensing process comes from community concerns about a rise in human trafficking and prostitution in the city of younger women from Asia being brought to the parlors. The regulation passed the city council in May and by June, inspections began being conducted.
The ordinance allows parlors once closed to reopen once they meet code compliance with the ordinance such as having all licensed massage therapists, but may face fines ranging from $250 up to $750 per offense.
Moredock also confirmed a city inspector had gone Friday morning to inspect the location of 452 S. Grand Ave., the closed Golden Relax Spa, which locals have called in recent activity at the closed spa in connection to 88 Relaxing Massage and Fitness spa.
Golden Relax and 88 Relaxing Massage on South Grand were raided by the FBI on April 11, 2024; Golden Relax closed shortly following the raids which lead to no arrests, while 88 Massage remained open until the building owner, David Zhang, was fined a total of $10,650 based on building code violations in mid-January of this year.

title: 'Civic-minded' Cox gets nod for Ward 1 alderman in Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: Cox, an attorney and chief compliance officer for a multi-state cannabis operator, took his seat at the horseshoe with the backing of all nine alderpersons.
content:
Jeff Cox was one of 12 candidates interviewed for the Ward 1 opening.
Cox grew up in Williamsville and has lived in Ward 1 since 2018.
Cox succeeds Chuck Redpath Sr., now the Springfield City Clerk.
Jeff Cox said Tuesday that the "civic minded" part of him led him to throw his hat into the ring for Ward 1 alderman.
Cox, an attorney and chief compliance officer for a multi-state cannabis operator, took his seat at the horseshoe with the backing of all nine alderpersons.
Cox succeeds Chuck Redpath Sr., who stepped into the city clerk role on Jan. 7.
"I was raised to give back to the community," said Cox, 43, who was joined by his wife, Megan, and their three children in the swearing-in ceremony by Sangamon County Associate Judge Christopher Perrin. "I feel like I missed that, working in the private sector."
Cox was on the Springfield Lake Shore Improvement Association and said he's very familiar with Lake Springfield, having lived in the ward since 2018.
"I'm familiar with the North Lake Shore area and the area off Hilltop. It is a big ward, a lot of space and a lot of doors to knock on," said Cox, who said he will run in 2027, when his term is up.
As for the city, "I want Springfield to grow," he added. "I want to help small businesses. I want to keep the businesses we have here. I want to keep the large businesses we have here and continue to build Springfield's economy as best we can."
Cox has been acknowledged as a critical component to the success of the Illinois Medical Cannabis Program and the launch of the state's recreational use in 2020.
State Rep. Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago, told a national cannabis industry newsletter that the state's medical cannabis program was Cox's "monumental achievement."
The company he works for, Progressive Treatment Solutions based in Palatine, has cultivation centers, processing facilities and dispensaries in four states, including Illinois.
Cox said he would consult with city attorney Gregory Moredock on the possibility of having to recuse himself from any cannabis-related votes for zoning or conditional use permits, for example.
Cox was one of 12 candidates interviewed by Mayor Misty Buscher and Chief of Staff Mike Disco.
One citizens group that addressed the committee of the whole was angling for a more transparent process involving the candidates.
"My primary concern was that the process be well-communicated, and that outreach occur, and the mayor did all of that in the process of appointing Jeffrey Cox to Ward 1," said Steven Simpson-Black, who was part of the group, but not a candidate himself.
Judge denies injunctive relief over clerk's motion
A Sangamon County judge last week refused to grant a court injunction in a motion filed against the appointment of Redpath as city clerk.
Calvin T. Christian III, who is behind the website Springfield Leaks, called Redpath's appointment "unlawful" in last month's filing.
Christian said that Redpath's vote for himself as clerk on Jan. 7 violated parts of the Illinois Public Officer Prohibited Activities Act and the Illinois Municipal Code and that it created "a direct financial conflict of interest."
Judge Adam Giganti ruled Feb. 14 that Christian's allegations were "vague and do not clearly present an ascertainable right in need of protection." Christian also failed "to articulate or present evidence which would indicate a likelihood of success (for the motion)," Giganti said.
The mayor was named in the complaint.

title: IHSA wrestling state finals 2025: Glenwood brothers lead Springfield area pairings, results
author: Bill Welt
description: Tyler and Cooper Clarke became the first brothers in Chatham Glenwood history to reach state together, plus all the first-round matches in the area as the tournament starts Thursday
content:
Senior Tyler Clarke will make his third appearance at the IHSA individual state wrestling finals this weekend, but first with his younger brother, Cooper.
The Chatham Glenwood tandem became the first brothers in program history to qualify in the same year during the Lincoln Sectional on Saturday.
Tyler watched Cooper, a freshman, earn second place at 106 pounds before winning the 120-pound championship match with a 6-5 decision over Troy Triad's Will Kelly.
'I think he motivates me to be better because I feel like it's a competition between us two — who's the better one out of us two,' Tyler said. 'It's pretty cool.'
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Cooper won the Illinois Elementary School Association Class AA state title last year at 85 pounds.
'I get to wrestle him sometimes in the (mat) room,' Tyler said of Cooper, 'but he works a lot with one of our other guys and it helps him a lot. He's gotten a lot better over the year.'
Tyler, who is 38-9 and will wrestle at St. Ambrose University, was among the program's three individual sectional champions.
Junior Cody Moss (35-5) repeated as a sectional champion, this time at heavyweight. Junior Jenna Tuxhorn (31-2) also won another girls sectional title after moving up to 145 in the Highland Sectional.
They all carry the mantle following the graduation of Drew Davis, who won two state titles before departing to Southern Illinois University-Edwardsville.
Both Tyler and Moss deferred credit to their coaches. Moss is ranked No. 4 statewide by Illinois Matmen. Moss said he especially worked with athletic trainer Jon Wiezorek to get acclimated to the bigger weight class.
'It's a little different at first because at 215 there's a lot of motion and moving around,' Moss said. 'But at heavyweight, it's a lot slower pace. It's a big jump because I'm only at 240-250 right now. I feel like I'm a lot quicker, so it's a lot easier to move around those big guys.'

title: Trump removes 150-year-old Resolute Desk from the Oval Office to be 'lightly refinished'
author: Greta Cross
description: President Donald Trump temporarily removes the 150-year-old Resolute Desk from the Oval Office to be refinished.
content:
President Donald Trump has temporarily taken the 150-year-old Resolute Desk out of the Oval Office for refinishing.
'A President, after election, gets a choice of 1 in 7 desks,' Trump wrote on social media. 'This desk, the 'C&O,' which is also very well known and was used by President George H.W. Bush and others, has been temporarily installed in the White House while the Resolute Desk is being lightly refinished —a very important job. This is a beautiful, but temporary replacement!'
When President Harry S. Truman first used the desk at the White House, it was brought into the Oval Office by President John F. Kennedy and became an iconic backdrop as his son, John F. Kennedy Jr., played inside the desk while his father was working.
What is the Resolute Desk?
Gifted to former President Rutherford B. Hayes by Queen Victoria in 1880, the Resolute Desk is a double pedestal partner's desk made from oak timbers of the British Shop HMS Resolute, according to The White House Historical Association.
For many years, the desk was used on the second floor of the White House, where the presidential offices were located before the addition of the West Wing in 1902.
In 1945, the Presidential Coat-of-Arms, the seal of the U.S. president, was fitted on the desk.
Between 1948-1952, the desk was moved to the Broadcast Room on the White House's ground floor and was used for a short period of time for radio and television broadcasts by former President Dwight D. Eisenhower, according to The White House Historical Association.
Former President John F. Kennedy was the first president to use the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.
When former President Lyndon B. Johnson took office in 1963, he requested another desk for the Oval Office, according to The White House Historical Association. Between 1966 and 1977, the Resolute Desk was part of a traveling exhibition before it was put on display at the Smithsonian.
Former President Jimmy Carter requested the return of the Resolute Desk in 1977, where it has remained since − except by George H.W Bush who used the C&O Desk.
Per The White House Historical Association, before its arrival to the White House, the Resolute Desk was a part of a British arctic expedition in 1852. During the expedition, the desk was abandoned and became trapped it ice. In 1855, the desk was recovered by an American whaler and Congress appropriated funding to refit the ship that the desk was on to England, as a gift to Queen Victoria.
Queen Victoria reaffirmed the U.S. friendship and constructed a new version of the desk, which was then given to Hayes, according to The White House Historical Association.
What presidents have used the Resolute Desk?
Beginning with the 19th president, Rutherford B. Hayes, every president has used the Resolute Desk, except George H.W Bush, who only used it for five months before requesting the C&O, according to The White House Historical Association.
What is the C&O Desk?
The Georgian-style C&O Desk is made of walnut and features golden handles. The desk's acronym stands for the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway because the desk was built for one of the railway's owners and later donated to the White House, according to Realtor.com.
George H.W. Bush was the first and only president − up until Trump − to utilize the C&O Desk.
What other desks can a sitting president choose from?
Theodore Roosevelt Desk
The Theodore Roosevelt Desk was crafted for the former president in 1903. It resided in the West Wing until 1929, in which it was stashed until former President Harry S. Truman took it out of storage in 1945, according to Realtor.com. Former Presidents Eisenhower, Woodrow Wilson and William Howard Taft are among others who signed legislation on the desk.
Today, the Theodore Roosevelt Desk is housed in the Vice President's Ceremonial Office in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building.
The Johnson Desk
Upon taking office, Johnson requested that a new desk be made for the Oval Office by the Senate's carpenters, according to Realtor.com. Johnson was the only president to ever use the desk.
Today, The Johnson Desk is located at the Lyndon Baines Johnson Library and Museum.
The Hoover Desk
During former President Herbert Hoover's presidency in 1929, a fire severely damaged the West Wing of the White House, including the Oval Office. The president's desk survived the fire, but when new furniture was installed, so was a new desk.
A gift from the Grand Rapids Michigan Furniture Manufacture's Association, Hoover's desk was made of American wood and a Michigan maple veneer, according to the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum.
When former President Franklin D. Roosevelt took the presidential office next, he continued to use Hoover's desk. On the desk he signed the New Deal, declarations of war with Japan and Germany and the GI Bill, according to the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum.
The Wilson Desk
Despite what folks may think, The Wilson Desk was not named after former President Woodrow Wilson. Perhaps it was named after the early Vice President Henry Wilson, Realtor.com hypothesizes.
Former Presidents Gerald Ford and Richard Nixon both used the mahogany desk. Today, it is on display in the Vice President's Room in the U.S. Capitol.
