title: Williamsville reigns with the raining of 3s: Bullets beat Auburn to finish Sangamo perfect
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Williamsville struggled shooting against Auburn for a fifth straight quarter, but unlike the January Sangamon County Tournament finale, the Bullets got hot.
content:
AUBURN — It would've been understandable to experience déjà vu after the opening quarter of Friday's Auburn and Williamsville Sangamo Conference boys basketball regular season finale game.
Although the gym was different, there were throwbacks to Auburn's three-point, low-scoring win over the Bullets in last month's Sangamon County Tournament title game: the standing-room only crowd, students quick to cheer for a great play or a play gone wrong and, of course, Williamsville's cold shooting start.
The final three quarters at Auburn's Doglio Gymnasium, however, were anything but that January game at Lincoln Land Community College's Cass Gym as Bullets, ranked No. 7 in the final Class 2A statewide Associated Press poll, drained 14 3-pointers in a 60-48 win.
Williamsville, with its 27 th win, tied the school record, set back in 1991 when the Carey McVickers-led Bullets finished fourth in the state tournament. The Bullets finished this regular season 27-3 and a perfect 9-0 record in the Sangamo Conference.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Auburn (27-4, 6-3 Sangamo and ranked No. 6 in the final 2A poll) jumped out to a 12-2 lead in the first quarter on the back of eight points from senior Cooper Carter, who finished with a game-high 21 points. Once Williamsville senior Carson Doran hit a 3-pointer with 30 seconds left, it opened the Bullets' floodgates.
'That's a heavyweight battle right there,' Williamsville coach Nick Beard said. 'That's two really good teams. (Auburn coach Seth McCoy) does a great job with them. They got us, obviously, at County. We didn't shoot it well that night — that was well-publicized, we were 9 of 42, that's been talked about a lot — and I told everybody after (the County) game, I'd shoot them again.
'These guys are too good of shooters, they put too much time in and those were the same shots we got in the County, and we made them tonight.'
Auburn won the Sangamon County Tournament championship over Williamsville 32-29 on Jan. 13.
Williamsville, which shot 2-for-15 in the first period, were 16 of 29 the rest of the way, including 13-for-21 from behind the 3-point line (14 of 27 overall from deep).
'They (struggled shooting early), but they're capable of not (struggling),' McCoy said. 'They showed that, especially in the second quarter, the third quarter.
'Sometimes, you get out to those early starts and it's almost a kiss of death (because) thongs are going kind of so easy. I still think, even in that (12-2) run, we kind of forced some things and weren't as patient as we should've, or could've, been.'
Even when the team started off cold, Brayden Saling said the team was concerned but refused to panic.
'Coach told us we have to keep our composure, and we've got to keep attacking,' Saling said. 'We got good looks, they just weren't falling early, we kept our heads, and we knew that we were going to get good shots, and they were going to start falling.'
The Bullets got 42 of their points from behind the arc and 10 more at the free-throw line. But Williamsville senior Blake Shoufler said the Bullets' inside threat with Jackson Sanders is good enough to force teams to guard everyone.
Shoufler and Brayden Saling both finished with 18 points apiece for Williamsville. Sanders and Garrett Timm each had eight and Doran finished with six.
'I felt like we got the same, exact shots we got at County,' Shoufler said. 'We knew that coming in that we can make those shots. It started off slow, but we stuck together and once we saw a couple fall, we really got going.'
Any potential third game would come in the Greenville Sectional finals — that is if Auburn wins the Greenville Regional and a sectional semifinal and Williamsville advances out of the Pittsfield Regional and its own sectional semifinal — on Friday, March 7.
McCoy said his team will be ready with a few new wrinkles. For instance, the Trojans played their 2-1-2 defense all night, despite Williamsville's barrage of 3s. Playing a man-to-man or different zone could be in the works if a season series tiebreaker comes to fruition.
'Hopefully we see them again in two weeks,' McCoy said. 'We honestly tried not to run a lot of stuff offensively (Friday), our sets and things. We played them tonight in that 2-1-2, it worked well for us the first time, it didn't work as well this time, but I thought we were better offensively, too. I think there are positives to grow from offensively and I think there are still a lot of areas offensively we can get better at.'
Carter Hunley added 13 points for Auburn and pulled down 10 rebounds for a double-double.

title: Here's where each of the 13 Springfield-area homicide cases from 2024 stand
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The State Journal-Register took a look back at the deaths and the latest information on rulings and court happenings. Here's what we found out.
content:
Of reported homicides in 2024, 11 people are charged and awaiting trial.
Four homicides have seen no arrests made.
In 2024, the Springfield Police Department handled nine homicides.
The Sangamon County Sheriff's Office investigated three alleged homicides, while Illinois State Police handled one.
The State Journal-Register looked at all the homicides and the latest on the court happenings.
Here's what we found out.
Alexandria Estrada, 36, was struck by a Jeep near Oaklane Road just east of Interstate 72 on the outskirts of Springfield, and her body was found Feb. 3. Preliminary findings at the time suggested Estrada died from multiple blunt force injuries sustained in the crash. Former Sangamon County Sheriff Jack Campbell said deputies were able to follow a trail of blood from the roadway to a lot in a mobile home park. Steven Mehundrew, 53, who lived with Estrada in Springfield, was charged with first-degree murder, aggravated domestic battery, leaving the scene of an accident involving personal injury and failure to report an accident/death. Mehundrew initially pleaded not guilty. He later withdrew his plea of not guilty to first-degree murder. Mehundrew was sentenced to 20 years in the Department of Corrections. Multiple charges were dismissed.
Teresa Ann Coleman, 54, of Springfield, was found dead near the southbound entrance ramp to Interstate 55 at Stevenson Drive on March 13 after she had been missing for several weeks. Preliminary autopsy findings at the time determined that Coleman's death was a homicide, but Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon could not divulge then how Coleman died. Illinois State Police is leading the investigation. ISP said recently the investigation is open and ongoing and they have no updates to provide. The Springfield Police Department took a missing person report on Coleman when the department was contacted by her family.
Michael Newton, 33, of Springfield, was fatally hot at a mobile home park in the 1000 block of North Edmond Street in an unincorporated area of Springfield on May 4. He died from a gunshot wound to the neck, an autopsy showed. The Sangamon County Sheriff's Office handled the investigation. Brandon L. Berner, 23, of Springfield was arrested and faces three counts of first-degree murder charges. Berner turned himself in after a warrant was issued for his arrest. Berner plead not guilty, and his next court date is Feb. 24.
Keyon Day, 16, was fatally shot across from Dreamland Park on Taylor Avenue on April 24. He was taken to the hospital but did not survive. Witnesses had told police they saw vehicles after the shooting that were driving fast and erratically. Two Springfield juveniles were charged with first-degree murder. Dremone Patterson, 16, allegedly fired the shots that killed Day, using a stolen firearm, Springfield Police officials said. Patterson has a known gang affiliation and was charged as an adult with three counts of first-degree murder, having a stolen vehicle, having a stolen firearm, and having a firearm as a street gang member. Patterson pleaded not guilty. His next court date is Feb. 24. A 15-year-old driver of one of the vehicles at the shooting scene is charged with first-degree murder under accountability.
Michael Gristy, 23, was found stabbed inside a vehicle in the 2500 block of North Grand Avenue East on June 1. Springfield Police Deputy Chief Sara Pickford at the time said the stabbing happened in the 3000 block of Louise Lane, which is about one minute away from where he was found. Gristy apparently drove himself. He later died at the hospital. Pickford said "a person of interest" was quickly located at the Louise Lane location by Springfield Police and was taken in for questioning. No arrests have been announced.
Misty Long, 51, was stabbed to death at her home in the 3000 block of Shadow Fax Drive in the Twin Lakes subdivision on June 29. Her adopted son, Jonathan Long, allegedly killed her by stabbing her over 100 times in her face, neck, abdomen, arms and legs. He was charged with first-degree murder and aggravated domestic battery. Long's next court date is March 20.
In what has been labeled a homicide-suicide, Renee Terry, 61, died from multiple gunshot wounds and her husband, Robert Terry Jr., 67, died from a single self-inflicted gunshot wound in their home in the 1800 block of Post Oak Court on June 13. Springfield Police Deputy Chief Sara Pickford at the time said evidence recovered from the scene, results of forensic examinations and interviews with family members led to the homicide-suicide finding.
Sonya Massey, 36, was fatally shot in the 2800 block of Hoover Street in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield on July 6. Former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy Sean P. Grayson and another sheriff's deputy responded to a 911 call from Massey, a Black woman and the mother of two children, about a possible prowler around her home. Grayson, who is white, shot Massey in the face, after words over a boiling pot of water quickly escalated. Grayson was charged with first-degree murder. His next court date is March 24.
Sammie Tyrone McClinton, 45, died from multiple gunshot wounds on July 25. Springfield Police found him at the 700 block of North Fifth Street, and he was taken to the hospital. Shelton A. Woolridge, 27, was arrested the day of the shooting. He was charged with three counts of first-degree murder, one count of aggravated battery with a firearm, and one count of aggravated unlawful use of a weapon. Woolridge pleaded not guilty, and his next court date is March 17. Keundra T. Daniels, 21, was also arrested in connection with the alleged homicide. Daniels was arrested Aug. 29. and charged with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit aggravated battery with a firearm. Daniels pleaded not guilty, and her next court date is Feb. 24.
Qrrey Bates died of multiple gunshot wounds and was found dead in his vehicle near the intersection of 13th Street and Cornell Avenue on Aug. 9. Springfield Police Deputy Chief Sara Pickford said the car was still idling when officers arrived. Detectives found shell casings inside the car. No arrests have been announced.
DayQuan Wiley, 17, was shot fatally in a home at the corner of 11 th and South streets on Aug. 4. He died from multiple gunshot wounds and died shortly after arriving at the hospital. Springfield Police Deputy Chief Sara Pickford said there were multiple people in the home at the time. Two teenage boys have been charged with first-degree murder. Larryoun Taylor, 17, and an unnamed 15-year-old face charges. Taylor was charged with three counts of first-degree murder, and home invasion. Taylor pleaded not guilty, and his next court date is March 3.
Telley Palmer, 29, of Columbus, Ohio, died from multiple gunshot wounds after Springfield Police found him in the 400 block of South Illinois Street in the early morning of Sept. 29. Palmer was taken to the hospital where he died from the injuries. In a news release at the time, police said the shooting happened after a fight involving multiple people at a Springfield bar earlier that night. Police said they were not notified of the fight. No arrests have been announced.
Antoine Williams, 39, of Springfield died from gunshot wounds. Springfield Police found Williams in the front seat of a vehicle with the wounds in the area of 17th and Cook streets on Oct. 13. Ventellis B. Cooper, 48, was arrested and charged with three counts of first-degree murder, aggravated and unlawful use of a weapon and possession of a weapon by a felon. Cooper pleaded not guilty. His trial is set for March 17.

title: Duolingo's make-believe mascot, Duo the Owl, duped his death
author: Greta Cross
description: Two weeks after Duo the Owl's demise, Duolingo's language learning app's mascot admitted that \
content:
Duo the Owl, Duolingo's make-believe mascot, is alive. The language-learning app announced on Monday that the mascot had faked his death.
Duolingo announced two weeks ago that the mascot was fatally struck by a Tesla Cybertruck, resulting in his "death."
Duo, introduced with the app in 2011, has grown increasingly popular in recent years as he has parodied pop culture referencing and appeared in outrageous memes.
Nearly two weeks after Duolingo announced the death of their beloved mascot, Duo the Owl, fans around the world learned they had been duped all along.
In an Instagram video released on Monday, the language learning app quickly recapped the owl's death before the bright green bird is seen bursting from flames with a comic book-style text bubble that reads, 'I'm back.'
'Faking my death was the test,' Duo wrote in the caption, 'and you all passed.'
The quick-paced video shows the completion of several in-app challenges, implying that users' increased activity on the app may have brought the beloved mascot back to life.
In fact, the stunt was part of a global campaign in which the app pawned different countries against one another to see which could earn the most XP (experience points) to save Duo. As of Monday, the top three performing countries were the United States, Germany and Brazil, according to the Bring Back Duolingo website.
'Our favorite green owl has returned − though how he came back varies across different markets,' a Duolingo spokesperson told USA TODAY. 'As always, we love leaning into creative storytelling that keeps our learners engaged, and this campaign was a fun way to do just that. We're not done telling this story just yet − more details on what really happened to Duo will be revealed soon.'
How is the internet reacting?
Many of the top comments on the TikTok video were left by brands, weighing in on the news.
'What was it all for tho?' mobile game Subway Surfers commented on the video. 'This Monday got so much better,' replied Microsoft Surface.
'So are my missed lessons forgiven or nah'? Tide Rescue said, followed by, 'It's magic fr (for real). Corpo (corporation) brand magic,' commented cereal brand Magic Spoon.
Who created the comeback video?
Video editor Mikey, known online as Kiuzr, began working with Duolingo to create social media videos in December. Mikey's first project was the brand's annual Duolingo Year in Review. This video is visually similar to the recent one announcing Duo's 'resurrection,' featuring fast-paced edits. Mikey, who is based in the Philippines, wished to be referred to only by first name for privacy reasons.
Duolingo became aware of Mikey's work after Mikey posted a 'silly, bored edit' they did that featured Duo the Owl last year.
'I then went to bed as soon as I posted it, not expecting anything crazy in return. I then woke up to Duolingo following me and telling me to check (my) DM (direct message) and there I was, offered ... multiple editing projects with them,' Mikey said. Today, Mikey is a contract video editor with the brand.
Who is Duo the Owl?
Duo Keyshauna Renee Lingo, more commonly known as Duo the Owl, was born in 1000 BC, according to an X post made by Duolingo. The silly, animated green owl is known for quite aggressively reminding users to complete their daily lessons.
While Duolingo jokes its mascot was born in 1000 BC, Duo actually debuted in 2011, the year the app launched, according to Apple Developer. But Duo looked different then. The original Duolingo logo featured a 2-D owl whose eyes and mouth spelled out 'DUO.' A year later, the first 3-D version of Duo was released with a realistic owl body and two wide eyes that seemingly stared right into a user's soul.
In 2014, Duolingo decided to 'gamify' its mascot, making him cuter and more animated, according to Apple Developer. By 2018, the Duo the Owl users know and love (or fear) was released.
In recent years, Duo grew increasingly popular as he parodied pop culture references, appeared in outrageous memes and even partnered with Netflix to promote 'Squid Game.'

title: Top takeaways: Rochester, Pleasant Plains, Havana reach girls basketball sectionals
author: Bill Welt
description: Pleasant Plains, Havana used defensive chops and depth to reach the girls basketball sectionals, plus Rochester's Cinderella run
content:
Here are the top takeaways from each girls basketball team advancing to sectionals in the Springfield area:
Just the scores: IHSA girls basketball playoffs: Springfield area schedule and results
Class 3A
Rochester
Taylor Offer has long been a staple at Rochester, even back to freshman year.
The three-year starter and senior point guard reached 1,000 career points near the end of the regular season and currently leads the Rockets with 12.3 points per game.
She most recently scored the go-ahead free throws with 2.1 seconds remaining in a 42-41 regional final win over Taylorville for another stunning upset after knocking off 2024 state runner-up Chatham Glenwood in Monday's semifinal.
No. 7 Rochester (11-22) next meets No. 1 Mahomet-Seymour in the Chatham Glenwood Sectional semifinals on Tuesday at 6 p.m. as the lowest seed remaining in the 3A bracket.
'All of our hard work that might not show up in our record, it's showing now,' Offer said.
Everything just clicked in the postseason.
Junior forward Delaney Farris has been a vital contributor with 9.2 points and 5.4 rebounds per game with not only a strong inside presence but also the unique ability to hit nylon from behind the arc.
Junior guard Alaina Stock (6.5 ppg.) has also supplied Offer support as another reliable ball-handler. She dialed up three 3s and finished with 13 points behind only Offer's 14 points against Taylorville.
'Taylor's my biggest role model and I've gotten to learn from her the past few years,' Stock said. 'That's how I've gotten to be where I am now.'
On the subject of 3s, junior Cami Tinder drilled a big one just before the buzzer at the end of the third quarter. Coach Brandon Rose said he only recently moved Tinder into the starting lineup. It's all coalesced at the right time and the Rockets are playing with nothing to lose.
'Glenwood and Taylorville, they're both unbelievable teams,' Rose said. 'We told the girls, 'You've just got to go out there, not worry about how talented they are and stick to the game plan,' and they did. I couldn't be prouder of the girls, I really couldn't.'
Class 2A
Pleasant Plains
The Cardinals stress defense every day in practice, said junior forward Anna Weber.
They are now 22-0 when holding opponents under 40 points following Thursday's 38-26 regional final win over Sacred Heart-Griffin.
Plains limited SHG to just one field goal in the third quarter for its second straight regional title, while Weber once again stood tall inside with eight points and 14 rebounds.
'We just play really hard and that's one of the most important things for us is getting after it every single night,' Weber said. 'I think that's why our defense is so good.'
One big family: Pleasant Plains' sisters act soars into Sangamon County tourney: What to know, schedule
It's not only their effort, but also their physicality, length, and quickness, said SHG coach David Andrews.
'They're going to knock you off your cuts and try to take away your pick-and-rolls and everything else,' Andrews said. 'They're young, too, which is amazing because usually when you're that young, it takes a couple years before they get to that point.'
Plains coach TJ Fraase said they are always on the same page defensively. It's a connection that extends beyond the court as classmates, friends, and sisters, according to junior forward Grace Sabatka.
'We're just so close with each other and that makes our team really tight-knit, so being able to communicate well on defense is our No. 1 priority,' Sabatka said.
The Cardinals (25-6) meet Carlinville (25-5) in the Waverly Sectional semifinals on Tuesday at 7:30 p.m. Plains won the previous meeting 54-34 in November.
Carlinville
Senior point guard Isabella Tiburzi totaled 16 points and 16 rebounds in Thursday's 45-40 regional final win over Hillsboro.
Tiburzi has exceeded several career benchmarks with more than 1,300 points, 1,000 rebounds, and 500 assists. She will next play at Lincoln Land Community College.
She also has a strong supporting cast, including Kaitlyn Reels.
The junior sharpshooter recently set a school record with seven 3s in a 75-46 regional semifinal win over Auburn. She also combined for eight 3s and 46 points in wins over North Mac and Staunton for first place in the Macoupin County Tournament earlier in the regular season.
Staunton
The Bulldogs missed a couple of key contributors but still came away with their third straight regional title following Friday's 43-28 win over Alton Marquette.
Sophomore Jenna Staggs is expected back, but senior guard and returning starter Grace Bekeske has been out since the holidays with a season-ending injury, the Alton Telegraph reported.
Seniors Ele Feldmann (19 points and 10 rebounds), Sam Anderson (three 3s and 12 points), and Lilly Bandy (6-for-6 on free-throw attempts and eight points) remain to carry the mantle.
No. 2 Staunton (27-5) meets No. 1 Camp Point Central next in the Waverly Sectional semifinals on Tuesday at 6 p.m. in a rematch of last year's sectional semifinals that CPC won 56-50.
The Panthers, ranked No. 6 in the final Class 2A Associated Press poll, bring back standouts Karly Peters and Lauren Miller after withstanding Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central 45-41. Miller, committed to Southern Illinois University-Edwardsville, scored 23 points in the last meeting against Staunton.
Class 1A
Havana
Senior point guard Josie Hughes is a student of the game.
She constantly watches film and finds a way to contribute no matter the circumstances — injuries notwithstanding.
Hughes, also committed to Lincoln Land Community College, still feels the lingering effects of a shoulder injury stretching back to junior year.
She can still rustle up buckets, to be sure. She also champions the intangibles more than ever as a floor general such was the case in Thursday's 48-27 regional final win over Mendon Unity.
It was the team's second regional title in the last three years after reaching the supersectionals in Hughes' sophomore year.
'Sometimes being a leader and one of the best players on the floor doesn't necessarily always equal scoring the most points — at least not on our team,' Havana coach and Hughes' mom, Michelle Brady, said. 'We talk a lot about having a team effort and everybody doing their job. Sometimes that job changes.'
Impact players: See what new names are making an impact in girls basketball around Springfield
Hughes ushered seven points, while six other players also found the net. Junior Kaydi Miller led the Ducks (22-10) with 17 points, while junior Olivia Kramer had eight and freshman Ava Kramer added six.
Hughes shifted more focus toward her ball distribution to take advantage of the team's newfound depth. It became a top priority with a heralded freshman class to boot.
'Our freshman class is very strong and high IQ'd,' Hughes said. 'They were very successful in junior high and then we have upperclassmen who have stayed together for a long time.
'We have more threats on the floor at all times. We can pretty much sub in and out as much as we need. A lot of teams can't do that, so they get really tired.'
The Ducks next tackle Abingdon-Avon in the Monmouth United Sectional on Tuesday at 6 p.m. Abingdon is ranked No. 2 statewide in Class 1A, according to the final Associated Press poll.
'I've played with her my whole life,' Hughes said of her mom, 'so senior year and her being my coach, it's bittersweet almost.'

title: Pritzker pushes to ban cellphones in Illinois schools
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Gov. JB Pritzker announced efforts that would ban cellphones in Illinois classrooms. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Gov. JB Pritzker announced efforts that would ban cellphones in Illinois classrooms.
The governor made the announcement during the State of the State address Wednesday afternoon.
'This session, I'll move forward with legislation requiring all school districts in Illinois to adopt a cell phone policy that bans the use of phones during classroom instruction,' Gov. Pritzker said.
Bills introduced in both houses of the General Assembly would require school districts to create policy that bans personal cell phones during class, with some exceptions, the Associated Press reported.
The proposed legislation would require schools implement the policies by the 2026-2027 school year. The districts would be allowed to develop policies that best suit them, according to the AP.
The AP also reported eight states already ban or limit cellphone use, while 15 states have proposed similar measures.
The effort aims to improve student achievement, social interaction and the mental health of public-school students, according to AP.
In step, large school districts across the U.S. have taken the initiative to ban the distracting screens. Los Angeles Unified, the second-largest school district in the country, voted this past summer to ban smartphones.
Schools from Seattle to St. Louis are taking such initiatives, USA Today reported.

title: Illinois health insurance provider ending coverage for hundreds of thousands of patients
author: Claire Grant
description: A central Illinois-based health insurance provider plans on closing down the majority of its health plans at the end of the end of the year.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Carle Health announced that it will be shutting down the majority of its health plans, including Health Alliance and FirstCarolinaCare, at the end of the year.
State Senator Chapin Rose expressed concern for affected employees and policyholders, pledging to assist with job training and healthcare options.
Are you insured by Health Alliance? It may be time to start perusing the market for next year.
One of Illinois' insurance providers, Carle Health announced on Feb. 25 its plan to close down the majority of its health plans. The end of coverage will take effect at the end of the year, leaving thousands without coverage.
Throughout the remainder of 2025, the health plans will maintain operations to support claims processing and meet ongoing business needs, regulatory mandates and contractual obligations. Membership information will continue to be available through the Hally/MyChart member platform beyond the end of the year.
Based in the Ubrana-Champaign area, Carle Health said Health Alliance and sister company FirstCarolinaCare are ceasing operations at the start of next year due to financial struggles competing with other for-profit health insurance companies.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
'In recent years, the health insurance industry has changed dramatically, particularly for provider-owned insurers,' Carle Health said on Feb. 25 announcing the planned closures. 'Medical inflation, rising prescription drug costs, increased utilization of healthcare services, higher volumes of chronic medical conditions, coupled with an increased demand for technology and broad networks have placed considerable financial strain on those organizations.'
First reported by Times News Global, 187,000 policy holders will lose insurance coverage with the change of the new year. In Illinois, Health Alliance offers individual and employer group plans, individual and group Medicare Advantage plans and Medicare Supplement plans.
Carle Health's Health Alliance employs over 600 employees, which received communication from the company about transitioning to other positions within the company.
State Senator Chapin Rose, R-Mahomet, expressed his sadness and shock to learn of the end of operation for the affected employees and the tens of thousands of locals who rely on Health Alliance.
'My office will stand by to try and help in any way we can in job training and recruitment efforts for the impacted employees,' Sen. Rose said. 'Continuity of care and access to trusted physicians must be the priority as thousands of local members will now be forced to find a new insurance carrier.'
Sen. Rose said his team has already connected with the Central Management Services director for group health insurance to see what healthcare options will be available next May enrollment cycle for the families affected.
Health Alliance insurance plans first launched in 1980, as CarleCare HMO. It changed its name to Health Alliance in 1989 and it was reorganized as a for-profit insurance company owned by Carle Clinic.
Health Alliance is the largest healthcare provider in downstate Illinois.
Almost 250,000 people are insurance through the company in Champaign; FirstCarolinaCare in North Carolina will process claims until the end of the year.

title: Coroner identifies two people killed in crash rural Sangamon County
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Two people who were killed in a head-on collision on Illinois 97 in rural Sangamon County on Saturday have been identified.
content:
Two people who were killed in a head-on collision on Illinois 97, just west of Farmington Cemetery Road in rural Sangamon County on Saturday, have been identified.
Leslie Foggy, 63, of Springfield, and Tammy Boyer, 43, of Peterburg, died from the collision, confirmed Sangamon County Coroner, Jim Allmon.
Foggy died by the time first responders got to the crash site, while Boyer was taken to the Springfield Memorial Hospital but died shortly after arriving.
Preliminary findings show both people died from blunt force injuries from the collision, Allmon said.
The crash happened around 2:30 a.m., according to Illinois State Police officials.
A driver in a Mitsubishi Outlander headed east on Route 97 crossed the centerline and struck the driver of a Hyundai Sonata traveling the opposite direction.
The reason for why the driver crossed the centerline, according to a report provided by Trooper Jayme Bufford of the ISP, was "unknown."
Bufford said there were a couple witnesses that had stopped at the crash site, though no one witnessed the actual crash.
Traffic in both directions was shut down on Route 97 for about six hours Saturday morning, according to ISP.

title: Pritzker wants Dems to focus on 'making it easier to just live a little more affordably'
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker discussed multiple topics during a podcast appearance this week, including minimum wage and what Democrats should focus on.
content:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker spoke on a political podcast this week, touching on issues facing the country and the Democratic party.
The governor believes the Democratic party should focus on issues related to affordability.
Gov. Pritzker acknowledged a "rigged system" against working-class Americans.
The governor of Illinois has continued to garner attention with appearances on national news programs as he spoke with MSNBC this week -- this time on a podcast.
Gov. JB Pritzker spoke about the Democratic party amidst the U.S. political landscape, and he talked about how he might have campaigned he if were in those shoes. He talked multiple times about 'standing up for people' or 'fighting for people's rights' on the political podcast, The Blueprint with Jen Psaki.
The podcast is billed as one where Psaki examines what's next for the Democratic party after big losses in 2024.
Psaki previously worked as the White House press secretary for Former President Joe Biden's administration. Prior, she served as a traveling press secretary to former U.S. Senator Barack Obama as well as deputy press secretary after he became president and later serving as the deputy communications director.
Psaki asked Gov. Pritzker, if he were to have 'things on the agenda of how democrats would run in 2026, what would they be?'
'Well, it wouldn't be imposing tariffs on our friends to the north and the south,' he said.
'But what are we for? Let me start with – let's make it easier for people to get the education that they need, go to community college to get skills that they need for a better paying job. Let's make it cheaper for people to get their drugs. PBMs (Pharmacy Benefit Managers) have taken terrible advantage of people who are sick – making them pay much higher drug prices.'
Gov. Pritzker went on to say that every point he would list has to do with 'making it easier to just live a little more affordably.'
'I think if we work on those all the time – if we think about what makes it a little bit easier for everybody to just survive and live – to save for retirement, to get a better job, to get a higher wage…I think that's what the Democratic party should really be all about.'
The governor questioned why Democrats did not campaign with the point of raising the minimum wage, which is currently set at $7.25 per hour.
'You can't live on that,' he said, adding that Republicans want to keep that number stagnant, and some want to eliminate the minimum wage altogether.
'If you poll the question, it's very popular. People want to raise the minimum wage,' Gov. Pritzker said.
In addition to kitchen table issues that he said should be brought to the forefront for the Democratic party, the governor talked about how he prioritizes his time in office.
'Prioritizing means asking the question, first, are we addressing the problems of the most vulnerable people and working-class people?...Second, is it something that has long-term benefit for the people of my state, or in this instance as you're talking about, federally, for the people of the country.'
When asked to respond to the notion that some Americans feel that 'the system is rigged against' them, referring to government and big businesses like pharmaceuticals, Gov. Pritzker said he mostly agreed that the 'system is rigged in the sense of it leans toward not working-class people, not toward vulnerable people, but toward the wealthiest. It leans toward the powerful. So, you've got to counteract that.'
He went on to highlight his efforts to advocate for early childhood education in years past.
'It was clear to me that if you wanted to make real change, you had to focus on these very young children and particularly very young children in the most vulnerable situations,' Gov. Pritzker said.
Almost no resources were going to children younger than kindergarten age several decades ago, he said.
'No one wanted to put any money in. Why? Because the powerful special interests are not with very young, vulnerable children. In fact, they have no, powerful, special interests working for them. The powerful special interests for children are in the later ages, right? Teachers' unions and advocates for education and education reform…I had to work really hard to try to change the attitude toward that by pointing out to Republicans and Democrats that you save money by investing in the youngest children.
He said early investment in children makes them more likely to succeed in their academics and in turn, more likely to get a job and less likely to become incarcerated.
'Frankly, I'm a Democrat, in part because we're the ones who fight hardest for those people. We are the ones who fight hardest against the rigged system.'

title: Readers should demand accountability from lawmakers amid USAID cuts
author: Deborah Greiser
description: A Springfield-native and former USAID worker weighs in on cuts made by the Trump administration.
content:
Born and raised in Springfield, I am a proud graduate of Sacred Heart Academy and the University of Illinois. As a Peace Corps Volunteer in Malawi, I worked on a USAID project supporting credit unions where members pooled savings and borrowed against them to pay school fees for their children or to start small businesses.
Inspired by this experience, I joined USAID where I worked for more than 30 years, living in Rwanda, Guinea, Senegal, Ghana, Uganda, Ukraine and Armenia. I saw firsthand the difference that USAID programs made in peoples' lives and the enormous goodwill they engendered.
USAID health programs help fight infectious disease and provide treatments and preventive measures that help avert millions of deaths from AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria. When we help prevent disease such as Ebola or avian flu abroad, we also help keep the U.S. population safe and healthy and prevent these diseases from spreading to our shores.
USAID's education programs engage youth, create opportunity, and build resilience. They provide high-risk youth with training that connects them to jobs in their own countries, and less inclined to migrate to the United States. Combined with civic engagement opportunities, they provide alternatives to extremism.
USAID also provides humanitarian assistance to victims of disasters, providing power and water to people in Ukraine, and food to address the famine in Sudan. And the food aid that USAID provides — more than 40% of it is purchased from American farmers.
USAID partners with U.S. businesses, including those in Illinois, to enhance livelihoods across the globe through activities that expand their markets and create American jobs. USAID's partnership with John Deere helped Zambians mechanize their farming and increase productivity. This built demand for John Deere products, and contributed to a more resilient global food system.
USAID also partners with U.S. universities, three in Illinois. The U of I Soybean Innovation Lab identifies potential markets for soybeans in Africa and conducts research on African soybean diseases that helps U.S. farmers combat diseases that can decimate soybean crops. Last week the Lab's Director reported that his lab will close in April since USAID funding has been cut. As a result, U.S. soybean farmers will lose one of their best tools to expand their markets.
At less than 1% of the U.S. budget, U.S. Foreign Assistance is in the American interest. It promotes American values and goodwill between the United States and more than 100 partner countries.
It provides more than 50,000 American jobs and invests a significant portion of its budget in the American economy. It promotes American business overseas and educational and research partnerships that enhance American productivity. USAID's work helps keep Americans safe by managing public health risks overseas.
It promotes American security by providing economic opportunities as alternatives to migration or terrorism. USAID's work represents the best that we are as American people.

title: Two arrested after travelling to Springfield to try to kill someone, authorities say
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Two people traveled from New York to Springfield to allegedly attempt to murder one of their parents.
content:
Two people traveled from New York to allegedly attempt to murder one of their parents.
Emily E. Getman, 21, and Dylan A. Romer, 29, both of Mohawk, New York, were arrested after allegedly attempting to lure a man to "a specific location." Police found them near the area of Sangamon Avenue and North Dirksen Parkway.
Getman, whose father was allegedly in the pair's sights to murder, was arrested for attempted first-degree murder, conspiracy to commit murder, unlawful use of a weapon, aggravated assault, aggravated battery, and criminal damage to property.
Getman's preliminary hearing is scheduled for March 7.
Romer was arrested for conspiracy to commit murder but has since been released.
A shotgun was recovered from the vehicle that the two had been living in for several days, police said.
Getman was taken to a local hospital prior to being taken to the Sangamon County Jail, police said.
The Springfield Police Department received information about the two people with intent to murder on Feb. 21, officials said in a news release.

title: Readers should demand accountability from lawmakers amid USAID cuts
author: Deborah Greiser
description: A Springfield-native and former USAID worker weighs in on cuts made by the Trump administration.
content:
Born and raised in Springfield, I am a proud graduate of Sacred Heart Academy and the University of Illinois. As a Peace Corps Volunteer in Malawi, I worked on a USAID project supporting credit unions where members pooled savings and borrowed against them to pay school fees for their children or to start small businesses.
Inspired by this experience, I joined USAID where I worked for more than 30 years, living in Rwanda, Guinea, Senegal, Ghana, Uganda, Ukraine and Armenia. I saw firsthand the difference that USAID programs made in peoples' lives and the enormous goodwill they engendered.
USAID health programs help fight infectious disease and provide treatments and preventive measures that help avert millions of deaths from AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria. When we help prevent disease such as Ebola or avian flu abroad, we also help keep the U.S. population safe and healthy and prevent these diseases from spreading to our shores.
USAID's education programs engage youth, create opportunity, and build resilience. They provide high-risk youth with training that connects them to jobs in their own countries, and less inclined to migrate to the United States. Combined with civic engagement opportunities, they provide alternatives to extremism.
USAID also provides humanitarian assistance to victims of disasters, providing power and water to people in Ukraine, and food to address the famine in Sudan. And the food aid that USAID provides — more than 40% of it is purchased from American farmers.
USAID partners with U.S. businesses, including those in Illinois, to enhance livelihoods across the globe through activities that expand their markets and create American jobs. USAID's partnership with John Deere helped Zambians mechanize their farming and increase productivity. This built demand for John Deere products, and contributed to a more resilient global food system.
USAID also partners with U.S. universities, three in Illinois. The U of I Soybean Innovation Lab identifies potential markets for soybeans in Africa and conducts research on African soybean diseases that helps U.S. farmers combat diseases that can decimate soybean crops. Last week the Lab's Director reported that his lab will close in April since USAID funding has been cut. As a result, U.S. soybean farmers will lose one of their best tools to expand their markets.
At less than 1% of the U.S. budget, U.S. Foreign Assistance is in the American interest. It promotes American values and goodwill between the United States and more than 100 partner countries.
It provides more than 50,000 American jobs and invests a significant portion of its budget in the American economy. It promotes American business overseas and educational and research partnerships that enhance American productivity. USAID's work helps keep Americans safe by managing public health risks overseas.
It promotes American security by providing economic opportunities as alternatives to migration or terrorism. USAID's work represents the best that we are as American people.
The Trump Administration has essentially shuttered USAID, frozen life-saving assistance programs, and eliminated 12,000 American jobs.
I ask you, readers, to demand accountability from your Senators and Representatives. Demand that they stand up to the Administration, to end the freeze on foreign assistance, and to insist that the Administration respect the rule of law. Congress authorized the establishment of USAID. The Executive Branch cannot shut it down.

title: Midwest region gas prices declined from last week: See how much here
author: USA TODAY Network
description: Here's a look at how weekly regional gas prices changed in Midwest region last week compared with the week prior.
content:
Regional gas prices declined for the second consecutive week and reached an average of $2.94 per gallon of regular fuel on Monday, down from last week's price of $2.98 per gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
The average fuel price in the Midwest region is about the same price as a month earlier. According to the EIA, gas prices across the region in the last year have been as low as $2.77 on Jan. 8, 2024, and as high as $3.48 on July 29, 2024.
A year ago, the average gas price in the Midwest region was 5% lower at $2.80 per gallon.
The average gas price in the United States last week was $3.12, making prices in the Midwest region about 6.0% lower than the nation's average. The average national gas price is slightly lower than last week's average of $3.15 per gallon.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration's tally of prices in the Midwest states includes Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Tennessee and Wisconsin.

title: DOGE cuts target 4 Springfield locations among 20+ Illinois facilities
author: Steven Spearie
description: Leases for five Springfield-area federal agencies were among the 20-plus statewide being cancelled. Here's what we know.
content:
The Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) website lists five lease cancellations in the Springfield area.
The cancellation of leases purports to save nearly $15 million in Illinois.
Leases for five Springfield-area federal agencies were among the 20-plus statewide being cancelled, according to the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) website.
The cost savings from those five leases was $443,980, it claimed.
Four of the leases being eliminated are in Springfield, along with a field office in Litchfield.
Statewide, there are 24 cuts in Chicago, Champaign, O'Fallon, Hoffman Estates, Rockford, Joliet, Naperville, Fairview Heights, Peoria, Lisle, Rock Island, Tinley Park and Quincy with a savings of $14,876,081.
The website listed a total of 748 federal facility leases that are scheduled for termination. The leases account for more than 9.5 million square feet in property and $660 million in savings, the site said.
DOGE, which is headed by billionaire Elon Musk, was created by the President Donald Trump Administration to find ways to cut spending.
In addition to the termination of leases, the website listed cutbacks in federal agencies and cancellations of contracts.
Here are the Springfield-area offices on the DOGE cut list:

title: Democrats chant 'January 6' as Trump gives speech before Congress
author: James Powel
description: Congressional Democrats invoked the memory of the January 6 attack on the Capitol during Trump's address on Tuesday night.
content:
Democratic lawmakers that remained in the Joint Session of Congress invoked the memory of the January 6th insurrection that tore through the same chamber President Donald Trump spoke on Tuesday night.
Several House Democrats began shouting and then chanting "January 6" as Trump talked about defending law enforcement officers during his speech.
Some Democrats left the speech before the interruption, turning their back on the president to reveal black T-shirts with the word "RESIST" in white letters. Others continued to head for the exits during the remainder of the speech.
California Democratic Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove was one of the Democrats who left. She wrote on X, formerly Twitter, that 'there's only so much (expletive) a person can tolerate.'
'Through walking out, my message to Donald Trump is simple: stop the lies, stop the cheating, and stop the stealing - enough is enough. The American people deserve better,' she wrote in a statement.
Representative Al Green, a Texas Democrat, stood and yelled, " You don't have a mandate," before Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson ordered him removed. Green announced in February that he would file articles of impeachment against Trump over 'injustice in Gaza.'
"I'll accept the punishment. It's worth it to let people know that there's some of us who are going to stand up to against this president's desire to cut Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security," Green told a media scrum captured by CSPAN.
As Trump was complaining about Democratic support, California Democratic Rep. Gil Cisneros yelled: "But the stock market," while Michigan Democratic Rep. Rashida Tlaib yelled, "Save Medicaid."
Trump and Jan. 6 insurrection, pardons
More than 140 police officers guarding the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, were injured when a mob of Trump supporters broke into the Capitol building as lawmakers met inside to formalize the results of the 2020 presidential election, which Trump falsely claimed he won.
One Capitol Police officer, Brian Sicknick, died due to injuries related to the attack. Two other police officers, Howard Liebengood and Jeffrey Smith, died by suicide a few days after the riot.
Trump approved pardons for nearly 1,600 people charged in the riot as a part of the early days of his second term.

title: Sexual and racial harassment investigations among those halted in Illinois schools
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Hundreds of civil rights investigations have been halted at schools in Illinois since the Trump administration took office.
content:
The U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights has halted more than 10,000 student complaints nationwide.
The federal office is only pursuing investigations that involve disability -- leaving out categories like sexual and racial harassment.
The U.S. Office for Civil Rights enforces civil rights laws in schools and any other entity that receives funding from the Department of Education.
Hundreds of civil rights investigations have been halted at schools in Illinois since the Trump administration took office.
The U.S. Department of Education placed more than 10,000 student complaints related to disability access and sexual and racial harassment on hold since Inauguration Day, ProPublica reported last month.
The U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights has since told employees last week that the agency would only be pursuing existing investigations that involve disability discrimination, according to a report from ProPublica.
What does this mean for Illinois? Here's what you need to know.
What is the Office for Civil Rights?
The U.S. Office for Civil Rights enforces federal civil rights laws in schools and any other entity that receives funding from the Department of Education.
What's happening in Illinois schools?
In Illinois, there are 330 pending cases in total that are currently under investigation at the kindergarten through high school level (elementary-secondary) as well as post-high school education (post-secondary).
129 of the cases in Illinois involve disability, so those investigations will resume. Some of those are titled 'restraint and seclusion', 'disability harassment,' and 'denial of benefits," to name a few. Of the 129 cases involving disability, 106 of the investigations are attached to K-12 schools, while 23 investigations are attached to post-secondary schools.
What investigations remain on hold?
201 investigations remain halted. Some of those listed are labeled as "racial harassment", "sexual violence" and "sexual harassment", and "Title IX athletics," to name a few.
What K-12 districts have the most civil rights investigations?
The Office for Civil Rights publishes a list of institutions that are currently under investigation, and they update the list weekly. Publication on the list means OCR has started an investigation of a case concerning that institution.
Chicago School District 299 shows 18 investigations.
Champaign Community Unit School District 4 shows 12 investigations.
Springfield District 186 shows nine investigations.
Rochester Community Unit School District shows eight investigations.
Waukegan Community Unit School District 60 shows eight investigations.
Riverside Brookfield Township School District 208 shows five investigations.
Which post-secondary schools have the most civil rights investigations?
University of Illinois at Chicago shows 10 investigations.
Lake Forest College shows 10 investigations.
University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign shows seven investigations.
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale shows eight investigations.
Find a list of all open investigations at ocrcas.ed.gov/open-investigations.
Why were the investigations paused?
The focus of the investigations since President Donald Trump took office has shifted to "directed investigations," meaning that the Trump administration ordered those inquiries, according to ProPublica. The report said the bulk of investigations previously launched following students or families filing complaints.
The few investigations that the administration has opened so far reflect some of the president's priorities, the report said, like "getting rid of gender-neutral bathrooms, banning transgender athletes from participating in women's sports and alleged antisemitism or discrimination against white students."

title: Marches, markets and memoirs. What to know about International Women's Day.
author: Hannah Hudnall
description: From marches, markets and memoirs, here's what to know about International Women's Day, including how it started and how you can celebrate.
content:
Show Caption
March 8 is International Women's Day, and with that comes a chance to celebrate the strength and accomplishments of women around the globe while advocating for their rights. This year's theme is "accelerate action" for gender equality.
Here's what to know about the upcoming holiday.
What is International Women's Day?
The first official National Woman's Day took place in New York City on Feb. 28, 1909, and was organized by members of the Socialist Party of America, according to History.com. Thousands of women's suffrage advocates and supporters of socialist ideals showed up to demonstrate and listen to addresses by labor organizer Leonora O'Reilly and other speakers.
The idea soon caught on in Europe, and the first International Women's Day was on March 19, 1911, drawing more than 1 million demonstrators globally. Countries including Russia, China and Spain soon adopted the holiday, and it was celebrated primarily in socialist countries until the mid-1970s.
The United Nations General Assembly recognized 1975 as International Women's Year and began celebrating March 8 as International Women's Day.
By 2014, the day became regularly celebrated in more than 100 countries and was made an official holiday in more than 25. It is now a day to advocate for equality, women's education, reproductive rights and more, and garners demonstrations in cities across the globe.
Ways to celebrate International Women's Day
Your celebration can start at home by honoring the important women in your life. You can buy them a bouquet of flowers, write them a handwritten card or treat them to dinner.
You can also donate to a women's rights organization or charity, such as the Center for Reproductive Rights, the Global Fund for Women or the Malala Fund. There's an endless number of nonprofits who advocate for women's education, reproductive rights, equality and empowerment, and would benefit from a donation.
If you want to use your money differently, you can support a women-owned business. USA TODAY published a list of various shops founded by women who sell homemade pasta, plants, makeup and more.
Those who want to educate themselves about powerful women — past and present — can pick up a biography and read their stories too. You can learn about the achievements and struggles of former first lady Michelle Obama, the late Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O'Connor or the female pilot Amelia Earhart.
Story continues after gallery.
Events happening in Illinois
Women's March is teaming up with Gemmes for Femmes to host an International Women's Day march in Chicago on Saturday, March 8. The march kicks off at 11 a.m. at Daley Plaza and will head towards Trump Tower near 98 E. Wacker Drive, according to the organization's website. Participants are encouraged to bring friends, signs and passion.
The Lincoln Square Ravenswood Chamber of Commerce is holding its 4th annual International Women's Day market at Artifact Events, located at 4325 N Ravenswood Avenue. The market will take place from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on March 8 and 9, and admission is free. It will feature a variety of pop-up shops run by women-owned businesses selling jewelry, food, home goods and more.
Read and Run Chicago is hosting a running tour in Chicago's West Loop to celebrate International Women's Day. The 4-mile "easy paced" guided running tour will focus on important women in West Loop's history and feature discussions with several stops. Tickets range from $15-35, and runners meet at Madison Street Books at 10 a.m. on March 8.
We the People Fitness Studio is holding an International Women's Day retreat from 12:30-3:30 p.m. on March 8. The 18+ event will feature yoga, massages, discussions and more, and tickets are $65.
Chicago Socialist Alternativeis organizing a speakout for International Women's Day at the University of Illinois Chicago quad on March 8. The event will feature discussions about women's rights and is open to all – including non-UIC students.
Why isn't International Women's Day on the Google calendar?
Google removed a variety of cultural holidays from its calendar in 2024, including the start of Women's History Month and International Women's Day.
The company said in a February statement that maintaining hundreds of international and national holidays globally "wasn't feasible." It said that though it had reverted to only displaying public holidays and national observance from timeanddate.com globally, users are encouraged to manually add other important moments.
Other holidays cut from the calendar include the start of , Lunar New Year, Holocaust Remembrance Day and Indigenous Peoples' Day.

title: Tariffs on aluminum will impact breweries across Illinois—and you may be paying for it
author: Claire Grant
description: 'Our craft breweries could see a $10.2 million increase in packaging costs, testing their already delicate supply chains and razor-thin margins.\
content:
With the calendar turning to March and the weather feeling more spring-like, you may be wanting to get a beer and sit outside to enjoy it. If that sounds good to you, just plan on paying more for the beer.
President Trump's tariffs on aluminum imports will likely impact both craft and domestic beer.
Importers were expected to pay the 25% tariffs starting March 4.
The Illinois Craft Brewers Guild believes the 25% tariff will greatly impact small brewery owners and its customers.
'Our craft breweries could see a $10.2 million increase in packaging costs, testing their already delicate supply chains and razor-thin margins,' the Brewers Guild posted to X.
Roughly half of all aluminum used in the states is imported, and almost all of it comes from Canada – roughly 3.2 million tons in 2024 in Canadian imports. According to Industrial Quick Search directories, Illinois has five aluminum producers, but none are in Sangamon County for local brewers – the closest is in Peoria.
While two decades ago there were none, Springfield is now home to several small to large breweries with ranging spicy to sweet flavors.
Brent Schwoerer, owner of Engrained Brewing Co. and board member of the Illinois Craft Brewers Guild, says the larger the brewery is on distribution, the harder the hit.
'In terms of what goes up our cans will by 25%, cans are a relatively small cost percentage for a case of beer,' Schwoerer said. 'Everything has gone up over the last two years as we continue to see the biggest increase in 2023. Grain prices went up 25 to 30 percent.'
Schwoerer says every packaged drink Engrained produces can vary in range, but ballparks at about 20 cents a can. In 2024, Engrained produced 15,000 cans of craft beer with 10,000 for distribution – about 5% of total business sales.
Ryan Kunken is another brewmaster in Springfield whose keeping Prairie State beer history alive through partnership with Reisch Charities to bring back Reisch beer with master brewer George Reisch.
The beer, which will be released later this year, will be canned in Springfield.
Rebecca Kunken, on behalf of her husband Ryan, and Schwoerer both agree prices going up mean amendments to how the businesses operate. Kunken said for the first time since opening in 2019 their brewery has increased prices, even without aluminum being a factor.
The rising costs can also be found in electric bills and air gas for the brewing process, which had six significant spikes in price last year.
'A lot of us are eating the majority of it,' Schwoerer said. '(Consumer) prices really haven't gone up in alignment with food in restaurants or other areas of the economy.'
Those broad rising costs and mounting fear about price increases cutting into thin margins of profit isn't just in the beer industry, too.
In a recent survey from business platform Alignable, one third of all small businesses in Illinois are afraid of revenue loss. In the same study, 18% of small businesses nationally foresee a boost in sales, while 40% said they didn't see tariffs having impacts on their sales.
'I think I can speak on every business out there we're just trying to make it and be cost efficient as possible,' Kunken said. 'The other side of it is you don't want the integrity and the taste of beer to go down. You just need to be mindful of where your expenses are going out.'

title: The federal government could shut down this week. Here's what that means for Illinois
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A possible government shutdown is looming. Here's what a shutdown would mean for Illinois.
content:
The federal government will shut down if a funding bill is not passed by the end of Friday.
Illinois has over 40,000 federal civilian employees who could be working with pay, working without pay, or furloughed with no income.
A possible government shutdown is looming.
Current funding for the federal government expires at the end of this Friday. If a funding bill is not passed, then the government will be forced to furlough thousands of federal workers and reduce federal services.
Here's what that means for Illinois.
How many federal employees are in Illinois?
Illinois has 44,784 federal civilian employees as of December 2024, according to data from the U.S. Office of Personnel Management.
Would all federal workers in Illinois stop working?
If the government shuts down, federal employees throughout the country would be working with pay, working without pay, or furloughed with no income.
Some federal employees would be deemed essential and not stop working, such as law enforcement and those involved in national defense.
Do state employees stop working under a federal government shutdown?
State employees whose employers depend on federal funds to operate could be out of work during a shutdown if their work is deemed by the government to be non-necessary, according to a USA Today report from 2023.
State employees who receive salaries from private employers who do not rely on federal funds wouldn't necessarily be impacted, though certain state employees could be furloughed until a shutdown passes.
How many state employees are in Illinois?
Illinois employs more than 76,000 people at state agencies and departments, according to a 2022 report from The State Journal-Register.
U.S. Postal Service
The U.S. Postal Service would not be affected because it does not depend on Congress for funding.
Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid
These agencies and programs would continue because some of their mandatory spending is not subject to annual appropriations by Congress.
National Parks
National parks, monuments, and other sites would close to the public, with rangers furloughed and facilities shut down. Some states may temporarily fund park operations, as seen during the 2018-2019 shutdown, according to USA Today.
TSA and air traffic controllers
Any travel plans are unlikely to be disrupted.
Transportation Security Administration agents who operate security at airports, as well as air-traffic control workers would be required to work.
Some airports in past shutdowns have struggled with staffers not showing up to work, though, which forced some operations to be suspended.
Why might the Republican proposal not pass?
Actions taken by the Department of Government Efficiency and Musk are top of mind for Democrats, who warned that a shutdown could be looming as they push back against Republicans' proposal, endorsed by President Donald Trump.

title: Student interest 'very strong' as District 186 adds American Sign Language
author: Steven Spearie
description: The addition of American Sign Language by School District 186 comes as the state mandates students take two years of a world language.
content:
In addition to American Sign Language, School District 186 offers Spanish, French, German and Latin.
Around one million people use ASL as their main way to communicate, according to Communication Service for the Deaf.
District officials studied the addition of ASL before it passed through the curriculum council in December.
Carrie Sluga, a deaf and hard of hearing teacher for Springfield School District 186, said when a board of education member expressed interest in the district adding American Sign Language to the curriculum several years ago, she knew she had to seize the momentum.
Sluga and one of her colleagues, Heather Gibson, had worked behind the scenes for years wanting to get ASL into the district's three high schools, Lanphier, Southeast and Springfield.
"Sarah Blissett made that comment (at a board meeting in 2022), and we took that spark and ran with it," Sluga said in a recent interview at District 186's administrative office. "We brought it forward and said, 'This is what we need to do.'"
Three years later, after studying what other high schools have done and wading through different curricula, the district will be offering ASL as a "world language" option to high schoolers this fall.
It comes at an opportune time after the Illinois State Board of Education made it a graduation requirement for all high schoolers enrolling this fall to have two years of a world language.
The addition has piqued student interest. More than 50 students at each of the high schools have signed up for ASL, meaning that in all likelihood different sections of it will be offered at each school, said Lance Thurman, the district's executive director of secondary schools & programs.
The district currently offers Spanish, French, German and Latin, all at four-year levels, said Rachel Dyas, a spokeswoman for the district.
Sluga said the idea is to get ASL to that level.
Around one million people use ASL as their main way to communicate, according to Communication Service for the Deaf.
Only a handful of school districts offer it, though. ISBE fully began counting it as a world language in 2021.
Sluga, Gibson and Thurman, along with two other deaf and hard of hearing teachers for the district, Carol Galusha and Rachel Cowle-Healy, visited ASL high school programs in Jacksonville, Peoria, Lyons Township and Hinsdale South, among other places.
Some also were able to attend the World Languages Conference put on by the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages in Chicago in 2023.
"We asked them all the questions: how you got started, how you got to where you were, what worked and what didn't, curriculums and everything, so when we were ready to bring this to the next level, we had all of our i's dotted and all of our t's crossed," Sluga said.
The plan was vetted by the district's foreign language group before being signed off by the curriculum council, Thurman said.
"It was probably the most positively received program I had been involved with moving through curriculum council," he added.
Thurman called student interest "very strong." The number of students who have signed up will determine how many teaching positions the district will add, he said.
That interest, said Sluga, who studied deaf education at MacMurray College and formerly served as a deaf interpreter for the district, "makes me smile from ear to ear. It makes all this hard work worth it."
Sluga said it could have other benefits, too, like connecting higher-level students with some of the district's life skills kids and promoting deaf education as a career.
For Blissett, the issue was personal. A close family member was recently tested for hearing problems, leaving Blissett wondering how she and other family members were going to communicate with him.
Blissett credited former school board president Judy Johnson for also championing the idea of adding ASL.
"I had the right people listening at the right time," she said.

title: Springfield fine dining restaurant reopens weeks after closing
author: Claire Grant
description: A fine dining restaurant in Springfield reopened about three weeks after it was closed until further notice.
content:
Loukinens' on 4th reopened its doors on March 2 after a brief stint of closing down to the public in February.
The reopening comes after a series of missteps for the casual fine-dining restaurant, which closed suddenly on Feb. 13 until further notice.
A foreclosure filed on Dec. 8 of last year by a Chicago-based law firm on the property led to the temporary closing of the location at 517 S. Fourth St.
Prior to Feb. 13, on Jan. 12 the business had posted on its Facebook alcohol would no longer be offered at the establishment, moving the restaurant to a bring-your-own-beer status.
Concurrently, the business is now serving lunches and dinner with soft drinks, as the bar works back up to its full-service status.
'Chef Keith has been working diligently with a solid group of long-term local business owners and banks to guide Loukinens' to correction and recovery,' Loukinens' stated in a social media post Feb. 23. 'Should Loukinens' be miraculously blessed with the opportunity to reset, know that it will come with a love and humility that most people never get to experience. Bruised but wiser.'
As the public found out about the unexpected closing of Loukinens', a GoFundMe started by Loukinens' owners Keith and Laurie Loukinen garnered $2,900 in donations before ending the donation period.
According to the business' website, the hours of operation have returned to 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., then 4 p.m. to 9 p.m.

title: Why Pritzker holds 'degree of skepticism' on new carbon capture bill
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: New legislation would help decarbonize Illinois. But the governor, along with some environmental groups, aren't fully on board yet.
content:
Illinois is attempting to completely decarbonize energy production by 2045, and, without carbon capture storage, advocates say it will be hard-pressed to meet that goal.
Several Democrat lawmakers, along with a selection of business and agriculture groups, are putting their weight behind recently introduced carbon capture storage legislation.
The Climate and Landowner Protection Act, its language contained in Senate Bill 3311 and House Bill 569, specifically targets the usage and ownership of pore space — empty underground areas between sand and sediment — plus creates new sources of funding for first responders.
"With this legislation, we can decarbonize without deindustrializing our state," said Illinois Manufacturers' Association president and CEO Mark Denzler during a press conference Wednesday.
Climate Jobs Illinois also supports the legislation, sponsored by Sen. Bill Cunningham, D-Chicago and Rep. Jay Hoffman, D-Swansea.
Sierra Club of Illinois however says the legislation is too limited, focusing solely on sequestration, and is instead backing legislation that would regulate CO2 pipelines and prohibit the use of eminent domain.
Denzler contended pipeline regulation is a federal matter for the U.S. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, currently crafting updated rules following a 2020 pipeline burst in Satartia, Mississippi causing over 40 people hospitalizations and more than 200 evacuations.
The bill would clarify that the owner of the surface estate would also own the beneath pore space, but would still allow for easements of the property. Securing easements proved to be difficult for the now cancelled Navigator Heartland Greenway — only receiving 13.4% of easements to construct its pipeline.
Local municipalities would also be eligible for grant funding, calculated by 1 cent for every ton of carbon dioxide injected into a sequestration facility for each fiscal year. The money could be used to cover emergency response plan expenses along with the purchase of new equipment.
Having funds to purchase new equipment, particularly electric vehicles, has been of particular importance to the Sangamon County Board who previously approved a moratorium on CO2 pipeline sequestration projects. Local officials have said EVs will be necessary in the case of a pipeline burst since gas-powered vehicles cannot start without oxygen.
Asked by reporters at an unrelated press conference, Gov. JB Pritzker said he had not yet reviewed the legislation. Essential to its passage, he said, were ensuring that business and landowner perspectives are represented.
"We're going to be working through how if he would, we would implement carbon capture in the state of Illinois," he said at the governor's office. "Is it going to be safe for people who are living in areas where carbon capture will be taking place? How would we implement it to make sure that in the construction of that, that it would be safe?"
Despite being seen as a prime geologic region for carbon capture, projects have struggled to gain footing in Illinois.
Both Navigator CO2 Ventures and Wolf Carbon Solutions LLC pulled applications with the Illinois Commerce Commission last year, with Navigator ultimately cancelling its 1,350-mile pipeline. The ICC is currently reviewing a much smaller scale project in Ford and McLean counties.
