title: Springfield pulls ordinance that would give city authority to address homeless encampments
author: Steven Spearie
description: The ordinance would give police and city staff legal authority to address encampments that pose significant health and safety risks.
content:
A Springfield City Council ordinance some people saw as an infringement on homeless individuals was pulled by its sponsor from emergency passage at Tuesday's meeting.
By a voice vote, it was sent to the regular committee route in front of a standing-room only crowd.
The ordinance came in light of a U.S. Supreme Court ruling this summer that bans prohibiting homeless individuals from camping on public property are not unconstitutional.
Mayor Misty Buscher said the ordinance was put on "emergency passage" because two "campers" have died with the past couple of weeks and Springfield Police were "concerned about the safety of campers."
But Buscher, who proposed the ordinance with Ward 5 Ald. Lakeisha Purchase, also acknowledged that route created "angst within the community."
The "germane part of the ordinance," Buscher insisted, was to help people in danger.
It would give police and city staff legal authority to address encampments that pose significant health and safety risks and to encourage applicants to accept other alternatives of shelters, drug treatment programs and mental health facilities.
"Campers" would have to be given 24 hours notice of removal and if they were still there 24 hours later, social service agencies that would serve them would be alerted by SPD and their personal belongings would be held for 30 days if they had nowhere to put them.
Violators could also face fines and jail time.
Keegan Otwell, who said he lost "everything except the clothes off me twice," said the ordinance sought to criminalize homelessness.
"This is not a motivation to get off the streets," Otwell said. "This is a condemnation to stay on the streets."
Ward 6 Ald. Jennifer Notariano said the city was "rushing to add this tool to our toolbox without an understanding of how it will affect our city."
Dozens of municipalities across the country have added some similar ordinances to their city codes.
Springfield should approach the homelessness problem with "persistence, compassion and respect," Notariano added.
Jenna Broom called the ordinance "vile, callous and abhorrent."
City attorney Gregory Moredock said the ordinance didn't punish the status of being homeless and that it was "equally applicable to individuals without regard to their housing status."
He said the ordinance was drafted using the recent Supreme Court decision, "Grants Pass (Oregon) v. Johnson," and several other templates, including one from the Illinois Municipal League (IML).
Buscher is a board member of the IML.

title: Former Springfield police sergeant arrested after crash as residents protest
author: Steven Spearie
description: A former police sergeant with the Springfield Police Department has been arrested after he was involved in a crash that seriously hurt two people.
content:
A former police sergeant with the Springfield Police Department has officially been arrested after he was involved in a crash that seriously hurt two people last week.
Michael Egan, 50, has been charged with aggravated DUI causing great bodily harm, a Class 4 felony. Authorities said Egan's vehicle was traveling northbound on East Lake Shore Drive and made a left turn in front of a motorcycle which crashed into Egan's SUV.
Egan was taken into custody by Illinois State Police troopers and U.S. Marshals around 12:45 p.m. Monday.
Egan will make his first appearance in Sangamon County Tuesday afternoon.
Meanwhile, about 30 or so protesters at the Municipal Building East briefly made it into the foyer before being turned back by police. A line of officers emerged with shields.
The two people, Trevor Hopkins and Chelsey Farley, were both seriously hurt in Thursday's crash. Hopkins was discharged from HSHS St. John's Hospital on Friday.
Deputy Chief Sara Pickford of Springfield Police said Egan's last day of employment with the department was Thursday.
Egan had 20 years of experience with the department and was promoted to sergeant in 2022, according to a State Journal-Register file story.
Egan was initially cited in the crash.
Residents rallied outside of the Springfield police headquarters, 800 E. Monroe St., on Monday after the crash. One of the residents was detained.

title: Downtown Springfield business launches fundraiser to keep doors open
author: Claire Grant
description: It's been nearly three months since the fire on Adams Street in downtown Springfield, but nearby businesses are still feeling the impact.
content:
The fallout continues nearly three months after a fire in the 400 block of East Adams Street in downtown Springfield.
While the anchor restaurant at 413 E. Adams St., Cafe Moxo, remains closed and other businesses have moved locations entirely, The Keep Store, a block away at 314 E. Adams St., recently launched a fundraising effort to help keep the business' doors open.
The business is struggling to cover basic expenses such as rent, utilities, and restocking popular items according to the fundraiser set up by owner Ami Shelton.
"Our Saturday sales, which used to be what kept us afloat during market season are now often less than our slower weekday sales," Shelton said. "We signed on to lease this space because of this location, not in spite of it."
According to Shelton, the movement of the Farmer's Market has had a negative reaction to the location, as sales have dropped by 50-60% since June without foot traffic.
The goal of the donations is to raise enough funds to continue providing refillable products and sustainable solutions to reduce single-use plastics in the area.
A donation goal of $5,500 has been set by Shelton, who says the goal will fund a few months of rent and enough to start restocking items.
The business did not request financial assistance from the Adams Street Fire fund Shelton said, because so many were directly impacted in devastating losses, while The Keep Store has been seeing decline in foot traffic due to the long-term effects of shutting down Adams.
'As many of you know, we have never crowd funded or asked for donations, fronting this business using 25 years' worth of our hard-earned money and savings,' Shelton said. 'However, those funds are now depleted.'

title: Former Springfield Police sergeant pleads not guilty in aggravated DUI case
author: Steven Spearie
description: Witnesses and others maintain a former Springfield Police sergeant got preferential treatment at a crash site Thursday.
content:
Making a brief first appearance in Sangamon County Court Tuesday, former Springfield Police Sgt. Michael Egan pleaded not guilty to a single charge of aggravated DUI causing great bodily harm.
Egan was wearing an orange-striped Sangamon County Jail issued uniform when he appeared before Associate Judge Rudolph Braud.
Braud set an Oct. 3 preliminary hearing for Egan, who faces 1 to 12 years behind bars if convicted. The charge is probation eligible.
Illinois State Police said Egan's vehicle was traveling northbound on East Lake Shore Drive Thursday evening and made a left turn in front of a motorcycle, which crashed into Egan's SUV.
Chelsey Farley, a passenger on the motorcycle, had multiple broken bones and fractures and damaged organs from the crash. She underwent an 11-hour surgery on Saturday and was scheduled for another surgery on Monday.
Farley's boyfriend, Trevor Hopkins, who was operating the motorcycle, had a head injury but has been discharged from the hospital, according to Farley's sister, Caitlyn Weiss.
A Springfield Police lieutenant at the crash scene called in ISP to take over the crash and subsequent DUI investigation.
Witnesses to the crash said it appeared that Egan, who had retired that day and whose retirement party was set for Friday, got preferential treatment.
Jason Rule, a motorcyclist who was following Hopkins and Farley but did not know the couple, saw Egan sitting in the front seat of an ISP cruiser.
"He was leaning out of the window, laughing at us," Rule told The State Journal-Register Monday.
Rule said he was close enough to Egan that he could "smell liquor on his breath, for sure."
A representative speaking for ABATE of Illinois, Josh Witkowski, said Monday that even though the sergeant showed visible signs of impairment, SPD officers appeared to be "palling around with their colleague rather than acknowledging the seriousness of the situation.
"Palling around does not build trust," Witkowski added. "That does not lead one to believe that we will all be treated equally under the eyes of the law."
SPD Chief Ken Scarlette said an internal investigation about conduct of officers at the crash scene had been started.
Egan was arrested Monday by ISP troopers and U.S. Marshals as a confrontational protest at the Municipal Building East, which headquarters SPD, erupted.
About 30 protesters, some banging on the building's windows and shouting "No justice, no peace, prosecute the police!", briefly made it into the foyer before they were turned away.
Officers later appeared with shields to prevent them from re-entering the building.
One person was arrested and one person was cited at the scene.
Egan had 23 years with SPD.
According to the Illinois Law Enforcement Training and Standards Board, Egan was an officer with the Springfield Park District Police Department for about a year-and-a-half beginning in 1998. He then worked for the Loami and Leland Grove police departments on a part-time basis before being hired by SPD in 2001.

title: 10 fall festivals and outings in the Springfield area you won't want to miss
author: Steven Spearie
description: From carving pumpkins to walking in Lincoln's footsteps, fall festivals and outings in the Springfield area are on tap.
content:
Check out some fine art, tour a historic (and some say haunted) mansion or be part of a bicentennial celebration.
There's a fall festival or outing for you in and around Springfield.
Here's a sampling of what's going on.
Edwards Place Fine Art Fair
The 36th annual Edwards Place Fine Art Fair features artists from around the country exhibiting a variety of media Sept. 21 (10 a.m. to 5 p.m.) and Sept. 22 (10 a.m. to 4 p.m.)
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
There are tours of the historic Edwards Place, a 190-year-old Italianate mansion. The fair features live music and food and beverage vendors. A used book sale benefits the Michael Victor II Art Library. 700 N. Fourth St. springfieldart.org. 217-523-2631. Free.
While in the neighborhood, visit historic homes in the Enos Park neighborhood in various stages of renovation. Tours are from 1 to 5 p.m. Sept. 21. Tickets available at the booth at the art fair. 217-553-4629. $10.
Clayville Fall Festival
Visitors to the Clayville Fall Festival Sept. 21-22 (10 a.m. to 5 p.m.) can join in on the bicentennial celebration of the Broadwell Inn and Tavern. The inn, according to an online history, served as a stagecoach stop and public house catering to stagecoach passengers, freight caravans, freight carriers, cattle drivers, circuit riders and others.
The name stems from Whig Party statesman Henry Clay and the Broadwells, the namesake of the inn, were prominent Whig participants. An 1842 Fourth of July celebration there drew another early Whig advocate, Abraham Lincoln.
The fall festival includes Civil War camps with the 10th Illinois Infantry Regiment, the 108th Illinois Infantry Field Hospital and others. Chris Camp (The Whip Guy) will be giving demonstrations and Batterton and Edwards will provide the music. Pleasant Plains, Illinois 125. clayville.org. 217-481-4430. Free.
Buzz Bomb Oktoberfest
Oktoberfest in September? Why not, especially when Buzz Bomb Brewing Company will be serving up several German styles of beers, along with other local breweries, and the musical headliner is the legendary Supersuckers.
The Sept. 21 outdoor festival will also include food, vendors, games and children's activities.
Other bands include Left Lane Cruiser, Aage Birch, Sonic Sunday, Master Bastard and Prairie State of Mind. Minors are allowed outside but must be accompanied by a parent/guardian to go inside Buzz Bomb. 406 E. Adams St. buzzbombbrewingco.com. 217-679-4157. $10.
International Route 66 Mother Road Festival
The Mother Road Festival routinely draws some 1,200 classic and antique cars and other vintage vehicles to downtown between Washington and Capitol streets and Fourth and Seventh streets Sept. 27-29.
It kicks off with the Route 66 City Nights Cruise from the Capitol City Shopping Center on Dirksen Parkway to downtown at 6:15 p.m. Friday. Dennis Gage will be filming an episode of Motor Trend TV's "My Classic Car on Saturday. Chris Jacobs, a host of "Overhaulin'" on Motor Trend TV, will also be appearing.
There's a burnout competition, a 5K run and a Miss Mother Road contest. Wowie Zowie, Wreckless Whiskey, Pizzazz Dance Band and Horizon Band will provide the music over Friday and Saturday. Route66Fest.com. 217-553-5271. Free to spectators.
Oak Ridge Cemetery Walk
Dead men (and dead women) do tell tales. Some of the best will be heard on 'Echoes of Yesteryear: A Walk Through Oak Ridge Cemetery' sponsored by the Sangamon County Historical Society.
Actors dressed in period costumes will portray figures at his or her gravesite. That includes con artist and international hustler Reed 'Kid' Waddell (1860-1895), who actually sold the Brooklyn Bridge. He will be portrayed by Pat Foster. Ellen Huntington Henkle(1853-1919) was, in her day, considered to be Springfield's best singer. She will be portrayed by Linda Schneider.
The walk between gravesites is about half a mile. Sept. 29. Noon. Oak Ridge Cemetery, 1441 Monument Ave. sangamonhistory.org. 217-525-1961. Free but donations are welcome.
Fall Harvest Festival
Lincoln Memorial Garden's annual Fall Harvest Festival includes artisan demonstrations and exhibits and gets started on Oct. 12 with a concert by duo Tater Tots (Kristi Lecocq and Micah Walk).
It runs Oct. 12 (9 a.m. to 4 p.m.) and Oct. 13 (10 a.m. to 4 p.m.) Lincoln Memorial Garden, 2301 East Lake Shore Drive. lincolnmemorialgarden.org. 217-529-1111. $8.
Artisan & Antique Market
The Artisan & Antique Market, put together by the owners of the Ursuline Music Conservatory, the Dream Center and the Brinkerhoff Mansion, offers up over 150 vendors, food trucks, a jump house, live music and more from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Oct. 5.
Some say the mansion, built for a contemporary of Abraham Lincoln's and known as "the Castle," is haunted by George Madoc Brinkerhoff Sr. himself.
Sixth Street between Keys Avenue and Eastman Avenue. Visit the Brinkerhoff Mansion Facebook page. Free.
Carve for the Carillon/Jack-O-Lantern Spectacular
Bring your carving tools and your imaginations to Carve for the Carillon from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Oct. 12-13 as a run-up to the Jack-O-Lantern Spectacular the following weekend around the Thomas Rees Memorial Carillon and Washington Park Botanical Garden.
The Springfield Park District supplies the pumpkins (while they last). It's a free event, but donations will be accepted.
The pumpkins will be on display from 6:30 to 9:30 p.m. Oct. 18-19. On Oct. 20, you can take away a decorated pumpkin for a donation. 1740 W. Fayette Ave. carillon-rees.org. $7-$10 (discount tickets at Ashley HomeStore Outlet, 1987 Wabash Ave.).
Springfield Area Highland Games & Celtic Festival
You can experience Scottish culture without having to cross the pond at the Springfield Area Highland Games & Celtic Festival at the Sangamon County Fairgrounds in New Berlin Oct. 19.
Athletes compete in traditional Scottish sporting events like the caber toss, hammer throw and stone put. Enjoy live performances of bagpipe music and Scottish dances, food and drink, like haggis and single malt whisky, plus crafts and storytelling.
316 W. Birch St., New Berlin. centralillinoiscelts.com. $8-$20.
New Salem Fall Festival
Period-clothed interpreters demonstrate daily tasks at the reconstructed village, such as candle dipping, soap making, blacksmithing, spinning wool, gardening and natural dyeing at the Fall Festival at Lincoln's New Salem from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Oct. 26.
Abraham Lincoln spent about six years of his early adulthood living in the village, about 20 miles northwest of Springfield.

title: Insurance coverage of abortion care protected by Illinois judge. What to know
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: The Illinois Baptist State Association filed suit in 2020, claiming the law violated their religious beliefs.
content:
A Sangamon County judge upheld a provision of the Illinois Reproductive Health Act in a ruling last week, maintaining that state-regulated health insurance plans that cover pregnancy care must also do so for abortion services.
The Illinois Baptist State Association filed suit in 2020 against the law passed by state lawmakers in the prior year, claiming it violated their religious beliefs. Named in the suit was the Illinois Department of Insurance.
Judge Christopher Perrin, however, sided with the state since the not for profit is not required by law to purchase health insurance regulated by the insurance department. Thus, he wrote, they have the option to have insurance plans excluding abortion care.
"These alternatives provide flexibility for organizations to maintain insurance coverage without conflicting with their religious beliefs," wrote Perrin.
Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, whose office filed for summary judgement on the behalf of the state insurance department, said on Friday that the decision was a "win in a years-long fight."
"My office is continuing to fight for reproductive care on all fronts because abortion care is health care. Full stop," he said in a statement. "We are committed to protecting access to comprehensive reproductive health care that includes abortion."
IBSA expressed their disappointment with the Seventh Judicial Circuit Court ruling on Monday. The Springfield-based association said in a statement they are reviewing the ruling with their attorneys and are likely to appeal the decision.
"The Sept. 4 ruling discounts the beliefs of over 150,000 Illinois Baptists, as well as all Illinoisans who hold these same sacred convictions, by requiring all insurance coverage in our state to pay for abortion on demand, without a clear pathway for religious exemptions for churches or faith-based ministries," the association said.
State lawmakers passed the Reproductive Health Act in 2019 with the intention to counteract a potential overturn of Roe v. Wade, which the U.S. Supreme Court ultimately did in 2022. It codified abortion rights into law, making abortion a "fundamental right" of people in Illinois.

title: Illinois Republican claims new state flag would 'advance the far-left's political ideology'
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: The Illinois Flag Commission began accepting submissions of new flag designs last week, but not everyone is on board with changing the flag.
content:
The Illinois Flag Commission began accepting submissions of new flag designs last week, opening up a process that could result in a change to a 55-year-old flag.
The original flag, designed by Rockford native Lucy Derwent in 1915, featured the state seal in front of a white background. It has remained the same since with exception for the addition of the word "Illinois" placed below the seal in 1969.
State lawmakers could ultimately decide to keep the flag as is, Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, noted during a press conference last week in Springfield. After a constituent of hers introduced the idea, she and Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, led the legislation which created the commission later signed into law by Gov. JB Pritzker.
But at the very least, she sees the discussion as a healthy way to activate young people across Illinois to get involved in state government.
"I have always said that history is living, breathing and ever evolving, and I think we need to ensure that government is also evolving so people are engaged," Turner said.
Following a public vote starting Jan. 1, the commission will submit 10 flags in addition to the current flag with the Illinois General Assembly by April 1, 2025. They are expected to take-up a vote on the matter during the spring session.
Not all state lawmakers are enthusiastic at the prospect of a new state flag.
Certainly not is Rep. Adam Niemerg, R-Dieterich, who is leading a petition to fight a new state flag. He believes a new flag could "advance the far left's political ideology," while Buckner noted on X, formerly known as Twitter, the commission is composed of Republicans and Democrats alike.
"Will we highlight the Governor's efforts to partner with Chinese-owned companies? Or will the flag become a state-sponsored tribute to the Pride flag?," Niemerg, a member of the far-right Illinois Freedom Caucus, said in a statement. "We need patriotic citizens to take a stand against this clear attempt to rebrand our state."
As for Turner, a change is something she could get behind.
"The seal represents the government," she said. "And I believe that the flag should be a symbol that represents the people and not the government."
A Secretary of State official said there have been more than 370 designs submitted so far. Submissions will be accepted until Oct. 18.

title: 30 years later: Springfield residents continue to speak out against the 1994 Crime Bill
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A group of Springfield residents recognized the 30th anniversary of the Crime Bill by advocating for change.
content:
About a dozen people marched through downtown Springfield Friday to protest the Violent Crime and Control Law Enforcement Act of 1994, more commonly known as the Crime Bill.
The Freedom Walk was held to recognize the bill's 30th anniversary — it was signed into law Sept. 13, 1994, by President Bill Clinton — and to advocate for reform against what some have blamed for the mass incarceration of Blacks and Hispanics in the United States.
'We're against those harsh sentences for low-level, non-violent offenses that many people during that time were opposed with,' said Margaritta Fultz, one of the leaders of the Transformational Justice Task Force that organized the event.
The task force is associated with the Faith Coalition for the Common Good, located at 2208 E. Kansas St. in Springfield.
The march began at the Illinois Police Memorial Park and ended at the Sangamon County Building, which group leaders said was intentional, reflecting their desire to build positive relationships with law enforcement agencies as they work toward change.
The Crime Bill of 1994 is the largest-ever crime bill in U.S. history, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. It provided 100,000 new police officers and allocated $9.7 billion for prisons and $6.1 billion for prevention programs, according to the department's web site.
Fultz and Tyshianna Bankhead, who is executive director of the group, said the Crime Bill predominately affects Black and Hispanic communities.
Bankhead offered that there are better ways to handle lower-level crimes and expressed her support for the Justice Reinvestment Initiative, which facilitates a collaborative process among stakeholders and system leaders to address incarcerations and recidivism.

title: 'Your hurting — we've heard it.' Massey Commission holds first listening session
author: Steven Spearie
description: The deaths of Sonya Massey and Earl Moore Jr., have 'shaken Springfield and Sangamon County to its moral core,' said a Massey Commision co-chair.
content:
Several people expressed concern about the proposed makeup and representation of the 12-member Massey Commission as it held its first public listening session at Union Baptist Church Monday.
While the full slate is expected to be announced later this week, one of the co-chairs of the commission, the Rev. T. Ray McJunkins acknowledged that nine people have already affirmed that they have agreed to serve, including a family member of Sonya Massey, the namesake of the commission, who was fatally shot in her home in an unincorporated part of Woodside Township after reporting a possible intruder on July 6.
Former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy Sean P. Grayson, 30, was charged with Massey's murder. Grayson has pleaded not guilty.
More than two dozen speakers addressed issues like police reform, accountability, training and crisis intervention in Monday's open forum.
"Your desires, your personal experiences, your hurting — we've heard it," said commission co-chair Dr. Jerry Kruse, dean and provost of the SIU School of Medicine in Springfield.
Kruse earlier said that the deaths of Massey and Earl Moore Jr., in late 2022 at the hands of two emergency medical workers charged with his murder, have "shaken Springfield and Sangamon County to its moral core and has become a collective toxic stress."
Both Massey and Moore were Black.
Several members of Massey's family, including her mother, Donna Massey, attended the hearing.
Kruse said mistrust of law enforcement and health care particularly was an issue he saw the commission addressing.
JoAnn Johnson, a former Illinois State Police trooper who does police training, said she hoped the commission would have "the teeth that it needs."
"I pray that this commission does everything that it hopes and is tasked to do," Johnson said.
Beth Langen was one of several speakers encouraging the establishment of a permanent citizens commission that would have oversight authority over the sheriff's office.
In announcing the commission last month, the goal was to create "tangible, practical and equitable solutions for the betterment of all who call Sangamon County home."
The commission will produce a comprehensive report outlining findings, recommendations and proposed actions within a year.
But the parade of speakers Monday also questioned what the makeup of the commission might be.
Kruse, McJunkins and another co-chair, Nina Harris of the Illinois Commission on Equity and Inclusion, sifted through over 200 applications for the dozen spots.
Breonna Roberts said with "the right people, leadership and resources, (I believe the commission) can be a transformative step in Springfield's future."
That came with a caution, though.
"I urge the co-chairs," Roberts said, "to deeply reflect on whether their actions align with the community's best interests. My hope is for fair representation of Black people, of Black women, of the Massey family. Those who have lived experiences with police brutality, being arrested, going to jail. Are they going to be on the commission? Are their voices of diverse walks of life going to be heard?"
Langen also had a prayer for the co-chairs.
"I hope that every decision you make," she said, "honors Sonya Massey."

title: East side grocery store closing in November
author: Claire Grant
description: An east side grocery store is shutting down. Here's what's going on at Kent Plaza.
content:
A grocery store the serves neighborhoods on the city's east side is shutting its doors in early November.
According to Niemann Foods director of consumer affairs Gerry Kettler, the County Market store at 2777 S. Sixth St. has not been able to renew its lease.
Staff was given notice of the closing on Sep. 12. Employees were then contacted by Niemann Foods that when the store closes, employees will be transferred to other County Markets in the area.
'The good news will be that all of our associates will be employed at our stores,' Kettler said. 'We're not necessarily closing it. We are, but we don't have a lease. We can't operate.'
The store plans to close Nov. 2, 2024, according to employees. If stock runs out, they may close earlier, they said.
The store is located in Kent Plaza.
Cleeman Realty Group arranged the $6,300,000 sale of Kent Plaza in July of 2020 in an off-market transaction to a private investment firm based out of Maryland.
Cleeman Realty's Michael Cleeman and Sam Seelenfreund represented both the buyer and the seller of the 94,260 square-foot center during the sale.
Kettler said the owners of Kent Plaza want to perform upgrades, including improvements in the space occupied by County Market.
'I don't know what they were going to be fixing but I know there are a lot of problems with the electronic things and the doors,' said County Market associate Meg Alexander. 'It's just an old store. This happens. Things get worn out. … I think Neimanns is trying to take care of their valued employees because they have a record of doing that.'

title: Witnesses: Murder defendant was at a party at a house where three people were later found dead
author: Steven Spearie
description: A state's witness called one of the victims 'caring and big-hearted.'
content:
Several people testified at a murder trial in Sangamon County court Wednesday that they attended a party at a house where three people were found shot to death on Aug. 9, 2021.
Some said they saw defendant Larry McClain Jr. at the Aug. 8 gathering, held after a Celebration of Life earlier that day at Regency Court.
Savante English, 27, and Keyera Gant, 25, of Springfield, and Bryant K. Williams, 27, of Houston, were all shot multiple times in a house being rented by English in the 2500 block of South 10th Street in the Harvard Park neighborhood.
Shunderika Price of Springfield, who was engaged to Williams, found the bodies when she stopped by the house after being unable to reach either Williams or English.
McClain, who is from Springfield, is on trial with Kelton Galmore of Jacksonville. A third defendant in the case, Joseph Hembrough, also of Jacksonville, pleaded guilty last week and is expected to testify against McClain and Galmore.
State's witness Davosia Whiteside identified Williams as his "best friend" and said he was "caring and big-hearted, a kind person."
Despite moving to California and then Houston, Williams, Whiteside said, often came back to Springfield.
Whiteside was at the Aug. 8 party and people were filtering in and out "all day. It was a good vibe. It was cool."
Whiteside said McLain, who he knew through a cousin, was at the party.
Shyra Daniels, who said she arrived at the party with her cousin around 7 or 8 p.m., also said she saw McLain, who had the street name of "Junior," there.
Michael A. Smith, who testified to being a childhood friend of Williams', said he told Springfield Police that McLain was at the party, but he didn't see him there.
Whiteside testified that he was with a group that included Williams, English, Gant and Smith and left the house around midnight to get something to eat at IHOP on Dirksen Parkway.
Smith said he was with the last group to leave the house to go to the restaurant.
Smith went to Whiteside's girlfriend's house with Whiteside afterwards, where they stayed all night.
Earlier, Dr. Nathaniel Patterson, a forensic pathologist for the Sangamon County Coroner, testified that both Williams and English were struck by gunfire eight times and Gant five times.
On cross-examination by McClain's attorney, Mark Wykoff, Patterson said it was "unclear" if there was more than one shooter or more than one firearm used, questions, he added, he would leave up to a ballistics expert.
The state's case was expected to last through the week.

title: Springfield police officer resigns following drug, steroid charges
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Deputies found $5,000 in cash along with more than 3 pounds of marijuana along inside the officer's home after being called for a domestic dispute.
content:
A Springfield police officer resigned after he was indicted on drug charges.
Clayton Hadley was indicted for possession of larger than legal amounts of marijuana as well as possession of testosterone.
Deputies searched Hadley's home on July 31 and found more than three pounds of marijuana along with multiple vials of suspected testosterone. Deputies also found roughly $5,000 in cash at Hadley's home.
Hadley was not arrested that day, but he was indicted last week by a grand jury.
Deputies searched Hadley's home after police were called to the home for a domestic dispute. Officers with the Springfield Police Department initially responded but later called in the Sangamon County Sheriff's office after they learned Hadley lived in the home.
Springfield Police Department Deputy Chief Sara Pickford told the State Journal-Register Hadley was taken to the hospital the night of the domestic for unknown reasons and remains hospitalized.
Pickford said the police department placed Hadley on administrative leave the day of the domestic disturbance after testing positive for marijuana. Pickford said the department tried to dismiss Hadley but was delayed due to his hospitalization.
Hadley is scheduled to appear in court on Oct. 10.

title: Defendant who pleaded guilty in Springfield triple murder testifies to scene inside the home
author: Steven Spearie
description: A defendant who pleaded guilty two weeks ago in a 2021 triple homicide in the Harvard Park neighborhood in Springfield said last week that two defendants currently on trial for murder shot the victims.
content:
A defendant who pleaded guilty two weeks ago in a 2021 triple homicide in the Harvard Park neighborhood in Springfield said last week that two defendants currently on trial for murder shot the victims.
Joseph Hembrough admitted in Sangamon County court that he brought a gun into the home in the 2500 block of South 10th Street in the early morning hours of Aug. 9, 2021, but he never shot it.
But attorneys for the two defendants, Larry McClain Jr. of Springfield and Kelton Galmore of Jacksonville, tried to poke holes in Hembrough's testimony, saying the Jacksonville man offered inconsistent statements in the past, making what he told to the seven-man and five-woman jury dubious.
Also on the witness stand for the state Friday was Taylor Rosenberger, Hembrough's ex-girlfriend.
Savante English, 27, and Keyera Gant, 25, who lived in the 10th Street home, and Bryant K. Williams, 27, of Houston, were all shot multiple times.
English and Williams, who was set to return to Texas the day he was murdered, were childhood friends. English and Gant were cousins.
Hembrough pleaded guilty under the "accountability theory," and received a 20-year sentence.
Under Illinois law, people can be convicted of crimes with which they were associated but did not actually commit.
Special prosecutor Derek Dion said in Friday's proceeding that Hembrough had to give "an honest and truthful statement" in court and that if he didn't, the plea could be revoked.
Monroe McWard, Galmore's attorney, said Hembrough "didn't want to come forward with a truthful statement until he was promised 20 years."
Hembrough, dressed in a black and white-striped jail-issued uniform and sporting dark-rim glasses, testified that Galmore texted him shortly before the shooting, saying he was looking for "a new connection" or drug supplier.
Hembrough, who also dealt drugs and was a convicted felon, said Galmore showed him a Snapchat post of a red car and large sums of money and told Hembrough they could buy methamphetamine from Williams or "get it for free," meaning they could rob him.
On the way to the 10th Street house late on Aug. 8, Hembrough and Galmore picked up McClain in Springfield. Hembrough said he did not know McClain at the time.
McClain, Galmore and Hembrough entered through the front door around 1 a.m. on Aug. 9. It was English, Hembrough said, who brought out bags of methamphetamine and scales to complete the sale.
When Williams appeared, he started yelling at McClain for showing up unannounced and bringing other people with him, Hembrough recalled.
Galmore produced a Glock 34, which had a switch on it to make it fire automatically, Hembrough said. Williams chuckled and tried to knock the gun out of Galmore's hand before he was shot multiple times, Hembrough said.
McClain then shot English in the kitchen, Hembrough testified.
Hembrough said he was "completely shocked" by the scene.
After all three got into Hembrough's car, McClain went back to retrieve a bag that contained five pounds of meth and nine ounces of fentanyl.
The group was about halfway to Jacksonville before returning to the house where Galmore had dropped his cell phone.
Hembrough was arrested and his drugs confiscated early on Aug. 13 in just outside of Rushville after Rosenberger got into a single-car accident. That was just hours after Rosenberger had totaled the Mercury Milan, used by Hembrough to go to Springfield, in an accident at Fifth Street and South Grand Avenue.
Hembrough was later arrested on a weapons charge in Jacksonville and implicated in the murder.
On cross examination, Mark Wykoff, McClain's attorney, tried to seize on earlier statements Hembrough made to police about having not been present at the scene but staying in Jacksonville and "smoking weed."
Wykoff reminded Hembrough about a gun magazine he left at the crime scene, though Hembrough told police in an interview that it wouldn't come back to him. He testified that it was his.
"You repeatedly lie," Wykoff told Hembrough.
Rosenberger earlier testified to seeing McClain at her Jacksonville home on Aug. 9.
She said she never heard Hembrough mention the names of the victims and that he didn't connections with Springfield.
The state is continuing with its case Monday. The trial could wrap up by mid-week.

title: Park service searches for Yellowstone employee who went missing after summit of Eagle Peak
author: Eric Lagatta
description: Austin King, 22, has been missing since he failed to return from a week-long solo excursion to summit Eagle Peak, the highest point in Yellowstone.
content:
Rescuers in Yellowstone National Park are searching for a park employee who has been missing since he failed to return last week from a week-long solo excursion through a remote area of the wilderness.
Austin King, 22, was last heard from on Tuesday, Sept. 17 when he called friends and family from the summit of Eagle Peak, the highest point in the Wyoming park, according to a news bulletin from the National Park Service. King was due to return Friday for his boat pickup near Yellowstone Lake's southeast arm, but never returned, the park service said.
A search and rescue effort began the following Saturday morning involving both aerial reconnaissance and ground operations. King's camp and personal effects were discovered Saturday evening, leading to a larger operation Sunday involving 20 ground searchers, two helicopters, unmanned air systems and a search dog team, the park service said.
As of Tuesday, King remained missing and park service officials are asking for information from other hikers who may have crossed paths with him.
Hiker summits Eagle Peak before vanishing
King, a concession worker at Yellowstone, was dropped off via boat on Saturday, Sept. 14 at Yellowstone Lake for what was to be a 7-day hike to summit Eagle Peak.
Located six miles from the lake's eastern shores, the remote mountain in Wyoming's Absaroka Range peaks at 11,372 feet, making it the highest point in Yellowstone National Park.
Two days after he began his hike, King spoke to a park ranger at Howell Creek cabin in the backcountry, which was not part of his planned route. At the time, King was planning to camp overnight in the area before climbing Eagle Peak on Tuesday, the park service said.
When King last made contact with anyone, he had reached the summit of Eagle Peak, where he described fog, rain, sleet, hail and windy conditions, according to the park service.
Rescuers from Yellowstone are concentrating their search efforts around Eagle Peak, including the 7.2-mile trailhead. Search teams from Grand Teton national parks and elsewhere also widened the search to areas such as the Shoshone National Forest.
National Park Service circulates photos of King
The park service is circulating a missing person flier for King, which includes identifying information and two photos of the hiker, including one from the day he was dropped off for the excursion.
According to the flier, King is about six feet tall, weighing 160 pounds. He has brown hair, hazel eyes and was thought to be wearing glasses, a black sweatshirt and gray pants when he vanished.
The park service said that anyone who has traveled around Eagle Peak since Sept. 14 may have crossed paths with King.
Anyone with information regarding his whereabouts can call the Yellowstone Interagency Communications Center at 307-344-2643.

title: Few know the heroic story of Albert Cashier. Looking for Lincoln hopes to change that
author: Erich Murphy
description: Albert Cashier lived in Belvidere before going off to fight in the Civil War in 1862. What no one knew at the time was Cashier was born a woman.
content:
The story of an Illinois soldier in the U.S. Civil War who was born a woman and took on the identity of a man may soon get its own historic marker as part of the state's expansive Looking for Lincoln program.
The Abraham Lincoln National Heritage Area covers 43 counties and 32 communities and allows Lincoln's story — and the stories of others who played significant roles in Illinois history during Lincoln's time — to be easily shared with visitors and the next generation of Illinoisans.
There are 260 such wayside exhibits in the state, and according Liz Vincent, Pontiac's director of community enrichment, there's talk of adding more — more specifically a storyboard for Albert Cashier, who has ties to both Belvidere and Saunemin, Illinois.
Vincent recently updated Pontiac city leaders on the expansion, informing them that while Cashier's home is located in nearby Saunemin, the marker could end up in Pontiac, where Looking for Lincoln already has nine storyboards marking everything from the courthouse where Lincoln won his first lawsuit to the historic Strevell House, the home of a fellow lawyer whom Lincoln visited.
'Recently, the Abraham Lincoln National Heritage Area, which is Looking For Lincoln, (was) granted funding from Union Pacific to create some new wayside exhibits,' Vincent told the council. 'The Albert Cashier story was one of the exhibits.'
Wayside exhibits also are located in Freeport, Galesburg, Macomb, Lincoln and Springfield among dozens of other Illinois communities.
Cashier's house was almost destroyed
Jennie Hodgers was born on Christmas Day in 1843 in Ireland.
Hodgers adopted a male identity in order to gain employment after moving from Ireland to Belvidere, Illinois.
In 1862, Albert D. J. Cashier enlisted to fight with U.S. Army during the Civil War. Cashier went through training at Rockford's Camp Grant and was assigned to the 95th Illinois Infantry, which eventually became part of the Army of Tennessee under the command of General Ulysses S. Grant.
After the war, Cashier returned to Illinois and continued to live as a man, working and voting in elections as well as receiving a pension as veteran. Cashier worked as a farmhand and a laborer in Belvidere and Saunemin, which is about 12 miles east of Pontiac.
Cashier died at the age of 71 and was buried with full military honors in Saunemin.
Cashier's house in Saunemin house ended up in Pontiac for a short time and was destined for destruction by the Pontiac Fire Department, who planned to use it as during a training exercise. But then the house was saved and moved back to Saunemin, where it remains today.
Pontiac's Strevell House chosen for marker
Although the Cashier house is in Saunemin, Pontiac was chosen as the storyboard site because the local groups involved felt it was better suited for visitors.
'I spoke with the people in Saunemin, and they thought it would be better served to actually be in Pontiac with the rest of our Looking For Lincoln-Livingston County exhibits,' Vincent said. 'So, Dale Maley, representing the Livingston County Historical Society, we worked together and came up with the idea that it would be best suited to be at the Strevell House due to the time period it is discussing.'
The Strevell House, located at 401 W. Livingston St., was owned by local attorney Jason Strevell, who moved to Pontiac in 1855. Strevell and Lincoln were friends.
According to the Visit Pontiac website, after speaking at the Pontiac Young Men's Literary Society, Lincoln spent the night as Strevell's guest at the Strevell home, which is one of the Lincoln exhibits in Pontiac.
A memorandum of understanding between the City of Pontiac and Looking For Lincoln, as was an agreement between the city and the Livingston County Historical Society, expresses the parties intent to place the Albert Cashier exhibit in front of the Strevell House.

title: Sonya Massey's cousin named a new co-chair of Massey Commission in leadership shake-up
author: Steven Spearie
description: The new leadership for the Massey Commission will delay a scheduled Sept. 30 listening session. Here's a look at the changes.
content:
After only one listening session, the Massey Commission has new leadership.
One of the newest co-chairs is Shadia Massey, a cousin of Sonya Massey, the namesake of the commission, who was fatally shot by a now former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy in her home in an unincorporated part of Woodside Township on July 6.
In light of the leadership change, a Sept. 30 gathering has been postponed.
Yet to be publicly announced are the 12 commissioners.
JoAnn Johnson, the first Black woman to reach the rank of colonel with the Illinois State Police and a law enforcement trainer in police bias, is the other new co-chair.
Dr. Jerry Kruse, dean and provost of SIU School of Medicine and CEO of SIU Medicine, will serve as the other co-chair.
More than two dozen speakers addressed the Sept. 16 session on issues like police reform, accountability, training and crisis intervention in Monday's open forum.
But some of those speakers also scrutinized the leadership of the commission and called for members of the Massey family to be included in the commission.
Also in question are resolutions that doled out over $78,000 to two different communications and consulting companies. They were tabled at a Sept. 18 special meeting of the county board.
'As we have been from the beginning, we will continue to be responsive to community voices in this process," said State Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, who helped form the commission, along with Sangamon County Board chairman Andy Van Meter.
The commission seeks to address systemic issues in law enforcement practices, mental health responses and community relations, with the goal of creating "tangible, practical and equitable solutions for the betterment of all who call Sangamon County home."
It will look to produce a comprehensive report outlining findings, recommendations and proposed actions within a year.
'Have to have a direction'
Johnson was with the State Police for nearly 30 years and came to Springfield in 2010.
Speaking at the session on Sept. 16, Johnson said she helped, through a company she now works for, train Springfield Police officers in "implicit bias."
Implicit bias is any bias a person holds on a level that they are not consciously aware of and can affect a person's behavior and decision-making without realizing it.
Johnson said the commission "will not get far if it is just a group of angry voices. We absolutely have to have direction, focus, come from a place of composure and bring these important issues to the forefront."
The commission, Johnson added "has to be diverse not only in race gender, culture and background, but also experience and expertise."
Johnson said she was one of just 200 people who applied to be on the commission.
Former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy Sean P. Grayson, 30, was charged with Sonya Massey's murder.

title: New Springfield-area sheriff is intent on listening to Massey Commission
author: Steven Spearie
description: In a one-on-one interview, new sheriff Paula Crouch discussed the Massey commission and what it means to be first woman sheriff in Sangamon County.
content:
New Sangamon County Sheriff Paula Crouch told The State Journal-Register in a one-on-one interview last week that she is intent on listening to the Massey Commission and suggestions it might offer regarding policing in the community going forward.
"I think the most important thing is for me right now to hear what the Massey Commission has identified as what our community thinks is a big problem with law enforcement," Crouch said. "I don't think it's going to be just the county. It's law enforcement in general, though our focus with this issue is the county.
The Massey Commission, called for last month by Sangamon County Board Chairman Andy Van Meter and State Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, seeks to address systemic issues in law enforcement practices, mental health responses and community relations, with the goal of creating "tangible, practical and equitable solutions for the betterment of all who call Sangamon County home."
It will look to produce a comprehensive report outlining findings, recommendations and proposed actions within a year.
The commission had its first listening session on Sept. 16, but yet has to publicly name its 12 commissioners.
"I feel with the commission, we have to have a partnership. As far as what they want me to do, I don't have all those answers. I'm sure we will review the suggestions that come up and I think we'll work together to come up with resolutions that will be satisfying to them and to law enforcement."
Crouch, the first female sheriff in the county, said if the history she has made brings encouragement to females in law enforcement, all the better.
"While I'm honored and it's amazing and I'm happy to be here and I hope it encourages others that you can achieve and you can be," Crouch said. "I think my resume--and I'm lucky enough with all the experience I had at SPD with the training and education there and just repetition of calls and opportunity--that it stands on its own and its shows I'm where I should be because of that."
A nearly 25-year veteran of the Springfield Police Department, Crouch's appointment was approved by a Sangamon County Board vote on Sept. 18.
She takes over for Jack Campbell who retired in the aftermath of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey by a now-former sheriff's deputy. Sean P. Grayson was charged with Massey's murder and remains behind bars.
At a recent county board meeting, Teresa Haley said she hoped Crouch would be willing to meet with the Black community on a regular basis, voices, Haley contested "I don't believe (are) being heard."
As a Springfield Police officer, Crouch said she worked with "the most vulnerable of our community," including serving as a neighborhood officer on the city's eastside and participating in a number of activities at Feitshans Elementary School, including providing students with books they could take home and having traditional Thanksgiving dinners.
During her eight years with the Child Advocacy Center, Crouch said she investigated over 500 child sex crimes.
"Sometimes, they don't have a voice of their own and they need a strong law enforcement support and really the CAC works on a team concept," including the Department of Children and Family Services and the Sangamon County State's Attorney, plus several police agencies, Crouch said.
On the other end of the age spectrum, Crouch worked with Senior Services of Central Illinois as an elder abuse officer.
Crouch said she would encourage deputies and staffers "to focus a little more on some community outreach type stuff and getting to know the community agencies and how they can help us."
Springfield Police Chief Ken Scarlette said Crouch was an excellent police officer who will serve Sangamon County well.
"I've already had a conversation with her offering my support any way I can help to help her as she gets her feet wet with this new assignment," Scarlette said recently. "Whatever we can do to work for the betterment of the citizens of Sangamon County, I'm all for that."
Crouch didn't tip her hand about a possible run in 2026 when the office is up for election.

title: Hurricane Helene: Workers from Springfield head to Georgia for assistance
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Springfield will be in a wind advisory starting at 1 p.m. Friday thanks to Hurricane Helene. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Crews from the City Water Light and Power division of the City of Springfield are heading to assist people with the effects of Hurricane Helene in Georgia.
Two crews and a supervisor left Thursday afternoon to assist in Douglas, Georgia. The crews were initially headed to assist the City of Marietta but were reassigned. They were originally tasked to assist with power restoration from Hurricane Helene making landfall, according to CWLP.
The hurricane was expected to hit the area around 3 a.m. to 5 a.m. Friday morning.
"Through mutual aid agreements like this, utilities are able to pool resources to restore power more quickly while staying safe when a big disaster hits," said Amber Sabin, director of customer and media relations at CWLP.
This mutual aid agreement is through the American Public Power Association and the Illinois Municipal Utility Association, she said.
Springfield is in a wind advisory
The National Weather Service has issued a wind advisory from 1 p.m. Friday until 1 a.m. Saturday.
Wind gusts will be at least 40 to 45 miles per hour but could be as high as 50 mph, according to Meteorologist John Bumgardner with the NWS based in Lincoln.
The peak of the winds will be from 5 p.m. to 1 a.m., he said. Weather effects from the hurricane will taper off after that.
Springfield will likely see light rain throughout Friday with intermittent showers on Saturday.
Bumgardner advises people to secure lawn items and to drive cautiously.
University of Illinois Springfield's Homecoming Pep Rally Block Party has been canceled due to the weather.

title: A Springfield high school was on lockdown Thursday. Here's what happened
author: Steven Spearie
description: No, no one was stabbed at Lanphier High School on Thursday, but the school was on lockdown momentarily. Here's what really happened.
content:
A series of fights at Lanphier High School Thursday morning created a number of headaches.
But a new badging system put in place this fall by District 186 summoned help to the scene quickly.
Here's what happened:
Three fights
Three fights broke out at Lanphier shortly before 11:30 a.m.
Superintendent Jennifer Gill said a teacher depressed a badge with a built-in security system triggering a hard lockdown. The more times the badge is depressed, the more heightened the situation. Springfield Police got the call and responded within minutes, Gill confirmed.
The hard lockdown was cleared at 11:40 a.m., said Jason Wind, the district's executive director of school support, but by 11:30 a.m. district personnel had determined it wasn't a true hard lockdown, defined as an intruder with a weapon or someone in the building seeking to do harm.
"We deemed it wasn't a hard lockdown scenario because staff immediately engaged with the fighters and separated them and broke that situation up," Wind said.
Social media rumors
One of those headaches, Gill said, was addressing social media rumors which spread quickly.
There was never a weapon and no one was ever stabbed, Gill said.
"These were all things that were being said on Facebook today that were 100% untrue and then being shared rapidly by other people not involved in the situation," she said.
"When Facebook is allowed to run rampant and people are allowed to call us liars--no, we know somebody taken out of there--we have to stand up for ourselves as a district and allow us to communicate what happened and allow us to take care of the situation."
Were parents and guardians notified?
Gill said the district got a message to parents and guardians that the lockdown was only momentarily.
"Our first job," Gill said, "is to secure the site, take care of the situation at hand and make sure everybody is safe."
What is Centegix?
School District 186 voted to approve the Centegix badging security system in February to the tune of about $2 million. Other school districts, like Jacksonville, have been using it.
Teachers and staff members have been training on it this month, Gill said.
"We're trying to get the knack of it," she said.
One of the advantages of the system, Gill said, is that it pinpoints where the call is in the building.
"It was an honest and thoughtful effort (by the district) to do right by the teachers and all staff members," said Springfield Education Association President Aaron Graves. "I think they were responsive in this manner."

title: City of Springfield cites public safety concerns for removal of items from unhoused camp
author: Claire Grant
description: The city cited "tragic incidents, including loss of life, reports of battery and increased drug activity" as reasons to remove the unhoused camp.
content:
The unhoused encampment on the corner of North Grand and Fifth Street had items removed by the city of Springfield early Wednesday morning.
Around 8 a.m. Sept. 25, members of Memorial Behavioral Health, the city of Springfield's community care coordinator Shannon Allen, and Springfield Police Department's homeless outreach team under officer Michael Newman arrived at the camp where tents, and living spaces were set up.
A gazebo, a small tent and abandoned belongings were removed by the Office of Public works. Allen said all items taken were given with consent from the community.
"When public works arrived on the scene, I let them know to not touch anything until the individuals let us know what was not theirs," Allen said. "Then public works preceded to discard the items that were abandoned."
The mayor's office released a statement Wednesday afternoon that the large tents posed safety risks to the unhoused individuals near the roadside, and cited "tragic incidents, including loss of life, reports of battery and increased drug activity" as reasons to remove the unhoused campground.
Director of community relations Ethan Posey said Thursday that a member of the unhoused community died in proximity to a business close to the camp, but did not provide additional details.
The statement from the mayor's office went on to say coordinators were dispatched on-site to connect with individuals for resources, and that members of the community were given the opportunity to collect their belongings. The unhoused however were not given notice until day-of the city was removing unclaimed items from the property.
No citations, tickets, or arrests were made according to the city.
"This was not some SPD operation," Posey said. "I have talked to community members that own property there, who are managers of businesses there ... and saw their concerns."
Even as the members of the unhoused community had to collect their belongings and point out what was abandoned, with some items left behind for the office of public works to collect, the group of unhoused have not been ousted from the lot and are still living on the corner of the intersection.
Posey plans to have a presentation on what public works covers on a daily basis with the unhoused community at Tuesday's city council meeting.

title: Senators in the clutch: Thurman, Scheffler lead last-minute drive as SHS beats Jacksonville
author: Adrian Dater
description: Jacksonville took a 29-28 lead with 62 seconds left. That turned out to be plenty of time for Brody Scheffler and Kale Thurman in Springfield High's win.
content:
Trying to describe Springfield High's 36-29 victory over Jacksonville Friday night? You definitely had to be there, because words alone make that difficult.
Having just taken a 29-28 lead with 1 minute, 2 seconds left in the game following a gutsy decision by Crimsons coach Mark Grounds to go for a two-point conversion, the Crimsons' sideline and Memorial Stadium's visiting partisan crowd were euphoric. Just prevent a Senators touchdown, and the Crimsons would be a 5-1 team celebrating a huge win on the road in this Central State Eight Conference matchup.
Springfield quarterback Brody Scheffler and receiver Kale Thurman would not let that happen. Going 80 yards in four plays — all catches by Thurman, including a 40-yard TD reception with 35 seconds left — the Senators pulled out the improbable victory to improve to 5-1 overall (3-1 CS8's west division) and become playoff-eligible.
'Listen, they punched us in the mouth, but we responded,' said Thurman, whose final TD reception was after a gorgeous timing-pattern by Scheffler down the right sideline that hit him fully in stride. 'The offense really just came together at the end. I mean, it couldn't have been a better pass by Brody.'
Scheffler's eye-popping statistics: 27-for-37, 428 yards and four TD passes.
'I put the ball in the air and trust my guys to come down with it, and that's what they did,' said Scheffler. 'We were in the same situation last week, but stalled out at the 20-yard line. Tonight, we finished the job. I couldn't be more proud of my teammates.'
Talk about a game of contrasting styles: Jacksonville 4-2 (2-2 CS8's west division) had 408 yards of total offense, but 316 of them came on the ground. Springfield had 454 yards of total offense, but only 36 came on the ground.
Jacksonville seemed to have the game won when Jeremiah Jackson (121 yards, 15 carries, and two TDs) ran it in from 7-yards out to make it a 28-27 game, then Jacksonville got the two-point conversion — and the lead — after a La'Marion Williams run.
But then Scheffler and Thurman combined to steal the show. Four plays, 80 yards. Still time on the clock for Jacksonville, but valiant Crimsons QB Braden Hutchison's Hail Mary attempt fizzled at the buzzer.
Normally, Springfield coach Jon Hebb calls the offensive plays on behalf of Scheffler. But not on the game-winner.
'Brody called that one,' Hebb said. 'That call takes some guts, but he made a perfect throw. A credit to our kids. They finished tonight.'
Asked if his 5-1 team has exceeded his expectations to this point, Hebb said: 'Maybe a little bit. But these guys have really grown. They've taken some huge strides toward the culture that we're trying to build here at Springfield High. They exemplified it tonight.'
The Crimsons had 182 yards of offense at the half — all on the ground. Hutchinson had 80 of the yards on just seven carries, doing much of the work on a drive in which Williams, a senior, capped with a 2-yard TD run.
Behind 6-foot-5, 290-pound center Ryan McCombs, Jacksonville runners had big holes to jump through. Jacksonville looked like it would take a 13-0 lead when it got the ball deep into the red zone on its next possession, but Springfield defensive back Jaiyden Wilson made a drive-stopping tackle near the goal line.
Springfield got down to the Jacksonville 2 on its first drive, but QB Brody Scheffler nearly was picked off on passes on third- and fourth-down. Mehki Newman, however, got the Senators even at 7-7 with a 49-yard touchdown run down the left side.
Williams ran for 75 yards and two TDs for the Crimsons, who only attempted eight passes in the whole game. For the Senators, Armanze Lewis had the second-most crowd-pleasing play of the night. Lewis, a big fullback, only ran the ball one time in the game, but it was for 65 yards and a touchdown that gave Springfield a 21-14 lead as the third-quarter buzzer expired.
The buzz, clearly, is back with the Senators' program after a few tough years. Can it continue on toward a great state playoff position?
'We're learning more as a team, I think,' Scheffler said. 'What we've been through before is starting to help us now.'
Adrian Dater is a freelance writer for The State Journal-Register. He can be reached through the sports department at sports@sj-r.com.

title: Official: Witnesses say boy, 10, wasn't intended target in fatal shooting
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Witnesses have told officials the boy who was fatally shot in Peoria who had ties to Springfield was not the intended target. Here's the latest.
content:
A botched drug deal may have led to the fatal shooting of Torres L. Johnson II, a 10-year-old boy who lived in Peoria but had ties to Springfield.
Witnesses said the shooting happened after a drug deal involving cannabis went wrong and led to an attempted armed robbery between the suspect Maurice Sargent, 33, and two juveniles, according to the Peoria County State's Attorney's Office.
The State's Attorney's Office said Johnson not involved in the drug deal and was simply walking by when the shooting occurred in the middle of an attempted robbery.
Sargent was charged with first-degree murder and armed habitual criminal in the shooting.
'My office will do everything we can to get justice for Torres and his family,' Jodi M. Hoos, Peoria County State's Attorney, said in a news release.
Peoria Police said that in addition to Sargent, a 14-year-old boy was identified as a suspect in the case. The teen was arrested for attempted armed robbery.
Johnson was shot at an apartment complex Sunday evening in Peoria. He was found, lying in the grass with a gunshot wound to the chest.
Police took Sargent into custody on Oct. 1.

title: College football rankings: Big Ten teams in updated Coaches Poll, AP Top 25 after Week 6
author: John Leuzzi
description: How will a crazy week in the Big Ten be reflected in the Coaches Poll and AP Top 25? Here's an updated look at where Big Ten teams stands:
content:
This story was updated with new information
Week 6 of the college football schedule featured some historic losses and upsets, including in the Big Ten conference.
Michigan dropped its second game of the season in a rematch of last year's College Football Playoff national championship, losing 27-17 to Washington in Husky Stadium. Even so, Michigan may have seen a glimpse into the remainder of the season with quarterback Jack Tuttle coming in and leading the Wolverines to 17 unanswered points.
In the Big Ten's other marquee matchup of the weekend, No. 3 Ohio State continued to show it is the team to beat in the conference, scoring 28 second-half points to beat Iowa 35-7. Buckeyes star freshman wide receiver Jeremiah Smith had another impressive one-handed touchdown catch vs. the Hawkeyes, putting him at six receiving touchdowns on the season.
No. 6 Oregon and No. 7 Penn State dominated in their games against Michigan State and UCLA, respectively. Jordan James had a career day for the Ducks, as he finished with a career-high 166 yards and a touchdown on 24 carries. Meanwhile, quarterback Drew Allar came up big for the Nittany Lions with 237 passing yards and two combined touchdowns.
Elsewhere, No. 15 USC suffered an upset loss to Minnesota as Gophers quarterback Max Brosmer scored the game-winning touchdown on a quarterback sneak on fourth-and-goal in the game's final minute. No. 24 Indiana moved to 6-0 on the season with a 41-24 win over Northwestern.

title: Remaining Neuhoff owned radio stations officially sold in Springfield area
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Woodward Communication, Inc. officially acquired the final 7 Neuhoff family-owned radio stations in Springfield and Bloomington. Here's what to know.
content:
The acquisition is complete and the Neuhoff family is officially out of local radio after nearly 70 years.
Woodward Communication, Inc. officially acquired seven radio station brands from Neuhoff Media in Springfield and Bloomington on Sept. 30, according to a press release from WCI.
'We are pleased to announce that today we successfully consummated the acquisition of Neuhoff Media's radio stations and brands based in Springfield and Bloomington, IL,' stated WCI President/CEO Tom Woodward in the news release. 'Over the past couple of months, we have gotten to know each other better, shared ideas, aspirations, etc. which in turn has created positive momentum and energy on which we can enhance our capabilities to serve our customers and communities."
The stations sold in Springfield include country music station 104.5 WFMB, Sports Radio 92.3FM and 1450AM, adult contemporary station 99-7 The Mix, adult hits station 96.7 BOB FM, and Channel 1450, a digital platform covering high school sports.
The Springfield channels are broadcasted from the radio station on South Fourth Street.
In Bloomington, WCI adds Rock 96.7, adult contemporary NOW 100.7, and BOB FM 97.9.
No layoffs are expected, and programming as of now will remain the same, said Kevin O'Dea, General Manager of Woodward Community Media in Springfield.
'All employees of Neuhoff Media Springfield and Bloomington are all remaining on board and we're moving forward with business as usual," he told The State Journal-Register.
Neuhoff Family Limited Partnership announced in July an agreement between Neuhoff Media LLC in Springfield and Bloomington to sell the seven different channels to WCI.
WCI is an employee-owned company which operates several radio stations in Wisconsin among other properties owned in Wisconsin, Illinois, and Rhode Island.
In February of this year, Neuhoff sold nine radio and website channels in Decatur and Danville to Champaign Media group, marking the company's first leap to exit the broadcast industry.

title: Camp Point Central escapes with close win over Jacksonville Routt after wild ending
author: Bill Welt
description: Jacksonville Routt's upset bid was dashed in the final seconds against Class 1A defending champion Camp Point Central
content:
JACKSONVILLE — An offsides penalty erased Jacksonville Routt's succesful go-ahead field goal attempt in the waning seconds in a 22-21 loss to Class 1A defending champion Camp Point Central at Freesen Field on Saturday.
Brock Runyon drilled a 27-yard field goal attempt through the uprights with nine seconds left, but confusion immediately reigned on the field with the offsides flag against the Panthers.
The Rockets initially celebrated amid the uncertainty, but the pre-snap penalty nixed the initial attempt and moved the ball forward for a second attempt from 22 yards out. This second field goal attempt missed the mark, and No. 5-ranked CPC (5-1 overall, 4-0 Western Illinois Valley Conference North) escaped with the win.
"We told our guys, 'Jump the snap count,'" CPC coach Brad Dixon said. "They're going to kick it anyway, so we went offsides, and of course it's loud. The official blows the whistle because offsides in high school is a dead-ball penalty. In the NFL, it's a free play, and in high school once you encroach the line of scrimmage, it's a dead ball. The referee didn't get the information from the side judge I'm assuming, so we told them, 'Hey, that's a dead ball,' and it was, and they had to try to make it again."
Week 6 takeaways: New Berlin, Springfield High come up clutch, and other Week 6 football takeaways
Routt (4-2, 3-1) moved the ball with ease on its final possession in the final 86 seconds, led by senior quarterback Kellen Creviston. The Rockets reeled off three first downs and reached as close as the CPC 7-yard line with 27 seconds left before settling for a field goal attempt.
Routt was initially stopped at midfield on its previous possession, but the defense forced a three-and-out to allow one more chance to win.
Creviston completed 24 of 40 passing attempts for 333 yards and two scores. Senior receiver Jace Lautemann caught a 52-yard TD pass down the near sideline in the first quarter and finished with five receptions for 95 yards. Senior wideout Eli Olson had eight catches for 85 yards, while senior running back Charlie Alan had four catches for 74 yards and a score.
"It was just a series of things we've done in practice a hundred times with our hurry-up offense," Routt coach Barry Creviston said of the final drive. "We just go up and down the field, and everybody's kind of on their heels, so get the ball down the field, get out of bounds and stop the clock. We put ourselves in a position to win the game, and it just didn't work out for us.
"It's going to be a hard one to swallow. But it's football, and it's a life lesson. We're going to have to definitely bounce back because it doesn't get easier in the next three weeks."
CPC initially trailed 14-0 but quickly rebounded with Zack Wear's 80-yard TD run early in the second quarter before finally rallying ahead on Nate Peters' 3-yard touchdown run with 5:38 left in the fourth quarter to cap a 16-play drive.
Wear led the Panthers with 92 rushing yards on eight carries. Elijah Genenbacher ushered 51 rushing yards, while Kadin Niekamp had 47 yards and the team's other score.
"It was a big grind every single play," Peters said. "Their defense is really good. They've got No. 54 (Trey Gause) and 68 (Henry Rawe) on the edge — they were blowing us up all day. Their offense has gotten so much better, too, with No. 2 (Eli Olson) and 88 (Jace Lautemann) as their receivers. They're really good."

title: Here's what our photographer saw during an impromptu visit at Lincoln Park in Springfield
author: Thomas J. Turney
description: A Walk in the Park is an ongoing series from The State Journal-Register. Check out what our photographer saw when he visited Lincoln Park.
content:
A Walk in the Park is an ongoing series from The State Journal-Register photographer Thomas Turney, who plans to explore the Springfield area — one park at a time — to capture all of the beauty and recreation Springfield area parks have to offer. If you have a suggestion of a park he should visit, email him at tturney@gannett.com.
Lincoln Park is the spot to get a workout in or play a sport. According to the Springfield Park District, the park has the greatest variety of sports-oriented facilities of any park in the district. The roadway network, trails and open space are used for walking, running, bicycling, training and school district cross-country meets. The northern half of the park has a soccer field, 6 baseball/softball diamonds, 3 tennis courts, 3 shuffleboard courts and 21 horseshoe courts. Also in this area, the Nelson Recreation Center has an outdoor swimming pool, 2 indoor ice rinks, rooms for special events, a concession area and restrooms. South of the building is a small bandstand, a picnic area with shelters and a large playground. You can also play frisbee golf at the park as well.
Founded: 1905
Address: 1601 N. Fifth St., Springfield
Acres: 88
History: This is one of the historic parks, developed as termini of the urban trolley line in use at the time.

title: 'It should have surfaced.' Debate over allegation against sheriff's husband boils over
author: Steven Spearie
description: A Sangamon County Board member contended a 2021 allegation against the sheriff's husband should have surfaced publicly.
content:
Speakers at Tuesday's Sangamon County Board meeting and a board member himself reiterated concerns that an allegation of unwanted physical contact against the husband of current Sangamon County Sheriff Paula Crouch wasn't brought to the public's attention during a background search last month.
Board chairman Andy Van Meter said the investigation of battery against Robert S. Crouch Jr., now the Riverton Police Chief, wasn't relevant to the determination of Paula Crouch's fitness for office.
Also Tuesday, the board sent a resolution initiating and authorizing a referendum to be submitted to county voters about recall of the sheriff's office to the election committee for additional study.
'We still don't believe women'
The 2021 allegation against Crouch made by Elizabeth Drea, a worker with the Police Benevolent & Protection Agency,"is why we've been asking for departments to FOIA their employees or board members to actually look extensively into people's backgrounds," said Breonna Roberts, during the public comment section.
Van Meter told The State Journal-Register that he was informed of the allegation as a committee was trying to finalize candidates as a successor to Sheriff Jack Campbell, who retired on Aug. 31 in the wake of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey in her home in an unincorporated area of Woodside Township.
A former sheriff's deputy was charged with the murder of Massey, though Campbell initially refused to resign.
"When you conduct a background check," Van Meter said, "there is lots of information that is deduced. You have to make a determination on what of that information is relevant and what of that information is not relevant."
The information Van Meter had, Roberts said, "wasn't something we were able to discuss as a community. It makes me a concerned citizen."
Board member Marc Ayers insisted the information was relevant and that it should have been up to the board to decide.
"It's a serious allegation and that really should have surfaced," said Ayers, a Democrat.
Sheriff Crouch attended the meeting but did not speak.
The Illinois State's Attorneys Appellate Prosecutor declined to press charges against Crouch. Drea told the SJ-R that she didn't want to relive the experience in court and that she was in therapy.
"It's frustrating we went through intensive background checks and we still don't believe women," said Ken Pacha, also in public comment.
The lack of formal charges, he added, "shouldn't mean we ignore that accusation."
'Like sending it to the graveyard'
Sam Cahnman, the board member sponsoring the recall resolution, joked that sending it to the election committee was "like sending it to the graveyard."
Another resolution of Cahnman's that went to the committee was never acted upon.
Cahnman is hoping the recall resolution gets before voters on the April 1 ballot.
The recall power, said Vanessa Knox, would be "a quick and tangible action" to resolve matters that might arise with a sheriff.
