title: Presto chango: Glenwood dominates Lincoln a week after Titans thrashed by U-High
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Glenwood scores four times in the air, four times on the ground as Titans use balance to blank Lincoln in CS8 matchup.
content:
CHATHAM — David Hay doesn't mince words, nor does he say more than he usually needs. The Chatham Glenwood football coach's postgame admonishment to his players following a 20-point loss to Normal U-High in Week 6 seemed to resonate with his Titans.
Glenwood scored four times on the ground and four touchdowns in the air to earn a well-deserved 57-0 Central State Eight Conference shutout of Lincoln on Friday.
'I think we executed pretty well today,' Hay said. 'We'll obviously have to check it and break down the film and get better, but definitely (it was) a bounce back. Our kids were focused — despite homecoming and all the things that go with that — they were focused on coming out here and playing good football.
'As a coach, you're certainly looking to (use a loss as a chance to improve): you have no choice, you lost and you have to go do something with it. There were plenty of things to find to improve on last week, and I sure hope we did. We've got to get better every week moving forward in the season.'
Glenwood junior running back Grady Mueller ran 13 times for 82 yards and three touchdowns, while senior wide receiver Gavin Simmons caught four passes for 60 yards and two touchdowns.
'Last week was just a slip-up,' Simmons said. 'We've been struggling to come off the bus all year. It really comes down to getting in the film room the next day, fixing things and coming out the next week and executing.'
Titans off and running
The Titans rushed for 230 yards on 26 carries.
'We reestablished the run game,' Glenwood junior quarterback Colten Knoedler said. 'A big thing for us all week was we needed to run the football better, more effectively, because you can't throw the ball 40 times in a high school football game. I thought coaches did a great job this week preparing us.'
It was a far cry from the road loss the Titans (5-2 overall, 4-1 CS8 East division) at U-High on Oct. 4. Last week, Glenwood nearly entered halftime without a score, before a recovered fumble led to the Titans' first touchdown to cut the Pioneers' lead to 26-7.
For all the accoladed the offense received after putting up 57 points, the defense could also take a bow. The Titans held Lincoln to 57 yards of total offense.
'They're really good and just a lot better than us,' Lincoln coach Matt Silkowski said. 'We have a lot of respect for Glenwood: we think they're a very good team and it's a challenge when your enrollment is half the size and they've got double the kids to pick from. It's a dangerous spot for us: that's just the reality of it. I thought our kids gave it their best shot, and I'm happy with the effort that our kids put in.'
On Friday, Simmons grabbed a 4-yard touchdown pass from Knoedler with 32 seconds left in the half to give Glenwood a 43-0 lead and a running clock for the entire second half.
Simmons is one reception from becoming the third Glenwood player with 100 catches in a career. He has 34 catches for 513 yards and seven TDs this season and 99 receptions for 1,412 yards and 18 scores in his career.
Railers struggle to move ball
Lincoln opened the game by getting a pair of first downs and moving the ball. Quarterback Tate Johnston hit Gabe Smith for a 24-yard completion, but three plays later, Johnston was picked off by Dylan Huff.
Less than two minutes later, Mueller capped off a five-play, 55-yard drive with a 4-yard TD run and Mia Gerger's point after kick was good for a 7-0 lead.
The Railers showed their desperation early when they went for it on fourth-and-one from their own 29, but a bad snap resulted in Glenwood taking over at the Lincoln 24. The Titans needed three plays for Knoedler to find Simmons for a 22-yard score and a 13-0 lead.
'Ever since summer of (2023) — Colten's first year — I could feel the connection that we had,' Simmons said of Knoedler. 'The second year of him throwing the ball to me makes everything so much easier. I trust him and I'm sure he trusts me.'
Glenwood tacked on one more score following a Lincoln punt when Knoedler hit Mason Neumann for a 47-yard TD throw before a fumbled snap in the end zone led to a Lincoln safety and a Titans' 22-0 lead after one quarter.
The Railers (4-3, 2-3 CS8 East) had three first downs in the first quarter, five in the first half and still finished the game with only those five. Lincoln has two more shots to get its fifth win and qualify for a postseason berth for the second season in a row. The Railers travel to Quincy Notre Dame (6-1) in Week 8 before hosting Jacksonville (4-3) in Week 9. Last year, Lincoln beat Jacksonville 41-28 to earn its first playoff spot since 1984.
'I told them at halftime that I was proud of them and I love them,' Silkowski said of getting his team past Friday's shutout loss. 'I told them the reality of the situation. We flushed it already, we're looking ahead to QND and this one is over as far as we're concerned.'
Knoedler was 7-for-8 passing for 124 yards. Tristan Schwindt also threw a 4-yard touchdown, this one in the third quarter to David Helm.

title: Teammates battle: Shankland beats Surges in all-Glenwood CS8 tennis meet
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Chatham Glenwood, the defending champion, took second place with 25 points and Sacred Heart-Griffin was third with 23 at Saturday's CS8 girls tennis meet.
content:
Normal U-High put both of its doubles teams into the championship final and the Pioneers rolled up 31½ points to win the Central State Eight Conference girls tennis tournament on Saturday at the Velasco Tennis Center in Washington Park.
Chatham Glenwood, the defending champion, took second place with 25 points and Sacred Heart-Griffin was third with 23. Upstart Jacksonville was next with 15½, followed by Rochester (15), Lincoln (9), Springfield High (9) and Southeast (6).
Here are four takeaways from the two-day tournament:
Glenwood goes 1-2 again
Chatham Glenwood teammates Samantha Shankland and Ellie Surges squared off for the conference singles title for the second straight season, and it was Shankland repeating as champ with a 6-4, 6-3 victory.
Shankland, the No. 1 seed, reached the final after beating unseeded Angel Yin of Normal U-High 6-2, 6-2 in the semifinals. Surges, seeded second, posted a 6-0, 6-2 victory over third seed Caroline Sheehan of SHG in the other semifinal.
The Titans, top-heavy in singles this season, received 20 points in the draw. Glenwood got five points in the doubles draw when unseeded Lydia Ryherd and Stella Lopp got to the quarterfinals. Fifth seed Natalie Alexander and Kiki Mander, however, were sent to the back draw after a 3-6, 7-5, 6-4 loss to unseeded Norah Alexander and Finley York of Jacksonville in the second round.
Sheehan proving her status
After losing to Surges in the semifinals, Sheehan rebounded with a resounding 6-0, 6-0 victory over Yin in the third-place match.
The senior has been a solid No. 1 for the Cyclones and confirmed that missing the tennis postseason last fall was due to her primary sport of soccer where she will continue to play for SHG in the spring as a center midfielder.
'I missed a couple tournaments for soccer (practice), and we had a lot of seniors last year, so coach Hayden (Esker) wanted to give them an opportunity to play since I missed,' Sheehan said. 'Someone else got to play singles and they moved our doubles team up, so they got to experience that.'
Sheehan appears grateful for the opportunity this season. She placed second in the No. 1 singles draw at the Central Illinois Invitational, defeated Rochester's best, Julia Musgrave, at a dual meet, and helped the Cyclones beat Quincy 5-4 in a meet with a win in doubles.
'Honestly, I was just wanting to have fun this year,' Sheehan said. 'I've played varsity since my freshman year I joined, just to have fun for a fall sport. I've always been able to move well. I've gotten better with my shots and my placement and gotten more consistent.'
Sheehan said she started playing tennis during the winter of eighth grade, and didn't have state tournament aspirations before this season.
'I can get to state if I work hard and do well, so I'm excited about that but it's not entirely my goal,' she said. 'I'm really happy with how well I did overall in the (CS8) tournament. I think sophomore year I got fourth, so I was glad I got to improve on that.'
U-High's depth leads to title
Top seed Haley Martin and Emma Eovaldi defeated teammates and sixth seed Risha Patel and Alison Storm 6-4, 6-1 in the doubles title match.
Patel and Storm got by the second-seeded team of Musgrave and Cora Haupt of Rochester 4-6, 6-3, 6-3 in the semifinals. Martin and Eovaldi downed unseeded Lucia Hassebrock and Catalina Mosquera of SHG 6-0, 6-1 in the semis.
Thanks to Yin's fourth-place finish in singles, the Pioneers were able carve out the title.
Area teams bracing for tough sectionals
Shankland and Surges will be two of the top singles players when Glenwood hosts the Class 2A Sectional that includes traditionally tough schools in Edwardsville, Belleville West and Alton.
Shankland, who did not qualify for the IHSA state finals after a loss in the quarterfinals at last season's Belleville West Sectional, said this time will be a great opportunity for her and the team to make some noise.
'I'm really excited that we're hosting sectionals this year,' Shankland said. 'It's definitely a higher level of competition than conference, but ever since we've been in 2A, it's good to play stronger people. It makes me stronger and everyone else gets better after playing them. They are definitely tough.'
With their strong CS8 showing, the Cyclones may have put themselves as one of the favorites to win the Class 1A Jacksonville Sectional. Quincy Notre Dame and Jerseyville usually put themselves in the running.
With Sheehan, Hassebrock and Mosquera and sixth-place singles finisher Laney Aleman, SHG has a core of players to compete.
Jacksonville's fourth-place finish has put the Crimsons on the map. Olivia Dobson reached the quarterfinals before losing to Sheehan, while Norah Alexander and York also advanced to the quarters before falling to Springfield High's Myla Shannon and Madisyn Williams 1-6, 6-2, 10-8 in the fifth-place doubles match.

title: Man faces multiple charges in fatal shooting of Springfield resident
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A man is in custody and charges have been filed after a fatal shooting in Springfield last weekend. Here's what we know.
content:
A man is in custody and charges have been filed after a fatal shooting in Springfield last weekend.
Ventellis B. Cooper, 48, faces three counts of first-degree murder, one count of aggravated unlawful use of a firearm and one count of felon in possession of a firearm.
Cooper was charged in connection to the fatal shooting of Antoine Williams, 39, on Oct. 13.
Police were called to the area of 17 and Cook streets just after 1 a.m. Sunday morning for reports of shots fired. Officers said they found Williams in the front seat of a vehicle with multiple gun shot wounds.
He was taken to the hospital where he later died from his injuries, authorities said.
Cooper was taken into custody on Oct. 14 after authorities searched his residence in the 2000 block of South 15th Street and found a firearm inside the home without owning a FOID card.
The fatal shooting was the eighth homicide in Springfield in 2024.

title: 'Millionaire surcharge': What to know about the property tax relief question on the ballot
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: Voters in Illinois will see a question regarding property taxes on their ballots next month. Here's what you need to know.
content:
In addition to candidates' names, Illinois voters will also see three advisory questions on their ballots.
One question would take a look at potential income tax reform, which its advocates like former Gov. Pat Quinn say is needed to fix a "upside-down" system.
'Right now, there are tax breaks for millionaires and tax bills, high property tax bills for everyday people,' Quinn said at a Capitol news conference Oct. 9. "That's not a fair system."
Here's what you need to know:
What is the specific language that will appear on my ballot?
The question reads as followed: "Should the Illinois Constitution be amended to create an additional 3% tax on income greater than $1,000,000 for the purpose of dedicating funds raised to property tax relief?"
Why is the question being asked in the first place?
Gov. JB Pritzker signed legislation in May that placed the income tax question, in addition to ones regarding election interference and insurance coverage of reproductive services such as in-vitro fertilization.
It also gives lawmakers insight into what tax reform their constituents, burdened by the second-highest property taxes in the nation, want. Per the latest data from the Illinois Department of Revenue, the 3 million households paid $23.2 billion in residential property taxes in 2022.
Will passage of the measure have any impact on property taxes?
There will be no immediate impact if voters support the measure, however, it could shape another vote for a constitutional amendment as early as 2026.
Quinn cites data collected by the state revenue department and says the tax would collect an additional $4.5 billion in revenues if enacted. That money would go into the state's property tax relief trust fund and be dispersed to homeowners in the form of rebates.
For those with incomes less than $1 million, there would be no change to their property taxes.
"Giving money back to homeowners in the form of a property tax rebate, they're going to spend that money and generate economic activity for the benefit of Illinois," he said.
Have there been similar questions asked of voters?
In 2020, Illinois voters turned down a constitutional amendment that would have done with the state's flat income tax. It would have installed a graduated income tax instead, but after a battle of billionaires — Citadel founder Ken Griffin and Pritzker — it was Griffin in the winner's circle.
Voters in 2014, however, did approve an advisory referendum that similarly placed a 3% tax on incomes exceeding $1 million to provide more resources to school districts.

title: Illinois launches new DMV kiosks for license renewal and stickers. What you need to know
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Illinois is making it easier for you to renew your driver's license and get your new license plate stickers. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Need to renew your license but don't want to wait in line at the DMV or go online to do it? Good news, many Illinois residents have a faster way they can get their license plate stickers.
The state launched a new pilot program where residents can renew their license and get their license plate stickers right from a kiosk.
Here's what you need to know.
What can the kiosks do?
The kiosks can quickly print vehicle registration renewals and plate stickers. Customers seeking a driver's license or state ID renewal can receive temporary documents from the kiosk while their new card is mailed to them.
How many Kiosks will be part of the pilot program?
There will be 15 Fast-Lane kiosks initially rolled out.

title: Central Illinois microbrewery debuting new beer supporting Hurricane Helene relief efforts
author: Claire Grant
description: The central Illinois brewery has partnered with the North Carolina Brewers Guild to help displaced people from Hurricane Helene.
content:
For Karen Conn, watching news updates from Hurricane Helene hit too close to home, knowing her family was dealing with the fallout of the hurricane in Asheville, North Carolina.
Conn's daughter, Amanda, has been working in the local hospital pretty much nonstop since the hurricane.
When Conn had a chance to help out, she did not hesitate.
Obed & Isaac's Microbrewery & Eatery at 500 S. Sixth St. announced sales from its new Appalachia Strong IPA will support the relief efforts following the devastating impacts of Hurricane Helene.
The massive storm Helene hit six states in late September of this year, claiming over 300 lives – many in North and West Carolina's Mountain region which had villages flattened, and leaving people without resources.
The central Illinois brewery has partnered with the North Carolina Brewers Guild to help displaced people from Hurricane Helene, alongside eight to 10 other brewers across the Prairie State. Through the Pouring for Neighbors initiative, Obed & Isaac's aims to rally the central Illinois community to contribute to the rebuilding efforts.
'My daughter and her wife and children live in Asheville and although they are without water and electricity, they didn't suffer any more damage,' Conn said. 'When we saw what we could do, this was just a perfect opportunity to jump on and just pour some beers for friends.'
The hurricane hits close to home for the downtown business too, according to Conn. Two prior bartenders moved down to Asheville after living in central Illinois. One of the bartenders is struggling now after the hurricane with extensive home damages.
The beer will officially launch on Oct. 25, with a portion of proceeds going directly toward the recovery efforts as part of the Pouring for Neighbors initiative.
A $1 of every pint of the specially brewed IPA will be donated to the Western North Carolina Relief fund with the Conn family matching each donation dollar for dollar.
The funds raised will support local organizations working on the ground to provide vital services, including shelter, food, and reconstruction efforts in the hardest-hit areas.
The Conn family is asking Illinoisians to come out and support the ale on Oct. 25 by spreading the word on social media with hashtags #AppalachiaStrong, #PouringForNeighbors, and #Obed&Isaacs.
Appalachia Strong IPA
According to the local brewers, Appalachia Strong IPA is an American-style India Pale Ale brewed to embody the resilience and spirit of the Appalachian Mountains and the people. The beer features notes of pine and citrus, layered with hints of candy stone fruit, creating a refreshing and aromatic experience.
'We think of North Carolina with pine trees, outdoorsy, so we were trying to craft our ale around that refreshing grainy,' Conn said. 'It's very hoppy. It's going to be a very hopps-style beer which is strong like Appalachia so – we put a little bit of thought into it.'
The brew will be available in draft at both Obed & Isaac's locations in Springfield and Peoria. Not a beer fan? The Conn family still urges donations directly to the Pouring for Neighbors campaign and supporting relief efforts at drinkncbeer.org under the North Carolina beer relief page.

title: Williamsville flexes run game, Maroa forges ahead, and other Week 8 football takeaways
author: Bill Welt
description: Why Williamsville football coach Aaron Kunz is excited about the team's prospects, plus other Week 8 takeaways from around Springfield
content:
Here are the top takeaways from Week 8 high school football games from around Springfield:
Mamma Mia! Glenwood kicker Gerger sends Titans past SHG for first time since 2019
Williamsville's offense takes shape
A pre-snap penalty tripped up Williamsville's opening drive.
The offense clicked after that despite falling behind 14-0 en route to a 28-21 victory over Class 2A top-ranked Maroa-Forsyth at Paul Jenkins Field on Friday.
The Bullets (7-1, 7-0) clinched at least a share of the Sangamo Conference title with the win and visit Pleasant Plains in the regular-season finale with a chance to claim first place outright.
Williamsville totaled 384 rushing yards. All-state senior running back Braddock Cates led the way with 199 rushing yards and a touchdown while fellow tailbacks Gage Paul and Matthew Miller combined for 126 yards and three TDs.
Each brings a big burst, while Cates also adds a wallop against would-be tacklers out of the Wing-T and wishbone formations.
Williamsville coach Aaron Kunz began installing the look last season and the offensive line has, by all appearances, learned to mesh since falling to Class 3A defending champion Bryon early in the season.
Williamsville's offense is a different beast these days and kept Maroa's prolific pass game off the field to come away with the home win.
'This offensive line is pretty darn good and they have not hit their stride yet,' Kunz said. 'We saw it in the second half last week and I think we saw it tonight, and we've got some really good running backs. We've got some special kids.
"It's coming together at the right time. Four weeks ago when you would've talked to me, I was pretty discouraged even after wins. I feel very excited about where we've gone and where we're headed.'
Maroa not mourning over loss
Maroa-Forsyth and Williamsville never seem to disappoint whenever they meet up. Ever since Maroa joined the Sangamo Conference in 2016, the two teams have sparred for first place.
After Williamsville won three straight from 2019 to the 2021 fall season, Maroa claimed the next two by a combined eight points to claim consecutive conference titles.
The Class 2A No. 1 Trojans (7-1, 6-1) dashed to a 14-0 lead in this latest chapter. Only turnovers and Williamsville's time of possession turned out to be the difference in their 28-21 loss.
Maroa indeed reach as far as the Williamsville 9-yard line before yielding a pivotal sack and throwing an interception on fourth down in the third quarter. The Trojans still came back and took less than four minutes to score on a 96-yard drive that included a highlight reel touchdown catch by senior receiver Mitch Williams in the corner of the end zone with 5 minutes, 1 second left in the fourth period.
Maroa just couldn' get a stop in the end.
Junior Ryne Sheppard finished 27 of 41 for 285 yards and three TDs with two picks, one on a deflected pass at the line of scrimmage and the other facing fourth-and-long. Williams also starred with 12 receptions for 132 yards and a score.
'The bottom line is we have to be better in all facets of the game,' Maroa coach Josh Jostes said. 'We needed a game like this. We're November-built and this game is going to make us better in November.'
Panthers, Lions light up scoreboard
Lanphier senior running back A'Jeont Lee showcased his talent.
But Decatur Eisenhower junior back Jaterryon Moore had the final word when the Panthers defeated the Lions 76-42 in a Central State Eight Conference game at Memorial Stadium.
The game featured two winless teams, yet there were plenty of fireworks.
Lee ran for six touchdowns, finishing with 226 yards on 25 carries. He kept Lanphier (0-8, 0-6) in the game with four first-half touchdowns as the Lions trailed 42-28 at halftime.
Moore scored five touchdowns, including returning a kickoff 78 yards in the first quarter. His first rushing TD was a 57-yard run with 11 minutes 28 seconds remaining in the second period. He added a 5-yard TD before the half and tacked on two 12-yard TD runs in the third period.
Moore finished with 276 yards on 24 attempts as Eisenhower (1-7, 1-5) outgained Lanphier 448-220 on the ground.
Eisenhower quarterback/cornerback Garryon Henderson had two rushing TDs offensively and picked up a fumble and ran 22 yards for a score on the defensive end. Henderson contributed 78 yards on six carries.
Don't sleep on Staunton's passing game
With Staunton seeking its fifth win, and a playoff berth, the Bulldogs forced overtime in an unlikely way: a 40-yard pass from Elliot Frank to Hunter Wallace. That touchdown, along with Carter Legendre's extra-point kick, pulled Staunton into a fourth-quarter tie.
It was just Frank's fourth touchdown pass of the season. He has 23 completions.
"Passing was something we really wanted to improve on this year," Staunton coach Austin Sherfy said. "We've got a lot of new kids in the passing game and new pieces on the (offensive) line.
"It's been slow and methodical. Early in the year, we had four picks off the bat in Greenville and ... we've had (three) since then. Luckily, Elliot is a junior. It's all great stuff we can build on for next week and next season."
Staunton (4-4) heads to Pana (7-1) needing a big upset to qualify for the postseason for the first time since 2018. Sherfy will hope that the Bulldogs don't need to come back from a two-score deficit to do it, but if they find themselves in that position, he says there isn't any quit in his team.
"That's two weeks in a row now that we've been down 13-0 in the first half and come back to take a lead," Sherfy said. "The boys got fight and we've got to hope and pray and drag out a little more fight so we can go on the road in Pana and get that fifth win."
Mueller proves electric
Chatham Glenwood junior Grady Mueller showed glimpses of his athleticism last season.
He ran for 235 yards and two touchdowns, while also netting nine catches for 109 yards and another score in 2023. He has been able to star among a host of other playmakers this season.
Mueller scored three touchdowns, including a 98-yard kickoff return in the first quarter, and ran for 165 yards on 24 carries in a 34-31 overtime victory over Sacred Heart-Griffin. Entering the week, he ranked second on the team in rushing with 203 yards and four TDs and third in receiving with 16 catches for 284 yards and two scores.
The previous week, he led the Titans with 13 carries for 82 yards and three scores in a 57-0 rout over Lincoln.

title: New hearing date set for former sheriff's deputy charged with Massey's murder
author: Steven Spearie
description: The hearing for the former sheriff's deputy charged with Sonya Massey's murder came on the same day as the first Massey Commission hearing.
content:
Family members and friends of Sonya Massey, who was fatally shot in her home by a f ormer Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy on July 6, were still finding seats in a courtroom when Monday's hearing ended.
In the less than 90-second proceeding before Presiding Circuit Judge Ryan Cadagin, Sean P. Grayson, charged with Massey's murder, was given a new status hearing for Dec. 2.
That is expected to be closer to a Fourth District Appellate Court ruling regarding Grayson's ongoing detention in Menard County.
As with his previous hearing, Grayson wasn't in court but appeared by Zoom seated next to his attorney, Daniel Fultz.
Another of Grayson's attorneys, Mark Wykoff, was present in the courtroom and asked for the new date.
Cadagin has ruled Grayson, 30, be jailed in accordance with the Pre-Trial Fairness Act.
At Grayson's July 18 arraignment, Cadagin cited the former deputy's callousness during and after the shooting of Massey, a 36-year-old Black mother of two who had called 911 about a prowler, including not rendering help to her.
The defense appealed the decision.
About 25 to 30 members of Massey's family and other friends attended Monday's hearing, but some weren't even seated when the hearing finished.
After the hearing, family members huddled in the state's attorney's office to debrief.
Among those attending Monday was Donna Massey, Sonya Massey's mother.
"The family is definitely committed (to this trial)," said Teresa Haley of Haley & Associates, speaking for the Massey family afterwards. "We had more family members here than at the first and second hearings."
Haley admitted the Massey family is "struggling," but is getting educated on the court process.
"It's definitely justice being delayed, but it's process," Haley admitted. "We all have to go through something to get to something and we're hoping in the end we receive victory and that (Grayson) is fully prosecuted for first-degree murder."
The hearing came on the same day as the first Massey Commission hearing, which will consider testimony regarding a proposal for an independent review of the Sangamon County Sheriff's department's procedures.
Shadia Massey, a cousin of Sonya Massey's who is serving as a commission co-chair, attended the court hearing as did another cousin and commission, Sontae Massey.
Grayson has pleaded not guilty.

title: Public gets a look at new master plan for downtown Springfield, medical district
author: Steven Spearie
description: The master plan, nearly three years in the making, is the first of its kind for downtown Springfield.
content:
John Stremsterfer, the president and CEO of the Community Foundation for the Land of Lincoln, said a newly minted master plan for downtown Springfield and the Mid-Illinois Medical District "creates an incredible framework for all kinds of flowers to grow."
The master plan, nearly three years in the making, is the first of its kind for downtown Springfield and a successor to one adopted by the medical district in nearly two decades.
It came after residents identified "downtown revitalization" as one of their priority issues through The Next 10 community visioning initiative spearheaded by the Community Foundation.
The 278-page document was recently rolled out online, but members of the public got a close-up of specifics at an open house at Memorial Learning Center on Oct. 24.
In addition to the medical district and the Community Foundation, the plan was put together by the city of Springfield, the Springfield Sangamon Growth Alliance and Downtown Springfield, Inc.
The plan will be presented at the committee of the whole meeting on Nov. 12, confirmed Val Yazell, director of the city's Office of Planning and Economic Development.
It isn't clear when the full city council would move on a final vote.
The medical district is a one-square mile designation just north of downtown and the Illinois Capitol Building. It was established in 2003 by an act of the Illinois General Assembly and is anchored by Springfield Memorial Hospital, HSHS St. John's Hospital, Springfield Clinic and Southern Illinois University School of Medicine.
"It is a blueprint, it is a guideline for us to use to reference when development's going to happen, for this particular area," Yazell said of the master plan at Thursday's open house. "We want to reference it and make sure we're in alignment with some of the recommendations."
Stremsterfer said those developers and companies interested in doing business might lean more towards a community that has a plan than one that doesn't.
"We all kind of want to see, in my opinion, the end result. We want cool shops. We want good restaurants," Stremsterfer said. "We do have a lot of those great things already. We just want more of them.
"How do we incentivize those things to happen? That's where I do think policymakers and economic development groups have incentives they can deploy to make that a more attractive endeavor for private investment."
While over the last few decades, a lot of the commercial businesses have moved to the west side for retail, "we still have incredible growth in the medical industry in this district kind of creating incentives to bring the two (districts) together more intentionally," Stremsterfer said.
"I think that was the idea of doing it together."

title: 'Most Wanted' fugitive arrested in Mexico in Illinois attorney's 2016 strangling death
author: Anthony Robledo
description: John Panaligan, 57, was arrested Monday in Tepic, Mexico, ending a nearly eight-year manhunt after attorney Victor Jigar Patel was strangled in his office.
content:
John Panaligan, 57, was arrested Monday in Tepic, Mexico, ending a nearly eight-year manhunt after attorney Victor Patel was strangled in his office. Patel was representing clients suing Panaligan.
Police in Mexico have arrested a man in connection with the strangling death of an Illinois attorney in 2016, U.S. officials announced Wednesday.
John Panaligan, 57, was arrested Monday in Tepic, Mexico, ending a nearly eight-year manhunt, the U.S. Marshals Service said in a news release.
Panaligan, who made the 15 Most Wanted fugitives list in 2020, was deported back to the U.S. on Tuesday, the service confirmed.
Panaligan is accused of killing attorney Victor Jigar Patel, 36, in his Northbrook, Illinois, office on Dec. 7, 2016. At the time Patel was representing clients who were suing Panaligan in civil court, according to the news release.
"I hope this arrest brings some measure of comfort to the Patel family and serves as a stark reminder to fugitives from justice that there is no place to hide," Marshals Service Director Ronald Davis said in a statement.
USA TODAY was unable to reach an attorney for Panaligan for comment.
Panaligan allegedly scheduled appointment to lure Patel
The Marshals Service allege that Panaligan scheduled an appointment under an alias to make an appointment with Patel at his law office.
Security cameras captured Panaligan wearing a disguise upon arrival before allegedly killing the attorney in his office, the Marshals Service says. Evidence collected by authorities led to him being the lead suspect in the murder investigation, according to U.S. Marshall Service.
Authorities detained Panaligan at the Canadian border two days later for allegedly attempting to smuggle a firearm into Canada. However, he was allowed to return to the U.S. so the Northbrook Police Department could interview him in the investigation into Patel's death.
On Feb. 8, 2017, a warrant for Panaligan's arrest was filed so he could be charged for first-degree murder but he presumably fled to Mexico before he authorities could find him.
On Nov. 23, 2020, the U.S. Marshals Service placed him on its 15 Most Wanted, offering a reward of up to $25,000 for information that led to his capture, according to the service. Speculation into Panaligan's whereabouts were complicated due to his dual citizenship between the U.S. and the Republic of the Philippines.

title: Here's why nearly 140K Illinois residents getting checks in the mail
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Nearly 140,000 Illinoisans will be receiving a check in the mail as the state tries to return more than $13 million to residents. What to know.
content:
Show Caption
Thousands of Illinois residents may have some free money coming their way.
Illinois Treasurer Michael Frerichs said 138,561 residents have checks coming in the mail for unclaimed property.
In total, the state's treasurer's office is trying to return $13.2 million to residents.
Here's what you need to know.
Where are the checks coming from?
The checks are from the latest round of the Enhanced Money Match program, which allows the Treasurer's Office to automatically return missing money to people without the need to file a claim.
How much are the checks worth?
The majority of the checks in this round are for $50 to $100.
How do the checks get sent to the right people?
The program leverages data already collected by the state and crossmatches it with the State Treasurer's unclaimed property database. The Treasurer's Office then sends a letter to the unclaimed property owner after confirming their identity.
What is the Enhanced Money Match program?
The program focuses on simple claims, or cash owed to a single person. This does not include cash owned by multiple parties, including a joint holding of a parent and minor child, as well as shares of stocks and bonds, escrow accounts, and the contents of bank safe deposit boxes. The program is part of the state's Unclaimed Property program, also known as I-CASH.
Why are checks being mailed?
The state treasurer is legally required to return unclaimed property to its owners or heirs, no matter how long it takes.
How much money has been returned through the program?
Since 2018, the Illinois Treasurer's Office has returned more than $102 million to nearly 422,000 people through the Enhanced Money Match program.

title: Bistro Verde ready to roll out a new menu for the fall
author: Joshua Dineen
description: Lincoln Land Community College's student-run restaurant is ready to roll out a new menu for the fall.
content:
I don't know where the last two months have gone; it happened so fast. LLCC's last Bistro Verde menu and class were quite successful and are now done. To the many of you who joined us for lunch and allowed the students to share their talents and learning experiences — thank you.
We are now on to the next menu, which offers plated dishes that are a little more upscale casual, but very reasonable. Service just began on Oct. 22 and will go through Nov. 21. We are open Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. (closed Nov. 5).
This class is focused on more challenging techniques and timings. In addition to our regular menu every week, each of the students will take turns being responsible for creating a three-course lunch menu that includes an appetizer, entree and dessert for $16.
Speaking of the regular menu, let's discuss the appetizers. We are doing a version of pad kaprow, a quick sauteed dish with lots of basil and a little garlic, chilis and soy sauce but using cauliflower instead of meat. We are making traditional Japanese gyoza, or pork dumplings, which provide a great opportunity for the students to practice the tedious task of folding tiny pleats of dough while keeping the delicious filling inside.
I also thought it would be fun to have some southern flavors and offer a homemade chicken tender served with a fried macaroni and cheese ball sitting on braised greens with a candied yam sauce and a drizzle of honey. Making this involves many cooking methods and timings. For the last appetizer, the students are butterflying shrimp and giving them a coconut breading. We serve this with yellow curry sauce, fresh pineapple and a little cilantro.
We go back to Japan for the first soup on the menu. We are making miso soup topped with tempura mushrooms. The second soup is a chicken and coconut soup from Thailand called tom kha gai. We are also going to have a version of a wedge salad using a variety of smaller lettuce heads and adding a pepperjack croquette for texture and fun.
Of course we are also offering a rotation of smashburger choices: Oklahoma, Flapper, Carolina, Santa Fe Hatch and the Luther burgers. Each of these regional smashburgers will be offered for one week respectively and can be enjoyed as a horseshoe if you prefer.
For a grilled cheese, we are having caramelized onions and mushrooms with Swiss cheese on sourdough. It seems simple, but it takes almost an hour to properly caramelize onions then melt the cheese just right without burning the bread while doing 10 other things. It is a little more challenging than you might think.
For the fish sandwich, we coat a large cod filet with crunchy course panko. It is served with pickled vegetables and homemade katsu sauce, all on a brioche bun.
For our pasta-themed entrée, we are taking the idea of a Cajun seafood boil and tossing it with homemade sweet corn gnocchi. Don't worry, all the seafood will already be shelled and ready to enjoy.
The grilled steak choice for this menu is petit filet mignon. This gives the students another opportunity to butcher larger expensive cuts of meat down to an individual steak. They then sous vide the steak to make sure it is flavorful and perfectly cooked and finally finish it on the grill. It is served with romesco sauce, a roasted tomato and red pepper sauce, topped with a poached egg, a side of broccolini and homemade shoestring potatoes for a little crunch.
Lastly, they are making a version of cassoulet, though we are making it with chicken instead of duck. They will sear thinly sliced chicken breast and serve it over a white bean stew, crispy potatoes, sauteed green beans, a couple slices of chicken sausage and finished with a very rich chicken and herb sauce.
I tried to use as many cooking methods as possible and introduce international flavors while helping the students make delicious food to share with our guests at Bistro Verde.
Hopefully we will see many of you and look forward to your feedback as our students learn about running a restaurant that offers plated foods in courses.
Sweet corn gnocchi
10 ounces sweet corn
2 eggs
5 ounces ricotta
1 cup grated parmesan
3/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon pepper
1 cup flour
Directions
Place sweet corn and eggs into a blender until smooth.
Combine with the rest of the ingredients in a bowl with a spatula.
Shape the dough into long ropes about 1 inch in diameter, using lots of flour to avoid sticking.
Cut into 1-inch pieces.
Drop the gnocchi into boiling water for 1 minute.
Carefully remove, and gently rinse in cold water.
You can freeze these for a later time or for a quick dinner. Space them out on a tray in the freezer until they completely freeze, and then transfer them to a freezer bag. This will prevent them from sticking together while frozen.
To finish:
Use a little butter or olive oil to sauté the gnocchi just to a light golden brown. They are a little delicate, so turn gently.
It is fun to add a little minced garlic, a splash of cream, grated parmesan and chopped parsley to make a quick and delicious dish.
Or add them to any sauce with the meat and/or vegetables of your choice.
Joshua Dineen is the chef specialist at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management and Baking/Pastry, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: Franklin's Bergschneider elected National FFA president
author: Steven Spearie
description: Bergschneider, who grew up in a farm in Franklin, was selected for the year-long position from 37 candidates.
content:
Thaddeus Bergschneider, who grew up on a fourth-generation farm in Franklin in Morgan County, was elected National FFA President at its conventional and expo in Indianapolis last week.
The Illinois FFA State President, Bergschneider is a freshman at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign where he is pursuing a degree in agricultural and consumer economics in the College of Agricultural, Consumer and Environmental Sciences (ACES).
A former member of the Franklin FFA Chapter, Bergschneider, 19, is the first Illinois student to lead the national organization in three decades.
He was selected for the year-long position from 37 candidates, who participated in an extensive interview process with the National FFA Officer Nominating Committee before the selection.
As National FFA President, Bergschneider will represent and lead more than a million FFA members across the country, working alongside a team of five other officers to drive the organization's mission of developing future leaders through agricultural education.
The National FFA Organization includes more than 9,000 local chapters across all 50 states, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
At Franklin, Bergschneider did his senior project on U.S. reliance on China for ag products.
"What really (interested) me about that," Bergschneider told The State Journal-Register in 2023, "(was) seeing ag on an economic level nationwide and locally and seeing how trade works with grain or any other commodity."
His family's farm, JP Bergschneider Farms, grows corn and soybeans and raises cattle and turkeys. The farm has a sister company, Yeoman Farms, that sells eggs year-round.
'Thaddeus embodies the core values of our college and the spirit of agricultural leadership," College of ACES Dean Germán Bollero said in a release from the U of I. "His dedication to serving others and his drive to elevate the future of agriculture make him an outstanding choice for this role."

title: Springfield bus driver faces several charges of child porn
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Illinois Attorney General has charged a Springfield bus driver with multiple counts of child porn.
content:
A school bus driver in Springfield faces child porn charges.
The office of Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul has charged Anthony J. Marconi, 58, with eight counts of possession of child porn.
Springfield Police officers along with investigators from Raoul's office searched Marconi's home in the 3000 block of East Enos Avenue on Oct. 23. He was arrested after law enforcement found evidence of child sexual abuse material, according to Raoul's office.
'Survivors of sexual assault and exploitation may never fully heal from the trauma they have experienced, making it imperative that the perpetrators of these crimes be stopped,' Raoul said in a news release.
Chris Coyle, the general manager for First Student, Inc., said Marconi was immediately placed on administrative leave.
Officials are encouraging residents who may have additional information to submit a tip by calling Special Investigator Tom Ritter at 217-685-7905
Marconi is being held at the Sangamon County Jail and his next scheduled court date is Nov. 14 in the Sangamon County Circuit Court.

title: Letter: A 'thank you' to those who helped get the Race Riot site as a national monument
author: Austin Randolph
description: Ken Page and Austin Randolph say \
content:
On Oct. 9, a great celebration was held at HSHS St. John's Children's Hospital in Springfield for the 1908 race riot site's federal designation as a national monument, which establishes it as a unit of the National Park Service.
In 2014, a search for buried historical items in a part of land purchased for the Springfield Rail Improvements Project uncovered the remains of the brick foundations of five homes destroyed by fire during the race riot.
The discovery at this site disrupted the landscape and became the driver for bringing a race riot memorial to Springfield.
If it had not been for the rail project uncovering the remnants of a horrible event from our city's past, we likely would not be delivering its story through a national monument today — nor celebrating the stories of greatness from that time, such as the black firefighters who battled homes set ablaze during the riot, the formation of the NAACP and one of the NAACP's co-founders, Ida B. Wells-Barnett.
No unit of the National Park Service has presented these stories before.
Over the past few decades, there have been efforts to recognize this part of our history. And for more than the past two years, a coalition of local and national organizations grew over time and worked, via consensus, toward the designation and future landscape for the memorial.
We want to call attention to the multifaceted, diverse team that strived to push for the site's federal designation and progress the endeavor through advocacy, community outreach, property matters and philanthropy.
The organizations in this coalition, and key representatives, include:
American Civil Liberties Union of Illinois – Springfield Chapter; Ken Page
City of Springfield; Nathan Bottom
Fever River Research; Floyd Mansberger
Hanson Professional Services Inc.; Kevin Seals
Hospital Sisters Health System; Damond Boatwright, Matthew Fry and Camille Rodriguez
Lincoln Presidential Foundation; Erin Carlson Mast
NAACP – Springfield Branch; Austin Randolph Jr., president and Teresa Haley, former president
National Religious Partnership for the Environment (NRPE); Cassandra Carmichael
Sakura Conservation Strategies; Dan Sakura
Sierra Club; Athan Manuel and Jackie Feinberg
This effort extends beyond political affiliations.
It has always been bipartisan, as seen in examples such as the city land donation process occurring across mayoral administrations, from former Mayor Jim Langfelder (D) to current Mayor Misty Buscher (R), and in community advocacy from Illinois Sen. Doris Turner (D). The congressional delegation has been supportive from the start, across terms and parties.
U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R) and former U.S. Rep. Rodney Davis (R) were early advocates — Rep. Davis proposed a bill to place the monument under the National Parks Service. U.S. Rep. Nikki Budzinski (D) and U.S. Sens. Dick Durbin (D) and Tammy Duckworth (D) have been staunch supporters.
We commend the support from a range of organizations, including Black Lives Matter Springfield, the Coalition to Protect America's National Parks, the National Park Foundation, Prince Hall Mason of Central Lodge #3, the Springfield and Central Illinois African American History Museum and the Springfield-Decatur Area Alumnae Chapter of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority Inc. In addition, we acknowledge the late Leroy Jordan, who held several volunteer leadership roles related to advocacy around the rail project and the race riot site's designation before he passed in 2020.
Just as Springfield's rail project has become a model for the nation, the monument and future memorial will serve as an example for this country, illustrating the collaboration between local and national groups.
Leaders in Springfield connected with the federal government on the race riot site project.
In 2020, Sergio 'Satch' Pecori, Hanson's chairman and CEO, testified before the House Subcommittee on Highways and Transit on the importance of timely and efficient federal assistance and coordination on infrastructure projects and preserving historic resources, such as those uncovered at the race riot site.
In 2022, Teresa Haley, former president of the Springfield Branch of the NAACP, hosted a public meeting convened by the NPS as part of the agency's special resource study on the site.
In June of this year, the Rev. T. Ray McJunkins graciously hosted hundreds of citizens at Union Baptist Church for a meeting convened by the U.S. Department of the Interior and the Council on Environmental Quality to hear the public's support for the designation.
National leadership included Ben Jealous, Sierra Club's executive director and past NAACP CEO, as well as NAACP's current CEO, Derrick Johnson.
And, in addition to the NRPE and Union Baptist Church, local and national faith communities were engaged in the process, including the Faith Coalition for the Common Good, the Jewish Federation of Springfield and the National Council of the Churches of Christ in the USA.
We have reached significant milestones this year, but we must be committed to staying involved — it has taken a lot of people to get this far, and it will take a lot of people to see this project to completion. This is an advocacy effort calling everyone to continue to urge making this monument a national treasure with the creation of a memorial to commemorate this tragic event in American history.

title: Williamsville senior provides playoff advantage for boys soccer, football
author: Bill Welt
description: Williamsville's Will Zinn faces back-to-back days of playoff action in football and boys soccer, plus other top kickers to know around Springfield
content:
VIRDEN — Will Zinn has a busy weekend ahead.
The Williamsville senior will serve as the football team's placekicker in a Class 3A first-round home playoff game against Carlinville on Friday at 7 p.m. He will later man the back line in the boys soccer team's Class 1A supersectional against host Columbia on Saturday at 11 a.m.
As long as he's not doing anything else for the football team, Zinn expects to be just fine.
He dabbled as a receiver earlier this season and even has a touchdown reception under his belt but after a few weeks, 'My legs were just cooked I guess.'
Zinn has still continued to star on the proverbial gridiron and pitch. In football, Zinn has drilled 2 of 3 field-goal attempts, along with 34 of 38 extra-point attempts.
In soccer, he has contributed six goals and seven assists as a defender and midfielder. On Wednesday, he helped usher this season's 17 th shutout in a 2-0 sectional final win over Pleasant Plains in Virden.
If the opportunity presents itself like against the Cardinals, he will also help facilitate the offense and push the ball forward.
'I just really like getting into the offense, it's really fun I think,' Zinn said.
Zinn, otherwise, said he has been a defender for most of his life.
'I've started some games freshman year and I've started sophomore, junior year and now senior year, it's just the guys who came before me taught me well and how to lead the team,' Zinn said of being a captain.
He began building chemistry with this thriving senior class as early as 4 years old. Seniors Reid Bodine and Bryson Trickey lead the offensive front with 52 goals and 16 assists combined.
Last season, Zinn was named all-Sangamo Conference first team alongside Bodine as well as fellow seniors Sawyer Woods and Drew Farnsworth. Zinn also picked up all-Sangamo second team honors in football by making 43 of 45 extra-point attempts.
'That's just always something I've wanted to do,' Zinn said of playing soccer and football in high school.
Here are other top kickers in the Springfield area going into the playoffs:
Brandon Sims, Jacksonville
The senior kicker converted three field goals in a 51-21 Week 9 win over Lincoln. His 55-yard field goal tied for seventh in IHSA history for longest ever made before tacking two more from 48 and 20 yards. He has so far converted 6 of 8 field goal attempts to go along with 33 of 35 extra-point attempts. Last season, he went 31-for-31 on PATs with two field goals, including a long of 40 yards. According to Chris Sailer Kicking, which is partnered with the Adidas All-American Bowl on NBC, he is ranked as a five-star kicker as well as a capable punter, which includes a long of 64 yards.
Lach Sullivan, Rochester
The senior kicker showed a good leg in a 41-27 Week 9 win over Sacred Heart-Griffin. He converted a pair of field goal attempts from 27 and 30 yards out. He has made 8 of 9 field goal attempts this season with a long of 42 yards. He is also 42 of 44 on PAT attempts.
Mia Gerger, Chatham Glenwood
The senior kicker loves stepping into the spotlight. She delivered the game-winning 21-yard field goal in a 34-31 overtime victory over Sacred Heart-Griffin in Week 8. She also previously knocked in a game-tying 20-yard field goal that forced overtime and led to a 52-51 playoff win over Oak Lawn Richards last season in Class 6A. She has made all three field goal attempts this season and is 40 of 42 on PATs after going 53 of 54 as a junior. Her 173 career PATs is a school record. Junior teammate Tristan Schwindt handles the punting duties and has a long of 67 yards.
Tom Davis, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The senior kicker also stepped up in the overtime loss to Glenwood. He tied the game at 31-all as the regulation clock expired with a 50-yard field goal that hit the crossbar and bounced inside the left goalpost. He chipped in eight goals and six assists on the boys soccer team this fall.

title: All systems go: Lehnen's return has Glenwood happy and healthy after 6A win over Crete-Monee
author: Ryan Mahan
description: The Titans celebrated the return of Blake Lehnen with a Class 6A first-round win over Crete-Monee.
content:
CHATHAM — Welcome back parties for the Chatham Glenwood football team don't involve coach David Hay bringing in cake and ice cream.
The Titans celebrate by having junior quarterback Colten Knoedler find his best friend and junior receiver Blake Lehnen for a touchdown in the first quarter.
Lehnen was on the field in a game for the first time this season as No. 5 Glenwood beat No. 12 Crete-Monee, 49-34, in a Class 6A first-round playoff game on Saturday after he missed the entire regular season with a torn quad. He caught five passes for 110 yards and a touchdown while also running four times for seven yards and a 3-yard touchdown.
'It feels great,' Lehnen said. 'I'm so happy to be back here battling with the family we have created here at Glenwood High School. Those two touchdowns don't happen without my teammates blocking for me."
That has to be a lot better than any sweets.
It came part of Knoedler's 475-yard passing performance where he was 23-for-31 with six touchdown passes. For every touchdown Crete-Monee scored, Glenwood had an answer each time, leading to the Titans' first win over the Warriors in four postseason meetings.
'It's really, really nice,' Knoedler said. 'I hope they're (former players who lost to Crete-Monee) smiling somewhere. If they were here watching, I hope they've got a little grin on their face.'
The Titans (8-2) travel to No. 13 Oak Forest for a second round game. Oak Forest toppled No. 4 Chicago Kennedy 44-0 to earn a home game in the next round.
Grady Mueller and Lehnen fueled Glenwood's 21-0 start. With 11 seconds gone in the second quarter, Knoedler found Mueller for a second TD between the pair, this time a 61-yard strike for the three-touchdown lead.
'We got Blake Lehnen back today, too: the fastest guy on the field,' Knoedler said. 'The fastest guy on the field was huge. That's my best friend: him back on the field, me throwing to him, that was fun.'
Glenwood senior kicker Mia Gerger was 7-for-7 on her extra-point kicks.
The Titans' defense helped the team take a three-touchdown cushion and prevent a serious Crete-Monee threat.
Gino Greco, Larry Wills and Cole Prost each had six solo tackles while Jonathan Helm had five. Becklin Anderson and Dylan Huff each pulled down an interception. Anderson picked off Patterson with less than four minutes left to seal the victory.
'(The Warriors) do a lot of screens and stuff, and we were ready for that,' Anderson said. 'That (interception) felt really good, like, 'Dang, we don't have to stop them one more time.'
The Warriors (6-4) showed plenty of resolve, despite an injury to starting quarterback Derrin Couch. Couch found Dorian Patterson for a 7-yard touchdown to pull within 21-7 before Knoedler and Brady Dwyer responded with a one-play, 60-yard touchdown possession to reclaim a 28-7 lead. But three plays later, Couch scored on a 71-yard run with 8 minutes, 38 seconds left in the second.
Once again, those pesky Titans couldn't let Crete-Monee's celebration last long. On the second play of the ensuing Glenwood drive, Knoedler found Gavin Simmons for a 64-yard touchdown pass. One play later, Couch was injured, and Patterson took his spot at QB. Patterson finished a 12-play, 80-yard drive with a 10-yard touchdown scamper. After a blocked point-after try, Glenwood headed into the locker room with a 35-20 advantage.
Grady Mueller caught four passes for 103 yards and two touchdowns while Gavin Simmons had five catches for 99 yards and a TD.
While Knoedler had a great day with his arm, he also turned into a running back on a 21-yard carry to get the Titans to a first-and-goal from the Crete-Monee 7 when he put his head down, followed his lead blocker and used the offensive line to generate momentum, despite several Warriors clinging to him. On the first play of the fourth quarter, Knoedler polished off the Titans' scoring by finding Jonathan Helm for a 3-yard touchdown pass.
'I was a little angry because I missed a throw to Blake (two plays earlier), so when coach (offensive coordinator Trevor Lehnen) called my number — he called a great game — when he called my number, it was an angry run,' Knoedler said.
Hay said Lehnen's return gives the Titans its receiving corps together.
'Him and Gavin can make such amazing plays together on the inside and you put (Mason Neumann and Andrew Schwartz) on the outside and you've got Grady in the backfield, you've got a lot to deal with,' Hay said of Lehnen's return. 'We're working at full-capacity now.
'You're going to have to pick your poison and coach Lehnen does such a great job finding the guys who they (defenses) aren't taking away. Colten out there is an operator and making plays and making it hard on a defense.
Glenwood and Oak Forest have never met in the postseason. The Bengals haven't gotten out of the second round since 2012. The Titans are looking for their second quarterfinal appearance in a row. Glenwood is 9-6 in 15 second-round games.

title: All incumbents on Sangamon County Board returned by voters; Milhiser, Roesch other winners
author: Steven Spearie
description: All seven incumbent Sangamon County Board members in contested races prevailed on Tuesday, including one cliffhanger.
content:
All seven incumbent Sangamon County Board members in contested races prevailed on Tuesday, including one cliffhanger.
State's Attorney John Milhiser and Circuit Clerk Joe Roesch both easily held on to their seats, while Recorder Josh Langfelder, the only Democrat to hold county-wide office, trails challenger Frank Lesko by 68 votes.
Eight county board seats up Tuesday were uncontested.
County Auditor Andy Goleman and Coroner Jim Allmon, both Republican incumbents, were unchallenged in reelection.
More:Rhetoric ratchets up in election for Sangamon County Recorder
Jennifer Ghesquiere Deaner, picked to succeed George Preckwinkle in District 25 in February, scored a nine-vote win over challenger Jennifer Merritt while third-party candidate Russ Clark finished a distant third.
It wasn't immediately known how many mail-in ballots or provisional ballots were in play in the race.
Sangamon County Clerk Don Gray pointed out that ballots postmarked by Tuesday and received by Nov. 19 still could be counted.
In a 2022 rematch with board chairman A.D. "Andy" Van Meter, Maureen Duffy Bommarito made a huge dent but came up a little more than four percentage points short Tuesday.
Van Meter, who has spent 30 years on the county board and 24 years as chairman, helped form the Massey Commission in the aftermath of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman, in her home by a now-former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy.
Four Republican incumbents--Tom Madonia Jr. in District 9, Greg Stumpf in District 16, Justin Davsko in District 26 and Abe Forsyth in District 27--scored double-digit victories.
Davsko's seat is for an unexpired two-year term.
Marc Ayers, the lone Democrat incumbent, staved off a challenge from Republican Colleen Lucas Cavanagh and won by 5.5%.
Lesko, the Springfield Clerk and former Ward 4 Alderman, clings to a lead, though over 3,500 votes by mail are still outstanding, Gray said.
Langfelder has been in office since 2008.
Milhiser, a Republican who returned as state's attorney a little less than a year ago replacing Dan Wright, soundly defeated Kimberly Talken, a Springfield trial attorney.
Roesch, also a Republican and also an appointee, defeated Democrat challenger Juwanda M. Burrage, who is director of staff development and training for the Illinois Department of Human Services, Mental Health.

title: How did swimmers from the Springfield area fare in girls sectional meets?
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Chatham Glenwood took second place as a team in the Edwardsville Sectional in girls swimming on Saturday
content:
Chatham Glenwood took second place as a team but did not advance an individual or a relay to the Illinois High School Association girls state swimming and diving finals.
Glenwood finished with 199 points behind first-place Edwardsville, which piled up 330 points on Saturday at the Chuck Fruit Aquatic Center of the Edwardsville Sectional.
The state finals are Nov. 15-16 at the FMC Natatorium in Westmont. A swimmer must win an event or beat the state qualifying time to advance. Divers must win the event or be among the top 32 sectional scores to receive an at-large berth.
Both Springfield High and Sacred Heart-Griffin also failed to qualify an individual or relay to state in Edwardsville. At Normal West, Addison Wherley of Petersburg PORTA didn't qualify and got ninth in the 200 freestyle (2:18.07).
Individuals, relay fall short for Glenwood
Glenwood sophomore Kylie Sullens placed fifth in the 200 IM in 2 minutes, 15.31 seconds with the qualifying time sitting at 2:10.54. She was fourth in the 100 breaststroke in 1:10.34, missing the cut of 1:07.17.
Senior Erin Turk finished eighth in the 200 freestyle (2:03.35) and third in the 500 freestyle (5:23.24). The state times are 1:56.21 and 5:13.64 for the 200 and 500, respectively.
Junior Maddy Yom had a time of 1:00.64 for third place in the 100 breaststroke with the time to advance at 58.38. Yom was seventh in the 50 freestyle (25.67) and the state cut is 24.38.
Sophomore Laynie Ryan, who has come on lately for Glenwood, took sixth place in the 100 freestyle in 56.86 with the cut at 52.98, and senior Ashleigh Maender was seventh in 56.91 in the same event. Ryan then came in fourth place in the 100 backstroke (state time of 58.56) in 1:04.31 ahead of senior teammate Hannah Poppenhouse (1:04.68, who finished fifth. In addition, Poppenhouse was sixth in the 500 free (5:42.42) and Maender was eighth in the 50 free (26.13).
The last time Glenwood sent an individual swimmer to state was in 2015 when Alexis Preski advanced in the 500 free and 100 breast and teammate Sharon Kok made it in the 100 free.
Glenwood junior Delaney Batton finished second with a score of 342.05 and did not receive an at-large bid in 1-meter diving. Edwardsville's McLaren Seaton won the event with 373.20. Freshman diver Marlow Burger of New Berlin was third with 341.75, followed by SHG senior Olivia Paul, who grabbed fourth place with 309.40. Springfield junior Reese Jennings, the City Meet champion, placed fifth with a score of 306.80.
Glenwood's best chance for a state berth came in the 200 freestyle relay when Sullens, Yom, Maender and Turk broke a school record. The foursome touched in second place in 1:41.27, breaking last year's mark of 1:42.22. The qualifying time is 1:39.00, and Edwardsville won the race in 1:35.41.
Springfield High, SHG have room to grow
Springfield and SHG can look to the future after finishing fourth and fifth with 77 and 49 points, respectively.
Springfield freshman Chloe Scheffler was seventh in the 100 back (1:05.33) and 10th in the 200 free (2:11.87), while junior Abby Myers took eighth in the 100 fly (1:08.40). With Scheffler, Myers, Miriam O'Brien and sophomore Lila Martin, the Senators were fourth and fifth in the 200 and 400 freestyle relays.
SHG junior Hope Speiser turned in another good swim in the 50 free and placed sixth in 25.44 before finishing 11th in the 100 breaststroke (1:15.54). Speiser had a time of 25.72 in the 50 free at City.
Junior Karigan Books was ninth in the 200 IM (2:26.59) and freshman Paityn Brady took 10th in the 100 butterfly (1:09.20). Brady, also on the cross country team, finished in 12th place at the Class 1A state meet in Peoria earlier in the day.
Books, sophomore Corrine Secrist, Brady and Speiser, led SHG to a fifth-place showing in the 200 free relay (1:52.82).
Springfield has not had an individual swimmer reach state since 2016 when graduate Caitlin Tierney made it in the 100 and 200 freestyles as a senior, and Haley Rivera advanced in the 200 IM as a junior.
Olivia Viele was the last SHG swimmer to reach state when she advanced in the 100 butterfly as a sophomore in 2018.
Meet reveals fast times
Overall, 21 times that were turned in beat the state qualifying standards and three pool records were set.
Edwardsville, which won the 200 medley and 200 and 400 freestyle relays, shattered the state times and established a pool record in the medley and 200 free. Junior Alyssa Albertyn of O'Fallon set a pool record in the 100 freestyle with a time of 49.94. The previous record was 50.96.
By event, the 200 freestyle had four swimmers qualify for state. The 200 IM and 100 breaststroke had three apiece, while the 100 butterfly, 100 freestyle and 100 backstroke had two each.

title: Gillespie's Chaz Oberkfell, Williamsville girls capture Class 1A cross country state glory
author: Bill Welt
description: Gillespie's Chaz Oberkfell, Williamsville girls cross country team each made history at the 1A state finals on Saturday.
content:
PEORIA — Chaz Oberkfell's morning started with a slight hitch.
"I put my coach through a lot this morning,' Oberkfell said, 'forgetting my jersey in the hotel room."
Gillespie's standout junior more than atoned by winning the individual Class 1A boys cross country state title at Detweiller Park in Peoria on Saturday. He crossed the finish line in 14 minutes, 31.87 seconds, a couple of seconds ahead of Winnebago's Nicolai Martino (14:33.88).
He's the school's first-ever state champion after previously achieving all-state medalist honors last season in 21 st place.
"In my mind, the first mile kind of has to be your fastest one because you're feeling the best during it," Oberkfell said.
"(Being a state champion is) sinking in a lot. It's kind of awesome."
Pleasant Plains junior Elijah Teefey ascended to eighth place in 15:03.33, while Williamsville sophomore Lucas Hollinshead was 17 th in 15:11.95 as the other 1A boys state medalists from the Springfield area.
Chatham Glenwood junior Van Schneider had the best performance in the 2A boys race. He posted a time of 15:25.50 for 53 rd place. Taylorville's Liam Bettis was 58 th.
Top girls performers
Williamsville senior Louisa Wilson became a four-time all-state medalist in 11th place individually and led the Bullets to the Class 1A girls team title.
Williamsville scored 171 points, just ahead of Tolono Unity (173) and Anna-Jonesboro (177). The program's previous best finish was fifth place in 2016.
Wilson, named The State Journal-Register's Small School Girls Cross Country Runner of the Year the past three seasons, reached the finish line in 17:26.60.
"I did everyone's hair, so I wasn't really thinking about the race at all,' Louisa said. 'I just know what I can do. I really didn't have to mentally prepare. I just went out and did it like I have in the past.
"It's really surreal (being a state champion) and I probably won't be able to like comprehend it for a few weeks."
Her younger sister, Joelle, had the team's next best time in 17:59.30 for 28 th place. Senior Hannah Nation (18:41.90) was 50 th in 18:41.90, followed by teammates Kaylea Hollinshead (18:56.70), Brooklyn Turley (19:09.20), Alaina Woolsey (20:29.80) and Maddie Overmeyer (20:31.10).
"It's really amazing,' Louisa said. 'They're all amazing people. It makes me even more happy. Like if I was a sophomore like winning state, I would still be so grateful, but I wouldn't feel all the emotions that I feel now as a senior."
Chatham Glenwood also garnered third place as a team in the 2A girls race as the defending champion. Chicago St. Ignatius ran away with first place.
Glenwood junior Ashlyn Chopra led the way in 20 th place in 17:40.23, followed by teammates Ali Broaddus (18:05.64), Ali Londrigan (18:33.74), Ally Knudson (18:44.96), Sophie Rentmeister (19:04.12), Brenna Sloman (19:22.69) and Addie Hamrick (19:38.86).
Rochester senior Brooke Zeibert, committed to Illinois State University, had the best performance individually out of the 2A girls field. She was 19 th in 17:38.50. The Rockets took fifth place as a team.

title: Holiday markets, Thanksgiving dinners among 5 things to do this weekend in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: Still need some weekend plans? Here are five things going on in the Springfield area.
content:
Show Caption
Dreary days at work don't feel as long when there's something to look forward to at the end of the week – what do you have planned?
Go on, get out and enjoy the weather before the leaves turn brown and Thanksgiving sneaks up on you. There's plenty to do around the capital city while also supporting local businesses who are gearing up for the holiday season for unique events around town.
Don't get caught on a Friday with no plans, here are five things to do around Springfield this weekend.
LMG Holiday Market
What: The Lincoln Memorial Garden will be hosting their annual Holiday Market this Saturday and Sunday serving complimentary hot apple cider and donuts to everyone who passes through. Peruse local artisans featured in the discovery room selling anything from bowls to jewelry, the Springfield Civic Garden Club Poinsettia sale and so much more. Three silent auction items will be available including an LED Christmas tree made of hand-forged horseshoes.
When: 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday and Sunday
Where: 2301 E. Lake Shore Drive, Springfield
More: A full list of participating vendors can be found on the Facebook page event.
Gather dining experience
What: As the holiday season approaches, the stress of planning the perfect family meal can overwhelm even the most seasoned hosts. Gather offers a chance to relax with friends before the holiday proper and share a four-course dinner catered by chefs. For those looking to enhance their hosting skills, an optional Holiday-themed Cocktail Master Class presents a delightful and interactive opportunity to learn how to mix a unique cocktail to enjoy with your dinner and complements your next holiday feast. Each attendee will be given a recipe card for all the courses, so when Thanksgiving rolls around, there'll be less hassle in the kitchen.
When: 6 to 8 p.m. Saturday
Where: 525 S. Pasfield St., Springfield
More: A general ticket is $61.50, with an added cocktail class tickets are $70.70.
Engelbach-Hart festival
What: Looking to hear some classical music? Illinois College welcomes the public to attend a serenade of music as part of its Fine Art Series. This admission-free music festival will consist of three exceptional concerts by outstanding artists in IC's Rammelkamp Chapel. The Engelbach-Hart Music Festival is possible through a generous gift to the community by the Engelbach and Hart families. The internationally renowned Vienna Boys Choir will kick off the festival on Wednesday, while Friday's concert will feature Grammy-nominated piano duo ZOFO, short for 20-finger orchestra.
When: 7:30 p.m. Friday for ZOFO, the piano duo.
Where: 215 Park St., Jacksonville, Rammelkamp Chapel
More: A full festival schedule including concert times and more information can be found at ic.edu/fas. All festival concerts are free.
Black Joy Thanksgiving Potluck
What: Join The Culture Experience and Ad Astra Wine & Tapas Bar for an evening of reflection and community where guests are welcomed to share stories of gratitude and the enduring spirit of Black joy over a heaping hot plate of soul food. Key features of the event include a keynote address from inspiring Black speakers as they share personal stories of thanksgiving, panel discussions, Q&A for thoughtful questions for how everyone can build a stronger community and of course, delicious food.
When: 4 p.m. Sunday
Where: 308 E. Adams St., Springfield inside Ad Astra
More: This event is free and while not required, it's a potluck – bring a piece of food to the table.
Deja Voodoo Heads at Curve
What: Down a drink with some electric sound in the background to liven your night! Deja Voodoo is back in town and is swinging by Curve Inn in Southern View for a night of loud music and rocking vocals. Deja Voodoo Band plays late '70s music, and previously played at Rock the Dock this year in July.
When: 6 p.m. Friday
Where: 3219 S. Sixth St., Southern View
