title: From stroke to State: Gillespie's Garwood fights back from medical emergency to run again
author: Ryan Mahan
description: For many people who have suffered a stroke, competing at the highest levels again isn't a top priority. But Gillespie's Marshall Garwood made it happen.
content:
Marshall Garwood's path to the Class 1A cross-country state meet last month took a wild deviation.
Just days after helping the Gillespie boys team qualify for the Toledo Cumberland Sectional with a third-place finish in the Shelbyville Regional, Garwood was sitting in Michelle Smith's Anatomy and Physiology class on Wednesday, Oct. 30 when something didn't seem right.
'I remember my eyes not looking the right way,' Marshall said. 'I don't know which way I was looking, but the lights were all messed up. Then I asked Hank (Fletcher), 'What was going on.' Everything was disoriented; different directions.'
In about an hour, Marshall was transported to St. Louis Children's Hospital. There, he and his parents learned that the 16-year-old had a stroke.
'He got up, and then he sat down and said he was dizzy,' Hank recalled about his best friend and cross-country teammate. 'And then he says his eyes were looking the wrong way.'
Miraculously, the stroke didn't end Marshall's cross-country season. Despite the loss at sectionals of the Miners' No. 2 runner, everyone else stepped up to get Gillespie a berth at the state meet on Nov. 9 with a sixth-place team finish.
At Peoria's Detweiller Park, Marshall returned to racing. While he didn't have the best time of his career, Marshall still posted a time of 17 minutes, 3.30 seconds in the three-mile race for a 191th-place finish.
Pretty impressive for being discharged from the hospital earlier that week.
It wouldn't even be the last visit to the hospital. He returned on Nov. 14 for surgery to repair a hole found in his heart. His mother, Nadine Garwood, said Marshall's surgery was a success and he was able to return to running on Wednesday.
'I was thinking I was tired or something like that,' Marshall said, 'I didn't really know what to think at first. I was thinking maybe I sneezed a little too hard, and (something) lodged out of the place. I was hoping if I waited long enough, it would just go away.'
Realization sets in
Minutes after Marshall arrived at the office of school nurse Whitney Page, Nadine arrived. Marshall and Nadine were put in the back of an ambulance for a drive to the Gillespie football field. Marshall was loaded into an awaiting helicopter, and Nadine and her husband, Shawn Garwood, made the hour-long drive to the hospital.
'The school nurse thought at first it was one of his ocular migraines,' Nadine said, adding Marshall has a history of migraine headaches.
While Marshall's parents were looking for a place to park at the hospital, Nadine got a call from a doctor saying they needed to take him back for an MRI. What she heard next was her first full realization of what was taking place.
'(The doctor said), 'We're calling in the stroke team,'' Nadine said. 'Even though I kind of recognized the symptoms, my mind wouldn't let me (think it was one).
'When she said they were calling in a stroke team I was like, 'Oh my gosh, it really was a stroke.' And then I told my husband to let me out; 'I've got to find my way in there.' I just got there in time to see him off to the MRI.'
With everything happening so quickly, Nadine taken aback with that news.
'I worked in a nursing home for a long time, and I guess I've never seen (a stroke),' Nadine said. 'I've taken care of people with strokes, but I guess I've never seen one happen. My brain wouldn't let me see what was right there. I think everybody knew but me.'
Gillespie cross country coach Jay Weber was the first one to reach the hospital.
'As soon as I got the call at the school that something had happened, I knew there'd be about 50 people there, including our wonderful, wonderful school nurse Whitney Page, who was absolutely amazing,' Jay said. 'I knew there'd be 50 people here, so I just never came to the school. As soon as I got the call, I just started driving right down to St. Louis because I knew nobody else would be down there.'
In the days following the stroke, Jay became much more than just a coach.
'Wednesday, I was there for a long time,' Jay said. 'I went home for just an hour to take care of my wife and then stayed Wednesday night, and I stayed well into Thursday. I came back (to Gillespie) to have practice with the team Thursday and then went back Thursday night.'
Running for Marshall
On Saturday, Marshall enjoyed the company of his teammates and celebrated their achievement at sectionals from earlier that day. Teammate Chaz Oberkfell won the race in 15:11.8 while Carter Sies was the Miners' No. 2 runner in 16:56.7 for a 44 th -place finish. Freshman Nolan Hostettler ran a time of 17:33.6 to finish just two spots ahead of Hank, who ran a 17:34.7 for 68 th place. Sophomore Lucca Kapp helped the Miners punch their ticket to state with an 82 nd -place finish in 17:46.8. It was Nolan's finish that surprised everyone, including Marshall and his mom, who were watching live from the hospital.
'He had just a huge breakthrough race that day,' Jay said of Nolan's race.
Jay said that night, he noticed Marshall had made big strides in his recovery.
'That Saturday night after sectionals when the guys all came down, they ate more candy and laughed more than I think I've ever seen,' Weber said. 'Before that, you could see he was back in terms of doing well, but that was when even the full personality was back, and he got to be himself.'
Marshall laughed at that.
'The doctor comes and sees all this candy on my table and goes, 'Oh, you've got to stop eating candy,'' Marshall said while laughing. 'I can't convince the doctor that I didn't eat all this candy.'
Prepped for state
One thing that was constantly on Marshall's mind during his hospital stay was getting back to racing again — soon.
He originally thought he could participate at sectionals, but when the team punched its ticket to state, Marshall had a new target.
'The doctors came in that Sunday morning and said they wanted to get him ready to run state,' Jay said. 'I think it seems so counterintuitive to us on the outside to think, 'Oh my gosh, how could he do that?'
'But when you think, a stroke is a blood clot, and activities that open up your veins, get your arteries bigger, capillaries, and get blood pumping, and get your heart beating ... I think it makes a lot of sense that that type of activity is really great prevention.'
Marshall was released from the hospital on Monday, Nov. 4, and joined his teammates the following day for a practice run on a bike trail. Marshall said his knees hurt after that, but he and the coach chalked that up to laying in a hospital bed for six days.
'Tuesday it was raining and my knees hurt,' Marshall said. 'I couldn't run much. I only just ran down the bike trail to the area where we were running, and then I ran back.'
By the time of Thursday's pre-state workout, Marshall was in much better shape.
'The only drawback was I hadn't consecutively ran three miles yet,' Marshall said of the looming state run. 'So, I didn't know if I could actually do it, physically. This is the only thing.'
Marshall's first three uninterrupted three-mile race since the stroke was at state. He started from the back because he wasn't sure if he would have enough speed to keep up.
While he celebrated being back at home with his parents and older brothers Wyatt, 20, and Hudson, 18, and being able to race at state, he wasn't done with being in the hospital just yet.
During his first stay, the doctors noticed Marshall had a patent foramen ovale, a tiny hole in the heart's wall of the upper chambers that usually closes at birth. While surgery isn't necessary for everyone with the condition, the doctors told the Garwoods that because of a stroke at such a young age, they recommended surgery to close it.
'A third of the population walks around with it and don't even know,' Nadine said. 'The only reason they look is if somebody has a stroke. But even when they find it, they continue testing.
'They said it's too tiny really to have been the problem, but since we know and he's had a stroke, we're going to close it.'
Marshall said he was overwhelmed by the amount of missed homework and tests he needed to finish.
'I came back to school, and they tell me I have all this homework and stuff,' Marshall said. 'It was just awful. And then they tell me I have to make up all these tests.
'It was just terrible.'
Marshall said he's looking forward to a healthy senior season already, especially since the team will return its entire roster.
'I cannot wait,' he said. 'It's going to be amazing.'

title: Media company that bought Neuhoff buys 4 more Springfield-area radio stations
author: Claire Grant
description: Four more radio stations in the Springfield area have been sold. Here's what you need to know.
content:
The same media company that bought the Neuhoff stations in Bloomington and Springfield in October has now acquired the Mid-West Family radio group in Springfield.
Woodward Communications, Inc. announced an agreement with Mid-West Family radio to purchase four radio stations in the Springfield market. Springfield now is WCI second radio market, alongside Appleton, WI.
Under the acquisitions, WNNS-FM, WQLZ-FM, WMAY-FM and WMAY-AM will operate under WCI.
These four radio stations join WXAJ-FM, WFMB-FM, WCVS-FM and WFMB-AM in Sangamon County, which were previously owned by Neuhoff Family Limited Partnership before being acquired by WCI on Oct. 1.
WCI is an employee-owned company which owns 15 radio stations and Insight Publications in Northeastern Wisconsin.
WCI said in a news release the purchases were strategic and that by merging the two operations, listener and customer experiences will be enhanced as well as advertiser value.
'We are excited about this opportunity and look forward to integrating Mid-West's solid brands into our Springfield operations,' Tom Woodward, CEO and President of WCI said. 'Over a period of time our plan is to co-locate all of the stations and related operations into Mid-West Family's current office and studios, which we believe will create synergies that will benefit our employee owners, our customers, and the community.'
In order to conform with Federal Communications Commission ownership rules, WCI has entered into an agreement to divest WCVS-FM.
WCI also has entered into agreements to divest two of its recently acquired radio stations in Bloomington, IL: WIHN and WWHX. Further, WCI has entered into a Local Marketing Agreement, or LMA, with Great Plains Media to operate WBBE.
Great Plains Media currently owns and operates three radio stations in Bloomington, IL. WCI stated the divestitures and the LMA agreement in Bloomington will allow it to better focus its resources in the Springfield marketplace.
Kevin O'Dea, market manager for Woodward's Springfield marketplace, will continue in his role with the company following the acquisition. O'Dea started his radio career in 1978 as an account executive with Mid-West Family Broadcasting's WMAY-AM in Springfield and has since been awarded the Illinois Broadcaster Association's 2024 'Vincent T. Wasilewski Broadcaster of the Year.'
O'Dea said in an interview that the radio team had met with Woodward already online and will keep their jobs under WCI. The new broadcasting schedule once cleared with the FCC might not be exactly what's on the radio today, but will be "best local programming we can," according to O'Dea.

title: Walks this way: Old Capitol Holiday Walks return to downtown Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: 'We're working to make it as engaging as we can,' said DSI executive director Carlos Ortega about the Old Capitol Holiday Walks.
content:
Springfield's downtown was central to Carlos Ortega growing up here.
Now he will oversee the Old Capitol Holiday Walks for the first time as executive director for Downtown Springfield, Inc.
"It's the ability to come together as a community in our downtown to facilitate an environment that is positive and engaging for our residents and visitors," Ortega said.
The walks kick off with Small Business Saturday on Nov. 30 with the Christmas Tree Lighting supported by Ace Sign Co. on the Old State Capitol Plaza at 4:30 p.m.
There are special activities on Wednesdays and Saturdays through Dec. 21.
In addition to the holiday lights downtown, some of the streets temporarily have been renamed, like Candy Cane Lane, Gingerbread Boulevard and Jingle Bell Drive. High school students have decorated some of the storefronts to correspond with the names.
It's an important stretch for downtown businesses, Ortega acknowledged, and a chance to welcome visitors downtown wouldn't ordinarily see.
"We're working to make it as engaging as we can," he said.
Here's what's happening over the next three weeks.
What's going on Small Business Saturday?
Ugly Sweater Festive Sports, noon to 4 p.m., Old State Capitol
Santa Claus, noon to 6 p.m., Old State Capitol
Abe & Mary Saturdays, noon to 6 p.m., Tinsley Dry Goods Room, Springfield Visitors Center, 1 Old State Capitol Plaza
Ice Skating, noon to 8 p.m., ALPLM Union Station Plaza
Abraham Lincoln Presidential Museum, 212 N. Sixth St., free admission with family friendly crafts and activities, 4 to 8 p.m. (also each Wednesday and Saturday of the walks)
Tree Lighting, with performance by Sangamon Youth Performance Group, Old State Capitol Plaza, 4:30 p.m.
Sounds of the Season, Old State Capitol, 4:30 p.m.; ALPLM, 6 p.m.
Dino-mite Holiday Sale, Kidzeum of Health & Science, 412 E. Adams St.
Special appearances by Tiana ("The Princess and the Frog") and Elsa ("Frozen") and "Holly," the SMTD Holiday Bus
Free hot chocolate for first 250 attendees
How about the man in the red suit?
Santa Claus will be at the Old State Capitol from 4 to 7 p.m. on Wednesdays and from noon to 6 p.m. on Saturdays.
You can have breakfast with Santa at Kidzeum from 9 a.m. to noon on Dec. 7.
Ice skating is back
The ALPLM purchased the LRS Ice Rink from the Sangamon CEO (Creating Entrepreneurial Opportunities) and it will be kept at Union Station Plaza.
The rink's surface is a polymer material that doesn't melt like ice but still lets people glide around on regular ice skates.
It will operate during the walks from 4 to 8 p.m. on Wednesdays and noon to 8 p.m. on Saturdays.
What bands and choirs are performing?
The Williamsville High School show choir will perform at the Old State Capitol at 4:30 p.m. and the ALPLM at 5:30 p.m. on Dec. 4. The Lanphier High School band will play at the ALPLM at 4:30 p.m. and the Old State Capitol at 6 p.m., also on Dec. 4.
On Dec. 11, it's the Taylorville High School band performing at the ALPLM at 4:30 p.m. and the Old State Capitol at 6 p.m.
The Pleasant Plains High School band plays at the ALPLM at 4:30 p.m. and the Old State Capitol at 6 p.m. on Dec. 14.
The Southeast High School performs at the ALPLM at 4:30 p.m. on Dec. 21.
Who doesn't love a parade?
The Jaycees Holiday Parade returns at 5:30 p.m. on Dec. 7.
The paraderoute proceeds west on Jefferson Street from the Horace Mann lot to Fifth Street, south on Fifth to Monroe Street, east on Monroe to Sixth Street and north on Sixth to Washington Street. Staging begins at 3:30 p.m.
Events at Kidzeum
Events at Kidzeum include a gingerbread house competition from 4:30 to 7 p.m. (Dec. 7), a holiday tea party (Dec. 14) and an ugly sweater day (Dec. 21).
Nutcracker performances
The Sangamon Youth Performance Group will also put on scenes from The Nutcracker at the ALPLM at 5:30 and 6:30 p.m. Dec. 11, 14, 18 and 21.
Red ticket giveaway
Make a $5 purchase at downtown shops and you will get a red ticket, which can be entered into a drawing for a Downtown Springfield gift card.
Three drawings will take place during the holidays walks.
Personal care drive
The ALPLM will be accepting personal care items, such as travel-sized shampoo, deodorant, soap and toothpaste, disposable razors, tampons and sanitary pads and socks and gloves, for the unhoused community through the holiday season.
All items must be new.

title: 'Good luck, I love you': Olivia Kratochvil continues to forge ahead a year after father's death
author: Ryan Mahan
description: On Sept. 23, 2023, Olivia Kratochvil had her life turned upside down after her father, a popular principal and former coach, suddenly died. A year later, she's still finding strength through him.
content:
On Sept. 23, 2023, Olivia Kratochvil had her life turned upside down.
Tim Kratochvil was the Pawnee schools superintendent and served as the junior high and high school principal. Those who knew and loved Tim saw a man with a larger-than-life personality who loved to laugh and joke.
But on that Saturday morning, Olivia was in a state of shock and trying to process what just happened. Her 49-year-old father was found unresponsive after suffering a heart attack at his home.
A year later, she's still trying to adjust, living with her mom, Wendy, in Rochester. She changed schools, played volleyball this fall, and maybe softball in the spring, with new teammates and newer friends.
'I feel like it can be normal at some times and then sometimes, I feel like he should still be here, that I can text him and he'll come pick me up at my mom's or something,' Olivia said. 'I'm still adjusting to that just because it doesn't feel real sometimes. But I definitely have adapted a lot better.'
Memories of her father
Olivia was the youngest of Tim and Wendy's three children. Jack graduated from Pawnee in 2020 and Luke in 2022. Luke displayed a broad smile when he summed up his father's relationship with Olivia, compared to him or Jack.
'He definitely has a sweet spot for Olivia for sure out of all of us, I feel,' Luke said. 'He was always very active in all of our sports, but I probably think that, well, it's hard for me to admit this, but Olivia probably was his favorite child.'
After Tim's death, Olivia took a week off from school and the Pawnee volleyball team. When she returned, her old routine helped take her mind off everything, but she always knew there was a huge absence everywhere around her.
In the hallways at Pawnee.
'I could hear his voice, in a sense,' she said. 'He was everywhere in that school. I mean, he was (always) talking to everybody.'
At her sporting events, as well.
'It was hard not seeing him watching me,' Olivia said. 'When I went back right after he passed and not seeing him in his usual spot, standing on the side, it was difficult. I would always look over to him and just make eye contact.
'Before a game or anything, he would say, 'Good luck, I love you, play hard, good attitude,' because I used to have a bad attitude problem, so he'd always tell me, have a good attitude.'
Even school lunches were far different without her dad around.
'For lunch, he would make me bagels,' Olivia said. 'I'd text him, like five minutes before lunch, 'Can you put me a bagel in the toaster?' Because he'd have a toaster (in his office).
'And no matter if he had a conference going, a meeting, or anything, he would walk out of his office, put it on the secretary's desk, and put cream cheese out for me. And then he'd go back in his office, shut his door, and go back to what he's doing.'
New town, new school, new friends
At the winter break, Olivia transferred to Rochester High School.
She didn't play basketball last winter because of the timing of the move between schools. She also decided not to play softball, partly because of the new school, but also because her dad wasn't around.
'I just didn't feel comfortable yet; I just needed to adjust to school, and I just couldn't think of playing without him watching me on the side,' Olivia said of softball, though she said she plans to play for the Rockets this season. She's been a shortstop and first baseman for much of her career.
Not only was changing teams a drastic difference, but changing schools meant a major adjustment.
'I think it was very difficult, just because I've gone (to Pawnee) all my life, I knew all the kids, and I grew up with the kids in my grade, so we had that kind of bond,' Olivia said. 'When I moved to Rochester, I felt like I didn't have any friends that knew me, because we didn't grow up together, we didn't really hang out.
'Trying to bond with your teachers and trying to learn how they teach is also another part that's difficult. And the coaches, getting adjusted to their coaching style was difficult.'
Growing up Kratochvil
All three of the Kratochvil children have played sports. Jack and Luke were both standouts in football and baseball. They all looked up to their dad's athletic feats.
Tim wasn't just an educator. He is the all-time winningest baseball coach at Taylorville with 164 wins. He was an all-state baseball player at Mount Olive before a successful career at Southern Illinois University, where he was inducted in the athletic hall of fame there in 2019. He also played two seasons in the Boston Red Sox organization.
'Grandpa (Roger Kratochvil) has all (Tim's) old game film tapes, you know, football, basketball, whatever, and the one that I love to see is his dunk in a game,' said Luke, who purchased his father's house outside of Pawnee. 'I don't know who they were playing, but ... he gets a breakaway, and just slams it down.
'It was like, 'Dad, I didn't even know you could jump that high. I didn't even know you could get off the ground like that.''
Olivia said she got much of her love of sports from her dad. But her tenacity and fighting spirit come from two older brothers.
'Well, Jack and Luke would always, you know, beat on me all the time,' Olivia said while Luke half-heartedly tried to protest. 'It was mainly Luke, to be honest. Jack kind of protected me sometimes, and then sometimes if I was being really annoying, he would give me a good old kick.
'I also feel like having brothers made me stronger because they would beat on me sometimes ... so I gained some strength from that.
'Sports was always a topic we talked about in our house. There was never a moment where we weren't really talking about sports, so it was definitely always around.'
It continues to be painful without her father, Olivia said. But she tries to focus on the good memories.
'My dad, he just always was funny and always making me laugh, coming in my room and stuff and just talking,' Olivia said. 'We'd always sit on the couch and watch TV and stuff; there was never a bad moment at home.'
All that changed just more than a year ago. From the moment Tim was found until she went back to school, many of her memories remain behind a foggy cloud.
'It just kind of like all blurred together,' Olivia said. 'From the hospital to the funeral and the week off, it just kind of mixed together.
'I just remember shaking a lot of people's hands and hugging people — some of the people, I didn't even know who they were. And they tell me their connection to my dad. I just remember, there were two days of it, so the first day (the visitation) was everybody coming (and) saying hi. And the open casket, which I tried to not be around that as much as I could, because it was just difficult.'
Olivia said she is fortunate that she's still able to hear her father.
'Whenever I'm missing him or something, I like to listen to his voicemails that he sent me, just so I can hear his voice."

title: 'Humbled, honored': Land of Lincoln Honor Flight's Joan Bortolon is First Citizen recipient
author: Steven Spearie
description: "There are so many people out there doing so much good without recognition ... we just want to help whatever target we're helping."
content:
Joan Bortolon said receiving the First Citizen award recently at a ceremony at Erin's Pavilion at Southwind Park reinforced for her the power of volunteering.
That's why Bortolon, the president of the Land of Lincoln Honor Flight, made sure to thank her board and a cadre of volunteers that put on multiple day-long trips annually for veterans to visit war memorials free of charge in Washington, D.C.
"There are so many people out there doing so much good without recognition," admitted Bortolon, in an interview with The State Journal-Register. "None of us want the recognition. We just want to help whatever target we're helping.
"It's a team effort to put the flights on. I'm humbled, but honored, to be singled out for the award."
The First Citizen award has been given out annually since 1963, but this is the first year it wasn't associated with the SJ-R. First Citizen Award was incorporated as a 501(c)3 nonprofit organization earlier this year.
The award honors individuals whose service, outside of their paid employment, has "significantly contributed to the betterment of the Springfield area."
A number of past recipients were in attendance at the award ceremony, including the 2023 SJ-R First Citizen, Patricia Benanti, a volunteer at the St. Martin de Porres Center.
Bortolon, 71, who is retired from the Illinois Department of Human Services, has been on all 72 of the Honor Flights that have originated out of Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport over the past 15 years.
She said a driving force in getting involved was that she wasn't able to take her father, John Bortolon of Dolton, Ill., to visit the newly-opened World War II Memorial before he died in 2004. John Bortolon served with the U.S. Army's 101st Airborne and was at the D-Day landing at Normandy and the Battle of the Bulge and participated in the liberation of the Netherlands.
"I never thought (instead)," Bortolon said, "that I would take almost 6,000 fathers, sons, brothers and meet them all. I'd be running down the runway behind the plane if they didn't let me on. I can't imagine not being with the veterans all day. Yes, we go to the same stops (every time), but each flight has a personality and that's cool.
"And why would anyone say 'no' to spending the day with 92 American heroes?"
Bortolon said an emotionally charged moment during each trip is the changing of the guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery.
That's bookended by a thunderous welcome home the veterans receive at the Springfield airport, one they may not have received after their tour of duty.
"They'll say, 'That welcome home was the best day of my life,'" Bortolon said.
In between, there are more private and tender moments.
One World War II veteran, Bortolon recalled, was bowled over by a cache of "thank you" letters as part of an on-flight mail call.
"He told me, 'I've been so cranky the last couple of years, I was sure nobody loved me anymore. Now I know they still love me,'" she said.
First Citizen board president and 2008 SJ-R First Citizen Garth "Butch" Elzea said Bortolon's service to veterans embodied the spirit of the award.
"Volunteering countless hours in the service of others, especially thousands of veterans, that have sacrificed so much, made her a deserving winner," Elzea said.
"When you find something you love," Bortolon said, "you keep doing it and that's kind of where I'm at (with Honor Flight)."

title: Santa's wish list: What Springfield area nonprofits are hoping for this holiday season
author: Steven Spearie
description: From foodbanks to animal rescue groups to veterans groups, Springfield area nonprofits make their wish lists for this holiday season.
content:
Feeling charitable this holiday season?
The State Journal-Register reached out to a number of Springfield-area nonprofits and asked them what they were hoping Santa ... or readers.... would bring them this year.
Hospital Sisters Mission Outreach
The agency's work: The Springfield-based Hospital Sisters Mission Outreach works with healthcare providers around the world to provide the best possible clinical care to patients, especially in areas where there are few resources.
Wish List: Executive director Erica Smith said the agency is asking for funds to send 2,000 'clean birth kits' to midwives and traditional birth attendants to give them the tools they need for safe, clean deliveries in places where there are no hospitals. It also would like to be able to buy parts for incubators and ultrasounds to get them in good condition for prenatal care because in some places, she said, access to an ultrasound isn't available for hundreds of miles.
Animal Protective League
The agency's work: APL is dedicated to caring for ill, injured and abused homeless animals and coordinating the adoption of animals by responsible pet owners. Its shelter provides a pet food bank, performs various pet therapy programs for nursing homes and schools, hosts a summer program for kids and runs low-cost vaccine clinics.
Wish List: Adopters, said executive director Deana Corbin, is APL's first wish. "We want to remind people looking for a pet to consider adoption from their local animal shelter versus buying their pet," Corbin said. Requests for pet food have steadily increased, she said, and APL needs dry cat and dog food for its food bank. Lastly, APL is asking for monetary donations to help provide special food and veterinary care to the animals at APL, along with gift cards from such stores as Walmart, Sam's Club and Farm & Home Supply where it can buy everyday cleaning and maintenance supplies.
Fifth Street Renaissance/SARA Center
The agency's work: Fifth Street Renaissance/SARA Center provides a number of outreach services, including transitional housing, homelessness, veterans services and health-related services.
Wish List: Executive director Penny Powell said, "dreaming really big," the agency's car, used for outreach, client transportation and deliveries to its various properties, could be replaced. It would also like to finish the Veterans Family Renaissance property, the city's first permanent supportive housing for unhoused female veterans and unhoused veterans' families. Ongoing, the agency, she said, needs fresh or frozen meats for its pantries as well as food staples, paper goods and cleaning supplies.
More information: 217-544-5040; fsr-sara.org
Sparc
The agency's work: Sparc's mission is to enrich the lives of persons with intellectual and developmental disabilities by enabling them to successfully live, learn, work and socialize in the community. Sparc's support services include 24-hour residential support; developmental training; supported living; supported employment and competitive employment.
Wish List: If Santa could bring Sparc something special this holiday, said Denise Corcoran-Schainker, its director of communications and fund development, "we would wish for support in enriching the lives of those we serve through community-based programs and resources." Contributions to help fund "transportation, activity programs and social events for the people we support would be incredibly meaningful," she added.
More information: 217-793-2100; spfldsparc.org
Wooden It Be Lovely
The agency's work: Wooden It Be Lovely (WIBL) provides women recovering from different forms of addiction, poverty or abuse jobs refurbishing furniture, sewing or making candles, which are then sold to the public. WIBL's Be Lovely House is a residential housing program for women who do not have children or do not have custody of their children and operates a year-round boutique store.
Wish List: A wish list for Santa, said WIBL founder, the Rev. Margaret Ann Jessup, would include a vacuum sweeper for the residence, a new pneumatic staple gun and air compressor for upholstery, a new industrial electric sander and pads and an industrial shop vac for cleaning. "Mostly," Jessup said, "our biggest wish is for lots of new monthly donors so we can hire more women healing from poverty, addiction and abuse."
Refuge Ranch
The agency's work: Located on a 17-acre campus just outside of Lake Sangchris State Park in Rochester, Refuge Ranch pairs at-risk youths with rescued horses. Its Bits of Hope mentoring program and its Freedom Reins special needs riding program serve over 50 children each season.
Wish List: On the wish list, said Refuge Ranch co-founder Chris Daniels, would be a farm utility vehicle used for feeding animals and chores around the ranch. Other wishes include riding helmets, saddles and gift cards to Farm & Home Supply, Tractor Supply and Menards to purchase feed for the animals, tools, fencing and other supplies. And don't forget the hay. Daniels said the average horse eats 15 to 20 pounds of hay daily and the ranch has 18 horses.
Mini O'Beirne Crisis Nursery
The agency's work: The Mini O'Beirne Crisis Nursery provides free, 24-hour emergency childcare to families in need. It also offers family support services, like parenting education classes, and has a basic needs pantry with items like diapers, wipes and formula. Its popular Holiday Store, where children can shop with the assistance of volunteers, returns to Fairhills Mall on Nov. 30.
Wish List:"Wishing big," said executive director Chriss Wilson, the crisis nursery would ask Santa for "a larger space so that we can assist more families." Wilson said the crisis nursery needs a continuous supply of diapers and wipes both at the nursery and through its basic needs pantry.
More information: 217-525-6800; miniobeirne.org
Central Illinois Foodbank
The agency's work: Central Illinois Foodbank's mission is to provide food and develop awareness of and creative solutions for food insecurity. The foodbank serves over 140 partner agencies across 21 counties in central and southern Illinois. One of its most popular food giveaways is with Friend-in-Deed, which served over 800 families last year.
Wish List: Items the foodbank would "love to receive," said executive director Pam Molitoris, are pasta, pasta sauce, low sodium canned vegetables, low sodium canned soup, canned fruit in juice, canned meat in water, peanut butter, whole grain cereal crackers, feminine products, laundry soap, bath soap, toilet paper, travel Kleenex, toothpaste, diapers and deodorant.
Midwest Mission
The agency's work: Midwest Mission Distribution Center, located in Pawnee, sends disaster relief, health, education and microbusiness resources to those in need. In 2023, Midwest Mission made almost 300 domestic disbursements and 44 international shipments, assisting more than 2.7 million people.
Wish List: Midwest Mission's big ask, said development manager Lisa Rigoni, is for a semi to help it fulfill the additional demand for off-site events, like its Blessings Bag Pack, which consists of rice, soy and dried veggies. Other requests include bicycles with wide tires used for delivery jobs and transportation to jobs and sewing machines (electric, not computerized) in good working order. Midwest Mission takes all treadle sewing machines. There is a need for volunteers, especially for the sewing machine shop. Rigoni said supplies are also needed for its layette, student and personal dignity kits.
More information: 217-483-7911; midwestmission.org
St. Martin de Porres Center
The agency's work: A Catholic agency named for a 16th century Dominican, St. Martin de Porres gives away free food, clothing and household items. All items are made available through donations and the agency is run by volunteers.
Wish List: Volunteer Leslie Sgro said the agency's first wish is additional funding to purchase food for the families it serves. "Money is always tight, even without staff," Sgro said. A second wish is assistance in fixing up the 40-year-old plus building. "We could desperately use air conditioning in the summer, new flooring and a coat of paint on the inside of the structure," Sgro added. "We try to keep it up, but we prioritize buying food first so upgrades must often take a back seat to our primary mission."
Forever Home Feline Ranch
The agency's work: Forever Home Feline Ranch is a sanctuary where cats will have a second chance to live a full life in a no-cage, no-kill environment. There are adoption and fostering options available.
Wish List: Forever Home Feline Ranch president and co-founder Cheryl Johnston said having a new roof for the barn and having vet bills paid off are on the wish list. The agency is seeking volunteers and fosters. Other items on the list include Purina cat chow and kitten chow, Friskies pâté, clumping litter, Capstar (flea treatment), paper towels, Clorox wipes and laundry detergent.
More information: felineranch.org
Land of Lincoln Honor Flight
The agency's work: Land of Lincoln Honor Flight provides round-trip transportation from Springfield to Washington, D.C. for veterans in order of their service (World War II Korean Era and Vietnam Era) who wish to visit their memorials. The one-day trip is free of charge to the veteran in honor of his/her service to our country.
Wish List: President Joan Bortolon, who has been on all 72 of the Land of Lincoln Honor Flights, has a simple wish for Santa: "to bring us all the eligible World War II, Korean and Vietnam era veterans so they can be shown our gratitude and given the welcome home they earned, deserve but did not receive."
Boys & Girls Clubs of Central Illinois
The agency's work: Boys & Girls Clubs of Central Illinois serves students ages 6 to 18 and operates at 21 elementary and middle schools throughout Sangamon and Morgan counties in addition to its main club facility. Each day, it serves roughly 1,500 youths, providing character building activities, academic programs and healthy activities.
Wish List: Number one on BGCCI's wish list said CEO and executive director Tiffany Mathis Posey is a new club facility "so we could focus on serving teens in a more robust way and have plenty of space to expand our program access at the central unit." Several new 15 passenger vans to transport kids to the Central Unit from their schools is also on list. BGCCI is looking for new winter coats for the kids as well as around 800 toys, dolls and other kid-friendly toys it will hand out at its annual holiday party.
More information: 217-544-0548; bgccil.org
Rutledge Youth Foundation
The agency's work: The Rutledge Youth Foundation serves approximately 300 abused/neglected youths annually up to age 21. The primary focus of services is protecting youths and teaching them independent living skills so that they become productive members of society.
Wish List: Executive director Marty Michelson said the youth foundation has an Angel Tree with gift suggestions for about 150 youths in its foster care, intact family and independent living programs. Michelson said some families are in need of essentials such as blankets, coats and food. Another idea, Michelson said, is to "adopt" a family and provide groceries and other essentials for a special holiday meal.

title: Here are this week's results in high school boys and girls basketball hoops for Dec. 3-7
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Pleasant Plains' Anna Weber rained in the buzzer beater in overtime to knock off Morton, plus other high school results around Springfield this week
content:
This is a daily list of top performers from Springfield-area high school sports teams for Dec. 2-7, compiled from information provided to The State Journal-Register by coaches, athletic directors, and team statisticians.
To have your team's athletes included, email results to sports@sj-r.com.
Monday, Dec. 2
⭐ Game of the Night
Pleasant Plains 49, Morton 47 (OT): At Pleasant Plains, junior forward Anna Weber made the game-winning basket at the buzzer in overtime and the Cardinals outscored the Potters 4-2 to record a nonconference girls basketball victory.
Weber's bucket on an inbounds pass from junior Madison Burke underneath the basket with 0.9 seconds remaining produced the win. Burke's two free throws added to Plains' scoring in OT.
Weber finished with a team-high 15 points, scoring 10 in the second period to keep the Cardinals close as Morton led 28-25 at halftime.
Sophomore Jada Leach helped Plains take a 42-37 lead into the final quarter when she knocked down three of her four 3-pointers in the third period.
Morton then outscored Plains 8-3 in the fourth and Abby Brooks' 3-pointer tied the game at 45 apiece to force overtime. Junior Grace Sabatka (eight points) made a 3 for the Cardinals' only points in the fourth.
Jada Leach finished with 12 points and junior Bailey Leach added nine for Plains (4-3).
Paige Selke scored a game-high 16 points and teammate Ellie VanMeenen hit three 3s and added 14 for Morton (3-1), which lost its first game of the season. VanMeenen had a chance to win the game in regulation, but her shot just inside the 3-point line hit off the rim as time expired.
The Potters, a successful program recently, won three out of four state championships in Class 3A in the 2015-18 seasons. They finished runner-up in the 2019-20 season.
🏀 Girls Basketball
Isabella Tiburzi, Carlinville: The senior made a pair of 3-pointers and scored 17 points to lead Carlinville past host Carrollton 45-40 in a nonconference game. She had 12 points at halftime, helping the Cavaliers (4-1) take a 20-13 lead.
Addison Wheatley, Auburn: The senior scored 13 of her game-high 16 points in the second half as the Trojans (5-1) broke a halftime tie and outscored Pawnee 34-16 for a 51-33 victory.
Kinley Stolte/Alivia Sabol, Nokomis: The junior-sophomore tandem combined to make 11 of 15 shots and scored 14 points apiece to lead Nokomis past Greenville 57-41 in a nonconference game. Sabol had a team-high eight rebounds and Stolte grabbed five boards for unbeaten Nokomis (5-0).
Amari Vickery, Gillespie: The sophomore tallied 12 of her 16 points in the first half as Gillespie defeated visiting Mount Olive 47-37 in nonconference play.
Josie Hughes, Havana: The senior guard totaled 22 points with three 3-pointers in a 54-48 win over Athens.
Addie Stadsholt, Athens: The senior contributed 16 points with three 3s in the loss to Havana.

Carson Doran/Blake Shoufler, Williamsville: Doran scored a team-high 15 points and Shoufler had 14 points and eight rebounds as Williamsville defeated host Taylorville 51-38 in its season opener. The Bullets outscored the Tornadoes 34-16 in the second half.

title: Springfield's Director of Planning and Economic Development is retiring
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The city's Director of Planning and Economic Development announced her retirement on Monday.
content:
The city's Director of Planning and Economic Development, Val Yazell, has announced her retirement for the end of this year.
Yazell began in the role in November 2017 when Former Mayor Jim Langfelder appointed her. She served as a contract employee for a time until the position was restored and Yazell was hired as a full-time employee.
Langfelder fired Yazell in 2021, but Mayor Misty Buscher hired her again in 2023.
The city announced Yazell's retirement Monday, saying she will retire on Dec. 31. Information about the incoming interim director is forthcoming, a city spokesperson said.
'Serving the City of Springfield has been one of the greatest honors of my career,' Yazell stated. 'I believe the city is well-positioned for ongoing growth. I look forward to watching Springfield flourish in the years ahead."
Mayor Misty Buscher stated that she is grateful for Yazell's service.
"Val's leadership has been instrumental in preparing Springfield for future success. Her dedication to economic growth and community development has made a lasting impression on our city,' she wrote.

title: Dorm Makeover Made Easy: How a Mom Used Temu to Cozy Up Her Daughter's Space
author: Hilary Tetenbaum
description: Decorating on a tight budget was no small feat.
content:
For Carrie Wait (@girlfam on TikTok), a mother of four, sending her eldest daughter, Taylen, off to college in Illinois was a bittersweet milestone. While Taylen looked forward to starting her freshman year, Carrie took on the mission of turning her daughter's dorm room into a cozy and inviting space—a true home away from home.
Decorating on a tight budget was no small feat. The rising costs of college essentials have made such endeavors even more challenging. According to the National Retail Federation, families are spending nearly double on dorm décor compared to a decade ago, with average expenditures per student exceeding $1,300 this year.
True to her motto, 'I love to shop but hate spending money,' Carrie got creative. She turned to Temu, an online marketplace known for affordable finds, and managed to completely transform Taylen's dorm room for just $200.
She started with the essentials: bedding and pillows. She found a set of floral blankets and coordinating fluffy pillows, transforming the bed into a warm and cozy retreat after a long day of classes and cheerleader practices. For lighting, she chose a trendy neon sign that says, "Good Vibes Only," which lit up above the bed. To combat the plain, sterile dorm walls, Carrie picked out colorful canvas posters. These simple touches instantly brightened the space, giving the room an inviting and chic vibe. Every piece was thoughtfully chosen and surprisingly affordable.
Carrie documented the entire dorm room transformation on her TikTok account, sharing the before-and-after reveal with her followers. The video quickly gathered thousands of views and resonated with both parents and students seeking affordable ways to personalize their dorm rooms.
'It was like a fun challenge trying to fit everything into the tiny room!' Carrie shared in the TikTok video, exuding her signature enthusiasm. 'We got a lot of these amazing items from Temu, and it all came together perfectly!'
The transformation left her followers in awe, with Taylen commenting, 'It turned out better than I ever imagined!' For Carrie, it wasn't just about finding budget-friendly décor—it was about creating a space where Taylen could truly feel at home, even when miles away from her family.
By blending style, savings, and creativity, Carrie's dorm room makeover has inspired countless families looking for ways to make their students' dorm experiences more comfortable and personalized—without overspending.

title: Can SHG basketball learn lessons after tall test against St. Louis powerhouse?
author: Adrian Dater
description: SHG boys basketball coach Tim Allen has a young team with some serious speed and athleticism, one that led for the majority of this entertaining game.
content:
What it lacked in size to St. Louis Christian Brothers College High School — which was considerable — Sacred Heart-Griffin's boys basketball team made up for with speed and smarts for much of Friday night's interstate matchup at Jim Belz Gymnasium. In the end, though, the height and muscle of the visiting school from Missouri proved the winning difference.
The final was 57-51 in favor of CBC, a team with three regular players 6-foot-7 or above, while the Cyclones' tallest player was senior reserve forward Chuck Lanier, at 6-6.
Don't sleep on the Cyclones moving forward, though. Coach Tim Allen has a young team with some serious speed and athleticism, one that led for the majority of this entertaining game. If they can correct some of the decision-making and turnovers that plagued them in the second half, the Cyclones (2-2) will make some noise in the Central State Eight Conference.
'I feel like it's one that we let slip away. But that's a heck of a home opener, to play against CBC,' Allen said. 'We want to play against the best; you want to go out and get competition. This team can do special things, as long as we keep growing.'
The Cyclones came out hot, hitting their first four shots, with sophomore guard Myles Montgomery creating open looks with his speed and skilled ball-handling. They led 31-25 at the half, with Montgomery scoring 10 points and junior guard Zion Lee hitting two shots from 3-point land.
But the Cadets (1-0) opened the second half on a 10-2 run, with 6-3, 215-pound junior guard Devin Houston getting four of his team-leading 16 points. Senior swingman Nikola Radovic, a native of Serbia, tied the game 33-33 with a three-point play and the Cadets took a 43-40 lead into the fourth quarter.
The Cadets extended their defensive pressure and started forcing rushed shots and turnovers. That was a big part of coach Sam Briscoe's adjustments after the half.
'We always talk about defense is where we want to hang our hat,' said Briscoe, in his second year at CBC. 'If you can guard and defend, you can give yourself a chance in any game, especially when your offense isn't going. And, our offense wasn't going whatsoever in the first half.'
The Cadets did a better job of denying Montgomery (a team-leading 13 points) the ball in the second half, and when he or other Cyclones were able to penetrate the paint, 6-foot-10 senior center Matt Michalski was there to swat shots away. He finished with five blocks.
Montgomery, who had an ice bag on his right hand after the game for an injury that otherwise seemed minor, said his team gained some potentially invaluable lessons.
Lee finished with nine points for the Cyclones, while senior Jamarion Bardwell added eight and sophomore guard Cam Brinkman added seven.
'We've got to just learn to keep our foot on the gas,' Montgomery said. 'I know we're going to be a dangerous team. I've been with these boys practically my whole life. We're going to make a run. Believe it.'

title: Second Sgt. Pepper's Cafe will not be returning to Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: The restaurant has been closed since the summer after a fire broke out at the business.
content:
After being open only a handful of months, the second location of a popular Springfield will not be reopening its doors.
Sgt. Pepper's Cafe opened a second location at 700 W. Jefferson St. in 2023 but closed after a fire at the business on June 21.
Ziyard Samara, whose son Muhammad started the second Sgt. Pepper's, after his own legacy location, confirmed the business would not be reopening after the fire.
Samara said the insurance did not fully cover everything lost to the blaze and after only being open for three months, the time investment to start again was too much for his son, who also has businesses in real estate.
The new Sgt. Pepper's Cafe featured a menu familiar to the first with comfort foods, and an addition for a full coffee bar.
The word "DEMO" has been spray painted over the front of the hollowed out building on Jefferson Street, but Samara hasn't confirmed when the building will be coming down.

title: Springfield receives nearly $3M to replace lead water service lines
author: Tom Ackerman
description: City Water, Light, and Power will replace lead water service lines that service around 400 Springfield homes.
content:
City Water, Light, and Power will replace lead water service lines that service around 400 Springfield homes, thanks to $2.9 million provided by federal funds.
The homes are located in low-income areas within wards 2 and 3 where CWLP has identified a high density of the lines, according to a news release.
CWLP is scheduled to begin the work in March 2025 and is expected to take two years to complete.
There will be an open house and public meeting for residents of the ward to learn about the program and sign up to be on the replacement list, which will be at the Salvation Army at 1600 E. Clear Lake Ave. on Dec. 12 from 4-6 p.m.
Residents who are unable to attend the meeting may sign up to be on a contact list for the program at surveymonkey.com or call 217-789-2116 ext. 2632.
The funds are provided by the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency's Public Water Supply Loan Program State Revolving Fund.
CWLP operations and maintenance funds are covering the cost of replacement for the utility-owned portion of lead service lines, the release read.
CWLP's lead service line replacement work began in 2019 and has accomplished over 800 replacements to date. There are 10,000 additional estimated lines needing replacement, CWLP said in a release.
Lead service lines in Springfield are located in homes or buildings constructed prior to 1930. Congress banned the use of lead pipes in 1986.
The Biden administration has finalized a landmark rule that would require water utilities to replace virtually every lead pipe in the country within 10 years, according to a report from Reuters.

title: New report finds Illinois in better spot to handle recession than recent past
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Illinois is better positioned to withstand a potential recession than it was in 2007 and 2020, a recent report says.
content:
Illinois is better positioned to withstand a potential recession than it was in 2007 and 2020, a recent report says.
Many economists predict that the U.S. could fall into a recession within the next few years, but if it happens, Illinois is in a better place than it was in December 2007 and March 2020, which saw the "Great Recession" and the "COVID-19 Recession."
Who wrote the report?
Researchers at the Illinois Economic Policy Institute and the Project for Middle Class Renewal at the at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign authored the report.
How does the report support its claim?
Researchers examined nine core fiscal and economic metrics 'on which the state has made dramatic gains over the past several years.'
'From significant improvements in budgeting and fiscal management to long-term investments in infrastructure, education, healthcare, and the stability of its pension system, Illinois has developed a far stronger resilience to economic downturns than at any time in recent history,' stated Illinois Economic Policy Institute economist and report coauthor Frank Manzo IV. 'Collectively, these improvements will help to mute the impact of any future national recession on critical public services, employment, and the economy as a whole.'
Did the report cite more specific evidence?
The report cited the following information as key indicators. The report provides greater detail for each indicator that can be viewed online.
Illinois eliminated the General Fund deficit and bill backlog, earning a total of nine credit rating upgrades since 2020 that will allow the State to borrow at lower interest rates.
Illinois achieved its largest ever Budget Stabilization Fund (or 'Rainy Day' Fund) balance at more than $2 billion--nearly 700 percent larger than it was prior to the Great Recession.
Illinois improved the funded ratio of its State retirement systems to its highest level since 2008.
Illinois rebuilt its Unemployment Insurance Trust Fund balance to $2 billion.
Illinois implemented a work-share program that allows employers to avoid layoffs by temporarily reducing employees' hours while enabling workers to receive prorated unemployment insurance benefits.
Illinois invested $2 billion more annually in public education—reducing the number of school districts in financial deficit by 55%—while increasing grants to make college more affordable by 77%.
Illinois established dedicated revenue streams that, together with federal funding, will invest $41 billion in roads, bridges, public transit systems, rail, and aviation infrastructure over the next six years.
Illinois committed to investments in climate resiliency and carbon-free nuclear power that are creating thousands of jobs on the path to 100 percent clean energy.
Through the expansion of Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act, Illinois has reduced its number of residents without health insurance by nearly 1 million, a 56% decrease.

title: US deploys resources on drone sightings; NY to receive 'state-of-the-art' detection system
author: John Bacon
description: For the last few weeks, people in New Jersey have reported repeated drone sightings, which have expanded to New York and Maryland.
content:
Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer has requested that "special detection systems" be deployed in New York and New Jersey after recent drone sightings fueled anxiety among residents in the region.
Schumer told reporters on Sunday that he made the request to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and pushed for Robin Radar Systems, which he said has a better chance of detecting drones because of their "360-degree technology." Schumer's request comes after a series of reported drone sightings in the Northeast over the last month, including ones that caused a New York airport to shut down on Friday.
"We've seen lots of recent sightings in New York, New Jersey, Long Island, Staten Island. So it's remarkable, with all these sightings over the last while, why do we have more questions than answers?" Schumer said Sunday. "If the technology exists for a drone to make it up into the sky, there certainly is the technology that can track the craft with precision."
Earlier Sunday, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas said the federal government is "deploying additional resources" to address the aerial drones.
"There's no question that people are seeing drones," Mayorkas said on ABC News "This Week.""I want to assure the American public that we in the federal government have deployed additional resources, personnel, technology to assist the New Jersey State Police in addressing the drone sightings."
Mayorkas said more than 1 million drones are registered in the U.S. A Chinese national living in Northern California was arrested last week on suspicion of flying a drone over restricted airspace — over Vandenberg Space Force Base, according to Mayorkas.
"It is our job to be vigilant," he said. "If there is any reason for concern, if we identify any foreign involvement or criminal activity we will communicate with the American public accordingly. Right now we are not aware of any."
Witnesses have described clusters of lights, saying they look like drones hovering over populated areas around New Jersey. The reported sightings have expanded to New York and Maryland and have attracted the attention of residents and politicians.
President-elect Donald Trump chimed in Friday, posting on social media: "Can this really be happening without our government's knowledge. I don't thinks so!"
New York to get 'state-of-the-art' detection system
Also Sunday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said the federal government will deploy a new drone detection system in her state. Drones forced runways at Stewart International Airport, 60 miles north of New York City, to shut down for about an hour Friday night. The airport serves commercial and military air traffic and is adjacent to the New York Air National Guard Base.
"In response to my calls for additional resources, our federal partners are deploying a state-of-the-art drone detection system to New York State," Hochul said in a statement. "This system will support state and federal law enforcement in their investigations."
Hochul provided no details on the new system.
Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-New York, sparked controversy last week when she said she does not believe the federal government does not know what the objects are. She urged the Biden administration to "be straight with us and just tell us what is going on."
Malliotakis doubled down on her claims Sunday, saying on Newsmax Sunday that lawmakers are getting "zero answers" from the White House, which she said shows the government "knows exactly what is going on."
Drone sightings won't be a 'Hollywood movie'
Rep. James Himes, D-Connecticut, in an interview with Fox News Sunday, was asked about the emerging conspiracy theories. Himes said he understood why people are anxious, and he chastised the FAA for failing to explain to the public that the large number of commercial, private and military aircraft that fly over New Jersey in any 24-hour period could be confused with drones.
"Now, let me say something that I know with confidence. It is not the Iranians. It is not the Chinese. They aren't Martians," Himes said. "I know that's very unsatisfying for people who want a Hollywood movie out of this."
Last week, White House National Security Communications Adviser John Kirby said the drone sightings appeared to be piloted aircraft, adding that there was no evidence the sightings "pose a national security or a public safety threat or have a foreign nexus."
Kirby did say the Department of Homeland Security and the FBI were working closely with state and local law enforcement to provide "numerous detection methods" to solve the mystery.
Chinese-built drones drawing scrutiny
Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Illinois, ranking member of the House Subcommittee on China, told Sunday Morning Futures he was concerned about the influx of Chinese-made drones into the U.S. Krishnamoorthi said even the U.S. military buys them "because they are cheap." He said he was concerned China could access data from the drones "in a backdoor manner" and so they ultimately could spy on Americans.
"The problem is, you are basically sacrificing our national security in the name of buying more inexpensive drones," he said.
Chris Christie sees a drone from his yard
Add former Gov. Chris Christie to the list of New Jersey residents reporting mysterious "drone" sightings outside of their homes. Christie said during an interview Sunday on ABC's "This Week," he believes he saw a drone over his house last week.
"I've never seen anything like that before, and I've been living at that house for 30 years," Christie said.'You can see why people are concerned, and it's a lack of communication from the government at the federal and state level that's at fault here," Christie said.
Christie said he wants the state police to have authority to "bring those drones down and find out why they're doing what they're doing." He said he understood why people are concerned.
− Zac Anderson
Some sightings may not be drones
The FBI and the Department of Homeland Security have said such sightings mostly appear to not be drones at all. 'Historically, we have experienced cases of mistaken identity, where reported drones are, in fact, manned aircraft or facilities,' the agencies said in a joint statement.
Harry Direen, an electronic and software engineering expert at DireenTech, said he wouldn't be surprised if people were seeing drones at first, but that once the notion of drones took hold, people assumed any aircraft they couldn't identify was a drone.
'After what were likely valid sightings of possibly hobbyist drones, every aircraft can then become suspicious,' he said.
− Jeanine Santucci

title: It's cold outside but winter sports are heating up: Vote for the SJ-R's athlete of the week
author: Ryan Mahan

content:

The senior scored 25 points on 10-for-13 shooting and had eight rebounds as the Titans defeated Decatur Eisenhower 67-47.

title: Springfield-area dive bar named one of best in nation for food
author: Claire Grant
description: America's grungiest dive bars for food have been named and a Springfield-area bar cracked the top 100.
content:
America's grungiest dive bars have been named – and Southern View's own Curve Inn has one of the best for food across the country.
In a recent poll from Geek Nexus, an entertainment and media website, 3,000 adults across America were surveyed to uncover the best dive bars in their locale for unexpected menu items and reasons to return again, and again, and again.
In total, 120 dive bars were named among the best for food, including four total in Illinois.
According to Geek Nexus, dive bars have adapted over the past two and a half decades from just cheap drinks and gritty charm to food destinations as well.
The Curve Inn, 3219 S. Sixth St. Road, is a historic bar and grill established in 1932.
Bought in 2002 by husband-wife duo Ray and Ami Merchant, the locale is known for its vibrant atmosphere, the love of all things grunge, pony shoes and national acts on its state-of-the-art beer garden stage.
'(Ami and Ray) are proud to be a dive bar and they revel in that,' marketing representative for The Curve Perry Zubeck said. 'Ray and Ami were the first ones to have live entertainment and they started doing that ten, twelve years ago and now there's so many bars.'
The Merchant family dig into the vibes and all things dive about their bar, which had a scandalous history offering prostitution and illegal gambling in the fifties, before turning into a piano bar in 1972. The current iteration of The Curve Inn still features live music on stage weekly.
The menu at Curve features American fare, including burgers, lasagna, and fish tacos.
Amenities such as live music, darts, karaoke and staff that've been there for decades contribute to its reputation as a favored spot for both locals and visitors.
'When you walk in and you just kind of know that feeling when you're there,' Zubeck said. 'Most people will tell you they're on a first name basis and if you don't know anybody there you will very soon. And that's what makes it a good dive bar.'
The Curve Inn is currently open from 11 a.m. until 3 a.m. but will soon be closing at 2 a.m. after the village of Southern View voted to reduce bar hours in the area to follow suit with Sangamon County.
Of the four Illinois locations that cracked the top 120, The Curve Inn is the only one in the central Illinois area.

title: President of Michigan company stabbed by employee during staff meeting, police say
author: Jonathan Limehouse
description: Erik Denslow, president of Anderson Express Inc., is in stable condition after allegedly being stabbed by a 31-year-old employee during a staff meeting.
content:
The president of a Michigan-based manufacturer was stabbed by one of the company's employees during a staff meeting, police said.
Nathan Joseph Mahoney, 31, has been charged with assault with intent to murder and fleeing and eluding a police officer in connection to the stabbing of Erik Denslow, the president of Anderson Express Inc., according to the Fruitport Township Police Department and Michigan court records.
Mahoney allegedly stabbed Denslow around 9:20 a.m. on Tuesday at Anderson Express Inc. in Muskegon, Michigan, Fruitport Township police said in a news release.
Muskegon is about a 40-mile drive northwest of Grand Rapids.
Fruitpot Township police officers were dispatched to the business at 9:23 a.m. after receiving a 911 call about a reported stabbing, according to the department.
Denslow was stabbed in his side with a knife, allegedly by Mahoney, who subsequently ran away from the business, entered his vehicle and fled the scene, police said. Mahoney was eventually stopped by police and taken into custody about 15 minutes after the incident, according to the department.
USA TODAY contacted Mahoney's public defender on Thursday but did not receive a response.
'We remain in shock over the incident'
Police said fellow employees described Mahoney as "having a quiet demeanor." Witnesses of the incident told police Mahoney entered the conference room wearing a black medical mask before walking up to Denslow and sticking a red-handled knife with a four-inch blade into his side, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by MLive.
A motive for the stabbing has not been determined, the department said. Denslow is currently out of surgery and remains in serious yet stable condition, according to police.
Mahoney had only worked for Anderson Express Inc. for two weeks and was being trained to replace a retiring employee at a high position in the company, police said, per WOOD.
'We remain in shock over the incident that happened at our plant yesterday,' a spokesperson for Anderson Express said in a statement to MLive. 'Our first thought is with our president, who has a good prognosis for a full and speedy recovery. We are also focused on supporting our employees as they process this senseless assault.'
Inmate records show that Mahoney, who lives in Walker, Michigan, is still in custody with a $500,000 bond. His next hearing is scheduled for Dec. 26.

title: Sangamon County home listings asked for less money in November - see the current median price here
author: The State Journal-Register
description: Here's a look at how monthly real estate listings changed in Sangamon County last month.
content:
The median home in Sangamon County listed for $199,900 in November, down 3.6% from the previous month's $207,450, an analysis of data from Realtor.com shows.
Compared to November 2023, the median home list price increased 8.1% from $184,925.
The statistics in this article only pertain to houses listed for sale in Sangamon County, not houses that were sold. Information on your local housing market, along with other useful community data, is available at data.sj-r.com.
Sangamon County's median home was 1,800 square feet, listed at $110 per square foot. The price per square foot of homes for sale is up 6.2% from November 2023.
Listings in Sangamon County moved briskly, at a median 40 days listed compared to the November national median of 62 days on the market. In the previous month, homes had a median of 38 days on the market. Around 220 homes were newly listed on the market in November, a 14.6% increase from 192 new listings in November 2023.
The median home prices issued by Realtor.com may exclude many, or even most, of a market's homes. The price and volume represent only single-family homes, condominiums or townhomes. They include existing homes, but exclude most new construction as well as pending and contingent sales.
Across the Springfield metro area, median home prices fell to $189,950, slightly lower than a month earlier. The median home had 1,777 square feet, at a list price of $109 per square foot.
In Illinois, median home prices were $303,000, a slight decrease from October. The median Illinois home listed for sale had 1,700 square feet, with a price of $180 per square foot.
Throughout the United States, the median home price was $416,880, a slight decrease from the month prior. The median American home for sale was listed at 1,821 square feet, with a price of $224 per square foot.
The median home list price used in this report represents the midway point of all the houses or units listed over the given period of time. Experts say the median offers a more accurate view of what's happening in a market than the average list price, which would mean taking the sum of all listing prices then dividing by the number of homes sold. The average can be skewed by one particularly low or high price.

title: Open for business: Fire Station 6 moves into new home for first time since 1954
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Moving just a few blocks from its home of 70 years, fire Station 6 is the latest and final of three firehouses built in Springfield this year.
content:
Moving just a few blocks from its home of 70 years, fire Station 6 is the latest and final of three firehouses built in Springfield this year.
Station 8 and 13 both opened this past summer. Before that, the newest station was built in 1996.
Located near the intersection of East Ash and South 11 th streets, the new firehouse is expansive, clean, and state of the art.
The station, located at 2121 S. 11th St., will welcome visitors for an open house on Dec. 21 from 9 a.m. to noon.
Though the crew is still getting used to their new home away from home, they say the move has improved morale and decreased response times. It also provides amenities that make working and living at No. 6 much safer.
For starters, firefighters are better rested and enjoy coming to work, said Battalion Chief Mark Ballinger, who helps oversee the south half of the city's fire operations.
While many of the upgrades are obvious in both size and modernity, Fire Chief Ed Canny says the biggest benefit is a new decontamination area to wash and store duds after a fire, in addition to multiple showers—rather than having just one to share.
Each of the new stations are equipped with the specialized washing machines that remove cancer causing chemicals, bloodborne pathogens, and anything else crews wouldn't want to trek into the house. The storage and de-con are also located on the other side of the garage from the living quarters, which is important.
Cancer has become one of the biggest killers for the profession, Canny and Captain Kainan Rinaberger explained. Canny compared waiting to take a shower after a fire to marinating a chicken.
'If you leave it in the bag for five minutes, it's not very seasoned. But if you leave it in that bag for a couple of hours, the seasoning permeates the whole chicken. Well, that's no different than when we go into a house that's full of smoke and carcinogens.'
If a firefighter can't wash for one or two hours, the smoke and chemicals start to enter the skin, Canny said.
'And then you get into the shower when you get home the next day, and your body heats up and you can smell all that smoke coming out of your pores. So the sooner we can get it off, the better because we don't know what we're putting in us and what's going to kill us 10 years, 20 years from now.'
In the former house at 2156 S. Ninth St., gear was stored not far from the living room. The department takes care of its properties, but there were issues to be expected for a building of its age. The department and its equipment have also changed since the firehouse was built.
Canny recalled visiting the firehouse as a kid because his dad was stationed there for a number of years.
Looking at the fire engine that sat parked in front of one of the two bays, he noted that the engines and trucks keep getting bigger with new technologies. At the new firehouse, crews can drive into the garage rather than having to reverse.
Also at the new facility, there is a gym, and there are now dorm-style bedrooms, so crews no longer have to sleep in a single room with a sprawl of beds.
The city's choice to purchase the property for the new station was controversial when it was decided in 2022. The site called for an environmental cleanup before the firehouse could be built.
The site was formerly inhabited by Honeywell-Hobbs that produced controls, switches, lighting systems, battery indicators and meters for the transportation industry on the site before it was shut down for good in late 2010.

title: Mystery drones are being seen some places. Can you shoot one down in Illinois?
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A series of reported drone sightings have taken place in the Northeast over the last month, what about in Illinois?
content:
A series of reported drone sightings have taken place in the Northeast over the last month, including ones that caused a New York airport to shut down briefly last week. Concern over the drones led to an investigation involving multiple police agencies and the Federal Bureau of Investigation in Newark, USA TODAY reported.
The news has raised questions about how airspace is monitored around the country.
Have there been any reports in Illinois?
A spokesperson for the Federal Aviation Administration did not respond to a question about possible suspicious drone activity in the state, but there have been no suspicious drones reported in Central Illinois.
Chris Mueller, Sangamon County's executive director of the county's central 911 dispatch center, said there have not been any calls made about suspicious drones since late October.
What do drone operators say?
Nic Hancock, who heads Aerial Elite Solutions, based in Decatur, said he has been following the news closely about the drones.
His company utilizes drones for inspection of wind turbine blades, telecom towers, solar field inspections, and crop health analysis, among other things.
Hancock received a call from a farmer last week asking whether his company or others in the area were flying drones over the farmer's property. Hancock said the farmer also asked about the legality in shooting down a drone.
Is it legal to shoot a drone?
The FAA says shooting any aircraft, including drones, is illegal.
Where is it legal to fly?
'Generally speaking, it is legal to fly a drone in most locations if you're operating under 400 feet, but there are rules — including safety tests, keeping below 400 feet, keeping the drone in sight, avoiding all other aircraft, not causing a hazard to any people or property, and avoiding restricted airspace,' a spokesperson for the FAA wrote in an email.
Do drone operators think anything suspicious is going on?
'I'm confident that around here, it is just people, drone service providers -- just doing a job,' Hancock said.
Hancock sometimes gets the police called on him for drone usage, he said, which prompts him to simply present his license to fly it.
For Hancock, the news is interesting because the drones in question appear to break several rules as far as entering restricted airspace, lacking remote ID, and not displaying proper lighting. He explained remote ID as being similar to a digital driver's license for drones.
'I think that's what makes it all be a big question mark -- where they're doing everything wrong. Who is it?', he said.

title: Illinois sees most significant wage drop in the country since 1935, data shows
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Nearly 100 years ago, Illinois could boast the highest national average for an entry level hourly wage. But now? Not so much.
content:
Illinois nearly 100 years ago could boast the highest national average for an entry level hourly wage, but it is currently ranks close to last amongst other states.
Coming from the top spot in 1935, Illinois now ranks 39th.
Average entry level workers earn $14.06 hourly in Illinois, but in 1935 they would have earned $15.43 hourly with inflation adjustments.
A mapping of the data on brilliantmaps.com illustrates that change as subsequently being the most significant drop, nationwide. Illinois saw an 8.9% decrease in Increase Above Inflation.
Where does the data come from?
Data comes from ZipRecruiter as well as the U.S. Department of Labor.
How did other states compare?
South Carolina, Georgia, Mississippi, Alabama, and Arkansas were the biggest winners, increasing their average entry level hourly wages by 150% or more over and above inflation.
Many northern and western states only slightly saw their inflation adjusted started wages improve over the period.
Isn't minimum wage increasing in Illinois?
Yes. On Jan. 1, 2025, minimum wage will increase to $15 an hour. The minimum wage for tipped workers will rise to $9 per hour and youth workers (under 18) working fewer than 650 hours per calendar year will see their hourly wage increase to $13 per hour.
