title: New Springfield restaurant has a friendly staff and good food, but confusing menu
author: Kathryn Rem
description: This new business offers a variety of dishes with generous portions. But, our restaurant reviewer thought there could be some improvements.
content:
Name: Pinoy Pride Cuisine
Address: 2501 Wabash Ave., Springfield (White Oaks Mall food court)
Phone: 217-685-2832
Website: pinoypridecuisine.com
Credit/debit cards accepted: Yes
Hours: 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Friday and Saturday, noon to 6 p.m. Sunday
Entrée price range: $5.99-$13.99
Children's menu: No, but there is a grilled cheese sandwich and a chicken salad sandwich on the menu.
My order: This new business offers a variety of Filipino dishes, including Pork Adobo ($11.99), considered by many the star of the cuisine of the Philippines. This version featured a generous portion of marinated and braised pork chunks in a garlic sauce over white rice and with a whole cooked egg in the center of the dish. My friend dined on an order of vegetarian Pancit Noodles ($9.95), which were mixed with carrots and green beans. She thought the dish would have been better without the large amount of oil in it. I also got the Halo Halo ($4.99 for the small size), a blend of tropical fruit, ice cream and shaved ice, which was quite delicious.
Likes: The staff was helpful in explaining what each dish was.
Dislikes: There are many different menus and promotions on the front counter, which I found confusing.
What would I order next time? Eight pieces of fried lumpia (spring rolls) are $8.99.

title: Elon Musk's 'odd-looking' salute sure looked like a 'Sieg heil' to me
author: The State Journal-Register
description: Elon Musk was so happy about Donald Trump's inauguration he gave two stiff-armed salutes that looked like what the bad guys in World War II movies do.
content:
Upon seeing a billionaire who appears to be the American president's right-hand man excitedly give what can most charitably be called a 'fascist salute,' the correct reaction is: Gulp.
Show Caption
Elon Musk (R-Billionaireville) was so excited about President Donald Trump's inauguration Monday he threw out two stiff-armed salutes that looked just like what the bad guys in World War II movies do.
Before appearing to 'heil' the crowd, Musk told Trump supporters at a post-inauguration rally in Capitol One Arena: 'There are elections that come and go, and some elections are important and some are not, but this one really mattered. And I just want to say thank you for making it happen.'
He then thumped his heart with his right hand and thrust the same arm into the air at an angle that, quite frankly, I did Nazi coming. Then he did it a second time, with a big, dopey grin on his face. The move sent "Nazi salute" trending on Google and various social media platforms.
The Anti-Defamation League posted a statement on social media saying: "It seems that @elonmusk made an awkward gesture in a moment of enthusiasm, not a Nazi salute, but again, we appreciate that people are on edge. In this moment, all sides should give one another a bit of grace, perhaps even the benefit of the doubt, and take a breath."
I'm no historian, but Elon Musk's weird salute sure looked ... WWII-era?
That's sure not how I or a slew of others saw it. The ADL was criticized last year by its former head, Abe Foxman, for going easy on Trump in the wake of a wildly racist rally at Madison Square Garden in New York City.
The bottom line is this: Upon seeing a billionaire who appears to be the American president's right-hand man excitedly give what can most charitably be called a 'fascist salute,' the correct reaction is: Gulp. ('Uh-oh' would also be accepted.)
The incorrect reaction is what CNN's Erin Burnett said of Musk: 'You saw him come out with that odd-looking salute.'
'Odd looking' is the Hamburglar-style hat Melania Trump wore to the inauguration. Letting one's inner fascist loose in a moment of excitement is something else altogether.
Some tried to defend Musk's salute as 'Roman.' That's not a thing.
Some ran to Musk's defense, saying what he did was 'a Roman salute,' like the kind of thing you'd see in a gladiator movie. The problem with that is the pop-culture-ized Roman salute lacks a historical basis. According to 'The Roman Salute: Cinema, History, Ideology' by Martin Winkler: 'Not a single Roman work of art ‒ sculpture, coinage, or painting ‒ displays a salute of the kind that is found in Fascism, Nazism, and related ideologies.'
Suffice it to say that when anyone sees that style of salute, the first thing they think of isn't ancient Rome.
So did Musk mean to do a Nazi salute or was he just ... excited?
So was this an intentional provocation by Musk or a momentary revelation of what lurks inside him? Who knows?
Whatever Musk intended with his whatever-you-want-to-call-it salute, some far-right extremists immediately got excited about it, which seems non-ideal.
And Musk's recent embrace of the far-right Alternative for Germany party, which the German government considers an extremist group and whose leader was fined twice last year for using a banned Nazi slogan, doesn't do him any favors.
There's also just this simple question: Who, regardless of their level of excitement, just fires off a salute that even resembles the one used by Adolf Hitler?
When it comes to fascism, I'd rather overreact than underreact
You're welcome to parse Musk's arm motions however you like, and you're also welcome to label me an overreacting liberal ninny.
But I'm guessing there were plenty of folks in the country where that salute gained its infamy who, at a particular moment in history, thought some were overreacting as well.
So I'll stick with my reaction and say maybe Americans should be more than a little concerned that the guy who cozies up to fascists and embraces a U.S. president who routinely talks like a fascist is so close to the halls of power.
If it walks like a duck, talks like a duck and salutes like a cosplaying Nazi … well, you figure it out from there.
This column was updated to add new information.

title: The 48 players picked for the 2025 McDonald's All-American high school basketball games
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Here are the 48 players named to the 2025 McDonalds's All-American Game rosters for 2025. The game is set for April 1 in Brooklyn.
content:
For the second consecutive year, no Illinois high school basketball players were selected to the 2025 McDonald's All-American game.
Rosters for the 46th annual prep hoops event were released Monday afternoon for the games on April 1 at the Barclays Center in Brooklyn. Ten Illinois girls were among the nominees, but no Illinois boys were nominated.
Michigan State redshirt freshman Jeremy Fears Jr. (Joliet West) in 2023 was the last player from Illinois to be named a McDonald's All-American.

title: How these guards make up the ‘heart and soul' of the Lincoln Land women's basketball team
author: Bill Welt
description: The Lincoln Land Community College women's basketball team knows it can trust these guards with the ball in their hands
content:
The Lincoln Land Community College women's basketball team is coming off a banner year.
The NJCAA Division II Loggers not only earned their second-ever national tournament berth but also reached seventh place for their highest finish in program history.
The pressure still remains high for the No. 9 Loggers, even after winning their first 16 games.
Next gen: Why basketball is king for this three-sport standout at Carlinville
Springfield area top performers: Anna Weber, Plains capture Sangamon County girls title
Other Region 24 contenders such as No. 8 Illinois Central College, No. 11 Lake Land College, and No. 24 Parkland College loom just as large as before and leave little margin of error on the road back to the NJCAA tournament.
Sophomore point guard Durbin Thomas doesn't shudder from the challenge — far from it.
'It's exciting, I love playing competition,' Thomas said. 'It's a lot more fun when you face adversity. It just proves a lot as a team that we can play together and overcome obstacles.'
Invaluable facilitator
The Mahomet-Seymour High School graduate certainly handled Parkland's pressure with poise in a 66-54 win on Wednesday. She didn't commit a single turnover despite 35 minutes on the floor while contributing eight points and four assists.
Thomas, committed to NAIA Indiana Tech, averages 6 points, 3.4 assists, and 0.8 turnovers per game. That ball control is what makes her so invaluable, according to coach Chad Jones.
'She's had a bunch of goose eggs from a turnover standpoint, she's so steady out there,' Jones said. 'If you look at her (scoring) stat line, you're like, 'She's an OK player,' but she's the heart and soul of what we're doing right now.'
Title game rematch: What to know from Chatham Glenwood girls basketball OT win over Lincoln in 3A title rematch
Instant impact
Thomas and sophomore guard Sam Lindhorst instantly took over the backcourt last season. Thomas said she only needed to pick up the pace and sharpen her defense out of high school.
Lindhorst predominantly played point guard out of Waterloo High School, too. But she has assumed a larger scoring role this season following the graduation of leading scorer Marley Smith.
Lindhorst, committed to NCAA Division I Northern Kentucky University, is averaging 13.6 points, 5.1 rebounds, 4 steals and 3.6 assists through her first 19 appearances.
She especially excels at getting to the rim where she can score or provide the assist.
Even if shots aren't falling, Lindhorst said she doesn't get discouraged. She knows there are other options available, most notably sophomore forward Megan Harrell, who leads the frontcourt with 14.9 points, 7.9 rebounds, and 2.5 assists per game. Sophomore forward Whitney Rumbold also pitches in 9.4 points and 5.9 rebounds per game.
Harrell, a Quincy University transfer, was named all-Region 24 second team last season.
'She's one of those kids where you can throw it up and she can go get it,' Lindhorst said. 'And if you throw up a bad shot, she's going to get that board and put it back up. She's aggressive and that's what you need in there.
'I look good just because I'm passing it to them and they work with me.'
The Region 24 tournament begins on March 4.

title: Illinois Supreme Court will take up State's petition on Sean Grayson's detention
author: Steven Spearie
description: The petition filed by the Sangamon County State's Attorney centers around an appellate court decision saying Sean Grayson should be released.
content:
The Illinois Supreme Court has agreed take up a Petition for Leave to Appeal filed by Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser regarding the detention of a former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy charged with first-degree murder in the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey.
Oral arguments will be heard by the high court after the State and defense attorneys for Sean P. Grayson file briefs.
The petition, or PLA, asks the Supreme Court to address a Nov. 27 ruling from the Fourth District Appellate Court that would have cleared the way for Grayson's release from detention under the Pre-Trial Fairness Act, which is part of the Safety, Accountability, Fairness and Equity-Today, or SAFE-T Act.
A March 24 hearing for Grayson in Sangamon County Court will stand.
On Dec. 10, the Supreme Court ordered Grayson remain jailed until a decision is made in the case. He is currently jailed in Decatur.
Grayson and another sheriff's deputy responded to Massey's residence for a purported prowler early on the morning of July 6.
Grayson shot Massey in the face while in her home, even as Massey put her arms in the air and said "I'm sorry" while ducking for cover. Grayson aggressively yelled for Massey to put down a pot of boiling water.
Body worn camera footage of the shooting sparked international outrage.
Grayson has pleaded not guilty to all counts.

title: Springfield may have new procedure for appointing vacant city positions
author: Claire Grant
description: If the new process is approved, public comment would be an active part of the process prior to a vote.
content:
An ordinance about a new procedure to appoint certain vacant positions within the city of Springfield is up for debate after a debate of its own at Tuesday's committee of the whole meeting.
The ordinance, which will be taken up by the full city council on Feb. 4, seeks to create a formal appointment procedure when appointing a new mayor, treasurer or clerk.
Public comment would be an active part of the process prior to a vote.
Any vote for those offices would require a three-fifths majority.
Ward 10 Ald. Ralph Hanauer argued against the ordinance, saying the new process would make appointments to critical city positions, specifically the mayor, take too long.
'In the event, let's say for the mayor, you're looking at what could be three weeks,' Hanauer said. 'You're talking about stymying the process and I just think that it's good we're trying to put something together but what it's gonna do is handcuff future councils in the event something like this happens. I don't think the city can go that long without a mayor.'
Ward 6 Ald. Jennifer Notariano, who brought forth the ordinance which was seconded by Ward 3 Ald. Roy Williams Jr. professed skepticism with Hanauer's timeline.
'Three weeks? Since when--it's been three weeks since we've had someone sitting in the Ward 1 seat,' she said. 'There should be a professional, not an appointed, management-level staffer in each of these offices who can make sure the city doesn't fall apart if we take our time and do our due diligence to appoint someone with public input to these positions.'
Hanauer also said the ordinance should be held in committee, due to the Ward 1 seat being vacant, leaving the around 12,000 constituents without a vote.
'We've got one ward that wouldn't be able to weigh in on this,' Hanauer said. 'I'd really like to hold this.'
Williams shot back it should be voted on.
'I think we shouldn't hold it and stick to our guns like they would if it was flipped around,' Williams said, referencing the Jan. 7 special meeting during which Ward 1 Ald. Chuck Redpath Sr. was appointed clerk, leaving the alderman position empty.
'I hope what's not going on here is people are upset about the process of what's been going on the past few weeks,' Ward 7 Ald. Brad Carlson said. 'We've known the process. … If we are purposely trying to ramrod through without the full representation (of Ward 1).'
Redpath, in his final term as Ward 1 alderman because of term limits, garnered five "yes" votes, including his own, for clerk.
At the original meeting, Redpath's name was put forward as an amendment to an ordinance declaring the office vacant.
Gregory, Williams, Rockford and Notariano all questioned the process of gathering candidates' names and having a more robust vetting system.
City council members nominate candidates for clerk. The mayor appoints aldermanic positions with a vote of the city council.
Williams made a motion to send the ordinance back to the committee of the whole, in essence to delay the vote for Redpath, but it ended up in a 5-5 tie with Mayor Misty Buscher casting a "no" vote to break the tie.
Ward 7 Ald. Brad Carlson, Ward 8 Ald. Erin Conley, Ward 9 Ald. Jim Donelan and Hanauer supported Redpath to become clerk.
Conley and Donelan both said at the special meeting that a process to replace a mayor was already in place, referencing when the city council appointed Frank Edwards to be mayor after the death of Mayor Tim Davlin in 2010.

title: This popular high-end, sushi restaurant in Springfield is overhauling its menu
author: Claire Grant
description: A popular Springfield restaurant is overhauling its menu and will be known by a new name. Here's what we know.
content:
Show Caption
A popular Springfield restaurant is remodeling and rebranding.
Empire Korean Steakhouse, 2100 W. White Oaks Drive, has been serving hibachi and the experience of cooking your own meat and veggies at the table since opening in 2022.
But according to two servers at the restaurant, customers will soon be getting a new experience.
Here's what we know.
What does the rebranding look like?
Among the changes, the servers said the restaurant will now be known as Japan House.
Along with the new name, owner Kevin Huang will be taking a backseat in operations while his father, Peter Huang revises the selections.
Peter Huang has more than two decades in experience across the dining industry across several states, including Pacific Spice in Cumming, Georgia, where Kevin worked before taking the reins of his own business.
Is the menu changing?
Yes. The restaurant will be adding dishes, including sushi, soups and Chinese food to be ordered at the table and made in the kitchen—a drastic shift from the Empire Korean Steakhouse.
Why is the restaurant eliminating the make your own BBQ?
According to Peter Huang, the switch up should help keep the restaurant profitable. Each table which currently has a BBQ pit will now keep the lid on top for food service while dishes are prepared inside of the kitchen.
Wasn't the restaurant looking to move locations?
The building was listed for sale last spring, but the restaurant never moved locations. Kevin Huang at the time told the SJ-R, "It was just to see how much the property is worth."

title: Springfield attorney, cannabis compliance regulator mayor's pick for Ward 1 alderman
author: Steven Spearie
description: More than a dozen people were interested in becoming the Ward 1 alderman in Springfield, including 12 people being interviewed.
content:
A full city council vote on Cox's appointment could come as early as Feb. 18.
Mayor Misty Buscher said a dozen people interested in the Ward 1 opening were interviewed.
Jeffrey G. Cox, acknowledged as a critical component to the success of the Illinois Medical Cannabis Program and the launch of the state's recreational use five years ago, will be put up before the Springfield City Council as the Ward 1 alderman candidate.
The appointment by Mayor Misty Buscher will be on first reading Tuesday. It could go to a vote by Feb. 18.
Cox would replace current City Clerk Chuck Redpath Sr., who served for nearly three decades on the city council but cannot run again in 2027 because of term limits.
Redpath resigned from the Ward 1 seat before he was sworn in as clerk.
An attorney, Cox has been in regulatory compliance guidance since he left his position as chief of the Illinois Department of Agriculture's Bureau of Medicinal Plants in mid-2020. He had joined that department during Gov. Bruce Rauner's term.
The former Sangamon County State's Attorney assistant has been vice president with Palatine, Illinois-based Progressive Treatment Solutions a little over two and a half years. Before that, Cox was with another cannabis application and operations consulting firm, NMI Management.
State Rep. Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago, told a national cannabis industry newsletter that the state's medical cannabis program was Cox's "monumental achievement."
Cox grew up around Williamsville and attended Truman State University for his undergraduate degree and Florida Coastal School of Law.
Buscher told The State Journal-Register that there were 16 applicants for the position, 12 of whom were interviewed by Chief of Staff Mike Disco and her. The other four did not live in the ward.
The sprawling ward covers the southeast part of the city, including the area around Lake Springfield.
Redpath's appointment as clerk got several groups talking about the process for filling each position.
One citizens group that addressed the committee of the whole was angling for a public forum involving the candidates.
The full city council will debate an ordinance Tuesday that seeks to create a formal appointment procedure when appointing a new mayor, treasurer or clerk.
Last month, a Springfield man filed a motion seeking a court injunction against the "unlawful appointment" of Redpath.
A hearing before Circuit Court Judge Adam Giganti is set for Feb. 14.

title: 'Chasing greatness': Lanphier boys basketball continues to roll with win over Glenwood
author: Bill Welt
description: JaiQuan Holman and Shaunassey Hatchett Jr. combined for 43 points in the win over Chatham Glenwood on Tuesday
content:
Lanphier seniors JaiQuan Holman and Shaunassey Hatchett Jr. immediately went to work.
They combined to score the team's first 17 points for the early lead and the Lions notched a 58-49 Central State Eight Conference win over Chatham Glenwood at Lober-Nika Gymnasium on Tuesday.
Holman totaled 23 points, while Hatchett supplied 20. Both combined to shoot 14-for-14 from the free throw line.
'Nothing you tell me about them will surprise me,' Lanphier coach Blake Turner said. 'Those are my two senior leaders. Those guys have been on varsity for multiple years. I really expect more from them. If you look at me during the game, I'm all over both of them all the time.
'We're chasing greatness and we're chasing perfection. When you stop doing those things, that's when bad things start happening.'
Hatchett indeed scored 10 points in the first period before residing on the bench for largely the remainder of the first half due to early foul trouble. He didn't pick up any more fouls after the break.
Hatchett said they were ready to take care of business after last year's 55-30 letdown loss at Glenwood after winning the City tournament.
The Lions (18-9, 5-3) have now won eight of their last nine games since the forfeits against Southeast and Jacksonville, including a second straight City crown.
'We're going to continue to do what we do,' Hatchett said. 'We came into the locker room, we weren't cheering. We've got more business to handle, we've got (CS8 leader) MacArthur and U-High.'
Glenwood senior Cam Appenzeller hit three of his four 3s in the fourth period. He came up with a steal and layup to trail by just seven points with under five minutes left. He led the Titans (15-7, 5-2) with a game-high 24 points.
Lanphier had no turnovers in the first half before finishing with eight.
'Second half we got a little sloppy,' Turner said. 'They turned their pressure up when they were down and started trapping us all over the floor. I thought we were passing out of the press just for safety reasons and when you break pressure, you have to attack the basket. I think that once we were able to do that, we were able to get the lead back up to double digits and secure the victory.'

title: Illinois eighth grade students are ahead of the curve nationwide in reading, math
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A nationwide report found eighth grade Illinois students are ahead of the curve when it comes to reading and math. Here's what to know.
content:
NAEP, also known as the nation's report card, released results last week.
Illinois eighth grade students outperformed national averages in reading, math.
Fourth grade, eighth grade, and the 12th grade are tested, but the 12th grade results have not yet been released.
Illinois students are ahead of the curve, according to a nationwide assessment that released its scores from 2024 this week.
The National Assessment of Educational Progress, also known as the nation's report card, tests students in each state bi-annually to provide a common measure of student achievement.
Here's how Illinois scored in 2024, and also how the Land of Lincoln stacked up against other states.
What is NAEP?
The organization claims to be the largest nationally representative and continuing assessment 'of what students in public and private schools in the United States know and are able to do in various subjects,' according to their site.
They began handing out exams in 1969.
NAEP is a congressionally mandated project of the National Center for Education Statistics that is part of the Department of Education.
Highlights from Illinois
Eighth grade students from Illinois have outperformed the national averages in both reading and math.
Fourth grade students from Illinois tested on par with national averages.
In both grade levels and all subjects, Illinois students held steady in their performance since 2022, while the nation showed 'significant' reading declines for students in grades 4 and 8, according to a news release from the Illinois State Board of Education.
Eighth grade reading
Only one state outperformed Illinois in eighth grade reading.
Also, Hispanic students are bridging the gap for reading achievement scores with their white peers. Hispanic eighth graders scored 26 points lower than white eighth graders in Illinois in 2003, but that number decreased to an 18-point difference in the recent results.
70% of the grade level performed at or above NAEP Basic. Also, 33% of the eighth-grade students performed at or above NAEP Proficient.
Basic means partial mastery of the knowledge and skills that are fundamental for proficient work at a given grade. NAEP denotes three achievement levels: Basic, proficient, and advanced.
Eighth grade math
Only four states exceeded Illinois' performance in eighth grade math.
Illinois students earned an average scale score of 277, surpassing the national average of 272.
The percentage of Illinois students who performed at or above NAEP Basic was 62% and who performed at or above NAEP Proficient was 32% — a six-percentage point improvement over 2022.
Fourth grade reading
Illinois students achieved an average scale score of 214, equivalent to the national average of 214.
The percentage of Illinois students who performed at or above NAEP Basic was 59% and who performed at or above NAEP Proficient was 30%.
Fourth grade math
The Illinois students earned an average scale score of 236, statistically equivalent to the national average of 237.
The percentage of Illinois students who performed at or above NAEP Basic was 74% and who performed at or above NAEP Proficient was 38%.
Who and what does the test measure?
Fourth grade, eighth grade, and the 12th grade are tested, but the 12th grade results have not yet been released. That is expected to happen this summer.
For grade 12, only national results are released, not the state level data, according to a spokesperson from ISBE. 12th grade is also only tested every four years.
Does every student take the test?
A sample of students take the assessment.
What do the scores mean?
For the fourth and eighth grades, scores are given on a 0-500 scale for reading, mathematics, history and geography.
The 12th grade is scored on a 0-300 scale.
Where can I learn more about the Illinois report?
"Snapshots" or key findings from the report can be found on the Illinois State Board of Education website by searching for National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) & International Assessments.

title: Top takeaways: Sean Lee keeps Decatur MacArthur boys basketball atop the CS8
author: Bill Welt
description: Decatur MacArthur boys basketball is now 18-1 in the CS8 stretching back to last season and is repeat champs, plus other top takeaways in hoops
content:
Here are the weekend's top takeaways from boys and girls basketball in the Springfield area as conference champions are crowned and the playoffs loom closer ahead:
This story will be updated following Saturday's results.
Boys basketball
MacArthur captures CS8 title with Lee, defense
Decatur MacArthur coach Terise Bryson said it was probably the best first half so far this season following a 57-27 win over Rochester on Friday.
The Generals opened with an 11-0 run and led the Rockets 33-6 after the first quarter en route to a second straight outright Central State Eight Conference title. MacArthur (19-7, 8-1 CS8) forced nine turnovers in the frame, while also converting four 3s from three different sources.
Junior point guard Khymir Carson scored all of his eight points in the opening period, including two 3s. The Generals thrived with two freshmen in the starting lineup: guards Tylin Cook and Kennall Howell.
Bryson said he introduced Cook to the starting rotation so the defense could press throughout the game. Howell finished with 11 points.
'Sean (Lee and (King) Dees led our team with the energy on defense and we were making some shots,' Bryson said. 'We were so unselfish and then the freshman Kennall Howell hit a couple shots.'
The 6-5 junior Lee was in attack mode early and starred with 29 points and 10 rebounds. Lee and Carson scored the team's first 13 points.
'That was just the goal,' Lee said. 'We knew there were going to be opportunities and open lanes in the paint.'
The Generals previously went 10-0 last season in conference play before reaching the sectional finals. Junior guard Khorbin Gregory led Rochester (16-9, 4-5) with nine points.

title: Coroner identifies 15-year-old who died in weekend shooting outside of Petersburg
author: Steven Spearie
description: Illinois State Police said the investigation into the shooting just east of Petersburg was \
content:
Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon confirmed that a teenager involved in a shooting just east of Petersburg Saturday was pronounced "clinically dead" on Tuesday.
Allmon said Wednesday that preliminary findings showed Grant Withers, 15, a student at PORTA High School in Petersburg, died from a gunshot wound.
Withers' father, Richard Withers, 40, also died from a gunshot wound.
In an email Wednesday, Illinois State Police spokesperson Trooper Shafer McKune said that the investigation is "active" and no further information is available.
Menard County Sheriff's deputies responded to the home in the 15000 block of Tice Road, just off Illinois 123, around 12:30 p.m. Saturday.
Grant Withers was taken from the home by ambulance to HSHS St. John's Hospital.
Withers liked to ride dirt bikes and four-wheelers, and hunt, according to a GoFundMe page set up to support funeral and additional expenses related to his passing.
Students in the school district have been wearing camo to support the Withers family.
PORTA Superintendent Shannon Duling told The State Journal-Register that counselors have been made available to students.

title: Letter: Massey Commission should request independent investigation into sheriff's office
author: Steven Spearie
description: Six Sangamon County Board members said the agreement with the DOJ didn't specifically address sheriff department hiring practices.
content:
The letter to the Massey Commission was signed by six Sangamon County Board members.
The Massey Commission made a request to the DOJ for an independent investigation in November.
Six Sangamon County Board members have requested the Massey Commission to renew its call for an independent review of the hiring practices and the policies of the Sangamon County Sheriff's Department.
While the U.S. Department of Justice Civil Rights Division wrapped up an investigation into the sheriff's office and central dispatch with an agreement on Jan. 16, the letter noted that it didn't specifically address department hiring practices.
Those hiring practices have been criticized in the aftermath of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey, a 36-year Black woman and the mother of two children, in her home in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield on July 6.
The Democrats also called for the county and the sheriff's department to release any and all information requested as part of the review.
A former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy, Sean P. Grayson, has been charged with first-degree murder in an internationally celebrated case.
The request comes as the county board Tuesday will consider a $10 million out-of-court settlement with the Massey family.
Grayson's criminal history shows he had two DUIs and a questionable discharge from the military. Grayson had also been with six different law enforcement agencies within four years before catching on with Sangamon County in May 2023.
Grayson used his future father-in-law, Scott Butterfield, a former Sangamon County sheriff's deputy for 25-plus years, as an employment reference.
The letter, dated Feb. 5 but only shared with the media on Feb. 9, was authored by Tony DelGiorno, the leader of the Democratic caucus who represents District 23. It was also signed by Marc Ayers (District 12), Sam Cahnman (District 18), Vera Small (District 19), Gina Lathan (District 22) and Kevin McGuire (District 28).
DelGiorno said his "gut reaction" was that the investigation was short circuited "likely due to the impending restoration of the Trump presidency."
Two days after the agreement was signed, USA Today reported that the outgoing DOJ Civil Rights Division Director Kristen Clarke conceded that the division sought to wrap up as many investigations as possible at the end of the Biden Administration and enter into police reform agreements that might have the best chance of success.
DelGiorno and Lathan in October had implored the Massey Commission, an independent group formed in the aftermath of shooting, to request an independent investigation of the hiring practices and the policies of the sheriff's department. After voting in favor of the recommendation, it sent a request to the DOJ, the Illinois Attorney General and the Illinois State Police.
The Massey Commission meets at Ruby Recreational Community Center, 101 N. 16th St., at 6 p.m. Monday.
At its November meeting, Massey Commission co-chair Dr. Jerry Kruse couldn't say if the investigation was a result of the commission's letter.
The two-year agreement between the DOJ and the county requires review of the county's policies, practices, and procedures while relaying reports to the DOJ made of discriminatory conduct.
"It is obvious that the agreement between Sangamon County and the DOJ will not be adequately enforced, if it is enforced at all," DelGiorno wrote.
"The Massey Commission, the Massey family and the people of Sangamon County deserve the answers that a timely, thorough, and thoughtful investigation would yield."

title: What is the definition of a ‘true North Side kid?' Meet Lanphier's star forward Shaun Hatchett Jr.
author: Bill Welt
description: Shaunassey Hatchett Jr. has long been a staple for Lanphier boys basketball and is soaring even higher as one of the top players in the area
content:
Show Caption
Lanphier boys basketball coach Blake Turner has all the confidence in the world in Shaunassey Hatchett Jr.
'He's the captain and one of the leaders on our team and when he plays well, we're pretty unbeatable,' Turner said of the 6-3 senior forward.
And Hatchett has been on a tear lately.
He doled out 27 points in an 82-60 nonconference win over Sacred Heart-Griffin, while shooting 9 of 11 from the floor before delivering 20 points (including 10 in the first quarter) in a 58-49 Central State Eight Conference win over Chatham Glenwood last week to put the Lions (18-9) on a torrid stretch that includes winning nine of their last 11 games.
He is an indomitable force in the paint, but that confidence extends to the perimeter. Hatchett pulled up and knocked down a big 3 while trailing late in the first half before dialing up another trey early in the fourth against SHG.
'It's really my teammates,' Hatchett said. 'Last year when we lost to them (SHG) in regionals, Chuck (Lanier) would have me at the 3-point line and just leave me and I'd just pass the ball up. And they're like, 'Get open and shoot the ball.' I'm like, 'All right, I got you. I'm going to shoot some 3s.''
Comfort zone
It's a testament to his work ethic, Turner said.
Hatchett has spent countless hours in the gym and weight room with his older brother, Corrington Jones, a former forward himself on Lanphier's fourth-place team in the 2017 Class 3A state finals.
'We really love to be in the gym together,' said Hatchett, who is undecided. 'We argue, we love each other — it's what we love doing.'
Hatchett only appeared in two games as a freshman but quickly ascended into the starting rotation the following season. He has twice been tabbed to The State Journal-Register's all-area team alongside senior guard JaiQuan Holman, who was named the SJ-R's Large School Boys Basketball Player of the Year last season.
Hatchett said it was initially challenging coming through the doors of the old Lober-Nika Gymnasium against the likes of Tye Banks and Austin Robinson.
'Shaunassey was a kid who came into the program and the only thing he could do was jump and he really couldn't even make free throws,' Turner said. 'He just got in the gym, lived in the gym and started working on it and started knocking down shots and he was able to stretch it to the 3-point line now.'
He is not only a definition of a 'true North Side kid' in Turner's words, but he is also a model of consistency.
Over his career, he has averaged 13.2 points and 6.7 rebounds per game. He has also garnered more than 1,200 points, 600 rebounds, and 120 blocks while shooting 56.6% from the field.
'They have more trust in me,' Hatchett said of his teammates. 'They feel like once I get in the paint, nobody can really be as physical as me. They feel like I can get my shot off or if I really get in there, one or two of them will be cutting and I can hit them. They're getting more and more comfortable with me just getting shots up in the paint.'
With Hatchett and also junior forward Soriano Hayes, the team presents a daunting frontcourt. Hayes is averaging 11.7 points and 5.3 rebounds per game this season.
If just two of those three staples — Holman, Hatchett, and Hayes — can get going, Turner likes his chances.
'He's one of the big men that came in and really started helping us rebound,' Hatchett said of Hayes. 'He leads us in rebounding right now, he's a good shooter, he's good all-around and he's a good defensive player at the blocks down low, so we really needed him to come down, so I can have a break sometimes a little bit and I can come back and help.
'He's a big, big help.'

title: Here are the 10 most dangerous intersections in Springfield
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Three intersections in Springfield have seen more than 200 crashes over a ten-year period. Here's a look at the top 10 most dangerous intersections.
content:
Show Caption
Unless you're a traffic engineer or very observational person, you probably haven't considered what intersections are the most dangerous in Springfield.
Crashes, while unfortunate, can consequently inform municipalities like Springfield about how to make an intersection safer.
The State Journal-Register reached out to the state and the city to find what intersections see the most crashes. Here's what we found out.
Most crashes at intersections
The data below shows the intersections with the highest reported crashes from 2013 to 2023.
Dirksen Parkway at Sangamon Avenue: 509
MacArthur Boulevard at Lawrence Avenue: 349
South Grand Avenue at Martin Luther King Jr. Drive: 202
Stevenson Drive at Dirksen Parkway: 171
Madison Street at 11th Street: 150
South Grand Avenue at Fifth Street: 127
Veterans Parkway at Washington Street: 118
Cook Street at Fifth Street: 118
11 th Street at Stanford Avenue: 118
North Grand Avenue at 19 th Street: 101
Where is the data from?
The data comes from the Illinois Department of Transportation, though some of the intersections are managed by the city of Springfield, and others by IDOT.
Where are the most fatalities taking place?
Here are the intersections from above, but this time showing what crashes resulted in people dying. Data is from the years 2014 through 2023.
MacArthur Boulevard at Lawrence Avenue: 3
11th Street at Stanford Avenue: 2
South Grand Avenue at Martin Luther King Jr. Drive: 1
South Grand Avenue at Fifth Street: 1
Veterans Parkway at Washington Street: 1
Cook Street at Fifth Street: 1
Dirksen Parkway at Sangamon Avenue: 0
Stevenson Drive at Dirksen Parkway: 0
Madison Street at 11th Street: 0
North Grand Avenue at 19th Street: 0
How is the data used by municipalities?
When agencies look to invest in roadway safety, they analyze factors like the number of crashes, fatalities, injuries, and property damage, as well as the speed of a given roadway, said City of Springfield Traffic Engineer T.J. Heavisides.
Heavisides said the city is aware that these intersections are seeing a high number of crashes. Safety funds have been awarded specifically for the intersections of MacArthur and Lawrence, and for South Grand and MLK. Consultants are working on designs to improve those intersections, he said.

title: Why Lincoln boys basketball appears stronger than ever ahead of the playoffs
author: Bill Welt
description: Lincoln starters Drew Hayes, Karson Komnick and Frank Sanders certainly took their fair share of lumps and bruises this season, but all is well now
content:
Drew Hayes traces the genesis of his basketball roots to his grandfather, Bob Meeker.
'My grandpa would take me to his shed where he had a nice basketball hoop and fresh concrete floor that he put in just for me to shoot baskets in,' Hayes said. 'That's where I found my love for the game.'
It's ultimately how the senior forward formed a lasting camaraderie with the rest of the Lincoln boys basketball team.
Hayes originally attended Hartsburg-Emden in grade school but became acquainted with his future high school teammates beginning with rec ball as early as first and second grade.
He eventually transferred to West Lincoln-Broadwell in eighth grade where he played with current seniors Blake Horn and Brady Miller and sophomores Bryce Vlahovich and Preston Short.
Chatham Glenwood's Cam Appenzeller: How this star pitching prospect elevated Chatham Glenwood boys basketball to win over Rochester
Hayes, the nephew of distinguished Hartsburg-Emden volleyball coach Jennifer Hayes, reached The State Journal-Register's all-area team last season with 9.2 points, 4.5 rebounds and 3.1 assists per game but has taken his share of lumps and bruises this season.
Hayes missed the first half of the season initially due to a concussion before encountering a high ankle sprain.
Hayes, who doesn't plan on playing sports after high school, said it was hard to miss so many games as a senior.
'It's been a battle to go through mentally, but we're getting through it as a team,' Hayes said.
Injury bug
Hayes wasn't alone in the injury department.
Junior guard Karson Komnick (wrist) and senior forward Frank Sanders (knee) also sat out for long stretches early in the season.
It's all in the past now.
The Railers appear stronger than ever with all three back in the starting lineup.
'I think we had a lot of guys step up in a big role to help everybody out,' Komnick said. 'People stepped up and I think that's what made us successful. We didn't win every game, but we got better and that's what matters — to play our best ball in March.'
Hayes and Komnick combined for all the team's 16 third quarter points in a 36-29 Central State Eight Conference win over Chatham Glenwood on Thursday. Lincoln trailed 11-7 at halftime until Hayes provided the spark with back-to-back 3s for his only points of the game, while Komnick finished with a game-high 11 points.
Lincoln subsequently won at Decatur Eisenhower 39-36 and rival Lanphier 43-36 on consecutive days to extend its win streak to eight games and improve to 18-8 overall.
It illustrates the team's resilience in a nutshell.
'We were hurt in the beginning of the year,' said Komnick, who missed eight games with a broken wrist, 'and it feels good to have everybody back and winning.'
Big presence
It's not just the offensive production, but their impact is especially pronounced defensively down low with the 6-5 forwards Hayes and Sanders.
Sanders recently committed to be a defensive lineman on the NCAA Division II Quincy University football team. He totaled 50 tackles, including 16 for loss and nine sacks this past fall. He also forced five fumbles with two recoveries and eight pass deflections.
He also helped end the football team's 39-year playoff spell the previous season.
Sanders first began playing basketball in eighth grade before trying football in high school. He started out as a receiver and defensive back before moving to the front lines.
'It was definitely a weird transition,' Sanders said. 'It was a lot more physical. I was used to running free and trying to catch balls, but now I'm dealing with 6-5 dudes who are 280 pounds trying to block me.
'I wouldn't have it any other way.'
That's also true working with Hayes.
'He's always finding me in the low post and stuff,' Sanders said of Hayes. 'He found me twice late in the game (against Glenwood) to go up by seven or nine points. He's always finding me, I know he'll find me.'

title: 'There are no words:' Three dead in house fire south of Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: A 34-year-old man and his two sons, 13 and 10, died in a house fire in Virden over the weekend, according to officials.
content:
As Michelle Clevenger tied a black and blue ribbon to a utility pole, Glenda Garrett placed balloons to railing on the front porch of a house in the 200 block of West Dean Street in Virden, about 35 minutes southwest of Springfield.
Garrett also tacked up a handwritten note that read "Loving prayers."
The house was the site was the site of fatal fire Saturday. A 34-year-old and his two sons, 13 and 10, died.
"It's to show respect to the family, that they're going to be missed," Clevenger said of the gesture. "They are loved. We want to put this up for the children, and the father, who passed away, to let them know we're thinking of them."
Two teddy bears, along with LED lights, were also placed in the yard.
"It's just terrible. There are no words," Garrett said. "There's nothing you can say."
A family member at the scene told The State Journal-Register that the three had moved into the rental house in November. The family member confirmed the ages of the children and the family relationship.
In a news release Saturday, Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon confirmed the father and the 13-year-old were pulled from the fire and taken by ambulance to Springfield Memorial Hospital.
Both were pronounced dead by hospital staff shortly after their arrival, Allmon said.
The 10-year-old was pronounced dead at the scene shortly after 10 a.m. Saturday, said Macoupin County Coroner Anthony Kravanya.
Neither coroner has officially identified the people who died in the fire.
Several area fire departments, including Chatham, responded to the fire.
The State Fire Marshal is handling the investigation.

title: 'No confidence': Massey family have misgivings about citizens commission
author: Steven Spearie
description: A Massey family member acknowledged the Masseys could still take their name off the Massey Commission.
content:
A cousin of Sonya Massey has left as co-chair of the Massey Commission.
The Massey family could still strip the commission of its name.
Sontae Massey said he was "actively defying" his family's wishes by staying as a member of the Massey Commission, formed in the aftermath of the July 6 fatally shooting of his cousin, Sonya Massey.
Addressing the commission Monday, Massey said his family "sent me here today to leave this commission and take our name with it."
Massey told The State Journal-Register that family members he spoke with Monday, including Sonya's mother, Donna Massey, "had no confidence in this (commission) whatsoever, but I do. I do see a glimmer of hope.
"I'm a Springfield kid. I'm not going anywhere and I'm here to fight."
It came on a night when Shadia Massey, also a cousin of Sonya Massey, resigned as one of the commission's three co-chairs. Sontae Massey said his cousin's departure was on a more personal note "and I respected her decision."
Several public commenters, in a lengthy and sometimes raw and uninhibited meeting at the Ruby Community Recreational Center, criticized the commission for being "unrepresentative" of the community and too pro-police.
Massey said he was "cautiously optimistic" about moving forward, though he acknowledged the family could still try to strip the commission of its name.
Massey planned again to talk to family members Tuesday, when the Sangamon County Board takes up a vote on a $10 million out-of-court settlement with the family.
Sonya Massey, a Black woman and the mother of two children, was shot in the face inside of her home in the 2800 block of Hoover Avenue of in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield.
Sangamon County Sheriff's deputies were dispatched to the home after Massey called 911 about a potential prowler.
Former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy Sean P. Grayson shot Massey even as she put her arms in the air and said "I'm sorry" while ducking for cover. Grayson aggressively yelled for Massey to put down a pot of boiling water.
Grayson, who is white, has been charged with first-degree murder. He is currently being jailed in Decatur and is next due in court on March 24.
Sonya Massey would have turned 37 years old Wednesday.
People "don't have faith in the commission," said Sontae Massey, witnessed by dwindling attendance at the meetings.
"But the people who showed up tonight convinced me that this can grow, this can be something," he said.
The commission, which has four workgroups, has sought to address systemic issues in law enforcement practices, mental health responses and community relations, with the goal of creating "tangible, practical and equitable solutions for the betterment of all who call Sangamon County home," according to its setup.
It is charged with producing a comprehensive report outlining findings, recommendations and proposed actions by the end of September.
Massey said he would like to see the commission extended by five years "at least."
Co-chair JoAnn Johnson, the first Black woman to reach the rank of colonel with the Illinois State Police and a law enforcement trainer in police bias, noted it was "the citizens' commission.
"I am here because I believe things need to change," Johnson added. "I will do what's in my power to help those things change."
Breonna Roberts said the "bad apple narrative" about Grayson is "a distraction."
"If there are bad apples, who's planting them?" Roberts said. "Who is letting them rot and why, time and time again, do those bad apples end up killing people who look like us?
"We are tired of being failed. We are tired of feeling let down and we are tired of watching our people die while those responsible get a slap on the wrist, a long drawn-out case and a system that continues to protect them."
Some of the commission's efforts have been hit and miss.
It recommended the county board set up a mental health board. A commission will study its formation with the idea that it would go before the voters in 2026.
But the board voted down a ballot initiative on sheriff recall that the commission favored and a move asking Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser to ask the Illinois Attorney General's office for its opinion on recall.
On Monday, county board member Sam Cahnman urged the commission to direct Milhiser to seek the AG's opinion.
Another county board member, Tony DelGiorno, speaking on behalf of six Democrats on the board, requested the commission renew its call for an independent review of the hiring practices and the policies of the Sangamon County Sheriff's Office.
The U.S. Department of Justice Civil Rights Division wrapped up an investigation into the sheriff's office and central dispatch with an agreement on Jan. 16, but DelGiorno said the DOJ didn't specifically address department hiring practices.
The commission's co-chairs, Johnson said, recently met with county board chairman Andy Van Meter, Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser and Sheriff Paula Crouch.
Johnson said the work of the commission "should and will continue full steam ahead" despite the agreement.
But Johnson also acknowledged "that we do understand that the timing of the DOJ's work and the agreement with Sangamon County leaves many to question whether the investigation was complete and sufficient to meet the discovery needs of the county and the commission."

title: Illinois lawmaker wants to lower legal drinking age to 18 if a parent is present
author: Tom Ackerman
description: An Illinois lawmaker wants to lower the drinking age when a parent or guardian is present. Do you think this a good idea?
content:
An Illinois lawmaker wants to lower the drinking age when a parent or guardian is present.
State Rep. John Cabello, R-Machesney Park, proposed legislation in late December that would enable 18-year-olds to drink alcohol in the presence of a guardian.
Rep. Cabello, who is also the Assistant Minority Leader in the Illinois House, argues that 18-year-olds are already contributing members of society. He also says the change would boost economic activity in the state.
'Many 18-year-olds are already contributing members of society, working full-time jobs, attending college, and serving – and in some cases dying for – our country in the military,' Rep. Cabello said in a news release. 'By lowering the drinking age, we are acknowledging their maturity and ability to make responsible decisions, just as we do in other aspects of their lives.'
Rep. Cabello also believes the measure would bring more families to eat at restaurants that would generate economic activity.
Rep. Cabello further argued that the law would encourage responsible drinking habits and avoid dangerous binge drinking.
The bill would amend the Liquor Control Act of 1934. The bill was first read on Jan. 9 and on the same day was referred to Rules Committee.

title: If you're looking a flavor packed salsa, check out this recipe
author: Jay Kitterman
description: Yes, the plate may look beautiful and served at the correct temperature, but if it does not taste good, then all is lost.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Arielle Johnson's "Flavorama: A Guide to Unlocking the Art and Science of Flavor" explores the complexities of flavor, combining taste and smell.
The book breaks down the five distinct tastes and the vast world of smell, explaining how they interact to create flavor.
"Flavorama" includes recipes and practical advice, encouraging readers to experiment and understand flavor profiles.
Part of what we teach our students in the culinary program at Lincoln Land Community College is the importance of flavor. Yes, the plate may look beautiful and served at the correct temperature, but if it does not taste good, then all is lost. Arielle Johnson has written a new text all about flavor, and the title is 'Flavorama: a guide to unlocking the art and science of flavor.'
Flavor is a combination of taste and smell, and this makes it a challenge for people who want to master it. There are five distinct tastes — salty, sour, sweet, umami and bitter. Our tongues have receptors for detecting each one. Johnson delves into all five.
Smell is more complicated, with about 400 types of smell receptors in the nose that capture signals from many, many different molecules taken together. This means a near-infinite number of flavors exist.
Arielle Johnson has a Ph.D. in chemistry and was the resident scientist at Noma, a fine-dining establishment in Copenhagen that has been named the World's Best Restaurant five times since it opened in 2003.
The colorful hand drawn illustrations in 'Flavorama' help one understand flavor science. Some of the illustrations of the human brain and nasal cavity explain how nerve cells that line the roof of the nasal cavity detect scent molecules and send signals directly to a part of the brain that handles feelings and memories.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
What about smell? Johnson organizes the building blocks of smell into categories — her main ones are fruity, herbal, spiced, meaty and vegetal, each further broken down into subcategories. Johnson writes, 'Smell — our most underrated, underappreciated sense — has everything to do with the way we experience flavor.' She further writes that 'taste plus smell equals flavor.'
Included in her book are close to 100 recipes. Most of these recipes have just a handful of ingredients. They are written in paragraph form with boldfaced ingredients labeled within the instructions.
I love lemon-flavored dishes, and Johnson asks the question, what is a lemon? The answer she writes, '… is a round yellow citrus, the fruit of the citrus lemon tree, a hybrid between a sour orange and citron. What gives us the flavor is the three distinct layers, the zest, the pith and the juice-infused flesh.' Each one has its on distinct flavor. Depending on the recipe, the lemon can add a citrusy aroma or sour taste. A lime, on the other hand, may 'match the sourness of the lemon, but its aromas are much more herbal.'
Her book teaches us how to improvise when cooking and identify alternative ingredients when at the last minute you run out of one. 'Flavorama' has been named one of the best cookbooks of the year by the New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, Science News and the Washington Post. If you are intrigued by how science impacts your cooking, I highly recommend purchasing this book. My thanks to Emily at Prentice Hall Publishers for her assistance and providing permission to include the following recipe.
Cilantro-Parsley-Tarragon Salsa Verde
In a powerful blender, combine:
1 bunch (about 90 g) cilantro (washed well and dried, large stems removed)
1 bunch (90 g) flat-leaf parsley (washed, dried, and large and medium stems removed)
1 small bunch (10 g) tarragon (leaves plucked from stems and stems discarded)
1 cup (240 ml) light and grassy extra-virgin olive oil
1 tablespoon (15 g) Dijon mustard
2 cured anchovies
1 tablespoon (12 g) capers
1 tablespoon (15 ml) lemon juice (from half a lemon)
1 peeled clove garlic
1 teaspoon (6 g) of sea salt and 1/2 teaspoon (1 g) ground black pepper
Blend at medium-high speed until combined, with all herb leaves broken down and emulsified in. It should be a thick-bodied, medium-fluid sauce; add more olive oil gradually to thin out the texture if necessary. Taste and add more salt, black pepper or lemon juice if necessary.
Store for 2 to 3 days in the fridge or up to 3 to 4 months frozen.
Makes about 2 cups.
Jay Kitterman is a culinary specialist at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management and Baking/Pastry, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: Pritzker proposes $2B in spending growth without new income or service taxes
author: Jerry Nowicki
description: Gov. JB Pritzker has proposed growing spending by about $2 billion without new income or service taxes in the upcoming fiscal year.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker has proposed a $55.2 billion budget, a 3% increase from the previous year.
Pritzker's plan would eliminate a health care program for low-income noncitizens aged 42-64 who are in the U.S. without legal permission.
The budget proposal includes revenue-generating measures such as adjusting tax rates on electronic gambling and offering temporary amnesty for delinquent tax payments.
Gov. JB Pritzker has proposed growing spending by about $2 billion without new income or service taxes in the upcoming fiscal year – though his administration acknowledged policy changes by the Trump administration could drastically alter the fiscal landscape.
Spending and revenues would each grow by about 3% under the proposal laid out Wednesday during the governor's annual budget address, with total general revenue fund spending growing to $55.2 billion.
The proposal is balanced, in part, because the governor's budgeting office expects to collect about $1.5 billion more in base tax revenue than it did when it issued its first fiscal year 2026 forecast in November.
That November forecast from the Governor's Office of Management and Budget had projected revenues to remain flat, driving a deficit of $3.2 billion. But it relied on a September economic forecast from the financial services company S&P Global. The governor's office says S&P has since revised its forecasts – but the numbers released Wednesday are ultimately likely to fluctuate amid the rapid pace of policy changes happening in Washington, D.C.
The governor's proposal would increase K-12 funding by $350 million and boost higher education funding by 3%. He'd keep funding flat for the Early Childhood Block Grant, however, which is a major driver of his effort to increase access to publicly supported preschool in Illinois.
Ultimately, lawmakers and the governor will have to come to an agreement on a spending plan by the end of May. But the governor's opening salvo could meet opposition from Democratic lawmakers in the General Assembly – especially members of the Illinois Legislative Latino Caucus – due what it doesn't fund.
The proposal would eliminate a health care program for low-income noncitizens aged 42-64 who are in the U.S. without legal permission. The Health Benefits for Immigrant Adults program, which was implemented in 2022, provided Medicaid-like and costs the state general revenue fund roughly $330 million, or less than 1 percent of the overall budget.
'As always, I stand ready to work with members of the General Assembly to deliberate and negotiate the final budget, but let's be clear, I will only sign a balance budget. If you come to the table, looking to spend more, I'm going to ask you where you want to cut,' Pritzker said in his address.
Advocates say that program is a key public health measure that drives down emergency room care costs and ultimately saves money. The governor's office says its decision not to propose funding reflects the state's fiscal reality.
The budget proposal maintains funding for a similar program serving immigrants aged 65 and older, passed by the legislature during the early months of the pandemic in 2020.
The governor's plan would raise another $469 million in revenue through other changes to law, including adjusting tax rates on electronic gambling and table games at casinos to generate $100 million in revenue. The plan also calls for pausing the transfer of $171 million in sales tax collected on motor fuel to the road fund, and raising $198 million by providing temporary amnesty for individuals making delinquent tax payments.

title: Richard Ringeisen, who led UIS as chancellor from 2001 to 2010, is dead
author: Steven Spearie
description: The University of Illinois Springfield admitted freshmen for the first time under Chancellor Richard Ringeisen.
content:
Richard Ringeisen was the University of Illinois Springfield's second chancellor.
Freshmen were admitted to UIS for the first time under Ringeisen.
Ringeisen oversaw the building of The Recreation and Athletic Center (TRAC) on campus.
Richard D. Ringeisen, who served as chancellor of the University of Illinois Springfield from 2001 to 2010 and oversaw the building of The Recreation and Athletic Center (TRAC) on campus, among other buildings, died in South Carolina on Feb. 18.
He was 80.
UIS Chancellor Janet Gooch made the announcement in a campus-wide letter shared with The State Journal-Register.
Ringeisen and his wife, Carolyn, retired to Clemson, S.C., in 2010. He was a mathematics professor and department head at Clemson University for 14 years.
During Ringeisen's tenure, UIS transitioned from the National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics (NAIA) to NCAA Division II.
An Indiana native, Ringeisen was vice chancellor for academic affairs at East Carolina University in Greenville, N.C., when he was chosen to succeed Naomi Lynn, when she retired in 2001.
Lynn was the university's first chancellor and last president. Founded in 1970 as Sangamon State University, it became part of the University of Illinois system in 1995.
Just months into Ringeisen's tenure, UIS admitted freshmen for the first time in the "Capital Scholars" honors program. It began admitting freshmen under the general education curriculum in 2006.
Before that, the university was only open to "upper division" students.
Ringeisen oversaw the construction of Founders Hall, University Hall, the quad and the university's colonnade.
Under Ringeisen, enrollment increased by more than 16 percent and topped 5,000 for the first time in 2010.
In addition to raising the profile of athletics, Ringeisen raised the profile of the fine arts, adding music and theatre programs.
Gooch said Ringeisen strengthened the school's academic programs, grew its faculty and expanded online education, "initiatives that continue to define UIS today."
"He cared about the students, faculty and staff who make this university special, and his impact will not be forgotten," Gooch said in the letter.
Ringeisen was succeeded by Susan Koch.
Funeral arrangements for Ringeisen are pending.

title: Who can make state? Here are the Springfield area's best swimmers and divers at sectionals
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Springfield High, Chatham Glenwood and Jacksonville will usher the area's best swimming and diving athletes at sectionals this weekend
content:
One swimmer and one diver qualified for the Illinois High School Association boys state swimming and diving finals in the 2024 season.
The area's best will attempt to advance even more this season on Saturday. The majority of the area schools will travel to the Chuck Fruit Aquatic Center at the Edwardsville Sectional. Taylorville will be the main representative at the Urbana Sectional.
To qualify for state, a swimmer must win the event or beat the state qualifying time. Divers must win the event or be among the top 32 sectional scores to advance.
Here are the top swimmers and divers to watch at this season's sectionals in alphabetical order:
Jack Borgman, Jacksonville
The senior swam his best times this season in the 50 and 100 freestyles at the Central State Eight Conference meet at Eisenhower Pool. Borgman won the 100 free in 50.84 seconds and placed second in the 50 free in 22.97. He finished sixth in the 50 free (22.77) and seventh in the 100 butterfly (58.84) at the Edwardsville Sectional last season.
Riley Herr, Springfield High
The junior is one of the main cogs on the team, including swimming the breaststroke on the 200 medley relay that SHS is eyeing to qualify for state. The relay includes sophomores Kishan Ugrappa, James Maeda and Oliver Havey.
Herr won the 200 IM (2:07.52) and took second in the 100 breaststroke (1:02.80) at the CS8 meet. He also competes in the 500 freestyle. He was sixth in both the IM (2:08.29) and breaststroke (1:03.32) at last season's Champaign Centennial Sectional.
Andrew Kotner, Springfield High
With a score of 396.05, the junior won the 1-meter diving competition at Eisenhower Pool. He also took first place at the 11-dive (363.05) Swim of Hope Invite in Edwardsville on Jan. 25 and won the six-dive event at City. Kotner finished in third place with 347.85 points at last season's Centennial Sectional.
James Maeda, Springfield High
The sophomore grabbed a fifth-place finish in the 200 IM (2:08.17) at the 2024 sectional in Champaign. Maeda finished second in both the IM (2:10.69) and 100 butterfly (57.51) at the CS8 meet and was a winner in the butterfly at City.
Jackson Vinzant, Chatham Glenwood
The senior has proven to be steady when he knocked off four seconds of his seeded time to win the 200 freestyle (1:50.81) at the CS8 meet. He was a double-winner after also winning the 100 backstroke (58.87). Vinzant swam for the Titans as a sophomore but did not swim high school his junior season.
Colin Wilson, Jacksonville
The senior touched in second place in the 100 breaststroke (1:01.30) and was sixth in the 100 freestyle (51.07) at last season's Edwardsville Sectional. The qualifying time for the breaststroke was 59.22. Wilson took third in the 100 free (51.25) and breaststroke (1:03.47) at conference.
Abdu Zeino, Chatham Glenwood
The senior sprint swimmer won the 50 free (22.91) and placed second in the 100 free (50.84) at the conference meet. He anchored the winning 200 freestyle relay (1:32.25) that included sophomore Kareem Zeino, Vinzant and senior Will Patzia. In addition, he swims a leg in the 400 freestyle relay. This will be his first sectional meet.
Kareem Zeino, Chatham Glenwood
The sophomore picked up two wins at the CS8 meet, capturing the 100 butterfly (56.22) and 100 breaststroke (1:02.39). Zeino won the butterfly at the Swim of Hope Invite. He swam the anchor leg and joined Abdu Zeino, senior David Helm and Vinzant in taking the 400 freestyle relay at conference, which Glenwood won with 413 points.

title: Weather in central Illinois to take a major turn. Here's what to know
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Central Illinois may get a taste of spring next week, following a bitter cold snap that changed its tune.
content:
Central Illinois may get a taste of spring next week, following a bitter cold snap that changed its tune.
Temperatures Friday are warming and will see a high near 28 in Springfield. The weather will get warmer through the weekend and by Monday, a high near 57 is predicted, according to the National Weather Service.
The past week has seen temperatures that are around 15 to 25 degrees below normal, said Alex Erwin, a meteorologist with the NWS.
The warmest period in the warmup will be Monday through Wednesday, with highs in the mid to upper 50s. That would be around 10 to 15 degrees above normal, but not quite approaching record levels.
River flooding is not much of a concern in the Springfield area.
Weather will cool again, possibly see rain
No rain is expected through Tuesday, but a cold front moving through on Wednesday will also bring a 40 or 50% chance of rain. No severe thunderstorms are expected.
The temperature will dip from the mid-50s – likely back into the 40s on Thursday.
'Highs in the mid-40s is actually pretty close to normal for this time of year,' Ewin said. 'While we cool down behind that front, it's not going to be any kind of bitter cold like we were dealing with.'

title: City of Springfield requests restraining order against two closed massage establishments
author: Claire Grant
description: Two massage establishments previously closed in are having further action taken by the city to keep the doors locked.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Two Springfield massage parlors, Illinois Relax Spa and Cozy Cabin Spa, are facing further legal action from the city for operating without licenses.
The city is seeking an emergency temporary restraining order to prohibit occupancy and use of the properties.
These businesses were among 11 massage establishments shut down in Springfield for failing to obtain the required massage establishment licenses.
Two massage establishments previously closed in Springfield are having further action taken by the city to keep the doors locked.
Illinois Relax Spa and Cozy Cabin Spa on Sangamon Avenue, two of the 11 spas previously shut down by the city for failing to pass inspections for a massage establishment license, were found by the city to be operating without a license.
City of Springfield senior assistant to corporation counsel Michael Hampleman confirmed the city has requested an emergency temporary restraining order through the Sangamon County Circuit Court. The order would prohibit occupancy inside the location and any use of the space.
A hearing on the plenary restraining order to Illinois circuit courts is set for Feb. 28.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Cozy Cabin and Illinois Relax have been under scrutiny alongside other spas like Q2 Asian Massage following a slew of closures on Jan. 31. City attorney Greg Moredock said on Feb. 17 the city was aware of the situation at Q2 and was keeping a watchful eye at the certain establishments.
'On the civil side we can't get an injunction over the weekend,' Moredock said Feb. 17. 'We are keeping an eye on that location and all the locations we have placards at.'
The businesses were closed due to a new ordinance requiring licenses to operate a massage location in the city. The new licensing process comes from community concerns about a rise in human trafficking and prostitution in the city of younger women from Asia being brought to the parlors. The regulation passed the city council last May and by June, inspections began being conducted.
What were the 11 establishments closed by the city?
