title: Man found unresponsive in Sangamon County Jail cell who later died is identified
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Sangamon County Coroner said earlier that Lapping died of 'natural causes.'
content:
Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon has identified the Sangamon County Jail inmate who was found unresponsive in his cell and later died at HSHS St. John's Hospital.
Jeffrey T. Lapping, 55, had been admitted to the jail on Feb. 14.
Lapping was alone in his cell, according to Allmon, and was discovered unresponsive right around 8:30 a.m.
Medical assistance was requested, and correctional staff began life saving measures by initiating CPR and utilizing an automated external defibrillator, or AED, until medical personnel arrived.
Lapping was pronounced dead by St. John's staff right around 9 a.m.
Allmon said in a news release that findings suggest that the man died from "natural causes." An autopsy performed Tuesday showed "no evidence of injury or trauma," he added.
Preliminary findings from the autopsy are officially 'pending toxicology studies," Allmon added.
Lapping had earlier been arrested for possession of drug paraphernalia and violation of an order of protection.

title: Tiburzi uses all her weaponry to lift Carlinville past Hillsboro for girls regional title
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Carlinville senior Isabella Tiburzi can do just about anything on a basketball court, and on Thursday night, the Cavaliers needed it all to beat Hillsboro for a regional title.
content:
CARLINVILLE — Few elite basketball players have the versatility, skill and unselfishness to do anything a team needs to win.
Carlinville senior Isabella Tiburzi has the whole package.
The Cavaliers' 5-foot-10 Tiburzi is listed as a guard/center combo. Coach Darrin DeNeve could, if brevity wasn't his thing, list all five positions next to Tiburzi's name.
Tiburzi, who has surpassed 1,000 points, 1,000 rebounds and 500 assists in her Carlinville career isn't done yet, nor are the rest of her Cavaliers teammates after Tiburzi led Carlinville's second-half turnaround to beat Hillsboro 45-40 on the Cavs' home floor to win the Class 2A Carlinville Regional championship on Thursday. It is the first regional title for Carlinville since 2022.
Tiburzi set a lot of individual goals for herself throughout her career and hoped that they would pay off with team success. She's ready for her final postseason.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
'I feel like that's what I've worked for my whole life,' Tiburzi said. 'Mr. DeNeve talked to me going into sophomore year: we had just lost our biggest player (Jill Stayton) and he (said), 'We're going to have to move the ball' and I said I'd much rather have more assists than points.'
No. 1 seed Carlinville (25-5) will face No. 2 Pleasant Plains (25-6) in the Waverly Sectional semifinals on Tuesday at 7:30 p.m. Plains beat Sacred Heart-Griffin 38-28 to win the Williamsville Regional title on Thursday. The Cavaliers hope to win their first sectional title since 2009, but Plains beat Carlinville 54-34 on Nov. 25 in Carlinville.
Hillsboro coach Bret Tuetken drew up a successful strategy in the first half, and his players hit shots necessary to take a 16-11 lead midway through the second quarter. The Hiltoppers' five-out offense kept the Cavaliers' defenders further away from the rim and allowed Hillsboro (20-11) eight offensive rebounds while Carlinville mostly stuck to a 2-3 defensive zone.
That changed in the second half. DeNeve watched his team give up 13 offensive boards the week prior — as was also the case on Thursday — in a 37-34 loss to Gillespie that kept the Cavaliers from winning the South Central Conference title. Ella Greenwood, who hit three 3-pointers in the first half for nine points, didn't get off another 3-point attempt in the entire second half, thanks to DeNeve's box-and-one defense on her.
'Sometimes that stuff is not about taking away one of their shooters or one of their players, it's sort of taking away their rhythm a little bit,' DeNeve said of the strategic change before adding about being better on the defensive glass, 'that may, honestly, have been the biggest difference in the whole (game).'
Tuetken was quick to credit the Carlinville players and coaching staff for the right strategy.
'They did a better job on the defensive boards in the second half ... and we weren't knocking shots down as well in the second half,' Tuetken said. 'They went to that box-and-one. We have other shots that can make the shots from the perimeter, we just didn't in the second half tonight and they were able to cut our lead down, get ahead and we were getting frustrated (because) we couldn't get the ball to Ella.'
And Tiburzi, who was a facilitator, stubborn defender and rebounder in the first half, added the additional load of scoring in the second half and scored 12 of her game-high 16 points over the final 16 minutes to give the Cavaliers a lift. Tiburzi finished with a 16-point, 16-rebound double-double, which included five offensive boards.
Hannah Gibson added 11 points — eight in the second half — for the Cavs while Kaitlyn Reels scored all seven of her points in the third and fourth periods.
'I think our energy changed (in the second half),' Reels said. 'We knew that we had to come out of the locker room with a lot of energy. Everyone had big rebounds, everyone contributed in some sort of way for us to create energy.'
Reels gave Carlinville its first multi-possession lead when she took a pass, curled around and hit a 3-pointer with 1 minute, 14 seconds left in the third. Hillsboro scored four straight points in the final minute to pull back even before Tiburzi knocked down a 3 from Reels just prior to time expiring.
'We knew we were ready for the second half,' Tiburzi said. 'I kind of felt that change in momentum when I hit that 3 at the end of the quarter — this is our time now. We weren't losing our final game on this court. We've been saying that all week and we proved that. We came out that fourth quarter really ready to go.'
Carlinville led the rest of the way, but that doesn't mean Hillsboro didn't make it interesting.
Tiburzi went to the free-throw line when she was fouled on a putback attempt, made both shots and gave Carlinville what seemed to be a safe eight-point, 41-33, lead with just 1:39 remaining. But, Hillsboro's Delaney Adams (five points), hit a 3, and Kearstynn Davis (10 points) made a layup to get within 42-38 and with 13 seconds left, Amya Greenwood made another layup to get back within 43-40. With 9.4 seconds left, Tiburzi sealed the victory by sinking both of her free throws.
'I thought we were real patient in the first half,' Tuetken said. 'I think we also ran out of gas a little bit to run down rebounds in the second half because when you're in five-out, you've got farther you have to go, we're playing really hard on defense and we just couldn't run those rebounds down and (Carlinville) did a better job of boxing us out, too.'

title: Pleasant Plains reaches Sweet 16 with win over Carlinville, plus other sectional results
author: Bill Welt
description: Pleasant Plains is the only girls basketball team from the Springfield area to reach the Sweet 16
content:
WAVERLY — Bailey Leach provided the spark before her younger sister, Jada, whipped up more breathing room from long distance.
Jada rained in four 3s — including three in the second period — for a team-high 14 points in a 52-37 win over Carlinville on Tuesday.
The Cardinals (26-6) advance to the Class 2A Waverly Sectional final against Camp Point Central/Augusta Southeastern (29-3) on Thursday at 6:30 p.m.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Jada said her teammates drew defenders away to set up the open 3.
'Whenever I see one that goes in, it gives me a lot of confidence; it gets me going,' the sophomore guard said.
Bailey, a junior, scored six of her 13 points in the first quarter and Plains led by as much as 33-12 early in the third period.
Anna Weber contributed 12 points and seven rebounds, while Grace Sabatka had seven points and nine rebounds. Madison Burke chipped in six points and seven rebounds.
Carlinville senior guard Isabella Tiburzi found her groove in the third and the Cavaliers pared the deficit to 10 points early in the fourth.
Tiburzi led Carlinville (25-6) with a game-high 17 points. Junior teammate Kaitlyn Reels had six points.
'We just got ourselves in too big of a hole,' Carlinville coach Darrin DeNeve said. 'They hit some shots and I thought we rushed ours — a lot of that is due to their terrific defense. You've got to give them credit for that. We just couldn't get any offense going early and then we had to play catch up the rest of the way.'
Tiburzi, who will play at Lincoln Land Community College, departs with more than 1,300 points, 1,000 rebounds and 500 assists in her career. DeNeve said Tiburzi and the rest of that senior class — including starters Jordyn Loveless, Braley Wiser and Hannah Gibson — left their marks all over the record book.
'They're a special group, they've played so much,' DeNeve said. 'It's going to be really odd not having them around.'
CAMP POINT CENTRAL/SOUTHEASTERN 58, STAUNTON 22: Senior guards Lauren Miller and Karly Peters generated all the offense for a 22-6 advantage by the end of the first quarter.
The Panthers later limited Staunton to just three field goals in the second half to trigger the running clock. Miller led CSE with 22 points, while Peters had 18.
Staunton senior teammates Ele Feldmann and Lilly Bandy had six points apiece. The Bulldogs (27-6) tied last season's school record for most wins in season in addition to a third straight regional title.
Class 1A
ABINGDON-AVON 61, HAVANA 53: Junior Kaydi Miller led the Ducks with 18 points, while senior Josie Hughes contributed 16 in the loss.
Freshman Ava Kramer added 11 and Havana (22-11) exits after winning its second regional title in the last three years.

title: Hatchett shoulders Lanphier load while Appenzeller, Neumann carry Glenwood in regional semis
author: Ryan Mahan
description: On Wednesday, Lanphier's Shaunassey Hatchett Jr. scored 24 points to lead the Lions past SHG. In the second game, Glenwood topped Springfield High.
content:
Lanphier senior Shaunassey Hatchett Jr. is tired of watching the boys basketball postseason after his Lions have been eliminated in regional play.
With 24 points and 13 rebounds, Hatchett put the No. 2 Lions on his back and to a 59-41 win over No. 6 Sacred Heart-Griffin at Lober-Nika Gymnasium on Wednesday in the Class 3A Lanphier Regional semifinals.
He really wanted to get past Sacred Heart-Griffin, the team which has ended the Lions' season in two of Hatchett's first three seasons: last year, SHG beat Lanphier 53-48 in the regional championship game; in 2022, SHG again won a regional title at Lanphier's expense with a 63-57 victory. Hatchett's Lions lost to Southeast in the 2023 regional semifinals.
'I'm determined to go to state. I really want to win something,' Hatchett said. 'I've been here for so long and we haven't made it past regionals. I just feel like we need to take it a step farther.'
Lanphier will face No. 3 Chatham Glenwood in the regional title game on Friday at 7 p.m. after the Titans' turned up the offensive aggressiveness in the second half to topple Springfield High 44-36 in the second game Wednesday.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Lanphier coach Blake Turner knows he can put the onus of the moment on Hatchett's broad shoulders.
'His determination, his drive, that's the reason he's the captain of this team, because he's who we want to follow: we want to follow that determination and that drive that he has,' Turner said. 'He plays with a different kind of energy, he wants to win by all costs and when you're a senior in this program, I expect the world from you.'
JaiQuan Holman added 13 points as Lanphier improved to 21-11. The Lions broke open a 36-29 game by outscoring the Cyclones (15-17) 23-12 in the fourth quarter.
The Lions had 18 offensive rebounds, 40 total boards and outscored SHG 19-7 on second-chance points.
Part of that advantage on the glass came due to an unfortunate twist when SHG junior Zion Lee seemed to injure his knee in the layup line in pre-game warmups. While he went up for a layup, someone affiliated with Lanphier stopped underneath the basket to shake the hands of several Lanphier assistant coaches. Lee came down and got entangled with the Lanphier fan.
Without Lee, the Cyclones were at a disadvantage.
'We were missing a big part of our team,' SHG coach Tim Allen said. 'He got hurt so we had guys playing different positions. I thought we battled pretty good for the first half.
'We felt like we had a chance, but we had to do things right and then we couldn't have a pre-game injury or we couldn't get in foul trouble.
'To be honest, I've never seen nothing like this. You're going into a game and you've got a coach or whoever on the floor. I'm glad (Lee) has another year, but if I were a senior, that would be crushing. Can you imagine going into the playoffs and you lose your whole postseason because an assistant coach from another team accidently is on the court?'
Glenwood pushes to beat SHS
Springfield High may have had the swagger when the No. 5 Senators were ahead 10-4 after the first quarter, but Glenwood had some tricks up its sleeve.
The Titans battled back to tie Springfield High 12-12 by halftime, then outscored the Senators 22-11 in the third quarter to take control for good.
Cameron Appenzeller led Glenwood with 13 points while Mason Neumann had 10 to power the Titans (20-9).
Glenwood's fortunes changed when they got aggressive offensively based on better ball movement.
'We practiced it for two days, we just didn't get to the high post,' Glenwood coach Todd Blakeman said. 'The guys didn't move. I think they were a little nervous at the beginning. Second half, we moved the ball much better. We were just waiting in the first half to get trapped.'
Blakeman said the Titans had to contend with a strong, quick and athletic Springfield High team that causes challenges.
'The first half, we came out slow and weren't really running our offense like we talked about,' Appenzeller said. 'We came out (in the second half) and executed like (Blakeman) wanted us to.'
Jonathan Helm, who had six points and six rebounds, was locked in a fierce, physical battle down low with Springfield High's Valor Komolafe. Though Komolafe had the height and weight advantage (6 foot 6 and 215 pounds compared to Helm's 6-4, 200-pound frame), Helm kept Komolafe busy, limited to three rebounds and in foul trouble before the Senators' senior fouled out with 2 minutes, 27 seconds left in a six-point game.
'I love being physical down there,' Helm said. 'I love the contact of it. Doing football and having older brothers, I'm kind of used to it.'
SHS coach Marques Warfield, who had two players foul out, including Noah Wade, thought his team didn't get the benefit of some calls.
"In the third quarter, some timely calls impacted some runs we were trying to make," Warfield said. "Those points in the game, I think deterred our guys, frustrated our guys a bit. There were fouls being called — I'm fine with fouls being called — but on the flip side, the same types of plays on the other end have to be called."

title: Camp Point Central's freshman, defense weather Pleasant Plains girls hoops in OT sectional win
author: Bill Welt
description: Pleasant Plains' Bailey Leach drained a game-tying 3 before Camp Point Central rallied for OT girls basketball sectional final win on Thursday
content:
WAVERLY — Pleasant Plains' Bailey Leach drilled a game-tying 3 in the final seconds of regulation.
But Camp Point Central/Augusta Southeastern freshman Lexi Niekamp stayed hot and the Panthers prevailed 51-44 in overtime in the Class 2A Waverly Sectional final on Thursday.
Boys hoops roundup: Pearse's heroics send Taylorville to regional final, plus more area results
Niekamp triggered a 16-0 run from 3-point range beginning in the third quarter before hitting the go-ahead 3 in overtime. She scored all of her four 3s and 16 points after halftime. Senior teammate Lauren Miller led CSE (30-3) with 20 points. Karly Peters added 12 points.
CSE advances to the Vandalia Supersectional against last year's state runner-up, Nashville, on Monday at 6 p.m.
"She's a great 3-point shooter; she's a huge threat, so I just kept telling her, 'Let it fly,'" Miller said of Niekamp. "That's what they were giving us and man, she stepped up big. I don't think as a freshman she knows how big of a game this is, but I'm just glad she was able to knock those down. I'm really happy for her."
Niekamp said the entire team was telling her to shoot.
"If we ever get down, our mentality always is we're going to get back up and bring each other up," Niekamp said. "We're just going to push to be the best versions of ourselves every day."
'It doesn't feel real sometimes': Calvary's Josh Long begins to thrive again after family tragedy
Junior forward Anna Weber led Plains (26-7) with 17 points and 12 rebounds. Leach summoned two 3s and 13 points, while junior Grace Sabatka had three 3s and 11 points.
The Cardinals jumped to a 14-4 lead by the end of the first quarter and led by as much as 12 points following back-to-back 3s by Sabatka early in the third period.
Niekamp and a flurry of turnovers reversed the momentum in CSE's favor and the Panthers took a four-point lead with under two minutes left in regulation.
"We thought maybe we could wear them down," CSE coach Matt Long said of his team's full-court press. "They've got a pretty shallow bench and a couple smaller guards on there. We thought when they brought them in to give them (the starters) a break that we could maybe force them into turnovers, which we did."
One big family: Pleasant Plains' sisters act soars into Sangamon County tourney: What to know, schedule
Sabatka converted the putback for a one-point deficit with less than 30 seconds left before Leach knocked down her tying 3 off a Weber screen.
"I told them this is fun, you get four minutes of free basketball," Long said of going into OT. "They kind of came into the huddle, 'Oh gosh.' I'm like, 'No, this is what it's about. This builds character,' and it did. That extra four minutes made us better and the good thing is you noticed how we responded in overtime."
Plains coach TJ Fraase said his team can glean one positive — the entire lineup will be back next season.
"They've got to be willing to remember this, come in and work and improve on one or two things to make them better individually so that this team can be better," Fraase said.

title: Daylight saving time right around the corner. What you need to know
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Are you ready for daylight saving time to begin? The quirky time change feat is coming soon. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Daylight savings starts early in the morning of March 9.
Illinois lawmakers have tried to get rid of the practice for several years, including this year.
President Donald Trump said DST is 'inconvenient' and 'very costly' before he was re-elected.
Spring forward, fall back.
In other words, most Americans will lose an hour of sleep on the second Sunday of March, thanks to daylight saving time.
Here are a few reminders about the quirky time change.
When is daylight saving?
Daylight saving time begins March 9.
What time does it happen?
Clocks will need to spring forward at 2 a.m.
When does daylight saving end?
The daylight-saving measure ends on the first Sunday of November, which falls on Nov. 2.
Hasn't Illinois tried to do away with DST?
Under the Uniform Time Act, States may choose to exempt themselves from observing Daylight Saving Time, but states do not have the authority to choose to be on permanent DST, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation that oversees the Nation's time zones.
Illinois lawmakers have tried to get rid of daylight saving for several years, with the most recent effort happening this year. State Rep. Brad Halbrook, R-Shelbyville, filed such a bill in early February that has been referred to the Rules Committee.
'The rationale for switching clocks twice per year to aid in the war effort was laudable over 100 years ago, but modern and scientific research now clearly favors the institution of Daylight Saving Time year round, eliminating the stress and negative health effects caused by changing clocks,' reads a segment of the bill's text.
Hasn't Trump talked about DST?
Before taking office, President Donald Trump said in December that he aims to put an end to daylight saving time.
"The Republican Party will use its best efforts to eliminate Daylight Saving Time, which has a small but strong constituency, but shouldn't!" Trump wrote in a Dec. 13 Truth Social post. "Daylight Saving Time is inconvenient, and very costly to our Nation."
In 2022, the U.S. Senate unanimously approved the Sunshine Protection Act that would make daylight saving time permanent, however the U.S. House of Representatives did not pass it, and former President Joe Biden did not sign it.
Why do we have daylight saving?
Benjamin Franklin's 'An Economical Project,' written in 1784, is the earliest known proposal to save daylight, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac.
But the idea did not gain support until after World War I when people recognized a need to conserve coal that was used for heating homes, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac. Germany was the first country to adopt the measure, and the U.S. was among those that followed in 1918 when Congress passed the Standard Time Act that established time zones.
Does every U.S. state have DST?
Hawaii and most of Arizona do not observe daylight saving time.
Because of its desert climate, Arizona doesn't follow daylight saving time (with the exception of the Navajo Nation), according to USA Today.
For Hawaii, the state is close to the equator and there is not a lot of variance between hours of daylight during the year.
Additionally, the following do not participate:
American Somoa
Guam
Northern Mariana Islands
Puerto Rico
U.S. Virgin Islands

title: Popular Springfield-area farmers market coming back this summer following closure
author: Claire Grant
description: After announced a summer farmers market won't be returning in 2025, a generous donation now has organizers shifting gears.
content:
AI-assisted summary
The Rochester Public Library's farmers market, which was shut down due to budget cuts, will reopen this summer thanks to a generous sponsorship.
Cattle farmer and former market vendor Noah Gregurich donated $1,500 to cover the wages of two library employees who work the event.
While the summer market has been saved, the library's fall festival remains canceled due to ongoing budget constraints.
A popular farmers market that said goodbye last year to the Rochester community is making a surprise return this summer season.
On Nov. 22, 2024, Rochester's Public Library announced significant budget cuts were coming to the library starting in January 2025.
The library announced the first program to be cut was going to be the farmer's market.
In 2024, the market featured 27 vendors selling anything from fresh produce to crafted goods. More than 2,000 people visited the market last year, according to the library.
'We want to extend our deepest gratitude to our vendors, attendees, patrons, and community members,' The social media post announcing the closure said. 'Whether you were a newcomer last year or have been part of our journey since the beginning, your participation and support have been the cornerstone of our Farmers Market.'
Following the referendum, farmers market coordinator Kendall Tracey says the library has made the choice to cut hours of operation, limit the amount of supplies for the library as well as cut the fall festival.
'The library has been struggling for a very long time, with no budget increase in 20 years,' Tracey said. 'We were attempting to make the most with what we've had for our communities and were going for referendums for building expansion and operation fund increases.'
After the closure, cattle farmer and small business owner Noah Gregurich reached out to the Rochester Public Library, seeing what he could do.
After making some calls, library staff announced on Feb. 24 the market would go on after a sponsorship for $1,500 from Gregurich Beef.
The funding would go into payment for the two library employees working the event over the course of the summer – funds from vendor spots would go toward marketing.
'Generally, we have a budget for $1,000 and now it's up to $2,000. It's a wash, the money comes in and also goes out,' Rochester Public Library director Janet McAllister said. 'The only thing we were short on is we did not have the funds to pay two people on a Sunday when the library is closed … We are one of the only libraries that does this kind of thing. Libraries might be at a market but running is not a typical library program.'
Gregurich Beef Company was started in 2015 by Gregurich and his wife Brooke to raise cattle in the Sangamon and Christian counties on a fourth-generation farm.
He was previously one of the vendors at the market and had been in conversation with the library since late November about plans to get the event running again.
The market, now reinvigorated, will take place every second and fourth Sunday from June through September, with usual start times of noon to 3 p.m. The market is held at One Community Drive in Rochester, right next to the Rochester Library.

title: Oscars 2025: How to watch the show and our picks and predictions
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The 2025 Academy Awards are Sunday night on ABC. Here is how to watch the Oscars and our predictions for all 23 categories.
content:
The 97th annual Academy Awards are here. The 2025 Oscars are tonight, with he Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Sciences awarding gold statuettes in 23 categories to mark the best in film for 2024.
Here is what you need to know about the 2025 Oscars show and our predictions for every award in the 97th annual Academy Awards:
What time are the 2025 Oscars?
The 97th Oscars are set for 6 p.m. CT Sunday, March 2, at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles. The show will air from 6-9 p.m. The red carpet show is one hour before.
Who is hosting the Oscars?
Emmy-winning talk show host Conan O'Brien is host of the 2025 Oscars. He takes over for Jimmy Kimmel, who hosted the show the last year.
What channel are the Oscars on tonight?
The Oscars for the 97th Academy Awards will air live on ABC starting at 6 p.m.
How can I stream the Oscars online?
You can stream the awards ceremony live on ABC.com, the ABC app, Hulu, YouTubeTV, AT&T TV and FuboTV (free trial).
What movies are nominated for Oscars in 2025?
This year's Oscar nominees feature an array of films from Best Picture favorite " Anora," to religious thriller ' Conclave,' historical drama ' The Brutalist ' to fantasy musical 'Wicked' and body horror movie ' The Substance.' Netflix musical thriller ' Emilia Pérez ' leads the pack with 13 nominations.
2025 Oscar predictions
There is still some intrigue for the top award of the night, Best Picture. At least three films could win, with Anora, Conclave and The Brutalist all among films to win major precursors. Here are our predictions in each category.
Picture: "Anora"
Actor: Adrien Brody, "The Brutalist"
Actress: Demi Moore, "The Substance"

Adapted screenplay: "Conclave"

Sound: "Dune: Part Two"
Visual effects: "Dune: Part Two"
Editing: "Conclave"
Makeup and hairstyling: "The Substance"
Score: "The Brutalist"

Animated picture: "Flow"
Animated short: "Yuck!"

International feature film: "I'm Still Here"

title: What to know about each boys basketball regional champion from the Springfield area
author: Bill Welt
description: Here are the seven boys basketball teams from the Springfield area sailing into sectionals
content:
A total of seven teams from the Springfield area advanced to the IHSA boys basketball sectional semifinals after Friday's regional final games.
At least one team from the area is guaranteed to reach the Class 2A supersectionals hosted by the Bank of Springfield Center on Monday, March 10 at 6 p.m.
Williamsville, Auburn, Pleasant Plains and Staunton will each appear in the Greenville Sectional beginning Tuesday and Wednesday. Lincoln and Chatham Glenwood, meanwhile, remain the last teams in the Class 3A bracket hailing from the Central State Eight Conference.
Here's what to know about each regional champion from the Springfield area:
Class 3A
Lincoln
Lincoln always seems to know what adjustments to make at the break. The top-seeded Railsplitters forged an 11-0 run in the third quarter en route to a 38-23 win over Taylorville for its first regional title since the 2020 playoffs (later canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic).
It was no mere anomaly. Lincoln (23-10) similarly staged its 'third-quarter push' in wins over Chatham Glenwood and Lanphier as well. The Railers have now won 13 of their last 15 games going into the Decatur Eisenhower Sectional semifinals against No. 2 Mount Zion (24-9) on Wednesday at 7 p.m.
It all hinges on their trademark 1-2-2 zone defense. Lincoln has limited opponents to just 32.1 ppg. in its last 15 games. Junior guard Brody Tungate leads the point on defense, while 6-5 senior forwards Drew Hayes and Frank Sanders make life difficult inside.
Both Hayes and Sanders — along with leading-scorer Karson Komnick with 13.4 points per game — missed the first few weeks of the season due to injuries before coming back to galvanize the Railers down the stretch.
Chatham Glenwood
The Titans also took advantage of their size in a 43-39 regional final win over host Lanphier. Six-foot-five senior guard Cam Appenzeller continues to show why he's The State Journal-Register's reigning Male Athlete of the Year. The prized pitching prospect ranks not only among the area's top scorers (13.7 ppg.) but also rebounders (6.1 rpg.).
Senior forwards Jonathan Helm (12.8 ppg., 7.3 rpg.) and Mason Neumann (8.2 ppg., 4.8 rpg.) provide even more length. Neumann stepped up big while Appenzeller was tethered to the bench due to foul trouble, finishing with 12 points against the Lions. Junior guard Jack Kurmann also stands at 6-5 and is among the top 3-point shooters (35.8%) in the area to further compensate for the loss of injured senior guard Mason Marshall.
Glenwood (21-9) meets No. 4 Champaign Central (17-12) in the Decatur Eisenhower Sectional semifinals on Tuesday at 7 p.m. The Maroons upset CS8 champion Decatur MacArthur 60-54 in their regional final.
Class 2A
Auburn
The top-seeded Trojans survived a proverbial trap game and Nolan Tabor's torrent of 3s with a 56-43 win over host Greenville for their second straight regional title. Tabor churned out six 3s for a game-high 20 points. Auburn (29-4) still prevailed with a balanced scoring effort, led by Jacob Barth (14 points), Clayton Kessler (13 points) and Cooper Carter (10 points).
It means the Trojans know the terrain better than the rest ahead of the sectional semifinals where they return to Greenville to meet No. 3 Pleasant Plains (22-10) on Tuesday at 7 p.m. The Cardinals won the previous meeting 51-43.
Pleasant Plains
Plains has had an excellent 2025, said head coach Kyle Weber. The Cardinals have indeed won 12 of their last 13 games since settling for fourth place in the Sangamon County Tournament in January and they recently nabbed their third straight regional title with a 48-41 win over Warsaw/Hamilton West Hancock.
Plains may be undersized than most, but its plethora of guards have shown over multiple games they can hold their own against anyone, including against Warsaw's 6-foot-9 junior forward, Cooper Knowles, or even Auburn's lengthy forwards, Clayton Kessler and Ryan Lash.
'We played a really tough schedule to get us ready for games like that,' Weber said, referring to the physical challenge presented by Warsaw. 'Our record wasn't as pretty as some of the other teams, but I think it prepared us for games like this.'
Williamsville
Quincy Notre Dame's 66-44 regional semifinal win over Petersburg-PORTA/A-C Central certainly presented an ominous specter of a possible upset in the Pittsfield Regional final. It all came to naught after senior guard Brayden Saling doled out all his 21 points in the second half for a 55-33 win over QND in the team's quest to return to the state finals after taking fourth place last season.
It's what makes the Bullets (29-3) so dangerous. Not only Saling, the SJ-R's reigning Small School Boys Basketball Player of the Year, but other prolific guards such as seniors Blake Shoufler and Carson Doran also lurk with big-game potential. Each averages double figures: Shoufler (14.1 ppg.), Doran (13.8) and Saling (12.2 ppg.).
Senior forward Reid Bodine has also surfaced with significant scoring production lately. He scored seven of his eight points in the first half for an 19-14 halftime lead against QND after logging 17 points and seven rebounds in a 52-43 win over PORTA.
They meet Staunton (28-4) in the Greenville Sectional semifinals on Wednesday at 7 p.m. to set up a showdown between the Sangamo and South Central conference champions.
Staunton
The Bulldogs won their first regional title since 2009 and third since winning the Class A state title in 1993 with a 50-32 win over Piasa Southwestern.
Staunton connected from long distance on its home floor. The Bulldogs totaled nine 3s in the 52-28 regional semifinal win over Roxana where sophomore standout Isiah Laux converted four from behind the arc. Staunton later summoned six 3s against Piasa — one apiece from Aaron Bodner, Ethan Sharp, Bryce Coalson and Zander Machota in the first quarter.
Class 1A
Mason City Illini Central
The Cougars champion a couple of prolific guards with more than 1,000 career points: senior David Bard (1,301) and junior Brody Folkes (1,020).
Folkes reached the milestone on his first bucket in a 46-37 regional final win over Mendon Unity and finished with 23 points for the program's first regional title since winning the state title in 2013.
Bard earlier set the school record for most points in a game with 41 in an 83-82 double overtime win over Lutheran. No. 3 Illini Central (17-16) meets No. 1 Peoria Christian in the Brimfield Sectional on Wednesday at 7 p.m.

title: Massachusetts authorities investigate 'suspicious' fires at Tesla charging stations
author: Taylor Ardrey
description: The fires comes amid other attacks against Tesla dealerships and car owners.
content:
Authorities in Littleton, Massachusetts, have launched an investigation into fires at a Tesla charging station that they deem "suspicious."
According to a news release, members of the local police and fire departments responded to the blaze at a shopping center on Monday around 1 p.m. The Littleton Electric Light & Water Department was also called to shut down the power.
Littleton is about 35 miles from Boston.
At the scene, officials discovered "several Tesla charging stations were engulfed in flames and heavy, dark smoke." Seven stations underwent fire-related damage.
No injuries were reported
Police said no one was injured as a result of the incident.
According to the news release, during their investigation, officials determined "that the fires appear to have been intentionally set."
They are urging the public to call the Arson Watch Reward Program Hotline (1800-682-9229), which offers up to $5,000 for tips that solve or prevent arson-related crimes.
The incident comes amid a growing trend of vandals targeting Tesla dealerships and drivers, seemingly due to Elon Musk's political ties to President Donald Trump.

title: Opening dates set for Cafe Moxo and the city's first conveyor belt sushi restaurant
author: Natalie Morris
description: Three big pieces of restaurant news in the Springfield area, including opening dates for a popular cafe and a new restaurant.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Cafe Moxo will reopen in a new location after a fire shut down their original location.
Izumi Rotary & Bar, Springfield's first conveyor belt sushi restaurant, opens next week.
Cousins Maine Lobster, a popular food truck, will be in Springfield twice in March.
Cafe Moxo opens Saturday in its new Montvale Junction home, just shy of nine months after a fire in the 400 block of East Adams Street shut down the downtown dining darling.
'We're staying true to who we are,' Mark Forinash, who co-owns Cafe Moxo with his wife Shawna, said of the move. 'We want to be the same restaurant that closed last June, opening March 8.
'At our core are the same hand-rolled noodles in our soup, scratch chicken pot pies, sandwiches and cookies.'
That said, the new address at 2661 Chatham Road (formerly home to Three Twigs & Co.) places Cafe Moxo in a very different neighborhood than its original home of 17 years at 411 E. Adams St.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Montvale Junction is a retail oasis surrounded by thick residential areas sitting alongside one of Springfield's main commuter arteries.
To provide the same quick service, Forinash has created a coffee bar and to-go pick up area for advance online orders with its own door and check out area to quickly serve on-the-go commuters. There's also curbside service for orders placed online at cafemoxo.com.
This new central location allows Cafe Moxo to offer in-house delivery service throughout Springfield for orders of $50 or more.
'Our goal is to provide the best service possible,' he said.
Hours are 6:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. daily. Services include dine in and al fresco seating, to go, curbside side pickup and in-house delivery service throughout Springfield. Phone: 217-788-8084.
More: 'Supporting the community that's supported us.' Cafe Moxo workers volunteer post Adams St. fire
The menu offers breakfast selections ranging from Cinnamon Toast Crunch French toast to avocado toast, breakfast burritos to Divine Swine – ham, bacon and sausage patty with egg on toasted sourdough. Lunch offerings include soups, sandwiches, salads and scratch pot pies. Bakery items feature scratch-made cookies, biscuits, bagels and croissants.
Forinash called the new address Cafe Moxo's 'national headquarters.' That said, he hasn't forgotten where the business came from.
'We have not forgotten the downtown. We haven't abandoned the downtown,' he said. 'We do fully anticipate opening another location downtown. We just need to get our feet underneath us here first.'
New sushi restaurant opening
Izumi Rotary & Bar – Springfield's first conveyor belt sushi restaurant – opens March 13 on Springfield's west side. And to encourage the uninitiated, free meals will be given to the first 30 patrons through the door.
The opening special – a $15 coupon for the first 30 customers – will be available for the first three days of business, March 13-15.
Owner Yong Wu, a former U.S. Marine who most recently worked as a sushi chef in Dallas, came to Springfield to be closer to family.
'I noticed there wasn't a conveyor belt concept,' Wu said. 'And I thought that was an experience I could bring to my new home.'
Dine-in customers have two automated ways to select their meal. Menu items can be ordered on a tablet located at each of the 42 tables with dishes delivered via robot. Meanwhile, a variety of other dishes parade by on the conveyor belt that snakes past every table. Color coded plates indicate price point (black plates $2.59, red/blue/orange plates $3.59). The cashier rings up the bill based on the tablet order and plate colors.
Menu selections include teriyaki and hibachi dishes with rice or stir-fried noodles. Appetizers range from crab rangoon and egg rolls to the more exotic like takoyaki (an octopus-filled dumpling.) Items tempting from the conveyor belt range from sushi rolls, sashimi, sushi nigiri, as well as a variety of desserts like creme brulee and cheesecakes.
A separate bar area specializes in martinis and margaritas.
Take-out service also is available. Orders can be placed in advance at izumirotary.com. Phone: 217-679-1317.
Izumi, Japanese for spring or fountain, occupies half of the new duplex at 3061 Wabash Ave. that recently rose from the parking lot in front of Gordon Food Service. Potbelly Sandwich Shop is slated to fill the other half of the duplex later this year.
Cousins Maine Lobster
A recent press release from Cousins Maine Lobster announced the Shark Tank-famed mobile eatery was launching its first food truck with a Springfield-Peoria route.
But the rolling eatery's actual itinerary indicates the business will be appearing in the Capital City about as frequently as the perfect summer day its signature sandwiches – lobster rolls – conjure up.
The black food truck adorned with a giant red crustacean is scheduled to be in Springfield twice in March, March 8 in the Scheels' parking lot (3801 S. MacArthur Blvd.) from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. and March 15 in downtown Springfield (1 S. Old State Capitol Plaza, starting at 11 a.m.) for the St. Patrick's Day festivities.
'We will not restrict our operations only in Springfield,' emailed Varun Salveru, operations manager for the Chicago-based franchise with the license for the Illinois market. 'We will be visiting all the cities and counties in central Illinois, making occasional visits to southern Illinois.'
The Chicago franchise's March itinerary for its fleet showed 8 visits scheduled for central Illinois communities, stretching from Peoria Heights to Springfield, Petersburg to Decatur.
Cousins posts a 30-day itinerary on its Facebook page of communities where their food trucks will be visiting.
The menu features two versions of lobster rolls: Maine (with the lobster served chilled with mayo on a New England roll) and Connecticut (with the lobster served warm with butter and lemon on a New England roll). Both cost $25 each.
Fresh lobster also is featured in a lobster bisque soup ($8/cup, $11/bowl), blended with macaroni and cheese or topping tater tots and tucked in tacos or quesadillas. Other selections include New England Clam Chowder ($8/cup, $11/bowl) and shrimp tacos. Kids menu has grilled cheese or cheese quesadilla w/ tots ($11).
Take home options include a do-it-yourself lobster roll kit (1-pound for $120, 2-pounds for $230).
Company founders Sabin Lomac and Jim Tselikis had one food truck operating in California when they pitched their business in 2012 on the ABC's Shark Tank. Today, the Los Angeles-based company has more than 60 trucks operating across the country, as well as four brick and mortar stores.
Pizzeria closes
Sorrento's Pizzeria in Lincoln has closed after a half century of serving its signature pizza from the Logan County square.
But the pizzeria's departure might not be the last word on this family-owned business.
'It is with mixed emotions that I must tell you Sorrento's is closing,' owner Lisa Drew posted on the restaurant's social media. 'Whether this will be a permanent or temporary closing remains to be determined but I will be sure to keep you informed.'
Final day of operations, at least for now, was Feb. 28.
Drew said the building at 1614 Broadway St., as well as the Sorrento's Pizzeria name and recipes, remains on the market with the potential for someone else to reopen the business.
Drew's in-laws, Sicilian natives Giovanni and Anna Curcuru served Sorrento's first slice in 1969 from its original home on the north side of the Logan County square. Their son Serafino 'Sammy' Curcuru took over the business, running it until his death in 1998. Drew and her second husband, Jim Drew, currently own the business.

title: Illinois unveils winning design of state flag. See which design won
author: Claire Grant
description: There were nearly 400,000 votes over a five-week period. Take a look at what design won the Illinois state flag contest.
content:
Illinois residents have spoken and when it comes to the state flag, the message is clear: if it's not broke, don't fix it.
After a five-week voting period for a new state flag, residents determined to keep the state's current flag, Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias announced on March 6.
Of the nearly 385,000 votes that were received, more than 165,000, or 43 percent, were cast for the current state flag, which received more votes than the next five top designs combined.
'Some may call it an SOB – a seal on a bedsheet – and the vexillogical community may hate it, but people overwhelmingly prefer our current state flag,' Giannoulias said. 'Thank you to everyone who made their voice heard on the future of this important symbol of state pride.'
Moving forward, the Illinois Flag Commission will prepare a report detailing its findings and recommendations to the General Assembly by April 1. Lawmakers will then vote on whether to adopt a new flag, return to a previous iteration or keep the current one.
Why was there voting on a new state flag?
Senate Bill 1818, sponsored by State Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, and State Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, was signed into law by Gov. Pritzker in 2023, creating the commission to gauge public desire for a new flag.
The commission selected its top 10 finalists in December of 2024 from the 4,844 entries it received during the six-week submission period that closed in October.
Among some of the top 10 entries included a cutout silhouette of Abraham Lincoln and the state border, a corn-focused flag and a butterfly flag.
State flag history
The original flag, designed by Rockford native Lucy Derwent in 1915, featured the state seal in front of a white background. It has remained the same since with exception for the addition of the word "Illinois" placed below the seal in 1969.

title: Springfield restaurant raising prices on egg dishes to combat inflated costs
author: Claire Grant
description: 'We tried to absorb it for several months and we just got to the point we couldn't absorb it anymore.\
content:
Show Caption
Due to a nationwide egg shortage, businesses that rely heavily on eggs are facing difficult decisions.
The avian flu, which has killed millions of birds, is the main factor contributing to the rising cost of eggs.
While some businesses have had to raise prices, others are absorbing the increased costs, impacting their profit margins.
We're all feeling the impact of rising egg prices, businesses included.
Ritz's Lil Fryer at 2148 N. Grand Ave. is one of the locations that serves sunny side up eggs every day of the week starting at 6 a.m., using over 430 dozen cartons of eggs a week.
To offset the rising cost of eggs, the business has made the hard choice to raise the price of dishes with eggs in them.
Vicky Ritz has owned and run Ritz's Lil Fryer on the east side since opening in 1978.
Initially, her business tried to eat the cost for the first three months of raised prices until profit took a deep enough swing south.
'I had to increase the pricing onto my customers,' Ritz said. 'We tried to absorb it for several months and we just got to the point we couldn't absorb it anymore. My customers aren't happy about it. Do they understand it? Yes, but they're not happy when you have to raise it that much.'
The average price of a dozen eggs went up 237% or from $1.47 in January of 2021 to $4.95 in late January of this year, according to Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins. Avian influenza, or the bird flu is the main reason behind the rising egg prices.
The bird flu has killed or led to the killing of more than 58 million birds since 2022 in 47 different states and according to recent data from the Center for Disease Control, is causing outbreaks in dairy cows and several recent human cases in U.S. dairy and poultry workers.
Eating the costs
For Springfield residents, that could mean eating less eggs or choosing to cook meals not requiring the ingredient. Brunch spots, however, can't take the classic omelet off the menu.
For the Farmhouse Restaurant inside Harvest Market, their menu is spackled with one egg combos, omelets and breakfast platters. The cost of one egg served with bread of choice will set you back $3.50, a price that hasn't changed, despite the rising costs.
Assistant General Manager Christi Stieren says luckily being a part of the larger grocery store, Farmhouse has been able to eat the inflated cost at a deficit to keep prices affordable for patrons.
On average, the breakfast spot will use anywhere from 300 to 400 eggs per week and are feeling the full brunt effects of the price climb.
'We have really, really taken a hit with our gross profit margins because we haven't been able to change our prices to keep things affordable for our guests,' Stieren said. 'We have the luxury of being inside of a grocery store so if we have to take a hit it's not that horrible. I couldn't imagine being a small mom and pop owning your own brick and mortar with the prices.'
End in sight?
No one can say just when cases of the bird flu will track downward but tailing back to Rollins, the Department of Agriculture plans to make a $1 billion investment to lower the price of eggs in the country over the course of the next three-to-six months.
According to the editorial first reported by The Washington Post, half of the billion-dollar plan will go into biosecurity for poultry producers.
Four-hundred million will be used as financial relief to farmers who have had to cull their flocks in response to the bird flu outbreak and do not have the funding to repurchase birds. The final $100 million will be used in research of vaccines for chickens to curb further infection rates.
The Farms of Illinois and Bland Family Farms are a group of farmers in the central and downstate Illinois communities; the farmers group says their price remains almost half of what many are currently paying for eggs have seen demand surge to the point they cannot keep up.
"The restaurant industry is one we love to serve, and we deeply respect the dedication of those who keep it going," marketing manager for the Farms of Illinois Serena Basham said. "This moment underscores the importance of strong relationships between our local farmer alliance and local restaurants."
Ritz is looking forward to lowering prices but until then, every side of hashbrowns is served with 75 cents per egg served.
'We try to keep our prices lower so a family can come in and not, you know, spend a fortune to come in and eat,' Ritz said. 'If you want eggs, even chicken is starting to go up now. We'll have to adjust prices again. It's awful, we've never had to change it so much before.'

title: Illinois residents likely to see total lunar eclipse. Here's what you need to know
author: Tom Ackerman
description: If you stay up late enough this week, you will be able to see a total lunar eclipse – also known as a blood moon.
content:
A total lunar eclipse will be visible on the night of March 13 for most of the Americas, as well as parts of Europe and the United Kingdom, depending on weather.
There are zero to three lunar eclipses per year, though they may not all be viewable from the same place on Earth.
The weather in central Illinois is expected to be clear and pleasant for viewing.
If you stay up late enough this week, you will be able to see a total lunar eclipse – also known as a blood moon – that becomes visible about every two and a half years.
The weather is expected to be clear and pleasant for those who aim to see the event or photograph it.
Here's more about the total lunar eclipse and how to spot it.
What is a total lunar eclipse?
A total lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth is positioned exactly between the moon and sun. The moon passes through the Earth's shadow. As this happens, the moon will darken and take on a dark shade of orange and red.
In other words, the moon doesn't produce its own light. It shines because its surface reflects the sun's rays. A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth blocks the sun.
When is the eclipse?
The total eclipse begins at 1:26 a.m. central time on Friday morning. The event of totality lasts about an hour.
Here's the timeline for Illinoisans to view the eclipse, starting Thursday night, according to NASA:
10:57 p.m., Penumbral eclipse begins. The moon enters the Earth's penumbra, the outer part of the shadow. The moon begins to dim, but the effect is subtle.
12:09 a.m., Partial eclipse begins. The Moon begins to enter Earth's umbra and the partial eclipse begins. To the naked eye, as the moon moves in the umbra, it looks like a bite is being taken out of the lunar disk. The part of the moon inside the umbra appears very dark.
1:26 a.m., Totality begins. The entire moon is now in the Earth's umbra. The moon is tinted a coppery red.
2:31 a.m., Totality ends. As the moon exits Earth's umbra, the red color fades. It looks as if a bite is being taken out of the opposite side of the lunar disk from before.
3:47 a.m., Partial eclipse ends. The whole moon is in Earth's penumbra, but again, the dimming is subtle.
5 a.m., Penumbral eclipse ends. The eclipse is over.
How to view it?
The eclipse can be safely observed with the naked eye, but a better view can be achieved with binoculars or a telescope.
What is the weather forecast?
The spring like week will lead to a nice viewing experience for majority of the state—from as far north from Rockford down to Springfield.
How often does the total lunar eclipse happen?
There are zero to three lunar eclipses per year, according to NWS, though they may not all be viewable from the same place on Earth.

title: How helping customers on hard times earned this Springfield diner national recognition
author: Claire Grant
description: The chance to be featured on a national show meant giving the opportunity to showcase Springfield, something important to the owners of Lulu's Diner.
content:
A Springfield diner is going to be featured on a national show.
A film crew from America's Best Restaurants stopped in at Lulu's Diner to record and share some of the diner's famous dishes online.
'So far we think they're going to go for the French toast since everybody says we have the greatest French toast,' co-owner Klorida Skenderi said. 'And we have a very good gyro horseshoe. … Which is toast or pita at the bottom, the gyro meat with fries and cheese sauce and all of the toppings – just like they come on the sandwich.'
A gyro is a Greek specialty sandwich with minced beef and lamb, coated in tomato, onion and a yogurt sauce typically on pita bread.
America's Best Restaurants is a national marketing company that spotlights independent and locally owned restaurants all across the continental United States.
Operated by CEO Matt Plapp, America's Best Restaurants was tipped off about Lulu's diner from a regular of the diner who knew of the premiums the owners of the restaurant would give to some of their customers on hard times.
'You never really know since some people are going through very rough times,' Skenderi said. 'Some people have little kids involved and no one should ever go to bed hungry.'
Skenderi said a customer reached out to America's Best Restaurants after they received a free meal from the diner.
'They walk in, we give them a meal if they need it," Skenderi said.
The America's Best Restaurants marketing team works alongside restaurants who want to be featured on the company's social media platform and website.
So far, America's Best Restaurants has published 842 episodes since its inception. Previously, another Springfield eatery, Burger Bar, was featured in March of last year.
While filming around the diner, guests were encouraged to watch and participate with their orders as the camera crew rolled tapes.
Klorida Skenderi will be joined on the Lulu's episode by her husband, Landi. The couple reopened the diner in 2017 after purchasing it from the diner's first owner, Ali Saleh Hussein.
The couple transformed the menu from middle eastern inspired to an American with Greek flavor. Despite the changes, the business struggled out of the gate.
'The first year was very rough as a new business and we kept the name from the previous owner,' Klorida Skenderi said. 'Only the first year was the hardest one and then with the virus of course it hurt a lot; but as soon as we opened back up everyone gave us so much support. It helped us to survive technically.'
For Skenderi, the opportunity to show the city she loves is important to her. Ever since she had moved to the United States from Albania in 2009, Springfield has felt more like home than anywhere else – because of the people.
'I feel like in Springfield everyone is very friendly,' Skenderi said. 'I don't have any family here – it's just my husband and my son and it's very warm. It's like I come to work and it's very exciting. … I don't know if it's just me and my restaurant but that's how I feel.'
The episode will be available online on ABR's social media platforms – Tiktok, Facebook, Youtube and website at americasbestrestaurants.com to stream online.

title: Ben & Jerry's annual Free Cone Day returns in 2024: Here's when it is and what to know
author: Gabe Hauari
description: Ben & Jerry's announced Wednesday it is bringing back its annual Free Cone Day celebration. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Ben & Jerry's is bringing back its annual Free Cone Day celebration this spring and is asking fans to help them beat a lofty goal.
The company wants this year's Free Cone Day to be the "biggest and best yet with 1 million scoops served," it announced Wednesday.
This year's celebration will take place on Tuesday, April 16, the company said in a news release. Free Cone Day made its return last year after a four-year hiatus.
'It was nothing short of amazing to see our fans back in our shops in their full Free Cone Day glory,' said Dave Stever, Ben & Jerry's CEO, who dished out ice cream at Ben & Jerry's shops in Vermont last year. 'We gave out over 970,000 scoops across the globe, but we know together with our fans we can break 1 million scoops,' Stever said in the news release.
The company said its Free Cone Day tradition began in 1979 as a way to give back to the community and thank fans for their support.
Flavors may vary by location but fans are welcome to try all available flavors and are encouraged to get back in line as many times as they'd like, Ben & Jerry's said in the announcement.
https://www.benjerry.com/scoop-shops/free-cone-day.
Free Cone Day is BACK! 🍦 Join us April 16, 12-8pm for a free cup or cone of your favorite Ben & Jerry's flavor! No fine print, no catch, just a sweet celebration of our incredible fans (that's you). Learn more: https://t.co/btgkdnfiED pic.twitter.com/JBCnAEvjww
— Ben & Jerry's (@benandjerrys)
Dairy Queen's Free Cone Day also returns this spring
Ben & Jerry's isn't the only ice cream maker offering customers freebies this spring.
Back by popular demand, Dairy Queen announced last week it will once again offer a free ice cream cone in March.
But the offer is for one day only, the business said.
'Nothing says warmer weather is around the corner quite like Free Cone Day," DQ posted on X. "We're inviting fans everywhere to grab their friends and families and get their ‘Treat Szn' started with something sweet – on us!'
Free Cone Day will take place at participating restaurants nationwide March 19 − on the first day of spring.
Customers will receive one free small vanilla soft-serve cone.
If you are a DQ Rewards member, the business said, you will receive double points on any food purchase that day, too.
The treat is limited to one cone per person while supplies last, DQ said.

title: Pritzker's new $900M plan would demolish, rebuild state prison near Springfield
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: The governor's office projects construction costs will range between $805 and $935 million, but save the state $34 million annually long-term.
content:
Two state prisons, including the Logan Correctional Center in Lincoln, would be demolished and rebuilt under a new plan unveiled by Gov. JB Pritzker on Friday.
A multi-year project, the $900 million proposal would be part of the upcoming fiscal year capital budget if approved by lawmakers. Also being targeted in the plan would be the Stateville Correctional Center in suburban Chicago, another prison state officials say has suffered from years of divestment and deferred maintenance.
Whether Logan, located 30 miles north of Springfield and employing approximately 500 workers, will remain open in the interim is still unknown. A location for a new facility is also still being considered.
'These investments will allow staff to work in modern and safe facilities, ensure those who are incarcerated can safely serve out their sentences, and save taxpayers hundreds of millions in deferred maintenance costs from years of neglect,' Pritzker said in a statement.
Both union leadership and county officials swiftly voiced concerns with the plan.
Sen. Sally Turner, R-Beason; Rep. Bill Hauter, R-Morton; Logan County Board Chairman Emily Davenport and Lincoln Mayor Tracy Welch called the decision "devastating and infuriating."
"While we recognize that Logan Correctional is in need of repairs, it is only in its current state of disrepair because of neglect and the misplaced priorities of this Administration," they said in a joint statement. 'Logan Correctional is an instrumental part of Lincoln and its surrounding communities. It provides more than 500 direct jobs, hundreds more indirect jobs, and immeasurable local economic benefits."
AFSCME Council 31, the state employee union representing corrections employees, said the plan is sparse on details regarding relocation for inmates and would lead to a loss of jobs. Logan being one of two facilities housing medium to maximum security female inmates, the union is concerned of overcrowding at the other if that is where they are transferred.
'We have grave concerns,' said Roberta Lynch, executive director of AFSCME Council 31. 'Closing facilities even temporarily would disrupt and potentially destabilize the prison system, while bringing upheaval to the lives of affected employees and individuals in custody.'
The governor's office projects construction costs will range between $805 and $935 million, but save the state $34 million annually long-term due to lower maintenance and utility costs. Design and construction for the new facilities is expected to be completed over the next three to five years.
Gov. Pat Quinn also tried to close down the Logan Correctional Center in 2011, seen as a necessary budget cut at the time. Lawmakers rebuked the governor's request, ultimately permitting the facility to remain open.

title: US senators urge Biden to create national monument to honor Springfield philanthropist
author: Steven Spearie
description: Some U.S. senators are asking for a monument to honor a Springfield native and philanthropist for his work during the Jim Crow era.
content:
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin has authored a letter to President Joe Biden urging him to employ his authority under the Antiquities Act to create a national monument in honor of Springfield native and philanthropist Julius Rosenwald.
As one of its owners, Rosenwald made Sears, Roebuck and Company a retail powerhouse, but during the Jim Crow era, he partnered with Booker T. Washington and nearly 5,000 Black communities in the South to build schools across 15 states for children without educational opportunities.
A total of 5,357 "Rosenwald Schools" educated some 600,000 Black Americans in the South, including alumni Congressman John Lewis, Medgar Evers and Maya Angelou.
U.S. Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Illinois., Ben Cardin, D-Maryland, Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, Cory Booker, D-New Jersey, Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, Kirsten Gillibrand, D-New York, Tim Kaine, D-Virginia and Mark Warner, D-Virginia, also signed the letter.
The National Park Service's Special Resource Study on Rosenwald is scheduled to wrap up later this year.
Rosenwald's boyhood home on Eighth Street is being considered for the national monument. It serves as the headquarters for the Lincoln Home National Historic Site, which consists of several residences in Abraham Lincoln's Springfield neighborhood.
Rosenwald, who was born in 1862 to German Jewish immigrants, lived in a house on Seventh Street until his family moved to the Eighth Street home in 1869.
Other sites in the North Lawndale neighborhood of Chicago and in Maryland also are being considered for the national monument.
Rosenwald served on the Chicago Commission on Race Relations. He was also the principal founder and backer for the Museum of Science and Industry.
'Julius Rosenwald's philanthropy changed the course of African American education in the South and had significant impacts on our society. We support elevating the story, people, and schools that facilitated that change through the creation of a national monument,' the senators wrote.
'A national monument would be of national historical significance and the first to commemorate the life and legacy of a Jewish American. It also would acknowledge the impact of Rosenwald Schools in the segregated South and address early Black-Jewish partnerships and the role of philanthropy in the United States. Importantly, a national monument also would pay tribute to the value of education as an equalizing force. As Julius Rosenwald so aptly stated, ‘I do not see how America can go forward if part of its people are left behind,'' wrote the senators.
The Antiquities Act gives the president the authority by proclamation to create national monuments from federal lands. The act has been used more than 100 times.

title: Don't feel like cooking on Easter? Try one of these specials in the Springfield area
author: Natalie Morris
description: These Springfield area businesses are serving up signature sweets and brunch buffets Easter weekend.
content:
Concerned Peter Cottontail might just be as capricious as the on-and-off again spring temperatures? If so, the following local businesses are ready to hop in as a replacement with everything from signature spring sweets to brunch buffets served Easter weekend, March 30 and 31.
Engrained Brewing Co.

Ham and turkey will grace the carving station at The Farmhouse Restaurant at Harvest Market's Easter brunch buffet.
The spread will be served from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. Easter Sunday.

title: Makers Madness enters Sweet 16, winner to be announced at Governor's Mansion
author: Claire Grant
description: Illinois voices have been heard about who will take the trophy in this year's Maker's Madness, a contest to find out which Illinois product is king.
content:
Illinois voices have been heard about who will take the trophy in this year's Makers Madness, a tournament-style contest to find out which product is "The Coolest Thing Made" in Illinois.
With preliminary voting done, the Makers Madness Sweet 16 has been set after more than 122,000 people cast their vote over more than 200 different products manufactured around the state in the contest hosted by the Illinois Manufacturers' Association.
If basketball isn't your thing or this season the team to cheer for is already on the bench, consider cheering for one of these sweet 16 to head towards the top 8.
The Top Four seeds for this tournament bracket from initial voting rounds are BoulePro 200AX manufactured by USACH in Elgin; Mullen's Imitation French Dressing made by Mullen's in Palatine; the P15 Tamper Evident Cap and Spout for Flexible Pouch Packaging manufactured by Hoffer Plastics Corporation in South Elgin; and Gindo's Hot Sauce made by Gindo's Spice of Life in St. Charles.
Voting for the Sweet 16 will take place on the IMA website at makersmadnessil.com until March 24 where the Top 8 competitors will move on.
Final Four voting will begin on March 25 until the 31; the final round of voting will be held April second to the seventh.
The winner for the contest will be announced April 10 at the Governor's Mansion at 410 E Jackson St. in Springfield, winning the title of The Coolest Thing Made in Illinois and the bragging rights that come with it.

title: Baseball roundup: Mount Pulaski pitcher's 15 Ks down Williamsville, and other Friday results

content:

title: March Madness, egg painting, Holi and more: 5 things to do in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: Looking for something to do this weekend in the Springfield area? Check out one of these 5 things to do.
content:
Looking for a low-key weekend after Saint Patrick's Day? Well, if you missed out on getting John Mellencamp tickets as he performs in Springfield this weekend, there's still plenty for you to do.
Here are five things we found.
March Madness with Motorheads Bar & Grill
What: The NCAA 2024 Men's Basketball Championship is finally here, so Motorheads Bar & Grill's entertainment complex will be Springfield's March Madness Headquarters all season long. With the first-round finishing on Friday, basketball fans can cheer on their teams in the second round all weekend long.
When: Route 66 Motorheads Bar & Grill is open from 11 a.m. to close at 10 p.m. Friday's game schedule starts at 12:15 p.m., while Saturday and Sunday games have yet to be determined.
Where: 600 Toronto Rd.
Pastel egg painting with the Easter Bunny at B's Creative Studio
What: The Easter Bunny 'Brushes" has hopped his way to Springfield just in time for kids to share a weekend before Easter learning arts and crafts. Offering open crafting tables and egg painting, children can take pictures with the bunny while adults can test their creativity by decorating cookies with colored frosting.
When:
More: Tickets are $35 per person and must be purchased 24 hours prior to the event. The tickets and additional information can be found online at bscreative.studio.
Women's History Month with Mary Lincoln: Springfield's First Lady
What: Learn about the tenacious Mary Lincoln's life in the 1800s as Springfield's First Lady; through triumph and tragedy Mary's passion for politics has left a historical impact on Women's Rights in America. Celebrate her life and legacy in a seated program that takes place inside the Vachel Lindsay Home State Historic Site, a home Mary Lincoln often visited during the time she lived in Springfield.
When: Sunday, March 24 with two time slots: 1 p.m. and 3 p.m.
Where: The Vachel-Lindsay House is located at 603 S 5th St.
More: Tickets are free but limited in quantity. To reserve a seat guests can go on the Vachel-Lindsay eventbrite page, or on the official website with Illinois Historic Preservation.
Sensory Friendly Easter with the Easter Bunny
What: Hosted by the Autism Support Center of Illinois, anyone and everyone is welcome to take pictures with the Easter Bunny in a time-controlled event to limit large crowds. Organizers say the event is designed to be sensory-friendly, making it a welcoming environment for individuals with sensory sensitivities. Photos can be taken with the bunny and sensory-friendly activities will be available.
When: Saturday, March 23 from noon to 2 p.m.
Where: Hope Pavilion located at 5220 South 6th St.
Neon Holi night at Jaalsa
What: Celebrate Holi in Springfield this weekend by painting the dance floor neon. With free facepainting and $1 pina coladas, Jaalsa intends for guests to paint the night away. Holi, or the festival of colors, is an Indian two-day holiday celebrating the love between Lord Krishna and his beloved Radha. To honor love and triumph over evil in tradition, fistfuls of paint are thrown in crowds, each color with their own meaning:
Red for love and fertility
Yellow is the color of turmeric, a spice important to South Asian culture
Blue for the Hindu God of protection, Krishna
Green for new beginnings
When: The party will start March 23 at 9 p.m., with free face painting and reduced-price drinks until 10 p.m.
Where: Jaalsa, 3114 6th St.

title: Springfield approves settlement with former transgender employee
author: Steven Spearie
description: A complaint filed 4 years ago over the denial of gender-affirming health care to a former Springfield city employee has been resolved.
content:
The City of Springfield has approved a settlement in a complaint filed in 2020 over the denial of gender-affirming health care to a former city employee.
Under terms of the settlement, the city will pay $95,000 to Katherine Anastacia Holt, who worked for Lincoln Library, for harm she suffered as well as legal fees.
The library is a department of the city.
Amber Sabin, a city spokeswoman, said the settlement will come out of the city's self-insurance fund.
Holt sought coverage for medications and other medical care prescribed by her physician to treat her gender dysphoria, which is generally the feeling of discomfort or distress that might occur in people whose gender identity differs from their sex assigned at birth or sex-related physical characteristics.
Holt later learned that the city's insurance plan specifically denied coverage for 'sex transformation and hormones related to such treatment.'
In February 2022, the Illinois Human Rights Commission ruled in Holt's favor. Several months later, the city changed its health insurance plan for employees to cover gender-affirming care.
The decision was the first time that excluding gender-affirming care from employee insurance plans was declared to violate Illinois' civil rights law, including protections for sex and gender identity.
Hanauer said his concern was about other areas the city's insurance doesn't cover that it could liable for.
"I've had people reach out to me and say when people come (to work for the city), they know what the insurance covers and just because it doesn't cover what they want, to me I think a lot of people feel that this isn't right," Hanauer said.
City attorney Gregory Moredock said that after the suit was filed in November 2020, Illinois changed the insurance code to define and cover the types of claims that were at issue in the lawsuit.
"We do now address those issues," he said. "We did move to dismiss this case because these items were not required by the insurance code when this lawsuit was filed, but I do think that subsequent changes to the insurance code have better clarified what we need to cover, and the city does cover that now."
Holt, through the ACLU of Illinois who represented her in the case, said the settlement was "a win for me and for every transgender employee across Illinois. It brings closure to my personal struggle after Springfield denied me coverage simply because of who I am. That was wrong.
'But this outcome also sends a strong signal to all employers including towns, cities, and counties across Illinois that they are violating the law if they do not provide coverage for gender-affirming care for their employees.'

title: See why a Springfield-area family has been invited to the White House

content:
More than 40,000 people are expected to attend this year's White House Easter Egg Roll. Among them is a Springfield-area family.
The family of Illinois National Guard Lt. Col. Nicholas Krzesinski, of Chatham, has been invited to participate in the White House Easter Egg Roll on Monday, April 1.
