title: Prep Spotlight: Irie Lohrenz fans 12 as Glenwood softball beats Belleville East
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Irie Lohrenz struck out 12 and walked just one in Glenwood's nonconference win over Belleville East, plus other regular season results from May 17-18.
content:
Here are regular-season baseball and softball results for May 17-18:
Friday's results
SOFTBALL
CHATHAM GLENWOOD 9, BELLEVILLE EAST 5: At Belleville, Ryleigh Kiel, Karmen Edwards and Cassandra Feld collected two hits apiece as the Titans won a nonconference game.
Kiel had an RBI single in the first inning and Sophia Feld drove in two runs with a single in the second. Taryn Griffith and Cassandra Feld both had RBI doubles and Kate Feld delivered a run-scoring single in Glenwood's three-run fourth.
Belleville East scored five unearned runs in the fourth to get within 6-5 until the Titans plated three in the seventh. Mollie Cascio had a run-scoring single and Edwards drove in two with a double for Glenwood.
Pitcher Irie Lohrenz fanned 12 and walked one in a complete-game effort. She allowed six hits and no earned runs.
LINCOLN 1, SPRINGFIELD 0: At Lincoln, pitchers Madison Wurth and Regan Kutz combined on a four-hit shutout and the Railers scratched a run across in the fifth inning to collect the win.
Faith Eckhardt singled to start the fifth and she stole third after Morgan Sheley walked. Eckhardt scored on a bunt by Kate Farnam.
Wurth, the winning pitcher, went 5 1/3 innings and allowed four hits to go with four strikeouts and two walks. Kutz pitched a flawless 1 2/3 innings.
Mia Volpert took the loss for Springfield. She struck out 11, walked two and gave up three hits.
MOUNT ZION 7, ROCHESTER 6: At Mount Zion, Chloe Williams plated a run on a walk-off groundout and the Braves scored four runs in the bottom of the seventh inning to get by the Rockets.
Trailing 6-3 in the seventh, Joelie Shafer stole home, and Ashlynn Dover scored on an error as Mount Zion got within one run. Kyleigh Garber tied the game with an RBI single before Williams (2-for-4, two RBIs) drove in the game-winner with two outs. Ella Fink went 3-for-4 in the win.
Jaelyn Watts was the losing pitcher for Rochester. She struck out 10, walked three and allowed nine hits and seven earned runs.
Brooklyn Thompson had a two-run single in Rochester's four-run third and Peyton Purves belted a two-run home run in a two-run fourth.
BASEBALL
CHATHAM GLENWOOD 7, O'FALLON 0: At O'Fallon, Cru Erickson went 3-for-4 with four RBIs and Cam Appenzeller dazzled on the mound in a nonconference win for the Titans.
Appenzeller struck out 12, walked one and gave up just three hits in a complete-game masterpiece.
Erickson popped a three-run home run in a four-run third inning. Erickson added a run-scoring single and Colten Knoedler and Bryce Murphy both had RBI singles for Glenwood.
SOUTHEAST 3, KANKAKEE 2 (9 innings): At Eisenhower Park, Miles Leininger scored on a walk-off error in the bottom of the ninth inning and the Spartans won a nonconference game.
Leininger doubled with one out and came home on an error from second base on a ground ball that was hit by Carter Hood. Southeast scored a run on a sacrifice fly by Brayden Twist that scored Tim Herrington in the first.
With the game tied 1-1, Herrington gave the Spartans a 2-1 lead with an RBI single in the second before Kankakee tied it with a run in the third.
Herrington threw one relief inning for the win. Ethan Murphy did most of the heavy lifting on the mound, throwing eight innings for a no-decision. Murphy struck out seven, walked two and gave up six hits and two earned runs.
TAYLORVILLE 1, MATTOON 0: At Taylorville, Maxx Greime hit a walk-off single to drive in Kason Pembroke in the bottom of the seventh inning in the Charlie Due wooden bat tournament.
Pembroke walked to start the seventh and reached third on a Mattoon error and a walk by Clark Durbin, who walked three times.
Pitcher Blake Ladage hurled a complete game for Taylorville. Ladage struck out one, walked two and threw a four-hit shutout.
BARTONVILLE LIMESTONE 6, SPRINGFIELD HIGH 2: At Bartonville, Springfield was limited to just two hits in the first game of a doubleheader loss.
Brody Scheffler scored on an error in the first inning and had an RBI single in the fifth for Springfield.
BARTONVILLE LIMESTONE 2, SPRINGFIELD HIGH 1 (9 innings): In Game 2 at Bartonville, Gino Holt scored on a walk-off error in the bottom of the ninth inning and Limestone completed the sweep.
Levi Friedrich stole home in the fourth to account for Springfield's one run. The Senators finished with three hits.

title: Eyeing expansion: Springfield airport looks to build more runways, FAA control tower
author: Claire Grant
description: The Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport in Springfield is looking to expand and build on more than 1,000 acres of land. Here's what the airport has planned.
content:
The Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport in Springfield is looking to expand and build on more than 47 million square feet of land, but not everyone is on board with the expansion.
The Springfield Airport Authority petitioned for a reclassification of zoning several properties totaling over 1,000 acres currently owned by the airport from R-1 residential zoning to I-2 industrial.
However, members of the Val-E-Vue subdivision south of the airport had issue with changing nine acres of farmland between Horseshoe Drive and Pulliam Road that connects the collection of houses to the airport. The Airport Authority wanted to turn that land into a heavy industry zoning space.
Lawyer Don Craven, representing the Airport Authority, assured locals the field would not be used as industrial and would be zone changed to keep consistency, but families from the rural division objected to the notion of potentially waking up to a warehouse across their street, instead of trees and corn with many houses not getting a notification letter.
'I think one of the issues that has come out of this is the airport board needs to do a better job of notifying and making the community aware when they're going to do something,' retired CEO of Illinois Educators Credit Union Gene Taylors, who objected to the zoning, said after the commission meeting.
In agreement to keep the nine acres of farmland R-1 residential, more than 25 other properties around and owned by the Airport Authority passed the zoning commission's vote to become I-2 industrial zones, with a follow up meeting next month at the municipal building.
The planned improvements for the properties are runways, an FAA traffic control tower, hangers for planes, a U.S. Department of Transportation standards office and the Illinois State Police air operations branch just a dash from the runways.
The Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport opened in 1947 in Sangamon County and over the years with expansion, has bought land annexed by the city of Springfield, making certain properties listed under the airport as residential zoning – which cannot be used as groundwork to establish factories, warehouses and other airport facilities.
In 2023, Abraham Lincoln Capital airport expanded to start providing service with Breeze Airways, which provides nonstop service to Florida; the airport since 2021 has seen the completion of $20.7 million in infrastructure upgrades for current buildings.

title: Meet the new athletic director at University of Illinois Springfield: Mike Hermann
author: Bill Welt
description: University of Illinois Springfield announced Mike Hermann as the next athletic director beginning June 17
content:
Mike Hermann was announced as the new University of Illinois Springfield athletic director on Thursday.
Hermann, who will take over June 17 following approval by the board of trustees, is wrapping up his third year as the senior associate athletic director for external operations at University of the Pacific.
He has previously served as AD at Niagara University, Towson University and Kansas Wesleyan University in addition to other roles at Norfolk State University, Seattle University, Xavier University and the Horizon League, according to the UIS press release.
At Norfolk State, Hermann oversaw corporate sales, media relations, marketing and ticket sales strategies, according to bio on the Pacific web site.
He was also previously named one of the NAIA athletic directors of the year in 2019 by the National Association of Collegiate Directors of Athletics while at Kansas Wesleyan.
Hermann, orginally from Ohio, earned his bachelor's degree at John Carroll University in Cleveland and a master's degree from Kent State University.
Jamarco Clark, the vice chancellor for student affairs, took over as the interim AD following Laura Liesman's resignation in the fall. Two other ADs have left since 2019 beginning with Jim Sarra and later Peyton Deterding.
UIS is currently searching for head coaches for the women's basketball and women's soccer teams. Graham Shaw, previously an assistant coach at Marquette University, was hired as the new men's soccer coach in April.

title: Demolition derby, rodeos and more: See what events will be at the 2024 Illinois State Fair
author: Hope Gadson
description: The 2024 Illinois State Fair is now less than three months away. Here's a look at what events will be happening at this year's fair.
content:
The event lineup for the Illinois State Fair has been announced for 2024.
This year's State Fair, now less than three months away, has something fun for everyone, young and old. From a monster truck show to a rodeo and a demolition derby, the main events have something for everyone.
Tickets for all of the events are now on sale. Fair admission is not included with event tickets. For more information on these events visit the State Fair website.
Aug. 8
What: Monster of Destruction takes over the arena on the first day of the fair with an all-out monster truck show with battles between Against the Grain, Redneck Rampage, American Scout, Crusharoo and War Wizard. There will also be a Tuff Trucks competition and a side-by-side competition. Guests will also have an opportunity to meet the drivers before the show, plus sit in the truck and have monster truck rides during intermission.
Cost: Advanced pricing tickets cost $25 for adults and $20 for children 11 years old and younger. Day of tickets cost $28 for adults and $23 for children.
Aug. 10
What: Fairgoers will be able to experience a full rodeo by Wooten Rodeo. There will be nine activities during the rodeo including, Bareback, Saddle Bronc, Bull Riding, Tie Down Roping, Over 40 Tie Down Roping, Breakaway Roping, Team Roping, Steer Wrestling and Barrel Racing.
Cost: Tickets for adults start at $10 and $5 for children 12 and under.
Aug. 12-14
What: The Illinois Tractor Pulling Association will host a three-day event of nonstop action to see which of the machines can pull the farthest. Guests can hear the roar of the engines and capture the excitement of this popular event.
Cost: Tickets for adults start at $10 and $5 for children 12 and under.
Aug. 17
What: Guests can enjoy destruction at the demolition derby as drivers crash into each other until one remains, earning the title of Illinois State Fair Demolition Derby Champion. The derby is a crowd favorite as drivers compete to test strength and durability in automotive combat.

title: Fauser: United Way of Illinois tried to enhance well-being of residents across the state
author: Marne Fauser
description: From supporting 211 services to addressing predatory lending practices, the UWI's Lobby Day showcased a comprehensive agenda aimed at advancing the well-being of Illinois residents, Marne Fauser writes.
content:
In a bustling day of advocacy at the state capitol, the United Way of Illinois (UWI), the Association of United Ways across the state of Illinois, spearheaded discussions on critical issues affecting communities across the state. From supporting 211 services to addressing predatory lending practices, the UWI's Lobby Day showcased a comprehensive agenda aimed at advancing the well-being of Illinois residents.
Strengthening 211 Services
One of the notable achievements highlighted during the Lobby Day was UWI's success in securing an additional $3 million in the FY'24 state budget for 211 services. This allocation, coupled with the $1.8 million appropriated in FY'23, marks a significant step forward in expanding access to vital resources for individuals and families in need. With Illinois having over 90% 211 coverage which now encompasses the Chicago metropolitan area population, UWI continues to advocate for steady state funding to further maximize and leverage this invaluable resource. Efforts are underway to secure $5 million in this year's state budget to sustain and enhance 211 services statewide.
Championing the Child Tax Credit
Addressing the importance of the Child Tax Credit (CTC), UWI underscored its role in advocating for policies that support low- and moderate-income families. The CTC, a refundable tax credit, has proven instrumental in lifting millions of children out of poverty and reducing food insecurity. Despite the expiration of the American Rescue Plan of 2021, UWI remains committed to ensuring that Illinois implements a state-wide CTC to prevent households from slipping into deep poverty. With a leadership position within the coalition, UWI continues to amplify the voices of communities across Illinois in advocating for policies that promote economic stability and security.
Combatting Predatory Lending Practices
Another pressing issue addressed during the Lobby Day was the continued prevalence of predatory lending practices in Illinois. Despite the passage of the Predatory Loan Prevention Act in 2022, which established a 36% interest rate cap on consumer loans, loopholes persist. This is unfortunately allowing pawn brokers to charge triple-digit interest rates. This affects those who are already struggling in our community including ALICE (Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed) individuals and families at an extremely high rate. UWI, in collaboration with coalition partners, remains steadfast in its efforts to reign in predatory lending practices that disproportionately impact ALICE and low-income households, hindering their path to financial security.
Expanding Dolly Parton's Imagination Library
In a bid to foster early childhood literacy, UWI celebrated the $1.6 million appropriation in the FY'24 budget for Dolly Parton's Imagination Library (DPIL). This funding will effectively double the size of the program in the state, offering more children access to free books. As education and early childhood experts and administrators of the program at a local level, UWI is actively collaborating with the Governor's office and the Illinois State Board of Education to facilitate the seamless implementation of this program expansion.
As the UWI and local United Ways continue to champion these vital initiatives, our commitment to serving as a catalyst for positive change in Central Illinois remains unwavering. Through advocacy, collaboration, and community engagement, UWI is striving to build a brighter and more equitable future for all residents across the state.
Marne Fauser is the President & CEO of United Way of Central Illinois. You can find out more about how United Way is mobilizing our community to create transformative change here: www.uwcil.org.

title: Construction of new multi-million dollar hotel underway in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: Springfield will soon have a new $13 million hotel near a new $40+ million sports plaza. What you need to know.
content:
Springfield will soon see a new $13 million hotel on South MacArthur Boulevard, just a short walk away from the future Scheels Sports Park complex.
Construction of the new Fairfield Inn hotel is currently set to be complete in July 2025. Once complete, the hotel will create up to 35 new jobs with more than 70% of those being full-time hospitality employees.
The Fairfield Inn will be only a stone's throw south of the Springhill Suites by Marriott at 3921 S. MacArthur Boulevard, which needed another hotel as backup for the projected traffic to Scheels Sports Park, according to Springhill Suites General Manager Darin Dame.
The sporting arena at Legacy Pointe hopes to be Springfield's hottest destination for competitive games. The sporting plaza is building eight multipurpose outdoor lighted turf fields with a 190,000-square-foot indoor sports dome.
The project will cost an estimated $42 million in development costs and is all set to open in 2025.
While the cost of the new Fairfield Inn is separate from the development of Scheels Sports Park, the construction going on at Legacy Pointe helped tip Marriott into the decision for the new hotel.
'With the announcement and the movement of construction over at the sports park,' Dame said. 'It did help us to make a decision for construction, yes.'
Contracted by Horve Construction company, the Fairfield Inn & Suites by Marriott will provide 91 new rooms for guests to the hotel with a pool, workout room and other amenities.
The hotel is owned by Legacy Hospitality at Legacy Pointe, where Scheels Sports Complex has been in construction for seven months. Ehrhardt Hospitality, an award-winning hospitality company in Illinois and Missouri, will run the location alongside Springhill.
With the sports park opening by next summer, Dame sees a necessary need for more hotels in the city to cover the need for lodging for tourists to Springfield.
'Currently I feel like we have enough, with our occupancy in the city of Springfield, we have enough hotel rooms to cover,' Dame said. 'They are projecting (the sports park) will be increasing occupancy for the entire city, so at that point we could be a little bit short. We are not really sure until we see what kind of volume that brings.'

Credit/debit cards accepted: Yes.
Hours: 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. Monday; 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday, 11 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday; noon to 7 p.m. Sunday
Entrée price range: $13.95-24.95
Children's menu: Yes.
My order: This quaint, rural restaurant just outside Springfield offers quite an extensive menu with well over 100 items with a variety of appetizers, salads, pizza, pasta dishes, and even vegan and gluten free options. We were told nearly everything is scratch made, an exception being the gluten-free pasta. I chose the Eggplant Rollatini, a breaded eggplant stuffed with ricotta cheese, rolled and topped with marinara sauce and mozzarella cheese ($13.95). My friend ordered gluten-free pasta with meat sauce ($13.95). Our meals came with hot, garlic butter rolls fresh out of the oven.
Likes: The rolls had that delightful, yeasty sweet taste with a chewy texture. The sauce had a good flavor with plenty of meat. I was impressed with so many menu offerings.
Dislikes: My friend thought her pasta was overdone, which is a drawback with some gluten-free pasta because it can break down quicker than regular pasta. She suggested next time the pasta be a bit underdone and let the sauce further cook it. I could not find a menu online, which is a drawback if I would like to order take out. The website listed on their Facebook page has a broken link.
What would I order next time? It's hard to know where to start there are so many choices. I might try a Stromboli or Calzone ($13.95) or perhaps the Lobster and Shrimp Ravioli ($21.95).

title: Litchfield magically keeps record-setting season alive with win over SHG
author: Adrian Dater
description: The Saathoff brothers on the mound benefitted from timely defensive plays behind them to give Litchfield a 2-1 win over SHG in the 2A Pleasant Plains Sectional.
content:
PLEASANT PLAINS — The baseball pinged loudly off the aluminum bat and seemed surely ticketed for center field. With it, a tie game — if not the lead — would be forthcoming for the Sacred Heart-Griffin Cyclones. Fate, however, would favor the Litchfield Purple Panthers, who used a freak double-play as part of a Houdini-esque 2-1 victory over SHG to win the Class 2A Pleasant Plains Regional title game Saturday.
The dream season for the Purple Panthers continues. Litchfield (28-7) will face Maroa-Forsyth (25-4) in the 2A Springfield Supersectional on Monday at Lincoln Land Community College's Claude Kracik Field. The game begins at 4 p.m. The winner will advance to the state semifinals at Peoria's Dozer Park on Friday. Maroa-Forsyth blanked Monticello 5-0 to win the Decatur Sectional on Saturday.
Litchfield, which won just nine games a season ago, set the school record for wins with its 25th victory in the Class 2A Gillespie Regional semifinals.
After stranding the bases loaded with nobody out in the top of the sixth in a 2-1 game, things still looked good for the Cyclones in the top of the seventh when sophomore Tye Springer stepped to the plate against Litchfield sophomore pitcher Ethan Saathoff with runners on second and third and nobody out. Springer smoked a line drive up the middle, but the ball caromed off the left wrist of Saathoff.
The ball deflected from there into a softer line drive toward Panthers second baseman Titan Hires, who gloved it for the out on Springer and quickly threw to shortstop Matthew Bywater to double up the runner on second. It almost was a triple play, but Cyclones sophomore Drew Ward hustled back to third. That set up a matchup between Saathoff and SHG's Thomas Lauterbach, with Saathoff getting him to hit another comebacker, only this time it was on one hop, and Saathoff underhanded the ball to first to end the game.
'I got confused and started looking for the ball, and I saw my second baseman had the ball, and I was so happy,' said Saathoff, who pitched the final two innings to save the win for his brother, senior Carson Saathoff. 'I definitely owe (Hires) a dinner on me.'
Litchfield coach Rocky Giannuzzi thanked 'the baseball gods for being with us today.'
'I won't lie and say I wasn't a little nervous in the sixth and seventh innings, but we found a way out of it, with a little luck, too. But that's been our team all year, led by pitching and defense, and I think that showed today,' Giannuzzi said.
The sophomore second baseman Hires said he was moving toward the middle of the diamond when the ball left Springer's bat but had enough time to correct himself and grab the ball as it caromed his way for the 1-4-6 double play.
'I knew I had to catch that one, then everybody was yelling to throw it to (second base), and we got him,' Hires said. 'We had to come up with some big plays, but we got it done. We're just going to keep going. Nobody at the beginning of the season thought we could do it, but we're here now. If we can get No. 1, we've got to go for it.'
Bywater tripled and scored on a passed ball to score the Purple Panthers' first run, and they manufactured another to get enough support for the Saathoff brothers.
Giannuzzi said he feels his team is capable of going even deeper in the state tournament with a pitching staff that he said, 'has five guys I'd feel comfortable using.'
Over at the SHG dugout, Cyclones coach Nick Naumovich said it came down to just too many missed opportunities, most especially in the final two innings.
'You have to tip your hat to them. They did enough to beat us,' Naumovich said. 'We had the bases loaded, nobody out, top of the sixth with our big guys up. But we just couldn't do it. That's baseball. We had moments this year when we couldn't string hits together, and today was one of those days. But these kids worked hard and were fun to be around.'

title: Springfield area man who made threats against Biden, Obama, sentenced in federal court
author: Steven Spearie
description: A Jacksonville man who made multiple threats against the lives of President Joe Biden and former president Barack Obama was sentenced Wednesday.
content:
A Jacksonville man who made multiple threats against the lives of President Joe Biden and former president Barack Obama was sentenced Wednesday to 14 months in prison at a hearing in federal court in Springfield.
Adam Ray Mouser, 40, of the 500 block of Brooklyn Avenue in Jacksonville, will also serve two years of supervised release following his term.
He pleaded guilty on Jan. 19.
Mouser posted on X, formerly Twitter, expletive-laced threats against Biden, his wife, Jill, and son, Hunter, on Aug. 10, 2023. Mouser's account has since been suspended.
Mouser also made threats against former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton and various members of the U.S. Congress.
Mouser taunted police by saying that they were too scared to come to his house because he was armed.
U.S. District Court Judge Colleen R. Lawless noted that 'words do matter' and that Mouser's threats repeated and escalated, even with the U.S. Secret Service going to his Jacksonville home.
Jacksonville man charged with threatening Biden, Obama, Hillary Clinton on social media
Mouser was arrested on Aug. 28.
The statutory penalties for threats against the president are up to five years imprisonment, up to three years supervised release, up to a $250,000 fine and a $100 mandatory special assessment.
The U.S. Marshals Service and Jacksonville Police assisted in the case.

title: Protests calling for Israel-Hamas ceasefire scheduled outside Budzinski district offices
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: Ahead of a scheduled protest outside her Springfield office, U.S. Rep. Nikki Budzinski renewed her call for a "mutually agreed upon" ceasefire in the Israel-Hamas war.
content:
Ahead of a scheduled protest outside her Springfield office, U.S. Rep. Nikki Budzinski renewed her call for a "mutually agreed upon" ceasefire in the Israel-Hamas war.
The Springfield Democrat will not be at her 133 S. Fourth St. office when the protest begins Wednesday morning, instead meeting with officials in Champaign that will similarly call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire, in addition to no further military spending to Israel.
Protests will be held throughout the Illinois 13th Congressional District at her other offices in Decatur and Bellevue as well.
On Tuesday, Budzinski admitted she holds deep concerns, especially after an Israeli airstrike killed at least 45 Palestinians at a temporary refugee camp near the besieged southern Gaza city of Rafah this weekend. The Israeli military maintains the fire that broke out was not directly caused by the airstrike.
"We have to have, as part of that negotiation, the release of all hostages," Budzinski said an unrelated event in Pawnee. "I've also really prioritized the need for humanitarian relief within Gaza."
A temporary ceasefire was reached in late November but talks for further pauses or a permanent end to the war that has resulted in more 36,000 Palestinian deaths and 1,400 Israeli deaths since Oct. 7 has largely stalled. U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Springfield, was the first senator to call for a ceasefire.
As of May 24, The New York Times reports 125 living and dead hostages remain in Gaza according to Israeli authorities. Another 9,000 Palestinians are being detained in Israel.
Budzinski voted in April to send $26.3 billion to Israel and Gaza - providing $15 billion in military aid to Israel and $9 billion in humanitarian aid for Gaza. The measure finally went through with bipartisan support after months of delay as part of a broader $95 billion package also sending aid to Ukraine and Taiwan.

title: This recipe provides a taste of Italy and will be a hit at your next dinner party
author: Sheridan Lane
description: A group of 17 community members and Lincoln Land Community College students traveled to Italy and got try this special recipe along the way.
content:
A group of 17 community members and Lincoln Land Community College students traveled to Italy and are enjoying an auspicious experience — two weeks of rich history, culture, food, wine and friendships in the making throughout the Marche and Emelio Romani regions of northeastern Italy.
One of many stops was to visit the Terracruda Winery in Fratte Rossa, a small town outside the UNESCO heritage site in Urbino and just about an hour off of the Adriatic coast. The winding roads took us high up the hillside where arbors of blooming roses greeted us before sitting down to learn more about the wonderful wines the Avenanti and Berti families are producing in their certified organic vineyards.
Maintaining a certified organic winery takes time, and sulfur is dusted on the vines nearly once a week to prevent mildew which can harm the grapes. Bianchello, Aleatico and Sangiovese are the three grape varieties in production at Catina Terracruda.
Bianchello di Metauro is the variety most famous in the Marche region, and this white grape varietal results in wines that are pale straw in color with plenty of aromatics and a delicate dryness perfect for the patio on a hot day alongside delicate seafood dishes.
The second variety, called Aleatico, is a lesser-known grape that previously was more typically used in blending, but that has been resurrected as a standalone wine in the last decade.
One of the wines we tasted, the Terracruda Ortaia made from nearly 100% Aleatico grapes, was a fantastically floral red with a bouquet that was as if we had gathered up the roses and jasmine hanging along the winery's arbors and stuffed them into the glass. This lightweight, easy drinking red would seamlessly pair with many dishes from charcuterie to ragu.
Another floral touch that was a highlight for many was the lovely accoutrement to the cured prosciutto and salumi we were served. The rose petal jam, homemade by the matriarch of the winery herself, was delicious with the soft, young Pecorino Toscana.
Finally, a common thread among the presentations at both Terracruda as well as from other agritourism sessions we experienced was the commitment to organic practices that not only avoid chemicals and pesticides but also cherish and uplift the age-old heritage of the product itself, making what is old somehow new again.
That notion is exactly what traveling to another country is supposed to evoke — renewed inspiration to celebrate the roots that run deep. Slowing down, taking the time and making the effort to bring to fruition the traditions in time honored craftmanship.
If you would like to join us in May of 2026 when we again embark on a food, wine and cultural experience, please email Sheridan.Lane@llcc.edu to be added to the list to receive more information.
Rose Petal Jam
1.5 cups filtered water
2 oz. or roughly 2 cups lightly packed fresh rose petals
2 cups organic cane sugar
3 tablespoons fresh lemon juice
1 tsp. pectin
Directions
Pick the rose petals, and gently submerge in a bowl of cool water to wash and/or remove any bugs or debris.
Lay rose petals out on a towel, and pat dry.
Place rose petals and fresh water (see amounts above) in a saucepan. Gently simmer uncovered for approximately 10 minutes.
Stir in 1.5 cups of sugar (save ½ cup of sugar) and continue stirring until dissolved. Add lemon juice.
Stir the remaining ½ cup of sugar and the pectin together, and slowly sprinkle into the cooking jam to avoid clumping.
Allow the mixture to continue gently cooking for another 20 minutes until it begins to thicken.
Serve with a Pecorino Toscano — a young, soft, sheep's milk cheese.
Sheridan Lane is director of culinary programs and operations at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management, Baking/Pastry, and Value-Added Local Food, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: UIS tabs former Pana star Olivia Lett as next women's basketball coach
author: Bill Welt
description: Olivia Lett has had a stellar basketball career as a player and coach. She will take that expertise to the DII level
content:
Former Pana star Olivia Lett was announced as the next head coach of the University of Illinois Springfield women's basketball team on Friday.
She replaces Summer Quesenberry after two seasons, pending approval by the board of trustees.
'I'm excited to stay in central Illinois and collaborate to build something great at UIS,' Lett said, according to a press release. 'I'm forever grateful for an amazing six years at Millikin University and all the support of the Decatur community.'
Lett was a three-time all-area girls basketball player by the State Journal-Register and left as the school's all-time scoring leader with 2,439 career points in 2008 before ushering a stellar collegiate career that included stops at Southern Illinois University in Carbondale and later Illinois Wesleyan University.
In 2012, she led IWU to the NCAA Division III title averaging 21.8 points and 6.8 rebounds per game and was named the national player of the year by D3hoops.com.
'In a playing and coaching career that has now spanned over 20 years, no one has made a bigger impact on basketball in central Illinois than Olivia,' said her former high school coach J.R. Boudouris, now the athletic director at Rochester. 'While she achieved both all-state and all-American accolades, she has always had a 'team first' mentality, which she has passed along to the teams she coached at Millikin.
'She will bring the same energy and passion for the game to the UIS program that she's always had as a player and coach."
1A baseball finals: Jacksonville Routt baseball falls to Ottawa Marquette in 1A state semifinals
Lett jumpstarted her coaching career at IWU and the University of Chicago as an assistant before becoming the head coach at Millikin University, where she compiled a 105-48 record across six seasons. The Big Blue finished this past season 23-6 overall and reached the NCAA tournament under Lett.

title: 'Ladies and gentlemen, we won' Springfield Chuck E. Cheese will keep its animatronics
author: Claire Grant
description: Chuck E. Cheese announced they'll be phasing out animatronic bands from more than 400 locations. The Springfield location, however, won't be one of them.
content:
The animatronics of Munch's Make Believe Band aren't going anywhere from Springfield's Chuck E. Cheese at 2369 S. MacArthur Blvd., performing on stage eternally in motion thanks to the pushback from the people.
CEC Entertainment, which owns the children's pizza joint has gone back on their decision to phase out all animatronic characters from more than 400 chain retail locations.
Originally, CEC planned on leaving only two bands across the country with talking metal rodents and drummer chefs in the nation.
The company said in a detailed plan by the end of 2024 animatronics would be phased out in place for more screens, trampolines and digital floors to dance on. The aggressive shift in company image would cater to new-generation youth, who grew up with technology that outpaced the robotic band.
The public outcried.
Chief Executive of Chuck E. Cheese David McKillips told The New York Times had die-hard fans of the band calling his personal phone number to criticize the decision, while other fans of the vintage animatronics sent letters, emails and phone calls to the company to see Pasqually the drummer keep on playing.
In response, Chuck E. Cheese announced in November the locations in Los Angeles and Nanuet N.Y. would keep their bands, but since backlash from local communities only three more locations (Springfield, Pineville, N.C. and Hicksville, N.Y.) have joined the list, saving Munch's band from decommissioning.
Fans of the characters took to Facebook to celebrate the news. Animatronic enthusiast Jake Suchman said, "Ladies and gentlemen, we WON," in regard to the Muncher's encore on stage.
The five bands that remain across the decades range from the 1980's to the 2010s. Springfield's animatronic band is the last CU 1-stage in the country, and last animatronic Chuck E. Cheese in the state. A CU 1-stage is a full character special stage type that uses 3-Stage characters with a 1-Stage-like format. The stage is unique to other Chuck E. Cheese stages, as the band is called ‘Chuck E.'s Make Believe Band' rather than the namesake ‘Munch's Make Believe Band.'
According to The New York Times, Chief Marketing Officer for Chuck E. Cheese Mark Kuferman said the decision to keep three more of the aging bands around was less about business and more about paying tribute to the children who have sustained the company through its 47-year history.

title: Willie Nelson's 75th solo album drops on Friday. Here's what to know about the country star.
author: Katie Wiseman
description: Willie Nelson, the 91 year-old country legend will release his 152nd album, 75th solo album on Friday. Here's what to know about him.
content:
Willie Nelson's new album "The Border" comes out on Friday.
Here's what to know about the country music legend.
How old is Willie Nelson?
Willie Nelson was born April 29, 1933, meaning he is currently 91 years old.
When does Willie Nelson's new album come out?
Nelson's newest album, "The Border" comes out Friday May 31, 2024.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
How many albums does Willie Nelson have?
"The Border" will be Nelson's 152nd album, according to Texas Monthly. This includes collaborative albums. His latest album is his 75th solo album.
Is Willie Nelson touring in 2024?
Yes, Nelson is currently touring. He's got upcoming shows during the month of June in Georgia, North Carolina, Virgina, New York and New Jersey.
You can find information about his tour dates at willienelson.com/pages/tour.
How many kids does Willie Nelson have?
Nelson has eight children, six whom are still alive, according to People. He had five daughters and three sons.
His children Paula, Amy, Lukas and Micah all followed in their father's footsteps and pursued careers in music.

title: Popular bakery near Springfield shuts its doors for good
author: Claire Grant
description: After closing for the day on May 25, Bakin' Me Happy in Riverton will not be reopening their doors to the public.
content:
After closing for the day on May 25, Bakin' Me Happy in Riverton will not be reopening their doors to the public.
Owner of Bakin' Me Happy Tina Aten said a personal decision led to the closing of the store.
The bakery and breakfast shop on North 7th street in Riverton had originally planned to reopen after Memorial Day, but a post made on social media May 30 said the store had closed because of an unexpected event, leading to the permanent closure.
'I'm just asking for my privacy at this time,' Aten said in a post announcing the closure to Facebook. 'This past year has certainly been a whirlwhind of emotions for me as well as my staff. We've met some pretty amazing people and made some pretty amazing memories, and our appreciation could never be stressed enough.'
Aten thanked the communities of Springfield and Riverton for their support of her local business and apologized for the sudden changes made to the store after Memorial Day.
According to the Office of the Illinois Secretary of State, Bakin' Me Happy LLC has been active since January 20 of last year under Aten, the sole employee of the bakeshop.
Bakery merchandise and equipment will be available for purchase the weekend of June 7 to 9 at Aten's house, alongside furniture and other household items.
Updates about the bakery equipment and times will be made available to the public via Aten's Facebook page.

title: Second suspect in fatal shooting of Springfield teenager to be tried as an adult
author: Steven Spearie
description: In addition to Cordae Curb, Dremone Patterson has been charged in the murder of Keyon Day, a Southeast High School student.
content:
A teenager charged in the fatal shooting of Southeast High School student Keyon Day in April will stand trial as an adult.
Cordae Curb of Springfield had his case transferred from juvenile court to adult court, Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser announced Tuesday.
Curb was 15 at the time of the shooting but is now 16.
Milhiser had petitioned the juvenile court for the transfer. Circuit Court Judge Karen Sue Tharp ruled on the case Monday.
The charges made against Curb in juvenile court, including first-degree murder, now stand in adult court.
Following the transfer, Curb was arraigned and ordered detained. His next court appearance is June 20.
Under Illinois law, transfers from juvenile court to adult court for first-degree murder are "discretionary" until individuals reach the age of 16, Milhiser said.
Curb is alleged to be the driver of the stolen vehicle from which shots were fired at Day.
Day, a 16-year-old sophomore at Southeast, was walking on Taylor Avenue across from Dreamland Park to school the morning of April 24. Day was coming from his grandmother's house.
Dremone Patterson, 16, of Springfield is the only other person charged in the shooting.
Patterson is alleged to have fired the shots that killed Day using a stolen firearm. Patterson has pleaded not guilty and is being detained.
Patterson's next court date is June 24.
Both Curb and Patterson face 20 to 60 years in the Illinois Department of Corrections. There is an enhancement of 25 years to life for discharge of a firearm.

title: 'A happy return:' New music director of the Illinois Symphony Orchestra has ties to state
author: Steven Spearie
content:
Taichi Fukumura, the assistant conductor of the Fort Worth Symphony Orchestra who has directed and worked with orchestras in Chicago, has been named music director of the Illinois Symphony Orchestra after an international search.
The orchestra has home bases in Springfield and Bloomington-Normal.
One of four finalists to succeed Kenneth Lam, now the director of orchestral studies at the Tianjin Juilliard School and resident conductor of the Tianjin Juilliard Orchestra in China, Fukumura guest conducted the ISO's "Fire & Fanfare" season-opening concert in October and the "Holiday Pops in the Heartland" concert in December.
The selection as director, Fukumura admitted earlier this week, marked "a happy return (to Illinois)."
"What was most attractive is the organization and the people itself," Fukumura added. "This is a very unique orchestra in that it has a very dynamic setup being a double home orchestra, both in Springfield and Bloomington-Normal."
In Chicago, Fukumura was the assistant conductor of the Chicago Sinfonietta and the Chicago Philharmonic, while directing two youth orchestras at the Merit School of Music. He also conducted the Northwestern Medical Orchestra, made up of students, faculty, residents, researchers and staff members in the Northwestern medical community.
Fukumura joined the Fort Worth Symphony Orchestra as its assistant conductor in 2022. He is the music director finalist for the Eugene (Ore.) Symphony, the Delaware Symphony Orchestra and the Colorado Springs Philharmonic and will guest conduct each during the 2024-25 season.
A native of Tokyo who grew up in Boston and started his musical studies on the violin at age 3, Fukumura is acclaimed for his dynamic stage presence and musical finesse.
At the "Fire & Fanfare" concert, Fukumura led the Illinois Symphony Orchestra through Márquez's "Danzón No. 2," Shostakovich's "First Cello Concerto" and Tchaikovsky's "Fourth Symphony."
Springfield concertgoers, he said, can expect a mixture of traditional works and newly written works or pieces the orchestra has never played before.
"I think longtime concertgoers of the Illinois Symphony will really find the season special and it's going to be an attractive season for newcomers as well," Fukumura said. "My goal is to really bring everybody in the room together and make an impact, create an evening of experience. I do that in many ways. I do speak with the audience and share with them what it is we love about what we do, why we chose to perform what we chose and why we feel it is important for people to hear it is what we do."
Post-pandemic concertgoers, Fukumura said, are choosier about what they are going out for and are more likely to show up to something they know is going to be an enjoyable experience.
"I think that is something we should keep in mind as performers and presenters, that every event we put together matters because what that experience felt like is going to be the determining factor for people to return in the future," he said.
The challenge now, Orthmann added, is "how can we make (the orchestra) relevant and important in the communities."
Immediate tasks at hand for Fukumura are filling a number of orchestra players' seats and programming for the upcoming season which starts Oct. 18.
"Both of those have been fun and fruitful discussions," Fukumura said. "They are just the first steps. We are looking years down the road of how to do we get there? How do we make sure this orchestra is thriving and growing and doing very, very well in years to come?"

title: 14-year-old driving go-kart killed after colliding with SUV outside of Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: Authorities said the 14-year-old boy lost control of his go-kart and an SUV was unable to avoid the collision. Here's what we know.
content:
A Morrisonville teenager was killed Wednesday evening when his motorized go-kart was struck by the driver of an SUV in Christian County.
Nicholas Debrun, 14, died at Taylorville Memorial Hospital from injuries in the crash.
According to a Christian County Sheriff's Department investigation, Debrun was traveling westbound on County Highway 10, just west of Morrisonville, and lost control of the go-kart, which went into the eastbound lane.
The driver of the SUV attempted to stop, Chief Deputy Jim Baker said, but was unable to avoid hitting the go-kart.
Sheriff's deputies were alerted to the crash shortly before 7 p.m. Tuesday by a 911 caller.
Baker, reached Wednesday, said there were no weather- or lighting-related issues that factored into the crash.
There were no other injuries in the crash.
Baker said no citations have been issued and that the investigation is continuing.
Morrisonville is about 40 minutes southeast of Springfield.

title: Sangamon County home listings asked for more money in May – see the current median price here
author: USA TODAY Network
description: Here's a look at how monthly real estate listings changed in Sangamon County last month.
content:
The median home in Sangamon County listed for $224,675 in May, up 13.9% from the previous month's $197,200, an analysis of data from Realtor.com shows.
Compared to May 2023, the median home list price increased 23.5% from $182,000.
The statistics in this article only pertain to houses listed for sale in Sangamon County, not houses that were sold. Information on your local housing market, along with other useful community data, is available at data.sj-r.com.
Sangamon County's median home was 1,788 square feet, listed at $108 per square foot. The price per square foot of homes for sale is up 2.5% from May 2023.
Listings in Sangamon County moved briskly, at a median 24 days listed compared to the May national median of 44 days on the market. In the previous month, homes had a median of 32 days on the market. Around 220 homes were newly listed on the market in May, a 3.8% increase from 212 new listings in May 2023.
The median home prices issued by Realtor.com may exclude many, or even most, of a market's homes. The price and volume represent only single-family homes, condominiums or townhomes. They include existing homes, but exclude most new construction as well as pending and contingent sales.
Across the Springfield metro area, median home prices rose to $216,225, up 0.1% from a month earlier. The median home had 1,808 square feet, at a list price of $107 per square foot.
In Illinois, median home prices were $340,000, a slight increase from April. The median Illinois home listed for sale had 1,795 square feet, with a price of $189 per square foot.
Throughout the United States, the median home price was $442,450, a slight increase from the month prior. The median American home for sale was listed at 1,859 square feet, with a price of $233 per square foot.
The median home list price used in this report represents the midway point of all the houses or units listed over the given period of time. Experts say the median offers a more accurate view of what's happening in a market than the average list price, which would mean taking the sum of all listing prices then dividing by the number of homes sold. The average can be skewed by one particularly low or high price.

title: Former Gov. James R. Thompson remembered as ‘titan' in state government
author: Brenden Moore
description: Former Illinois Gov. Jim Thompson, a figure who literally and figuratively towered over state government and politics...
content:
Former Illinois Gov. Jim Thompson, a figure who literally and figuratively towered over state government and politics for more than a decade, died Friday evening from an apparent heart attack. He was 84.
Thompson, a moderate Republican from Chicago, was the state's longest-serving governor, holding the office from 1977 to 1991. He was affectionately known as 'Big Jim,' both referencing his six-foot-six frame and his larger-than-life personality.
'He was someone who was a U.S. Attorney, had never run for public office and yet was this commanding physical presence just in terms of his just his size and his presence,' said Kent Redfield, a retired professor of political science at the University of Illinois Springfield. 'And then (he) turned out to have a real feel for politics and operated very easily between the folksy down home and being part of Springfield.'
Longtime observers of Illinois government and politics credit Thompson with presiding over the modernization of state government and spearheading what was at the time the largest capital construction program in the state's history. He was also known to be an effective administrator with an ability to eye and attract talented people to work in state government.
Before running for political office, Thompson made his name as the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois. In that office, he secured several high-profile convictions for public corruption, including that of former Gov. Otto Kerner and Chicago Ald. Tom Keane, who was Mayor Richard J. Daley's floor leader. He also took part in the investigation of Republican Vice President Spiro T. Agnew, who eventually pleaded no contest to tax evasion.
Thompson used this record as a springboard to run for political office. Though Thompson was a newcomer, he quickly displayed a natural skill for retail politics.
With a divided Democratic Party — Illinois Secretary of State Michael Howlett, backed by the Chicago Democratic machine, knocked off incumbent Gov. Dan Walker in the Democratic primary — Thompson was elected with 65% of the vote in 1977. He would go on to be reelected three more times.
Former Gov. Jim Edgar, who succeeded Thompson in 1991, said his predecessor was 'the best retail politician I've ever met' and that 'he turned out to be a very effective administrator.'
'His instincts were as good as anyone I've ever dealt with in politics or in life,' Edgar said. 'He had the ability to listen to everything but then to sort it out and to come up with what was the best policy.'
Edgar, who was elected to the Illinois House the same year as Thompson was elected governor, credited Thompson with springboarding his career and eventually allowing him to run for governor. But it didn't start out that way.
'I was a legislator and I was mad at him,' Edgar recalls. 'We were fighting over something and I thought he kind of pulled the rug out from under us. And he called me and I thought 'I don't want to talk to him. This is the last guy I want to talk to.''
At the insistence of his wife, Edgar returned the call. Thompson wanted Edgar to become his legislative liaison. Knowing the freshman lawmaker's future political ambitions, Thompson promised he would eventually find a place on the statewide ticket for Edgar.
After some negotiation, Edgar accepted the offer. A couple years later, Thompson tapped Edgar to be Illinois Secretary of State after incumbent Alan Dixon was elected to the U.S. Senate.
'He kept his word on that and that also gave me the opportunity to be governor,' Edgar said. 'I was just kind of an obscure freshman legislator. I worked in the legislature before and knew people, but the fact that he kind of took a chance on me, that that was a huge thing.'
Taking a chance on people he considered talented — even if the person's resume wasn't as long — would become a theme throughout Thompson's tenure. Many credit him for finding effective department heads who would often shape state government and politics for decades to come.
Among them was Greg Baise, who served Thompson as a traveling aide, scheduler and personnel director, where he oversaw the governor's patronage-related hires. Thompson later appointed him director of the Illinois Department of Transportation.
'He was a skilled person in handling the levers of power on the governmental side,' Baise said. 'His political instincts were second to none. And he had an ability to recognize talent … and he brought good people to government.'
Baise, who managed President Ronald Reagan's Illinois presidential campaign in 1984 and Thompson's final reelection campaign in 1986, said that Thompson had a unique understanding of how to win as a Republican in Illinois.
'He understood that he couldn't get elected with just Republican votes in this state, that he had to appeal obviously to the independents, but he also had to go out there and get the labor votes,' Baise said. 'Remember, this is a guy who gets the AFL-CIO to go neutral in 1986, in his last election.'
Thompson's ability to break bread with Democrats as well as his fellow Republicans was also fondly recalled. A Chicago native, Thompson knew how to work within the rough-and-tumble politics of the nation's third largest city. But, he also knew his way around the state and county fair circuit in central and southern Illinois.
'There's sort of an irony that he passes away the week of what would have been the State Fair, an event that he truly loved and enjoyed in that regard,' Baise said.
In 1988, Thompson teamed up with House Speaker Michael Madigan to secure votes for a plan to publicly fund a new stadium for the Chicago White Sox, whose ownership was threatening to move the team to Tampa, Florida if a deal wasn't struck.
On June 30, with minutes to spare before midnight, when votes needed for passage would increase from 60 to 71, Thompson worked the House floor, twisting Republican arms to switch votes from ‘nay' to ‘aye.'
Those opposed to the plan were singing 'Na, Na, Na, Hey, Hey Goodbye' to the Sox. But Thompson had the last laugh.
The legislation passed 60-55, with the official time marked 11:59 p.m. Though the actual time was 12:03 a.m. As a result, new Comiskey Park, now known as Guaranteed Rate Field, was constructed and the White Sox remained in Chicago.
Thompson also had a legacy as a builder, spearheading the effort to pass and implement Build Illinois, which was the largest capital construction program in the state's history at the time.
Among the buildings constructed during his tenure was the James R. Thompson Center, which opened in downtown Chicago in 1985. The building, designed by architect Helmut Jahn, was renamed in Thompson's honor in 1993.
It was considered an important statement of architecture by some and an eyesore by others. Thompson defended the building to his death. The state has been attempting to sell the structure in recent years.
Like the modern design of the building that bears his name, Thompson's legacy includes modernizing state government.
'Thompson clearly gets credit for — in that long period of time that he was governor — professionalizing state government, for bringing in directors that had expertise,' Redfield said. 'And the state government expanded in terms of its functions and its size.'
'State government looked much different after Thompson than before,' he added.
Thompson also had a hand in the expansion of Chicago's McCormick Place convention center and the construction of what is now the United Center, home to the NBA's Bulls and the NHL's Blackhawks.
He also played a role in the restoration of Navy Pier, which now consistently ranks among the state's top sites for tourism.
Those from all over the Illinois political world have chimed in on Thompson's passing and the legacy he leaves behind.
In a statement, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said that Thompson will be remembered 'as one of the titans in the history of state government.'
'As the longest-serving governor in Illinois history, ‘Big Jim' was known to treat people he encountered with kindness and decency,' Pritzker said. 'He dedicated himself to building positive change for Illinois, and he set an example for public service of which Illinoisans should be proud.'
Illinois Republican Party Chairman Tim Schneider said that Thompson 'treated others with legendary kindness, and created lasting positive change for Illinois over his 14 years as Governor.'
'He helped send a corrupt governor to jail as a prosecutor, rebuilt the state's infrastructure, saved the White Sox, and presided over a healthy and prosperous Illinois,' Schneider said. 'Our thoughts and prayers are with Jayne and his family at this time.'
Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan and his wife, Shirley, said they considered Thompson 'a cherished friend' and that he 'should be credited with the modernization of Illinois government.'
'He was a hard-nosed political figure and a compassionate leader,' they said in a statement. 'We were honored to serve with him.'
'Governor Thompson was a friend, mentor and an exemplary statesman who loved Illinois,' said Illinois House Minority Leader Jim Durkin, R-Western Springs. 'He was a hands-on Governor who loved the process of getting things done in Springfield, and his accomplishments still stand strong today. Our state was fortunate to have such a dedicated leader.'
Thompson is survived by his wife, Jayne, and daughter, Samantha.
The Associated Press contributed to this article. Contact Brenden Moore: 788-1526, brenden.moore@sj-r.com, twitter.com/brendenmoore13.
A Thompson timeline:
* 1936: Born May 8 in Chicago.
* 1959-64: Prosecutor, Cook County state's attorney's office.
*1964-69: Associate professor, Northwestern University Law School.
* 1969-70: Department chief, Illinois attorney general's office.
* 1970-71: First assistant U.S. attorney.
* 1971-75: U.S. attorney for Northern Illinois.
* 1976: Married June 19 to Jayne Ann Carr.
* 1976: Elected 39th governor of Illinois by defeating Democrat Michael J. Howlett.
* 1978: Re-elected governor by defeating Democrat Michael Bakalis.
*1982: Re-elected to third term by narrowly defeating Democrat Adlai Stevenson III.
* 1985: Becomes the longest-serving governor in state history on Feb. 4.
* 1986: Re-elected to fourth term by defeating Stevenson.

title: Everything Illinoisans need to know about the Real ID ahead of 2025 deadline
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: We're less than a year away from a federal deadline to have a Real ID. Here's everything you need to know about the ID and how to get one.
content:
In less than one year, Illinois residents 18 and older will be required to have a Real ID card in order to board planes and to enter certain federal facilities.
'I strongly encourage residents who intend to fly to get their REAL ID as soon as possible to avoid future headaches,' Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias said in a news release. 'Our DMV facilities stand readyto help customers get their new driver's licenses and identification cards before the federal deadline.'
In charge of administering the licenses in the state is the Illinois secretary of state's office, who said only 23.5% of Illinoisans had the license as of May.
Here's everything you need to know about the Real ID.
When is the deadline to have a Real ID?
May 7, 2025, is the deadline set by the federal government to have the license created under the REAL ID Act in 2005 — a post-9/11 security measure.
Are Real ID's mandatory?
No, if you have a valid passport, military ID or other federally approved identification, you don't need a Real ID to board a plane or enter certain federal buildings.
How do I apply for the license?
Those applying for a REAL ID card first need to either make an appointment or walk-in to a secretary of state DMV facility. The SOS website shows what facilities require appointments.
What do I need to apply for a Real ID?
You will need to provide proof of your identity, your full Social Security number, signature and have two documents showing your current residency. A full checklist of requirements can also be found at the SOS website.
How much does a Real ID cost?
The fees for a Real ID are the same as a standard driver's license/ID. More information can be found on the SOS website.
Who needs a REAL ID?
The Transportation Security Administration will not any accept identification besides the Real ID, meaning no passengers attempting to board planes without it will be permitted. It is also required to enter military bases or visit nuclear power plants, per the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
Air travel and visiting these facilities will still be allowed if the individual can present a valid US passport, which is compliant with the REAL ID.
Do I need a Real ID to vote?
No. You don't need a Real ID to vote or do any of the following:
Drive
Open a bank account
Apply for/receive federal benefits
Enter a federal facility that does not require IDs like a post office
Visit a hospital

title: Maroa-Forsyth baseball's Kaiden Maurer triples to give Area All-Stars win over CS8
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Once Kaiden Maurer gave the Area All-Stars the lead, they never let up to beat the CS8 in the annual Baseball Classic.
content:
Kaiden Maurer's big swing with two outs in the bottom of the second inning put the Area All-Stars up 3-1 against the Central State Eight All-Star team on Tuesday.
But would the Area pitchers and defense be able to quell the CS8's prolific hitters for long? They sure did.
Maurer, a senior from Maroa-Forsyth, hit a two-run triple to core Jacksonville Routt teammates Isaac Long and Conrad Charpentier and the Area All-Stars never looked back in a 6-1 victory over the CS8 in the annual Baseball Classic at Lincoln Land Community College's Claude Kracik Field.
'It was good,' Maurer said. 'The CS8, they have a lot of talent out there and the pitcher (Lincoln senior Wyatt Mammen) was throwing hard. It was sitting right-center (of the plate) and I just took it that way.'
Rochester senior Jack Swaney took the second pitch of the game deep over the fence in right field to put the Central State Eight crew up 1-0 quickly. If it looked like it could be a rout early, the Area team had other plans.
'Sometimes, playing the bigger schools and you see that (Swaney's early homer), things can unravel pretty quick,' Area coach Joel Washko said. 'We had an error in the first inning, but our pitcher (Litchfield's Tate Dobrinich), bounced back really strong and then we had some really good pitching backing him up.'
Maurer's Maroa-Forsyth teammate, senior Zayn Giles, hit a two-out RBI single in the bottom of the first to score New Berlin senior Lucas Bixby to pull the Area squad into a 1-1 tie.
'Answering in the bottom of the first was huge, I think,' said Washko, who put on his Mount Pulaski pants and windbreaker on for the last time after 10 seasons at the Hilltoppers' coach. Washko was recently hired as a dean of students at Lincoln Community High School.
In the bottom of the seventh — of the nine-inning game — Williamsville senior Josh Cates scored on an RBI single from Charpentier. In the eighth, New Berlin junior Rockman Prince drove in Maroa-Forsyth's Tate Brandenburg with an RBI triple then scored on an RBI ground out one batter later.
Better final memories at Kracik
For Litchfield seniors Dobrinich and Drake Gasperson, their trip back to Claude Kracik Field had a better result than their last one — a 10-4 loss to Maurer and Maroa-Forsyth in the Class 2A Springfield Supersectional on May 27.
With more than two weeks since the Purple Panthers' historic season came to a close, the two seniors were better able to relish their season rather than focus on the disappointing loss.
'It definitely means a lot because it's my senior year and I'm not going to be able to come back (and get redemption here),' Gasperson said. 'Just knowing I had one of my favorite teammates on and off the field (in Dobrinich) and knowing I can share the field with him one last time, it's happy memories.'
Litchfield set a school record with 28 wins, surpassing the previous mark of 24. The Panthers won just nine games a year ago and had single-digit wins in each of the three years Dobrinich and Gasperson were in school before their final campaign.
The Purple Panthers' supersectional berth was the furthest the program had gone since a second-place Class A finish in 1985.
'It feels a lot better winning on this field,' Dobrinich said, who added there is still a buzz around town about the turnaround of all three of Dobrinich's sports: the football team made the playoffs for the first time since 2006 and the basketball team won 20 games for the first time since 2018-19.
'Today before the game, some guy stopped me at the gas station and he's been following me for a long time, I guess, and he said, ‘Man, you've had one heck of a senior year ... 28 wins, a regional championship, a sectional championship; you have a lot to be proud of.''

title: One person killed in early morning fire outside of Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: Authorities were alerted about the fire when a neighbor noticed smoke coming from the Sangamon County home.
content:
One person is dead following a fire in the Village of Dawson early Sunday morning.
Sangamon County Sheriff's Sergeant Andrew Henton said fire crews were called after a neighbor noticed smoke coming from the home in the 300 block of Walnut Street around 5:30 a.m. Sunday.
Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon confirmed that it was a 63-year-old man who was found in the home.
The man's identity is being withheld pending next of kin notification, Allmon said.
Calls went out to multiple fire departments in the area.
The Illinois State Fire Marshal was called to the scene, Henton said.
Allmon said an autopsy is slated for Monday.
Dawson is about 20 minutes northeast of Springfield.

title: Death investigation in Springfield now ruled a homicide-suicide
author: Steven Spearie
description: The couple was found dead in the west side home early Thursday morning. Here's what we know.
content:
A death investigation on the west side of Springfield is now being called a homicide-suicide.
According to an autopsy and preliminary findings from the Sangamon County Coroner's office, Renee Terry, 61, died from multiple gunshot wounds and her husband, Robert Terry Jr., 67, died from a single self-inflicted gunshot wound in their home in the 1800 block of Post Oak Court Thursday.
Springfield Police were alerted to the scene shortly before 7:30 a.m. Thursday.
Post Oak is a cul-de-sac off Greenbriar Drive, west of Veterans Parkway.
It is the third homicide case in the city in 2024.
Neighbors talked to by The State Journal-Register said they did not hear any gunshots from the home.
Springfield Police are continuing an investigation.

title: Springfield City Council votes to end 3 a.m. alcohol sales—with one major change
author: Claire Grant
description: While Springfield bars won't be able to sell alcohol until 3 a.m., they won't have to end sales as early as initially thought.
content:
The days of alcohol being sold until 3 a.m. are officially numbered in Springfield.
Springfield City Council voted 8-2 in favor of ordinance 2024-231. However, there was a slight modification to the ordinance ahead of the vote.
The ordinance initially called for alcohol sales to end at 1 a.m., but an amendment passed 9 to 1 during Tuesday night's city council meeting will allow alcohol sales to go until 2 a.m. Ald. Roy Williams Jr. was the only one to vote against the amendment.
The approved amendment to the ordinance means there will only be one liquor license for all bars in the city.
Springfield bars will have to pay an additional $100 to renew their license come January, which will allow them to choose when they want to close with 2 a.m. being the latest.
Clique co-owner Justin Rebbe thanked the city for listening to the local bars when he stood at the podium, as well as The Alamo owner Barry Friedman.
'As a bar we would like to keep our 3 a.m. license but we're happy to not have it taken back to 1 o'clock and allowing us to keep the 2 o'clock,' Rebbe said. 'I don't think it was going to pass if we tried to maintain the 3 o'clock so I think the 2 a.m. is a good compromise for now. We'll definitely still have a loss of revenue in that time, at least it's one hour and not two; that also speaks for our gaming revenue in those hours.'
Bars rolling back hours are The Alamo on North 5th Street, The Gin Mill on South 5th Street, Clique on East Washington Street, Bourbon Street Rhythm & Ribs on South Grand Avenue, Celtic Mist on South 7th Street and Unique's Bar & Grill on East Cook Street. The listed bars all either operate with a sub-class license for 3 a.m. or a Class F license currently, and will not longer be able to starting next January.
Ward 5 Ald. Lakeisha Purchase and Ward 2 Ald. Shawn Gregory represent the two wards with the 3 a.m. bars. Purchase, who was not present during the Committee of the Whole meeting last week, supported the amendment for 2 a.m. closing as a compromise.
'I know it is not as favorable to move to 2 a.m. but as I stated to (bars in her ward) last night, I did not want it to be all or nothing,' Purchase said. 'So, this was the compromising.'
The leadup to this decision dates back to early April, when the Sangamon County Board in a 21-5 vote ended 3 a.m. liquor sales, eliminating the selling of alcohol after 1 a.m.. The new code went into effect this month, and by the end of June several taverns in the county will have rolled back hours.
The change goes into effect starting Jan. 1, 2025.
Steven Spearie contributed to this article.

title: Disney settles Magic Key class action lawsuit, find out if you qualify
author: Amaris Encinas
description: There's still a chance to see if you qualify for a cut of a $9.5 million lawsuit settlement paid out to Disney's Dream Key Passholders.
content:
A cut of a $9.5 million settlement from Walt Disney Parks & Resorts might not make you a millionaire, but will grant the opportunity for select Magic Key passholders to walk away with a little bit of extra cash.
The company in March settled claims made nearly two earlier, when a California woman alleged that they 'mislead consumers about the nature, benefits, and restrictions of Dream Key Passes,' the complaint states.
Disney, according to the plaintiff, misrepresented one key feature of the Dream Key Pass option, which was one of three Magic Key Pass options that provides purchasers with a 'variety of reservation-based admission opportunities, discounts and prices.'
Dream Key Passholders were not allowed to make admission reservations anytime, instead they were forced to make park plans around 'blockout dates' despite an advertisement of the pass option claiming the opposite, according to the complaint.
'(The plaintiff), and others similarly situated, have not received the benefits of the Dream Key passes that were promised to them,' the complaint states. 'Instead of receiving a ‘no blockout date' pass that would allow them to reserve admission to the parks whenever the parks had capacity, Ms. Nielsen and her fellow Dream Key pass holders received a much more limited right to make reservations for a limited class of Dream Key tickets. This is a far cry from what Disney advertised to consumers and from what Disney sold to its customers.'
Disney has denied any wrongdoing, instead offering to pay around $67 to any customers who purchased a Dream Key pass from Aug. 25, 2021 through Oct. 25, 2021, according to the Disney Dream Key Settlement website.
Here's what we know.
What did the class action lawsuit against Disney seek?
Jenale Nielsen, who brought forth the lawsuit on behalf of an estimated 103,431 Dream Key Pass holders in November 2021, in an attempt to stop Disney from 'engaging in unlawful trade practices' through the offer and sale of the $1,399 pass option, according to the complaint.
As well as the practice of 'promising' purchasers that they would not be subject to 'blockout dates' when making theme park reservations.
Nielsen sought 'injunctive relief' to prevent and deter Disney from engaging 'in these and similar' deceptions in the near future. She also asked the court to order Disney to cover attorney fees, damages and restitution owed to any purchasers who may have been harmed by the company's conduct.
How do I sign up?
It's not too late to determine if you are eligible for compensation, but most, if not all, Dream Key Passholders, received a cut of the settlement payment in the mail or via email on June 14.
Dream Key Passholders, who were contacted by the settlement administrator, but have not claimed their payment have until Sept. 12 to do so, according to reporting by the Los Angeles Daily News.
You can contact the settlement administrator by phone at 877-894-4029, via email info@dreamkeysettlement.com, or send an inquiry by mail at Nielsen v. Walt Disney Parks and Resorts U.S., Inc. c/o Settlement Administrator, P.O. Box 2318, Portland, OR 97208-2318 to find out if you are an eligible Dream Key Passholder.

title: Party infighting leads to Illinois GOP chairman stepping down
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: Republicans elected Tracy in February 2021, becoming the first chairman from downstate since fellow Springfield resident Donald "Doc" Adams' term from 1973 to 1988.
content:
A tall task awaits Illinois Republicans in November as the party tries to capture a foothold in the deep blue state. It will be doing so, however, without its chairman.
Springfield attorney and businessman Don Tracy, the former head of the Illinois Gaming Board, announced on June 18 that he will be stepping down as party chairman.
His decision comes less than one month away from the Republican National Convention in Milwaukee, where his resignation will go into effect no later than July 19 — the last day of the convention. The party will send 64 delegates to the convention including Tracy.
Republicans elected Tracy in , becoming the first chairman from downstate since fellow Springfield resident Donald "Doc" Adams' term from 1973 to 1988. He said then that he planned on "making Illinois a two-party state again," a goal he ultimately did not fulfill. Democrats continued their hold of all statewide offices during the 2022 midterm elections, while adding seats in the Illinois General Assembly and having 14 out of the state's 17 congressmen.
What pushed him to make the decision, Tracy wrote in a resignation letter, was infighting among party members.
'When I took on this full-time volunteer job in February 2021, I thought I would be spending most of my time fighting Democrats, helping elect Republicans, raising money to pay for more Party infrastructure, and advocating for Party unity," Tracy wrote to fellow Republicans. "Unfortunately, however, I have had to spend far too much time dealing with intra party power struggles, and local intra party animosities that continued after primaries and County Chair elections.'
Tracy wanted Republicans to make up grounds in previously competitive counties surrounding Chicago, well-populated areas that could turn elections in their favor. Instead, the party has largely won the land game particularly downstate but not the votes.
Such was the case in 2022 when Gov. JB Pritzker needed just 12 out of the state's 102 counties to dispatch Republican challenger and then-state Sen. Darren Bailey of Xenia handily.
The Democratic Party of Illinois pounced on the opportunity to assert Republicans were in disarray, adding the party had followed a "strict adherence to a losing set of anti-choice, anti-worker, pro-Trump policies" in a statement. It projects the next chair will be a "MAGA extremist" although no official plans for Tracy's replacement had been announced as of Thursday morning.
Tracy's resignation comes after Republicans voted to remove state party vice chair Mark Shaw two days prior. The decision to remove Shaw, previously gunning to be a Republican National Committeeman during a contentious state party convention in Collinsville last month, Tracy maintained lacked due process and "portends a direction of the state party I am not comfortable with."

title: Kite festival, rodeo among 5 things going on in Springfield this weekend
author: Claire Grant
description: While temperatures are on the rise and on track to mull around 90 degrees this week, there's still plenty of family-fun activities in Springfield.
content:
While temperatures are on the rise and on track to mull around 90 degrees this week, weather can't stop a good time.
Beat the summer heat with these five events happening around Springfield; remember to listen to your body when to step out of the sun and cool down before jumping back into the action.
The Great Lawn Kite Festival
What: This national festival will bring all eyes to the sky. Presented by the Springfield Park District as part of Hopeapalooza, the Southwind Park Great Lawn Kite Festival brings togethers kite-fliers of all skill levels from beginner to professional. Send kites soaring and fill the Springfield skies with billowing red tapers, multicolored diamonds and unique designs. This event includes inflatables, a live DJ, petting zoo and food vendors.
When: 10 a.m. Saturday, with a rainout date on Sunday in case of bad weather.
Where: Southwind Park, 4755 S. 2nd St., Springfield
Day of Fae Magic Market
What: A wholly unique event will be turning a popular downtown spot into a woodland wonderland for one night. Ad Astra will be hosting their first Magic Market this Saturday for the fae-folk of Springfield to trade coins for witchy wares. Dressing up in elf ears, wings and ethereal dresses is encouraged for this magical market which will have vendors feeding into the fantasy setting.
