title: Porsche, MINI rate high in JD Power satisfaction survey, non-Tesla EV owners happier
author: James Powel
description: J.D. Power has released its annual satisfaction survey ratings, see how car owners rated the 2024 models.
content:
J.D. Power 's 2024 U.S. Automotive Performance, Execution and Layout (APEAL) Study shows a slight improvement in driver satisfaction with 2024 offerings from car manufacturers.
Drivers rated their satisfaction with the latest car models at 847 on a 1,000-point scale on average, a two-point increase over 2023.
Porsche led the premium brand category and MINI led the mass market brand category. Hyundai Motor Group took the most segment-level awards while the BMW 7 Series was the highest-ranking model in the survey.
"Traditional manufacturers have listened to the Voice of the Customer," Frank Hanley, senior director of auto benchmarking at J.D. Power said in a press release. "They're launching enhanced vehicles that are more in line with what customers want, including improved interior storage and higher quality materials, as well as ensuring features have ease of use."
The study is based on responses from just under 100,000 owners of new 2024 model-year vehicles, who had owned their car for at least 90 days between July 2023 through May 2024.
Here's what the J.D. Power APEAL survey found:
J.D. Power APEAL top brands and models
Non-Tesla electric vehicle owners happier than Tesla owners
Owners of electric vehicles made by manufacturers other than Tesla reported higher levels of satisfaction than owners from the electric-vehicle giant.
Non-Tesla vehicles scored 877 points in the survey — an all time high — while Tesla scored 870. J.D. Power reported that Tesla brand loyalists remained satisfied with their cars, but the Elon Musk-owned company struggled with new customers.
The improvement in satisfaction was attributed to the improvement in driving range and improved interiors.
Consumers find entertainment systems too complicated
J.D. Power reported that it found drivers are less than thrilled with infotainment systems provided by carmakers.
The survey found that 25% of owners said switching between sources caused a "poor audio experience" and 23% blamed menu set-up for audio problems. Drivers who used systems that were extensions of mobile devices, such as Apple Car Play and Android Auto, reported higher levels of satisfaction.
"Owners struggle to perform simple audio-related tasks, so it begs the question whether automakers are actually in tune with the desires and needs of their customers," Hanley said.

title: Reports: 1 man dead from canyon fall at Starved Rock State Park in Illinois
author: Eric Lagatta
description: A person died Saturday afternoon from a fall at a canyon at Starved Rock State Park in northwest Illinois, according to reports.
content:
A person died Saturday afternoon from a fall at a canyon at Starved Rock State Park in northwest Illinois, according to reports.
The fatal fall occurred about 4:30 p.m. at Illinois Canyon, one of 18 such canyons located at the park – a popular Midwest destination along the Illinois River for hikers, fishers, campers and hunters. CBS News identified the victim as a man.
It was not immediately clear what caused the man to fall. USA TODAY left messages Monday morning with both the Illinois Conservation Police in LaSalle County and also the Illinois Department of Natural Resources – the agency that maintains the park – that were not immediately returned.
Starved Rock popular among visitors for its canyons, waterfalls
Located about 100 miles southwest of Chicago in the town of Oglesby, Starved Rock has earned a reputation as one of Illinois' most popular attractions, according to the Peoria Journal Star, a USA TODAY Network publication.
The state park's 18 canyons feature vertical sandstone walls covered in moss that were formed by glacial meltwater, according to the Illinois DNR's website.
Hikers also flock to the park for its rain-fed waterfalls and more-than 13 miles of trails through "lush vegetation" and "spectacular overlooks," the DNR says.

title: Jr. Blues' do-everything Defreitas remembered with cancer, youth hockey benefit
author: Adrian Dater
description: Zack Defreitas is never far from his brother's mind. The hockey-crazed family started this charity in his honor.
content:
Brad Defreitas knows there will be no physical response from brother Zack Defreitas. That was made cruelly impossible in March of last year when colorectal cancer took Zack's life at age 30. But that doesn't stop his older brother from texting Zack two or three times a week.
'I usually text him something about hockey,' Brad said Saturday, while the second annual Zack Defreitas Skate For A Cure was happening at the Nelson Center ice rink. 'We both grew up on the Peoria Rivermen, and they won the (Southern Professional Hockey League) title this year, and me and my dad watched it. Sometimes I just type out the text and don't send it, but this one I did. He was very opinionated about hockey, so I would text something like 'Hey, did you see who the (St. Louis) Blues signed this week?' I used to rile him up pretty good, just for fun.'
Zack Defreitas's true hockey love was the Springfield Jr. Blues. He was both a player and, later, the team's jack-of-all-trades. He ran the marketing department. He was the traveling secretary. And, best of all, he was the team's voice, broadcasting games via the team's streaming feed.
He had dreams of becoming the next John Kelly, the longtime St. Louis Blues broadcaster, or anything close. After being hired in 2018 as the team's marketing and communications director, Defreitas impressed owner Dan Ferguson Jr., so much that, starting with the 2022-23 Jr. Blues season, he was to be the team's full-time broadcaster for home and road games.
But, in March of 2022, he was diagnosed with a rare form of colorectal cancer. Despite a brave battle against the disease, he passed away a year later, leaving a wife whom he'd married not long before.
'It's still tough,' Brad Defreitas said. 'It kind of comes and goes. I don't really feel like it's real, and I probably never will. He never really shared much with me about his treatments, because he didn't want me to get upset about it. He was supposed to have gotten surgery in January of '23, but they did a scan and it had just spread too far. He was put into hospice the morning of (March) 17, and he passed that night.'
Zack Defreitas story:'He loved everything about the Jr. Blues': Fan favorite, hockey team's do-everything dies
Said Kelly: 'I didn't know him, but I'm very sorry to hear this. He seemed to have the right passion for the game and for broadcasting."
Brad set up a website — Gonzoslegacy.net — and organized the Skate For A Cure events to accomplish two things: to raise awareness of colorectal cancer among younger people, and to raise money to buy hockey equipment for Springfield-area youth who want to get into the game.
Tyler Gansky, who was a teammate of Zack's for several years on different teams, was part of Saturday's second annual event that included a 3-on-3 tournament. In its first year, the event raised thousands of dollars and, judging by the crowded Nelson Center Saturday, this year's did very well too.
'That's been kind of the reasoning for all this, because he would have done it for any of us,' Gansky said. 'We lost him too soon. The one thing he loved more than anything was hockey, and we felt the best way to help push what Zack would have wanted is to help kids get into the sport he loved.'
More:Central Illinois team back at Senior League Softball World Series, looks to defend title
The way the foundation works is, kids get free hockey equipment (except skates), and if they keep participating in youth hockey beyond a year, the equipment is theirs forever. If not, they can turn it back in for someone else. Some other funds go to cancer research.
'We're trying to grow the sport more in Springfield. We think it can be growing faster,' Gansky said. 'Across the country, it's growing at a huge pace, and we want to maintain that pace in Springfield. We don't want kids to have to go to Peoria or St. Louis to play more competitive hockey. We want to keep them here.'
Asked about his last visit in hospice with his friend, Gansky gets choked up.
'It's a terrible disease. He didn't deserve that,' Gansky said. 'But he was the same Zack he always was, right to the last breath.'

title: Illinois State Fairgrounds looks 'better than it's looked in decades', official says
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: The Illinois State Fair kicks off next week and officials say fairgoers will notice massive improvements thanks to$85.3 million in renovations.
content:
Ahead the start of the Illinois State Fair next week, state officials are once again touting major improvements and renovations to the fairgrounds.
Through the Rebuild Illinois Infrastructure Program — Gov. JB Pritzker's 2019 capital improvements plan — $85.3 million has been allocated towards the Springfield fairgrounds as part of a multi-year and ongoing upgrades and repair plan.
So far, Illinois Department of Agriculture director Jerry Costello said more than $65 million has been spent on renovations plus another $8.3 million in improvements completed by the building and grounds staff over the last five years. Fairgoers, he said, will particularly notice improved roads and roofs and a modernized Coliseum.
"It's a massive investment," he told reporters during a fair media day event on Monday. "A lot of people, certainly anybody that has been coming to the fair for years realizes, prior, that not a lot was done on the fairgrounds for a few years. There's some deferred maintenance that had to take place, but there is so much renovation being done outside of that."
"When people get on the grounds, I'm telling you, I think it looks better than it's looked in decades," Costello added.
Costello said work at the Coliseum, the "crown jewel of the fairgrounds" where $31.5 million is dedicated in renovations, is ongoing. The 60,000-square-foot structure, constructed in 1901, will now feature two elevators, new restrooms and improved Americans with Disabilities Act accessibility.
The renovations also include $14 million towards resurfacing roadways and sidewalks; $9.3 million in roof repairs; $3 million to tuck-pointing and bridge repairs; and $8.6 million for a new canopy, concession stands, restrooms and structural repairs to the foundation and terraced walls at the Multi-Purpose Arena.
For Pritzker, who Costello said has invested in the fairgrounds and agriculture at levels not seen since the days of Govs. Jim Thompson and Jim Edgar, the need for the improvements comes after years of neglect.
"I said my first year in office to my staff, I want out fair to be, first of all I want it to be profitable for the state because it should be," Pritzker said during a May Citizens Club of Springfield event. "And I want it to be something that people love going to and that we build up."
Last year's fair saw attendance top 700,000, breaking a one-year record. This year's state fair runs from Aug. 8 through Aug. 18.

title: New, conveyor belt style restaurant opening in Springfield will be city's first
author: Natalie Morris
description: Conveyor belt style restaurants originated in Japan in the 1950s. A new restaurant opening will bring the concept to Springfield.
content:
Conveyor belt sushi restaurants where diners select their meal from a variety of dishes paraded by them on a conveyor belt originated in Japan in the 1950s.
And now the automated dining concept is finally making its way to Springfield with construction underway at 3061 Wabash Ave. for the new restaurant slated to be called Izumi.
Steve Zhao, who co-owns the 5,300-square-foot building rising out of the parking lot between Gordon Food Service and the strip mall that houses Jo-Ann Fabrics and Bard Optical, confirmed details about the tenant signed for the spot.
'He's an ex-Marine from Hawaii and a sushi chef, most recently operating in the Dallas area who is bringing a conveyor belt restaurant to Springfield,' said Zhao. 'It will offer sushi and other Asian cuisine.'
Izumi is Japanese for spring or fountain.
Zhao said building construction is on track to be completed by late August, which would position the restaurant for an opening in the fourth quarter of 2024 or first quarter 2025.
This work site is only one construction zone on Wabash Avenue Zhao is overseeing this summer. He is also one of the partners involved in The Feast Buffet that is expected to open in the expanded footprint of the former Show-Me's on South MacArthur Boulevard this fall.
Both of these newcomers into the local dining scene highlight Asian cuisine but offer very different dining concepts.
The Feast Buffet will be serving up an all-you-can-eat spread featuring a variety of Asian cuisine and meat carving stations, as well as a full arcade known as Funkiddo. The vibe is aimed at mimicking the Dallas-based Dave and Buster's chain that serves food with a side of fun.
The conveyor belt concept, however, combines food and tech in a whole different way.
The story goes that concept inventor Yoshiaki Shiraishi struggled to staff his small sushi establishment. Inspiration hit while visiting a brewery and watching beer bottles travel along a conveyor belt.
Shiraishi opened his first conveyor belt restaurant, known in Japan as Kaiten-sushi, which translates as 'rotation sushi', in Higashiosaka, Japan in 1958. Upon his death in 2001, he operated 11 conveyor belt restaurants throughout Japan.
Conveyor belt restaurants boomed in 1970 after the dining concept was used at the Osaka World Expo.
Shiraishi's other fast food staffing workaround, a sushi restaurant where robots delivered dishes, never gained similar traction.
Today, chains such as Sushiro and Kura Sushi operate more than 500 locations throughout Japan.
Cafe renovations
The Ariston Cafe in Litchfield recently underwent a $75,000 renovation. But don't worry because the Route 66 landmark still feels like a time capsule back to the Mother Road's heydays.
'We've kept it age appropriate,' said William 'Will' Law, who co-owns the renowned spot with wife Michele Law and Marty and Kara Steffens, 'We didn't take anything away, if anything, we've restored some of the 1930's charm.'
The work, done with the help of a grant aimed at shining up Route 66 attractions before the famous road's 100th birthday in 2026, included some structural repair to the 1935 art deco building, as well as freshening up the interior.
But the 'Remember Where Good Food Is Served' neon sign still hangs over the lunch counter and the original, chrome hat racks mounted to the booths harken back to another era.
Renovations were completed just in time for the cafe to celebrate its centennial anniversary in July.
Greek immigrant Pete Adams originally opened his cafe in Carlinville on Route 4 in 1924, before Route 66 carved across the country from Chicago to LA. Adams eventually relocated The Ariston Cafe to its current home in 1935.
The stop offered Route 66 travelers a rest from the road, a bite to eat and fuel. The two gas pumps in front of the building were later removed by Pete's son Nick Adams, who with his wife Demi, ran the business until 2018.
The building was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2006 with this written in its application: 'The Ariston Cafe remains a rare survivor of the type of family-owned restaurants that flourished along Route 66 in Illinois during the mid-20th century. It is a well-known landmark and a direct link to the history of Route 66.'
'An investment in our future'
Customers have gathered around the soda fountain at Docs Just Off 66 in Girard since 1884. A $50,000 grant, awarded Tuesday, in part, by American Express, aims to ensure this central Illinois landmark continues to thrive well into the future.
Funds from the Backing Historic Small Restaurant Grant Program will be spent converting an 1870s era outbuilding behind Docs Just Off 66 into a bar and meat smokehouse, as well as creating an outdoor seating area.
'My first thought was, 'How fantastic this is going to be for our community,'' Casey Claypool, who owns Docs with her husband Steve, said of receiving the grant money. 'It's an investment in our future.
'Our kitchen is at capacity and our cooks are dying to get into that (smoked meats) realm.'
Claypool said the outbuilding has been vacant since the 1940s. But the structure was used to store horse equipment when it was built in the 1870s, before being converted into bathrooms in the early 1900s, she said.
Construction is scheduled to begin later this month and wrap up by January 2025.
Docs Just Off 66 was one of 50 small restaurants throughout the country to be awarded the grant in 2024. This is the fourth year for the grant – issued in conjunction by the not-for-profit National Trust for Historic Preservation and American Express.
Only four other Illinois businesses have received this grant. Old Fashioned Donuts in Chicago was also named this week and Flesor's Candy Kitchen in Tuscola and Jeff's Red Hots in Chicago were among the 2023 recipients.
The Girard business began as Deck's Store, a pharmacy and soda fountain, in 1884. It continued doing business as Doc's Soda Fountain from 2001 through 2021 under the operation of various owners, until the Claypools purchased and rechristened the business.
The local draw still displays artifacts from early medical practice from its predecessors, as well as a considerable collection of Coca Cola memorabilia. Offerings include a full lunch and dinner menu, bar and soda fountain.
This is the second grant the Girard business has been awarded this year. Work began this week to replace some of the original windows to the building on the Girard square. The $10,000 grant for the project was part of the National Trust for Historic Preservation's Route 66 Legacy Grant.

title: Illinois House Speaker's staff continues attempt to unionize
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: Staffers attempting to unionize in House Speaker Emanuel 'Chris' Welch's office are continuing their suit against the Hillside Democrat.
content:
Staffers attempting to unionize in House Speaker Emanuel 'Chris' Welch's office are continuing their suit against the Hillside Democrat.
The Illinois Legislative Staff Association filed a response on July 31 to the speaker's motion to dismiss their case, alleging Welch has failed to engage in collective bargaining. The association formed in 2022 after voters approved the Workers' Rights Amendment that November — codifying a worker's ability to organize and collectively bargain in the state constitution.
"Until adoption of the Workers' Rights Amendment, the Speaker's own legislative staff had no legal right like other employees to bargain with their employer over wages, hours, and working conditions," the staff association wrote in their motion in Cook County Circuit Court. "Now they do."
The Illinois Public Labor Relations Act, Welch's attorneys write in their motion to dismiss, excludes employees of the Illinois General Assembly from its definition of a "public employee" thus providing them no pathway to unionize. This was also the finding of the Illinois Labor Relations Board when they denied the association's petition to form a bargaining unit in March 2023.
Taking their case beyond the state labor relations board was "forum shopping" by the staffers, defendants wrote in their June 24 motion. The staffers contend, however, the labor relations board does not have the ability to conduct constitutional analysis and only courts can properly rule on the matter.
'Through this suit, Plaintiffs are attempting to bypass the carefully crafted labor representation process set forth in IPLRA and 40 years of case law,' the defendant's filing said.
The battle to unionize legislative staff comes after the Illinois House passed House Bill 4148, allowing the unionization to move forward, during last year's fall veto session. The bill has since languished in the Senate, never making it to a committee vote during the spring session.
While previously thanking Welch for introducing the bill and pushing it through to the next chamber, the staffers now say it is the speaker who is blocking that effort. They have accused him of working with Senate President Don Harmon, D-Oak Park, to guarantee the bill does not move in the Senate.
ILSA announced their filing hours after Gov. JB Pritzker signed into law legislation limiting employers' use of "captive audience" meetings where employees are effectively forced to listen to the political or religious views of their boss.
The " Worker Freedom of Speech Act" passed in the Illinois General Assembly mostly along party lines this spring, 79-30 in the House and 39-18 in the Senate, and was led by Sen. Robert Peters, D-Chicago.
The new law goes into effect on Jan. 1, 2025, and does not prohibit businesses from holding these meetings, but rather prevents employers from punishing workers if they choose not to attend them. Illinois became the eighth state, joining states like New York and Minnesota, to pass such a law.

title: Fishing tournament, beer school among 5 things to do in Springfield area
author: Claire Grant
description: It's the first weekend of August, which means summer is slowly winding down. Despite that, there's still plenty to do in the Springfield area.
content:
August is here and with it comes thoughts about back to school, late summer camping and the Illinois State Fair.
But there's still plenty to do before the fair kicks off on Aug. 8. Here's five things we found to do this weekend.
Magical Garden Party
What: Join Incredibly Delicious for complimentary cake as it celebrates 29 years of serving the community. While not required, fancy dresses are encouraged to add a level of mystical wonder to the party in the yard of the historic downtown house the bakery and store resides in.
When: 11:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. Saturday
Where: Incredibly Delicious, 925 S. Seventh St., Springfield
More: A list of cakes, and more information about the delicacy bakery can be found online on their Facebook page.
Redneck Fishing Tournament
What: The Village of Bath is putting man against fish in this invasive fishing competition. The Redneck Fishing Tournament has two, 2-hour heats in which teams, many in costumes, go out on the water to see how many flying invasive carp they can net out of the air or jump in the boat. Winning teams often collect hundreds of the fish.
When: Gates open at 8 a.m. Friday, and 9 a.m. Saturday.
Where: 218 W. First St., Bath, Ill.
TableScape Celebration
What: The Springfield Civic Garden Club and host sponsor Lincoln Land Community College Foundation will present A TableScape Celebration for fantastic designs. The creatively decorated tables will be presented by talented members of community groups like Lincoln Memorial Garden, the Dana Thomas House Foundation, Springfield Art Association, Sangamon Watercolor Society and others. Over 30 tables with different designs will be displayed at the event, with 20 gift baskets valued between $50 to $100. All proceeds support the community grants of the club and LLCC scholarships.
When: Noon to 4 p.m. Friday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday
Where: Lincoln Land Community College, 5250 Shepherd Road, Springfield
More: Admission to the event is $10, but students of LLCC have free admission.
Wizarding Weekend at the Wakery
What: For all those who love alliteration as much as spell incantation, meet up at the Wakery this weekend for a slew of spell craft and non-boozy drinks to enjoy. A full menu of wizarding drinks including the Wakery's famous butter beer and pumpkin juice will be served alongside different events each day hosted by local businesses. Friday will host Witches Hat Burning and Decorating with Wildflowers and Barley and tarot reading. Saturday will have Glitter Potion Bottles with Dabble Springfield, aromatherapy and lip gloss potions with The Aromatic Dragon and spell bottles with That Wyrd Place. Sunday features a wizard tea party with Passions by Bryce, mini curio domes by Severyn Designs, and a patronus discovery event for fans of the book series Harry Potter.
When: All weekend with different dates coinciding with events that can be found online on Facebook.
Where: 5 W. Old State Capitol Plaza, Springfield
More: A flash by the Wakery's Facebook event will give all the details intrigued readers will need.
Beer School 101
What: While school is in session, students can learn about the brewing process, take a tour of the brewing facilities and sample some of the freshest ales available. Attendees must be 21+ and attend under the explicit acknowledgement that they will be touring an operating brewery, where wet surfaces and other moving equipment may be present.
When: 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. Saturday
More: Spots for the event are limited but free – if missing out this time around, next month the class will open up again.

title: Freeman: Personal, school and community safety are needed to help students grow
author: Tina Freeman
description: Tina Freeman writes about the importance of valuing children in the classroom.
content:
I am an English Language Arts Educator with Springfield Public Schools at Jefferson Middle School. My psychology degree and educator certification are from the University of Illinois Springfield.
I have joined the Faith Coalition for the Common Good as a board member and co-chair of the Education Equity Task Force. I became an educator to be one person in a student's life that knows, respects, and values them. I have come to learn three things:
Greeting a student with a smile and their name could make them smile.
It is okay to show respect to students first. Some may not know what respect looks like.
It is also ok to repeat respectful acts as often as necessary.
My fire for knowing, respecting, and valuing students started while volunteering as a classroom parent in Springfield.
As I extended an invitation to one student to join the learning station, the classroom teacher told me, as an announcement to the whole class, 'Do not worry about him. He will not conform to [the rules of the class].'
I slowly rose and walked back to the small group, leaving the one student at his disheveled desk. Upon my next visit, the student who had been singled out by the teacher greeted my youngest daughter (at the time) and me and led us to his now organized desk.
He told my daughter that she could sit there while he joined the learning station. That student satisfied his need to exert responsibility (an expectation) before 'conforming."
While pursuing my degree at UIS, I encountered a quote like Pam Leo's, "Children need at least one person in their life who thinks the sun rises and sets on them, someone who delights in their existence and loves them unconditionally.'
Children need that one person. Unfortunately, some children do not have that one person. As a teacher in District 186, I heard a comment regarding how we value all children. It was a simple comment. 'We have always known about Jefferson.'
I have been at Jefferson Middle School since 2019. There has been opportunity for improvement for years prior to my start date. The opportunity to value what students are capable of producing by increasing expectations is paramount.
In my classroom, I hold safety as the number one priority to foster community. We need that same directive to take actions toward personal safety, school safety, and community safety. The introduction of social emotional learning for students and staff was an important addition to the District 186 curriculum for personal and school safety.
Relationship building between community members and the police department is a step toward community safety.
Ensuring that families have access to resources also builds community safety. Can I have your thoughts about the nextquestion? What is the first thing you do when you feel safe?
After you answer, keep asking yourself that same question and replace it with the answer you gave to the previous question. Keep going.
Personal, school, and community safety at a fundamental level will spark additional improvements. Currently, dates are set for community canvassing, prayer walks, and focus groups to discuss solutions that can be enacted to build personal, school, and community safety.
Valuing a student is setting high expectations for them to reach.
Tina Freeman is the co-chair of Faith Coalition's Educational Equity Task force. If you have any questions or want more information on how to get involved, email tyshianna@faithcoalition-il.or g.

title: This Springfield park offers sites to visitors all-year round with miles worth of trails
author: Thomas J. Turney
description: The State Journal-Register photographer Thomas Turney continues our A Walk in a Park series at Lincoln Memorial Garden and Nature Center.
content:
A Walk in the Park is an ongoing series from The State Journal-Register photographer Thomas Turney, who plans to explore the Springfield area — one park at a time — to capture all of the beauty and recreation Springfield area parks have to offer. If you have a suggestion of a park he should visit, email him at tturney@gannett.com.
The Lincoln Memorial Garden and Nature Center offers more than 5 miles of trails to explore. The park, which pays homage to President Abraham Lincoln, is a self-governing woodland and prairie garden owned by the city of Springfield. Depending on when you check out the park, you might see springtime dogwoods in full bloom, the colorful prairie wildflowers in the summer, burnished autumn leaves or snow-covered maple trees. The park features six miles of interconnected trails that wind through the Garden's restored prairies, woodlands and wetlands. The Garden also contains a dozen footbridges, a pond, and eight stone council rings, most with views of the lake. Trail surfaces are either wood-chipped or grass. Visitors are asked to stay on the marked trails.
Founded: 1936, Nature Center opened in 1965
Address: 2301 E. Lake Shore Drive, Springfield
Acres: 61
History: Civic leader Harriet Knudson began coming up with the idea of honoring President Abraham Lincoln as the city was in the midst of building a 4,000-acre lake. Knudson was able to get the city on board along with the Garden Clubs of Illinois. The park was designed by architect Jens Jenson.

title: New, but nostalgic: Springfield arcade hopes updated look will help spark business
author: Claire Grant
description: A popular kids arcade in Springfield went retro with its $250,000 renovations. Here's what's new, and what's sticking around.
content:
Classic pizza and arcade nostalgia await you at Chuck E. Cheese, along with a quarter of a million dollars in renovations.
The new renovations at 2369 S. MacArthur Blvd. include a retro-style paint job around the building, digitized menu boards, an interactive dance floor and a new trampoline wall coming in September.
The renovations took place in the middle of the night after the store had closed down for the day, being able to be completed in a matter of three weeks without impacting the sales or hours of operation for the location.
What didn't change? The kid-friendly arcade's Make Believe Band is still playing hits on the banjo and drums. The over four decades old animatronic band is one of the last handful remaining in the entire country and is the last original band in Illinois and the Midwest.
CEC Entertainment, which owns the children's pizza joint, has gone back on their decision to phase out all animatronic characters from more than 400 chain retail locations.
It's because of these swinging chefs and Chuck E. Cheese himself onstage, that Springfield chose to not follow suit with the contemporary 2020's remodels happening across the country
'In this case we thought it was a unique idea to say every store in Illinois is going to have the new look,' District Manager Reggie Donovan said. 'Why not take the full show and make it a retro remodel?'
Making the Springfield location unique will helpfully benefit the store, which has been on the lower end of sales in the district according to Donovan, who attributes the opening of Malibu Jacks, a popular children's entertainment destination which opened in the White Oaks mall in October of last year, to be a factor in driving sales down.
A typical 2020's remodel can cost upwards of half a million dollars, which means besides attracting nostalgic superfans from across the state to see the old show in a way they'd remember it, the revamp also saves money.

title: Complaint filed against Springfield Police Department following July arrest
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: The family of a 20-year-old Springfield man pulled over for having a car with tinted windows has filed a complaint against the Springfield Police Department.
content:
The family of a 20-year-old Springfield man pulled over for having a car with tinted windows has filed a complaint against the Springfield Police Department.
Ardell Hampton Jr. is facing misdemeanor charges for resisting arrest and obstructing a peace officer following a July 8 traffic stop. The family, however, is alleging the tactics used by the Springfield Police Department are part of a broader issue experienced by people in low-income parts of the city.
"We identify the actions that the officers did as the same actions they typically do in the community," said family spokesperson Samuel Johnson during a Monday evening news conference.
Per the police report, Sgt. Michael Raynolds and an officer only identified by a last name Cortes spotted a black Nissan heading south on Ninth Street at 7:47 p.m. on July 8. The officers allegedly took a U-turn after spotting the tinted windows and followed Hampton into the Oscar's Tavern and Package Liquor parking lot.
Hampton got out of the vehicle, despite police saying they instructed him to stay, and they tackled him when they thought he could be attempting to flee by foot.
The family maintains that Hampton was not trying to run-away and was simply trying to pick-up his car keys that he had accidentally dropped.
Johnson referred to the tactic as what he describes as the "jump-out boys," where officers get out of their vehicles and search for contraband inside vehicles they pull over. A search of Hampton's person and vehicle found no contraband.
Hampton received a citation in lieu to arrest and has court date set for Aug. 13.
Emails to the Springfield Police Department were not returned Tuesday night.

title: 'Full justice.' Family, friends gather to recall Sonya Massey a month after fatal shooting
author: Steven Spearie
description: Sonya Massey's mom, Donna, reiterated during a vigil Tuesday night that the family's top priority is justice for Sonya.
content:
Theresa Mercado's 11-year-old daughter, Maleyah, recalled making tea with some friends one time when she asked her neighbor, Sonya Massey, for some honey.
"She said, 'Here you go, sweetie,'" recalled Maleyah, of Massey. "She's a nice person."
About 100 or so friends and neighbors gathered at Massey's home in the 2800 block of Hoover Avenue Tuesday night to mark the one-month anniversary of her fatal shooting at the hands of a Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy.
After a moment of silence and prayer, the crowd released purple balloons, Massey's favorite color. They also lit candles for her on the front porch of her home and left flowers and artwork.
The gathering came on the same day Gov. JB Pritzker, at a press conference in a Chicago, expressed frustration with embattled Sheriff Jack Campbell.
Shadia Massey, a cousin who likened herself to Sonya's older sister, admitted the last month has been hard on the family "and it's getting harder, actually. We are dealing with it day by day."
The family, she said, has kept its eyes on "full justice for her. We won't change in this for the community, for the world, for the nation."
Jimmie Crawford Jr., who was the first family member, along with Shadia, to arrive at Massey's home the morning of July 6, said he still hoped her death could be a catalyst for change in gun reform and civil rights "that we need."
Abbie Giganti, who is white, said police in Springfield treat Blacks like "sub-humans."
"They look at people who are different from them," Giganti said, "and they shame them and punish them."
Erin Pacha, who has been a stalwart with Giganti at local protests and rallies that cropped up within a week of Massey's murder, said police should have sent someone who could have dealt with Massey mental health issues "and not someone who was going to punish her for it."
"But it's important to us to be out here and be here for the family. I want the family to know there is support for them."
An emotional Donna Massey reiterated it was about getting justice for her daughter.
"That's all this is about. It's not just about Sonya," she said. "There have been thousands of us killed by the hands of the police. She's the straw the broke the camel's back."
Earlier, Pritzker said he was "disappointed with the answers" he was hearing from Campbell over the hiring of Sean P. Grayson, who is being held on first-degree murder charges.
"How did the sheriff end up hiring this person?" Pritzker said. "(He) must have known their background, must have."
An advisory referendum, even if it makes it to the ballot and gets a majority of the votes on Nov. 5, still might not be Campbell's undoing because he would not be bound by it.
Campbell is next up for election in 2026.

title: Business forced to close after Adams Street fire nears reopening at new location
author: Claire Grant
description: A business that was forced to a close after the June fire on East Adams Street is about to reopen at a new location.
content:
A business that was forced to a close after the June fire on East Adams Street is close to reopening at a new location.
The Cat's Pyjamas Cat Cafe has already opened the doors for a select few customers at the cafe's new location at 524 E. Capitol Ave.
Owners of the cafe, Tom Raymond and Samantha Enz, said the cafe won't fully be open for a few weeks.
It's been nearly two months since a fire at 413 E. Adams St. caused several businesses to close along with the cat cafe.
Multiple forms of fundraising events have happened since the fire to help residents and businesses impacted by the fire.
On July 15, the INB Benefit for the Businesses Affected by the Adams Family Fire fund distributed $15,750 in donations to seven businesses and 12 residents. The funds were collectively donated by community members, and a second round of donation checks will be distributed later in August.
'The community support really did help bring this cafe back to life,' Raymond said. 'I worked a lot on this project for three years and during this time I've had a lot of encouragement saying this was a great idea and was really going to happen.'
Doing what any business owner can do following the destruction of his cafe, Raymond set out and successfully adopted the remaining cats the cafe had hosted for the Animal Protective League, then set his eyes on "what next?"
With the help of Steve Myers, the president of Myers Commercial Real Estate who reached out after the fire, Raymond secured the new space on East Capitol Avenue.
Previously Harders Law Offices, the storefront needs a new set of paint and certainly a few comfy cat towers, but it's already a place Raymond can see the cafe coming together with the ample spacing of the office.
'I did a lot of research on locations downtown and this was one of the locations I had researched a couple years ago,' Raymond said. 'It seemed the most viable and after being in it for the last week and a half it's really starting to feel like something we could have long term.'
The cafe held a soft-open house on Aug. 1 asking for donations of items like chairs and cat toys and according to Facebook, are thrilled to announce their first four new furry residents into the building soon.
The couple did say they were able to get all nine cats at the cafe at the time of the fire adopted. The couple is now looking ahead.
'I started a cafe, I got 18 adoptions, I built my goal, and I could just move on,' Raymond said about a conversation he had post-fire. 'I said no, the community really wants this, and they really want it back and I should at least attempt to bring back the cat cafe.'

title: Embattled Springfield-area sheriff will retire following Sonya Massey shooting
author: Steven Spearie
description: Embattled Sangamon County Sheriff Jack Campbell will retire by the end of the month, he announced Friday.
content:
Sangamon County Sheriff Jack Campbell, embroiled in controversy following the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey by a sheriff's deputy, said he is stepping away.
Campbell, who has been sheriff since 2018 but whose family roots run deep in the department, is retiring no later than Aug. 31 he said in a statement issued Friday afternoon.
Former deputy Sean P. Grayson has been charged with Massey's murder. He has pleaded not guilty and remains in custody.
It will be up to Chairman Andy Van Meter to name an interim replacement. The current second in command is Chief Deputy Anthony Mayfield.
Calls for Campbell's resignation had come from many sides, including Gov. JB Pritzker and Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton earlier this week. Massey's family members also called for his ouster.
In a statement provided, Pritzker hoped a fresh start with new leadership "will usher in a new era of reform and rebuilt the trust lost between the Sangamon County community and sheriff's office."
Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who the Massey family has retained, said Campbell's retirement "marks a turning point in the ongoing pursuit of justice for Sonya Massey."
"Although the pain of her loss is still fresh, Sonya's family is willing to work with the outgoing sheriff for the remainder of his tenure to help heal the community and achieve full justice for Sonya," Crump said in a statement. "The Massey family also hopes to work with Sangamon County's next sheriff to examine how this tragedy happened and to ensure that a tragedy like this never happens again in this community.'
Questions have centered around the hiring of Grayson who worked for six different agencies in four years.
Grayson had two DUI convictions in Macoupin County, including one while he was still enlisted in the U.S. Army. Both occurred before he was employed as a police officer.
Grayson's separation from the Army noted a "serious misconduct" Campbell said he construed to be the first DUI charge.
Campbell acknowledged that Scott Butterfield, a former Sangamon County sheriff's deputy for 25-plus years, was listed as a reference for Grayson and that he was contacted by the department prior to Grayson employment with the county in May 2023.
In his reference, Butterfield noted his daughter was dating Grayson.
Grayson and another deputy, who has not been charged in the case, responded to Massey's home in the 2800 block of Hoover Avenue after a 911 call was made about a possible prowler.
County deputies responded because the home is in an unincorporated area of Woodside Township.
In an earlier inte rview, Campbell said he felt Grayson "betrayed" members of sheriff's department.
Campbell said the department "failed the community, we failed Sonya, we failed Sonya's family and friends," at a U.S. Department of Justice hearing in Springfield last month.
"While it is painful to say goodbye, I do so knowing I have fulfilled my duties and served to the best of my ability," Campbell said Friday.
Campbell, a former undersheriff, has been around the department most of his life. His father, Jim Campbell, was with the sheriff's office 20 years and rose to sergeant and his great-uncle, Hugh Campbell, was sheriff.
Like Pritzker, State Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, said the hiring practices of the sheriff's office needed to be reviewed and is calling for an independent investigation.
'This was absolutely the right decision,' Turner said of Campbell's move, in a statement. 'It doesn't do any good to remove the sheriff unless we look into the hiring practices that led to Sonya Massey's murder.'
Three Sangamon County Board members, all Democrats, also asked for his ouster.
But the 60-year-old Campbell maintained his stepping down would be "irresponsible."
"I was overwhelmingly elected to lead the Sheriff's Office through both good times and bad," Campbell said. "I am fully prepared to continue leading my office and serving the residents of Sangamon County through this difficult period, ensuring we learn from this tragedy and work toward a better future."
Since the shooting, Campbell insisted he has been "proactive and transparent, working tirelessly to present all of the facts to the public. I have committed to making changes to our standards and collaborating with other units of government on ways to prevent incidents like this in the future."
Van Meter said in a text that he respected Campbell's decision.
"The Jack Campbell I know," Van Meter said, "has always done what he thinks is best for the community."
Board member Kevin McGuire, who called for Campbell's ouster, said his leaving was a first step.
McGuire is also calling for an outside investigative team to look at the sheriff's department's hiring practices.
"I would say that's paramount," McGuire said.
Sunshine Clemons, a co-founder of the Black Lives Matter group in Springfield, said she was "saddened" that Campbell appeared to be taking no responsibility for the situation.
"His lack of accountability is a major issue," Clemons acknowledged. "If he doesn't see a role that he played in this, I don't believe he's able to bring in the change that is actually needed."
Board member Marc Ayers said what happened to Sonya Massey can never happen again in Sangamon County.
"I invite the community to heal and come together as we fight for justice, not just for Sonya Massey," Ayers said.
This story will be updated.

title: Longtime Illinois Auditor General Bill Holland dead at 72
author: William G. "Bill" Holland
description: While he was the Auditor General for 23 years, William \
content:
, who served as Illinois Auditor General for 23 years in a public service career that spanned four decades, died at his home in Seattle on Saturday.
He was 72.
According to an obituary supplied by the family, Holland had been diagnosed with colon cancer.
A native of Joliet but raised in Kansas, Holland served as chief of staff to then-Senate President Phil Rock, D-Chicago, before his appointment as auditor general by the Illinois General Assembly in 1992.
The office, created as part of the 1970 Illinois Constitution, analyzes state agencies to ensure money is spent appropriately.
Holland's tenure overlapped five different governors, both Democrat and Republican.
According to a 2015 State Journal-Register story, Holland's 2005 audit of the Department of Central Management Services brought into question suspicious activities of former Gov. Rod Blagojevich. He was impeached in 2009.
Gov. Jim Edgar told the SJ-R in 2015 that Holland never let partisan politics play into his role.
"He came at Republicans and Democrats with equal gusto," Edgar said.
Before joining Rock's staff, Holland served as director of the Illinois House Majority Appropriations Committee Staff and as first director of the Illinois General Assembly's Washington, D.C., office.
He is survived by three children and five grandchildren.

title: Time to dust off those cleats: high school football practices have returned
author: Ryan Mahan
description: August brings football practices back to high school fields across Illinois.
content:
Another year, and another first day of practices for high school football teams around the state.
Or is it?
Football coaches have 25 opportunities during the summer to practice with their players, teach plays to newcomers and sharpen up skills for those returning. There are even some competitions thrown in the mix with various 7-on-7 camps and linemen challenges.
'From summer, it doesn't really feel that different; it's just a continuation,' Glenwood coach David Hay said on the first day of practice. 'But we're in helmets only, so we kind of go back to the basics a little bit — they did have 10 days off and they are teenage boys, so you've got to kind of reset them a little bit in terms of what they're doing. Teachers started school today and it's like you just jump into the regular season.'
While some coaches and players say Monday wasn't unlike other days during the summer, Aug. 12 also served as a reminder that the first games of the season aren't too far away.
'It's closer to game time now,' Athens senior Davis Ishmael said. 'You've got goosebumps, your hairs are up and you're a little nervous now because it matters now.'
Ishmael, who was hurt for the season last year in Week 3, is the starting nickelback for the Warriors and is also competing for the starting quarterback job.
'School is starting Wednesday and when school starts, football starts,' Glenwood junior quarterback Colten Knoedler said. 'I felt like we showed up today with a different mentality.'
No more two-a-days
What was one an end-of-summer ritual — the two-a-day practices — have mostly gone the same way as the BlackBerry phone. Hay credits all the instruction time the coaches are allowed during the summer practice sessions.
'We do so much in the summer now that the whole olden-day thing I did for a long time, the two-a-day concept, doesn't really apply,' Hay said. 'We don't need to go two-a-days right now, we've got darned near everything installed. Now it's just a matter of going back to the basics, brushing it back up and then prepping for competition.'
Glenwood senior receiver Gavin Simmons agreed with his coach that Monday didn't feel that different.
'Not really, we're still doing all the same stuff, fine-tuning all of our run plays today and pass plays tomorrow,' Simmons said. 'It's just good to get back out here; it's a slow start after dead week, but it's also good to take a step back and go back to the basics before we pick up speed.'
Happy to be back out there
The postseason was a little shorter than Athens coach Ryan Knox is used to. In 2023, the Warriors finished second in the Illinois High School Association Class 2A state football tournament, the highest finish in school history. Shorter or not, he's always excited for the season practices to begin.
'I like going in the evening on the first day of practice, but I also don't like the anxiety of waiting around for practice to start,' Knox said with a smile. 'I don't care when it is, the first day is always special.'
The first two days of practice this week are helmets only, followed by helmets and shoulder pads for days 3-5. After that, players can start practicing in full gear.
'These first two days, it's kind of to see how we're moving; there's some fundamentals since we're just in lids,' Knox said.
It's also a time for senior leadership to really kick into gear. Kody Walsh, a senior in his third year starting at center for Athens, said due to numerous graduation losses, he's excited to see how the younger players develop.
'The different feeling is there's not as many returning starters as there normally would be, so it's just a lot of fresh meat out here: getting to see them play, what they can do,' Walsh said. 'They'll be returning next year as well, so preparing all of them to get ready (is the responsibility of the seniors).'
That sentiment was echoed by teammate Chris Dillon, returning to his spot at right tackle with Walsh on the offensive line. He wants to pass down the lessons he learned from last year's run to the state title game.
'We learned we could be great, you just got to put in the effort,' Dillon said. 'It took a lot last year: hitting, injuries, work, study the plays, give it their best.'
With the entry of Quincy Notre Dame as a football-only school into the Central State Eight Conference, the schedule structure for those 12 teams is totally revamped. This season, the CS8 will introduce two six-team divisions and four nonconference games. The Titans start the season with Edwardsville and North County in Bonne Terre, Missouri.
That excites Glenwood senior tight end and linebacker Jonathan Helm: 'Seeing more difficult teams and seeing different teams in general so it's not the whole thing every time.'

title: What are the biggest questions heading into the 2024 football season around Springfield?
author: Bill Welt
description: How much will Quincy Notre Dame impact the Central State Eight Conference, and other top questions around Springfield this high school football season
content:
Teams around the state officially kickstarted the high school football season with the first day of practice on Monday.
Here are some of the biggest questions around the Springfield area going into Week 1 on Aug. 30:
How will Quincy Notre Dame impact the Central State Eight Conference?
The CS8 welcomes QND to the fold — well, in football anyway. That means each CS8 team will open the 2024 season with two nonconference games before diving into conference play.
The Raiders finished 5-6 last season but reached the second round of the Class 2A playoffs. It was their 25 th playoff appearance in the last 29 seasons, led by returning all-state linebacker Taylin Scott.
QND certainly wields the potential to wreak all kinds of havoc in the CS8, which boasted six playoff teams last season.
What does the rest of the CS8 look like?
Rochester graduated all but five starters after winning the Class 4A state title last season and opens against Chicago Simeon at Gately Stadium on Saturday, Aug. 31 at 1:30 p.m. and Missouri Class 5 state champion St. Louis Cardinal Ritter Prep at Rocket Booster Stadium the following Friday in Week 2.
Sacred Heart-Griffin will roll out a new quarterback after reaching the second round of the Class 5A playoffs in John Allison's head coaching debut.
Chatham Glenwood may bristle with the most experience, including all-CS8 quarterback Colten Knoedler and a gamut of talented receivers such as Gavin Simmons and Blake Lehnen.
Normal University's tandem featuring quarterback Alek Weiland and wide receiver Cade Cunningham also can't be overlooked this year after leading the team to its first playoff appearance since 2015.
Lincoln made its first playoff appearance in nearly four decades but graduated twin tailbacks Ki'on and Kani Carson.
Decatur MacArthur also made the playoffs last season, while Jacksonville missed the cut by one game. But MacArthur's Myson Johnson-Cook moved to Texas after leading the Generals into the postseason as a nationally heralded freshman tailback.
How will Maroa-Forsyth defend its Sangamo Conference title?
Maroa claimed its second straight outright Sangamo title and reached as far as the Class 2A state semifinals before falling to eventual state champion Wilmington.
But the Trojans graduated a spate of all-conference players, most notably all-state quarterback Kaiden Maurer. That said, all-conference seniors Mitch Williams and Grant Smith very much still loom large.
Smith, who recently committed to Illinois State University, helped secure last year's outright Sangamo title with a forced fumble against eventual 2A runnerup Athens, who made their first state final appearance in program history but lost prolific running backs Cory Craig Jr. and Camren Bigard — not to mention all-state linebacker/offensive lineman Brayden Leathers. Craig was the State Journal-Register's Small School Football Player of the Year.
Perennial contender Williamsville will usher in a new quarterback but heralds all-state running back Braddock Cates.
How will the South Central Conference shake out this year?
Litchfield, not unlike Lincoln, nixed its playoff drought last season and made its first postseason appearance in 18 years.
The Purple Panthers subsequently hired defensive coordinator Colton Faure as their next head coach and will summon a new nucleus of players this season.
Gillespie also hired new head coach Cory Bonstead over the offseason. Elsewhere, Hillsboro coach Joe Reed will serve a six-game suspension for an off-campus incident.
Greenville won its first SCC title since 2014 and retains all-conference running backs Dayton Oliver and Declan Graber.
Pana may up for the challenge to reclaim the throne with quarterback Wyatt Kile and running back Isaiah Harbert in tow.
