title: Sonya Massey recalled at historic church on monumental day in Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: Attorney Ben Crump said during a memorial for Sonya Massey, \
content:
Even if she didn't know, Lisa Clanton said she felt a connection to Sonya Massey, who was fatally shot by a Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy in her home on July 6.
"We're Black women," Clanton said before Wednesday's memorial for Massey at Pleasant Grove Baptist Church. "She called for help. Unfortunately, help did not come to her. Quite the opposite, she lost her life to someone who was supposed to protect and to serve.
"I see myself reflected in her in that dire situation."
The church, and faith, also connected Clanton, 46, and Massey, 36. She called Massey "my sister in Christ."
Both grew up in the church and Clanton well understood Massey's directive at Sean Grayson—"I rebuke you in the name of Jesus"—before he shot her in the face inside her home after she called 911 for a possible prowler.
"She was rebuking an evil presence that she recognized in the sheriff deputy," Clanton said. "He was confused and didn't understand cultural reference."
About 100 people gathered for the service, which featured civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who also represents the Massey family.
Wednesday also marked the 116th anniversary of the start of the Springfield Race Riot. It was announced earlier in the week that President Joe Biden intended to use the Antiquities Act to make the site, along the 10th Street railroad tracks at Madison Street, a national monument under the National Park Service.
Fittingly, Sontae Massey, Sonya's first cousin, explained to the gathering that the family had ties to William Donnegan, an elderly Black man and one of the city's best-known citizens, whose throat was slit and body hung during the riot.
Crump, reciting a long list of Black victims who had been shot by police or others in authority, cautioned that it was time for Springfield to stand up for Massey.
"We can't be scared," Crump challenged. "We have to speak truth to power."
Recalling a quote from the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., Crump said the coward will ask the question, Is it safe? Expediency, he said, will ask the question, Is it politically correct? Vanity will come along and ask, Is it popular?
"Conscience comes along," Crump said quoting King, "and asks the question, Is it right? My brothers and sisters, it is the right thing to do to stand up for Sonya Massey. It's the right thing to do to speak up for Sonya Massey. It is the right thing to do to fight for Sonya Massey."
Pleasant Grove pastor, the Rev. William DeShone Rosser, said the evening struck "a 10 out of 10."
"Everything I had in mind came about and more," Rosser admitted. "The choir lifted us and got us inspired. (Ben) Crump preached tonight, and he touched our spirits, touched out hearts."
Clanton said a fallout from Massey's death is that it has brought the Springfield community together, evident at rallies and gatherings supporting the Massey family. Clanton said she took part in a rally at Comer Cox Park on a National Day of Mourning for Massey on July 28.
"She gave her life," Clanton said of Massey, "hopefully to move us forward, to call for reform, everything from the sheriff retiring to reform in hiring practices to transparency in background checks."

title: Pritzker calls Trump a 'loser' as Dems champion Harris, Walz during Governor's Day
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: After former President Donald Trump called Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker a "loser" on Tuesday, the Illinois governor responded during on Wednesday.
content:
A precursor to the Democratic National Convention in Chicago next week, Illinois Democrats rallied in Springfield on Wednesday — vowing to again keep the Land of Lincoln blue this November.
At both the Illinois Democratic County Chairs' Association brunch and Governor's Day events, elected officials and party leaders drummed up support for Vice President Kamala Harris and running mate Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and levied attacks against Republicans up and down the ballot.
In Harris, Democrats accounted for the historical significance in having the first woman in the Oval Office. Still, they say it's the platform, advocating for nationwide abortion protections and promoting gun control, that she would strive for as president in addition to her identity that make her the best candidate.
And with national polling showing Harris moving ahead of former President Donald Trump, Democrats say the momentum is palpable.
"This is an energy that you can't buy and can't fake," U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Springfield, said during the morning brunch at the Bank of Springfield Center. "And that's what's driving Donald Trump bat crazy."
Democrats see Harris and Walz as unifying figures not just for the party, but for the country as a whole. It's a stark contrast to what they say Republicans would bring to the table.
Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, donning a "Kamala For Everybody" shirt, repeated Walz's "weird" tagline to describe former President Donald Trump and his running mate Ohio U.S. Sen. JD Vance. For Gov. JB Pritzker, Illinois Republicans are in the position they are in due to their continued backing of the Trump-Vance ticket.
"It's almost if Illinois Republicans don't want Illinois families to succeed," Pritzker said. "They seem focused on other things like explaining away the 34 felony fraud convictions of Donald Trump or whitewashing the fact that JD Vance said that he hates police and wants to raise taxes on people that don't have children."
Trump attacked Pritzker Tuesday during a virtual interview on X with Tesla founder Elon Musk and called the governor a "loser." Having won his two gubernatorial elections comfortably, and noting Trump's loss in 2020 to President Joe Biden, Pritzker responded Wednesday that term doesn't apply to him.
"We're gonna have Kamala Harris winning this race all over the country," the governor, a Harris surrogate, told reporters following his Governor's Day speech. "We know who the winners are, and Donald Trump is the loser."
While the focus has largely been on the presidential election, also at-stake are all 17 congressional seats and seats in the Illinois General Assembly. And looking to maintain if not add to its grip over Springfield, Democrats again touted their accomplishments during the first five-plus years of the Pritzker administration.
Those accomplishments — raising the minimum wage, eliminating the grocery tax and cancelling medical debt — were done without Republican support in the state legislature. The governor added that, with these 'no' votes, it's "no wonder the Illinois GOP is a super-minority party."
Illinois Democrats don't have much to fret when it comes to Harris winning the state, voters supporting the Democratic presidential candidate in every election since 1992. The same, however, can't be said of fellow Midwest swing-states like Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
The state party is making plans to help build a "Midwest Blue Wall," which could prove to be essential for Democrats to retain the presidency. Already, Pritzker's Think Big America pro-abortion advocacy group purchased billboard ads to run in Milwaukee during the Republican National Convention last month.

title: New commission being formed after Massey shooting will address police practices
author: Steven Spearie
description: The new commission will look to address systemic issues in law enforcement practices, mental health responses and more. Here's what to know.
content:
A citizens' commission is being formed in the aftermath of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey.
The Massey Commission's proposed mission, according to a statement released Friday, is to address systemic issues in law enforcement practices, mental health responses and community relations, with the goal of creating "tangible, practical and equitable solutions for the betterment of all who call Sangamon County home."
It will look to produce a comprehensive report outlining findings, recommendations and proposed actions within a year.
The commission will be co-chaired by Jerry Kruse, dean and provost of the SIU School of Medicine; the Rev. T. Ray McJunkins, pastor of Union Baptist Church and Nina Harris, chair of the Illinois Commission on Equity and Inclusion.
While Sangamon County Board Chairman Andy Van Meter and State Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, called for the commission, it won't have any elected officials on it.
Van Meter said the commission was in part a response to the public commentary from Tuesday's board meeting. The public commentary part lasted more than three hours, many calling for an independent investigation.
He added that public officials have reached out to counterparts in other communities, like Ferguson, Missouri, where similar tragedies have occurred.
In the months after the shooting of teenager Michael Brown on Aug. 9, 2014, then-Gov. Jay Nixon appointed an independent group to address the situation.
"The consistent advice (from those communities) has been careful listening, absolute transparency and a firm resolve to adopt best practices," Van Meter said. "Many of the thoughtful comments at Tuesday's county board meeting confirm the wisdom of this advice."
Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman and mother of two children, called 911 in the early morning hours of July 6 because she thought she heard someone outside of her house, which is technically not part of the city of Springfield.
Now-former sheriff's deputy Sean P. Grayson shot Massey in the face after a situation over a pot of boiling water quickly escalated.
An Illinois State Police investigation "did not support a finding" that Grayson, whose hiring by the department has been called into question, was justified in his use of deadly force. He was indicted and charged with murder on July 18.
Sheriff Jack Campbell eventually announced his retirement over the situation.
McJunkins' church hosted a U.S. Department of Justice community relations service listening session over the fatal shooting.
"My hope is that the work of this commission creates space for Sangamon County to be able to move toward what the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. called the beloved community, a community governed by a shared commitment to equitable policies and systems for all," said McJunkins, one of the founders of the Faith Coalition for the Common Good.
In the statement, Kruse said in addition to the Massey shooting, the death of Earl Moore Jr. and the shooting of Gregory Small Jr. in Chatham have "shaken Sangamon County to its moral core."
Two emergency medical services workers were charged with Moore's death on Dec. 18, 2022. Small was shot by Chatham police responding to a mental health crisis on March 7, 2021.
The officer, Adam Hahn, was cleared by ISP. Small was found not guilty of aggravated assault by reason of insanity in 2022.
'The people of Sangamon County must now engage in meaningful and sustained actions to address the issues related to these events," Kruse said. "The Massey Commission will guide the process to engage the community; to hear, respect and understand all voices; to begin a process to develop mutual trust; to repair fragmented and inequitable systems, and to ensure safety for those in need of help."
Civil rights attorney Ben Crump of Florida, who represents the Massey family, welcomed the creation of the commission.
"Efforts like these go beyond addressing past injustice," Crump said in a statement. "They help create a future where the relationship between law enforcement and the communities it serves is one of trust and mutual respect, and where every individual is treated with the fairness and dignity they deserve."
Those wishing to serve on the Massey Commission can apply at SangamonIL.Gov/MasseyCommission. The application deadline is Aug. 30.

title: New Mexican restaurant on track to open in Springfield; popular eatery expands menu
author: Natalie Morris
description: Owners of a popular food truck are on track to open a sit-down restaurant in Springfield.\n\nAlso, a popular eatery has reopened with an expanded menu.
content:
The Taco Joint is known already for its elevated food. Now its operators are looking to serve similar Mexican fusion fare in an elevated environment.
Ramona – Tacos & Mezcales is on track to open at 4403 Yucan Drive on Springfield's west side as a full-service, sit-down restaurant, in contrast to The Taco Joint's options of take out or al fresco dining.
'I'm not going to say (Ramona is) fancier (than The Taco Joint),' owner Hector Lopez said. 'But it is a newer, elevated version of what we do here.
'The plating, creativity will be more elevated. The cocktails will be elevated, smokey drinks. And we will do everything in-house. If it's on the plate, it's going to be made in-house.'
Fans of The Taco Joint will be able to find its signature tacos and burritos on the menu at Ramona. But Lopez said the majority of dishes will be new creations with flavors influenced by his birthplace, the Jalisco region of Mexico.
Mane Jerez, who oversees the kitchen at The Taco Joint, also will serve as head chef at Ramona.
Both establishments also share murals done by Springfield artist Spencer Stokes, who created the Dia de los Muertos-inspired murals at The Taco Joint. Stokes was commissioned for a 40-by-10-foot mural at Ramona that features a hummingbird. The diminutive bird, known in Spanish as Colibri, represents remembrance of past loved ones.
Ramona gets its name from Lopez's maternal grandmother.
'She had the spirit of cooking in her,' Lopez said, describing the inspiration behind his new establishment. 'And a lot of recipes in our home were from her.'
This new establishment marks the second opening for Lopez in the past eight months. The Taco Joint moved into a permanent home at 710 South Grand Ave. E. in December after operating from a shed on the same strip since 2017.
The fast casual establishment is known for blending the cultural lines dividing cuisines with items like the birria pizza and chorizo-chicken egg rolls. SJ-R readers voted the eatery the 2021 Readers Choice in the food truck category.
Reopened with expanded menu
The Foundry Pizza Kitchen reopened this week after a six-week kitchen revamp with a greatly expanded menu.
You'll still find the signature pizza and flatbreads, for which the establishment—located in Anvil & Forge Brewing & Distilling Company at 625 E. Washington St.—is known. But a new kitchen fryer opened the door for some more traditional tavern fare such as onion rings and mozzarella sticks, burgers and horseshoes, fry baskets and an array of sandwiches.
But while the menu sounds familiar, the technique isn't.
A scratch-made white cheddar-and-beer cheese sauce is featured in everything from the dipping sauce served with the house-made, fried pretzels to the macaroni and cheese, the hand-cut cheese fries to the horseshoe.
Sandwiches—everything from a Cubano to grilled cheese, smash burgers to hand-breaded fried chicken—are served on either scratch-made focaccia or brioche.
And for those who are looking for more than tavern staples, there is scratch-made gnocchi served with asparagus tips in a cream sauce and the house-smoked pork belly that comes with a sweet potato puree. Dessert selections include a skillet cookie a la mode and olive oil cake served with whipped mascarpone.
Kitchen hours are 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Friday and Saturday and 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Sunday. Inside seating is available.
The Foundry Pizza Kitchen first opened in December 2021.
Drive-through window coming soon
A run to Dolphin Food Market is about to get a little more convenient.
Construction has begun at the 2611 Adlai Stevenson Drive business to add a drive-through window. Owner Siad Zedan said daily operations won't be affected during construction.
Dolphin Food Market has been serving a selection of burgers, gyros, fried chicken and desserts from the address since April 2023. Zedan also owns Dolphin Chicken Fish and Grill at 409 North Grand Ave. E.
McDonald's renovations
The McDonald's at 2303 W. Monroe St. is getting a refresh, leaving the fast-food chain operating drive-through service only starting Monday.
The dining room will close at 3 p.m. Aug. 19 for a complete renovation. Construction work is expected to last two weeks, leaving the fast-food business operating only its drive-through window and mobile orders only during this time.
The renovated dining room will feature new decor and seating, as well as the removal of the self-serve drink station in favor of a new automatic system that fills drink orders. Franchise operator Kim Derringer said dine-in customers will still be able to get free refills at the counter.
Make-your-own Mimosa bar
Pease's at BUNN Gourmet is expanding the ways to treat yourself throughout the week.
Sunday brunch hours have been extended to 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. with options like the make-your-own Mimosa bar and a new chef salad on the menu.
Need a weekday pick-me-up? A new shared plate menu has been added for the weekday happy hour served 4 to 6 p.m. Monday through Friday at The Gables eatery. Features include a soft pretzel charcuterie board, peach barbecue pulled pork sliders and Margherita flatbread. Prices range from $14 to $18.
And for those who just can't wait to get their freak on, a paired down version of Pease's Freak Shake is now a permanent part of the menu. The Freak Shake Junior – like the original – comes as a 16-ounce treat, but with fewer garnishments. Cost is $9.99. Current flavors are Butterbeer and Raggedy Ann. Rotating flavors will be posted on Pease's social media.
Pease's at BUNN Gourmet is at 2941 Plaza Drive.
Not to be outdone with new temptations, the original Pease's store at 1701 S. State St. has added Dippin' Dots ice cream to its sweet treat lineup. Flavors include chocolate chip, cookie dough, rainbow, banana split, birthday cake, cookies and cream, and cotton candy. Cost is $5 for a 2.5-ounce cup.

title: Springfield-area teachers, staff get pay bump under new contract
author: Steven Spearie
description: The contract covers more than 300 certified staff members, including teachers, counselors, social workers, instructional coaches and more.
content:
The Ball-Chatham Board of Education last week unanimously approved a three-year teachers contract hammered out after four months of negotiation.
Ball-Chatham Education Association (BCEA) members ratified the agreement with an 85.4% favorable vote in late July.
The current contract expires Aug. 15, just after students come back for the school year.
Federal mediators were called in for the last couple of sessions.
The contract covers more than 300 certified staff members, including teachers, counselors, the head librarian, instructional coaches, instructional technology coordinators, speech and language pathologists, social workers, psychologists and the certified school nurse.
The district has over 4,600 students in pre-kindergarten through high school.
Here's a look at some key points of the contract:
Salaries
Certified staff members will receive a 4% raise and an average of a 1.87% step for a total average raise of 5.87% annually for the period of the contract.
Insurance
All staff members who elect insurance coverage will receive $950 in Year 1, $975 in Year 2 and $1,000 in Year 3 in Board dollars toward their premium. The $1,125,000 increase in Board dollars represents a 26.67% increase in Year 1 and up to a 33% increase by Year 3 of the contract, based on today's insurance offerings.
Compensation
The step scale was modified to provide greater equity and recognize the hard work of teachers at the beginning, middle and end of their careers. The scale for extracurricular and athletic stipend was raised in Years 2 and 3 of the contract, and the district will pay the employee TRS contribution for extracurricular/athletic activities.
Working conditions
Topics related to safety, time off, bereavement leave and professional development were addressed in the contract.
What the school board is saying
'A compromise was reached due to a commitment on all sides,' board president Tiffani Saunders said. 'This contract represents the board's commitment to responsible fiscal leadership of the district while also showing support and appreciation for the outstanding work of our teachers.'
What the teachers union is saying
"We're pleased that we were able to come to an agreement before school started so our teachers could start the year with a current contract, (but) it wasn't a very easy bargain," said Julie McAllister, the union president and a school counselor in the district. "The one thing we were disappointed that wasn't included in this contract was class size language (K-5). (The district) didn't follow their policy in multiple instances."

title: Springfield-area ice cream shop's special sweet treat wins award at Illinois State Fair
author: Claire Grant
description: The Olympics may be over, but it didn't stop a Chatham ice cream shop from taking home the gold at the Illinois State Fair.
content:
For a state fair debut, a local ice cream shop is taking home gold to Chatham.
Well, the Golden Abe award, that's for sure.
Chatham's own Scoop Du Jour is the winner of the 2024 Golden Abe Fantastic Fair Food Contest, a hotly contested race every year at the Illinois State Fair.
The winning item was a fair exclusive: the donut ice cream sandwich which consists of a sprinkle donut with a cookies and cream ice cream scoop wedged in between.
Co-owners Shannon McAuley and Fran Abbott said they were surprised to take home first place.
'We got a call back later and were told 'you're in the finals so come back to the stage' and we were like okay!' Abbott said. 'There was a second round, and we wound up winning the Golden Abe award and the sweet category. It's pretty exciting.'
McAuley has been a part of the state fair for decades and since the opening of the old-fashioned ice cream shop at 95 W Plummer Blvd. in Chatham, he knew he wanted to be a part of it.
'I've always wanted to work at the fair and I used to sell sodas when I was a kid, so I love the fair and been here almost every year of my life,' McAuley said. 'I'm a really big fair supporter so it was kind of a no brainer when they asked if they wanted us to be a vendor out here.'
The pair was originally offered a spot at the fair in 2023 but had to decline due to worker shortage. This year was different thanks to the help of locals last minute signing up to work with the ice cream shop at Adventure Village.
Because the donut ice cream sandwich was such a hit and score at the state fair, Abbott says it'll be added to the menu at their shop after the fair has come to an end so no matter what time of year it is, there'll be a taste of the fair right around the corner.
'We love Chatham as our community and we would love to see more local business out here,' Abbott said. 'We know how hard it is to stretch those employees and stretch your time and I'm just really happy we were able to do that this year.'

title: Flowers, cocktails, dogs and more: 5 things to do in the Springfield area
author: Claire Grant
description: The Illinois State Fair is in full swing. But there's still plenty to do around the Springfield area outside of the fair.
content:
With week two of the Illinois State Fair underway, thousands of visitors from across the state have come down to Springfield to see the world famous butter cow, rock out to Lil' Wayne, and try the new fair foods.
Wanting to take a break from walking around the carnival rides and see what else the capital city has to offer?
Check out these five things to do around the Springfield area this weekend.
Scheels Outdoor DockDogs
What: A day when all dogs are welcome no matter their shape, size and breed – every dog over six months old is welcome to Scheels sports park for DogDocks, a competitive dog jumping competition for airborne pups to jump for prizes. Whether you're considering signing up your dog for jumping in part of the competition or want to see the fanfare and animal companionship at the event as part of Scheel's weekend scheduled events, a break from the summer heat at the state fair can be found poolside by the pups.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
When: 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Friday, Saturday and Sunday.
Plants & Pints Beer Garden Plant Swap
What: After a successful first plant swap, Conn's Hospitality group has put together another swap for plants, pints and eco-friendly ideas. The swap requires plants be pest-free, rooted or cuttings of plants that are labeled. The swap will have plenty of cider, beer and cocktails to sip on while bartering cuttings and plant pieces. Alive on 66 will be selling plants for anyone to start their fauna and foliage journey, with Dabble Art of Springfield ready to help make terrariums.
When: 2 p.m. Sunday
Where: 7th Street Cidery, 503 S. Seventh St., Springfield
More: More information can be found online on a Facebook post for the event.
Smashing Pumpkins
What: We mentioned Lil' Wayne in the intro at the state fair but wanted to mention one other performer this week. An alternative rock band from Chicago popular in the '90s, Smashing Pumpkins is regarded as one of the best gothic rock bands. The band has continuously evolved since their creation in 1988 adding elements of gothic rock, heavy metal, grunge, psychedelic rock, progressive rock, shoegaze, dream pop, and electronica into their music.
When: 8 p.m. Friday
Where: Illinois State Fair Grandstand, 801 E. Sangamon Ave., Springfield
More: Tickets range from $55 to $125 before fees and can be purchased on TicketMaster.
Widow Von Du at Clique
What: Returning from the runway of RuPaul's Drag Race Season 12, Widow Von Du is performing at clique with local drag legend Mahogany Knight. The show stopping queens will be joined by drag performers Alicia Markstone, Lulu Stiletto, Tonia Mazzerati Steele, and Teresa Holiday.
When: 10:30 p.m. Saturday
Where: Clique, 411 E. Washington St., Springfield
More: This event is $10 general admission with a $25 VIP Meet and Greet with Widow. The Meet and Greet is an hour before the performance. Tickets can be purchased on the Clique website.
Blooms-n-Brews
What: Here's a good opportunity for insta-worthy photos and a breath of fresh air. Bring your friends and family for a fun day of picking your own zinnias and capturing beautiful photos among the vibrant blooms. The u-pick field will be filled with a variety of zinnias in all different colors, creating the perfect backdrop for your photos. After you've finished picking your zinnias and snapping photos, head over to Harvest Brew Coffee Shop for a refreshing strawberry lemonade slushie signature latte or the original and Ultimate Silo. While you're there, be sure to browse the selection of unique gifts and goodies for sale.
When: 3 p.m. Saturday
More: This event is no admission, and flowers are free – just don't take more than you can handle.

title: New school year, new laws: See how your child's classroom will look different this year
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: It's the start of a new school year and classrooms throughout Illinois could be looking different through these new laws.
content:
It's the start of a new school year and classrooms throughout Illinois could be looking different through new laws going into effect now and in the near future.
Whether it be a preschool classroom, all the way to college, here are some changes you can expect.
Native American education
Through legislation signed into law last year, public elementary and high schools will include a unit of Native American history this school year in their social studies curriculum.
Each school district is in-charge of actually creating the curriculum, but the Illinois State Board of Education will provide guidelines for how to develop it. Per the bill, the lessons should detail Native American contributions in "government and the arts, humanities, and sciences, as well as the contributions of Native Americans to the economic, cultural, social, and political development of their own nations and of the United States.'
Fentanyl education
Similarly, all public high school students will also receive instruction on the dangers of fentanyl. In every state-required health course, curriculum will cover the legal and illegal uses of fentanyl and explain the reasons why it is often laced with other drugs such as cocaine or heroin.
In 2022 alone, there were 3,261 fatal opioid overdoses in the state according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. A large share of these overdoses were caused by synthetic opioids like fentanyl.
Legacy admissions
Gov. JB Pritzker signed legislation on Aug. 9 that prohibits public colleges and universities from considering an applicant's relation to any past, current or prospective donors during the application process.
It also bars those schools from considering an applicant's 'legacy status,' or whether they are related to former students. The practice of legacy admissions came under fire at Ivy League schools like Harvard University particularly after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled against affirmative action in 2023.
Corporal punishment
Illinois has banned corporal punishment in public schools since 1994. That same policy has not been applied to private schools, yet a newly signed law will change that.
The law, which keeps nonpublic schools from slapping or paddling a student, placing a student in a physically painful position and the intentional infliction of bodily harm on a student; goes into effect on Jan. 1, 2025.
Intentional down-time
Aiming to reduce stress and keeping kids focused, another law will emphasize giving them down-time during the school week.
The new law requires all public school districts to offer relaxation time or relaxation activities for at least 20 minutes a week. The time would be used to emphasize self-care and downtime as a way to improve overall health.
Defibrillators on-hand
Legislation going into effect in January will require schools to have automated external defibrillators on the premises during both the school day and during extracurricular activities.
These types of defibrillators are used to revive someone after they suffer from a sudden cardiac arrest, such as during a heart attack. They are already required in fitness centers and gyms, including those in schools.

title: Opposing measures to expand or limit abortion access in Nebraska make November's ballot
author: Maya Marchel Hoff
description: Voters in Nebraska will decide to broaden or limit abortion access in the state after two dueling measures made it onto the November ballot Friday.
content:
The state's set of conflicting initiatives are the first to pop up since the overturn of Roe v. Wade in 2022.
Show Caption
LINCOLN - Voters in Nebraska will get to decide if abortion access should be broadened or limited in the state after two opposing measures made it onto the November ballot on Friday.
While a handful of states will see abortion on the ballot, Nebraska will be the first state to have competing measures since the overturn of Roe V. Wade in 2022 after Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen announced the certification on Friday of two ballot measures: one aiming to enshrine the state's current 12-week abortion ban in the Nebraska Constitution, and the other seeking to extend abortion access up to fetal viability.
'I applaud our county election offices and election workers who are working hard to process several petitions and meet important election deadlines,' Evnen said in a statement. 'Barring any legal challenges, this November general election ballot will host two ballot measures that appear in direct conflict with each other, which could be the first time this has happened in Nebraska's history.'
The measure sponsored by Protect Our Rights, a coalition of local reproductive health rights groups, would enshrine the right to abortion when it is 'needed to protect the life or health of the pregnant patient,' as well extend abortion access up to fetal viability, which is typically around 24 weeks.
The other measure backed by the anti-abortion group Protect Women and Children aims to enshrine Nebraska's current 12-week ban in the state constitution in opposition to the Protect Our Rights initiative. Since its launch in March, the measure has received backing from conservative lawmakers in the state, including Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, who has contributed more than $2 million to the petition.
Both campaigns collected record-breaking amounts of signatures for ballot initiatives in the state, over 136,000 of which were valid for each measure, according to the secretary of state. To qualify for the ballot, each group had to collect signatures from roughly 123,000, or 10% of the state's registered voters, and signatures from 5% in at least 38 of Nebraska's 93 counties.
The winning measure must garner at least 35% of the vote this fall. If both measures surpass that threshold, the one that receives the most votes in November will pass.
Nebraska is the latest state to certify abortion-related ballot measures, following Missouri and Arizona, which put their own on the ballot earlier this month. But not all initiatives have seen the same success. Abortion rights supporters in Arkansas were on track to get their own measure on the ballot but were blocked by an Arkansas Supreme Court decision Thursday ruling that the measure is invalid because of a paperwork error.

title: 'Confrontational and reactive': UIS outlines expectations for men's and women's golf coach
author: Bill Welt
description: The UIS golf coach says in a statement he looks forward to addressing concerns and making himself a better coach
content:
The University of Illinois Springfield administration conveyed its concerns and expectations to men's and women's golf coach Michael Leotta in a redacted July 24 document obtained by the State Journal-Register through a Freedom of Information Act request.
Anonymous allegations surfaced against Leotta in a 2aDays.com report on July 9 before a former player supported those claims in a subsequent State Journal-Register article on July 30.
The allegations ranged from verbal and emotional abuse to reckless driving.
Preseason poll: Vote for the preseason top high school golfer in the Springfield area for 2024
UIS vice chancellor for student affairs Jamarco Clark addresses Leotta with the redacted heading, 'Letter of Expectations regarding Conduct,' in the two-page document.
The opening paragraph alludes to conversations on May 31 and adds that Leotta's conduct led to a UIS Access and Equity Office finding, along with concerns of 'other behaviors that do not align with university expectations or the Code of Conduct.'
Clark then lists 'detailed expectations for your position moving forward,' but those are redacted. The university declined to comment on the AEO finding, citing that it is a personnel matter.
Leotta's salary as the men's and women's golf coach was $42,892 before Aug. 15, and the university said that appointment notices are being administratively processed for the upcoming academic year.
Leotta took over the UIS men's and women's golf teams in 2021 after previously serving as an assistant from 2013-16. He also acted as head coach at Wittenberg University for two years before returning to UIS.
Leotta emailed a statement to the SJ-R.
"Student-athlete experience has always been of the utmost importance to me,' Leotta said. 'It is always disappointing when any student-athlete doesn't have a positive experience. I have always prioritized and provided the appropriate resources to ensure student-athlete well-being both mentally and physically.
'I continue to look forward to addressing any concerns and making myself a better coach to help enhance the experience of our student-athletes and continue to elevate this program.'
'They're still here': Lanphier football stays on track with new interim head coach
The document delves deeper into Leotta's interpersonal skills, professional behavior and interactions with players on the ensuing page, to an extent.
'Behaviors such as raising your voice, engaging in arguments, and using intimidating language are unacceptable and cannot continue,' Clark says in the document. 'It is crucial that you treat others with respect and maintain professionalism in all interactions.
'While you are recognized for your knowledge, there have been concerns about being confrontational and reactive. It is expected that you take responsibility for managing your behavior, interactions, and reactions.'
Clark later adds in the document, 'You are expected to all times comply with all university policies and procedures. This includes specifically the University Non-Discrimination Policy. Your recent conduct was the subject of an internal investigation that led to a finding. This is a direct reflection of your judgment and decision making.'
Clark took over as the interim athletic director following Laura Liesman's resignation in November. Mike Hermann began as the new AD in June.

title: Earthquake reported off the coast of Portugal Monday morning measuring 5.4
author: Max Hauptman
description: An earthquake measuring 5.4 on the Richter scale was recorded off the coast of Portugal early Monday morning and was felt in Lisbon.
content:
An earthquake rattled southern Portugal Monday morning, according to the United States Geological Survey.
The earthquake, which registered a magnitude of 5.4, was recorded at 5:11 a.m. local time off the coast of Portugal, about 32 miles west of the town of Sines.
Data from the USGS showed that the earthquake was recorded at a depth of almost 11 miles.
Earthquake felt in Lisbon, throughout Portugal's coast
No injuries were reported, but light to moderate shaking was felt up and down Portugal's coast, including in the capital city of Lisbon
Portugal's Institute of the Sea and Atmosphere reported that at least four aftershocks of minimal intensity had been recorded.

title: Rarely before seen Abraham Lincoln-related images now available to public. What to know
author: Steven Spearie
description: More than 1,000 high-resolution photos connected to Abraham Lincoln are now available online. The images have previously only been seen by researchers.
content:
More than 1,000 high-resolution photos connected to Abraham Lincoln are now available online through an initiative by the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum.
Most of the photos in 'Picturing Lincoln' have never been online before and only available to researchers.
Here's what to know.
Are all of the photos of Abraham Lincoln?
According to the library, 129 of the photos are of Lincoln. Some are from his time in Springfield, and some are from his presidency.
Almost 200 of the photos are of Lincoln's Tomb in Oak Ridge Cemetery, including some of Lincoln's coffin when it was unearthed during a construction project in 1901.
Dozens of photos are related to Lincoln's assassination in 1865, his funeral and the execution of the conspirators who plotted his death.
Are there other Lincoln family members represented?
There are also photos of Robert Lincoln, the only son of Lincoln and Mary Todd Lincoln to survive past his teenage years, as well as Lincoln's grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
What about Lincoln's animals and pets?
Old Bob, Lincoln's carriage horse, is represented in an 1865 photo with then owner John Flynn. Old Bob was part of the cortège preceding Lincoln's funeral in Springfield,
There is also a photo of the Lincoln family dog, Fido.
What is Daniel Day-Lewis doing in the collection?
Oscar-winning actor Daniel Day-Lewis is pictured with historian and author Doris Kearns Goodwin in the vault beneath the presidential library in 2010.
Day-Lewis was then researching the president who he played in Steven Spielberg's 2012 film, "Lincoln." The film was based in part on Goodwin's 2005 book 'Team of Rivals.'
What's the resolution of the photos?
The images have a resolution of 600 dpi (dots per inch).
What are they saying about the photos?
'Abraham Lincoln's legacy belongs to the world, so the whole world should be able to see these images. They show the highs and lows of President Lincoln's life, remind us of the nation's deep mourning at his death, and give us a glimpse into the lives of descendants he would never see," Christina Shutt, executive director of the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum, said.
Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias said, "these photos represent a virtual treasure trove that tells a rich and vibrant story of one of our nation's most influential leaders."
Where can I see the images?
Go to the Illinois State Library's website.

title: 2 North Carolina high school football players killed in 'devastating' ATV accident
author: Saleen Martin
description: Calling the boys "young, vibrant lives," Transylvania County Schools Superintendent Lisa Fletcher said this is a reminder of how precious life is.
content:
Two North Carolina teenagers were killed in an ATV crash over the weekend, leaving community members reeling with grief.
The two teens, Layne Jones and Jayden Reynaldo, were killed Saturday in a four-wheeler crash in Transylvania County, a spokesperson from Transylvania County Schools confirmed to USA TODAY Tuesday afternoon.
The teens were driving a 2015 Polaris sportsman four-wheeler, tried to go around a curve and ran off the road, hitting a tree, FOX Carolina reported.
Transylvania County Schools Superintendent Lisa Fletcher said in a statement posted online that the boys died in a "devastating accident."
'Young, vibrant lives'
The teens went to Rosman High School. Photos of the two shared on the school's Facebook Sunday showed the boys wearing football uniforms. In a press release Sunday, Fletcher called the boys 'young, vibrant lives,' and said their passing is a reminder of how precious life is.
Counseling has been set up at the school, and Fletcher encouraged community members to lean on one another.
'Please keep the families of our dear students in your thoughts and prayers,' Fletcher wrote.
Community rallies around family, offers condolences
Community members changed their social media display photos in honor of the teens, including the Transylvania County Sheriff's Office.
'On behalf of Sheriff Owenby and the men and women of the Transylvania County Sheriff's Office we offer our condolences, sympathies and regards to the families and friends of these two young men,' the sheriff's office wrote. 'Our prayers will be with you all during this difficult time.'
Other schools in the area also offered condolences online.
'We extend our heartfelt condolences to the Rosman community and football team as they mourn the devastating loss of two young lives,' shared Franklin High School. 'Our thoughts and prayers are with Rosman High School during this difficult time.'
Community members plan to wear orange at Friday's football game in honor of the teens."Come support our school and remember Jayden and Layne by helping us ORANGE OUT our stadium at Friday Night's game against North Henderson," RHMS Cheer shared in a post, which was later shared on the high school's Facebook page. "These boys will surely be missed and our team will need your support. Let's do this for our boys! GOOOOOOOOO Tigers!"

title: Labor Day in Springfield: What's open, what's closed and when's the parade
author: Steven Spearie
description: You ready for the holiday weekend? Here's what's open and what's closed on Monday. And a look at where you can go for Labor Day parades.
content:
Two central Illinois communities will renew their long-standing Labor Day parades.
The Greenview Civic Improvement Association will put on the town's 55th Annual Labor Day Celebration, including its parade, at 10 a.m. Monday.
In Pana, the theme for its 91st annual Labor Day Parade, billed as "the largest parade on Labor Day in downstate Illinois," is 'Family Game Night." It steps off from Second and Poplar streets at 10 a.m.
The Springfield and Central Illinois Trades & Labor Council will hold its Labor Day Picnic at the Illinois AFL-CIO, 534 S. Second St., at 5:30 p.m. on Sept. 6.
Monday is a federal holiday, meaning banks and post offices will be closed and there will be no mail delivery.
Government buildings
Federal buildings and courts, state of Illinois offices and courts, the Sangamon County buildings and courts and the Municipal Building, along with Lincoln Library and Oak Ridge Cemetery offices, will be closed.
Schools
Springfield School District 186 administrative offices are closed Monday and there are no classes. The board of education meeting will be held at 6:30 p.m. Tuesday.
There are no classes at the University of Illinois Springfield, Lincoln Land Community College or Midwest Institute of Technology. Offices at all three campuses are also closed.
Public transportation
Sangamon Mass Transit District buses will not be running Monday. That also includes ACCESS paratransit service. SMTD administrative offices will be closed.
What is open in Springfield on Monday?
Tourist sites, such as the Lincoln Home, the Lincoln Tomb, the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum and the Dana-Thomas House are all open during normal hours on Monday.

title: DCFS worker from Springfield was 'doing her job protecting kids' on day of fatal stabbing
author: Steven Spearie
description: Deidre (Graham) Silas had been called to investigate "a report of abuse and neglect" in Thayer, in southern Sangamon County, on Jan. 4, 2022.
content:
A former first assistant in the Sangamon County State's Attorney's office said Deidre (Graham) Silas was "just doing her job protecting kids" when the child protection specialist was fatally stabbed in a home on the southern tip of Sangamon County on Jan. 4, 2022.
Benjamin Howard Reed, 35, is accused of killing the Illinois Department of Children and Family Services worker.
Reed's trial, delayed earlier this year, began in Sangamon County court on Monday with opening statements and several witnesses, including Reed's mother, Jennifer Askins, who admitted through tears to calling police after Reed told her "he lost it" and killed Silas.
Reed, sporting a long black beard and wearing a striped jail-issue uniform, sat at the defense table and appeared to make little eye contact with witnesses. Reed did not speak at the trial.
Several of Silas' family members were in court along with some of her former DCFS workers.
Askins testified that Reed and his wife, Amanda, and her four children stopped by her apartment in Decatur late in the afternoon of Jan. 4, 2022.
Askins said Reed didn't say who he killed, but his wife told her it was "the DCFS lady."
"I almost dropped my grandbaby," Askins said in response to what Reed did.
Askins testified she told Reed and his wife that they couldn't stay at the apartment. Both went to HSHS St. Mary's Hospital where Reed was getting treated for a knife cut.
Askins then called police and told them where Reed was headed.
Earlier, Silas' former supervisor, Jamie Bramblett, testified that Silas was called in to investigate "a report of abuse and neglect" at the home in Thayer, a village of about 700 people 22 miles south of Springfield, where Reed resided, though the complaint wasn't about Reed or his children.
Since the environment was a concern, Bramblett said Silas had a responsibility to assess all six children living in the home, including Reed's.
Bramblett said there were "no plans to remove children" from the home that day.
In the opening statement, Derek Dion, who is now with the Office of the State's Attorneys Appellate Prosecutor but is trying the case with Kendra Hansel, said that Reed's wife told Silas she couldn't see her kids. That's when Reed armed himself with a knife, Dion said, and stabbed Silas 43 times.
Reed also struck Silas in the head with "a shot hammer," Dion said.
The autopsy photos, with forensic pathologist Dr. Nathaniel Patterson narrating, were viewed in open court.
In a brief opening remark, defense attorney Mark Wykoff said "the only question for the court was what was (Reed's) mental state at the commission of the crime."
The defense could call Terry Killian, a psychologist, as an expert witness to speak to that mental state.
The state has filed a motion indicating that rebuttal witnesses have been contacted to match Killian's potential testimony.

title: Pana football puts Rench in Carlinville plans: defense leads Panthers to key SCC win
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Pana defenders Cash Lynch and Tyler Rench created plenty of havoc for Carlinville's offense in a South Central Conference Week 2 matchup.
content:
PANA — The Pana defense suffocated the Carlinville offense for much of the Panthers' 26-14 South Central Conference football victory on Friday.
The Carlinville run game was limited to 56 yards, one week after the Cavaliers produced 215 in a win over Litchfield. And though the Cavs' passing game totaled 184 yards at Brummett Field on Friday, Pana intercepted Carlinville quarterback Noah Byots three times.
Panthers' junior Cash Lynch had two of them and had a potential third go right through his hands. Hayden Blackwell came down with the other.
Fellow junior Tyler Rench was seemingly in every defensive stop for Pana. The 6-foot-3 defensive end sniffed out the Carlinville run game and helped hold Carlinville to nine rushing yards in the first half.
'I can't sing (Rench's) praises enough: he flies around, he's ready, willing to go out and block people and then dishing it out on defense,' Pana senior running back Isaiah Harbert said. 'That mentality is what we need in every player.'
Pana opened the scoring on a fourth-and-10 from the Carlinville 28-yard line. Quarterback Wyatt Kile found tight end in the back of the end zone for a touchdown.
Two possessions later, Byots threw the first of his three picks. Blackwell took the ball to the CHS 7-yard line. Two plays later, Harbert punched in a 1-yard touchdown run to give Pana a 14-0 lead midway through the second quarter.
Brotherly advice
Harbert finished with 98 yards on 18 carries with a pair of TDs.
Pana's offensive game plan, Harbert said, 'was to out-physical them: let our (offensive line) do the job and I just follow them.
'They do all the work. If I could give my touchdowns to them, I would every time.'
Harbert remembers the advice his brother gave him to help on second efforts. Ian Harbert was a running back for Pana and graduated in 2018.
'It's just always keep moving forward,' Harbert said. 'My brother Ian taught me that, no matter what, you fall forward.'
Lynch also has plenty of lessons from his older brother. Max Lynch was the Pana QB and graduated in 2023.
'Try as hard as you can,' Lynch said he remembers Max saying. 'Don't ever feed into anyone ever doubting you. Always work hard; work your best.'
Pana Cashes in on defense
In the second half, Carlinville found the end zone with a 33-yard pass from Byots to Triston Thompson, cutting Pana's lead in half. The Panthers responded on the next drive with Harbert's second 1-yard score, capping off a nine-play drive.
Any momentum Carlinville gained was lost from there. A Byots interception led to Lynch's 2-yard touchdown catch for a 26-7 lead. On the first play of the next Cavaliers' drive, Byots was again picked off by Lynch.
'Every day in practice, our secondary works so hard and it's a huge improvement from last year,' Rench said. 'Last year, our secondary was scary (but) this year, they've really stepped it up and they know how to cover.'
Carlinville's best success came on medium-range passes. Byots completed 20 passes — including eight in a row — and finished with 184 yards. Mason Gilpin had eight catches for 62 yards while Thompson made eight receptions for 66.
'Higgins and I have very similar philosophies: we take what they give you and we were trying to play games by jumping in and out,' Carlinville coach Chad Easterday said. 'We had some success a couple of times but shot ourselves in the foot a couple of times in some very, very key areas that cost us the game.
'We didn't help ourselves there a lot, we gave them one short field and, if you take that score off the board, we've got a ballgame going on here.'

title: New state of the art luxury car facility coming to downtown Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: A new luxury car center is officially in the works in downtown Springfield after construction started over the weekend.
content:
A new luxury car center is officially in the works in downtown Springfield.
Right across from the Isringhausen BMW center and city Amtrak station, Isringhausen Imports of Illinois started construction of a new state of the art Porsche Center.
The new facility is an investment into the local community and economy through architecture and employment, dealer principal Geoff Isringhausen said.
'Investing into our community, and specifically our downtown, has historically been one of Isringhausen's top priorities,' Isringhausen said. 'For over 40 years, we have continued to call downtown Springfield our home. … We pride ourselves on delivering world class experiences to those that trust us with their automotive journey while also focusing our investments on the local community.'
Porsche Sales and Service will continue to operate at the current location of 229 E. Jefferson St. with an anticipated transition to the new facility slated for the end of 2025. The new location will feature the Porsche corporate architecture concept 'Destination Porsche."
According to Isringhausen, the new facility will have a customer cafe, virtual reality imaging for ordering new vehicles and more features.
Isringhausen Imports, a Springfield brand delivering luxury cars across America, has previously won the Porsche Premier Dealer award and is frequently ranked among the top 25 Porsche centers in the nation for customer service.
According to Isringhausen, the new building will cement the company's reputation as one of the leading Porsche centers in the country, as well as continue to support local customers around central Illinois.
'This new exclusive Porsche Center is a continuation of a dream that began over 40 years ago, to provide delightful experiences to our customers, and to share our automotive passion with the world,' Isringhausen said. 'We are excited for this chapter of our story and look forward to welcoming our customers to the new facility.'

title: Former Springfield police sergeant cited in crash that seriously injures two people
author: Steven Spearie
description: A former Springfield Police sergeant was cited in a crash with a motorcycle that seriously injured two people by Lake Springfield. Here's what we know.
content:
A former Springfield Police sergeant was cited in a crash with a motorcycle that seriously injured two people by Lake Springfield around 9:20 p.m. Thursday.
Michael Egan, 50, who had just retired from the police department, was ticketed for failure to yield the right of way, according to a release from the Illinois State Police.
Deputy Chief Sara Pickford of Springfield Police said the on-duty lieutenant at the time, Lt. Grant Barksdale, contacted state police to conduct the traffic crash and a DUI investigation. Pickford said three ISP troopers arrived at the scene at 10:08 p.m.
An ISP spokesperson did not immediately indicate whether Egan was given a field sobriety test.
ISP contacted the Sangamon County State's Attorney's Office and additional charges against Egan may be filed pending toxicology report results.
State's Attorney John Milhiser, reached Friday afternoon, said the investigation is "ongoing and will be completed as expeditiously as possible."
Pickford said Egan's last day of employment with the department was Thursday. Egan had 20 years of experience with the department and was promoted to sergeant in 2022, according to a State Journal-Register file story.
An internal investigation was started by SPD "to ensure that all policies and procedures were adhered to by Springfield Police personnel at the scene," according to a release provided by SPD.
'Both and active and retired law enforcement officers must be held to the same standards to maintain public trust and uphold the integrity of the Springfield Police Department,' SPD Chief Ken Scarlette said.
Injured in the crash were Trevor Hopkins and Chelsey Farley both from Springfield. A family member of Farley's provided the names.
According to ISP, Egan was traveling northbound on East Lake Shore Drive and made a left turn in front of Hopkins and Farley and the motorcycle struck the side of Egan's vehicle. Both Hopkins and Farley were ejected from the motorcycle.
Pickford said officers who arrived on the scene minutes after the crash began to render aid to Hopkins and Farley.
East Lake Shore Drive was shut down following the crash and reconstruction.

title: New buffet style restaurant opens in Springfield while popular chicken, fish eatery reopens
author: Natalie Morris
description: A new buffet style restaurant has officially opened in Springfield. Meanwhile, a popular chicken, fish eatery has officially reopened.
content:
Steve Zhao established two fast casual brands since the pandemic turned the dining industry on its head. But now the local restaurateur is betting that the public is ready to eat out again with the recent opening of Feast Buffet.
'Everybody misses dining out,' said Zhao, managing partner of MacArthur Boulevard Place LLC, which owns the new, all-you-can-eat establishment at 3101 S. MacArthur Blvd. 'Over the (Labor Day) weekend we had a big, big group.
'It just confirms, a lot of people want to come out again.'
And the Feast Buffet tempts customers to do just that with more than 100 selections on the smorgasbord. There is an array of Chinese and Japanese dishes, two dozen sushi selections and a hibachi grill station.
For those inclined more to home cooking, there is brisket, ham and sausage with side dishes like macaroni and cheese and fries. Steak joins the dinner lineup. Top it off with a fruit and salad bar, as well as desserts made in-house.
And more is still planned. The coming months will see the addition of soft serve ice cream and bottled beer, as well as the roll out of a full arcade known as Funkiddo.
Feast Buffet is open from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily. Dine in, take out only. A set cost is in place for lunch and dinner dine-in service. Adults eat for $13.99 for lunch, $17.99 for dinner. Seniors get a $1 discount off the adult price. Children prices are $8.99 for kids 8 to 11 and $6.99 for kids 3-7. Children two and younger eat for free.
Take-out prices are $6.99 a pound for lunch and $8.99 a pound for dinner.
Phone: 217-971-4031. The Feast Buffet accepts reservations.
Zhao's fast casual brands include two Hibachi Madness locations at 4318 Wabash Ave. and 2811 N. Dirksen Parkway, as well as Bowl Plus at 1745 Wabash Ave. Neither brand is owned by the Feast Buffet's parent company.
Springfield diners associated Zhao with all-you-can-eat buffet spreads long before the fast-casual concept was coined. Zhao once owned the Hibachi Grill & Supreme Buffet at 2309 S. MacArthur Blvd. He sold his interest in the restaurant in 2018. The new owners unexpectedly closed the business last month.
Long-waited reopening
MJ's Fish and Chicken Express reopened Wednesday in Enos Park after a two-year hiatus from offering regular operating hours.
'It feels really, really good,' Margaret Taylor, whose given name provides the 'M' in MJ's Fish and Chicken Express. She co-owns the business with her husband, Jerome. 'We really missed our customers, seeing our customers.'
The restaurant at 716 E. Enos St. is open from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday with dine in and carry out service. Phone: 217-572-0257.
Seafood options include fried walleye, as well as choice of fried or grilled catfish and shrimp. A variety of combo platters mix all of the above options. Party wings are the sole chicken option on the regular menu, but yet-to-be-established daily features will include fried chicken dinners.
Sandwich selections include hamburgers and pork tenderloin, either fried or grilled. The appetizer menu features fried okra, fried cauliflower, onion rings and clam strips. Side dishes include fries, green beans, coleslaw, potato salad, macaroni and cheese and greens with cornbread.
It has been a decade since Jerome began frying for the public in 2014 when he opened MJ's Fish and Chicken Express as a food trailer at 11th Street and South Grand Avenue East. Three years later, MJ's found a permanent home in the Enos Park address when the Taylors purchased the former Suzi Q's building with the help of tax increment financing money from the city.
Sandwich shop reopening
Toasty-Subs is poised to open in its new home at 2120 S. MacArthur Blvd. eight months after a burst water pipe shut down the sandwich shop's operation across the street at 2025 S. MacArthur Blvd.
Navee Singh, who co-owns Toasty-Subs, said the business is on-track to open Sept. 10, although that date could be pushed back a day or two depending on the results of a final city inspection Monday.
'We are excited and cannot wait to see our regulars and take pride in making something that's exciting and tasty,' Singh wrote in a text.
Toasty-Subs is announcing its return with a 'grand offer,' rather than a grand opening celebration.
Discounts Tuesday feature the entire sandwich menu for $5 each and soups and salads for $3, as well as unlimited refills on soft drinks.
The sandwich discounts amount to roughly half price whether you are craving Toasty-Subs' Italian Stallion or the Classic Cubano, the Bombay or the vegetarian Buffalo Cauliflower.
Hours are 10:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday through Saturday and 10:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Sundays. Phone: 217-679-5459.
The new location doesn't represent a big move – only a block south of its former home. But the new address does mean more space for seating, parking and back of house, as well as locating the eatery directly across from Hy-Vee.
The building was previously home to Fink's Cleaners.
Toasty-Subs opened at 2025 S. MacArthur Blvd. in 2020.
Outdoor patio coming soon
Construction is set to begin at Charro Mexican Restaurant for an all-weather outdoor patio.
The al fresco dining spot, once completed, will add 30 seats to the Whitney Business Park eatery.
Owner Ezequiel Camacho said the concrete pad will be poured on the east side of the building at 2500 Sunrise Drive and will feature a retractable awning. The design will be similar to that of the Charro Mexican Restaurant in Decatur.
The project is estimated at $41,500, according to the building permit filed with the city.
Construction is not expected to affect daily operations at the establishment.
Charro Mexican Restaurant opened in the former home of Springfield Char House in May.
Temporary closure
The Taco Bell at 731 Adlai Stevenson Drive is expected to be closed for the entire month of September for extensive renovation work.
A representative with the Peoria-based franchise operator LucWork Enterprises said the goal is to reopen the fast food establishment in early October.

title: From Pulitzer Prize winners to Grammy winners: 11 notable UIS alumni
author: Steven Spearie
description: An American Idol. A Pulitzer Prize winner. A Tiananmen Square participant. Meet these University of Illinois Springfield alumni.
content:
University of Illinois Springfield students are back in class, and you never know who will go on to accomplish big time things once they graduate.
For instance, some of the school's most noteworthy alumni range from a Grammy winner to Pulitzer Prize recipients.
The list includes former students from Sangamon State University, which was established in 1969. SSU merged with the University of Illinois system in 1995.
The school considers "anyone who took a class to be an alum," said UIS spokesman Blake Wood. The list includes traditional undergraduates, graduate students and others who took classes.
Here's our list in no particular order:
A real 'American Idol'
A 2022 graduate (B.A. in exercise science), Hannah Nicolaisen won the Atrium national singing contest earlier this summer.
Most notably, the Montgomery, Ala.-based Nicolaisen was a Top 20 finisher on Season 21 of "American Idol," when judge Lionel Richie told Nicolaisen her "unique voice...is what you pray for in this business.'
Along with her singing acumen, Nicolaisen was a highly-regarded hitter/middle hitter for UIS volleyball for three seasons.
Producer behind 'Juno'
A Lanphier High School product, Russell Smith earned a bachelor's degree in political science from 1974 to 1977. He also studied at Eastern Illinois University, where his roommate, John Malkovich, became his future partner (along with Lianne Halfon) in a production company, Mr. Mudd.
The one-time executive director of Steppenwolf Theatre Company in Chicago would go on to produce "Juno," "Of Mice and Men," "The Man in the Iron Mask," "The Libertine" and "The Perks of Being A Wallflower."
According to IMDb, Smith, 69, also served as executive producer for "Ripley's Game" and "Which Way Home."
Fox News political commentator
Dana Perino has been a political commentator for Fox News since leaving the White House, where she served as President George W. Bush's press secretary from 2007 to 2009.
The author of three books, central Illinois viewers got an early glimpse of Perino when she served as the statehouse reporter for WCIA-TV.
Perino is a graduate of the university's Public Affairs Reporting (PAR) program.
Chicago Bulls front office person
A former Prairie Star hoopster, 2012 UIS graduate Chigozie Umeadi (bachelor's in business administration) is the director of basketball operations for the Chicago Bulls.
Umeadi also serves as general manager for the Bulls' NBA G League affiliate, the Windy City Bulls. Prior to that, the Bensenville, Ill., product worked for eight years as an associate manager in Basketball Strategies and Analytics with the NBA.
Umeadi played in 73 games for the Prairie Stars over three seasons.
Former Illinois congresswoman
Cheri Bustos (PAR program graduate) served five terms in the U.S. House of Representatives, representing the 17th congressional district in the northwest part of Illinois.
Before beginning her public service, Bustos was a reporter and editor for the Quad-City Times. Her father, the late Gene Callahan, was a reporter for the SJ-R, who went on to work for Major League Baseball.
Bustos is now a consultant for Mercury Public Affairs, which has an office at Sixth and Monroe streets. In February, she will receive the university's Alumni Achievement Award.
A soccer MVP
Bill Becher was a member of the first at SSU men's soccer team to win the NAIA national championship, in 1986. The All-American from St. Louis was named the NAIA national tournament Most Valuable Player.
Becher played professionally for several indoor and outdoor teams. He scored over 200 goals with the Harrisburg Heat as part of the National Professional Soccer League. He also played for the St. Louis Ambush.
He also had a long coaching career with the Harrisburg City Islanders.
Singer behind 'Don't Worry, Be Happy'
Bobby McFerrin, the writer and singer of 'Don't Worry, Be Happy," attended SSU in 1975-76 as part of its Individual Option Program.
McFerrin played at several different venues around Springfield, most notably with guitarist Greg Pasenko.
"Don't Worry, Be Happy" won Song of the Year and Record of the Year at the 1989 Grammy Awards. Now 74, McFerrin has worked through the years with Herbie Hancock, Chick Corea and Yo-Yo Ma, among other musicians.
'The diva of dish'
One of four PAR alumni to have won a Pulitzer Prize, Deborah "Deb" (Singer) Peterson had a celebrated reporting career at the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. A gossip column in her later years earned her the nickname "the diva of dish."
Peterson, a Chicago native, was at the Kansas City Star when she helped cover the collapse of the Kansas City Hyatt Hotel skywalks in 1981.
Peterson was also an editor, home interiors writer, movie reviewer and feature writer.
Tiananmen Square participant
A PAR alum in 1991, Wenguang Huang participated in the student pro-democracy movement in Tiananmen Square in 1989 and shortly thereafter left his home for Springfield.
Huang's 2012 memoir 'The Little Red Guard' chronicles his growing up in northern China during the 1970s. His writing has appeared in the Paris Review, Harper's, the Christian Science Monitor, the Chicago Tribune and the Asia Literary Review.
He was the commencement speaker at UIS in 2012.
Prairie Stars' first MLB pick
Pitcher Andrew Dean became the first Prairie Stars' player selected in the Major League Baseball in 2021 draft.
Dean was drafted by the San Diego Padres in the 18th round and got to Class A before being released.
Two other UIS players are playing in independent baseball leagues: Quinn Gudaitis, a 16th-round pick of the Detroit Tigers in 2022 and Zion Pettigrew, an undrafted free agent.
The man in charge of the Chicago Tribune
Mitch Pugh, the executive editor of the Chicago Tribune since 2021, is a Riverton native who got his start at the SJ-R as a part-time sports writer.
A 1998 graduate with a bachelor's degree in English, Pugh was executive editor at The Post and Courier of Charleston, S.C., when it was awarded the 2015 Pulitzer Prize award for public service.
In addition to Peterson and Pugh, two other PAR alumni, Trif Alatzas (1989) and Kathy Best (1990), have won Pulitzer Prizes.

title: Springfield wine shop celebrates 30 years by popping corks for a cause
author: Claire Grant
description: This Springfield business celebrated 30 years of being open with a fundraiser to give back to the community.
content:
There's a place in Springfield serving drinks and laid back, French bistro vibes just a walk from Washington Park on the south side of town. The large emporium of spirits and wines is The Corkscrew on Chatham Road, a quiet and quaint spot for a drink after work.
Their latest pairing? Three dozen flights of wine and fundraising for a good cause.
To celebrate the store's 30th anniversary, husband-wife owners David and Danielle Anderson held an event Aug. 31 to celebrate the milestone with food from Maldaners and over 35 wines for tasting in the back lounge of the store.
All of the proceeds of the event went toward Autism Support of Central Illinois, a charity close to David Anderson's heart.
'We have a granddaughter who is autistic, and that is why we chose the Autism Support Center of Illinois as our beneficiary this year," Anderson said.
The Autism Program of Illinois helps serve and support people with autism and their families through a coordinated network of providers.
While the duo bought the business in 2016 from original owner Geoffrey Bland, both Andersons have been part of the store since 1994.
It's a lucrative business the couple has managed for three decades now, and Anderson says the key to it is the mix of customer care and wine knowledge their employees have picked up over the years.
'We are built on customer service and that is what we set apart from big box stores,' Anderson said. 'Our people have gained wine knowledge over a period of years working here so yeah, I'd say our customers like the service. What we hear a lot is people appreciate the ownership presence and that makes a big difference.'
Anderson was able to walk around the store and point out one by one the most popular wine by continent in the store: from North American chardonnay to South American carmenere.
Along with gaining knowledge over the years, Anderson said the other big change has been the rise of mobile t-go orders, especially during the pandemic.
'Nobody could go out to drink at a bar or at a restaurant because the restaurants weren't open,' Anderson said. 'We were an essential business, and we were open the whole time. We did an awful lot of delivery and curbside – for three months it was just Danielle and I. … I hate to say it, but it was good.'

title: Sangamon County Fair Fall Festival among 5 things to do this weekend
author: Claire Grant
description: Still looking for something to do this weekend? We have you covered with these five events around the Springfield area.
content:
What's on your autumn bucket list? While it may still feel a little warm outside right now, fall is quickly approaching and there's plenty going on in the capital city.
From fall festivals to a grand ball sending you back in time, there's plenty of things to experience this weekend.
Her Majesty's Regency Ball
What: Dearest Readers, the town is abuzz with the latest gossip, and so it is our honor to impart to you: The Queen herself is hosting a grand ball, and you are invited. This once-in-a-lifetime evening will be full of delightful food, drinks, dancing, and activities, in what will surely be the event of the season.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
More: The event is 21+ and meant to be a dress up ball in regency wear. Tickets are available online for $30 each before tax on the Pasfield House website.
Beyond the stage at the Pillsbury Factory
What: Go Beyond the Stage with your Illinois Symphony Orchestra at the Pillsbury Factory. Listen live to the symphony's percussion trio and piano trio as they perform in the C-mill of the old Pillsbury Mill. The musicians will be surrounded by the spray-painted murals created by local artists, as well as the rich patina of the 87-year-old factory floor, which will provide for a unique acoustic experience beyond the traditional concert hall. The event includes snacks catered by Conn's Catering and a cash bar.
When: Gates open at 6 p.m. Saturday

More: The event is co-hosted by Moving Pillsbury Forward with all the event proceeds supporting the Illinois Symphony Orchestra. Tickets are $40 per person before the event, and $50 day of.
Sangamon County Fair Fall Festival
What: Dust off your boots for line dancing, drinks and plenty of food to go around. Choose from Italian Beef, pulled pork sandwiches and pair them with baked beans or chips, with spiced fall drinks on the menu. Local band UNCHAiNED will take the stage to rock you with the best of the '90s and original music from their collection.
When: 4 p.m., Saturday
Where: 316 W. Birch St., New Berlin
More: The event is free admission for all ages and held in the outdoor Warren Boynton State Bank Pavilion.
Rocky Horror at The Wakery
What: Join the cast of Rocky Horror for a weird adventure into the night with Springfield's local non-alcoholic bar. Learn the Time Warp, sing along with the cast, get a preview of the show, and enter the costume contest. Special themed beverages will be available for purchase throughout the evening: the flavors are a spooky surprise.
Where: The Wakery, 5 W. Old State Capitol Plaza, Springfield
Pine Mountain Logs at Motorheads
What: Grab a drink, a bite to eat and settle back to enjoy some music for a good cause. This event is a benefit for the Mary Bryant Home, which helps visually impaired peoples in Illinois. The Mary Bryant Home facility is the first in Illinois and is designed for residents to live independently with visual impairment.
