title: CWLP crews return to Springfield after restoring power in Georgia following Hurricane Helene
author: Tom Ackerman
description: City Water, Light and Power crews have returned to Springfield after a nearly two-week trip to Georgia following Hurricane Helene.
content:
City Water, Light and Power crews have returned to Springfield after a nearly two-week trip to Georgia where they helped restore power after Hurricane Helene had hit.
Two crews and a supervisor traveled to Douglas, a town with a population around 12,000 that is near the center of the state. Initially headed for the city of Marietta, crews were reassigned mid-journey based on needs in the region.
CWLP participates in a mutual aid agreement through the American Public Power Association and the Illinois Municipal Utility Association that shares resources when disasters happen.
The crews arrived in Douglas the night of Sept. 27 after the hurricane tore through the area earlier that morning.
The two job foremen that traveled there described the town as having trees down everywhere and lines down. They said roads were largely impassable. There was no electricity, running water, cell service, or maps when crews arrived.
The crews joined a peak total of around 160 other linemen in the town, though there were 70 to 90 linemen there for most of the time. Crews worked to repair larger circuits on major transmission lines and poles to restore power to the community.
'One thing that touched me in a way – the community, even though it was mass devastation – the community was very giving,' said Bill Lewis, one of the CWLP foremen. 'We had laundry service for an example. They went and washed our clothes. While I thought that was going to be a commercial laundry service, I had no idea until we got our clothes back that it was individual families that were washing our laundry in their house.'
Children left notes in the laundry, thanking the workers, he added.
Local churches, too, offered goody bags with water, energy drinks, deodorant, and more thank you notes.
Power was restored to Douglas by the time the crews left, CWLP said. A local news outlet further detailed that on Oct. 4, the distribution lines had been restored and crews were able to restore power to individual homes.
The crews from Springfield all ventured on a volunteer-basis. Lewis said a lot of it has to do with pride in his work.
Most of the crews have assisted in disasters before, the linemen said who spoke to The State Journal-Register. They recalled traveling to Hurricanes like Irma in 2017 and Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
'It's pretty devastating,' Huff said. 'You're there to help serve the public get the lights on, but then at the same time, you've got this gut-wrenching feeling for all of these customers that lost their house, their roof, their everything.'
But while the hours are long, from 16 to 18 hours daily while assisting, the work is otherwise what the workers are accustomed to, said Kyle Clark, the other foremen on the trip.
The crews could be called to Hurricane Milton as the storm begins to thrash Florida's west coast.

title: 'It should have surfaced.' Debate over allegation against sheriff's husband boils over
author: Steven Spearie
description: A Sangamon County Board member contended a 2021 allegation against the sheriff's husband should have surfaced publicly.
content:
Speakers at Tuesday's Sangamon County Board meeting and a board member himself reiterated concerns that an allegation of unwanted physical contact against the husband of current Sangamon County Sheriff Paula Crouch wasn't brought to the public's attention during a background search last month.
Board chairman Andy Van Meter said the investigation of battery against Robert S. Crouch Jr., now the Riverton Police Chief, wasn't relevant to the determination of Paula Crouch's fitness for office.
Also Tuesday, the board sent a resolution initiating and authorizing a referendum to be submitted to county voters about recall of the sheriff's office to the election committee for additional study.
'We still don't believe women'
The 2021 allegation against Crouch made by Elizabeth Drea, a worker with the Police Benevolent & Protection Agency,"is why we've been asking for departments to FOIA their employees or board members to actually look extensively into people's backgrounds," said Breonna Roberts, during the public comment section.
Van Meter told The State Journal-Register that he was informed of the allegation as a committee was trying to finalize candidates as a successor to Sheriff Jack Campbell, who retired on Aug. 31 in the wake of the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey in her home in an unincorporated area of Woodside Township.
A former sheriff's deputy was charged with the murder of Massey, though Campbell initially refused to resign.
"When you conduct a background check," Van Meter said, "there is lots of information that is deduced. You have to make a determination on what of that information is relevant and what of that information is not relevant."
The information Van Meter had, Roberts said, "wasn't something we were able to discuss as a community. It makes me a concerned citizen."
Board member Marc Ayers insisted the information was relevant and that it should have been up to the board to decide.
"It's a serious allegation and that really should have surfaced," said Ayers, a Democrat.
Sheriff Crouch attended the meeting but did not speak.
The Illinois State's Attorneys Appellate Prosecutor declined to press charges against Crouch. Drea told the SJ-R that she didn't want to relive the experience in court and that she was in therapy.
"It's frustrating we went through intensive background checks and we still don't believe women," said Ken Pacha, also in public comment.
The lack of formal charges, he added, "shouldn't mean we ignore that accusation."
'Like sending it to the graveyard'
Sam Cahnman, the board member sponsoring the recall resolution, joked that sending it to the election committee was "like sending it to the graveyard."
Another resolution of Cahnman's that went to the committee was never acted upon.
Cahnman is hoping the recall resolution gets before voters on the April 1 ballot.
The recall power, said Vanessa Knox, would be "a quick and tangible action" to resolve matters that might arise with a sheriff.

title: Central Illinois first responder dies in two-vehicle crash
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A first responder in central Illinois died after being involved in a crash last week. Here's what we know.
content:
A first responder in central Illinois died after being involved in a crash last week.
Chelsie M. Sonneborn, 32, was an emergency medical technician in Franklin. Sonneborn was driving on IL Route 104 near Ress Station Road on Oct. 3 when her vehicle collided head-on with a pickup truck, according to the Morgan County Coroner's Office. The crash happened around 4 p.m.
The coroner said Sonneborn died at the scene of the crash.
Sonneborn worked as an EMT for seven years for America Ambulance while she worked towards becoming a paramedic.
'She absolutely loved being a first responder and helping others,' her obituary reads.
Sonneborn graduated from Jacksonville High School in 2010. She also worked for the Murrayville Fire Department for two years, as well as volunteering for the Murrayville Woodson Ambulance Service for a few years.
'Chelsie was not just a co-worker but was a friend to many in our community, and her loss has come with a tremendous amount of grief and devastation,' according to a Facebook post from America Ambulance. 'Chelsie's dedication and expertise as an EMT will be sorely missed by all that knew her. We ask that you keep her family, friends, and EMS family in your thoughts and prayers.'
A funeral service is set for Oct. 9 at 12 p.m. at the Buchanan & Cody Funeral Home in Jacksonville.
The crash is being investigated by the Illinois State Police and the Morgan County Coroner's Office.

title: Miller time: Williamsville football stuns New Berlin before halftime in Sangamo win
author: Bill Welt
description: Everything changed suddenly in the final seconds of the first half and Williamsville knocked off New Berlin in a key Sangamo football game
content:
(This story was updated to add new information.)
NEW BERLIN — It wasn't exactly designed that way.
It still worked in the end.
Williamsville senior running back Braddock Cates hurled a 30-yard touchdown pass to junior Matthew Miller on a trick play as time expired to end the first half ahead 14-7 and catapult the Bullets to a 39-7 Sangamo Conference win over previously unbeaten New Berlin at Pretzel Field on Friday.
"It definitely was not supposed to go to him," Cates said. "I was looking down the field and he was the only dude who was kind of open, so I was running and I just tossed it down there and luckily found him in the end zone. I don't know if it was luck or skill, or a little bit of both, but we got it done."
None of that would've transpired if not for quarterback Jackson Sanders' game-tying 6-yard touchdown pass to Mason Johnson with 8.3 seconds remaining in the second quarter and Nathan Tonellato's recovery on the ensuing kickoff.
Tonellato also recovered a fumble jarred loose by Gage Paul earlier in the second quarter.
"That was awesome," Tonellato said of his kickoff recovery that set up Cates' pass to Miller. "It was a great feeling — very electric."
Williamsville (6-1 overall, 6-0 Sangamo) initially lined up for a Will Zinn field goal attempt, but personnel issues led to a delay of game penalty and the Bullets opted to go with a desperate heave that turned out gravy.
"The special teams unit did a great job," Sanders said. "They had a fumble recovery for us and we knew we had to punch it in and make a difference before half. Braddock did that and put on a great ball and now he's gunning for my job at quarterback."
That was in jest, of course. Sanders orchestrated the first-scoring drive with less than 3 minutes left in the first half beginning at midfield. Sanders eventually found Johnson after scrambling out of the pocket with no timeouts remaining. Sanders finished 6 of 9 for 36 yards.
"He got really shifty in that space," Sanders said of Johnson's run after the catch. "I had to scramble and make something happen and luckily I was able to find him and he did his magic and got in the end zone."
Cates, a Class 3A all-state honoree last season, had 22 carries for 179 yards and two touchdowns. Miller ran for 33 yards and another score.
Clark Nelson led New Berlin (6-1 overall and Sangamo) with 85 rushing yards and a score. The Pretzels reached inside the Williamsville 10-yard line behind 20-7 in the third quarter but stalled as the Bullets scored on all four of their possessions in the second half to pull away with the win.
Williamsville next meets 2A top-ranked Maroa-Forsyth (7-0, 6-0) at Paul Jenkins Field on Friday, Oct. 18 for the outright Sangamo lead. The Trojans are chasing their third straight outright Sangamo title.
"We knew it was going to be a battle going into it and luckily our defense bailed us out and got some stops," Sanders said. "Once we got in the end zone one or two times, the train started from there and we built our momentum."

title: Here's what our photographer saw during an impromptu visit at Lincoln Park in Springfield
author: Thomas J. Turney
description: A Walk in the Park is an ongoing series from The State Journal-Register. Check out what our photographer saw when he visited Lincoln Park.
content:
A Walk in the Park is an ongoing series from The State Journal-Register photographer Thomas Turney, who plans to explore the Springfield area — one park at a time — to capture all of the beauty and recreation Springfield area parks have to offer. If you have a suggestion of a park he should visit, email him at tturney@gannett.com.
Lincoln Park is the spot to get a workout in or play a sport. According to the Springfield Park District, the park has the greatest variety of sports-oriented facilities of any park in the district. The roadway network, trails and open space are used for walking, running, bicycling, training and school district cross-country meets. The northern half of the park has a soccer field, 6 baseball/softball diamonds, 3 tennis courts, 3 shuffleboard courts and 21 horseshoe courts. Also in this area, the Nelson Recreation Center has an outdoor swimming pool, 2 indoor ice rinks, rooms for special events, a concession area and restrooms. South of the building is a small bandstand, a picnic area with shelters and a large playground. You can also play frisbee golf at the park as well.
Founded: 1905
Address: 1601 N. Fifth St., Springfield
Acres: 88
History: This is one of the historic parks, developed as termini of the urban trolley line in use at the time.

title: Springfield-area airport recognized as one of the best airports in the state
author: Claire Grant
description: A local airport has been named one of the best airports of the year in the state. Here's what you need to know.
content:
A local airport has been named one of the best airports of the year in the state.
The Illinois Department of Transportation announced the winners of the Airport of the Year award at the Illinois Public Airports Association fall conference in Galena last week.
The Jacksonville Municipal Airport ​won the Large General Aviation airport of the year category. A general aviation airport is a public-use airport that does not have scheduled service or has scheduled service with less than 2,500 passenger boardings each year, according to the FAA.
The awards reflect outstanding achievements of the state's aviation community in different aspects. The awards also celebrate the contribution of airports to the state's overall economy and transportation system. ​
What plays into Illinois' success as an airport hub? According to IDOT, Gov. JB Pritzker's bipartisan Rebuild Illinois capitol program could help strengthen airports outside of O'Hare.
The Rebuild Illinois capital program has been investing into the Illinois transportation through IDOT since 2021.
In that year, IDOT released the $20.7 billion six-year plan aiming to improve roads, bridges and help ensure Illinois remains a top transportation network in the U.S. Pritzker announced a $94 million commitment to airports throughout the state in the program, with an added $11.5 million in local contributions, the largest statewide capital investment for airports in the prairie state's history.
Currently, IDOT is investing a total of $150 million into the aviation industry.
Illinois Airports
Illinois is home to 100 public-use airports and heliports, with nearly 3,000 registered aircraft. The system of airports supports more than 492,000 jobs, with a combined payroll of $21.9 billion and a total economic impact of $95.5 billion according to Illinois.gov.

title: McDonald's McRib sandwich returning in 2024. Here's when and how to find it
author: Claire Grant
description: One of McDonald's most vaulted and iconic sandwiches is coming back to central Illinois – for a limited time of course.
content:
One of McDonald's most vaulted and iconic sandwiches is coming back to central Illinois – for a limited time of course.
The McRib will likely appear on Springfield McDonald's menus in mid-November, according to a local general manager.
A second general manager for a separate Springfield location confirmed that while a date would not be given until the end of October, the sandwich served hot with crispy fries would likely be returning next month.
For those who aren't in the know, the McRib consists of a restricted boneless pork patty shaped to be like a miniature rack of ribs for the aesthetic, which is then dunked in barbecue sauce and placed on a sandwich roll with onions and pickles. McDonald's first Executive Chef René Arend, who created the McNugget, also created the McRib.
The saucy sandwich was created in 1981 to curb chicken shortages, due to high demands for chicken nuggets and raised price for fowl. The item was sold until 1985 when it was taken off the menu for infrequent buying, and has since been a recurring intermittent dish best served swimming in it.
It would be back – it always comes back.
The last time the McRib was seen on the menu was a week out from Thanksgiving in 2023, after the golden arches had said their November 2022 Farewell Tour of the McRib would be the last appearance of the sandwich.
The sandwich garnered such a following, a super-fan named Alan created the McRib Locator in 2008. The website allows users to track McRibs nearest to them. The "most recent sighting" was logged by a user in the United Kingdom on Sept. 30.
While not confirmed, the meal usually hits stores around the country around Thanksgiving and has been confirmed in Missouri to return on Nov. 27, 2024.

title: 'This is not transparency': Alderwoman objects to commenters not being seen
author: Steven Spearie
description: Some are questioning why the city of Springfield has not shown public commentary during city meetings the last two weeks.
content:
For a second straight week, public commentary has not been part of video broadcasts of city of Springfield meetings, leaving some to believe the decision veered into questionable territory.
Haley Wilson, a spokeswoman for the city, said it was "a mayoral decision," while Ward 6 Ald. Jennifer Notariano countered that city council members weren't informed of the decision ahead of time.
The video broadcast of this week's city council meeting cut to the speaker's name. Last week's committee of the whole meeting showed small snippets of some speakers.
The audio portion has remained intact.
Wilson said lately some individuals have "screen recorded" their comments and shared them on social media platforms.
"Technically, (recordings are) considered intellectual property of the city of Springfield," Wilson said. 'Publicly recorded meetings must remain unaltered to preserve their context and maintain broadcast integrity. This adjustment helps protect the content from violating any Open Meeting or FCC violations.'
Wilson said the decision to block speakers' images was a temporary solution, though she couldn't say how long it would be.
It comes at a time when commentary has become more heated over a variety of topics, including the clearing of an unhoused encampment near Fifth Street and North Grand Avenue on Sept. 26 and the Sept. 9 arrest of recently retired Springfield Police Sgt. Michael Egan.
Wilson couldn't say whether that was reason or not for the city's not showing the video.
Notariano said there is no reason to alter the video broadcast.
"People who take time from their day to come out and address (the city council and the mayor) deserve more respect than this, and viewers at home shouldn't be prevented from seeing what's happening at meetings," Notariano said via Facebook. "This is not transparency."
Ken Pacha of Springfield, who frequently comments at city council meetings, agreed.
"If this is the response by the mayor, it's the opposite of transparency and a rather childish use of her authority," Pacha said Thursday.
Noting that the video broadcast was not on the speakers Tuesday, Breonna Roberts began describing what she looked like and what she was wearing when she took to the microphone.
The city clerk's website lists prohibited conduct while addressing the horseshoe, including vulgar or profane language; racial attacks; personal slurs; name calling and allegations of personal wrongdoing.
Failure to follow guidelines could result in citizens being banned from meetings or prohibited from making public comments.

title: Opinion: The Democratic Party has clearly nominated the best choice
author: Paula Coulahan
content:
On Jan. 6, 2021, I stopped by my parents' grave site on the way home from work.
I got out of the car and stood over their grave stones. It was brutally cold. The trees looked stark and violent. I said, 'I'd tell you what happened today, but you'd never believe it.' I got in my car and drove away.
My parents were proud Americans, descendants of Swedish and Irish immigrants who knew hardship and hard work, loved their community and gave to others in endless ways. They were 'dyed in the wool' union Democrats. They knew, and loved, all of our neighborhood families. Ours was a true working class neighborhood that had boasted WWII Victory Gardens across the street from our house when my father was young.
Never, in their wildest dreams could my parents have imagined some of the events of recent history in America: the violent insurrection in our Capitol; Charlottesville; the election of a president who would disrespect veterans or mock a reporter with a disability from the bully pulpit.
One of the things my parents taught me was to respect the president, no matter which party won. They also expected that presidents would conduct themselves with a certain decorum. They held dinner table discussions about how the president is just a person too, with a family, hopes and dreams, and one of the hardest jobs in the world. They analyzed. They empathized.
When President Ronald Reagan had surgery, my parents wrote him a letter wishing him well and relating it to my father's own experience. The president wrote back and sent a heartfelt letter that seemed he must have written and signed it personally. My father, the lifelong union Democrat, was thrilled. 'We're more alike than we are different.' (President Barack Obama).
Following demonstrations regarding George Floyd's murder, I wrote to Representative Adam Kinzinger addressing policing and expressing concern. He wrote a two-page reply explaining his own concerns and his plan to address the issues that were made clear by public outcry. It arrived not in email, but in the mailbox.
Kinzinger was a true representative of the people, no matter party affiliation, and it is the Republican Party's loss that he walked away from politics, except for occasional appearances.
Kinzinger would have made a great Republican nominee for president. Unfortunately, some in the party have veered so far to the right that they don't recognize someone who would serve the best interests of the country at large.
Now it is time for all American voters to think about the expectations for 'presidential' behavior.
Do we want a president who bad mouths veterans and disparages immigrants?
Do we want a president who dismisses the Constitution and feels he is above the law?
Do we want a president who responded to this question — 'What do you think is the biggest threat to car manufacturing?' with the answer 'Nuclear weapons?"
The Democratic Party has nominated the person who is clearly the best choice, Vice President Kamala Harris.
As a lawyer, former Attorney General of California, former senator, and Vice President, she has the first-hand experience and knowledge it takes to be a resilient and successful president and to solve complex problems.
She leads with strength, clarity and intelligence. She is a compassionate leader who cares about all Americans.
In November, vote your conscience.
Remember, it's not about just you and me. Democracy is about giving all Americans a chance to live in freedom and improve their lives. If it wasn't, it wouldn't be worth saving.

title: Use veggies right from your garden for this vegetarian chili recipe
author: Sheridan Lane
description: It's starting to feel like fall, which means it's chili time! Check out this recipe to try this year.
content:
Wednesday marks an internationally important day, World Food Day. For those unfamiliar with World Food Day, Oct. 16, is recognized annually in more than 150 countries worldwide with the mission of raising awareness of global hunger and food insecurities.
According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations (UN), all people have 'the right to foods for a better life and a better future.' Statistically speaking the UN FAO notes on their website that, 'Over 2.8 billion people in the world are unable to afford a healthy diet. Unhealthy diets are the leading cause of all forms of malnutrition — undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies and obesity, which now exist in most countries, cutting across socio-economic classes.'
The World Food Day mission stretches far beyond just extinguishing hunger but also addresses quality, basic nutrition as well as supply chain challenges associated with the foods the world eats.
A three-ingredient 'recipe' in honor of World Food Day:
1. Take a moment to learn more about great ideas for tackling this mission in the 'stories' section at fao.org. Creative thinkers, scientists, entrepreneurs and community members are taking one step at a time to move this mission forward, and just maybe you might have a great idea for your community.
2. Donate, support or volunteer to help organizations globally, nationally or right here at home that also share values with FAO such as the Illinois Stewardship Alliance, the Central Illinois Food Bank and other reputable organizations supporting heathy communities, farmers and eating.
3. Connect with food directly. Gather up the last of this season's garden production by snagging what is left straight from the source! Many fall markets and roadside stands still have many items left to eat. Continue to support local producers and farmers so that those small businesses stay in business for seasons to come. Below is a recipe that just might fit the bill for including locally produced ingredients in a healthy and nutritional way.
Vegetarian Chili with Blistered Tomatoes & Roasted Fall Veggies
First, gather up your end-of-season prep:
2.5 lbs. of end-of-season tomatoes, roasted (wash, rinse, toss in olive oil and broil on high until slightly blistered but soft; run roasted tomatoes through a food mill, and set aside until ready to add below.)
2 lbs. of the assorted diced vegetables below, roasted (wash, dice, toss in olive oil and roast on 400 degrees, stirring occasionally until caramelized but still firm.)
1 medium-to-large, sweet potato, peeled and cut into ½-in. cube1 medium-sized fresh canning pumpkin, peeled and cut into ½-in. cubes
1 medium butternut, acorn or other squash, cut into ½-in. cubes
When the end of season prep is complete, continue with the ingredients and instructions below.
1 tablespoon olive oil
3 cloves garlic, minced
1 yellow onion, diced
1 large carrot, diced
1 red bell pepper, diced
6 oz. diced fresh green chilis or jalapenos (seeds and ribs removed)
2 1/2 tablespoons mild chili powder
1 tablespoon cumin
½ teaspoon dried oregano
¼ teaspoon garlic powder
¼ teaspoon paprika
¼ teaspoon cayenne pepper
¼ teaspoon salt
½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
2 cups vegetable broth
1 (15-ounce) can black beans, rinsed and drained
1 (15-ounce) can kidney beans, rinsed and drained
Directions: Place oil in a large pot, and place over medium-high heat. Add in garlic, onion, diced carrot, red bell pepper and green chiles; sauté for 5-7 minutes, stirring frequently. Nearing the end of the sauté, add the spices and stir into the sauté. On medium heat, add broth, tomatoes, black beans and kidney beans. Bring to a boil. Then reduce heat and simmer for 30-40 minutes or until chili thickens and flavors come together. Stir in remaining roasted fall vegetables, and simmer for 15 minutes more. Taste and adjust seasonings and salt as necessary. Garnish as desired.
Sheridan Lane is director of culinary programs and operations at Lincoln Land Community College.

title: Video shows police officers saving man from radio tower hundreds of feet in the air
author: Saleen Martin
description: Police rescued the man from a 250-foot radio towe in Eagan, about 16 miles southeast of Minneapolis.
content:
Police in southeastern Minnesota saved a man from a 250-foot radio tower this month, and a video captured shows the daring rescue.
Authorities made the rescue in Eagan, about 16 miles southeast of Minneapolis. The footage was released on Oct. 17, but the rescue was made on Oct. 10, according to a news release issued by the Eagan Police Department and Storyful, where the footage was shared.
Neighbors called Eagan police around 5:51 a.m. on Oct. 10 for a welfare check. They told police they heard someone yelling for help, according to the press release. When officers arrived, they found a 51-year-old man at the top of the radio tower.
Watch officer rescue man from radio tower
To the rescue
Eagan Fire and Dakota County Special Operations Team (SOT) were called for help. An SOT officer climbed to the top of the tower and rescued the man by rappelling him down.
According to Eagan police, the man was "in a mental health crisis and had been exposed to the cold weather." He was taken to the hospital for treatment. Authorities were not able to offer any updates on the man's condition Wednesday afternoon.
The Rosemount Police Department also helped that day. Rosemount Police Chief Mikael Dahlstrom said Wednesday afternoon that the man was in the early stages of being hypothermic when he was rescued.
"In order to access the tower, he had to climb over a fence that included barbed wire across the top of the fenced sections," Dahlstrom said.
The six-minute body cam video of the rescue shows an officer climbing the tower to reach the 51-year-old man, securing himself to the tower so he didn't fall. According to television station KVRR, a Dakota County Special Operations Team member was also there and used high-angle rope rescue techniques to climb the tower and save the man.
The body cam footage was shot from the perspective of a police officer helping with the rescue.
'Alright, let's take a break,' the officer said in the video, briefly resting his arms on the tower's bars before resuming his climb.
'You're doing awesome buddy'
As the officer inched closer to the man, he told him 'You're doing awesome, buddy" and reminded the man to keep breathing.
As the wind picked up, the man appeared to yell, prompting the officer to comfort him and let him know they were doing everything they could to get him down to safety.
The video also showed the man clinging and attached to a rescue team member.
The task seemed to have worn out the officer involved, who said his arms were 'dead' and later added 'I need an IV bag' once he was closer to the ground.
'I don't need to work out for the next two months,' the officer said at the end of the video.

title: Sangamon County Juvenile Detention Center has been approved to reopen. What's the hold up?
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Sangamon County Juvenile Detention Center has been approved to reopen more than a year after detainee fired a weapon at officers.
content:
The Sangamon County Juvenile Detention Center could reopen once enough staff are hired to operate the facility, officials said.
Juveniles previously detained at the center at 2201 S. Dirksen Parkway were transferred elsewhere after 17-year-old Camren Darden, a detainee at the center, fired a gun several times inside the facility. He attempted to escape with a 16-year-old girl before he was shot by responding Springfield police officers on Sept. 30 of last year.
The Administrative Office of Illinois courts has approved all of the center's measures to increase security, including the addition of a body scanner, said Kent Holsopple, who is the Director of Probation and Court Services for Sangamon County.
The reopening plan requires a set-minimum staffing level to operate the facility 24 hours a day and seven days a week, he said in a statement to the SJR.
'Sangamon County like many detention centers around the state has struggled to fill openings. The Administrative Office will not approve reopening until we meet the appropriate staffing level,' Holsopple said.
The county has worked closely with the Administrative Office of Illinois Courts to prepare for the reopening, he said.
Darden at the time fired at least four shots at three different people inside the detention center, authorities said.
Officials said the teen pointed a handgun at the Springfield police officers responding to the active shooter call when a veteran officer opened fire and shot the boy. Darden was taken to the hospital where he later died.

title: EPA announces stricter lead paint policies impacting millions of American homes
author: Max Hauptman
description: In a ruling issued Thursday, the EPA is cracking down on lead paint dust that remains in millions of homes and poses a health risk to young children.
content:
The Environmental Protection Agency announced Thursday that it had finalized a new set of requirements aimed at eliminating lead-based paint dust from older homes and childcare facilities.
The new ruling declares any amount of lead exposure as harmful, and limits the amount of lead-based paint dust in homes constructed before 1978 to levels low enough that they cannot be detected.
"Too often our children, the most vulnerable residents of already overburdened communities, are the most profoundly impacted by the toxic legacy of lead-based paint," EPA Administrator Michael Regan said in a statement on Thursday, adding that "These protections will reduce lead exposures for hundreds of thousands of people every year, helping kids grow up healthy and meet their full potential."
The EPA estimates that the new rule will limit exposure to lead for nearly 1.2 million people every year, including 178,000 to 326,000 children under the age of 6.
Banned for 46 years, but still a heath hazard
Lead-based paint was banned in 1978. The EPA estimates, however, that as many as 31 million housing units − single-family homes and multi-unit apartments -- still contain some level of lead paint, including 3.8 million homes with one or more children under the age of 6 living in them.
Exposure to lead, and lead dust created by deteriorating or disturbed lead-based paint, can cause serious and lifelong adverse health impacts, and young children are especially vulnerable to ingesting lead dust. Even small amounts of exposure can severely harm mental and physical development for young children and cause lifelong adverse health effects, including behavioral problems, lower IQ, slowed growth, and irreversible damage to the brain.
In adults, lead exposure can lead to increased blood pressure, heart disease, decreased kidney function, and may cause cancer.
Lower income communities are also considered especially vulnerable to these risks, given that lead-based paint is more commonly found in lower-income neighborhoods.
Ruling mandates undetectable levels of lead paint
The current standards consider hazardous levels of lead-based paint dust to be 10 micrograms per square foot on floors, 100 micrograms per square foot for window sills, and 400 micrograms per square foot for window troughs.
The new rule, which goes into effect next year, reduces those levels across the board to an essentially undetectable level − the lowest amount that can be accurately measured in a laboratory setting − after lead paint abatement has occurred.
That abatement process could be triggered by determining that a child has an elevated level of lead in their blood, or through requirements for receiving federal housing funding.
'We can all breathe a little easier now that the EPA has significantly lowered its dust lead standard to protect children,' said Peggy Shepard, Co-Founder & Executive Director of the New York-based advocacy group WE ACT for Environmental Justice.
Earlier this month, the Biden administration also announced a ruling requiring water utilities to identify and remove all lead pipes from homes within the next decade.

title: Who is Bill Pope? Meet the new owner of Gabatoni's in Springfield
author: Natalie Morris
description: The thought of owning Gabatoni's Restaurant was once laughable for William \
content:
William 'Bill' Pope had no sooner purchased Charlie Parker's Diner seven years ago when his dad suggested another signature Springfield establishment that should be on his radar.
'My dad made the comment that if I should ever buy another restaurant, it should be Gabatoni's,' Pope said. 'I laughed at him.'
Last week that offhanded prediction came true.
Pope purchased the familiar, green-roofed pizza parlor at 300 E. Laurel St. that until Oct. 16 always has been owned by a member of the Lynn family since it opened in 1951.
The sale – which included the name and recipes, as well as the building and facilities – seamlessly transferred the business from owner Rosalie Beck without missing a day of operation.
Beck's parents Johnny and Rosemary Lynn founded the pizzeria, which was only the third pizza joint in Springfield at the time.
Pope said the only change planned is reopening Gabatoni's dining room that has been closed since the pandemic in 2020. The business has operated solely as take out and delivery service since. Hours are 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday.
The goal is to reopen the dining room in December.
A new, custom-made bar is in the works before Gabatoni's front-of-house can once again welcome dine-in customers. The original island bar fell into disrepair while the dining room had been closed. Its replacement will maintain the same aesthetic, but be flush to the wall with bar seating available.
The rest of the Gabatoni's old school ambiance will remain untouched.
Pope has a history of buying local dining hangouts that built their reputation a little off the main drag. And he isn't one to mess with the character of a business that already has stood the test of time.
That was the same philosophy he embraced when purchasing the '50 diner Charlie Parker's at 700 North St. in 2017 and later Parkway Cafe at 2715 N. Dirksen Parkway in 2022.
Both establishments opened in the early 1990s when the addresses were considered rural, rather than the retail hubs they are today.
Pope recently sold Parkway Cafe to his brother Larry Pope, who has managed the business since 2022.
Both establishments built their reputations on comfort food and friendly faces.
'Rosalie was a regular (at Charlie Parker's). Every Wednesday she'd be here for meatloaf,' Pope said. 'I noticed when she'd missed a few weeks and heard she'd put the business up for sale.
'She knew me. I knew her. She knew I'd keep it the same. Everyone else wants to change stuff. Why change what works?'
New cafe officially open
Beth's Rx Cafe opened on the SIU School of Medicine campus Monday, serving breakfast, lunch and caffeinated beverages.
The cafe, which is open to the public, operates from the atrium in the campus' Springfield Combined Laboratory building at 825 N. Rutledge St. from 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. weekdays.
The cafe is operated by the Springfield-based Three Gen Hospitality Group LLC, which also owns westside hotspots Curate and VELE.
Three Gen Hospitality Group's website describes the cafe as a 'coffeehouse that serves breakfast and lunch bites, as well as afternoon pick-me-ups in a modern industrial space.'
Breakfast selections range from oatmeal cups to build-your-own breakfast sandwiches to pastries. Lunch offerings range from a bacon-mac panini to Nashville hot chicken sandwich, kale and Quinoa salad to minestrone. The beverage menu lists signature espressos, teas, Lotus drinks and seasonal sips.
Dine in and online ordering available. Phone: 217-378-0386.
The atrium previously served as home to a Subway franchise from 2002 to 2005.
While Three Gen Hospitality Group is better known for its fine dining offerings, this is its second eatery in a Springfield medical facility. Soleil Cafe serves up breakfast and lunch selections from Springfield Clinic's main campus.
Beth's Rx Cafe was named after 2011 SIU School of Medicine graduate Dr. Elizabeth 'Beth' Nielsen.
Rebranding
Conn's Hospitality Group is again fine tuning its stable of dining and drinking establishments.
The relative newcomer 7th Street Cidery which has operated at 503 S. Seventh St. since 2022 has been rebranded Obed & Isaac's The Cidery.
The establishment, known for its selection of ciders and meads, has been rechristened, taking on its neighboring sister business's name, as well as access to the food menu at Obed & Isaac's Microbrewery & Eatery, across the street at 500 S. Sixth St.
'Customers can order food from Obed & Isaac's and enjoy it at The Cidery, making it a prevailing spot for a full dining and drinking experience,' reads a press release issued by Conn Hospitality Group last week, announcing the rebranding.
Obed & Isaac's Microbrewery & Eatery is open from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily. Obed & Isaac's The Cidery is open 4 to 10 p.m. Tuesday through Friday, 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. Saturday and noon to 10 p.m. Sunday.
The Springfield-based hospitality group also is the force behind the Vinegar Hill Mall renovation, which now houses Trish & Mary's Public House, as well as Wm. Van's Coffee House, which previously called the Seventh Street address home.

title: Jacksonville improves playoff position by denying Lincoln a postseason spot
author: Adrian Dater
description: Brandon Sims booted a 55-yard field goal and kicked three through the uprights in Jacksonville's win over Lincoln in the regular season finale.
content:
LINCOLN — Last year around this time, the Lincoln Railsplitters broke a 39-year football playoff drought with a victory over visiting Jacksonville. That same playoff opportunity was there for the Railers against the same visiting school Friday night at Handlin Field.
All this week, Crimsons players wore a sticker on their helmets with the numbers '41-28' — the score of last year's game. The message from Jacksonville coach Mark Grounds: 'Let's not let them punch their playoff ticket at our expense two years in a row.'
It was a close game for three quarters, but Jacksonville's ground game finally wore out the Railers' defense, en route to a 51-21 Week 9 victory that ended Lincoln's season. The Crimsons will likely start the playoffs on the road next week, but as Grounds told his huddled players afterward, 'You guys are a very dangerous 6-3 team.'
Indeed, it will take a very good defense to stop the Jacksonville running game. Senior La'Marion Williams ran for 112 yards on 19 carries and two touchdowns, and freshman Jeremiah Jackson ran for 142 yards on just seven carries in leading Jacksonville (6-3 overall). Last week, the Crimsons ran for more than 500 yards and Friday they ran for 412 more.
The runners were the stars, but the Jacksonville kicker was a major factor too. Senior Brandon Sims had a night that got him close to the all-time Illinois state record for longest field goal in a regular-season game. As it stood, Sims had to settle for a seventh-place tie for his 55-yard kick that got Jacksonville a very important three points, when it was a 7-0 game for Lincoln in the first quarter.
Sims, who also added a 48-yarder to end the first half, tied three others in state history for seventh-longest, with Tucker McCann's 60-yarder in 2014 for O'Fallon still the record.
'I knew I was capable of it,' Sims said. 'I could feel the heart racing, but as soon as I hit it, I knew it was good.'
Lincoln was guilty of some bad clock management to end the first half, and it cost them those three big points. The Railers had the ball deep at their own 20 with 26.5 seconds left, down 17-7. But the Railers started throwing the ball down the field in a hurry. All that mostly did was keep stopping the clock.
The Railers had a fourth-and-four about their own 40, with four seconds left. A run play was called, and in just two seconds, the run was stuffed in the backfield. Those two seconds still on the clock allowed Sims to come back on the field and attempt the 48-yard field goal, which sailed through the uprights. Instead of being down 10 at the half, with the ball to start the third, Lincoln trudged off the field down 20-7.
Lincoln senior running back Gabe Smith, however, made two runs totaling 40 yards to get in the end zone to start that third quarter, making it a 20-14 game.
The Railers got the ball back with a chance to take the lead, but were stopped on a third down play, bringing out the punter. Railers coach Matt Silkowski called for a fake punt, but the pass was broken up by Jacksonville's speedy freshman two-way player, Darren Henry.
On the first play from scrimmage, another freshman with speed, Jackson, burst up the middle for a 53-yard TD run to make it more comfortable again for Jacksonville at 27-14.
Back the Railers came, however. Senior quarterback Tate Johnston rediscovered his own running game, and he had some good runs that he capped off with a 3-yard scoring plunge, pulling Lincoln within 27-21 with 2:02 left in the third.
But it was all Jacksonville from there. Sims had a chip-shot 20-yarder that made it 30-21, then the Jacksonville defense stopped Johnston on a fourth-and-three at the Railers' 28. On the next play, Williams ran it in from 28 yards and suddenly it was 37-21 Crimsons with time running out in the fourth.
'We just had to stay patient and keep plugging away,' Grounds said. 'Our running game is about body blows. With our big guys leaning on you, you're going to be a step slower and you're going to blink, and our backs run hard.'
Said Williams about next week: 'I feel like, our biggest thing is we've got to come out strong at the gate. We got to pick it up from the jump and get moving.'
The Railers (4-5, 4-4 CS8) got a valiant effort from senior Paytan Bunner (111 yards on 14 carries) and Johnston had a 30-yard scoring run to open the scoring. Despite the loss, Silkowski said his team will be back.
'I think this is one of the greatest senior classes to ever go through here,' Silkowski said. 'We gave it everything we had. No regrets. That was our motto coming in.'

title: Notice a stench in the air this week in Springfield? Here's the likely cause
author: Tom Ackerman
description: If you stepped outside over the last couple of days in Springfield and thought it smelled a little weird, you're not alone.
content:
If you stepped outside over the last couple of days in Springfield and thought it smelled a little weird, you're not alone.
Social media users complained about a foul smell Wednesday morning in the area.
Most people theorized that it had something to do with farmers fertilizing their fields, or farm products in some capacity.
But a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Lincoln said the best and simplest explanation is a phenomenon known as petrichor, which is an earthy smell that occurs after a rain, especially after a dry period.
That smell can be perceived as chemical or oily, and as radiating upward from the ground, said Mike Albano, a staff meteorologist with the NWS.
He didn't smell the odor, but he said that petrichor would make sense because harvest took place early this year on top of the area being in a drought.
Peoria, for example, experienced its fourth driest September since 1883, with .72' of rain.
Lincon saw its 8 th driest September since 1883, with .98' of rain. Springfield fared wetter with 1.66' of rain.
A second explanation for the smell is that a scent was carried by a cold front from southcentral Iowa or southeast Iowa, Albano said.
Residents may be dealing with the smell again Friday morning after rain rolled through the area Thursday night and Friday morning.

title: Former deputy in Sonya Massey shooting moved to Macon County Jail
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy charged in the fatal of Sonya Massey has been transferred to a different jail.
content:
The former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy charged in the fatal of Sonya Massey has been transferred to the Macon County Jail in Decatur from the Menard County Jail in Petersburg.
Sean P. Grayson was moved to Decatur because it is a larger facility, Menard County Sheriff Mark Oller said Monday.
The move was decided mostly because Presiding Circuit Judge Ryan Cadagin ruled that Grayson would continue to be detained in accordance with the Pre-Trial Fairness Act, leading sheriffs to decide where best to place Grayson while he awaits trial.
Grayson has a new status hearing for Dec. 2. A Fourth District Appellate Court ruling regarding Grayson's ongoing detention is expected around the time of the hearing.
Oller said he and former Sangamon County Sheriff Jack Campbell had arranged for Grayson to be jailed in Menard County rather than in Sangamon County as a security precaution, but it was their intention to only hold Grayson in Menard County for a short-term stay.
'I think some of (former Sheriff Campbell's) concerns were that he had worked in Sangamon County, so his arrestees could have possibly been in the jail," Oller said. "Some of the staff could have been familiar with him. None of our staff knew him."
Oller said he had some concerns about holding Grayson because of the notoriety in the case, but he wanted to assist neighboring sheriffs. Jails holding inmates for neighboring counties is not an uncommon practice.
Sangamon County Sheriff Paula Crouch and Macon County Sheriff Jim Root were unable to be reached for comment. Grayson's defense attorney Daniel Fultz did not immediately return messages to The State Journal-Register.
During the time that Grayson was held in Menard County, Sangamon County was responsible for any expenses such as medical expenses, Oller said, though Grayson experienced no major medical issues while in the Menard County Jail.
Grayson was dealing with complications from a diagnosis of Stage 3 colon cancer, Fultz said in court in late August.

title: Trickey fast: Senior forward carries Williamsville boys soccer to 1A sectional title
author: Bill Welt
description: Williamsville's Bryson Trickey treated the boys soccer team to a 2-0 sectional final win over Pleasant Plains, plus other sectional results
content:
VIRDEN — Williamsville's Bryson Trickey wanted to contribute more than last season.
The senior forward/midfielder has proceeded to elevate the Bullets to a second straight Class 1A sectional title with a goal and assist in a 2-0 victory over Pleasant Plains on Wednesday.
"We've been playing fantastic," Trickey said. "Last year we had a really great season, too, and I've felt we've kept that going into this season and we've done really well."
Trickey punched in the go-ahead goal in the first minute before assisting to senior teammate Brett Mizeur late in the second half to secure a third victory this season over their Sangamo Conference rival.
Trickey said the team's speed set up the first goal, assisted by senior teammate Sawyer Woods.
Williamsville advances to the Columbia Supersectional to set up a rematch against the host Eagles on Saturday at 11 a.m. Columbia, which previously nicked the Bullets 1-0 at last year's supersectionals, knocked off Glen Carbon Father McGivney 3-2.
"He's been making things happen and he sneaks up on people sometimes with his speed," Williamsville coach Joe Fandel said of Trickey. "I think they look at him and they respect him, but they don't realize he's got another gear. He gets going and sometimes it's hard to catch him."
Trickey poured in 11 goals and 15 assists last season and has nearly doubled that production this fall with 22 goals and 19 assists following Wednesday's triumph.
"I feel like last season I was kind of disappointed in myself to be honest," Trickey said. "I knew I could be better, so I spent a lot of time in the offseason and it's really paying off for me."

title: Williamsville football finally heats up to knock off Carlinville in IHSA playoff opener
author: Bill Welt
description: Carlinville flustered Williamsville at the start before the Bullets reeled off three quick touchdowns in the second quarter
content:
WILLIAMSVILLE — The Williamsville football team took a little longer than it wanted but eventually warmed up in a 49-14 victory over Carlinville in the first round of the Class 3A playoffs at Paul Jenkins Field on Friday.
The Bullets (9-1) erased a scoreless tie with three touchdown runs in the second quarter. Senior Braddock Cates summoned 107 rushing yards and two touchdowns on 20 carries while junior QB Jackson Sanders also had two scoring runs.
Williamsville senior offensive lineman Corbin Stewart credited everyone from the fans to his fellow linemen for sparking the team.
"I feel like you always see us cheering for something no matter what," Stewart said. "Even if we have a bad play, we cheer our guys up. I think that's what really gets us going."
Williamsville, seeded No. 3, advances to the second round against Saturday's winner between No. 6 Monticello (7-2) and No. 11 DuQuoin (6-3).
Matthew Miller and Gage Paul combined for 98 rushing yards, while Mason Johnson surged in the second half and finished with 88 rushing yards and a TD on five carries.
Carlinville (5-5) chewed up almost 11 minutes on its first drive, beginning on its own 6-yard line, but punted after 19 plays following one of two Griffin Liles sacks.
"You don't play an 8-1 team without trying to eat that clock and manage it," Carlinville coach Chad Easterday said. "We knew they could score some points even in the (run-heavy) offense they're in, so we were trying our best to make sure to manage that situation."
Williamsville didn't score until Miller's short TD run with less than five minutes left in the second quarter. Cates scored on the ensuing possession before Anthony Beckman recovered a muffed kickoff return to set up Sanders' first TD plunge with 48 seconds remaining in the half.
"Carlinville came out and played harder than us in the first quarter, and they did a lot of good things and they owned that first quarter," Williamsville coach Aaron Kunz said. "But we did hold them and we got the ball back twice. Once we did go down and score, I think it took some pressure off."
Carlinville senior running back Nate Dyer ran for 51 yards on 21 attempts. Junior receiver Triston Thompson scored on a 67-yard touchdown pass from junior quarterback Kip Reels, while also rushing for 31 yards. Senior lineman/fullback Weston Kuykendall chipped in 42 rushing yards and a score.

title: Popular record store opens second location in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: A popular record store in Springfield has opened a second location. Here's what you need to know about Dumber Records.
content:
Brat summer is over, but Dumb Records fall is in full swing.
Expanding on the success Record Store Day has had between community and business downtown, Dumb Records is expanding to a second location on the city's west side.
Dumber Records opened last week inside the White Oaks Mall. The store is on the first floor between Off the Wall and across from Kay Jewelers.
The second record store still sells all the latest records and merchandise fans of the indie business love but have a chiller atmosphere to the rock 'n' roll stage of the main location.
Brian Galecki, who co-owns Dumb Records at 418 E. Monroe St., felt confident in opening a second location thanks to community support.
'Really it was the Record Store Day events that really made us feel we have to do something to expand or get a bigger space in general,' Galecki said. 'This past April when we had over 200 people in line, that really made us start thinking, what if we had two locations to split up the crowd here?'
Record Store Day celebrates the culture of independently owned record stores and began in 2007.
Record Store Day will take place on Black Friday, Nov. 29 and again in late spring with both locations of Dumb Records offering deals on the latest music to classic oldies.
Galecki hopes the new location will be a place to shop, sit back and chill to music listening parties, and scratch that itch for older generations who remember record shops in the mall.
'Moving to the mall is a throwback in the same way that a record store is,' Galecki said. 'A certain generation has fond memories of going to the mall for Music Land … so we want to try and bring that back I would say.'
Even a few of the arcade games will make a forever home in the new store.
The store is open Monday through Thursday from noon to 7 p.m.; Friday and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. and Sundays from noon until 6 p.m.

title: Belleville Althoff boys soccer nicks Chatham Glenwood with rally, penalty kicks
author: Bill Welt
description: Belleville Althoff boys soccer clinched its 2A state berth in penalty kicks against Chatham Glenwood
content:
JACKSONVILLE — Tyler Pollock had never been in this situation before in high school, but he knew exactly what to do.
The Belleville Althoff sophomore midfielder catapulted the Crusaders to the Class 2A state semifinals with the final penalty kick for a 4-2 PK victory over Chatham Glenwood in the Illinois College Supersectional on Tuesday.
Althoff meets Lemont on Friday at 1:30 p.m. at Hoffman Estates for its third trip to the state finals in the last four years, but first ever in 2A.
"I knew where I was going the whole time, so I didn't have to think about it too much," Pollock said. "I took my time and waited to see where he would go, and I just placed where he wasn't."
Althoff (24-4) rallied from a 2-0 deficit beginning with an own goal prompted by a Nate Pitre free kick less than a minute after Glenwood senior Miles Calderon's goal early in the second half.
Althoff senior midfielder Bo Gomric then outmaneuvered the Glenwood defense along the goal line before finding the far post for the game-tying goal with 17 minutes, 4 seconds left in regulation.
"It's just a great individual effort," Althoff coach Skip Birdsong said of Gomric. "That was all him. I'd love to take credit like, 'Yeah, that's how I drew it up,' but that was just him."
Glenwood's Luke Baxter headed in the opening goal on a Lucas Smith throw-in for a 1-0 halftime lead. The Titans exit 19-6-3.
"That's a really talented team," Glenwood coach Kyle Franke said of Althoff. "We fought, fought and fought. We gave ourselves a chance in the end. In PKs, it's a 50/50 chance there. Like I told the boys, I'm proud of their effort. No one lacked any effort. They gave it all they had."
Glenwood was seeking its second state berth in the last three years.
"I feel bad for the seniors," Franke said. "We do have a lot of juniors and some sophomores, but the seniors led this team. My heart goes out to the seniors because they were so close making that return trip back to state."

title: Springfield residents have mixed feelings about Trump's return to the White House
author: Steven Spearie
description: "I would recommend that people spend more time trying to find the truth and not listening to the same rhetoric over and over again."
content:
The day after a monumental victory by Donald Trump, Calvin Mabus of Springfield was more guarded than ever.
Standing feet away from the Trump/Vance sign in the front yard of his home on West Lawrence Avenue, said a battle "is yet ahead" involving Democrats.
"Dems are endorsing their 'woke' policies," Mabus said. "A lot of shenanigans are going to start happening. That's my opinion anyway. (The oppressed side) will blame (things) on Russia. They'll blame it on China. They'll blame it on Iran. They'll blame it on somebody, but there's going to be some stuff going on."
With enough electoral votes in hand, Trump will become the first president to serve terms non-consecutively since Grover Cleveland.
Trump's Democrat challenger, Vice President Kamala Harris, conceded Wednesday.
Republicans also reclaimed control of the Senate, picking up seats in West Virginia and Ohio.
That sat well with David and Laura Johnson, who had just visited the Lincoln Home Wednesday afternoon as part of a Route 66 tour.
David Johnson, a former small business owner from Shrewsbury, Mass., described himself as "one of the few Republicans in Massachusetts."
"I was very happy to see the results," Johnson said. "We got up in the middle of the night to turn it back on. We're excited. Most of my neighbors are not Trump people, to the point where you're afraid to say anything. I live my life in the shadows."
Johnson said he was particularly concerned about illegal immigration and the high crime he claimed it generated.
"We have an open border," he said. "They kept letting more and more people in. It's unbelievable what is happening in this country. It's gotta change."
Laura Johnson added she was all in on Trump's plan of deporting illegal immigrants who are criminals.
"He's said he committed to fighting those criminals so we can cut back on all of the horrible crimes that are being committed on unsuspecting U.S. citizens," she said.
Mabus said immigration issues and "the inflationary raking we're going through (from) the 'scamdemic,'" his word for the COVID pandemic, were reasons he was supporting Trump.
Trump's win didn't sit well with Dan Horowitz, who moved to Springfield from Chicago about a year ago.
Horowitz said Trump's bullying and rhetoric was distasteful and wondered why he was voted in again after serving from 2016 to 2020.
"The hate in general (really worries me)," said Horowitz, waiting for his bus downtown. "It's almost like a nihilism. It doesn't matter what happens ultimately, it's just about getting back at people you don't like, and that strikes me as a bad way to go in life.
"I get that people are frustrated about change not happening and not liking how things are, but I don't see how going in the direction they chose to is going to make things any better. We've seen what happened (before), yet people decided they wanted to do it again and I just don't get why."
Laura Johnson suggested people should tamp things down regarding Trump.
"I would recommend that people spend more time trying to find the truth and not listening to the same rhetoric over and over again," she said. "Look what he did during his last term. I know several Democrats who benefitted financially his last term. Still, they can't get beyond the hate of him. They can't put aside the distaste of his personality.
"It gets back to let's all get back to some common sense and some common decency towards each other."

title: FBI investigating as Black students in Texas, nationwide targeted in racist texts
author: Laura A. Bischoff
description: The FBI is investigating racist messages sent to Black students nationwide, including Texas. Texts follow election victory of Donald Trump.
content:
Black college students in several states, including Texas, reported to authorities Wednesday they had received anonymous text messages using racist references to the era of U.S. slavery. The FBI is investigating the incidents.
The messages varied in detail, but followed the same basic script, saying the recipient had "been selected to pick cotton at the nearest plantation."
Officials could not say where the messages originated.
The Southern Poverty Law Center, which tracks hate incidents nationwide, and authorities in Texas, Ohio, Alabama, South Carolina and other states were investigating the messages, which were sent out after the announcement of Donald Trump's election as president.
It's unclear who sent the messages and how many were sent. At least some of the messages claimed to have come from "A Trump supporter."
Where are students receiving racist text messages?
Authorities began investigating the text messages after reports that students from Clemson University in South Carolina, Ohio State University, the University of Alabama and other schools had received them.
Students appear to be the primary target of the messages — but not all the recipients were in college.
High school and even middle school students from across the U.S. have reported receiving the malicious messages. A 13-year-old in Austin was among those who received such a message.
"You have been selected to become a slave at your nearest plantation," the text read. "Please be ready by 12 a.m. with all your necessary belongings. You will be picked up in a white van with a Trump representative from your area."
"You are in slave group B," the message continued.
Shaun Hopkins, a Spanish teacher at Small Middle School in Austin, has had some of his students of color — and he knows of other students in the Austin district — who received racist texts asking them to report to a location, he said.
The students receiving the messages didn't know what to do with them, but some are concerned, he said.
"Kids can't learn if they're scared," Hopkins said.
The texts that Hopkins has seen appear similar to those sent to other students across the county, but some include students' names in the message, he said. For students of immigrant families, the fear of someone coming to take a family member away could be real, he said.
"For Latino students, the idea of ICE coming into their community, creating some disruptions, is not outlandish," Hopkins said. "It's a very real possibility."
Mary Banks, who has a daughter in Columbus, Ohio, said the 16-year-old received one of the hateful text messages Wednesday evening that included her full name. A few of her daughter's friends in the Columbus City school district received similar messages, she said.
Banks said she's not surprised that racist hatred would surface at this moment in history.
"I feel white supremacy got stronger after the election," she said.
Ohio State University spokesman Ben Johnson told The Columbus Dispatch, part of the USA TODAY Network, that hateful messages were sent to "several students."
Bethany McCorkle, a spokesperson for Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost's office, said the office was aware of the text messages and was looking into them.
Columbus NAACP President Nana Watson told the Dispatch that she believes the text messages are a hate crime.
"This is racism at its highest," Watson said.
Diedre Simmons, a spokesperson for the University of Alabama, told The Crimson White school newspaper that university officials informed local authorities about similar messages sent to students there. Authorities at Clemson University also are investigating racist text messages sent to Black students in South Carolina, according to the Greenville News, part of the USA TODAY Network.
R.J. Polite, a senior at Clemson who received a version of the text, said he was shocked by the message and mentioned the negativity he's seeing on social media after Trump's results."It was ignorant and kind of childish." Polite said. 'I really tried to stay off of my phone and off the internet for the day because it was just so much going on. It was just bad.'
Who is sending the messages?
It's unclear who sent the text messages.
Alejandra Caraballo, a clinical instructor at the Harvard Law School Cyberlaw Clinic, said this is the first time she has seen a widespread racist attack using text messages. Tracking the culprit who perpetrated the campaign might be complicated, depending on how extensive it is, she said.
'It remains to be seen how widespread this is,' Caraballo said. 'If this is a few hundred texts it could be done by a local racist group in an afternoon as a trolling tactic, but if it's thousands or tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of people, then it would have to be automated and involve a fair degree of sophistication.'
If the attack is that widespread, Caraballo said, she wouldn't rule out foreign actors seeking to foment discord in the United States in the days after the presidential election. She said bomb threats to majority Black polling places on Election Day were reported to have come from Russian email addresses.
Bad actors can quite easily purchase lists of phone numbers — some categorized by race or other demographic characteristics — on the dark web, to be used for anything from sales campaigns to cybercrime, Caraballo said.
In some states voter registration information is public, including a voter's race, she said, and that information could be combined with phone records to create a targeted attack like this.
An FBI statement said the bureau is 'aware of the offensive and racist text messages sent to individuals around the country and is in contact with the Justice Department and other federal authorities on the matter."
The FBI also encouraged people to contact their local law enforcement agencies if they are physically threatened.
Civil rights leaders urge politicians to condemn 'public spectacle of hatred'
Representatives from civil rights advocacy organizations, including the Southern Poverty Law Center and the NAACP's Columbus chapter, said the contents of the messages constituted hate crimes.
Margaret Huang, president and CEO of the law center, called them "a public spectacle of hatred and racism that makes a mockery of our civil rights history" in a statement Thursday.
Huang called on political leaders to "condemn anti-Black racism, in any form, whenever we see it."
Experts on domestic extremism were shocked by the messages Wednesday, telling USA TODAY the campaign appears to represent a tactic that has not previously been employed by white supremacists or hate groups.
'This is the first I've ever seen of this kind of racist attack using texts. It's frighteningly personal and harrowing,' said Heidi Beirich, co-founder of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism. 'I've also never seen this kind of racist messaging threatening people directly.'

title: Racist text messages spamming Black Americans in Ohio, across U.S.
author: Laura A. Bischoff
description: Racist text messages are being sent to Black Americans in multiple states, including Ohio.
content:
Racist text messages are being sent to Black Americans in Ohio and around the nation, telling them they're selected to be enslaved and assigned to pick cotton on a plantation.
The widespread messages are being reported in multiple states and screenshots are going viral on social media sites. The messages vary in details, but follow the same basic script.
Students seem to be some of the targeted recipients.
"Some students have received these hateful text messages," said Ohio State University spokesman Ben Johnson. "We have reported the messages to the Office of Institutional Equity and are offering support services. We are aware that this is happening nationally."
Columbus State Community College spokesperson Brent Wilder confirmed students at the college have received spam messages. College officials weren't able to quantify how many students.
"This is racism at its highest," said Columbus NAACP President Nana Watson. "I believe it is a hate crime as I see it."
Mary Banks said her 16-year-old daughter received a hate text message at 8:12 p.m. Wednesday and it included her full name. A few of her daughter's friends in the Columbus City Schools received similar messages.
Banks said she's not surprised that racist hatred would surface. "I feel white supremacy got stronger after the election. That's my personal opinion."
FBI, Ohio Attorney General's Office aware of racist text messages
In a tweet on its X account, the FBI said it "is aware of the racist and offensive text messages sent to individuals around the country and is in contact with the Justice Department and other federal agencies about the matter.
"As always, we encourage members of the public to report threats of physical violence to local law enforcement agencies."
In response to the FBI tweet, Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican representing Kentucky's 4th Congressional district, replied on his X account: "It's probably y'all sending them. Pack your bags."
Republican Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost's office is also aware of the text messages and has a team looking into it, his spokeswoman said.
The messages appear to be coming from phone numbers with Ohio area codes. A check of some of the numbers show they are landlines, which cannot send text messages. That could be a sign that the text messages are part of a spoofing scam.
Spoofing makes it look like a call or text is coming from a known contact or local entity.
The Southern Poverty Law Center, which tracks hate incidents nationwide, said in a statement that the text sent to young Black people "is a public spectacle of hatred and racism that makes a mockery of our civil rights history."
'Leaders at all levels must condemn anti-Black racism, in any form, whenever we see it — and we must follow our words with actions that advance racial justice and build an inclusive democracy where every person feels safe and welcome in their community,' said Margaret Huang, SPLC president and CEO.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Late to the party: Budzinski comfortably wins reelection to U.S. House seat as numbers unfold
author: Steven Spearie
description: Rep. Budzinski won in all but two counties in the district that snakes from Champaign to the Metro East area and includes Springfield.
content:
U.S. Rep. Nikki Budzinski easily defeated political newcomer Joshua Loyd in the 13th District race, although numbers were late developing.
The district includes Springfield where the 47-year-old Budzinski, who formerly worked in President Joe Biden's administration, resides.
Budzinski held a 58% to 42% lead over Loyd, who is from Virden, Wednesday morning.
That's a bigger margin than Budzinski won by over Regan Deering in 2022, when the 13th District was newly drawn.
Sangamon County went Budzinski's way with a 54% vote.
Budzinski had been scheduled to address a watch party at the Hoogland Center for the Arts at around 8:30 p.m. Tuesday.
But numbers, including those in Champaign County, were late developing because of technical issues with electronic poll books earlier Tuesday. There, Budzinski held 74% of the vote.
Associated Press declared Budzinski the winner shortly before 10:30 a.m. Wednesday.
'Two years ago, voters in central and southern Illinois placed their faith in me to go to Congress and work across the aisle to get things done for our communities," Budzinski said in a release issued by her campaign Wednesday. "I'm so honored that my constituents have seen my record of results and given me the opportunity to keep fighting for them. I'll continue to cut through the political noise and nonsense to support working families, lower costs and secure our southern border."
Budzinski advocated during her first term to make the site of the 1908 Springfield Race Riot a national monument. On Aug. 16, President Joe Biden signed a proclamation doing just that under the Antiquities Act.
Loyd, a West Point graduate who positioned himself as a political outsider, defeated Thomas Clatterbuck in the March primary.
Loyd won only Macoupin and Piatt counties.

title: Illinois 2024 election results: Ballot measure on election interference
author: Mike Kramer
description: One of three non-binding advisory questions on Illinois ballots is a measure to penalize political candidates for election interference.
content:
One of three non-binding measures put to Illinois voters on Tuesday asked whether candidates interfering with or attempting to interfere with an election worker's duties should be subject to civil penalties.
Illinois State Sen. Don Harmon and Illinois State Rep. Jay Hoffman sponsored Illinois Senate Bill 2412, which included the three advisory questions, this spring. The bill passed in the Illinois House and Illinois Senate in early May. Non-binding advisory questions like this have no legal effect on a state's laws, but allow government officials to gauge public opinion.
The wording of the election interference question on the ballot reads:
'Should any candidate appearing on the Illinois ballot for federal, State, or local office be subject to civil penalties if the candidate interferes or attempts to interfere with an election worker's official duties?'
With 40.5% of the expected vote reported, the Associated Press has projected "Yes" to carry the day. 89.5% of Illinois voters have voted "Yes" on the question, while 10.5% cast "No" votes.
