title: City Council approves $85.6M for new coal supplier for City Water, Light & Power
author: Claire Grant
description: The four-year coal contract with Foresight Energy passed in a vote 9 to 1, with Ward 3 Ald. Roy Williams Jr. voting no.
content:
The nearly $86 million contract with Foresight Energy to power Springfield's coal power plant passed in city council chambers Tuesday night.
The four-year coal contract with Foresight Energy passed in a vote 9 to 1, with Ward 3 Ald. Roy Williams Jr. voting no.
The contract would set the price of coal at $40 per ton until 2027, when the price would increase to $44.50 per ton and $46.75 per ton in 2028; however, the contract would not include the cost of hauling the coal over fifty miles from Hillsboro to Springfield.
That would be a separate contract.
Changing Springfield's coal supplier
City Water, Light and Power chief utility engineer Doug Brown previously said Knight Hawk Coa l, which owns Viper Mine, the current mine CWLP uses for fossil fuel, raised their prices from 2020 $45 per ton to $65 per ton. Brown said CWLP instead looked toward the fossil fuel market for competitors to Knight Hawk and was offered two different proposals, one of which was Foresight and the other Peabody Energy.
CWLP estimates the coal burn of Dallman 4 at 500,000 tons per year.
Brown previously said part of the uncertainty of renewing a contract with Viper mine are recent unconfirmed rumors of the location shutting down, and mixed with the raised rates, the city could save $39 million over the length of the contract with the lower rates at Foresight.
Integrated Resource Plan concerns
During an Oct. 29 committee of the whole meeting, local environmental activist Lori McKiernan voiced hesitation about the city entering an agreement with Foresight Energy without an Integrated Resource Plan, or IRP, to plan for the future energy needs of the city and the environmental impact of resources, like coal in this case, used.
At Tuesday's city council meeting, Anne Logue of Sustainable Springfield said it was time for an outside insight into the city's environmental plans with an IRP.
Nick Dodson of Helping Hands Springfield said there was a level of cognitive dissonance between CWLP and constituents of wards about the need of an IRP.
'Let's also remember that the last IRP reportedly saved CWLP and ratepayers tens of millions of dollars over the last five years,' Dodson said. 'If an IRP offers such clear financial benefits, why is it missing from the priorities of this council and CWLP's leadership? Ignoring the potential benefits as a new IRP seems at best disingenuous and at worst, deceptive.'
Dodson and several other environmental activists have organized a petition to tell City Council to plan Springfield's utility feature, which has accrued close to 400 signatures since its creation.
Dodson says the plan should include public engagement, consultation with independent energy experts, evaluations of the most cost-effective way to move to clean energy and away from coal.
The plan suggested by activists would pass an ordinance this year for an IRP in the next budget and to be completed in 2025.

title: 1 dead, 2 children injured in wrong-way crash; driver suspected of DWI: Reports
author: Julia Gomez
description: A woman is dead and two children are injured after a person suspected of driving under the influence drove down the wrong way of a freeway.
content:
A woman was killed and two children were injured in Houston, Texas after a pickup truck heading the wrong way crashed into the SUV she was driving, according to multiple reports.
Early Sunday at 3 a.m. local time, a pickup truck was driving south on the Eastex Freeway's northbound lanes crashed into an SUV that was traveling north, according to news stations Fox 26 and KHOU.
A woman, the driver of the SUV, was pronounced dead at the scene of the crash.
Two children, ages 6 and 14, were passengers in the truck when the crash occurred, according to KHOU. They were taken to the hospital for their injuries.
The driver of the pickup truck suffered from a broken leg, and police believe they may have been driving while intoxicated, Fox 26 reported.
Who were the crash victims?
The names of the driver and the victims have not been released.
The Houston Police Department and the Harris County Institute of Forensic Sciences did not immediately respond to USA TODAY.

title: Man sentenced for murder of 2022 Illinois DCFS worker in Sangamon County
author: Steven Spearie
description: At the time of the verdict in August, the judge called it \
content:
A Sangamon County man who was found"guilty but mentally ill" in the Jan. 4, 2022, slaying of Illinois Department of Children and Family Services child protection services worker Deidre (Graham) Silas of Springfield was sentenced to 100 years behind bars last week.
Benjamin Howard Reed stabbed Silas, a 36-year-old mother of two children, 43 times in his home on the southern tip of the county and also bludgeoned her to death with a sledgehammer.
Sangamon County Presiding Circuit Judge John Madonia told Reed, a 35-year-old former roofer, that whatever rehabilitative potential he had, "you neglected, you ignored, you let it consume you, and it cost Ms. Silas her life."
In handing down the verdict Aug. 29, Madonia called it "one of the most brutal and heinous" cases he has seen in his legal career.
Reed is not eligible for parole.
Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser had asked Madonia to impose a prison sentence "sufficient in length to ensure (Reed) cannot get out and hurt anyone else."
Silas had been called to the home in Thayer, about 35 minutes southwest of Springfield, to investigate "a report of abuse and neglect" against the parents of two children living in the home.
The report didn't initially involve Reed or his wife's four children and stepchildren, but since the environment was a concern, Silas had a responsibility to assess all the children. Twelve people, six adults and six children, lived in the two-bedroom home, which witnesses described as "chaotic" during Reed's trial.
Reed was later apprehended and arrested the day of the murder in Decatur, where his mother lived.
Reed told Dr. Terry Killian in a 2023 interview to determine sanity, that he saw Silas as "an intruder." Voices inside and outside his head, Reed said, told him that Silas was there to kidnap his kids "and hurt us."
Killian, a Springfield psychiatrist, testified that Reed had "bona fide (Diagnostic Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders)-documented mental health conditions and disorders."
Silas' death put more of a spotlight on the faces of DCFS workers.
Both Sen. Steve McClure, R-Springfield, and Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, introduced legislation addressing worker safety and providing survivor benefits for a DCFS worker's family if the worker dies on the job.
"The court's sentence (Friday) holds the defendant accountable for this brutal murder," Milhiser said. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the family of Deidre Silas and with child protection workers across the state who work each day to keep the most vulnerable members of our community safe."

title: Downtown Springfield bar getting a face-lift. Here's what customers can expect to see
author: Claire Grant
description: One of downtown Springfield's most popular bars is getting a face-lift just in time for holiday sips and cheer.
content:
One of downtown Springfield's most popular bars is getting a face-lift just in time for holiday sips and cheer.
Anyone who's been downtown has probably noticed the white-walled off exterior of Floyd's Thirst Parlor, 210 S. Fifth St., and the construction going on inside next to Third Shift Kitchen.
Jeremy Bredemeyer, the co-owner of the bar, said the fishbowl with windows near the bar is coming down for a rolling wall to open to the outdoors.
"When we put it in that kitchen, we lost some of our occupancy, so we have to regain that occupancy we had lost,' Bredemeyer said. 'Those windows used to be displays for an old department store that sold women's clothing in the sixties, so it broke up the space."
The major change comes from the building's current lack of a beer garden, Bredemeyer said. He said while other businesses can hold events in the back outside sitting, Floyd's doesn't have that back bar space, so the solution to provide outside seating was this new renovation.
According to architect Dave Leonatti, principal architect of Melotte, Morse, Leonatti and Parker, the whole facade of the building will be improved starting with the first-floor storefront. The cobbled together set of wooden and glass doors have been overhauled and insulated to be ADA compliant.
'The idea was to open up the front of the bar and we removed a bunch of infill wall between the two sides,' Leonatti said. 'We'll put in a large folding storefront so the full height from the floor to the canopy will be a bifold wall in sections. It rolls on the top and bottom tracks.'
Leonatti related the trifold wall folds into flat sections and stacks like a convention room divider.
'On the part of the bar where there was a bunch of cut up compartments is now wide open,' Leonatti said. 'So, we'll have tables there and it'll be wide open and spill out onto the sidewalk.'
Construction should wrap up by the end of November according to Leonatti, who says time of completion can shift due to moving parts.
This is the second phase of three redeveloping Floyd's. The first phase was the addition of Third Shift, the second phase is reshaping the exterior by adding more airy, open space with light, while phase three will be the elusive rooftop bar and elevator to it.

title: New study finds Illinois residents most interested in Black Friday
author: Tom Ackerman
description: If you've been looking for some Black Friday deals, you're definitely not alone, at least according to this new study.
content:
Will you be one of the early birds in line at your favorite store on Black Friday? One study suggests that you are more likely to be if you live in Illinois.
Illinois is the most interested state in the discounted shopping day after Thanksgiving, a recent study found by using Google keyword metrics.
Who conducted the study?
Coupon site BravoDeal utilized Google Keyword Planner to track how often Americans search for Black Friday related terms in the span of a year. The rank is based on the number of searches divided by the population of each state.
How often does Illinois search for Black Friday?
Illinois recorded over 1,400 keyword searches each month on average per 100,000 people. Overall, Illinois residents searched for the related keywords over 178,000 times each month.
What are the most searched phrases?
In Illinois, the most searched term was 'black friday deal' followed by 'black friday' and then 'black friday deals Walmart.'
What other states ranked high or low?
Many of the states in the top 10 are in the Midwest. Missouri ranked second. Minnesota and Kentucky tied for third. Alaska ranked last.
Were certain stores searched?
Americans inquired about Walmart the most in related keyword searches with over 167,000 monthly searches for "black friday deals walmart." Best Buy and Target received the second and third most related searches.

title: Taking Riverton by Stormy. Daniels yuks it up at The Donald's expense
author: Steven Spearie
description: Adult film star Stormy Daniels took several shots at President-elect Donald Trump during a comedy routine in central Illinois.
content:
For as many digs as Stormy Daniels got in at President-elect Donald Trump, "the orange elephant in the room," the biggest applause line the adult film star and director got Monday dealt with her own political affiliation.
"People ask, 'Why are you still a Republican? Why haven't you changed?" Daniels said during her 50-minute comedy set at The Backroom Lounge in Riverton. "Because it makes (Republicans) so mad, and I am that kind of petty."
Not that Daniels was enthralled with Tuesday's matchup between Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris.
"How are those our only options (for president)?" Daniels demurred. "It's the hypocrisy of the whole thing."
Daniels' alleged affair with Trump in 2006 led to him being found guilty of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records as part of a conspiracy to unlawfully interfere in the 2016 election.
A Manhattan judge has said he will issue an opinion on Trump's request to toss his conviction and either order a new trial or dismiss the case out of hand.
Trump has denied the sexual encounter.
Trump, Daniels pointed out, called President Joe Biden "Sleepy Joe," yet "(Trump) falls asleep at his own trial, except when I was on the stand. Lucky me."
When Daniels decided to tour doing standup, some comedians became incensed, she admitted.
"We all know I do my best work laying down," Daniels said. "It's way more fun."
Daniels said after the show that comedians like Kathy Griffin encouraged her endeavor.
Copenhagen Bandit, one of two comedians who opened the show for Daniels Monday, said he wasn't averse to Daniels "jumping the line" comedically.
"When it comes to standup comedy," said the Joplin, Mo.-based performer, "the only thing it takes is if you can make people laugh. I think she's very good at that. She's got a lot of funny stories.
"Comedy's different than it used to be. We have a lot of famous people who are doing it (now) and if they want to come in and get in the ballgame, it's a beautiful thing."
All of the comedians were donating, after costs, proceeds to local veterans groups.

title: Springfield-area woman raising funds for injured soldiers as she trains for Boston Marathon
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A Waverly High School graduate is looking to raise money injured soldiers while she trains for the Boston Marathon.
content:
In April of 2013, a senior at Waverly High School was so moved by the tragedy of the Boston Marathon bombings that she laced up her running shoes and ran 26.2 miles along Illinois 104.
Now a U.S. Marine Corps Staff Sergeant and a mom, Brennan Barrett (formerly Schneider) will be re-running that route as she trains for the Boston Marathon and raises money for military families in need.
Barrett aims to raise $10,000 for Semper Fi & America's Fund that supports veterans and their families after sustaining life-changing injuries or critical illnesses.
'It feels like a full-picture moment,' Barrett said. 'Running the Boston Marathon has always been a goal, but I think it's such a small part of what I'm doing because I'm raising all of these funds for such an amazing organization.'
Barrett didn't know at the time of the bombings that she wanted to pursue military service or that she would still be talking about that trek along Illinois 104 over a decade later.
But she is still talking about it, as she plans to run in Waverly on March 15 a month before she will run the Boston Marathon in April.
She aims to raise awareness for the cause and raise money for the charity with events scheduled as soon as Dec. 7 at the Jacksonville VFW from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., where Barrett and her family will host 'The Warm Up." A ticket will get participants an assortment of homemade soups, rolls, drinks, and sweets.
There will be also raffles, silent auctions, and T-shirts for sale. All the money raised will go to the non-profit. Barrett will also pay for her own flight to Boston.
Barrett said she is in good company as she gears up to train, being stationed in Indianapolis with fellow Marines who regularly compete with one another.
Barrett and some of those Marines once ran a 50-kilometer race – that's 31 miles – with many of them never having ran anywhere close to that distance.
'We were like, 'hey, let's do this.' None of us trained for it but we all finished it. They're just like, 'that's nuts, I never want to do that distance again, and you're just willing to sign up and do it again?'"
The answer is yes.
Barrett in the last 10 years has run marathons and even longer distances in Chicago, Honolulu, Little Rock, Maine, San Diego, and Indianapolis.
After running the initial marathon distance in Waverly – sporting a t-shirt that read "Boston 26.2" on the front and 'Honk for Boston' on the back, Barrett told the SJ-R the following:
'When I heard (the bombings) happened, as a runner, running being my life, I felt I had to do something,' says Brennan. 'I couldn't think of anything better to do than run – finish the race for those who didn't finish.'

title: Mark your calendars: Illinois State Fair announces first two headliners for 2025
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Thinking of heading to the 2025 Illinois State Fair? The first two music headliners have been announced. Here's what you need to know.
content:
We know what you're thinking: didn't the Illinois State Fair just end? Yes, the annual fair ended in August, but it's never too late to start thinking the 2025 Illinois State Fair.
State fair organizers are thinking the same thing, it's why the state fair already announced two headliners for next year's fair.
Here's what you need to know.
Who are the two headliners?
State fair organizers announced country star Megan Moroney and music group Def Leppard will be performing at the 2025 Illinois State Fair.
How much are the tickets?
Tickets for Def Leppard range from $85 to $115, and after the new year will range from $85 to $125.
Tickets for Megan Moroney range from $47 to $122.
Why did they announce the act so early?
The move comes from thinking outside of the box to provide fairgoers a chance to get discounted rates during the holiday season, said Illinois State Fair Manager Rebecca Clark.
Why are these acts appealing to fair organizers?
The fair aims to book acts that appeal to everyone, Clark said.
'Def leopard has a catalog that's spans so many years, and it has so many cross generational appeals,' she said.
On Moroney, organizers shared that the fair has a long tradition of showcasing artists early in their careers. "She has a bright future in Country music," stated Illinois Department of Agriculture Director Jerry Costello II.
When can I get a ticket?
Tickets for both acts will be on sale Saturday morning.
Where can I get a ticket?
Tickets can be purchased at ticketmaster.com.
Lil Wayne, Keith Urban, the Jonas Brothers, Motley Crue, and Jordan Davis headlined, among other big names. Lil Wayne broke the attendance record by selling more than 15,000 tickets.

title: Illinois crime victim bill turns 10. Meet one of the biggest proponents of Marsy's Law
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Jennifer Bishop-Jenkins's sister and brother-in-law were killed in 1990, but never have a chance to speak in court. She helped make sure that changed 10 years ago in Illinois.
content:
Jennifer Bishop-Jenkins and others' efforts succeeded 10 years ago when Illinois voters decided to amend the state constitution and afford more rights to victims of violent crimes.
That choice has since resulted in a cultural shift in courtrooms throughout the state, she said.
Bishop-Jenkins recalled an instance prior to the amendment passing when victims were referred to as 'pieces of evidence.'
Now, every county in the state has victim advocate staff, she told The State Journal-Register. There are now automatic notification systems in place to keep victims in the loop if they opt for it, and there are mandatory meetings between victims of violence and the prosecutors. The victims now are guaranteed the right to make their victim impact statements if they choose.
Bishop-Jenkins is currently the director for Marsy's Law for Illinois, but she became involved in efforts to get the amendment on the ballot after a teenager murdered her sister, her sister's husband, and their unborn child in 1990.
Bishop-Jenkins was on her way to the killer's sentencing hearing when she was told that she and her parents would not be allowed to provide a victim impact statement because the sentence was mandatory life in prison.
'Don't come to court. Don't bother. We don't have time for you," she said. "After all the process, it was just like, 'What? What do you mean?'' she said.
She had cooperated with attorneys and the legal system for years awaiting the day. But she wasn't just deflated. She was confused as to why it happened.
Bishop-Jenkins began looking into the existing language of the constitution and in that time learned of then Attorney General Lisa Madigan's push to give that language teeth.
She was invited to join a meeting with the Illinois Coalition Against Sexual Assault who were already working with Madigan and the Illinois Coalition Against Domestic Violence. Bishop-Jenkins came to represent the murder-victim-families community, she said, noting that it is 'sadly, a significant group.'
Illinois became the second state to enact changes following California, and today a dozen states have adopted some version of Marsy's Law in their state constitutions, she said.
These days, Bishop-Jenkins handles the role in a part time capacity as most of the work was done in the years leading up to the amendment. Still, she connects people with resources and keeps tabs on how the amendment is being implemented.
Bishop-Jenkins did testify against a bill last year that would abolish life sentences for any incarcerated individual who was under the age of 21.
She argued it didn't do enough to make sure that victims or their families would be notified when an individual becomes eligible for parole.
Bishop-Jenkins continues to attend court as the killer of her sister and her family seeks a lesser sentence.
But now, Bishop-Jenkins finds some peace in knowing that she is tweaking the system so that victims no longer become re-victimized after a tragedy.

title: Sangamon County sheriff's department subject of a Department of Justice civil rights probe
author: Steven Spearie
description: The fatal shooting of Sonya Massey has led to the Department of Justice launching a civil rights investigation of the Sangamon County sheriff's office.
content:
A scathing letter from the U.S. Department of Justice said the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey by a now former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy in her home this past summer "raises serious concerns about (the sheriff department's) interactions with Black people and people with behavioral health disabilities" along with a host of practices and procedures.
The eight-page letter directed to Sheriff Paula Crouch and State's Attorney John Milhiser among others and dated on Nov. 14, asks for the department's cooperation in providing records in nearly 30 different areas.
Crouch, in a statement released Friday, said her department "pledged full cooperation with the Department of Justice in its review."
A representative from the office of civil rights attorney Ben Crump didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The Florida-based Crump represents the Massey family.
The DOJ probe is outside of the criminal prosecution of former deputy Sean Grayson, who is charged with Massey's murder.
The letter added that Massey's killing incident brings into question the sheriff's department's "policies, practices, procedures, and training regarding community policing, bias-free policing, response to behavioral health crises, use of force, de-escalation, affirmative duty to intervene, affirmative duty to render medical aid, and body-worn camera policies and compliance."
The fatal incident and prior 911 calls involving Massey in the days before her death indicate "possible issues" with Sangamon County, the sheriff's department and the sheriff's department emergency response and dispatch system, the letter added.
The DOJ also has reviewed reports "concerning (the sheriff's department employment practices, including allegations that a lack of racial diversity at (the department) impacts (its) provision of policing services in communities of color."
In addition to seeking all records related to the fatal shooting of Massey, the sheriff's department was asked to identify whether it "has provided or currently provides any form of alternative response models when responding to behavioral health crises or interacting with someone with a behavioral healthdisability."
That includes any co-responder teams, mobile crisis teams or Crisis Intervention Training (CIT) programs.
With regards to its hiring process for deputies and lateral transfers, the department was asked to produce information on recruitment, background check, psychometricevaluation, reference, and selection processes.
Grayson's hiring process has been brought into question. His criminal history shows he had two DUIs and a questionable discharge from the military. Grayson had also been with six different law enforcement agencies within four years.
Grayson used his future father-in-law, Scott Butterfield, a former county sheriff's deputy, as an employment reference in 2023.
Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman and the mother of two children, called 911 about a would-be prowler at her home on Hoover Street early on the morning of July 6. Massey was the subject of a 911 call shortly after 9 a.m. on July 5 made by her mother, Donna Massey, who said she was having "a mental breakdown."
Springfield Police responded because Donna Massey's home was within the city. Sonya Massey's Hoover Street home is an unincorporated part of Woodside Township.
The Massey Commission was called for in August by Sangamon County Board Chairman Andy Van Meter and State Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, with an eye towards addressing systemic issues in law enforcement practices, mental health responses and community relations.

title: Store allowing children to buy, wrap and tag gifts reopening soon in Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: The popular store allowing children to buy, wrap and tag gifts for parents, grandparents and more reopens for the season soon in Springfield.
content:
The Mini O'Beirne Crisis Nursery Holiday Store returns to Fairhills Mall, 1919 W. Monroe St., beginning Nov. 30.
The store allows children to purchase, wrap and tag gifts for parents, grandparents, siblings and even their pets with the assistance of volunteer shoppers.
The gifts range in price from $1 to $15.
Here are all the details:
What are the shopping times and dates?
The store is open from Nov. 30 through Dec. 21.
Shopping times are from 4 to 7 p.m. Thursday and Friday; 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturday and noon to 6 p.m. Sunday.
Special hours can be scheduled for groups.
Is the store looking for volunteers?
Yes. Shopping assistants or elves must 14 years of age or older. You can sign up at the Holiday Store website MOCN.org or call 217-525-6800, Ext. 5 for more details.
Does the store have another location?
There will be a pop-up store at Chatham United Methodist Church, 104 W. Chestnut St., from 6 to 8:30 p.m., on Dec. 6. There will be carriage rides, hot cocoa, carolers and the lighting of the tree.
Are there other ways to help the nursery?
New this year is a holiday cash raffle with a grand prize of $2,500.
Tickets are $25 each and available online, by mail or in person at the Holiday Store. A limit of 500 tickets will be sold.
What does the Crisis Nursery do?
Founded nearly 40 years ago, the Crisis Nursery, 1011 N. Seventh St., provides free, 24-hour emergency childcare to families in need. It also offers family support services, like parenting education classes, and has a basic needs pantry with items like diapers, wipes and formula.

title: Here's some chances to shop small business this holiday season
author: Claire Grant
description: Seasonal business ventures are one of the top ways small businesses create opportunities to boost growth during the holiday season, when major competitors like big box stores are ramping up sales.
content:
Don't wait until Black Friday, because deals and steals are already popping up around Springfield.
Seasonal business ventures are one of the top ways small businesses create opportunities to boost growth during the holiday season, when major competitors like big box stores are ramping up sales.
According to the Small Business Index, eight in 10 small businesses say the holiday season is important for their overall profit. Constant Contact reports that the majority of small businesses rely on holiday shopping for at least one quarter of their annual revenue.

Featured at the event is make and take crafts, face painting, live music, hot drinks and a picture with the one and only Grinch.

Where: 1500 N. Fifth St., Springfield

Most local businesses downtown will be holding shopping deals during the day, like District 23 Boutique which will have a hot chocolate and sweet treat bar, as well as in-store giveaways.

title: Breakdown of the top 12 girls basketball teams in the Springfield area this winter
author: Bill Welt
description: Lincoln and Chatham Glenwood's girls basketball teams made last season epic. This year promises to be another good one in the Springfield area
content:
More than a few high school girls basketball teams around Springfield bring back winning experience this season.
Class 3A state runnerup Chatham Glenwood perhaps looms the largest, along with Taylorville.
Here are the top teams to watch for the 2024-25 season beginning with Class 3A:
Class 3A
🏀 Chatham Glenwood
A bevy of newcomers blended right in and elevated the Titans to their first sectional title since 2003 and best season in program history with second place in Class 3A and a 28-8 overall record. That starting lineup graduated Makenna Yeager and Karley Hawkins but features senior track star Katelyn Lehnen and sophomores Alexis Neumann and Ava Bobb. Neumann was tops in the league in rebounding and third in total scoring with 11.8 points and 8.5 rebounds per game. She nearly had a double-double with 15 points and eight rebounds in the 60-44 loss in the 3A championship game against Lincoln.
🏀 Taylorville
Only a turnover and Makenna Yeager layup thwarted Taylorville from the 3A regional title against Glenwood. That core will look to close out games and make a deeper postseason run this winter. Senior guard/forward and Southeast Missouri State commit Addison Tarr (14.9 ppg.), senior guard Kyleigh Heimsness (10.9 ppg.) and senior center Mazie Fleming (10.3 ppg., 7.1 rpg.) each averaged double figures. They will be reinforced by juniors Peyton DeMichael and Baileigh Wernz, and sophomores Grace Rogers, Hope Kietzman, Gianna Tarr and McKynlee Siempelkamp.
🏀 Springfield High
The Senators won their first City title since 2019. Coach Brad Scheffler will now call on a number of veterans to assume larger roles this season, including seniors Ariana Williams (7.6 ppg., 6.8 rpg.) and Keziah Toran (8.9 ppg., 5.3 rpg.). Junior forward Aniyah Rhinehouse (6 ppg., 4.6 rpg.) will enhance the front court. A host of newcomers may enter the mix: Jameara Townsend, Abby Borders, Zoe Luhtala, Lydia Auble and Oriona Nichols-Holman.
Class 2A
🏀 Sacred Heart-Griffin
New head coach David Andrews takes the helm after previously assisting Steve Klunick. Last season, the Cyclones drew a tough Class 2A regional final against host Camp Point Central, which later knocked off Staunton and Pleasant Plains in the Beardstown Sectional. SHG graduated top scorers and rebounders Maggie Fleischli and Callie Huston, but four battled-tested seniors remain. That includes three-year starters Izzy Hassebrock and Reese Watson.
🏀 Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central
Jayce Privia, The State Journal-Register's Small School Girls Basketball Player of the Year, has departed for McKendree University after winning the outright Sangamo Conference title. The Bluejays still retain one of the area's top ball-handlers: junior guard Aubrey Vogel. A consummate shortstop committed to Eastern Illinois University's softball team, she averaged 5.9 points, 3.2 assists, 3.1 rebounds and 2.3 steals per game. She will mesh seamlessly with PORTA's interior: seniors Carson Arthalony and Cassie Cox. Arthalony, who will play at Illinois College, contributed 10.8 points and 5.7 rebounds per game.
🏀 Pleasant Plains
The Cardinals secured their fifth Sangamon County title in the last seven years before coming up just short against Camp Point Central in the 2A sectional finals. Most of that lineup returns, including junior forward Madison Burke (8.7 ppg.) from injury. Junior forward Anna Weber (14.1 ppg., 14.1 rpg.) dominated the paint, while junior guard Bailey Leach (12.1 ppg.) surfaced as a perimeter threat. Her younger sister, Jada Leach, also stepped up following Burke's injury. Bailey and Jada are among three sister combos on the team.
🏀 Staunton
Nearly Staunton's entire lineup comes back to defend the South Central Conference title. Senior all-SCC first team picks Ele Feldmann and Grace Bekeske form the vanguard after leading the volleyball team to a fifth straight league title. Feldmann averaged 10.9 points, seven rebounds and 3.3 assists per game. Senior Lilly Bandy was all-SCC second team.
🏀 Carlinville
Senior guard/center Isabella Tiburzi may reach 1,000 points, 1,000 rebounds and 500 assists before she heads off to Lincoln Land Community College. She has a strong supporting cast that includes junior Kaitlyn Reels (9.4 ppg., 5.4 rpg.), senior Jordyn Loveless (7.8 ppg.), senior Hannah Gibson (5.3 ppg., 5.4 rpg.) and senior Braley Wiser (4.5 ppg.). Reels dialed up 70 3-pointers and shot 36.5% from long range last year.
🏀 Gillespie
Former assistant Nikki Brawner replaces longtime coach Kevin Gray after 16 seasons. The Miners are also coming off their first regional title since 2012 and most wins since 2002, led by Nikki's daughter, senior Mia Brawner. She averaged 16.2 points and 6.1 rebounds per game. Junior guard Amari Vickery was also all-SCC second team, while senior forward Delaney Taylor was on the third team. The Miners tied Carlinville and Greenville for second place in the SCC.
Class 1A
🏀 Havana
The Ducks hope to compensate for their lack of size with speed and athleticism. Senior guard Josie Hughes certainly brings that to the table with 15 points, five rebounds and four steals per game, along with junior Kaydi Miller's nine points, six rebounds and three steals per game. Seniors Hannah Hodgson and Alexis Richardson will provide support, along with juniors Olivia Kramer and Lindsay Greer and sophomore Taylor Lindsey. A talented freshman class, coming off back-to-back IESA Class 2A state titles, add another edge.
🏀 Nokomis
Coach Brandon Engelman's options are limitless. NHS graduated just one senior from last year's roster. That experience extends across different grade levels. There's senior Natalie Brownback (8.4 ppg.), but also junior Kinley Stolte (6.9 ppg., 7.8 rpg.) and sophomore Alivia Sabol (6.3 ppg., 5.7 rpg.) to name a few. They will attempt to break the regional title dry spell that stretches back to 2001.
🏀 Kincaid South Fork/Edinburg
South Fork's 20-12 season and Waverly Thanksgiving Tournament championship run were unprecedented in program history. Angelina Ippolito totaled 24 points in the Waverly championship win over Auburn and continued to flourish with 15 points per game. Ippolito, now a junior guard, was named all-MSM Conference first team, along with returning senior point guard Lilly Wake. Senior forward Jara Shoulders was all-MSM second team. It's now a matter of capitalizing on last year's success.

title: 'The people have spoken:' Lesko bests Langfelder by 31 votes in Recorder's race
author: Steven Spearie
description: There were 456 provisional and late-arriving vote by mail ballots counted by the Sangamon County Clerk's office Tuesday.
content:
With over 100,000 votes cast, challenger Frank Lesko bested incumbent Josh Langfelder in the Sangamon County Recorder's race after the clerk's office counted 456 provisional and late-arriving vote by mail ballots.
Lesko's lead from Election Night shrank by 37 votes, but the Springfield City Clerk and former city council member held on for the win.
"I think the people have spoken," Lesko said afterwards. "I wanted all the ballots counted. I wanted to hear what the people of Sangamon County wished for. I'm very humbled."
There were 212 provisional ballots and 244 late-arriving vote by mail ballots.
Lesko's vote total stood at 49,124 to Langfelder's 49,093 with 2,320 "under votes" after the count.
In another close election, Jennifer Ghesquiere Deaner clung on to a win over challenger Jennifer Merritt in the District 25 Sangamon County Board race.
Clerk Don Gray said any candidate who lost an election by a 5% or less margin is able to apply for a discovery recount.
This story will be updated.

title: 9 Springfield-area establishments found selling alcohol to underage people
author: Claire Grant
description: Of the nine establishments that were found selling alcohol to underage people, three of them had failed a previous compliance check.
content:
Nine Springfield-area establishments sold alcohol to underage people earlier this month.
On Nov. 7, the Illinois Liquor Control Commission, or ILCC, in coordination with Springfield Police Department, conducted 25 underage compliance checks at businesses across the county.
During the operation, there were six prior violators which had sold alcohol to minors re-tested for compliance.
What businesses sold alcohol to underage people?
The Winner's Circle, 2327 N. Fifth St.
Main Gate Bar & Grill, 2143 N. 11th St.,
La Fiesta Grande, 2830 Adlai Stevenson Drive
Lucy's Place IV, 1822 Adlai Stevenson Drive
Jaalsa, 3114 S. Sixth St.
Crows Mill Bar & Grill, 1220 Toronto Road
Taqueria El Dorado, 1386 Toronto Road
Miss Kimmees, 1933 W. Iles Ave.
709 Cut Rate Package Liquors, 2710 E. Clearlake Ave.
The Crows Mill Bar, Miss Kimmees and 709 Cut Rate Package Liquor previously failed an underage compliance check during last inspection.
In July, Crows Mill was visited by the ILCC and sold alcohol to underage people – but it wasn't the first time. Crows Mill Bar and Grill failed previous compliance checks in 2014 and 2017.
Passing the check
Establishments which previously failed an underage compliance check but passed this time include the Northender Package Liquors on North Ninth Street, Crossing Too on East Clearlake and The Office Sports Bar on West Iles Avenue.
How operations are conducted
The report is a result of ongoing undercover and cooperative law enforcement operations conducted by agents of the ILCC, local law enforcement officials and underage participants recruited from area high schools and colleges.
The teams randomly visit liquor stores, restaurants and bars in communities around the state to check for ongoing compliance with state laws mandating that no liquor is sold to persons under 21 years old.
ILCC agents also work with local and state law enforcement agents to focus on communities with a high incidence of underage liquor sales.

title: Senior outside hitter from Greece is living American dream with UIS volleyball
author: Bill Welt
description: Here's everything you need to know about this UIS hitter from Greece and the Great Lakes Valley Conference volleyball tournament at Williamsville, which runs Friday through Sunday
content:
University of Illinois Springfield's Eirini Glynou already has one ring.
The senior outside hitter previously won the Sun Belt Conference tournament in her only season at NCAA Division I South Alabama. She hopes to pry another one at this weekend's Great Lakes Valley Conference tournament at the Williamsville High School Fieldhouse.
The No. 5-seeded Prairie Stars (18-9) open against No. 4 Rockhurst (19-6) in the quarterfinals on Friday at 2:30 p.m.
It was already a long journey before she even transferred to UIS — literally and figuratively.
Glynou originally hails from Athens, Greece. Economic hardship led her family to move to the Chicago area — where her dad, George, was born — about five years ago. The COVID-19 pandemic put the world to a halt just a few months later.
It threw her senior season into disarray with a shortened schedule, but she still found reprieve through the Sports Performance volleyball club in Aurora. She also found solace through her younger brother, Vasilis.
'I remember my mom (Eleni) when we moved here, she told me everything would be OK no matter how difficult it is right now because we were struggling,' Glynou said. 'It was hard, but I look back now and we made it through. Everything happens for a reason. No matter how hard life is, you just don't give up.'
It quickly dawned on Glynou that she had to prove herself.
'I wasn't worried that somebody would take my place (in Greece),' Glynou said of her time playing club volleyball at home. 'But when I came here, I realized, 'Oh, things are different here. I need to work really hard for that.' It was a good motivation for me to keep working hard because everything happens for a reason.'
Last season, Glynou was named all-GLVC second team with a team-high 419 kills and second-best 306 digs. She currently has 352 kills and team-high 39 aces to go along with 322 digs and 31 blocks.
This is Glynou's final season as a player at UIS, but the exercise science major still plans to stick around with a master's degree in mind. She said she may also pursue professional volleyball once school is done, not unlike her dad back in Greece.
He still remains a constant source of help. She wasn't too sure if he would be able to attend the tournament, but either way, her family is never far from mind.
'But no matter what, I always feel like they're there for me,' Glynou said. 'They're also a motivation for me. They really want the best for me. They also know it's my last year, so I'm going to give it everything.'
🏐 Quick facts about the tournament
The Great Lakes Valley Conference tournament will take place at the Williamsville High School Fieldhouse for a second straight year, running Friday through Sunday.
No. 1 Quincy kicks off against No. 8 McKendree at 11:30 a.m. on Friday, followed by No. 4 Rockhurst versus No. 5 UIS at 2:30 p.m. The championship is Sunday at noon.
Of the league's 14 teams, only the top eight earn a conference tournament bid. UIS is making its sixth appearance in the last eight years after missing last year's tournament.
Lewis, the No. 3 seed, is vying for its fourth straight conference tournament and 13 th overall. Top seed Quincy and No. 2 Maryville split the regular season title.
The tournament champion earns an automatic bid to the NCAA Division II tournament. Last year, four GLVC teams earned an NCAA berth and Missouri St. Louis reached the NCAA semifinals. UMSL is the No. 6 seed in this year's GLVC tournament.
UIS has only made one NCAA appearance since it transitioned from the NAIA in 2009. That occurred in 2018.
Quincy (No. 21) and UMSL (No. 22) are ranked in the latest American Volleyball Coaches Association poll.
Tickets must be purchased in advance at this link. Single-Day tickets are $15 for adults; $5 for students with ID and ages 6-17; and free for children 5 and under. Doors open one hour before the first game.

title: Experts: At the holiday table, pass the pumpkin pie, pass up the political talk
author: Steven Spearie
description: At the holidays, getting caught up in politics or other topics that are highly fueled is \
content:
Several years ago, Dan and Sherry Frachey of Springfield took a trip to visit relatives on the East Coast, some of whom they had strained relationships with because of political squabbles in the past.
Before the trip though, the couple made an "intentional effort" to rekindle personal ties, minus the political talk.
"We could feel like our family ties were thinning out," Dan Frachey said. "We needed to get together and build up some of the goodwill. It happened and we did remember why we liked these people."
Frachey, a spiritual director and a newly ordained priest for an independent Roman Catholic church in Springfield, said he understands the fractiousness families face as Americans travel for holiday gatherings.
When it comes to talk around the dinner table about the fallout from the recent presidential election or other volatile issues, Frachey has a word of advice.
"In response to those families having that conversation, I'd say please don't," Frachey cautioned. "(Most) who would have that conversation are probably not going to have a happier, productive outcome and it will likely exacerbate already strained relationships."
Dr. Sara Bahn, a co-owner of Behavioral Health Center of Illinois in Springfield, said while most families have a wide range of what they all look like, the focus should be on commonality and what brings them together, not getting sidetracked on things that are less important in a shared celebration.
"The whole point of getting together is to connect to other people and to keep it simple," Bahn said. "If you get caught up in politics or other topics that are highly fueled, it's like a runaway train."
Kristin Deneal, who moved to Springfield last year, said she knows that all too well.
"We have certain subjects we don't talk about, including politics, and that keeps it civil and respectful," Deneal said.
Bahn suggested falling back on a classic therapy line if political talk does come up: choose your battles.
"If something becomes challenging or there could be disagreement or conflict or even different political views, my suggestion is step back and try to understand or be an observer and remember the simple things and what's most important," she said.
Frachey acknowledged that it may take a little assertiveness to lay some ground rules for getting together. And if there needs to be "a cease fire" of sorts, so be it, he said.
"Let's call that humanitarian assistance a Thanksgiving meal," Frachey said. "We need to be together because we need to face so much together."
Frachey said sometimes the wounds are so deep that it might be best for some families not to get together now, but he cautioned that shouldn't be a permanent thing.
Bahn agreed.
"Everyone's an adult and you make your own decisions, your own choices," she said. "I think it's OK for people to take breaks or say, 'Hey, no thank you.' But a forever deal, I would sit with that a little bit longer."
That trip Frachey and his wife took proved to be a balm, but not without some soul-searching and planning.
"It was everything we hoped," he admitted. "We made the very conscious choice: we weren't going to try to initiate anything difficult. The mission was to re-see our family. We did that and we spent some really lovely time together and it did everything we hoped.
"Since then, it's restored what was lost. We were really glad for having made the effort. It was so worth it."

title: Two Lanphier High School students tased after fighting
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A school resource officer tased two students to end a fist fight at Lanphier High School earlier this week.
content:
A school resource officer tased two students to end a fist fight at Lanphier High School around 1 p.m. Wednesday.
Both students were arrested for aggravated battery, but neither met points for incarceration and were released to a parent or guardian.
The students did not respond to the school resource officer's commands, Lanphier principal Alicia Miller wrote in a message to parents and guardians.
Miller wrote that the officer 'deployed his taser and one prong struck each of the students fighting."
Springfield police said the students were taken to the hospital and later released.
Video of the fight obtained by the SJ-R shows at least two boys repeatedly throwing each other to the ground and punching each other.
The sound of a taser is heard along with a voice saying, 'Oh my god, he just tased him.'
Security officers can be seen in the video trying to pull the two boys away from each other in the hectic scene.
When asked about the school's taser policy, the school referred the SJ-R to the Springfield Police Department, who did not respond to phone calls from the SJ-R.

title: Cooley steps away from Springfield LGBTQ center after nearly two decades
author: Steven Spearie
description: Jonna Cooley helped launch the city's first PrideFest in 2011.
content:
Jonna J. Cooley, who had been with the Phoenix Center in Springfield for 18 years as its executive director and its development director, has retired effective Nov. 22.
Whether the parting was forced or not hasn't been confirmed.
The board of directors' president for the LGBTQ center, Karen Reynolds, reached Tuesday by The State Journal-Register, would only say that Cooley, 62, submitted her resignation and that she is retired.
A source close to the center but not authorized to go on the record said the board has another emergency meeting about Cooley's situation on Dec. 1 after meeting on Nov. 18.
Cooley, posting on social media Monday, acknowledged that losing her wife, Lisa Tomasino in 2022 after years of battling cancer, an identity theft and losing her nephew over the summer have "taken a toll on my physical and mental health. My doctor said I need to take care of me and spend more time with my granddaughter."
A post from the Phoenix Center said it was "a bittersweet day."
"Jonna has done so much and influenced so many in our community," the post read. "She leaves big shoes to fill."
Cooley helped launch PrideFest in 2011 to mark the center's 10th anniversary and oversaw the opening of its latest facility, OUT on East at 704 S. Dirksen Parkway, in the spring.
Cooley came to the Phoenix Center in 2006 after resigning from the Sangamon County Child Advocacy Center under suspicion of alleged misuse of the center's funds.
Eventually, Cooley pleaded guilty to a single charge of forgery on Feb. 2, 2009, and was sentenced to 30 months probation and fined $1,500. Cooley also was ordered to pay $8,000 in restitution.
Reynolds said the Phoenix Center's work would continue.
It offers various groups public health services, training, social and educational events and transitional housing.

title: How Central Illinois became a hotbed for esports on high school, college levels
author: Bill Welt
description: With a new computer arena for the Springfield high schools' championship-level esports program, as well as more players at Glenwood and Illinois College, the video game competition is growing by leaps and bounds locally.
content:
Chatham Glenwood junior Nikash Madanagopal appreciates all that esports has to offer in high school.
The excitement, adrenaline and camaraderie rival any other sport.
'It does feel pretty intense when you're in the game when the rounds are really close," Madanagopal said. 'At the end of the day, everyone wants to win, so it gets pretty intense, especially when you're playing with all your friends.
'When someone has a huge play, everyone will get excited, so it's just really fun. You can really feel the intensity, especially when it's in the playoffs. You need to win this to go on.'
Esports has been teaching life skills beyond the classroom as well.
It's dispelling old notions long associated with video games that Glenwood coach Rashid Bibb and Springfield Capitols interim coach Adam Martin perhaps grew up with.
Bibb said he has seen kids break out of their proverbial shells in his four years at the helm.
'I had to adjust my mindset to what this was,' Bibb said, ''Oh, competitive video games. How competitive could it be?' You get in there and see these kids are as determined to win this game as a football or a basketball player.'
Skeptics may think esports is just kids playing video games, Bibb said, 'but there's also a lot of strategy that goes into it.'
Teamwork is imperative. It's something that becomes especially visible in an esports arena.
The Capitols, a co-op between Springfield High, Southeast and Lanphier that began in 2019, recently settled into its decked-out arena at Lanphier last winter. Part of the school's $93.5 million renovation, it resembles a computer lab, but the space is exclusive to the Capitols.
Springfield High senior Christian Schneider said it promotes a stronger team environment.
'The difference between preparedness and coaching staff from the other schools and having everyone in the single room, you can tell,' Schneider said. 'There are a couple times their captains won't even be there on time, it's just a real blessing that we have this and we're able to go somewhere to actually compete.'
What is the high school esports experience?
Schneider, who also participates in the SHS marching and pep bands, has been with the Capitols since he started high school.
He has competed in a variety of games through the Illinois High School Esports Association and the Illinois High School Association. The former looms the largest.
The IHSEA serves up a fall and spring season. Each spans eight weeks with a different array of games that culminate in the state finals at Northern Illinois University in DeKalb or remotely. The IHSA subsequently hosts sectionals and state finals toward the end of the school year in April and May.
Each participating team typically ranges between 4-6 players, depending on the game's parameters.
A player may dabble in multiple games simultaneously, perhaps occasionally competing and practicing on the same day. Schneider, who acted as the captain of the Fortnite team this fall, intends to play both Pokémon Unite and League of Legends in the spring.
The practice schedules are typically flexible, but they certainly still require time commitment.
The Capitols alternate games each day — each practicing twice a week — and have the advantage of being able to huddle together and strategize over a whiteboard and large-screen TV in their new accommodations.
Due to the medley of esports titles across different platforms, Martin's staff includes four other coaches.
Martin emphasized these players are held to the same academic standards as any other student-athlete.
'It's not necessarily that we're coaching the games,' said Martin, who has a proclivity for Call of Duty. 'We're coaching the students as well to kind of come into their own and fill those spots in the game.'
Players assume leadership roles
Captains also point the way.
That includes Glenwood students Madanagopal in Valorant and Brady Daniels in Super Smash Bros. Ultimate.
Madanagopal, who also plays tennis, first started esports as a freshman.
'As a captain, I'm kind of the in-game leader,' Madanagopal said, 'so when we're playing, I kind of direct the strategy that we're taking. When we're having matches against other teams, I talk to them to set up the time. It's a good aspect to be able communicate with other people, it kind of helps.'
Daniels, a senior, said it was a little intimidating when he first came aboard as a sophomore.
He now instructs teammates on the nuances of the aforementioned Nintendo Switch game, which Daniels described as more fast-paced and intense than chess.
'You can study it down to one specific interaction between your opponent and what move beats out this other move, or how you can avoid one move to counterattack back,' Daniels said.
Glenwood sophomore Szymom Dynda, who also assists the football team, not only wants to reach the Overwatch 2 varsity lineup this spring, he also harbors state title ambitions. Last year's Overwatch team took third place in the IHSEA finals.
'Through esports, I've gained friends who are a lot better than me and they've given me some tips,' Dynda said. 'I've also learned to have a wide variety of characters to play.'
A few of these students said they may pursue esports in college.
Illinois College figures most prominently in the region. It launched its program and Meraki Gaming Center in 2016. It's directly funded by the athletics department and offers scholarships.
It's a prospect that so many high school students overlook, according to IC coach David Seering.
Seering was a former player himself at IC before taking the reins in 2023. Esports may still be relatively new ground, but Seering has seen improvements on the recruiting front with more resources available such as the web site Stay Plugged In.
It's just a matter of growing the world of esports from the bottom up.
'I think the momentum is building the same as it's been since 2016,' Seering said. 'IC has been consistent with it the entire time. We have done what we've needed to do to make sure we're a competitive team.
'It's more so just seeing other high schools invest in esports. That's what I'm looking forward to because the more people who get into it and realize there are scholarships available, competitions are going to be more fierce and I think that's just going to make everything more fun in the long run.'
Players can also take the intramural route at University of Illinois Springfield, which has a sleek, new arena at Founders Residence Hall. The UIS teams compete in the National Esports Collegiate Conference, separate from IC's Midwest Valley Esports Conference and Midwest Esports Conference.
It may be more relaxed, but that's only true to an extent.
'Definitely this semester I've noticed some players have shown frustration from losing, so I'd say it's very competitive for some of these students,' UIS coach John Nguyen said. "When you're competing in something, everybody wants to win. Everybody's competitive in their own mindset.'
Nguyen was a former player at UIS before becoming a coach at the start of the fall semester, primarily Valorant and Overwatch 2.
The workload took the 2024 alum by surprise balancing multiple teams, practices and matches all in a week's effort. And not unlike Seering, Nguyen sees plenty of room for growth. These games, after all, are global in scope.
'It's definitely different than as a player for sure,' Nguyen said. 'I didn't do any research as a player, so whenever it was match play, I just played to the best of my ability. As a coach, you look at the other team — what they play and how they play it — and then try to prep your players as best as possible.'

title: Carving up a storm: One artist's woodworking pieces popping up across Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: A Springfield man has been turning tree stumps into a work of art on South Grand Avenue West. Have you seen them yet?
content:
A giraffe, a penguin, an eagle and a flamingo.
These bright and colorful creatures aren't the real thing on South Grand Avenue West, but the work of a local artisan is bringing tree stumps to life around Springfield.
Meet Jon Morrissette, the lead pastor at Lakeside Christian Church at 225 Toronto Road. When not saying grace or having sermons, Morrissette is around town is making unique art with his chainsaw with his side business, JMCreative.
For people driving by on Grand Avenue watching a mini zoo come to life, that's Morrissette hard at work for his latest client, Ty Milner of Milner Dentistry.
According to Morrissette, Milner asked him to take two different stumps and turn them into art. The first stump he completed took 45 hours and featured animals Milner's child picked out.
The stump Morrissette is still working on will feature three teeth in the front showing dental tips to stay healthy, while in the back carved into the wood will be the family's golden doodle, a dentist in comic-book style, a cardinal for the St. Louis Cardinals and a big cutout of the state of Illinois at the top.
The love for woodworking stems back to his father Morrissette said, who he would spend hours with as a child carving wood with.
'I use vacations and extra time as a side job,' Morrissette said. 'It's art, so the more people buy stuff, I buy bigger tools.'
The art takes inspiration from Abraham Lincoln and the mother road, which Maid-Rite in Springfield made history as the first drive-thru on the route.
This isn't the first, and nowhere near the last of Morrissette's work in Springfield. For the Route 66 centennial in 2026, the City of Springfield commissioned him to carve and paint the stump outside of Maid-Rite Sandwich Shop at 118 N. Pasfield St.
Other art installations he's made can be found on Meadowbrook Road with a Narnia memorial featuring the Lion Aslan and dozens of references special for the family that commissioned it, or in the backyard of his house.
Morrissette says his commissions are open for more art pieces on his website jmcreativeshop.com, but wants to work through all of his current projects before tackling new ones, and is happy his art style has been continuously growing with the better equipment he has.
'I wouldn't have been able to do this a few years ago,' Morrissette said. 'It's very expensive cause all the saws can be $500 to $1,000 depending on what your setup is and all your little tools. It just takes a while to get all the tools you need to get that done.'

title: Fully recovered from ACL injury, senior Chloe Crawford ready to lead Southeast girls hoops
author: Bill Welt
description: Chloe Crawford has only provided small snippets of her potential on the Southeast girls basketball team after coping with an injury last year.
content:
It's easy to see why Chloe Crawford is considered the heartbeat of the Southeast girls basketball team.
Crawford indeed conveyed nothing but unbridled enthusiasm after a 73-48 win over Lanphier on Tuesday. She also provided a small hint of her full potential.
She battled through early foul trouble and scored eight of her 10 points in the fourth quarter at Lober-Nika Gym — all the while brushing off a slight injury scare with a laugh after the game.
'What she brings to the team is just unmatched with her energy and leadership,' coach Jasmine Woolfolk said.
Top teams in the area: Breakdown of the top 12 girls basketball teams in the Springfield area this winter
Nothing but smiles
Crawford only appeared in a trace amount of games last season due to a torn ACL the previous spring in soccer.
Now she can finally show everyone what she can do beyond the intangibles.
'It was a rough season last year,' Crawford said. 'It was difficult, I thought my body would be back 100%. Once I got back out there, I soon realized I was nowhere near 100%. I just had to work my way back up and this season I'm 10 times better than before.'
Crawford champions all that is incumbent of a point guard, even more critically as the only senior on the roster.
'You see me right now, I'm smiling,' Crawford said. 'I'm just excited to think about how much I can do compared to my previous seasons. I'm so ready for the rest of this season.'
Next up
The Spartans certainly buckled down following Crawford's fourth foul and turned a 26-24 halftime deficit into a 55-37 advantage by the end of the third quarter against Lanphier.
Crawford said she wasn't stressed with such a deep bench.
'The only word that I can think of is proud,' Crawford said. 'I'm so excited to see them play their game. I'm happy to have this last year with them, but I'm going to miss them.'
Junior guard Zaria Weston tallied 17 of her game-high 20 points in the third quarter, while defensive pressure churned out a slew of turnovers. Sophomore guard Navehua Collier and junior guard Corrine Pickett supplied 11 and eight points, respectively, as well. Six other players also scored.
Collier averaged 9.5 points and 5.7 rebounds per game as a freshman.
'The energy's amazing from the coaches to the players, everybody's picking up the energy and it helps in games like this because we kind of need that energy to get back,' Crawford said.
'It was great to see. Everybody was getting on the boards, everybody was doing something to contribute. It was amazing.'
Soccer star
Crawford said she gravitates more toward soccer.
She was named to The State Journal-Register's all-area girls soccer team in 2022 with 24 goals and three assists before her injury the following year.
'I think I'm just more natural at it,' Crawford said.
But she is open to the idea of remaining a dual athlete in college.
She credited both her parents, Howard and Carly, for supporting her along the way. She said her dad always talks to her after a game on how to improve, win or lose.
'I'm always talking to him and I think that's what makes me a better player,' Crawford said. 'Even if he's tired and his back is hurting, he's there. He's always in the crowd somewhere.'

title: Here's how to get the perfect sear on scallops
author: Channing Fullaway-Johnson
description: Making seafood at home can be tricky sometimes, so we want to offer some help. Here's how to get the perfect sear on scallops.
content:
My family, most simply put, is a blended family. With so many people coming together at the holidays with roots and traditions ranging from Illinois to the coast of Florida, it can get a little crazy.
However, we all agree it is not a holiday dinner without a seafood feast! Half the family does not like turkey, and the other does not like ham.
So, we started the tradition of a seafood feast many years ago. The family has grown, faces have changed, friends became family, and some are now missing, but we all find a way to fit around the dining room table for one big meal each year.
Of course, there are some family favorites that make the menu every year: baked salmon, seared scallops with garlic butter sauce, St. Augustine fried shrimp with famous pink sauce, poached white fish and some kind of crab dip. Everyone brings a side dish or dessert, and no one goes away hungry.
A few months ago, I shared the St. Augustine shrimp recipe and story from my hometown, and it is a crowd favorite. Coming in a close second are the seared scallops with garlic butter.
Choosing the right scallops can make or break the dish. I look for dry-packed scallops, which are free of added water or preservatives. There are many sizes to choose from, but do not let that overwhelm you.
I like using U10 scallops for this dish. "U,' meaning under, indicates that there are less than 10 scallops per pound.
On average, U10 scallops weigh about 1.5 to 2 ounces and are roughly 2-inches in diameter. The larger size makes them perfect to achieve that golden crust when searing them for your next dinner.
Make sure to remove the scallop foot, which is a small piece of tissue on the side of the scallop that connects it to the shell.
This piece is edible; however, it can be very chewy and not enjoyable. Next, I pat them dry with paper towels to remove excess moisture. This step and placing them in a pre-heated pan are the keys to achieving a golden crust.
Tips for the perfect sear: Use a large, heavy-bottomed skillet (preferably stainless steel or cast iron) to ensure even heat distribution and cooking. Also, do not rush the cooking. If you pre-heat your pan before placing the seasoned scallop and at 2 minutes it is sticking, give it more time. As they cook, they will naturally release from the pan and will be very easy to flip.
Garlic Seared Scallops
Ingredients
1 lb. dry-packed sea scallops
2 tbsp. olive oil
2 tbsp. unsalted butter
4 garlic cloves, minced
Salt and freshly ground pepper (to taste)
Fresh parsley, chopped (optional)
Lemon wedges (for serving)
Instructions:
Pat the scallops dry, and season with salt and pepper.
Heat a skillet over medium-high heat. Add olive oil and butter.
Once the butter is foamy, place scallops in the pan. Sear for 2-3 minutes on one side until golden brown.
Flip and cook for another 1-2 minutes. Then reduce the heat, add garlic and baste scallops with garlic butter.
Remove scallops from the pan, and drizzle with the remaining garlic butter.
Garnish with freshly chopped parsley and a squeeze of lemon juice for brightness.
Serve immediately.
Channing Fullaway-Johnson is the culinary coordinator at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management and Baking/Pastry, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: Bridgestone grant provides Springfield Boys & Girls Clubs much-needed passenger van
author: Steven Spearie
description: Officials from Bridgestone's Chicago office were in Springfield Wednesday to officially make the gift to the Boys & Girls Clubs.
content:
Jackie Davis of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Central Illinois (BGCCI) said a 15-passenger van, made possible by a grant from Bridgestone Retail Operations, "drives like new money."
"It's like the feeling of luxury," said Davis, a unit director, who picks up kids from several schools for the after-school program at the clubhouse at 300 S. 15th St.
Officials from Bridgestone's Chicago office were in Springfield Wednesday to officially make the gift.
The Springfield club was one of 10 clubs nationwide to receive the $60,000 grant, said Tony Halas, a region manager for Bridgestone.
Funds raised for Driving Great Futures, its partnership with Boys & Girls Clubs of America, come directly from customers and employees from Bridgestone's 2,200 company-owned retail operations nationwide. Bridgestone has contributed $25 million to address transportation-related and technology needs through the partnership, Halas said.
The van from Bridgestone arrived, said club CEO and executive director Tiffany Mathis Posey, right around the time another new passenger van, made possible by the Boys & Girls Clubs of Springfield Foundation, also docked.
The vans had been on Mathis Posey's wish list, so now two-thirds of the club's aging fleet is brand new.
"Transportation is costly, so I feel lucky we were able to access that," she admitted.
The most impactful part in putting together the application to Bridgestone, Mathis Posey said, was a video where club kids gave feedback about why they felt the club deserved a new van and things they wanted to see in it, like air conditioning and individual seating.
"Kids are learning how to advocate," she said. "I love that the kids are using their voice (resulting) in something so big."
It was a bright spot in a week when BGCCI learned that free after-school programming could end at eight sites after the Illinois State Board of Education declined to renew a $1.2 million grant.
The absence of programs could leave roughly 900 BGCCI and Springfield Urban League students and their families in a lurch.
"We become family to our families," said Mathis Posey, who has a child attending one of the targeted sites. "There is a huge need. It's very, very, very devastating to see this happen."
