title: We need a plan to re-empower Central and Southern Illinois
author: Ken Anderson
description: Ken Anderson, director of Southern Illinois University Carbondale's Advanced Energy Institute, says it's time for a new plan to power Illinois.
content:
Flipping a switch to turn on the lights, or any of the other electrical devices that we use every day, is something that most of us take for granted.
But behind that switch is our electrical grid, a complex web of engineering that generates, regulates and transmits the energy that powers our devices, and those of us living in Southern and Central Illinois need to start paying more attention to it, or face the social and economic consequences of failing to do so.
According to data from the U.S. Department of Energy, over about the last decade, the southern half of Illinois has suffered a net loss of about 4.8 gigawatts (34%) of our generation capacity.
With further closures planned, in four years, Southern Illinois will have about half the electrical generation capacity it had 10 years ago.
The situation is better in northern parts of the state, where capacity additions (8.5 GW) have outstripped closures (6.0 GW), but even there, supply is struggling to keep up with increasing demand.
Aside from higher prices, the greater impact for consumers over the next few years may well be decreased reliability.
The National Electric Reliability Council assesses that much of the Midwest, including Central and Southern Illinois, is already at high risk of being unable to meet normal peak demand, and the problem is expected to worsen as further plant retirements go into effect.
Many factors have combined to bring us to this point. Recent opinion pieces in Springfield and Chicago blame the 2021 Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA), but the reality is more nuanced.
The typical design-life expectancy for a traditional power plant is about 40 years. That can be, and often is, extended with retrofits and upgrades, etc., but the useful life of these facilities cannot be extended indefinitely, as recent failures of generators in Grand Tower and Springfield demonstrate.
The average age of the power plants in Southern Illinois that have been retired recently was about 53 years, and the age of those to be retired is about 55 years.
CEJA may have moved the needle slightly with respect to the timing of these retirements, but this problem is ultimately the result of decades of inadequate infrastructure planning and investment, especially in southern parts of the state.
There's another acute aspect to this problem: The transmission system in rural parts of the state is not designed to accommodate many small, distributed generators.
Historically, our transmission system was designed a bit like a spider web, with large generators in the center, sending power out to consumers through a series of progressively smaller substations.
That's not well suited to accommodating many relatively small generators distributed over a wide area (like most solar and wind-powered generators), and there doesn't seem to be any real effort to upgrade it in a planned or thoughtful way.
So, what are our options? That's not an easy question to answer. Keeping aging generators open longer than planned is not really a solution.
Replacing them with new coal- or gas-fired generators probably doesn't make economic sense, would face an uphill battle over environmental concerns and probably couldn't secure financing anyway.
Nuclear power is technically viable, but it's expensive and would certainly face permitting and public acceptance challenges. Geothermal power and wind energy are not viable options in Southern Illinois.
Solar energy is viable here. That's why solar developers have been expressing keen interest in Southern Illinois for several years now.
But even this option has its challenges. Deploying solar energy on the scale that will be needed requires large amounts of land, preferably flat, open land, with good existing access and no trees to shade the panels.
Unfortunately, most of the land that fits that description is already in use – for agriculture, which is creating conflict between energy developers and the agricultural community.
Farmers have legitimate concerns regarding the loss of prime farmland, which is causing many agricultural communities to resist solar developments.
One thing is clear: We need to look for solutions and invest in getting those solutions deployed – sooner rather than later.
Allowing the electric supply system to become more expensive and less reliable will only widen the economic disparities within the state, driving businesses, and people, out of Central and Southern Illinois.
We need a plan for generating and distributing power to where it's needed. A plan that takes into account the short- and long-term goals of largely rural communities in Central and Southern Illinois and provides them with the infrastructure they need to take advantage of opportunities to thrive and prosper.
A well-thought out, pragmatic plan based on the best available science and engineering, not politics. A plan that treats all Illinoisians as equal citizens of the state.
And we need it soon.

title: Carson Arthalony leads PORTA, Gillespie girls beat Auburn, plus area top performers
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Carson Arthalony scores 21 in PORTA loss; Mia Brawner leads Gillespie past Auburn with 19 in area girls basketball.
content:
This is a daily list of top performers from Springfield-area high school sports teams for Dec. 9-14, compiled from information provided to The State Journal-Register by coaches, athletic directors and team statisticians.
To have your team's athletes included, email results to sports@sj-r.com.
Monday, Dec. 9
Girls basketball
Game of the night: Pittsfield 45, Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central 39
PETERSBURG — Carson Arthalony scored eight points in each of the first two quarters and led Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central with a team-high 21 points in a nonconference loss to unbeaten Pittsfield on Monday.
Junior cousins Aubrey Vogel and Allison Vogel combined for 14 points for the Bluejays (7-3 overall). Aubrey Vogel had eight points, six in the second half.
Pittsfield (9-0) got a game-high 23 points from freshman Reese Ramsey. She had eight points at halftime, nearly doubled her output with seven more in the third quarter and added another eight points in the final period.
'They're good. They've got a really balanced team,' PORTA coach Derek Schnapp said. 'They've got quickness. Obviously, Ramsey is a heck of a ballplayer who can shoot from outside and drive to the hoop.
'But she's got a lot of teammates that can really distribute the ball well. They've got young pieces and older pieces; they've got a very bright future.'
Senior Lila Simon added eight for Pittsfield, hitting two 3-pointers in the opening quarter.
PORTA led 22-21 at halftime but were outscored 11-7 in the third and 13-10 in the fourth.
— Ryan Mahan
Stars of the night
Mia Brawner, Gillespie: The Miners' senior notched 15 of her game-high 19 points in the second half as Gillespie turned a one-point halftime lead into a 71-65 nonconference win over Auburn in Gillespie. Brawner was 7-for-10 at the free-throw line, including hitting five of six in the fourth quarter as the Miners improved to 7-3 and grew their winning streak to seven games after starting out 0-3. Amari Vickery added 17 points for Gillespie while teammate Delaney Taylor scored 11.
Addison Wheatley, Auburn: The Trojans' senior center scored a team-best 18 points and was one of three players to reach double figures in Auburn's 71-65 road loss at Gillespie. Emme Divjak netted 12 points and hit two 3-pointers while Grayson Allen chipped in with 11.
Taylor Kiers, North Mac: The senior guard spearheaded a big second quarter and finished with a game-high 19 points in the Panthers' 46-31 nonconference win at Jacksonville at The Bowl. Keirs ended with two 3-pointers, went 5-for-6 from the foul line and had 15 first-half points and North Mac outscored the Crimsons 19-6 in the second quarter.
Natalie Brownback, Nokomis: The senior scored a game-high 12 points on 5 of 9 shooting and added three steals in Nokomis' 51-11 win over Ramsey. Sophomore Alivia Sabol had nine points and 12 rebounds and junior Kinley Stolte chipped in eight points and nine boards for NHS, which improved to 7-0.
Savana Howell, South County: She made two 3-pointers and scored 10 of her 16 points in the first period before South County rallied and defeated Kincaid South Fork 51-41. The Vipers outscored the Ponies 32-16 in the second half after trailing 25-19 at halftime.
Angelina Ippolito, Kincaid South Fork: The junior made a couple of 3-pointers and netted 14 of her 16 points in the first half in Kincaid's home loss to South County.
Maressa Williams, Jacksonville: She finished with a team-high 16 points in Jacksonville's home loss to North Mac.
Boys Swimming and Diving
Jackson Vinzant, Chatham Glenwood: The senior won the 200 and 500-yard freestyles and anchored Glenwood's winning 200 freestyle relay as the Titans finished second with 155 points in a quadrangular meet against first-place O'Fallon (181 points), Springfield High (133) and Sacred Heart-Griffin (29) at Eisenhower Pool.
Riley Herr, Springfield High: The junior won the 100 breaststroke and swam the breast on the Senators' second-place finish in the 200 medley relay in the quadrangular meet.

title: Nonprofit's raffle makes a dream come true for one Springfield woman
author: Claire Grant
description: A Springfield woman moved back to the area 3 years ago to be with her daughter. Now, the woman will be a homeowner thanks to a local nonprofit.
content:
The dream to call a house your own has come true for a Springfield woman thanks to a raffle.
Yvonne Williams was the lucky winner of the Little House of Hope raffle organized by Wooden It Be Lovely, a local nonprofit enterprise designed to give women in need employment and empowerment with job training and housing.
The house, donated by the O'Shea family to the nonprofit, features a two-bed, one-bath bungalow layout on the city's west side. Members of Wooden It Be Lovely, all women who are overcoming addiction or hardship, hand painted several parts of the home from the yard to the living room furniture pieces.
Williams moved back to Springfield to be with her daughter, a District 186 schoolteacher three years ago, according to a post made on social media by the nonprofit.
Previously living in an apartment, Williams had been one of the first to snag a ticket the day they went on sale with her daughter for the chance at a real place to call home.
Tickets for the housing raffle were sold for $100 each and capped out at 2,250 tickets. The tickets sold out before the drawing, in which the winner would be able to choose between $100,000 or the house.
All proceeds from the 2,250 tickets sold will go toward future program and housing expenses for women in need, according to Executive Director Rev. Margaret Ann Jessup.
Wooden It Be Lovely provides women in transition with a part-time job up to 20 hours a week in a supportive work environment, linking counsellors and filling the holes on the road to recovery.
Rev. Jessup said the opportunity to give a home to a member of the community was already a blessing, but knowing Williams had been dreaming of the house, made it all the more special.
'The winner couldn't have been more perfect,' Jessup said. 'She has been dreaming about it since she bought her ticket … we just couldn't be more happy for her and by the end of the year, hopefully it'll be her house.'
Jessup noted the raffle was only possible from the home being donated and from help from several local businesses supplying tools to help complete the makeover so the home would be move-in ready.
'We also had a lot of help for Little House of Hope with local businesses,' Jessup said. 'We couldn't have done it without our sponsors, and it was a learning opportunity and a unique way to get more exposure in the community.'

title: Having a Christmas feast but don't want to cook? These restaurants have you covered
author: Natalie Morris
description: Want more time to fa la la la la this holiday season and less time in the kitchen? These Springfield restaurants are here to help.
content:
Want more time to fa la la la la this holiday season and less time in the kitchen? The following compilation of local businesses offering Christmas dining and catering specials will keep you on the nice list without being tied to the oven all December.
Interfaith Holiday Breakfast
The 19th Annual Interfaith Holiday Breakfast will be served at Temple B'rith Sholom Christmas Day from 8:30 a.m. to noon with all proceeds going to SPARC.
Breakfast selections are scrambled eggs, pancakes, turkey sausage, assorted pastries, fruit, orange juice, tea and coffee. Cost is $10 for adults, $5 for children age 5 to 12. Kids four and younger eat for free.
The Temple B'rith Sholom and Temple Israel are jointly hosting the event that will take place at Temple B'rith Sholom located at 1004 S. Fourth St. SPARC, a non-profit, works to enrich the lives of those with intellectual and developmental disabilities by enabling them to successfully live, learn, work and socialize in the community.
Sgt. Pepper's Cafe
Sgt. Pepper's Cafe is open Christmas Day for its regular free holiday meal.
Ziyad and Souad Samara – owners of Sgt. Pepper's Cafe – are again inviting the public to spend the holiday meal with them at the 3141 Baker Drive cafe.
The meal, served from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m, includes turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes and gravy, sweet potatoes, cranberry sauce, a vegetable, bread and dessert.
Take out meals are limited to two per person and must be called in advance between 10 and 11 a.m. Phone: 217-525-5939.
The Samaras have served the free holiday meal since 2001.
Feast Buffet
Feast Buffet is adding steak and crab legs to its all-you-can-eat spread on Christmas Day, as well as a meet-and-greet with the Jolly ol' Elf himself Dec. 20.
The Christmas Day buffet will be served from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. The endless buffet costs $18.99.
Free photos with Santa Claus Dec. 20 from 5 to 8 p.m. Feast Buffet is at 3125 S. MacArthur Blvd.
Chatham Cafe
Chatham Cafe is open Christmas Day serving up three special entrees.
Christmas dinner specials include prime rib, baked ham with sweet potatoes and lasagna. The featured dinners come with a choice of potato, soup or salad, vegetable and dessert.
The cafe will be open Christmas Day from 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. Selections from the regular menu also will be available.
The Chatham Cafe is at 414 N. Main St. in Chatham. Reservations requested for parties of 5 or larger. Phone: 217/697-1101.
Cracker Barrel
Cracker Barrel is closed Christmas Day, but the Tennessee-based chain is taking preorders on holiday heat-and-serve meals to ensure you don't spend the whole day in the kitchen.
The Holiday Family Package features a spiral sliced sugar cured ham, cornbread dressing, cranberry relish, macaroni and cheese, green beans, rolls and gravy. The package costs $124.99 and feeds 4-6.
The Holiday Feast Package builds on the Holiday Family Package menu, adding mashed potatoes and two pies – apple streusel and pecan. The package costs $184.99 and feeds up to 10 people.
The Prime Rib heat and serve family dinner costs $149.99 and serves up to 6. The meal comes with au jus and horseradish sauce, mashed potatoes and gravy, macaroni and cheese, green beans and yeast rolls.
Add to your spread with a line up of a la carte selections. Extra meat selections include turkey breast ($44.99) and ham ($69.99). Side dishes range from Cracker Barrel signatures like fried apples and hashbrown casserole to broccoli cheese casserole and French toast bake. Sides can be purchased in two quantities that serve up to 6 and up to 10 individuals. Prices range from $15.99 to $31.49.
Pie selections include pumpkin, apple-streusel, pecan, chocolate-pecan and cinnamon roll pie. Cost $13.99.
All of these heat-and-serve meals are available for sale from Dec. 21-28 with 24hour advance notice. All Cracker Barrels are closed Christmas Day, but open Christmas Eve until 2 p.m. Place orders online at crackerbarrel.com/about-heat-n-serve.
Golden Corral
Celebrating your Christmas meal early? Golden Corral Buffet & Grill is highlighting its traditional holiday feast buffet lineup that expands the regular spread throughout December.
The 1038 Lejune Drive business is closed Christmas Day, but won't leave you slaving in the kitchen. There are two ways to take Golden Corral's holiday spread home: heat-and-serve or ready-to-eat. The family feast feeds 6 to 8 people with prices starting at $109.
Customize with choice of turkey, ham or roast beef. The meal also comes with mashed potatoes and gravy, stuffing, a side dish of choice, cranberry sauce, a dozen yeast rolls and choice of dessert.
Additional a la carte items can be added for an additional fee. Orders should be placed online at goldencorral.com under the holiday meal tab 48 hours before desired pickup time. Golden Corral will be open 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Christmas Eve.
Harvest Market
The Harvest Market deli isn't offering a heat-and-serve catered meal this Christmas season, but the grocery's in-house restaurant Farmhouse Restaurant has added holiday-themed entrees to its grab-and-go dinners throughout December.
Ham, turkey and roast beef have been added as entree to the regular line up for the single serve meals. The prepackaged meals include a protein, starch and vegetable for $11.99. Bone-in wings in a variety of sauces also join the lineup with 10 jumbo wings for $11.99.
Holiday-themed side dishes also have been added such as au gratin potatoes, green beans and glazed carrots. Sides are sold in a variety of quantities that serve anywhere from 5-10 individuals. A variety of prepackaged soups – ranging from tomato bisque to butternut squash – also are available by the cup, bowl or quart. Prices range from $4 to $14.
These grab-and-go options are located outside the Farmhouse Restaurant entrance by the deli during regular store hours. Harvest Market is at 3001 Veterans Parkway.
Mimi's Kitchen
Getting your photo with the big guy in the red suit too traditional? How about grabbing pancakes with the Grinch instead?
You don't have to travel to Mount Crumpit for the occasion. Mimi's Kitchen in Divernon is hosting an event featuring everyone's favorite green grump Dec. 21 and 22. Three seatings are available each day at 8 a.m., 10 a.m. and noon. Call 217-705-4573 to reserve a seat by Dec. 14.
The buffet meal includes green pancakes, scrambled eggs, hash browns, Tater tots, ham, biscuits and gravy, sausage patties, omelets, fresh fruit and assorted scratch desserts. Cost is $18.99 for adults, $8.99 for children 12 or younger. Price includes photo ops with the Grinch.
Golden Hour Bake House
Pre order your holiday sweets at Golden Hour Bake House in downtown Springfield.
Featured selections include Christmas cake donuts, layered cakes, pies and cookies. Orders due Dec. 17 for pickups Dec. 21.
Holiday cake donuts come in three flavors (white chocolate-peppermint, sugared orange-cranberry and double chocolate sprinkles) and are available in regular ($15/half dozen) or gluten free ($20/half dozen).
Featured cakes are white chocolate-raspberry, spark chocolate-peppermint and Winter Wonderland (a white cake with blue buttercream and decorated with snowflakes). Cost for the 6-inch, three layer cakes range from $50 to $60. Pies come in cherry, crumble apple, toast S'mores, peppermint French silk and whipped gingerbread. Cost range from $28 to $32.
Christmas cookie flavors include iced sugar cookies, chocolate chip, Bourbon snickerdoodle, chocolate-hazelnut thumbprint, holiday M&M sugar and 'Ninjabread' men. Cookies are available by the dozen for $30 to $32. Or opt for an assorted cookie platter for $48 for a dozen. Place orders online at goldenhourbakehouse.com under the Christmas preorder tab.
Incredibly Delicious
Incredibly Delicious has your holiday shopping – as well as noshing – all wrapped up.
Pre-order packages for the French bakery range from hot cocoa and cookies for two ($16.95) to Santa's brunch box ($20) to Mrs. Claus' cake box ($42). And don't forget the Elves macaron box with the cloud-like cookies in flavors like candy cane, gingerbread and chocolate-cherry-rum ($15 for half dozen, $30 for a dozen).
Orders must be placed by midnight Dec. 16. Orders should be placed online only at incrediblydelicious.com. A direct link to the order site is under the Christmas tab. Pick up available at the 925 S. Seventh St. bakery Dec. 24 from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m.
Incredibly Delicious also has its signature holiday Buche de Noel cakes. Selections this year feature chocolate-blood orange and spiced apple-cookie butter ($48.95 small/$64.95 large).
Holiday cakes flavors unveiled this season are chocolate-peppermint, coconut snowball, gingerbread-hot cocoa, red velvet, snowman and winter wonderland. The 8-inch iced layer cakes range in price from $51.11 to $57.36.
Want to roll up your own sleeves this holiday season? Try the DIY cookie kits that come in two options: Christmas cookie or gingerbread men. Kits include 10 cookies, icing and sprinkles ($27). Or there is the DIY hot cocoa kit with Belgian hot cocoa, marshmallows, sprinkles, crushed candy cane and festive trimmings. ($25, serves 6).
The pastry shop has Christmas eclairs, peppermint mouse, lemon meringue tarts, cheesecake brownies and Paris-Brest – puff pastry shell filled with hazelnut cream and caramel. Prices range from $21-$23 for a box of 4.
Don't have sugar plums dancing in your head? Try the bulk chicken salad $14.25/pint, $25.95/quart) or the quiche selections ($29/half pie, $54/whole pie).
Also available for preorder, stuffing mix, dinner rolls and breads. Featured selections include French, multigrain, brioche, baguette, rye, Kalamata Olive, pepper Parmesan, and the traditional Italian holiday sweet bread, Panettone. Prices range from $3.75 to $12.95.
Pease's at BUNN Gourmet
Pease's at BUNN Gourmet in The Gables Shopping Center has holiday-themed cakes, cheesecakes, cookies and mini tarts to deck your Christmas table.
Cheesecake selections include peppermint, gingerbread, Raggedy Ann and New York-style. The 10-inch cheesecakes range in rice from $59.99 to $62.99. The 10-inch Hot Cocoa layer cake is $52.99.
Smaller bites include decorated sugar cookies or decorated gingerbread cookies ($3.49 each) or mini lemon-gingerbread tarts or mini eggnog tarts ($1.99 each).
All selections come decorated for the holidays unless otherwise specified. Call 217/793-1840 to place orders, which are due by Dec. 19.
Apple Barn
The Apple Barn in Chatham is taking orders for holiday pies, cookies and candy trays for holiday festivities.
A variety of 10-inch pies are available with prices ranging from $12 to $14. Choose pies either pre-baked or scratch-made, frozen pies that can be baked at home.
Selections include apple or apple crumb, cherry or cherry crumb, chocolate cream, coconut cream, lemon meringue, peach or peach crumb, pumpkin, pecan and strawberry rhubarb. Cream pies are available with a choice of cream topping or meringue.
Assorted cookie and candy trays come in three sizes: small for $27, medium for $47 and large for $67. Or, opt for a bulk candy order. Selections include peppermint bark ($5.50 for 5 ounces), buckeyes or pecan clusters ($7 for 7 ounces) or peanut brittle ($14.95 for 12 ounces).
All items are in stock at the Chatham store, but 48-hours advance notice suggested for large orders.

title: Springfield school buses see improved staffing, wage increases
author: Tom Ackerman
description: While the COVID-19 pandemic created staffing shortages for school bus companies; Springfield District 186 is nearly fully staffed again.
content:
While the COVID-19 pandemic created staffing shortages for school bus companies; First Student Inc. that services Springfield District 186 schools is nearly fully staffed again.
185 drivers are now employed to operate across 175 routes in place for District 186, marking the first time in years that all routes are consistently covered, and with spare wheelmen and women available to assist with arising day-to-day needs.
Extra drivers fill in for one another when they get sick, and the increase also allows for drivers to standby throughout the city to pick up students who may be running late.
The company locally aims to hire a total of 192 drivers, which is 10% more than the number of routes in place, First Student Location Manager Daniel Thompson told The State Journal-Register.
How short-staffed were the drivers before?
When COVID-19 took hold, staffing at bus companies fell because schools were practicing remote and hybrid learning. Drivers servicing the district dwindled to as low as 160 to start the school year, making it harder to deliver timeliness for the students and families they transport.
What does the boost mean for students and parents?
Hopefully, more drivers equate to improved punctuality.
Thompson said in November data from the week prior showed buses getting to school by the bell 92% of the time, but he wants to see that number closer to 95%.
What are parents saying?
Lauren Tomten, a parent of twins in seventh grade, has seen a mixed bag for timeliness this school year.
In two conversations with the SJ-R, she shared that the beginning of the year was problematic, but there was later improvement with timeliness and also with communication through the First Student app, FirstView.
In the second conversation with Tomten, she expressed frustration after buses had been late for two days in a row. She ended up driving her kids to school.
'I looked at the app this morning and it looked like they were in kind of a weird place, so I don't know if they had to pick up other kids or maybe somebody dropped a route or something. But they would have been late to school if I didn't take them,' she said.
Tomten said her kids at times have observed their bus driver being re-routed by the driver's tablet device throughout the drive to or from school. They also often noticed taking different routes to get home.
Tomten's children are part of a gifted program at Franklin Middle School, and they are bused from outside of the school's normal district to get there, she said.
Are there other variables for punctuality?
The district last year approved a new routing software service for the school buses it contracts with through First Student. Superintendent Jennifer Gill at the time said the district will realize more efficiency and a cost savings by using the new program.
When asked about the software, Steve Miller, who is Director of Business, Finance & Operations for the district, wrote in an email that the software replaces routing that was done using physical maps and pencils. The hand-routed sheets were distributed to the drivers.
The technology manifests in the way of a tablet device in each bus that provides drivers with turn-by-turn directions for the routes.
The software makes use of Google Maps data to estimate travel times between stops, which allows routers to better estimate the total time of a route, Miller said.
Certain buses began using the software last winter, and this year it has been implemented on all bus routes.
"This has allowed route changes to be processed faster. We are also able to look at the student population and reduce stops that are no longer necessary due to students not living near those locations," Miller wrote.
He added that the district and First Student will be assessing all of the routes to see if any changes could be more efficient.
What has drawn drivers back to the bus?
Drivers are making more money and there is consequently more retention from year to year, Thompson said. The company is receiving more job applications, so First Student can be more selective about what drivers they hire to service the district.
Drivers now earn a starting pay of $25 per hour, which was set at $19 in recent years, Thompson said. That increase came through negotiations with the union that represents the drivers and in competing with other wage increases in the area.
Drivers are also now guaranteed six hours of work per day instead of four.

title: Illinois among worst states to celebrate Christmas, new report finds
author: Tom Ackerman
description: When it comes to Christmas celebrations, a new report found Illinois is among the worst states to do so.
content:
Show Caption
Looking to get in the holiday spirit? You may need to leave Illinois to do so.
A new report from 24/7 Games ranks Illinois 45th of the 50 U.S. states for Christmas celebrations.
Here's what to know about the report.
How were states graded?
The ranking is based on traditions and activities, affordability, community presence, generosity, and shopping options, with some of the categories weighing more heavily than others in the total score. Scores for each factor were scaled from 0 to 100, where 100 represents the best performance.
How did Illinois do?
Illinois had an overall score of 23.56, narrowly edging out Georgia at 23.55.
Why did Illinois receive a low grade?
Here's a look at where Illinois ranked in the five categories:
Traditions and activities: 26th
Affordability: 38th
Community presence: 42nd
Generosity: 42nd
Shopping options: 46th
Who were the highest scoring states?
Vermont: 51.43
South Dakota: 49.49
Wyoming: 48.93
North Dakota: 46.77
Delaware: 46.00
The report said Vermont 'numerous Christmas tree farms, holiday events, and a vibrant shopping scene, all while keeping costs like hotels and drinks affordable.'
Who scored lowest?
California and Florida rank last with the report citing 'high costs, low traditions, weak observance, and a hot climate that lacks festive winter charm.'
How were the rankings determined?
Traditions and activities looked at Christmas Tree Production, number of ice-skating rinks, and number of Christmas events.
Affordability looks at hotel costs, dining affordability, drink prices, cost of movie tickets, and holiday spending budget.
Community presence looked at religious demographics.
Generosity looked at the number of local Christmas-specific charities and share of income donated to charity.
Shopping options looked at shopping centers, Christmas stores, toy stores and hobby shops, and more factors.
The research team at 24/7 games cited the following sources: TripAdvisor, EventBrite, Google Maps, Booking.com, Numbeo, Expatistan, Wisevoter, Need Help Paying Bills CNN Money, and GoCraft.

title: Staunton girls want to make history, but quietly
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Staunton's girls basketball program has reached new heights with 53 wins and two regional titles in the previous two seasons, but the Bulldogs want more.
content:
The Staunton girls basketball team would prefer to play basketball, practice and focus on getting better. The Bulldogs' mentality — spearheaded by sixth-year coach Corrie Allan — isn't concerned much by stats or publicity.
Staunton itself is a quiet Macoupin County community nestled off Interstate 55. The girls basketball program has flown under the radar for the most part, but that's more due to the lack of overall success than anything else.
But this group of players, along with Allan, have started to change the latter. Five seniors — Sam Anderson, Lilly Bandy, Grace Bekeske, Ele Feldmann and Lilly Troeckler — brought the school its first girls regional championship ever in 2023 and finished with a then-record 26 wins. Last season, the Bulldogs repeated as regional champs and set another record with 27 wins.
Allan said the team still prefers to exist in anonymity.
'We've never been into any of that, we've never been into talking to (media) or anybody or any type of interviews or blasting stats,' Allan said. 'We don't do a lot of social media stuff. Our social media is if we dress up in dresses when we take our team picture. I mean, that's how we'll do that.
'We are just low key, and we want to come in, do it on the court, and go home.'
Just because they don't seek the limelight doesn't mean they don't want the success that will bring the notoriety, the media attention and — the ultimate goal — would be to play the biggest games when the lights are brightest. There's no more next year for the seniors. They want to maximize their potential this season.
Allan said that had to begin on the defensive end.
'Something that we have truly focused on this year is our defense, so we had to get better at our defense,' Allan said minutes after Staunton beat host Riverton 57-19 on Dec. 4. 'It couldn't get much worse than what it's been in the past, so we've really been working on a lot of defensive drills. I think the girls can tell, and I think they feel more comfortable and confident in what they're doing.'
Building a program
Russell White, who took over the Riverton girls program this season, is looking to rebuild the Hawks program. He said Staunton provides a great example.
'They run a pretty good program,' White said. 'Whatever they're doing with a size school like that to be able to get numbers like they do, I would love to try to do something like that here. And that's been my goal when I coached the middle school for the last five years over here.'
But just having more numbers throughout the program is one thing. Turning those numbers into more wins is another, he said.
'We're trying to get our numbers up and our numbers are doing well there now so I think eventually we can get to the point where we have that,' White said. 'Numbers are always a great start, then when you start getting the numbers to start working all the fundamental stuff at the bottom on your way up — which I see coming for us — they do very well.
'When they do something really well like that, you either try to beat them with something else or you join what they're doing. I see them do that. I see Lincoln do that up north. I see a lot of good teams doing those things, building it from the bottom and having just numbers and fundamentals. They do so well with that kind of stuff.'
Allan, who is also the Staunton athletic director, encourages her players to be as well-rounded as possible and play multiple sports. That culminated with a Class 2A Litchfield Regional title this fall in volleyball and several of those players also play softball.
'They all play multiple sports, so it's really a struggle (to schedule practice time in the offseason),' Allan said. 'And never would I ever want them to just play one sport because they are so athletic in everything that they do.'
Making a statement
After a 4-0 start, the Bulldogs faced their biggest test of the young season on Dec. 2 on the road against a taller Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central squad. Staunton survived the Bluejays in overtime, 59-53. Two nights later, Staunton improved to 6-0 by beating Riverton.
'They're balanced,' PORTA's first-year coach Derek Schnapp said. 'When I say balanced, against us … they had four girls almost in double digits — one had nine. They had a girl with 16, 14, 11, nine. Another girl with six. Another girl with three.'
But Schnapp said they're dangerous for other reasons.
'They can go full court on you because they're all about the same size,' Schnapp said. 'They have that basketball size where they can do a lot of things. They can press you. They can play a full court on you.
'All five can shoot the ball from the outside and they do a good job and … are selfless. They can distribute the ball to one another … (and) they do a great job just sharing the basketball because all five can shoot it.'
The unbeaten streak ended the next day when Gillespie upset Staunton 50-46 on Dec. 5. Currently, Staunton sits at 8-1.
Chemistry makers
Bandy said her group of seniors hasn't just been playing together through high school, but their days go back much further.
'We've been playing basketball since we were in second grade; it's such a positive environment to be around,' Bandy said.
Given that, it's no surprise the team says chemistry is one of its biggest assets.
'We're a very close team,' Feldmann said. 'I feel like we have a lot of connections. We like the team bonding and stuff, and I feel like that just makes us better as a team, on the court and off the court. I feel like that's one of the big things for our team.'
The Bulldogs have chemistry, talent and they've bought into Allan's coaching. Is there anything they lack? Sure, but they find ways to work around it.
'We don't really have a lot of height, so I think we've got to be quick and aggressive,' Allan said. 'They work really hard; they're a good group that listens and works hard. And talking about defense, Lilly Bandy's defense has improved tremendously, and I think she'll tell you that too, and Ele's has as well.
'They listen much better and want to get better at defense because they know that's going to win ballgames.'
Bandy and Feldmann both say there's still plenty of improvement the team can make between now and when regionals begin in February.
Bandy said her No. 1 priority was better communication.
'Both on and off the court, we have to talk on defense and offense, but we also have to communicate to our coaches about how we're feeling (and) our emotions.'
Feldmann added that the team also needs to stay positive.
'I would say we get really down on ourselves; not as a team, but as an individual,' Feldmann said. 'I feel like that's one of our big struggles.'
But Bandy said she feels they've put themselves in a place to reach their goals.
'Because we've played together for so long, we've always wanted to improve after every single season,' Bandy said. 'We worked hard, so we're really happy with where we are right now.'

title: Double-double for Noah Wade, rebounding help Springfield High basketball top Lanphier
author: Adrian Dater
content:
A large crowd escaped the frigid outside temperatures to gather inside Willard Duey Gymnasium Friday night for a Lanphier vs. Springfield High boys basketball game.
They didn't witness a classic, but they did see a good, tough, gritty city game between the crosstown rivals, with the host Senators prevailing 60-54.
Springfield coach Marques Warfield's team got a team-high 17 points and 13 rebounds from 6-foot-4 sophomore Noah Wade, while two other Senators hit double figures to get the team its first victory in the Central State Eight Conference against two losses, and upping their overall record to 3-5. The Lions, who jumped out to a 5-0 nonconference start, have now lost three straight — all within the CS8.
Down three points at halftime, the Senators hit Lanphier with a 21-4 third quarter to take a 48-34 lead into the fourth. A big rebounding edge — especially on the offensive glass — was probably the biggest factor in the victory for Springfield.
'Rebounding is crucial for our success,' said Warfield, an alum of Lanphier in his second season at the Springfield helm. 'That's one thing we work on in practice and work on game-to-game — who can win the rebounding war.'
Springfield had a 19-7 rebound edge in the first half and finished 38-19 overall. Wade, with several strong putbacks after missed shots, did the majority of the work, but he had plenty of help from teammates such as brother Elijah Wade and 6-6 senior Valor Komolafe.
Still, the Lions led at the half, led by Jaiquan Holman's nine points, with seven each from Amari Anderson and Soriano Hayes.
'We had to lock in. We knew what we had to do. We just had to come out and do it,' Noah Wade said. 'Whatever I have to do to help our team win, I'll do. If I have to score, I'll score. If I have to rebound, I'll get a rebound.'
Noah Wade hit six of his first eight shots, many of the aforementioned rebound putback variety. He had a running dunk to put Springfield up by 12 at 46-34, then finished off the third quarter in style by stealing an inbounds pass and putting in a layup for the 48-34 lead.
For Lanphier coach Blake Turner, the third quarter was a 'disaster' for his team.
'We're just not competing at the level that I want us to compete at. This is a program that's built on playing championship basketball, and everybody knows that defense wins championships, and we really struggled defensively,' Turner said. 'Our effort on 50-50 balls was just going through the motions until things start feeling too late, then they get that sense of urgency and want to start doing things the right way. That's just not good enough to win, and that's what they have to realize.'
Sophomore guard Ed Horton scored 10 points for the Senators, and the 5-7 point man even blocked a shot in the first half. Elijah Wade had 12 points, while Jaiyden Wilson added eight.
Warfield thinks his team is better than its 3-5 record, in part, he said, because they 'play one of the toughest schedules in the state.'
'We've been battle-tested. Everything on our schedule has been to help build toward February,' Warfield said. 'As a sophomore, I think (Noah Wade) is one of the better players in the state. Once he puts it together, as far as his foundation, the sky's the limit for him. You're looking at a scholarship (collegiate) player.'
Holman had a game-high 19 points for the Lions, who got as close as five points late in the fourth before running out of time. Hayes finished with nine points, as did Anderson and Shaunassey Hatchett Jr.
Adrian Dater is a freelance writer for The State Journal-Register. He can be reached through the sports department at sports@sj-r.com.

title: 'It could have been my son': Parents to protest over students' treatment at Maryland Cracker Barrel
author: Greta Cross
description: Parents have organized a protest at a Cracker Barrel in Waldorf, Maryland after special education students were denied dine-in service.
content:
"It's helpful, seeing other people supporting and wanting to be a part of this," protest organizer and parent Dustin Reed said.
School officials and parents say a group of students and teachers, on a special education field trip, were denied dine-in service at the Cracker Barrel in Waldorf, Maryland on Dec. 3.
Parent Dustin Reed organized a protest to be held at the restaurant on Sunday afternoon.
More than 200 Facebook users have expressed interest in attending the protest.
Family members and protesters are set to gather Sunday afternoon at a Cracker Barrel in Maryland, where a group of special education students received what the restaurant later called "unacceptable" service earlier this month.
The protest was organized by Dustin Reed, father of 7-year-old Madelynn. She was one of 11 special needs students who were turned away from dine-in service at the Cracker Barrel restaurant in Waldorf, Maryland during a field trip on Dec. 3, parents and school officials say. The protest is set to be held at the restaurant from 1-5 p.m. EST on Sunday, Dec. 15.
More than 200 users have expressed interest in attending the protest on Facebook, while countless users have commented support for the students, parents and teachers affected. Users who report being anywhere from Chicago to Brazil have left a comment on the event.
"It's helpful, seeing other people supporting and wanting to be a part of this," Reed told USA TODAY on Wednesday. "But it's also sad at the same moment because reading and hearing all of these people's stories and hearing about what really goes on and a lot of it, it doesn't get talked about because there's not enough media coverage or there's not enough people willing to want to stand up for whoever needs a voice."
Elise Horne, co-founder of the Charles County Autism & Developmental Disabilities Parent Support Group, told USA TODAY on Thursday that she plans to attend the Sunday protest. Horne has a 9-year-old, nonverbal autistic son who also attends the Charles County Public Schools District. Though he wasn't on the field trip to Cracker Barrel, he also regularly participates in community-based instruction outings.
"It is very important to me that the orgs in my community understand and they get the message that it is not okay to discriminate against my son's community," Horne said. "I really want to go so I can help send that message and I feel like there is a strength in numbers and the more of us that show up, the louder our voices will be. I am standing in solidarity of these parents because it could have been my son."
What happened?
Last Tuesday, a group of 11 students and seven staff members from the Charles County Public Schools District visited the Waldorf Cracker Barrel. The outing was a part of community-based instruction, which allows students in special education programs to practice practical skills and socialize in public.
Charles County Public Schools District special education teacher Katie Schneider informed parents in an email that the group was denied service. Schneider said the group was told that the restaurant couldn't accommodate them and they were asked to remove the location from an approved list of restaurants for such field trips.
The restaurant permitted students and staff to place a to-go order, Schneider said in her email. After about an hour of waiting for the carryout meals, the students moved outside to the school bus to wait and ultimately ate their lunch back at the elementary school, Schneider said.
The students attend Dr. James Craik Elementary School and belong to the district's ACHIEVE program, for students with "significant cognitive disabilities" and SOAR program, for students with autism.
Following last week's events, three employees at the Waldorf Cracker Barrel were let go, a Cracker Barrel statement shared with USA TODAY said. An internal investigation with guest and employee interviews was also opened.
"We strive to create a welcoming environment and great experience for guests of all abilities, and we have a zero-tolerance policy against any form of discrimination," the statement said. "We did not refuse service to this student group, but operational breakdowns caused by staffing shortages and poor communication on our part led us to fall well short of our service standards that day. This is unacceptable."

title: First look: State unveils 10 finalists for new Illinois flag
author: Tom Ackerman
description: One has a butterfly on it. Others nod to Chicago, the Mississippi River and other Illinois waterways, Abraham Lincoln, and agriculture. Which is your favorite?
content:
The top 10 designs for a new possible state flag may surprise you.
One has a butterfly on it. Others nod to Chicago, the Mississippi River and other Illinois waterways, Abraham Lincoln, and agriculture.
The Illinois Flag Commission has selected its top 10 finalists out of nearly 5,000 submissions for the state flag redesign contest.
Are we getting a new flag for certain?
Beginning in January, the public will be able to vote for one of the 10 new designs, or for one of the three former flag designs including the current state flag, the 1918 Centennial Flag and the 1968 Sesquicentennial Flag.
How will the winner be decided?
After the public votes, the commission will then report these results to the Illinois General Assembly by April 1. Assembly members will vote on whether to adopt a new flag, return to a previous version of the flag or retain the current flag.
Why is the state considering a new flag design?
A constituent of Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, introduced the idea, leading she and Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago to move forward the legislation which created the commission later signed into law by Gov. JB Pritzker.
"I have always said that history is living, breathing and ever evolving, and I think we need to ensure that government is also evolving so people are engaged," Turner previously said.
The original flag, designed by Rockford native Lucy Derwent in 1915, featured the state seal in front of a white background. It has remained the same since with exception for the addition of the word "Illinois" placed below the seal in 1969.

title: Crouch: Merit commission part of new hiring process for sheriff's department
author: Steven Spearie
description: Sangamon County Sheriff Paula Crouch detailed the office's new hiring practices at Monday's Massey Commission meeting.
content:
Sangamon County Sheriff Paula Crouch said a newly created background investigation manual could close holes that allowed the hiring of a now former sheriff's deputy charged with first-degree murder of Sonya Massey in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield this summer.
Crouch, who took over as sheriff on Sept. 18 following the retirement of Jack Campbell, told members of the Massey Commission at the Bank of Springfield Center Monday that she didn't know if the process would have out and out prohibited the hiring of Sean P. Grayson, who shot Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman, in the face in her home after she placed a 911 call about a potential prowler.
Among the most pertinent hiring changes under Crouch are a sheriff's merit commission and a mandate that investigators review records in person if an applicant worked at another law enforcement agency.
Those changes come as the U.S. Department of Justice last month launched an investigation into the sheriff's department and other county offices. The offices had to comply in turning over records by Dec. 14.
Also on Monday, co-chair Dr. Jerry Kruse reiterated the Massey Commission's support for two proposals before the Sangamon County Board: a resolution that would give voters a voice in the possible recall of the sheriff and the creation of a county mental health board.
A work in progress
Crouch admitted the four-person merit commission was still a work in progress. One of its benefits might be taking the sheen off the county's "reputation for political hires," said Massey Commissioner Gerry Castles.
One of Grayson's references in his application to the Sangamon County Sheriff's Department was longtime deputy Scott Butterfield, the father of Grayson's now-fiancée.
The merit commission would review the written test scores of applicants and recommend if the sheriff should proceed with the background process. It would also determine whether the applicant goes on the merit list.
Crouch said if she thought a candidate still had too many red flags, she could halt the hiring process.
In addition to filing a Freedom of Information Act request for personnel records if an applicant previously worked as an officer, investigators would have to go to that agency in person with a signed waiver from the candidate to review records.
Crouch said that would also give investigators a chance to talk to the candidate's supervisors.
Asked by commissioner the Rev. Susan Phillips whether multiple DUIs or a questionable military discharge, both part of Grayson's record, would have raised red flags for Crouch had she been sheriff at the time, Crouch said "the military discharge, more than the DUIs, would cause concern for me."
Both DUIs came before Grayson was hired as a police officer.
"It would be my hope," Phillips said, "that when you have tweaked this hiring process that you would have a high degree of confidence that a person like Grayson would never be hired again by the sheriff's department."
Sheriff's recall question
Kruse said he was hoping the county board would take "positive action" on the recall matter.
"I'll be very disappointed, and I know the commissioners share that sentiment, too (if the county board doesn't pass the resolution)," he said.
The resolution failed to make it out of committee last week, so its sponsor, Democrat Sam Cahnman, has one last crack at it on Jan. 13.
"The best information we have is we don't have the authority under the (Illinois) Constitution to recall an elected official," contended board chairman Andy Van Meter. "The state legislature has to create that right."
Cahnman countered that if people lose confidence in their elected officials, they need a mechanism to remove them "and recall is the way."
Crouch, asked by commissioner Sontae Massey, a first cousin of Sonya Massey's, how she felt about recall, sided with Van Meter. Republicans control 21 of the board's 29 seats.
Evan Brown, a member of one of the commission's workgroups, chastised Crouch for her stance in public comment.
"The simple thing," he said, "would be not politicize this, to not side with the county Republicans who are politicizing this, and to be bold and be brave and say I support the recall."

title: Morgan County to pay $6M in settlement over inmate's death in 2022
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Morgan County has agreed to a settlement of $6 million after the 2022 death of inmate Brian Downs. Here's what happened.
content:
Show Caption
Morgan County has agreed to settle a lawsuit by paying $6 million after the death of a former inmate at the Morgan County Detention Facility.
Brian Downs died in April 2022 from complications related to heroin withdrawal while in jail, according to a complaint filed in the U.S. District Court in Springfield. The lawsuit argued Downs did not receive appropriate medical care.
Downs was arrested and jailed on April 22, 2022. One day later, he started vomiting, including blood, over the course of 34 hours, according to the complaint.
Downs died on April 25 after going into cardiac arrest while he was locked in a medical holding cell at the jail, the complaint read.
"During this time period, no employee of the jail notified a qualified health provider, nor did they transport Brian to the emergency department at [Jacksonville Memorial Hospital]," the complaint read.
Julie Downs, the administrator of Brian Downs' estate, and attorney Richard Frazier filed a motion for finding a good faith settlement. The collective parties in defense of the county agreed on the settlement with Frazier and Downs on June 6.
Frazier said he expects the settlement to be approved soon.
The groups agreed to the settlement "to avoid the uncertainty, expense, and burden associated with further litigation" the motion reads.
Downs died of dehydration as well as septic shock due to bowel obstruction as a consequence of small bowel intussusception in the setting of opioid withdrawal syndrome, the complaint said, citing the autopsy.

title: Here are 5 things to do the last weekend before Christmas in the Springfield area
author: Claire Grant
description: In case you haven't had a chance to look at the calendar, this weekend is the final one before Christmas. Here are 5 things to do in Springfield.
content:
Christmas Day falls on a Wednesday this year, so this is your last weekend chance to get out and enjoy the winter festivities before the turn of the New Year.
Here are five things you can do this weekend whether you're done with your shopping or not.
Old Winter Capitol Farmers Market
What: The Winter Farmers Market will be hosted at the historic Union Station with swaths of baked goods, meat and produce to even furniture and crafting items for that last minute holiday shopping. Enjoy cookies and check out what local businesses nearby are offering.
When: 8 a.m. to noon Saturday
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Where: 212 N. Sixth St., Springfield
More: Can't make it out? Why not visit downtownspringfield.org for the full calendar.
Capital City Improv Ha-Ha Holiday
What: It's improv, with a twist! The Seventh annual Ha-Ha Holiday Show is this weekend, put on by the Capital City Improv group at the Hoogland. Guests should bring a jolly attitude and their voice, as this improv troupe utilizes guest participation with fun improv games.
When: 8 p.m. Saturday
Where: 420 S. Sixth St., Springfield, inside the Hoogland Center for the Arts.
More: This is a ticketed event, tickets can be found online at HCFTA.org/tickets.
Christmas at Motorheads
What: In an event by Off the Wall, Motorheads Bar & Grill, meet Santa over a pint of something good and dance the night away to keep the cold at bay.
When: 8 p.m. Friday
Where: 600 Toronto Road, Springfield
More: While there, check out Big Ron, Route 66 latest marvel and giant on the road that was installed earlier this year.
Chatham Friends light up the park
What: Drive out to Chatham for a dazzling mile of iridescent lights, glittering all the way through multiple holiday displays. title: 'Senseless acts of violence': 5 dead in apparent Utah murder-suicide identified by family
author: Natalie Neysa Alund
description: The deceased are: Bu Meh, 38, her daughters Kristina Ree, 8, and Nyay Meh, 2, and her son Boe Reh, 11, according to a statement released by the family.
content:
This story contains mention of possible domestic violence. Those facing domestic abuse can call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-SAFE (7233) or visit its website for a virtual chat.
Extended family members of five people fatally shot in what police believe to be a murder -suicide case in Utah released the victim's names Thursday.
They are: Bu Meh, 38, her daughters Kristina Ree, 8, and Nyay Meh, 2, and her son Boe Reh, 11, according to a statement released by the West Valley City Police Department on behalf of the family. In the statement, the family called it "senseless acts of violence."
Their bodies were found Tuesday in their home in West Valley City, a Salt Lake City suburb. A handgun was found under the body of husband and father, 42-year-old Dae Reh. Police said they believe he was the shooter.
The couple's teenage son was also shot in the head and, on Thursday, remained in critical condition unable to communicate with authorities.
"Sha Rey is our 17-year-old hero," the family wrote in the statement. "He has a long and complex road to recovery. He needs our full attention, our unconditional love and the Savior's gifts of healing and peace."
As of Friday, a motive in the killing remained under investigation, according to police.
Mother killed was refugee who came to US to flee violence
According to the family, the mother was a refugee who fled violence in Myanmar, an Asian country northwest of Thailand.
The mother came to the United States with her husband and young family "with little more than clothing on their backs, where she taught herself English, learned new skills and worked to support her family.
She achieved a way of life "far beyond the nightmare of her former country or the refugee camp," her family said in the statement.
"For reasons that we cannot comprehend, her husband robbed her and their children of that security and their very lives," her extended family wrote. "While the perpetrator of these heinous acts is deceased, we know that God's justice is not."
No note found at slain Utah family's home
The discovery took place after the mother failed to report to work this week, according to the West Valley Police Department, the lead agency on the case. A concerned relative entered the garage of the home, found the17-year-old boy critically injured, and notified police.
Police said they believe the killings took place over the weekend, police spokesperson Roxeanne Vainuku announced during a news conference this week.
Officers found no note at the crime scene, and there is no history of domestic violence on records at that home, Vainuku said.
"We understand how frustrating it is for an incident of this magnitude to happen and to not understand why. We know people want to know why. We want to know why," Vainuku said. "The truth is we may never know. It's hard to comprehend."
Anyone with information about the killings is asked to contact West Valley police.

title: CS8 boys basketball: Sacred Heart-Griffin, Rochester leap into holidays
author: Bill Welt
description: Sacred Heart-Griffin's Cam Brinkman and Terrion Wallace combined for eight 3s, while Rochester moves to 3-1 in CS8 boys hoops on Saturday
content:
Here's what we learned from Central State Eight Conference boys basketball action featuring Sacred Heart-Griffin's win at Chatham Glenwood and Rochester's triumph at Lincoln on Saturday.
Rochester 47, Lincoln 36
Rochester found the slightest wrinkles in the 1-2-2 zone defense before taking over in the third quarter.
The Rockets (5-3, 3-1 Central State Eight) outscored Lincoln 18-4 in the decisive third quarter beginning with back-to-back 3-pointers by sophomore Eli Cox and junior Kai Bruce.
Freshman guard Khordell Gregory also delivered a three in the frame and led Rochester with 14 points off the bench.
'We got it inside,' Rochester coach Tony Gavin said. 'Once we got it inside, we were able to kick it out and most kids can knock down shots.'
Gavin said he couldn't remember the last time when – or if – Rochester began 3-1 in the league.
'We're starting to handle the teams that we've struggled with in the past,' Gavin said. 'I think we're on the right track. I think we still have a very long ways to go, but 5-3 I'll take it all day.'
Cox and senior Jack Melton had 11 points apiece. Junior Tanner Beal added eight.
'We're trying to turn the basketball program around,' Cox said. 'We're known as a football school, but we're trying to change it to a basketball school, too.'
Lincoln (7-3, 2-2) was coming off a 57-53 overtime win over Mahomet-Seymour on Friday, but its starting lineup has been decimated early in the season.
The Railers were without junior guard Karson Komnick, senior forward Drew Hayes and senior forward Frank Sanders due to injury.
Hayes sprained his ankle against Mahomet, while Komnick also recently injured his hand and coach Neil Alexander said he will be out until the start of January. Sanders dressed for the first time this season.
'We're doing the best we can, it's the only thing we can do and hopefully we'll get through it,' Alexander said. 'The kids played hard and executed, we just got beat by a better basketball team.'
Senior Blake Horn scored eight of his team-high 13 points in the fourth quarter. Freshman Bryce Vlahovich chipped in eight.
'He knows every position,' Alexander said of Horn. 'The only one he really doesn't know is the point guard, but I imagine if I put him out there, he could run it. He's a good type of player to have on our team.'
Sacred Heart-Griffin 59, Chatham Glenwood 55
Sophomore guard Cam Brinkman nearly matched a career-high with 19 points for the team's third straight win of the season.
He hit 3-pointers in the first quarter and totaled five threes against Glenwood's zone defense. He converted a pivotal three in the third quarter for a two-possession cushion and the Cyclones (6-4, 2-2 CS8) led 40-32 by the end of the third quarter.
Brinkman's previous high was 20 points against Decatur Eisenhower last December.
'Once the first one fell, I knew I was going to be on,' Brinkman said. 'I was shooting well during the warmups. I had a nice feel in my shot and when I just kept making them, I kept shooting them and they went in.'
SHG sophomore guard Terrion Wallace drained three threes and finished with 11 points off the bench. He heeded to his coaches after passing up his first open look.
'They basically screamed at me, 'Just let it fly,'' Wallace said. 'I just let it fly. I had confidence in myself to shoot the shot.'
He converted back-to-back three to end the first half ahead 24-19.
'I've been struggling shooting the three in the season, so basically that's a confidence booster for me to keep going. I'm just going to keep going,' Wallace said.
Fellow sophomore guards Myles Montgomery and Tereik Hurd supplied 11 and nine points, respectively, while junior foward Zion Lee had eight.
Hurd drilled a contested jumper at the buzzer to end the first quarter, and SHG's backcourt circumvented Glenwood's trap defense despite senior guard Jamarion Bardwell's foul trouble.
'They're really fast and shifty,' Brinkman said of his fellow guards. 'They pass the ball well and when you're open for 3 and they see you, that's all you can ask for. You've just got to knock shots down.'
The Titans (5-4, 2-1) missed Mason Marshall in the lineup and just couldn't connect from long range most of the game. Senior Cam Appenzeller hit two from long range in the first quarter and led the Titans (5-4, 2-1) with 16 points in a gritty effort on both sides of the ball.
Jonathan Helm scored all his 11 points in the second half. Mason Neumann, battling foul trouble, and Brody Green each had 10 points.

title: IRS to send unclaimed stimulus checks to 1 million taxpayers worth up to $1,400
author: Julia Gomez
description: The IRS will send out stimulus checks worth up to $1,400 to eligible taxpayers who missed theirs in 2021.
content:
Did you miss out on receiving the Recovery Rebate Credit in 2021?
The IRS just announced its plans to issue the payments starting later this month to 1 million taxpayers who didn't claim it while filing for their 2021 tax returns.
"The IRS announced the special step after reviewing internal data showing many eligible taxpayers who filed a return but did not claim the credit," the agency said in a press release.
While most eligible taxpayers received their stimulus checks or credit, those who haven't can expect to receive their 2021 Recovery Rebate Credit in late January if they didn't receive a stimulus check before.
Here's what to know.
How money much will be sent out?
Taxpayers can expect to receive a maximum of $1,400, according to the IRS. A total of $2.4 billion will be sent to those who missed receiving the credit.
How do I receive my stimulus payment?
People do not have to do anything to receive their payments, as they will automatically be sent out to taxpayers in December and will arrive in most cases by late January.
Eligible taxpayers will receive a separate letter notifying them of the payment.
Payments will be automatically direct deposited or sent by a paper check, according to the IRS.
The payment will be direct deposited into the bank account provided on the eligible person's 2023 tax return or sent to the address of record.
What if I didn't file my 2021 taxes?
People who didn't file their taxes in 2021 can still be eligible to receive their stimulus checks, the IRS stated.
But, they only have until April 15, 2025 to "file their returns to claim the credit and any other refund they might be owed."
Who is eligible for the special payment?
People who placed a $0 on the field for the Recovery Rebate Credit on their 2021 tax forms or left the section blank are eligible for the credit.
According to the IRS, those receiving the payment are "taxpayers where IRS data demonstrates a taxpayer qualifies for the credit."
(This story was updated with headline changes.)

title: 'Difficult decision': Big Lots will begin going out of business sales at all stores
author: Cassidy Waigand
description: The retailer said its plans will affect all remaining storefronts, including those in Illinois.
content:
Show Caption
Just over three months after filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, Big Lots, Inc. announced plans to initiate going out of business sales at all of its remaining locations. The retail chain has already closed more than 10 Illinois storefronts in recent months.
Big Lots announced it had filed for bankruptcy and entered into a sale agreement with Nexus Capital Management LP in September. The court approved the company's planned sale in late November, with Big Lots expecting to close the sale in early December.
In a Dec. 19 news release, however, the company said that "it does not anticipate completing its previously announced asset purchase agreement with Nexus Capital Management." The business is exploring its options and said that it still aims "to complete a sale by early January."
"We all have worked extremely hard and have taken every step to complete a going concern sale," said Bruce Thorn, CEO and president of Big Lots, in a statement. "While we remain hopeful that we can close an alternative going concern transaction, in order to protect the value of the Big Lots estate, we have made the difficult decision to begin the (going out of business) process."
The retail chain operates 963 locations throughout the United States, according to its website. This includes 17 storefronts in Illinois. Peoria-area stores include:
8901 N. Knoxville Ave., Peoria
2500 E. Washington St., East Peoria
Big Lots also operates one location in Galesburg, one location in Machesney Park and two locations in Springfield.
The Journal Star called the media contact listed on the Dec. 19 press release and has not yet received a response. Employees at the Peoria and East Peoria storefronts both directed the Journal Star to reach out to the company's media relations.

title: Jimmy Carter was no stranger to the Springfield area
author: Steven Spearie
description: Jimmy Carter was one of four sitting U.S. presidents to address the Illinois General Assembly. Here's a look back at his trips to the capital city.
content:
The late President Jimmy Carter was no stranger to Springfield.
Carter, the Nobel Peace Prize winner who died in hospice care in his hometown of Plains, Georgia, at age 100 on Dec. 29, made at least six trips to the capital city, including two as president and four during his first campaign for president in 1975-76.
During his Sept. 22, 1980, visit to Lincoln Land Community College, Carter gave a major energy address at Menard Hall to over 1,100 students, staff and visitors.
Carter also toured during his two-hour visit the campus' alcohol fuels plant, viewed a demonstration of a corn mash gasohol still and visited with state and local political leaders, including former Sangamon County Democrats chairman Todd Renfrow, in Logan Hall.
Carter was one of four sitting U.S. presidents to address the Illinois General Assembly.
Carter gave the address on May 26, 1978, and was introduced by the Speaker of the House, William A. Redmond, D-Bensenville.
Other presidents to address the legislature were William Howard Taft in 1911, Herbert Hoover in 1931 and Barack Obama in 2016.
The same day Carter attended a fundraiser for Illinois Comptroller Michael Bakalis, who was running for governor, at the Holiday Inn East. Bakalis was trying to unseat Gov. James Thompson.
Carter last visited the Springfield area on October 14, 2014, when helped launch the 'Pathways to Peace' initiative at Illinois College in Jacksonville.
There, he was with Khalaf Ahmad al Habtoor, the Dubai-based leader of the Al Habtoor Group LLC, and owner of the President Abraham Lincoln Hotel, and former U.S. Paul Findley, R-Jacksonville.
In 2013, Carter weighed in on the '272 Words' project, organized by the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library Foundation.
That collected essays from people from all walks of life who sent in their thoughts about Abraham Lincoln in observance of the 150th anniversary of the Gettysburg Address.
The essays made up the book 'On Lincoln's Mind: Leading the Nation to the Gettysburg Address," which is available at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum.
In November 2023, the Carter's wife of 77 years, Rosalynn, also passed away in the modest house they built together in 1961, when he had taken over his father's peanut warehouse business and was only beginning to consider a political career.
The longest-lived president in U.S. history, Carter is survived by his children, Jack, Chip, Jeff, and Amy; 11 grandchildren and 14 great-grandchildren.
'Jimmy Carter proved that excellence in public service can extend beyond the White House," said U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Springfield, in a statement Sunday. "His life was an inspiration to those of us who aspire to lead a life of service.
'I offer my condolences to the entire Carter family, to his friends and former staff members, and to the untold millions of people throughout the world whose lives are better because Jimmy Carter lived.'
Carter, said U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Chicago, via X, "lived a long life of service to our nation...a legacy we will never forget."
Added U.S. Rep. Nikki Budzinski, D-Springfield, also via X: "President Jimmy Carter dedicated his life to making the world a better place. His legacy as a peace builder will live on for eternity."
Gov. JB Pritzker said Carter "truly exemplified what it meant to live a life full of service. His towering legacy of compassion for others set a standard that will always be remembered."

title: Here's why these 9 Springfield-area nursing homes were fined for thousands of dollars

content:

Several Springfield and Springfield area nursing homes are the subjects of violations in a quarterly finding made by the Illinois Department of Public Health.
In all, 312 violation reports were found across the state in the third quarter of 2024.
To file a complaint against a healthcare facility in Illinois that is licensed by IDPH, go to the IDPH website.
Here are local nursing homes that incurred fines:
Aperion Care Capitol, 555 W. Carpenter St., Springfield
Fined: $25,000
Survey date: May 16, 2024
The facility failed to treat a urinary tract infection in a timely manner for a resident, which led to the resident's admittance to the intensive care unit for septic shock.
Concordia Village Care, 4101 West Iles Ave., Springfield
Fined: $2,200
Survey date: June 26, 2024
The facility failed to provide timely assessment and treatment of a humeral fracture for a resident.
Arcadia Care Auburn, 304 Maple Ave., Auburn
Fined: $25,000

The facility failed to prevent a resident from overdosing on medication, which led to the resident's hospitalization and then death.
Carlinville Rehab & HCC, 751 North Oak St., Carlinville
Fined: $25,000
Survey date: May 26, 2024
The facility failed to monitor and treat a resident with the type 2 diabetes, which resulted in the resident being sent to the Emergency Room for Uncontrolled Diabetes Mellitus.
Additionally, the facility received fines from a survey date of July 1, 2024, that totaled $2,700.
The facility failed to obtain or conduct certain pre-employment screening to determine if employees had prior criminal history that would disqualify them from employment.
The facility also failed to identify, assess, and implement interventions for pain in a resident, which resulted in the patient moaning in pain due to not being assessed and treated with the medication for nearly 45 minutes.
Grove Health & Rehab Center, 873 Grove St., Jacksonville
Fined: $2,200
Survey date: May 9, 2024
The facility failed to answer call lights and address the consequent needs of four residents. The facility also failed to provide 'complete incontinent care' to prevent urinary tract infections for two residents.
Skld Nur & Rehab, 1517 W. Walnut St., Jacksonville
Fined: $2,200
Survey date: May 22, 2024
The facility failed to provide oxygen to two residents who needed it, which caused one of the residents to become cyanotic with a low oxygen saturation.
Lincoln Terrace, 2324 North Kickapoo St., Lincoln
Fine: $2,150
Survey date: June 4, 2024
The facility failed to provide evidence that they completed required screening within 24 hours of multiple new residents, including the Illinois Sex Offender Registration search and the Illinois Department of Corrections.
Following a resident being identified as an offender, the facility failed to provide evidence of the required Department of State Police notification and fingerprinting completion.
The facility also failed to provide evidence that they verified an employee's licensure status with the state, in addition to other background checks for employees.
Lincoln Village Healthcare, 2202 N. Kickapoo St., Lincoln
Fine: $25,000
Survey date: April 25, 2024

Taylorville Care Center, 600 South Houston St., Taylorville

The facility also failed to use alternatives to bed rails and assess and monitor for related risks. This resulted in one resident's arm being fractured by being caught in the bedrail.

Four state facilities listed below were cited with type 'AA' violations when there is a condition or occurrence at the facility that proximately caused a resident's death.
The facilities included Alden Lakeland Rehabilitation & Health Care center, Chicago, fined $50,000; ALIYA on 87 th, Chicago fined $50,000 for an 'AA' violation and $25,000 for an 'A' violation; Allure of Pinecrest, Mount Morris, fined $50,000 for an 'AA' violation and $2,200 for a B violation; St. Paul's Senior Community, Belleville, fined $50,000.
The IDPH was not immediately able to comment about why the Auburn resident's death did not amount to an "AA" violation.

title: Snow likely in Springfield Thursday and this weekend. What you need to know
author: Tom Ackerman
description: It may be time to find your snow shovels and get your snowblowers ready in the Springfield area. What you need to know.
content:
It may be time to find your snow shovels and get your snowblowers ready.
Snow is coming this week, with large amounts of snow likely on Sunday.
Here's what you need to know.
The highest chances for snow this week will be Sunday afternoon and through the evening hours, according to Alex Erwin, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Lincoln.
Snow is very likely in that timeframe with current estimates showing the Springfield area receiving 4", with an 80% chance. There is a 70% chance that the area will receive six inches of snow.
Precipitation may begin late Saturday night, but it will most likely begin early Sunday morning.
The weather system containing the heaviest band of snow could shift north or south, but the models have stayed relatively consistent in the last day or so, Erwin said.
The heaviest snow amounts will be oriented from west to east, so the predicted amounts are also true from Quincy to Indianapolis.
Areas closer to I-70 may potentially see freezing rain or sleet.
Is there snow today?
There is a chance of rain and snow in Springfield Thursday, mainly after 4 p.m. There is a 40% chance of precipitation, according to the National Weather Service. The high is near 40.
Rain and snow are likely before 9 p.m. tonight. There is also a chance of snow between 9 and 11 p.m. There is a 60% chance of precipitation, but little or no snow accumulation is expected.
No snow is in Friday's forecast. There is no snow forecast for Saturday during the day, but Saturday night will see a 40% chance of snow after midnight.
