title: City of Springfield releases names of 11 massage parlors that were shut down
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Several massage parlors are no longer allowed to operate in Springfield, and 11 of them have been named.
content:
Show Caption
11 massage establishments close for failing to apply for permit and for lacking licensed massage therapists.
Concerns about human trafficking and prostitution prompted the regulation in May.
No arrests have been announced as of Feb. 4, 2025.
Days after announcing the closure of multiple massage parlors in Springfield, officials have revealed more information.
The city announced Tuesday that a total of 11 parlors were closed down.
The businesses are now restricted from working in Springfield, as result of ongoing efforts by the city to make sure the parlors are adhering to local laws and licensing requirements.
Here's what we know.
Which massage parlors are closing?
Healthy Spa
Capital Spa
Cozy Cabin Spa
Jade Spa
Illinois Relax Spa
Q2 Asian Massage
Royal Massage
Sunshine Massage/Providence Massage
Sunflower Massage
Red Bean Spa
Fitness Massage
Authorities did not provide addresses to the parlors that were shut down.
Why is the city stopping these businesses from operating?
These businesses either failed to apply for necessary permits with the city or did not have a licensed massage therapist on-site during inspections, according to a press release from the city.
"This is an ongoing effort to ensure businesses operating in Springfield adhere to local laws and maintain the proper credentials to provide services safely and legally," Mayor Misty Buscher said in a news release. 'We will continue to monitor compliance and take necessary action to protect the well-being of our community."
City attorney Greg Moredock last week told The State Journal-Register that several of the businesses closed Jan. 31 after a slew of inspections on that day. Three of the closed locations had never submitted an application for a license in the first place and inspectors had found the places remaining in operation.
If a closed location fails their inspection and continues operating, Moredock said the city can take administrative action with fines, or enforcement of closure through circuit courts.
Was there concern about human trafficking and prostitution?
Yes. This past May, concerns about human trafficking and prostitution prompted the working committee of the Springfield City Council to send an ordinance to the consent agenda, requiring the parlors to register annually with the city.
Some of the parlors or spas also reportedly advertised on illicit adult websites.
The city passed the new ordinance last June which requires all massage parlors in the city to be licensed and up to code with licensed massage therapists and inspections from multiple city branches.
48 of the parlors were determined to be unlicensed from September to Dec. 21. After three rounds of letters from the city regarding inspection, three locations closed voluntarily.
Did anyone get arrested?
The issue sparked public comment and conversation among City Council members at a late January Committee of the Whole meeting, where Springfield Police Chief Ken Scarlette was asked to talk about what police were doing about it.
The FBI division of the State Police has conducted investigations into human trafficking and continues to conduct those investigations, Scarlette said. In such an investigation, Scarlette said he aims to deconflict with other agencies involved.
'The last thing I want to do, is number one get up here and say something that may impact an ongoing investigation, so I try to be very careful when it comes to that,' the chief said.
Scarlette added that he doesn't always have the luxury of knowing what's going on when it comes to federal investigations.
'They don't call the local leaders and share some of that sometimes.'
Chief Scarlette emphasized, though, that the SPD is aware of alleged illegal activity happening at some of the parlors.
'I'm going to do my damndest to make sure that that doesn't happen in the city of Springfield,' he said.
A public information officer with the Illinois State Police referred the SJ-R to local law enforcement for information when asked about whether any arrests have been made, but police have not responded.

title: Spring is quickly approaching. Here's what The Old Farmer's Almanac is predicting
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A long-running weather publication has announced its predictions for spring, which is less than two months away. Here's the outlook for Illinois.
content:
A long-running weather publication has announced its predictions for spring, which is less than two months away.
The Old Farmer's Almanac, which has been around since 1792, released its predictions for the U.S. last week.
Here's the outlook we can expect in Illinois.
What is the prediction for Illinois?
The Old Farmer's Almanac predicts most of Illinois will see a dry spring with normal temperatures.
The southern part of the state is predicted to see a cool and dry spring, and the northwestern section will see a warm and dry season.
How about the U.S. overall?
'The U.S. spring outlook predicts warmer-than-normal temperatures for most of the country, with a few exceptions: southern and central California, Desert Southwest, southern Florida, and western Ohio Valley, where it will be near to below normal," the outlook read.
Is Old Farmer's Almanac accurate?
The publication claims to predict the weather about 80% of the time.
The publication gauges the weather trends and events by comparing solar patterns and historical weather conditions with current solar activity.
"Our extended winter weather forecasts emphasize temperature and precipitation deviations from averages, or normals," an article from the organization read from this past September. "These are based on 30-year statistical averages prepared by government meteorological agencies."

title: Illinois protestors among those nationwide against actions of President Trump, Elon Musk
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A nationwide protest at state capitols consequently drew about 200 people to Springfield, Illinois by Wednesday afternoon.
content:
Hundreds met at the state Capitol in Springfield to protest Pres. Trump and his administration.
Protests were organized at every state capitol in the U.S.
Many of the protestors said it was their first time at such a demonstration.
A nationwide protest at state capitols consequently drew about 200 people to Springfield, Illinois by Wednesday afternoon.
Organized by the 50501 Movement and apparently taken up by volunteers in each state, the Springfield protest saw people from throughout Illinois that sought to push back on actions being taken by President Donald Trump and his administration.
Protestors gathered at the Lincoln statue -- carrying signs, chanting, and evoking honks from cars driving by.
More than one protestor interviewed by the State Journal-Register said it was their first time protesting, but that recent actions by President Trump as well as Elon Musk motivated them escalate their voice from social media platforms to an in-person protest.
'We're concerned about American democracy,' said Katie Carlson of Springfield, adding that 'we're fearful that there are so many intrusions on our legal process,' citing Musk's alleged access to the U.S. Treasury's payment systems.
Carlson has never gone to a protest, but she has become more engaged with politics because of recent happenings on the national level.
'I love family and friends who are conservative, but I think we need to unite on this to save our democracy,' she said.
An organizer who identified herself by her first name, Skye, from Southern Illinois, said she obtained a permit for the protest. She had seen the movement advertised and decided to spearhead the organization in Illinois with other like-minded people.
Skye and others were setup with microphones and speakers at the top of the steps beside the statute. Skye motioned towards the crowd in an interview and said the crowd was a lot bigger than she anticipated, especially because the group began planning it just three days ago.
The group's main agenda is to push back on President Trump and his administration's overreach of executive orders, she said.
'We believe that they are infringing on our rights, and they are overstepping a lot of the constitution."
Victoria Lee Rosario, who traveled from Bloomingdale, IL, said she was protesting because she is concerned about transgender representation, as well as healthcare that supports gender identity and expression. Rosario transitioned in 2004 but in recent years says she felt discriminated against in the workplace, which prompted her to become more politically active.
Rosario and her partner said they were afraid to make the step to join a physical protest as opposed to speaking up on social media forums, but they said now is more important than ever to advocate for people's rights. The day marked their first time protesting and they didn't know what to expect.
'I thought we could have been the only ones…even if we were going to be the only ones, we were still going to do it,' she said.

title: Having their say: Ordinance will allow more public input when citywide office vacancies occur
author: Steven Spearie
description: An ordinance addressing the filling of 3 citywide offices when a vacancy occurs that will allow for greater public input passed the full city council.
content:
The public will get to see a list of candidates if the offices of mayor, treasurer or clerk are vacated.
An amendment to Tuesday's ordinance also addresses who should fill the offices of clerk and treasurer in the interim process.
An ordinance addressing the filling of three citywide offices when a vacancy occurs that will allow for greater public input passed the full city council Tuesday.
Fresh in their minds was the tumult the occurred when former City Clerk Frank Lesko held onto the seat after being elected and sworn in as Sangamon County Recorder and then-Ward 1 Ald. Chuck Redpath Sr. was quickly voted on to fill the seat without public discussion.
An amendment to the ordinance also addresses who should fill the offices of clerk and treasurer in the interim process.
The city already has a mayor tem. That person operates as mayor when the mayor is out.
The ordinance's sponsors, Ward 6 Ald. Jennifer Notoriano, Ward 5 Ald. Lakeisha Purchase and Ward 2 Ald. Shawn Gregory, were joined by Ward 3 Ald. Roy Williams Jr. and Ward 8 Ald. Erin Conley in affirming it.
The discussion, sometimes intense and spirited, lasted over 90 minutes.
Some alderpersons intent on addressing some of the language of the ordinance and amendment wanted to hold it in committee, but that was voted down.
Ward 4 Ald. Larry Rockford, a "no" vote, reasoned that there weren't any current vacancies.
"We're setting this up for the future, if something happens," Rockford said.
Rockford pointed out he talked to city attorney Gregory Moredock "to get something in writing" if Lesko won the election as recorder and had to resign.
Rushing the ordinance to a vote Tuesday, said Ward 7 Ald. Brad Carlson, was "disingenuous."
Notariano said after the meeting that the public "deserves to be part of that deliberative process and they deserve the opportunity to weigh in on it.
"I'm happy that we could compromise."
In Redpath's case, there was an ordinance that was amended to insert his name and then a city council vote was taken, all at the Jan. 7 meeting.
Calvin T. Christian III, who was present at Tuesday's meeting, filed a motion in Sangamon County court seeking a court injunction against Redpath's appointment being "unlawful," citing a number of legal and ethical violations.
Should a vacancy in one of the offices occur, a posting will be brought to the public to allow anyone who qualifies for the office--a resident in good standing with the city--to put their name forward.
City council members will winnow down the names, with the help of the public, she said.
"They'll get to speak to their alderpeople. They'll get to come to city council to speak on the different nominees and have their say," Notoriano said. "They don't get to vote, but at least they get to have their voices heard."

title: 'A great kid': Students, sports teams honor late Petersburg teen in a personal way
author: Steven Spearie
description: The PORTA school district has provided counselors and therapy dogs to students and staff in the aftermath of Saturday's shooting.
content:
Grant Withers was known for his competitiveness but also as a "super kind" student.
Richard Withers, 40, also died of a gunshot wound, according to the Sangamon County Coroner's office.
Illinois State Police are still investigating the shooting.
Just before the start of basketball practice last fall, PORTA boys coach Steven Price heard Grant Withers, a tall, lanky, but athletic kid still growing into his body, didn't plan on coming out for the team.
In a story related by Brett Leischner, the assistant principal for the junior/senior high school in Petersburg, Price, who saw potential in Withers' athletic ability, approached the 15-year-old at school about what was behind his decision.
"(Withers) said, 'Well, coach, I'm real sorry, but I just want to hunt more,'" Leischner recalled. "And that's what he did."
On Monday, two days after Withers sustained a gunshot wound that would prove fatal at his family's home in the 15000 block of Tice Road just east of Petersburg, students honored Withers and his family by wearing camo shirts, jackets and pants to school.
The idea caught on.
PORTA's girls' basketball team donned camo warmups, as did its Sangamo Conference opponent, Williamsville. Porta's wrestlers and teams from Beardstown and Farmington also saluted Withers at a meet on Tuesday.
Withers also liked to ride dirt bikes and four-wheelers, according to a GoFundMe page set up to support funeral and additional expenses related to his passing.
Illinois State Police, which is leading the investigation, has not divulged details of the fatal shooting. Menard County Sheriff's deputies were called to the scene around 12:30 p.m. on Feb. 1.
Withers' father, Richard Withers, 40, also died of a gunshot wound, according to Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon.
PORTA brought in counselors for students for the week, Leischner said, including its former high school principal, Amy McMahan, who was a guidance counselor and now works in the Havana school system. Surrounding school districts, he added, volunteered to send in help.
The district also made therapy dogs available to students, said PORTA Superintendent Shannon Duling.
"We had a lot of supports on Monday," Duling said. "Kids and staff leaned on each other throughout the day and just kind of remembered Grant.
"We had lots of different areas for kids to talk to one another. Fortunately, we had a nice (weather) day, so we had kids who walked the track and tried to get some physical movement."
"It was amazing to see some kids you really didn't think Grant interacted with a lot who were really affected by it, too," Leischner added. "I think that just really speaks to how well Grant was liked and just that everyone knew he was a great kid."
Leischner taught Withers as a seventh grader and coached him in basketball and baseball. Withers played football at PORTA.
Withers, he remembered, had a competitive side, even in recess or PE class, but he was "super kind and a good teammate. He would do anything to help out the team."
Like Withers had a close-knit circle of friends, Leischner said, Petersburg is a close-knit community.
That's what's made the situation so devastating, he said.
"This hurt a lot of people. I'm not going to sugarcoat that," said Leischner, a PORTA graduate. "But I think it's going as well as it can. I've been incredibly, incredibly impressed by our staff here. They've gone above and beyond for our kids, checking in with them, understanding what they're going through.
"But it's hard. It hit our staff hard, and the kids, obviously. One of the great things about our community and our school and our district is that we wrap around each other, and we make sure that we get through things together."

title: Former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan convicted in corruption trial
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Chicago Democrat who holds the title of the longest-serving legislative leader in U.S. history was convicted of bribery and wire fraud Wednesday.
content:
The Chicago Democrat who holds the title of the longest-serving legislative leader in U.S. history was convicted of bribery and wire fraud Wednesday.
Jurors convicted former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan of 10 counts and acquitted him of seven. The jury could not reach a decision on six, according to the Associated Press.
The jury had deliberated for over 10 days.

title: How much snow will Illinois see this week? Here's the forecast
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A snowstorm this week is predicted to bring around at least four inches of snow to a sizable part of Illinois. Here's what to know.
content:
A snowstorm this week is predicted to bring at least four inches of snow to a sizable part of Illinois.
Most places near and west of Illinois 55 are expected to receive at least four inches of snow Wednesday, according to latest predictions from the National Weather Service.
The storm could also bring a mix of rain and freezing rain to central Illinois.
Here's the outlook for throughout Illinois.
Northern Illinois
The northern part of the state largely sees strong probabilities of receiving at least three or four inches of snow Wednesday, which will start around noon and stop around midnight.
While the weather is always subject to change, that prediction for the northern part of the state should remain fairly accurate, said Mike Albano, who is a meteorologist with the NWS.
Light snow will start around noon and the snow is expected to be falling heavily by the evening commute time.
Chicago, Peoria and Rockford all fit within the storm's path traveling from southwest to northeast that could bring three to five inches.
Central Illinois
Places in central Illinois currently are predicted to see anywhere from one inch to four inches on the low end.
Central Illinois sits in the transition zone of the storm that is especially subject to change as it gets closer, Albano said. That could mean variations of snow, freezing rain, sleet, and rain alone, in moving south.
Areas in that transition zone are from Quincy to Kankakee, including Springfield.
Southern Illinois
Areas along and south of I-70 could see freezing rain and the further south will see only rain.

title: Schallenberg steps into a Plains' game-winner, plus Williamsville drops game against Benton
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Cooper Schallenberg couldn't have made it look better if his idea was to make the shot in Pleasant Plains' buzzer-beating win over El Paso-Gridley.
content:
RIVERTON — Cooper Schallenberg couldn't have made it look better if his idea was to seal Pleasant Plains' 49-46 win over El Paso-Gridley with the shot that he made at the Riverton Shootout on Saturday.
With the game tied, time running out in regulation and El Paso-Gridley having three fouls to give, the ball found the hands of the Cardinals' senior.
Facing a double team, Schallenberg stepped through two Titans' defenders and let the ball leave his hands from behind the 3-point line. The ball cleanly went through nothing but net as time expired and touched off a Pleasant Plains' celebration for a fourth-straight game.
"Honestly, what happened is I heard a bunch of their bench yelling, 'Foul,' so I was kind of trying to draw a foul on the shot so I could get some free throws to win the game," Schallenberg said. "I ended up just stepping through and shooting a little one-handed floater."
Plains coach Kyle Weber said it was a smart strategy by his senior.
"He knew they had a foul to give, and I'm not so sure he didn't get fouled," Weber said. "He did a great job playing through it. Great players make great plays at the right time and that's just kind of what we did. He was able to make a play and kind of save us there."
Schallenberg finished with a game-high 27 points. Schallenberg hit six 3-pointers, but none were bigger than the last one. While he's practiced the move that led to his game-winner, he doesn't believe he's used it to hit a shot at the buzzer before.
"It's mainly to get out of pressure, not necessarily to shoot the ball after stepping through," Schallenberg said. "I'll be honest, that was kind of luck. Practice stepping through to make a pass."
It's just another way the Cardinals keep winning. Since the calendar flipped from 2024 to 2025, so too have the Cards' wins. In the first five weeks of the season, Pleasant Plains went 5-7. During 2025, Plains is 13-3 for an overall record of 18-10.
"We've just got to come into every game like we're the underdogs," Schallenberg said. "We're really good when we're up against good teams and we think people are doubting us."
The Cardinals are a veteran team, and that experience has helped the team with the midseason turnaround. Weber used just seven players on Saturday: senior starters Schallenberg, Trager Shultz and Sean Lowder, junior starters Grady Grisham and Owen Johnson and juniors off the bench Xander Smith and Nolan Scott.
Scott hit three 3-pointers and finished with nine points, including one after El Paso-Gridley took a 44-43 lead. Plains never trailed again.
"(Scott) has hit a couple of really big shots for us here lately," Weber said. "We've got a lot of experience playing in really close games. It seems like whether we're up five or down five, somehow it gets really close at the end. Credit our guys for making some plays down the stretch."
Benton beats Williamsville in state-ranked matchup
Chicago Phillips beat both Williamsville and Benton in last year's Class 2A state tournament finals. Williamsville, without leading scorer Blake Shoufler, lost to Phillips 60-56 in the 2A semifinals. Phillips beat Benton 54-47 in the state title game.
On Saturday, both teams were eager for the matchup of two teams that each have ambitions to get back to Champaign.
Benton's height and defense helped carry the Rangers, ranked No. 7 in the most recent Associated Press Class 2A poll, past No. 3 Williamsville 47-32.
"We talked about (Williamsville's) three-headed monster — Shoufler, (Carson) Doran and (Brayden) Saling — and I thought our guys, all seven guys that played, really, really, really bought into guarding," Benton coach Ron Winemiller said. "Then you've got our eraser at the rim (the 6-foot-9 Docker Tedeschi), and they didn't want to challenge him that much."
Both teams are now 25-3, but it was the worst loss of the season for Williamsville and the Bullets are 2-2 in their last four games.
This kind of game, against the height and talent of Benton, is a good one a week before the postseason begins, Williamsville coach Nick Beard said.
"We knew the schedule we're playing was really difficult," Beard said. "We're hoping this gets us prepared for the postseason. A week from now, if this happens, your season is over."
Waltonville 56, Riverton 46: Riverton sophomore Julian Rice scored 22 points, but the Class 1A sixth-ranked Spartans were too much for the Hawks. Player of the game Kyle Cooper led the way for the Spartans (22-4) got 18 from Kyle Cooper while Jagger Mayville had 13 points to go with 11 rebounds.
Bloomington Central Catholic 52, New Berlin 42: In the day's opening game, Wyatt Frantz scored 11 points for the Pretzels while Aydin Littig had 10 in the loss. Keshaun Manney led BCC with 18.

title: Get ready for Valentine's Day with these classic chocolate truffles
author: Josh Dineen
description: If you're looking to make a little sweet treat for a loved one this Valentine's Day, consider these classic chocolate truffles.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Chocolate truffles likely originated when hot cream was accidentally mixed with chocolate instead of pastry cream ingredients.
In 1923, chocolatier Russell Stover began selling heart-shaped boxes of chocolate, linking chocolate to Valentine's Day.
Valentine's Day is just a couple of days away, and chocolate is often associated with this hopefully romantic holiday. I am really picky when it comes to sweet foods. As a kid I didn't care much about sugary sweets, which my sister loved.
She would have only consumed sugar and candy if allowed, so I always gave her my candies. But with chocolate — I distinctly remember looking forward to savoring chocolates of any kind, not in large amounts, but just enough to satisfy that craving.
My wife often teases me about the way I pronounce the word chocolate. She says I slow down the word a bit, which is comical as I am known for speaking rapidly, and I guess I always give a little smile in the middle of the word. All I know is that I really enjoy the flavors and creamy textures of quality chocolates. I love finding a new brand or batch from a small producer. It's fun to pick through the flavor tones, just like a quality wine, bourbon or scotch.
I first learned about the science of manipulating chocolate when I was 18 working at Incredibly Delicious. Patrick taught me my first lessons on heating and cooling chocolate to control the behaviors of cocoa fats and the way they crystallize, which is known as tempering.
This was the beginning of creating various textures and fillings for truffles. While at culinary school in New York and throughout the decades of my career, I learned that these ideas can be translated indefinitely into parts of other pastries.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
My wife and I are always on the lookout for new chocolate as we travel, which is as often as possible. I often cook when we travel, and recently we were grocery shopping on a trip and came across Scharffen Berger 70% chocolate. It was delicious, with delicate fruit and floral tones. I immediately sent a text to Patrick explaining my thoughts and excitement, and even after almost 30 years, we both still enjoy discovering chocolates that we haven't had or reminded us of old favorites.
Noel chocolates were the first quality I was exposed to, and they are still one of my favorites. It is most of the chocolate we use at Lincoln Land Community College now. Over the years, I have worked with Callebaut, Valrhona and Ghirardelli chocolates, which are also great products that we also occasionally use now. Guittard chocolate is great too, and I have had the pleasure of taking classes with their company at conferences the last couple years.
The origins of foods always provide many fun and debatable ideas. The most accepted beginning of truffles comes from the kitchens of Auguste Escoffier, who standardized French recipes and the way restaurant kitchens are organized and ran. It is said that one of his apprentices was making pastry cream and accidentally poured the hot cream into a bowl of chocolate rather than eggs, sugar and starch.
Chocolate is expensive and not wasted. As a result, the mistake was later checked, and the beginnings of ganache were discovered. They rolled it into balls and tossed it in cocoa powder. The sweet creamy inside was balanced by the bitter coating, and it looked like a black truffle mushroom, which is where the name was derived. Currently, there are chocolate truffles in flavors only bound by imagination.
As far as chocolate in connection with Valentine's Day, there are two major ideas. Chocolate contains phenylethylamine, which when consumed releases endorphins in the brain resulting in a happy feeling that some may say is like the feeling of love.
Russell Stover, a chocolatier, started selling heart-shaped boxes filled with chocolate confections, including truffles, in 1923. The heart-shaped box easily attached to the romance surrounding Valentine's Day, and the rest is history.
Classic Chocolate Truffles
Ingredients
1 cup dark chocolate, roughly chopped into smaller pieces
1 cup heavy cream
Flavorings – optional, I will explain the lack of measurement in a moment
1/4 cup cocoa powder
Directions
Place the chocolate in a bowl. Then place the heavy cream in a pot and bring to a boil.
As soon as it comes to boil, pour it over the chocolate and let sit 60 seconds. Then stir gently, just until combined and creamy. Some chocolatiers say to only stir in one direction.
Cover and place it in the fridge until firm.
Use a small cookie scoop, maybe ¾-1 ounce in measurement, to scoop out the truffles. Gently roll them between your hands to make a pleasant looking ball.
Place the cocoa powder in a bowl and gently toss the truffle balls in the cocoa powder to coat.
(I always eat the first one immediately.)
They should be wrapped or stored in an airtight container in the fridge for the best results. Though the taste is best at room temperature in my opinion.
Notes on chocolate types: If you want to use milk chocolate, change the amount of chocolate to 1 ½ cups. For white chocolate, change the amount of chocolate to 2 cups. If you want a softer truffle filling, increase the heavy cream to 1 ¼ cup.
You can add more flavors after the chocolate and cream have been stirred together. You can use a flavored liquor, a little Nutella, chopped or ground nuts, dried fruits or just about anything you can imagine. Food is very subjective, so I would suggest having a little fun and experimenting with the amounts to find your favorite ratio. In the spirit of Valentine's Day, maybe cater the ratio and flavorings to further increase the feelings of happiness for the person you are celebrating with.
Enjoy!
Joshua Dineen is a chef specialist at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management and Baking/Pastry, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: This Springfield tearoom has more than just tasty beverages and pastries
author: Janet Seitz
description: While this tearoom may be known for its teas, scones and other fresh baked sweet treats, the lunch menu is well worth it, our reviewer says.
content:
Name: Whimsy Tea Company
Address: 316 E. Adams St., Springfield
Phone: 217-331-6920
Website/Facebook: whimsyteacompany.com
Credit/debit cards accepted: Yes.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Hours: 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday
Entrée price range: $5-10.50
Children's menu: No.
My order: While this tearoom may be known for its teas, scones and other fresh baked sweet treats, my friend and I opted to try out their lunch menu which had been implemented in the fall offering soups and sandwiches. My friend had an Autumn Market sandwich with roasted vegetables and turkey on house made focaccia ($8.50), and I had the Reubenesque Panini ($10.50), a take on the classic Reuben.
Likes: The made-from-scratch flavorful sandwiches were served on china, which made for a nice touch. The chef/owner asked us how we were enjoying our meals, so we appreciated the interest in our satisfaction.
Dislikes: My friend thought the atmosphere could be improved upon and made a little more inviting. Perhaps it was the many tea jars spaced out on multiple shelving units which made for an apothecary-like setting and slightly cramped seating.
What would I order next time? Tea. There are many options to choose from with whimsical names. I'd pair a cup with one of their many sweet treats ($4-6.50).

title: Coroner: Findings suggest Sangamon County Jail inmate died of 'natural causes'
author: Steven Spearie
description: Correctional officers gave the jail inmate life-saving measures, according to the county coroner.
content:
Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon said a 55-year-old Sangamon County Jail inmate who was found unresponsive in his cell Tuesday morning later died at HSHS St. John's Hospital.
Allmon did not release his name pending notification of next of kin.
Allmon said in a news release that findings suggest that the man died from "natural causes." An autopsy performed Tuesday showed "no evidence of injury or trauma," he added.
Preliminary findings from the autopsy are officially 'pending toxicology studies," Allmon added.
The inmate had been alone in his cell, according to Allmon, and was discovered unresponsive right around 8:30 a.m.
Medical assistance was requested, and correctional staff began life saving measures by initiating CPR and utilizing an automated external defibrillator, or AED, until medical personnel arrived.
The man was pronounced dead by St. John's staff right around 9 a.m.
Sangamon County law enforcement has been in the national spotlight, especially since the July 6 shooting death of Sonya Massey by a sheriff's deputy.
There have been at least eight deaths in the custody of deputies and corrections officers, in addition to Massey, according to a report by CBS News.
That includes Jaimeson Cody, who died April 27, 2021, as a result of "restraint asphyxia in the setting of methamphetamine intoxication."
While Allmon classified Cody's death as a homicide, then-Sangamon County State's Attorney Dan Wright said it "does not equate to a legal determination that an act of murder, manslaughter, or other crime occurred."
Wright did not seek criminal charges in Cody's case. That decision was preceded by an independent investigation led by Patrick Delfino, director of the Illinois Office of the State's Attorney Appellate Prosecutor.
Cody's family has sued the county and has been vocal lately at county board meetings, saying jail personnel should be held accountable for his death.

title: Illinois is among the best states to raise a family, according to a recent report
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Are you happiest when in the Land of Lincoln, or have you ever thought about moving out of state?
content:
AI-assisted summary
WalletHub ranked Illinois the 7th best state to raise a family in 2025.
The ranking was determined by analyzing 50 key indicators across five categories: Family Fun, Health & Safety, Education & Child Care, Affordability, and Socioeconomics.
The study used data from various sources, including the U.S. Census Bureau, Bureau of Labor Statistics, and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Are you happiest when in the Land of Lincoln, or have you ever thought about moving out of state?
WalletHub ranked each state in the U.S. to see the best and worst places to raise a family in 2025.
Here's where Illinois landed.
What is WalletHub?
WalletHub is a website and app that helps people manage personal finances.
How did Illinois stack up?
Illinois is the seventh best state in the U.S. to raise a family, according to the report.
How was the ranking determined?
Authors looked 50 'key indicators' and compared them across the 50 states. Those indicators include Family Fun, Health & Safety, Education & Child Care, Affordability, and Socioeconomics.
'Raising a family has become significantly more expensive in recent years as the cost of living has risen quickly," wrote Chip Lupo, an analyst with WalletHub. "In light of the expensive nature of being a parent and the responsibility it entails, it's important to live in a city that is affordable while still providing quality health care, education, safety and opportunities for enrichment."
Lupo added that raising a child to the age of 18 can cost well over $300,000, citing the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
In what areas did Illinois score well? Where can it look to improve?
Illinois ranked second in the country for Family Fun.
Illinois ranked third highest in Median Family Income (authors of the study adjusted for cost of living in the category).
Illinois ranked 11th in Education & Child Care.
Illinois ranked 12th in Affordability.
Illinois ranked 30 th in Health & Safety.
Illinois ranked 45 th in Socioeconomics.
What other states ranked well?
Here are the top 10 states from the report:
Massachusetts
Minnesota
North Dakota
Nebraska
New Hampshire
New York
Illinois
Wisconsin
Maine
Connecticut
Massachusetts took the top spot for the third year in a row. It took the cake this year because "it provides a good blend of economic opportunities and safe conditions for children," the report read.
Where did the data come from?
Data came from this past September from the following sources, according to WalletHub: U.S. Census Bureau, Bureau of Labor Statistics, National Center for Education Statistics, Child Care Aware of America, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Council for Community and Economic Research, Federal Bureau of Investigation, U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, National Partnership for Women & Families, TransUnion, The Pew Charitable Trusts, United Health Foundation, Indeed, U.S. News & World Report, Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, National Climatic Data Center, FINRA Investor Education Foundation, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Kaiser Family Foundation, ATTOM, a property data provider - U.S. Foreclosure Market Report, Zendrive, TripAdvisor, PlushCare and WalletHub research.

title: 3 skiers killed in 2 separate avalanches in Oregon and California
author: Zach Urness
description: Police ask people to "use extreme caution" and be aware of weather conditions before recreating outside.
content:
A couple in Central Oregon was found dead after being caught in an avalanche while skiing the day after another person was killed in a separate avalanche in California.
"I am deeply saddened by the tragic loss of the couple who lost their lives in the avalanche while enjoying the Central Oregon backcountry," said Deschutes County Sheriff Kent van der Kamp in a statement. "Their long history in our community and the lives they touched are a testament to the spirit and resilience that make Central Oregon such a special place to live. "
On Tuesday, the Deschutes County Sheriff's Office responded to a reported avalanche burial near Broken Top, Oregon, around 185 miles southeast of Portland, the Deschutes County Sheriff's Office said in a statement. Two bodies were recovered at the scene.
Authorities believe the couple was skiing when the avalanche occurred, according to the Central Oregon Avalanche Center.
"We extend our deepest condolences to all who loved the couple who tragically lost their lives while doing what they loved," the center wrote in a statement. "As longtime residents of Central Oregon, they have touched many lives, and their legacy will continue to live on in our community."
The victim's identities will not be released at this time, police said.
Where did the avalanche happen?
The Deschutes County Sheriff's Office Search and Rescue Unit recovered the couple from Trail 8 on snow-covered Forest Service Road 370, between the Bend Watershed and Broken Top area in an area known as Happy Valley.
"The avalanche occurred at 6,700 ft. on a South facing slope," according to the Avalanche Center.
The avalanche was rated as a D2, according to the center.
D2 avalanches are typically the length of a football field and are capable of burying, injuring, or killing a person, according to Avalanche.org.
Police asked people to stay away from the area and to know that avalanche danger in the Central Cascades area "is moderate to considerable."
"Please use extreme caution when recreating in the areas and check coavalanche.org for more information, including forecasts and observations," police said.
Skier killed in California
Another skier, in an avalanche separate from the one in Oregon, was killed near Powderhouse Peak in California, around 111 miles east of Sacramento, according to the El Dorado County Sheriff's Office.
On Monday, the victim was reported overdue to the county's dispatch, police said. The skier was later found dead by friends in an avalanche area.
Dangerous snow conditions caused the recovery to be delayed until Tuesday morning. At 5 p.m. Tuesday, the victim's body was recovered after further avalanche danger was mitigated, police said.
"The El Dorado County Sheriff's Office wishes to remind everyone to be safe and exercise caution when recreating in the outdoors," the sheriff's office said in a statement.
The victim's identity will not be released at this time, police said.

title: Former Springfield USAID worker thinks agency's emergency response will 're-emerge'
author: Steven Spearie
description: LeGrand 'Lee' Malany worked for an arm of USAID for two decades. He talked to the SJ-R about what he believes will happen to the agency.
content:
Work of USAID will likely re-emerge in different governmental departments.
Some believe the takedown of USAID is undermining national security.
A Springfield resident and former longtime worker for the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) believes the Cold War-era program will be gone, but that some of its work might get moved around under different governmental departments.
LeGrand "Lee" Malany was a personal service contractor with USAID whose work over two decades took him to Haiti, Pakistan and Afghanistan, among other places, dealing with emergency responses.
The 83-year-old Malany left the agency in September to re-join Shelter For Life, an international non-governmental organization for whom he worked in the early 1990s.
President Donald Trump accused USAID of being corrupt by spending money on projects the White House termed wasteful.
Only a few hundred workers for "mission-critical functions" were expected to be kept on, leading to a lawsuit against the Trump administration filed by groups representing the foreign aid workers.
U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols of Washington, D.C., recently temporarily halted plans that would have put thousands of USAID workers on leave. A court order by the judge will keep the stay in place for at least another week.
U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., a member of the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said the dismantling of USAID undermined U.S. national security, empowered adversaries and jeopardized Americans' economic security.
"Trump's destructive actions are causing real harm to people's lives and their livelihoods," Duckworth said recently.
Malany, who works out of modest office on West Jefferson Street, said "the fight of whether we should have USAID has been going on for a long time.
"We've been arguing ever since the creation of the country about how wasteful government is. I don't think Trump is our problem. Trump is our symptom. He's a symptom of our problem and part of that symptom is the other things the government has done overseas."
Trump and Elon Musk, who heads the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), may not be able to get rid of the USAID name, but "they can make it a shell," Malany said. "It's not like getting rid of the Department of Education, which they cannot get rid of without Congress. USAID, you could make a shell and the things they're doing are going to be reallocated (perhaps to the U.S. Department of Agriculture)."
Malany has a background in engineering, which came into play after being dispatched to Pakistan after its 2005 earthquake and Haiti after the 2010 earthquake. He had seven assignments in Afghanistan between 2002 and 2007.
Malany worked in the U.S. Office of Foreign Disaster Assistance (OFDA), which was a separate part of USAID, and had its own security force. While in the office, Malany carried a diplomatic passport.
While its mission was different than the greater whole of USAID--emergency response versus development, Malany said "there's always been bipartisan support for OFDA activities and still is. Sen. Lindsay Graham, R-South Carolina, has always thought (OFDA) was one of our greatest 'soft goods,' and would be supportive of us, even though he might not like the bureau or the rest of USAID."
Around 2018, OFDA joined with the Food for Peace program to form the Bureau of Humanitarian Assistance.
The emergency response function of OFDA, Malany surmised," will re-emerge somewhere in government. We need it. It's great. It doesn't expend a lot of money, and it has a tremendous image impact around the world (for) what America is."
Shelter For Life, based out of Minnesota, does response-related work and development in war-torn countries like Senegal, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Iraq and Ukraine, Malany said.
But like at USAID, uncertainty in the Trump era has meant two postponed trips for Malany.
"As siloed as the American government operates and is at times, it is still really linked together when these kinds of financial issues hit and this confusion hits" he said. "Like everybody, we have to regroup and redesign what it is that we can do based on what is happening."

title: 'Just incredible': Chatham Glenwood wrestler Cody Moss wins Class 2A heavyweight state title
author: Bill Welt
description: Chatham Glenwood's Cody Moss' wrestling dream came true at the state finals on Saturday
content:
Show Caption
Chatham Glenwood junior Cody Moss became the school's second-ever boys wrestling state champion at the State Farm Center in Champaign on Saturday.
Moss jumped ahead 7-3 during the first period before withstanding East Peoria's Jose Del Toro (48-3) for a 9-7 decision for the Class 2A title at 285 pounds.
Former Glenwood standout Drew Davis won the school's first title at 106 pounds in 2022 before becoming a repeat champion at 113 pounds in 2023.
Moss was the only wrestler from the Springfield area to reach the championship round.
"I've been dreaming of this since I was a kid: being a state champ," Moss said. "This is just incredible. Just incredible. It's so surreal to actually be here and experiencing it."
Moss (39-5) initially fell behind 3-0 in the first 30 seconds before registering a takedown and near fall for the lead. He opened the third period with an 8-4 cushion.
Moss said he needed to get control right away.
"I was trying to score early; I didn't want to have to come back at the end," Moss said. "I heard my coaches counting it down at the end and that excitement started to really build. It's just an incredible feeling."
Moss previously appeared at 215 pounds and finished 2-2 at last year's state finals after winning his first sectional title. He dominated this year's Lincoln Sectional in the heavyweight class and won two of his first three matches via pin to reach the championship match.
Moss, ranked No. 3 by Illinois Matmen ahead of the state finals, pinned Cary-Grove's top-ranked wrestler, Lucas Burton, in the third period, while Del Toro was ranked second.
Other state medalists in the area hailed from the Petersburg PORTA co-op in Class 1A. Junior Justin Zimmerman won an 8-2 decision over Olney Richland's Carson Bissey for fifth place at 157 pounds, while fellow junior Zach Bryant earned sixth at 132.

title: Overcoming sexual stigma: Springfield massage therapist shares experiences, hardships
author: Claire Grant
description: If you can expect a safe and clean environment at a local eatery, shouldn't the same be said for all massage establishments?
content:
Massage therapists work to overcome sexual stigma brought on by unlicensed massage parlors.
Alicia Depew is an award-winning licensed massage therapist who has seen the stigma firsthand.
When you go to a restaurant, you want your food cooked by a chef who knows what they're doing in a clean kitchen. If you go to a bar, you expect to see a license on a wall.
If you can expect a safe and clean environment at a local eatery, shouldn't the same be said for all massage establishments?
Less than one year following an ordinance requiring massage establishments to be licensed, 11 locations have been shut down by the city.
The closures are a step forward for practitioners of bodywork and licensed professionals like Alicia Depew.
'It's more frustrating we have to continually fight and educate and it's more since people still view massage therapy in general as a sexual thing,' Depew said. 'We work really hard for our licenses here and it's frustrating when there are places that operate like that.'
Last week, the city requested an emergency restraining order against Illinois Relax Spa and Cozy Cabin Spa for continuing to operate despite being forced.
Depew has been a licensed massage therapist for almost two decades. She says she first found her love for the form of medical care when going on a trip to Chicago to shadow different medical providers and feeling the relaxing and positive effects massage had in that moment.
While attending St. Charles School of Massage Therapy in Missouri to obtain her license, she was taught about massage parlors, different to licensed establishments, and how to tell if a location is legit.
Depew said some of the biggest red flags for establishments are obvious like provocative pictures on doors, covered windows, but there are other ones you may not think of.
'Sanitation is also part of license practice,' Depew said. 'It's important to have safe sanitation practices because if you're touching one person and touching another person you can transfer what that first person had. It happens unfortunately and it's incredibly important to go somewhere that is licensed who follows continued education.'
In June of 2024, the City of Springfield passed an ordinance requiring massage establishments within the city to apply for a business license to curb the rise of spots dotting the map offering prostitution. To obtain a license, locations must pass several branches of city inspections as well as have documentation for licensed massage therapists onsight.
Depew says she's relieved to see the new licensing process in the city to better differentiate parlors from therapy clinics and spas.
Overcoming the sexualized stigma
Depew admitted she had been sexually assaulted on more than occasion while working on a patient who expected more from her.
'Even though it's taught in school how to handle these situations by the book, when you're in these situations you don't know what to do,' Depew said. 'I didn't tell anybody ... because I felt like I did something wrong. Looking back years, it's like, I did nothing wrong ... but I was in a very vulnerable spot.'
Depew said after winning an award for her medical work, she received an influx of emails requesting to see provocative photos of her or requesting for a massage that was more sexual in nature.
'Massage has this sexualized stigma with it and we're trying to break free from that,' Depew said.' 'But people who continue to patron those establishments that do offer those services continue to sexualize this career. It's why I'm so passionate about this … I'm not into that and people still presume. … It's very frustrating.'
Lack of information can be dangerous
Depew says massage can cause long-term nerve damage if done incorrectly and unlicensed establishments can be predatory toward customers who don't know the difference between parlors and spas.
'I had a client who was sending her son to me, and he accidentally went to the wrong location,' Depew said. 'He said he was there for me, and they took him and told him he was in the right place … luckily nothing sexual happened but he felt uneasy and uncomfortable the whole time.'
When looking to get a massage, the internet is a key factor. Most locations listed on Google maps have an attached website or phone number: search online the name of the establishment and be wary of provocative images, or websites not containing the names of licensed massage therapists – not masseuse – on the website.
If a name pops up, you can use the online verification tool provided by the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation.
'(The massage clinics are) trying to branch out away from establishments like that,' Depew said. 'And then you have people who have no idea because the (parlors) say massage. Even if they do not receive any sexual services they should not be able to perform those services.'
Depew enjoys working as a freelance massage therapist at Waggener Chiropractic and Wellness Center at 7012 Kingsmill Court and says it's been a while since the encounters at the workplace happened.

title: Springfield City Council approves of FY26 budget with little debate, little fanfare
author: Steven Spearie
description: The city council approved several "technical amendments," giving it budgetary discretion, though the programs still need to be voted on later.
content:
City council unanimously approved the FY26 budget.
Several "technical amendments'" were added, like a barricade system.
With little debate, and little fanfare, the Springfield City Council unanimously approved the FY2026 budget Tuesday with a corporate fund just over $184.5 million.
That figure did not include several "technical amendments" added to the budget, including a $635,000 barricade system to help block streets and reduce the risk of vehicular attacks.
While added to the budget, the barricade system will still require full city council approval to be implemented.
The corporate fund is the principal operating fund for the city and excludes CWLP.
Ward 9 Ald. Jim Donelan complimented Mayor Misty Buscher and city department directors for getting budget books into the hands of city council members more than two months before it needed to be passed.
Hearings and meetings with the mayor, Office of Budget and Management Director Ramona Metzger and department heads, he said, cut down on the drama of passing this budget.
While voting for the budget, Ward 2 Ald. Shawn Gregory cautioned directors that they might want to hold off on equipment and personnel for FY27.
"It's getting tight," Gregory said, "and we don't want to put the city in the position to take on debt, raise taxes, etc."
Donelan said he was reminded of having to go through previous budgets line by line to make cuts, sometimes hundreds of dollars at a time, because it was so tight.
"We don't want to be in a position where we have to make dramatic cuts or anything of that nature in the near future, let alone in the long term," he said.
The barricade system came in response to an attack in New Orleans when a man drove a pickup truck into a crowd on Bourbon Street, then exited the truck and engaged in a shootout with police before being fatally shot. Fifteen people were killed.
"I think it's important that we look at purchasing this and having this available for our citizens," said Springfield Police Chief Ken Scarlette.
It was first budget for Ward 1 Ald. Jeff Cox, who was sworn in at last week's city council meeting.
"I was very nervous about the budget, and I had a lot of people help me understand what was in it," he said.

title: New bill would raise age in which Illinois seniors need to take a driving test
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Currently, Illinois residents 79 years old and above need to take a behind-the-wheel driving test. New legislation would raise the age to 87.
content:
Bill would align driving laws with other states, supporters say.
Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias drafted the legislation.
Crash rate for senior drivers is the lowest, legislators say, citing IDOT data.
Drivers who are between 79 and 86 years old would no longer have to take a behind-the-wheel driving test to maintain a driver's license in Illinois under proposed legislation.
Rep. Jay Hoffman, D-Swansea, filed House Bill 1226 along with a long list of House sponsors showing support.
Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias drafted the legislation, according to a news release.
The Land of Lincoln is the only state that requires the driving test based on age, both Giannoulias' office and Rep. Hoffman said. They also said Illinois is one of five states that does not allow immediate family members to report concerns about a relative's driving ability, which the bill would change.
'Our state's crash data indicates that the crash rate for drivers aged 75 and older is lower than any other age range of drivers,' Rep. Hoffman wrote in a press release, citing 2023 crash rate data from the Illinois Department of Transportation.
The bill has been placed on the calendar for a second reading and short debate.
What would the law change?
Legislation would amend the Illinois Vehicle Code to raise the age from 79 to 87 when drivers need to take a behind-the-wheel test to renew their license, in addition to creating a process for family members to report any concerns about driving ability.
What is the law currently?
Drivers aged 79 and 80 must currently renew their license every four years, in addition to taking a behind-the-wheel test and a vision test.
Drivers between the ages of 81 and 86 years old must currently renew their license every two years as well as take a behind-the-wheel test and a vision test.
And drivers over 87 years-old must renew their license annually. To pass, they need to take a behind-the-wheel test and a vision test.
How did the Secretary of State get involved?
Giannoulias and the American Association of Retired Persons both support the initiative, according to a release from Giannoulias' office. The Act seeks to make Illinois consistent with other states, they wrote.
'AARP Illinois has heard for years from our members about how the driving test requirement disproportionately affects older drivers and perpetuates false narratives about their driving abilities,' stated AARP Illinois State Director Philippe Largent.

title: Pleasant Plains boys basketball capitalizes on ball movement to reach regional finals
author: Bill Welt
description: Pleasant Plains boys basketball harbored a little trepidation until a four-point play put the Cardinals at ease
content:
Show Caption
PLEASANT PLAINS — Sometimes the first bucket can be the hardest to come by.
Pleasant Plains senior guard Cooper Schallenberg quashed those initial fears with a four-point play. It not only ended the early dry spell but also sparked the host Cardinals in a 61-47 win over Riverton in the Class 2A regional semifinal on Wednesday.
No. 3-seeded Plains (21-10) advances to the regional final against No. 2 Warsaw/Hamilton West Hancock on Friday at 7 p.m.
'We were down 6-0 at the time and missed a couple layups; I thought it was going to be one of those games,' Schallenberg said. 'It was just good to see one go through and get us going.'
Cardinals dish up 3s
Schallenberg and three other Cardinals combined for nine 3s. That included three treys from junior reserve Nolan Scott.
Senior guard Trager Shultz generated a game-high 15 points, while junior guard Grady Grisham supplied 12 points. Scott and junior guard Owen Johnson had 11 points apiece.
Shultz and Co. didn't buckle against Riverton's pressure after the previous two meetings were decided by five points combined during the regular season.
'He handled the ball super well tonight,' Schallenberg said of Shultz. 'We've got to handle the ball against them because they were pressuring us like crazy everywhere. Being calm under pressure and seeing the open man is huge and Trager did a good job tonight.'
Shultz said it comes down to being strong with the ball and refraining from over-dribbling.
'It's good to see your passes actually fall through with the shot,' Shultz said, 'it's good to see all of us work together cohesively.'
'It doesn't feel real sometimes': Calvary's Josh Long begins to thrive again after family tragedy
Plains coach Kyle Weber indeed described the offense as opportunistic and hopes the Cardinals can duplicate that success in a rematch of last year's regional final that Plains won 64-60.
'If they're going to play aggressive and trap, that gives you opportunities on the back end where if you can make that first pass, you're a couple passes away from a wide open 3 or a layup and I thought we did a good job of handling that,' Weber said.
Riverton hopes to build on experience
Plains surged ahead with 12 unanswered points and led 26-12 by halftime. The Hawks just couldn't hit their open looks, Riverton coach Matt Mead said.
Junior Colton Johnson led Riverton with eight points, while sophomore standout Julian Rice and senior Jaxson Miller had six apiece.
Riverton finishes 22-10 with just two seniors in the starting lineup, twins Carter and Jaxson Miller.
'We kind of figured this year we would be one of the younger teams around,' Mead said. 'I'm really proud of our four seniors, I know Jaxson and Carter (Miller) had a lot to do with our success, so were Gage Werner and Tristan Tolley. They didn't see the floor quite as much as the Millers did, but they were there every day at practice working hard and helping to sharpen us all year long.
'I'm thankful for their effort and for our younger guys, I told them, 'Look, you've got to try to learn from it and get motivated to come back even better next year.''
NO. 2 WARSAW/HAMILTON WEST HANCOCK 84, NO. 8 ATHENS 36: Six-foot-nine junior forward Cooper Knowles led the Titans with 18 points, while Gavin Grothuas and Lewis Siegfried each had 17.
Isaac Brown paced Athens with eight points.

title: Two business owners, longtime friends team up to buy former Alexander's Steakhouse
author: Claire Grant
description: Two longtime friends, business owners have purchased the former Alexander's Restaurant location in Springfield.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Alexander's Steakhouse was purchased by Marcus McGlasson and Andrew Cochran, two local businessmen.
Alexander's Steakhouse closed in February of 2024 after nearly four decades in business.
The owners of several coffee locations across Illinois are the new owners of a former popular steakhouse location in Springfield.
According to Sangamon County property tax records, Marcus McGlasson and Andrew Cochran of Pleasant Plains have purchased the old Alexander's Steakhouse at 620 N. Bruns Lane.
If one of those names ring a bell for readers, Marcus McGlasson and his wife, Lauryn, run several franchised Scooter's Coffee locations across Illinois and Indiana, including the Springfield-area Scooters and the still in development Chatham Scooter's Coffee.
McGlasson also co-owns Just Right Easing, a meal delivery service in Edwardsville and Springfield and is a financial advisor for LPL Financial. According to the Illinois Secretary of State, Cochran, Brian Brewer, Stephanie Johnson and Dominic Podeschi are listed as managers for the meal prep kit business.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Cochran, who is a homebuilder in Springfield and owns Andrew Cochran Construction, has been lifelong high school friends with McGlasson.
'We bought it as an investment and haven't finalized plans yet,' Cochran said. 'We look to get together mid-March and come together with some (business) options.'
The two friends' choice to go all in on purchasing the close to million-dollar building is an investment into the future, while keeping a part of the local food scene's history active and not left to sit on the market.
The steakhouse business closed a year ago this month of Feb. 29, 2024, citing poor customer retention, inflation of service costs and competition between other steakhouses as the reason. The 5,000 square foot building was sold to Cochran and McGlasson on Jan. 16, 2025.
Before closing, Alexander's Steakhouse had been open for almost four decades and been a piece of Springfield's high profile dining experiences for customers.
In the following weeks, Cochran said to expect an update on the commercial direction the building will take and what the two friends cook up for the area.

title: 'You couldn't ask for a better gentleman': Former circuit judge Lewis dead at 77
author: Steven Spearie
description: Theodis "Ted" Lewis, the first Black judge to be appointed to the Seventh Judicial Circuit, died at his home in Chatham last week.
content:
Theodis Lewis was in private law practice and an assistant public defender before becoming a judge.
He was last recommended for reappointment in 2007, months before his retirement.
Theodis "Ted" Lewis, the first Black judge to be appointed to the Seventh Judicial Circuit, died at his home in Chatham on Feb. 17.
He was 77.
A native of Little Rock, Ark., who attended Illinois Institute of Technology and the University of Illinois Law School, Lewis was appointed an associate circuit judge for Sangamon County in 1991.
More: Richard Ringeisen, who led UIS as chancellor from 2001 to 2010, is dead
The judicial circuit covers Greene, Jersey, Macoupin, Morgan, Sangamon and Scott counties.
For years before that, Black leaders in Springfield, like then-Ald. Frank McNeil, had called for the appointment of a Black judge, citing the need for ethnic diversity and fair representation on the bench.
Lewis' appointment came on the heels of the landmark Voting Rights lawsuit, of which McNeil was a plaintiff. It alleged Springfield's commission form of government, with a mayor and four commissioners elected at-large, curtailed Black voting strength.
In 1987, a consent decree established the present form of government with 10 alderpersons representing wards based on geography.
"It was about inclusiveness," McNeil said about Lewis' appointment. "A large percentage of our young people were being sentenced to (prison) terms in the Illinois Department of Corrections. We felt there was a lack of understanding of the things they had endured coming into it."
Lewis practiced in several areas of the law, including traffic, misdemeanor, small claims and civil and felony cases, as well as being an assistant public defender in Sangamon County before ascending to the bench.
Lewis was last recommended for reappointment in May 2007, a few months before he retired.
In 2014, Lewis became a railroad-relocation ombudsman in an agreement between the county and the Illinois Department of Transportation.
Lewis worked for several months, but the state failed to complete a contract for the position. He was later compensated for his work.
Lewis served on the boards of numerous youth-related organizations, including the Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts, the Springfield Urban League and Springfield College in Illinois.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Byron Cudmore said Lewis was a respected attorney when the two met in Springfield in the late 1970s.
"I watched his career as he became an associate circuit judge sitting in Sangamon County," Cudmore said. "I always respected his approach to decisions and his soft-spoken manner in court.
"Ted was a good man."
McNeil said he knew Lewis' wife, Judy, and their four children from attending Zion Missionary Baptist Church together. Lewis, McNeil added, served as a good role model.
"He took seriously his job as a judge but understood the lives of African Americans who had come from very difficult circumstances," McNeil added. "Outside of a judge, he was a very, very good human being.
"You couldn't ask for a better gentleman, a better man, a better family man."

title: Springfield man found guilty of sexually assaulting 6-year-old granddaughter

A Springfield man has been found guilty of sexually assaulting his granddaughter.

Lord assaulted his granddaughter, who was around six years old at the time of the assaults, between 2017 and 2020, according to the Sangamon County State's Attorney's Office.

Court records show that Lord was born in 1951, making him around 74 years old.

title: Attorneys for Sean Grayson want his trial moved out of Sangamon County
author: Steven Spearie
description: It is anticipated that Sean Grayson's attorneys will ask Judge Ryan Cadagin to set a hearing for a venue change at Grayson's next court appearance.
content:
Show Caption
Attorneys for Sean Grayson say he can't get a fair trial in Sangamon County.
Any court change would be approved by Circuit Judge Ryan Cadagin, who has Sean Grayson's case.
The attorneys for a former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy charged in the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey don't believe the defendant can get a fair trial in Sangamon County, so they are asking the court for a change of place of trial, commonly known as a change of venue.
Daniel Fultz and Mark Wykoff, both of Springfield, filed the motion on behalf of Sean P. Grayson of Riverton on Wednesday.
Grayson, who is being jailed in Decatur, is charged with first-degree murder.
The motion stated that, among other things, extensive media coverage of the case established "a prima facie showing of prejudice against (Grayson) by the inhabitants of Sangamon County such that a fair trial cannot be obtained without a change of place of trial."
Nearly "everyone is aware of and has an opinion on the matter and has discussed the case with fellow community members," the motion read.
The State Journal-Register was among media outlets cited in the motion.
Any change would have to be decided by Circuit Judge Ryan Cadagin, who is trying the case.
It is anticipated that Grayson's attorneys will ask Cadagin to set a hearing for the change at Grayson's next court appearance on March 24.
Grayson does not have a trial date yet.
The Massey Commission, a citizens' commission established with an eye towards addressing systemic issues in law enforcement practices, mental health responses and community relations, the renaming of the Jefferson Bridge the Massey Memorial Bridge and a GoFundMe page were all brought up in the motion as possibly tilting public opinion.
"The prejudgment of this case–whether through direct knowledge, media influence, or social pressure–poses a significant threat to the defendant's right to a fair trial," the motion read.
Changing the setting of a trial has taken place in a number of high-profile cases in the area.
In 2002, Dale Lash, accused of carjacking, sexually assaulting and murdering Lori Hayes, had his case moved from Sangamon County to Peoria County.
A circuit judge granted the attorneys for Christopher Harris, one of two brothers accused of slaying five members of Beason's Gee family in 2009, a change of venue. They said the Logan County jury pool was too tainted because of extensive media coverage.
The murder trial of Ashland grandmother Shirley Skinner was moved out of Cass County to a court in Quincy in 2009. She was accused in the shooting death of Steven Paul Watkins.
A case moved to Sangamon County was Curtis Lovelace, a former Adams County assistant state's attorney and University of Illinois football standout, accused of killing his first wife, Cory Lovelace. His first trial, in Quincy, ended with a deadlocked jury. The second trial was moved on a change-of-venue request.
Grayson and another sheriff's deputy responded to Massey's residence in an unincorporated neighborhood just off Stevenson Drive for a purported prowler early on the morning of July 6.
Grayson, who is white, shot Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman and the mother of two children, in the face while in her home. The incident was captured on Grayson's partner's body-worn camera.
The Massey family recently agreed to a $10 million out-of-court settlement with the county.

title: Glenwood packs regional title win over Lanphier
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Despite losing Cam Appenzeller for nearly half the fourth quarter, Glenwood got timely plays and key points to beat Lanphier to win a 3A regional title.
content:
When Cam Appenzeller picked up his fourth foul with 5 minutes, 33 seconds left in a four-point game, Chatham Glenwood coach Todd Blakeman subbed out his leading scorer and main ball handler.
When the Titans struggled offensively to break through Lanphier's defense without Appenzeller, Blakeman gambled and sent Appenzeller back in the game, but the senior quickly picked up his fifth foul with 3:45 left.
While it seemed as if that would be the opening Lanphier needed, the rest of the Titans stepped up to beat Lanphier 43-39 for the Class 3A Lanphier Regional title on the Lions' home floor, Lober-Nika Gymnasium, on Friday.
'We just had to have grit,' Glenwood senior Gavin Simmons said. 'Basketball is a game of runs and whenever Lanphier went on a run, we just had to slow down, play our game and just weather the storm.'
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
No. 3 Chatham Glenwood (21-9) will now face No. 4 Champaign Central in the Decatur Eisenhower Sectional semifinals at 7 p.m. on Tuesday. The Maroons (17-12) toppled No. 1 Decatur MacArthur 60-54 to win the Champaign Centennial Regional, also on Friday. The semifinal winner will face either No. 1 Lincoln or No. 2 Mount Zion in the sectional championship game on Friday.
'Their defense was phenomenal,' Lanphier coach Blake Turner said. 'We had trouble penetrating their defense, I didn't think we were aggressive enough attacking the paint. They killed us on the glass, almost two to one (29 rebounds for Glenwood compared to 15 for Lanphier).
'Chatham came in and earned it, my hat's off to them and I'm going to wish them luck next week.'
Mason Neumann, who finished with 12 points to lead Glenwood, had five of his points on free throws after Appenzeller fouled out. The Titans, who knocked down four 3-pointers in a 44-36 win over Springfield High on Wednesday in the regional semis, went three quarters without a made outside shot. Jack Kurmann got one to drop for the Titans when he opened up the fourth quarter with a 3 to give the Titans their biggest lead, 28-22.
'We stayed confident in ourselves and we fought until the end,' said Appenzeller, who truly prefers playing to watching. 'Every second, the game stopped and it felt like it took 20 minutes to play the last minute. Every time we came down the court, I was confident in my team.'
Lanphier had chances to go ahead. Soriano Hayes scored a fastbreak layup and was fouled with 5:11 left but missed the free throw. Lanphier struggled at the line, going 11-for-20. Down two when Appenzeller picked up his fifth personal, Holman missed the second free throw, then missed a second free throw with 1:45 left and Glenwood leading 32-30.
Simmons and Kurmann, who handled the point guard duties without Appenzeller, combined to hit four free throws and put Glenwood up 36-30 with 45.4 seconds left. Simmons had all four of his points over the final 1:41 of the game.
'We practice without Cam a lot, just for that reason, and still, we don't have a true point guard,' Glenwood coach Todd Blakeman said. 'It's point guard by committee (without Appenzeller). We were able to step up and win this game.'
Shaunassey Hatchett Jr., a 6-foot-4 Lanphier senior, had the Lions' first three field goals, but didn't have another until he hit a 3 with 30 seconds left and finished with 12 points. He went a full three quarters, from 1:53 to go in the first until that late 3 in the fourth, without a field goal. Much of that responsibility was up to Glenwood's fellow 6-4 senior, Jonathan Helm.
'I watched film, I thought (Hatchett would) spin a lot more, but and he didn't — he just took it to the hole on me,' Helm said. 'Luckily, I was able to stop him for some of the drives. He's very talented, very skilled; I respect that guy a lot.'
Blakeman said the goal was to make Hatchett feel uncomfortable, but it was Blakeman and the Titans who were feeling the pain when Hatchett scored three buckets in the opening quarter.
'It was like, 'What are we doing,' Blakeman said. 'But at the same time, I told Johnny, 'Stay in front of him. Nothing's going to be easy. We bowed out last year: a little bit of adversity here and there and we didn't have the fight in us we have now. These guys are a team and they're going to pick each other up.'
Turner said his team just couldn't beat Glenwood's pack-line defense.
'We didn't do a good job getting the ball to (Hatchett) and finding him, but also I think (Glenwood) made adjustments and they really turned up the pressure and worked hard to take him away. Chatham's known for their pack-line defense and when it's effective, they're hard to beat and tonight it was effective.'
Appenzeller finished with 11 points, Kurmann and seven and Helm scored six. Hatchett led Lanphier (22-12) with 12 points while JaiQuan Holman had 10 and Amari Anderson scored six off the bench.

title: Trump: US deal with Ukraine's Zelenskyy over 'raw earth' looks to be on hold
author: Mike Snider
description: President Trump wants rare-earth minerals deal to help the US recoup its support to Ukraine. He's said it's about 'raw earth.' What does that mean?
content:
Show Caption
President Donald Trump wants Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal with the U.S. over the country's "raw earth" minerals.
But what does that actually mean?
Zelenskyy came to the White House on Friday under expectations he and Trump would reach a deal with Ukraine that would put 50% of future revenue from mineral resources, oil, natural gas, and other materials into a joint Ukraine-U.S. investment fund.
Trump described the potential deal on Friday, saying, "We don't know exactly how much because we're going to be putting some money in a fund that we're going to get from the raw earth that we're going to be taking and sharing in terms of revenues, so it's going to be a lot of money,' Bloomberg reported.
Potential profits from the deal could satisfy Trump's request that Ukraine repay the U.S. for its help defending the country since Russia's invasion in 2022.
This wasn't the first time Trump described the deal as involving "raw earth." Earlier this week, Trump suggested Zelenskyy would sign an agreement in Washington on Friday. "We've pretty much negotiated our deal on raw Earth and various other things," said Trump on Tuesday.
And again on Friday, Trump said the deal covers minerals vital to industry. "This has just about every component of the raw Earth that we need for computers for all of the things we do. This puts us in great shape," he said The National News Desk reported.
Ukraine doesn't currently produce any rare earth metals but, according to Ukraine's Institute of Geology, possesses large deposits of such minerals, including lanthanum, cerium, neodymium and yttrium. Detailed data about those reserves is classified, Reuters reported.
Ukraine also has one of the largest lithium reserves in Europe – amounting to about 3% of global total reserves – but is not currently mining it, NPR reported. Lithium is used in batteries for smartphones and many other devices.
'Raw earth': What does it mean?
So, what is "raw earth"? Well, that's a good question. Here's a possible answer. Rare-earth metals and elements such as lanthanum and lutetium are raw materials of which there are limited concentrated deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
What President Trump may be doing is using a shorthand phrase of "raw earth" to cover all the rare-earth elements and raw materials covered by the proposed agreement.
That could be a suitable description because Ukraine has a lot of raw materials on its own. 'About 5% of all the world's 'critical raw materials' are located in Ukraine, which occupies only 0.4 percent of the Earth's surface,' Ukraine's deputy minister of environmental protection and natural resources, Svetlana Grinchuk, said in 2022, reported CNBC.
Whether the deal will come about remains to be seen before the planned joint press conference with Trump and Zelenskyy, which was canceled after a discordant meeting with Trump, Zelenskyy and Vice President JD Vance. During the meeting, Vance told Zelenskyy he was being "disrespectful" to Trump and should be thanking the U.S. for its support, rather than lecturing it on the cause of the war.
