description: President Trump wants rare-earth minerals deal to help the US recoup its support to Ukraine. He's said it's about 'raw earth.' What does that mean?
content:
President Donald Trump wants Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal with the U.S. over the country's "raw earth" minerals.
But what does that actually mean?
Zelenskyy came to the White House on Friday under expectations he and Trump would reach a deal with Ukraine that would put 50% of future revenue from mineral resources, oil, natural gas, and other materials into a joint Ukraine-U.S. investment fund.
Trump described the potential deal on Friday, saying, "We don't know exactly how much because we're going to be putting some money in a fund that we're going to get from the raw earth that we're going to be taking and sharing in terms of revenues, so it's going to be a lot of money,' Bloomberg reported.
Potential profits from the deal could satisfy Trump's request that Ukraine repay the U.S. for its help defending the country since Russia's invasion in 2022.
This wasn't the first time Trump described the deal as involving "raw earth." Earlier this week, Trump suggested Zelenskyy would sign an agreement in Washington on Friday. "We've pretty much negotiated our deal on raw Earth and various other things," said Trump on Tuesday.
And again on Friday, Trump said the deal covers minerals vital to industry. "This has just about every component of the raw Earth that we need for computers for all of the things we do. This puts us in great shape," he said The National News Desk reported.
Ukraine doesn't currently produce any rare earth metals but, according to Ukraine's Institute of Geology, possesses large deposits of such minerals, including lanthanum, cerium, neodymium and yttrium. Detailed data about those reserves is classified, Reuters reported.
Ukraine also has one of the largest lithium reserves in Europe – amounting to about 3% of global total reserves – but is not currently mining it, NPR reported. Lithium is used in batteries for smartphones and many other devices.
'Raw earth': What does it mean?
So, what is "raw earth"? Well, that's a good question. Here's a possible answer. Rare-earth metals and elements such as lanthanum and lutetium are raw materials of which there are limited concentrated deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
What President Trump may be doing is using a shorthand phrase of "raw earth" to cover all the rare-earth elements and raw materials covered by the proposed agreement.
That could be a suitable description because Ukraine has a lot of raw materials on its own. 'About 5% of all the world's 'critical raw materials' are located in Ukraine, which occupies only 0.4 percent of the Earth's surface,' Ukraine's deputy minister of environmental protection and natural resources, Svetlana Grinchuk, said in 2022, reported CNBC.
Whether the deal will come about remains to be seen before the planned joint press conference with Trump and Zelenskyy, which was canceled after a discordant meeting with Trump, Zelenskyy and Vice President JD Vance. During the meeting, Vance told Zelenskyy he was being "disrespectful" to Trump and should be thanking the U.S. for its support, rather than lecturing it on the cause of the war.

title: Here are the final Big Ten women's basketball power rankings before postseason play
author: Dargan Southard
description: Here are the final USA TODAY Sports Big Ten women's basketball power rankings before the conference tournament begins on Wednesday.
content:
The bright lights of March are finally here. Big Ten women's basketball plans to make a significant splash with its numerous postseason opportunities.
With the possibility of landing a stunning 13 NCAA Tournament bids later this month, this league is full of teams with potential for lengthy postseason runs. From now until Selection Sunday, it's all about that final bit of positioning for bigger things ahead.
With that in mind, here are the final USA TODAY Sports Network Big Ten women's basketball power rankings before the conference tournament begins on Wednesday in Indianapolis.
1. USC (26-2)
What to know: The Trojans sent a loud statement Sunday with their resounding road win at UCLA to clinch the outright Big Ten regular-season title. USC will be the No. 1 seed in Indy.
2. UCLA (27-2)
Previously: No. 2
What to know: The Bruins didn't look their best down the stretch and will head to Indy as the No. 2 seed, looking to restore momentum entering the NCAA Tournament.
3. Maryland (23-6)
Previously: No. 4
What to know: Wins over Indiana and Ohio State this past week has Maryland heading to Indy as the No. 4 seed on the NCAA Tournament hosting bubble.
4. Ohio State (24-5)
Previously: No. 3
What to know: A strong win last Wednesday over Michigan State, coupled with Sunday's overtime loss to Maryland, has Ohio State as the No. 3 seed in Indy. The Buckeyes are firmly on the NCAA Tournament hosting bubble as well.
5. Michigan State (21-8)
Previously: No. 6
What to know: The Spartans rebounded from last Wednesday's loss at Ohio State with a strong home win Saturday over Minnesota. Michigan State will head to Indy as the No. 6 seed.
6. Iowa (20-9)
Previously: No. 9
What to know: The Hawkeyes finished the regular season strong with a road win at Michigan and a home victory over Wisconsin. Iowa will be the No. 11 seed in Indy.
7. Michigan (20-9)
Previously: No. 7
What to know: The Wolverines shook off last Wednesday's loss to Iowa and rebounded with a strong rally Sunday at Illinois. Michigan will be the No. 5 seed in Indy.
8. Illinois (21-8)
Previously: No. 5
What to know: A crushing loss Sunday to Michigan has Illinois entering the Big Ten Tournament on a three-game losing streak. The Fighting Illini are the No. 7 seed in Indy.
9. Indiana (18-11)
Previously: No. 8
What to know: The Hoosiers bounced back Sunday with a win at Purdue following last Thursday's home loss to Maryland. Indiana is the No. 9 seed in Indy.
10. Nebraska (19-10)
Previously: No. 10
What to know: Nebraska got back on track with a resounding win Sunday at Northwestern. The Cornhuskers will be the No. 10 seed in Indy.
11. Oregon (19-10)
Previously: No. 11
What to know: After stumbling Sunday at Washington, Oregon will be the No. 8 seed at the Big Ten Tournament in Indy.
12. Washington (18-12)
Previously: No. 13
What to know: Washington looks poised to snag an NCAA Tournament at-large bid, now on a four-game winning streak entering the Big Ten Tournament. The Huskies are the No. 12 seed.
13. Minnesota (20-10)
Previously: No. 12
What to know: Having lost seven of nine, the Golden Gophers will be playing for their NCAA Tournament lives this week in Indy. Minnesota is the No. 13 seed this week.
14. Wisconsin (13-16)
Previously: No. 14
What to know: The Badgers backed into the Big Ten Tournament as the No. 14 seed and will face Iowa for the second time in four days on Wednesday.
15. Rutgers (11-18)
Previously: No. 15
What to know: The Scarlet Knights also backed into the Big Ten Tournament as the No. 15 seed and will face Nebraska to open postseason play on Wednesday.
16. Northwestern (9-18)
Previously: No. 16
What to know: The Wildcats' season has ended after falling short of making the Big Ten Tournament.
17. Purdue (10-19)
Previously: No. 17
What to know: The Boilermakers' season has ended after falling short of making the Big Ten Tournament.
18. Penn State (10-19)
Previously: No. 18
What to know: Penn State's season has ended after falling short of making the Big Ten Tournament.

title: Regional champs, buzzer-beaters: Vote for the SJ-R's athlete of the week
author: Bill Welt
description: Here are this week's nominees. The poll closes at noon on Friday.
content:
Here are The State Journal-Register's athlete of the week nominees.
The poll closes at noon on Friday. Information about the nominees is below. Staunton's Ele Feldmann won last week's poll.
If you have trouble viewing the poll, click on this link.
Jacob Barth, Auburn, boys basketball
The senior guard generated a team-high 14 points in a 56-43 win over host Greenville for the Class 2A regional title.
Brody Folkes, Mason City Illini Central, boys basketball
The junior guard reached 1,000 career points and supplied 23 points for the host Cougars in a 46-37 win over Mendon Unity for the program's first regional title since 2013.
Grady Grisham, Pleasant Plains, boys basketball
The junior guard provided a team-high 15 points and nine rebounds for the host Cardinals in a 48-41 win over Warsaw/Hamilton West Hancock for the Class 2A regional title.
Karson Komnick, Lincoln, boys basketball
The junior guard totaled 19 points in a 38-23 win over Taylorville for the Class 3A Southeast Regional title.
Bailey Leach, Pleasant Plains, girls basketball
The junior guard beat the buzzer with a game-tying 3 in regulation and finished with 13 points in the 51-44 overtime loss to Camp Point Central/Augusta Southeastern in the Class 2A Waverly Sectional final.
Mason Neumann, Chatham Glenwood, boys basketball
The senior forward ushered a team-high 12 points in a 43-39 win over host Lanphier for the Class 3A regional title.
Malique Pearse, Taylorville, boys basketball
The junior guard Malique Pearse stole the ball with less than two seconds left and hit the game-winner from midcourt to give the Tornadoes a 40-37 Class 3A regional semifinal victory over Rochester. It was the team's only 3 in the game.
Brayden Saling, Williamsville, boys basketball
The senior guard doled out all his 21 points in the second half for a 55-33 win over Quincy Notre Dame for the Class 2A Pittsfield Regional title.
Ethan Sharp, Staunton, boys basketball
The senior guard converted both his 3s for a 28-18 halftime lead and led the host Bulldogs with 12 points in a 50-32 win over Piasa Southwestern for the Class 2A regional title.
Jenna Tuxhorn, Chatham Glenwood, girls wrestling
The junior earned third place at 145 pounds following a 5-3 decision against South Elgin's Allison Garbacz at the girls wrestling state finals in Bloomington. She finished with a 35-3 record.

title: Leistikow: Announcer Robbie Hummel is seemingly everywhere at once as March Madness begins
author: Chad Leistikow
description: Detailing how the former Purdue star has quickly become an elite broadcaster and will be "the face of college hoops for years to come."
content:
Late in the first half of an Illinois vs. Iowa men's basketball game, officials gathered around courtside monitors to potentially reverse a call over a rarely called violation.
'I haven't seen a cylinder review all year long in a game that I've done,' Robbie Hummel, the TV analyst for that Fox Sports 1 broadcast, told play-by-play man Brandon Gaudin. 'Even though that is the rule.'
Gaudin retorted in jest, 'And you've done every game in college basketball this year. So you would know.'
Similarly, during a recent Michigan-Michigan State game on FOX, legendary analyst Bill Raftery mused that Hummel probably had the call on the rivals' managers game the previous night in Ann Arbor.
Hummel's on-air omnipresence during college basketball season has become a running gag, especially in Big Ten Conference country. Cue up the TV on a day that ends in y, and Hummel has seemingly teleported into yet another arena three states away, calling yet another 2-hour basketball game with total expertise on whichever two teams are playing.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
It is probably underselling it to say Hummel, who turns 36 this month, is a rising star in basketball broadcasting. He's already a highly respected voice in the sport who will, all told, call 85 games this season for FOX, Fox Sports 1, Big Ten Network, Peacock, Turner Sports (for the NCAA Tournament's first and second rounds) and Westwood One Radio.
'It's a challenge,' Hummel said. 'The way I look at it is I don't work for seven months. For the five months that I do, it's full go.'
This week kicks off one of Hummel's busiest stretches of the year, and why not? March Madness has arrived.
Here's the itinerary leading up to the five-day Big Ten men's tournament March 12-16 in Indianapolis:
Tuesday: Drive from his Lincoln Park home in downtown Chicago to West Lafayette (2 hours) for the 7 p.m. ET Purdue-Rutgers game on Peacock, then drive back to Chicago.
Wednesday: Fly to Minneapolis for the 7:30 p.m. CT Minnesota-Wisconsin game on BTN.
Thursday: Fly to Cedar Rapids and drive 25 minutes to Iowa City for the 7 p.m. CT Iowa-Michigan State game on FS1.
Friday: Fly back to Chicago, Uber 20 to 55 minutes (depending on traffic) home to re-pack, grab a rental car and drive 1½-2 hours to Milwaukee. (He was originally slated for that night's 7 p.m. CT Illinois-Purdue game in Champaign, but even Hummel conceded that was overly ambitious.)
Saturday (his birthday): Call the 11 a.m. CT Marquette-St. John's showdown for FOX, then zoom the rental car back to O'Hare to catch an evening flight to Newark, N.J.
Sunday: Call the 1 p.m. ET Rutgers-Minnesota game for BTN, then hustle 40 minutes from Piscataway to Newark to jump on an evening flight to Asheville, North Carolina, via Charlotte.
Monday: Call the 7 p.m. ET Southern Conference championship game for Westwood One.
Tuesday: Board the first of two flights at 6 a.m., land at O'Hare hopefully around 10, hurry home to do laundry and pack a few fresh suits, then return to O'Hare for an 8 p.m. flight to Indianapolis, where the next day he'll call three games on Peacock to open the Big Ten Tournament and more games for BTN as the week goes on.
Hummel has the travel part down to a science. He refuses to check a bag, a time-saving strategy. A special carry-on allows multiple suits to fold around separated sections of other clothes – including sweat-soaked T-shirts and shorts from his daily workouts – like an omelet. He leaves enough room to include a fresh shirt and tie for every game, and his dress shoes slide into the backpack with his MacBook, iPad and volumes of game notes.
The most impressive part, though, is Hummel's intricate knowledge of every single team he covers.
'He's never unprepared,' said Jason Benetti, one of FOX's leading sports voices and a frequent Hummel partner in basketball. 'I have never done a game next to Robbie Hummel and felt anything other than he's 99th-percentile prepared.'
The meticulous homework Robbie Hummel does in game preparation
Benetti chuckled (and raved) about the only analyst he's worked with who brings a color-coded spotting board 'that you feel like has been created by an accountant.'
Hummel's "board" for each team is truly an organized, chaotic work of art − typed out jersey numbers, years, measurements, stats and detailed pronunciations for anyone who might play (or is injured). The secret sauce to his knowledge is the scribbled notes in black ink with his own scouting report on every player, the previous game's results, team trends, what defenses the coach might use, three keys to the game and pretty much anything interesting he learns ... until almost every corner of white on each team's page is covered.
With such a hectic travel schedule, how does Hummel find time to research every team, every player, every matchup?
Flying always beats driving, if possible. As soon as he gets through security, he'll open the MacBook and get to work. Flights are prime time to study, too. FOX will send him packets of locally produced articles ahead of each matchup. The most valuable tool is the same scouting technology that most teams use, called Synergy. One search can instantly provide a single stream of, say, every Payton Sandfort shot this season. From November through March, he keeps and adds notes on every player he covers.
'You can get a pretty good feel for what guys want to do by watching 50 or 60 clips, just watching their field-goal attempts,' Hummel said. 'Like, 'Wow, he goes to his right a lot.' Or, 'Man, he likes to jump-stop to get to his turnaround jumper.' I wish I had done that (homework) as a player.'
Before heading to the arena, he'll take 30 final minutes in his hotel room to review his detailed spotting board. In pregame coaches meetings, he'll press for specifics, especially when it comes to injuries. More than what is happening on the floor, an elite broadcaster describes why something is happening, without hesitation.
'I don't think you can not be on top of it,' Hummel said. 'The fans will be like, 'Why don't you know?' It's not an excuse that, 'Oh, I've done four games this week.''
Benetti, a master of impressions of fellow broadcasters, does a great Hummel. The easiest hook, he said, is to use the phrase, 'That's his deal" − which Hummel absorbed from Matt Painter, his college coach at Purdue.
An example for Iowa fans would be Hummel saying something like, 'Josh Dix likes to get to the mid-range jumper with a step-back in transition. That's his deal.'
'I give him grief all the time for it,' Benetti said. 'But the reason I love the phrase so much – and it's really out of love – is 'that's his deal' means he knows the tendency of every player on the court.
'Quite a few people study broadcasters. Quite a few people study basketball. He studies both. And I think it creates magic.'
How Robbie Hummel turned from player to elite broadcaster
Hummel has the work ethic and ability to one day call Final Fours, like Raftery (still going at age 81) does for Turner Sports, a remarkable statement considering he just got into broadcasting full-time in late 2017.
Hummel considered himself a milquetoast interview as a player, which included five years and two ACL tears at Purdue, where he remains top 10 all-time in rebounds. Thus, his path to becoming a knowledgeable, deadpan humorous storyteller behind the mic is fascinating.
Here's the brief back story.
During his two years with the Minnesota Timberwolves (2013-15), Hummel participated in the NBA's 'Sportscaster U' training program at Syracuse, known for churning out broadcasting talent. ('I wasn't good,' he mused.) Then after dislocating his shoulder while playing in Milan, Painter invited him to rehab at Purdue and help the team out … and stay in his house. During that time, BTN reached out to Hummel for occasional help on its studio shows. After a few airings, someone noticed Hummel's talent and connected him with the agent Maury Gostfrand (who represents many big-time announcers such as Doris Burke) that he still uses today.
His shoulder healed, Hummel was the last cut for the Denver Nuggets and played the summer of 2017 in Moscow, an experience he said 'drove me out of playing.' A new back injury served as a final sign that he should transition from playing basketball to talking about it. In his first full basketball season as a broadcaster, at age 28, he was tapped to call 55 events for BTN and ESPN.
He's been on the ascent ever since. He is engaged to actress Logan Andrews, who spends a lot of time in Los Angeles and understands the grueling nature of TV work.
NBC's Noah Eagle, who calls play-by-play with Hummel on Peacock's Big Ten package, said working with Hummel is 'a cheat code' because he's a walking, talking encyclopedia.
'What stands out is how much admiration he's rightfully earned in such a short time,' Eagle said. 'I've never seen a Purdue legend go to (Indiana's) Assembly Hall and get showered with love like him. And the coolest part is every person that comes up to him, he remembers the previous conversation they had and picks up like they never stopped.
'Elite storyteller with elite stories. (He) will be the face of college hoops for years to come.'
Hummel was a third-grader in Valparaiso, Indiana, when Bryce Drew's miracle shot sparked a Cinderella run for Valpo in the 1998 NCAA Tournament. He remembers the joy he felt during that national story and would become a ball boy for Homer Drew at Valpo. His father played tennis at Illinois, so he inevitably watched and was surrounded by Big Ten and big-time basketball.
Flash forward to today, as Hummel gets to be at the forefront of announcing March Madness moments. He's living out a dream job that he's really good at … for five frenetic months every year.
'There are a lot harder things you could be doing,' Hummel said. 'That's important to keep in perspective. I mean, you are watching basketball, and you're sitting courtside at Big Ten games, where it would cost you a lot of money to buy those seats. I'm very lucky to get to do what I'm doing.'
.

title: Chatham Glenwood boys basketball summons another late rally for elusive sectional title
author: Bill Welt
description: The Chatham Glenwood boys basketball team found another way to win late for 3A sectional title over Mount Zion on Friday
content:
Show Caption
DECATUR — This was the goal stretching back to last year.
The Chatham Glenwood boys basketball team is here now.
The Titans finished on a 10-0 run en route to a 39-32 victory over Mount Zion in the Class 3A Decatur Eisenhower Sectional final on Friday.
Glenwood (23-9) advances to its first supersectional appearance since 2013 against Troy Triad at the Bank of Springfield Center on Monday at 7:30 p.m.
"I know we always have a chance," senior guard Cam Appenzeller said of the program's third sectional title all-time. "The whole team knows we always have a chance and we just fought to the end. That's what we've been doing every game and it's a good feeling."
Mount Zion (25-10) committed four straight turnovers down the stretch after taking a 30-26 lead early in the fourth quarter.
Glenwood senior forward Mason Neumann nabbed a steal for a raucous dunk before Cam Appenzeller delivered the go-ahead basket off the glass for a 33-32 advantage with just over a minute remaining.
Appenzeller delivered his own emphatic dunk after a steal to end the game. The Braves had seven of their 12 turnovers in the final period.
"That's one of our biggest things is our defense," Neumann said. "We like to hold teams under 45 points every game. We did that tonight and if we keep doing that, it's going to be hard to beat us."
Neumann led Glenwood with 14 points, while Appenzeller had nine. Jack Kurmann scored both of his 3s in the first quarter for six points, while Jonathan Helm had five.
"We were confident," Kurmann said. "We've been shooting all day in practice every day. That's what we did today."
Glenwood led 20-16 at halftime after Neumann drained his two 3s in the second frame. The Titans totaled eight 3s, including Gavin Simmons' only trey early in the fourth quarter to end a scoring drought that lasted nearly 11 minutes.
Mount Zion's Lyncoln Koester scored 11 of his 14 points in the second half.
"Neumann, Kurmann — they all did," Glenwood coach Todd Blakeman said of the pivotal 3s. "You've got to get some 3s against these guys, they were sagging (on defense). But I'm telling you, our defense — Matt Held came in and did a great job. We just followed the game plan."
Glenwood also overcame a 13-point deficit in a 57-45 overtime win over Champaign Central in the sectional semifinals on Tuesday.
"We just battled," said Blakeman, who came out of retirement last season. "We battled the night before, we got down tonight. These kids are relentless. I'm just thrilled to have them."

title: Tariffs on aluminum will impact breweries across Illinois—and you may be paying for it
author: Claire Grant
description: 'Our craft breweries could see a $10.2 million increase in packaging costs, testing their already delicate supply chains and razor-thin margins."
content:
A 25% tariff on imported steel and aluminum could significantly impact local breweries, increasing packaging costs and straining already tight margins.
Brewery owners are grappling with rising costs across the board, including grain, electricity, and air gas, forcing them to consider price increases or absorb the added expenses.
With the calendar turning to March and the weather feeling more spring-like, you may be wanting to get a beer and sit outside to enjoy it. If that sounds good to you, just plan on paying more for the beer.
President Trump's tariffs on aluminum imports will likely impact both craft and domestic beer.
Importers were expected to pay the 25% tariffs starting March 4.
The Illinois Craft Brewers Guild believes the 25% tariff will greatly impact small brewery owners and its customers.
'Our craft breweries could see a $10.2 million increase in packaging costs, testing their already delicate supply chains and razor-thin margins,' the Brewers Guild posted to X.
Roughly half of all aluminum used in the states is imported, and almost all of it comes from Canada – roughly 3.2 million tons in 2024 in Canadian imports. According to Industrial Quick Search directories, Illinois has five aluminum producers, but none are in Sangamon County for local brewers – the closest is in Peoria.
While two decades ago there were none, Springfield is now home to several small to large breweries with ranging spicy to sweet flavors.
Brent Schwoerer, owner of Engrained Brewing Co. and board member of the Illinois Craft Brewers Guild, says the larger the brewery is on distribution, the harder the hit.
'In terms of what goes up our cans will by 25%, cans are a relatively small cost percentage for a case of beer,' Schwoerer said. 'Everything has gone up over the last two years as we continue to see the biggest increase in 2023. Grain prices went up 25 to 30 percent.'
Schwoerer says every packaged drink Engrained produces can vary in range, but ballparks at about 20 cents a can. In 2024, Engrained produced 15,000 cans of craft beer with 10,000 for distribution – about 5% of total business sales.
Ryan Kunken is another brewmaster in Springfield whose keeping Prairie State beer history alive through partnership with Reisch Charities to bring back Reisch beer with master brewer George Reisch.
The beer, which will be released later this year, will be canned in Springfield.
Rebecca Kunken, on behalf of her husband Ryan, and Schwoerer both agree prices going up mean amendments to how the businesses operate. Kunken said for the first time since opening in 2019 their brewery has increased prices, even without aluminum being a factor.
The rising costs can also be found in electric bills and air gas for the brewing process, which had six significant spikes in price last year.
'A lot of us are eating the majority of it,' Schwoerer said. '(Consumer) prices really haven't gone up in alignment with food in restaurants or other areas of the economy.'
Those broad rising costs and mounting fear about price increases cutting into thin margins of profit isn't just in the beer industry, too.
In a recent survey from business platform Alignable, one third of all small businesses in Illinois are afraid of revenue loss. In the same study, 18% of small businesses nationally foresee a boost in sales, while 40% said they didn't see tariffs having impacts on their sales.
'I think I can speak on every business out there we're just trying to make it and be cost efficient as possible,' Kunken said. 'The other side of it is you don't want the integrity and the taste of beer to go down. You just need to be mindful of where your expenses are going out.'

title: Illinois high school girls basketball all-state teams: Coaches pick top IHSA players
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The Illinois Basketball Coaches Association announced its all-state teams for the 2024-25 IHSA girls basketball season.
content:

title: Coroner: Springfield man identified as homicide victim from last weekend
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A Springfield man who was shot and killed last weekend has been identified by the authorities. Here's what we know.
content:
A Springfield man who was shot and killed last weekend has been identified by the authorities.
Calvin Bell, 47, died of a gunshot wound early Saturday morning, according to Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon.
An autopsy was completed Monday.
According to a release issued by Deputy Chief Sara Pickford of the Springfield Police Department, officers responded to a large fight in the 800 block of Stevenson Drive on the city's far south side right around 2 a.m.
A witness said 20 to 30 people were involved in a disturbance in the 800 block of Stevenson Drive.
Pickford said gunshots could be heard during the 911 call to dispatch.
A number of people administered aid to Bell before he was transported by an ambulance to HSHS St. John's Hospital.
Bell died shortly after he arrived at the hospital around 2:30 a.m.
Two persons were taken in for questioning by the Springfield Emergency Response Team (ERT) around 7:30 a.m. Saturday after serving a search warrant in the 1500 block of North Grand Avenue West.

title: Live updates: Chatham Glenwood, Troy Triad boys hoops vie for state berth in 3A supersectional
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Check here for the live updates and final recap of Chatham Glenwood's Class 3A boys basketball supersectional against Troy Triad
content:
Chatham Glenwood Cam Appenzeller reeled off three 3-pointers before dishing the game-winning assist to Jonathan Helm in a 43-41 victory over Troy Triad in the Class 3A supersectional at the Bank of Springfield Center on Monday.
Glenwood (24-9) advances to its first state appearance since 1975 and second overall against Chicago DePaul College Prep at the State Farm Center in Champaign on Thursday at 8:15 p.m. Triad finishes 29-7.
Appenzeller led the Titans with 18 points, while Helm had nine points and 11 rebounds. Mason Neumann added nine points.

title: Springfield man faces first-degree murder charges following fatal shooting
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A Springfield man has been arrested for allegedly shooting and killing another Springfield man over the weekend.
content:
A Springfield man has been arrested for allegedly shooting and killing another man last weekend.
Springfield Police arrested Emmanuel K. Watts, 30, for the shooting death of Calvin Bell, 47, of Springfield.
Watts has not yet been charged by the Sangamon County State's Attorney's office, but he is behind bars in the Sangamon County Jail.
Deputy Chief Sara Pickford said in a news release that detectives arrested Watts for first-degree murder, aggravated battery/discharge of a firearm, aggravated discharge of a firearm, and unlawful possession of a weapon by a convicted felon.
Officers responded to a large fight in the 800 block of Stevenson Drive on the city's far south side right around 2 a.m. on March 8.
A witness said 20 to 30 people were involved in a disturbance in the 800 block of Stevenson Drive.
Pickford said gunshots could be heard during the 911 call to dispatch.
A number of people administered aid to Bell before he was taken by an ambulance to HSHS St. John's Hospital.
Bell died shortly after he arrived at the hospital around 2:30 a.m.

title: New book reinforces Lincoln was an abolitionist long before his presidency
author: Steven Spearie
description: A new book revisits the case of Nance Legins-Costley, a Pekin woman who was freed from indenture servitude in 1841.
content:
Abraham Lincoln argued Nance Legins-Costley's case before the Illinois Supreme Court.
Indentured servitude, the equivalency of slavery, was allowed in Illinois.
Legins-Costley lived for many years in Pekin, where she is commemorated with a downtown memorial.
A Pekin woman who gained her freedom from indentured servitude with the help of Abraham Lincoln more than two decades before he issued the Emancipation Proclamation as president is the subject of a major new book.
"Nance: A Girl of Color and Her Lawyer Abraham Lincoln" (Pangaeus Press) details the story of Nance Legins-Costley, whose case has long been a footnote in history.
The book's author Kevin Orlin Johnson has written extensively about Lincoln and in a 2022 book claimed that Lincoln owned slaves through his marriage to Mary Todd of Kentucky.
Johnson said Lincoln sold the slaves after the death of his father-in-law, Robert Smith Todd.
Legins-Costley's case from 1841 was one of Lincoln's earliest before the Illinois Supreme Court, which then met in the Old State Capitol in Springfield. The case had been before the state's high court twice previously.
Johnson argued that Legins-Costley "championed racial justice as effectively as Harriet Tubman, Sojourner Truth and Rosa Parks."
Legins-Costley was born in 1813 in Kaskaskia, then the capital of the Illinois Territory, some five years before statehood. Her parents were indentured servants, basically equivalent to slaves.
The family's owner, Col. Thomas Cox, moved the household to Springfield in 1822. Facing debt several years later, a Sangamon County court ordered the sale of Cox's possessions, including his indentured servants.
That began a protracted fight for Legins-Costley's freedom, culminating in the Illinois Supreme Court decision Bailey v. Cromwell. The ruling not only had implications for Legins-Costley's station, but for the slavery and indentured servitude questions in Illinois.
Some historians suggest the case pushed Lincoln toward a more anti-slavery stance.
In a promotional release, Johnson said he found the case while researching his earlier books on Lincoln.
Legins-Costley has been the subject of at least two other books.
A placard memorializes the purported burial place of Legins-Costley in South Peoria while a recently unveiled monument honors her and her son, William Henry Costley, in a park in downtown Pekin.

title: Unemployment claims in Illinois stayed the same last week
author: USA TODAY Network
description: Here's a look at how weekly unemployment claims changed in Illinois last week compared with the week prior.
content:
Initial filings for unemployment benefits in Illinois were unchanged last week compared with the week prior, the U.S. Department of Labor said Thursday.
New jobless claims, a proxy for layoffs, hovered at 8,123 in the week ending March 9, in line with the week before, the Labor Department said.
U.S. unemployment claims dropped to 209,000 last week, down 1,000 claims from 210,000 the week prior on a seasonally adjusted basis.
Oregon saw the largest percentage increase in weekly claims, with claims jumping by 33.7%. New Hampshire, meanwhile, saw the largest percentage drop in new claims, with claims dropping by 60.6%.

title: Remains found near highway identified as missing Springfield woman
author: Steven Spearie
description: The woman found dead near the southbound entrance ramp to Interstate 55 at Stevenson Drive Wednesday afternoon had been missing for several weeks.
content:
The woman found dead near the southbound entrance ramp to Interstate 55 at Stevenson Drive Wednesday afternoon had been missing for several weeks.
Teresa Ann Coleman, 54, of Springfield, was last seen on Feb. 17 according to a flyer shared by Coleman's family on social media.
In a news release issued Thursday, Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon said that preliminary autopsy findings determined Coleman's death was a homicide.
Reached by The State Journal-Register Thursday, Allmon said he couldn't divulge how Coleman died.
Springfield Police Deputy Chief Sara Pickford said that ISP is leading the investigation.
Pickford confirmed that SPD took a missing person report on Coleman when the department was contacted by her family.
An Illinois Department of Transportation work crew discovered Coleman's remains early Wednesday afternoon. That is when Illinois State Police were summoned to the site.
The death remains under investigation by the ISP, the Springfield Police Department and the coroner's office.

title: Happy Easter, Happy Passover or Happy Ramadan: Show respect no matter what
author: The Rev. Glen VanderKloot
description: Let's show respect to each of these traditions and holy days.
content:
Each year Jews, Muslims and Christians celebrate their most holy days around the same time of spring. Each of these three religions trace their religion to Abraham who lived around 4,100 years ago.
They each use the new moon in determining the date of their holy day. The specific date changes each year.
Easter this year is March 31, 2024. Easter is the culmination of the work Jesus was sent to do. All of Christianity revolves around the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
It takes place over a week with four major events. It begins with Jesus' triumphant entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday.
On Maundy Thursday, Jesus celebrates the Passover with his disciples and institutes Holy Communion.
Then Jesus and his disciples went to the Garden of Gethsemane where Jesus prayed. That night Jesus was betrayed by Judas and put under arrest.
On Good Friday, Jesus was tried, mocked, beaten and then crucified. Friday evening, he was laid in the tomb.
On Easter Sunday, the tomb was empty, and Jesus appeared to Mary, two disciples on the road to Emmaus and that evening to 10 disciples. You can greet Christians with 'Happy Easter.'
The Passover holy day begins this year before sundown on Monday, April 22, 2024, and ends after nightfall on April 30.
Passover is one of the most sacred Jewish holy days. It celebrates the Israelites' freedom from slavery in Egypt. The final plague of God was the death of the firstborn son in all of Egypt.
However, the angel of God passed over every Jewish household where they placed the blood of the lamb on the door post.
Moses then led the Jewish people out of Egypt and began a 40-year journey to the Promised Land. Jewish people observe a weeklong festival with a number of important rituals, including a traditional
Passover meal, known as the seder meal. You can greet Jewish people with 'chag Pesach samech' which is greeting someone to have a kosher and joyous Passover. You could also greet them 'Happy Passover.'
Muslims around the world are welcoming the arrival of Ramadan. This is a month of dawn-to-dusk fasting, communal prayer, charity and feasts. This is the holiest month of the Muslim calendar.
The exact timing depends on when local Islamic authorities around the world declare the sighting of the new moon.
Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. Muslims believe that the first verses of the Quran were revealed to the Prophet Muhammad at this time of the year.
You can greet Muslims with 'Ramadan Mubarak' which translated means 'Happy Ramadan.'
Let's show respect to each of these traditions and holy days.
This is my last column in the SJ-R. Thank you for listening. May you have a Happy Easter, a Happy Passover or a Happy Ramadan.
The Rev. Glen VanderKloot is the retired pastor of Faith Lutheran Church, where he had served since 1989.

title: Two Springfield women to be recognized for work in their community
author: Steven Spearie
description: The Illinois Jaycees will honor two Springfield women as part of its Outstanding Young Persons of Illinois awards program.
content:
The Illinois Jaycees will honor two Springfield women as part of its Outstanding Young Persons of Illinois awards program.
The program annually recognizes young people who excel in their chosen fields, endeavors and show a great commitment to their respective communities.
Haley Wilson, the director of communications for the city of Springfield, was recognized for cultural achievement while Erin Burneson of Williamsville was recognized for humanitarian and/or voluntary leadership.
Wilson and Burneson will be recognized at an awards banquet in East Peoria on April 27.
Wilson, 33, is the founder of The Culture Experience LLC, an organization with a mission, according to a news release, "to create a cultured and comfortable environment for minority groups to embrace the joy of new and unique experiences by facilitating fulfilling cultural collisions to happen."
Wilson recently told The State Journal-Register that The Culture Experience was born out of the city's history of segregation traditionally divided east and west by the Ninth Street railroad tracks.
Wilson is a member of Kiwanis, Together Women Rise, Illinois Women in Leadership and the Informal Educators Group and serves on the United Way of Central Illinois marketing committee.
Burneson is co-founder of BHAYLI, a project that empowers women in rural Indian villages by helping them to secure sustainable livelihoods through opportunities in up-cycling.
She also founded Studio Rachanā, a creative consulting company whose mission is to work alongside individuals, communities and businesses to catalyze creativity for social and environmental impact and collaboratively solve complex humanitarian problems.
While in India, Burneson co-founded a collaborative learning program designed for adults from different religio-cultural communities to learn with and from one another.

title: Homes in Sangamon County sold for lower prices recently: See how much here
author: USA TODAY Network
description: Here's a look at the prices of sold homes changed in Sangamon County in December 2023.
content:
Newly released data for December shows that potential buyers and sellers in Sangamon County saw houses sell for lower than the previous month's median sale price of $188,000.
The median home sold for $177,500, an analysis of data from Realtor.com shows. That means December, the most recent month for which figures are available, was down 5.6% from November.
Compared to December 2022, the median home sale price was up 7.9% at $177,500 compared to $164,450.
Realtor.com sources sales data from real estate deeds, resulting in a few months' delay in up-to-date data. The statistics don't include homes currently listed for sale, and aren't directly comparable to listings data.
Information on your local housing market, along with other useful community data, is available at data.sj-r.com.
Looking only at single-family homes, the $176,250 median selling price in Sangamon County was down 7% in December from $189,500 the month prior. Since December 2022, the sale price of single-family homes was up 6.8% from a median of $165,000.
One single family home sold for $1 million or more during the month, compared to one recorded transactions of at least $1 million in December 2022.
Condominiums and townhomes increased by 31.3% in sales price during December to a median of $220,000 from $167,500 in November. Compared to December 2022, the sales price of condominiums and townhomes was up 150% from $88,000. One​ condominium or townhouse sold for $1 million or more during the month, compared to zero recorded transactions of at least $1 million in December 2022.
In December, the number of recorded sales in Sangamon County dropped by 15.1% since December 2022 from 146 to 124. All residential home sales totaled to $28.5 million.
In Illinois, homes sold at a median of $260,000 during December, up 2% from $255,000 in November. There were 9,774 recorded sales across the state during December, down 4.4% from 10,219 recorded sales in December 2022.
The total value of recorded residential home sales in Illinois increased by 14.6% from $3.3 billion in November to $3.7 billion this December.
Out of all residential home sales in Illinois, 3.99% of homes sold for at least $1 million in December, down from 7.37% in December 2022.
Sales prices of single-family homes across Illinois increased by 0.9% from a median of $253,542 in November to $255,782 in December. Since December 2022, the sale price of single-family homes across the state was up 4.4% from $245,000.
Across the state, the sale price of condominiums and townhomes rose 1.6% from a median of $256,850 in November to $260,916 during December. The median sale price of condominiums and townhomes is up 1.1% from the median of $258,211 in December 2022.
The median home sale price used in this report represents the midway point of all the houses or units listed over the given period of time. The median offers a more accurate view of what's happening in a market than the average sale price, which would mean taking the sum of all sale prices then dividing by the number of homes sold. The average can be skewed by one particularly low or high sale.

title: President, CEO of Springfield hospital to retire next year. Here's who will replace him
author: Steven Spearie
description: After more than 15 years, change in leadership is coming for a Springfield-based hospital.
content:
Memorial Health president and chief executive officer Ed Curtis will be stepping down next year with Kevin England, the health system's senior vice president and chief administrative officer, taking over.
England will become Memorial Health's president in July. He will report directly to Curtis and is expected to be named president and CEO within a year, when Curtis retires.
A Springfield native, Curtis spent his entire career with the health system, starting out as a register nurse at Springfield Memorial Hospital, then known as Memorial Medical Center, in 1975.
Curtis became the president and CEO on Jan. 1, 2008, succeeding Robert Clarke. Curtis had been the senior vice president and chief operating officer of the health system before taking over the top spot.
The Memorial Health board of directors approved the plan.
Memorial Health operates five hospitals located in Decatur, Jacksonville, Lincoln, Springfield and Taylorville, as well as 70 primary care, urgent care and specialty care clinics; behavioral health services; and home health services. It is based in Springfield.
'One of Memorial Health's greatest strengths is the stability and the continuity of our leadership,' Curtis said, in a news release. 'Throughout our history, we have created succession plans to ensure that leadership transitions are as seamless as possible. This succession plan marks the beginning of a new chapter for Memorial, and I look forward to working with Kevin to ensure we continue to fulfill our mission for many years to come.'
England has spent 35 years with Memorial Health. He began his leadership career as director of clinical resource management at Memorial Medical Center and went on to oversee a wide range of clinical areas as well as business development functions.
He graduated from the University of Illinois Springfield with a bachelor of arts degree in management and from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign with a master's degree in business administration. He is a member of the board of trustees for the Springfield YMCA and served on the board of directors of the Central Illinois Community Blood Center (now ImpactLife) for 14 years, 12 of those years as board chair.
'This is a time of rapid change in the field of health care, and Memorial is well-positioned to meet the challenges of the future thanks to our tradition of strong, visionary leadership,' England said. 'It's an honor to be chosen to carry that tradition forward.'
Michael Aiello, chair of the board of directors, said that England exemplified the qualities the board is seeking in a leader.
'Kevin has shown a strong commitment to Memorial and our communities over the years,' Aiello said. 'We believe his leadership, vision and deep understanding of the organization's culture make him the ideal person to guide Memorial in the coming years.'

title: Honor roll, athletes and drama club: Vote for this week's Student of the Week

content:
Voting for The State Journal-Register Student of the Week is now open after principals and administrators from local and area schools put forth another three nominations.
The students were nominated based on academic achievement, leadership, citizenship, character, public service and participation in clubs and activities.
We will publish a list of Student of the Week nominees every Monday morning at sj-r.com and in print on Tuesday. Voting closes at 10 a.m. on Thursday.

"We are so lucky to have a student like Emma represent our school," Ellis said.
Diveley plans to attend the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign to study applied health sciences in the fall.

Heiple, a senior at Rochester High School, carries a 4.298 grade point average (weighted) and has achieved high honor roll all four years.
She is a member of the National Honor Society, the Rochester High School Club U, Student of the Month award winner and Central State Eight Conference Athletic Academic award winner all four years.
Heiple lettered in golf this past fall.
Heiple's nominator was high school principal Jeff Reed.
Aleesa Jones, Brown Co.

title: Painting from Springfield Art Association headed to Smithsonian Institute
author: Steven Spearie
description: "Woman with a Monkey" by Ethel Mars, believed to be a self-portrait created in Paris between 1906 and 1909.
content:
A painting in the Springfield Art Association 's permanent collection by a local artist who gained international acclaim is headed to the Smithsonian Institute in Washington, D.C.
"Woman with a Monkey" by Ethel Mars, believed to be a self-portrait created in Paris between 1906 and 1909, will be shown at the National Portrait Gallery as part of the exhibit"Brilliant Exiles: American Women in Paris, 1900-1939," which runs from April 26 through February 23, 2025.
'I am thrilled that an important institution like the Smithsonian is bringing attention to artists such as Ethel Mars and other young women who chose to go to Europe in the early 20th century because they were not taken seriously as artists in the United States,' said Betsy Dollar, executive director of the Springfield Art Association.
Born in 1876, Mars grew up and was educated in Springfield before attending art school in Cincinnati.
According to SangamonLink, Mars got her first artistic recognition in the pages of the Illinois State Journal (a forerunner of The State Journal-Register) in April 1891, when a crayon drawing she did went on display in the window of Frank Simmons' bookstore and art gallery in Springfield. 'The picture is said to be the finest of its kind ever exhibited by an amateur,' the newspaper said.
After working as a book illustrator in New York City, Mars and her partner, Maud Hunt Squire, relocated to Paris, where they were frequent attendees of Gertrude Stein's salon, which also included Paul Cézanne, Pablo Picasso and F. Scott Fitzgerald.
The couple was the subject of Stein's 1922 prose poem "Miss Furr and Miss Skeene," containing what was believed to be the first published use of the word "gay" to refer to a homosexual relationship.
In addition to painting in France, Mars made chalk drawings and woodblock prints.
For a 2000 exhibition of her work, a New York Times critic wrote that Mars' work was distinguished by "its flat forms, bold simplicity of design and lively color."
'Woman with a Monkey' was featured in Harper's Weekly magazine.
The Illinois State Museum has a number of Mars' paintings.

title: 'It's local. It's here.' Springfield-area group fundraising for Edgar Lee Masters museum
author: Steven Spearie
description: "They were so into it. I had only planned on teaching like 20 of them, but they asked to keep going."
content:
Springfield High School English teacher Lydia Negele dusted off Edgar Lee Masters' "Spoon River Anthology." Literally.
"I was back in the bookroom and there was a very dusty, old, yellow stack of (the books which) had been taught in the 1940s, 50s, 60s," Negele said. "I wasn't familiar with it, but I'm a huge fan of teaching the classics.
"Currently, in our department, in our district, there's more of a push for kids to read modern stuff that is more relevant to them, that (kids) can see themselves in. I think the classics can do that, especially if the teacher works hard to make those connections."
Did she ever.
Negele soon found her sophomores and junior jostling over some very contemporary issues within the pages of Masters' 1915 masterpiece, a compilation of some 200 or so short, free-verse epitaphs spoken from the cemetery of the fictional town of Spoon River, some based on real people he knew growing up in Petersburg and Lewistown.
"It was by far better than I had anticipated," said Negele of the students' reception to the poems. "They were so into it. I had only planned on teaching like 20 of them, but they asked to keep going."
In his poetry, Masters called Petersburg his "heart's home."
Fundraiser will contribute to boyhood home of Edgar Lee Masters
The board of directors that operates the Masters museum that was once his boyhood home is having a dinner and auction fundraiser at Indian Creek Farmstead on April 6.
Edgar Lee Masters' granddaughter, Catherine Masters, a visual artist who lives in Maine, will be the guest speaker.
President Kathy Olesen said the board doesn't receive any funding except through donations. It has to pay the monthly bills and upkeep on the home, which is owned by the city. Money raised through "Party with a Poet" will most likely go towards replacing the home's wood shingle roof.
This summer, the board is starting a Chautauqua series with speakers and music at First and Third Wine Bar and Boutique in Petersburg on the third Sunday from May through September.
The July 21 speaker is Western Illinois University professor John Hallwas, who edited and wrote an introduction to annotated edition of "Spoon River Anthology."
In 2016, the home and museum donated about 300 manuscripts and letters, unpublished poetry, photographs and other works to the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library. One of the largest collections of Masters' work for scholars is at the University of Texas at Austin.
Catherine Masters is making her first trip back to central Illinois since the coronavirus pandemic.
Although her grandfather died before she was born, Masters said she is gratified there are those who is still celebrate the poet's work, though readers grapple with some weighty issues, like murder, alcoholism, rejection and isolation, in "Spoon River Anthology."
"There's something in me that gets great joy," Masters said, "that this poetry, that is about people's lives and what lies beneath the surface, is still so interesting to people and it's because that is all of us. It's not just those people he wrote about. It's everybody.
"(There are serious issues but) there are a few who talk about enjoying life and grabbing onto it. It's still relevant today."
Phil Funkenbusch has directed "Spoon River Anthology" several times. With the Masters' family's permission, Funkenbusch adapted a musical based on poems Masters wrote later in life, works that were more pastoral and nostalgic about his one-time home.
"I always wanted to do 'Spoon River' because it's our roots. It's local. It's here," he said. "These people were real people."
Finding meaning in 'Spoon River Anthology'
With her students, Negele said she didn't shy away "from the darker, controversial stories that hit you in the gut." Pointedly frank conversations came up in the class, she said, around adoption and bullying, for instance.
Also appealing to students, she said, was that Masters wasn't preachy and they had to play a bit of detective to understand what the characters were saying.
"It's magic what happens with this book, and I think it's because the kids have to find it," Negele said. "There's no answer key to it."
The Edgar Lee Masters Home and Museum is located at Eighth and Jackson streets in Petersburg. Its hours of operation are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday and Saturday or by appointment.

title: Tuesday roundup: Chatham Glenwood girls soccer remains unbeaten in CS8 with win over SHG
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Caroline Cody sparked Chatham Glenwood to another CS8 girls soccer win, and other spring results from Tuesday
content:
Here are the high school spring results around Springfield from Monday and Tuesday:
Tuesday's results
GIRLS SOCCER
CHATHAM GLENWOOD 3, SACRED HEART-GRIFFIN 1: At Ken Leonard Field, Caroline Cody ended a scoreless tie after intermission to keep the Titans unbeaten in the Central State Eight Conference.
Makenna Yeager rebounded a header by Kinsley Zellers that went off the crossbar for a 2-0 advantage. Rowann Law added another insurance goal unassisted and Glenwood improved 3-2 overall and 3-0 in the league.
Caroline Sheehan delivered the only goal for the Cyclones (5-1, 2-1 CS8).
RIVERTON 6, WARRENSBURG-LATHAM 0: At Riverton, Genevieve Anning's first-half goal was all the Hawknadoes needed — but not all they'd get — as Riverton peppered the Cardinals' defense in a nonconference win.
Anning put away an Abby Churchill assist to give the Hawknadoes (2-4-1) a 1-0 halftime lead.
Keirstan Shamblin and Stevi Fuess each scored twice in Riverton's five-goal second half. Miami Bryant had the final goal in the 70 th minute.
Riverton's Briannah Walker needed to make one save for the shutout. Meanwhile, Riverton had 14 shots on goal.
AUBURN 1, CARLINVILLE 1: At Carlinville, two goals in the final three minutes of the first half were all the teams could muster in a nonconference tie match.
Emme Divjak put Auburn on top 1-0 in the 38 th minute of the first half. With 36 seconds left before the break, Mia Smith pulled the Cavaliers into a 1-1 tie.
Auburn goalkeeper Abby Divjak and Carlinville's Savanna Siglock — along with their teams' respective defenses — kept both teams scoreless over the final 40 minutes on a cold, windy evening.
Carlinville put 12 shots on goal and Abby Divjak made 11 saves for the Trojans (5-1-1). Siglock made two saves for the Cavs (2-2-1).
BASEBALL
JERSEYVILLE 10, CARLINVILLE 0 (5 innings): At Jerseyville, Carlinville managed just two hits and dropped to 0-4 on the season.
Mason Wise and Dom Alepra both singled to make up the two hits for Carlinville. Alepra was the losing pitcher, allowing five hits and six runs (five earned) with three strikeouts and no walks in three innings.
Winning pitcher Jude Jones threw all five innings and handled Carlinville with 10 strikeouts and three walks. Jerseyville's Gage Walker (3-for-3, three runs) hit a three-run home run, doubled and drove in four runs, and teammate Zach Weiner doubled and finished 3-for-3 with three RBIs.
Monday's results
SOFTBALL
AUBURN 5, HILLSBORO 1: At Auburn, Meena Taylor allowed just one hit and one unearned run in a complete-game victory.
She struck out eight and walked just one hitter. She also doubled with two RBIs. Addison Wheatley mustered three hits, including two doubles. Taylor Patterson and Piper Taylor each had two hits.
CARROLLTON 12, STAUNTON 8: At Staunton, Lauren Flowers generated two home runs and three RBIs in a nonconference win. She also threw two innings with four strikeouts.
Megan Camden doubled and tripled with four RBIs.
Ele Feldmann went 4-for-4 with two RBIs and two runs for Staunton. Taylor Nolan had two hits, two RBIs and three runs.
BASEBALL
HILLSBORO 5, STAUNTON 4: At Hillsboro, Ketch Mills hit into a double play but scored Jackson Tuetken for the go-ahead run in the sixth inning.
Jace Stewart hit the game-tying RBI in the previous at-bat. Eli Zaidi produced two hits and earned the win on the rubber in the final 2/3 innings. He allowed one hit and two walks for the Hiltoppers' (1-6) first win of the season.
Stewart lasted five innings with eight strikeouts. He gave up two runs, three walks and three hits.
Matthew Overby had a double for the Bulldogs.
AUBURN 8, GREENFIELD/NORTHWESTERN 6: At Greenfield, Clayton Carter recorded the win in 4 2/3 innings. He struck out seven and allowed four hits, five runs and five walks.

Morrow pitched all three innings, struck out three and allowed two hits, two walks and one run.

title: Solar eclipse forecast: What the weather may look like in central Illinois
author: Claire Grant
description: The solar eclipse is right around the corner. Will the rain and gray get in the way of the solar phenomenon in the Springfield area?
content:
On Monday, Springfield will be in line for partial totality of the solar eclipse, a rare solar phenomenon which has only crossed over the Midwest twice since 1918; with the last partial solar eclipse setting over Springfield in 2017.
With weather as dreary as it has been, these April showers will bring May flowers—but will they bring down the atmosphere on eclipse day?
According to Hydrologist for the National Weather Service Darrin Hansing, Monday may actually be the best day of the whole week.
'We are expecting sunny skies so viewing at this point is looking quite good,' Hansing said. 'With temperatures in the mid 70's so really, it's looking quite nice for eclipse day.'
According to AccuWeather, the weather forecast from April 1 through April 7 had a high of 66 degrees Fahrenheit and low of 31 on April 4, with dispersed rain through the start of the week and thunderstorms on Sunday.
But the forecast for Monday is shaping up to be perfect: 72 degrees and clear skies throughout the duration of the solar event.
But on Monday on the day of the eclipse, weather is projected to peak at 72 degrees and clear skies throughout the duration of the solar event.
'Viewing is at this point looking quite good,' Hansing said. 'There should be opportunities for viewing in the Springfield area as well with temperatures a little bit cooler.'
Springfield will have a partial eclipse which will start at 12:45 p.m. and last until 3:18, with a peak at 2:02 p.m.; Carbondale will have a total eclipse lasting four minutes and nine seconds. A total eclipse means only certain locations will be in the perfect line of the moon's shadow as it's trajectory changes across the country.
It's important to remember for the solar eclipse while sunscreen will help – sunglasses won't. Mylar-based eclipse glasses are needed to view the sun, or risk scalding your eyes.

title: IRS has $1B tax refund funds waiting to be claimed. See if you're eligible for any of it
author: Claire Grant
description: The IRS has $1 billion set aside and waiting to be claimed. Find out if you're eligible for any of it.
content:
With Tax Day looming over the country, by April 15 most households in America will file their tax return. For Illinoisians, tax time can be especially difficult, as a yearly report from WalletHub on States with the Highest & Lowest Tax Rates found Illinois at the very top of the totem pole with the highest tax rates in the country.
There may be a way to lift that weight off of households' shoulders, as according to the IRS more than $1 billion in federal tax refunds are still unclaimed from COVID-19 era policy.
Here's what you need to know.
Am I eligible?
If households did not file a tax return during the height of the pandemic for the 2020 tax return year and believe they missed a tax return, the agency said the roughly $1 billion is still on hold for eligible filers to claim and retake for the lost year.
When is the deadline to make a claim?
The window created by the pandemic made filing strange in 2020 with an extension of the common three-year filing window but the open window is starting to shut. Households only have until May 17 of this year to claim their tax refund for 2020 before it's too late.
Is filing any different?
To file for a 2020 tax refund, it's like filing any other tax refund for previous years; residents of Illinois can file themselves or go to professional help like TurboTax or H&R Block using documents from the 2020 tax refund year.
What if I'm missing documents?
For missing documents since it's been almost half a decade, the IRS resources allow transcripts online on IRS.gov or last ditch, asking for copies of old documents from employers' works too.
Yes, Illinois taxes are as bad as you think
The IRS says the median refund for the pandemic fiscal year is around $932; which may help Illinoisians who have yet to file their 2020 return and are filing for 2023 at the same time.
In the study conducted by WalletHub, tax rates were determined on a median household income of $75,586 with a $281,900 house and car valued at $26,420.
By overall effective state & local tax rates, income tax, real-estate tax and sales taxes on a scale from one (lowest) to 51 (highest) with 25 as average.
In the studies finding, Illinois ranks overall 51 (including District of Columbia) in the country for tax rates.
Illinois ranked 51 in Overall Effective State & Local tax rates
Illinois ranked 47 in Income tax
Illinois ranked 50 in Real-Estate tax
Illinois ranked 32 in Sales & Excise tax
Currently, Illinois has a 4.95% individual income tax rate, a 9.50% corporate income tax rate, a 6.25% state sales tax rate and a 4.75% local sales tax rate.
On Feb. 21, Gov. J.B. Pritzker proposed his 2025 budget which outlined proposed tax changes for the upcoming year. In an effort to increase state tax revenue by $900 million, tax increases are proposed to help fill budget holes while increasing spending in the state.
The forms of taxes which would see an increase are state sales tax, sports betting tax, individual and corporate taxes. On the flip side, Pritzker proposed a substantial reduction to reduce local revenue tax.
