title: Springfield-area village makes compromise in changing its liquor license laws
author: Claire Grant
description: Community support for a Sangamon County bar helped lead to a village modifying its liquor laws.
content:
Show Caption
Local support for a Sangamon County bar helped lead to a village modifying its liquor laws.
The Village of Southern View had planned on ending alcohol sales at 1 a.m. for the three bars in the village. However, a petition was started by Springfield local and labor relations manager for the Illinois Department of Insurance Lisa Badger on behalf of The Curve Inn, a historical family-owned bar at 3219 S. Sixth St.
The bar currently operates until 3 a.m. and the petition called for hours to remain extended at the bar, which currently operates from 11 a.m. to 3 a.m. The petition garnished hundreds of signatures in the first two days it was launched.
The community support was heard by the Southern View Village Board, which voted to modify the liquor law to 2 a.m. rather than 1 a.m. so The Curve Inn could stay open an hour later than anticipated.
Badger said in the petition the decision to reduce its operating hours to 1 a.m. would have significant detrimental effects, leading to the elimination of 12 positions at the location.
'We urge for the need to retain the existing operating hours of The Curve Inn to ensure its survival,' Badger wrote on the website ahead of the vote. 'We believe in the power of small businesses as the backbone of our economy and are reaching out for your support.'
After the vote, The Curve Inn posted on its Facebook page thanking the community for their support.
Badger went on to say she was happy to hear the Village Board trustees took the time to listen to the Curve and decided to shift the closing time back only one hour, saving the positions.
"I would've felt terrible for them if they had just had the rug pulled out from under them," Badger said.
Changing liquor license laws
Southern View isn't the first community to rework their liquor license laws. The City of Springfield and Sangamon County both voted to reduce bar hours over the summer.
Previously, both the county and city had operating licenses for bars to stay open and sell liquor until 3 a.m. but on April 4, the Sangamon County Board voted to end 2 a.m. licenses, pushing back closing time to 1 a.m.
Following the county board, the Springfield City Council voted 8-2 in favor of ending 3 a.m. liquor licenses, with the modification that now all bars operate under one liquor license, capping closing time at 2 a.m.

title: Bistro Verde ready to roll out a new menu for the fall
author: Joshua Dineen
description: Lincoln Land Community College's student-run restaurant is ready to roll out a new menu for the fall.
content:
I don't know where the last two months have gone; it happened so fast. LLCC's last Bistro Verde menu and class were quite successful and are now done. To the many of you who joined us for lunch and allowed the students to share their talents and learning experiences — thank you.
We are now on to the next menu, which offers plated dishes that are a little more upscale casual, but very reasonable. Service just began on Oct. 22 and will go through Nov. 21. We are open Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. (closed Nov. 5).
This class is focused on more challenging techniques and timings. In addition to our regular menu every week, each of the students will take turns being responsible for creating a three-course lunch menu that includes an appetizer, entree and dessert for $16.
Speaking of the regular menu, let's discuss the appetizers. We are doing a version of pad kaprow, a quick sauteed dish with lots of basil and a little garlic, chilis and soy sauce but using cauliflower instead of meat. We are making traditional Japanese gyoza, or pork dumplings, which provide a great opportunity for the students to practice the tedious task of folding tiny pleats of dough while keeping the delicious filling inside.
I also thought it would be fun to have some southern flavors and offer a homemade chicken tender served with a fried macaroni and cheese ball sitting on braised greens with a candied yam sauce and a drizzle of honey. Making this involves many cooking methods and timings. For the last appetizer, the students are butterflying shrimp and giving them a coconut breading. We serve this with yellow curry sauce, fresh pineapple and a little cilantro.
We go back to Japan for the first soup on the menu. We are making miso soup topped with tempura mushrooms. The second soup is a chicken and coconut soup from Thailand called tom kha gai. We are also going to have a version of a wedge salad using a variety of smaller lettuce heads and adding a pepperjack croquette for texture and fun.
Of course we are also offering a rotation of smashburger choices: Oklahoma, Flapper, Carolina, Santa Fe Hatch and the Luther burgers. Each of these regional smashburgers will be offered for one week respectively and can be enjoyed as a horseshoe if you prefer.
For a grilled cheese, we are having caramelized onions and mushrooms with Swiss cheese on sourdough. It seems simple, but it takes almost an hour to properly caramelize onions then melt the cheese just right without burning the bread while doing 10 other things. It is a little more challenging than you might think.
For the fish sandwich, we coat a large cod filet with crunchy course panko. It is served with pickled vegetables and homemade katsu sauce, all on a brioche bun.
For our pasta-themed entrée, we are taking the idea of a Cajun seafood boil and tossing it with homemade sweet corn gnocchi. Don't worry, all the seafood will already be shelled and ready to enjoy.
The grilled steak choice for this menu is petit filet mignon. This gives the students another opportunity to butcher larger expensive cuts of meat down to an individual steak. They then sous vide the steak to make sure it is flavorful and perfectly cooked and finally finish it on the grill. It is served with romesco sauce, a roasted tomato and red pepper sauce, topped with a poached egg, a side of broccolini and homemade shoestring potatoes for a little crunch.
Lastly, they are making a version of cassoulet, though we are making it with chicken instead of duck. They will sear thinly sliced chicken breast and serve it over a white bean stew, crispy potatoes, sauteed green beans, a couple slices of chicken sausage and finished with a very rich chicken and herb sauce.
I tried to use as many cooking methods as possible and introduce international flavors while helping the students make delicious food to share with our guests at Bistro Verde.
Hopefully we will see many of you and look forward to your feedback as our students learn about running a restaurant that offers plated foods in courses.
Sweet corn gnocchi
10 ounces sweet corn
2 eggs
5 ounces ricotta
1 cup grated parmesan
3/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon pepper
1 cup flour
Directions
Place sweet corn and eggs into a blender until smooth.
Combine with the rest of the ingredients in a bowl with a spatula.
Shape the dough into long ropes about 1 inch in diameter, using lots of flour to avoid sticking.
Cut into 1-inch pieces.
Drop the gnocchi into boiling water for 1 minute.
Carefully remove, and gently rinse in cold water.
You can freeze these for a later time or for a quick dinner. Space them out on a tray in the freezer until they completely freeze, and then transfer them to a freezer bag. This will prevent them from sticking together while frozen.
To finish:
Use a little butter or olive oil to sauté the gnocchi just to a light golden brown. They are a little delicate, so turn gently.
It is fun to add a little minced garlic, a splash of cream, grated parmesan and chopped parsley to make a quick and delicious dish.
Or add them to any sauce with the meat and/or vegetables of your choice.
Joshua Dineen is the chef specialist at Lincoln Land Community College.
Lincoln Land Community College offers credit programs in Culinary Arts, Hospitality Management and Baking/Pastry, and non-credit cooking and food classes through LLCC Community Education.

title: 'Most Wanted' fugitive arrested in Mexico in Illinois attorney's 2016 strangling death
author: Anthony Robledo
description: John Panaligan, 57, was arrested Monday in Tepic, Mexico, ending a nearly eight-year manhunt after attorney Victor Jigar Patel was strangled in his office.
content:
Police in Mexico have arrested a man in connection with the strangling death of an Illinois attorney in 2016, U.S. officials announced Wednesday.
John Panaligan, 57, was arrested Monday in Tepic, Mexico, ending a nearly eight-year manhunt, the U.S. Marshals Service said in a news release.
Panaligan, who made the 15 Most Wanted fugitives list in 2020, was deported back to the U.S. on Tuesday, the service confirmed.
Panaligan is accused of killing attorney Victor Jigar Patel, 36, in his Northbrook, Illinois, office on Dec. 7, 2016. At the time Patel was representing clients who were suing Panaligan in civil court, according to the news release.
"I hope this arrest brings some measure of comfort to the Patel family and serves as a stark reminder to fugitives from justice that there is no place to hide," Marshals Service Director Ronald Davis said in a statement.
USA TODAY was unable to reach an attorney for Panaligan for comment.
Panaligan allegedly scheduled appointment to lure Patel
The Marshals Service allege that Panaligan scheduled an appointment under an alias to make an appointment with Patel at his law office.
Security cameras captured Panaligan wearing a disguise upon arrival before allegedly killing the attorney in his office, the Marshals Service says. Evidence collected by authorities led to him being the lead suspect in the murder investigation, according to U.S. Marshall Service.
Authorities detained Panaligan at the Canadian border two days later for allegedly attempting to smuggle a firearm into Canada. However, he was allowed to return to the U.S. so the Northbrook Police Department could interview him in the investigation into Patel's death.
On Feb. 8, 2017, a warrant for Panaligan's arrest was filed so he could be charged for first-degree murder but he presumably fled to Mexico before he authorities could find him.
On Nov. 23, 2020, the U.S. Marshals Service placed him on its 15 Most Wanted, offering a reward of up to $25,000 for information that led to his capture, according to the service. Speculation into Panaligan's whereabouts were complicated due to his dual citizenship between the U.S. and the Republic of the Philippines.

title: Chatham Glenwood grad Maggie Joos reflects on grand time with UIS women's soccer
author: Bill Welt
description: Chatham Glenwood grad Maggie Joos and teammate Madison Grandys have helped turn the UIS women's soccer team into a competitive program
content:
Maggie Joos just might have the most minutes ever logged by a University of Illinois Springfield women's soccer player.
The fifth-year senior out of Chatham Glenwood High School has compiled an astronomical 6,782 minutes with the Prairie Stars — and counting.
Over that span, the tenacious defender has become a more confident leader all the while transforming UIS into a more competitive Great Lakes Valley Conference program.
'Freshman year, I don't think I really said much,' Joos reflected on the opening 2021 spring season. 'I just kind of played soccer and that's all I focused on, but as I've earned my way to be a leader, I've grown the most in that aspect I feel.'
That growth and assertiveness naturally came with time — some of that due to being a newcomer at the NCAA Division II level but also the challenges wrought by the COVID-19 pandemic, which canceled her senior season in high school.
'Once you get more minutes under your belt, it becomes easier to gain a voice,' Joos said. 'I'm not the loudest person, so I think it had to kind of be worked on for me — just saying stuff off the field and being someone that people can go to off the field. That's kind of the biggest thing that has changed from freshman year to now.'
Fellow fifth-year player Madison Grandys, of Yorkville, could also attest how much their first year was a challenge trying to mesh as a team when social distancing, masks and regular health checks were the norm.
Grandys said she earned her way on the field after battling through an ankle injury her freshman year and has rotated through a medley of positions over the years from target forward to winger to attacking mid.
It all just depends on the matchup, she said.
'I feel really comfortable playing any of those positions,' Grandys said. 'I feel like I have pretty good soccer knowledge and I've played different positions my whole life — literally every position on the field.'
UIS volleyball: How newcomers like Lutheran grad Makenna Cox have sparked torrid start for UIS volleyball
Joos and Grandys won't have to dig too deep to find motivation for the end of the season. They are among 13 different seniors or graduate students listed on the roster. That includes fifth-year midfielder Abby Dellamonte, who led the team in points the past two seasons.
On Friday, senior goalkeeper Allison Mirimanian was named GLVC Defensive Player of the Week with five saves in a 2-0 win over Indianapolis to reach 6-6-3 overall.
Last season, Dellamonte, Joos and Grandys were each named academic all-GLVC, while Joos and Grandys each won the GLVC Brother James Gaffney Distinguished Scholar Award with a 4.0 GPA.
Joos intends to pursue physical therapy at Washington University in St. Louis, while Grandys plans to use her marketing chops in London and possibly resume soccer on a semi-pro basis.
The Stars conclude the regular season at home against Upper Iowa University on Friday at 5 p.m. and Lewis University on Sunday at noon.
Joos initially didn't expect to return for another season at last year's home finale, but she knows this one is for real — along with so many of her other teammates.
'We've been a family for four-plus years, so not getting to see each other every day, that's probably going to be the hardest part,' Joos said.
Here are other notes from around UIS sports:
Volleyball
The Stars split their matches over the weekend to move to 14-7 overall and 4-3 in the GLVC. UIS will celebrate the volleyball program's 35 anniversary in its home match against Missouri St. Louis on Saturday, Nov. 9 at 3 p.m. with alumni invited to attend.
Men's Golf
Springfield High grad Jake Baldin was named GLVC Men's Golfer of the Week at the start of October. The sophomore tied for second place individually in the Flyers Fall Intercollegiate with a 2-over-par 146 total with six birdies and an eagle on Oct. 7-8. The team tied for fourth place overall before concluding the fall season at the Bill Crabtree Invitational in Kentucky in 10th place. Brady Wilson led the Stars in 25th place (72-76), while Baldin was 29th (77-72).
Women's Golf
Junior Elanie Grant ascended to fifth place individually at the Flyers Fall Intercollegiate firing 1-over 73 in the second and final round. She finished with a 9-over total and the Stars took third place as a team. The Stars ended the fall season in fifth place at the Kentucky Wesleyan Invitational with Grant in third place individually (78-69).
Men's Cross Country
Isaac Cortes ran 24:36.11 for eighth place individually, while teammate Briar Nevills was 11 th place in 24:42.04 at the GLVC Championships 8K run hosted by UIS on Saturday. The Stars took third place as a team.
Women's Cross Country
Maddie Miller posted 21:33.82 for eighth place individually, while teammate Kaleigh Inniss was 14 th in 22:08.71 at the GLVC Championships 6K run hosted by UIS on Saturday. The Stars finished fourth place as a team.
Men's Soccer
UIS moved to 4-6-5 overall after a scoreless tie with Indianapolis on Friday and a 3-2 loss to St. Cloud State University on Sunday. Joey Fitzgerald has a team-high 13 points with three goals and seven assists. Corne Boshoff and Anton Aduwa-Emovon also have three goals apiece this season.

title: 4A shake-up: Peoria Notre Dame bounces nine-time state champ Rochester in first round
author: Adrian Dater
description: A blocked extra-point kick in overtime led to Rochester's first-round ousting by Peoria Notre Dame.
content:
ROCHESTER — Ben Mullens seemed almost in shock when he limped to the Peoria Notre Dame bench while his teammates celebrated on the battered turf of Rocket Booster Stadium following his team's unbelievable 59-58 Friday night victory that ended the season of defending Class 4A champion Rochester.
Mullens, it turned out, wanted to take it all in for just a few more moments, to comprehend what his team had just pulled off.
In one of the most epic playoff games probably in all of state history, the visiting No. 13-seeded Irish just barely outlasted a valiant, banged-up Rockets squad in a game that both teams seemed to have locked up just a few minutes earlier. In the end, it went the Irish's way thanks to Mullen's quarterbacking, the running of halfback Jack Hanley, and the right leg and right arm of fullback, linebacker and kicker Lawson Alwan.
'That was such a great game. I'm going to remember this game forever,' said Mullens, whose white and Kelly green uniform was caked in dirt. 'It's just an unbelievable feeling to actually win it.'
For the first time since 2008, the nine-time state champion Rockets are bounced in the first round. Not only was it the first opening-round playoff loss for No. 4 Rochester in that span, but the Rockets had not failed to make at least the quarterfinals in any playoff run since 2008.
While Hanley probably deserved the game ball after scoring five touchdowns, including a 33-yard run with 3:07 left in regulation, the Irish's real hero at the end was Alwan. Not only did he kick a 30-yard field goal with 1.8 seconds left in regulation to tie it at 52-52, but he then blocked the extra point after Rochester's Tanner Beal scored on the Rockets' first possession in OT to keep the Irish six points back with four downs from the 10-yard line to get seven points.
On 4th down, about three inches from the goal line, Mullens called an audible and handed the ball to Alwan, who barely got the ball over the white stripe. With the score now tied 58-58, Alwan booted the extra point well past the uprights.
Rochester players fell to their knees, while Irish players danced in jubilation along with a sizable contingent of fans that made the drive from Peoria.
Alwan credited junior lineman teammate Jacob Khoury for helping him block the extra point in OT.
'He got the guard opened up a little bit and gave me a small, little window and I was able to get my right hand up and block it,' Alwan said. 'After that field goal to tie the game, that (extra point kick) was easy. I felt the nerves go away and I knew we had it.'
Rochester, which lost starting quarterback Bryan Zulauf at the start of the season, became an offensive juggernaut as the season wore on. The Rockets were averaging 39 points a game entering this one. But, no, the defense just wasn't as good as last season's dominant squad. Not that the effort wasn't there.
'This is a young team, and they played their butts off,' Rockets coach Derek Leonard said. 'We just didn't play our best game tonight. They were physical and out-physicaled us, but you know what man? I love these kids and love these seniors and people can't assume that winning just happens. It doesn't, and I think this was a real lesson for everybody.'
The first half saw touchdowns on the first 11 combined possessions, with the Irish holding a 42-38 lead. Rochester's defensive line got much tougher in the second half, and it took the Irish more than 15 minutes to get another point. The Irish's running game was just too tough for Rochester to deal with in the end, as the visitors ran for 460 yards. Mullens only threw three passes in the game, but they were big ones toward the end, for 56 yards.
Kaiden Stout had a strong game for the Rockets, running for 127 yards on 19 carries and a 9-yard TD run in OT. Tanner Beal scored three touchdowns for the Rockets, and three quarterbacks combined for 230 yards on 12-for-19 passing.
Hanley not only ran for 212 yards, but he also caught a big pass on the Irish's field-goal drive that tied it 52-52. He also ran back a kickoff 88 yards for a touchdown.
'He's our superstar,' Alwan said. 'That's our guy. He does it all for us. But it was a team effort for us all the way through.'
Rochester finished the season 7-3. The loss snapped a five-game win streak.
'In the playoffs, there are no good lessons, but this will be eventually for some of our young kids," Leonard said. "For our seniors, they can walk off this field with their heads up high.'
Adrian Dater is a freelance writer for The State Journal-Register. He can be reached through the sports department at sports@sj-r.com.

title: The short version: Who won, what passed in Springfield area election
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Not sure who won a certain race last night? Here's a quick recap of results from the Springfield area.
content:
Some argue that this national election is of monumental significance, and it's consequently coming at a time of a great political division in the U.S.
Locally, the race is important, too.
Here's a quick recap of what happened Tuesday night.
County races
There were several uncontested seats in which incumbents remain, including Sangamon Coroner Jim Allmon, Sangamon County Auditor Andy Goleman, and several county board seats.
County Board
No new faces have surfaced on the Sangamon County Board, but there were a few close races.
Democrat Marc Ayers retained his district 12 seat after defeating Republican Colleen Lucas Cavanagh with a margin of 219 votes.
Republican A.D. "Andy" VanMeter will retain his district 24 seat after defeating Democrat Duffy Bommarito with a margin of 181 votes.
Republican Jennifer Ghesquiere Deaner will retain her district 25 seat after defeating Democrat Jennifer Merritt with a margin of nine votes.
Circuit Clerk
Republican Joe Roesch retained his position after defeating Democrat Juwanda M. Burrage.
Recorder
One of the few intriguing races leading into the election, Republican Frank J. Lesko led incumbent Democrat Joshua Langfelder with a margin of 68 votes as of Tuesday night. Don Gray, the Sangamon County Clerk, told the SJ-R there were still more than 3,000 mail-in ballots that needed to be counted.
State's Attorney
Republican John C. Milhiser retained his position after defeating Democrat Kimberly Talken.
Kenny Naughton, exiting So. Side Christian Church, after voting Nov. 5, 2024.
Kenny Naughton of Springfield talks about the anxiety and divisiveness of the nation going to the polls on Nov. 5, 2024.
U.S. House of Representatives
U.S. Rep. Nikki Budzinski held a slim lead over political newcomer Joshua Loyd in the 13th District race as of 11:45 p.m. Tuesday. With an estimated 63% of the vote in, Budzinski had 132,758 votes to Loyd's 118,437.
Statewide referendums
All three of the statewide referendums passed, including the advisory question on property tax relief. Despite the question receiving more "yes" votes than "no", there will be no immediate impact, however, it could shape another vote for a constitutional amendment as early as 2026. The tax would impact Illinois residents whose income is greater than $1 million.

Election Day is finally here, which means the political ads online and on TV are coming to an end, thankfully.
The presidential election is obviously the biggest race of the day across the country, but there are plenty of races in Illinois and in the Springfield area that are worth keeping an eye on and monitoring throughout the day.
The State Journal-Register will have live updates online at the sj-r.com and on The State Journal-Register mobile app.
6 a.m. polls opened
Polls have officially opened in Illinois. Polls will be open throughout the state until 7 p.m.
If you are going out to vote Tuesday, keep an umbrella handy. Rain is predicted for most of the day in the Springfield area.
If you are voting in person Tuesday, you can find your polling place online at ova.elections.il.gov. Even if you aren't registered to vote, you can do so at your designated polling place Tuesday.
For Sangamon County results, click here. For Illinois results, click here.
8:45 a.m. Voter registration technical issue
Sangamon County Clerk Don Gray said there was a vendor issue delaying same-day voter registration, but the issue was quickly resolved.

He encouraged people who wanted to register to vote Tuesday to go to the county building at 200 S. Ninth St.
9 a.m. A look at early voting in Sangamon County

title: How Sacred Heart-Griffin football's pass game has learned to jell at the right time
author: Bill Welt
description: Sacred Heart-Griffin receivers Seamus O'Brien and Jamarion Bardwell always had trust in sophomore QB Cam Brinkman from the beginning
content:
It doesn't matter how a team begins the season because it all boils down to the postseason.
Sacred Heart-Griffin's pass game has certainly found another gear going into its Class 5A second-round matchup against behemoth Joliet Catholic at Ken Leonard Field. Kickoff is Saturday at 2 p.m.
First round takeaways:
'It's been way better over the last few weeks,' senior receiver/cornerback Jamarion Bardwell said. 'Our quarterback is getting a lot of confidence. He's developing into the QB I know he can be, so that's great for him. I know he's probably one of the best quarterbacks in the CS8 in my opinion. I'm just seeing greatness from him, that's all.'
Bardwell was referring to none other than sophomore QB Cam Brinkman, who recently led the No. 14-seeded Cyclones (6-4) to a 24-21 upset win over No. 3 Mahomet-Seymour in the first round by completing 22 of 33 passing attempts for 292 yards and three touchdowns.
Brinkman previously went 25 of 39 for 322 yards and four TDs in a 41-27 Week 9 loss to Rochester. Despite another sluggish start against Mahomet, the Cyclones went to the air with an empty backfield and prevailed with Brinkman's go-ahead 78-yard touchdown pass to senior wideout Seamus O'Brien with less than four minutes remaining.
It not only exhibited the team's trust in Brinkman but also his increasing confidence.
'I think the biggest challenge is not being too nervous and overwhelmed,' Brinkman said. 'I think coming in my first few games, I just kind of felt like I had to do everything so perfect to kind of prove myself and do things the right way.
'But as I've moved on, I feel like I haven't really been as nervous, and I've just kind of gone out and played my game. I think it's been working. I think I've been playing pretty good as of late, and hopefully, I can keep doing it.'
He has particularly developed a strong connection with O'Brien, who leads the team with 36 catches for 594 yards and nine touchdowns. Over the last two weeks, O'Brien has reeled in 20 receptions for 202 yards and four TDs.
'He's been big,' Brinkman said. 'He's really good at getting open, and he's always available for the ball. He's been a really good target for me. When nothing's open and the play is not going according to plan ... he's always trying to get open and find ways to get the ball. That's really big because it keeps the play alive, and we have a chance to get a first down.'
It's something the two have incessantly worked on together after practice.
'You stay after and you start to build that relationship,' O'Brien said. 'I know what he's doing when he rolls out right, he knows how many steps I'm taking on a comeback. I think we've really grown to be so cohesive that it's starting to really come together.'
Volleyball sectionals: SHG, Nokomis remain as Springfield area's last teams
Last season, O'Brien had 21 catches for 333 yards and two TDs. His dad, Matthew Fitzgerald, previously played football at SHG.
'He made me more competitive than anyone else,' O'Brien said.
Brinkman began playing quarterback in seventh grade and said he largely learned on his own until working with head coach John Allison as well as assistant coaches Todd Chance and Doug Martin — not to mention trainer Rob Garcia in the Peoria region.
He knows the No. 5 Hilltoppers (7-3) just might be their toughest test yet. JCA, brandishing a potent Wing-T offense, previously defeated SHG 56-27 in the 2021 Class 4A state finals.
Bardwell, a triple jump state champion in Class 2A, said the Cyclones just need to be physical and strong after overcoming injury himself during the regular season. It may be a boring game for most corners, but Bardwell is an exception.

Veterans Day is a federal holiday meaning most government buildings and schools will be closed on Monday.

Federal, State of Illinois, Sangamon County and city of Springfield offices and courts will be closed Monday.

title: Illinois, DoorDash agree to $11.25M settlement over misused tips
author: Claire Grant
description: DoorDash has agreed to more than an $11 million settlement providing relief for nearly 80,000 DoorDash drivers in Illinois. Here's what we know.
content:
An over $11 million settlement has been made between Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul and food delivery service, DoorDash.
The $11.25 million settlement which was agreed upon on Nov. 8 is still pending judicial approval. The settlement addresses the allegation DoorDash violated Section 2 of the Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act, by representing to consumers tips and how they would affect driver's earnings.
The settlement includes relief for almost 80,000 drivers in Illinois, and requires DoorDash to maintain a pay model which does not use consumer tips as a factor in calculating its own contributions to driver's pay.
The office of the Attorney General alleges instead of allowing drivers to keep tips made by deliveries as well as the guaranteed payment of the app whereas DoorDash used customer tips toward guaranteed pay promised in driver deliveries. The practice, which ended before COVID-19, saw customer tips rarely impact the real overall pay of the driver while reducing DoorDash's contribution.
'DoorDash encouraged customers to tip as much as possible, indicating that all of their tip would go to workers,' Raoul said in a statement. 'Instead, DoorDash used tips to reduce the amount the company paid workers. By putting tips toward driver pay, DoorDash could get away with contributing as little as $1 toward a worker's pay and allow tips to make up the rest. This settlement ensures tips from customers end up where they were intended to go: into the pockets of delivery drivers.'
The business model took place between July 2017 to September of 2019. Under the new settlement, the company will be required to make clear disclosures to both workers and customers regarding its pay model.
The Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act (ICFA) is comprehensive legislation designed to protect consumers, borrowers, and businessmen against fraud, unfair methods of competition, and deceptive practices in trade or business.

title: Wisconsin authorities believe kayaker staged his disappearance and fled to Europe
author: Justin Marville
description: In a shocking turn of events, Wisconsin authorities believe Ryan Borgwardt, 44, staged his disappearance and fled to Europe.
content:
GREEN LAKE, Wisc. – Authorities in Wisconsin believe a kayaker who was reported missing for several months may be alive and staged his disappearance before fleeing the country.
Ryan Borgwardt, a 44-year-old married father of three, according to WBAY, initially went missing on Aug. 12 after kayaking on Green Lake, a natural inland lake about 100 miles northwest of Milwaukee. Local authorities located Borgwardt's kayak overturned with a lifejacket that same day.
An extensive search for Borgwardt's body, which involved underwater drones, towable submersible sonar, divers and three K-9 cadaver teams, continued for about 54 days, but "there was nothing we could find," Green Lake County Sheriff Mark Podoll said during a news conference Friday.
In a shocking turn of events, Podoll said further investigation revealed that it was likely Borgwardt staged his disappearance and fled to Europe. After regrouping with his team on Oct. 7, Podoll said they decided to "go a different direction" and discovered that Borgwardt's name was "run" on Aug. 13.
"That was something we didn't expect," Podoll said, adding that authorities recovered evidence of Borgwardt taking out a life insurance policy and that he was communicating with a woman from Uzbekistan.
Ryan Borgwardt initially reported missing on Green Lake
Borgwardt's wife previously told authorities that she received a text message from him on the night of Aug. 11 saying he was heading to shore and that his last known location was Green Lake.
Deputies found Borgwardt's vehicle, along with his trailer parked in Dodge County Memorial Park on the southwest end of the lake, according to Podoll. Deputies immediately deployed a boat and discovered a capsized kayak in the western part of the lake, where the water was about 220 feet deep, Podoll said.
Bruce's Legacy, a nonprofit search-and-rescue organization, and multiple law enforcement agencies searched the area "extensively" and found a fishing rod that was identified as Borgwardt's by his wife, according to Podoll. Authorities also found a tackle box containing Borgwardt's wallet, keys and license.
Podoll recalled that on Oct. 4, Keith Cormican − who started Bruce's Legacy in 2013 − had told him that he searched the western part of Green Lake but was unable to find Borgwardt's body. But Podoll noted that Cormican was not ready to give up on the search.
"So Oct. 7, I got my crew together," Podoll said. "We met and we talked and we said, 'We got to go a different direction.' And the direction we went was offline, and we found out that Borgwardt's name was run on Aug. 13."
'We believe that Ryan is alive and likely in Eastern Europe'
The new investigation revealed that Borgwardt's name had been checked by Canadian law enforcement on Aug. 13 and showed he had a second passport after reporting his original passport lost.
With help from Customs and Border Patrol, Homeland Security, the FBI and the Wisconsin Department of Criminal Investigations, Podoll said investigators conducted a digital forensic analysis of Borgwardt's laptop.
"We recovered that he replaced his hard drive on the laptop," Podoll said. "He cleared the browser on the day of his disappearance. He synced the laptop into the cloud on Aug. 11. He took photos of his passport."
Podoll said authorities also found that Borgwardt inquired about moving funds to foreign banks, changed email addresses associated with financial accounts on the day of his disappearance and was communicating with a woman from Uzbekistan.
Podoll added that in January, Borgwardt took out a $375,000 life insurance policy and purchased an airline gift card.
'Due to the discovery of this new evidence, we are confident that Ryan is not located in Green Lake and we have ended all search efforts associated with Green Lake,' Podoll said. 'At this time, we believe that Ryan is alive and likely in Eastern Europe.'
'Our investigation has many more steps to take to put this puzzle together,' Podoll added, noting that authorities are in the process of reviewing charges that might be brought against Borgwardt.
The Green Lake County Sheriff's Office urged the public to come forward with any information on Borgwardt. Podoll also pleaded with Borgwardt.
"Ryan, if you're viewing this, I plea that you contact us or contact your family. We understand that things can happen, but there's a family that wants their daddy back," Podoll said.

title: 'Best of both worlds': Chatham Glenwood senior shines in slot ahead of football quarters
author: Bill Welt
description: Gavin Simmons has totaled nearly 1,500 receiving yards over the past two seasons with the Chatham Glenwood football team.
content:
The Chatham Glenwood football team will figuratively throw anything at you.
Senior Gavin Simmons said the playbook itself contains hundreds of plays — so much, he said, 'I can't even count how many plays we have.'
That extensive playbook is complemented by a gamut of players who each bring something different to the table. It starts with junior dual-threat quarterback Colten Knoedler.
Knoedler can turn to speedy slot receivers Simmons and junior Blake Lehnen or bigger targets such as 6-7 senior Mason Nuemann and 6-4 senior Jonathan Helm.
That doesn't even include the tailback combo of electric junior Grady Mueller and bruising senior Herchel Walker.
'We have a little bit of everything that you could ever want in the offense,' Simmons said.
Last season, Simmons led the Titans with 53 receptions for 725 yards and nine touchdowns. This season has been much the same in the slot with 50 grabs for 767 yards and nine TDs.
Simmons has dabbled a little bit of everywhere over his career, but the slot is unquestionably his preferred position with jet sweeps and screens potentially in the offing.
'It's more of a hybrid receiver/running back player compared to the outside,' said Simmons, who has ambitions to play at the next level, 'so I'd say I like it a little bit more because you get the best of both worlds playing running back and slot.'
Mueller is also a threat in more ways than one.
He has a team-high 699 rushing yards and nine scores on 122 carries. He is also second-best on the team with 26 catches for 507 yards and six scores. He began the season as a slot receiver before pivoting back to what he considers his more natural position.
'I knew that was my spot,' Mueller said of being a running back. 'I just kept at it and kept working.
'Herchel Walker, he's been competing with me all year. We definitely help each other get better.'
Last week, Mueller rushed for 217 yards and three touchdowns on 22 carries in a 42-21 win over Oak Forest in the second round of the Class 6A playoffs. In Week 8, he totaled three touchdowns — including a 98-yard kickoff return — and 165 rushing yards in a 34-31 overtime victory over Sacred Heart-Griffin.
'I've just been working hard every day at practice — shoutout to my line, they're just working hard as me,' Mueller said. 'We've been getting better every week.'
Knoedler has been shattering records along the way himself. He went 23 of 31 for 475 yards and six touchdowns in the 49-34 win over Crete-Monee in the playoff opener to set a record for most completions and passing yards in a game while also tying for most touchdowns. Last week, he broke his own record for most passing yards in a season with 2,430.
Lehnen's return has further galvanized the offense. He missed most of the season due to injury.
The No. 5-seeded Titans (9-2) next welcome top-seeded East St. Louis (10-1) in the 6A quarterfinals on Saturday at 2 p.m.
Glenwood lost the last meeting 50-28 in the 2019 6A semifinals before the Flyers captured the state title. East St. Louis has subsequently returned to the state finals the past three seasons with one additional title in 2022 — a stretch only interrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic.
Simmons is keenly aware of the challenge ahead but said the team's mental approach remains the same.

title: Springfield-area woman raising funds for injured soldiers as she trains for Boston Marathon
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A Waverly High School graduate is looking to raise money injured soldiers while she trains for the Boston Marathon.
content:
In April of 2013, a senior at Waverly High School was so moved by the tragedy of the Boston Marathon bombings that she laced up her running shoes and ran 26.2 miles along Illinois 104.
Now a U.S. Marine Corps Staff Sergeant and a mom, Brennan Barrett (formerly Schneider) will be re-running that route as she trains for the Boston Marathon and raises money for military families in need.
Barrett aims to raise $10,000 for Semper Fi & America's Fund that supports veterans and their families after sustaining life-changing injuries or critical illnesses.
'It feels like a full-picture moment,' Barrett said. 'Running the Boston Marathon has always been a goal, but I think it's such a small part of what I'm doing because I'm raising all of these funds for such an amazing organization.'
Barrett didn't know at the time of the bombings that she wanted to pursue military service or that she would still be talking about that trek along Illinois 104 over a decade later.
But she is still talking about it, as she plans to run in Waverly on March 15 a month before she will run the Boston Marathon in April.
She aims to raise awareness for the cause and raise money for the charity with events scheduled as soon as Dec. 7 at the Jacksonville VFW from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., where Barrett and her family will host 'The Warm Up." A ticket will get participants an assortment of homemade soups, rolls, drinks, and sweets.
There will be also raffles, silent auctions, and T-shirts for sale. All the money raised will go to the non-profit. Barrett will also pay for her own flight to Boston.
Barrett said she is in good company as she gears up to train, being stationed in Indianapolis with fellow Marines who regularly compete with one another.
Barrett and some of those Marines once ran a 50-kilometer race – that's 31 miles – with many of them never having ran anywhere close to that distance.
'We were like, 'hey, let's do this.' None of us trained for it but we all finished it. They're just like, 'that's nuts, I never want to do that distance again, and you're just willing to sign up and do it again?'"
The answer is yes.
Barrett in the last 10 years has run marathons and even longer distances in Chicago, Honolulu, Little Rock, Maine, San Diego, and Indianapolis.
After running the initial marathon distance in Waverly – sporting a t-shirt that read "Boston 26.2" on the front and 'Honk for Boston' on the back, Barrett told the SJ-R the following:
'When I heard (the bombings) happened, as a runner, running being my life, I felt I had to do something,' says Brennan. 'I couldn't think of anything better to do than run – finish the race for those who didn't finish.'
For more information and to donate, go to givengain.com.

title: Pawnee football falls to defending champ Amboy in first 8-Man semifinal appearance
author: Bill Welt
description: A one-handed grab put Amboy on track to win over Pawnee and third straight state final appearance in the Illinois 8-Man Football Association playoffs
content:
PAWNEE — It was just a matter of instincts.
Junior tight end Rylen McNinch pulled down a one-handed catch before barreling into the end zone on Amboy's opening possession and the Clippers sailed to a 52-8 victory over Pawnee in the Illinois 8-Man Football Association semifinals.
Amboy, the defending state champion, will meet Milledgeville in its third straight state final appearance on Friday at 7 p.m. in Monmouth.
The Clippers (11-1) quickly surged ahead 22-0. After McNinch's 31-yard touchdown reception, a blocked punt set up senior running back Brayden Klein's first of three touchdown runs. He ran for 103 yards on 11 carries.
Senior quarterback/defensive back Eddie Jones picked off Pawnee QB Caden Ward before throwing a 77-yard touchdown screen pass to senior tight end Caleb Yanos.
The Clippers led 30-8 by halftime.
Pawnee was making its first ever semifinal appearance and concluded with the most wins in program history at 11-1. Senior running back Carson Wort totaled 91 rushing yards and a touchdown, along with four catches for 39 yards.

title: Looking for Santa Claus? Here's where you can find Saint Nick in the Springfield area
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Santa Claus arrives in Springfield Friday night. Here's where and when you can find him ahead of Christmas.
content:
Show Caption
It wasn't so long ago that we saw princesses, superheroes and skeletons ringing our doorbells.
Yet, rumor has it that Santa will be making stops in Springfield before Christmas.
Here are a few places you can see Santa as the holiday season approaches.
Holiday Extravaganza at the Illinois State Fairgrounds
What: This is a craft show featuring over 100 vendors. Santa will be there from 1 to 4 p.m. There will be a cake walk, and concessions will be available. Kids under 13 can get in for free. Entry fee for adults is $4. Seniors receive a discount from 9 to 11 a.m. Proceeds go to an art or music program in a local school.

Time: 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Date: Nov. 24
For more: Springfield Illinois Holiday Extravaganza on Facebook
Light up the Gables Parade
This parade features Santa and Mrs. Claus, in addition to Abe and Mary Todd Lincoln, the elves, and more.
Place: The Gables shopping mall at 2800 Plaza Drive, Springfield
Time: 5 p.m.
Date: Nov. 29
For more: VisitSpringfieldIllinois.com
Illinois Product Holiday Market
What: Santa and his sleigh will be present. The event also offers activities for children, local food and goods, and live music.
Place:"Y Block" North of the Governor's Mansion
Time: Varies
Date: Dec. 6-8
For more: Agr.Illinois.gov
Holiday Open House
What: A "Civil War era" Santa Claus will be at this free open house, where visitors can see the Edwards Place Historic Home decorated for the holidays. Visitors can also sing and listen to carols around a piano once heard by Abraham Lincoln.
Place: 700 N. Fourth St., Springfield
Time: 1 to 4 p.m.

title: The Winter Farmers Market returns to Springfield this weekend
author: Claire Grant
description: Looking to get a head start on some Christmas shopping? You may want to consider some of these events in Springfield this weekend.
content:
With only one week out from Thanksgiving meals, Black Friday deals and small biz Saturday steals, what are you doing this weekend?
Find something around Springfield with these five things to do.
Pink Friday Downtown
What: Mark your calendar and make plans with friends to kick off your holiday shopping on Pink Friday your favorite downtown businesses for a fun Friday filled with sales and specials. Businesses The Keep Store and Whimsy Tea Company are ringing in Pink Friday with sales and enthusiasm to make East Adams Street stronger with the season.
Where: Downtown Springfield, start at 312 E. Adams St., Springfield
More: Pink Friday is a nationwide event celebrating and supporting small and local businesses. It's held annually on the Friday before Black Friday, encouraging shoppers to discover and shop from small retailers first during the holiday season.
Winter Old Capitol Farmers Market
What: The Holiday & Winter Farmers Market will be hosted at the historic Union Station. The former train station, now part of the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum, will provide a dedicated sheltered outdoor and heated indoor space for the winter season and dedicated parking. Sip on some hot cocoa and enjoy the nearing end of the farmers market with friends and good finds.
When: 8 a.m. to noon Saturday
Where: 547 E. Jefferson St., Springfield
Pre-Thanksgiving bash at Casey's Pub
What: Celebrate the season with Soul Experience Band and have a gobbling good time at Casey's Pub. Other performing artists on the dance floor include Reggie B and the Price Sista's as part of the New Experience in Soul night.
When: 7 p.m. to 10 p.m. Saturday
Where: 2200 S. Meadowbrook Road, Springfield
More: Soul Experience Band plays around Sangamon County and is a R&B, funk, jazz Motown and blues flavored band.
BYOB - Bring Your Own Book
What: When was the last time you opened up a book and read more than a page? Putting down the phone and picking a good book will help relieve stress and help you focus better during the day. Head on over to Obed & Isaac's The Cidery for a lowkey book club with quiet music, drink specials and no talking needed.
When: Quiet reading time honored 4:30 to 6 p.m. every Sunday.
Annual Sherman Holiday Wonderland
What: Shop local craft artists and ring in the season at the 16th Annual Sherman Holiday Wonderland. There's something sweet about picking up sweets at the market filled with holiday cheer.
When: 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Sunday
Where: 300 S. First St., Sherman, inside the Sherman Athletic Club.

title: Illinois Innocence Project based in Springfield helps free man after 32 years behind bars
author: Steven Spearie
description: A southern Illinois man who spent over three decades behind bars for a murder evidence proves he did not commit was freed last week.
content:
A southern Illinois man who spent over three decades behind bars for a murder evidence proves he did not commit was freed last week thanks in part to the Springfield-based Illinois Innocence Project (IIP).
The court vacated the sentence of Danny Davis, 52, of Cairo, and ordered him freed from the Department of Corrections. The state is appealing the ruling of Circuit Court Associate Judge Tyler Edmonds' made last week in Alexander County.
Davis pleaded guilty to the 1992 murder and robbery of a woman who ran a small convenience store out of her home at the southern tip of the state. The woman was stabbed nearly 40 times in her home.
The IIP, housed at the University of Illinois Springfield, and the Innocence Project in New York took on Davis' case in 2015.
The Exoneration Project at the University of Chicago Law School later joined the team. One of its attorneys representing Davis is Lauren Myerscough-Mueller, the daughter of U.S. District Judge Sue Myerscough. Myerscough-Mueller, a graduate of Chatham Glenwood High School, formerly worked at the IIP.
Lauren Kaeseberg, a co-director of the IIP reached over the weekend, said via text that Davis' legal team wasn't conducting any press interviews about the case.
According to the Innocence Project website, Davis endured "psychological and physical abuse" after being brought in for initial questioning, including being threatened with the death penalty.
Davis and his brother, Isaac, signed false confession statements implicating themselves and an acquaintance, DeVoe Johnson, in the crime. Danny Davis pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life without parole. Isaac Davis also pleaded guilty, but Johnson was acquitted in a bench trial.
In its post-conviction investigation, attorneys obtained information that had not been turned over to the defense during the original investigation, including critical witness statements and potential alternate suspects.
DNA obtained from the victim excluded both Davis brothers and Johnson.
Davis was released from Menard Correctional Center.

title: Springfield woman faces murder charges in connection to 2019 homicide
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A Springfield woman faces murder charges in connection to the death of a man five years ago.
content:
A Springfield woman faces murder charges in connection to the death of a man five years ago.
Morgan C. Allin, 36, was arrested and indicted on three counts of first-degree murder, aggravated battery of a firearm and other charges in connection to the death of Joseph Sommer II.
Police responded to the 1600 block of North Seventh Street on April 19, 2019, for reports of a man down. Officers arrived and found Sommer II with a single gunshot wound to his upper body.
Sommer lived alone at the time of his death, but police confirmed they were investigating the death as a homicide.
'The arrest of Allin was the result of complex investigative follow-up to include countless hours of interviews and the processing and analysis of physical evidence,' police said in a news release.
Allin was arrested on Nov. 8, indicted by a grand jury on Nov. 13 and arraigned on Nov. 21.
Allin is not expected to appear in court again until January 2025.

title: Signings and commits around Springfield so far, including Chatham Glenwood girls hoops
author: Bill Welt
description: Chatham Glenwood girls basketball brims with next-level talent, plus other signings and commits in the Springfield area so far
content:
CHATHAM — Katelyn Lehnen loves basketball. Especially the team camaraderie that comes with the sport.
'You just can't get anything better than that,' the Chatham Glenwood senior guard said.
This is the last basketball season of her career after signing with the University of Illinois women's track and field team earlier this month.
It's anything but a surprise.
Her résumé includes three sprint titles — in Class 3A no less. She won the 200-meter dash in her first ever state meet as a freshman before reaching the top podium in the 100 and 400 last spring.
She not only connected with the Illini coaching staff but also liked how the strength and conditioning paralleled Glenwood's under Caleb Cox.
Lehnen looks forward to the day when she knows which sprint beckons her the most.
'I'm excited whatever the coaches want me to do,' Lehnen said. 'Anything that they have for me, I'm ready to work at.'
Lehnen said she will still keep tabs on her senior teammates after graduation: Makaela Diamond, Rowann Law and Macy Martynowski. They have played basketball together since at least grade school.
'Saying goodbye to those group of girls that I've been playing with my whole life is definitely going to be hard,' Lehnen said.
That senior corps just brims with talent.
Diamond and Martynowksi will play basketball at Lake Land College and College of DuPage, respectively, while Law will go to Missouri State University for soccer.
'This group of four, we've bonded and we've had some great experiences together,' Martynowski said. 'Just being able to all say that we get to pursue our dreams is kind of insane, but it's really awesome.'
Law, of course, won the Class 2A girls soccer state title with her twin sister, Rylann, in 2023.
Last season, Rylann was named The State Journal-Register's Large School Girls Soccer Player of the Yea r. She will play at Illinois State University, also part of the Missouri Valley Conference. Rowann said they both thought it would be fun to compete against each other on occasion.
There's no question how quick this basketball team can strike with all that athleticism on the floor.
Glenwood ascended to the Class 3A state finals last season and the state runnerups aspire to be even better this year under second-year coach Alyssa Riley.
'It just shows how good our team is and the athletes that we have all around at Glenwood,' Rowann said. 'It shows our programs are really good here.'
Martynowski said her dad, John, introduced her to basketball.
She may be listed as a 5-10 senior forward, but she can also play guard as a utility player. But with so many other guards on the team, she largely camps out in the post and pairs up against prolific 6-1 sophomore forward Alexis Neumann in practice.
'We have fun; she mainly blocks me, but it's OK,' Martynowski said with a laugh.
Diamond said her older brother, Kyle, has helped her improve as a shooter virtually every day. Defense is another top priority.
'Everything starts with defense,' Diamond said. 'We believe that defense fuels our offense, so I've just been trying to get better on defense.'
Lehnen's speed does wonders defensively. It can also have a downside.
'It's hard for me to slow down on offense a little bit, but I'm working on it,' she said with a laugh.

title: Furniture outlet store closing its doors in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: A furniture outlet store that opened up a few years ago in Springfield is closing its doors.
content:
A furniture outlet store that opened up a few years ago in Springfield is closing its doors.
The third-generation business Ashley Furniture Outlet Store has been operating for three years now at 1987 W. Wabash Ave., in the old Barney's Furniture, which closed in 2020.
The store will remain open until most of the inventory of the location is sold, according to an employee at Ashley Outlet. Black Friday will ramp up deals, as business owner Barry Seidman seeks to close the outlet location to focus on the main Ashley HomeStore at 2325 ChuckWagon Drive.
The difference between an Ashley Outlet store and the HomeStore is the price point of entry: for the outlet, customers can buy single pieces of sets or items not constructed to build themselves at home.
Seidman's grandfather opened Barney's Furniture in 1939 at the corner of Seventh and Washington streets in downtown Springfield. By 1974, the store moved to the east side of the city on South Grand Avenue East, where it stayed a staple of the east side for four decades.
The Seidman family has owned the location on W. Wabash since 2016, then the local business was converted into an Ashley Furniture Outlet following the pandemic.

title: Thanksgiving traditions: Here are some of our holiday traditions
author: Claire Grant
description: In spirit of the holidays, we wanted to share some of our favorite Thanksgiving memories and traditions. What are some of your favorite traditions?
content:
It's a little day at the end of November that I used to dread every year, but as I've gotten older, I've found myself looking forward to being around my family again, after moving states away.
The tradition of Thanksgiving goes back hundreds of years, but it was in 1863 Sarah Josepha Hale, who wrote 'Mary Had a Little Lamb', lobbied President Abraham Lincoln to make the final Thursday of November an official American holiday.
Since then, plenty of turkeys have been baked, casseroles have been burnt and bickering matches over bread rolls have made the holiday something to look forward to along with a myriad of family traditions.
Here's a look at some of our Thanksgiving traditions.
Many years ago, my brother was hospitalized with a severe bacterial infection right around Thanksgiving. The thought of the disruption of a family gathering--especially when one of your own was fighting an illness--was jarring. That's all I could think of, sitting in a church at an ecumenical service the night before Thanksgiving, that we wouldn't fully be together as a family the next day.
In the years since, I've tried to make a Thanksgiving service, usually put on by the Greater Springfield Interfaith Association or the Springfield Ministerial Alliance, part of the season. It's a way of expressing thanks in a communal setting.
It's also a reminder of all those years ago when things weren't so great and a reminder that when family is fully together, what more do you need?
Tom Ackerman
As a kid who grew up near a fantastic park, our neighborhood always gravitated to it throughout the year. On Thanksgiving, that meant throwing the football around.
The turnout has decreased in recent years, but we recall a time when the fields were full of people of all ages. The games were and are, for some reason, always competitive. Sometimes it's accompanied by hot chocolate and donuts.
A related, consequent tradition is that I usually end up getting injured at 'the Turkey Bowl.' I remember walking home early one year with my wrist bent too far towards the bottom side of my arm, and shyly telling my parents that it might be broken. 'Not again!' my mom said.
This year, I plan to see another side of the family in Connecticut, where I lived for a few years. I want to visit them, but I already have some regrets as the cold mornings come and remind me of the football games before our Thanksgiving meals.
Claire Grant
Thanksgiving morning used to mean hot, fresh baked bread. My mom would always try to make the day a little bit better if she ended up yelling at my sister and I to get dressed on the way to Aunt Pam's or Uncle Jim's for our 2 p.m. dinner.
It was a decently long drive from Detroit to Okemos, around an hour and a half, but it was always worth it to run through the front door and see my family; it wasn't often I'd see my mom's side of the family – only on Easter, Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve.
Dad's side lives much closer to Detroit in St. Clair Shores, and every weekend was a weekend with Grandma Grant.
It's on Thanksgiving I can be fussed over, and maybe picked over a little bit – too – much by Grandma Houthoofd.
Since celebration starts so early, snacks and charcuterie are the table setters. Mini pumpernickel cracker pizzas, salamis and cheeses galore, with around two pounds of shrimp.
The dinner plate is a pretty solid mess of ham, turkey, stuffing, potatoes, salad, dinner rolls and plenty of green bean casserole. Minimal yams. I do not like yams.
After dinner and laying comatose on the couch for a few hours, I head back home with my sister to her apartment in the Cass Corridor of Detroit and we get ready for ice skating the next day at Campus Martius Park and exploring all the new exhibits at the Detroit Institute of Art.

title: Illinois Innocence Project founder sees students' lives 'changed by this work'
author: Steven Spearie
description: The Illinois Innocence Project in Springfield has helped secure the release of 25 innocent people and was recently recognized for its work.
content:
Larry Golden points out that the Illinois Innocence Project (IIP) at the University of Illinois Springfield uses undergraduate students in researching and reviewing cases, making it the only innocence project in the nation to do so.
"The young people who are coming in, their lives are being changed (by this work) and they're telling us (that) right now," said Golden, a professor emeritus at UIS and the founding director of IIP in 2001, who is still involved in classes being taught at UIS. "We're seeing the results of the seeds that got planted."
Golden accepted the Humanitarian of the Year award presented by the Greater Springfield Interfaith Association at its annual Thanksgiving Service at Temple B'rith Sholom on Nov. 24.
Also at the presentation was longtime IIP executive director John Hanlon.
The award comes on the heels of IIP, along with two other groups, working for the release of Danny Davis, a Cairo, Illinois, man who spent 32 years behind bars after pleading guilty to the murder and robbery of a woman who ran a convenience store in the town.
Davis, according to the Innocence Project website, endured "psychological and physical abuse" after being brought in for initial questioning, including being threatened with the death penalty.
Davis and his brother, Isaac, signed false confession statements implicating themselves and another person. Davis pleaded guilty, he told a judge, because "I (wanted) to live."
IIP has helped secure the release of 25 innocent people.
GSIA cited the project for its work for reform at "all levels of policy, policing and government to reduce and eliminate wrong convictions in Illinois."
Golden said receiving recognition from people outside "who don't fully understand what we do but do understand the justice that comes out of the work that we do is so satisfying."
Several faith-based and justice-oriented groups, like the Springfield Dominicans, were particularly helpful to IIP in the early days, Golden said, when it had little funding outside of the university.
IIP also received the Humanitarian of the Year award in 2015. The second award reflected "the continued significance and statewide impact of their persistent and courageous advocacy for justice for the wrongfully convicted," according to GSIA.

title: New report finds two Springfield hospitals aren't fully compliant with price rules
author: Springfield State Journal
description: The report found of 65 hospitals reviewed in Illinois, only 15 were found to be in compliance with the federal rules.
content:
Both hospitals in Springfield failed to adequately update and publicize their prices online this year, according to a recent nonprofit report.
The nonprofit, Patient Rights Advocate, semi-annually examines 2,000 hospitals nationwide to identify compliance or not with a law that requires U.S. hospitals to make public a list of their standard charges. The law also requires hospitals to publish the list online and update annually.
The Hospital Price Transparency Rule was enacted in 2008 as part of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act.
Here's what you need to know.
Why did Springfield hospitals fail?
HSHS St. John's Hospital and Springfield Memorial Hospital both failed to fully comply, according to the report.
Springfield Memorial passed in most of the metrics but failed in the categories of Pricing Data Sufficiency Rating and CMS Validator Tool. There are 15 categories total.
St John's failed in the categories of Header Information, MRF Filename Format, and TXT File and Content.
What were overall results?
Of the 2,000 hospitals across the country reviewed, only 421 were found compliant.
How did other Illinois hospitals do?
Only 15 of 65 Illinois hospitals reviewed were fully complying with the rule, according to the report.
Who is Patient Rights Advocate?
The nonprofit is focused on systemwide healthcare price transparency, according to their site. 'Through advocacy, testimony, media, legal research, and grassroots campaigns, our organization seeks actual, upfront healthcare prices that will greatly lower costs through a functional, competitive healthcare marketplace,' their site reads.
It is worth noting that some criticism can be found of the organization from the American Hospital Association and the Healthcare Financial Management Association.
Do any other groups monitor this?
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, a federal agency, audits a 'sample of hospitals' related to the Hospital Price Transparency Rule. They also investigate any related, submitted complaints.
CMS enforces a national standard for the rule, and in 2019 added to the 2008 mandate by requiring hospitals to publish the list online and update it annually. Initially, hospitals only needed to provide the information upon request.
The agency has issued a total of 15 civil monetary penalties to U.S. hospitals.
In a search of publicly available data from CMS, the agency issued three separate actions following Hospital Transparency Compliance Reviews. They are only titled "Warning Notice", "CAP Request", and "Closure Notice."
HSHS St. John's does not appear in a search.
CMS did not immediately respond to requests from the SJ-R for available data of compliance in Illinois or the U.S.

title: Apple and Android users on notice from FBI about texts amid 'massive espionage campaign'
author: Mike Snider
description: FBI and homeland security officials suggest the use of encrypted texts on smartphones because texts between Apple and Android devices are not secure.
content:
Hackers could be after your text messages. Especially vulnerable: texts between Android and Apple devices.
Three weeks ago the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) revealed that hackers connected with the People's Republic of China had infiltrated the U.S. telecom infrastructure as part of "a broad and significant cyber espionage campaign."
Those targeted were "a limited number of individuals who are primarily involved in government or political activity," the agencies said at the time. Stolen were customer call records data and "certain information that was subject to U.S. law enforcement requests pursuant to court orders," the agencies said.
However, the hackers are apparently still at work and cybersecurity officials said this week they haven't been able to evict them from the networks of some telecom and internet firms.
On top of that, officials with those agencies are making a special point to remind smartphone users that text messages between Android devices and Apple devices are especially vulnerable, as they are not encrypted.
"Encryption is your friend, whether it is on text messaging or if you have the capacity to use encrypted voice communications, even if the adversary is able to intercept the data, if it is encrypted, it will make it impossible, if not really hard, for them to detect it. So, our advice is to try to avoid using plain text," said Jeff Greene, CISA executive assistant director for cybersecurity, during a press briefing held Tuesday.
Hackers have been able to steal a large amount of records including information on where, when and with whom people were communicating with, but no audio or actual text messages, a senior FBI official said during the briefing. However, some in the Washington, D.C. area did have audio and texts captured by the hackers, the official said.
Hackers still have access to the networks, officials said. And, Greene said, "We don't have any illusion that, once we're successful in evicting these actors, that they are not going to come back."
Text messages: What to know about security
In addition to seeking help from private companies to assess the reach of the attacks, officials suggested that people concerned about the security of their messaging should use encrypted messaging systems – think WhatsApp and Signal.
That's because if you are like most of us, some of our texting pals have Apple devices and some have Android devices. Messages sent between two Apple gadgets are encrypted, as are messages sent between users of Google Messages. But those between Android and Apple devices are not.
Federal Communications Commission Chair Jessica Rosenworcel on Thursday proposed agency action to ensure telecommunication companies be required to secure their networks.
"As technology continues to advance, so does the capabilities of adversaries, which means the U.S. must adapt and reinforce our defenses," said Rosenworcel in a press release.
Chinese hacking attack 'absolutely mind-boggling'
The Director of National Intelligence Avril Haines, the National Security Council, Rosenworcel, the FBI and CISA held a closed-door briefing for the U.S. Senate on Wednesday. Senators were updated on the long-running investigation into PRC-connected "threat actors" including a hacking group known as Salt Typhoon, which has infiltrated several telecom and internet firms including "at least" eight telecom firms in the U.S., including AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile.
"The extent and depth and breadth of Chinese hacking is absolutely mind-boggling – that we would permit as much as has happened in just the last year is terrifying," said Sen. Richard Blumenthal.
"This was part of a massive espionage campaign that has affected dozens of countries," the FCC said in a fact sheet.
Incoming FCC Chair Brendan Carr said Wednesday he will work "with national security agencies through the transition and next year in an effort to root out the threat and secure our networks."
Rosenworcel, a Democrat named as FCC chair by President Joe Biden, has announced she will leave the agency next month.
US companies respond to hacking attack
Among the companies infiltrated, Verizon said "several weeks ago, we became aware that a highly sophisticated, nation-state actor accessed several of the nation's telecom company networks, including Verizon" adding the incident was focused on a very small subset of individuals in government and politics.
AT&T said it is "working in close coordination with federal law enforcement, industry peers and cyber security experts to identify and remediate any impact on our networks."
T-Mobile and Lumen (formerly known as CenturyLink) both said there was no evidence hackers got access to customer data.
Chinese officials have previously described the allegations as disinformation and said Beijing "firmly opposes and combats cyber attacks and cyber theft in all forms."

title: Here's how to get the perfect sear on scallops
author: Channing Fullaway-Johnson
description: Making seafood at home can be tricky sometimes, so we want to offer some help. Here's how to get the perfect sear on scallops.
content:
My family, most simply put, is a blended family. With so many people coming together at the holidays with roots and traditions ranging from Illinois to the coast of Florida, it can get a little crazy.
However, we all agree it is not a holiday dinner without a seafood feast! Half the family does not like turkey, and the other does not like ham.
So, we started the tradition of a seafood feast many years ago. The family has grown, faces have changed, friends became family, and some are now missing, but we all find a way to fit around the dining room table for one big meal each year.
Of course, there are some family favorites that make the menu every year: baked salmon, seared scallops with garlic butter sauce, St. Augustine fried shrimp with famous pink sauce, poached white fish and some kind of crab dip. Everyone brings a side dish or dessert, and no one goes away hungry.
A few months ago, I shared the St. Augustine shrimp recipe and story from my hometown, and it is a crowd favorite. Coming in a close second are the seared scallops with garlic butter.
Choosing the right scallops can make or break the dish. I look for dry-packed scallops, which are free of added water or preservatives. There are many sizes to choose from, but do not let that overwhelm you.
I like using U10 scallops for this dish. "U,' meaning under, indicates that there are less than 10 scallops per pound.
On average, U10 scallops weigh about 1.5 to 2 ounces and are roughly 2-inches in diameter. The larger size makes them perfect to achieve that golden crust when searing them for your next dinner.
Make sure to remove the scallop foot, which is a small piece of tissue on the side of the scallop that connects it to the shell.
This piece is edible; however, it can be very chewy and not enjoyable. Next, I pat them dry with paper towels to remove excess moisture. This step and placing them in a pre-heated pan are the keys to achieving a golden crust.
Tips for the perfect sear: Use a large, heavy-bottomed skillet (preferably stainless steel or cast iron) to ensure even heat distribution and cooking. Also, do not rush the cooking. If you pre-heat your pan before placing the seasoned scallop and at 2 minutes it is sticking, give it more time. As they cook, they will naturally release from the pan and will be very easy to flip.
Garlic Seared Scallops
Ingredients
1 lb. dry-packed sea scallops
2 tbsp. olive oil
2 tbsp. unsalted butter
4 garlic cloves, minced
Salt and freshly ground pepper (to taste)
Fresh parsley, chopped (optional)
Lemon wedges (for serving)
Instructions:
Pat the scallops dry, and season with salt and pepper.
Heat a skillet over medium-high heat. Add olive oil and butter.
Once the butter is foamy, place scallops in the pan. Sear for 2-3 minutes on one side until golden brown.
Flip and cook for another 1-2 minutes. Then reduce the heat, add garlic and baste scallops with garlic butter.
Remove scallops from the pan, and drizzle with the remaining garlic butter.
Garnish with freshly chopped parsley and a squeeze of lemon juice for brightness.
Serve immediately.
Channing Fullaway-Johnson is the culinary coordinator at Lincoln Land Community College.
