The FBI did not respond to questions about the specific location of sightings along the 70-mile Raritan River, which at one point passes within about 10 miles of Trump National Golf Club
The FBI said it is launching an investigation into large drones that have been spotted flying over central New Jersey in the last several weeks.
On Tuesday, the FBI issued a joint statement with the New Jersey State Police and the State Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness asking for information related to "the recent sightings of possible drones flying in several areas along the Raritan River."
"Witnesses have spotted the cluster of what look to be drones and a possible fixed-wing aircraft," FBI spokesperson Amy Thoreson said. "We have reports from the public and law enforcement dating back several weeks."
The FBI is also investigating reports of a 'fixed-wing aircraft' seen flying along the Raritan River, according to reporting from The Daily Record, part of the USA TODAY Network.
The FBI did not respond to follow-up inquiries about the specific location of sightings along the 70-mile Raritan River, which flows through Somerset County, at one point passing within about 10 miles of Trump National Golf Club, the president-elect's frequent summer getaway in Bedminster, before flowing into Middlesex County and onto the Atlantic Coast.
The FAA bans drones in the area
Last month the Federal Aviation Administration issued a temporary flight restriction prohibiting drone flights over Trump National and the Picatinny Arsenal military research and manufacturing facility in Morris County. The move came "at the request of federal security partners," the FAA said.
Officials say there is no threat to public safety
Morris County Sheriff James Gannon said there was no current threat to the public in a statement published on Facebook on Monday.
'The recent drone activity observed by many in our communities is being actively investigated," Gannon said. "There is no advisable immediate danger to the public at this time, and the Sheriff's Office, along with many law enforcement agencies, are working in partnership on this matter."
But that does not mean that local residents haven't been spooked. Jonelle Ferentinos is one witness looking for more answers. Ferentinos told the Daily Record that she had seen the drones for several weeks when out for nightly dog walks. On Sunday night, she says she saw five of them.
"It was dark, so I really couldn't see where they were coming from or going to," she said. "They just seemed to be flying around."
The drones were back in her neighborhood Monday night, up to four at a time, hovering and moving about in different directions, she said.

title: Carson Arthalony leads PORTA, Gillespie girls beat Auburn, plus area top performers
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Carson Arthalony scores 21 in PORTA loss; Mia Brawner leads Gillespie past Auburn with 19 in area girls basketball.
content:
This is a daily list of top performers from Springfield-area high school sports teams for Dec. 9-14, compiled from information provided to The State Journal-Register by coaches, athletic directors and team statisticians.
To have your team's athletes included, email results to sports@sj-r.com.
Monday, Dec. 9
Girls basketball
Game of the night: Pittsfield 45, Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central 39
PETERSBURG — Carson Arthalony scored eight points in each of the first two quarters and led Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central with a team-high 21 points in a nonconference loss to unbeaten Pittsfield on Monday.
Junior cousins Aubrey Vogel and Allison Vogel combined for 14 points for the Bluejays (7-3 overall). Aubrey Vogel had eight points, six in the second half.
Pittsfield (9-0) got a game-high 23 points from freshman Reese Ramsey. She had eight points at halftime, nearly doubled her output with seven more in the third quarter and added another eight points in the final period.
'They're good. They've got a really balanced team,' PORTA coach Derek Schnapp said. 'They've got quickness. Obviously, Ramsey is a heck of a ballplayer who can shoot from outside and drive to the hoop.
'But she's got a lot of teammates that can really distribute the ball well. They've got young pieces and older pieces; they've got a very bright future.'
Senior Lila Simon added eight for Pittsfield, hitting two 3-pointers in the opening quarter.
PORTA led 22-21 at halftime but were outscored 11-7 in the third and 13-10 in the fourth.
— Ryan Mahan
Stars of the night
Mia Brawner, Gillespie: The Miners' senior notched 15 of her game-high 19 points in the second half as Gillespie turned a one-point halftime lead into a 71-65 nonconference win over Auburn in Gillespie. Brawner was 7-for-10 at the free-throw line, including hitting five of six in the fourth quarter as the Miners improved to 7-3 and grew their winning streak to seven games after starting out 0-3. Amari Vickery added 17 points for Gillespie while teammate Delaney Taylor scored 11.
Addison Wheatley, Auburn: The Trojans' senior center scored a team-best 18 points and was one of three players to reach double figures in Auburn's 71-65 road loss at Gillespie. Emme Divjak netted 12 points and hit two 3-pointers while Grayson Allen chipped in with 11.
Taylor Kiers, North Mac: The senior guard spearheaded a big second quarter and finished with a game-high 19 points in the Panthers' 46-31 nonconference win at Jacksonville at The Bowl. Keirs ended with two 3-pointers, went 5-for-6 from the foul line and had 15 first-half points and North Mac outscored the Crimsons 19-6 in the second quarter.
Natalie Brownback, Nokomis: The senior scored a game-high 12 points on 5 of 9 shooting and added three steals in Nokomis' 51-11 win over Ramsey. Sophomore Alivia Sabol had nine points and 12 rebounds and junior Kinley Stolte chipped in eight points and nine boards for NHS, which improved to 7-0.
Savana Howell, South County: She made two 3-pointers and scored 10 of her 16 points in the first period before South County rallied and defeated Kincaid South Fork 51-41. The Vipers outscored the Ponies 32-16 in the second half after trailing 25-19 at halftime.
Angelina Ippolito, Kincaid South Fork: The junior made a couple of 3-pointers and netted 14 of her 16 points in the first half in Kincaid's home loss to South County.
Maressa Williams, Jacksonville: She finished with a team-high 16 points in Jacksonville's home loss to North Mac.
Boys Swimming and Diving
Jackson Vinzant, Chatham Glenwood: The senior won the 200 and 500-yard freestyles and anchored Glenwood's winning 200 freestyle relay as the Titans finished second with 155 points in a quadrangular meet against first-place O'Fallon (181 points), Springfield High (133) and Sacred Heart-Griffin (29) at Eisenhower Pool.
Riley Herr, Springfield High: The junior won the 100 breaststroke and swam the breast on the Senators' second-place finish in the 200 medley relay in the quadrangular meet.

title: Rocky start, but Southeast's Hamilton vows improvement is the process
author: Ryan Mahan
description: While Southeast's boys basketball team is off to an 0-4 start, first-year head coach Wayne Hamilton promises improvement.
content:
For the first time since 2008, another coach other than Lawrence Thomas is guiding the Southeast boys basketball program.
When Wayne Hamilton Jr. took the court in the Spartans' season opener on Nov. 27 at Stephen Decatur Middle School, the 46-year-old first-time head coach was ready to put into practice all he had learned.
'It was a complete and total honor to be in this position,' Hamilton said. 'I've worked a long time to be able to get in this position, and I'm just blessed and honored to be in this position to be mentioned with the name of somebody like L.T. (Thomas).'
In terms of wins and losses, things haven't gone well for the 0-4 Spartans, but Hamilton is in it for the long haul, and he said the team will get better throughout the season.
'We've got some young talent on the team, and they got to learn the system and what we want to be trying to do,' Hamilton said. 'Two weeks is a little quick, so it's going to be a process for us this year.'
Thomas said he had hoped Hamilton would be the one to succeed him at Southeast.
'I'm about loyalty and Wayne's been with me for 12 years,' Thomas said. 'If I'm not respectful of everything that he's given me to the point where I can't support him in total for the position of head basketball coach at this school where I know he's grinded just as much as me, it's a no brainer.'
Hamilton and Thomas aren't the only ones who have faith. Lanphier coach Blake Turner, who worked with Hamilton when the two were assistants under then-Lanphier coach Chuck Shanklin, said Southeast made a great hire to replace L.T.
'They're going through some growing pains early, but I think he's doing the right thing, playing a bunch of young guys that can buy into his system and be able to come out and contribute,' Turner said. 'I know him, I know that he's not going to say a lot, he's not going to complain a lot, he's just going to put his head down and watch film, and get to work and keep working.
'In the conversations that I've had with him, that's what it sounds like he's been doing and I'm confident that that's what he'll do, and he'll get the program where it needs to be.'
Hamilton is a social studies teacher at Jefferson Middle School, and that will serve him well also, Turner and Thomas said.
"He teaches. He's a good coach. He likes the game," Thomas said. "He likes teaching the game. He's very positive. P.J. (Hamilton's nickname), his coaching style, he charts in every column. He's very competitive. He's smart. He's got all the intangibles that it takes to be successful in coaching. Regardless if we're talking basketball. He's great. He's patient. He's got a lot of traits that I wish I had."
Turner added, "I think that P.J. is a laid-back, no-nonsense kind of guy. He's quiet, but he's one of those guys where you can't mistake his kindness for weakness.
'He's a teacher, so he's really invested in kids, he does a good job teaching, teaching basketball to kids, teaching the offense, teaching the defense, and I just think that once he gets a class of kids to come through there that learn his terminology, learn the way that he wants them to play and learn his system, I think that he'll be good.'
Southeast opened the Decatur Turkey Tournament with a 67-37 loss to Decatur MacArthur, then dropped a 69-33 decision to another Central State Eight Conference member, Sacred Heart-Griffin. In the seventh-place game, Southeast fell to O'Fallon, 71-39. The Spartans were off until a 52-31 loss to Rochester in the CS8-opening Showcase Saturday at the Bank of Springfield Center on Saturday.
'It's a lot of things that are correctable,' Hamilton said. 'We've just got to put in the effort and look at the film and get back to the drawing board.'
Two recent Southeast alumni are on the bench helping Hamilton: 2019 graduate Anthony Fairlee, The State Journal-Register's Large School Boys Basketball Player of the Year in 2018, and Trevyon Williams, a 2017 Southeast graduate.
Despite their youth, Hamilton praised their maturity and said they were big assets to the program.
'I don't see these guys as kids (or) I wouldn't have hired them,' Hamilton said. 'These guys, when I went through the hiring process, I saw the hunger that they have. I saw the passion that they have for our school and our team, because they've been through the fire and everything like that.
'I surprisingly saw some maturity from them as talking to them and being around them. Anthony has a young son right now, and he's being a wonderful, tremendous father. These guys have matured, and they're going to continue to mature, and they're going to learn how to be good coaches.'
What's Hamilton's biggest takeaway from the start of the season?
'We've just got to get better,' he said.

title: Two men convicted in triple homicide sentenced to natural life behind bars
author: Steven Spearie
description: At the time, Sangamon County Coroner\u00a0Jim Allmon\u00a0called it \
content:
Two defendants found guilty of first-degree murder on Sept. 25 for their roles in a 2021 triple homicide in the 2500 block of South 10th Street in Springfield both received natural life sentences in Sangamon County court Monday.
Kelton Galmore of Jacksonville and Larry McClain Jr. of Springfield were sentenced by Presiding Circuit Judge Ryan Cadagin.
A third defendant, Joseph Hembrough of Jacksonville, pleaded guilty to first-degree murder on Sept. 9 and was sentenced to 20 years in prison. He testified against both defendants.
Galmore and McClain were also found guilty of armed violence and armed robbery. The jury trial lasted nine days.
Galmore fatally shot Bryant K. Williams, 27, of Houston and formerly of Springfield. McClain fatally shot Savante English, 27. Both were found guilty of shooting Keyera Gant, 25.
At the time, Sangamon County Coroner Jim Allmon called it "one of the most horrific scenes" he had ever witnessed in his career.
Family members of Williams and English testified at Monday's sentencing.
English and Gant, who were cousins, lived in the rental home in the Harvard Park neighborhood.
English and Williams, a budding rapper who went by the name BK Yola, were childhood friends in Springfield. Williams was scheduled to return home the day of the murder.
English, Williams and Gant were found in the home on Aug. 9, 2021.
At trial, Hembrough testified that Galmore texted him shortly before the shooting, saying he was looking for "a new connection" or drug supplier. Hembrough said Galmore showed him a Snapchat post of a red car and large sums of money and told Hembrough they could buy methamphetamine from Williams or "get it for free," meaning they could rob him.
As a deal was being made, Hembrough testified that Williams started yelling at McClain about showing up late and bringing other people, leading to the shooting.
Neither Mark Wykoff nor Monroe McWard, defense attorneys for McClain and Galmore respectively, put on witnesses. Neither defendant took the stand.
"Our thoughts and prayers are with the grieving families of the victims in this case," Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser said in a text statement. "Let the sentences today serve as a message that if you commit violent crimes, we will use all the tools available to bring you to justice.
"These defendants can no longer cause harm in our community and will remain locked up for the rest of their lives."
Handling the case for the State were special Assistant State's Attorney Derek Dion and Assistant State's Attorneys Meghan McCarthy and Kaylan Beard.

title: First look: State unveils 10 finalists for new Illinois flag
author: Tom Ackerman
description: One has a butterfly on it. Others nod to Chicago, the Mississippi River and other Illinois waterways, Abraham Lincoln, and agriculture. Which is your favorite?
content:
The top 10 designs for a new possible state flag may surprise you.
One has a butterfly on it. Others nod to Chicago, the Mississippi River and other Illinois waterways, Abraham Lincoln, and agriculture.
The Illinois Flag Commission has selected its top 10 finalists out of nearly 5,000 submissions for the state flag redesign contest.
Are we getting a new flag for certain?
Beginning in January, the public will be able to vote for one of the 10 new designs, or for one of the three former flag designs including the current state flag, the 1918 Centennial Flag and the 1968 Sesquicentennial Flag.
How will the winner be decided?
After the public votes, the commission will then report these results to the Illinois General Assembly by April 1. Assembly members will vote on whether to adopt a new flag, return to a previous version of the flag or retain the current flag.
Why is the state considering a new flag design?
A constituent of Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, introduced the idea, leading she and Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago to move forward the legislation which created the commission later signed into law by Gov. JB Pritzker.
"I have always said that history is living, breathing and ever evolving, and I think we need to ensure that government is also evolving so people are engaged," Turner previously said.
The original flag, designed by Rockford native Lucy Derwent in 1915, featured the state seal in front of a white background. It has remained the same since with exception for the addition of the word "Illinois" placed below the seal in 1969.
Where can I view the flag designs?
You can view the 10 designs at the ilsos.gov. website.

title: From festive lights to old world markets, these destinations are worth the drive from Springfield
author: Steven Spearie
description: From light displays to holiday markets, these Midwest events will put you in a festive mood and are worth the drive from Springfield.
content:
From light displays to holiday markets, these Midwest events will put you in a festive mood.
Kids can meet Santa Claus, in a town named after him. Families can glide along the ice or even duck the cold weather in a heated igloo.
Check out these holiday destinations, all within short drives of Springfield.
Christkindlmarkt
Christkindlmarkts ("Christkind" translates into "Christ child") date back to the early 18th century in Germany.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Belleville replicates the Nuremburg Christkindlmarkt on the Public Square (Illinois 159 and Main Street) through Dec. 23.
Some 20 vendors will be featuring unique European and handcrafted items. The are German bands and folk dancers; gingerbread creation displays; horse-drawn trolley rides; a cookie stroll, a petting zoo and Santa on the Square.
The Christkindlmarkt operates from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Thursday through Saturday; 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Sunday and 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Dec. 23.
Visit bellevillechristkindlmarkt.com for more information.
A Christkindlmarkt in Carmel, Ind., about 45 minutes north of Indianapolis, features German artisans and craftsmen, an ice-skating rink, German food and drink and a children's area in the town's center. A 33-foot-tall "Christmas pyramid" features over 3,000 lights.
It runs through Christmas Eve. For days and hours of operation, visit christkindlmarkt.com.
Chicago's Christkindlmarket in Daley Plaza, 50 W. Washington St., runs through Dec. 24.
The market is open from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Friday and Saturday.
Way of Lights, Belleville
The Way of Lights at Our Lady of the Snows, a Catholic shrine in Belleville operated by the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate, uses over 1.5 million lights to depict the journey of Mary and Joseph as they travel to Bethlehem.
Other activities include area bands and choirs; camel, donkey and pony rides for the kids; a LEGO brick display; a selfie stand and a food stand.
The drive-through display is open nightly from 5 to 9 p.m. through Dec. 31. Donations are accepted.
Santa Claus, Indiana
How can you go wrong with a town named after the Big Guy himself?
Located at the southwestern tip of the Hoosier State and about a four-and-a-half-hour drive from Springfield, family-friendly favorites include a 1.2-mile Christmas light drive-through at Sun Outdoors Lake Rudolph ($20 per vehicle through Dec. 23) and a live reindeer exhibit at Santa's TOYS.
There's also a Santa Claus Christmas Parade (Dec. 14) and ongoing activities like Christmas cookie decorating, dinner with Santa and roasting chestnuts.
Since the post office there gets letters to Santa from all over the world, it's a tradition for "volunteer elves" to reply to children's letters with a postmark from Santa Claus, Ind.
For more information, visit santaclausind.org
East Peoria Festival of Lights
The East Peoria Festival of Lights celebrates its 40th anniversary this year with the lighted display running through Jan. 5.
Forty floats that made up the Nov. 23 parade are now part of the drive-through portion at 123 Par 3 Lane.
Crowd favorites include a 160-foot Steam Train, a replica of a Clydesdale horse team pulling a wagon, a Chinese Dragon and a Giant Blue Whale.
Admission is $10 per regular vehicle. You can also see the display via a horse-drawn wagon.
For more all the details, visit folepi.org or call 1-855-833-5327.
Winterfest in St. Louis
Winterfest returns to Kiener Plaza in St. Louis through New Year's Eve.
There's ice skating, s'mores stations, holiday-themed karaoke and even heated igloos for rent underneath 100,000 twinkling lights.
For more information, visit archpark.org.
While in St. Louis, there are holiday light displays at Grant's Farm (10501 Gravois Rd.) and the Anheuser-Busch Brewery (721 Pestalozzi St.), both drive-through and walk-through, and Missouri Botanical Garden (4344 Shaw Ave.), walk-through.

title: Here are The State Journal-Register's All-Area boys, girls golfers of the year and teams
author: Bill Welt
description: Sacred Heart-Griffin's Izzy Hassebrock again leads the best high school golfers in the Springfield area. Who else joined her on the boys and girls all-area teams this fall?
content:
Here are The State Journal-Register's boys and girls golfers of the year, plus other members of the Springfield all-area team.
Boys Golf
➤ Drew Downen, Chatham Glenwood
Everything clicked at the right time for Downen.
He tied for third place individually at the Class 3A Decatur MacArthur Sectional and the Titans celebrated an elusive team state berth at Hickory Point Golf Course.
Downen shot even-par 72 at sectionals after shooting 2-over 74 in the Collinsville Regional, where the Titans captured the team title.
Downen, The State Journal-Register's Large School Boys Golfer of the Year, also won the individual Central State Eight Conference title, shooting even-par 71 at the Lincoln Elks Club.
➤ Sam Schwab, Litchfield
The junior ushered the best state performance among boys golfers in the area.
He finished 12-over 156 after two rounds and tied for 21st place in the Class 1A state finals at Prairie Vista.
He also tied for third place in the Mount Olive Regional with junior teammate Tucker Maguire, shooting 76. He later carded an even-par 71 for second place at the Ziegler-Royalton Sectional.
He is The State Journal-Register's Small School Boys Golfer of the Year after his older brother, Tug, won the award in 2022.
➤ Colton Barr, Jacksonville
The senior won the Class 2A Canton Regional title with a 2-under 70 before taking 36th place at the 2A state finals at Weibring Golf Club.
➤ A.J. Charpentier, Jacksonville
The junior nearly catapulted the Crimsons to the Class 2A team sectional title at the University of Illinois. He tied for fifth place individually, shooting 73. Charpentier also tied for second place at the Central State Eight Conference meet. He wound up 44th at the 2A state finals.
➤ Derek Dulceak, Chatham Glenwood
The senior pieced together a strong postseason run: A 3-under 69 for fourth place at the Class 3A Collinsville Regional before a 76 at the Decatur MacArthur Sectional to make the state finals at The Den at Fox Creek, where he opened with a 75 before tying for 76th.
➤ Brayden Mueller, Chatham Glenwood
The senior shot a team-best 68 at the Collinsville regional for third place. He helped cement a team state berth with a 78 at sectionals.
Girls Golf
➤ Izzy Hassebrock, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The senior's stellar high school career concluded with another individual state medal and team trophy at Red Tail Run in Decatur.
The Idaho State University commit finished at 3-over-par 147 and tied for second place in the 1A state finals. She became the school's first girls golf state champion with the same score last year.
The Cyclones also repeated as state runners-up behind four-time champion Mount Carmel.
During the regular season, Hassebrock captured the Central State Eight Conference individual championship and spurred the team to first place. SHG also claimed its second consecutive regional and sectional team titles.
Hassebrock is The State Journal-Register's back-to-back Large School Girls Golfer of the Year.
"We practiced really hard every day," Hassebrock said after the state finals. "We had great coaches who led us here. Everyone worked really hard, especially in the postseason. Everyone just knows what they need to work on and how to practice in order to improve."
➤ Alaina Ervin, Pleasant Plains
The senior improved on last year's state performance and tied Hassebrock for second place in the Class 1A state finals.
Ervin took seventh a year ago.
She grabbed the individual Sangamo Conference title in each of her four seasons and won this year's Williamsville Regional at The Rail.
She departs as The State Journal-Register's Small School Girls Golfer of the Year, her first after former Athens standout Catalina Easley won the award the previous two seasons.
'I'm very happy about it,' Ervin said of her high school career. 'I don't even know what else to say about it, I've had so much support over the past couple years and especially this year. It's surreal.'
➤ Lilly Bandy, Staunton
The senior eked into the Class 1A state finals and tied for 68th place.
➤ Maddy Johnston, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The sophomore fell just shy of the individual Class 1A Rochester Sectional title in a playoff that also included Hassebrock. The two led SHG to the team title despite bowing to Carlyle's Sarah Hyten. Johnston placed 17th at the state finals and returns to the all-area team for a second straight year.
➤ Macie Petropoulos, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The senior is also back on the all-area team. She tied for 38th at the state finals to round out the team score. She finished among the top 10 individually in the Rochester Sectional and Williamsville Regional.
➤ Natalie Zak, Sacred Heart-Griffin
The junior scored a team-best 77 to lead the Cyclones to a second straight Class 1A regional title at The Rail. The two-time all-area honoree also missed the sectional playoff by just two strokes before tying for 30th at the state finals.

title: Morgan County to pay $6M in settlement over inmate's death in 2022
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Morgan County has agreed to a settlement of $6 million after the 2022 death of inmate Brian Downs. Here's what happened.
content:
Morgan County has agreed to settle a lawsuit by paying $6 million after the death of a former inmate at the Morgan County Detention Facility.
Brian Downs died in April 2022 from complications related to heroin withdrawal while in jail, according to a complaint filed in the U.S. District Court in Springfield. The lawsuit argued Downs did not receive appropriate medical care.
Downs was arrested and jailed on April 22, 2022. One day later, he started vomiting, including blood, over the course of 34 hours, according to the complaint.
Downs died on April 25 after going into cardiac arrest while he was locked in a medical holding cell at the jail, the complaint read.
"During this time period, no employee of the jail notified a qualified health provider, nor did they transport Brian to the emergency department at [Jacksonville Memorial Hospital]," the complaint read.
Julie Downs, the administrator of Brian Downs' estate, and attorney Richard Frazier filed a motion for finding a good faith settlement. The collective parties in defense of the county agreed on the settlement with Frazier and Downs on June 6.
Frazier said he expects the settlement to be approved soon.
The groups agreed to the settlement "to avoid the uncertainty, expense, and burden associated with further litigation" the motion reads.
Downs died of dehydration as well as septic shock due to bowel obstruction as a consequence of small bowel intussusception in the setting of opioid withdrawal syndrome, the complaint said, citing the autopsy.

title: 'Great fun': Lincoln girls basketball coach sees progress in new team after state run
author: Adrian Dater
description: Defending 3A champion Lincoln girls basketball continues to trend in right direction with new lineup and defeated Rochester on Friday
content:
LINCOLN – Taylor Rohrer's voice could be heard by everyone, even up in the nosebleeds of the Lincoln High School gym, for most of Friday night's Railsplitters girls basketball game against Rochester. Rohrer paced up and down the length of her team's bench, at times screaming in exasperation and sharing anguish over her team's play with equally vociferous assistant coach Cory Farmer.
For the coach of the defending Class 3A state champion Railers, this constituted, in her words, 'great fun.'
'It's fun, because it's a different way, a different style. I get to really help and teach these kids in doing what I love,' Rohrer said after Lincoln's 45-35 victory over Rochester. 'Right now, we coach a lot in the games, and maybe the last two years we coached a lot more in practice than they did it in the games. But both are fun and exciting in their own right.'
All-area volleyball: Here are The State Journal-Register's All-Area volleyball players of the year and teams
Lincoln went unbeaten last season at 38-0 and won the state title with a 60-44 win over Chatham Glenwood, and Rohrer was named The State Journal-Register's Coach of the Year for 2023-24. That senior-laden team is now populated with more juniors and new seniors so things haven't come as easy for the Railers, now 5-4 overall after this victory.
Rohrer, however, is seeing progress and a fresh identity forming in her team.
'When you're coaching, you're just trying to improve your team every game, every practice, no matter what team you have. And, I see that in our girls. I see them showing up and wanting to work hard and get better, and I think we've seen that in our games, where the things we're doing in practice is starting to transfer onto the floor,' Rohrer said. 'You want to play your best basketball in February, and we're working toward that.'
Despite a 3-9 overall record coming in, Rochester took a lead in the second quarter after falling behind 15-14, thanks in part to a couple of 3-point field goals from senior Taylor Offer. That's when the voices of Rohrer and Farmer went up many decibels, and that had the right effect on her players.
Up 35-27 after three quarters, the Railers got the ball inside more to 5-foot-9 senior forward Makinley Knapp, and she put home several shots in the paint as part of a 16-point effort. Junior guard/forward Lily Holmes made some key free throws down the stretch as well, and she scored a game-high 19 points. Lincoln junior Mia Clark had five points, five assists and six rebounds.
Knapp, who has played all four years for the Railers in her high-school career, said her younger teammates are learning.
'We definitely had a couple of really good years (74-1 overall), but this year we've just had to kind of get in that groove of 'OK, it's us now.' We've got to really work hard in practice and push ourselves and keep playing good defense the whole game, not just the first half,'' Knapp said.
The Rockets got 15 points from junior Delaney Farris, with nine from Offer and five from Alaina Stock. Rochester had good ball movement throughout and plenty of good looks at the basket, but went through too many cold stretches with their shooting.
'We just couldn't string enough offensive possessions together,' Rochester coach Brandon Rose said. 'We just didn't have that flow. We got the lead, but it just didn't continue on. But I'm proud of our team for coming into a tough place to play and giving them a tough game. It's something we can build on moving forward.'

title: How Springfield High boys hoops answered the bell with comeback win over Jacksonville
author: Adrian Dater
description: Sink or swim? Springfield High's Jaiyden Wilson, Valor Komolafe show mettle in comeback win over Jacksonville
content:
The Springfield Senators trailed for most of the first 29 minutes of Saturday's Central State Eight boys basketball game with visiting Jacksonville.
The Senators trailed by eight points after three quarters, and the noise level inside Willard Duey Gymnasium was only slightly above that of, say, Lincoln Library.
And then, everything went Springfield's way. Marques Warfield's Senators wound up walking off the court to a rousing cheer from the home fans, after a stunning 14-point fourth quarter turnaround that gave Springfield a 69-62 victory.
Whereas there were plenty of turnovers in the first three quarters, suddenly Springfield took great care of the ball. Whereas there were moments when Springfield seemed uninterested on defense, suddenly the Senators were ball hawks who forced the Crimsons into rushed shots and turnovers.
For Springfield (5-5, 2-1 Central State Eight), it was another teaching moment in the young season. The lesson being, when they want, the Senators can be an explosive, dominant team.
'At halftime (down 41-34) I went in and I challenged them. I told them, 'they're only in the game based on our mistakes.' We had almost 20 turnovers in the first half, we shot poorly from the free-throw line and didn't capitalize on layups and stuff like that,' Warfield said. 'That's all mental. So, my challenge to them was: are you going to respond or are you going to make excuses? We had a bunch of guys that wanted to make excuses, but we wouldn't let them. I'm not going to let them off the hook.'
Warfield got balanced scoring, with senior Valor Komolafe leading the way with 16 points and 14 rebounds. The player who really sparked Springfield in the fourth quarter comeback, though, was senior guard Jaiyden Wilson.
Wilson scored eight of his 12 points in the fourth, and gave Springfield its first lead (62-61) since the opening minutes. Wilson used a quick first step off the dribble to hit some mid-range jumpers from the right side as a featured part of his repertoire.
'Everything for us starts with defense with us, so basically I think we started from there,' said Wilson, when asked how his team was able to mount such a big, late comeback. 'I think we just played together, played as a team for once in the game.'
Komolafe, a 6-foot-6 center, was strong on the boards at both ends in the fourth quarter and showed a soft touch from the free-throw line, hitting three big ones in the final minutes.
'At halftime, our coach said, hey, you're either going to sink or swim and we decided to swim,' Komolafe said. 'We were able to play better defense and had less turnovers, and hit our shots.'
Springfield also got a big second half contribution from junior Logan Peach, who came off the bench to score 11 points. Noah Wade had a somewhat sluggish first half, but finished with 14 points, while Arielle Robinson added eight and Elijah Wade six.
Jacksonville (3-5, 1-2) played a solid first three quarters, spreading the floor well and getting good production from senior guard Amaree Burries, whose game-high 23 points included a rousing dunk off the fast break.
But the Senators did a better job on him defensively in the fourth.
'I think we just settled too much, with our lead, instead of keeping our foot on the gas,' Burries said. 'They sped us up a little bit and forced some turnovers.'
Junior guard Masen Johnson had 15 points for Jacksonville, while Troy DeFrates added eight.
Springfield will get a strong test on Monday when they play East St. Louis in a nonconference game.
'Our schedule is set up the way it is to set us up for February,' Warfield said. 'Everybody starts 0-0. We're learning that when we get some adversity, if we challenge our minds, we can overcome it.'

title: Springfield bar and grill catches fire on Christmas Day
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A bar and grill at the corner of North Grand Avenue and MacArthur Boulevard caught fire on Wednesday morning.
content:
(This story was updated to meet our standards and to add new information.)
A bar and grill at the corner of North Grand Avenue and MacArthur Boulevard caught fire on Wednesday morning.
The driver of a Toyota Camry crashed into the building causing the fire around 4:30 a.m.
Before slamming into MVPs Bar & Grill, the driver knocked down a traffic signal, Springfield Fire Chief Ed Canny said.
More: Open for business: Fire Station 6 moves into new home for first time since 1954
The burning vehicle lit the west side of the building on fire. The flames spread into the rest of the building and into the attic, Canny said.
The car most likely caught fire due to impact, but the cause remains under investigation. Cars often hit buildings, but they seldom catch fire as a result, Canny added.
No injuries were reported.
Fire crews were on scene until 7:30 or 8 a.m.
The barbecue/soul food restaurant had operated at the site since September. There was no immediate word if the restaurant was a total loss.
Neither Springfield Police officials nor the bar and grill's owner were able to be reached immediately for comment.

title: Springfield officer cleared in shooting of 19-year-old as police release bodycam footage
author: Steven Spearie
description: Along with authorities announcing no charges will be filed against the officer, police released bodycam footage from the shooting.
content:
Show Caption
Sangamon County State's Attorney John Milhiser said no charges will be filed against a Springfield Police officer involved in the shooting of a Springfield teen outside of a restaurant at South Martin Luther King Jr. Drive and Kansas Street on Sept. 4.
On Dec. 20, Springfield Police released footage from body cameras worn by four different SPD officers at the scene.
Milhiser's decision followed the completion of an Illinois State Police independent investigation.
In a letter dated Friday, Milhiser said he reviewed "applicable law and thoroughly examined all of the evidence based in the Illinois State Police investigation."
Milhiser said "taking into consideration the totality of the circumstances" that SPD Officer Jesse Schmillen "was justified in the use of deadly force and the discharge of his firearm" against Carrington James, 19.
In the aftermath of the shooting, the scene was described by SPD Chief Ken Scarlette as "extremely chaotic...in which frustration and anger were boiling over."
The ISP investigation determined that James, a passenger in a vehicle that had been stopped at Mr. Gyro's in the 1100 block MLK Drive, fired a shot from his gun as he exited the vehicle and began to run away from the officers.
Bodycam footage reviewed by The State Journal-Register showed James verbally sparring with the officer and clutching his waistband as he ran away.
Schmillen fired five shots, striking James in the head, spine and leg.
James was identified by SPD as a suspect in a shooting in the 1600 block of South 16th Street earlier on the afternoon of Sept. 4.
In that shooting, a picture window of a home was struck with gunfire from James from inside a vehicle. Five people were inside the home at the time.
A 14-year-old who was playing outside gave police a physical description of the gunman and another person in the car and vehicle information.
Schmillen, in a report detailed in Milhiser's finding, said he believed the shot from James was "directed at myself and other officers on the scene."
"The reasonable belief by Officer Schmillen (that James was an imminent deadly threat to officers and the public) justifies his subsequent use of deadly force in discharging his firearm," Milhiser concluded.
Scarlette, reached Friday by The State Journal-Register, said Schmillen remained on restricted duty.
The department, Scarlette said, still needs to conduct a use of force review and a fit for duty/psychological evaluation before Schmillen returns to normal duty.
Schmillen has been with the department for four years, according to Scarlette.
Scarlette said his thoughts and prayers were with the officers at the scene along with their families and James and his family.
Black Lives Matter SPI, the Springfield Community Roundtable and Springfield Coalition for Dismantling Racism were among the groups that viewed body worn camera footage the day after the shooting.
To see the body cam footage, go to the city of Springfield's webpage. (Please note the video contains disturbing content and may not be appropriate for all viewers.

title: President Biden commutes sentences of most federal death row inmates
author: Francesca Chambers
description: President Joe Biden commuted the sentences of all but three inmates on federal death row to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
content:
WASHINGTON − President Joe Biden said he was commuting the sentences of nearly every inmate on federal death row, a move meant to stop President-elect Donald Trump from restarting stalled executions
"In good conscience, I cannot stand back and let a new administration resume executions that I halted," Biden said in a statement Monday.
The move reduces the sentences of 37 of 40 federal death row prisoners, in keeping with a moratorium his administration imposed on executions. The 37 now face sentences of life without parole. The moratorium excludes people convicted of terrorism and hate-motivated mass murder.
The list of commutations released by the White House does not include Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, who was convicted in the Boston Marathon bombing in 2013 that killed three people and injured more than 260, or Robert Bowers, who was convicted in the 2018 Tree of Life synagogue mass shooting in Pittsburgh that killed 11 people.
Biden also declined to commute the sentence of Dylann Roof, who was convicted in the mass shooting in Charleston, South Carolina, at Mother Emanuel, an African American church, in 2015. Nine people were killed.
Among the death row prisoners who had their sentences commuted and will now face life in prison: Thomas Steven Sanders, sentenced to death for the kidnapping and murder of a 12-year-old girl in Louisiana; Len Davis, a former police officer sentenced to death for ordering the killing of a woman after she filed a complaint against him at the New Orleans Police Department; and Richard Allen Jackson, who was convicted of the kidnapping, rape and murder of a 22-year-old jogger in Asheville, North Carolina.
Biden had pledged to end the death penalty during his presidential campaign and had been under pressure from progressive lawmakers and criminal justice activists to commute the sentences of federal death row inmates before Trump takes office.
"Make no mistake: I condemn these murderers, grieve for the victims of their despicable acts, and ache for all the families who have suffered unimaginable and irreparable loss," Biden said in a statement.
But, he said, "I am more convinced than ever that we must stop the use of the death penalty at the federal level."
Trump has said he would seek to expand the death penalty in his second term. In Trump's first term at the White House, his administration carried out 13 federal executions, ending a 17-year hiatus.
All but three of the 16 people who have been executed for federal crimes since 1988 were put to death during Trump's term in office. No prisoners on federal death row were executed during Biden's presidency or vice presidency.
A spokesman for Trump criticized the commutations in a Monday afternoon statement.
"These are among the worst killers in the world and this abhorrent decision by Joe Biden is a slap in the face to the victims, their families, and their loved ones," Trump communications director Steven Cheung said. "President Trump stands for the rule of law, which will return when he is back in the White House after he was elected with a massive mandate from the American people."
Biden's commutations met with mixed reaction
Pope Francis had publicly urged Biden, who is Catholic, to stop the executions. Biden and Francis spoke by phone last week.
After the White House's announcement, advocates and lawmakers who had pleaded with Biden not to execute death row inmates praised the commutations.
Patrick Gaspard, president and CEO of the liberal Center for American Progress, said Biden had "cemented his legacy as a champion for mercy, compassion and justice for all."
Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., who is among more than five dozen Democratic lawmakers who urged Biden to use his clemency power on his way out, said Biden's decision would "save lives, address the deep racial disparities in our criminal legal system, and send a powerful message about redemption, decency, and humanity."
'The death penalty is a racist, flawed, and fundamentally unjust punishment that has no place in any society," she said.
According to the Legal Defense Fund, as of January of 2024, roughly 40% of the inmates on death row in the United States were Black, 42% were white and 14% were Hispanic. Another 3% were Asian or Native American.
Republicans in Congress blasted Biden for the move.
A "horrific betrayal of justice," Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, said in an X post.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., called the decision "horrifying." He detailed several of the inmates' crimes in a string of posts and said: "Their victims deserve better, and justice demands more."
The commutations were "senseless" and an "outrageous example of this administration's upside down and backwards ideology," added Rep. Dan Meuser, R-Pa.
Biden has vigorously exercised his clemency powers as he prepares to exit office. He commuted the sentences of nearly 1,500 people who had been on home confinement since the COVID-19 pandemic earlier in the month in what the White House called "the largest single-day act of clemency in modern history."
Biden also pardoned 39 people who were convicted of nonviolent crimes. He issued a sweeping pardon to his son Hunter Biden in early December for charges that included gun and tax offenses.
Trump also made use of his clemency power near the end of his presidency. He issued 74 pardons and 70 commutations on his last full day in office.
Contributing: Joey Garrison

title: New plan to strengthen power grid will likely mean higher bills for Illinois residents
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A $3.3 billion plan to strengthen power grid reliability and support the electrification of the state's power system will likely mean higher bills.
content:
A newly approved $3.3 billion plan to strengthen power grid reliability and support the electrification of the state's power system will likely mean higher energy bills for Illinois consumers.
The Illinois Commerce Commission approved Commonwealth Edison's plan this week as well as that of Ameren Illinois.
The Climate and Equitable Jobs Act required the state's largest investor-owned utilities to progress towards Illinois' clean energy goals and hold electric companies accountable for their performance, according to a press release from the ICC.
Per ICC's decision, ComEd customers will pay for an increase of $606 million over the next four years, while Ameren's customers will pay $309 million.
The impact of the decision on individual customers will vary based on service class and energy usage.
The two companies' plans are respectively consolidated with their multi-year rate plans 'to determine which system maintenance and upgrade costs can be passed on to ratepayers, at a reasonable cost,' the release read.
'After extensive review, the Commission is confident that both ComEd and Ameren have the tools necessary to make needed investments to drive the clean energy transition and continue modernizing Illinois' electric grid,' ICC Chairman Doug Scott said in a news release. 'These plans are a key component to meeting the goals of CEJA and represent significant improvement in meeting its requirements.'
Scott also said the investments approved will deliver significant benefits to customers in an affordable, cost-effective manner.
ComEd's rate increases are 11% lower than requested per the ICC decision and Ameren's rate increases are 7% lower than requested, according to the release.

title: Dee-Mack wins tussle over PORTA between girls basketball championship rivals
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Last month, Petersburg PORTA held Dalia DeJesus to three points to win the Clinton Turkey Tussle. On Saturday, DeJesus led the Chiefs to beat PORTA for Riverton title.
content:
RIVERTON — Deer Creek-Mackinaw wanted a rematch with Petersburg PORTA. The Chiefs' 5-foot-11 junior Dalia DeJesus really wanted a rematch with the Bluejays.
After being held to just three points in PORTA's win over Dee-Mack to take home the Clinton Turkey Tussle championship on Nov. 23, DeJesus gave a much better performance to lead Dee-Mack to a 43-35 win over top-seeded PORTA to win the Riverton Christmas Classic tournament on Saturday.
DeJesus had 14 points, including eight in the final period to hold off a potential PORTA rally.
'I did the watch the (Nov. 23) game about three times to critique myself,' DeJesus said. 'I think overall, how aggressive I was tonight did not at all match how I played before. Even though it was three weeks ago, I have much more trust in myself and my teammates and I really owe it all to them.'
The Chiefs (13-2) have won 10 straight. On Saturday at the Hawk Center, Dee-Mack was dialed in from behind the 3-point line and finished 7-for-21 (33%). Sophomore Kate Schmidgall's first 3-point attempt, from the corner, managed to bank off the glass and drop in to start Dee-Mack's scoring. DeJesus got on the board with a putback bucket before Jaelyn Nunley, a junior, tied the game 8-8 with a corner 3 of her own.
'Part of it was we weren't prepared for the defense we saw the first time,' Dee-Mack coach Joni Nightingale said. 'This time we were a little educated in what they might throw at us.
'It just speaks to the resiliency of not only Dalia, but this whole team, to trust this process and know we have plans in place for a reason.'
PORTA (12-4) struggled in the second quarter. Freshman Regan Heubner had two buckets in the period to account for the Bluejays' only scoring as Dee-Mack took a 21-14 halftime lead. Meanwhile, the Chiefs hit three 3s by three different players.
'Dee-Mack's a good team,' PORTA coach Derek Schnapp said of the tournament's third seed. 'I think I was the only coach who seeded them first in this tournament because I know they're a good ballclub.
'They're balanced, they go deep and all of them can shoot the 3. They're hard to guard. We tried to throw a junk defense: it worked the first time, not so much the second time.'
With the Bluejays trailing 29-17 in the third, junior Aubrey Vogel (team-high 14 points) sparked an 8-0 PORTA rally as the Bluejays closed the game to 29-25, but DeJesus hit a runner in the final seconds to push the Chiefs' lead back to six points after three quarters.
'Our biggest thing the last few weeks is being composed and being smart,' DeJesus said. 'I think we did a very good job of that and, in turn, we got some very good looks.'
PORTA senior Carson Arthalony (12 points) tried to spark another run in the fourth when she hit a 3-pointer with 4 minutes, 23 seconds left to cut Dee-Mack's lead to 35-29. PORTA had a chance to trim that in half when Vogel took another 3, but a referee blew the play dead and said she traveled, despite the ball falling in the net.
Both Schnapp and DeJesus said they'd embrace a chance at a best-of-three tiebreaker.
'I would (like to play PORTA once more),' DeJesus said. 'They're a good team and I think if we play them again, it would be a lot more competitive because we're tied now.'
Schnapp saw a bigger picture with the question.
'It would be great to see it, because if it happens, it would be in the big house (the state tournament in Normal,' Schnapp said.
Third-place game
ROANOKE-BENSON 47, HILLSBORO 46: In a game that went down to the wire, the undermanned Hiltoppers still put three players in double figures despite the loss of the injured Tatum Christian, who suffered an ankle injury late in Friday's semifinal loss to Petersburg PORTA. Ella Greenwood led Hillsboro with 13 points, Amya Greenwood had 11 and Kearstynn Davis finished with 10. Brianna Harms led the Rockets with 17 points.
Fifth-place game
PAWNEE 61, MOUNT PULASKI 44: Adalyn Boblitt connected on three 3-pointers and finished with a game-high 18 points as Pawnee outscored the Hilltoppers in each quarter. Ava Rodriguez and Greenlee Dust each added 14 for Pawnee. Meanwhile, Elayna Murphy led Pulaski with 16, Addison Brown finished with 13 and Alyson Murphy had 11.
Consolation title
MOWEAQUA CENTRAL A&M 56, RIVERTON 38: Freshman Skyler Stokes led the Hawks with 11 points but Riverton's two-game win streak came to an end against the Raiders. Gwyn Hardimon led A&M with 13 points.
Consolation third-place game
LITCHFIELD 58, NORTH MAC 45: Lynzie Reid, a freshman, scored a day-best 20 points to lead Litchfield to the win over fellow South Central Conference member North Mac. Reid was 7-for-11 at the free-throw line and had three 3s. Teammate Adia Melchert, another freshman for the Purple Panthers, added 18. North Mac junior Carla Nogueroles led the Panthers with 14.

title: Illinois State Trooper struck and killed by vehicle in northern Illinois
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The driver of the other vehicle faces a Class 4 felony charge on a Scott's Law violation. Here's what authorities said happened.
content:
Show Caption
An Illinois State Police trooper was struck and killed by a vehicle near Joliet Monday evening.
Trooper Clay M. Carns, 35, was removing debris from a lane on southbound I-55 when he was hit by a passing pickup truck around 9:42 p.m., according to a news release from the agency.
The crash was north of Blodgett Road, near Channahon.
Carns died from injuries around 10:45 p.m. after being taken to St. Joseph Hospital in Joliet.
John Fleet, 69, of Wilmington, was arrested and faces a Class 4 felony charge.
At the time of the crash, Carns had observed debris on the interstate, so he turned on his emergency lights and pulled over to the right shoulder. Carns was standing in the lane to grab the debris when he was struck.
Fleet was not injured and waited for additional authorities to arrive, according to the release.
The death marks the second fatal crash this year involving a state police trooper this year. A trooper was struck and killed in Champaign County in late October.
Carns was assigned to Troop 3 and had served as an officer with ISP for 11 years. He is survived by his wife Meghan, children Gray and Ally, parents Patti and Danny Carns, and siblings Chad Carns, Erica (Carns) Raciack, and Elyssa Carns.
ISP Director Brendan F. Kelly announced the death Tuesday morning.
'Please keep Trooper Carns, his family, loved ones, and his ISP family in your thoughts, prayers, and hearts during this most difficult time,' he stated.
The crash is under investigation.

title: Jimmy Carter, 39th US president and noted humanitarian, has died
author: Susan Page
description: Jimmy Carter, the 39th president of the United States and a global force for peace after his presidency, has died at 100.
content:
Former President Jimmy Carter, honored more widely for his humanitarian work around the globe after his presidency than for his White House tenure during a tumultuous time, has died. He was 100.
'My father was a hero, not only to me but to everyone who believes in peace, human rights, and unselfish love,' said Chip Carter, the former president's son. 'My brothers, sister, and I shared him with the rest of the world through these common beliefs. The world is our family because of the way he brought people together, and we thank you for honoring his memory by continuing to live these shared beliefs.'
Carter died Sunday in his hometown of Plains, Georgia. In November 2023, the Nobel Peace Prize-winner's wife of 77 years, Rosalynn, also passed away in the modest house they built together in 1961, when he had taken over his father's peanut warehouse business and was only beginning to consider a political career.
In February 2023, he had announced he was ending medical intervention and moving to hospice care.
Jason Carter had visited his grandparents at the time of the announcement and said "They are at peace and – as always – their home is full of love," he posted on Twitter.
At peace, perhaps, but still political: The former president vowed he wanted to cast a ballot for Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.
After serving a single term in the White House, Jimmy Carter became one of the most durable figures in modern American politics. Evicted from the White House at age 56, he would hold the status of former president longer than anyone in U.S. history, and in 2019 he surpassed George H. W. Bush as the nation's oldest living ex-president.
Carter remained remarkably active in charitable causes through a series of health challenges during his final years, including a bout with brain cancer in 2015. He was admitted to Emory University Hospital in Atlanta in November 2019 for a procedure to relieve pressure on his brain, a consequence of bleeding that followed a series of falls. A few months earlier, in May, he had undergone surgery after breaking his hip.
In the White House from 1977 to 1981, Carter negotiated the landmark Camp David peace accords between Israel and Egypt, transferred the Panama Canal to Panamanian ownership, dramatically expanded public lands in Alaska and established formal diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China.
But the 39th president governed at a time of soaring inflation and gasoline shortages, and his failure to secure the release of Americans held hostage by Iran helped cost him the second term he sought.
'He's never going to be ranked as a great president; he's middling as a president,' said historian Douglas Brinkley, author of a 1998 book on Carter, "The Unfinished Presidency." 'But as an American figure, he's a giant.'
After losing his reelection bid to Ronald Reagan, and until well into his 90s, Carter continued working as an observer of elections in developing countries, building houses through the nonprofit Habitat for Humanity and teaching Sunday school at the tiny Maranatha Baptist Church in Plains, Georgia, his hometown.
He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002, 22 years after he left the White House.
"I can't deny that I was a better ex-president than I was a president," he said with a wry laugh at a breakfast with reporters in Washington in 2005.
"My former boss was humiliated when he lost in 1980; he felt he let himself and the American people down," David Rubenstein, a young White House staffer for Carter who became founder of the Carlyle Group and a billionaire philanthropist, told USA TODAY in an interview in 2019.
"For a long time, he was basically the symbol of a weak president and a terrible person. And today, 40-some years later, he's seen as a very incredible person who has had many good things he did, though he didn't get reelected," Rubenstein said.
Peanut farms and nuclear subs
James Earl Carter Jr. was born on Oct. 1, 1924, in Plains to Earl Carter, a peanut warehouser who had served in the Georgia Legislature, and 'Miss Lillian' Carter, a registered nurse and formidable figure who joined the Peace Corps when she was in her 60s.
He grew up on a peanut farm in Plains, then graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy. In the years after World War II, he served in the Navy's submarine service in the Atlantic and Pacific fleets. After doing graduate work in nuclear physics, he became a pioneer in the introduction of nuclear power in submarines.
When his father died in 1953, Carter resigned his naval commission and took over operation of the family peanut farms with Rosalynn, his hometown sweetheart. After a rough early patch, the business flourished, and Carter became increasingly active in community affairs and politics.
During two terms in the Georgia state Senate, he gained a reputation as an independent voice who attacked wasteful government practices and helped repeal laws designed to discourage Black Americans from voting.
But in 1966, he lost a race for governor to segregationist Lester Maddox in an election that analysts said reflected a Southern backlash against national civil rights legislation enacted in 1964 and 1965. In a second bid for governor in 1970, Carter minimized his appearances before Black audiences and won endorsements from some segregationists.
After he was elected, though, Carter declared that the era of segregation in Georgia was over, and he was hailed as a symbol of a new, more inclusive South.
Still, he was an unlikely presidential contender. When he launched his bid for the 1976 Democratic nomination, the former one-term governor was so obscure outside the Peach State that 'Jimmy who?' became a campaign trope. He perfected the meticulous cultivation of voters in Iowa, and his unexpected victory in the opening presidential caucuses there provided a launching pad that long-shot contenders tried to emulate for decades.
The Watergate scandal boosted Carter's prospects. In the aftermath of President Richard Nixon's decision to resign in 1974 rather than be impeached, Carter pitched himself to voters as an outsider who would reject Washington's unsavory ways. 'I'll never lie to you,' he told them.
In 1976, he narrowly defeated President Gerald Ford, whose campaign was damaged by verbal missteps and by controversy over his decision to pardon Nixon.
Four years later, Carter would be ousted himself. He faced a damaging challenge for the Democratic nomination from the left by Massachusetts Sen. Edward Kennedy and then a landslide defeat in the general election from the right by Reagan.
The former California governor tapped into discontent with Carter's leadership. 'Are you better off than you were four years ago?' Reagan asked voters in the iconic closing of their only campaign debate.
Presidential achievements eclipsed?
Carter's defenders argue that he was a better president than generally recognized.
"I think that he is the most underappreciated modern president that we've had," said Stuart Eizenstat, a veteran Washington official and ambassador who was Carter's chief domestic policy adviser in the White House.
"The reason for that is the lingering memories of his presidency are negative ones – gasoline lines, high interest rates and inflation, the Iran hostage crisis, the Desert One failed rescue effort – and those totally obscure a really remarkable set of accomplishments both at home and abroad, which in many ways didn't materialize until after he left office."
Eizenstat, author of "President Carter: The White House Years," published in 2018, said Carter's policies and appointments laid the groundwork for a stronger economy, energy independence, environmental protection, business innovation in transportation and more.
On foreign policy, Carter painstakingly negotiated the 1978 Camp David Accords, a historic agreement between Israel's Menachem Begin and Egypt's Anwar Sadat that led to a formal peace treaty between the two countries the next year.
But he stumbled when he came to the politics of the job.
Despite having the advantage of a solidly Democratic Congress, many of his legislative proposals, including a consumer protection bill, stalled. The no-backroom-deals approach that helped him win the White House contributed to his difficulties in actually governing once he got there. He was mocked for charging members of Congress for their breakfast when invited to meet with him at the White House and for eliminating alcohol from most evening events.
He was seen by some, then and later, as prickly and sanctimonious.
Meanwhile, unemployment rose, interest rates for home mortgages climbed into double digits and Americans found themselves waiting in lines to buy gas in an oil crisis created by OPEC, the powerful international energy cartel. In a speech to the nation in July 1979, Carter described a 'crisis of confidence" among the American people. Although he never said the word, it became short-handed as his 'malaise' speech.
"He lacked the political and managerial skills needed to make best use of the office he held," said Robert McClure, a political scientist at Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs.
Damaged by the hostage crisis
Most damaging of all was the Iranian hostage crisis.
Carter had agreed to allow Iran's deposed shah, a former U.S. ally who was living in exile, to receive cancer treatment in the United States. In protest, Iranian Islamist radicals overran the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and took 52 Americans captive. The confrontation, which began on Nov. 4, 1979, would end only as Reagan was being inaugurated 444 days later.
Carter chose diplomacy and economic sanctions over military action. He halted oil imports from Iran and froze Iranian assets in the U.S. He severed diplomatic relations with Iran and imposed a full economic embargo on the country.
Finally, he approved a top-secret military mission to free the hostages, but it ended in catastrophe. Three helicopters developed engine trouble in a remote staging area in the Iranian desert, forcing the mission to be aborted. Eight U.S. troops were killed when a helicopter and a plane collided while forces were being withdrawn.
It all added to the impression that Carter was out of his depth.
"The hostage crisis left a bitter taste in voters' mouths, which Carter was never able to overcome," said Stephen Hess, a Brookings Institution scholar who worked on Carter's transition team when he was president-elect.
On the day of Reagan's inauguration, Jan. 20, 1981, Iran agreed to accept $8 billion in frozen assets and a promise by the U.S. to lift trade sanctions in exchange for the release of the hostages. Minutes after Carter's successor took the oath of office, the hostages were freed.
Finally, a Nobel Peace Prize
Carter left the White House, but he didn't retire.
Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter established the Carter Center in Atlanta, their home base for decades as they worked on global health and democracy. He helped negotiate an end to the long civil war in Nicaragua between the Contra rebels and the Sandinistas. He met with North Korean leaders to try to end its nuclear weapons program. He mediated conflicts in Ethiopia, Liberia, Haiti, Bosnia, Sudan, Uganda and Venezuela. He led dozens of delegations of international observers to various countries to help assure elections were free and fair.
For decades, the Carter Center also led an international campaign to eradicate Guinea worm disease, a devastating tropical ailment that in 1986 afflicted an estimated 3.5 million people in Africa and Asia. In 2020, it was on the verge of eradication; just 27 cases were reported in six African countries.
For a week each year, the Carters volunteered with Habitat for Humanity, a charitable group that renovates and builds homes for poor people around the world.
He also wrote more than 30 books – controversial ones on the Palestinian territories and the Middle East and less controversial ones on Christmas memories and fly-fishing. He published a collection of his poems and a collection of his paintings. Again and again, he returned to writing about the lessons and demands of his Christian faith.
Carter, who attended Donald Trump's inauguration in 2017, at times criticized the 45th president. In June 2019, at a Carter Center conference in suburban Virginia, he questioned the legitimacy of Trump's election, citing allegations of Russian interference that were later called into question.
Trump responded at a news conference by calling Carter a "nice man, terrible president."
But there were also times when Carter reached out to Trump. On the 40th anniversary of the normalization of U.S.-China relations, in 2019, he sent Trump a letter offering advice on managing that relationship. Carter said the phone conversation that followed was the first time the two men had spoken.
In 2002, Carter was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize that supporters thought he had deserved years earlier, when it had been presented to Begin and Sadat. The Nobel committee honored Carter "for his decades of untiring effort to find peaceful solutions to international conflicts, to advance democracy and human rights and to promote economic and social development."
"The bond of our common humanity is stronger than the divisiveness of our fears and prejudices," Carter said in accepting the prestigious award. "God gives us the capacity for choice. We can choose to alleviate suffering. We can choose to work together for peace. We can make these changes – and we must."
When he left the White House, Carter moved back home to Plains. Unlike most other modern presidents, he didn't choose to make money by delivering high-priced speeches or serving on corporate boards. But he did regularly speak to hundreds of visitors who would gather for his Sunday school class at Maranatha Baptist Church.
In November 2019, he told those gathered that he didn't fear death.
"It's incompatible for any Christian not to believe in life after death," Carter, then 95, told them, although he acknowledged he had wrestled with doubts throughout his life. In his prayers, he said, "I didn't ask God to let me live, but I just asked God to give me a proper attitude toward death. And I found that I was absolutely and completely at ease with death."
In July 2021, he and his wife hosted a 75th anniversary party in Plains attended by about 300 friends, family members and fellow pols, among them Bill and Hillary Clinton. Carter, his fragility apparent, made a point of greeting the guests at each table for what many of them assumed would be the last time they saw him.
"He was not a self-promoter in the White House or afterwards, and I think that hurt, because it leaves all the sour tastes from the failures and didn't allow the positives to shine through," Eizenstat said. When Eizenstat visited Carter in Plains in 2018, Carter told his former aide he was comfortable with letting history judge.
As he approached his 90th birthday, Carter mused about his legacy in an interview with USA TODAY.
"One is peace," he said. "I kept peace when I was president and I try to promote peace between other people and us, and between countries that were potentially at war, between Israel and Egypt for instance. And human rights. ... I think human rights and peace are the two things I'd like to be remembered for – as well as being a good grandfather."

title: Williamsville boys basketball closes lid on Warrensburg-Latham to win own holiday tournament
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Williamsville finds stroke just in time to overcome Warrensburg-Latham to win Williamsville Holiday Tournament championship.
content:
WILLIAMSVILLE — Williamsville had jumped out to a 11-0 start behind its shooting and defensive prowess.
Warrensburg-Latham's 14-0 start was in large part to its scorching-hot offense, averaging 70 points per game.
On Monday, it was the Bullets who overcame cold shooting as Williamsville won its own Williamsville Holiday Tournament title with a 40-32 win over the Cardinals for the Bullets' first own tournament title since 2017.
The Bullets (12-0) didn't stop shooting 3-pointers just because they started off 0-for-8 and were trailing 15-4 nearly 11 minutes into the game.
'We just got to get that lid off (the basket) first and when that first one goes down, you gain that confidence,' Williamsville senior Carson Doran said. 'We just keep shooting with confidence, keep moving the ball, keep attacking the zone and we knew shots were going to fall at some point.'
When senior Brayden Saling, The State Journal-Register's reigning Small School Boys Basketball Player of the Year, splashed in from the corner his first made 3 with 5 minutes, 17 seconds left in the first half, it opened the floodgates as he and fellow senior Blake Shoufler drained three in a row combined. By the time the second quarter clock ended, the Williamsville players were within 19-16.
'We knew sometime shots were going to fall and we just (needed to) keep putting them up,' Shoufler said, 'keep making the right play, get some layups in there, get to the free-throw line and eventually they'll fall, and they eventually did.'
Even after the Bullets clanged several 3s, Saling and Shoufler tried from even further behind the 3-point line. Williamsville coach Nick Beard said, while it may look counterintuitive to many observers, he has the utmost confidence in his players' ability to dial in sooner than later.
'We've got too good of shooters to talk about shot selection or how far they're back,' Beard said. 'They make those all the time, and I don't want them to think about it. We just tell them to keep shooting.
'We felt at halftime that (the first half) was our bad half. That's about as bad as we could have played. We didn't make anything, and we were only down three.'
The shooting struggles returned in earnest for both teams in the third quarter, even though Williamsville was able to take its first lead when Carson Doran and Shoufler started the period on a 5-0 run. But the teams were just 6-for-25 shooting combined in the third, with Williamsville going three of 14 and 1-for-6 from behind the 3-point arc.
Shoufler, who missed the holiday event last season through the Bullets' run to a fourth-place finish in the Class 2A state tournament due to a broken right ankle, scored eight of his game-high 17 points in the fourth quarter alone as Williamsville turned a 27-25 deficit into an eight-point win over the final eight minutes.
Doran and Saling each finished with nine.
Williamsville finished 14 of 41 from the floor, including 6-for-23 from behind the arc. Warrensburg-Latham was 14 of 39, but 1-for-7 on 3s.
'We knew they were going to hit,' Warrensburg-Latham coach Tim Martin said. 'We kept telling them, 'They're not going to keep missing. These guys are shooters. They're going to keep shooting. They're going to eventually make it, so we've got to be able to weather the storm.''
For as timely of shots as the Bullets had, it was their defense that kept the home team from facing a larger margin when the shots weren't falling.
Warrensburg-Latham senior Brayden Hickey scored 11 points for the Cardinals (14-1). No other player had more than seven as the Cards were held to their lowest offensive output this season. The Cardinals' previous lowest score was 51, done twice. The team has only failed to reach the 60s just three times, including Monday.
'Coach Beard does a great job with his team,' Warrensburg-Latham coach Tim Martin said. 'The way they hedge any type of ball screen, he knew a lot of our plays, he was very prepared for that, so we had to try and adjust how we did some things.
'But just credit to him, his defense, that pressure, we haven't seen any of that yet this year. I mean, there's a reason why a lot of polls are ranking them second in the state. That team's been there and experienced it, and our team's trying to come up and experience environments like this. I mean, it was incredible tonight.'
Shoufler said the packed house made the win even more special.
'It was electric in there; surreal,' Shoufler said during an interview inside the makeshift media room next to the boys locker room, normally used by athletic trainer Kurt Turner. 'It's awesome to get these fans out here and I appreciate every single one of them.'

title: Auburn completes dominant run in the 2024 Waverly Holiday Tournament, plus other results
author: Bill Welt
description: Auburn, Jacksonville Routt met in the Waverly Holiday Tournament championship game on Monday with a combined 26-1 record.
content:
WAVERLY — The Auburn boys basketball team turned to an unexpected source for a hot start.
Senior forward Ryan Lash scored nine of his 14 points in the first quarter. The top-seeded Trojans (14-1) then went on to capture their first Waverly Holiday Tournament title since 2009 with a 55-37 win over No. 2 Jacksonville Routt on Monday.
"We say earned, not given," Lash said. "Every game is a championship game. We just brought that kind of energy to every single one, and here we are."
Lash delivered eight of the team's first 11 points, and Auburn raced ahead 31-13 by halftime. Senior guard Carter Hunley converted four 3-pointers for a game-high 21 points.
"I wouldn't necessarily say this was my moment," Lash said. "I would just say I found the open looks and as a team, we all contribute. Tonight, we just did well."
Auburn, which last season won its first Sangamon County Tournament since 1986, won by an average margin of 19.7 points over four games in Waverly.
"It wasn't part of the plan," Hunley said of Lash, "but he started stepping up and balling out. That's what you want. It's what you want out of all of your players.
"We're happy we got it done."
Junior guard Bryson Mossman, the tournament MVP, led Routt (13-1) with 14 points.
NO. 12 SOUTH COUNTY 59, NO. 3 WINCHESTER WEST CENTRAL 37: Junior guard Caden Colwell delivered 18 points and the Vipers captured third place for their highest finish in the tournament since the advent of the co-op between Waverly and Franklin in 2015. South County previously took fourth place last year but features new head coach Josh Krumwiede this season. Junior Owen Paluska and senior Bishop McDannald had nine points apiece.
NO. 6 EDINBURG 67, NO. 7 CONCORD TRIOPIA 49: Senior Alex Peacock scored 23 of his game-high 29 points in the second half and the Wildcats earned fifth place. Peacock converted 12 field goals and shot 5 of 7 from the free throw line. Junior Treyton Davis added 11 points. It similarly signaled a step forward from last season, not unlike South County. Edinburg won the consolation final last year.
Consolation final
