title: Here is The State Journal-Register's Small School All-Area football team for 2024
author: Bill Welt
description: 24 players made the SJ-R's All-Area Small School football team for classes 1A through 3A. Read about them here.
content:
Show Caption
Here is The State Journal-Register's Small School All-Area football team, listed in alphabetical order:
Carson Beattie, Williamsville
The senior defensive end totaled 47 tackles, including 14 for loss and five sacks, with one forced fumble to earn all-Sangamo first team on the defensive front. He ended his career with 77 tackles and nine sacks. He was also all-Sangamo second team as a blocking tight end.
Braddock Cates, Williamsville
The senior running back/linebacker garnered Illinois High School Football Association all-state honors in Class 3A for a second straight season, the first in program history. He carried the Bullets to their first Sangamo Conference title since 2021 with 1,605 rushing yards and 20 touchdowns. He also led the offense with 18 catches for 282 yards and three scores — all the while delivering 52 tackles, including six for loss. He was unanimous all-Sangamo first team both ways. He finished with 3,479 career rushing yards, 4,416 all-purpose yards and 48 TDs.
Kellen Creviston, Jacksonville Routt
The senior quarterback once again set school records across the board. He shattered last year's benchmarks by throwing for 2,987 yards and 31 touchdowns — not to mention piling up 3,336 yards of total offense and 37 total TDs. He was named IHSFCA all-state in Class 1A. He was not only tabbed all-Western Illinois Valley Conference North Division first team for a second straight season but also the WIVC-North Offensive Player of the Year. He also finished with career school records for most passing yards (6,075), passing TDs (63), most completions (424), most passing attempts (686), total offense (6,954 yards) and total TDs (77).
Matthew Crouch, Williamsville
The senior offensive tackle was named all-Sangamo first team for a second straight season. This is also his second appearance on the all-area team. He started at left tackle over three seasons in 35 games.
Nate Dyer, Carlinville
The senior running back/linebacker posted 734 rushing yards and four touchdowns while also leading the defense with 98 tackles and one interception. He was all-South Central Conference second team on both sides of the ball.
All-area girls tennis:
Trey Gause, Jacksonville Routt
The senior defensive end totaled 89 tackles, including 23 for loss and 12 sacks. He tied a state record with eight sacks against Mendon Unity. He was selected all-WIVC North first team defensively.
Isaiah Harbert, Pana
The senior running back/linebacker won the team MVP award. He was also all-SCC first team defensively with 129 tackles (60 solo), including seven for loss. He also ran for 621 yards and 11 scores to pick up all-SCC second team honors on that side of the ball.
Nolan Herpstreith, Nokomis
The junior running back ran for 1,171 yards and 14 touchdowns. He registered six games with more than 100 rushing yards. He was all-conference first team offensively and second team defensively in the Lincoln Prairie.
Jaeger Hill, Niantic Sangamon Valley
The senior quarterback/linebacker vaulted the Storm to the playoffs with 424 rushing yards and nine touchdowns while also giving out 27 tackles.
Carter Hunley, Auburn
Unanimous all-Sangamo first team, the senior receiver hauled in 58 catches for 829 yards and four scores. He was all-conference second team at safety with 37 tackles and a pick.
All-area cross country: Here are the SJ-R's 2024 cross country runners of the year and all-area teams
Caden Kahl, Williamsville
The senior left guard was named all-Sangamo Conference first team and will play at Monmouth College.
Wyatt Kile, Pana
The senior quarterback earned all-SCC first team acclaim and was named the team's offensive player of the year. He went 117-for-210 for 2,010 yards and 22 touchdowns with two picks. He also ran for 350 yards and six scores.
Weston Kuykendall, Carlinville
The senior lineman was all-SCC first team both ways. He registered 56 tackles, including 12 for loss and three sacks. He also ran for 300 yards and five touchdowns.
Roaran Lees, Pana
The senior lineman was heralded as the team's top offensive lineman at right guard. The three-year starter was all-SCC first team offensively.
Roark Lewis, North Mac
The senior running back set a school record with 1,347 rushing yards and 10 touchdowns to launch the Panthers back into the playoff picture. He was IHSFCA all-state in Class 2A and all-SCC first team on offense.
Cash Lynch, Pana
The junior defensive back/receiver achieved IHSFCA all-state accolades in Class 2A. He corralled 48 catches for 685 yards and 10 touchdowns. Defensively, he tied a school record with seven interceptions to go with 52 tackles (29 solo) with four for loss. He was all-SCC first team both ways.
Clark Nelson, New Berlin
The senior running back/linebacker totaled 1,239 rushing yards and 19 touchdowns. He was unanimous all-Sangamo first team offensively and second team defensively in the program's best season since 2015.
Eli Olson, Jacksonville Routt
The senior receiver pulled down 51 catches for 920 yards and 10 touchdowns. He was named unanimous all-WIVC North first team on offense. He finished his career with 109 receptions for 1,665 yards and 19 scores.
Gage Paul, Williamsville
The senior linebacker was all-Sangamo first team with 89 tackles, including seven for loss. He also recorded a pick with five forced fumbles and one recovery. He also pitched in 383 rushing yards with seven total scores. He departs with 173 career tackles.
Rylan Reimolds, Rushville-Industry
The junior running back ran for 1,219 yards and 16 touchdowns to lead the Rockets to an 8-2 season. He was unanimous all-conference first team offensively in the Lincoln Trail-Prairieland Conference Small Division. He was also named all-conference first team at linebacker.
Tyler Rench, Pana
The junior was credited as the best defensive lineman on the team with 66 tackles, including 15 for loss and a school-record 11 sacks. He was all-SCC first team on defense.
Sam Sims, Pana
The senior receiver/defensive back chalked up 35 catches for 710 yards and eight touchdowns. Defensively, he pried away five interceptions and totaled 62 tackles, including five for loss. He was all-SCC second team both ways.
Kaiden Watts, Pawnee
The senior lineman helped pave the way for Pawnee's historic 11-1 season and was named all-state by the IHSFCA. Defensively, Watts had 31 tackles, including six for loss and two sacks. PHS reached its first ever state semifinals and set a school record for most wins in the Illinois 8-Man Football Association.
Carson Wort, Pawnee
The senior running back/linebacker was tabbed all-state by the IHSFCA and ran for 2,130 yards and 37 touchdowns. He ran for 490 yards and seven touchdowns in a 64-24 quarterfinal win over St. Anne.

title: The readers have spoken: Magic Kitchen tabbed city's most iconic restaurant
author: Steven Spearie
description: Magic Kitchen Thai Restaurant was a favorite with readers, garnering 40% of nearly 7,100 votes cast in a recent online poll.
content:
Sitting in his Bangkok hotel room, Brian DeLay said the thought of Magic Kitchen in Springfield, halfway around the world, made him drool.
"Still one of the finest Thai dining experiences in my life," said DeLay, a Springfield High School graduate who formerly taught music in southern China, via Facebook.
Many stumping for the family-run Thai restaurant, voted the "most iconic" in Springfield in a recent poll by State Journal-Register readers, spoke about its degrees of heat in its dishes.
"Hot is devastating," the restaurant's own menu advises.
"Pie," said the former Springfield judge, counting apple and cherry among his favorites.
Waiting for a table at Magic Kitchen's 4112 N. Peoria Road location could create its own kinship. There is also a location at 115 N. Lewis St.
A tried-and-true maxim has kept Paul Truax a regular customer.
"I go back cause it's good food at a good price," he said.
Magic Kitchen garnered nearly 40% of the nearly 7,100 votes cast. Runners-up in the poll were Saputo's, the Old Lux, Chesapeake Seafood House, Maldaner's and Bella Milano.

title: First Black US Attorney for Central District of Illinois announces retirement
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Central Illinois' chief federal prosecutor announced his retirement this week. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Central Illinois' chief federal prosecutor has announced his retirement.
U.S. Attorney Gregory K. Harris, who leads the Central District of Illinois submitted his resignation Monday to President Joe Biden and stated that he would retire afterwards, effective mid-day Jan. 2.
Harris was confirmed in 2021 by the U.S. Senate to fill the role, which made him the first Black person to lead the district as U.S. Attorney.
Harris took office following former U.S. Attorney John Milhiser who is now the Sangamon County State's Attorney. Milhiser at the time submitted his resignation to President Biden, which was connected with Biden, a Democrat, defeating Republican incumbent Donald Trump in November 2020.
Both Harris and Milhiser received support from U.S. Sens. Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth in attaining the position.
'Having served for nearly 30 years as an assistant U.S. attorney, more than a decade in private practice and several years in the Illinois Office of the State Appellate Defender, Greg Harris is well-qualified and an excellent choice,' the two said in a joint statement at the time of Harris' confirmation.
Harris' tenure in the U.S. attorney's office has included serving as chief of the criminal division. He also served as an assistant U.S. attorney in the Central District from 1980 to 1988. From 1988 to 2001, he was a litigator in the Springfield law firm of Giffin, Winning, Cohen & Bodewes. Harris returned to the U.S. Attorney's Office in 2001.
From 1976 to 1979, Harris worked in the Illinois Office of the State Appellate Defender.
He was chief legal council for the Illinois governor's office of manpower and human development and the Illinois Department of Commerce and Community Development from 1978 to 1980.
Harris earned his law degree from the University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, formerly known as The John Marshall Law School, in 1976, and he received a bachelor's degree from Howard University in 1971.
In 2022, U.S. Attorney General Merrick Garland appointed Harris to the Attorney General's Advisory Commission, where Harris was one of 13 U.S. Attorneys to represent the nationwide community of 93 U.S. Attorneys.
'Serving as United States Attorney after more than thirty years with the office has been the honor of a lifetime,' Harris wrote in a statement. 'Words cannot express my gratitude to the public servants in law enforcement who have dedicated their careers to protecting our community and to the prosecutors and staff in my office who work tirelessly every day in pursuit of justice.'

title: Illinois EPA has begun moving into the White Oaks Mall
author: Claire Grant
description: It's official – employees of the Illinois EPA are clearing out their desks and moving into the new location inside the White Oaks Mall.
content:
It's official – employees of the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency are clearing out their desks and moving into the new location inside the White Oaks Mall.
In an email confirmation with Capital Development Board Public Information Officer Lauren Grenlund, the transition to the new facility is in progress and will be over the next few months.
The price tag to move into the mall is hefty – around $430 per square-foot according to Grenlund for the 186,000-square-foot space. In total $80 million over the last four years has gone into the project run by the CDB, which oversees state construction projects.
The construction project, originally set to finish last year in July, took longer to finish due to unidentified issues at purchase.
Grenlund said the cost encompasses the project which underwent a competitive bidding process for design and construction inside the old Sears Center, which went out of business in 2018.
The center was chosen instead of a downtown location, as the Central Management Services and CDB evaluated existing state-owned and leased properties in the county before settling on the locale inside the White Oaks Mall. The state purchased the Sears building in 2020 for $3.5 million.
A deciding factor was the floor plan inside the Sears, as well as the extensive parking lot outside.
'The open floor plan of Sears allowed for a more flexible and efficient layout of office spaces and cubicles to meet the agency's needs.'
In response to the movement of 559 EPA employees, the food court inside the mall is adapting to cater to its new, stable customer base. Just this July, 710 Rippy G's Chicago style & Soul Food opened up shop inside the food court while Pinoy Pride, a Filipino restaurant, opened this month with full breakfast to dinner menus.
Eventually, once the EPA, Department of Innovation and Technology and Illinois Pollution Control Board move into the mall officially through the next several months, the current EPA location at 1021 N. Grand Ave. E. will be demolished to make room for railroad improvements.

title: Springfield area could see up to 10 inches of snow. What you need to know
author: Steven Spearie
description: A winter storm warning remains in effect for the Springfield area until noon Monday. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Mother Nature is promising to put on a show in the Springfield area.
Officials at the National Weather Service in Lincoln said the central Illinois area could see two different snow events into Monday that could deliver up to 10 inches of snow.
A winter storm warning remains in effect for a wide swath of central Illinois, including Springfield, until noon on Monday.
Freezing drizzle, said NWS meteorologist Mike Albano, could cause its own set of impacts on highways and other roads into the evening hours Sunday.
Bands of heavier snow along Interstate 72 corridor, Albano said, could reduce visibility to about half a mile. The Springfield area could get two to five inches of snow in that first sequence before tapering off around 3 to 4 p.m., he said.
"In the evening, could see a lull where heavier snow shuts off and we start to transition to freezing drizzle or flurries," Albano said.
A secondary push after midnight could impact the Monday morning commute while layering on another two to five inches of snow, Albano added.
Snow emergency for Springfield
The city of Springfield's Office of Public Works has declared a snow emergency for designated snow routes until 11 p.m. on Monday.
Residents must remove all parked vehicles from marked snow emergency routes. Visit springfield.il.us/snow to view the route map and the city's snow and ice removal policy.
Persons clearing private parking lots and sidewalks are reminded not to plow the snow into the streets, which is a violation of city ordinance.
Residents and businesses are encouraged to keep their sidewalks clear as a safety measure during inclement winter weather. All sidewalks adjacent to properties must be cleared of snow by 10 a.m. each morning following a snow event. Non-compliance may result in a fine.
The village of Jerome and the cities of Jacksonville and Lincoln have also declared snow emergencies.
Sangamon County has declared a Level 1 winter weather emergency, which is in effect until further notice.
The declaration applies only to county highways.
Under Level 1, roadways are hazardous and drivers may encounter blowing and drifting snow. Drivers should use caution.
Driving tips in winter weather conditions
Here are some driving tips from the Illinois State Police to navigate winter weather conditions:
Plan your travel, selecting both primary and alternate routes;
Let someone know your travel routes and itinerary so that, if you don't arrive on time, officials will know where to search for you;
Check latest weather information;
Try to travel with another vehicle, if possible;
Drive carefully and defensively. Watch for ice patches, especially on bridges and overpasses;
If a storm begins to be too much for you to handle, seek refuge immediately;
If your car should become disabled, stay with the vehicle, running your engine and heater for short intervals. Be sure to "crack" a window in the vehicle to avoid carbon monoxide build-up.

title: Springfield closing in on $1.4M settlement over 2022 car accident involving policeman
author: Steven Spearie
description: The Springfield City Council will look to settle a 2022 court case involving a city man injured by a Springfield Police Department officer.
content:
The Springfield City Council will look to settle a 2022 court case involving a city man injured by a Springfield Police Department officer.
The settlement is for $1.4 million for Kevin Heffington of Chicago who was injured in a Jan. 20, 2022, accident at Illinois 4 and Browning Road involving Officer George Wayda.
Wayda, a five-year veteran of the force, was on duty at the time and responding to a call about a possible subject with a gun.
The city council put the ordinance for the settlement on the consent agenda at its Jan. 7 meeting.
That means unless it is pulled, it will be part of an omnibus vote.
With council consent, the settlement will be paid out of the city's self-insurance fund, said city attorney Gregory Moredock.
According to the lawsuit, Wayda was southbound on Route 4 when he approached the intersection. Heffington was eastbound on Browning Road.
The lawsuit said Wayda failed to activate his emergency lights and siren at the intersection and failed to reduce speed to avoid the collision.
Heffington suffered "severe and permanent injuries."
Heffington's attorney, David Rabinowitz of Dworkin & Maciariello, did not immediately return messages from The State Journal-Register.

title: City of Springfield unveils first proposed budget for FY26. What you need to know
author: Steven Spearie
description: A look at what agencies are asking for and what the headcount might be in the city of Springfield's FY26 budget.
content:
The public is getting a first look at the city of Springfield budget while departments will lay out particular programs in workshops beginning Jan. 14.
The overall ask is $350,232,993 by agencies outside of City, Water, Light & Power. The utility is seeking $318,611,749.
In both cases, that excludes American Rescue Plan Act, or ARPA, expenses.
The city's Office of Budget and Management (OBM) released the tentative budget at the end of December. It is the second budget under Mayor Misty Buscher's administration.
The corporate fund (corporate expense budget, including ARPA transfers out, and minus CWLP) is $194.7 million.
The first of three budget workshops, presented by the heads of the departments, is Jan. 14.
"It's important to hear what programs and projects are going to be focused on, that the city council will have a chance to get in with the directors," said Ward 9 Ald. Jim Donelan, who will be chairing the budget workshops.
Final amendments are due to OBM by Jan. 25.
A public hearing on the budget is scheduled for Feb. 11, with a final version set to go before the full city council on Feb. 18.

Lincoln Library, $5,787,299, from $6,591,063, down 12.2%
Mayor, $4,395,015, from $4,057,799, up 8.3%
CWLP, $318,611,749 from 315,598,208, up 1%
Who is going up in headcount?
The city's overall number of budgeted employees goes from 1,469.50 to 1,490.50, an increase of 21.
CWLP's proposed headcount swings from 525 to 540, which includes called for additional water department employees for new infrastructure work--lead service line replacements and other work--under the water rate increase, said CWLP spokesperson Amber Sabin.
There is additional budgeted staff for succession planning for positions among mainly apprentices and engineers in the electric division.
The offices of the mayor, clerk, treasurer and planning and economic development all go up by one position.
The fire department and police department also go up by one person each but in personnel other than sworn firefighters or sworn officers.
Who is going down in headcount?
The fire department is down three sworn firefighters due to normal work force attrition, Chief Ed Canny said.
Budget presentations
All hearings will be held in City Council Chambers (Municipal Building West) and begin at 5:30 p.m.
Jan. 14: Overview, Mayor's Office, Treasurer's Office, City Clerk, City Council, Springfield Convention & Visitors Bureau and Lincoln Library.
Jan. 16: Human Resources, Office of Planning and Economic Development, Office of Budget and Management, and Public Works.

title: The people of Sangamon County should have their voices heard
author: Andy Carrigan
description: Monday, Jan. 13, 2025, is last time for the County Board to put a binding referendum on a recall for the office of County Sheriff in the April election.
content:
Monday, Jan. 13, 2025, is last time for the County Board to put a binding referendum on a recall for the office of County Sheriff on the ballot in the April election.
The County Board meets at the Sangamon South Auditorium on 9th, between Monroe and Capitol streets. The meeting begins at 6 p.m.
Citizens wishing to address the County Board on this should sign up on the County Board's website or call the Board Office 217-753-6650 by 4:30 p.m. Sunday, Jan. 12.
The Massey Commission unanimously recommended that the County Board adopt Recall for the office of Sheriff by placing a binding referendum on the ballot a the earliest possible election.
The Commission was created by County Board Chair Andy Van Meter, State Sen. Doris Turner (D-Springfield) and the County Board to heal the community and find solutions to the problems that led to the tragic killing of Sonya Massey by a now former deputy sheriff.
Ironically, the primary opponent of Recall is Chairman Van Meter.
He claims the Board lacks the power to enact Recall, relying on the opinion of an assistant state's attorney and a part-time professor at the University of Illinois College of Law, who worked 34 years for the corporate Chicago law firm of Winston & Strawn.
This is in the face of a 2016 Appellate Court opinion clearly ruling that local governments have the right to adopt Recall via a binding referendum. Arlington Heights, Buffalo Grove and Wheeling adopted Recall under this power
State's Attorney John Milhiser declined a request to seek an opinion on this from the Illinois Attorney General's Opinion Bureau, which exists for this very purpose.
The County Board was elected to carry out the will of the people. We are not Judges. The People of Sangamon County overwhelmingly want us to adopt Recall for the office of Sheriff.
We should do that Monday. If someone wants to challenge that in Court, they are free to do so. Then the real judges will decide the legal issue.

title: Fallout announced from Tuesday's Lanphier-Southeast basketball stoppage
author: Ryan Mahan
description: District 186 quickly made a decision and announced its discipline for the Southeast and Lanphier boys basketball teams after their Tuesday game ended in less than four minutes because of a fracas between the players.
content:
The Lanphier and Southeast boys basketball teams will be feeling the repercussions beyond this week from Tuesday's stopped game between the Springfield rivals.
On Thursday, it was announced that both teams will receive a pair of forfeit losses ― not only for the incident between the teams which led to the cancellation of that game, but for their next matchups as well.
Three players also will serve further suspensions.
District 186 officials confirmed that Lanphier's game at Jacksonville and Southeast's home game against Sacred Heart-Griffin, both scheduled for Friday, were canceled. Jacksonville and SHG will receive forfeit wins.
According to an official with one of the involved teams, three players will serve additional penalties. One Lanphier player is suspended for two additional games for making physical contact with a Southeast player; another Lanphier will be suspended three games for leaving the bench and making contact with a Southeast player; and one Southeast player will serve a three-game suspension for leaving the bench and making contact with a Lanphier player.
Additionally, all athletes from both teams must participate in a "restorative circle" on Jan. 15 at the District 186 office. If an athlete does not attend, he will be ineligible for the City Tournament, which is scheduled for Jan. 22-25 at the Bank of Springfield Center.
Tuesday's game at Lanphier's Lober-Nika Gymnasium was called off with 4 minutes, 44 seconds to go in the first quarter with Lanphier leading 3-2. Lanphier's JaiQuan Holman scored a basket and was fouled, resulting in an altercation which spilled over to the sidelines. Players from both teams came off the benches before the fracas was stopped. Southeast coach Wayne Hamilton sent his team to the locker room and Lanphier coach Blake Turner quickly did the same.
On Thursday, District 186 Executive Director of School Support Jason Wind issued the following statement:
"Springfield Public Schools District 186 holds our student-athletes to high standards of accountability for their actions, both on and off the court. On Tuesday, January 7th, the boys' basketball game between Southeast High School and Lanphier High School was stopped in the first quarter due to a physical altercation on the floor that led to players from both team leaving the bench and entering the court. After reporting to the IHSA, the game was declared a double forfeit.
"Following this incident, District 186 Administration, along with school administrators, and coaches from Lanphier and Southeast High Schools, have determined that both teams will also forfeit their next scheduled games on January 10th. Southeast will forfeit their game against SHG, and Lanphier will forfeit their game against Jacksonville High School. In addition, individual disciplinary actions have been taken for players involved in the most serious physical contact.
"District 186, alongside our community, does not condone this type of behavior. To support our students in making better choices, both teams will participate in a restorative practice event next week. This initiative aims to promote accountability, reflection, and growth while reinforcing the importance of sportsmanship and good citizenship between our schools.
"We remain committed to helping our student-athletes learn from this incident and supporting the efforts of our administrators and coaches to guide our students toward making positive decisions. By working together, we aim to build a culture of respect and excellence that reflects the values of our schools and community."
Matt Troha, an assistant executive director with the Illinois High School Association, said in an email Thursday that the IHSA was aware of the situation and it would meet either Friday or Monday to discuss the next steps in the process.
The last time a District 186 basketball team was involved in a double forfeit occurred during the 2014-15 season, after an incident at the end of a game involving Decatur MacArthur and Lanphier.
Both teams were issued a forfeit loss and the IHSA's statement, in part, included: "… in light of the lack of available players to finish this contest and the seriousness of the incident, declaring one school the winner of this contest doesn't seem appropriate. In accordance with IHSA By-law 1.460, this contest shall be considered a double forfeit, and both schools will need to report this as a loss on its record.'

title: What to know from Chatham Glenwood girls basketball OT win over Lincoln in 3A title rematch
author: Bill Welt
description: Neither team was fully healthy, but Chatham Glenwood and Lincoln battled to the wire in the 3A girls basketball title game rematch
content:
LINCOLN — Chatham Glenwood's seniors had never beaten Lincoln. Until now.
The Titans escaped with a rollicking 66-56 overtime win over Lincoln at Roy S. Anderson Gym in Saturday's rematch of last year's Class 3A girls basketball state final.
'They're fighters, they're not going to give up,' Glenwood coach Alyssa Riley said. 'They wanted this game. The seniors have never beaten Lincoln before, so regardless of the state playoffs just for my senior kids being able to go out and win is huge.'
Where they're going: Signings and commits around Springfield so far, including Chatham Glenwood girls hoops
It was a much-anticipated Central State Eight Conference showdown, but neither team was entirely healthy.
Lincoln junior guard/forward Mia Clark drained a 3-pointer in the final seconds of regulation to force overtime. Glenwood senior guard Rowann Law answered with a 3 to begin the extra period as the Titans survived without leading scorer and rebounder Alexis Neumann.
Lincoln senior guard/forward Piper Whiteman was also making just her second appearance this season after an ACL tear in June.
Here are the top takeaways from the seesaw clash for first place in the CS8:
Filling Neumann's shoes
Neumann, The State Journal-Register's Large School Volleyball Player of the Year, has been unavailable since the holidays due to a fractured wrist on her shooting hand. She is expected to return at some point during the season, according to Riley.
The sophomore forward averaged team-highs 11.8 points and 8.5 rebounds last season.
Glenwood's frontcourt turned to sophomore Hope Gilmore and senior Macy Martynowski in her absence.
Martynowski scored a team-high 15 points, while Gilmore nearly recorded a double-double with 10 points and eight rebounds. Gilmore, listed as a guard, said she realized just last season she could be a strong rebounder.
She also had a difficult assignment going up against Clark and senior forward Makinley Knapp.
'It was hard but it's doable,' Gilmore said of being in the interior. 'Everything is possible, it takes heart. We're missing Lex, but we work hard in practice, me and Macy. I trusted Macy, so I knew if I couldn't do it and if me and Macy switch, then we're good.'
Gilmore became the fulcrum of the offense against Lincoln's 1-2-2 zone defense and found Law open for the go-ahead 3 in overtime.
'I know if I'm not open and I can't make a move, I know I have shooters who I can trust,' Gilmore said. 'I trust all of them, so I know I don't need to force anything.'
Riley trusts Gilmore to handle any task.
'She just has the energy down there,' Riley said. 'She's got the aggressiveness she needs down there and she's stronger than she looks.'
Law, Diamond turn up clutch
The Titans (10-6, 5-1 CS8) had contributions throughout the lineup with five players in double figures.
'That shows we have other people who can step up even when people are injured,' Law said. 'Our depth and bench on our team is good.'
Law and Diamond especially delivered in crunch time. Law scored 12 of her 14 points after the third quarter (including six in OT), while Diamond hit a pair of timely 3s.
Diamond converted her first 3 before the end of the first half for a 23-22 halftime lead and hit another go-ahead trey with just over two minutes left in the fourth.
Diamond and sophomore guard Ava Bobb, who scored the team's first seven points, finished with 11 points apiece.
Riley also said senior guard Katelyn Lehnen was battling an illness, too.
'We're not 100% right now,' Riley said, 'but it's good to win games when you're not because it makes everybody else step up and then your better players when they're all healthy, then it's a good thing.'
Lincoln's Whiteman eases back to action
Whiteman was the proverbial sixth man on last year's state championship team, averaging six points a game.
She provided all of her six points in the second quarter off the bench.
'She worked really hard to get back on the floor,' Lincoln coach Taylor Rohrer said, 'so I'm really proud of her and all the work she put in to get that knee back in shape. She's still working at it and we're going to take it slow.'
Clark and Knapp have surfaced as a productive combo so far this season. Knapp and Clark finished with 17 and 12 points, respectively. Senior guard/forward Lily Holmes added 11 points.
Adding Whiteman to the mix provides an additional boost after the Railers (8-9, 4-2 CS8) knocked off 3A state-ranked Morton 52-50 to open the new year.
'Mia and Mak do a nice job inside,' Rohrer said, 'but they do a good job because we have good guards who give them the ball. It's a team effort out there.'

title: Riley's heroics buoy Tri-City in overtime, plus Riverton, Calvary have what the other needs
author: Ryan Mahan
description: On the opening night of the Sangamon County Tournament, Donavyn Riley's buzzer-beater gets tourney started on exciting note.
content:
The Buffalo Tri-City/Sangamon Valley locker room was in quite the mood after Monday's 50-44 win over Pawnee in the first game of the 99 th Sangamon County Tournament.
The eighth-seeded Tornadoes players were still basking in their overtime victory that seemed improbable after Ryder Smith gave No. 9 Pawnee a 41-38 lead with 6.4 seconds remaining.
If Tri-City coach Steve Dilley had a priority list to take a last-second 3-pointer, junior Donavyn Riley wouldn't be the first couple of options, at least.
'We drew something up for two dudes in the corner to shoot it and it didn't really go as planned,' Riley said. 'I caught it, and I shot it. I can hit (3s), but it's not what I usually do.'
But there he was, at the top of the key with the ball and the clock nearly all zeroes. There he was knocking in the shot to send the game to an extra four minutes.
'I was a little worried, then I saw it going down and I was like, 'That's in,'' Riley said of what he felt in that moment. 'When it left my hand, at first it kind of went off wrong, but it went in.'
And there he was scoring the final basket of the six-point win, losing his shoe and suffering a minor injury to his ankle.
Even with the momentum on their side, the Tornadoes still have an overtime to play. R.J. Sullivan scored five points — including his only 3-pointer of the game — and Riley and Jackson Nibbe each had two points.
'Anything didn't fall all night, but I hit that 3 when it counted,' Sullivan said. 'That's what went through my head when I shot that.'
In Tri-City's locker room, the emotions of such a win were still high. Gone was the anxiety of the Tornadoes watching their 28-17 and 30-20 leads evaporate, nor were there thoughts yet of the tall task ahead for TCSV on Tuesday: a date with No. 1-seeded Williamsville.
'You can hear them over here. Gosh, you'd think we just won a state tournament,' Dilley said before joking, 'You know, we get to play Williamsville tomorrow. Maybe they don't know that.'
Nope, the players couldn't have cared less if they were told they were playing the Boston Celtics, Williamsville, a 6-under team or even hockey next.
'After this game, all this energy, I think we're going to have a high confidence level tomorrow,' Sullivan said.
Steve Dilley, in his 21 st year coaching, said one benefit of being a veteran is being able to appreciate those moments.
'When I was younger, I'd have been losing my mind on the sideline,' Dilley, the dean of the county coaches, said. 'There at the end, I just kind of sat down and watched it. You just watch, because at the end of the day, it's in their hands.
'We wanted to get Donnie (Riley) downhill and look to kick it, but I'll joke and say that's how I drew it up; that was the play we drew up.'
Riverton, Calvary seek different improvements
Riverton coach Matt Mead and Calvary coach Tives Gardner could probably put together a heck of a team if the Hawks and Saints joined forces.
Mead is very happy with his team's ability to play defense but would love to get more offensive output. Gardner knows his team's offense makes his Saints a nightly threat, but his team's defensive struggles mean they can also be beaten by any team as well.
Following No. 3 Riverton's 57-46 win over No. 6 Athens, Mead marveled at his team's defense, especially when the Hawks held the Warriors to just three points in the second quarter.
'I felt like defensively we had a lot of energy, a lot of juice tonight, but offensively we've got to take care of the ball better,' Mead said. 'I feel like even though we were playing so hard defensively, we may have ended up with as many or more turnovers than they did, and that's not good.
'Turnovers are only good on defense if you can do something with it on offense. I felt like at times we were really out of control tonight, so we've got to correct that.'
Riverton sophomore Julian Rice, who finished with 19 points, agreed.
'It just depends on the moment,' Rice said. 'We've just got to work on defense to keep our game up because that's where we're best at. We're a pretty small team, so we have to work 10 times harder than everyone else. We work on defense a lot at practice and it translates to the game.'
At Calvary, Gardner wishes that was the case, though the 11-5 Saints have been known to put on a show, like on Saturday when Calvary went on the road to beat Peoria Christian 81-80. On Monday at Lincoln Land Community College's Cass Gymnasium, junior Luke Blackford scored 33 in No. 7 Calvary's 55-47 win over No. 10 Lutheran.
'The whole game we struggled to play defense. We couldn't get the stops that we needed,' Gardner said. 'In order to play it, it takes some effort. It takes some heart.
'I always say you can't coach defense. Defense has to come with inside of you. We play it in spurts, but we're not consistent with it, and that comes with youth, the inexperience.'
Blackford was very frank in his assessment.
'We don't play no defense; it's a huge problem right now,' Blackford said. 'It's just something that we're taking slowly ... and it's hurting us. Right now, it looks like any team could keep up with us.'
Gardner joins a club
Gardner won his 200th game on Monday. He is in his 12th season as the Saints' coach. When asked how he felt about it, the lack of defensive intensity was still on his mind.
"Well, I'm happy, but, I stay focused on my boys; I don't worry about that," Gardner said. "I'm trying to get this defensive thing corrected. Until we get it right, I'll probably never think about the 200."

title: Jeannette Slover, convicted of 1996 murder of former daughter-in-law, dies at 77
author: Steven Spearie
description: The Illinois Innocence Project claims new DNA test results on 11 items of evidence exclude Jeannette Slover of the 1996 murder.
content:
Jeannette Slover, who was convicted of the 1996 murder of her former daughter-in-law in Decatur but whose innocence was championed by several groups, died on Jan. 8.
Slover was 77.
Slover's death was confirmed by Illinois Department of Corrections spokeswoman Naomi Puzzello and by members of the Illinois Innocence Project (IIP). The project based at the University of Illinois Springfield represented Slover on her post-conviction claim.
Slover was serving a 60-year sentence and was incarcerated at the Decatur Correctional Center, but was on a medical furlough, according to the IDOC website.
The Karyn Hearn Slover murder case grabbed national headlines after the aspiring model's dismembered body was found in garbage bags in Lake Shelbyville just days after her disappearance on Sept. 27, 1996. She had been shot in the head several times.
Jeannette Slover, her husband, Michael Slover Sr., and their son and Karyn Slover's ex-husband, Michael Slover Jr., were arrested in 2000 after a four-year investigation. All three were convicted of murder in 2002.
Michael Slover Sr. died in prison in 2022. His son was paroled in 2024, according to the IDOC website.
Karyn Slover disappeared after leaving her job in Decatur. Her car was found abandoned on Interstate 72 just outside of Champaign the same day.
The prosecutor's case centered around the custody of Michael Jr. and Karyn Slover's then-three-year-old son.
In a joint statement Thursday, the IIP, the Exoneration Project, the Steve Beckett Law Office and Springfield attorney Peter Wise said they will carry on the fight to prove her innocence.
A second supplemental petition for post-conviction relief filed in Macon County court in October claimed new DNA test results on 11 items of evidence excluded Jeannette Slover and revealed unknown DNA profiles found at the crime scene. The tests also exclude Michael Slover Sr., and Michael Slover Jr., according to the petition.
"Jeannette and her family deserve justice. The victim of this murder, Karyn Slover, also deserves justice by having the actual perpetrators held accountable for her death," the statement read.
A status hearing in the case is set for Feb. 20.

title: Springfield residents press for 'public process' to fill alderperson vacancy
author: Steven Spearie

Some Ward 1 residents are hoping that a process to fill a vacancy for alderperson can include a public forum of potential candidates.
The city of Springfield is accepting resumés for the opening through the end of the workday Tuesday.
Ward 1 Ald. Chuck Redpath Sr. was appointed by the city council as clerk on Dec. 7 forcing him to resign from the city council seat.
Steven Simpson-Black, a Ward 1 resident addressing the committee of the whole on Tuesday, said he and others wanted to avoid "the confusion and consternation that was around the clerk's appointment."
A petition calling for transparency and posted at www.change.org had gathered 100 signatures by Wednesday.
Several alderpersons questioned the process of gathering clerk candidates' names while favoring a more robust vetting system.
City council members nominate candidates for clerk. Redpath, who served on the city council for nearly 30 years, was one of two names voted on after Frank Lesko's resignation.
Jane Ford, also from Ward 1, said residents of the ward have "a right to expect a public process that will...hear what candidates for the position have to say." Ford also angled for a public forum where candidates can be heard and questioned.
The sprawling ward covers the southeast part of the city, including the area around Lake Springfield.
Mayor Misty Buscher said the vacancy is a mayoral appointment and that she and her chief of staff, Mike Disco, would be having conversations with candidates.
Two members of the city council--Ward 3 Ald. Roy Williams Jr. and Ward 5 Ald. Lakeisha Purchase--were appointed, Buscher said, by her predecessor, Mayor Jim Langfelder.
Neither of them had public forums, she said.
"I'm being asked to do things Mayor Langfelder was never asked to do by the community," Buscher said after Tuesday's meeting. "He didn't hold (forums). He didn't have candidates debate each other. He didn't do any of those things."
Buscher added she read into the record an ordinance to appoint a clerk on Nov. 19, the day provisional and late-arriving vote by mail ballots in the recorder's race were tabulated and when Lesko was declared the winner.
Lesko was sworn in as recorder on Dec. 2 but stayed on as clerk when Josh Langfelder filed for a discovery recount. Langfelder opted not to press for a full recount.
As for the alderperson vacancy, Buscher said she wouldn't require anyone to say whether they would or wouldn't run for the office in 2027.
The appointment needs city council approval.
Simpson-Black served on the city's planning & zoning commission before resigning in 2023 and ran unsuccessfully for the Springfield Metropolitan Exposition and Auditorium Authority (SMEAA) board in 2023. He said he would not be an alderperson candidate this time around.
"I think there are going to be some very big decisions that are going to be in front of the city in the next few years," Simpson-Black said. "It's really important that we have good representation, especially in Ward 1. It's a very big ward. Having a strong alderman or alderwoman is really important for us to be connected to the city."
County Board vacancy
The Sangamon County Board also has a vacancy, following the death of Clyde Bunch on Dec. 3.
Bunch represented District 21, which encompasses the south-central part of Springfield.
The candidate will be appointed on Feb. 11. There is a special election for the seat on Nov. 3, 2026.
Candidates must be Democrats and registered voters within the district and have resided in Sangamon County for at least one year prior to the appointment.
Interested individuals may submit their resumé, a letter of interest and any supporting documents via email to County@SangamonIL.gov or deliver them in person to the Sangamon County Board Office at 300 S. Ninth St. The office is on the second floor.

title: Beardstown forces out Elliott Craig as football coach, will remain as AD, teacher
author: Bill Welt
description: Elliott Craig stepped down as Beardstown's football coach just before the holidays, saying he was given little choice by his bosses
content:
BEARDSTOWN — Elliott Craig resigned as Beardstown's football coach at the Dec. 18 school board meeting.
He still remains as the school's athletic director and driver's ed teacher.
Craig said he was told by the school administration and board that they wanted to move in a different direction with the football program.
'Your two choices as a coach at that point are either resign ... or you say no and you make the board actually vote you out,' Craig said this week. 'At the end of the day, I was told it was going to be the same result.'
In an email response to The State Journal-Register, superintendent Brent O'Daniell said the resignation has no impact on his employment as an AD or teacher but did not provide additional comment.
Craig was previously the head coach at North Fulton for 14 seasons. Over his 18 years as a head coach, he has made seven playoff appearances. He arrived at Beardstown after the COVID-shortened season and led the Tigers to the playoffs over the first two seasons. Beardstown went 1-8 in 2024 after missing playoff eligibility by one game the previous year.
Craig said he would consider coaching again, if the opportunity was right. Otherwise, he plans on staying put.
'I felt like we did a pretty good job,' Craig said. 'Like I said, I don't have any regrets. They felt like they wanted to hire someone else, so that's what they're going to do. I just chose to step down and will continue to teach and be the AD and go from there.'

title: King Breakfast at 50: Illinois Supreme Court justice to keynote event at new location
author: Steven Spearie
description: For its golden anniversary, the Martin Luther King Jr. Breakfast moves to the Crowne Plaza.
content:
Lisa Holder White, the first Black woman to serve as a justice on the Illinois Supreme Court, will keynote the golden anniversary of the Martin Luther King Jr. Day Breakfast in Springfield on Jan. 20.
The event, held annually on the day commemorating the civil rights leader and sponsored by the Springfield Frontiers International Club, moves to the Crowne Plaza, 3000 S. Dirksen Parkway, for the first time.
The breakfast starts at 8:30 a.m. Tickets are $40 and may be purchased from Frontiers Club members or by calling 217-494-0189.
Frontiers member Allan Woodson said the core purpose of the breakfast is "to foster and promote racial harmony by bringing together diverse ethnic groups from the Springfield metro area to fellowship, celebrate and keep the King dream alive.
"Each of the past 49 years, our members have identified and invited individuals to come share their experiences and visions with a focus on how Dr. King's life and beliefs have impacted today's world.'
Holder White was sworn in as a Supreme Court justice in July 2022 replacing Justice Rita B. Garman, who retired.
Holder White won reelection in November.
In 2013, Holder White was sworn in as the first Black justice on the Fourth District Appellate Court.
She first became a judge in 2001 after practicing family and criminal law with Brinkoetter & White Law and serving as an assistant public defender in her hometown of Decatur.
The Frontiers Club will use a portion of the breakfast proceeds along with the proceeds from its annual golf outing to generate financial support for the Positive Youth Development Program for sixth, seventh and eighth graders and the Junior Frontiers for high schoolers.
The funds are also used to help with Frontiers Club scholarships named for two deceased members of the organization, J.D. Washington and James Forstall, the 2016 State Journal-Register First Citizen Award winner.
This fall marks the 60th anniversary of the only speech King delivered in Springfield. He addressed some 4,000 delegates at an AFL-CIO convention at the Illinois State Armory on Oct. 7, 1965. The downtown armory is undergoing a three-year, $122 million renovation set to be completed later this year.
Past breakfast speakers include Mamie Till-Mobley, mother of Emmett Till (1997); the Rev. C.T. Vivian, minister and author who worked with King (1993); Martin L. King III, King's eldest son (1984); Rosa Parks, whose refusal to give up a bus seat to a white passenger sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1983) and Yale University Law School professor and presidential advisor Tracey Meares of Springfield (2019).
Unity March
A Unity March under the Visions 1908 - University of Illinois Springfield banner will be held at noon on Jan. 20.
The march will begin at Pilgrim Rest Missionary Baptist Church, 1800 S. Martin Luther King Jr. Dr., and go to Pleasant Grove Baptist Church nine blocks directly north.
There will be a program there, said Teresa Haley, the founder of Visions 1908, centered around what King would have to say about current issues in America.
The roundtable is usually led by UIS students.
Cold weather scuttled last year's march, though the roundtable was held.
Jacksonville NAACP event
The Jacksonville chapter of the NAACP will hold its MLK celebration also on Jan 20.
A march starts from Mt. Emory Baptist Church, 426 S. Church St., to Jacksonville Community Park, 1309 S. Main St., at 10 a.m. A program will start there at 11 a.m.

title: Supreme Court upholds law that could ban TikTok in the U.S., leaving the matter to Trump
author: Maureen Groppe
description: In an unsigned opinion, the Court sided with the national security concerns about TikTok rather than the First Amendment rights. There were no noted dissents.
content:
Looming over the Supreme Court's TikTok decision is what could happen after Donald Trump takes office. Trump promised to "save" the popular platform.
Show Caption
WASHINGTON − The Supreme Court on Friday unanimously upheld a law that would effectively ban TikTok in the United States on Sunday, siding with the government's national security concerns over the First Amendment rights of the company and its 170 million TikTok users.
That decision shifts the focus to whether President-elect Donald Trump can intervene after he takes office on Monday.
Trump, who tried to ban TikTok during his first administration, has since promised to 'save' the wildly popular platform, though it's unclear how he could do so.
Minutes before the court released its decision, Trump said on social media he'd just spoken with Chinese President Xi Jinping about TikTok and other issues.
'It is my expectation that we will solve many problems together, and starting immediately,' Trump posted.
After the court upheld the law, Trump said he will decide what to do "in the not too distant future."
"Stay tuned!" Trump posted.
Alan Rozenshtein, an expert on the law and technology policy at the University of Minnesota Law School, said none of Trump's options are 'particularly promising.'
'The bottom line?' Rozenshtein wrote in an analysis posted on Lawfare. 'There are a lot of moving pieces and it's foolish to make particularly confident predictions, but the most likely outcome is that TikTok goes dark on the 19th and stays that way for the immediate future.'
The company has said that even a temporary ban on the short-term video app would have 'devastating' effects on TikTok's ability to attract users and content creators. About 170 million Americans − and more than 1 billion people worldwide − use TikTok, according to the company.
The court's decision came a week after the justices heard more than two hours of heated debate on Jan. 10 on whether the government can require the short-form video app to divest from its parent company, China-based ByteDance.
TikTok called that a "massive, unprecedented restriction" of free speech.
"One of America's most popular speech platforms will shut down in nine days," Noel Francisco, an attorney for TikTok who served as solicitor general during Trump's first administration, told the justices on Jan. 10. "That shouldn't happen."
In an unsigned opinion, the court said that while TikTok offers a 'distinctive and expansive outlet for expression, means of engagement, and source of community,' Congress has determined that divestiture is needed because of 'well-supported national security concerns.'
There were no noted dissents, although Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Neil Gorsuch gave their own explanations for why the law should be upheld.
A majority of the court rejected TikTok's argument that the law must meet the toughest test for overcoming a 1st Amendment challenge.
The sell-or-be-banned provision addresses an important government interest unrelated to the suppression of free expression and doesn't go farther than it needs to address that goal, the court said.
The court also cautioned that its analysis is 'narrowly focused' on how the law applies to TikTok, given the abbreviated amount of time the justices had to evaluate it because of the impending deadline.
Still, free speech advocates said the court's decision paves the way for additional 'repressive policies."
Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute, said the court has 'weakened the 1st Amendment and markedly expanded the government's power to restrict speech in the name of national security.'
The Department of Justice had argued the restriction is not on speech but on a foreign adversary's ability to control a widely used means of communication. Unless TikTok is sold, the government said, China can gather data on Americans or manipulate the content on TikTok to shape U.S. opinion.
"The Chinese government's control of TikTok poses a grave threat to national security," Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar told the court last week.
She said before Trump steps in, he should review all the updated national security information since he was last in office.
In Friday's opinion, the court described Trump's efforts during his first administration to separate TikTok from ByteDance.
Despite his past concerns, the "Art of the Deal" president-elect had urged the Supreme Court to pause the ban to give him time to "negotiate a resolution."
Once in office, Trump could direct his attorney general not to enforce the law. But it's uncertain if Apple, Google and other conduits for the app will feel that's enough protection from the law's stiff penalties.
Pam Bondi, Trump's choice for attorney general, declined during her confirmation hearing Wednesday to commit to enforcing the law.
Bondi said she would "in general" defend U.S. laws against constitutional attacks, but said she couldn't make that specific pledge about the TikTok ban.
Trump could try to take advantage of ambiguity in the law as to whether the president can declare that TikTok is no longer controlled by a Chinese entity.
And there are questions about whether Trump can extend the deadline for TikTok to be divested from ByteDance.
Asked about that during the Supreme Court's debate, Prelogar called it a "statutory interpretation question."
She also said TikTok may have been playing a game of chicken with the U.S. and would find a way to divest once it was clear whether the deadline would hold.
Francisco, TikTok's attorney, told the court the platform would "go dark" on Sunday unless the law was blocked.
'Essentially, the platform shuts down," he said.
But the law doesn't require TikTok to act. The penalties fall on the app stores and companies such as Oracle that host TikTok's content in the U.S. Changes by those companies would make the platform harder to use over time but wouldn't necessarily stop its immediate use for people who already have the app.
On Friday, Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco said enforcing the law "will be a process that plays out over time."
Trump's change of heart on TikTok may, in part, be related to the app's use in connecting him to young voters. His account had 14.8 million followers as of last week.
'TikTok's a great platform that many Americans use and was great for his campaign and getting his message out,' Rep. Mike Waltz, Trump's incoming national security adviser told Fox News Thursday.
Trump also had good things to say about TikTok after he met last year with billionaire Jeff Yass, a major conservative donor with financial ties to ByteDance.

title: Springfield man sentenced to federal prison for punching postal worker in the face
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A Springfield man is being sentenced to prison for punching a postal carrier who authorities said was being a Good Samaritan.
content:
A Springfield man was sentenced to prison for punching a postal carrier in the face.
Larry French Jr., 23, was sentenced to 18 months in federal prison this week for assaulting a U.S. postal carrier in Springfield during May of last year.
Authorities said French was having a "physical interaction" with his sister in the roadway which prevented the mail carrier from driving through an intersection.
The carrier yelled to French that he was going to call the police when French approached the carrier and punched the carrier through an open window in the mail truck.
The mail carrier needed corrective surgery following the punch, according to authorities.
At the sentencing hearing, presiding U.S. District Judge Colleen Lawless said French acted irrationally by punching the carrier and that his actions caused the victim serious bodily injury. Judge Lawless also said the carrier acted as Good Samaritan by stopping the initial attack and trying to call the police.
A federal grand jury indicted French with the assault in July 2024 and French pleaded guilty in September. He has remained in custody of the United States Marshal.
The United States Postal Inspection Service and the Springfield Police Department investigated the case.
Statutory penalties for assaulting federal officers are up to 20 years of prison time, up to three years of supervised release, and up to a $250,000 fine. French's sentence will be followed by two years of supervised release.

title: DOJ reaches agreement with sheriff's department, dispatch over investigation
author: Steven Spearie
description: The investigation was launched in the months after the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey by a former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy.
content:
Show Caption
Under an agreement reached with the U.S. Department of Justice, the Sangamon County Sheriff's Office will "review and update policies, rules and procedures" with the State's Attorney's Office.
The agreement, announced by the DOJ on Thursday, resolves an investigation launched in November of race and disability discrimination in the provision of policing and dispatch services.
That investigation was based on complaints and reports about the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey, a Black woman who had called 911 about a potential prowler.
Former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy Sean P. Grayson is charged with first-degree murder in the case.
Massey, who lived in an unincorporated neighborhood of Springfield, had been the subject of a mental health call in Springfield just hours before the fatal shooting.
The DOJ's Civil Rights Division investigated the sheriff's department's and Sangamon County Dispatch's compliance with certain parts of the Civil Rights Act, nondiscrimination provisions of the Safe Streets Act and parts of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).
The Civil Rights Act and the Safe Streets Act collectively prohibit discrimination on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex and religion by recipients of federal financial assistance, such as the sheriff's office. Title II of the ADA prohibits discrimination on the basis of disability by public entities.
'The death of Sonya Massey was a terrible tragedy for a woman experiencing a mental health crisis, her family and the entire Sangamon County community,' said Assistant Attorney General Kristen Clarke of the DOJ, in a statement released by the DOJ. 'This agreement reflects Sangamon County's commitment to instituting reform and taking action that will help improve public safety and restore trust with the community in the road ahead.'
The state's attorney's office worked, according to the statement, to ensure the sheriff's department has "the tools and training to conduct its policing activities in a nondiscriminatory manner and that the county and dispatch provide dispatch services in a nondiscriminatory manner."
Among the most pertinent hiring changes under Sheriff Paula Crouch are a sheriff's merit commission and a mandate that investigators review records in person if a department applicant worked at another law enforcement agency.
Part of the agreement requires county development and implementation of a mobile crisis team program, which will include trained behavioral health staff who timely respond to individuals needing urgent behavioral health assistance.
The Massey Commission was formed in the aftermath of the shooting. It endorsed the formation of a 708 Mental Health Board county-wide. The Sangamon County Board on Monday agreed to form a commission to study its implementation with the possibility of a referendum going before the voters on the Nov. 3, 2026, ballot.

title: Springfield police link 3 juveniles to more than 40 burglaries, car thefts
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Springfield Police Department said three juveniles are tied to more than 40 burglaries and car thefts.
content:
The Springfield Police Department believes three juveniles have been responsible for numerous vehicle thefts and burglaries.
An investigation following the recent arrests of three juveniles linked the juveniles to over 40 burglaries and vehicle thefts, with one of the juveniles responsible for 25 previous cases, according to a Facebook post from the Springfield Police Department.
'Calls for service regarding burglaries and vehicle theft nearly stopped after their arrests,' the department said.
Police arrested two juveniles for the theft of a Hyundai Dec. 9 around 7:20 a.m., also finding a stolen firearm. Another juvenile ran off but was later caught and arrested, police said.
Officers on the midnight shift of Dec. 8 were called to multiple vehicle thefts and break-ins, including a stolen silver Hyundai that was seen fleeing from another crime scene.
The police department said an officer saw a Hyundai the next day that matched the description. Another Hyundai was chasing it, which was later found to also be stolen, according to police.
A different officer found the silver Hyundai around 7:20 a.m. when two of the arrests were made.
Springfield saw an increase in car thefts and burglaries in 2024, according to data released by the police department. From January through November in 2024, there were 574 vehicles stolen, up from 504 during the same time frame in 2023.
In data from November, which is the most recent data available, 115 motor vehicles were stolen. November from the year prior saw 56 motor vehicles stolen.
1,654 instances of burglaries and breaking and entering are reported for January through November of 2024. That's up from 1,082 in 2023.
November saw 142 offenses of that crime, which was down from the year prior, which saw 185 offenses.
The two officers were awarded a Certificate of Commendation.
The Springfield Police Department did not provide additional information on the three juveniles who were arrested.

title: Macoupin County preview: How this junior became a key guard for Staunton boys basketball
author: Bill Welt
description: Here's the blueprint for success for this junior guard and Staunton boys basketball, and what else to know about the 106th Macoupin County Tournament
content:
It's all a matter of effort and the Staunton boys basketball team is reaping the rewards.
The Bulldogs won their first Carlinville Holiday Tournament title since 2009 and now have a chance to secure their first Macoupin County Tournament crown since 2012 as the No. 1 seed.
Staunton has the bye and meets either No. 4 North Mac or No. 5 Bunker Hill in the semifinals on Wednesday at 6 p.m., also hosted by Carlinville. The championship game is Friday at 7:30 p.m.
The Bulldogs (14-4) have already nearly matched last year's 16-win total with losses only coming against Class 3A schools Centralia, Rochester, Jerseyville and Bethalto Civic Memorial — all wins generated with just one senior, Ethan Sharp, in the starting lineup.
In their previous trip to Carlinville, sophomore guard Isiah Laux and junior guard Bryce Coalson averaged 14.3 and 13.7 points, respectively, over the three-game stretch. They combined for a staggering 21 3s in those games and both were named to the all-tournament team.
'He can really shoot the ball,' Coalson of Laux said following a 52-47 win over Hardin Calhoun at the Big House. 'It's great whenever we have so many guys on the floor who can shoot it, it's tough for teams to guard us and we really like to get down and guard, too.'
Sangamon County results: Auburn, Williamsville set up ranked showdown for County title, plus schedule and results
It may be hard to believe, but Coalson said he hardly saw any time on the varsity floor last season. Coach Ty Laux, Isiah's dad, said Coalson put up nearly 30,000 shots over the offseason and added 20 pounds of muscle.
That's been the recipe for his success.
'Every time I have the ball in my hands, I'm confident that I'm going to score the ball,' Coalson said. 'It's just a great moment for us (to win the tournament).'
Other teammates stood out along the way. Sophomore Jeremiah Graham poured in three 3s for a game-high 19 points in a 56-42 win over Carlinville in the semifinals, while junior Aaron Bodner did the same in a 70-27 win over Gillespie in the quarterfinals.
'No one out there is like, 'I'm going to go get my points,'' Coalson said. 'Everyone wants to win the basketball game, that's the No. 1 priority. I think that's why we're so good this year.'
Added Isiah, 'None of us are selfish, we're always sharing the ball.'
How to watch
The Macoupin County boys and girls tournament will take place in Carlinville. Tickets are $4 for adults and $2 for students at the door. Games can also be streamed online via subscription on the NFHS Network web site.
Tournament history
This is the 106 th Macoupin County Tournament and it is one of the oldest continuous high school sports events throughout the state, according to local historian Tom Emery. The first tournament was held in 1919. It later handed out the first girls title in 1980. By comparison, the Winchester Invitational Tournament gave out its first trophy in 1923 while the Waverly Holiday Tournament started in 1951. The Sangamon County Tournament recently celebrated its 100 th anniversary, according to information supplied by Phil Shadid. Elsewhere, the 113th McLean County Tournament began over the weekend after its debut in 1911.
Past boys champions
Gillespie has raked in the most titles with 17, followed by Piasa Southwestern (17), Staunton (15), Mount Olive (12) and Carlinville (9). Southwestern has won the previous three titles.
Past girls champions
Piasa Southwestern touts the most titles with 17, followed by Carlinville (10), Gillespie (8), Staunton (5) and Bunker Hill (2). Gillespie won last year's title following back-to-back Staunton titles.

title: Siberia, Iceland and other places where it's warmer today than it is in Evansville
author: Ryan Reynolds
description: Temperatures dipped to 5 degrees in Evansville early Monday morning, and the wind chill reached minus-6 degrees.
content:
A brutal cold snap is underway in the Tri-State − and in a lot of the rest of the country, frankly.
Temperatures dipped to 5 degrees in Evansville early Monday morning, and the wind chill reached minus-6 degrees.
And it's going to be cold for a few more days. The National Weather Service forecast doesn't bring the Tri-State above 32 degrees until Thursday.
It got us wondering: Where is it warmer today than it is in Evansville and Henderson?
Here are four such places.
Barrow, Alaska
Barrow (also known as Utqiagvik) is the northernmost city in the United States. The town is surrounded on three sides by the Arctic Ocean. From October through May, the temperature rarely gets above freezing.
For a couple of months each winter, the sun sets and doesn't come back up. It's dark all 24 hours of the day.
Yes, there are polar bears.
At 9 a.m. Monday, it was 26 degrees in Barrow, about 20 degrees warmer than it was in Evansville.
Novosibirsk, Siberia (Russia)
Siberia, with its long, brutal winters, has been a favorite spot for Russian leaders to send convicts for labor-camp sentences for the past four to five centuries.
There are large expanses of wilderness in Siberia, and around Novosibirsk, the locals point to a lack of mountains to keep Arctic winds at bay.
The city's Wikipedia page likens it to Winnipeg, Canada.
Yes, there are polar bears. (They're at the city zoo.)
It was 32 degrees this morning in Novosibirsk.
Reykjavik, Iceland
It's the capital of a place called Iceland, for heavens sake. And it was 32 degrees there this morning, 25 degrees warmer than it was in Evansville.
Pituffik Space Base, Greenland
Formerly known as Thule Air Base, Pituffik is on the northwest coast of Greenland.
The place gets so cold that they have to use tugboats to move icebergs around to get ships in with supplies. And that's in the summer, when you can actually get ships into the port.
The place is 750 miles north of the Arctic Circle.
Yes, there are polar bears.
It was 10 degrees this morning at Pituffik, five degrees warmer than it was in Evansville.

title: Cougar that roamed west side of Springfield soon to have new digs in Indiana
author: Steven Spearie
description: In the fall of 2022, a 150-pound cougar roaming around the west side of Springfield captivated the public. The big cat will soon have new digs.
content:
roaming around the west side of Springfield captivated the public.
The big cat soon will have a lot more ground to roam at the Exotic Feline Rescue Center, a little over an hour southeast of Indianapolis, where he's been since being captured in Springfield.
"His health is good," said center director Joe Taft of the four-year-old Capone, who got the gangster-inspired name in a 2023 online naming contest run by the center. "With luck, he can live to between 15 and 18, maybe up to 20 years old."
The nonprofit center takes in and cares for exotic cats from abuse situations or have been abandoned or find themselves without homes.
Taft thought Capone would have a smooth transition into his new home, which has been a couple of years in the works.
It will just be Capone in the digs for now.
"Unless somebody springs a wild female (cougar) on us," Taft quipped.
Here's an update.
The backstory
Capone had been tracked and observed on the city's west side for several days in late October 2022.
Originating in Nebraska, Capone, his mother and his brother had been live trapped and collared there by that state's Game and Parks Commission. His mother, Taft said, purportedly still lives in the wild in Nebraska, though his brother was killed by a car.
Cougars or mountain lions--the names are interchangeable, said Taft--can travel long distances and often on their own. Illinois doesn't have breeding or resident populations of cougars, he said.
While Capone appeared to be comfortable in the city, officials with the Illinois Department of Natural Resources, Illinois Conservation Police, the U.S. Department of Agriculture and Springfield Police Department considered his presence to be a public safety issue.
The center stepped in when officials from both Nebraska and Illinois wouldn't relocate the animal for various reasons. Capone was immobilized and transported to Indiana by a convoy of state and federal agents.
Life in Indiana
Taft remembered being surprised at how well-fed Capone was when he arrived at the center, probably reflective of his hunting skills.
Capone gets a dose of Ivamet every month to kill fleas as well as a number of other parasites, Taft said. He's been vaccinated and boosted for feline distemper and a variety of feline upper respiratory diseases, as well as canine distemper, which cougars are susceptible to.
Vets at the center have also done a blood draw on him, Taft added.
Capone is currently in an enclosure built several years ago for a group of leopards that were confiscated by the USDA and taken in by the center, Taft said. The cage is about 50 to 60 feet long and about 20 feet wide with several elevated platforms and walkways.
Where Capone is going
The new 250-foot-by-250-foot enclosure includes some dense vegetation that might offer Capone, Taft said, a perfect hiding place. And something more.
"He'll certainly be able to hunt rabbits," Taft said. "We're bringing in piles of large dead trees he can climb on."
There's a large tower in the middle and a series of 4x8 platforms, some as high as 12-feet off the ground, for Capone to explore.
Taft said Capone has even shown a propensity to play with a Boomer Ball made out of shatter-resistant plastic.
"One morning, I went out (to his enclosure) and I could not find the ball," Taft said. "He had taken it and put it inside a deer carcass. I don't know if he batted it in there out of mere chance or if he planned on it."

title: Illinois schools prepare for immigration enforcement
author: Peter Hancock
description: The 'non-regulatory guidance' on immigration enforcement actions was issued two days after President Trump was inaugurated for his second term.
content:
The Illinois State Board of Education is encouraging local school districts to adopt clear policies spelling out how and when their staff should cooperate with federal immigration officials carrying out enforcement actions or seeking information from school officials.
The 'non-regulatory guidance' on immigration enforcement actions was issued Wednesday, Jan. 22, two days after President Donald Trump was inaugurated for his second term in the White House.
Almost immediately after the inauguration, Trump's new head of the Department of Homeland Security, acting Secretary Benjamine Huffman, rescinded a Biden administration policy that had limited immigration enforcement actions in or near 'sensitive locations' such as schools, playgrounds, child care centers and school bus stops.
'All children in the United States are entitled to equal access to a basic public elementary and secondary education, regardless of their actual or perceived immigration status, or the status of their parents/guardians,' State Superintendent of Education Tony Sanders said in his weekly message posted on the ISBE website.
Sanders cited a 1982 U.S. Supreme Court case, Plyler v. Doe, which struck down a Texas statute that barred children who were not 'legally admitted' into the United States from enrolling in public schools, saying the law violated the 14 th Amendment's equal protection clause.
In announcing the policy change, however, DHS said the Biden administration's policy had hampered legitimate law enforcement efforts.
'This action empowers the brave men and women in CBP (Customs and Border Protection) and ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) to enforce our immigration laws and catch criminal aliens—including murders and rapists—who have illegally come into our country,' the agency said. 'Criminals will no longer be able to hide in America's schools and churches to avoid arrest. The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement, and instead trusts them to use common sense.'
During the 2024 presidential campaign, Trump vowed to crack down on illegal immigration into the United States. That included promises to carry out the largest mass deportation operation in U.S. history.
In his message, Sanders reminded school officials that they are not allowed to inquire about a student's or parent's citizenship status. But he said the guidance was being issued to respond to the 'numerous requests' for information the agency had received from local officials about how to handle enforcement actions that federal agents might carry out on school grounds.
The guidance notes that federal law authorizes DHS to deputize state and local law enforcement officers to enforce federal immigration law. But it also reminds school officials that under a 2019 state law known as the Keep Illinois Families Together Act, no Illinois law enforcement agency or official is allowed to take part in such an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
In addition, the guidance notes, the Illinois TRUST Act restricts the way law enforcement agencies and officials may participate in federal civil immigration matters.
'These pieces of legislation would apply to law enforcement agencies that might otherwise have a relationship or presence on the school's property,' the document states.
The document advises districts to name a point person or department where federal authorities can be directed should they arrive on campus. It also advises designating a point person to review records requests or subpoenas from immigration agencies and to keep track of requests they receive in case that information is needed for future reference.
It also describes the differences between various types of documents that immigration officials might serve on school officials, such as federal court warrants, federal court orders, judicial subpoenas, civil immigration warrants, notices to appear and administrative subpoenas.
'ISBE strongly encourages school districts to work directly with their legal counsel to create board policies and administrative guidelines so school districts can ensure any potential response to a warrant or subpoena described above is legally compliant and aligns with that school district's policies,' the document states.
Leaders of the state's two largest teachers unions issued statements criticizing the new Trump administration policy.
Illinois Federation of Teachers President Dan Montgomery called it a 'sad and shameful day when schools, meant to educate and support students, are turned into sites of fear and chaos.'
Illinois Education Association President Al Llorens issued a statement saying all children should have access to 'an equitable, high-quality public education.'
'Our educators should not be put in the crosshairs of these political policies,' he said. 'School employees should be allowed to focus on supporting and educating all our students. We will do whatever it takes to protect ALL students, our teachers, our school support staff, our communities.'
