title: How No. 2 Williamsville boys basketball passed stingy test against Pleasant Plains
author: Adrian Dater
description: Williamsville guard Blake Shoufler is back on the floor and lapped up a tough Sangamo win over Pleasant Plains
content:
WILLIAMSVILLE – A year ago, Blake Shoufler was just a guy in street clothes and a knee brace at the end of the Williamsville bench. Outwardly, he was the team's biggest cheerleader. Inwardly, he was without cheer.
Friday night, Shoufler casually talked with a recruiter from Illinois College after helping his Bullets team to a 46-41 win over Pleasant Plains. A reporter stood nearby, patiently waiting for his turn to talk to the senior guard, while other Bullets fans gazed on admiringly.
For Shoufler, the good life he'd always enjoyed as an athlete is back after a trying several months rehabilitating from the injury that ruined his junior year.
'It's just so nice to be on the floor and contribute again,' said Shoufler, who didn't have as good a shooting night as normal but still finished with 12 points for the Bullets (23-1, 5-0) in a Sangamo Conference matchup with Pleasant Plains. 'It really sucked not being able to play, but I think I worked hard to get better and I feel great.'
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Shoufler, the point guard of the Bullets, who seems to be involved in every play at both ends, has had a tremendous senior season. He's averaging about 15 points, six assists and three rebounds a game for a Bullets team that will be dangerous in the postseason. He has re-established himself as a top player in the conference after an injury that had about an eight-month rehab timetable.
'It definitely tested him, but he was a great teammate,' Williamsville coach Nick Beard said. 'He was almost a second coach for us on the bench. I think he learned a lot. He learned not to take things for granted, and he relishes every opportunity he has to come out and put the uniform on. He's a great kid, a great competitor and a great leader. I'm glad he's on our team.'
While this was a competitive game throughout, Williamsville pretty much always had a four to six-point lead and where Pleasant Plains (14-10, 4-1) couldn't get any closer. The Cardinals, not a big team, didn't convert enough of their open-look shots developed from their usual good ball movement. A 1-3-1 trap defense early on seemed to stifle the Cardinals, and No. 2 state-ranked Williamsville built first-half leads into the double digits.
Pleasant Plains had chances to get even at the end but just couldn't finish enough of their chances.
'I was proud of the way we played in the second half, in a tough environment here,' Cardinals coach Kyle Weber said. 'We're right there, but we've just got to be a little better on each possession. A shot goes in here and there, who knows? We need to cash in more on our opportunities.'
Brayden Saling led the Bullets with 15 points, while Reid Bodine added eight and Garrett Tim added five.
Senior Cooper Schallenberg led the Cardinals with 17 points, while Grady Grisham added 14.
Beard, who has been at the Bullets helm since 2013, likes how his team has competed throughout the season.
'We've worked hard defensively, and we've got three or four guys who can lead us in scoring,' Beard said. 'We didn't shoot it well tonight, but we did enough of the other things. We shared the basketball and our defense created some opportunities for us.'

title: Illinois lawmakers try again to ban certain food additives
author: Lily Carey
description: An Illinois lawmaker is once again pushing to ban several chemicals from Illinois food items. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Illinois Senator Willie Preston has proposed the Food Safety Act for the second time, aiming to ban four potentially harmful chemicals from food products in the state.
The bill has gained momentum due to recent FDA bans on two of the chemicals, brominated vegetable oil and red dye No. 3.
Opponents believe that food additive regulations should be handled at the federal level and that recent FDA actions indicate a shift towards quicker action.
For the second legislative session in a row, Sen. Willie Preston, D-Chicago, is pushing to ban several chemicals from Illinois food items.
But this time, Preston and his bipartisan backers have momentum from the federal government on their side.
Senate Bill 93, dubbed the Food Safety Act, passed out of the Senate Public Health Committee Tuesday. It would ban the use of four chemicals in Illinois foods: brominated vegetable oil, red dye No. 3, potassium bromate and propylparaben. All four of these substances have been the subject of scientific studies linking them to elevated health risks over time, and red dye No. 3 has been linked to cancer in animals.
Preston proposed an essentially identical bill last year, which passed the Senate with bipartisan support but was not called for a vote House. However, this year's bill comes amid renewed national attention on the issue of food additives. In the past six months, the Food and Drug Administration has moved to ban two of the four substances that Preston's bill proposes banning in Illinois — brominated vegetable oil and red dye No. 3.
The latter ban was enacted on Jan. 15, just days after Preston reintroduced the Food Safety Act. He said in a news release he intends to amend his bill in line with the recent federal bans.
'Manufacturers already have to comply with California standards, the EU (European Union) standards and now the FDA,' said Sen. Rachel Ventura, D-Joliet, at a Senate Public Health Committee hearing Tuesday. 'We're just asking them to make sure that our state, Illinois, also has those same safe foods.'
The two recent federal bans came 'at lightning speed for the FDA,' Preston said. But the agency has a long history of missing deadlines, Melanie Benesh from the research and advocacy organization Environmental Working Group noted during the hearing.
The ban on red dye No. 3 has been in the works since 1990, when the FDA linked the chemical to cancer in lab rats and to behavioral problems in children. Meanwhile, all four substances that the Food Safety Act proposes banning have been outlawed in Europe and Australia for decades.
Given the FDA's history of regulatory delays, Preston and other members of the Senate Public Health Committee said Illinois needs to take food additive bans into its own hands.
'I want the FDA to be a leader on this issue, but I cannot allow them the time to be a leader on this issue at the expense of the people of Illinois,' Preston said.
California became the first state to ban red dye No. 3 and brominated vegetable oil in 2023, and several other states are currently considering similar bans on food and color additives, including New Jersey, New York, Arkansas, Oklahoma and Missouri.
But some legislators believe the recent FDA bans could signal a change to the federal food regulatory process. Sen. Andrew Chesney, R-Freeport, was one of three to vote against the act in committee. He said food additive regulations should be left to the federal government and he expects President Donald Trump 'will handle things differently' and move regulations along more quickly.
Sen. Seth Lewis, R-Bartlett, one of four Republicans to support the bill last session, is a chief co-sponsor on this year's effort.
'Make no mistake — food, and the security of our food and the quality of our food, is a bipartisan issue,' Lewis said at a Wednesday news conference. 'We need to make sure that what our children are eating helps them grow to be accomplished individuals here in our society. That is not partisan, that is bipartisan.'
Lily Carey is a graduate student in journalism with Northwestern University's Medill School of Journalism, Media, Integrated Marketing Communications, and a Fellow in its Medill Illinois News Bureau working in partnership with Capitol News Illinois.

title: Super Bowl LIX: What can you bet on in Illinois? Here's what you need to know
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Super Bowl is right around the corner, and with it comes the opportunity to make some fun bets in Illinois. Here's what you need to know.
content:
The Super Bowl features more prop bets than any other game of the year.
Not all prop bets are available to legally be bet on in Illinois.
The Super Bowl is right around the corner, and with it comes the opportunity to make some cash by wagering.
Whether you are itching to bet on the winning score -- or simply the color of the Gatorade that is poured over the winning coach -- there are opportunities for everyone.
Here's what you need to know about betting on the Super Bowl in Illinois.
What are some of the popular bets?
People place much more prop wagers on the Super Bowl than traditional bets, according to the sports betting site, BetOnline.
Prop wagers, also known as proposition bets, are wagers on an individual player or specific event in a game or a match that is not directly connected to the outcome of a game. These fun bets began as a way to entertain bettors during games that had probable winners. In time, however, prop wagers have evolved to becoming majorly popular in their own right.
Halftime show, first song
The most popular prop bet is the first song performed by the musician at the halftime show, though new bets are usually halted early because of leaks due to rehearsals.
Kendrick Lamar is performing at the halftime show.
You cannot bet on the halftime show in Illinois.
Coin Toss
This fan favorite boats the highest bet count of any Super Bowl prop.
"It's a 50-50 proposition so it's something we can set high limits for and allow our customers to wager on all year," BetOnline Brand Manager Dave Mason said in the release. "Bettors love the coin toss because we grade it immediately, so they're already hoping for a win before the game even kicks off."
National Anthem
People can bet on how long the anthem will last, whether it will include piano, and whether the play/coach will cry, according to the Sportsbook Review, which is a betting analysis website.
Jon Batiste is this year's performing artist.
Illinois residents cannot legally bet on the National Anthem.
Gatorade color
People can bet on what color of Gatorade that gets poured on the winning coach. The orange flavor/color has been the most popular for a Gatorade shower since 2001, occurring five times, according to Sports Illustrated. Blue and clear have each appeared four times and there was no Gatorade pouring on four occasions. Purple and yellow have each been seen three times.
Rules in Illinois
In October, the Illinois Gaming Board made some bets forbidden after the National Football League made a request to do so.
The NFL sought to stop wager types they determined to have a 'negative impact on game integrity, NFL players and consumers,' according to a news release at the time.
The bets in question are suspended for the Super Bowl. The prohibited items for wagering are:
Player injuries
Fan safety
Player misconduct
Penalties
Replay results
Officiating assignments
First play of the game
Roster or personnel decisions
Player to miss a field goal or extra point try
First pass to be incomplete
Any other wager that is pre-determined or 100% determinable by one person in one play.
'As articulated by the NFL…wagers of these nature introduce sport integrity concerns in contravention of public policy goals,' wrote Marcus D. Fruchter, who is the Illinois Gaming Board Administrator. 'Pre-determined choices and actions within the control of individual players, coaches, or league officials are susceptible to abuse and manipulation.'
The board will consider making these changes permanent at the Feb. 6 meeting, Beth Kaufman told the State Journal-Register, who is Director of Communications for the board.

title: Pleasant Plains junior reserve gets hot at the right time in OT win over Petersburg PORTA
author: Bill Welt
description: Pleasant Plains junior guard Nolan Scott continued to hit nylon after forcing OT in boys basketball win over Petersburg PORTA on Tuesday
content:
PLEASANT PLAINS — Pleasant Plains' Nolan Scott had a game to remember.
The junior reserve guard delivered the game-tying 3 to force overtime before totaling five treys and 19 points in a 67-63 overtime win over Petersburg PORTA/A-C Central in a Sangamo Conference boys basketball game on Tuesday.
'I've been able to shoot it,' Scott said, 'but I've never been hot like that.'
Plains (16-10, 5-1 Sangamo) trailed 60-56 in OT until back-to-back 3s by Scott for the lead. He banked the go-ahead 3 near the corner with 32.1 seconds remaining.
'I think I was just hot,' Scott said. 'That might've been a little luck, but it went in, so it counts.'
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
PORTA's Drew Marr answered with the tying layup before Scott launched the final go-ahead 3 from the wing with just a couple seconds to spare.
'I knew he was capable of a game like that and we thought this would be a good matchup for him to play in and he took full advantage,' Plains coach Kyle Weber said. 'What a big 3 that he hit to send it to overtime. He gave us a huge lift and I thought a lot of guys did.'
Junior guard Owen Johnson supplied four 3s and finished with 16 points. Cooper Schallenberg rallied Plains late with nine of his 11 points in the fourth quarter to set up Scott's game-tying trey with 11 seconds remaining.
Guards Grady Grisham and Trager Shultz added 10 and nine points, respectively.
'It was a big 3,' Scott said of the shot to end the fourth quarter. 'We saw the mismatch when I ball-screened Cooper and he (the defender) just left, so I was open and I shot it.'
PORTA (22-5, 5-1) surged ahead 48-42 with under four minutes left in regulation following a 15-2 run.
Senior guard Griffin McClure led the Bluejays with 22 points. Guards Marr and Jett Karrick provided 15 and 14 points, respectively.

title: New restaurant serving breakfast, lunch opens in Springfield
author: Claire Grant
description: A new restaurant has opened in Springfield offering breakfast and lunch every day. And the menu has something for everyone.
content:
A new Springfield restaurant has opened in a former cafe location.
Harvest Kitchen + Bar celebrated a soft-open of their upscale dining restaurant on Feb. 10, a month and several days later than their planned opening date of the first of the new year at 4241 Conestaga Drive.
Vivian Dominguez, who co-owns the business with Odette Yobal, said the staff decided to host a soft open to get the ball rolling until the business can operate at one hundred percent. The business is open from 7:30 a.m. until 2 p.m. seven days a week.
'We are still working on some details and making adjustments to add a few things,' Dominguez said. 'This allows for us to fine-tune all the details before expanding our hours. We kindly ask for our customers' patience as we are working for them and because of them.'
The restaurant advertises themselves as an American breakfast and brunch spot setting itself apart by having an elevated aesthetic compared to a regular diner. According to Dominguez, no dish on the morning menu hits over the $15 mark, while lunch menu items range from $10 to $20.
"We love to play with food presentation, making dishes look attractive and appetizing," Dominguez said. "I truly enjoy the experience of eating, and I want our customers to feel the same."
Yobal and Dominguez run a separate Mexican restaurant, but did not comment on which location in the city.
The menu offers breakfast staples like omelets, biscuits and gravy and avocado toast. Salads, cocktails and health juice drinks were also advertised by the restaurant. The decision to add gluten free, keto and vegetarian options and health-minded dishes was made by Dominguez, so dietary restricted customers could eat with friends and family at the table.
The location may be familiar for some readers. Sweet Basil Café held the space for several years before suddenly shuttering doors in late August. The closure followed an eviction notice served by the landlord for over $110,000 to owners Jim and Denise Karonis.
Before becoming Sweet Basil, the building housed O'Charley's, which closed in March 2019.

title: The US is leaving the World Health Organization. What does that mean for Illinois?
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The U.S. is pulling the plug on its membership with the World Health Organization. What does that mean for Illinois?
content:
The director of the IDPH speaks out about how the exit from the WHO will harm Illinois public health.
Pres. Trump seeks to leave the organization for the second time.
The U.S. is and has been the largest funder of the global health agency and has influenced its direction since its founding in 1948.
The U.S. is pulling the plug on its membership with the World Health Organization.
What does that mean for Illinois, and why does it matter?
The head of the Illinois Department of Public Health believes the decision will harm the state's public health. Here's more of what he said in a letter to colleagues last month.
Illinois DPH speaks out
Dr. Sameer Vohra, who is Director of IDPH, made a statement about President Donald Trump's executive order to leave the organization and it would mean for the Illinois IDPH.
Vohra also noted that the Trump administration instructed the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to stop communicating with WHO. Vohra said he felt it was important to share how the decision would harm the state's public health.
The U.S. may lose internal access to WHO's global surveillance system, which provides the U.S., including Illinois, with early warnings of outbreaks by monitoring disease activity in more than 150 countries, Vohra said. 'Without access to this network, Illinois could lose critical time detecting threats like new COVID-19 variants, Ebola, avian influenza, and more,' he wrote.
Illinois may become less able to monitor new or emerging diseases entering the state, Vohra stated. 'Chicago is home to O'Hare International Airport, the second busiest airport in the United States and a primary point of entry for international travelers. Public health teams at O'Hare, including those from the CDC, the Chicago Department of Public Health, and IDPH, could face incomplete data on infectious travelers, inconsistent health screenings, and greater risk of disease spread through one of the nation's key transit hubs.'
Vohra added that Illinois will now need to explore alternate tools and resources to understand and address global crises, obtain data, and quickly identify emerging threats in the absence of any confidential information provided by the WHO.
WHO also plays a 'critical role in identifying the right components of both our annual flu vaccine and other emerging disease threats."
What is the WHO?
The U.S. is and has historically been the largest funder of the global health agency headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. WHO, part of the United Nations, is tasked with preparing for and fighting health emergencies. The U.S. has influenced the agency since its founding after World War II.
Why is the U.S. leaving WHO?
President Trump criticized the WHO for its handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, even as his administration faced scrutiny for being slow to respond to the crisis, according to USA Today. In 2020, at the height of the pandemic, then-President Trump began the process of pulling out from WHO.
So, the U.S. tried to leave WHO once before?
The Trump administration previously failed to leave the organization under U.S. law governing the timeline for withdrawal and funding obligations to the agency. Former President Joe Biden reversed Trump's decision after taking office and restored funding to WHO.
What else did IDPH say?
Dr. Vohra said in the Jan. 31 letter that IDPH plans to meet with a coalition of global health experts in Illinois to "determine how to maximize our resources to protect the public health of Illinois residents."
In addition to using existing data systems to track health issues, the department will explore other tools to monitor global outbreaks and mitigate related threats in Illinois.

title: Crump: $10M settlement in Sonya Massey case 'bittersweet'
author: Steven Spearie
description: The $10 million to the Massey estate via the settlement is believed to be the single largest payout in Sangamon County history.
content:
Attorneys for the Sonya Massey estate called the $10 million settlement 'very significant.'
Sonya Massey would have turned 37 years old Wednesday.
Civil rights attorney Ben Crump said an out-of-court settlement between Sangamon County and the estate of Sonya Massey was "bittersweet" and hoped legislation would address "constitutional failures" in Illinois.
The Sangamon County Board unanimously agreed to a $10 million mediated settlement at its meeting Tuesday evening.
It is believed to be the largest single payout in the county's history.
The settlement, said County Administrator Brian McFadden on Tuesday, will be paid through cash reserves.
The mediation took place last week in Chicago and involved a retired Illinois judge, Kay Hanlon of ADR Solutions.
Wednesday marked the 37th birthday of Massey, who was fatally shot in her home by a Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy, Sean P. Grayson.
Grayson was charged with first-degree murder and remains jailed. His next court appearance is March 24.
Anthony Romanucci, an attorney working with Crump, called the settlement "very relevant and very significant."
"We're in Sangamon County," Romanucci said. "This settlement is in best interests of (Massey's children)."
A bill by State Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, to strengthen background checks and increase transparency in law enforcement hiring was expected to be introduced today.
Speaking from Pine Bluff, Arkansas, Massey's father James Wilburn, said his heart was "heavy," and maintained that Grayson was "a rogue cop" who should have never been hired by Sangamon County.
"No one should feel the hurt we're feeling today," Wilburn said.
"It is the hope of Sonya's family that her death can bring change," Crump added, "and that the community will continue to say her name, so no one ever needlessly loses their life again when all they are asking for is help."

title: Looking to get out of the house? Check out one of these 5 things in Springfield

Love is in the air this weekend as Friday marks Valentine's Day. While the day is often celebrated by couples, be sure to tell your friends and family how much you love and appreciate them.

Topsy Turvy painting

In this art class, all art supplies are included in a ticket as guests are guided through the art process with snacks and drinks.
Brews and Mews

title: Riverton's Allgaier looks ahead to new season as reigning NASCAR Xfinity champ
author: Ryan Mahan
description: Barely three months after winning his first NASCAR Xfinity Series championship, Riverton's Justin Allgaier is back — and ready for even more.
content:
After winning his first NASCAR Xfinity Cup title after 14 seasons in November, Riverton's Justin Allgaier was on top of the world.
The 38-year-old driver continues to have success. On Thursday, he beat out Martin Truex Jr., and J.J. Yeley in the first Daytona Duel race for a spot in Sunday's NASCAR Cup Series Daytona 500 in the No. 40 car owned by Dale Earnhardt Jr.'s JR Motorsports team.
The celebrations that followed his championship win won't put all his past struggles out of mind.
'I've told people that you have to have those deep, dark valleys to really understand how high those peaks really are,' Allgaier said. 'Would it have been great to win a championship earlier in my career? Absolutely, but I don't know if I could have fully enjoyed it, nor could I have fully appreciated what it means to me now.'
Following the 2024 season, Allgaier's celebration didn't last long. Just weeks after finishing second at Phoenix Raceway on Saturday, Nov. 9 to clinch the championship, Allgaier had shoulder surgery. Now healthy, the reigning Xfinity Series champion understands he'll have a target on his back. He's ready for it.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
'We want to take the fight to them, and not only do we want to have set the bar last year, but we want to be the bar all year this year and put ourselves in a position to try to try to go back-to-back,' Allgaier said. 'For me, the mindset's different this year: I'm no longer chasing that first title; I'm chasing a second title and I can go out each week and I can have more fun with it. I'm actually more excited about 2025 than I was 2024.'
Allgaier's talent was noticed early
Hal Pilger, who covered motorsports as part of his 35-year career as a sportswriter at The State Journal-Register before he retired in 2009, said he saw brilliance in Allgaier long ago.
'I think the first time I ever saw Justin race, he was probably about 13 or so, and you could tell right away that this guy was a natural; this kid was so far above what most people his age would be able to do,' Pilger said from his home in Florida.
'I think the first time I actually ever saw him in a big race was at the (Illinois State Fairgrounds in 2009), and I think it was an ARCA race, and he more than held his own with the track and with the other drivers.'
Allgaier, at 16, finished 17 th after starting 40 th in his first ARCA Series start.
"It was pretty impressive for being a teenager,' Pilger recalled. 'The first time I ever encountered anything like that was ... (NASCAR legend) Kenny Schrader, down in the Ozarks. I was sports editor at Rolla, Missouri, they had a half-mile asphalt track, and Kenny Schrader was either 15 or had just turned 16 ... and he was very competitive.'
It wasn't just stock car drivers that Pilger compared Allgaier with, but Springfield's Donnie Beechler, who raced 36 times in the Indy Racing League — including four starts in the Indianapolis 500.
'Donnie Beechler started out really young, too, and he of course progressed to being able to qualify and finished 12th (in the 2000) Indy 500,' Pilger said. "I guess you almost have to start really young to get that far, but you could tell (Allgaier) had more ability than probably anybody around at that stage of the game at his age. He's more than proved what he can do, and this championship certainly speaks to that.'
Wearing Brandt with pride
Most cars in NASCAR are adorned with some of the biggest household names and products in the world. It's a colorful ballet on wheels with name-brand restaurants, tool manufacturers, beverage companies, and other services with instant recognition.
Allgaier said he is delighted to wear his Brandt fire suit and the international agriculture fertilizer company's emblem, seen at their headquarters on Koke Mill Road in Springfield, on his car. Allgaier and Brandt paired up first for the 2011 Nationwide Series season.
The Springfield-based crop, fertilizer, and agricultural services company sponsored 17 of Allgaier's 34 races in 2011. That early investment helped pave the way for Allgaier's current success.
'I don't know if words can describe what that feeling is like, to represent a central Illinois to having the relationship that I do with (Brandt CEO) Rick Brandt, his wife Kristie, his aunt Evelyn, who was one of the founders of the company,' Allgaier said of winning the title with Brandt's logo being front and center.
'In sports, there's a lot of great sponsors there's a lot of great partners that are a part of it, and you don't always get to pick the companies ... to represent: some have different goals and agendas or meanings to a driver than others. The word Brandt, while it's red and white and a name, it's been something that has become prideful for me because it's home and — to your point, when you say when you see the word Brandt, you think of me: I would say it's inversely the same, when I hear somebody say my name, I hope that they think of Brandt because they've been as much of a part of my career and getting to where I'm at.
'Let's be honest: I wouldn't still be in the sport if it wasn't for the family and for the Brandt culture. It's something that means a lot to me.'
Two area drivers had main sponsors from Springfield companies: Allgaier and now-retired National Hot Rod Association Funny Car driver Tim Wilkerson. Wilkerson was sponsored by Levi, Ray & Shoup. For two national drivers from Sangamon County to have local sponsors was a blessing, Allgaier said.
'I don't know that there are many drivers that get an opportunity to represent brands that are near and dear to home like Tim and I do,' Allgaier said. 'To be honest with you, I was always jealous with LRS (and that partnership with Wilkerson). I always told everybody I would love to emulate that and to be able to represent a local home brand, something that is here and means something personally to me and I'm passionate about.
'Lo and behold a couple years later and I had the opportunity to do that.'
Ready for more
Just because Allgaier is 38 and can boast a championship, he said he's not ready to walk away. Last year, he and Brandt signed a two-year extension through 2026. He also hopes he hasn't even reached his racing prime, yet.
'They say that between 40 and 42 is kind of peak age for NASCAR,' Allgaier said. '(That) is when your talent and your experience kind of beats your aggression level and everything balances out.'
With his shoulder healed, Allgaier said physically, there are no issues climbing in the car. But as he gets older, Allgaier says drivers learn different ways to maintain a mental edge without taking as many risks.
"You prioritize things differently,' he said. 'When you're young, you're willing to take a lot more risks and sometimes that's good.'
Now retired, Pilger can root for Allgaier as strictly a fan: one of many who root for the top-notch driver who has successfully combined talent and affability.
'I'm just so happy for him because you want a guy like that who treats people the way they should be treated along the way and then doesn't forget about them afterwards,' Pilger said. 'I'm always very happy when somebody like that is very successful, whether it's in baseball, football, auto racing, anything really; it's just you like to see good people have good success.'

title: Cash App is ordered to pay millions in refunds. Here's how Illinois users can get paid.
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Do users need to do anything to receive funds? How much can they expect to receive Here's what you need to know as a Cash App user in Illinois.
content:
A federal agency ordered Cash App to pay users and the government to directly and indirectly compensate them for the mobile app's weak security procedures.
The dollar amount for refunds and when users can expect it is not yet known.
A $15 million settlement last year against Cash App paid users affected by a security breach upwards of $2,500.
Cash App users could be getting a paycheck since a federal agency has ordered the company to pay out $175 million for its weak security procedures.
Do users need to do anything to receive funds? How much can they expect to receive?
Here's what you need to know as a Cash App user in Illinois.
What is Cash App accused of doing?
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, which enforces federal consumer finance laws, claims Cash App 'tricked' its customers by allowing fraud to take place on the mobile app, according to USA TODAY.
The company closed cases of reported fraud without opening a legally required investigation, CFPB said.
The company also in some cases directed users who lost money to ask their bank to reverse the transactions. Block Inc., which is the mobile app's parent company, would then deny the request.
"Cash App created the conditions for fraud to proliferate on its popular payment platform,' said CFPB Director Rohit Chopra in a news release. 'When things went wrong, Cash App flouted its responsibilities and even burdened local banks with problems that the company caused.'
The company is additionally accused of misleading consumers to think that banks were responsible for disputes, which is against federal law.
The mobile app further failed to provide 'meaningful and effective customer service,' according to the CFPB, when users sought help from after being defrauded. This led to people searching online to speak with Cash App customer service representatives – and consequently running into scam artists.
"Block knew that its customers were being targeted by fraudsters in this way but failed to take timely action to address the issue," according to the CFPB.
How much money will Illinois Cash App users get?
It's not yet clear how many users will be refunded, who will qualify, how much users will receive, or when, according to the USA TODAY report.
A $15 million settl ement last year against Cash App paid users affected by a security breach upwards of $2,500.
The CFPB earlier this month ordered Cash App to pay out $175 million, which includes refunding users $120 million, as well as paying $55 million into a government relief fund to help those "harmed by companies that break federal consumer financial protection laws."
How do I sign up to receive the payment?
Users do not need to sign up or do anything at this time to receive a refund.
Am I eligible to receive money?
Cash App users who could qualify for the settlement include:
Consumers who did not receive refunds to which they were entitled for fraudulent transactions.
Consumers whose accounts had unauthorized transfers or transactions not adequately investigated by Cash App and Block.
Consumers who had accounts locked as a result.
Consumers who did not receive provisional credits during delayed investigations.
Can I contact someone if I have questions?
Cash app users can contact Block, Inc., according to the CFPB.
Toll-free phone: 1-888-488-1181
Email: CFPBinquiry@cash.app
Mail:
Cash App MSC 210
1955 Broadway, Suite 600
Oakland, CA 94612.

title: Inspector: Springfield restaurant 'on the verge of a roach infestation'
author: Claire Grant
description: Of the 150 inspections that took place in January, six establishments had more than 10 violations. Here's what health inspectors found.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Out of 150 Sangamon County restaurant inspections in January, six establishments had more than 10 health code violations.
Violations included improper food storage temperatures, pest control issues, and cross-contamination risks.
The Sangamon County Department of Public Health conducts routine inspections based on an establishment's risk level.
The first health inspections of the year are out, and the Springfield area is off to a good start.
Blackhawk Elementary, Early Learning Center and Southern View Elementary all received no violations in their first inspection of the year, but the same can't be said about several Springfield-area restaurants.
On Jan. 8, Top Cats at 3211 E. Sangamon Ave. racked up 16 health code violations during a routine inspection, causing a reinspection to fix the issues that were spotted during inspection.
Meat juices found at the bottom of a large cooler were found during the inspection and when asked, employees said the cooler was used for ribs prepared a few days before. In another cooler, a container of cottage cheese in one of the prep coolers was found two weeks out of date by the date of inspection.
In continuation of food safety, cross-contamination was corrected from coats and sweatshirts stored over food items used in the cooking process.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
How violations work
Food establishments are inspected by the Sangamon County Department of Public Health on an annual schedule that is determined by assigned risk type. The risk types are high, medium, or low risk, as defined by the Illinois Food Service Sanitation Code. These are determined by the complexity of food preparation taking place at the facility. Routine inspections are conducted unannounced. Follow up and complaint inspections are conducted as needed.
Critical violations concern hygiene, food temperatures, sanitizing procedures, and cross contamination. Non-critical violations concern the maintenance and cleanliness of a facility.
Here are the Sangamon County restaurants that received more than 10 violations from the health department during the month of January.
In January, 150 inspections took place across different establishments; six inspections resulted in over 10 violations.
Yummi Yummi Hibachi Express
Location: 2901 Ridge Ave., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Jan. 28, Complaint
What: Inspection found 15 violations, five risk factors.
Notes from inspection: During the inspection, a large tub of rice was found cooling on top of a dorm cooler close to 100 degrees Fahrenheit, instead of cooling in a safe cooling area. The rice was also measured to be four to six inches deep, making cooling uneven during the process.
Three bags of shrimp were also noticed thawing on a counter during the inspection, while large bags of rice and sugar in the shed were left open. The foods had no protection according to the inspector, from external contaminants as the vents in the facility do not prevent pest entrance.
Lime St. Cafe
Location: 951 S. Durkin Drive, Springfield
Date/inspection type: Jan. 23, Complaint
What: Inspection found 14 violations, four risk factors.
Notes from inspection: According to notes left by the inspector, the facility is "on the verge of a roach infestation."
There are pests observed throughout the facility in various life stages. The cleaning and maintenance of the facility is supporting the proliferation of these pests. The facility has grease, dust, food, and water standing in places throughout the bar and kitchen. Pests are observed primarily in the dish area, on the far side of the bar and the prep cooler.
Pink mold was observed on the deflector shield in the ice machine used by staff and the soda gun in the kitchen had mold inside the nozzle. Also, during the inspection, a sanitizer bucket in the same area had too low of cleaning solution in it to moderately clean surfaces.
Hunan Restaurant
Location: 1333 Wabash Ave., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Jan. 13, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 13 violations, five risk factors.
Notes from inspection: In a repeat violation, several foods in prep were stored uncovered in the walk-in coolers while several white powders like flour and cornstarch were stashed without a label, leading to possible food contamination.
The floor is in need of a good cleaning, the floor directly underneath the fryers has an accumulation of grease and food debris. The inspector suggests pulling out the fryers to clean underneath.
Mr. Gyro's Jefferson
Location: 2126 S. MacArthur Blvd., Springfield
Date/inspection type: Jan. 9, routine inspection
What: Inspection found 13 violations, five risk factors.
Notes from inspection: During this inspection the person in charge could not produce verification that employees were notified of their responsibility to report illnesses and symptoms related to foodborne illness. A copy of the Reporting Agreement given out by this facility was found in the paperwork given during the pre-opening.
In the prep room, raw chicken was found over raw vegetables while a tub of onions was found under a shelf of cleaners, degreasers and bleach.
Almadina Halal Restaurant
Location: 3109 Chatham Road, Springfield
Date/inspection type: Jan. 13, first inspection
What: Inspection found 11 violations, five risk factors.
Notes from inspection: Within the restaurant, no member of the staff was certified in food training or designated as a certified food manager.
No sanitizer, sanitizer test strips, or paper towels were present when the inspector arrived, while caulking was found needing to be repaired at the triple sink.
In the back of the kitchen a wall mounted potato press was found soiled in food water. According to the inspector, the press was not in use from the last restaurant and was then removed from the wall.

title: Here are the two Springfield area seniors advancing to boys state swimming and diving meet
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Chatham Glenwood's Jackson Vinzant tied for first to earn spot in the boys state swim meet, along with Sangamon Valley's Andrew Bellemare
content:
It came down to a touch at the wall and Chatham Glenwood senior Jackson Vinzant made the most of his opportunity at the Edwardsville Sectional boys swimming and diving meet at the Chuck Fruit Aquatic Center on Saturday.
At sectional, a swimmer must win the event or beat the state qualifying time to swim at the FMC Natatorium. Vinzant tied Edwardsville freshman Jackson Suhre for first place in 1 minute, 49.59 seconds in the 200-yard freestyle and both advanced to the Illinois High School Association state finals that runs on Friday and Saturday in Westmont.
Meanwhile at the Urbana Sectional, senior Andrew Bellemare of Niantic Sangamon Valley won two events, taking the 200 freestyle (1:45.35) and 500 freestyle (4:51.55) to qualify for state.
It's Vinzant's first trip to the state meet. He swam for the Titans as a sophomore in the 2022-23 season and finished in fifth place in the 200 freestyle at sectional, touching in 1:58.28. Vinzant was 10th in the 100 backstroke (1:00.33) that season and swam a leg on Glenwood's second-place 200 and 400 freestyle relays.
Vinzant did not swim high school last season but came back just in time to join Bellemare as the two area swimmers to qualify for state this season.
Close but no cigar
Glenwood was within striking distance of advancing a pair of relays to state, but the Titans were out touched by two traditional power schools. O'Fallon finished in 1:29.19 and defeated Glenwood in the 200 freestyle relay for first place. Sophomore Kareem Zeino and seniors William Patzia, Abdu Zeino and Vinzant clocked a time of 1:30.59 for Glenwood. The qualifying time was 1:27.47.
The same foursome came in second place behind first-place Edwardsville (3:19.37) in the 400 freestyle relay — the last event of the day. Glenwood finished in 3:21.89 and the qualifying time was 3:12.85.
Individually for the Titans, Abdu Zeino (22.45) was fifth and Kareem Zeino (22.72) took eighth in the 50 freestyle while the qualifying time was 21.73. Kareem Zeino earned third place in the 100 breaststroke (1:02.78), and the state time was 59.18. Abdu Zeino finished seventh in the 100 freestyle (51.02) with the qualifying time at 47.53.
Edwardsville won the sectional with 247.5 points, and second place O'Fallon had 233. Glenwood was third with 182.5, followed by Springfield High (162), Jacksonville (73), Sacred Heart-Griffin (62) and Southeast (2).
Senators, Crimsons get shut out
Springfield High and Jacksonville failed to qualify an individual swimmer or a relay.
Springfield junior Riley Herr placed third in the 200 IM (2:06.63) and fifth in the 100 breaststroke (1:03.93). To qualify in the IM, Herr needed 1:57.28. Sophomore James Maeda took fourth in the 100 butterfly (55.71), and the qualifying time was 51.95. With sophomore Kishan Ugrappa, Herr, Maeda and sophomore Oliver Havey, the Senators had their best finish in a relay with a third-place showing in the 200 medley relay (1:42.98). The state time was 1:36.78.
Springfield junior diver Andrew Kotner finished second in the 1-meter diving competition with a score of 389.30. Edwardsville junior Derek Ruehl was first with 482.85.
To advance to the state diving finals, a diver must win the competition or be among the top 32 sectional scores. Kotner's score was good for 40th place around the state, falling short of advancing.
Jacksonville junior Jack Borgman was fifth in the 100 freestyle (49.94) and ninth in the 50 freestyle (22.88). Senior Colin Wilson placed second in the 100 breaststroke (1:02.62), and he was sixth in the 100 freestyle (50.29).
The 200 freestyle relay team of sophomore Andrew Schumacher, Caleb Atkins, Wilson and Borgman placed third in 1:33.67 for the Crimsons.
Also, at Urbana
Taylorville sophomore Joseph Goodman was fourth in the 200 free (1:58.16) and seventh in the 50 free (23.41). Freshman Kade Guhlstorf placed seventh in the 100 free (51.94) and ninth in the 100 breaststroke (1:10.26) for the Tornadoes.

title: Audit: Illinois' noncitizen health care programs far outstripped original cost estimates
author: Hannah Meisel
description: The report also found more than 6,000 people enrolled in the state-funded programs were classified as 'undocumented' despite actually having social security numbers.
content:
Two Illinois healthcare programs for noncitizens cost the state $1.6 billion, far exceeding initial projections.
Governor Pritzker proposes defunding the program for adults aged 44-64, citing high costs and potential for work-based coverage.
The audit highlights discrepancies in enrollment data and the need for more accurate cost estimations in the future.
A pair of health care programs that benefit noncitizens – one of which is already on Gov. JB Pritzker's budgetary chopping block – far outstripped its original estimated price tag and cost the state of Illinois $1.6 billion through last summer, according to a new audit of the programs published Wednesday.
The report also found more than 6,000 people enrolled in the state-funded programs were classified as 'undocumented' despite actually having social security numbers. Some of those people were green card holders who would have instead qualified for health coverage like Medicaid or traditional insurance.
The audit, which lawmakers requested in late 2023, comes one week after Pritzker delivered his annual budget proposal to the General Assembly. The governor's plan would defund the newer of the two programs, which is aimed at noncitizens aged 44 to 64, while leaving in place the smaller program for noncitizen seniors aged 65 and older.
Asked about the audit at an unrelated Chicago news conference Wednesday, Pritzker defended the Department of Healthcare and Family Services' work on redeterminations in the program over the last year, which has brought down total enrollment in addition to the administration's freezes on enrollment in the programs in 2023.
'It's some evidence, anyway, that there are an awful lot of people out there who need coverage, who aren't getting it, or who will do anything to get it,' Pritzker said after reiterating his support for universal health care coverage. 'And I think that's a sad state of affairs in our society.'
Republicans, who've long criticized both the programs' ballooning costs and what they've characterized as a lack of transparency, said the audit proves them right about Illinois' first-in-the-nation programs.
'We're the only state that puts this burden on Illinois tax on their own state taxpayers taking this on and to not run it properly and to have these large cost overruns, that's how you end up with a budget deficit,' Senate Minority Leader John Curran, R-Downers Grove told reporters Wednesday at the Capitol. 'That's what's crowding out spending on education. That's what's crowding out spending on other components of the state budget. That's why we need an audit.'
Vastly underestimated costs
When progressive lawmakers first pushed for the creation of the Health Benefits for Immigrant Seniors, or HBIS, program for noncitizens aged 65 and older in the first few months of the COVID-19 pandemic, officials relied on advocates' $2 million cost estimate for the program's first year. Though that projection was later doubled to $4 million as the program was being set up in the latter half of 2020, the actual cost ended up at more than $67 million after HBIS began accepting enrollees in December of that year.
But while actual costs for the seniors' program in its first three years – $412 million – ended up being 84% higher than original estimates, the price tag for the expanded program for adults aged 44 to 64 was many times larger.
The Health Benefits for Immigrant Adults, or HBIA, program covered noncitizen adults age 55 to 64 and was later expanded to cover those as young as 44. It cost $485.3 million over its first two years – roughly 284% more than the combined original estimate for both programs.
The programs were designed with the same income eligibility thresholds as Medicaid. But since federal Medicaid dollars can't be spent on many types of non-citizens, the state has had to foot the bill itself instead of receiving a roughly 52% federal match like it does for traditional Medicaid coverage.
The audit noted that HFS began seeking federal reimbursement for some emergency services last year, which would be retroactive to mid-2022. But Pritzker last week said part of the reason he was proposing axing the program for adults – which would save an estimated $330 million next year – was due to the Trump administration signaling it would soon halt that reimbursement.
Enrollment has also far outstripped original estimates, especially in the program for adults aged 44 to 64. For fiscal year 2023, nearly 54,000 adults enrolled in the program – about twice the original projection of 26,800.
In 2023, after the Pritzker administration acknowledged the programs' cost had grown to $1.1 billion, the governor asked the General Assembly for authority to impose spending controls. After lawmakers followed his request, Pritzker quickly paused enrollment in the program for adults in July of 2023, followed by a pause in the program for seniors in November of that year.
The programs have not accepted any new enrollees since those pauses and redetermination efforts have decreased their headcounts in the last year. The audit cited an enrollment decline in the adults' program from a high of 53,936 in fiscal year 2023 to 41,537 in fiscal year 2024, which ended June 30.
The day after the second enrollment pause in November 2023, lawmakers approved a resolution calling for an audit of the programs, which authorized Auditor General Frank Mautino's office to begin work on the report published Wednesday.
Pritzker last week proposed defunding the program for adults, telling reporters that those aged 44 to 64 are still of working age and could get jobs with health care coverage.
Axing the program renews a disagreement between the governor and progressive members of the General Assembly's Latino Caucus, who opposed enrollment pauses and efforts to require co-pays for program participants.
But the governor framed his proposal as one of shared sacrifice.
'If you come to the table looking to spend more, I'm going to ask you where you want to cut,' the governor told lawmakers in his Budget Address. 'I have made difficult decisions – including to programs I have championed, which is hard for me, just as I know some of the difficult decisions you will have to make will be hard for you.'
Mis-enrollments
The audit also found inconsistencies in enrollment data, sometimes relying on misreporting from program participants.
Of the 6,098 enrollees with social security numbers who'd been mislabeled as undocumented, nearly 400 people had been in the U.S. for the five years it takes for legal permanent residents to qualify for Medicaid, according to the audit. Meanwhile, other green card holders who hadn't yet reached that five-year threshold but were enrolled in the state-run programs would have been eligible to purchase health coverage from the Affordable Care Act's insurance marketplace.
HFS last spring issued new rules clarifying that those noncitizens were not eligible for the state health coverage programs, and the agency's redetermination process has identified and disenrolled many.
Others who had social security numbers are in the U.S. legally but are not eligible for green cards. The HBIA and HBIS programs were designed to cover them but were not intended to cover asylum-seekers who've been sent to Illinois from southern border states in recent years.
Those mis-enrollments, which also included nearly 700 people who received coverage under the program for noncitizens 65 and older despite being too young to qualify, drove some of the ballooning costs in the health care initiative. But the audit points to the Pritzker administration relying on vastly underestimated figures when setting up the programs in 2020, 2021 and 2022.
'Actual enrollment and actual costs exceeded the initial program estimates for both the HBIS and HBIA program,' the audit said.
Jade Aubrey contributed.

title: See Gene Hackman's star-studded cast of co-stars: Clint Eastwood, Denzel Washington, more
author: Mike Snider
description: Gene Hackman, who was found dead on Feb. 26, along with his deceased wife, shared the screen with an admirable list of co-stars.
content:
Gene Hackman, whose acting career began in 1961, shared the screen with many phenomenal co-stars including Clint Eastwood (twice), Christopher Reeve (three times), Barbra Streisand and Ann-Margret.
Show Caption
In the wake of Gene Hackman's Feb. 26 death, a who's-who of Hollywood have offered tributes to his greatness.
Among them: Clint Eastwood, who directed and co-starred with Hackman in "Unforgiven," said of him in a statement to USA TODAY: "There was no finer actor than Gene. Intense and instinctive. Never a false note. He was also a dear friend whom I will miss very much."
Need more proof of his talent? During a five-decade career, Hackman held his own with a grand gallery of co-stars.
Hackman started early co-starring with Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway in 1967's "Bonnie and Clyde" – he got a supporting actor nomination for his role of Buck Barrow – and in 1970, Hackman got another supporting actor nod in "I Never Sang for My Father," which starred Melvyn Douglas.
But he would win a best actor award the following year for perhaps his most famous role and his co-star would get a nomination, too. Here's that combination and some more of Hackman's co-stars.
1971: Roy Scheider in 'The French Connection'
Hackman and Scheider play New York City detectives in the 1971 film, directed by William Friedkin. Hackman who won his first Oscar as best actor for his role as James "Popeye" Doyle; Scheider, in the role of Buddy "Cloudy" Russo, earned a supporting actor nomination. Friedkin, who would go on to direct "The Exorcist," won the Oscar for best director and the film won best picture.
"(Popeye) was a man who was very driven," Hackman told USA TODAY in 2005. He would return as Doyle four years later in the 1975 sequel, "French Connection II."
1972: Ernest Borgnine and Shelley Winters in 'The Poseidon Adventure'
In "The Poseidon Adventure," one of a slew of '70s blockbuster disaster films, Hackman played a reverend who led fellow passengers/co-stars including Shelley Winters, Ernest Borgnine, Stella Stevens, Red Buttons to the upper reaches of the capsized ship.
1972: Lee Marvin in 'Prime Cut'
Lee Marvin plays a mob enforcer sent to Kansas City to collected a debt from Hackman, whose role is that of a crooked slaughterhouse operator. Also in the film: Sissy Spacek.
1973: Al Pacino in 'Scarecrow'
In "Scarecrow," Hackman's just-released convict, Max, finds a kindred soul in the optimistic sailor Francis (Al Pacino). To prepare for their roles, the actors "literally dressed in old raggedy clothes and hung out on Market Street," in San Francisco, Hackman said.
1974: Robert Duvall and Harrison Ford in 'The Conversation'
The late film critic Roger Ebert in "The Great Movies II," wrote Hackman delivered "one of the key performances of a great career," as a surveillance expert in the Francis Ford Coppola-directed thriller.
Hackman's wiretapper worries that two people he is spying on will be killed. "You see that this compulsion to do this has left him a shallow guy in ways, and troubled. (He's) not a leading man but a character," he told USA TODAY. "Unfortunately, we don't see those anymore."
Also in the film: Duvall, Ford, John Cazale, Teri Garr and Frederic Forrest.
1978: Christopher Reeve and Ned Beatty in 'Superman'
Hackman's Lex Luthor served as the foil for Superman (Christopher Reeve) in three "Superman" films including 1980's "Superman II" and 1987's "Superman IV: The Quest for Peace."
Also in the films: Margot Kidder, Jackie Cooper and Marlon Brando ("Superman II").
1981: Barbra Streisand in 'All Night Long'
Hackman is a middle-aged man who has a fling with a married woman (Streisand).
Also in the film: Dennis Quaid and Diane Ladd.
1985: Ann-Margret in 'Twice in a Lifetime'
Hackman, who played a steelworker, and producer/director Bud Yorkin both drew on their real-life recent divorces in this film about a man who separates from his wife (Ellen Burstyn) to live with his new flame (Ann-Margret). "We were two men working closely together, going through that same experience," Hackman told USA TODAY.
Also in the film: Ally Sheedy and Amy Madigan.
1986: Dennis Hopper in 'Hoosiers'
A coach with a checkered past (Hackman) leads a small-town Indiana basketball team to the state finals with the help of reformed town drunk played by Dennis Hopper, who got a supporting actor Oscar nod.
Also in the film: Barbara Hershey.
1988: Willem Dafoe in 'Mississippi Burning'
Hackman and Dafoe play FBI agents investigating the disappearance of three civil rights workers. "I remember someone high in the civil rights movement telling me how disappointed they were in the movie that it didn't tell all the truth," said Hackman, who earned a best actor nomination. "I told them that movies are compromises."
Also in the film: Frances McDormand, who was nominated for best supporting actress, and Brad Dourif.
1992: Clint Eastwood, Morgan Freeman in 'Unforgiven'
Hackman as Sheriff "Little Bill" Daggett stands between Eastwood and Freeman, who are out to collect a bounty. The film won the Oscar for best picture.
Also in the film: Morgan Freeman and Richard Harris.
1993: Tom Cruise in 'The Firm'
As the head of a prestigious law firm, Hackman welcomes newcomer Cruise in this film based on a John Grisham bestseller. But Mitch (Cruise) soon learns the firm has a secret client.
Also in the film: Hal Holbrook, Holly Hunter, Ed Harris, Jeanne Tripplehorn, David Strathairn and Gary Busey.
1995: Denzel Washington in 'Crimson Tide'
International intrigue leads to a faceoff on a submarine between its captain (Hackman) and new executive officer (Denzel Washington). Also in the film: James Gandolfini and Viggo Mortensen.
1996: Robin Williams in 'The Birdcage'
Gay drag club owner Armand (Robin Williams) and the venue's star Albert (Nathan Lane) are a couple who must play it straight when meeting the family of Armand's son's wife-to-be which includes conservative U.S. senator Hackman. Also in the film: Dianne Wiest, Calista Flockhart, Hank Azaria and Christine Baranski.
1996: Chris O'Donnell in 'The Chamber'
In another film based on a John Grisham novel, O'Donnell is a young attorney seeking to prevent the execution of his grandfather, who is in prison for a past Ku Klux Klan bombing.
Also in the film: Faye Dunaway and Bo Jackson.
1997: Clint Eastwood in 'Absolute Power'
Clint Eastwood directed and starred in this film as a jewel thief who witnesses a murder involving the president (Hackman).
Also in the film: Ed Harris, Laura Linney, Scott Glenn, Dennis Haysbert, Judy Davis, E.G. Marshall and Penny Johnson Jerald.
1998: Will Smith in 'Enemy of the State'
Smith is a lawyer and Hackman is a surveillance expert who unknowingly get embroiled in the coverup of a politically motivated murder. Also in the film: Jon Voight, Regina King, Loren Dean, Jake Busey, Barry Pepper and Gabriel Byrne.
1998: Paul Newman in 'Twilight'
A retired private detective (Newman) is pulled into a long-buried crime by friends played by Gene Hackman and Susan Sarandon. Also in the film: Reese Witherspoon, Stockard Channing, James Garner, Giancarlo Esposito, Liev Schreiber and Margo Martindale.
2000: Keanu Reeves in 'The Replacements'
Hackman is hired to coach a team of replacement pro football players when the starters go on strike. He recruits Reeves as quarterback.
Also in the film: Jon Favreau and Orlando Jones.
2001: Gwyneth Paltrow, Ben Stiller, Danny Glover, more in 'The Royal Tenenbaums'
The patriarch of an dysfunctional family (Hackman) returns hoping to reconcile with his children (played Gwyneth Paltrow, Luke Wilson and Ben Stiller) and wife (Anjelica Huston).
Also in the film: Bill Murray, Danny Glover and Owen Wilson, who also co-wrote the script with director Wes Anderson.
2001: Danny DeVito in 'Heist'
A jewel thief (Hackman) who had planned to go into retirement is forced to complete another job by his fence (DeVito).
Also in the film: Sam Rockwell, Rebecca Pidgeon, Delroy Lindo and Patti LuPone.
2001: Sigourney Weaver in 'Heartbreakers'
Hackman is a rich man who gets caught up in a romantic con game run by a mother and daughter, played by Sigourney Weaver and Jennifer Love Hewitt.
Also in the film: Ray Liotta, Jason Lee, Anne Bancroft, Nora Dunn, Sarah Silverman and Zach Galifianakis.
2003: Dustin Hoffman in 'Runaway Jury'
Dustin Hoffman is a lawyer in a jury trial pitted against a jury consultant (Hackman) who is trying to guide the proceedings in favor of a firearms maker.
Also in the film: John Cusack, Rachel Weisz, Bruce McGill and Jeremy Piven.
2004: Ray Romano in 'Welcome to Mooseport'
Hackman plays the president again, but this time he's a former president running for mayor against hardware store owner Romano.
It was Hackman's last role. "Reality stares you in the face when you get to be my age," he said a year after the film came out. "You are playing the grandfather or the great-grandfather, and you're not used to playing those roles, and although I could, it just doesn't appeal to me."
Also in the film: Maura Tierney, Marcia Gay Harden, Christine Baranski, Fred Savage and Rip Torn.

title: 'Trademark Lincoln third quarter punch' upends Taylorville in 3A regional title game
author: Trevor Lawrence
description: Lincoln quickly ballooned its two-point lead with an 11-0 run and took control over Taylorville to win the Class 3A Southeast Regional title.
content:
In a matter of 1 minute, 11 seconds of a two-point ballgame, No. 1 seed Lincoln High School regained control and the Railsplitters knocked out seventh seed Taylorville 38-23 in the boys Class 3A Southeast Regional championship matchup on Friday night.
Lincoln (23-10) advanced to the Decatur Eisenhower Sectional semifinals and will meet No. 2 seed Mount Zion (24-9) on Wednesday at 7 p.m. The Braves defeated No. 6 Mahomet-Seymour 66-45 to win the Mount Zion Regional title.
It seemed Taylorville found life when sophomore Blake Ladage made a bucket to get the Tornadoes within 18-16 with 5:34 remaining in the third period.
But after a Lincoln timeout, junior guard Karson Komnick scored, and Gabe Smith's steal and layup upped the Railers' lead to 22-16 just 30 seconds later. A putback by senior Frank Sanders made it an eight-point game and when junior Brody Tungate collected another steal and layup, Lincoln forged ahead 26-16 at 4:23. It led to an 11-0 run and the Railers went into the final quarter leading 29-18.
'That trademark Lincoln third quarter punch that they've done for decades got the best of us,' Taylorville coach Ryan Brown said. 'You know it's coming, and can you just withstand it and make sure you guys are ready and prepared for it? We can talk about it until we're blue in the face — but until you see it — that just stung us. Three or four minutes lost us the game.'
From there, Lincoln outscored Taylorville 9-5 in the fourth quarter and collected its first regional title since the 2019-20 season, which was cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
'It's been up-and-down, we fought COVID for a few years,' Lincoln coach Neil Alexander said. 'We played hard, the kids knew how long it had been, and it's been unusual that we've gone this long without a regional, so it's pretty happy right now.'
Komnick delivers in prime time
Komnick's 3-pointer gave Lincoln a 3-0 lead in the first period and the Railers never trailed. He had two 3s, including a traditional 3-point play and scored nine points in the quarter when Lincoln led 11-8 after one.
'Let's get to a hot start because (Taylorville) pulled the ball out and held the ball for a long time, and we didn't want that to affect us,' Komnick said. 'We got off to a hot start and they played catch up.'
Komnick finished with a game-high 19 points while hitting 7 of 9 free throws. Senior Drew Hayes made a 3-pointer and scored five of his seven points in the second period as Lincoln led 18-14 at intermission.
But it was the third quarter burst that sealed it for the Railers.
'Brody really picked it up at the point of press and he got a couple steals, and it really got us going,' Komnick said.
'It was our defense,' Alexander said. 'We don't score a lot of points, and we got to win with our defense. It definitely won tonight in that little spurt that we had.'
It will be Komnick's first trip to a sectional.
'I've never done this, so it feels good. I'm really happy right now,' Komnick said. '(The sectional's) tough, and we have to play better than we did tonight. I think we got a shot.'
Cinderella Taylorville holds heads high
The Tornadoes (15-18) got to the regional championship stage by needing a half-court buzzer-beater shot by Malique Pearse to beat No. 4 Rochester 40-37 on Wednesday.
Taylorville had its moments against Lincoln in the first half. Senior Drake Howard buried two 3-pointers in the first quarter and finished with a team-high 11 points. Ladage slipped through the Lincoln defense several times and added 10.
Brown commented on how Taylorville turned around a six-win campaign from last season to 15 wins this season.
'Our seniors been through some ups-and-downs in the program and to have seven of these guys still here, I think they wanted to get this ship righted and they did,' Brown said. 'To play in this game, a great experience. Those guys felt like kings for two days after the Rochester game. They'll never forget that.'
Inside the numbers
The Tornadoes turned the ball over on their first four possessions and finished with 17 overall, while the Railers ended with just six miscues.
Taylorville had attempted just 13 shots through three quarters, making eight of them. They went 10-for-22 from the floor and outrebounded Lincoln 17-10. Sanders (four points) had six of Lincoln's rebounds.
Lincoln shot 50% from the floor, hitting 13 of 26 shots, including 3 of 7 from 3-point territory.

title: Pleasant Plains boys basketball stays hot for third straight regional title
author: Bill Welt
description: Pleasant Plains boys basketball never relinquished its lead for a third straight regional title
content:
PLEASANT PLAINS — The Pleasant Plains boys basketball team picked up where it left off.
Owen Johnson kicked things off with the open 3-pointer on a Cooper Schallenberg assist and the No. 3-seeded Cardinals led from start to finish in a 48-41 victory over No. 2 Warsaw/Hamilton West Hancock in the Class 2A home regional final on Friday.
Regional semis vs. Riverton: Pleasant Plains boys basketball capitalizes on ball movement to reach regional finals
Plains (22-10) advances to the Greenville Sectional semifinals against fellow Sangamo Conference foe and No. 1 seed Auburn on Tuesday at 7 p.m. No. 1 Williamsville also meets No. 2 Staunton in the other semifinal on Wednesday at 7 p.m.
The Cardinals dialed up four of their six 3s in the first half, while Warsaw generated just two treys all night.
Junior guard Grady Grisham led Plains with 15 points and nine rebounds, while Schallenberg had 13 points. Johnson followed with 11 points.
Junior reserve Nolan Scott began the fourth quarter with his only 3 for a 29-21 cushion. Plains shot 12 of 21 from the free-throw line to close out the win.
Gavin Grothuas paced the Titans with 12 points.

title: Illinois high school swim team sets national record at IHSA state finals
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The stacked 200-meter medley relay from Hinsdale Central set a national record Friday at the 2025 IHSA state finals in Westmont.
content:
An Illinois high school boys swimming team set a national record at the Illinois High School Association state finals in Westmont.
The 200-meter medley relay team from Hinsdale Central teamed to swim 1 minute, 26.75 seconds in the preliminary round of the finals Friday at FMC Natatorium.
The mark was .13 seconds faster than the previous mark of 1:26.88, set by a relay team from Carmel (Indiana), according to The National Federation of State High School Associations. That Carmel team included Olympian Aaron Shackell, Sean Sullivan, Ryan Malicki and Christopher Holmes, according to swimswam.com.
The record propelled Hinsdale Central into the final, set for Saturday morning.
The record-setting run was started by sophomore backstroker Luke Vatev, followed by senior breaststroker Josh Bey, senior butterfly swimmer Henry Guo and junior freestyler Matt Vatev. Bey, a member of the U.S. Junior National Team, is headed to Indiana, while Guo and Matt Vatev are committed to Penn.

title: Nearly $2B has not been paid to Illinois by feds, Gov. Pritzker and others say
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The federal government owes Illinois nearly $2 billion in funding, the governor and legislators say, as they look to D.C. for answers.
content:
Some departments in Illinois have missed out on $1.88 billion in federal funds since late January, when that office directed federal agencies to "temporarily pause" certain financial assistance.
Gov. JB Pritzker and Illinois members of Congress have written to the Office of Management and Budget, seeking answers.
14 state agencies, boards, and commissions in Illinois have been affected, the letter said.
The federal government owes Illinois nearly $2 billion in funding, the governor and legislators say, as they look to D.C. for answers.
Gov. JB Pritzker along with Sens. Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth and the Illinois Democratic congressional delegation say several state departments are not receiving federal funds. They also say a lack of clarity has made the future uncertain concerning the funding of the agencies, per President Donald Trump's aim to pause certain grant, loan and other financial assistance programs.
The continual withholding of funding has 'forced many to pause operations, cancel projects, or cut staff,' according to a letter they wrote to the Russell Vought, who is the Director of the Office of Management and Budget.
What Illinois agencies are not receiving money and what do those agencies do? Here's what you need to know.
What agencies are not receiving funding?
Nine state agencies, boards, and commissions have a total of $692 million in federal funds 'obligated but not yet received, and they are unable to access those funds," according to the letter.
Also, 10 state agencies, boards, and commissions have a total of $1.19 billion in federal funds 'anticipated/awarded but not yet obligated, and the grants/programs are essentially paused.'
The departments include:
What is the purpose of the letter?
The funds in question were passed by Congress, signed into law, and promised to Illinois, the authors wrote.
They also said the funds have been "contractually agreed to, allocated, and planned around by their recipients—which include childcare providers, educational institutions, small businesses, community and economic development organizations, and more."
How long has this been happening?
Problems began on Jan. 28 following a directive from the White House Office of Management and Budget to federal agencies to the day prior to 'temporarily pause all activities related to obligation or disbursement of all federal financial assistance.'
That day saw 'widespread reports of system outages and lockouts that prevented grantees from accessing entitled funding. Attempted communications with government liaisons were often ignored and public statements from the White House were inconsistent with the experiences of our grantees.'
Since then, the legislators wrote, they have continued to receive reports from agencies and organizations detailing their inability to access funds.
What do these agencies do?
'These frozen funds impact programs that provide technical assistance for small businesses, provide affordable solar energy for low-income residents, improve roads and bridges,' the letter reads.
The mission of the Commerce and Economic Opportunity is 'to create equitable economic opportunities across the State of Illinois,' according to their website. "By attracting and supporting major job creators, investing in communities, strengthening Illinois' world-class workforce, fostering innovation, and ushering in the new clean energy economy, DCEO works to fortify Illinois' reputation as a global economic powerhouse while ensuring Illinois is the best state to live, work and do business.'
The Illinois General Assembly established the Illinois Community College Board in 1965 'to create a system of public community colleges that would be within easy reach of every resident,' according to their website.
Illinois Emergency Management Agency is responsible for better preparing the state for natural, manmade, or technological disasters, hazards, or acts of terrorism.
The mission of the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency is to 'safeguard environmental quality, consistent with the social and economic needs of the State of Illinois, so as to protect health, welfare, property, and the quality of life,' their website reads. The site also said that the Illinois General Assembly was the first state legislature in the U.S. to adopt a comprehensive EPA Act that in part created the state agency in 1970.
What else is Illinois doing about it?
Gov. Pritzker traveled to Washington D.C. this week to meet with Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and talk about the issue, among other reasons for the visit, according to the governor's office.
